question: What are subtle signs of autism and Asperger syndrome?
answer: Well, Asperger’s Syndrome is just autism, so we can get rid of the second half of the question. Thus, the question I’ll answer is: What are subtle signs of autism? There is the clinical, medical definition of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), and then there is the real, lived experiences that us autistics deal with all day, every day, and we’ve dealt with them our entire lives. And these signs are quite numerous, but be aware that not every autistic experiences these things, these are just the most common ones I’ve seen in my experience. So, here’s 63 subtle signs of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).Wearing bright colors/wearing subdued colors. We either crave stimulation, or we don’t want to be overwhelmed, so our clothes can be bright and attention seeking, or subdued. I insist on band shirts, jeans, and Vans.Hating phone calls. No, if I see a Rickenbacker bass that I want to buy, I will not call for a price, just let me know what it costs online.Not realizing you’re hungry or thirsty. Sometimes you just don’t feel or notice that you’re hungry or thirsty, even though you probably are very hungry or thirsty.Not replying to a text message. You want to choose your words carefully, so you think about it for a week, and then it’s too late to reply.Hating seams and tags in clothing. I hate clothing with tags or prominent seams. They feel stifling and itchy.Having an atypical sense of humor. Sometimes I say something I think is funny, but it just doesn’t land.Always telling the truth. I have a compulsive need for honesty, so I blurt out the truth even if it’s best for everyone if I keep my mouth shut.Feeling out of sync in groups. You always feel like an outsider in your friend groups.You have an aversion to or an obsession with popular culture. If pop culture is your special interest, you’ll be obsessed with it. If not, you just don’t “get” pop culture.Over-planning everything. You must schedule all tasks on a calendar, otherwise, nothing will get done. As someone that also has ADHD, this is a general feeling in ADHD as well, except it’s not for planning or setting schedules, it’s so you remember what you said you were going to do.Always feeling tired. Masking autism is mentally exhausting, so you always feel tired. Or you just feel tired all the time for no real reason.Don’t like being told what to do. We have a routine and schedule that works for us, don’t say it needs to be changed.You started reading at an early age. I was taught to read at 3 and a half years old.Finding comfort in repetition and routine. Routine is good. Routine is love. Routine is life. Except my ADHD wants something new and spontaneous too, so it’s a constant battle between the two.Struggling with crowds. You feel overwhelmed and overstimulated anywhere there’s a crowd.Seeing people as people. Because of how your brain is, you forget social expectations that other people have towards other people, and you default to treating people as people, regardless of who they are.Sensitive hearing. I’ve always had sensitive hearing, but I never found music to be triggering. In fact, I found it relaxing. I love music so much I decided to become a musician.High pain tolerance. I have a high pain tolerance. But the paradox is that I’m not indifferent to it, in fact, I feel pain more intensely, I just am able to tolerate it better.Over-apologizing. You apologize to people way too much over an issue because you perceive it’s due to you saying something and being misunderstood.Not caring what people think. The fun kind of autism where it’s just free and unmasked autism without a care in the world!Being really good at something that isn’t useful. I know a lot of dinosaur facts, data, and knowledge. I can give you the 100 million year evolutionary history of tyrannosauroids from memory, and if you’re lucky, with sources, but ask me to do my tax paperwork or expense reports and I fold like laundry. Another trait autism shares with ADHD, and for me, the two are reinforcing each other here.Being sarcastic. It’s not being sarcastic sometimes, you’re sarcastic all the time.Preferring face-to-face communication. Sometimes, people take a text message the wrong way, so you prefer discussing real matters face-to-face to avoid misunderstandings.Struggling to find appropriate gaps in conversation. You want to express your opinion on the subject, so you look for an opportunity, but none of them seem appropriate, and then the conversation moves on from that subject and you’re left there alone.Constant background anxiety. Masking autism or ADHD or any kind of neurodivergence breeds a specific kind of background anxiety that only people who are neurodivergent will understand. It’s more common than you think.Being overly empathic. In contrary to a popular myth, we autistic people actually have too much empathy and it becomes overwhelming to the point it comes off as overly literal or logical. We have so much empathy it creates so much emotion, that we have to use logic to make sense of it. That comes across as overly cold or logical, even when we may understand you and your situation more than you think we do.Relating to animals more than people. We love animals! I love all animals, but cats, dogs, lizards, and turtles are my favorites! They are completely non-judgmental, dogs and cats especially.Avoiding trying new things. Part of the rigid thinking pattern of autism. My routine works so well for me, why should I consider something new? That said, for me, it’s a constant battle between the autism wanting and craving the familiar, and my ADHD being curious and spontaneous and wanting something new and exciting. So how that ends up is that I spontaneously try something new, and if it works, I will make it a part of my routine, rigidly, and hate deviations from it.Eating the same food every day. We found the food we like, and it works for us. Some of us can be picky eaters, but again, my ADHD loves to try new things, so I’ve made food one of my special interests. How that looks is unless the food is meant to be mixed, it won’t be mixed and the food remains separate on my plate. That way I can try each individual thing on my own time. I’m like an autistic food critic. And yes, I loved the movie Ratatouille, why do you ask?Finding inappropriate things funny. I love Chris Tucker, Dave Chappelle, Monty Python, and Richard Pryor. I’d repeat their jokes, never understanding why repeating their jokes as a young, white, autistic and ADHD kid wasn’t appropriate. But I found them hilarious. Still do as an adult, quite frankly only now I learned there’s layers to the jokes they were telling that I didn’t see as a kid.Not liking to be touched. Only my wife, my family, and close friends can touch me. Everyone else must keep their distance, and stay out of my blood circle. For those that don’t know, the blood circle is a Scouting term that describes the area within the radius of the arm plus the length of a knife. Only a few people are allowed within my blood circle.Tendency to notice small details. For me, these are random, because, hey ADHD and autism linked up, so the small details I notice are small sounds that my brain fixates on and I have to respond to it.Hating florescent/down lights. I hate florescent lights. Even when other people don’t notice a flicker, I do, and it’s bothersome and overstimulating.Stimming. Flappy hands are happy hands. For me, my stims are cracking my knuckles, moving my leg rapidly, chewing my tongue, playing with my fidget cube, and squeezing my fists over and over.Always wanting to understand why. This is me with everything. Because of my logical thinking brain, everything happens due to some mechanism or reason, so my curiosity leads me to constantly ask questions. My ADHD side of me is also insanely curious, and since there’s no self-control, the two are reinforcing this curiosity.Enjoying repetition. When that dopamine hit from that new song hits, that song gets played on repeat for hours before I let Spotify continue on. Happened recently with the Zenith Passage’s song, “Synaptic Depravation.” That was on repeat for no less than three hours when I first heard it.Thinking in pictures. In other words, you’re a visual thinker and visual learner. You like to see something happen before you understand it. I’m an auditory thinker and learner myself, which isn’t shocking as I am a musician. But weirdly, I think in color when writing music, and unless music and optics are your special interests, that’s just going to seem weird to you, and a strange rabbit hole to fall down in. By the way, the note A is orange, and I won’t accept any counter-arguments on the matter.Having a flat affect. Otherwise known as “resting bitch face.” You have this look even if you’re just vibing. I don’t have this, personally.Preferring to pace around the room rather than sitting. Sitting can sometimes be weirdly painful, so we get up to move around. This is something that can overlap with ADHD, and in my case, having both, it just shows itself as that I can’t sit still and need to stim more.Imitating other people. Sometimes you learn something fun when imitating other people. I don’t do this anymore, but I did it as a kid all the time.Having a favorite thing. This thing you carry with you everywhere, no matter what. For me, it’s my fidget cube, but it used to be my $75 double action OTF knife, because I tend to always carry a knife on me, but it was confiscated when I went to my niece’s graduation, which bothered the hell out of me. I rather liked that knife a lot. There’s a whole other reason why I was bothered, but that’s personal stuff.Getting excited and interrupting people. Yeah, this is another trait autism and ADHD share, and yeah, the two don’t help each other out here. This leads to me info-dumping about my special interest for hours on end.Thinking over previous social interactions. You overthink about previous social interactions all the time.You see patterns in everything. Yep. For me it’s sonic patterns as I’m attuned to sound pretty strongly being a musician, so I perceive things as musical when they’re really random.You either have a good memory or a bad memory. You don’t have “normal” memory. Again, this is a trait autism shares with ADHD. For certain things, my mind’s like a steel trap, and nothing gets past it, but my working memory and executive functions aren’t the best, so I can lose my keys all the time and forget where I placed them.Preferring non-verbal communication. Some autistics are non-verbal, and may prefer to use other forms of communication, even if they can speak. I’m like the opposite, I can be a real motor mouth.Hating to brush your teeth. I hate to brush my teeth. I do it twice a day as dentists and doctors recommend, so my dental hygiene is good, but that doesn’t mean I like it. Admittedly, my Philips Sonicare toothbrush actually massages my gums, so that feels nice, but it still is part of the routine that is my least favorite. Showers? Love ‘em. Heeding nature’s call in the morning? Best part of the morning. Brushing my hair and styling my beard? Not as fun, but necessary, otherwise it gets unruly. But brushing my teeth? Nah, not the fun one, but I know it’s necessary.Having a monotone voice or a strange voice. Our voices can be strange at times.Difficulty identifying emotions/emotional dysregulation. A trait that autism also shares with ADHD. Our emotions can be overwhelming because it’s usually a combination of emotions at once, not one feeling. Worse yet, in my case, the ADHD leads me to be emotionally impulsive, so I just express emotion with no filter. The emotion is logical and rational, but there’s just no filter on it. This can make shutdowns and meltdowns worse, and easily, my least favorite part of being neurodivergent.Getting overwhelmed by too many tasks at once. This is an executive function challenge, something autism and ADHD share in common. The solution I’ve found is monotasking rather than multitasking. Focus on one task.Watching the same movies/TV shows all the time. There’s comfort in familiarity. There’s certain shows I go to that are comfort shows that put me in a better mood.Feeling awkward in groups. Social awkwardness is one of the quintessential autistic symptoms. Not that you’re not social, not that you don’t have friends, not that you’re introverted, you’re just a little socially awkward, and that can lead to misunderstandings.Thinking outside of the box. This is one of my favorite things about being autistic and ADHD is divergent thinking. Because the autism loves details my brain can come up with a detailed plan of action, and because the ADHD has millions of thoughts at once, those plans come out quickly, fully thought out, and detailed. Really a boon to creativity too, important for my job as a musician and songwriter.Having unique brilliant ideas. Same thing with problems, that divergent thinking also works with new and innovative ideas as well.Struggling to read between the lines. Socially, people don’t just say what they mean. Often, a lot of times, there’s a lot being said that’s not being said. I miss these all the time. For us autistic people, it’s a struggle because we think very logically and literally when it comes to communication. We’re assuming you’re saying what you’re actually saying, we don’t know if you meant something else between the words you said.Preferring written communication. Because it takes time and thought to write something out, some autistic people feel more comfortable with written communication.Two speed productivity. You’re either insanely productive you get 3 months worth of work done in 8 hours, or nothing gets attempted. There is no in between. This is a trait autism shares in common with ADHD.Compartmentalizing life experiences. We autistic people are really good with compartmentalizing everything, including our own life experiences.Comfortable being alone. You love the sweet embrace of solitude, because you can finally be yourself, no masks required.Happy with few material comforts. You love minimalism. You don’t need much, you don’t want much, and are happy with having few material comforts. Not a thing with me, as my autism came with ADHD, so my impulsivity came with special interest projects that… still need completing.Always finishing what you start. Hyperfixation and perseveration is real. This is something that autism shares in common with ADHD, when we’re hyper-productive, the project must get done start to finish, even though you should probably stop and take a break.Scripting conversations in advance. You have scripts that you practice for specific social interactions, or you think about hypothetical social situations and arguments and practice your responses to them.“How can someone so smart be so stupid?”. This isn’t what you think, but what others think of you. With my autism and ADHD I also was intelligent as a kid, and I still am intelligent as an adult, yet, there are so many strange and weird quirks about me, that my loved ones constantly think, “You’re so smart, why is this such an issue for you?” This points to the fact that, despite the positives of autism and ADHD, they really are disabilities, and they come with invisible struggles that no one sees.Hope this helps!EDIT: Two people took objection to me saying that Asperger’s Syndrome is just autism. Now, I’m coming from the DSM-V, because I’m from the United States, and one of the foremost authorities on mental conditions is the American Psychological Association. Here, Asperger’s is just a form of autism, as autism changed to become Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). In fact, there was other labels besides Asperger’s that further clouded the issue and lead to misunderstandings. I meant it quite literally that Asperger’s is just autism, and it’s to reflect that autism isn’t one thing. It was meant to be inclusive, as a lot of support aspies needed, weren’t all too dissimilar from ASD. So rather than have extra labels they just got rid of all those labels, including Asperger’s, PDD-NOS, Kanner Syndrome, and childhood disintegrative disorder (CDD). They realized these were all basically the same thing, so they’re all just Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). So that’s what I meant. I meant it in a very literal way that Asperger’s is just autism. Now, one commenter came at this very respectfully, intelligently, and clearly explained why they identify with the Asperger’s label. I’ve left their comments up for everyone to read, because they offered a unique perspective. Another commenter I deleted and blocked, something I don’t usually do, because he called autistic people the “R-word.” I don’t think I have to belabor the point that that’s offensive, it’s not speaking plainly or frankly, it’s just being an asshole for the sake of being an asshole, and doesn’t exactly encourage free and open discussion. So, I don’t usually block or delete someone’s comments. If you disagree, do what the other commenter did and just explain your point of view without insulting an entire group of people.Originally answered: What are subtle signs of autism and Asperger syndrome?

question: What is Asperger’s syndrome?
answer: Asperger’s is a neurological development disorder characterized by significant difficulties in social interaction and nonverbal communication, along with restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior and interests. It differs from other Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs) by relatively normal language and intelligence. Signs usually begin before two years old and typically last for a person's entire life. Someone asked me what was it like having Asperger's. I can't speak for my fellow ASD travelers since each one of us on the Spectrum is unique. I can describe my own life on the Spectrum, but don't ask me to explain it. Those who don't have ASD can't understand it and those of us who do can't explain it. PLEASE .... My anxiety goes up a notch or two when I am given the "PLEASE go get the..., find the..., bring me ..., it's in the...next to the...on the right...". The longer the instruction string, the least likely the instructor will get positive results from me. For example, I was helping a friend the other day with an outdoor project and she gave me a few of those type requests in one sitting. The pressure to find what she wanted in record speed put me on panic alert. I did find them but not with record speed and not without my friend repeating or rephrasing the directions. If I were quick on my feet, I would have asked, "Am I getting warmer?" meaning am I getting closer or further from the target of the safari hunt. The items were within a short, I do mean SHORT, distance from me. EMBARRASSING! If there had been a hole, I would have climbed in it until my friend talked me out of it. BED NECESSITIES Sleeping with five pillows instead of one. A miserable night if I was reduced to sleeping with the standard number of 1 or even 2. It is just one of my long held rituals to be surrounded by pillows at bedtime. I call it, for lack of a better explanation, my comfort food at bedtime. DIET ROUTINE - WRITTEN IN STONE My list of what I eat on a regular basis could be counted on two hands. Most of those items are high in starches. Thus, I am a big fan of bread, bagels, dry cereals, crackers, chips, and popcorn. No salt shaker but what I eat has plenty in it. When I eat my meals is beyond my understanding but I stick to my peculiar eating routine like SUPER glue. GOOGLE IMAGES WITHOUT WORDS I am in a conversation and have the floor. I am telling a story and come to a point where for the life of me I can't think of the name of the image in my head. I describe it in a haphazard way where I stutter all over myself. This is the part that frustrates me. A few minutes later, my brain pops the word up. Granted, this surely happens to most people, but in my life on the spectrum, it is the "norm" instead of the exception. OH CLUMSY ME! If there is something to trip over, stumble on, tumble over, then one of my toes, feet, or knees will find it. I don’t take daily inventory, but I don't think I've lived a day that I didn’t have a bruise on my person. I’ll only remember how I got a bruise if it hurt so much that I saw lights flashing. It is frustrating to no end when I bump, fall, and trip but I try to take ’em as they come and keep going with bruises galore. NOT SO FINE ON MOTOR! Fine motor skills have to do with the small stuff when it comes to movement. This is why my handwriting bears a strong resemblance to chicken scratch. It is why picking up objects between my thumb and finger is no small feat. Such as putting on or off pierced earrings. As hard as I try to hang on to the earring or "back", it happens without fail of one dropping. I have come so close at times to give up earrings entirely and forget about my two tiny ear holes. I give in against my better judgment and buy a pack of cheap earrings at the dollar store just to replace the missing "backs". WHY DID I SAY ALL THAT? I meet a total stranger who gives me an inch. I'll tell the stranger way more than I want to about myself. It was as if I had provided a total perfect stranger a chapter or two of my audiobook autobiography. Shortly thereafter, I'm kicking myself as to what in the world was I thinking telling a stranger my life story. Those are just some examples of what it is like to have Asperger's Syndrome. Sometimes I have a no-meltdown kind of day. Other times my autism slaps me in the face and lets me know it's around and is here to stay.

question: What are the advantages of having Asperger's syndrome?
answer: My son has Asperger’s. While he struggles socially, he has many, many incredible strengths associated with his ASD (autism spectrum disorder):Impressively accurate long-term recallWe recently struggled to remember the theme of his nursery. He effortlessly recalled that his very first room was filled with John Lennon’s “Imagine” bedding, lamps, and mobiles. He also reminded us that when he was 2, the dog next door crashed through our screen door to come play with our golden. I could go on… When in doubt, we always trust A’s memory over ours.Unusually sensitive hearingI’ve written elsewhere that his hearing was so acute, we thought his ears were broken (granted, we were new parents and knew nothing, but still…).He can hear a dog in distress or an unexpected sound from 4+ floors away. We half-jokingly call him our early-warning system. The downside, of course, is that he hears everything we say. We quickly learned we can only “safely” talk in the car. Without him. Blocks away.Insistence on logicHis unwavering need for logic helps keep us in check. “Because I said so” has never been an acceptable response. A’s need for things to “make sense” has pushed us to more thoroughly consider our responses, ensure that consequences are very clearly tied to an infraction, and helped us (virtually) eliminate knee-jerk reactions.We’re also far more aware of the arbitrary and sometimes contradictory nature of many social “rules”. Why should we say “I love it” when we despise the gift? Who says that adults are always right? And, why the hell should he be told to hug gramma when he so dislikes touch?When our neurologically impaired rescue dog went missing for 29 hours last week, A. was the first to state the obvious: “she’s probably dead and gone forever”. Though not what we wanted to hear, it was important to prepare ourselves.Extreme intelligence and verbal skillsWhile his precocious speech was unsettling at first, we quickly grew to appreciate his incredible brain. At 16, he’s reading at a grad-school level, has impeccable grammar, writes impressive poetry, and loves words. What’s not to love?His problem-solving skills, spatial relations, ability to generalize new concepts, and quickly grasp cause and effect are outstanding.While his parents are pretty freaking smart, he’s far brighter than we’ll ever be. His IQ was first formally assessed when he was about 6 and he’s consistently tested as (highly) superior over the years. Though I know IQ is just a measure of one’s potential, it’s pretty cool to have such an intensely smart kid.I’m finding it difficult to end this post. His gifts far outweigh his challenges. I could list a dozen more positive traits related to his ASD, though suppose I need to stop somewhere. This seems like a decent stopping point. With one more shout-out: Our resident Aspie has super-powers!

question: What, if anything, is wrong with having Asperger syndrome?
answer: Post 10 — What are the main problems that people with high-functioning autism face?There is nothing wrong with having Asperger syndrome, but I assume the question to mean, “What are the main problems that people with Asperger syndrome face?”, some of which are the following factors:Social deficits — People with ASD have a lesser need for social contact, as well as a lesser ability to socialize.Decreased prosocial behavior — Altered neurochemicals resulting in brain inflammation decrease social interest, and thus prosocial behavior[1]. This can be problematic, as socializing has been well proven to be conducive to interpersonal relationships which result in a more successful life in every domain (money, happiness, job satisfaction, etc.).Lack of social engagement — The more socially interactive you are, the more social support one gets. As such, people with ASD miss out on the benefits of prosocial behaviors.Lower social reward — Our brains do not get intrinsically rewarded by social interactions in the way neurotypicals do; neurotypicals are rewarded in social interactions with oxytocin and dopamine for neurotypicals, which is not the case in people with ASD[2].Self-presentation — Neurotypicals engage in positive self-presentation, prosocial lies, and negative emotion concealment for politeness purposes[3]. People with ASD don’t tend to engage in these acts, thereby decreasing their ‘likability’ and potenitial for relationships a known factor in lowering their quality of life.Bluntness — People with ASD can be overly blunt and brutally honest; two qualities that are appreciated by some, but in many cases causes social friction, as the diplomacy is low.Low agreeableness — People with ASD will be lower in ‘agreeableness’ (one of the Big Five personality traits) due to their reduced capacity to comprehend interpersonal cues; to relate to, empathize with, and feel compassion for others; and to engage in emotionally sensitive, reciprocal social responding[4].Theory of mind — People with ASD have a low theory of mind, which means they have a lower capacity to understand other people’s perspectives, feelings and states of mind.Blindness to emotional and mental states — Children with autism spectrum conditions (ASC) have major difficulties in recognizing and responding to emotional and mental states in others’ facial expressions. Such difficulties in empathy underlie their social-communication difficulties that form a core of the diagnosis[5].Weak theory of mind — A weak theory of mind decreases the quality of life due to a lack of perspective in the other, and a lack of social skills in general, causing social friction and even conflict. A decrease in quality of life due to a weak theory of mind has been found in individuals with ALS, schizophrenia, and ASD among others.Adherence to societal standards — People with ASD have problems adhering to societal standards, either because they don’t care to follow them, or have difficulties acknowledging them.Need to mask — In order to fit in, many people with ASD feel the need to mask in order to keep up appearances of normality. This creates a pressure, with exhaustion, challenging stereotypes, threats to self-perception, depression, and even suicidality as a result[6].Social inappropriateness — Autistic mannerisms are often perceived as socially inappropriate by neurotypical people, and this perception can undermine interaction/communication[7] as well as acceptance in mainstream society, which results in a decrease in quality of life.Low extraversion — People with ASD tend to score lower on ‘extraversion’ (one of the Big Five personality traits), given their difficulties with social interaction and communication, and their tendency to avoid social contact rather than pursue it as rewarding. As such, people with ASD are disadvantaged in a society where social contact has its benefits, and is often deemed necessary and even essential[8].Lack of conforming — People with ASD tend to have a reduced capacity to engage in emotionally sensitive, reciprocal social responding, which means they often find themselves on the edge of society, and hence the stereotype of the social outcast[9].Public perception — The public perception of ASD may not necessarily match with the traits and experience of an individual with ASD, which can be damaging in its own right, as it can perpetuate negative stereotypes. One possible consequence is challenges with getting a job, as people with high-functioning autism are seen as mentally incapable of executing certain jobs.Sensory deficits — People with ASD tend to have hypo- or hypersensitivity to sensory stimulation, as well as other sensory issues.Overstimulation — A study shows that social and sensory overstimulation drives autistic behaviors. What it comes down to is that the autistic brain is hyper-functional, and thus is prone to mental overstimulation[10].Sensory overload — People with ASD tend to get dysregulated due to sensory overload, where sensory experiences including smell, hearing, vision and touch are often too great for the nervous system to process[11].Sensory issues — Beyond sensory overload, there are other possible sensory issues, including negative effects from synesthesia[12]—which has been linked to autism[13].Sensory processing dysfunction — Reports on sensory processing dysfunction in people with ASD vary from 42–88% ; they often have difficulty regulating responses to sensations and specific stimuli, and may use self-stimulation to compensate for limited sensory input or to avoid overstimulation. This also decreases quality of life.Meltdowns — People with ASD are prone to meltdowns when they get dysregulated, where a build-up of emotions and stress results in an eventual release of emotions[14].Negative feelings — People with ASD tend to focus on their failures, and base their thinking on past experience, meaning they tend to become pessimists.Pessismism — We tend to focus heavily on our failures and magnify them, but when it comes to positive feelings, due to alexithymia—often comorbid with ASD—these are not always experienced. As such, positive feelings are short-lived while negative feelings are self-perpetuating and cyclical, and so negative thoughts, behavioral problems, and life interference are significantly higher in people with ASD[15].Lower happiness — Findings revealed that adolescents with AS, in contrast to their peers without AS, reported less subjective happiness, less positive affect, and lower affective balance[16].Paranoia — People with ASD tend to experience low-level paranoia symptoms. However, these paranoid symptoms arise as a consequence of different mechanisms than those involved in psychotic delusions[17]. Possible explanations for paranoia symptoms are likely to be found in deficits in social reasoning—particularly in the low theory of mind[18].Obsessiveness — Although not explicitly a negative trait, the obsessive nature of people with ASD can cause them to focus heavily on their failures, experience cyclical negative thoughts, and can sporadically think about past failures again—thus again focusing on negative emotions, which causes anxiety.Anxiety — Self- and parental reports revealed significantly higher levels of anxiety in both Asperger syndrome and classical autism. Negative thoughts, behavioral problems, and life interference were significantly higher for the group of people with Asperger syndrome than for the other two tested groups (autistics and neurotypicals)[19].Processing deficits — People with ASD often experience processing deficits, which are problems with the processes of recognizing and interpreting information taken in through the senses.Decreased empathy — The mind blindness theory of autism proposed that in ASD there are deficits in the normal process of empathy, relative to mental age[20]. While emotional empathy is intact and may even be increased, impairments in cognitive empathy often prevents emotional empathy from being brought into action, or with a delayed response.Working memory deficits — People with ASD often experience problems within the working memory system, particularly spatial working memory[21].Executive function deficits — People with ASD tend to have executive function deficits, which results in challenges with self-regulation and self-directed behavior toward a goal, the ability to break out of habits, the ability to make decisions and evaluate risks, the ability to plan for the future, the ability to prioritize and sequence actions, and the ability to cope with novel situations[22].Rigid thinking — People with ASD tend to show restricted and repetitive behaviors, and a propensity towards behavioral and environmental consistency[23]. question: Is Asperger Syndrome overdiagnosed?
answer: Contrary to every other anecdote based answer here, yep. Opinion | Asperger’s History of Overdiagnosis Is Asperger's Overdiagnosed? Many more like it. One explanation for the various anecdotes presented by all the answers is negativity bias. A person who was diagnosed correctly and received treatment is far less likely to write an answer for this question since it has no bearing on their situation. Only someone who was misdiagnosed would provide an answer, either with AS or with something else in lieu of AS. So far it seems all the answers are from the latter group. Diagnosing mental disorders is tricky since the lines are arbitrary and redrawn based on new data and ideas. The rough idea is that a mental disorder must disrupt daily life enough to have a severe negative impact. Every person struggles with mental health, it only becomes a disorder when the effects are severe enough. Many people fail to understand this distinction. Also, severity is highly subjective. This is why it is tricky. Being an Aspie has become trendy. People self-diagnose and self-identify as an Aspie proudly as if its a badge of honor. If we go by the rough definition of a mental disorder, then the negative impacts must be severe enough to disrupt daily life. That is usually not something one is happy to be diagnosed with. Many AS symptoms are also common among “neurotypical” adults or other mental disorders. Neurotypical is a terrible term since no one is neurotypical. Again. Every person struggles with mental health. For example, some excerpts from Gabi DiCiolli Boardman's answer to What is a person with Asperger syndrome like?Extreme social awkwardness. I take things literally & at face value unless I consciously focus on observing for signs of subtext. For example, my dog's vet once asked if my then-blue hair was natural. Without thinking I responded no, but my dark roots were... of course, 1 nanosecond later I realized he HAD to have been joking- cue the wave of embarrassment!!Gabi is actually able to understand context, almost instantly. This anecdote suggests she was just a nanosecond too slow. “NT” individuals can also struggle with social cues. No one is on 24/7. A miscue here and there is common. A better indication of AS would be if she completely failed to understand the social cue and someone had to explain it to her later.I avoid unstructured social situations whenever possible and have serious difficulty making friends or relating to people in person.Many “introverted” people are like this. Introvert is also a terrible term, but that is a whole ‘nother issue.I do not spontaneously share my interests with my coworkers and prefer to be left alone to my own devices as much as possible while working.Again. A private person would do the same. So would an “introvert”. Or even someone who is just diligent about his/her work. Or someone who is distracted easily. And so on…A love of knowledge, facts, lists (hehe), & objective data. I've collected binders of information since I was a child, and I recall once spending my hard-earned class points on an enormous complete, unabridged English dictionary in 3rd grade.Not all bookworms are Aspies. Not all Aspies are bookworms. NT people can have hobbies as well.Narrow, obsessive interests. For me this is currently genetics, animals and their behavior/psychology, speed & efficiency/time management, and matters of social justice.Obviously, narrow is subjective, but some of these do not sound very narrow.I can also spend several hours on a single task I find interesting without a break; some Aspies are known to get so highly absorbed in their projects they need to be reminded to eat!NT people can also lose track of time and get lost in a task. Hyperfocus is also a common symptom of ADHD. That is probably enough armchair psychology for now. Obviously, it is impossible to get an accurate picture of Gabi based on a few words in an online post, so my observations are just to illustrate a point and have no bearing on Gabi as an individual. There is no easy way to diagnose a mental disorder even with detailed information. Medical professionals must make a subjective call in many cases. Because of how AS was defined in the DSM IV and how its definition has become even broader since being included as part of the new ASD in the DSM V, misdiagnose is common. The other answers are incorrect about the general case as they are based on personal anecdotes.

question: How does Asperger syndrome affect driving?
answer: Everyone with Asperger's (aka Autism Spectrum Disorder with an attitude) is different, and some have the skills to be good drivers while others don't. You are probably on the road every day with Autistic drivers, whether or not they have an ASD diagnosis, as most people over a certain age who would be considered "Aspergers" graduated from K-12 before the diagnostic criteria existed. You probably know someone who never learned to drive and doesn't know the reason that driving seems too overwhelming is that they're an undiagnosed Autistic. (In my experience, that would be my mother, and some odd "fringe" members of various groups.) Generally, people on the Autistic spectrum are more likely to self-assess their strengths and weaknesses realistically, without rose-tinted glasses or succumbing to peer pressure. If an Autistic knows they have difficulty with visual processing or motor control, the idea of driving will be too frightening. They're not going to take lessons, let alone get a license. Taking formal lessons is particularly a good idea for Autistics because an instructor is accustomed to explicitly teaching "rules of the road" that a family member takes for granted. A family member may not be as well-versed in defensive driving, either. Many non-Autistics overestimate their driving skill and have bad habits they don't realize. Non-Autistics are also likelier to think "rules are for other people" and fail to signal turns, change lanes to weave through traffic, and tailgate. (The last is "physics is for other people"!) So an Autistic driver may be more courteous, if they're instructed well. I've been worried about parents overprotecting Asperger's/Autistic kids and limiting them with low expectations. If these individuals have the skills and wisdom to drive, then I'm glad to see them gaining their independence. Nobody should be dependent on getting rides from family, friends, or caregivers--or on public transit where it isn't the optimal method--just because of a diagnosis. They should have the same right to qualify for a license as anyone else. Driving makes independent living more feasible in most communities. Rent is usually higher near good transit, except in urban core areas that may be noisy and dangerous.Jobs are more difficult to find if you don't have your own transportation. You're limited geographically as well as which shifts you can work.Shopping may be difficult, particularly for large, heavy, or perishable items.

question: What is the hardest part of Asperger syndrome for you personally?
answer: Easy. It’s the obsession. I get obsessed with everything. Good and bad. If I like something, it will be all I can focus on until I lose sight of everything else. It is like tunnel vision. Your mind gets stuck in a mental loop. The thoughts are intrusive, repetitive and never stop. You get stuck on one topic of special interest and you rehash and rehash, over and over. You will become engrossed on an interest for hours on end. And because you think about it all of the time, it’s all you can talk about. That is where the theory of mind comes into play-Difficulty understanding other’s perspective. Understanding that others have their own interest, thoughts, feelings and affairs. I do not understand how obnoxious it must be for someone to listen to me talk about the same thing unless they spell it out to me. My communication becomes very repetitive, one-sided and monotonous. And if I am aware of it, it is very hard to stop, because that is just how I function naturally.Unlike OCD, the root of my obsession is not from anxiety, instead the obsession is from something that intrigues and captivates me. Rather than disturbing and anxiety inducing thoughts that people with OCD have. That’s you see them compensate with compulsions. But this is a very, very fine line. Obsessive interest can manifest easily into anxiety. My obsessive nature has repelled people away from me, made them judge me. After a while, you start to feel ashamed, once you slowly realize what you’re doing. People will tell you to stop talking about it. Cringe at how you could be so over passionate and single-minded. Think ‘How could you be so preoccupied with one thing and never get sick of it?’. I would feel humiliated after I look back months later and realize I had passed through another obsessive phase. It’s especially worse if I could reciprocate with no one who shared and appreciated my interest. After you realize no one takes it to the extreme you do, it becomes lonely. Fast. And can destroy your friendships. Sometimes the thoughts get tiresome, just thinking about it, but they always persist.

question: Should people with Asperger's syndrome not have children for fear that they will also have Asperger's syndrome?
answer: I think a lot of what needs to be said has been said here already. However, a point of interest that you might want to consider along with the answers that have already been posted here is this. In Biology, when a species is described, the specimen the description is based on is called the type, or more specifically, the holotype. If more than one specimen is necessary to describe it, these are called syntypes, and any supplemental specimens are called paratypes. Later, a better specimen may be found to represent the species, and would be designated a lectotype. In the event that a holotype specimen is damaged, lost or destroyed, a neotype may be named to replace the holotype. The idea is, species are actually represented by real, physical specimens, so that there is always a point of comparison. Why is this random bit of Biology relevant? Because the species Homo Sapiens, US, has no officially designated Type at all. There is a bit of a story about the guy who "fathered" modern taxonomy, Carl Linnaeus, but essentially, since the late 1770's, there has never been an official, actual human specified as being the best example, or even the most general example of us as a species. Take a moment to think about that. In 300 years, our own species has defied all scientific efforts to even come up with a standard model we could use to point at and say "this is a typical human". I find that pretty gratifying and empowering. What it means, is that it is ok to be different to each other. There is no definitive, perfect human. We cannot agree on what traits and elements should even begin to make up an ideal subject. What it means, is that I, with all my faults, my high functioning autism, my achey joints and bad habits, am no more, and no less perfect than the guy sat in the office opposite me, the woman next door, or anyone who happens to come across this post and take the time to read it. You ask me why I should not have children, because I am different, and because I have the capacity to do harm and cause suffering. I ask you the very same thing. You are not "ideal" either, because, scientifically, we have no ideal to compare ourselves to. You carry within you the means to cause harm and suffering to others, just as does any one else. How many times have you read in the paper about parents that have injured, even killed their kids, intentionally or otherwise, and how many times have you read quotes from their neighbours and friends saying something like "I don't believe it, they always seemed so happy/stable/etc" ? You don't need a learning disability, mental condition or chemical addiction to lash out or make a mistake and injure someone else. Some times all it takes is a bit of stress at the wrong time to make demons out of anyone. The key difference between NT's and those with a diagnosis is that we are usually aware that we can be different to other people, and that this can have an effect on our relationships with them, even if we don't understand how or why that is. Over the course of our lives we have developed strategies to mitigate those effects, where they are negative, and we are probably more aware of them than you are of similar issues in yourself. You as a parent are very likely no better than me, and I am very likely no worse than you. As for loving our kids. Don't mistake having problems communicating our feelings for not having any at all. When events conspired to see me moving away from my son when he was 3, I knew I was unlikely to see him again (his mother denied access for about 10 years as punishment after I objected to her sleeping around) I managed to hold my emotions in check on what felt like the longest train journey in the history of the universe as I travelled to my new flat alone, the sound of his crying at me not to leave echoing in my head in the way that any aspie reading will fully understand. When I got in through the door, closed it and then collapsed on the floor and lay there crying for the best part of a whole day. It felt like my insides had been ripped out. Believe me, I feel love for my child, and when we do chat now, on the phone, in person or on the computer, I make the greatest effort I can to ensure that he goes away knowing that if there is only one thing he can be certain of in his life, it's that I love him completely and utterly. As I said, I'm aware of the fact I don't communicate emotion well, so I make the intellectual choice to try my hardest to make sure that I do communicate those feelings to him. Are you a parent? When did you last tell your kids you loved them? I told mine last night. We make a game of it, at the end of every call we try to one-up each other... "I love you dad" "I love you plus 10" "Yeah well I love you times a million" "Well I love you times a millionzillion plus 12" etc etc.... the process takes a long time, we have a laugh and a joke and at the end of it he knows that no matter what, I love him. Is it difficult at times? Absolutely... but parenting is never easy, for anyone. You do the best you can, develop coping mechanisms where you must, and get support and help where you need it, which is the same for anyone, regardless of how they deviate from a non existent norm. When [sprog] is a little older we'll have a chat about why daddy is a bit different, sure, because I want him to understand his old man a bit, just like we had a chat about why it doesn't matter wether he finds he loves boys or girls (as long as they keep him safe and make him happy, that's all that matters to me) and why it's ok for him to like acting and doing stuff on tv and I'm glad he has a thing he really loves doing. By then he might have realised anyway, he might not. But he still knows I love him.

question: Did Elliot Rodger have Asperger Syndrome?
answer: I think he had two co-morbid personality disorders. I suspect narcissistic PD is the primary one. The other one is schizotypal PD, which shares allot of common features with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), such as poor rapport with others, social withdrawal, flattened affect, odd speech, etc. It is easy to see how the two can be confused, especially if a child is presenting with these traits. What Elliot Rodger did experience which is uncharacteristic of ASD (and should rule it out as a likely diagnosis), are strange beliefs, magical thinking, ideas of reference, paranoia, etc. ASD does not account for these, but schizotypal PD does. Plus, the comorbidity of narcissistic PD and schizotypal PD is fairly common. Narcissistic PD comorbid with ASD (which some users have proposed here) is very unlikely. Many of these traits are evident in his manifesto, where he expresses a belief in being destined to live a life of greatness and win the lottery; he believes that women - who don’t even know him - are “cruel and sadistic” and deliberately attempting to torment him by denying him sex. He reads malicious intent into innocuous interactions. He believes that once he goes on his terror rampage, people will somehow magically know why he is acting out. A person showing signs of schizotypal PD is probably going to be mistaken for someone with ASD by most people unfamiliar with schizotypy, especially someone who has no experience in differentiating between the two, especially parents of these kids.

question: How do you get Asperger Syndrome?
answer: My father was clearly on the spectrum, as am I, and I have three children diagnosed as being on the spectrum too. Beyond that their types of autism, as these vary a great deal too within the autistic spectrum, show some significant similarities to mine. It is well established that autistic spectrum parents tend to have autistic spectrum children so I think it is perfectly obvious that this is mainly genetic. Most of the alternative theories about stomach bacteria, vaccines, sunspots or whatever, if not all of them, are just junk science. Why is autism in the human genome is an interesting question, and I think the answer to that is also obvious. Increasing the size of human brains is very costly in evolutionary terms, and evolution is a careful shopper. How can one get more out of human brains without increasing their size? Well you could mess around with motivations, remove the neurotypical impulses towards mostly meaningless social interactions, add an increased aptitude for math and an obsessive nature and you have evolved better researchers. If you put an autistic spectrum person next to a neurotypical of equivalent intelligence and talent for a particular sphere of endeavour, and if the autistic person finds that sphere of endeavour interesting, the autistic person will likely outperform the neurotypical person pretty much every time. That is the power of focus, the positive side of obsession. People on the autistic spectrum are more likely to suffer from depression, nine times more likely to kill themselves, and many are lost to substance abuse. Many of the remainder though deliver much or most of the technological advancements made by humanity. Elon Musk just outed himself as an aspie yesterday, and most of the greatest scientists (and many of the artists) in history show clear autistic traits. That’s likely not an accident, it’s evolution. From the perspective of someone on the spectrum though, the ability to do really interesting and original work comes at a steep price. Van Gogh knew that, and many others. When my older son, then about ten years old, had just been diagnosed as being on the spectrum, he asked me what he should say about it at school. I half-jokingly replied that he should tell them that it is the price of genius, and for many people doing genius level work, I think that is likely true.

question: Is Asperger's syndrome worse than cancer?
answer: "Worse" implies "bad" - it means to have "more badness" than something else. There's the first problem: AS is a mixture of strengths and weaknesses, it is not simply a bad thing. Now for the comparison to cancer. Cancer is a group of physical diseases, varying widely in terms of cause, part of body affected, and prognosis. And curability. While cancers might give people the chance to show courage, compassion, and sincerity in the face of life-threatening illness, cancer in itself does not confer strengths, as far as I am aware. Asperger's syndrome, however, can confer strengths, and it also confers many neutral differences that only seem to be negatives because of social expectations by western neurotypical society. Some cultures, for example, avoid eye contact, and Aspies might not appear so different in those environments. Of course there are negatives - that is why AS appeared in DSM-IV - but even those negatives can often be reduced or overcome with education in life skills designed for Aspies rather than for neurotypicals. A neurotypical raised in an all-Aspie world would probably also display many signs of stress and impairment. Not all problems experienced by Aspies are caused by AS, they may simply be the result of growing up as an isolated individual or minority in a world full of people who are significantly different to Aspies. Among other things, Asperger's is a form of "Being Different" syndrome.

question: What is the difference between Schizoid personality disorder and Asperger Syndrome?
answer: They are different conditions with different mechanisms and causes behind them. I don’t know much about Asperger, since I am a schizoid, but I’ll try to give my view. Schizoid personality disorder exhibits an abnormal tenancy for loneliness and a lack of emotional expression. It is, mostly, an emotional disconnection from the real world, involving a split between the false self (living the in the real world, with low or null emotions, that we usually have to fake in order to be unnoticed as weirdos) and the real self (living in our inner world, where some emotions may happen). It is suspected to have a genetic base with that kind of tenancy, and then experiences in the first years of childhood pull the trigger. It happens along a spectrum, going from a neurotypical person to a 100% (almost a robot with no emotion) schizoid. Asperger (excuse my ignorance) would be a soft kind of autism. So, it would be entirely driven by genes, and it involves a significant deficit in terms of language, communication, empathy and dealing with other people. So, it is not strange that some schizoid people have been misunderstood as Asperger, and vice-versa, but I’ll point the next differences:Asperger would be a more severe problem than schizoid personality.Schizoids prefer loneliness since we don’t need other people and don’t feel the emotional reward of human relationships, but we can fake and have those relationships, and we can even look like normal and have a perfectly competent life. It would be an effort because we dislike it, but we are not unable to do it. I think this would not be possible for many Asperger's, or it would imply a huge education and effort.Schizoids have no problem with language and communication.Empathy is a complicated issue. We schizoids can have cognitive empathy, and we usually realize and understand what other people are feeling, even if we can’t feel it ourselves. This would be much harder for Asperger's.Some psychologists consider Asperger and SPD inside a continuum, where SPD would border with normal, and Asperger would place between SPD and Autism. Other people don’t give credit to this idea. Greetings.

question: How does Aspergers syndrome affect work?
answer: Aspersers (psssssst…. we’re not supposed to be using this term anymore… we now say the politically correct term of “Autism Spectrum Disorder”, or if we’re really being considerate to the socially and politically correct… we shorten that and just call it “ASD”, knowing full well that most NTs haven’t even broached the subject and aren’t fluent in our secret little private language of anagrams). ASD tends to yield a personality type that is thirsty for knowledge for knowledge sake, and grants an unfiltered determination to achieve it! The great side effect of this is laser focus. We can settle down on a topic or task (for me, trouble shooting a calculation error where an algorithm was misapplied, usually with my luck, four years ago with no real time data capture on an active account that has new interest yield calculations applied MONTHLY. Ugh) and go at it for hours, without a break, until we figure it out. That’s why we’re the programmers and the analysts in life. Doctors. Lawyers, Scientists… etc. Where this can become a stumbling block is that we do that with EVERYTHING that peaks our interest, regardless of time, or social setting. It’s just how we’re programmed. Aspies tend to have amazing performance results but we will get dinged right and left for something we’ve said or someone we’ve inadvertently pissed off. We’ll work a 12 hour day without breaks but then the next, get lost in a google escapade on the latest USDA APHIS update for the mid-western strangles rate for 2018, and repeat transmit-ability in equines with prior exposure verses inoculation (BTW if you live in Michigan, the USDA APHIS record shows 5 confirmed cases across a 5 county span in the last 90 days, get vaccinated and I’d refrain from hauling right now… but that’s just me). It happens. Keep your socializations to a minimum. We tend to feel obligated to socialize a lot in order to “fit in” and “appear normal”, but alas, we are not normal and inevitably we just end up exhausted from the effort and feeling awkward instead. I’ve learned over the years the more I keep to myself and just WORK, the happier I am in life in general. Great news is, though there will be times that you irritate your boss with this behavior, generally speaking your accomplishments will far outweigh your quirks and you will be a valued asset. Just be patient and approachable when you slip up, and you’ll do great.

question: When someone has Asperger's syndrome, is it obvious to other people?
answer: As an autistic person, it is easy for me to recognize autistic children and to a lesser extent, autistic adults. I suspect this has to do with the person’s ability, conditioning, and/or desire to blend in at the time. If the person is non or low verbal at the time I interact with them, it is also easier to notice that they are exhibiting autistic behaviors. On the other hand, if the person is exhibiting no stereotypically autistic behaviors when I interact with them, it’d probably not even cross my mind that they're on the spectrum. This is a common factor in the under diagnosis of autism in women - we’re skilled at camouflaging and adopting a set of unnatural behaviors for a social performance. Unfortunately wielding this “skill” is often done at the expense of our mental health, sense of self, and ability to set and maintain healthy boundaries in relationships. Back to cases that are obvious: I was sitting with the sea lions at the beach last week. I watched an autistic child and his father swim from the cove to the rock I was on. They walked around the rock and looked at the sea lions. Before they left, I recommended that the dad listen to my podcast. He clarified the name and thanked me. When I recounted the story to my boyfriend later, he asked me how the conversation went. I was confused. There was no conversation. I observed. I spoke to the dad, he understood the information and why it was given and was thankful. Then my boyfriend asked how I knew the kid was autistic in the first place. I just shrugged and said it seemed obvious. He probed and wanted to know more. Maybe that’s what you want to know too? What do I as an autistic person notice as giveaways about other autistic people? * has impressive skills but doesn’t behave like people in “cool person” database * hand flapping/rocking/flicking other stimming * non-standard vocalizations (echolalia/humming/grunting) * avoids eye contact/acts like...

question: What do people misunderstand about Asperger's Syndrome?
answer: Years ago I told an old friend about my diagnosis, and his reply is somewhat typical. He happens to be one of the smartest people I know, which leads me to believe that awareness in the United States could use some improvement. Anyway, here’s what he had to say (my own comments are enclosed in square brackets). I can see that a very mild form of Asperger's might fit, given some of the things you mentioned as well as a medium case of ADHD in certain settings, but I would beg you to consider this as simply a convenient label [people often say that it’s “just a label”] for your idiosyncratic gifts and difficulties rather than as a scientific designation, which it is certainly not. Today's psychologists and neurologists cannot even define what autism is , let alone pretend to understand its origins [be that as it may, the existence of autism is indisputable]. In the end their characterizations are still behavioral and narrative-dependent, versus empirical and physical [empirical evidence has actually shown that certain facial characteristics consistently turn up in people with autism, which is something that a good diagnostician will take into account] which basically means such terms are socially derived and applied for social ends - whether good or bad. Regarding the two characteristics you mentioned, I will give you that you do have a slower, low voice that can appear as monotone...but you also do excellent imitations of various kinds of accents and personages, which is something that someone who had Asperger's in any meaningful sense would likely not be able to do [it is actually well documented that people with ASD are excellent mimics]. Also, you have a developed sense of wit, humor and nuance [aspies are often the last people to get the joke, but they can make other people laugh], and an insight into the feelings and thought-worlds of those around you [via logic, not intuition]. These are social skills that many with Asperger's do not possess. Moreover, your own obsessions are not mono-maniacal but have included several, disparate subjects - it wasn't just Russian culture/language/history, it was that of Latin America [in both cases it was rooted in linguistics, and even so, aspies don’t have to stick with just one special interest]. It wasn't just one kind of music but many kinds of music, from Yngwie Malmsteen to Modest Mussorgsky and Mozart [aspies don’t necessarily listen to one genre]. You majored not just in Spanish but in Econ [major and a minor]. You worked in sales and in ESL [I sold language software and taught a language, so it was all rooted in linguistics. Regardless, who says that aspies always remain in the same line of work?]. Your conversations are sufficiently versatile and include personal subjects - which are not usually the provenance of Asperger patients [I’m not sure what he deems “sufficiently versatile”]. You've also always had a relatively easy time making friends - of many different kinds (e.g. W—, myself and M— are extremely different people) [having some friends doesn’t mean it’s easy to make friends]. You've not seemed to have a problem finding women to date [3 failed relationships at 37]. Asperger patients almost always have difficulties with friendship formation, romance and versatility [Japan is actually full of aspies who teach English, so it simply isn’t true that they can’t be versatile, live in other cultures, etc.] Furthermore, Asperger's sufferers are often insistent, unyielding and particular. You seem to have a more "laid back" and accepting attitude towards the minutiae of life [I talk in a slow monotone, which gives the false impression that I’m relaxed all the time]. Just some thoughts. Psychiatrists are woefully unsystematic, have been shown in the US to apply rules of thumb to treatment more often than any systematic protocol and rarely if ever are their specific judgments tested via independent assessments of other professionals. Take everything that comes your way from such a "professional" with an extreme grain of salt. My friend seems to know a little bit more than average about AS, but like many other people, he’s looking for something more severe and obvious. Most people imagine a child with severe developmental problems. My friend appears to imagine the stereotypical hermit with almost no friends, unable to maintain a conversation about anything besides his special interest. There are people like that on the spectrum, but not everyone. Children with autism have distinct facial features: Study

question: Is rage common in Asperger's syndrome/ASD?
answer: Here, again, is asked if something is common in autists. Here, again, I will say, autists are, by nature of their brains, being their selves, very individual. While some may experience rage, others may never. While rage, itself, may mean great internal anger to one, it may mean physical aggression fueled by great anger for another. So, to claim that rage is common, or not common, is to once again ignore the extremely individualist mind of the autist. That said, I can tell how my life has been, in terms of rage. In her infancy, this baby (me) was kept clean and dry, fed, played with a little, until Mother had other things to do, then she was stuck in the crib. All the important things a baby should get, according to the times (1950s), she got. When she expressed discomfort or displeasure by fussing or crying, she was put to bed, or left in bed. When she wanted to be awake and take in the world (all the damn time), if she was up, she was put back to bed after a very short time, well before she was tired. In her frustration, she cried. She was left to her crying. Sometimes she was afraid, becoming hysterical in her terror. The “overall atmosphere” in her family was good, when she was in her crib, being quiet. It was okay when she was up and active, until whomever took her out of her crib got tired of her and put her back down. Frustration built up because she wanted to see to feel to know what she was smelling to explore to find out what she was hearing to be with the family instead of in that crib!! There was so much she could do, but nobody would let her get her fill. As a toddler, she was that little girl who everyone thinks is adorable as long as she’s not any inconvenience. She was an accelerated learner, who pushed for more input, more input, even before anyone could understand what it was she wanted. She loved to learn. It drove her family to distraction, and to throw her back in the crib when they’d had enough. Y’know, back then, most people assumed babies were like empty buckets. Put in it what you please. There is nothing there, so you can make it whatever you want. And if the baby didn’t like it, well, they’d learn to, By God!!! Oh, but as we all now know, there IS something in there, A LOT OF SOMETHING!! Our self is in there. Parents, caregivers, medical professionals, teachers, most didn’t get that. Kids were viewed as incapable of thinking for themselves. WHAT A HUGE MISTAKE!! It caused extreme psychic dissonance, anxiety beyond imagining, constant fear driving that toddler insane, with no understanding of why. ANGER-BUILDING, TEMPER-FIRING, FRUSTRATION BUILT INTO A HORRIFYING PENT UP RAGE THAT SPEWED ALL OVER HER AND ANYONE AROUND HER!!! So, she was a brat. Yep. She got her ass paddled for every little infraction of the rules. Didn’t matter that she couldn’t understand why the rules were. They just were and she’d damn well follow them. Asking questions about rules was usually seen as challenging them, a bad behavior, and punished. Asking about things she was curious to learn about, okay, until the simple answers were not enough for her. Keep asking, time for a nap, or a spanking, or both. Talking about things she thought about would usually be met with ridicule and taunts, jokes made at her expense. She didn’t understand why the family did this when all she wanted was to share what she’d learned and to know more. The siblings were frequently vicious in their verbal attacks, she’d become overwhelmed and fall to the floor in utter despair, crying, miserable, with no idea why she was so devastated but, oh damn, she was having a TANTRUM! She must be over tired, put her to bed, OR, if the tantrum (autistic meltdown, no cognizant self-control) became too wild as she kicked and swung at whomever touched her, screaming bloody hell in her abject horror at being in this state, let’s PUNISH HER, that’ll teach her! Oh, yeah! It taught her. It taught her that she was awful. So disappointing. Such a bad child. Bad, bad, bad, bad, bad! SHE WAS A TERRIBLY BAD LITTLE GIRL! Maybe… Maybe we can give her away. Wouldn’t you like to live with the Pattersons? They can’t have any children and they really love having you around when they babysit you. The Berrys sure do like watching you, you think you want to live with them all the time? That shit went on, in various levels of seriousness, for several years. It’s a wonderful feeling to know there’s at least one couple who will take you when your family finally sends you away. One couple who actually WANTS you. Two caring people who ask you questions and answer all of yours the best they can and never just push you away because they are too busy, when you have been patiently waiting to show them something. Who love you, you have no doubt, because you can FEEL THE STRENGTH OF THEIR LOVE throughout your entire being. She learned a great deal from her family. She learned how to be quiet, regardless of how important what she had to say was, because it wasn’t important to anyone else, so, it wasn’t important. She learned that people would act nice in front of others, but then be mean to her when no one could see or hear them. She learned that people tell you things they don’t really mean. It’s called lying. and once you learn to do it yourself, because, well, you are learning to do everything your family does, you GET PUNISHED for it. Why doesn’t anyone else get punished for it, she wondered? Oh, she learned they didn’t get punished because no one knew they had lied. And when they turned things around so it seemed like she had lied, or done the wrong thing, she was the one who GOT PUNISHED. Being punished for almost everything that goes wrong in your family became accepted, because she was the BAD LITTLE GIRL! So, they gave her a nickname. MONSTER ANN. then, simply MONSTER. And used that nickname everywhere, in front of everyone, so the world knows what a HORRIBLY BAD LITTLE GIRL SHE IS and how she disgraces the family, and, for hell’s sake, don’t ever let up. Because… well, no reason, just don’t ever let up. God only knows what she might turn into if we let up on her for a second. So, KEEP HER DOWN.There you have it. The first few years of this autist’s life, in abbreviation. It continued on that way until my older siblings were gone and I was the only kid left. Then, I was fourteen and had long since begun to recklessly push beyond the boundaries, regardless of the consequences. Being my autistic self was all I could do, a lifelong struggle against an NA (non-autistic) society, but things began to change. That’s several other stories.What’s to be enraged about?
comment_answer: Wow, at last I can tell people about my life. Ive hid it from world cause of shame.

question: How did Asperger's Syndrome become so trendy?
answer: I don’tagree with you. I don’t think it is trendy and people want to be aspie to fit in, rather people have spent entire lives struggling and looking for answers. In the past, with books you would have less access to information and Medical Journals were not readily available nor diagnostic tools. Nowaday you can research your symptoms and find the diseases that fit the criteria, you can learn about them and even use diagnostic tools online ( similar to the tests you’d get done professionally). In this day and age you can learn a lot about anything on the internet using reliable sources , medical Journals and associations that spread information about ASD. Many people with high functioning Autism have been misdiagnosed or if they were suspected for ASD ( Like I was as a child) denied a diagnosis on technicalities like learning to speak earlier than usual for ASD. There are still many misconceptions about ASD, mainly regarding females on the spectrum. Some of us may know more about Autism than your average Psychiatrist. It is not easy. Many struggle for years and have no access to people who understand High Functioning Autism ( most psychiatrists are not prepared for people with Asperger’s or females that are masters of disguise and imitation and appear neurotypical. With that said and you may judge for yourself… I will leave some test results I took, some of them for the first time ever and I was unaware of the criteria and what those scores meant prior to taking htem. As you can see I wasn’t diagnosed, I’ve seeked help before and was dismissed by my psychiatrist because I’m too smart and appear normal… however if you look closely to my results they fall mostly well within ASD boundaries, except for one that doesn’t fit Either neurotypical or ASD ranges. Here: You can Judge for yourself. Am I trending or do I have reasonable grounds to be suspicious? The Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale-Revised (RAADS-R) The Friendship quotient The Empathy Quotient (EQ) The Systemising Quotient (SQ) Two-Factor Imagination Scale (TFIS) Reading the mind in films Part 2: Faces task ( there’s no link to part one because it redirects to the same page [it has both test scores anyway]) The Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) That’s what I wanted to say. It’s not that it’s trendy, diagnostic has just become more accessible and people who are looking for answers eventually find them Edit: It is not a disease, it has no possible cure . Aspergers is a developmental disorder. You may minimize the negative impacts but you cannot change the brain’s hardwiring… it’s just how the brain functions. It is not deffective it’s just geared differently and more efficient for different tasks that neurotypical brains are not prepared to preform optimaly and where neurotypicals excell ASD brains have shortcomings.
