question: My new flat-mate said she can't work because she has Asperger's Syndrome. She said she has difficulty interacting with people at a workplace. Why can't some people with Asperger's Syndrome (or high-functioning Autism) work?
answer: I once knew a chap, at the time we were friends, but because of this and a number of other reasons, we’re no longer speaking. He and I both received diagnoses for Asperger’s (which still existed then) - mine being marginally more severe - but we responded in different ways. He went into the testing almost determined to get diagnosed with something. I went in wondering what would happen, and whether the results would give me any answers to questions I’ve had about myself since I was a toddler. As it turned out, I was relieved that I now understood why I felt the way I did. The diagnosis helped me get in touch with myself a little better - understand my limitations, and my strengths. Just to have something logical “This happens because of X” was, in many ways, the beginning of the rest of my life. I explained it to my boss, assured him that I didn’t require anything but just wanted them to be aware - I asked for one small allowance - a tiny thing that they could do, which would make my life easier; a desk with a wall behind it, and which faced the door. They accommodated me, and said that they would do anything else they could to help me, and in fifteen years I have never taken up the offer him up on his offer. I became a better person, and I continue that struggle even now. I am proud of my achievements, both because they’re good achievements and because I fought for every single one. I am driven to make new ones, and to never stop challenging myself. That’s not how he reacted. He got what he “wanted” - his first act upon receiving the diagnosis was to research how much free stuff and special exemptions he could get himself. He didn’t want to know what was wrong and find ways to help himself; he wanted something he could use to turn his problems into everybody else’s problems. He fought for a disabled badge, parking spaces, free laptops, benefits, exam extensions, free transport, special treatment at work, and got them all. He took his Asperger’s and wielded it against the world, using it as a mallet to bash at anybody who ever expected him to take any kind of responsibility for his life. He was very open and honest that he was doing this. He openly mocked the system that looked out for him, because he was going to make “the man” work for him. He didn’t need a disabled badge; he simply realised that with it he could park where he wanted and save himself the effort of walking or using public transport. He didn’t need the free laptop - he already had a better one than what they were offering; but he fought tooth and nail for the free laptop, paid for by the taxpayer, sold it, and spent the money taking himself and his friends to the Download Festival. He didn’t need exam extensions; he was just lazy and didn’t want to study. He didn’t need special treatment at work; he resented going to work because he considered himself “too intelligent to abide the daily grind so beloved of other, average people” (his verbatim words) and because his colleagues were “knobs” - he found a way to leverage his Asperger’s to make his life easier. He objected to shift work, but was asked to attend to help cover a night shift for somebody who was critically ill (they had been hit by a car) in hospital, refused to do it, threatened to take his manager to HR because he was “discriminating against somebody because they’re disabled”, and then promptly resigned. “But, my Asperger’s!” became a mantra. He didn’t get another job - he searched for a little while but couldn’t understand why, as a man with no experience and no qualifications, he had to start in an entry level position. He considered himself a genius and thought they he should begin at the top. After evading “get a job” pressure from me and from other friends, he took out a large student loan because he said he wanted to get a degree in engineering (in actuality, he just wanted to move to Brighton to get drunk and have sex) so off he went, and he attended one class, told his professor that she was an imbecile and that the classes were “beneath him”, and never went back. He squandered the loan money on beer and kitting out his pathetic rusty Ford Fiesta with a floor-shaking sound system. Then, it was discovered that he never attended University, and the Student Loan Company started proceedings to get the money back - which he’d spent. “But, my Asperger’s, I have a disability!” he said at the age of 29, and his father paid off all his debt. Now his father is almost bankrupt and his mother is descending into depression. Meanwhile, he sleeps in until midday, watches Star Trek, and yells at his mother when she asks him to contribute some money towards the rent - which he still doesn’t, aged 32. (His mother is still friends with mine, so there is some news throughput - but not direct.) It was an utter disgrace - and far from being ashamed, or feeling guilty - he was overjoyed - he’d found a way to beat the system, and to get more in exchange for less. I worked - HARD - to get what I’ve got today. I’m not rich, but I’m comfortable. Every single posession (with the exception of the obvious things; Christmas and Birthday gifts, etc) I have, I bought with my own money which I earned through hard work, or I crafted by my own hand. I have never made my diagnosis somebody else’s problem, and I have never abused it to get an easier life. As a matter of fact, I have made a conscious effort to under-exploit it, and voluntarily take on the additional stress that it causes me. I am almost certainly dealing with more than I have to; but I would rather do that. Following my stroke, all sorts of benefits, freebies, additional time off work, and special treatment was offered; and I refused them all because I didn’t need them and I didn’t want them. I took the time I needed to recover, squared everything with my doctor, and I went back to work. It took me a little time to get back up to “full strength” but I did, and it was worth the effort. I wanted to get there on my own. I have always had to fight for everything, and I’ve got so good at fighting that people don’t realise that I’m fighting at all. I am the living embodiment of the famous Swan Metaphor; gliding gracefully over the water, but propelled by desperate flailing under the surface. I’m terrified of making a telephone call, but I present to a group of 80 executives, and I get applause. I’m terrified of travelling, but my company has an office in Switzerland, so I go to the airport, fly to Geneva, take a train and then a funicular and walk up a mountain to get to work, and everybody asks me how I’m doing and I tell them I’m doing just fine. Then I go and hide in the toilet for half an hour and cry. I’m terrible at interpreting body language and tone of voice. I’m crappy at conversation and I die a thousand deaths a minute in any social gathering. I’m bad at showing empathy. I’m obsessed with routines, and the prospect of change - any change - scares me to death. I speak the way I write, and people think I’m arrogant because of it - they don’t realise that it’s because I actually write out every sentence I’m about to say inside my head, edit it a thousand times, play it back in my head to make sure I’m getting the words and the tone correct, and then read it from my mental “script” - because the thought of speaking “off the cuff” paralyses me with fear. I am overly sensitive to light, noise, and heat, but I share an office with someone who keeps playing with the lights, banging and crashing around, and won’t open the window because they’re too cold. I’m physically clumsy - both as a result of the Asperger’s and worsened by a cerebellar stroke in 2015 - and have poor hand-eye coordination. Sometimes all the sensation just disappears in my right leg and is replaced with stabbing pains that run all the way up to my neck. I have sleep apnea, and on the rare occasions I can sleep, I have nightmares. Life isn’t easy. Especially the parts of life that look easy. But I shut up and I get on with it. And, when I realise just how well I’m doing, it makes it all a little easier. I feel like I can do it - because I am doing it, and if I can do what I’m doing now, maybe I can do a little more. I’m not saying people with Asperger’s shouldn’t seek help where they need it. Not for one moment. But I am very aware that, as with all disabilities, there is a number of people who will try to milk it for whatever they can - at the expense of the genuine people who really do need support and understanding. I don’t need help, I need an absence of hindrance. That’s a subtle but significant difference which many people don’t seem to appreciate.
comment_answer: “An absence of hindrance” would be a true gift to many of us, whether “neuro-typical” or not. Kudos to you for choosing to define yourself on your own terms, and for sharing your wonderful writing.

question: How do I tell if I have Asperger's Syndrome?
answer: You probably don’t. For one thing, you probably don’t. It’s fairly rare. For another, you definitely don’t. That diagnosis no longer exists, it is now just a part of the Autism spectrum. For another, you probably don’t. It’s difficult to self diagnose, since many of the symptoms involve not being able to see the cues that might inform you that you have that specific problem. For another, you probably don’t. It is the “high functioning” end of the spectrum, which means it looks a lot like you’re just not very good at social things and have a few odd quirks. So that was fun. I enjoyed the repetition. Did you? But lets take a closer look. If you suspect you are on the spectrum, you should try asking a friend to help you decide if it’s a possibility. 1 Ask them if they find they have to be very blunt with you to get you to understand what they’re saying. 2 Ask them if they find you to be exceptionally rude despite being very nice (turns out that particular combination is relatively rare in NT’s but fairly common to HFA folks) 3 Ask them how good you are at looking in their eyes when they talk to you. (note, the answer here isn’t really about looking in their eyes, it’s about doing it correctly. Do you look too long, not long enough, do you look at the wrong times, do you stare, do you… well, in other words, do you do it WRONG? Because it’s of course easy enough to look at someone’s eyes. Just not the way NT’s use it, as an added communication channel that most ASD folks don’t process) If you couldn’t find a friend honest enough to have that talk with, well, that’s a sign in and of itself. Try an online quiz. They aren’t by any means definitive, but they can be indicative. If you’re having significant issues dealing with other people, and you think having a diagnosis might help, then look around and find an affordable way of getting a professional assessment. Don’t lead with “I think I might be autistic.” Tell them you’re having some issues and want a generic assessment. Be honest but don’t lead. You can have a lot more faith in a diagnosis that doesn’t look like someone just confirming your suggestion. There isn’t an awful lot to be done, if the answer is yes, but it can be very comforting to know. You can get some counseling to help you deal with the issues entailed, you might be able to improve some of your social skills better with help…or you might be better off figuring that out on your own, your own way. Depends a lot on you and how you deal with authorities, I know they are useless to me. But at least you’ll know and knowing…. is half the battle. I had to say that. You may understand what I mean. (Occurs to me that you may have meant how do you know if someone ELSE is HFA. That’s probably easier to guess at if you’re NT. But remember, your guess is no more than a guess, there are lots of other reasons for those…I don’t even want to call them symptoms. Peculiarities? They’re just indicative.)

question: How are people with Asperger syndrome different from neurotypicals?
answer: I have observed these differences:Aspies can be a lot more sensitive to sensory stimuli. Sights, sounds and smells that neurotypicals may find pleasant, or at worst annoying can be distracting and overwhelming to Aspies. The sensory filter that helps people screen out unwanted stimuli and concentrate on a task or conversation doesn't seem to work as well for an Aspie, and this situation can create terrible stress and cause neurotypicals to misunderstand, misjudge or dislike the Aspie.Aspies don't socialize the way neurotypicals do. They may misread or not notice social cues to approach people, to stop talking or to apologize. These errors are often treated as deliberate acts of rudeness or worse, even though they are unintentional. Also, Aspies can be so topic oriented they fail to connect as well with neurotypicals as they would like. There can be mutual misunderstanding of the other's desires and intentions.Aspies are information collectors and this can have interesting and unexpected effects on the way they think and behave. They may be highly rule oriented and the usual hammer-nail cognitive bias problem all people have may present serious problems for them particularly in grey area experiences like critical thinking, social life and relationships. This tendency to hunt data can make them very well informed and competent but also may make them believe in a principle and rule-based world that doesn't actually exist. I read about an eye scan study done on autistics that revealed some subjects who read fictional texts the way most people read lists or data tables—eye fixations on the initial word or words of a line instead of the usual Z pattern. It suggests to me at least that sometimes people look for patterns that are observable and seem to make sense according to predictable or known rules they already believe and understand. A neurotypical might be more likely to make his principles fit the facts instead of hunting for the facts that fit his principles.Aspies can hurt others' feelings but aren't malicious. They don't take any pleasure in hurting others, aren't intentionally threatening, and indeed can often be relied on to act in ways that undeniably prove they care and want to help. They just often lack the social skills to communicate these feelings or feign interest using formulaic language.Aspies like people and want to have relationships with others, often trying too hard instead of not hard enough. They aren't necessarily shy, but their struggles with the social environment can leave them terribly anxious and depressed.

question: How is it different to have Asperger syndrome?
answer: High-functioning autistics can learn to appear "normal." Often, when I tell people that I have Asperger's Syndrome, that I'm shy, and that I'm extremely introverted, they are surprised. They have seen me at parties; they have seen me teaching classes and directing plays. At such times, I haven't struck them as awkward, upset, or fearful. What's really going on is that I'm old enough to realize what's required to function in the world, and I've developed coping strategies. Everyone does this to some extent, whether they have Asperger's or not. How many adults hate their jobs but are skilled at not showing it? How many have aches and pains but simply push through them? It's part of existing in the world. I don't hate all social gatherings. I'm not a fan of most parties, but I love teaching. I love socializing when it's structured (e.g. when I have a specific role, such as teacher or student), and I love one-on-one's with close friends. I work hard to arrange my life so that, most of the time, I'm either hanging out with a single friend or, if I'm in a large group, I have some specific task. So, if you see me doing this stuff (and not the sort of socializing I dislike), you'd never realize anything was amiss. You also probably wouldn't notice the ten minutes I spent in the bathroom at that party I couldn't get out of. Or that time when I went to a bar for a friend's birthday, how I slipped out and walked around the block a couple of times. I do what I need to do in order to cope, and most of the time I do it quietly without bothering anyone. I have a large group of friends who I love. I seem one of them maybe once every two or three weeks. The rest of the time I stay home, communicating with them on Facebook and through emails, which feels safe to me. From their points-of-view, it seems seamless. As far as I can tell, they don't see me as aloof. They seem me as that guy who chats with them everyday online and then hangs out with them in person every few weeks. Lots of people do that, simply because they have busy lives. So, I've found ways to "recharge" that don't seem odd. For me, the sensory-overload problems are way worse than the social ones. A huge number of things upset me: sounds that are too loud; sounds that are too quiet; the tastes of various foods; people drumming on the table; scraps of paper accidentally dropped on the floor... In many cases, I am unable to just ignore these things. But, again, if you hung out with me, you probably wouldn't notice, because I don't make a big deal about it. I simply find ways to avoid or solve the problems. If you see me pick a piece of paper up off the floor, you'll probably assume I dropped it. Or, if you know I didn't, you may momentarily think, "That's odd," but since I don't act oddly in general, you probably won't linger on the thought. My own behavior reminds me of an interview I once saw with a guy who stutters. That is, he supposedly suffers from stuttering, but I never once heard him stutter in the interview. When questioned, he said that he always could tell, about half a second before saying a word, that it was going to cause him trouble. And so, over the years, he had developed a sufficiently large vocabulary to allow him to switch to a synonym just in time. I've also read about people with involuntary tics--weird body movements they couldn't control. Many found ways to make them look like normal behaviour. For instance, a guy whose tic caused him to raise his arm would then extend the gesture purposefully, smoothing out his hair. So it wound up looking like his intention all along had been to groom himself. And the stand-up comedian Howie Mandel is a germaphobe. He can't stand to shake anyone's hand. So he does the fist-bump instead, and it just looks like "his thing." We're all under immense pressure to "act normal," and so most of us, unless we absolutely can't, find ways to do it (or appear to be doing it), even if we have to work hard at it or take a few extra steps.

(Along with other sensory issues...)

question: Are people with Asperger syndrome frequently misunderstood?
answer: Let me give you a sadly common example from my daily life. Hopefully, you’ll find it humorous. I’m a little bit old-fashioned. But, sometimes holding myself to certain standards reads like I hold others to the same standards and judge them when they “stray”. So, one morning a friend was very frustrated with how things were going at work. She was having quite a day. As she was telling me about what was going on, she used the f-word… and immediately turned around and said that I would never use words like that. So begins the rabbit wheel in my mind: she must think I judge her. What a silly thing for me to judge her for! What did I do to make her think this way? How can I make it better? Just because I don’t use the same words doesn’t mean I don’t experience the same frustration! In fact, I usually deal with my frustration in less productive ways than her! Naturally, I wasn’t able to process my thoughts and reduce them into a coherent, reassuring sentiment in the moment. So, I resolved that the next time I was frustrated and dealt with the situation terribly, I would tell her about it. To my mind, this would conclusively prove that I don’t judge her for swearing, since I deal with my frustrations in decidedly worse ways. Thus, I could not possibly be judging her. Fast forward about a week. I was starting a new job as a merchandiser at a division of Kroger. I showed up to the store dark and early in the morning, ready to put out the brand new products. Well, the store had lost the product. So, after about an hour of searching for it, I left. I coordinated with store personnel to let me know when they found it, so I could put it out before their corporate overlords came by the next day. A few hours later, they found the product and put it out. This was probably no big deal. But, it was my job. There was a planogram to be followed, there were merchandising standards, and I was familiar with the store management, who didn’t care so much about these things. Furthermore, they would probably have lost my backstock if left up to their own devices. They just don’t care—and I used to work with/for them, so I would know. Well, the whole thing caused quite a meltdown for me. As soon as I accepted the reality that it was being done, the store was setting my product and there was nothing I could do about it, I started to come up with passive aggressive plans to get my revenge and/or show that they should have just waited for me to do it. (I know I’m terrible). I thought about waiting until about noon and then resetting their fixture during the corporate visit. I thought about boxing it all back up and then resetting it during my usually scheduled hours the next week. I really enjoyed coming up with these plans, but of course, I would never go through with them. Soooo the next day, I showed up at the store, dark and early in the morning again. I took all the product off the fixture, set it to planogram and merchandised it properly so it would look good for the visit. I organized my backstock, found a place for it to live where it wouldn’t get lost, and was quite happy to have everything done properly. The store director even noted how much better the fixture looked. (← Can you tell I’m still a little salty about the whole situation? >;) ). Aaaaanyway, back to my friend. I told her about the situation and my horrible over-reaction to it. I told her that my reaction was terrible and that I need to be better about people messing with my stuff and doing things that aren’t in accordance with my rules. Buuut, she didn’t see it as me trying to show her that I don’t judge her. She still thought I judged her, and that I react in worse ways. She just thought I was a hypocrite!! Ugh!! I probably should have seen that reaction coming. *facepalm* Things like this happen to me all the time, where I over-think someone’s reaction to something, don’t have the words to resolve it in the moment, and strategize for how to deal with it over time. But, I am also misunderstood when I’m not being so calculating. I tend to hide in corners, which can be interpreted as standoffish, rather than shy. I don’t know the rules for introducing myself to new people, which can make me seem cliquey. I don’t know how to move a conversation past “Hi! How are you?”, which can make me seem rude or uncaring. Sometimes my reactions are too flat. Sometimes, I spend more time reading you than processing what you’re saying (that will come later), so I can’t respond in an accurate way. Sometimes I seem fake. Sometimes, I worry that I’ll come across as fake, which usually makes me seem faker. So, at least in my case, I am frequently misunderstood. It can be really frustrating, but it also keeps life interesting. It’s a puzzle I need to solve. Maybe, one day, I will! :)

question: What is the difference between Narcissism and Asperger's syndrome?
answer: People with Aspergers can experience empathy, but they have difficulty reading people. They cannot read body language, have very limited understanding of facial expressions, cannot see the signs that other peole are sad, upset, or annoyed. So they end up looking like assholes. As they realize they have been such (because the person gets angry or hurt and yells at them) they are profoundly ashamed of what happened. They tend to withdraw from society because of this, as it becomes repetitive, often developing anxiety disorders, depression, social phobia and inferiority complex. Narcissists cannot experience empathy. They cannot feel guilt or remorse. They cannot process shame, and never accept their own failures, always blaming others for them. They have an inflated sense of self-worth and others are always fools, incompetents and parasites. Since their graundious self-image is false, and deep inside, they know it, they have to constantly prove to themselves they are indeed that big deal and have total control about everything and everyone around them. They will abuse people to make them feel like sh*t, so then can feel like gods. They know they are being abusive, but they rationalize it by telling themselves that the person somehow deserves it. They also will do anything they can to control people and make them serve their purposes. When a person fails or refuses to serve them and boost their ego, they either dump the person or punish her, being extremely cruel and abusive, as they simply don't care about the consequences their actions will have on others.

question: What is the process like for getting diagnosed with Asperger syndrome?
answer: I went through three days of testing, several hours a day. Normally it is spread over more days, but because I had to travel to Helsinki to get it done, they arranged so that it could be done over consecutive days. I also had a behavioral therapist assessment, where I got to prepare a cooking task of my choice. I ended up making chicken wraps. I got the assessment that when we went to the grocery store, I didn’t realize I was supposed to use a basket because putting things in the shopping bag could look like I was going to run off without paying. Also I didn’t notice another shopper that needed to get past me. While cooking, I returned to the recipe to check multiple times and I forgot to close the doors of the cabinets after taking stuff out. Also every session took longer than planned, because I was so slow at getting dressed and leaving. The other behavioral therapy session involved a workshop where I made a belt. There I got marked for confusing other group members by advising them noisily when I should’ve left it to the group leaders, and it was often unclear who I was addressing. As for the testing, they tested my intelligence, language skills, maths, social skills and face recognition/remembering. There were tasks like draw a pattern according to a model, and every 10 seconds or so, you switch to a different colored pencil so that they can keep track of in which order you drew it. Later on you had to draw the same picture from memory.I can’t remember very clearly what the picture was like because it’s been several years, but it’s something like this. Then you had to memorize a list of 10 (or was it 20?) words and they kept repeating it until you could repeat all of them. Later they ask you to repeat as many as you can to check your long term memory. The most Asperger related tasks are arranging picture cards to make a story that makes sense, and answering questions about stories, that describe social situations. They might also have you look at pictures of faces, then look at a series of pictures where some pictures are new, and you have to say if you have seen this person before or not. They also ask you questions about what were you good at in school and what kind of play you liked when you were a child. They also ask questions to rule out psychosis and such. They also pay attention to if you have tics or fidgeting. If they ask you if you ever rock yourself, if you say yes, they ask you to show how, so if you don’t do it regularly, this might throw you off. Like I have this tendency to spin back and forth when I’m on a spinning chair, but if I sit in a normal chair, I’m mostly still. One of the tasks was to draw a bicycle that can be operated. You need to remember all the parts that make it move. There can be picture cards like: One guy pushes a door open while other guy watches. Guy approaching a door alone. Guy walking away from a door and another one approaching the door. Guy trying to pull a door open but it won’t budge. Rearrange these so that they make a story that makes sense. I won’t tell you the right answer but for most people it’s obvious after a moment. I think if you are very autistic then you might fail to make sense of it. Edit: I also had to get a blood test taken and pee in a cup to prove I wasn’t taking drugs, because smoking weed can cause symptoms similar to Asperger’s, and there has been an influx of people who were thought to have AS, only to turn out they were just potheads.

question: What are good techniques for communicating with people with Asperger's Syndrome?
answer: Do not talk in paragraphs: If you find a lot of your sentences begin with the word ‘and’ you are likely rambling and the person may be getting frustrated.Do not talk in a recollective narrative:Good example: I went to the pharmacy and my drug was not in stock, they’ll have it on Tuesday though.Poor example: I asked the pharmacist for my prescription. She said “oh hello, let me check on that. I said “okay thank you,” She said “Uh oh, it looks like it’s on backorder,” I said, “OH NO, when will you have it back, I need it!” She said, “Well you know the system, but probably next Tuesday.” I said, “Can you call me when it’s in?”…..etc.3. If we decide to share a story with you keep in mind:The person may feel ‘on the spot’ once they start talking and anxious to have to finish or what your response may be.To keep the conversation going, ask questions gently.Don’t ‘pick’ at the story with phrases that might sound like you’re questioning the story with openers like “But I thought…” rather, use openers like “Have you considered that..”4. Be polite if they seem nervous or act ‘strange’They may not want to look at you, may fidget, and may even visibly be sweating. They are just trying to process what you are saying and making an attempt to stay involved (or get away as soon as possible!).Be alert to the volume of your speech. The person may flinch or squint if you’re talking too loudly.5. Give positive reinforcementIf the person isn’t comfortable with you, they may be agonizing later worried they said the wrong thing or reacted the wrong way. A follow up later even by text saying “it was great talking to you, etc” can go a long way to ensure future conversations.6. Do not ask rhetorical questionsAsking a question like “How many times do we need to tell Steve not to….” might just get you a blank open mouth stare. I would be thinking in my own mind “Do you want an actual number?’, ‘are you waiting for me to answer this question?’, ‘I can’t possibly know what Steve requires before his behavior changes’. For me, these questions are the worst of all scenarios. I expect when someone asks me a question they want quantifiable data as an answer.
comment_answer: I am raising two children with Autism Spectrum Disorder. I have found that keeping directions concise helps them. Ex: Shoes. Room. Now. Replaced: Hey, I noticed that you left your shoes on the living room floor. I just tripped on them. Please pick them up and put them in your room. Following first, next, last: First, get your lunch box. Next put your lunch inside and zip it. Last put it in your backpack. Interrupt a routine at your own peril. Small talk while getting ready to leave the house may not distract a neurotypical person but it may paralyze a person with HFA because their routine is off track abd they don't know how to prioritize your small talk and their known routine. My boys give better, more complete answers to “think" questions than “feel" questions. Ex: what think about going out with Jack and Jill? As opposed to how do you feel about going out with Jack and Jill? With my boys phrases like “I notice….” “I am wondering..” “I get confused when…” “Please tell me about….” are good conversation starters. Using exclusive or inclusive words like always and never lead to perserevation on the topic looking for any exception to the always or never. Be prepared for lots and lots of half conversations or monologues….if someone or something is fascinating, my boys will research every single tidbit of information and share it at you when you least expect it.

question: Why is Asperger's syndrome considered a disorder and not the next stage in human evolution?
answer: What's a disability? Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, an individual with a disability is a person who: (1) has a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities; OR (2) has a record of such an impairment; OR (3) is regarded as having such an impairment. A physical impairment is in turn defined as "any physiological disorder or condition, cosmetic disfigurement, or anatomical loss affecting one or more of the following body systems: neurological, musculoskeletal, special sense organs, respiratory (including speech organs), cardiovascular, reproductive, digestive, genitourinary, hemic and lymphatic, skin, and endocrine." * The WHO defines a disability as "an umbrella term, covering impairments, activity limitations, and participation restrictions. An impairment is a problem in body function or structure; an activity limitation is a difficulty encountered by an individual in executing a task or action; while a participation restriction is a problem experienced by an individual in involvement in life situations. Disability is thus not just a health problem. It is a complex phenomenon, reflecting the interaction between features of a person’s body and features of the society in which he or she lives. Overcoming the difficulties faced by people with disabilities requires interventions to remove environmental and social barriers."** Why do we care? From a policy perspective, it is important to look at the difference between the medical model of disability and the social model of it. Perspectives leaning towards the medical model talk abotu cure and treatment, therapy and intervention; were support and services are needed, it focuses on fitting the indivisual with disabilities into the larger society and making them "better". The social model of disability maintains that "disability" is a socially/cultually created problem and a matter of achieving integration of the disabled into society, by whatever means are available up to and including changing society.Equal access for someone with an impairment/disability is from this point of view a human rights issue of major concern There are of course many others. But these two are the major players in the thought war raging at the moment. What should we do? If Autism (Aspergers having been defined out of existence recently) is an advantage then there should be no supports or help from society available, we don't pay tax dollars to provide support and help to people who are better at life than the average. In many places this debate rages also about gifted children and adults; in many states gifted programs fall under special education along with programs for the disabled. I myself am on balance for this approach, but it is controversial. But this is in general not the case , even for folks who are very "high functioning". People with autism are overrepresented in unemployment and underemployment figures amoung other things, some have issues with independent living which must be helped, there are a lot of issues and it is not as simple as it may appear at first blush. Whether this is from autism or from neurotypical people's issues with autism, it is what it is and redefining it will result oin a loss of help for many. A result oriented approach seems to be the most productive in terms of policymaking. * How does ADA define disability? ** WHO | Disabilities

question: What is adult life with Asperger’s like?
answer: Never even knew I am an Aspie until I had a major brain trauma from an accident. I had to have my cognitive skills assessed to see what was hindering/advancing my recovery. Growing up, I knew I was slightly different from other kids. I pegged myself as shy. I had an extremely hard time making eye contact with people as I became an adolescent. HATED word problems in math, because I would get caught up in the words and struggle to figure out what the question was really asking. Had never learned to study due to a photographic memory. (Something I miss now; that never fully returned after the accident.) An example of me with the boys in high school: gym class... Boy: "Hey Nin, what's your number?" Nin: (perplexed while trying to prefect her golf swing) "My number? You didn't get a locker when school started? I'm sure if you go to the office, they will give you one. I've already have a locker partner, sorry." Boy: looking at Nin strangely, laughing with his "wingmen." Nin: Not sure what is going on with those boys, and goes in search for a golf club that is not bent slightly to the left, disturbing the arch of her swing. I don't have friends, not in the TV "best-ies" sort of way. I trained myself to act calm and open, and can now hold someone's gaze easily. People say I'm gregarious and wickedly funny, but I most times I'm not joking when I say something. I didn't understand the need to go to coffee or lunch with people. It was something that seemed like too much energy/effort. I had my brothers and sisters and my parents. And now my husband and my children. Why did I need friends? My husband, frustrated over me not feeling the urge to make friends with the neighbours, said to me once "you have to make friends! Who will show up at your funeral?" I found this statement funny. He got angry when I laughed. I told him, "Why would I care? I'll be dead." Seriously, I am very content to be by myself. Now that I have Aspie children, I am WAYYY more sensitive to the ways to improve thought processes that help to build friendships. I want my kids to be happy, and since they have had early intervention, my son when he was 2 years old, my daughter when she was 6 years old (she was diagnosed late, unfortunately, so things are a little harder for her), they are very much aware of social gaffes around them where as when I was their age, I either a) didn't notice b) noticed but didn't understand it, so filed it away as "strange" c) didn't care. Constantly, I am encouraging my kids to see themselves as special for who they are and not "disabled" as some might think kids on the spectrum are. We have Asperger. Big deal. It like how someone might have blond hair, or brown eyes. It's just a part of us. Just the way God made us. Practicing the science of social cues and reacting to them is very normal in our house. But by teaching my babies, I am learning too, and at times, it is not very comfortable. Maybe going to coffee is important when someone asks you to. question: How is Aspergers Syndrome a learning disability?
answer: “Learning disability” is anything about you that interferes with your learning. It IS NOT defined as low IQ, although ID is one of many learning disabilities. ASD that was formerly called Aspergers has a number of behavioral symptoms that tend to interfere with learning. Here is a not so brief list:Inappropriate or minimal social interactionsConversations that almost always revolve around themselves or a certain topic, rather than othersNot understanding emotions well or having less facial expression than othersSpeech that sounds unusual, such as flat, high-pitched, quiet, loud, or roboticNot using or understanding nonverbal communication, such as gestures, body language and facial expressionAn intense obsession with one or two specific, narrow subjectsBecoming upset at any small changes in routinesMemorizing preferred information and facts easilyClumsy, uncoordinated movements, including difficulty with handwritingDifficulty managing emotions, sometimes leading to verbal or behavioral outbursts, self-injurious behaviors or tantrumsNot understanding other peoples’ feelings or perspectivesHypersensitivity to lights, sounds and texturesAsperger's Syndrome i should also note that there is a widespread but erroneous belief that people with mild or “high functioning” ASD (Aspergers) are more intelligent. ASD does not correlate with intelligence. Since ASD is a spectrum disorder, some of these may not apply in any given case, and there may be other ASD symptoms that do. How is Aspergers Syndrome a learning disability?

question: Asperger syndrome: What is your learning style?
answer: I don't like labels so I won't label myself with a "learning style". I love reading and I love learning by reading. I don't memorize everything (especially if the style is obscure and/or the content very dense) but I apparently tend to remember much more than other people from what I read. People are sometimes baffled that I remember a minor detail from something I read years ago (whatever it was fiction, a technical document or an academic book). The stranger thing is that I also learn by writing. When I was in high school I loved learning by listening to the teacher and taking notes. The point is, the notes themselves were almost useless afterwards ; I never tried to memorize them and barely skimmed through them before the exam. It was the process of writing down the lesson on a paper that made me memorize it almost instantly. It's quite efficient but it is also a liability because I don't really remember much from a talk if I don't take it in note, and sometimes I just don't feel like writing everything. I like charts, tables, schemas, etc. but I won't say that they are central to my learning. It is more that well-organized and structured information is something that feels comfortable and pleasant to me :) A last (maybe) interesting point is that I strongly dislike videos as a support for declarative knowledge. Videos are great for explaining practical, hands on tasks. When I want to know how to disassemble my laptop or how to work word with a chisel, videos are great. But when I am looking for products reviews, video game walkthrough or similar things that can efficiently be conveyed by text, I am quite annoyed when everything I find are videos, videos and more videos. Videos need a computer or a smartphone with a good signal to be viewed, they demand your complete attention, they can't be efficiently searched for a specific piece of information, you can't easily copy and save information for further reference, and often you have to put up with the video author lamely trying to be witty or funny when you just would like him to focus on the topic. I'm really disappointed by the web increasingly turning into a heap of videos.

question: What job do people with Asperger Syndrome on Quora have?
answer: I currently have three separate paid jobs: each one addresses different aspects of my interests and neurological abilities. After receiving my disappointing A level results from the local comprehensive school and at a local technical college, I started the first job just as I was starting my first degree. The job is in retail, which entails selling and fitting clothing (sometimes making the alterations myself), in addition to dealing with customer enquiries and stock reports: although some of the social, sensory and physical aspects are difficult, I have always found the processing of colour management / systemisation / categorisation quite calming. My second job came after I finished the first degree and before I started the second degree (my first postgraduate qualification). The job is as a policy, law and senior litigation advisor. This position has allowed me to specialise in very intricate areas of knowledge, including immigration, electoral law in Northern Ireland and housing policy, which requires a pedantic attention to detail and a precise application of language. Working in smaller groups and teams has made it easier for others to accept my 'behavioural quirks', but I suspect that this occupation attracts others of similar neurological leanings, so it is easier on several levels. My third job started with the onset of my third (but not final) degree. I started to teach and lecture undergraduates and postgraduates at universities, mostly teaching Cold War politics and comparative political systems, but later moving on to constitutional politics, public policy, development studies and social policy. I still enjoy research and the application of theory to practical situations, which led to positions as a Visiting Fellow at Oxford and as a Post Doctoral Research Fellow in Wales (strangely, I completed both tenures before I graduated with my PhD). I also studied American Foreign Policy and legal writing at Harvard, so I can legitimately say that I have attended both Oxford and Cambridge in an academic capacity. I once turned up to my PhD supervisory sessions in a long red wig and my supervisor didn't recognise me (I was having a bad hair day). I later waddled into my PhD viva five months pregnant, sat down and plonked an industrial size cup of coffee on my lump to help me get through the exam. I enjoy communicating through written papers, articles and debates, which allows me to focus on specific areas of interest at my own pace. I wrote the corrections for my thesis during my second maternity leave and went on to gain my legal qualifications and a PGCE whilst on my third maternity leave. I currently hold a position as a Senior Visiting Research Fellow at King's College London, where I am writing a paper on nuclear defence communication systems in the UK during the 1980s. I also have the rewarding (if challenging) job of being a single parent to three children (aged 8, 11 and 14), two of whom are diagnosed with Autistic Spectrum Disorder, ADHD, social communication difficulties and other co-morbidities linked to autism. The other is neurotypical, but with unusual role models. Due to some destructive tendencies of my children (combined with financial restrictions and an over-protective adopted rescue dog who dislikes workmen / engineers), I have learnt to do basic maintenance, including tiling, plastering, plumbing, electrical repairs and I even fixed the central heating system a couple of times. Over the years, I have taught myself to cook a variety of meals both indoors and outdoors: it is certainly not cordon bleu, but it is still (probably) healthier and definitely cheaper than takeaways. I also spend time acting as an advocate for autism at work, fighting unlawful discrimination (as part of my work, I wrote a Code of practice on the prevention of unlawful discrimination), following through on complaints and trying to secure support that my children are legally entitled to. In my spare time, I have attempted and completed various qualifications in welding, spraying, mechanical engineering (motorcycles mainly), teaching, psychology, Russian and French, playing the violin and piano, politics, history, civil and criminal law and educational applications of neuroscience. In terms of voluntary work, when I first moved to London, I regularly assisted in the administration of Karate training courses and grading, dealing with many visiting foreign dignitaries. More recently, I served for several years as a governor on a couple of local Governing bodies (one was as a local authority governor and the other was as a parent governor). Before I became a parent, I volunteered as a make-up artist and spotlight operator on productions at the Brighton and Edinburgh Festivals, as I enjoyed engaging with the technical element of theatrical productions. I have also performed in several events, including (memorably) a dance routine as part of a professional musical production on an Italian stage, wearing make-up, a large smile, fishnet stockings, high heels and very little else. I love the theatre and live music, so I usually go on my own to performances, prioritising those where my friends are performing or working behind the scenes. Starting at the age of 19, with no real experience of travelling abroad (a school day trip to Calais and Boulogne / booze cruise for teachers at the age of 12 hardly counts), I circumnavigated the world alone several times, including using Shinkansen to travel the length and breadth of Japan, a flight to the northern-most tip of Australia in a light aircraft and a nightmarish journey across the Sea of Japan to Vladivostok. I shared a taxi cab in Fiji with a jumping spider, I trekked around Zambia by bus and into British Columbia by coach carrying a banjo mandolin (I used to play Duelling Banjos, and a selection of REM, Beatles, Green Day and Led Zeppelin songs on it), risking a cavity search by Canadian officials at 3am. I also travelled across New Zealand, Russia and the United States by train (1 day, 6.5 days and 3.5 days respectively). I visited Hong Kong whilst it was under British control, I walked the Great Wall of China and made a trip to the four corners of North Korea whilst four months pregnant. I also managed to fit in a visit to Russia, the Ukraine, Estonia, Finland and Azerbaijan at six months pregnant: all of these trips were completed before the birth of my first child at the age of 30. Whilst I have many interests, qualifications and paid occupations, I believe that they are all dependent upon, and can actively benefit from, my neurological condition. A condition, I should point out, that I had no idea that I had until my middle child received his diagnosis. That is not to say that it is easy to do or manage all of these things: it is not, but I find it rewarding to try and I have made some very good friends over the years as a result. I have been single, planned my own wedding, got married, administered my own divorce and been (effectively) widowed during my life and I am still going. I have developed a single-mindedness and determination that has allowed me to identify and focus on specific goals; it has provided the means by which they might be achieved. It has also allowed me to develop, connect and correlate many different (seemingly unconnected) interests and areas of research. For the sake of balance, I can also say that over the years, I have suffered from severe levels of anxiety, insomnia, depression (anti-natal, post-natal and clinical), OCD and various other negative aspects of ASD. Hyperacusis can make both sleep and concentration on work difficult, with my home regularly suffering neglect from my failing executive function (or successful dysfunction, if you prefer). I find crowds difficult, and I have a tendency to dig my plastic travel card into the palm of my hand to help me focus when travelling on public transport and around busy cities on my own. I am monumentally awful at self-care and my inability to interpret intention and meaning through facial expression / voice / body language has led to abysmal performances at job interviews (a viable explanation of why I have chosen to keep the jobs that I managed to get into) and made me vulnerable to sexual assaults and other types of abuse, including being held at knife point when pregnant and trauma as a result of bullying. All said, I would prefer to focus upon what I have been enabled to do as a result of my condition, rather than concentrate upon the negative aspects, of which there are many.

question: How do people with Asperger syndrome study?
answer: This is going to be lengthy. I have Asperger's and I am sensitive to noises in particular. I also am a Nursing student and doing great in school. Here’s how I study: IN CLASS: During lectures I usually print out all the slides with 3 to the page and the other side to take notes. Whenever the instructor elaborates on points in the slide I would write down the information that I may not remember. I exclude things that are already learned so I don’t waste any note space. I sit in the front of the classroom at a far corner, so that I can hear well and not be distracted by things on either side of my peripheral vision. I do bring earplugs to my class and lightly put them in (I can still hear the teacher clearly for the most part, since I am in the front of the class, and I keep my hair down to hide the earplugs. I do tell my classmate that i’m sitting next to so that if she needs to ask me a question and whispers she can just tap my shoulder and i’ll pull an earplug out to talk to her. So far I haven’t had any bad reactions except “Can you hear the teacher?”, in which case always do so I’ll say yes my hearing is just very sensitive). STUDYING OUTSIDE CLASS: As for studying outside the classroom, I do it alone in my bedroom. I bought a pair of Bose noise cancelling headphones that I use with or without music depending on any distracting noise inside or outside. I like to buy candles and light one every time I study because It makes me feel calm and the smell relaxes me. I have my desk and printer in my room (but it doesn’t matter where, just away from anyone or any distractions). I close all the blinds, maybe the curtains too, and I’ll light my candle (or essential oil diffuser) and turn on one or two lamps so I can read without straining my eyes. If the light bulbs on the lamps are too bright I’ll just cover the top with a t shirt or something (they’re LED so they don’t get hot). If you have one of those lamps that don’t have a shade and are glass, I like to put colored paper around them and tape them together so it adds this nice ambiance to the room (Blue color helps me study well and it doesn’t hurt my eyes). Just make sure your bulbs are LED and don’t get hot, you don’t want any fires. I wear comfortable clothing and I NEVER sit in my bed to study. Don’t get too comfortable. Maybe turn your fan on to keep the air circulating or add any extra white noise. Create a relaxing, therapeutic work environment at home that makes you feel like you can sit down and focus for a long period of time and occasionally get up and walk around to rest your mind. Put your phone away somewhere, or put it on silent. Don’t open YouTube, Facebook, or any websites that will distract you unless you’re taking a break for a specific amount of time. Use a timer whenever you do. Take a break to have a healthy snack or a little bit of coffee or tea. Keep a water bottle in the room with you. For music I like to use soft piano study music, lo-fi hip hop beats, or binaural beats. There’s lots of playlists on YouTube that last for hours. Pick one that you think you can study to. For my personally I don’t like listening to drums or jazz because the noises may distract me whenever I’m in study mode. As for you study style it really depends on the individual. If you are visual then take whatever terms you have to learn and draw pictures (doesn’t matter if it’s stick people). Take a quiz online to learn your study style. You may be a mix of a few of them. But whatever you do, don’t Over study a subject in your material that you feel passionate about. ALWAYS focus on your objectives in your syllabus or study guide and directly answer them without going into too much detail. I know us Aspies tend to do things like that. Anyways that is what works for me! Good luck! -MG

question: As an aspie, what is your Myers-Briggs Type Indicator?
answer: INTJ, close to INTP in my case. Almost by definition anybody on the autism spectrum, including Asperger's syndrome, is an Introverted (I) and Thinking (T) type. Introverted not just because of the poor socialising skills, but especially because of the need for a quiet environment and the sensory overload caused by crowds or even by an animated conversation between a few people. The Thinking dimension is also obvious as Asperger's is a form of ‘extreme male brain' characterised by a very rational, logical and analytical mindset, which generally prime over the emotional and empathetic tendencies. Theoretically people on the spectrum have a higher likelihood of being Judging (J) types, a dimension associated with a preference for clear planning if activities, fixed rules, more organisation… However I think that this is mainly a coping mechanism to deal with anxiety. Not all Aspies require it. In fact it seems from other responses that quite a lot of Aspied are close to parity between J and P. As for the last dimension, it seems that Aspies are slightly more likely to be Intuitive (N) types while other autistic people (including highly functional types) are more Sensing (S) types. NT types are people who like to play with ideas, test hypotheses, develop theories… That fits more with the more verbal and scientific-minded Aspies. S types are more down-to-earth and practical and would be more attracted to raw numbers (maths), engineering and more likely to be obsessed with mechanical stuff like cars, trains and airplanes.

question: What's it like to have Asperger's Syndrome and ADHD?
answer: Well, First things first, I will have to give you the old chore that not all mental disabilities manifest in the same way. Sure, having ADHD and Asperger’s is definitely going to shape you and how you live your life, but it is NOT everything. Secondly, if you - as I did - became distraught and depressed from reading the answers to this question because you or someone you know has autism and ADHD, you must first realize, that often in these categories (mental illnesses) persons will use their (sometimes made up) diagnoses and their 15 minutes of fame to rant about personal problems that they may otherwise not rant about in their real life. Now, let’s get on with actually answering the question. What is it like having ADHD and Asperger’s? It is F****ing AMAZING, if you allow it to be. First of all, you spot every detail there is in every street, every painting, every face and everything else beautiful. A beautifully sculpted balcony or a perfectly formed rock can give you the same excitement and dopamine-kick a neurotypical can only get from extensive and time-consuming activities such as getting a kiss from drawn-out and boring date. You may not even realise it, but you get so much more from a day of looking and pondering, than most get from a whole year of partying and drama. Having ADHD and Asperger’s is also like having a private universe inside of your head filled with amazing songs, paintings, ideas and discussions. You might not bring all of them out of there so others get to enjoy them, but you’re definitely experiencing it. And if you one day do decide to bring out all of that amazingness inside of your head you might realise, that you can become ANYTHING you want. Yeah sure, neurotypicals can too, but the difference is that, not only are you going to be the person in the room at what you’re doing, you’re also darn sured guaranteed to be the most excited and happiest person at doing that job. In the sense that you might finally “combat” your autism by meeting someone who likes you for you, or getting a new job you’re happy with or finally finding a girlfriend that can keep you intellectually stimulated, your ADHD (the other weight) might make you scare off your friend, or make you lose interest in your job or make you bored of your girlfriend. But if you lift that weight long enough you will start to develop new strengths and skills. And you better believe me, when I am telling you those strengths and skills, whether they’re social-, economic- or technical skills, are gonna be so much greater than the skills of those born without those weights. Being born with ADHD and Asperger’s doesn’t mean you have to be a homeless, unemployed, 30 year old, lonely virgin like these answers would like you to be believe. You can be a 19 year old millionaire living the lifestyle of your dreams, a super genius working for NASA, the greatest pianist in the world OR the richest man in the US ( ;) ). question: Can a person with Asperger's Syndrome write romantic poetry?
answer: I once read a love poem - I cannot remember it exactly - but it went along the following lines: "I love you more than a mouse fears cats, I love you more than a businessman hates taxes..." In other words, it compared the strength of the writer's love to the strength of various well-known negative emotions. It was funny. If I ever change my mind, I'll let you know." Not sure how to turn that into poetry, but hopefully you get the idea. Someone (a psychologist well versed in Asperger's syndrome) once said that the Beach Boys song "In my room" was an Aspie love song - although it is a song about loving to be alone in one's room, rather than about loving another person. I could imagine a person with Asperger's syndrome writing a love poem about their special interest ("Volcanoes bring me inner peace, as ashes from the vent release, in volume to the air above...something something something love"). A person with Asperger's syndrome may well be obsessed with their partner when they are in the "just fallen in love" phase - the partner would be their special interest. In this state they may write romantic poetry, although it might be humorous as well - or have other idiosyncratic features e.g. mimicking existing romantic poetry. Maybe I could copy a medieval poem of courtly love from the troubadours and change the name... that might an Aspie way of expressing love. question: Do many Quora enthusiasts border on having Asperger syndrome?
answer: No. Unlikely. According to the National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NHAMCS) Asperger Syndrome happens in about 1 in 10,800 patients. Given that Quora probably has around 50,000 or so users since opening to the general public (when I joined in May, my Quora number was 15,000, so making a bit of an assumption), that would mean there are probably 5 people on Quora with Asperger Syndrome. Your actual question was are they borderline? Well, let's say the incidence of borderline is 3-5x the rate of actual cases. That would mean there are still only 15 to 25 people on Quora with borderline Asperger type behavior. Of course two things could be happening. First, let's assume true Quora enthusiasts are 1% of users (500 users). It could be possible users with Aspergers are more likely to become hardcore Quora users. Assuming of course they are not already obsessed with something else. Going from the above calculation, let's assume all of the borderline Asperger users become enthusiasts; then at best, this would mean only 5% or 25 of the enthusiasts would be borderline. A very small number. Second, within your social and topics graph, the 15-25 users who do have borderline Aspereger type behavior could be over represented relative to other user's experience with their own social and topics graphs. You may simply attract all the Asperger types. Unlikely, but possible. So, I don't believe Quora enthusiasts are any more predisposed to borderline Asperger behavior. I think two things are happening in the Quora community. First, is a version of the old cliche, "Everyone is either a fox or a hedgehog." If you are not familiar with the quote, it basically means Foxes are super generalists with broad knowledge, but very little depth, and Hedgehogs are individuals with very deep knowledge about a few subjects, but less breadth in their overall knowledge of the world. After using Quora for the last four months, it seems Hedgehogs are the dominant strain of user. These users have super specific areas of focus and incredibly deep knowledge. This is the part of Quora that is incredibly fun. For example, getting an answer from a world-renowned cancer researcher or a specialist in machine learning. Very cool. This also comes with a downside: many of the Hedgehogs don't actually know they are in fact, Hedgehogs and as a consequence, believe their expertise plus the values from their field of expertise transfer across all subjects. Sometimes this works for them, more often it just pisses off users from different perspectives or disciplines. The second thing happening is that many users on Quora are the epitome of the culture of their chosen discipline. Most professions, whether it is software engineer, economist, doctor, or lawyer, have cultures that are rigorously enforced in a very subtle way. As a result, you can expect some predictable answers and behaviors out of people based on their training and vocation. For instance, when you are negotiating a deal, sometimes (not always) having a lawyer around can be an impediment to getting the deal done because lawyers are trained to be risk averse and cover every contingency. It's not unfounded: often their license to practice law and means to make a living is on the line. So, lawyers during a deal negotiation can (not always) slow the deal process down as they focus on details and act over-cautiously. With that said, I think the answers and comments many of the Quora users give come from the perspective of their own professional culture and depending on how strong that professional culture is, it limits their ability to empathize with answers from users outside their discipline. As a result, they seem rigid, dogmatic, and inflexible and often exhibit some poor form when it comes to social interaction. Also, many professionals live very siloed work lives. I'm sure very few medical doctors spend much time with crossword puzzle or machine learning experts. As a result, these groups have very little social knowledge of each other, and tend to bump up against each other when interacting on Quora. I believe the recent attention Asperger Syndrome has received as a result of the pop diagnosis of Mark Zuckerberg and the actual diagnosis of Michael Burry (made famous in Michael Lewis's book The Big Short) has made Asperger Syndrome a fashionable excuse for poor and insensitive social behavior. Another version of "not my fault." In the last couple weeks, I've had no less than three people confide to me that they thought they had some symptoms of the disorder. Of course, this confession came after some insensitive behavior on their part and a half hearted attempt at apologizing or justifying their socially obnoxious behavior. Yes, the irony that this is a slightly Asperger-esque answer is not lost on me. LOL (Asperger Data from Wolfram Alpha http://bit.ly/bxwbec)

question: How do people with Asperger's Syndrome experience grief?
answer: This is a topic which really warrants some serious research and writing. I experienced a devastating loss recently, and found myself struggling to cope – not only with the loss itself, but with normative expectations about how I would process it, and with understanding how (or if) I was processing it. There’s a funny little circle that happens – autistic people tend to research things, both for comfort and in order to understand them as they become relevant. So I went and researched autistic mourning. One of the typical responses? Researching mourning. Go figure. In short, I basically had a very extended shut-down. I could barely respond to a text. Even when I made it clear to the people in my life that I wasn’t in a position to respond, they’d send me texts just to make me feel supported, knowing I wouldn’t respond. And even THAT was too much. Everything weighed on me; just having to accept condolences was emotional labor, and made me realize that this concept – the emotional labor of accepting condolences – deserved some thought and discussion in its own right. I had some such discussions with friends and strangers online, and it was the most productive thing I managed to do. Just getting a bunch of people talking about how hard all these things were that nobody understood. I came to feel that, as with so many things, most of the common ways of understanding and participating in mourning in the NT world were counter-productive, harmful, poorly-thought-through, and very often selfish. People were worried about me, so they expected me to keep them informed, to tell them I was okay. It wasn’t about me, it was about assuaging their anxiety. The notion that this ought to be my responsibility caused a great deal of resentment which I’ve tried very hard to work off. Autistic people can take longer to process things. Grief, for me, takes ages. It seems infinite and inescapable. Most of the comforts extended to me only made things worse. I needed time alone, time not under observation, but that’s the opposite of what everyone thought I needed. Grief is deep and conceptual for me as well as immediate and experiential. Feeling one death so acutely means confronting death itself in a more pronounced way. Maybe I’m lucky that I do this anyway as part of my philosophical and creative work. Maybe not. I had trouble hanging onto a thought. I had trouble remembering even very basic things. Names, recent events. I didn’t go through the typical stages at all. There was no denial, no bargaining. I was angry, but I was angry because in this instance there were factors which warranted blame. I didn’t want or need to talk. I needed to be able to step into this awful truth without being needled and prodded. Of course it varies, and I know I’ve said more about the social aspects of grieving amidst NTs. But the short answer is, it’s probably going to be more complicated, take longer, and perhaps be felt more deeply. Going through it in the neurotypical world will probably be more alienating, and require more work from you if you really want to carve out the space you need to do it in a way which makes sense for you. There’s not much out there about it, but I’d recommend scanning the various message boards, which, while anecdotal, sometimes really help when all you want to know is what it’s like for people like you. Here are a couple decent links: https://www.iidc.indiana.edu/pages/supporting-individuals-on-the-autism-spectrum-coping-with-grief-and-loss http://www.thinkingautismguide.com/2012/08/autistic-grief-is-not-like-neurotypical.html

question: Do people with Asperger's Syndrome enjoy sports?
answer: Do people with Asperger's Syndrome enjoy sports? - Yes.Do people with Asperger's Syndrome manage to play games that need team work? - Yes.Do they have problems with fine motor skills and hand eye coordination? - Yes.Can they predict the intentions and moves of the opposite team? - Yes.People with Asperger's are like any other population of people. We have varied interests and varied abilities. Do we enjoy sports? Yes. Many neurotypical people enjoy sports as spectators, many as casual players, and a very few at a high level of skill. Autism doesn't change the nature of that, although it skews the distribution a bit more towards the spectator side due to common motor skills issues. That said, there's nothing that says autism and sports ability are mutually exclusive, just a bit less prevalent than in other populations. Teamwork? Absolutely. Sports tend to organize as meritocracies. The autistic's quirky traits matter less on a team than skill and talent. It may be that we are more often in teams that utilize our technical abilities but if an autistic person happens to be really good at a sport most teams would welcome and value him or her. Where this falls apart it's not usually the autistic person but rather bullies on the team mistreating that person. Deficits in motor skills and coordination are a hallmark of autism but like any other trait these vary widely. As a kid my misproprioception was so bad I was like a puppy tripping over giant paws all the time. I was in the middle of the range and there were - and are - lots of autistic people with more or less motor deficit than me. Did that stop me from playing football or basketball with my neighborhood friends and enjoying it? No. I was often the worst player there but among my friends I was a player nonetheless. The game I was playing was recognizable as the same one they were playing, I was getting all the fun and benefit of exercise and I was among friends. It helped that I was just as amused by tripping over myself as my friends were since in laughing it off together I felt supported rather than bullied. (Contrast with non-friends from whom the same response might feel like derision or signal imminent danger.) As for predicting intentions this is easier in physical sports. I suck at poker since I'm totally blind to microexpressions. Hell, I can hardly parse macro-expressions that to others are as obvious as sledgehammers. But I do understand physics and all of Newton's laws of motion apply. People can't change direction without compensating for the inertia. It's relatively easy to see when someone tenses to pivot or push off. I don't look at their eyes or face for these signs, I look at their trajectory and whether their posture will result in preserving or changing it. This covers most of the prediction I need to function in the game. The most important part of any of this though has nothing to do with autistic deficits and all about personal beliefs. All other things being equal and surrounded by supportive or neutral people, it comes down to a person's expectations. Anybody, whether they are autistic or not, who believes they will not have fun playing a sport in which they are physically capable of participating at at least a rudimentary level, will most likely not have fun. Anyone who participates with the expectation of having fun will most likely have fun, even if they do not find they have a natural talent for the sport. At my house we have a birthday tradition of going out to eat at whatever restaurant the celebrant chooses. These are meant to be fun occasions so we want them to go well and everyone to have a good time. For many people this would mean picking a restaurant that is tried and reliable. We don't want bad food or service ruining the night. I take a different approach. I always pick restaurants we've never been to before. We fully expect some of these to be disasters and sadly they often are. Does that ruin the birthday? Not at all because the risk is part of the adventure and sometimes we discover new favorite places. In fact, the horror stories we tell years later continue to return fun experiences on the investment we made in taking that original chance. (Remind me sometime to tell the story of the place that gave us straws with our wine.) Whether at sports or picking restaurants, having fun means taking risks and accepting what comes. If you go into it unprepared to accept a poor result those expectations can be crushing. But if you let fear of failure or performance anxiety stop you from even trying then you never find that new favorite restaurant or discover unexpected talent for some new sport. When you go into something new with the intention of exploring and having fun then these goals are achievable regardless of how well you perform at the task. This is because because your measurement for success comes down to whether you made the attempt or sat life out on the sidelines, and that choice has nothing whatsoever to do with autism. That comes down to character.

question: Are you born with Asperger Syndrome?
answer: Am I born with Asperger’s syndrome? Well, I am diagnosed with Asperger’s syndrome, so I have got it now. Asperger’s also may run in my family (I am the only member formally diagnosed, however). And there is evidence that “milder” forms of autism like Asperger’s tend to be more the result of many genes, each with a small effect on the development of the brain, whereas severe autism (e.g. with intellectually disability, epilepsy, and no speech) is more often the result of major mutations “out of the blue” (i.e. de novo — Rare mutations linked to severity of autism symptoms | Spectrum | Autism Research News) So the evidence seems to suggest that I was born with the genetics and prenatal neurological development that would eventually manifest as Asperger’s syndrome. But nobody realised my life experience was “autism” until I was in my fifties. It was most obvious back in my teen years and early twenties, though. In some ways, asking if a person is born with Asperger’s is like asking if they are born with language. They are born with all the genetics (e.g. FOXP2 gene) and brain structures (Broca's area) required for developing language, but language does not begin to manifest itself until age 1-2 years, and it has a strongly learned aspect, which is why we have so many different—and constantly changing—languages in the world. If you are autistic, you already have autistic genes and much of the autistic neurology when you are born (a lot happens neurologically after birth in all people too). But the characteristic autistic behaviours may not be clearly evident for some time, and early learning can have an influence on how they manifest, particularly in Asperger’s syndrome.

question: How are Asperger syndrome and psychopathy different?
answer: In many ways I see Asperger's and psychopathy as opposites. A core issue is "empathy", which is often misunderstood or oversimplified. I like to explain empathy - and its role in Asperger's and psychopathy - in terms of five questions:do you care about other people?are you affected by obvious displays of emotion (e.g. someone crying, or someone shouting angrily)?do you know what to do if someone is obviously expressing emotion?can you guess what other people are probably thinking and feeling when they are not obviously expressing emotion?do you know what to do about other people's thoughts and feelings when they are not obviously expressing emotion?A person with Asperger's might answer these questions with: Yes, Yes (possibly overwhelmed), No, No, No. We care about other people; we may be overwhelmed by the obvious expression of emotion; but we often don't know how to respond nor how to read subtle emotional cues. A psychopath might answer No, No, Yes, Yes, Yes. They might not care much about other people; they are not moved by obvious emotional expression, but they understand other people and know how to manipulate them. So a person with Asperger's may well be socially clumsy, but well-intentioned. The psychopath may well be socially very smooth and competent, but coldly calculating their own advantage. They have opposite problems with "empathy". They most certainly are not the same or "related" (whatever that means).
