question: Why is Asperger’s associated with intelligence?
answer: There’s no mystery about why Asperger’s and high intelligence are related; it’s just defined that way. Asperger’s is a now-outdated label for autism without speech delay or developmental delay; it’s outdated because psychologists realized that Asperger’s and autism really are the same phenomenon, and just put them together as autism spectrum disorder. So to be diagnosed with Asperger’s, you had to be autistic, but you also couldn’t have any speech delay or developmental delay. Developmental delay rules out Asperger’s. Removing all developmentally delayed people from a group automatically moves the average intelligence (as measured by IQ score or developmental progress) of the group to above average. Aspies are autistic people, and by definition, autistics have problems with communicating. However, they learned language at the same time as their peers. That means that even though they have problems with communicating, they learned language on time—and one good way to do that is being good at learning, period. (Or you could just have a relatively unaffected language-use ability.) It didn’t hurt that the original Asperger, the man after whom the disorder was named, was a bit of a eugenicist who was trying to prove to the Nazis that his “little professors” were not intellectually disabled, and thus perfectly capable of contributing to society. Asperger’s is an artificial category. It’s a subdivision of autism defined by language skills and at least low-average intelligence. If you’re autistic, can talk the hind leg off a mule, and understand that the mule is figurative, you would probably have been labeled with “Asperger’s”.

question: Would you date someone with Asperger's syndrome? Why, or why not?

question: Asperger's Syndrome: Are autistics more likely than neurotypicals to be atheists?
answer: Well. Those with ASD are united in viewing the world mechanistically. That is, the world as mechanism: a organised system of rules, that has certain input, outputs, and states. This is because they lack the theory of mind of others that so biases neurotypicals to see thinking minds in both animate and inanimate entities and processes alike. That, then, yields the answer : yes, they are more likely to be atheists. If they are not, then they will most likely be deists. This too is compatible with universe-as-mechanism. If they are still religious in the traditional sense (theism), they'll probably be fundamentalist, as that too offers a strong set of rules which are mostly internally consistent (if not externally). And this is what the research has found. Pretty consistently. (There is also the fact that those with ASD generally really like detailed learning, and well, thoroughly learning a religion usually results in atheism or extremism.) As for me, I have ASD, and I am an athiest. Always have been. I do not believe myself capable of being religious, and again, always have been - the very idea seemed absurd, I remember thinking in my early days of primary schooling, quite confused at what others seemed to get out of it (along with many other parts of human behaviour!). Most of my family isn't very religious, but then they aren't identified atheists (except my sister). I certainly don't talk about it much (unless prompted directly, or if it's of contextual interest), and neither does anyone else.

question: How does meditation affect those with Asperger syndrome?
answer: My wife uses meditation a lot with teenagers with autism and aspergers, and she has pretty much universally had positive feedback. question: What are some examples of stims of people with Asperger's Syndrome?
answer: How do I stim, let me count the ways! Shortly after I learned I was on the Autism Spectrum, I had a conversation about "stimming" with a special education teacher. She said something that stuck in my brain like glue: any repetitive movement is stimming. Well, it isn’t limited to only hand flapping, spinning, and rocking. I am big on rocking myself which is a big help when the "meltdowner" pays me a visit. I have more ways to stim than I probably realize. For example, during my summer break from my school job, my sweet 80-something year-old Mom said, "If you're looking for something to do..." I interrupted and said, "No, I wasn't on the hunt." HA! She was suggesting some other yard chore - a new one on me. Well, that pricked up my ears. Her suggestion was trimming a hedge in the backyard. I got excited at the prospect. I know ... I live such an exciting life. The hedge trimmer and I were not well-acquainted since I lived in apartments most my adult life and didn’t have to touch the shrubs. I was eager to give it a whirl though. After my Mom left to do errands, I took off outside with the manual trimmer and went to work. Cut, cut, cut! Repetitive movement all right! It was an instant gratification to see the hedge taking shape. I was like a sculptress with a chisel. As I often do thanks to my Autism, when I like something, I go overboard. I have since obtained battery-charged trimmers to “yard stim” without so much wear and tear on my upper limbs. In addition to pacing the floor, I jog in place. Well, jogging in place is repetitive. The advantage to jogging in place is I can do it indoors too. That's a definite advantage in 90-something temps with 50% humidity or a wind chill of 20 degrees. The other day a friend came by while I was on a date with the clippers. She said smiling, "I saw you trimming and jogging at the same time. Is that, by chance, an Autism thing?" I told her, "Yeah." She asked if I wondered what people were thinking when they drove by. I live on a busy three-lane two way street with traffic fitting a major thoroughfare. I told her I just face the hedge and keep my back to the traffic whizzing by while telling myself it doesn't matter what the passer-by's think. She laughed and said, "Whatever gets you through your day." Like someone once said, "Dance like nobody's watching." Well, even if they are, I'll stim by jogging in place while trimming the front yard hedge if I want to.

question: What is the difference between Asperger's syndrome and antisocial personality disorder?
answer: While I can understand where you might be coming from when you compare the two conditions, there are clear differences between Asperger’s Syndrome/Autism and antisocial personality disorder. Asperger’s Syndrome/Autism is a neurological developmental disorder, characterised by someone’s social, emotional, communication and sensory development in comparison to their peers. Someone with this condition will lack the understanding about these things, and may not be able to detect when someone is doing something manipulative or rude. People with Asperger’s Syndrome/Autism may also act in a similar manner, or come off as being that way because they’re unable to hold eye contact or understand the way a conversation works, but more often than not, this is because they do not understand how to act around neurotypical people as opposed to doing it to purposely bring someone around to their point of view. However, someone with antisocial personality disorder is likely to understand social rules. They’ll know what is and isn’t acceptable and how social rules work, but they’ll want to defy them and use them to their advantage in any way possible. Unlike autistic people, people with antisocial personality disorder will weigh up a situation and purposely sway it in a direction that benefits them. They will be aware of their manipulation techniques, and won’t take the opinions of another person into account when carrying out actions. People with this condition, formerly known as sociopathy, will put themselves above everyone else. It’s a common misconception that people with Asperger’s Syndrome/Autism will manipulate a situation because they have no empathy for other people, but this is actually more characteristic of antisocial personality disorder, as mentioned above. Someone with Asperger’s/Autism is more likely to feel too much empathy for others, which is why they often suffer from conditions like social anxiety disorder and depression, which comes as a result of excessively overthinking how they come across to other people. People with Asperger’s Syndrome/Autism will find it harder than others to make friends due to their delayed social development and other possible deficiencies; however, it is likely that they will want to make friends. Talking from personal experience, observing other people’s interpersonal relationships and realising I didn’t have anyone like that in my own life hurt for a number of years. I was lucky enough to find friends who value me and respect me, for all my good and bad abilities, and the last thing I would want to do is hurt them, even if meant it would push me further towards my personal goal. People who have antisocial personality disorder, on the other hand, aren’t very good at making friends. Not because they don’t know how to, because they’re very skilled in that department, but because they don’t see the point in making friends. They’ll befriend someone on a temporary basis if they can see it as advancing their current goals, or getting them to where they want to be, but when someone better comes along, or the situation passes that said ‘friend’ was needed for, the person will quickly be forgotten about within the person’s mind. I hope this has helped answer your question! If you have any more, feel free to leave them in the comments below or contact me via the contact information on my blog, and I’ll be happy to try and help in the best way I can.

question: Are people with Asperger's shy?
answer: I have been thinking about this a lot recently, and have come to the conclusion that it is because many of us are somewhat uninhibited, that probably causes us to be also somewhat shy. We are afraid of what we might say to people that might offend them. I find that most intelligent people find me intelligent, often more so than themselves, and are not offended by my uninhibited conversational style, possibly why they think I am more intelligent than I am. On the other hand, unintelligent people tend to think I am considerably less intelligent than themselves. Both kinds, when they are stupid, tend to agree I am stupid. It is navigating within these two or three groups that leads to our shyness. We have to make sure that what we say (and do) is OK first. If everybody was highly intelligent, without a shred of stupidity, we would be completely OK socially. If we think back to childhood, and remember who we tended to prefer as our most likely peers, most aspies would agree we preferred certain elderly folk. They were usually intelligent kind people, who mostly listened to us with great interest and good humour. It is probably this childhood experience that has formed the reason for our present shyness, and continued friendships with older people. These good elderly folk were OK with us, but the rest were not, and even openly hostile to us saying things which were often outrageous to their young minds. This is written with some humour, and I am sure there are other very good reason for our shyness.

question: Is it possible for a person with Aspergers Syndrome to be in a satisfying and committed relationship?
answer: Of course it is. All these previous answers prove that. I'll start by stating that I do not have a formal diagnosis, but I have all the symptoms (including my mom's having had a severe strep infection while she was pregnant with me), and I self identify as an Aspie. Also, I am bisexual but I typically favor men (particularly older men around 50-60, which apparently is a sexual orientation in itself). By NT standards, I have not had many relationships (there have only been 3 serious ones), and they have all been with males. I identify as “mostly female” in that my body is female, but I think of myself as both male and female, but mostly female. Basically, I don't need surgery or hormones or counseling. I'm completely happy living as a woman, but I don't consider myself fully woman. I'm very secure in this knowledge, and don't wish to do anything about it, nor do I wish to talk about it all the time, as some with varying degrees of gender dysphoria seem to. But I shared this information about myself because it is possibly relevant. I got married in 2009 to a man I truly loved, and who I believe really loved me. We had already had a long history by the time we got married. He has a problem, though. He is a career criminal and loves crime. He “went into retirement” when our daughter was born, and stayed in retirement for a couple years. But by 2014, he'd been to prison twice since our wedding day, and three times since we met in 2005. I gave up on him, plain and simple. He's still in prison. I won't reunite with him after he is released. At the end of 2014, I embarked on a relationship with another man (who is definitely not on the spectrum) and we consider ourselves married, though we don't have a piece of paper from the government saying as much. We don't always get along, due to our mutual intelligence, highly stubborn natures, and our occasionally nasty personalities, but we love each other intensely. We've built a beautiful life together and we are committed for life. Now, I consider myself a failure for my first marriage failing, and I don't know if it is partly due to my ASD or my sexual orientation or gender dysphoria, or if it was 100% his fault. I always wonder if I should blame myself or not. If he could've stayed out of prison, I’m sure he and I would still be together. But I was tired of getting in trouble with the law, due to things he did and got me involved with. I don't want my daughter having that kind of example growing up. My current marriage is just shy of 3 years old. I've never had a relationship last more than 5 years, but I've never had one last less than 3. And, I'm only 30. I am unable to have a relationship that's lasted longer than I've been alive. Though my track record doesn't really reflect it, I am capable of having a committed, fulfilling, satisfying relationship. It's not in my nature to end a relationship―if I love them and they love me (and neither party poses a danger to the other), I won't leave. It's just that simple. Abandonment, heartbreak and having to move on is just too traumatic for me, not to mention inconvenient. If there's a problem in the relationship, fix it. Don’t break up. Change the burned out lightbulb, don't move!

question: Is synesthesia common among those with autism and Asperger syndrome?
answer: Not common, but quite prevalent compared to the prevalence of synesthesia among the general public.ASD and synesthesia comorbidity Synesthesia occurs in 4% of the population[1], and ASD has a prevalence of 1%.[2] If there were no correlation between the two conditions, then synesthesia and ASD should co-occur in only 4 in 10,000 people (0.04%).[3]Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. question: How does someone with Asperger's syndrome get and stay employed?
answer: First, learn to mask well when necessary. Practice by masking so well in school that peers and teachers consider you a suck-up. Joining things like Theater or Debate Clubs will help advance the skill beyond merely being a suck-up, which is desirable. Then, choose a career in a field you are highly interested in. This is important, because you will need to become HIGHLY skilled and a VERY prolific worker. Get as many certifications and/or degrees in your chosen field as you can, and make sure they translate to usable skills. Become one of the best in the field— top quartile is necessary, top quintile preferred, top 10% even better. Along the way, build a personal life in which masking is minimally necessary. Masking is exhausting; if you have to do it at work and in your off hours you will burn out quickly. Either find friends and a partner who accept you without masking, or choose to be solitary and make your job your life. Check your emotions at the door when you go to work. Keep your personal life and your work life COMPLETELY separate. Do not socialize with coworkers outside the workplace unless it is necessary to do so; if it is, treat this time as work and perform accordingly. If your income allows it, save AGGRESSIVELY. Autism is not degenerative, but it does not age gracefully. You may find yourself unable to continue to perform at a younger age than a neurotypical person.

question: How do you convince a sociable, outgoing woman that she has Asperger's Syndrome?
answer: I am a sociable and outgoing woman (when I find it necessary). When I tell people I am on the spectrum they always say: "no you're not, you're so friendly and outgoing." Duh. It's not difficult to learn (read How to Win Friends and Influence People and then just try out a new trick every day - it's amazing how predictable human behavior is). It's just exhausting to do. That said, you would be hard pressed to convince me of ANYTHING. My closest friends and family members can confirm this. However, if you want me to learn something about myself (which I am open to when I am not confronted), you should address me very directly and with plenty of facts rather than emotional vagueness if you want me to take you seriously. Writing is best. I can re-read what you've said to make sure I didn't misunderstand or misinterpret something. I also have the exact words to show someone else to see if I am understanding the situation correctly or if I should consider a different perspective. My boyfriend generally sends me emails with links to prove his points. I often counter with emails showing the websites he's referencing to be invalid. But there are also plenty of times when I do consider what he's said and changed my mind (even when it was in conflict with my self identity) and behavior accordingly. He didn't tell me I am on the spectrum, but had he sent me the info, I would have taken the time to decide if it was applicable. We need people in our lives who care about us and want the best for us. It sounds like she has some good friends who have some information that may or may not help her. Encourage your friend to examine the information and make a decision for herself. Maybe she'll self identify, maybe she'll see an actual medical professional as the others have (wisely) suggested, maybe she won't. You cannot diagnose her. You can give her information and the power to make her own decision about her identity. Then you accept the decision she has come to - this can hold true for anything you want to share with her about herself. I think if you go about it in this way, the worst that can happen is she (and you and your friends) learn more about people on the spectrum and that doesn't hurt anyone at all.
comment_answer: Aspergers can mean quiet, shy, but it is a difference in how you think and process, NOT the personality type, though many aspies are pidgeon-holed in a very few types.

question: Which country’s culture is most friendly to people with Asperger Syndrome?
answer: Since you’re asking about “Asperger’s syndrome” or mild autism holistically, I won’t bore you with answers to the effect that “preferences differ among autistic people.” One of the standard frameworks for understanding autism was presented just a few years ago in the book Autism as Context blindness. Paraphrasing the author’s findings, I often explain autism as “hyperattention to detail, accompanied by occasional tunnel vision.” Autistics thus tend to be 1] detail oriented, 2] often but not always intellectual, 3] quirky, and 4] wanting to do their own thing[s]. I wouldn’t put the US [or even the anglophone countries taken as a whole] high on any list, but here are some possible localities: 1] Detail orientation: Scandinavia / the Nordic countries; Germany; some parts of Italy; the Czech Republic and Hungary; some parts of Asia, including possibly Korea and Japan; 2] Intellectualism: Big cities in general; universities and university towns; New York City and San Francisco; New England; France; Spain and some Latin American countries, at least in some quarters; Northern Italy; much of Eastern Europe; Japan and Korea; some pats of China; and some quarters of India. Notice I’m probably leaving a lot out by accident. 3] Quirky/tolerance for quirkiness: Texas [I liked it surprisingly]; California, especially the north; New England; some big cities; and - my only NOT - NOT any part of the American Midwest, and NOT most parts of the American South. 4] Individualism: Northern Europe; many cities; some parts of Latin America; Northern Europe. I wish I knew more about Africa. Perhaps others can comment on that great region. I think Canada would beat the US but I can’t put my finger on why.

question: What's the difference between Asperger's syndrome and HSP?
answer: I think this is the beginning of a much larger question which is how are AD/HD and Autistic Spectrum Disorders related and just what the heck does Highly Sensitive People mean. Having been diagnosed with With both at age 39, I have been researching, experiencing and living with this (at age 67) for 28 years. During that time I have seen many more variations in the terms and descriptions of cognitive differences. One thing is certain, their may be common symptoms and behaviors but the impact and how this is displayed seems to vary widely for those of us who “think different”. Based on some of the books by David Eagleman (and others), I think it is safe to say that who we are is based on how we were raised and who we hang out with. In addition perhaps we should look into how thinking and leaning different effects us developmentally and the patterns and behaviors it creates. First, my hypothesis for a long time is that All of this ADD/ADHD/Autism/Aspergers, etc. falls under the umbrella of Autistic Spectrum Disorders. (Since I don't spend much time these days reading the DSM I'm not sure what the current status is.) (DSM: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders). Some of the most common behaviors I see in myself and those I have worked with may include: distractibility, difficulty with recall, lack of social skills/innability to read social cues, difficulty sustaining attention over time, difficulty with active listening or sustained reading, sleep related issues, impulsive decisions, showing empathy, seeming selfish or self centered, compulsive lying or exaggeration, certain food or texture dislikes, poor sense of direction, reward deficiency syndrome/frequent need for praise, hyper focus, having favorite topics which they can talk about for hours, poor since of time (no past or future, everything is now), lack of deferred gratification, well anyway, its a long list. These, and other differences can and do have a profound impact on the developing patterns in the young brain because they represent an inaccurate or distorted view of reality-based behaviors and responses. As an example, as a Boy Scout leader and teacher, I used to take young people and teens with Autistic Spectrum Disorders on three day camping trips. It quickly became clear that skills these young people should have acquired in terms of self care (clothing, hygiene, food preparation, judging direction, reaction to weather changes, sharing resources, working in a team, learning from others, ability to listen and internalize) were often significantly deficient. Research indicates that the brain only scans small visual slices of the surrounding environment and mentally paints a picture of the rest which if fills in. These pictures are created during the developmental process, many of which occurs prior to two years of age. I believe that Autistic Spectrum Disorders create large gaps in the creation of these pictures and the recording of them within the brain. In other words their are simply experiential gaps which create situations that the brain has no idea how to react to. It is widely recognized that around 95% of the decisions our brain makes are on an uncouncious level we are not aware of, and it is in this lower legal of thinking that I think the problem is based developmentally. The goal of any behavior modification theraphy type approach I would suggest, would be the use of medication (what works varies widely based on the learning differences of the individual patient) and the identification of these developmental gaps so that skills based training (neural repatterning) can be applied. Current neurological research also supports that this can, and does occur in adults. In short, this is a pattern recognition and developmental pattern that is sustained by differences in the production and availablility of neurotransmitters and the long term effects on learned behavior. So I can see how most of this fits under the Autistic Spectrum Disorders Umbrella but I am unclear as to what HSP (Highly Sensitive People) really means. Within the four personality models •Highly Active, •Highly Emotional, •Highly Intellectual, •Highly structured, I have often heard HSP people described as Highly Emotional. One the extreme I have heard them described as highly predictive, psychic or even telepathic. In the personality model I presented, all of us have a balance of one primary and one secondary, and the other two to lesser degrees. For me, the HSP could easily be the highly emotional, or in extreme cases related to some types of mental issues.

question: What kind of jobs are good for people with Asperger's syndrome?
answer: This might surprise some people but... ...Truck driving. Seriously. I don't know how it is in other countries but I assume the trucking industry is more or less the same in the rest of the industrialized world as it is in America. Modern truck driving is a very regimented, rule-focused profession. The company tells you where to find your load, where it needs to go, and how it needs to get there. Every driver on the roads today has a GPS in his truck. Even if officially the company frowns on the use of GPS devices, I guarantee you every driver in their fleet has one and uses it. All your directions are set by other people, which basically means that so long as you don't do anything stupid anything that goes wrong along the way is not your fault. The nice thing about these rules is that there is very little ambiguity to them. If your truck fails the pre-trip inspection, game over. You are going nowhere until the company can figure out how to fix it. If you run out of driving hours (in America, truck drivers can only drive for a max of 11 hours per day) game over. You must stop and rest. Additionally, truck driving is a profession that all but requires a certain degree of anti-social tendencies. A person who enjoys being alone for extended periods of time will do well behind the wheel of a truck.

question: Does Elon Musk have Asperger's syndrome? If so, how does this affect his personal and professional lives?
answer: First off, in America we have something called HIPAA (see below), such that anyone who KNOWS he has Aspergers Syndrome/ASD can’t SAY he has ASD. Only way we would know is if Elon personally shared his diagnosis. If he does have ASD, he has obviously used his massive intellect and efforts to learn how to pass as NT for the most part, as have many other folks who are Aspies’ and “pass” as productive members of society without any public awareness of their ASD. For instance, if you find you are color blind.. you pick clothes that match via help! If you are ASD, you mimic, you watch others and model, and as long as the situation doesn’t go off script too much, you can often “pass” as NT. I call it driving blind by bumping off the curbs. If he does have it, I am sure it has and had and will affect his personal and professional life, but affect and “do in” are two different things! Obviously he is ok. HIPAA, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, sets the standard for protecting sensitive patient data. Any company that deals with protected health information (PHI) must ensure that all the required physical, network, and process security measures are in place and followed.

question: How do I flirt with a girl with Asperger syndrome?
answer: Flirting can be complicated with an aspie as our understanding of body language can be.. tricky.. never mind our own body language (eye contact is tricky and a lack of it does not mean she’s not listening). Be clear and direct when you flirt and make absolutely certain you don’t flirt with anyone else. .. Also talk to her about why you’re flirting with her (if she even noticed) and the fact that you like her and would like to date. .. and thats a good start. (once she’s aware of what flirting is and what you do when you flirt she’s more likely to notice it and perhaps also learn to reciprocate (perhaps through example or being told what you’d like her to do and why). And be very careful about her boundaries so any new steps (even as little as to give her a hug/holding her hand..) talk to her about it first so that you’re certain she’s comfortable with it. And remember.. Don’t expect her to know anything she has not done before (and you’ve seen her do) and or told you in her own words (preferably both.. even more so when it comes to actually doing things).. and then I wish you luck. question: Do people with Asperger syndrome dislike talking on the phone?
answer: I must start with the prerequisite response: “Not all people with Asperger's or autism respond the same way to social interactions”….BUT, in my case, the answer is a resounding “YES!” about talking on the phone. All social interaction tends to provoke anxiety for me. Obviously talking on the phone is better than a face to face meeting, but it still ranks high in my anxiety scale. I have always considered telephones to be an enormous disruption. I prefer to schedule calls a day in advance and keep the conversation to a minimum. You will never find me chatting on the phone for no reason; a phone call is a means to exchange information and that is all. This has caused enormous difficulty in my life, especially with people who don't understand me. I've actually lost friends because I don't call them enough or I ignore their calls. I screen nearly every call and often don't reply until I absolutely have to. When I worked, my secretary would have to hunt me down to take a phone call, and even then I usually would need to call the ringer back as I felt the need to “prepare” for the call. Once I got in a lot of trouble from a new boss when I didn't return his call the first thing in the morning; he didn't understand why I wouldn't make retrieving my messages a priority over other things. It wasn't until I received my diagnosis in my 40’S that I put my dislike of the telephone together with having Asperger's. It was an eye opening experience, however it didn't change the way I did things. If you are working with someone on The Spectrum, my advice would be to be patient. For me, it's just a “thing”. A quirk. It's not because I don't like you. I just don't like the phone.

question: Are people with high-functioning autism and Asperger syndrome ever gifted?

question: What are the differences between Asperger's syndrome, avoidant personality disorder, and social anxiety disorder?
answer: Avoidant personality disorder and social anxiety disorder are stand-alone conditions, as are other comorbid conditions such as dyspraxia, OCD, etc. If you have an ASC, which is sometimes considered a social communication disorder, then you may have social anxiety disorder but you also have much more going on than just that one disorder. Social anxiety is common in people on the spectrum but is not the only behavioural symptom evident in the person's profile and the same goes for any other comorbid condition. Social anxiety is also not part of the criteria for an ASC but it may be how difficulties with social processing make themselves evident in some people on the spectrum - my son is hypersocial, an unusual trait in an autistic person, but that hypersocialbility comes with a difficulty in understanding how to behave "appropriately" in social settings, in another person the social problems may cause heightened anxiety, or avoidance but they are a symptom of the same core problem. An ASC presents on the surface as a complex combination of symptoms which are sometimes bad enough to give an additional diagnosis (often a person will be given a stand-alone diagnosis such as dyspraxia before it is realised that there is more in their presentation than just the one condition) but it is never covered by just one of these other conditions because the reason for the presentation being more complex than a single comorbid is the internal processing systems which cause the surface symptoms. These processing differences affect the presentation in ways that can seem like other conditions but when you look more carefully at the person's history and additional symptoms, and especially their sensory processing, you see that there is a different root cause for those symptoms than would be expected in a disorder like social anxiety disorder. One of the main reasons that ASCs are complex to diagnose is that we are currently reliant on external behaviours for diagnosis rather than being able to tell from the neurology and processing that the condition is present. We do know that the condition must be present from birth so histories are taken very carefully to allow clinicians to trace the condition back to early childhood. Other conditions such as social anxiety disorder and avoidant personality disorder are not necessarily present from birth but can develop due to experience and circumstance.

question: Why would someone see the Asperger syndrome as a bad thing?
answer: Well, it can be debilitating, which is a bad thing. I’m autistic and I don’t want to change that about myself. I’ve spent 47 years working at being me and switching gears just isn’t my style. I can say that autism has prevented me from achieving as much as I could have in my life, but I don’t think there would really be any value in “more”. Fame, fortune, notoriety, glitz and glamour don’t appeal to me very much. I think autism has a bit to do with that attitude, but I wouldn’t trade it for a fatter bank account. I’m sure there are many who would, but I can only speak for myself. Since I’m autistic I see the world differently than others. This is clear to me in my interactions with other people, day to day. I think my brain paints a more vivid picture of the world, I'm more in tune with my environment and I can anticipate things others can’t even imagine. Those thing I wouldn’t trade for anything. The same goes for my visual thinking. I think in pictures and short movies, which I learned in later life, that most people do not do. I found that astonishing and I can’t imagine how they figure things out without seeing them in their heads. I love being a visual thinker. There are some negative aspects of autism though. I don’t get along well with lots of people. I don't build lasting relationships and I don’t “have fun” like others do. Not being “part of the crowd” stunts your professional growth, no matter how good you are at your job. That, meltdowns, sensitivities and anxiety due to changes in routines/unanticipated events are others. Funny story: The other day a drawer face fell off of a refrigerated drawer on my cook’s line. The cook who was working that station isn’t autistic but is definitely neurotic-divergent in some way. She’s a sweetheart and a good friend. question: What is the evolutionary advantage of Asperger's syndrome?
answer: "Evolution" and "purpose" are generally not well used together. Evolution doesn't have a "purpose". Questions about traits are a matter of history: how did trait X come into being? It's even harder to answer in this case because we really don't know what Asperger's Syndrome is. We can't even identify it reliably, or identify the biological mechanism that produces it, much less the genetics. We don't even know whether it is genetic or environmental. So we can only speculate on how it fits into evolutionary history. The best speculation at the moment is that it's some kind of developmental disorder of the brain. In that it's like any other birth defect. There may be genetic traits that predispose one to it, but not necessarily. A common question is how traits that make reproduction difficult aren't weeded out. Sometimes, it's because the trait isn't always deadly. A classic example is the gene for sickle cell anemia: with one copy of it, you get resistance to malaria. The gene is beneficial, but when you get two copies, it's deadly. That's a trivial example; biology and genetics are vastly more complicated than the simple models you get in high school. Individual genes get put to multiple purposes, and there's rarely a "gene for X". Metabolism is like a pile of coathangers: pull on any one and the rest of the pile comes with it. It may even be that there isn't a genetic component to Asperger's syndrome. The fact that it's much more common now means that it's almost certainly environmental. Brains developed in the absence of some element of the environment, and the environment has changed. Occasionally, that leads to Asperger's syndrome, but that's much too little evolutionary pressure to cause a wholesale restructure of the brain. The brain is a complex organ, the most complex structure in the universe, and its development will not change just to avoid a few rare defects. It's probable that Asperger's syndrome appears as a relatively small fault in one of the brain's vast numbers of feedback mechanisms. Nobody knows how they work, but it's known that everybody's are hooked up differently. Asperger's is likely simply an extreme case, some mechanism tuned too low or too high.

question: Why do people with Asperger syndrome tend to dislike fiction?
answer: We have this fantasy world of our own whereby we take in various stimuli may it be pictures, words, objects, patterns etc. from our environment for the purpose of creating this said world. This is the reason why we tend to have things taken literally as we do not make enough time to even understand the abstract. So if we read fiction, this only serves to defeat the purpose of having this inner world created as the author had their ideas laid down already. This on top of our atypical cognitive pattern making it difficult to understand moods, themes and contexts. While we can compensate by learning to focus on the philosophical and technical aspects of the works we are dealing with, this never quite goes away. Don’t get me wrong, while we are perfectly capable of feeling emotions and understanding human behaviour, our underdeveloped theory of mind makes it easier to grasp more concrete concepts. Even if we can feel an abstract concept, we tend to grasp it in a concrete manner. Nevertheless, we are capable of enjoying works of fiction provided that it’s more conductive of our personal interests and contains concepts which are more concrete. We also find authors and novels, which employs otherwise novel and sophisticated styles of writing, to be highly entertaining due to our penchant for analyzing things such as Umberto Eco. Otherwise, we easily get bored with literature. We already have our hands full mentally speaking.

question: Why are people with Asperger syndrome unenthusiastic?
answer: This question is from a very Amerocentric perspective. Aspies tend to take life quite seriously. There are a few reasons for this but the primary I think is that Aspies tend to have a greater understanding of the world around them and they often see problems and understand the consequences of these problems more than NT’s. For example: How U.S. road designs result in high crash rates and road deaths/injuries. But also how U.S. road designs lead to health problems and high costs of healthcare because walking and bicycling for local transportation, a key component of the better health of other cultures, is made at best dangerous and uncomfortable, and often impossible. In this way Aspies are not unlike many or most people in countries like Finland, Sweden, Netherlands and many others who similarly take life seriously. A get together of people in other countries may include some discussion of the local football club but will typically have more discussion on how their community can be improved. U.S. Americans on the other hand do not take things very seriously. They have a ‘whatever’ approach to life. So for example, while people in Sweden might fight for safer and better roads, people in the U.S. take a ‘whatever’ approach and rather just want to have fun and not be burdened with trying to understand something and then creating a better society. Perhaps a ‘U.S. people are fiddling while the U.S. burns’ kind of thing. So in this way Aspies may seem unenthusiastic compared to exuberantly enthusiastic people in the U.S., while compared to people in many other countries they have a more similar level of enthusiasm and don’t seem much different.There’s an additional layer on this though. In many other countries Aspies aren’t alone in their altruism or in seeing problems and wanting to see them fixed. A good chunk of the population around them is on the same page. So in Sweden for instance, an Aspie who desires a safer road will find over half the population fighting along with them. In the U.S. they feel much more alone. Rather than a lot of support for a safer road for instance, they get a lot of pushback from people around them that it’s unnecessary or will slow traffic or a long list of other ‘can’ts’. This can dampen the enthusiasm of even the most enthusiastic of people.

question: Can someone have Asperger’s syndrome without having all of the symptoms?
answer: People with ASD—or AS if you insist—are a diverse group. While you need a certain set of symptoms to get diagnosed, you certainly don’t require to have all of them to qualify for a diagnosis. In fact, there will be plenty of people who go through life with an autistic brain and certain challenges, without those challenges being prominent enough for them or those around them to have considered ASD. When I was 19 and I told my friends I likely had AS, they didn’t take it seriously. They joked about how I was indeed an ass burger. I didn’t appreciate not being taken serious, but at the same time the fact that they disbelieved my suspicions was indicative of me managing to compensate well for my symptoms. I had and still have my eccentricities, but at least people perceived me as more or less normal (i.e. perceived to be within the neurotypical range). But as I got older, I started struggling more. I was very ambitious and entrepreneurial, but when I moved out of my parents’ house to live on my own, I entered a downward spiral. Or rather, I didn’t quite know I was, until in 2011 I had a psychosis and broke down. Since then my life has been a lot smaller. I believe it was in 2012 that I was diagnosed. My psychologist told me I was “autistic in every way except for the capacity to communicate”. I compensate for some of the symptoms, but I would say they have gotten more pronounced compared to when I was 19. So there are two points I want to make here. The first is that symptoms don’t have to be easily noticeable for someone to have AS. Autism is in the brain, so as long as you have the capacity to compensate for your behaviors sufficiently, outwardly you will appear “normal”. But that doesn’t mean the struggle is not present. It usually is, and a breaking point can be reached, where the symptoms can no longer be camouflaged. The second point is that it’s often a matter of circumstances. If you have a stable life with a close community around you with people that support you, potentially you can go through life never realizing you are autistic. When that environment changes however, and more stress factors are introduced, the symptoms usually become more readily noticeable. Note also that autism is not an on-or-off switch. Autism as well as schizophrenia are defined by a lack of synaptic pruning[1], which means that a lot of redundant neurological connections are not streamlined. In sociopathy the opposite is true, where an excess of synaptic pruning occurs[2]. So you can imagine that the extent to which synaptic pruning occurs in greater or lesser amounts will indicate how prevalent autistic or sociopathic symptoms are. And although I’m simplifying the issue quite a bit and autism and sociopathy are likely not exactly at opposite ends of a spectrum, the point is that there are degrees to all these neurological conditions. People are not at all autistic or in varying degrees, and it will depend on degree whether you could be considered autistic, and it depends mainly on the extent of the problems the individual experiences whether a diagnosis is sought out and considered in the first place.For more information on (high-functioning) ASD, have a look at: Embrace AutismA blog about quantitative- and qualitative research on autism, by Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht ND RP and Eva Silvertant.Footnotes[1] https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/05/160502161118.htm[2] Synaptic growth, synesthesia & savant abilities

question: What would happen if everyone were to have Asperger's syndrome? Would society be much different?
answer: I am not a psychiatrist, but I would like to share some insights with the group. In addition, Wendy Hardeveld has helped me out by suggesting some edits. As for the question, it is a little behind the times. Officially Asperger's isn't a diagnosis any more since the DSM 5 (The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition) 2012. You now can only be diagnosed with Autistic Spectrum Disorder. Asperger's syndrome was a form of autism, except that the subject has a high intelligence to go along with the autism. But psychiatrists have decided that Asperger's is not a separate disease from autism. The character Sheldon (played by Jim Parsons) on the Big Bang Theory television program could be considered autistic, from which the program generates much of its humor. Autistic sufferers are not funny, however. They are sometimes deeply disturbed individuals who have trouble expressing their emotions to others. Which is why I say it sometimes seems like many people suffer from some degree of autism. Autists have trouble empathizing with others because they don't empathize with others. I don't mean to say they don't feel emotions. They do, but they don't understand what others are feeling. Many people in our society seem to have little concern for the suffering of others, which may be due to a lack of contact with their own emotions. Psychologists theorize that there is a continuum of autism, and that subjects exist with every level of intelligence. We really don't know enough about the human mind to answer the question yet. Since there are autistic persons at every level of intelligence, it could also be true that there are persons with normal intelligence who suffer from autism to varying degrees, from mild to extreme. If this is true, it would explain why many people seem unable to empathize with the sufferings of others and also why others only do so in a general catastrophe such as a hurricane or an earthquake. At those times, there is an outpouring of sympathy and donations. This could be a sign that many people ordinarily feel little empathy with others but have the ability to reason that they should be feeling pity or sorrow when they notice that many others are feeling the same. If everybody had a high degree of autism spectrum disorder, society would be a dismal place where there was little communication and not much joy--because happiness is also an emotion that requires empathy to experience.

question: How can people with Asperger syndrome improve their social skills?
answer: Social Stories are a useful technique. These are fictional stories, that focus on social situations featuring a person with autism. They can ask questions like ‘What do you think happens next?’ They are a vehicle for practicing social skills, but as an exercise. One theory of why they help is Baron-Cohen’s Theory of Mind. By exploring how other characters react to a person with autism, and how they react back, in story form helps that person develop ‘Theory of Mind’ . This is the notion that we all predict what we think others will think in response to our communications. I could imagine that if I said ‘Yes, you do look very fat in those clothes’, you might feel negatively. And because I can predict that, I might modify how I expressed that. Autism commonly presents without this theory of mind, and very literal communication occurs. Those clothes - which do not present you at your best - might well get the factual response. But the listener then uses their theory of mind and assumes that - as a normal person - you intended to hurt them. And then communication breaks down. The person with autism may then go into a spiral as they themselves get hurt, because this is not what they meant. In their head, there was just helpful information, intended to help you look your best. Social stories are one technique that allow this interaction to be safely explored, offline.

question: What is the role of mirror neurons in Asperger's Syndrome?
answer: Mirror neurons are brain cells that become active when an individual performs a certain behaviour and when he or she observes another person perform the same behaviour. Mirror neuron systems (MNS) is thus activated during imitation, action observation and intention understanding. Mirror neurons not only enable us to understand the actions and intentions of others but also allow us to understand other people’s mental/emotional states, thus facilitating empathy. Some aspects of ASD, such as difficulties with social relating, are thought to result from dysfunction of the MNS and the associated inability to understand other people’s mental states. In support of this claim, a number of studies using brain imaging techniques, such as fMRI, found reduced activation of the mirror neurons in individuals with ASD in response to watching others’ perform various behaviours. Dapretto and colleagues (2006)*, for instance, measured the activation of MNS in children, with and without ASD, during observation and imitation of emotional face expressions. While neurotypical children showed increased activity in the pars opercularis region of the inferior frontal gyrus, a brain region with identified mirror properties, no such activity was detected in children with ASD. Similarly, during observation of emotional face expressions the activity in the pars opercularis region was significantly stronger in the neurotypical children compared to children with ASD. Interestingly, there were no differences in the activation of fusiform gyrus (responsible for face processing) in both groups, indicating that children with ASD attended to the face stimuli just as neuroptypical children did. Researchers also found a negative correlation between the activity of pars opercularis and the severity of social difficulties experienced by children with ASD (less activation= more difficulties). *Dapretto et al. (2006). Understanding emotions in others: mirror neuron dysfunction in children with autism spectrum disorders. Nature Neuroscience, 9(1).

question: How can a man with Asperger's Syndrome get a girlfriend?
answer: Hmm - I'd say the same way everyone else does, but the truth is, it's probably harder (and certainly feels that way) to find a romantic relationship with Aspergers. Since I know nothing about you, I am going to speculate about people with this issue in general. First, you're probably older when entering into your first relationship - negotiating regular friendships takes so much time and work, by the time you have any real bandwidth for anything else, you're likely into your 20s. There's a certain amount of personal stigma (not necessarily externally derived, but possibly internally derived - feeling that one is "the last one without a boy/girlfriend", etc, regardless of the truth of this matter) that can make this even more difficult. Second, people with Aspergers tend to do better with rules and guidelines - and this area of relations, even more so than friendships - are simply fraught with ambiguity. Third, and this is so rarely addressed - it's not the getting, but the keeping that the hardest. Like a dog chasing a car, what do you do once you actually get the date? The second? The fifth? What does "dating" mean? What does it mean to be "in a relationship?" Why is this desirable, or why is the specific person desirable for this situation? When is it no longer worth the trouble, or when is it time to secure permanence? These things are not intuitive for those unhampered by Aspergers - once you add in the complication of Aspergers, it is incredibly difficult to shift from this abstract concept of "girlfriend" or "boyfriend" to "person sitting next to me expecting me to do things and interact. Regularly." So, I suspect what you are looking for is probably more practical, actionable advice. In this vein, I will suggest the following: First, think carefully about why you want to date someone or be in a relationship. Relationships are a lot of work - it's ALWAYS easier to be alone (unless you're very young, when you have little to no self-identity and are extremely malleable). People are in relationships for many reasons, but the best reasons tend to be ones that deal specifically with the person you are in a relationship with. Not "you want to be in a relationship," but "you want to be in a relationship with THAT SPECIFIC PERSON." It's really not worth it otherwise. Too many compromises are involved. Second, once you find a SPECIFIC person with whom you want to have a relationship, you need to be certain that person also wants to be in a relationship with you. How? Well, there are lots of schools of thought on this, but my suggestion would be: ask. Well, not if they want to be in a relationship - unless you're in high school, and have some formal "going out" language requirement. Let's talk about a relationship definition. A relationship is just a series of engagements with someone with whom you enjoy spending time with, who also enjoys spending time with you. This starts off with a date, which is a fixed social engagement that both parties agree is an appointment in which both parties will get to know one another with romantic intent. This differs from "hanging out," which is getting to know one another WITHOUT romantic intent. Who do you ask on a date? A person you feel comfortable spending time with, who accepts you for your quirks and bluntness (A note about bluntness in general: try to withhold bluntness that can be perceived as cruel - opinions that are unfavorable can be couched using moderate language, and never, ever offered without asking). At the very core, you need these elements: You should feel comfortable without having to explain yourself, You should feel good about yourself in this person's presence, You should be able to laugh comfortably, in general and at yourself, without feeling like your ego is at risk,You should have one or more shared interests, and You should feel physically attracted to this person.Once you find someone who meets these criteria (and you're not just looking "for someone to date" - a common problem among people, and never fair to yourself or the other person), now what? You ask them out on a date. How, where, what do you do? Pretty straightforward. First dates are generally the least fun ever. Awkward, you don't really know if you "click," or connect on a romantic level. So reduce the pressure by reducing the time. Ask the person to go for coffee, or dessert, or a drink. These are time limited, so easy to end if they are clearly not working on either end. Coffee can be in the morning or between 3 and 5, drinks are around 5-7 pm (or right after work), and a dessert is after dinner, so later in the evening - a good thing to do after a movie. Movies are questionable - you don't get to talk, so don't get to know one another, but do get to grow comfortable being physically close to one another - which, for an Asperger, is a plus. I'd save that for a second or third date. Note that you don't actually have to drink alcohol or coffee when you go to these things. If you get drinks, and you don't drink but your partner wants to drink, I suggest ordering one (like a beer), and just sip it. People don't like to drink alone, and it will make your partner more comfortable, which is what you're looking for. (Please, no hate on this one. I'm not advocating a change in ethics or moral issue - just trying to bring ease.) The other point: regardless of gender, I believe that you ask, you pay. What do you do? First, compliment her. Then, ask questions! Ask about your date's life - assuming this is a woman, ask where she is from, what brought her to her current location. What she does, why she chose that career. If she could pick any other, what would it be? What does she do with her spare time? Has she traveled lately? Where? Does she have a bucket list? What's the craziest thing on it? When you find topics in common, elaborate on them. You are not interviewing her, but are trying to make her comfortable and find out who she is, rather than who she appears to be or who you think she may be. You want her to find out about you, where it makes sense - don't force anything. Don't worry about making the first date too long. If you enjoyed it, after an hour, end the date ("that was really great - I had a lot of fun talking to you!"). If you want to see her again, plan another one ("I'd love to get together - do you want to get together next week? Maybe for dinner?") If she says yes, you call her, plan, etc, etc. A relationship evolves from these repeated events, and eventually you both mutually decide you don't want to see anyone else - just each other. Voila - relationship. If it doesn't work out, then you say "that's ok," and you move on. Most people will NOT work out in a relationship. Don't take it personally. Remember - they don't know you at all. They know some public version of you. And that's ok. You're looking for someone very specific, and it should be very hard to find that person. I can't say this enough - being in a relationship involves a lot of work and compromise. You have to account for someone else's thoughts and feelings. All the time. Do not buy into what movies and television sell you as "relationships" - remember that anyone can be easy to deal with for 2 hours and $2 mil. Even me. Don't sell yourself short. Open yourself up to a lot of friendships first. That will help you build positive relationships - and you'll need them if you decide to enter into just any romantic relationship (someone will have to bring over the Ben & Jerrys and wine). :) You'll do great!! Kind regards, Alexandra

question: Are there any billionaires with Aspergers syndrome?

question: Is social anxiety commonly a comorbid disorder in people with Asperger's syndrome?
answer: Thank you for the A2A. I was diagnosed as Aspie last year, at 57. Yes, social anxiety is ONE OF many comorbid issues related to the spectrum. However, many social anxieties are not apparent on the outside (as seen by others). Many manifest in areas of ‘routine’ issues one might not necessarily associate with the anxiety, such as a reluctance to speak on the telephone (or call others), or the inability to enjoy doing things alone. Of course, there are far more people with social anxieties (which are often masked under GAD until they become more specific and/or troublesome) who are not on the spectrum. There is a spectrum of functionality within the ASD spectrum, as there are Aspies on all ends of their own spectrums, as well. I’m extremely social and extroverted, but deal with internal (mental) anxieties about dealing with people, conversations, responsibilities that I battle with AFTER some interactions, but outwardly many (most) people wouldn’t see me as “stereotypical,” until I tried to ask a question. My questions, although intrinsic to my understanding or insight into a situation, often don’t “make sense” (even to me) when I try to ask them. That causes me to have to “collect my thoughts” before continuing, even when in the middle of an active discussion. I have to figure out how to “word” my query in a way that makes sense to both of us (me and the person I’m asking) … and will elicit a reply that I can understand in context to what I asked. It’s all part of the anxiety thing.

question: How (well) did you learn to hide your asperger syndrome?
answer: Honestly, I feel as through my autism is a glowing neon sign over my head, instantly visible to everyone I meet. Any time I’m slow to process, struggle to figure out what to say/do next, accidentally leave a conversation too early, mishear something, spend too much time reading and analyzing others’ opinions, react too flatly, talk to my self, visibly stim… I feel like everything I do shows that I’m an alien from another planet and not one of you. But, to my surprise, when I tell people that I’m an Aspie, they’re usually quite surprised. Sometimes, people don’t even believe me. So, I guess I hide it pretty well? But, here’s the thing: I’m a very shy, closed, and self-defensive person. So, it’s very rare for people to actually get to know me. I pick a couple of traits that seem “safe” (liking math, being addicted to knitting, wearing skirts, being sarcastic, being old-fashioned, enjoying skipping and being “care free,” etc) to hide behind. In a pinch, everything relates back to one of these traits. I spend so much time reading the person talking to me that I can’t even process the words they said until after the conversation ends and I have time on my own to think. I used to be obsessed with reacting/responding the “right” way, the way the speaker intended me to. So, I hunt for little facial/vocal/verbal cues as to what I should do and how I should be interpreting what they’re saying. If I’m caught off guard and pressed for a reaction to early, I’ll actually respond with what I’m reading off of the person, instead of what I actually think. So, I think I hide my Asperger’s well because I hide myself well. I’m trying to change that and be a more open person. My diagnosis helped me see that there is nothing wrong with me and that I’m just as human as everyone else. We all have our own quirks. There’s nothing wrong with being me.

question: How do people with Asperger syndrome experience music?
answer: I experience art in general, but specifically music, with overwhelm, it goes very deep inside me, as if it were a physical part of my body. It makes my cry often. If autists are hypersensitive, I absolutely experience that with music. When I am at live concert, I can’t talk to anyone when it’s over because I need to reflect and process what I have just listened to. I don’t think many music lovers can relate to that deep and intimate connection with music. I could live without loved ones —in a certain way I do—, but I would rather die without music.

question: Has Asperger's Syndrome officially changed its name since the symptoms of Asperger's Syndrome are now included in a condition called Autism Spectrum disorder (ASD)? In 2013 the name was reclassified but WHO still calls it Asperger's Syndrome.
answer: The USA DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders) leads the way in this field and the ICD (international Classification of Diseases) follows a few years later with a culturally corrected version. The most recent DSM 5 2013 lumped all autism together including Aspergers. It also moved Retts to a separate category reflecting that autism is not the dominant feature of that disorder. Autism Spectrum Disorder is now split into 3 categories, depending on how much support a person needs. Level 3 is for those with the greatest support needs. Level 2 is intermediate. Level 1 is for those who need a bit of state support to mostly pass as neurotypical (e.g., mutism in childhood which requires speech therapy etc). My understanding is you keep your historic diagnosis, but newly assessed people will only get an ASD diagnosis if they meet the new criteria. Also if you are autistic without clear repetitive behaviours, the description does not cover you. I think they will have to amend this aspect eventually given that repetitive behaviour is a stress adaptation that not everyone has. But it is what it is. There is also a new diagnosis of Social Communication (Pragmatic) Disorder. This boils down to failure to communicate effectively with neurotypical social context expectations. No mention of the double empathy gap findings, that it is a two way communication problem. It also pathologizes talking to children and social inferiors with the same respect as regular folk. Because this is obviously the sign of some kind of mental deficit!

question: What is the history of Asperger’s?
answer: The history of autism & Asperger syndrome1798 — French physician Jean-Marc Gaspard Itard described Victor of Aveyron, a young boy who was found after being isolated in the woods for 11 years, as being socially withdrawn in addition to having language and intellectual disabilities. question: What are the biggest difficulties that people with Asperger's Syndrome have with forming and keeping friendships?
answer: As far as I can tell from my personal experience there are several reasons. I do have friends, only few, but they have stayed friends for a very long time. So here are my difficulties in forming friends. Lack of small talk, I can't contain small talk for more than a few minutes and this is very off putting to most people. My friends either don't mind long silences or are happy to fill them themselves when they find the need. They are also content with me not paying attention to their small talk. Most people insist you listen an recall later on what they said. This I can only do for short sequences and so I retain that ability for strictly professional interactions where it matters. The thing is that my mind drifts away from immaterial noise very fast. Strong opinions, I have strong opinions about certain issues and will voice them when the opportunity presents itself. Many people are put of by that. I love debating things but most people get very emotional about that and I don't realise until after the fact if I have hurt their feelings. I'm also very passionate about certain things I believe in and will continue on and on if I start. I'm like a train in that it takes a bit to set of but an emergency break is not applicable so I can't easily stop once I have started. Inattention to emotional details, I miss the things that many care greatly about, like birthdays and returning calls or noticing/recognising (prosopagnosia) them in the street. This causes me to be called cold and uncaring etc which many do not care much for in their friends. Lack of self initiation, I find it hard to initiate contact. Call them out of the blue or suggest an activity. I usually just go about my day in the same way as the day before. The times that I need to do an errand outside my usual routine is complex and exhausting and frankly so is initiating contact with a friend. Difficulties in reading intentions, I find it hard to determine whether people are genuinely being friendly and not perhaps taking an advantage. I realise that many people are swindlers of some type or they are just being polite and following social protocols. I need factual based evidence to determine people's intentions, which can take a long time to gather and so many give up before then. Lack of interest by others, frankly most do not seem interested to be my friend at all so the above only applies to the rather few that appear to have shown interest. I hope this helps answer the question, you have received many other good answers here.

question: How do I live with Asperger's syndrome?
answer: Disclaimer: I’m not an academic Autism expert, I just have a lived in experience with Autism. Take it 1 day at a time. Living with Autism (Asperger’s is part of the spectrum) isn’t easy, I won’t sugar coat it. Some days you’ll wake up, go through it without so much as a bother ,and forget you have Autism. Other days, you might be fine for a little bit, then something might trigger your senses, turn them up to 11 and then lead to overload, where you might stim alot, such as repetitively shaking a body part, or making the same sound over and over. We can all have different triggers, but I find that getting to a quiet, dark room, away from other people, helps tremendously to speed up with recovering. The key thing when this happens, and even when it doesn’t, is to have people around you, that are open-hearted/empathetic towards your ups and downs. They don’t have to know everything about Autism, or have it, but being supportive of your needs is a massive help. Social interaction: We don’t tend to be societal conformists, thus, you’ll probably have your own way of doing things, bare in mind though, that this can lead to potential conflict with other people, including other Autists, as they will see they’re way of something as the most efficient way, and not yours. It goes without saying, that just being yourself and straight talking isn’t always up to most people’s tastes. That’s why we tend to mask (hiding your condition) alot, most often when around NT’s (Neurotypicals). Bare in mind though, that masking can be exhausting, and putting increasing pressure on yourself to look/act normally, will accelerate the likelihood of overload. Communication difficulties vary from person to person, but most can be hampered in one way or another, such as having an idea in your head for something, but not knowing how to communicate this idea to other people. One of the most common ones is finding facial expressions hard to understand. Daily living: You might need a personal assessment by an Occupational Therapist, who will try and find out your needs, such as if you can cook basic meals, walk unassisted, wash daily without being prompted etc. Yes, the last part is embarrassing, but it is still somewhat common amongst some of us. Just remember to wash, when you can. Mental Health: This is an area where problems often arise. We’re very prone to Anxiety disorders and Depression, (got both). This I also feel the need to mention. We’re at higher risk of suicide/suicidal intent then Neurotypicals. Fortunately your a woman, so the rate is lower, then that of men, but this doesn’t mean you might not be at risk, even if it’s just thoughts. If you’re ever feeling like your having uncontrollable suicidal thoughts. Dial your suicide helpline asap. Have their number, alongside any other mental health emergency numbers on your phone, even if you never ring them. Education and Work: Depending on your respective country’s laws, their may or may not be support that your educator/employer has to provide for you, such as here in the UK our workplaces and educational institutions are required by law, to make reasonable allowances for disabilities, such as providing you with an isolated workspace, if you’re in an office for example. If your country doesn’t have anything in the law about providing some sort of allowance for your condition, then I would recommend writing to your local Parliamentary representative about that, if possible. In the meantime you could try and see if you have a local/national Autism charity to help you. __________________ Unsure if it’s always applicable, but it might help others out.. Trust. I find that I can be too trusting of individuals and this has lead to my detriment in the past, such as being taken advantage of, however this is just my personal experience, and it might not be applicable to yourself. Don’t let other people abuse it. Give them a second chance, if they are genuine, but if they deliberately keep breaking your trust, then keep them out of your life. Your still an individual: Be Assertive, but not aggressive or passive. Standing up for yourself and knowing that your more than just a person with Autism, is small step in the right direction. Don’t build your entire identity around just being Autistic. Same as others do with things like sexuality, Nationality, Politics, Education etc. You define it. It doesn’t define you. It just one small part of a complex whole.

question: Are all autism or Asperger syndrome people introverts?
answer: I did not think of myself as having Asperger’s until I did an online test. One reason was this: the main person I knew locally who was diagnosed with Asperger’s was also an extrovert. I am not an extrovert. So I didn’t see myself as “like him” … as like someone (the only one I knew) with Asperger’s. And oddly enough, the completely different person who suggested doing the online test that changed my opinion of myself was also an extrovert. She said she loved social interaction, but it exhausted her too much. So by the time I recognised my introverted self as having Asperger’s, I already knew at least two people on the spectrum who were extroverts. On the other hand, Wrong Planet, a major online forum for people on the autism spectrum, has occasionally had an informal poll about Myers-Briggs personality types. In one poll with 270 votes in 2008, 92% of respondents belonged to one of the introverted M-B types. Perhaps that tells you something about the autism spectrum, or maybe it says something about the type of person who frequents Wrong Planet, or maybe about the type of person who votes in polls on Wrong Planet about M-B types. Not all people with Aspergers are introverts, But I suspect a lot are. I cannot give you an exact figure though.

question: Why do INTPs act like they have Asperger's?
answer: INTPs ( i.e., Introversion Intution Thinking Perceiving) are generally shy and introverted persons, especially around people they're not close to. Since INTPs always strive for logical conclusions and have little value and understanding for emotions, they tend to be overly critical and sarcastic while with others. They may not realize the moral standards of attending to people's feelings, which often results in clumsiness, inability to emotionally connect with others, and difficulty to interact in social gatherings. These aspects of social awkwardness and lack of empathy in an INTP is what's present in people with Asperger's syndrome too. Albert Einstein was a typical INTP. People of this personality type are thinkers, they love theories and are always eager to know about things and reasoning. Due to this, they always appear dreamy and distant to others, just like AS people. Both INTP and AS people become really curious at times, and thus can focus deeply on a single topic as long as it keeps them interested, tend to be good with patterns, think a lot and thus frequently seem to be uninterested. And of course, they are highly misunderstood individuals. I have a strong feeling that a large percentage of people with Asperger's are INTPs.
