question: How do people with Asperger syndrome memorize things?
answer: If this is a scheme about human memory:Source: Types of Memory - The Human Memory then, as a person with ASD: Sensory memory:“is the ability to retain impressions of sensory information after the original stimuli have ended. It acts as a kind of buffer for stimuli received through the five senses of sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, which are retained accurately, but very briefly. For example, the ability to look at something and remember what it looked like with just a second of observation is an example of sensory memory.”Some stimuli (inside the body f.i. hunger) I don’t feel when busy; so my system immediately ignores them; but some time later, when I stop an activity I can remember that I was f.i. hungry; other stimuli, once I’m aware, I remember ‘how the sensory stimulus was’ very accurately for a long time. So somebody could have called my attention while I was busy, I don’t hear it at the moment itself, but after half an hour, I can suddenly ‘hear’ that somebody spoke to me. My response is thus delayed. How the storage happens from ‘ignoring a stimulus’ to ‘remembering a stimulus’, I have no idea. The same for Short Term Memory. Short Term Memory:“Information is passed from the sensory memory into short-term memory via the process of attention (the cognitive process of selectively concentrating on one aspect of the environment while ignoring other things), which effectively filters the stimuli to only those which are of interest at any given time.”When people talk to me while I’m a little distracted, I forget immediately what I heard. This can have bad consequences when people expect me to do something. When the content interests me a lot, I’m like a sponge. At that moment I forget everything else (I forget how to behave, I forget what day it is, where I am); my focus is completely on the content. This is one of a few extremely pleasant states. Afterwords I can remember almost every word exactly; while I have a quite bad short term memory in general. Combining sensory memory with short term memory in an example: once I was doing examination. Every candidate was in a separate small room with a big window. It was winter time, but I found I needed some more air to think well. I opened the window (not a bit, completely) and started my test; the idea was to close the window after a while. The test absorbed me completely, I felt hot, so hard I threw myself on the case. When time was up and the person entered the room, she was shocked about the open window and closed it immediately. I had completely forgotten about the window; I didn’t feel any cold. Long Term Memory:“is intended for storage of information over a long period of time. Despite our everyday impressions of forgetting, it seems likely that long-term memory actually decays very little over time, and can store a seemingly unlimited amount of information almost indefinitely.”I have a good over-all long term memory, much better than my short term memory is and better compared to the average person. This is a thing I wonder about a lot: how is it possible that I don’t notice or remember things people said to me during the day, but I can keep situations and especially places in my mind for decades. As said in a previous post, I have prosopagnosia. I almost don’t recognise unfamiliar faces. Unlike this, I remember places and objects over very long times. It’s like there’s a magnet in me that navigates me, and I can’t explain this skill. I easily make a mental map of roads I have driven along. I also have a very clear mental image in my mind about things (things that exist, but also things I want to design); I can rotate the objects mentally before my eyes and look closely at them from all angles, I can change the design, replace elements with new ones. I have a good memory for licence plates and phone numbers. An example: mostly I return home at a specific time of the day. If one returns home at the same time daily, one can recognise patterns: many the same people are on their way too daily. One day I thought ‘something is wrong here’, I didn’t see the same licence plates crossing my way. Indeed, I then realised that I went home an hour earlier than usual. I often forget what I ate at noon or what I did the evening before. Since I know this is an important aspect of small talk, I do some effort to memorise what I do. I try to live more ‘outwardly’ instead of emerging myself in my own state of concentration.Short-term memories can become long-term memory through the process of consolidation, involving rehearsal and meaningful association.So, I don’t really understand why some things become long term memories while I don’t rehearse them. It is possible that ‘meaningful association’ is at work, but then not in its usual meaning of ‘meaningful’ as ‘generally important’.Short-term memory is supported by transient patterns of neuronal communication in the regions of the frontal, prefrontal and parietal lobes of the brainThe (pre)frontal and parietal lobes are brain regions that according to scientific research have shown to function differently in ASD.The hippocampus area of the brain essentially acts as a kind of temporary transit point for long-term memories, and is not itself used to store information. However, it is essential to the consolidation of information from short-term to long-term memory, and is thought to be involved in changing neural connections for a period of three months or more after the initial learning.Types of long term memory:Several different types of long-term memory have been distinguished, including explicit and implicit memory, declarative and procedural memory (with a further sub-division of declarative memory into episodic and semantic memory) and retrospective and prospective memory.I have both good explicit/declarative and implicit/procedural memory. In ASD, implicit memory (for movements) can be impaired; this isn’t the case with me. I can dance, sport, walk, play music with precision. Exercising music made me already wonder as a child about this type of memory: by times it seemed like my fingers still knew how to play a piece on the piano as long as my mind didn’t interfere or tried to retrieve the music. It was as if my fingers had a (superior) memory completely by themselves. Explicit/declarative memory contains episodic memory and semantic memory:Episodic memory is the memory of autobiographical events (times, places, associated emotions and other contextual knowledge) that can be explicitly stated.My memories go back at the age of 1 year, though these first memories are vague. Again, the places and objects I remember most clearly. I had the impression being at age 3-4 that my general consciousness was bigger than that of other toddlers. I was very aware about the phases of the day, the places, even politeness… which can make someone wonder because people with ASD are said not to be the most polite. I remember myself at age 3 looking around at those sleeping infants around me while the school-mistress was reading from a book. I found them so rude: how could they sleep while the book wasn’t finished? Afterwards, the school-mistress told my mother that she couldn’t stop reading for such a long time because I kept listening. With time, I must say that my long term memory starts to diminish. Some memories become more vague, some memories are gone. This is a strange thing, because not at all ‘me-like’.Semantic memory, on the other hand, is a more structured record of facts, meanings, concepts and knowledge about the external world that we have acquired. It refers to general factual knowledge, shared with others and independent of personal experience and of the spatial/temporal context in which it was acquired.About things that interest me, I know a lot. Connected with these special interests I learned a lot about completely useless facts. I make no effort at all to remember facts; this can be due to the fact that so much knowledge is within constant reach because of the internet/pc. If I had to go to the library for all this knowledge, I think I would do more effort to remember the content before bringing back the books. But again (and contrary to the theory that factual knowledge is independent of the spatial/temporal context), I remember where I learned something. When studying I use mind maps, I draw a lot, I use colors for each chapter/ notion that is important. All attached-colors belong to the same content-category, sometimes with nuances in the colors to show the hierarchy of the content.

question: How does Asperger's Syndrome affect someone's life?

question: Why are people with Asperger syndrome so frequently perceived as being creepy?
answer: I think the word “creepy” overstates it, since I prefer the word “uncanny,” but I will answer nonetheless. The book Autism as Context Blindness basically - to use my own paraphrase - defines autism as “hyperattention to detail, accompanied by tunnel vision.” Autistics often focus on details of the world deeply and persistently, and don’t always unpin from that detailed study easily, so we end up processing the world serially rather than “multitaskingly.” As poorly as most humans have been shown to multitask, they give it more of a go than autistics do, leading to a timing difference in body language, facial expressions, and even eye synching between many autistics and many neurotypicals. [Other atypicals, such as those with ADD and ADHD, can have timing issues, and so too can some neurotypicals, quite a few of whom are social duds.] I’m pretty good at reading body language - having learned it like an academic discipline - but my perceptions are often on a delay, making me seem slow-reacting socially. Likewise, many of us with autism project our emotions on a delay, which can incorrectly make us seem dispassionate, or even robotic. The overall picture autistics present can come across as unengaged, unfriendly, and even uncanny. Eye synching is an interesting case in point. Eye synching is just making eye contact with someone in a socially adept way. Even when we learn to “eye synch” the way so many mammals do - or NOT to eye synch when dealing with superiors - we aren’t doing it the way most people do, and that can make us seem shifty or furtive. Kiersey basically divides us into four personality types: entertainers; humanitarians; traditionalists [liberal or conservative]; and intellectuals. I by far have the most trouble - and tend to rub the wrong way - the traditionalists, and I gibe GREAT with intellectuals. Surprise, surprise - intellectuals by far care the least about what are basically remnants of our earlier evolutionary days, and they care the most about science and the life of the mind. Finally, it’s worth mentioning another framework that points to why some neurotypicals see autistics as creepy: the uncanny valley. “Uncanny” refers to something alien or unknown to us. Good examples are clowns, some dolls, and many mannequins. Paintings, robots, and cartoon characters are something we find appealing, and we like them more when they seem like us. We also don’t mind robots, animals, or even space aliens that are very different from us. Somewhere in the middle are the clowns and mannequins mentioned above: they aren’t quite enough like us to evoke comfortable familiarity, but nor are they enough different to dispel the “creepy” factor. The IEEE spectrum has a good article on this topic. In the article, you’ll see a graph of what I just talked about - the graph has a “valley” shape. Google “What Is the Uncanny Valley? - IEEE” for the article. In short, with all our human foibles and interesting quirks, those of us with autism are just different enough from “normal” people to instigate feelings of creepiness once in a while.

question: Is it ok to tell people that I have Asperger's Syndrome if I've never been formally diagnosed?

If you do not fully comprehend what Asperger Syndrome entails, then you are not qualified to determine whether or not you have Asperger Syndrome. Even if you were qualified to determine whether or not an individual other than yourself had Asperger Syndrome, attempting to diagnose yourself without seeking a qualified opinion from a second/third/fourth/fifth/sixth/seventh/as many different qualified individuals/as many different sources as possible would provide a biased result. Scientifically, medically, and legally speaking, you cannot unequivocally inform other people that you have Asperger Syndrome without an official diagnosis from an accredited psychologist. Now, IF you think you MAY have Asperger Syndrome, consult your GP Doctor. question: Why are people with Asperger syndrome so prone to black-and-white thinking?
answer: I can only speak for myself (though I've observed similar traits in other Aspies), but I'm not prone to black-and-white thinking. Rather, I'm prone to pinning things down as much as possible, because that helps me grasp them. So, for instance, if someone says, "We're going to meet every Monday," I'll ask "Does that include Labor Day?" And I may say, "I assume 'every Monday' doesn't mean forever, so do you mean indefinitely or is there some specific date at which we won't have Monday meetings any more?" If the answer is, "I have no idea how many Mondays we'll meet," I won't blow a gasket. I'm fine with that*. I'm cool with ambiguity, as long as I know that the subject is ambiguous, so that I can plan for it—so I can know it's an unknown. What bothers me is false ambiguity—stuff that's only ambiguous because no one is asking simple questions or giving simple answers. So I tend to ask "Why? ... why? ... why? ..." until I hit a bottom level of explanation where there's clear ambiguity. "Clear ambiguity" sounds like an oxymoron, I know, but I mean a level at which there's no point asking "Why?" because there's clearly no answer. When I get to that level, I don't freak out. I don't even find myself wishing there was an answer. I just accept that I've reached an unknown and put some elasticity in my plans. Many Aspies have poor working memories (poor abilities to hold multiple things in their head at once), and I'm no exception. So my goal is to simplify, so that I can practice purposeful forgetting. If of X, Y, and Z, only Z is ambiguous, I can forget about X and Y. If all three are ambiguous, I may need to be ready to deal with all of them at once, at any time, without warning. Yikes. I'll do it if I have to, but since that's hard for me, I'll first make damn sure X and Y really are ambiguous and not merely saddled with false-ambiguity that could be resolved with one last "Why?" Aspergers has also gifted me with infinite patience when it comes to working a single thing out in a super-exacting way: "Where exactly are these meetings? At what time? What should we bring? How long will they last?" Though this (understandably) irritates some people, it's also what makes Aspies good at extremely detail-oriented fields like computer programming. See Marcus Geduld's answer to Is it true that you either get programming or you don't? Why do I insist on precision? My theory is that it has to do with aversion to abrupt transitions. It takes everyone mental energy to go from one state to another—to be in the middle of reading a novel and to suddenly having to answer the phone ... but for many people on the autism spectrum, that's particularly challenging. We tend to be able to focus on a specific task for hours, but we generally suck at multi-tasking. Back when I taught kindergarten, I worked with a high-functioning autistic kid who would throw tantrums if you told him to "put the blocks away, right now." But he was fine if you said, "In five minutes it will be time for you to put the blocks away." He just needed a little time to make a mental transition. My wife sometimes complains that if she talks to me while I'm focused on something, such as writing a Quora answer, I'll look at her like she's a space alien. What happens, from my point of view, is that my entire world becomes only Quora**, so that when she talks (after being silent for a long time), she really is a space alien. She's not from planet Quora, which is the planet I'm currently on. There are a couple of moments when I literally can't comprehend what she's saying, as if she's speaking an alien language. When I've been typing for a long time, my brain seems to turn off spoken-language-parsing modules, and they can't start up again instantly. So we often have "conversations" like this: WIFE: I'm getting hungry. Let's make dinner. (Pause.) WIFE: Did you hear me? ME: Let's make dinner .... ? Dinner ... dinner ... (Pause.) Dinner? (I'm thinking, "What does 'dinner' mean?") WIFE: Yes! Let's make dinner. You know: dinner! ME: Let's ... Let's make ... Oh! Got it! Let's make dinner. Sure ... yeah! I'm hungry, too! It feels as if, in order to pump my cognition into the Quora answer, my brain has shut off all non-relevant modules, and they take a moment to boot back up when they're required. Aspies also tend to be hyper-sensitive to stimuli, such as rooms that are too dim or too bright and noises that are too loud or too quiet. We—or at least I—can't tune those things out. Which, coupled to bad multi-tasking skills, can be a nightmare. For instance, if I'm trying to focus on a book but there's a dripping faucet nearby, my brain insists on paying attention to the faucet and the book. There's no way I can just tune the faucet out. In fact, the more I try to "just not think about it," the more it intrudes on my thoughts. Which means that I'm multi-tasking, going back and forth between book and faucet, and each switch is exhausting. I'm nearly 50, and I've been like this my whole life, so I've developed lots of strategies to help me keep on task and avoid abrupt transitions. And, having done that for decades, and having become good at it, it's also developed into an aesthetic. So now it's not just that I like to pin things down so there are no big surprises. It's also that I have an aesthetic for pinning things down. I'm skilled at it and I enjoy it. I'll end by saying that this is one of my favorite paintings:"Mystery and Melancholy of a Street" by Giorgio de Chirico. What I specifically love about it is its ambiguity. I wouldn't like it if it was clear what was going to happen next, and I also wouldn't like it if it showed the source of the shadow. What I love about it is the fact that it will never resolve. It will always be a story without an ending. It will always be a delicious question mark. In fact, I generally dislike art that answers all its questions. I like stories, painting, poems etc that are highly nuanced, unresolved, mysterious, and ambiguous. That may seem to fly in the face of everything I've written above, and certainly not all Aspies share my tastes, but we're complex people. No Aspie is defined by Aspergers Syndrome. I find that if I feel safe, as I do when I'm interacting with art, I can tolerate and even revel in ambiguity. Art puts the ambiguous (and even the abrupt transition, which I enjoy in many films and symphonies) inside secure boundaries. So, in a sense, I become a person enjoying a lion at the zoo as opposed to a person being chased by a lion through the jungle.* Though it's amazing how often people claim to have "no idea" when, in fact, they do have an idea—they just don't have an exact one. They can give you a ballpark estimate, but for some reason they don't want to do that or don't think you'll want to hear it. Sometimes I find myself having conversations like this: PERSON: We're just going to have to sit here and wait, because the package could come at any time, and we need to be here when it arrives. ME: Literally any time? PERSON: Yup. (Pause.) ME: Sorry. I don't mean to be annoying, but are you saying it could come four days from now? PERSON: No. I didn't mean that. If it's not here by 3pm today, we'll just move on. ME: Oh, okay. So we'll wait for it between now and 3 ... PERSON: Yeah. And the delivery guys said it should be here sometime early in the day, but they didn't say exactly when. I'm guessing it will be before 3 ... probably before noon. ME (Thinking): That's a far cry from "the package could come at any time."** My planet is even smaller than that. It's a planet called "This Particular Quora Question." It drives me crazy when, while I'm in the middle of typing an answer, a Quora notification pops up. And it's even worse when an operating-system message pops up, saying I need to update some piece of software or telling me I have an email. Aspies may make good programmers, but there are many things about computers that are frustrating to me. I wish there was a way to force them to silence all popups for a set period of time.

question: How do you communicate with someone who has aspergers?
answer: This is a question that has challenged my non Aspie wife and I for many years. My short answer is that a non Aspie should try to base communication on understanding how a particular Aspie thinks (yeah, we keep saying no two of us are the same). Similarly Aspies need to understand their Aspie ways of thinking and responding so they can develop more flexible ways of responding. Until my recent diagnosis, my wife had come up with some solutions such as withdrawing from circular arguments, specifying one task at a time when she needed me to do something and accepting that sometimes communicating with me would become a brick wall experience. She worked with therapists to develop these solutions. To improve our communication my wife is trying to increase her understanding of how I think and how I attempt to get a clear message about what she is saying. At the same time I am trying to increase my currently vague understanding of what is in her mind when she is framing words to get something across to me. For me anything said is unclear if there is the slightest chance of ambiguity or vagueness. To the non Aspie this doesn’t make sense. To clarify, I typically respond by asking endless questions like ‘Do you mean this or that…?’ This often leads to my wife getting frustrated by numerous attempts to explain what she means. With my lack of empathy I don’t respond when her raised voice indicates frustration. I keep asking more questions and feed back to her what she has said to say why it is not clear etc., this conflict raises anxiety for both of us and we get more rigidly into circular arguments. Another example is when I ask a question and my wife indicates she doesn’t understand. Then I repeat the question using the exact same words and intonation which, with my logical thinking, seems very clear to me. I don’t re-frame the question. To help her to communicate with me I am trying to increase my understanding of how my mental processes are programmed to operate and what are the inherent limitations. As I increase this understanding I discuss this with my wife (when we are relaxed), so she can better understand my confusion with her supposedly clear statements. At the same time I am trying to find ways other than endless questions when I am unclear what she is saying, or repeating my questions in the same way when they are not understood. With both of us being aware of these patterns we can use this so both of us can feed to the other when these processes are occurring and break a potential impasse. Obviously this is still a work in progress for both of us. For us we see communicating with an Aspie involving the Aspie and the other person increasing their insight about the challenges, being flexible in the ways they respond to the other person and thinking out ways for both to change response patterns.

question: Asperger's Syndrome: How do you feel about public displays of affection?
answer: A2A. I have no idea whether this is an Asperger's trait - it could be age, culture, family, .... I am uncomfortable with displays of affection between other people in public - e.g. kissing and hugging. I think I find the emotional stuff too intense! I am rarely the object of any public displays of affection, nor do I initiate it, except for a quick kiss to my wife in appropriate circumstances (e.g. at the airport if she was going away without me). Usually if someone spontaneously initiates it (e.g. a niece of mine met me unexpectedly in the city and instantly gave me a hug), I am too busy processing what is going on to have time to think about its being in public. I have never been able to work out how people know when to hug or kiss socially. I see two acquaintances meet, and then suddenly they both lurch forward and hug or kiss, and I cannot see how they know when to do it. It is a complete mystery to me. It is not like they say out loud: "Shall we kiss? OK. After 'three' then, 1 ... 2 ... 3." I just freeze when I am in those circumstances: I have no idea whether I should or shouldn't, and no idea of "timing". question: Is it wrong to dislike people who have Asperger's syndrome?
answer: Here’s a scenario: You get taken to an unfamiliar place, and sat down to take a test on a subject that you have no idea about. (for this, let’s use bugs. I have no idea if you have knowledge about them, but just go with it for the sake of the scenario.) You are to look at a number of different specimens and say where they’re from, what gender they are, what species they are, and at least one fact about each unique species. But, many of the bugs look so similar you can hardly tell if they’re the same or not. There are judges watching you, and they are experts, not saying anything as you struggle with what they perceive as ‘the basics’ of bug identification. (They snicker as you make a mistake, to them it’s obvious that was a migratory locust, not a grasshopper. They make quiet remarks about how stupid you are from their desk.) After hours of struggling through the test, you learn that you got most of it wrong. After being booted out of the classroom that you were in, the halls are filled with people who have learned of your failing the test. They laugh, saying ‘You really are stupid! There are 16,000 different species of moths, not a measly 100!’ You try to explain, tell them that you had no idea of any of this, that you weren’t given any time to prepare or anything of the sort. They laugh and ridicule you more. ‘This should come naturally!’ ‘You really must be blind, there were so many obvious clues showing that Agrias Butterfly was a boy, not a girl!’ You feel miserable. After all, everyone else here seems to have gotten it right, and they didn’t look all that different from you, a few of them you even recognize. That is what it’s like. Except replace the bugs with social ques and interactions. It’s hard, confusing, and most of the time exhausting to someone with Apsergers, or autism of any kind. Yes, it’s wrong. (Another similar question would be ‘Is it wrong to dislike black people? I can’t see how anyone can’t be white.’ [I’m not saying you’re a racist, but I’m trying to prove a point.]) Now, if there was someone who stole something or did something you didn’t like, that just HAPPENED to be an Aspie, then it’d be fine to dislike that person, but not purely for the fact they have Aspergers syndrome.

question: Is Asperger's syndrome scientifically linked to immaturity?
answer: Scientifically? That’s a tough one. There have been no empirical studies to my knowledge that relate AS to immaturity. If you are thinking about people in general on the autism spectrum, about half of those with autism also have an intellectual disability. As such, they would be behind their peers in the areas of self-help and life skills as well as academics. But people with Asperger’s have intellectual ability within the average range or higher. I presume that you are talking about emotional and social maturity. Sometimes people on the spectrum seem to develop more slowly than their peers in these areas. While other small children instinctively watch others to pick up social cues to know what is expected of them and how to fit in, many with autism and Asperger’s are oblivious to these subtle and nonverbal cues. They have difficulty with Theory of Mind - understanding that other people have thoughts and feelings that differ from their own and being able to guess what mind be in someone else’s mind. That makes social understanding difficult. But, with time and practice people do get better at these skills. Since this development generally comes later than with their peers, someone on the spectrum can come across as immature. Integrating information can be difficult for people on the autism spectrum. They may process and store each piece of incoming information separately. While the knowledge might be nicely tucked away, retrieving it can be tricky, unless the new situation very closely resembles the initial learning. Over time, they will get better at integrating knowledge and being able to apply it in different situations but again, this skill often comes later than with same age peers, again, giving the impression of immaturity or lagging. Many people on the spectrum are plagued by sensory sensitivities. Thus while other children are sitting in class paying attention, the child with an ASD is trying hard to ignore that tag at the back of his neck, the humming and blinking of the fluorescent lights, the scratch of the pencil on paper and the squeaking of another child’s chair. Try devoting your full attention to new learning material under these stressors. In addition, many people on the spectrum take in information that they see far more easily than that which they hear. Schools are full of people lecturing, so some of this information will go over the head of the child who has autism. When you’re working hard to just hold it together and figure out what might be coming next, it’s hard to be as on top of things as other kids who don’t have these added difficulties. So yes, those on the spectrum could well lag behind in maturity.

question: Are witnesses with Asperger's syndrome more reliable?
answer: The topic tags say "Jehovah's Witnesses" and "Religion", but I assume that you meant witnesses of crimes and accidents and so on. As an Aspie myself, I'd say Aspies are definitely different witnesses than neurotypicals, but certainly not necessarily more reliable. The reliability depends a bit on how Aspie-proof the interviewer can formulate his questions. If a question covers too much ground---so, has to be summarized in the Aspie's mind too much---he might just feel as if he is asked too much for him to answer. He might feel overloaded, like a neurotypical person will feel overloaded from talking two conversations at the same time. Take some more time with an Aspie. An Aspie might have seen more than another person, as it is more easily distracted by a notable occurrance around him. Besides that, he might be able to tell more details of it too. You must ask him in detail too. Actually, sometimes you really have to squeeze the details out, some of which appear to be hidden deeply in the Aspie's mind. You see, usually Aspies have a history of being told not to tell too much detail in a conversation. So, they will not tell them by themselves---you really have to dig up these details from their minds by asking good questions. So, they're good witnesses, but you need to make an extra effort to pick the fruits of it. Rebecca Caverly is also very right in her answer.

question: As someone with Asperger's Syndrome, how do you deal with physical contact?
answer: *Note: I have PDD-NOS, not aspergers, which is still a part of the autistic spectrum. If you are looking for specifically aspergers, do not use this answer.* You know that feeling when someone sits next to you on the bus—and you’re not quite sure why they’re there because dude, there are at least four open seats— and the bus makes a sharp turn, slamming them into you? Erugh. Physical contact, as many of the other answers have said, is inevitable. My clothes have to be put on, shoes have to be worn (screw you, socks), my mom likes hugs from me, my friends expect hugs/some kind of touch, I’m going to bump into people, etc. I can’t avoid many of these things, so the only thing I can really do is mentally prepare for that and avoid as many of the bad touches as I can. My feelings on contact changes depending on the kind of day I’m having. Some are worse than others. Bad sensory days make it hell to even lay in bed, so I just lie on the floor or stand with as little clothing as I can get away with. Lately, I’ve been averse to touch and while I used to enjoy hugging people and the fabrics of my clothes, it doesn’t quite feel right anymore. The best way to describe it would be like claustrophobia. It goes from “Oh, this isn’t too bad” to “get me the fuck out of here” in a few seconds. I feel trapped and my skin is crawling—the touch is no longer pleasant. When it comes to clothes, I’m fairly picky. I don’t go for matching clothes or flattering clothes, I go for durability and comfort. Most of my clothes are stretchy, soft fabrics and are very, very loose on my body. Anything that is even slightly clingy is a big no. It explains my lack of fashion sense. My poor mother had to watch me go to school in a pink patterned shirt, a plaid overshirt, purple patterned pants, and crocs. Goodness knows that I’ll never be a fashion designer. There aren’t too many things I can really do to prepare for physical contact other than anticipating it and asking people not to do so. The vast majority of the people around me respect my decisions, so they leave me alone. If they forget, I just grin and bear it. It’s all I can do. If I have a fidget on hand, I’ll use it to stim (fidget cubes are a blessing) and that’s about it. A few off of my list of “bad” at the current moment:Kisses.I despise kisses of any kind and always have. I have never kissed anyone or anything, not even my parents. Kiss me without my consent anywhere and you just guaranteed that I will never come near you again. This is one of the absolute worst, if not the worst, physical contact I get. I hate it.My mom got away with it this morning, but she apologized after my numerous grunts and grumbles. I’ll usually say “No kisses!” but she got me before I could say it.The clingy shirtsHow do people stand to wear those things? The fabric rubs against you and is constantly sticking to your skin! I’m physically cringing right now at the thought of it.Socks.They’re like the chinese finger traps for feet that you can’t get out of. ‘Nuff said.When someone is touching me without any pre-warning or my consent.Yes, that includes hugging me from behind. Given my height, you’ll end up choking me anyway—or maybe that’s my friend’s plan…Winter coats/jackets/etcAt one point, the principal of my middle school had to threaten to come into my class and put the coat on herself in the -30C weather. It didn’t work, mind you, but they tried.Ever walk home in a snow storm in shorts and a t shirt? Parents got mad, 2/10 would not recommend.I may or may not be ditching my coat in my locker at this very moment.So those are just a few things that I can usually avoid, but I do immensely dislike. There are good things, of course, but since this is about how I “deal” with physical contact, I suppose I should stick with these. If you want the “good things” list, you can either message me or ask in the comments. Overall, I just have to mentally prepare and ask people to be respectful of my wishes. Luckily, I have supportive and (mostly) aware people around me. **Autistics are all different. Your milage may vary.**

question: Why does ABA therapy seem to be used primarily for autistic children?
answer: First, read David Andrews's answer to Why does ABA therapy seem to be used primarily for autistic children? It is succinct and accurate. I up voted and was going to comment, but once again my long-winded comment became its own answer. The thing is, behavioral therapy improves observable behavior. It doesn't consider how a person thinks or feels, just corrects behavior that the therapist has determined to be incorrect, through years of training and continuing education. A clinical psych needs 3 years internship after getting a doctorate. In addition, a certain number of hours of training are required each year for an active license. They are very good at what they do. But, as Mr. Andrews correctly stated, the only way to verify an outcome is through observable behavior. That's why behavioral “therapy” is the only therapy that can be demonstrated with an observable outcome. Because behavioral therapy is teaching behaviors. This is not a bad thing. The goal is a functional person who can take care of themselves. I personally do not think Aspergers is the same as “High-functioning Autism” because people I know with Asperger's, do not struggle to learn language. Rather, the common experience is to find oneself baffled when reprimanded for not following a social convention that one was not ever aware of. Nobody ever taught me that! It is the common refrain. We need it explained to us in words. We are good with words. Not so much with body language. Non verbal low-functioning Autism is a different story. They cannot function or take care of themselves. Behavioral therapy is teaching. I like that, David Andrews . If the goal is to teach Behavior, behavior therapy is where it's at. But if the goal is for the person to be healthy and happy, well, cognitive therapy is tried-and-true and proven to work, if your goal is for a person to have self-esteem and think highly of themselves. If your goal is their emotional well-being, rather than to teach behaviors. Notice these are different outcomes. The treatment is not for the same thing. There is a catch: one must be able to speak for cognitive therapy to apply, whether verbally, sign language, or even through writing. There is a movement towards online therapy for people who are more comfortable in their home, such as someone with agoraphobia, receiving therapy through writing. But a child with low-functioning autism who cannot speak, nor sign, nor write, cannot receive any other type of therapy other than behavioral therapy. Here is my controversial opinion. Please note it is only my opinion. Asperger's is not the same condition as “high functioning autism.” Low functioning autism is a different condition, it is a difference of type rather than scale. The difference being the ability to use language. It makes a world of difference. For child with autism, it is no wonder behavioral therapy is used instead of talk therapy to actually ask the child what they think. Because a child with severe autism cannot talk. But there are movements now towards play therapy or art therapy, where a child even with low-functioning autism can express themselves even if they are non-verbal. They are new so I don't know much about them or how they work or the long-term outcomes. ABA therapy has immediately observable outcomes, and it teaches the behaviors that the therapist wants to teach. There is nothing wrong with this in and of itself. Again, this is good if the goal is to teach Behavior. But who advocates for the child and their well-being? I'm proud to say I educate young people who will become parents someday, so parents of the future will hopefully be a little more educated than my parents generation. Obviously the parents should be the child's best advocate. I am on Quora because it is a place where people educate themselves, and parents of a child with low-functioning autism have resources to learn about different therapies available. I hope the parents educate themselves. There are lots of options and more of them are becoming available all the time.

question: Is ABA therapy only for autism?
answer: Of course, no. It is a myth that ABA therapy is only for children with autism. The treatment reflects how all human brains learn through positive and negative support, ABA therapy helps children and adults without autism adopt beneficial skills. The principles and techniques of ABA can foster basic skills, including social, motor and verbal skills. It can also help cultivate complex skills, such as reading and understanding another individual’s viewpoint. Autism was once a mysterious disorder. Some of these myths persist today, especially when it comes to treatment for this developmental condition. Many parents are interested in treatment for autism. ABA treatment is one of them used to cure the disease. This treatment is used both for children and adults. There are different ABA therapy techniques used by professionals. Therapists began using ABA in the early 60s as a way of teaching communication skills, social, academic, play, work and community living skills. They also used the approach to reduce problems using a variety of teaching methods, including Discrete Trial Training (DTT), often referred to as “drilling.” DTT breaks down complex skills into smaller, discrete tasks then combines skills to accomplish complex goals. A trainer teaching colours to a child might begin by presenting a red ball and a white ball, asking the child to point to the red ball, and then rewarding the behaviour.

question: Is ABA therapy made just for children with autism?
answer: No. Applied Behavioural Analysis is basically an advanced form of behaviour modification/conditioning which allows for cognition. If you know anything about the history of psychology, you know that there were pitched battles between the dog-trainers (behaviourists) and the computer nerds (cognitivists). Okay, not quite, but one behaviourist’s kids had to attend school under false names because of death threats, and a cognitivist also received death and rape threats. So attempts to get them playing nice together are a huge deal. Now, CBT (cognitive behaviour therapy - cognitive therapy with some behavioural techniques) is tremendously popular and effective. ABA should be, too - and it actually is in many settings, such as, for example, improving the lives and environments of non-vocal persons, including the severely and profoundly mentally handicapped. Given that, it would seem ideal for helping autists, many of whom are mentally handicapped and/or non-vocal. So, why isn’t it? Why do people call it “abuse”, instead? I think it’s a combination of poor professional standards and overweening hope. There was a time when anyone could take out an advert in the classifieds and call themselves a psychologist. That included a large period during which behaviourism was in its zenith. Behaviour modification is relatively easy: dog-trainers do it with no psychological training at all. The chap who trained my grandfather’s sheepdogs couldn’t even spell psychology, or anything else, really - he was a settled Traveller who’d never been to school. Increased professionalisation in psychology came in when cognitive psychology came to prominence - and cog psych is that wee bit more technical. So there were plenty of people out there performing perfectly competent phobia reduction, stop-smoking sessions, and so on using behavioural techniques without professional qualifications, doing no harm. But cognitive psychology can’t really be done without some professional background. And when desperate parents - who might have accepted a profoundly handicapped Downs baby, but were hung up on the fact that some autists can function almost like neurotypicals - were prepared to spend wodges of cash on anyone who offered the slightest hope… I think some people who didn’t really understand what they were doing, people who had read an article on ABA but lacked the professional chops to understand the creative and intuitive and pastoral side of ABA - some of those people did more harm than good. A good, trained, sensitive ABA therapist will make your autist a happier, more contented person - partly by training YOU, the parent, in how to keep them on an even keel. They won’t necessarily give you the autistic prodigy you read about in Reader’s Digest feel-good stories, and you shouldn’t expect them to try. And you definitely shouldn’t put your child in the hands of the dog-trainers who promise they can.

Many of us with ASD are extra sensitive to medications side effects, so often “let's try this" remedies from physicians end up making things much worse than if they did nothing. Then eventually, a breakdown or failure must occur. Many of us force ourselves into unnatural efforts to keep masking, sometimes for years, but eventually we do end up crashing. The crash that eventually stops most of us is called autistic burnout. question: What is the goal of ABA therapy for kids with Autism?

question: Should I listen to my occupational therapist's suggestion to drop ABA therapy for my child with autism?
answer: I would say it depends on how the ABA is used. ABA has a good research history of being one of the most successful interventions for children with autism (for teaching all sorts of skills non-occupational therapy related, including literacy, math, and life skills). Most good special education teachers have some background in it. I think the problem occurs when the ABA services are divorced from meaningful purpose. I have seen examples of this where the ABA intervention is provided in a totally segregated setting around meaningless tasks, like identifying “what is wrong” with a flashcard picture of a snake with bunny ears. That is not a meaningful skill the child will ever use and is based on a stupid developmental model that doesn’t account for the individual’s needs. Your therapist may similarly think that ABA skills don’t make sense for your child in the OT setting if they are doing things like sorting colored objects to acquire fine motor skills. This might not be a task that will ever be meaningful or helpful to your child and would be better to skip. ABA in a more successful/useful context might look like a task analysis (breaking down a task into all of its small component steps) for a task the child wants to learn. I have used ABA for things like teaching a young man with intellectual disabilities how to tie his shoes in middle school in the context of getting changed for gym in the locker room. A task analysis is very helpful for this work, because it tells the male paraprofessional helping him exactly what to do to help the child be successful. We paired this with “reverse chaining” which is starting with the last step, where the child experiences immediate success and works backward from that (so pulling the knot tight, success! then putting the hoop through the knot and pulling it tight, success! etc.). The important thing about using ABA is that it be in a MEANINGFUL context for a skill that is useful or interesting to the child, not based on some theory about the skills kids need to acquire to become “ready” to learn other skills. Many children with disabilities never go through the “normal” milestones of other children and may skip from things like understanding that letters make sounds, to just reading all of the words because they have memorized them all. Forcing kids to learn in the same way as their peers, when they have a different set of strengths and needs, is just unfair to the kid. In short, ABA is great, if done well, by someone who understands the values of the kid, the family, and the context (including school and home) and if the skills are targeted to be the most meaningful, important skills for the kiddo to learn. Best of luck!!

question: What is the difference between MRT and ABA therapy? Which do you think is better for treating autism and why?
answer: MRT (Modified Radial Tonic) and ABA (Applied Behavioral Analysis) are two different behavioral therapies that are used to treat autism spectrum disorder. Both approaches use the principles of learning and behavior modification in order to train children with autism to better interact with their environment. MRT is an approach that uses reward-based methods and focuses on self-management skills as well as reduction of repetitive or restricted behaviors. This approach aims to improve social, cognitive, self-care, and communication skills in an individual who has been diagnosed with autism by providing opportunities for reinforcement for desired behaviors and reducing the reinforcement for undesirable behaviors. This is accomplished through techniques such as praising desirable behaviors, ignoring undesired ones, redirecting inappropriate behavior, teaching new skills through imitation or modeling techniques, setting clear rules and expectations around target behaviors before they occur; while giving verbal comments or physical guidance when necessary. Conversely, ABA therapy emphasizes changing environmentally based responses to stimuli by manipulating environmental variables in order to obtain a desired outcome. It also utilizes positive reinforcement practices such as reward systems or token economies where individuals with Autism can be rewarded for completing targeted tasks correctly in order to increase desirable responses towards future activities within their environment. In addition,.ABA therapists frequently break down complex instructions into smaller steps so those affected by autism can better understand them--and then reinforce correct answers after completion of each step sequence until the entire task is complete. Overall both MRT and ABA treatments have shown great promise when it comes treating Autism Spectrum Disorder but which one works best will depend on the individual being treated due differences between people when it comes neurological functioning . Each treatment option has unique advantages so it is important for clinicians work closely together with family members of those affected by Autism Spectrum disorder in selecting a treatment plan that works best given the individual circumstances involved .

question: Are there therapies besides Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) that are effective for autism?
answer: I am a caregiver for a family member on the spectrum. I am not a medical professional. In my family member’s case, one year of ABA was of minimal effectiveness, which appeared to be because a lot of her therapy focused on trying to identify triggers/causes of unwanted/unhealthy behaviors. This is normal for ABA, but her problems were just not that simple. However, she did benefit by learning some adulting-type skills. Overall, with one year of ABA therapy we saw very little improvement. Psych meds have helped, but they are not a magic cure-all pill. She has reached a point where she has tried/eliminated pretty much all the psych meds available to her and she is nowhere near functional enough or free enough of symptoms to enjoy much of her life. Meds can only do so much. Hospitalizations help during a crises, primarily by keeping her safe, supervised, and monitoring her while any changes are made to her meds. However, that system is terribly overburdened and, at least in our state, inpatient stays are severely limited for her regardless of her symptoms, usually 4 - 7 days max. Recently, her psychiatrist has recommended a trial of DBT therapy. From my research, I like what I see and we will be giving it a try. Her doc told us it was designed for patients who are chronically suicidal, have chronic mood and thought disorders, and the resulting behaviors which accompany such problems. My limited understanding of DBT therapy is that it is intensive (~1x/week individual therapy & 1x/week group therapy), extra supportive (patients can have a 15 min phone consult in between sessions to direct them to/tweak skills learned in therapy), and teaches mindfulness as well as skills and copes designed specifically to improve intrusive thoughts, suicideality, out of control moods, etc. Their goals seem to include quality of life/learning to live with yourself as you are. Most of the therapies we’ve tried have really been designed to either push her towards activities she can’t yet do (full-time school, college, work programs, employment, etc.), or seem focused on issues which ignore her symptoms and side-effects of meds. The end result of these therapies for her have been minimal gains, while she ends up feeling as though no one listens to her voice while pushing her towards activities which will worsen her conditions. My further understanding from the doc & her therapist is that, while individual therapists can and do offer DBT therapy, they usually only offer one component (being the skills portion) of what is meant to be a much more comprehensive program (groups, phone consultants between sessions, specialized DBT therapists, the group of DBT therapists supporting each other in helping patients, etc.). If possible, it is recommended that patients try to locate a dedicated DBT center in their area. This therapy is a big commitment and my understanding is specialized DBT centers ask that the patient focus solely on therapy through them so the patient can better learn/focus/practice skills taught there. In addition, there may be problems with patients’ insurance paying for both DBT and other, concurrent therapies. Another benefit to attending a specialized DBT center is that they usually offer therapy for children, adolescents, and adults. Many traditional counselors/therapists in our area will not perform DBT if the patient is under 18 years of age. Keep seeking and don’t ever give up. This may or may not be our answer or your answer, but at least we can say we tried it. Either way you’ll end up with new knowledge, experience, friends, and hopefully skills. God bless and stay healthy, Lisa

question: What were the reasons you left your job as an RBT, BCABA, or BCBA providing ABA intervention/therapy for children with autism?
answer: I was hired on as a behavior technician (BT) and gave my 2 week notice after having worked only 3 months. I was going to work towards becoming an RBT after starting to work with clients. I was hired and began training that was mostly completed online at the site where trainers would check in after certain checkpoints. I had 2 encounters where I would practice the skills I was learning online, with a trainer who was role playing as a child with Autism, and then one encounter where I practiced what I had learned (things like DTT) with a child as the trainer observed me and gave me pointers about my delivery of the intervention. I completed this training in 40 hours, during one week, and then began working one-on-one with 3 different clients throughout the week. The first problem I faced was that I was trained with a binder and was told that each client had a binder where I could find all the information I needed to know about that child. It was supposed to include the unwanted behaviors that the child typically engages in and what to do if he/she engages in them and the specific steps to take for that child to deescalate any tantrums. The binder was also supposed to include information that was specific to the child including things like toileting routines, reinforcement plan, if and what time the child was supposed to meet with the speech therapist, etc. I was trained with a binder that had all those specifics, however after a week of training, I started working with clients and none of them had all the specifics in their binders. I tried asking for clarification on how I was supposed to deal with a specific behavior a child was engaging in and I would never be able to get an answer because I had never even met the BCBA for that child. When I would ask other people who would know about the child’s specifics they would tell me that the BCBA for that child was always in the other building, at a home visit, or elsewhere. So not only did I not have the appropriate materials/ information provided but there was no one ever available to ask. Each of my clients had a different BCBA, however I only ever met one of them and she called a team meeting which included the BCBA, 4 RBT/BT, and the child’s mother. I got the most support from this BCBA and felt more comfortable and confident when working with the child after having met with his team and knowing who I could ask for clarification on things. This BCBA would come in an observe me with the client and update his program and show me how to implement the new programs she was creating. She was very supportive; however, I never met the other client’s BCBA or other RBT/BT and was not able to get information I needed to be able to support the client to the best of my ability. Also, in the 3 months that I was there, the other 2 client’s programs were never updated after the children had reached mastery criterion for certain skills. I feel that there was a very big lack of support because there were so few BCBA’s and so many children they each had to be updating programs and binders and other things for, that there weren’t enough hours in the day for them to be able to support in the way they need to nor be updating the programs like the children needed them to be updated. Additionally, I was supposed to have a mentor assigned to me that I would meet with, however for the 3 months I was there, I was not assigned a mentor until after I gave my two week notice. I think another problem with the job was that they had very minimal requirements to apply. The job only required applicants to be 18 years or older, have a high school diploma, and be able to work between 25-40 hours a week. I luckily had knowledge about the development of children, because by the time I applied for the job, I was one semester away from graduating from a junior college with an AA degree in Early Childhood Education. However, I quickly found out that what I learned in my ECE college courses, was very different from how I was being trained to interact with the children at the ABA facility. An example of this was when I was giving a child a task to complete and they would engage in an unwanted behavior like swiping, I was trained to give that child a shape sorter and tell them “Finish” as a way to help the child deescalate their tantrum/unwanted behavior. However, if the child wouldn’t do it independently and would instead continue to engage in swiping or other unwanted behaviors, I would have to physically take the child’s hand in mine and make the child complete the shape sorter. This was completely opposite of what I had learned in my ECE classes. In a classroom with typically developing children, everything in a preschool setting is supposed to be an invitation to do something and a child will never be forced, much less physically, to do something they choose not to do. Skills I learned to help a child calm down from a tantrum or unwanted behavior included things like taking deep breaths, allowing that child to take time to themselves in a quiet area with sensory bottles, books, and other materials to help them calm down, and then have a conversation about it once the child has self-regulated. question: What are the benefits of ABA and SI therapy for autism?
answer: Sensory integration therapy is not evidence based. Many people will say that it helps. If anecdotal evidence is good enough for you, then I don't see the harm in trying (except for the time, money, and effort). ABA is the only evidence based service offered to autistic people. You have to be extremely cautious when selecting a provider. Many ABA practitioners are ableists. Some of them are abusive. Familiarize yourself with the BACBs ethical guidelines. If your practitioner.does.not follow them, then that's a massive red flag. For example, it is considered highly unethical to recommend punishment procedures without first exhausting all other options. If all else fails, punishment procedures might be used, but they should only be used alongside reinforcement strategies. I have worked with over 100 clients over the last 12 years. I have only recommended punishment strategies with 3 of them. It is almost never necessary to use punishment in order to support an individual. There are almost no circumstances where the use of positive punishment is acceptable..positive punishment is anytime an aversive stimulus is used (e.g. pain) to shape behavior. Most often, if punishment is used, it involves taking something away (ie response cost). For example, if someone is working towards a new video game, they might use a point system..once they earn enough points, they can buy their game. They can earn points by demonstrating skills that they are learning or strengthening (e.g. offering to help someone in need). A punishment component would involve losing points that were already earned. Once again, losing points would not be used unless it's been shown that the point system is ineffective without the use of response cost. In other words, the focus of ABA is never supposed to be on getting rid of undeseriable behaviors. The focus is supposed to be on skill acquisition (ie learning or strengthening of skills that matter to the autistic person receiving services).

question: Recently my 4 year old was diagnosed with autism level 1. All of this is still new to us and we have a lot to learn, but one of the therapies provided is ABA. I hear mixed feelings on this sort of therapy. From experience, should we let him do it?
answer: I speak as someone who was certified as an ABA therapist in 2008, chose not to work in that area after a few months, and has an autistic adult son (Level 1 autism). ABA is controversial. I wasn’t even comfortable with it for more neurodivergent children and adults with whom I (briefly) worked. I certainly wouldn’t have considered it for my Level 1 son. ABA asks autistic people to put a great deal of their focus and energy into learning how to behave more typically. Some of that can be helpful for them, especially if they wish to fit in more easily in a neurotypical environment. Most of it, though, I think is not about serving the needs of the autistic person. It becomes another hurdle placed in front of them for reasons that may not have value for them at all, but only for people in the neurotypical environment. I think there are much more positive and constructive supports available for neurodivergent people. I saw children and youth identified as being on the ASD spectrum become less confident and less happy as a result of the demands placed on them by ABA. Many found the “training” to be boring, aversive and a confirmation that they don’t “measure up.” Here is just one example from my training: We worked on teaching autistic people not to perform repetitive behaviours. The reason? Because it’s distracting to others and makes the ASD person stand out. The distracting-to-others part can be handled by first identifying who really is distracted by it (not everyone will be bothered by a fellow student rocking in his seat), and arranging seating so that the distracted person and the repetitive-motion person are not in one another’s sightlines. For me, that’s a solution that respects differences and approaches these in a practical spirit of comfort for all parties involved. Because - and this is important - the repetitive-motion person is not doing it to be annoying. They are doing it to self-soothe, combat anxiety, increase focus, and so on. The rocking serves a functional purpose. There are so many tools we have to help people with different needs and behaviours share a space more comfortably. I decided in 2009 that ABA was about making neurodivergent people try to learn to “pass” as “normal,” and even if some of the reasons for that were good reasons, the price was just too high. question: What is the difference between autism and Asperger’s syndrome, and could there be another category? What if you have most of the defining characteristics except you also possess empathy?
answer: As others have explained in varying ways, Asperger's Syndrome and a number of other diagnoses, including Pervasive Developmental Disorder - Not Otherwise Specified (PDD-NOS), were removed from the DSM-5 in 2013 and may well be removed from the ISD11 in 2022. The conditions described didn't cease to exist, and you may still find them mentioned in the diagnostic manuals, but instead of being a separate diagnosis they have all been subsumed into the single diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder. The word “spectrum” was intended to indicate the wide scope of variation possible within that diagnosis, which now includes what were formerly separate conditions. Unfortunately, it has more often than not been misunderstood by both neurotypicals and even autists, leading to confusion. Some have pictured it as a 2-dimensional line with “severe" autism at one end, neurotypical at the other, and “mild" autism somewhere in the middle, each kind of blending into the others at various points along the way. Under this misapprehension, some autists are seen as “almost neurotypical”, and some neurotypicals as “a bit autistic”. Others picture separate 2-dimensional lines, with the “autistic” one having “severe" or “low-functioning” autism at one end, and “mild" or “high-functioning” autism at the other end. This is almost as completely incorrect as the previously mentioned image. If you'd like to know what the word “spectrum” is meant to indicate, and how those formerly separate diagnoses can all fit into the current Autism Spectrum Disorder, then read this: "Autism is a Spectrum" Doesn't Mean What You Think » NeuroClastic In terms of empathy, what it boils down to is that there are different kinds of empathy. When scientists and researchers declared that autists have delays or deficits in empathy, they were talking about cognitive empathy, but what most lay people mean when they use the word is affective (or emotional) empathy. There are several other, less well-known, types of empathy too. So there is often a lack of clarity about which type of empathy (if any) is being referred to, and whether it's a lack, an impairment, or a delay. Then too, the internal lived experience of autists, their understanding, and their abilities have often been misunderstood and/or underestimated by well-intentioned researchers, caregivers, and families alike. If you want to know more about autists and empathy, you can get a taste of the issues in the following: Autism & empathy | Embrace Autism The double empathy problem ‘Theory of mind’ does not fade with age among autistic adults | Spectrum | Autism Research News Impairments in cognitive empathy and alexithymia occur independently of executive functioning in college students with autism - Tim Ziermans, Ymke de Bruijn, Renee Dijkhuis, Wouter Staal, Hanna Swaab, 2019 Empathy Impairment in Individuals With Autism Spectrum Conditions From a Multidimensional Perspective: A Meta-Analysis Edited to add: It was probably clear already, but just to be certain, the fact that you have empathy doesn't mean that you're not autistic, nor does it mean that another category of autism is needed. Autists do have empathy. It may not follow the same profile as a neurotypical, it may be delayed, an autist may be less likely to pick up nonverbal cues that there is a situation where empathy should be expressed, and they may express their empathy in atypical ways - but that doesn't mean that it isn't there. I won't argue that all autists are empathetic, but it shouldn't be automatically assumed that they're not.

question: What is your opinion of the "double empathy" theory regarding communication between people with autism and non-autistic people? Are these gaps unbridgeable?
answer: It’s not really a theory. It’s just a fact. It’s usually called the “double empathy problem.” It exists, undeniably. It happens when I don’t get you and you don’t get me. That’s not going to happen until you open your heart and begin to know what it’s like to be me, from the inside, and I do the same with you in return. Consider autism of the kind we encounter on a regular basis, (for example in folks with what we used to call “Aspergers.” Can you see it as a naturally occurring variation, like so called “AD/HD,” and “homosexuality” and eye color, and not first of all as a medicalized “disorder?” If so, you can begin to look far past diagnoses and differences and connect better, not neurotypical to autistic, but person to person. Like any therapist, I work hard to think non-diagnostically, avoiding categorization, when working alongside folks with any variations. Even with therapists the variations can trigger microfear and microavoidance, because there’s something about them that “doesn’t fit” average expectations. If we lump atypical humans into a discrete and separate category from ourselves and offer “treatment” (always designed to make them a more comfortable fit), true empathy becomes impossible. Sympathy, sure, and toleration, and even generic kindness, and foundations seeking a cure, but never empathy. I know a person with “ASD” might not get a joke, and take it literally. That’s a clinical observation, no empathy involved. If I drop my categories and open my heart, I may be able to appreciate what’s it’s like to be smart but not to get certain jokes, how it feels. I might accept and celebrate a person whose communication style interrupts and corrects me (quite correctly). I might appreciate that my friend is an expert in washing machines and finds them fascinating, and cultivate curiosity about the topic so I can share the fun. I have friends “on the spectrum,” and have had for years, and never think of them that way unless I’m writing about autism. They’re just who they are, not typical like me, maybe, but prized and precious, at least as much, no need for categorization. That is the double empathy problem, or my version of it, as it applies to interacting with folks with neurological differences, people we run into in many settings, people who do fit but could fit in better with better empathy. Certainly, some kids and adults are much more severely impacted, and not only don’t communicate typically, but barely communicate at all. Still, even with them, or perhaps most of all with them, the double empathy problem is very real. That’s a topic for another answer. question: Is it possible for a person with autism to excel in reading emotions and empathy, but still struggle in social situations due to their lack of self-awareness and poor communication skills?

question: What are the differences between lack of empathy, or difficulty showing empathy, in autism, narcissism, and psychopathy?
answer: Narcissist A narcissist knows what you are feeling, but does not care. The narcissist is interested in their own aggrandizement only; you are useful only to the degree you provide that aggrandizement. The narcissist has no sense of self and replaces that internal hole with external praise. However, the hole can never be filled so the search for aggrandizement never ends. Literally everything the narcissist says and does is insincere. Communication is a tool to get what they want, not a way to communicate needs and feelings. Truth and falsehood are irrelevant. The narcissist speaks with equal conviction when stating a lie or a truth because they are equally useful for earning aggrandizement. The narcissist is profoundly insensitive to the needs of others because only their own needs feel real. When the narcissist apparently panders to your needs, e.g., by flattering your intellect or beauty, it is only an investment to earn aggrandizement from you later. If the interaction is between a heterosexual male and a female, the reward isn’t necessarily sex. The narcissist may just want to use her as eye-candy at a party where the aggrandizement will come from the envy of other men. Now suppose the narcissist’s flattery has induced you to handover your life savings which the narcissist then lost or squandered. You are upset and confront them. They can see your hurt your feelings, but so what? Why does it matter? The narcissist can't even pretend to empathize because they can’t imagine your pain and summon a similar feeling inside. In reality, when you confront the narcissist in anger, the narcissist feels aggrieved by your verbal attacks (because his aggrandizement is challenged) and will usually play the victim in response, often vehemently. Donald Trump is the master of this pattern.Say something offensive or demonstrably falseGet criticizedPlay the victimWhile the narcissist says and does things which lead to benefit to him and harm for others without compunction, the narcissist is not in it for revenge. As long as the narcissist has his aggrandizement, he does not need to be nasty. That is why the narcissist does not hold on to bad feelings when a battle is over. The narcissist can flip-flop from bitter opponent to flatterer on a dime. “Lyin Ted” becomes a “tough and brilliant opponent” immediately after Ted endorses Donald. Psychopath A psychopath also knows what you are feeling but the psychopath lacks normal feelings. A psychopath does not experience feelings of caring or a need for social acceptance. A psychopath is willing to take actions like theft, intimidation and fraud because the social consequences don’t matter—the psychopath could not care less that others view him and his actions as contemptible, as long as they don’t express their disrespect in public. Suppose a psychopath threatened you with violence, insincerely but convincingly, to get something he wants. When arrested, the psycho won’t understand what the fuss is about. Yeah I scared you. So what? I wasn’t really going to hurt you, what are you whining about now? While lacking most other feelings, the psychopath does experience rage, particularly in response to disrespect. Interrupt a psychopath in speech a few times and you will summon that rage. The rage is often kept under wraps until the psychopath can dominate a situation. When that happens, look out. The psycho holds a grudge and his lack of limits means the revenge will be far out of proportion to the original offense. Anyone can feel annoyed by an interrupter, but it take a psychopath to use that anger as motivation to get him fired from a job, urinate in his car, burn his house down, etc. Lacking a need for regard, the psychopath can observe you and your statements with less distortion than normal people do. Normal people have instantaneous emotional reactions to the events they experience. If they see a reproachful look, their guilt circuit is triggered. They might instantly think "Oh my God, I offended him!" when the anger was unrelated. Psychopaths watch you dispassionately, taking notes to use in future. The psychopath learns to emulate normal emotional reactions by watching others. The psycho understands the importance of blending in to get their needs met so they train themselves to copy real emotions to better exploit the people around themselves. Autistic Spectrum Disorder (ASD) People An ASD person does not know what you are feeling. He or she literally can not see it. Autism-spectrum people must learn in a mechanical way to understand social consequences of actions. "Gee, I notice that the last three times I called someone stupid, they yelled at me. I don't like that, so I won't call them stupid anymore." But the autism-spectrum person does not truly get why the other person is angry--I was just stating a fact. Why would someone get mad at hearing a fact? ASD people do not use words to earn aggrandizement or to intimidate. They speak what feels like truth to them without a filter. When an ASD person calls someone stupid, they can always produce a reason based in that person’s actions—this is why the statement feels factual to them. When an NT person calls someone stupid, they often can not. The NT person felt hurt and used “stupid” as a way to express their anger, rather than because they saw stupidity in that other person’s actions. When the offensiveness of the word “stupid” is explained to the ASD person and when you ask how it would feel to know other people think you are stupid, the ASD person will understand his statement was insulting. Unlike narcissist and psychopath, the autistic person cares deeply about other people, and about how they regard the ASD person. The autist struggles with a perceptual barrier not an empathy barrier. They are sweet and guileless and believe that fairness is tremendously important. The ASD person will not cheat at a game, nor deceive. If your sales person has ASD, the product you are sold will be the best fit for your needs, not the one with the highest commission. The ASD person takes no pride in their honesty; to them that is just how the world is supposed to work. They are outraged when someone else breaks the rules, even if the rule was trivial, because in their view rules are so important. Rules are the frame that allows the ASD person to navigate a bewildering world. The ASD person understands the meaning of words literally. If you say, "I want my child supervised by an adult" the ASD person doesn't infer "Oh by 'adult' she meant ‘responsible person’." The ASD person thinks "over 18". On that basis the ASD person might dismiss the hyper-responsible 17-year-old babysitter, but accept the less responsible 19-year-old. The ASD person is the opposite of the psychopath. The ASD person feels empathy and may want to show that empathy, but has a hard time communicating empathy. They do not know how to use tone, body language and implicature to communicate emotional messages. When the ASD person tries to show sympathy for another, the gestures may seem oddly flat or muted. The autist may have a powerful internal experience of caring, but unless the non-autistic audience is well-attuned, they will miss the feeling. The ASD person shows his appreciation with gestures rather than words. Your ASD son remembers your birthday and paints a picture or makes an ashtray—he invested his time to show his love. But he won't jump into your arms with delight when you walk in the door—that is not his style. Autism occurs on a spectrum—a range of behaviors and symptoms varying from so mild they are almost invisible, to so extreme the person seems unaware of other people around them. My answer addresses the autism I have personally encountered—people who function socially but struggle with their perceptual barriers. I do not consider autism a disease or an abnormality. Autism is a label for internal wiring that differs from neurotypical wiring, that is all. Although neurotypical wiring is more common, autistic wiring is part of the normal range of human beings. And like most widespread human traits, autism exists for a reason—under the right conditions, it endowed survival benefits in the past. Conclusion Narcissists range from obnoxious to asshole. Psychopaths are manipulative, dangerous and despicable. Neither feels caring emotions for others and neither have real friends. The autist is a gentle, caring person often overflowing with feeling for others but having a social deficit interfering with reading emotion in others and communicating their own feelings. They need more time and understanding, but if you accept their communication without judgment, they will be your kind, loyal and true friend forever.
