question: What is the experience of empathy like for people with autism?
answer: Thank you for the A2A. Being that there is two different types of empathy (as others have explained), I’ll address my experience with both of them, because they are vastly different. Cognitive Empathy: This is the ability to ascertain another’s state of mind from their body language/tone of voice/facial cues. I have a lot of trouble with this. I can often determine if someone is happy or sad or angry, but the nuances within these broad categories trip me up, so all forms of upset (irritation through to rage) can seem similar to me. I can also miss mounting frustration/irritation and not really see it until someone explodes at me, so it seems like a blast of anger comes out of nowhere. However. I can learn one person very, very well if they become one of “my” people. This is where my brain kind of latches onto them and starts soaking up information like a sponge, as though they are one of my obsessive topics. There are maybe two people I can do this with (so it’s very rare) and they are also on the spectrum. I end up learning every bit of their “normal” and my pattern recognition goes into overdrive if an emotion I don’t immediately recognise flashes over their face, or they do something differently than they usually do. Whomever this happens with will not be able to keep anything from me because anything out of the ordinary will grab my attention like a neon sign, no matter how subtle it is. Sometimes I can mistake the cues for one emotion for another, or miss the context and give the wrong responses. Combined with my auditory processing disorder it can produce really painful results, like giving a polite laugh after someone has just told me their dog has passed away. (Around 90% of the time I can fake my way through a conversation where I’m getting very little actual information because I can’t process the auditory input in that moment. I learnt to fake it after finding people get very impatient and aggravated when you ask them to repeat themselves over and over.) If I’m deeply engrossed in doing/reading/learning something, zero non-essential (according to my brain) information will make it through, including emotions that I might have found fairly obvious otherwise. ONCE I LEARN that someone is distraught, hurting, angry and so on, this leads to the next form of empathy… Emotional Empathy: Almost as if to make up for my lack of cognitive empathy, I have far too much emotional empathy. I can very easily feel other’s emotions as my own, when it’s obvious that they are very upset or angry, or even joyous. When I hear of, read about or see violence and abuse towards people and animals, it’s horrifying and overwhelming to the point that I will shutdown or meltdown. People expressing anger in my vicinity will reduce me to a quivering mess. I cannot watch horror movies, or shows with excessive realistic gore in them. It’s incredibly traumatising to see images of animal abuse. My mind immediately puts myself in the place of the abused and helpless creature and how I/they would feel. I have deep compassion for people who endure mental illness, heartbreak, abuse and so on but I’m often useless to help them in person because I get overwhelmed very easily. I can more easily express support and comfort in text. The sheer magnitude of human and animal suffering on this planet is not something that I can ever put out of my mind and I am painfully aware that I can do very little about any of it. I try to advocate, explain and draw peoples’ attention towards it in various places online because that’s the only way I can do so, but it feels like a hopeless task. There are too many people with entirely different perspectives than mine and I can’t make people feel what I’m feeling in order to grab their attention. Frequently I’m ignored, belittled or abused for asking people to look at how their own behaviour affects others. I’ve been raked over the coals all my life for not responding to people “properly” in things like small talk and day to day interactions. I am horrified and apologise profusely if I make a mistake that hurts someone and do what I can to make it right and then try not to do it again. When I try to tell others about their behaviour however, I am usually met with a torrent of anger and a doubling down of the behaviour. It’s beyond frustrating, because in my mind hundreds (thousands?) of little social rules don’t mean anything because they are culturally dependent and pretty arbitrary (seriously, don’t get frustrated at ME because you asked me “how are you?” and didn’t actually want the answer), but treating animals and people ethically is everything.

question: What is the empathy imbalance hypothesis of autism?
answer: The empathy imbalance hypothesis (EIH) of autism posits that there is an imbalance between two kinds of empathy:Cognitive Empathy (CE) is the ability to understand another person’s feelings or behavior based on their ‘imagined’ mental state. Similar to Theory of Mind, it involves interpreting the outward, observable behavior or expression displayed by others in the context of their unique experience(s) in order to access and understand the other’s internal, unseen, emotional state. The interpretation of language including abstractions like metaphors, sarcasm, hyperbole, etc. are in the cognitive realm. It is hypothesized that autistic individuals have significant deficits in CE which interfere with effective social skill and empathy.Emotional Empathy (EE) is the ability to respond emotionally to the emotional expressions and demonstrations of the other. It is hypothesized that an over-arousal of this EE system in autistics creates a disproportionate response to the emotions of the other. Emotions take on an exaggerated magnitude that is more appropriate to the situation of the other. This over-sensitivity is likened to ‘emotional contagion.’ It is conjectured that the EE imbalance may explain the autistic’s avoidance of eye contact contact and perception of facial expressions which can be too intense or stimulating.For more information: https://opensiuc.lib.siu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1031&context=tpr

question: Is it true that everyone on the autism spectrum lacks empathy, including those with high functioning autism/Asperger's syndrome and synesthesia? If not, what factors contribute to the differences in empathy among individuals with these traits?
answer: Misconceptions about autism and empathy are rampant. It's a common belief that Autistic people lack empathy (the ability to feel along with others) and/or sympathy (the ability to feel for others). This is a stereotype, and not true of every Autistic person. The misconception comes from the fact that empathy is experienced on both a cognitive level—recognizing and understanding another’s mental state, and on an affective or emotional level—feeling for someone. Autistic people appear to struggle more with cognitive empathy because we're less able to recognize and name emotions based on other’s facial expressions and body language. However, affective empathy—based on instincts and involuntary responses to the emotions of others—may overwhelm us if we feel other's emotions too intensely. You might be surprised how many psychologists are Autistic. These cognitive and emotional differences do not mean Autistic people are uncaring. In fact, I believe empathy is a universal human problem. Most humans in most cultures are suspicious, perhaps even afraid, of anyone who seems different from them. Autistic people are neurologically different, and society has a very long way to go towards understanding, accepting and showing empathy towards us. question: Is it possible for someone with autism to have high cognitive empathy but low affective (emotional) empathy?

If I saw someone upset, I would rush to hug them. I ran up to bickering couples to wrap my arms around the legs of whoever looked the most distressed, and it never crossed my mind that they might not WANT a chubby sticky child interrupting. Hugs made me feel better, end of conversation. Once I got older, I had/ have to approach empathy in quite a calculating way. For example, I have a friend who once drank too much as a teenager and sobbed over an adult man that didn’t want to be with her (and rightly so). It wasn’t something I could relate to, and my initial emotion was frustration at what was happening in front of me. I had to very quickly run through a formula in my mind. Affection+rejection+embarrassment+frustration+the vulnerability of telling someone+the vulnerability of being drunk. Then I had to filter out what *I* would want versus what *she* would want, which wasn’t a massive, silent hug that lasted for several minutes, but verbal reassurances and slow shoulder stroking. I can do this sort of empathy with my best friend, or someone shown on the news, or an animal, or a book character who does something I don’t understand. I was able to successfully intervene when a friend yelled at their pet, because I could do the same process in both directions and both made good points (one with yelling, which is unhelpful and one with peeing, which is also unhelpful but less so) (the cat was in the right imo) i think my ability to “put myself in someone else’s shoes” is reduced because I’m autistic, but I think my ability to recognise that fact is greater than the average neurotypical person. I’m used to having to work through the steps required towards feeling someone else’s pain. Im used to having to work hard to understand what I’m seeing and hearing.

question: Is autism spectrum disorder more a disability of empathy or social intelligence?

There is now research going on to see what these differences are, so hopefully we’ll have more answers in the near future.You can stop reading now if that answered your question. What I type from this point forward is my biased opinion about how non-autistic people treat autistic people in regards to empathy. Autism encompasses a very broad spectrum. I am sure there are people who are autistic who are not capable of empathy, but I have yet to meet an autist who is not. Granted, I have not met that many who have severe disabilities and need help with many aspects of life, so I have limited first hand experience from which I can glean an understanding. However, I know quite a few people IRL who are on the spectrum but considered higher functioning or an Aspie. I am the latter. I have many more online, but I admit that I am not the autistim expert. I am empathetic. I think I always have been. I know I had to learn to stop and think what another human beings must feel like in certain circumstances, but we all have to do that. I remember being little (pre-kindergarten) and not liking other people hurting my sister’s feelings, so some of it I’m sure is at least partly innate. I have no idea really, but the point is that there was some degree of concern for another human being’s emotional well-being within me and has been for the majority of my life. But there are times when something is going on with a person, and it is difficult to tell. Or you don’t understand how important something is to the other person. But even going back to the car accident, to me, expressing condolences should be enough. If I am not close to that person, then I’m not going to go out of my way to help the hurt person live their life. I’m not going to cook for them, etc. Well, actually I might if they specifically asked me and I was capable of getting to their house, etc. Other than saying “sorry” and doing something if asked, then I don’t know what else to do. I am not close to a lot of people, which as an adult I now prefer, and I have a hard time knowing when I overstep. Boundaries are definitely an issue for me. I now just stay away because I’m afraid of doing something that isn’t called for. You’d be surprised how many people don’t want help, etc. but I was taught to help others. It was difficult growing up and trying to do stuff for people who didn’t want me to do anything for them. It is difficult to explain all of this here. It is the absolute fact that neurotypicals and society in general systemically do not treat non-neurotypicals in an empathetic manner that causes a lot of us to shut down (as adults) when around other people. Most of us do need clues such as “this is about me right now” “I need you to understand that right now I feel _________” “would you focus on me at the moment” and be very specific about what is needed. “I need ___________ from you.” Open and specific communication is needed from and between everyone in this world because we can’t read each other’s minds, but some of us especially need this communication. For me, I am a very blunt and honest person. I have learned that this is not really what society in general appreciates, but it is tremendously hard for me to be another way. I try to be diplomatic in the best way I know how. Even about things that I to this day do not understand is wrong. Even on Quora people can get upset just when sharing information. I don’t know where I overstep. However, each of you who asks about a person on the spectrum and empathy, which seems to be a popular topic on Quora, you need to ask yourself how you have treated a person on the spectrum. When it comes to empathy, please remember that many of us do have it. What we need is for you to realize that we may not need the obvious disability accommodations such as wheelchair ramps. What we need is for you to tell us that you need X from us while communicating with you. Or ask what we need from you because it’s obvious that we are not communicating well. Sometimes this is all we need, but sometimes it is not enough. The following is my experience: Our attention span may not be long enough to remain focused on you. Or we may not have the emotional or mental energy to remain focused on you. It can be exceedingly draining for a person on the spectrum to invest a lot of emotional energy. Also, some of us have a difficult time processing information. Some of us have a difficult time understanding words that are used. Sometimes there may be certain lights or sounds or smells that are present which can cause us to be very uncomfortable. Sensory processing disorders are very real for the majority of people on the spectrum, and this seems to be all along the spectrum from those who are considered to be low functioning to those considered to be high functioning. There is so much going on with us neurologically (please note this is not a mental disorder - it is very much a medical issue) at any given time that makes it difficult for us to remain focused on another person. Maybe some on the spectrum truly have no empathy, but consider that maybe some of us do have it but weren’t treated all that well throughout life. We just either need specific directions or simply shut down when dealing with others based on experience. If that makes sense. I’ve only relayed what happens for me. There can be more going on in regards to other people on the spectrum. Yes. Many of us are empathetic, but there is a whole lot more going on. What we need is for the medical community and our communities in general to be a little more empathetic toward us.

question: How do you teach men with high functioning autism empathy and communication?

To give some examplesDo people who are deaf lack empathy for those whose sleep is disrupted by noise? Do they lack communication because they cannot hear?Do hearing people lack empathy for the deaf when they do not respond to them? Do they lack communication because they do not see their distress?If you try to understand someone with high functioning autism, to respond to their distress, encourage their delight, accommodate their difficulties, and enjoy the things about which they are passionate, it’s almost certain your attempts will succeed. If instead, you decide they are tedious, and don’t bother to understand and help them when their perceptions become overwhelmed. If you slap down any response they may give as unacceptable and weird. If you choose to assume what they convey must be nuanced in the way that you would nuance things, both with an insatiable need for attention, and a focus primarily on your own self interest. If you do all these things, then it becomes clear that it is not the autistic person who is most lacking in empathy. If neurotypical people assume autistic people are unfeeling, then why are autistic people typically the first to react during emotionally charged family circumstances? Frankly, the problem seems to be mostly with neurotypical people, with their insatiable and absorbing focus on social stimulation that leads them to fail to appreciate the strengths the autistic person may have in compassion towards others; even towards others that are significantly different to them. Just because the compassion of autistic people differs in perception and expression from the neurotypical “norm” does not demonstrate that it is non existent. Autistic people, and particularly those with high functioning autism, are regularly interacting with neurotypical people. On the whole, they mostly get things right because they encounter such people every day. Neurotypical people struggle because they have little opportunity to develop a theory of mind capable of encompassing autistic people. They have so few interactions with autistic people, so it is the exceptional neurotypical person capable of extending their empathy to those who are on the autism spectrum. This can include autism researchers, very few of whom would consider making friends with autistic people. But that doesn’t mean all neurotypical people are so impaired. Some are able to reach past their limitations and interact with people on the spectrum. Those neurotypical people that succeed in such a way should be considered high functioning neurotypicals. I don’t believe we ought consider such high functioning individuals to lack empathy. They are trying their best. TL;DR: Demonstrate empathy to them and look for empathy that takes a slightly different form. Empathy is contagious when practiced without strings attached.

question: What is the reason that some people think that people with autism lack empathy or theory-of-mind? Is this a universal trait among people with autism?
answer: Speaking as a neurotypical here— Because there are two aspects to empathy. One is recognizing & being aware of/sensitive to the pain & distress of other human beings. From all that I’ve read by actual people with autism, they usually have that capacity—often to an overwhelming degree. But what often falters for them is in expressing their empathy, which is the crucial other aspect to empathy. It’s not enough to simply feel & be aware of another person’s suffering, as human & humane as that is—empathy has to be concretely shown, offered, given—and at the time that it’s most needed & in the way that it’s most needed. For the person suffering, it doesn’t matter how much the other person feels, however strongly & even overwhelmingly, if that feeling is not acted upon at that moment. It’s like someone dying of thirst & another feeling genuine compassion & pain for that person—but not being able to open up their canteen & help the person dying of thirst to drink, while cradling & soothing that person at the same time. It’s an imperfect analogy, but it’s basically true. All the intense feeling in the world is meaningless to another suffering person if that feeling isn’t acted upon. From the suffering person’s viewpoint, there is no empathy at all. And protesting that yes, you do feel empathy, comes across as empty words devoid of feeling. Because ultimately, empathy is not about how you feel. It’s about how the other person feels & what you can do to help.

question: Do those on the autism spectrum have empathy? What are some examples?
answer: One of the most misunderstood aspects of autism is the (in)ability to feel and to show empathy towards fellow humans and animals. They will show their empathy in convenient as well as unconvenient ways. Empathy doesn’t mean that people with autism will react how you wish it. They are not automatons. They can have a very different logic which leads to diverse empathic reactions. When I was a student, by some stupid mistake, I ended up in a practicum of psychology (as a philosopher) in which I got more than 200 hours of training based on Carl Rogers’ theory of empathic listening. By the time I had to do examination, it became clear I had been the whole year in the wrong course, to that extend that I didn’t have to do examination because I had 20 times too much practical training. In the course we learned how to listen with empathy by using simple techniques and by understanding the rationale behind empathy. Btw, most of the students were neurotypical, and the course was designed to meet their future needs to be able to cope empathically with what their clients would tell them. Though I have autism, I didn’t do less well than the other students (it is a technique, explainable and clear), and soon I became an expert in listening, nodding at the right time, facilitating the conversation with the right questions, pacing and leading etc. About being authentic. Though those learned skills were handsome, I only used them during work, and nowadays only when I think I can help someone actively. In general, when talking with a friend or colleague, I prefer to be myself (myself which includes of course learned behaviour but not to the extend of Rogers’ therapy). I’m convinced that being myself, not using any technique is better: it adds to world’s diversity. I also don’t apply Rogers’ techniques because I think it’s not fair to let my friends befriend a technique instead of a person with her own world of ideas, lived experiences and emotions. I’m a philosopher. I was born a philosopher and I’ll remain this my entire thinking life. Maybe autism ‘helped’ me becoming a philosopher. I can’t exclude a broader perspective even in moments of distress, I feel with more than only the person before me; sometimes I feel deeper with what is far away than the person in front of me, if this seems reasonable. Profound thoughts and logic can be (to me) very consoling; it’s difficult not being permitted to share this deep consolation with others when all they seem to need is a hug, someone who agrees even when they make thinking mistakes that make them grieve even more. It is hard to watch someone suffering when with different thoughts they could feel much better/more connection with others, instead of being pampered into a downward spiral of self-pity and finally loneliness. It’s not the same as saying ‘keep yourself together’, not at all. I know that going through the darkest thoughts first can bring a fresh spirit afterwards; but only being allowed to respond like the other one wishes is very narrowing and in fact dehumanizing. The eye never sleeps… …is a good book about zen attitude, to read in small doses. On a given moment the book describes it is better to let people find their own way and responses, maybe they find a new way. Exactly this passage had made me giving it a try: I knew that 2 people whom I cared for were running in a ‘relationship fallacy’. They were already for a longer time in a power struggle. To -in my opinion- resolve the struggle, they decided to marry. They took a year to exclamate their happiness about the coming plan (they already lived together for 10 years). The first time I responded in line with their showed feelings, a bit hesitating, but in line. But this period dured a whole year, every conversation with different people turned back on the coming marriage, and after a few times I couldn’t respond with the appropriate reaction. I thought for a moment it would be better to warn them for the possible unhappiness this marriage could bring when marrying for the wrong reasons. I kept my mouth; just in time. The book ‘the eye never sleeps’ helped me to let them go their way, even when I had my biggest doubts about their future happiness. And after all, my opinion and warnings would have been like a fly telling the buffalos they were about to run in a pit. What has it to do with empathy? I learned that my honest feelings and thoughts often don’t matter. The world can keep spinning with the same velocity when I put away my personality and respond in line with what others like. The world isn’t waiting for me to respond as a unique creature, it just wants to go on with what it was busy doing. This leads me to alienation of myself: am I supposed to be a liar and a feigner if I want to stay connected with others? Will others still know who I am if I act my way through it. It is deceptive and that must backfire. Examples of diverse empathy. I’ll give a few examples of spontaneous reactions on quite critical moments. These reactions were not appreciated as empathic, though I still think they were, or my reaction came too late. They were absolutely not meant to hurt or being rude, actually the inverse. Please, read the examples and go back to the lists here above to recognize the theory in them. Ex.1 A friend’s sister in law got cancer. My friend said that she admired the way her brother and sister in law came through that period together as a couple. They were so much further as adults because of having gone through all these difficulties together. She added that it was so unjust that exactly these two people, smart, nice, good for others.. wouldn’t be able to get children because of the cancer treatment. She was silent for a moment and she shook her head saying again ‘so unjust…’. I replied (softly, and not in a rude way) that there was nothing unjust in that. I told her: imagine that the already happy, good, rich people (like her brother and sister in law, both doctors) couldn’t get cancer, wouldn’t that be very unjust for people who were sad and in poverty? The blind mechanism of nature is a very just system. It’s when people mingle in it, it often becomes unjust. I didn’t want to be smartass, I actually said this not only because I believed truely what I said, I thought it would help her to look at it from a different angle. She didn’t, and it was I think a breaking point for her. I wasn’t the friend who would nod and cry with her, I was a different friend. Ex. 2 When I was 24, the person with whom I had a relation died by suicide. I was very much shocked about this sudden fact, but I know that in moments of shock I can become very rational. I can’t start grieving until I have all pieces of the puzzle sorted (which is not that uncommon). I went to the mortuary to greet the body and there I met a couple of whom I knew they were acquainted with my deceased friend. The woman was crying unstoppable, she almost fell around my neck, I could barely avoid that. I didn’t cry a tear, I was wondered about this extreme display of sadness. She sobbed how sad this was. I shrugged my shoulders in some kind of dispair of not finding my words and not knowing if this was objectively so sad. I said to her “if you look at this on a worldly scale, this is nothing”. Saying this, I was at the same time expressing my wonder about if I was really to grieve, or if I should put this in broader perspective. Looking back, I think I struggled giving the whole event a place. It was an expression of my doubt, but a doubt I shared with her. I guess angrily she stepped away. Maybe she had wanted to show and share empathy towards me, searching words and not finding any better than ‘this is so sad’, I replied on this as would it have been a real conversation; it wasn’t. The conversation she started was non-verbal, but I didn’t understand it like that. If I had shown empathy for her, I should have replied with a non-verbal, equal reaction. I still think I had empathy with her, but I didn’t show it as she wished; I showed my empathy on a verbal level by accepting her words for true; also by accepting the fact she cried and I didn’t. If she really showed empathy for me, she would have further elaborated my reply. We would have had a meaningful conversation. So both of us were not able to communicate empathy; a wall of differences stood in between us. With time and lazyness, I understood I’ld better mirror what I see in such situations to avoid social problems. But is it empathy then because the other one understands it as a wanted reply? It looks to me more like egoïsm (avoiding trouble, being rewarded with being liked for the right response) and hypocrisy (not true to one’s authentic thoughts). Ex. 3 A project coordinator (whom I liked for an occasional, funny chat) told me he was working his last day; after that he would start in a new job in another company. I watched his face; loose thoughts went through my mind about the strange fact his eyes were wet. Meanwhile, the conversation went further. I knew he had had a problem with his eyes already, yeah, but it was quite cold that day, he had probably been walking through the wind, he didn’t have heavy lower eyelids neither so eye fluid could easily flow overboard, he wasn’t really old, no, but elderly had more often damp eyes, well that was soon… All this crossed my mind while I said him goodbye, knowing it was probably the last time (for a very long time or never) I would see him again. With all this in mind, it was difficult to respond at the same time, so I don’t know what I said, I remember my thoughts and searching for an answer why his eyes were wet. It all went too fast to work through. Later I felt ashamed of myself, over my weak response and the stream of thoughts I had had. It suddenly came to my mind he had with big probability been crying because he was saing goodbye. Situations like this happen frequently, and I can slam my head afterwards for how slow I am in identifying accurately emotions based on visual and non-verbal cues, and thus letting slip the opportunity to be a good friend, colleague, person… My (in)appropriate reaction or questions can follow a long time after an event or communication has passed, when everybody has gone back to the usual. Ex. 4 One day during a meeting with my boss, I asked some questions. I saw the head of my boss becoming more and more red. He leaned with every word further over the table towards me, spoke louder and in a more ‘staccato’ way. I was so fascinated about what I saw that I had a smile on my face. Suddenly, and for the first time in my life, it came to my mind that he *might* be angry, and because I smiled, became even more angry. I immediately stopped smiling to prevent it from getting worse. I absolutely wasn’t laughing with him or with what he said. For me, the conversation was still an open discussion. The moment I realised he didn’t perceive it like I did, I stopped my reaction. I think this indicates no bad intentions, only difficulty identifying emotions in other people, too much focus on detail, and not seeing the whole picture. Thát something happened, or, what exactly happened? I suppose, for most people, it is sufficient to know thát ‘one will leave his job’, ‘is getting cancer treatment’, ‘will have a baby’…, to display an appropriate reaction that is conform to the other person’s emotions ánd their own emotions. People in general will transfer what they learned in one situation to another. If the situation belongs grovely to the same kind of events, they’ll react socially the same way; they don’t mind if it’s a platitude. For someone with autism, extra verbal explanation is often needed with enough facts and details to facilitate an empathic reaction. Autistic people are often natural born worriers: they won’t react much until they know for 100% sure that they have all information ; and this delay often makes people judge them as a having no empathy. Meanwhile, they are trying to respond as an artist would, with a highly personal, individualized gesture. A woman told me her husband had died a few years ago. One of my first questions was ‘did you get along well’. I would never express my condolences to the remaining half of a couple that has been fighting for years, instead I would congratulate it had finally finished. Not having sufficient information can make autistic people very anxious. They start to explore all possibilities and lose themselves in trivialities, in order to respond properly, especially when they care about the other person. The quantity and detail of the questions can come across as rude and insensitive, and finding out what exactly happens makes them lose time; responding out of time with something empathic is perceived as non-empathic. Special interests and routines. People with autism can question you on certain elements because these elements belong to their special interests. They’ll do this regardless of your feelings if you don’t communicate how you feel about this. It’s possible they’ll turn to their special interest when things get difficult. Notice that perceived distress can make people with autism roll back on what they know and what is sure and certain. Sometimes, people say ‘people with autism can become ‘more autistic’ under stress’, know that this is the key to empathic feelings in people with autism. They perceive difficulties, grief and commotion, but they’ll get away from it to seek solace in something unchangeable. It won’t say they don’t feel sorry or happy for you. Compared to NT people. I’ll seldom/never gossip behind peoples back, I’ll go out of my way to help when help is needed, I’ll give my best advice and am very loyal, I’ll listen with an (too) open mind, I’m not competitive in a way that would hurt others, I’ld rather leave than have a fight... This is empathy on a daily base. I won’t start complaining about all times I thought NT people really lacked understanding and empathy. Often the cause of this lack of empathy was lack of knowledge and being too much absorbed in one’s small circle of people telling only what they expect to hear; only being able to feel empathy with a small group, their incrowd; being too lazy to step out of their comfort zone to discover new mental horizons. For all humans, empathy with things we don’t fully understand, is difficult. If you search someone to howl with the pack, don’t turn to the person with autism. This doesn’t mean that autistic people don’t have empathic feelings. Not being empathetic is quite rare in humans, it is often related to psychopathy or narcissistic disorder. To a bad observer, these things can look the same as autism, but they aren’t. Very-very rarely I have seen someone who is honestly able to attune his/her emotional reaction to his/her -narrow and/or broader- surroundings. Being empathic is absolutely on a spectrum too, with the majority of people driven by tribal feelings. Those few people who amaze with their empathic reaction are not incrowders. And I make a distinction between empathy and altruïsm, the latter probably non-existant. Consider that for humans, being empathic with things we don’t fully understand, is difficult. It doesn’t matter if one is autistic or not.

question: I'm on the autism spectrum and I'm wondering why do my close relatives think I lack empathy?
answer: What have you been taught or trained on regarding empathy so far? Being on the autism spectrum you really need a Occupational Therapist or similar health care professional to develop empathy as your close relatives are describing. Dont give this too much worry. People with strong empathy skills develop incredibly high and low emotional capacity with those whom they love the most. This is only part of love. Love is also wide and long. If you connect to those you want to care about over time this strengthens the connections enormously. You can be their for others and compassionately help several and have strong empathy in that group or community. I think what your relatives are looking at is reconciling with those you feel close to. A great deal of the population thinks we are born this way. We are not. reconciling and the feelings that come with it are learned. An example may be a newly married couple is getting started in life when suddenly, one wrecks a car. The spouse, already dealing with the difficuties of a new marriage gets very upset. In anger they say things about the other being a poor driver or not caring about the new marriage and so on.. After the anger, the spouse settles down and their thoughts change from how angry they are to how important the new spouse is to their life. Over time the thoughts of being a bad driver go away and they start to think about how wonderful and lucky they are to have this new spouse in their life. Eventually they come to realize the relationship is far more important that the car. At some point the spouse who was offended may realize they could have lost their spouse in that accident forever. They go back to the spouse and apologize for being so hurtful, so angry and tell them how important this person is to them. The other reacts in a similar way saying they could be more cautious, that the issues leading up to the accident are not near as important as the new marriage. This is empathy that is reconciling. It is compassionate. For those reading this some of you grasp what I am saying and some have no idea. My point is, that your close relatives know this experience. Autism, which makes you very honest, also makes it very difficult for you to learn how this works. In the few words of your sentence I do believe you are loved unconditionally. You have skills, knowledge and capabilities others can only imagine.

question: Do people with autism lack empathy? If so, why do they often appear to be kind and considerate?
answer: I can only speak from personal experience while all of these (often stupid) questionsseem to want general, universal answers. I'm not sure that general answers are possible, because we are individuals. In my case if I am focused on something, I am not aware of interpersonal stuff so I may appear non empathetic. If what I'm focused on is an individual (and their problems) I can appear quite empathetic. I am focused on whatever I am focused on. People bring up that people with Aspergers don't look others in the eye. The fact us that neurotypicals apparently do a lot of non verbal communication and emotional synchronization through eye contact. I can't do that, so I get no information from looking people in the eyes. It doesn't bother me to do so and I can do so, but neurotypicals quickly get nervous if I do because I'm not giving the feedback they expect. As a result, I tend to frighten them (though I'm generally innocuous). If I can't read them, they also cannot read me. This scares them. This is also why I appear non empathetic as they cannot “read" empathy in my face. I do find that dark glasses help since they can't see my eyes easily. I think that the issue is not a lack of empathy, but rather an issue of focus and lack of expected non verbal communication.

question: Can you explain the experience of and brain changes (physical, chemical, activity) in terms of cognitive and emotional empathy in autism?
answer: Interesting question , there is a book I'm currently reading called the master and his emissary by Iain McGilchrist. He is a psychiatrist and the book discusses the structure and functionality of the brain in considerable detail while at the same time tying it with actual actions and perceptions on a high lvl. He compares autism and schizophrenia to observation of people with various brain damage and it appears that we have deficiencies mainly across the right hemisphere(RH). Empathy is apparently mainly in the frontal lopes. What is missing in autism is the ability of the RH do fluently read body language which impedes empathy because we are not always able to pick up on others feelings/moods but our ability to sympathy and feel others pain is intact when we are aware of it. There are also some RH functionality that enables theory of mind and impairment there results in difficulties to understand another perspective. Essentially Iain says that the LH handles detailed reasoning while the RH handles the greater perspective. So the LH sees the trees and knows the blueprint for a tree, it knows the functions and attributes of a tree and see a tree as no different than another item. So in the same way the LH sees a car and its functionality like it does for a tree. The RH on the other hand sees the forest and within the forest it sees many individual living trees and other living creatures and plants. It also sees the car as a non living thing and in a greater context to civilisation and science and pollution etc . The RH sees the unique individual and so does recognition of people while the LH sees items more as an abstract entity and so is not concerned withe telling individuals apart. Prosopagnosia, difficulties in recognising faces, that I have, is therefore a RH deficiency. It should be underlined that these are generic comments and in reality the hemispheres both work together. It is not binary in that LH just does X and RH just does Y. Therefore in the case of brain damage other parts are sometimes able to take over the functionality that was lost.

question: What is the double empathy problem in relation to autism spectrum disorder (ASD)?
answer: Autistic individuals struggle to see things from a neurotypical perspective and neurotypicals struggle to understand things from an autistic perspective. The is an empathy gap. Recent studies have shown that neurotypicals struggled to read the emotions of autistic participants, and/or form negative first impressions of autistic people. This is something autistic people have experience first hand and have found such a difficult experience as neurotypicals are the ones with power: they are the parents, family, the professionals, their peers, society - who decide what normal is (who also have the power to cause harm or to punish) - and these people naturally misunderstand autistics or form a negative impression of us. It is like a cultural difference 100 years ago - the way you grew up and viewed the entire world has been completely different to the other. Both groups really dont understand the other persons way of life or way of being - there is a real gap in natural empathy (though autistic people have not been agents of intentional harm towards neurotypicals - and have generally only sought to appease people they dont understand). I hope I do not cause offense to draw a parallel and say - Autistic people are like indigenous cultures: colonised. They have to suppress their natural self, and natural behaviour, which is completely integral to their wellbeing, and continuously apply effort to imitate the neurotypical way of being in the world and not give away any cue to being autistic or they risk social negativity. Unfortunately, its meant many autistics forced into submission and neurotypical conformity with ABA, social ostracism, rejection, bullying, abuse, and extremely harmful medical practices (electric collars, drinking bleach). They are a generally invisible, often silenced, second class citizen. You can see the rift clearly in the quite hostile relationship between organisations like Autism Speaks (which is run dominantly by parents of autistics) and the autistic community Neurotypicals set the diagnostic criteria - naturally deciding that autism is a pathology, and everything about the way an autistic person is has been labelled as an undesireable defect. The standard psychological theory has long said that autistic people dont have Theory of Mind - or ‘cognitive empathy’, because autistic people dont relate to, and cannot naturally or intuitively engage with normative social interaction, and cannot predict the intentions or mind of another person (which is a neurotypical skill akin to mind reading). Its lead to the widespead fallacy that autistic individuals have no empathy. Its now coming to light that the gap in empathy and natural understanding goes both ways. Neurotypicals need to listen to autistic experience (especially parents) in order to understand what is going on, or what the intention of the person is - rather than approaching the autistic individual from their view of the world, which has a negative bias towards autistics, and trying to correct it.

question: When someone cries in pain, I don’t feel empathy, but instead, I want them to shut up. Is this just because of my autism, or is this something worse?
answer: Raising an autistic child, I would contribute a good deal of what you are confused with and dealing with to that. The first thing to ask yourself is “have I ever cried out in pain?” and remember what caused it as well as why it resulted in crying out in pain. Now, I will agree with you to some extent. There are way more individuals in this world who are crying out in “pain” for no reason at all. Take this example:Where something is certainly bothering them, this person shows no self control and is ruled by their emotions. Don’t do that. A lot of what autistic children and adults deal with is analyzing by facts and evidence while leaving emotion in absence. It is a sensible way to deal with things, but in a world that is imperfect this method can end up leading people to believe you to be cold and unfeeling. When it comes to figuring out how to approach or even witness a situation where someone is crying out in pain, the best method is to analyze the severity of what is causing them to cry out in pain. For Example: if someone has just lost a limb and is crying out in pain it is probably because of the excruciating pain they are in from the trauma. If someone is crying out in pain because they just lost a loved one, we can analyze that the same way as someone losing a limb in its severity. One thing to always keep in mind is to remember a situation where you may have cried out in pain, take the severity of that pain, and associate it with someone else who is in pain (even for a different reason). There may not be much you can do about it, but you can always aim to understand that their pain is severe and that you can always ask if there is any way you can help.

question: Isn't the Intense World Theory of autism very different from Baron-Cohen's ideas of low empathy for autistics?
answer: Yup, those two ideas are pretty much complete opposites. The big difference: The Intense World people listened to autistic people. Simon Baron-Cohen merely observed autistic people. About half of autistics do have trouble understanding emotions, both in themselves and in others, but even these alexithymic autistics don’t lack the sort of empathy that makes you care what happens to others. Our moral frameworks are pretty well average. We bond with our caregivers just as securely as neurotypical kids. On the other hand, a large majority of autistic people experience sensory hypersensitivity. Most of the minority, who experience only hyposensitivity, still have unusual sensory processing. Presumably a few here and there have completely typical sensory processing, but honestly, I’ve never actually met one. The near-universal nature of unusual sensory processing does imply that it’s more fundamental to autism than the idea of empathy. How? No clue. It’s still a new theory. The trouble is that the idea of empathy is more fundamental to how neurotypicals perceive other people. The idea of a “systemizing” or “extreme male brain” is very social-focused, because neurotypicals are very social-focused and that was an idea that came from a thoroughly NT perspective. Our atypical social interaction is the first thing they notice about us, so they assume that atypical socializing must be fundamental to autism. But they’re biased by their own neurology.

question: My friend is 16 and he says he has autism so he can’t show empathy to anyone, but he shows empathy to all his friends but me. What should I do? Is he right?
answer: Short answer: He’s not entirely right. But he isn’t completely wrong either First off: people with autism do feel empathy. Many even feel a lot of empathy and may be considered ‘empaths’ (which basically means they feel more empathy than’s good for them). There is however an issue with showing empathy… And if he literally says he can’t show empathy than there might be a partial truth in that. People with autism often have issues with ‘reading’ what other people think or feel. So while the do empathise they may misinterpret what someone is feeling. On the other hand they’re also not really good at showing the body language (and also finding the right words) to show how they’re feeling. Since there can be a two-ways mismatch of how two people (one with autism and the other without) are feeling there is a chance that it seems the person with autism isn’t showing any empathy… It is however strange if he does show correct empathy towards others, however: is that really the case or is it just your interpretation and that interpretation possibly being wrong because again: he might not show his feelings as you might expect…. It’s quite complicated really… Basically you and him are thinking, feeling and possibly also speaking in a different ‘language’. That makes it hard for both parties to understand what’s going on in the head of the other. Or, he’s just lying and just doesn’t feel anything for you…. Now it is good to note that people with autism are usually not the best liars. But exception confirms the rule. All you can do is discuss your feelings with him. Be honest, be to the point. Consider his feelings and definitely do not be judgemental. It is perfectly fine to tell him you find this difficult (because it probably will be!). People with autism usually appreciate you being honest.

question: What are some of the differences in empathy and emotional reactions that people with autism have?
answer: Natalie: So I watched these commercials that User-10517941397103481147 put in an answer:Miranda Marcus’ answer to How would you explain emotional empathy to a psychopath?In her answer she speaks about how she started crying at certain points in the video. So while I am on the phone with you, I decide to watch those videos and I start crying—sobbing, really—and you think that I am playing a joke on you, however I am not. At some point you realize that I am genuinely crying, and you ask to watch the videos yourself, and you respond by laughing almost all the way through. The interesting thing is that it speaks a lot about our empathy reactions. Can you speak a bit about that? Martin: To be fair, I believe I only laughed at the second video. I might have chuckled at the first video, as I didn’t understand the strong emotional reactions about a video I considered to be rather dull. The second video, I admit, was quite hilarious to me, as the yelling father had some really funny expressions. Natalie: Now that is interesting. You missed empathy cues in both me and the video. And yet at the same time you immediately saw that the relationships was abusive, and you were able to communicate that clearly to me, such that I ‘woke up’, and saw what was happening. I mean, once you pointed it out it became clear to me that the video was showing an abusive parent that the child was reacting to, and honestly no wonder—who wants to be yelled at all the time? Think about what animals do when they are yelled at—cower or run; they basically try to escape by becoming submissive or by leaving. That is what the children in both videos were doing. It actually annoys me now thinking about it, because I think this is the classic abuse situation, where someone is treating you badly all the time, and somehow you become the bad person because as soon as they are nice you are not responding. I had that experience a lot with my mom growing up. For example, she was once relentlessly yelling at me for not spending enough time with her, and at the end of it, she threw a pair of boots I had been wanting on the bed and said in a disdainful way, “There—I got those boots for you.” I really felt guilty; I just felt like a horrible person. So it was a lot of those feelings that came up during the video. You know, this nonrealistic vision of how terrible I had been, and how she really loved me. You also said something about that, which was that someone loves you, it does not preclude that they may have abused you. I wonder if it is my ASD that makes that so difficult for me to understand. Martin: I’m not sure about how ‘immediate’ my understanding of the abuse displayed in the video was. At first I was focused on the funny expressions and hand gestures of the guy, and it wasn’t until a bit later that I focused on who he is supposed to be—an abusive father. It actually wasn’t until a quote near the end of the video that I understood the video properly. It said:There are no perfect fathers. [pause] But a father will always love perfectly.When I saw this, I felt something in this video really didn’t make sense. First of all, we saw a yelling father, which to me takes the notion of loving perfectly into question. I think the end of the video was supposed to be a great twist which causes emotional impact of some kind, but perhaps I was too keen on analyzing its content to be concerned with feeling what was going on in the video. To get back to the sentences above, though, I wonder what it is about this text that is supposed to induce strong emotions. To me, the punchline doesn’t make logical sense. I accept the premise, that there are no perfect fathers. But if we accept that to be true, then how does it follow that an imperfect father will always love perfectly? Is it the expression of affection that is perfect? Certainly not the dad’s behavior as a whole. But to be honest, the father didn’t even strike me as particularly abusive. I just saw a goofy individual having some tantrums. That’s why I laughed pretty much throughout the video. And then that drawing of the father and child… I’m puzzled as to how one person breaks down crying, while another breaks out in laughter. Those are two rather opposing reactions. Natalie: I am wondering if I was really empathizing with the character or if I was really thinking about issues I am currently experiencing. I was so consumed by the video images, thinking about my son—that was very much like my life as a child. They were my own feelings. I am not having empathy for the situation or those people, but for myself. Also, it is interesting that me being a visual thinker, I focused on the images and missed most of the words, while you being a verbal/abstract thinker, read the words. It is really interesting to see what your thoughts are, and how you make sense of those words—really I see that I lost a lot of what you picked up on because you were focused on the words while I was not. I think this is very autistic; there is all this emotional stuff going on, and you are thinking about the words not making sense and miss the emotional significance of the video. I on the other hand miss different information, as I am having what is called Intense World Syndrome—thus sobbing while my cognitive brain has shut down. I am basically hanging out with my amygdala, while you are in your cortex and frontal lobe. For example, I did not see that quote that you put above, nor did I know that he was practicing a speech with the birthday cake…I wonder if you may have missed some of the visual cues? Martin: I did. Having watched the video a second time, I realize the first time watching I was too focused on the things I considered to be antithetical to what I understood the meaning of the video to be (the video is entitled “This is the saddest commercial you will ever see”, after all), that I could only see the funny and the illogical. question: What is empathy? Can people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) be empathetic?
answer: Empathy is being capable of realising what someone else feels and realising it may not be the same as you feel, plus responding to these feelings showing love, care, understanding. It has an overlap with Theory of Mind: realising other people may have different feelings and thoughts than you do and being able to respond to those. Autism does not usually impact empathy or theory of mind, or just to a small degree. Most people with autism are therefore empathic. Actually most are very empathic to a degree where they could be considered ‘empaths’ (being more empathic than is good for a person). The common myth that people with autism supposedly lack empathy or Theory of mind is caused by what's called the double empathy problem. People with autism usually have some challenges correctly recognising social information, like facial expressions, body language and ‘reading between the lines’. So while they are empathic they may not always correctly identify what another person is feeling. Because of this same issue their response to certain emotions, feelings or behaviour may also be different than someone neurotypical would expect. At times it may therefore appear someone autistic doesn't understand people's feelings and is therefore incapable of feeling empathy. That's not the case, it's just the double empathy problem.

question: Is it true that people with Autism Spectrum disorder (ASD) lack empathy? How does ASD affect the way individuals express empathy?
answer: As with the rest of the qualities of humanity, empathy in people with autism exists somewhere on a spectrum. We (and people in general) seem to be more empathetic towards experiences we can relate to, and after all, that is the difference between sympathy and empathy. The more we can relate to an event or concern, the more we empathize. We can often empathize with situations, but empathizing to general emotions, I find more difficult if I don’t have the context. This leads directly into how we often express empathy. We often express our empathy not with consoling words or touch, but with sharing our experiences. I personally find small talk almost intolerable, and consoling words feel like small talk. This can come across as us trying to make the conversation all about ourselves or trying to one-up the distressed person, but that is how we show empathy; we demonstrate that we have been in a similar situation and thus understand the other’s distress. This can contribute to the perception that we lack empathy because the other does not feel like the focus is on their needs when we are expressing empathy the way that makes sense to us. Another part of it for me is that I tend to move away from emotional expression immediately into problem-solving mode. I want to fix it. I need to fix it. But often, the other person doesn’t want it fixed, they want a shoulder to cry on. I generally see that as time taken from solving the problem and getting the person to a better situation as quickly as possible. I am very efficient, and that efficiency can come across as brusque and unfeeling. It may appear to be short-tempered or victim blaming (why don't you do blank can be seen as accusatory), when in actuality, I just want to help make things better. I am trying actively to work on my verbal empathy skills, since most common empathetic responses grate on my nerves (i.e. “They’re in a better place.”). I make myself say, “I am so sorry you are going through this,” or “I’m sorry this happened to you,” and let the other person carry the conversation, but it is something I have had to learn and still struggle with at 50. Empathetic touch is almost out of the question: it feels forced and awkward as hell, and rejection sensitivity makes me fear that it is an unwelcome imposition if the person has not specifically asked for the touch or hug.

question: Have you also observed that a person with ASD (autism) actually has MORE empathy than typical people?

There's a certain group of folks online who have insisted autistic people are superior to other people in various ways. If someone has said people with autism lack empathy, then this group will insist autistic people have so much empathy they don't know what to do with it at all. I wish everything they said was true. Unfortunately it's not. And some people with autism have Intellectual Disability or Borderline Intellectual Functioning, both of which can also interfere with learning empathy as it makes it more difficult to learn, retain and apply information, experience and observations. Again, these discussions choose to ignore this group of artists and pretend they do not exist. Then there are the other constructs that ‘autism advocates’ have created about how people with autism are superior, that conforming to social norms is ‘masking’ and abhorrent, that small talk is repellant and autists have their ‘own way’ of doing things that is superior to what others do, that they are owed extensive work accommodations and should not have to do anything that they don’t want to do, and empathy is a fleeting thing indeed. An additional problem is that many autistic people have been bullied, teased or exploited. There is a tendency for a person who has experienced such things to be skeptical and wary in general, so that when someone reaches out they often go into ‘protection mode.’ That also interferes with empathy. There are many people with autism who have very intense emotions of their own, emotions such as anger, annoyance at being told what to do, inflexible thinking, and hostility towards a point of view different from theirs. These interfere greatly with empathy. Depression and anxiety also interfere with empathy as they focus a person more inwardly and sap their energy. These are not rare among people with autism. Unfortunately, empathy is not about being ‘sensitive to the emotions of others.’ It's not about noticing emotions or naming them, or having theories about what caused the emotion. Empathy is about ‘doing for other people.’ Further no one really agrees completely as to how much empathy one should ‘do.’ Most people draw a line in the sand very quickly and very early as to how much they are obligated to do for other people. We often hear both non-autistic people as well as autistic people, complain about ‘problem friends’ who have ‘too many problems’ and ‘only talk to me when they want sympathy’ and ‘never listen when I want to talk.’ Unfortunately, this kind of thinking interferes with empathy. Here, empathy is seen as a form of the other demanding exclusive attention that is not ‘50-50,’ and human interactions are never ‘50-50’ moment to moment or minute to minute. Unfortunately empathy is something one does, rather than something one simply has. This is the gravest error all people make in thinking and talking about empathy. Empathy is largely about recognizing what other people want and doing very specific things in response to what they want. Empathy requires oneself to put aside one's own needs for a time, and find out what someone else needs and act upon it. The toughest things about empathy and autism are that empathy often requires one to break a familiar routine, to socialize according to some difficult to divine patterns and to glean very scant hints from language, all challenges for people with autism, to varying degrees. Empathy is work. It's work for anyone. And I must emphasize, it's not a trait or an attribute. It's an activity.

question: Do people with ADHD, autism, OCD, or similar conditions usually have a lower, or higher empathy, and care for others compared to neurotypical?
answer: I will address autism because the neurological factors involved in other conditions don’t directly influence empathy in the same way. While these conditions are often comorbid—meaning they frequently occur alongside one another—they don't always co-occur. Each condition has its own distinct neurological profile, but autism specifically presents unique differences that can influence social interaction and emotional understanding. Autism can be considered a type of neurological difference, though it is often referred to as a "neurodevelopmental condition" rather than an aberration. Autism, or Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), involves differences in brain development that affect how individuals perceive, communicate, and interact with the world. These differences aren't necessarily considered "abnormal" in a negative sense but rather reflect a variation in how the brain processes information. Regarding research into autism, scientists have concluded that it is associated with an increased number of synaptic connections or branching in the brain. This over-connectivity is thought to contribute to the unique ways that autistic individuals process information and engage with their environment.In the image above, we see the process that occurs between ages 2 and 4. During this time, the brain begins to prune neural connections, meaning that the pathways that are used less frequently are gradually eliminated. As a result, the connections that are used more often become stronger and thicker, shaping the child's dominant social behaviors. This pruning allows the brain to refine its networks, enhancing the abilities that the child regularly engages in while letting go of those that are less necessary.As you can see, the synapses on the right—representing the brains of individuals with autism—retain their extra synapses later in life. In contrast, the neurotypical neuron on the left has undergone more significant pruning. This difference in synaptic density is due to variations in the pruning process. In individuals with autism, the pruning might be less extensive or occur differently, resulting in a greater number of connections. The biochemical involved in regulating this pruning process is mTOR, also known as mammalian target of rapamycin. mTOR plays a critical role in cell growth, proliferation, and synaptic plasticity, influencing how neural connections are maintained or eliminated. In the context of autism, mTOR signaling is often found to be dysregulated. Research suggests that in ASD brains, mTOR may be overactive, leading to excessive synaptic growth and reduced pruning. This overactivity can contribute to the retention of extra synapses, which might disrupt typical neural network organization and affect sensory processing and social interaction. In contrast, in neurotypical brains, mTOR activity is more balanced, facilitating appropriate pruning and maintaining a more streamlined synaptic network. This imbalance in mTOR signaling helps explain some of the unique cognitive and sensory processing traits observed in autism. The heightened synaptic connectivity in autism can lead to enhanced sensitivity to sensory stimuli and a more profound emotional response to certain situations. This may contribute to an increased capacity for empathy in some individuals with autism, as their heightened awareness of sensory inputs and emotional cues allows them to experience and understand others' feelings in a more nuanced way. However, this increased empathy can also come with challenges, such as being overwhelmed by intense sensory experiences or emotional overload. On the other hand, conditions like sociopathy or antisocial personality disorder often involve a reduction in mTOR activity or impaired regulation of synaptic pruning. This can result in reduced synaptic density in certain brain regions, which may affect the individual's ability to process emotional and social information. As a result, individuals with sociopathic traits might exhibit lower levels of empathy and a diminished capacity for emotional connection, leading to behaviors that are less responsive to social and emotional cues. This neural overconnectivity in autism and reduced connectivity in sociopathy highlight the complex interplay between brain development and emotional processing. Understanding these differences provides insight into the diverse ways individuals navigate and interpret their world, showcasing the rich complexity of human neurological development.

question: Since narcissists lack empathy to pick up social cues, how often does narcissism get misdiagnosed as autism or aspergers?

Neither one of the two types of empathy has anything to do with ones ability to pick up social cues. With autism spectrum disorder [including Asperger’s syndrome], autistic people have high levels of emotional empathy, but low levels of cognitive empathy. Now, for the social skills - it is true that autistic people are somewhat lacking in social skills and have difficulty picking them up. That is because autistic peoples brains are wired completely differently to non-autistic people’s brains. Autism is a neurological difference. question: What is the difference between cognitive empathy and affective empathy? Why do people with autism lack affective empathy but still have cognitive empathy?
answer: This is a common scientific misunderstanding, culturally rooted in ableism. Autistic people actually don’t lack either form of empathy. In fact, some autistic people have way more empathy than neurotypical people do. Some autistic people have a phenomenon called hyperempathy. Cognitive empathy is empathy based on understanding through knowledge/communication the other person’s predicament, and emotionally relating to it based on your understanding of it, and shared experiences. Affective empathy is sharing neurological similarities in the makeup with the other person, so that you pick up on their emotional reactions and feel what they’re feeling. Note how I phrased the latter. This is where the scientific misunderstanding happens. Neurotypical researchers in autism have pathologised the difficulties that autistic people have in affectively empathising with neurotypical people. What they didn’t take into account is that neurotypical people have just as much difficulty affectively empathising with autistic people. There is a disconnect exactly because we are a different neurotype.Autistic people have no problem affectively empathising with other autistic people (this has been recently proven in science, see “the double empathy problem”), just the same as neurotypical people have no problem affectively empathising with other neurotypical people. But put one autistic and one neurotypical person together in a room, and the only form of empathy that will be shared in plenty between them is cognitive empathy. They’ll need to understand each other’s different worlds before they can relate, before they can empathise — because, although they are both very much human, they are very-very different human beings, their neurology/bodies and experiences are very-very different in their workings. They are both human, but they are different human beings, and very different people. The way that autistic people affectively empathise, the nature, depth, and scope of that empathy, is also very different to neurotypical affective empathy, because our bodies work differently, and therefore our way of feeling/processing the world, our approach, our experiences, and our intuitive and rational perception and understanding of the world are also very different. Autistic people tend to have a form of empathy that is far wider than their own social circle, and encompasses all living creatures in their environment, regardless of differences. Expecting an autistic person to be able to affectively empathise with a neurotypical person (and vice versa!) is like expecting a cat to relate to the experiences of a dog. It goes only part-ways — it will never be on the level that a dog relates to a dog, or a cat relates to a cat. We can each learn to better empathise with the other by learning about each other, but an autistic person will never be neurotypical, and a neurotypical person will never be autistic. We are each born into a particular neurotype, a particular body — and this neurodivesity is key to the health and survival of the human species in nature. So it’s not autistic people that lack empathy, it’s neurotypical autism researchers that lack common sense and a wider awareness.

question: Can individuals with autism develop empathy? What factors may influence this development?
answer: Empathy is the ability to mirror another person’s emotions - to feel what they are feeling, so you understand it from the inside. Individuals with autism typically have a high level of empathy, in some cases even excessive empathy. But, since they are not necessarily psychic, their empathy relies on the same cues that most people’s empathy relies on. Tone of voice, body language, facial expressions… you know, all of the things that persons with autism are absolutely terrible at interpreting. But if you tell an autistic person that you’re extremely sad, and why, they’ll feel for you as much or more as anyone else, possibly to an uncomfortable degree. We’re just not as likely to know how you are feeling if you don’t tell us, because we are poor at interpreting your facial expressions, tone of voice, and body language. This is the reason why persons with autism were initially believed to lack empathy - if you don’t know a person is sad, you can’t feel sad along with them. So, people would be emoting, and we wouldn’t react, because we didn’t know what they were emoting, you see. But, no - nothing wrong with our empathy at all.

question: Can you explain the difference between cognitive and affective empathy? How might someone with autism experience these types of empathy differently from someone without autism?
answer: Cognitive Empathy is when you understand how someone is feeling a certain way and what they might be thinking in a certain situation. Affective Empathy (emotional empathy) is when you are actually able to feel what someone else is feeling. Although ASD people have a capacity for both, it’s often the case that people will not be obvious enough about how they’re feeling — with their social cues — for us to pick up on it, so we can be scored low in cognitive empathy. One reason why previous research on ASD people reported that we have inherently low cognitive empathy is because it’s more difficult for us to detect such social cues that NTs find obvious enough for them that they didn’t control for it. So, the research was flawed because it was erroneously based on testing the capacity for picking up on social cues rather than quantifying the empathy itself, and this translated as being unable to have cognitive empathy. Which has been proven false, and which ASD people have always understood as false. For the most part, once we understand what the other person is feeling, we’re able to have cognitive empathy just fine. For affective empathy, it’s often the case that we have a greater capacity for feeling and sharing the emotions of others. Just like just about everything else in this world, this will inevitable require more energy expenditure and need for recharging. Which can appear to an outsider as having less capacity for this kind of empathy. We speak the same emotional languages, but we have different accents and require different precision with grammar.

question: My friend is 16 and he says he has autism so he can’t show empathy to anyone, but he shows empathy to all his friends but me. What should I do? Is he right?
answer: May just be my theory but for some autistic people, empathy is something you learn from people telling you what empathy means and looks like. So there is a chance they show empathy but doesn't know that their action shows empathy. Maybe they are confused or unsure because afterall, empathy is many things and is very abstract. Like when I learn how to parent my son, I had to learn this technique called sportcasting: repeat exactly what happens and put a word describe it. Like “Wow you feel sad because your friend feels sad, that's very empathetic of you.” Repeat and repeat until they associate certain actions with an abstract words. This action is empathy, that action is also empathy, empathy means you do this when this happens. That gives him a concrete image of what empathy means. So in your friends' case, he may have been with his friends for long enough to establish a concrete image of what behaviours those friends are expected of him and understand those friends' needs enough to choose the appropriate course of actions or reactions when something happens to his friends. This is especially true if those friends are patient with him enough over the years to teach him what they expected of him. The fact that he doesn't show the same reaction to you may mean that he has not been able to get to know you yet and don't know what you expect from him. In the book “How to teach life skills to high-functioning autistic children" by Jennifer Mcilwee Myers, shw stated that even if an autistic child know what to do, they may not be able to apply what they know in different situations. They learn what to do in certain situations and environment and can't make the connection that it can also apply to every other similar situation. So the same empathy that your friend shows his friends may not be applied to you because you have never told him that you want the same treatment and give him solid example of what that even means. With autistic people, you have to be very clear of what you want, even break it down to small steps. For example, if you fall down in front of your friend, tell him “Hey man, help me standing up please.” “Can you fetch a bandage from the infirmary for me? Also ask them for some disinfectant.”

question: What is a situation where you thought your autism heightened your empathy beyond that of a neurotypical’s?
answer: There are many places. In fact one of the theories regarding autism is that we have too much empathy.
