I have hyper empathy syndrome (a term described in scientific literature). It means that I have a tremendous ability to feel other people’s emotions, even in books and TV. So you can imagine that this is an excellent tool to have for a therapist. People often think I am psychic because I can read them so well. Book shopping is always quite funny for me; I will ask the salesperson for a book that is not too sad, not too real, nothing where people die, nothing with diseases, nothing depressing… For me, this mirror-emotion empathy happens automatically and makes me very good at assessing my patients’ emotions, but it makes it unbearable to be friends with most people. I cannot tolerate someone feeling hurt or disappointed. If someone asks me to take a walk with them and I want to say no, it causes excruciating stress and anxiety, and a repetition over and over in my mind. Baron-Cohen does such good job describing my level of empathy, that you can switch Hannah for me.Hannah is a psychotherapist who has a natural gift for tuning into how others are feeling. As soon as you walk into her living room, she is already reading your face, your gait, your posture. The first thing she asks you is ‘How are you?’ but this is no perfunctory platitude. Her intonation—even before you have taken off your coat—suggests an invitation to confide, to disclose, to share. Even if you just answer with a short phrase, your tone of voice reveals to her your inner emotional state, and she quickly follows up your answer with ‘You sound a bit sad. What’s happened to upset you?’ Before you know it, you are opening up to this wonderful listener, who interjects only to offer sounds of comfort and concern, to mirror how you feel, occasionally offering soothing words to boost you and make you feel valued. Hannah is not doing this because it is her job to do so. She is like this with her clients, her friends, and even people she has only just met. Hannah’s friends feel cared for by her, and her friendships are built around sharing confidences and offering mutual support. She has an unstoppable drive to empathize.[1]I suspect this is why the people I am closest to are less emotional. One friend is a diagnosed psychopath, but they are easy to deal with as I cannot hurt their feelings, and they don’t experience intense feelings. Then there is Martin who is deeply empathetic to me, but not about things in general, so I am able to talk to him about everything.When I hear or see something that I perceive to be upsetting, then I have an immediate reaction of empathy, which recirculates over and over—which is why I don’t tend to watch or listen to the news. Let me demonstrate what hearing the news or seeing a disturbing image is like for me: A number of months ago I was on Quora and came across an answer with this image of Omayra Sánchez, a 13 year old girl killed in Aremeno by being trapped by the rubble caused by a volcano.Image Attribution: Omayra Sánchez Internal experience: Her eyes, her eyes--why are they black? My heart aches physically. Omayra’s legs were being held down by a brick door and clutched in the arms of her dead aunt. She was pinned down by a brink wall, and had a steel bar in her hip. I am horrified at hearing this. I imagine what it is like to have a dead person you love holding you in the water. I imagine the pain of a bar going through her leg. Omayra took 60 hours to die. I imagine being her, in the freezing water (I remember all the times water was so cold that it hurt), I imagine feeling her dead aunt’s hands on my ankles. I remember the time I was paralyzed for a day, I could not move. Rescuers tried to save her. I imagine being her again, trapped in the water, hoping that this time it will work; I will get out. Omayra was lucid for almost all of the 60 hours she took to die. My heart aches. She dies of exposure of gangrene, I imagine the pain. I see all the rescuers, imagine trying to save her, and not being able to, my despair, my disappointment. I see her joking and being in good spirits, and beginning to come to terms with the fact that she will die. I try to imagine what it is like to be that brave and dignified. I hear her bid goodbye to her mother. Many months later, I feel physical heart pain equal to what I felt when I first saw her. The horror. I imagine the nights, wonder how she slept. Did she sleep? And while she was in the water, she wondered if she was going to get in trouble for missing school—such an innocent concern. She shows such concern for the workers too. Telling them to go home and rest, and then come back. It is simply unbearable. This tragedy shook the world for a short time. For me it continues to shake my life.It is the same if I hear on the news someone has been shot. I imagine their fear, their pain. I imagine the pain of their family, the lives that are irrevocably altered. I imagine being the mother of this person, and I cannot bare it. Genes My genes in part make me more empathetic. I have rs53576 double GG SNP in my oxytocin receptor (OXTR) gene. Studies have demonstrated that individuals with the G allele are more empathetic, feel less lonely, employ more sensitive parenting techniques, and have lower rates of classical autism, but the G allele is associated with Asperger’s. Basically, I am built to be highly empathetic. Martin, on the other hand has A;G allele for the gene, making him more empathic to those he is bonded with like our dog Pluto and me, but less to other people.They found that G;G individuals performed significantly better on the behavioral measure of empathy and were 22.7% less likely to make a mistake on the "Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test" (RMET) (a behavioural measure of empathic accuracy) than A;A/A;G individuals (P = 0.005).To learn more about genetic effects of SNPs you can read a previous answer.Natalie Engelbrecht’s answer to What causes Autism Spectrum Disorders?Footnotes[1] Against Empathy

question: Do people with autism have empathy for inanimate objects?

question: What are some thoughts on autism and school?

I'm Dan, and today we're diving into a crucial discussion around education for individuals with autism. This journey through the revolution in autism education has been an evolving narrative—one that holds significant importance in the lives of countless individuals with autism, ADHD, and similar neurodivergent traits. Let's rewind a bit. When I was in school, there wasn't much in terms of support for autism. The educational landscape didn't accommodate neurodiverse learners, leaving us with large gaps in the curriculum. I recall being part of a reform initiative in the UK, pushing for better educational support, yet challenges persisted even in 2023. Back in the '80s and '90s, the lack of understanding and resources meant many of us, autistic individuals, were left isolated in the education system. We were often categorized as "special" or put in units where we weren't catered to effectively, resulting in missed learning opportunities. Early intervention emerged as a crucial factor in the developmental journey of autistic individuals. The call for early diagnosis to facilitate timely intervention is loud and clear. It's this intervention that paves the way for success in the lives of neurodivergent individuals. But times are changing. Over the last 15 years, there's been a noticeable shift—an educational revolution in autism. Funding allocations for autism education have surged across the UK, Wales, the US, and globally. With autism prevalence at 1 in 100 in the UK and 1 in 53 in the US, there's a growing need for inclusive education. The educational landscape is adapting. Schools are taking autism education seriously, investing in training staff, and equipping them with the tools to accommodate neurodivergent students. In the past, children with additional needs often had to attend specialized schools due to the lack of support in mainstream education. However, this is changing as mainstream schools undergo transformation to become more inclusive.It's been a long journey, but progress is visible. Advocates and legal actions have driven change, emphasizing the importance of specialized training within schools. Now, more than ever, autism is being understood in educational settings, and there's an increasing effort to support neurodivergent students effectively. There's still much to be done. Individuals can make a difference by engaging with their local educational boards, suggesting improvements, and highlighting the need for increased support for autistic students. question: Can autism schools be for high functioning autism and Asperger syndrome, too?
answer: I don’t know about private schools, but I can give some insight into public schools since I work as a substitute teacher’s aide for a suburban school district in the Dallas, Texas area. All of the K-12 grades have special education classes specifically for those with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). I’ve subbed in several elementary ASD classes since I started subbing four years ago. The students who are placed in these classes usually are non-verbal. They have learning difficulties that are such that they are not able to attend general education classes. There are also those who have behavior issues to the extent they must be in a special education class instead of general ed. A child with Asperger’s or hi-functioning Autism may not have learning disabilities, but they are in an autism special ed class because of behavior issues instead. Their behavior is severe enough that they are not ready for general ed. They are at the same level or even above their peers as far as intelligence, but severely lack social skills. I’ve seen some cases where such students do make the transition to general ed. A new program in the district is called “Bridge” which is aimed at 2nd grade down to kindergarten students who have severe behavior issues. The goal is to transition these children into general ed classes. It is heartbreaking to see how severe these cases are, but at least, they are getting behavior therapy and hopefully will be able to cross the bridge into general ed.

question: How do I help ease my son into middle school? He’s got high functioning autism and has difficulty making friends.
answer: First realize that middle school is tough for EVERYONE. It is even more turbulent for kids in the spectrum. Almost every family I’ve spoken with has some pretty “interesting” stories about their child during this time. It seems to peak around 15, so just understand that you are at the beginning of this tumultuous period. Expose him to a wide variety of opportunities inside and outside of school. That will give him a better chance that he will find a friend or two he can rely on during this wild time of growth and development. Next take a deep breath: inhale (2, 3, 4) and exhale (2, 3, 4). You will need to practice doing this frequently while your son is in middle school. As you have mentioned very little about what your son’s particular issues are, I can only make very general suggestions. There are 5 things that will be most helpful.The best thing that you can do is to focus on his particular interest or skill and find a club either at school or outside of school where he can be around other people who share that interest—as long as it doesn’t harm himself or others. What ended up working best for my son was the church youth group. And those kids are still his friends, even as they’ve graduated and scattered throughout the country on their various college/work paths.Find him a social skills group outside of school. You didn’t mention whether he has a 504 or IEP, so I’m not sure if he has access to supports while at school. the Social Thinking people have done a LOT of work in this area. Try to locate a speech pathologist or psychologist who has trained with them and is running a social skills group for middle schoolers. I would suggest that you even attend one of their conferences if you can.Teach him some kind of stress/anxiety management system. That could be meditation or biofeedback or heartmath or general mindfulness or yoga. . . ..He will need something. So will you. It would be better for you to find someone else who could teach it to him.Find a teacher to take him under his wing at school. This could be an arts teacher (band, orchestra, etc), a coach, a computer science teacher, a librarian etc. It could be the teacher who supervises the club that he joins. This is the time in his life when he needs to expand his circle of mentors beyond his parents. You MUST find someone else he can speak with about his worries because he won’t be talking much to you about most things.Set your bar a little lower during the next few years. Typically kids’ social development rockets ahead of kids in the spectrum, and just trying to keep up exhausts them. Sometimes getting through the day in junior high is a win.Good luck and God bless.

question: How do professionals detect and diagnose autism spectrum disorders with adults compared to how they diagnose it for preschoolers and school children? What are the assessments and inventories used? Who normally interprets the scores?
answer: I am not certain how all adults are assessed. The psychiatrist who diagnosed me was very experienced at diagnosing autism. He was actually treating my son at the time. And I would talk to him extensively about my concerns, recounting the similarities between myself and Harry back when I was a little girl. I did not call it 'autism'. I was terrified that Harry would be treated as badly as I had been by adults and started to describe aspects of my own sensations and behaviors that had always been challenging to my existence. I guess I provided so much detail that his assessment was very straightforward. The diagnosis was PDD-NOS, which would (these days) likely not be specified. I would simply be considered to be 'on the spectrum’. Interestingly, I ultimately left that psychiatrist because of his obvious disdain for some of my son's characteristics (ones I actually appreciated!) and how he insisted that I hospitalize him. I did not agree, as I knew I would ultimately be able to help Harry learn to self-soothe on my own (using a combination of medication plus behavioral techniques). Autistic people vary greatly in their capabilities. But I had the advantage of being highly intuitive and also exceedingly stubborn when it came to resolving our family challenges (like learning to manage aggressive impulses). I believe that the entire family must take responsibility for such problems and begin to heal before lasting change is possible for any one member. I don't see the autistic child as “the problem”. The whole family system must be altered for the better, in my opinion. I knew I was equally in need of changing the way I managed my emotions. And that is why I knew that our family would succeed. Harry and I have both come a very long way over the course of nearly fifteen years. I feel proud of us.

question: Is it common for someone to have mild autism and they have always been independent at school?
answer: Sure, but in today’s society, it’s not necessarily a good thing. Many high-functioning people with autism begin to choose, and pursue their chosen profession, from a very young age, without being prompted. But many also don’t know to ask for help with anything. I have autism, and I made it all the way through college without help from parents, tutors, friends, etc. By about 3rd grade, I was reading encyclopedias and building mechanical things in my spare time, eventually switching from mechanics to electronics after reading about transistors and such in encyclopedias. Regular school was really helpful in a couple of different things:It broke my spirit sufficiently to get me to hold still and stay silent.It kept me busy and stressed enough that I had to spend my spare time recovering in shutdown mode instead of pursuing extracurricular intellectual activities.College had even more benefits of its own:Accumulate student debt.Use up several years of my life.Taught me that in truth, I am actually privileged, and that I am unconsciously an oppressor of people that I’ve never even encountered.During the final month or two of college, I found out about something called an internship, and that groups of my classmates were currently in internships that either their friends had gotten them into, or where entire groups of them had gotten internships at the same company together.

question: How do schools accommodate students with special needs like autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)?
answer: My ADHD earned me “special attention”from my grade school teachers ie a seat at the front of the class,close by the teacher’s desk, and the closeness of the teacher as they taught the class,by them standing close to my seat during the class. It worked and my hyperactivity did settle with this proximity. I learned to contain myself that year ( grade 8) and in the subsequent years I was able to quiet myself and could be left a lot farther towards the back of the classroom. This was repeated the next year and by the time I entered high school ( grade ten) I was better able to be quiet and could be left in the seats farther back in the room. I still required stimulant meds to quiet my ADHD and took them for the rest of high school,and on entry into University,did no longer require such monitoring. I read articles about missionary doctors working in Africa and on cruise ships ..and this stoked my interest further..and I did get a two year residency for rural practice,aiming at exotic locations in the third world..but alas , I was recruited by a friend,an older GP, to join their large clinic in central Vancouver. I accepted this, since I could not find any overseas posts that year. The rest is history, for me. My wife and I moved to Vancouver and initially she worked in a hospital as a young head nurse and I joined the clinic where the re were a dozen GPs as well as half a dozen specialists. The next decade plus was a joyful time for me and my family. My wife worked as a young head nurse in one of the hospitals ,and soon we went on to have two daughters….who did grow up in Vancouver..plus skiied ( snowboarded in the local mountains ,then in Whistler for the ensuing decade plus.I finally returned to a residency in Psychiatry ,sub specialising in Adolescents. which got me recruited by an Institution for Court Ordered Adolescents ..the next two decades of my career.Through out those years, my ADHD was a contributing factor in my work in a Locked Program for court ordered adolescents…with a buddy who was the head psychiatrist…where I stayed till we both retired twenty years later! A varied and absorbing career..with fortuitous opportunities and work that fit my own ADHD!

question: Is there any psychological terms for the “weird kids” at school that clearly don’t have autism and seem to be normal until you talk to them?
answer: The question is too vague. I can’t understand what you’re talking about. What do you mean by ‘weird?’ What do you consider ‘normal?’ ‘Abnormal?’ The other problem is that the question over-simplifies a very broad area of knowledge. I think you might be asking about kids who you cannot point out as ‘weird’ based on their posture, way of walking or movement. But when you talk to them, ‘something is wrong.’ I just can’t figure out what you think ‘wrong’ ‘abnormal’ or ‘weird’ is. There are other disorders than autism. Autism affects only about 1.5% of people, and that statistic usually is arrived at through telephone questionnaires, so I do not know how accurate it is. Aside from autism there is a whole world out there of disorders and conditions that can affect people and affect how they seem to you. problem #1 many speech disorders have no effect on walking, posture, gait; they only affect speech. Many people have language disorders or speech disorders, yet physically walk and move like most people walk and move. So that’s your first problem. Language and speech disorders often affect speech only. problem #2 many disorders affect movement and speech, but not intelligence or mental processes. Many people have disorders that affect how they physically walk and move, yet have no Intellectual Disability. No problem with anything, actually, except movement. For example, Cerebral Palsy can affect movement(that includes speech) in a way you might notice, but many people with Cerebral Palsy have IQs above 85(the start of the ‘normal’ range of IQ), and think the same way other people do. So you can’t tell how ‘normal’ someone is mentally based on how they move or speak. That’s your second problem. problem #3 some people are normal in movement, intelligence and speech, but have mental illness that affects thinking. For example my friend walks normally, talks normally, is obviously very intelligent, even did very well in school, but has a mental illness that affects his thinking. So you might not notice anything ‘abnormal’ as he passes by you in the hall. However, as you started talking to him, perhaps you might notice(or you might not notice) that he is becoming more and more anxious, because if he talks to people for more than a few minutes he starts getting afraid someone will hurt him or the person he’s talking to. With ‘kids in school,’ often the mental illness is just starting at that age, or is still very slight, so it may not be obvious. problem #4 some kids are doing drugs or alcohol in school Drugs or alcohol can affect movement, speech, as well as how a person thinks and behaves. problem #5 some kids are in a bad mood or having a bad day problem #6 some kids are just messing with you

question: How many school accommodations are reasonable for a secondary school student with anxiety, OCD, autism, and depression on a 504 plan?
answer: I don’t think the question can be answered with a number. I think the accommodations should include all accommodations necessary to provide equal access to the benefits of a public education. When designing accommodations, they should be minimally intrusive, meaning that they should minimize the extent to which the student can be identified as different from his or her peers. For example, imagine that a hypothetical child needs to wear noise can ceiling earbuds. If this child was the only one in the class able to wear them, the accommodation singles the student out as disabled. Allowing anyone in the class to wear them minimizes this problem. Similarly, if a student needs to take tests at home because he or she needs to type responses, writing a take home, open notes and book test minimizes the identification of the student with the accommodation. Although the accommodations should be comprehensive in that they provide equal access to educational benefits, on practical terms, a student or a parent wants accommodations to be implemented with fidelity. “Fidelity” means implemented the way the writers intended. You can increase fidelity by simplifying the accommodations and limiting them to a manageable number. So this means that you have to balance being comprehensive with being practical and minimally invasive. I know this is not a direct answer, like saying “X is the magic number,” but I think it is the optimal answer. Thank you. question: What are the pros and cons of mainstream schooling vs. homeschooling for a child with autism and ADHD?
answer: The pros and cons are personal to each one of us, but I can tell you our story in hopes of giving a little insight. I homeschooled my autistic son (and his two brothers) through 8th grade. That allowed me to hone in on his specific needs and struggles and give him time to work them through. When you're in a classroom setting, the teacher, of course, has to consider the needs of all students. By 8th grade both he and I were ready to do something different. I had introduced teaching technology the last year we were together, as he was having a hard time separating mom from teacher. Then, he went to a private school where they claimed to treat their students like family. They said he wouldn't require an I.E.P. because they knew their students personally and were able to adapt to their needs at all times. Some of the teachers did a great job, but for others adapting meant getting rid of anything the students didn't like. That's not how education works in our home, so he spent his last two years with an I.E.P. at our local high school. This was invaluable, as it allowed him to participate in a program after high school that required an I.E.P. He also found his love for videography taking that as an elective both years. So, my advice — adapt to your child’s needs as he learns and grows. Find the best learning environment and help him discover his passion and purpose. Don't underestimate him. Push gently. Allow him to be who he is. Love him. Also, if you choose to homeschool, make sure to make time for yourself. It is not for the faint of heart. There were days when I wanted to run after the yellow school bus, toss my three boys on, and run away to Tahiti. 🤔 Finding a homeschool community at my church and through a homeschool hybrid worked for me., and I'm still mostly sane. Blessings on your journey. It will pass by fast. Enjoy the ride!

question: I was diagnosed with autism and ADHD by my school when I was a child. I'm 27 now. How would I know if I may have learning difficulties?
answer: Thank you for requested answer Nathan Locksdale. Like you, I also have autism and ADHD. You were diagnosed as a child. I was diagnosed in adulthood. I took the liberty of reading your profile and noted the two sensible comments reflecting life with these two conditions. You’re happy to accept edits to your Quora edits and you accept that you are not perfect. I accept edits (due to my ADHD carelessness). I accept that I am far from perfect. Learning difficulties may mean difficulties in acquiring knowledge and skills to the normal level expected of those of the same age, especially because of mental disability or cognitive disorder. Learning difficulties may accompany ADHD and autism, but not necessarily be a result of it. Neverthelesss, with ADHD and autism, you may experience some or all of the following: Trouble recognising other people’s feelings and “reading” nonverbal cues. There’s a tendency for literal speech accompanied by difficulties with understanding puns, riddles or figures of speech. These symptoms are also seen with social communication disorder, ADHD and receptive language issues. Difficulty with executive function. People with autism find it hard to get organized and solve problems. They can struggle to keep their emotions in check and change the way they do things without getting upset. Those with ADHD and executive functioning issues often have similar issues. As someone with both ADHD and ASD, executive function causes me great difficulty. A tendency to seek out or avoid sensory input. This is also common in people with sensory processing issues and ADHD. A tendency to be clumsy and uncoordinated. People may have trouble with handwriting, riding a bike, catching a ball or running. Trouble working with words. People with ADHD or autism may struggle to express themselves, follow conversations, and speak with the right volume and inflection. I tend to speak quickly, loudly and with needless enthusiasm. None of these are necessarily aspect of a learning disability. So if you have any doubts, see a professional and get help. I know about the daily difficulties of life with ADHD and autism. I write about them in a regular Quora blog No half measures. But the approach to your two conditions is everything. Self awareness, self management, research and periodic help. (And I really do not like asking for help).

question: After I have autism and I remember after I graduated in high school, I regressed in my development. Has anyone else had this issue?
answer: I experienced this a few years ago, which is when I got my (adult) diagnosis. I burned out so bad I could no longer compensate for masking and “keeping up with the neurotypical-Jones’s” so I regressed badly in self-care, ability to perform previously-acquired skills (physical or social), ability to tolerate over-stimulation, general social skills, energy to remember to / energy to perform manual emoting, ability to demonstrate intellectual abilities, overall mental stability and thus of course, overall confidence and self-esteem. I no longer had the energy reserves, which I call internal resources and is often referred to by many in the autistic community as spoons. The more energy we have to expend coping with hiding ourselves (and therefore worrying about doing so) and dealing with overstimulation (ex. the social jet-lag of having to “people” with NT’s and all their changing unwritten social rules and lack of forgiveness for social missteps, the energy-drain of flourescent lighting and loud volumes on our more-sensitive eyes and ears, uncomfortable clothing or foods, etc.) the less we have to simply function, let alone thrive. It’s like having an extreme, debilitating prescription-meds-worthy migraine every single day all day long. You can’t rest enough and refill your energy reserves (your health-bar, if you will) to equal and certainly not overcome the drain (the poison potion is taking more hp every few seconds than your [work breaks or days off] healing potions can make up for). Extended rest, and actually-useful-to-you-individually coping mechanisms are needed to recover (not masking, but compensating; this is the difference between hiding a weakness pretending it’s not there, and getting around a weakness by utilizing aids or personal strengths or leaving a situation or changing the requirements on you). Stress often is what “reveals” autism as we regress and stim to self-soothe in place of automatic bodily self-regulation (my goodness, how I wish I could tune out background noises automatically in self-regulation instead of having to have white noise override it so my brain will stop trying to hear everything at once!). Similarly, it reveals ADD/ADHD when a person who has been in circumstances making use of their strengths or compensating for their weaknesses (ex. being in a job that encourages hyperfocus on projects, or being a kid who had parents to keep track or organization of timeliness), suddenly finds themselves in an opposite-situation and fails to continue succeeding due to the inability to continue exploiting personal strengths or experience in offsetting weaknesses (like time-blindness). Find out what your energy-drains are (your forks, if you will), your sensitivities, your anxiety-inducers, and how to neutralize them. For example, I started wearing orange 100% blue-light-blocking sunglasses to counter flourescent lighting and overcast-sky days, which reduced my visual-overstimulation strain, which plugged up an energy-leak hole in my system (since I’m not an artist, the change in my overly-perceptive ability to perceive colour-shade differences, while wearing the glasses, was no loss). Make sure you know the effects of your diet on your body, as autistics tend towards having comorbidities, and commonly they include ADD/ADHD or gut / inflammation issues (the former being worsened by the excessive ingestion of artificial food dyes and extreme amounts of caffeine, the latter often complicated by unusual food intolerances such as bananas, chocolate, sunflower oil/butter, avacado, nightshade veggies, some citruses, some legumes, etc. and resulting in their respective intolerance-responses and overall malaise). If possible, reduce the “forks” in your life, or at least your exposure to them. Therapy is useful for achieving (and keeping tract of) the aforementioned, and supporting you through it, if it is possible to attend sessions in whatever your individual circumstances are. I wish you luck on finding stability and making that upward-climb back to better health and happiness.

question: If a school gives a student with level 2 autism and a 504 plan a truancy ticket, is that going against the 504 plan?
answer: Truancy means the student or his/her parents are choosing to not get the student to school on a regular or timely basis and that an acceptable excused absence has not been provided. 504 plans or IEPs are legal documents that require commitment and responsibilities for ALL that sign the documents. The school system certainly has responsibilities, but the parents and the student (if he/she is old enough to sign the document) have responsibilities, too. One of the main responsibilities of the parents and student is to actually attend the educational program (school). In addition having a 504 plan or IEP document does not suddenly make state laws about school attendance suddenly evaporate. A student can't arrive late, skip out, or just not come and then think having a 504 plan makes that okay. If there is a reason for late or truant behavior that is VALIDLY related to the reasons the student has a 504 plan, then the 504 committee needs to reconvene to address that. Otherwise a school system has every right to issue a “truancy ticket.”

question: What strategies can be used to help someone with autism and ADHD succeed in school?
answer: “What strategies can be used to help someone with autism and ADHD succeed in school?” Explaining principles behind the processes or the “facts” you are teaching can help a lot. Encouraging students to collaborate, and to recognise how their different ways of thinking and working can function better together than any one alone. Encourage neurodivergent staff members to be aware of how they can be mentoring and setting positive examples to neurodivergent students. There is unlikely to be any funding for a full-on mentoring program but teachers can help students to feel that they are recognised and accepted when so many people seem to marginalise them.

question: I have a little brother who is in middle school who has autism and he has extreme anger issues. What can I do to help him?
answer: Have worked with children with autism for 15 years and has a brother on the spectrum. The biggest thing is patience. If you realize that alot of his behavior truly are not his fault, then you wont blame him when he does act out. Growing up, I was always angry at my brother and that didnt help him at all. Others have mentioned a therapist that specializes in behavioral therapy, which I wholeheartedly support. Also, eating well and exercise are important. And, lastly WATCH FOR SCAMS. There are a ton of people that will offer cures (homeopathy, barium chambers, gluten free diets). Do NOT believe them. If any of them worked they would be part of the prescribed treatment. Eating gluten doesnt affect autism, neither does getting vaccines, eating canned tuna, red dye # 7, or a million other things you may be told. Children with autism often self limit their diets. If you further restrict their diets they can often suffer malnutrition. The truth is we DONT KNOW what causes autism. There is some really good work happening in the field of neuro science, but we arent there yet. We can treat symptoms by removing environmental stressors (individual to the client) and teach methods to better cope with social situation by giving them tools. Its extremely individual. Make sure you contact a professional trained in Applied Behavior Analysis. ABA observes behavior, attempts to predict the function of the behavior and offer replacement behavior that meets the same need while having less social impact.

question: I have HFA autism and a lot of girls like me at school. I also stutter. How can I talk to them without seeming weird?
answer: I’m in my mid 50′s and have not been diagnosed but recently came to suspect I have High Functioning Autism. As I researched autism, one of the things I remembered from being a teen is what my friends and I came to call “total lip failure.” This wasn’t stuttering but it was certainly noticeable. The words in my head have always tended to happen very rapidly. Way faster than I could talk. I’d start a sentence and about halfway through you’d hear … “and yeah, we should go to Mcdonaldfdhowffahsdfj … pbbt.” It was as if my tongue had just fallen down a set of stairs. There was no way I could control it or predict when it would happen. And it happened a lot. It became a running joke … and I decided I’d be in on the joke and laugh *with* the people about myself. For some reason, laughing at myself tended to disarm even bullies: I laughed uncontrollably as a pack of boys dragged me across a yard and smushed my hand into a pile of dog sh*t. I was even laughing as I wiped the crap off my hand into the yard. I was humiliated but kinda-not at the same time. I think I cried afterward but kids picked on me less after that. Okay … only a little less. ;-) My childhood was very weird but no one ever thought I was autistic … just quirky. (It’s was late 1960’s and early 1970’s … I don’t think we had ever heard the term autistic!) So … if the girls already like you … THEY LIKE YOU. Dude … that is way cool! I was also very well liked by girls because I wasn’t a total asshole and listened to them. So, if your words won’t come out and you stutter, smile, shrug and laugh it off. Girls will most likely find it endearing that you have a sense of humor. A potentially unintended side-effect — that may not be as true now as it was before girls started to realize a lot of jocks are jerks — if you are adorable, girls may not immediately consider you dating material. This is not necessarily a bad thing. Not rushing into heavy physical relationships can save you a lot of unnecessary emotional drama. As a friend told her kids, “You have to be emotionally ready to take on a physical or sexual relationship. Sex *always* effects one partner or the other emotionally.” And taking your time means you will tend to find nicer, more interesting girls to date. Oh … and if you are really interested in a girl you will probably have to tell them. No girl ever had a clue I was interested! That may also be a part of the HFA thing. I always feel like I’m expressing all sorts of emotions all the time … but for the most part people see Happy, Really Happy and Neutral. That’s it. Sad or worried or wicked attracted to a person? Nope. Nothing. And … there are plenty of really nice, quirky, intelligent (and frisky) women out there! Take it slow. Have a sense of humor about yourself. Embrace and shrug off your awkwardness and you will be fine.

question: I was diagnosed with mild autism and was bullied in high school over and over again by a guy. Why was he doing this? I am genuinely interested. What was going through his head?
answer: *If this sounds strange to some, move on. It's tailored to this writer. Bear with me, it rambles. One of the things we'll never understand, as people with Autism, is how or why others think. Bullies pick on vulnerable people they don't understand. Often, It's because they are scared or uncomfortable around you (us), but that doesn't mean you were wrong. It also doesn't mean they knew they were impacting your life so deeply, because we tend to be able to recall negative experiences in great detail. You won't necessarily ever know why he did or said something, because NTs are emotional, which means there is often no logical cause/effect factor in their choice of decisions. We can't know what someone else meant or said, (Autistic or otherwise) because we view things from one or more different perspectives. It's not just NT vs ASD, but it's also Introvert vs Extrovert, Male vs Female gender role identity, logical vs emotional thinking, inferred vs deferred knowledge, etc. We remember incidents, often to the finest detail. I know, for instance, that I often misread someone's tone of voice in writing. Because of that, I try to explain myself so someone can “sense” the tone of my writing as they would in my voice but it doesn't always work. Some people will always read my writing as a boring lecture and some will read with interest and, (hopefully) whatever I write brings a smile to someone's face. It might not be the person who asked the question who is smiling, but someone else reading will understand that I know what they're going through. I truly believe the only experts on Autism are people with Autism. You can't fix stupid (bullies) but you can do your best to overcome hard feelings. You don't have to like the people who bully you. People who treat you badly are not your friends. Allowing people to mistreat you is not ok, but that does not allow you to confront people you call friends and accuse them of bullying. It means that people should remove themselves from others who are mean to them. Confronting a bully instead of walking away is not a way to advocate for yourself. It will keep you mad or at risk for being used or further humiliated. You need to walk away. But, if you want, take the hurt you’re feeling and try helping to create an antibullying movement at school or in an area locally. Try asking your parents or a local Autism Society (Not Autism Speaks) to help. I used to make friends with the other kids that were made fun of. I didn't go where I wasn't wanted, but I'd find someone who looked sad and ask if they needed a friend. If they said no, or treated me mean, I stayed away. If you can't, that's ok, too. You might just need closure so you can let the issue go. Try writing a letter and sending it to yourself. Say everything you want, any way you want, even if it sounds really mean or nasty in your head. It's ok, because in this activity, no one else around you can tell how you are feeling when you write your email. No one's feelings will be hurt. When you are done, send it to yourself. Hitting “Send” will remove the negative energy and stress (and possible physical pain) from your body and sometimes your mind, including the obsession about wanting to know what happened. It might help you refocus away from dwelling on the “why.” Now, open up the e-mail you sent to yourself, and read it. Don't read it like you did when you wrote it. Try reading it as if you are telling yourself, “I was there, I lived through it. I am moving on, after I deal with this.” So, if you can, imagine you are reading it with contempt, as if you are lauding or reigning over a nobody in a faraway kingdom. Pretend you are (someone you admire or crush on), talking to someone who is lowly or insignificant, like a King to a peon. I don't know sci-fi references (smile). Think about Sheldon vs Wolowitz, Amy vs Penny, good and evil, etc. whatever works for you. When you watch tv or read anime, the minor fight is often over at the end of a scene, episode, season, etc. While characters have their issues, they may still be in each other's worlds, but their relationship changes because trust between them has been lost, even if they end up back together. So, in your head, imagine this letter is a conversation between the good you (victim) and bad you (hero). You are going to win this argument because the good person you are is going to rescue the victim you feel like. Make it a personal victory -- a winning moment. Instead of remembering every time someone has done you wrong (because I know I can), keep track of every time you proved yourself right, or something turned out well or better than expected. Thanks for reading. Hope this helps.

question: Our oldest child has autism and will be starting high school. He has been in a charter school but we are going to have to home school him now. Any tips on good programs and best practices? Thank you.
answer: In short, you asked about Home Schooling your child. As an experienced secondary professional educator, I will tell you about the common thing that I see with people who have been Home Schooled and I will make a suggestion as to how it can easily be handled. Students who have come to me who have been Home Schooled, are almost always ahead of the others and they know how to speak with adults, but they have no concept of deadlines or interacting with others. I have had them say things to me like, “I am not ready to take the exam so I will do it later” or “I did not attend your lecture/demonstration yesterday because my mother felt it best that we do something else; can you do it for me today?” Additionally I have noticed that formerly Home Schooled students do not have a concept of respecting the time of others. They are not intentionally being rude, it is just a foreign concept to them to be on time. It is normal that a Formerly Home Schooled student will come to class late and say, “I am sorry that I am late can you start over?” Parents that Home School their children can take a few simple steps to help the students. First, hold them fast to a deadline because the world desperately needs people who can meet deadlines. Second, help them learn to respect others by respecting their time —it is rude to be late as it says to the others who were on time, “I am more important than you are,” and Third, help them to learn how to respectfully deal with others when they are very rarely late due to circumstances beyond their control. It is common that I have do deal with the disruptive tardy student who has not been trained in how to enter a classroom or auditorium after the presentation has begun. I am Allen Morris and I approve of this dashed off first draft.

question: Is there a correlation between autism and IQ? Why do some individuals with autism struggle in school despite potentially having a higher IQ?
answer: There is both a positive and a negative correlation. High end aspergers autistics like me test out at the genius level in IQ tests. But the greater percentage of autistic people who lack that “high end advantage” would tend to test below and sometimes very far below average. This is why so many people don’t process the confusing word, Autism: because it can describe both genius’s as well as badly brain impaired people.

question: My brother has autism and he's already 22. He doesn't go to school because he can't talk and he is sometimes violent and having episodes. What can I do to entertain him everyday?
answer: You would need to talk to his behavioral therapist and people who around him all the time. Most people with autism hate changes in their routine. Sometimes loud noises, bright colors, new things can make them feel overwhelmed. If he cannot talk, some of his violent behavior may be from frustration of not being able to communicate. Instead of trying to entertain him, try to spend quality time with him. You will need to find his likes and dislikes. Take the time to get to know him as a person. Dont get so focused on autism that you forget he has feelings. Some questions to start with: Is there anything that makes him agitated or upset? What helps calm him down? What is his favorite food? What is his favorite TV show or movie? What’s his favorite kind of music? What are some things he likes to do? What kind of videos (animal/nature shows, cartoons, etc)?

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder. b. History of learning disorders after the 14th birthday. c. Autism spectrum disorders. d. History of disorders with psychotic features. e. History of bipolar disorders. f. Depressive disorder. g. History of a single adjustment disorder. h. History of conduct disorders. i. History of personality disorder. j. Encopresis after 13th birthday. k. History of any eating disorder. l. Any current communication disorder. m. History of suicidality. n. History of self-harm. o. History of obsessive-compulsive disorder. p. History of trauma or post-traumatic stress disorder. q. History of anxiety disorders. r. History of dissociative disorders. s. History of somatic symptoms disorders. t. History of gender dysphoria. u. History of paraphilic disorders. v. Any history of substance-related and addictive disorders. w. History of prescription with psychotropic medication. x. History of other mental disorders that may reasonably be expected to interfere with or prevent satisfactory performance of military duty. y. Prior psychiatric hospitalization for any cause. Reference. DoD Instruction 6130.03, Volume I, Medical Standards for Military Service: Appointment, Enlistment, or Induction; Section 6, Disqualifying Conditions § 6.28.

question: What should I do with my son still wearing diaper at home and school, my son has diagnosed with intermediate autism, he cannot expression when he want to go to the toilet, so I still let him wearing diaper to school, what should I do the next?
answer: First things first: Intermediate autism doesn’t exist. Autism just is. It’s not a disease you can have a little or a lot, just like you can’t be ‘intermediate pregnant’ for example…. So he has autism. Period. And it affects him intermediately (that sounds a bit weird, but I guess you understand what I’m trying to say here). With autism having issues with going to the toilet is quite common. There could be (at least) four different reasons for it, and usually it’s a combination of reasons.It could be a medical reason not even directly related to his autism. This should be discussed with a doctor.He genuinely doesn’t feel when he needs to go. People with autism may have certain sensory issues, and these can include not feeling properly when the bladder is full. If this is the case there isn’t really much you can do about it, except giving him a timer and saying he simply must ALWAYS go to the toilet when the timer is at zero. No matter if he thinks he should go, he must go and try to pee. He will hate that timer in time. But in time it’ll become a habit and it might work.He does feel the need to go but is distracted by other things. Also quite common with autism is certain activities or even thoughts taking up all attention. People with autism have a tendency to be hyper-focused about things, forgetting everything else around them. Including paying attention if they need to go the toilet. If this is the case with your son it’s again about making it a habit for him to regularly check if he doesn’t need to pee. Again a timer could do the trick.He just doesn’t care… People with autism often have a tendency to live very much at the moment. I think that’s actually a gift. But, certainly with kids it can also offer some challenges. For instance: delaying things they don’t really want to do. Including going to the toilet… Here the issue isn’t so much the kid not realising he needs to go, but simply not finding it important enough. That means a timer could help, but probably not… When the timer runs out they’ll probably decide to wait another minute because they’re right in the middle of something. And that minute becomes, 2, 3, 4, 5…. So here the kid will need to learn it’s important to go to the toilet in time. This requires a lot of parenting, educating, psychology. The kid needs to genuinely understand pee belongs in the toilet and not in a diaper. You could for instance take the diaper away. Maybe only at set times at first and only at home. And if he has an accident, do not punish him for it… But do make it very clear it is bad! He might not like walking around in wet, stinky clothes. If that’s the case: let him for just a bit longer than you normally would. Also make it clear to him it’s really a burden to you you now have to change his clothes, wash his clothes. Etcetera. You could even make him part of this process…. “You made it dirty, so you’re going to help me clean it!” (but only if this annoys him. If it’s a huge punishment to him than don’t… and if he likes washing clothes than obviously also don’t). This one is possibly the most difficult of the four and will require a lot of time and patience…Besides an ordinary timer there are also special tools that alert a person when it’s time to go. Bedwetting alarms and such. So you might want to check that out as well. Good luck!

question: Why do schools not care even after you show them the autism and ADHD diagnosis?
answer: The job of the teachers is to [successfully] impart knowledge. Having a challenge such as autism or ADHD can make learning more difficult for the student. However, the teacher’s job remains the same. Now the question becomes how to help the student. Most teachers have entire classrooms of students. They cannot devote one-on-one time to special needs students and they cannot alter their teaching styles and protocols to accommodate one student. So what do we do? For ADHD, there are meds that can help. There are behavioral and attention management tricks the student can learn. Sometimes a combination of therapies is recommended. Autistic students require different methodologies depending on where the student falls on the spectrum. Schools and teachers do care. However, they are not empowered to diagnose or treat individual conditions. They are tasked with teaching and they do so to the best of their abilities.

Ignore them, and don’t allow anyone else to ever share the posts’ contents with you. Think of them as hungry beasts that feed on your pain. Don’t feed them. Step three. Block them every place that you can. When their posts show up, block the senders. If they come under other names, block them too. If someone else forwards them to you, tell them to stop, and if they don’t, block them too. You may need to set up a new account that you privatize so that you only accept posts from a very small group of trusted friends. Step four. It may be necessary to get off of social media entirely for a while. Find another way to communicate with friends who treat you well and stay away from the ones who want to hurt you. Sooner or later, the kids from your old school will get tired of getting no response from you and will leave you alone.

question: How has the rise of autism and ADHD affected the educational landscape in Australia, particularly in terms of inclusion of students with disabilities in mainstream schools?
answer: There has not been a rise in either Autism's or ADHD in Australia at all in recent decades. In fact research has shown the the incidence of these conditions has actually declined and there are less issues like this in society than there were a few decades ago. What has increased is the diagnosis of these cases. There are no more of these cases in classrooms just a rise in the number of children diagnosed with them. Back in the 80’s and 90’s both ADHD and Austin’s were common diagnosis among children and schools have worked with these diagnosis in children for decades. The rise in diagnosis has two factors to it. The first is that cases that may been previously undiagnosed are now being recognised. This will generally make the situation in schools easier because children with these conditions were still in classrooms before but we’re not receiving treatment. ADHD was generally quite accurately diagnosed for those with combined type or Hyperactive/impulsive type in the 90’s-90’s but inattentive type tended to be over looked. This was (and still is) particularly for boys with inattentive type. Milder cases of Autism are also now being diagnosed. The other part of the rose of diagnosis of these conditions is due to overdiagnsis. This is not just limited to ADHD and Autism but happens with a lot of conditions like Anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder and PTSD. There are a number of reasons for this such as false information being spread on the internet, internet algorithms, advertising from drug companies in the US which has an indirect effect on Australian numbers, social media causing us to make too many comparisons and leading people to believe there is something wrong with their children, the rise of AI and technology meaning that a lot of jobs that didn’t require degrees become obsolete so there is more pressure on kids at school, NAPLAN, the NDIS has caused a rise in Autism diagnosis as it leads to funding etc. The over diagnosis of these conditions leads to many problems. People don’t necessarily realise this, they just think in the short term it means extra support for their children. But it leads to children having self limiting beliefs “I can’t do that because I have ADHD” “that will be hard for me because I have Autism”. Parents and teachers lowering expect which tends to lower outcomes, stigma being placed in these children, problems that arise not being addressed but often just being attributed to the condition, unnecessary medication leading to serious side effects, addiction and dependency and leading children to believe they can’t function without them and the limited resources available being stretched too far.

question: Should I mention my autism and autistic experiences in my college applications, or will it be a turnoff to the Ivy League Schools I plan on applying to, including Yale, Columbia, Cornell, and University of Pennsylvania?

I feel you should disclose, as it’s very important to have that on record to receive the accommodations you need to be successful. Because of the 1990 Americans With Disabilities Act, being turned away from a college because you are autistic would be legal violation. Each college will have a Disability Services department that can help you, but you need to let a college know what needs you have. Should I write about my autism in an application letter? That depends. Does it add anything meaningful to you as a person? If you feel you have a real story, then write about how you overcame adversity to become an Ivy League applicant. Overcoming adversity is a life skill that a lot of these school would like to see. question: Why would someone have an IQ of 120 when tested in elementary school and score an 82 at the age of 25? There is no history of brain injury or major trauma. She does have Autism and learning disabilities, and did very poorly in middle and high school.
answer: IQ tests are imperfect measures of knowledge and problem-solving abilities. At 25, she would have been assessed with a different set of tests from when she was under 10 or so. Also, if she's on medication that has cognitive side effects, her performance will be impaired. I experienced this personally. I have Autism and ADHD, plus Nonverbal Learning Disability (NVLD). As a child I tested in the 120 to 130 range. Shortly after graduating with a Master's degree and a severe case of burnout + exhaustion, my counselor told me all the psychological tests I'd taken were invalid. She put it this way: ‘Someone with an MA can't fail IQ tests.’ But I had “failed" them. Many years later, when my NVLD was diagnosed, I scored in the top percentile range for verbal and auditory communication, and below 80 on all the visual-spatial tests. Those probably used to be called “Performance IQ". I was baffled. How could such a difference come about? What I've come to believe is that my stress levels were “through the roof" when I was tested as an adult. I was struggling at work with things that neither my co-workers nor my supervisors could see. Even I didn't fully understand my struggle until someone managed to articulate my battle. I was working three times harder than anyone else to do my job. Nobody saw it because I took so much work home with me to complete. At that point, I was sooo tired. I couldn't focus in the office and signs of my ASD, ADHD, and NVLD really began to surface. I lost confidence in myself. I once read a little story about a cup of (something carbonated, I imagine) being jostled a little bit from morning to night. Every shake up in the course of a day builds pressure. And when the lid comes off--- It's a useful analogy for many situations. When I looked at my mental, physical and cognitive decline through that lens, I saw myself struggling through each grade in school with work that got harder and harder. The pressure on me was building. With help, I learned to add, subtract and multiply. Division remained difficult, and once I reached the point of studying the mandatory Algebra, my brain cells and neural synapses couldn't wrap themselves around ideas that were much more abstract. This might not answer your exact question, but I hope you can see the ways in which my story may be similar to that of the girl you mention. I, too, was about 25 when I failed my IQ tests.

question: Is it possible that I have trouble trying to retain my memory the moment I got out of high school or is it that I am getting older? Or if possible ADHD, Asperger/Autism, and learning disability is causing the deficit to get worse.

Even if not feeling stressed, are you having to “function” among non-autistics etc. in situations you don’t know well, including “masking”/”camouflaging” as non-autistic yourself as best you can? If so, these things can be pretty stressful! Sometimes I find myself so caught up in trying to camouflage that I don’t realize how stressed I am, it’s so all-consuming for me. I think that stress messes with our ability to encode memories, there are stress hormones involved. Plus having to focus-focus-focus on the camouflaging often doesn’t allow time for reflection and really taking in the situation, imho. It’s like, if you were having to sit and take math exams for 10 hours / day and then you were supposed to remember what was on the tv in the corner of the room too? Your brain was focused on the exam to remember much else. Oh, and right now, the real-life TVs have constant war, mass shootings, climate disasters… talk about stress. And many people have to deal with the stuff in real life. Just a theory, maybe, my speculations … but I’ve had the same issue for decades!!! I’m 58… I find regular exercise to help with my general memory, esp. if my heart rate gets up nice and high. Another detail: I also remember visual stuff way better than verbal stuff, which is relevant for workplace accommodation requests for me. Yay for captions! Plus my memory seems different from some peoples’, I am better at remembering things connected to my strong interests, in a web, rather than random stuff. Maybe, try to make correlations, notice (after the fact) which things, situations, might be making this worse, or which improve your memory? That is difficult for me but very helpful. It takes a long time sometimes - partly because I had to work it all out myself. I hope you have positive people around you, support can be great.

question: Why before DSM-5 people couldn't have both adhd and autism? will sometime exist a DSM-6? Context: i live at Brazil but in the 2013s, it was new in the whole world but everything heres came late, i was at primary school and doctors said that i couldn't have both, and they said i had adhd. nowadays, i came to a revalidation consult for adhd, (it's like a checkup every 10 years to see if the symptoms have improved or worsened) and the new psychiatrist claimed a suspect of autism and told me to go into further investigation, now i have both 🤡. even in these days some old doctors claim that can't have both they're ignorante but. at least i feel that everything is clear now
answer: I am a 66 year old woman with both. Didn’t know this about myself until last year. Please remember that the DSM is a listing of things that affect people’s brains and actions. There is a TON of stuff we do not know about how our brains function and why people do what they do. The reason it’s called a medical practice is because it’s always changing and always evolving. The things we are now learning about spectrum “disorders” are far outpacing the publishing of another DSM. Accumulated knowledge is way ahead of it. Doctors, for the most part are way behind. It’s not their fault. They are focused on pills, surgery and physical injury. Doctors have a lot of new info coming out everyday and they too are human. My own doctor, when I told her I was positive I have Autism and ADHD said, “Can you cope?” I told her most of the time. She didn’t even recommend an official diagnosis. She has so much more on her plate than if a patient HAS Autism. I managed ok to get to her appointment (she has no idea how many spoons that takes) then she figures it’s not a problem for her to push me to get a medical diagnosis. Now, if I suffered from extreme anxiety it would be different. In a way I can’t blame her. I think I don’t want to go through the hoops to get that official diagnosis. Others who can’t cope need the limited resources of the medical community more than I do. In 50 years you will be able to look back and see there were SO MANY things we didn’t know back in 2024 about spectrum disorders and many other things. And honestly, if I could tell your doctor, I don’t believe Autism or ADHD is going to “improve or worsen”. It’s not going to heal. It’s just the way our brains work. It’s the way we process info. We are the Androids in an iPhone world. I suspect someday in the future we will wonder why we called it a disability except in cases where people need a lot of continued intervention and help to cope with daily life. Yes, there are struggles. Most struggles are caused by the world we are forced to live in. When we minimize the things we can’t tolerate things can be pretty darn good. Over the years I learned various ways to cope. Some were helpful and others not as good. That is the only real way I believe that people on this spectrum can thrive right now. We are faced with a world that is set up for people who function differently from us. It’s up to us to find ways, ask for help, and figure out how to live in ways that support our different needs. Just like some animals eat meat, and some eat grass and some eat both…we need to find what helps us to thrive and figure out where to get what we need. Fortunately we are learning a lot about Autism and ADHD and how they interact on a daily basis. We are able to use the internet to talk to each other and learn from each other. The DSM is way behind the knowledge on the “street” that is out there in the community of people who are actually on the spectrum. We are learning to reach out and support each other. We are learning to ask for what we actually need and how can we get it. Gradually we are creating lives that give us the space and features that help us cope with our very individual trait presentations. And we are gradually going to teach the non-spectrum world how to help us, and help themselves also. Things that are good for us are often also good for everyone. Keep asking. Keep writing. Keep learning. Keep coping. Keep helping others when you can. Keep being kind. We got this!

question: What would it be like to have autism and ADHD at the same time?
answer: I have both autism and ADHD. Basically, they’re a life of antitheses. Autism means I hate chaos, ADHD means I can’t stand routine. Autism means special interests, ADHD hyperfixations. If I hyperfixate on a special interest, the world could go up in flames and I would continue to pursue it. I’m usually good at school, but always get the details wrong. On other times, I focus on the details and forget the big picture. I want to have a clean room, but tidying is overwhelming and boring. Basically, imagine a constant fight against yourself. If I had myself as a roommate, I would have moved out long ago, we’re not really compatible. It’s constant fights against yourself, and there’s not really anything you can do.

I would not take my toys out of their box after receiving them for my birthday or Christmas. If my mom forced me to let a friend play with one of my toys...I would remove the toy from the box, undo all of the twist-ties which hold it in the packaging and hand it to the friend. I would watch over them while they played with my toy. Then once they left, I would put the toy back exactly how it was, re-twisting all the twist-ties, place it perfectly in the box and put the box back under my bed where I had it previously. question: How do teenagers with autism/aspergers deal with school?
answer: Answered by my 17 year old daughter who is a Junior in HS. As I wake up in the morning, I feel completely fine. I wake up about an hour and a half before school starts so as well as getting ready for the day during that period of time, I have that much time to process what the day might look like. As I am on my way to school, I pass the same apartment complex which is not even a block from my school, but those apartments are a reminder to me that school is just about to begin. My hands then begin to sweat, my heart races extremely fast, my mouth starts to water, and I almost become faint. I realize that these sensations happen on a daily basis before school, however I also realize it's because I have a LOT of social anxiety and OCD. Most people who fall on the Autistic Spectrum and who have OCD will find themselves with social anxiety. With having OCD, my mind works by me having to know the outcome of every situation I am going into. Since there are tons of people at school, and me not knowing what any of them are thinking about me, I start to get anxious. I am a shy student and I pick up on every detail- something Autism has gifted me with. However, to answer your question: School is not a place where I feel any sort of comfort, since I do not know the outcome of how the day is going to end nor what is going to happen inside the classrooms. Things that help me are: taking deep breaths, telling myself not to worry and it will all turn out alright, and I just remind myself that I am not the only one who feels this way…or you can vape! Lol.

question: Why is school difficult for people with autism?
answer: Schools have to accommodate everyone in every academic area, and they expect students to be roughly equally able in all areas. Autistic people have what would be considered gaps in ability by neurotypical standards. I am what is now considered “twice exceptional” or “2e”. I am autistic (though not diagnosed until my 20s) and “gifted”. For nursery school and elementary/middle school, I was placed in private dual language immersion schools for the gifted. It seemed like a perfect fit: I loved to learn, especially languages, and I absorbed everything I could. The class sizes were also smaller than other schools, meaning fewer stimuli making me upset. The challenge was that a class full of gifted neurotypicals being taught by a neurotypical teacher didn’t really know what to do with a “gifted kid” who could do all the academic work, but was unable to learn unwritten social rules. I understood to stay in my seat because we were told to every day, and it was written on a poster. But no one ever told me how to start a conversation, how to manage topics, how to BE in social situations. It was made exceedingly clear to me that I was different, but I couldn’t grasp why, and I still can’t really explain what I was doing wrong. A couple kind peers had been willing to befriend me, but neither stayed at my school very long. There was one social group at the school where everyone knows everyone. And if you weren’t in it… you were me. The teachers didn’t seem to have a problem with my classmates not letting me sit at the lunch table or be in their group for a project or on their team in gym. The most powerful lesson I learned there was that my only value as a person was my ability to learn things well. I was not a person of value in my own right. People with autism who have higher support needs than I do are done a major disservice by schools that are at best set up to “manage behavior”, let alone help them discover what they want to learn. Just because someone does not use spoken language does not mean they are not intelligent and don’t have desires and preferences for what they learn. You never know until you take the time to see what they can do, and the child may not know how to show you in a way you’re expecting. I was extraordinarily lucky to have spoken language as a special skill; now I use it to help autistic kids learn to communicate more successfully in their lives, whether they use speech, sign, a communication device, picture cards, or often a combination. As a speech pathologist, I have the luxury of working with kids one on one, even if only for a short time. Getting “my kids” to speak is secondary to finding out what speaks to my kids. Classroom teachers are rarely given the time and resources to meet the needs of children who don’t fit the “expected” student profile.-Me, stealth stimming on my dad’s Bible. The pages had a really pleasing texture, and there were big capital letters at the beginning of each section that I liked.

question: What is autism burnout, and how does it affect you?
answer: I had what I called a total breakdown about 15 years ago. The pivital moment was when I broke the cycle of unresolved disputes between me and my husband. He could not understand how such a clever person could be so obtuse. He mistakenly thought I was full of lies and deceit. Dumb insolence. Thick as pig shit.A gas-lighter. Inconsiderate. Lazy. He was beside himself with dispair, until he came to hate me. I saw hatred distort his face. How could he not love me? I left that hour. Lived rough for 3 months. My son said he wanted to live with me, and with 2 of us we qualified for a place in a family hostel. I was astonished my son chose to leave his home and his father in order to look after me. I am choking up and tears are threateniing to burn my eyes. I had written myself off as a gonner. I had the biggest meltdown of my life. End of one life. Begining of seven years of hell on earth, and my gradual rebirth as someone I knew and recognised complete with Aspergers. Aspergers suddenly made sense of many mysteries that had puzzled me since my earliest years. I retreated inside myself. My stress levels were off the scale. At first my 15 yr old son was the only one who could communicate with me. He spent 6 weeks (summer holdays) with me 24 hrs a day, mostly in the bedsit we shared at the family hostel. When he got me so I could walk to the shop on my own and come back with milk or bread, he made that my special job. He prompted me to do everything I needed to do, but could not think of by myself. Then he said “I’ve got to go to school now Mum. I need you to look after me. Food, clean clothes, somewhere to live. You know, Mum, the whole deal.” He had given me respite, and then given me a purpose. I could make myself do things for my son, that I would not have done for myself. I still experienced:increased meltdowns and sensory sensitivityphysical pain and headaches, bewilderment, deep anxiety and depressionphysically shutting down, including the loss of speech. I was heartbroken.Autistic burnout affected all aspects of my life, and this makes it different from professional burnout, which is related to work. That was then and this is now. My work life had always been the successful part of my life. I am a good earner. I worked my socks off, and sent my son away to university when he was old enough. I told him it was his duty to himself. His rite of passage. I made sure he had a home to come back to. Free, like a bird. Free to fly away, and free to come home again. People like me. They make friends with me. I am now thriving and take my place to give a hand up in our mutual support network. I like myself, and will never feel I have to apologise for myself again. question: Is autistic burnout permanent?
answer: The short answer is no, but I have heard of some people going through it for several years. One thing I learned when I was studying autism and how it effects specifically females is that some (but of course, not all) women on the spectrum will be on overdrive during their 20s and 30s. They may have a job that they're excelling in, taking on multiple projects outside of work, having children too perhaps, etc. Then when they reach their middle-aged years they will go into burnout for quite a long while since they practically lived a full life in that span of 10–20 years in the way that they kept themselves busy and focused. I believe this can absolutely happen for males too regardless of the fact that I was researching women. I also don't think it takes a state of overdrive in order to trigger an excessively long burn out. It could also be prolonged forms of stress or abuse. Burn out can feel really draining, but the important thing to remember is that this is still a state of being. We can use burnout as an opportunity to treat ourselves with the kindness and care that we would if we were addressing a dear friend. And in turn, become closer with ourselves than we ever have been before.

question: What is autism burnout, and how does it affect you?
answer: Burnout in autistic individuals is characterized by a profound inability to make decisions, coupled with exhaustion and a lack of motivation. This state can persist for days, weeks, or even months, depending on the duration the individual has masked their challenges. Burnout results from prolonged cognitive and social demands that exceed their capacity, necessitating an extended recovery period. Recovery often involves significant rest, such as sleeping throughout the day, and requiring assistance with basic tasks like eating and laundry. Burnout can also arise from denial or a lack of self-awareness, leading the individual to neglect their need for rest and self-care.

question: How do you explain to your friends and family about autism burnouts? No one has heard of it and I think they should know.
answer: I agree - few have heard of it, which makes it difficult to explain to others, especially employers and offended spouses. I have endeavoured to describe it using a selection of synonyms designed to elicit an empathic response from my listeners, on account of the fact that they themselves almost certainly will, at one time or another, have experienced one, some or all of them: exhaustion, fatigue, general malaise, ennui, all mixed in with a listless lack of energy or motivation that borders on rendering one comatose. If they need more, I go on to say it’s a combination of mental and physical exhaustion that is the cost of spending too highly from the overdraft I have with the Sociability Bank. Or that it is the state of having not just few, but NO spoons in the cutlery drawer. If they remain inquisitive, I posit that they will have felt something similar if they’ve ever had the flu. Subtract all the cold-like symptoms and body-aches, and you have it: empty batteries, broken plug, faulty connector, broken-down generator etc etc. I have been asked if it’s not just simply depression, and I have always said, depression can certainly be present co-morbidly, but that it is not a sufficient or necessary feature, such as to make the two tantamount to one another. I have said it is perfectly possible - and I have myself experienced it as such - to be in a state of autistic burnout without feeling in the least bit depressed. No, one isn’t bouncing around the room in spasms of ecstatic euphoria, either, but certainly I have been in the state of burnout and been perfectly alright in terms of my mood. Ultimately, any functional, effective description must appeal to what your listener knows themselves: that is, similar experiences they are likely to have had. We’ve all been bored, listless, energiless and so on. Tell them it’s that multiplied by a thousand, with the drained, exhausted, utterly spent mein of an ultramarathon runner seconds acter completing a course, thrown in for good measure. If all that still fails to move your listener to the dizzy heights of basic human compassion, tell them you are in the midst of a nervous breakdown. I did that once, and instantly got a much more understanding response. And let’s face it, they are not a million miles apart, from everything I’ve read.
