question: How can I deal with feeling that I can’t talk freely with anyone about my feelings including psychologist and psychiatrist (autism, burnout, depression, jobless and close to being homeless)?

question: For those of you with autism, have you experienced autistic burnout? How long did it last and did you do anything to stop it or just let it run its course?
answer: For clarity, I’m going to distinguish between burnout and shutdown. Not everyone using these terms the same way, so here’s how I and folks I hang with use them: Shutdown is a temporary state which is triggered by immediate factors in our situation or environment. Many have described it as a meltdown turned inward — all that screaming and lashing out happen, just on the inside where you can’t see it. Like meltdown, shutdown typically only lasts for a few minutes, maybe half hour-hour max. Burnout is long term. Burnout isn’t the result of immediate factors, but of ongoing factors. For all I disagree with other parts of her answer, Celina Thommesen-Kähler is absolutely right that burnout is NOT depression. (I have had chronic depression (caused by B12 defeciency) and have bipolar disorder, the experience of depression is VERY distinct from that of burnout.) The longest I have been in burnout was nearly two years. Right now I’m approaching a month. What is burnout? Okay, I’m honestly not sure how comprehensible this will be to allistic folks, but I’ll try. Every autistic person is constantly doing mental ‘work’ every day to deal with stuff that allistics never even think about: coping with sensory shit, deciphering social and emotional cues, masking, forcing ourselves to speak when it doesn’t come naturally to us or navigating the world while non-verbal when folks expect you to be able to speak, controlling or restricting our not-socially-acceptable stims, etc Burnout is what happens when we do those things too hard for too long. It’s the mental equivalent of exercising too hard while not doing enough self care (ie, eating protien, warming up, etc) and ending up with a torn muscle or ligament. Not only can you no longer push yourself to that level, you can no longer do even your regular day-to-day stuff until the injury has time to heal. And because you can easily re-injure it if you aren’t careful, it can take a long fucking time to heal. When parents of autistic kids talk about their kid reverting or regressing, they are probably talking about burnout. Adults show the same symptoms, becoming nonverbal when they had been verbal, no longer able to care for ourselves, needing help go to the bathroom, resurgence of previously surpressed stims… obviously, it varies person to person. My highly burnout state is going to be another person’s best state, and my best state is going to be another autistic person’s highly burnout state, because it’s all relative to our normal and our capabilities.

question: Is burnout common among individuals with autism and their interests?

question: What is the difference between autistic burnout and ADHD burnout? I have both autism and ADHD so I’d like to know the differences whenever I get them.

When you get burnout, identify your specific needs and make changes in your lifestyle and environment so those needs can be met, rather than try to figure out whether a doctor or psychologist would put it into one box or the other.

question: Can people with Autism/Aspergers work as psychologists or therapists? Id love to but am worried of the emotional/communication overload. Do autistic therapists experience burnout? Meltdowns? Sensory overload/emotional overload from client's problems?

I think the nature of the job is emotionally draining for anyone whether autistic or not. That's why therapists that deal with depression often have to have long intervals to decompress. question: I was never really aware of my sensory intolerance to sunlight until I began to go through burnout and was in the process of receiving an autism diagnosis. Why is this?
answer: As kids many of us were faced with parents and adults in authority who DEMANDED we “behave”. Sensory intolerance wasn't something that they could relate to, so we inevitably taught ourselves to deeply and instinctively mask all manner of intolerances and discomforts to survive. The alternative would have been to deal with even more invalidation from all sides, but in most cases that was already extremely harsh/abusive on a daily basis. Autistic burnout involuntarily strips away so much of our ability to mask that long buried powerful sensitivities can re-emerge with a significant amount of surprise to us. If you're like me, you lived with chronic fatigue and depression for years or decades while masking far too much. Masking accounts for the fatigue, but all the buried pieces of ourselves seem to be where the depression originates. In theory, getting out a shovel and digging up all these missing buried pieces of ourselves is how we start to heal.

question: Is it common for adults with high-functioning autism to experience "burnouts" where their symptoms become more severe than normal? What could be the cause of these episodes?
answer: Yes, autistic burnout is not uncommon in high masking/ low support needs autistic people. Many autistic people with low support needs learn to suppress their autistic traits ( masking) in order to fit in and appear „normal“. Masking helps many to escape bullying but prevents them from getting the accommodations they need. An autistic person with higher support needs or without the ability to mask has a higher chance of being diagnosed and offered accommodations. Even a diagnosed masking person can be denied these accommodations. The lack of help can put a strain on a person’s mental health and become extremely exhausting. Additionally, masking itself is associated with depression, autistic burnout, anxiety and other things. The reason for that is that constantly monitoring your every word and action in order to not get labeled as „weird“ or „rude“ is incredibly energy consuming. During autistic burnout a person may lose their ability to mask, additionally their sensory issues may increase which could appear as their „symptoms“ becoming more severe. The later in life a person is diagnosed ,the later they are able to receive help. This is part of the reason so many low support needs autistic people deal with depression or burnout during their adult life or during adolescence.

question: Can autistic burnout be mistaken for depression by professionals? How might one distinguish between the two?
answer: Medical and psychology professionals (including autism specialists) are not necessarily aware of the “autism burnout” syndrome idea. So they are much more likely to diagnose a situation that can be described as “autism burnout” as depression (or something else like “vocational burnout”). “Autism burnout” as a concept is very poorly documented at present. In my opinion, the two aren’t mutually exclusive. As answerer William Isaacson says, depression is always a symptom of something else. It is likely that your “depression” is a symptom of “autism burnout” which is a consequence of having an ASD mind and an episode of cortisol overload (aka excessive stress). So a diagnosis of “depression” isn’t wrong, it’s just not nearly as helpful as other diagnoses would be. The best truth is the most useful. See https://www.seattlechildrens.org/globalassets/documents/health-and-safety/autism/autism_206_raymaker_slides.pdf for more information.

question: What does 'autistic burnout' really mean?
answer: When an autistic person is exposed to prolonged stress (which can be caused by camouflaging their autism, taking on more activities/commitments than they can handle, major life changes, etc.), the coping skills they have learned may no longer be enough to help them manage the stress of daily life. When this happens, the brain kind of "shuts down" and goes into emergency survival mode. Kind of like a city having a brown-out due to too much strain on its electrical resources. Autistic burnout can look a lot like a depressive episode, and it may or may not be accompanied by depression. Many people also report feeling or acting "more autistic." It can take years for a person to recover from a burnout, and they may never fully return to their former levels of executive functioning. I've been struggling with autistic burnout for about 3 years now. It majorly sucks and has affected my academic performance. I used to be a full-time student and part of my school's honors program, but now I can barely handle 1 or 2 classes per semester due to anxiety and struggling with time management and task initiation. I'm trying to be patient with myself, but it really is hard.

question: Why are women less likely to have an Autism diagnosis?
answer: Gender disparities exist in the identification of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), with females being consistently under-diagnosed compared to males. This discrepancy has been attributed to a variety of factors, including differences in symptom presentation, diagnostic criteria, and societal and cultural biases.One of the primary reasons for the gender disparity is that the diagnostic criteria for Autistic Spectrum Disorder (ASD) are based on male-centric characteristics. For instance, many of the classic symptoms of autism, such as difficulty with social interaction, narrow interests, and repetitive behaviors, may be more easily identifiable in males. As a result, females may not meet the diagnostic criteria for ASD, even though they have significant difficulties in social communication and interaction. Another reason for the under-diagnosis of females with ASD is that they may present with different symptom profiles than males. Females may be more likely to have better social communication skills and less severe repetitive behaviors, leading to a perception that they are "less autistic." For instance, some studies have suggested that girls with ASD may be more likely to have interests in animals or people, rather than inanimate objects or systems. Furthermore, there may be societal and cultural biases at play, as many clinicians and educators may not associate autism with females. As a result, females may be less likely to be referred for diagnostic assessment or may be misdiagnosed with other conditions, such as anxiety or depression.For example, a study conducted in the UK found that girls with autism were more likely to receive a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa or depression, and less likely to be diagnosed with autism, compared to boys. This is concerning because a delay in diagnosis can result in delayed access to appropriate services and interventions, which can impact long-term outcomes. It is therefore crucial to increase awareness of the gender disparities in autism diagnosis, improve diagnostic tools and criteria, and ensure that clinicians and educators are equipped to recognize the signs of autism in both males and females. Please note this is National Autism Awareness Month (April 2023).

question: What are the reasons behind the difference in diagnosis rates of high functioning autism between men and women?
answer: Well, the term ‘high functioning’ does have a few problems. The internet community assumes that means ‘genius.’ It does not. It means needs less support or help to get through simple activities of daily living. Since autism was redefined in 2012, the term ‘high functioning’ makes less sense than it did before, which was ‘not much sense.’ And as far as characterizing what might be considered to be high functioning autism in males vs females, studies are inconclusive, which means that every study you read says something different(and they often contradict each other) about what autism is like in females vs males. Usually this is because they are studying small groups of people and the way they recruit people isn’t consistent between the studies. They also may be measuring different end points or using different definitions for things. And studies prior to 2012 were using a very different definition of autism. With autism in general, there are people who say that autism was, and even still is, often missed in females. The research on that is so deficient that I can’t put a percentage on it(to be abundantly clear, the research on many aspects of autism is rather poor, especially when it comes to severe autism, as it is getting more and more common to exclude severely autistic people from research). However, we do have to be careful with this subject, as the criteria for autism has been markedly reduced/relaxed 12 years ago, so we should see some people getting diagnosed as adults because when they were children, the diagnostic criteria was much stricter. When we find women whose diagnosis was ‘missed’ in childhood, we may be looking at people who now qualify for the broader current diagnosis when they did not prior to the changes in the diagnosis. And there are other things going on. As an example, look at the RORA gene. This is a gene that’s often miscoded in autism. Funny thing is, it has an observably more severe effect on males than females. So there are actual differences between how this gene miscoding affects males vs females. And I think more such differences have been observed since I read that first study, which I would expect due to slight biological differences between males and females. Over the course of the past 50 years, I’ve definitely met more autistic males than females. Since I was initially doing respite care, it could be that fewer autistic females require respite care. Or it could be that they simply were not diagnosed. My female friend has a high IQ. She was(very legitimately) diagnosed with schizophrenia as an adult. She was also diagnosed with autism as an adult. She had not been diagnosed with autism as a child. When she told her father of her autism diagnosis, he said, ‘And here I always thought you were just an a******.’ Keep in mind this was BEFORE the loosening up of the autism diagnosis, not after. So, ignoring the change in autism diagnosis in 2012, are there women who were, or even still are, not diagnosed with autism because they have a high IQ? Let me put it this way. I was not diagnosed with kidney stones because I did not say the magic words: ‘flank pain.’ Because I didn’t have flank pain. And while I’ve only talked to a few women about this, all of them told me, ‘I didn’t have flank pain either! And it took a long time(and a lot of pain) to get diagnosed with kidney stones.’ People who do not fit the expected symptom pattern don’t get diagnosed promptly. That much I know. How many people with a high IQ are not diagnosed with autism when they should be? Can’t find anything definitive on that. Not a popular research topic.

question: If a child has a subtle form of autism, is it usually picked up through a public school system? Or do many on the spectrum slip through the cracks?
answer: When I saw this, I knew I had to answer it. A lot of people who have no understanding of how the system around diagnosing and supporting autistic people works. The truth is that so many people fall through the cracks. It’s quite common for autistic girls to slip through the cracks when they’re younger. We’re more likely to observe social skills from our peers, and while they aren’t complicated, it’s quite easy to go undiscovered. For me, the problems started when I hit puberty, at eleven years old. From what I’ve read from other autistic people—girls in particular—this is not uncommon. In the UK, this coincides with when girls go into secondary school. But wherever you live, the beginning of puberty is when social rules from your childhood go out of the window and things become far more complicated. You need to know how to discuss more complex subject matters. How do you feel about that boy? What that girl did was so stupid, right? What happened to the girl code? But we’re not judgemental, at all. It’s hard to understand the right way to answer that. A lot of it is about context, but I still got it wrong. As teenagers, autistic people’s fixations also become more obvious, because neurotypical people quickly move from one thing to the next because they want to fit in and follow the latest crazes. Guess what, though? I still fell under the cracks. Even after I left mainstream education because of my mental health, they didn’t detect that there might be something else at play, too. But I was lucky… I received my autism diagnosis when I was seventeen. In fact, it was three days after my seventeenth birthday. That’s a fact I like to tell people a lot. I don’t know if you’re asking this question because you’re curious whether you could have fallen through the cracks, or because you suspect a loved one might have, but there’s every chance this is the case. There’s stories of people who are many decades older than I am (I’m currently 20) receiving diagnosis’ after going through life knowing there was something wrong with them but not knowing what. It’s something that’s been prevalent in both genders in recent years, but females especially. In fact, some people have dubbed us ‘The Lost Generation of Women’ because we have been all but forgotten about in autism research for so long. If this is you, or someone you care about, I wrote this piece about whether getting an autism diagnosis is worth it. I’m sharing this in the hopes that it could help you, a loved one, or even a stranger who just so happens to come across this post. With that being said, I just wanted to add one more thing: If you feel like you could have grounds for an autism diagnosis—and you want to go for it—don’t be put off. You are perfectly entitled to find out as much, or as little, about your neurology as you desire, regardless of anything else going on in your life.

I wanted to talk to someone I trusted on that topic — a well-recommended specialist in ASD. I went back to my GP after I was diagnosed to get a referral for more services (help with misophonia). I could afford to pay for my own diagnosis without national health insurance (I would have needed the GP’s referral for that). Not everyone can do that.

question: As an adult, is it worth getting an autism diagnosis?
answer: As an adult, is it worth getting an autism diagnosis? There are pros and cons — it depends on how that pans out for the particular adult. Some examples of pros and cons are: CONS An autism diagnosis may affect the availability of certain careers, including police and armed forces, depending on your nationality and the policy in your location. An autism diagnosis may affect your health coverage depending on your health insurance scheme. An autism diagnosis may cause other people to view you differently (stigma) and may cause you to experience internalised stigma (feel bad about yourself). It is possible to deal with these negatives, but you should be aware of their possibility. An autism diagnosis might be too threatening for someone in denial about themselves. It might have negative consequences if forced upon them. An autism diagnosis might be too expensive or there might not be adequate, very experienced, professional resources available to perform a reliable diagnosis (especially for women). PROS An autism diagnosis may confirm your suspicions and remove uncertainty about yourself. An autism diagnosis may help you to develop a greater understanding of yourself, your strengths and weaknesses. It can change your whole concept of yourself, and lead you to be more natural (mask less) in your behaviour — which may help your mental health longer term. An autism diagnosis may help you feel part of the wider “actually autistic” community. You are not alone. An autism diagnosis may convince some other people that you are not “just making up” your differences — you really are different (inside your brain) and a professional has checked it out and confirmed it. An autism diagnosis may lead you to overcome stigma — both internalised and from other people. You may see people with other disabilities and disorders differently … i.e as fellow human beings rather than “strange” and “other”. CONCLUSION It is up to each adult to work out whether they want to be diagnosed — and when and why. Hopefully, if an adult is diagnosed, they will use it to develop greater knowledge of themselves and of other people, and it will help them grow as a person and be more true to themselves.

question: Is autism easier to diagnose in men and why?
answer: As a woman with Asperger’s, I can relate to the belief that women on the autism spectrum are invisible. In my job as a substitute teacher’s aide, I am often assigned to autism units. It didn’t take me long to realize that the overwhelming majority of students in these classes are male. Their behaviors are usually more visible than the few female students there are. In answer to the question of why are men more likely than women to have autistic traits, or receive a diagnosis of autism, Professor Simon Baron-Cohen, director of the Autism Research Centre who, along with PhD student Emily Ruzich, led the Cambridge/Channel 4 study. They found there’s a lot of research showing that testosterone changes brain development. Males on average produce more testosterone than females, even when in the womb, and the data shows that children with autism on average have higher levels of the hormone than typically developing kids. This backs up a 2009 study that looked into the prenatal testosterone levels of typical four-year-olds. “The higher the child’s prenatal testosterone, the more autistic traits they had,” says Professor Baron-Cohen. These findings suggest the critical factor may be hormone levels rather than gender, and could be pivotal to further understand the higher rates of autism diagnosis in men. But, as Professor Baron-Cohen points out, “It’s only one piece of the puzzle.” He adds: “The nature of science means one new finding opens up a hundred new questions.” Wendy Lawson, author of "Build Your Own Life: A Self-Help Guide For Individuals With Asperger Syndrome" and a self-described autistic woman, believes girls on the spectrum may be underdiagnosed because if they have obsessive interests (often a feature of spectrum disorders), these are more likely to be socially acceptable than the obsessions of boys with autism. Girls, she says, might get into reading or animals, which seem normal, "so people don't pick up on our social difficulties." Jennifer McIlwee Myers, who has Asperger's and is the author of "How to Teach Life Skills to Kids with Autism or Asperger's," concurs. She says boys on the spectrum are more likely to respond to their difficulties with anger and aggression, while girls are more likely to "deal with issues quietly," cultivating extreme "niceness" and imitating other girls' behavior. Boys who have the vision problems that sometimes go with autism spectrum disorders may hit other boys, she explains, while girls might instead cling to other girls. And a boy who attacks other kids is going to get intervention a lot faster than a girl who cries quietly every day. Myers says there are "a lot of invisible girls" who are autistic but never get help, because nobody notices. I can relate to trying to act like other people. It is about not making people mad and not being singled out as different — when they're diagnosed as adults, they have to build a whole identity from scratch. That’s what I am going through now at the age of 59. Finding out I was on the spectrum was like finding out the name of the street I had been living on for close to six decades.

question: Can someone with Aspergers fake normal on an autism test?
answer: Yes, sure, assuming they’re familiar with the symptoms and are smart enough to catch any questions that are repeated with different phrasing to catch people who are falsifying answers. Since I always notice the repeated questions and would be answering systematically even if I couldn’t, I could make the diagnostic tests come out any way I wanted. Really, the questions are typically pretty obvious. For example, here are the first five questions from the AQ test, a screening instrument: 1 I prefer to do things with others rather than on my own. 2 I prefer to do things the same way over and over again. 3 If I try to imagine something, I find it very easy to create a picture in my mind. 4 I frequently get so strongly absorbed in one thing that I lose sight of other things. 5 I often notice small sounds when others do not. Anyone familiar with Asperger’s knows that Aspies tend to be loners, like to stick to routines, focus strongly on special interests, have unusually acute senses, etc. Hell, we live it as well as know it. It would be easy to “fool” the test by giving the answers that an Aspie would be least likely to give and you wouldn’t have to guess right all of the time, since there’s overlap between autistic and non-autistic traits. An Aspie would actually be less likely to fool an expert in autism in person, since they’re very familiar with the cues that point to Asperger’s — hesitation in speech, lack of eye contact, unusual posture, speaking in a monotone or with exaggerated intonation, poor coordination, etc. Observation by an expert familiar with these signs from numerous interactions with autistic people is an important part of autism diagnosis and I’ve read some experts say that after a time they can spot an Aspie a mile away. However, Aspies cover a wide range, with some showing obvious signs and others just subtle ones. And, as you point out, we Aspies tend to become more adept at emulating neurotypicals as we age. Women in particular are good at mastering neurotypical behaviors, and it makes them harder to diagnose. That said, what purpose would fooling the psychiatrist serve? Accurate diagnosis serves the patient, not the shrink.

The only people who can diagnose you with autism are those who are specicially qualified to and they know a lot about autism so they’re unlikely to give a diagnosis unless they’re really confident. question: How do you get a diagnosis of high functioning autism in a girl?

question: Why does there seem to be so much autism being diagnosed these days?
answer: The diagnostic criteria for autism was way different than it was about several decades ago. It’s just that the high support needs autistics were at first diagnosed and put in institutions and before they were labeled, they were considered “idiots” or “retarded” while the low support needs autistics slipped under the radar and were considered “weird”, “annoying”, “creepy”, “childish”. Back in the early 20th century, when autism was discovered, it was originally applied to high support needs people, the ones who couldn’t live independently, the ones who were nonspeaking, the one who were put in asylums, and the one who probably had low IQ test scores (does not necessarily equate to lower actual intelligence). It was even once considered to be another branch of schizophrenia as in “childhood schizophrenia”. Later on, somewhere in the 1980s, asylums and institutions were shut down, so more people who were originally diagnosed as “mentally retarded” at that time, some of them turned out to be autistic. Furthermore, in the 1980s to the 1990s, the autism spectrum was further expanded to include people who were speaking, those who could probably live independently, and the ones who scored higher on IQ tests (does not necessarily equate to higher actual intelligence). Then, in 2013, the diagnostic criteria was even further expanded as diagnoses of Asperger’s syndrome and PDD-NOS were lumped together into ASD diagnoses, making the autism diagnosis rate even bigger. As of today, even though the autism diagnosis criteria hasn’t changed since 2013, what’s also making the autism diagnosis rate higher is when more adults, women, and POC are getting diagnosed with autism due to the fact that autism may look different in those types of people, but it’s still autism nonetheless. More to add, autism rates are “increasing” not because they’re actually increasing. It’s the diagnosis rate that is increasing. Actual autism rates are not the same as diagnosis rates. Diagnosis is basically an estimation of what conditions a person has. As an analogy to the previous paragraph, diagnosis of health conditions in people is basically akin to the carbon dating of artifacts and fossils. Neither of these actions are perfect. It’s all just an educated, significant guess. Even more to add, autism has been proven countless numbers of times that it’s not caused by vaccines, gut biomes, diets, pollution, or many types of environmental factors. The cause of autism is actually unknown, but according to many certified, verified research done around the world, it’s said to be 92% genetic, even more than height! In conclusion to all of this, autism diagnosis rates are getting higher because of significant changes in the diagnostic criteria throughout history and more research and services done for autistic people. As a side effect, it also led to less stigma and more people disclosing and being open about it, urging more people to get diagnosed.

But X did not understand context and did all of this out of time, until her peers began to move away from X. They said she was boring and it made her feel a weirdo again. At this age, she began to be interested in boys, but didn’t know how to flirt. Sometimes she kept staring at them. She also didn't know when she was being flirted with. If no one spoke, no matter what clues the boy gave, she didn't realise he was interested. So X was the only one in her class who hadn't kissed a boy. She felt that something was wrong, thought she must be ugly, but she wasn't. [issues interpreting nonverbal communication] X felt lonely, ugly and like a weirdo. She didn't understand how a fast learner who got good grades at school and was called smart could not know how to behave in social situations. Feeling so out of place, she began to change each of her characteristics, including how she ate. Before, she always ate little, but now she forced herself to eat a lot. She gained weight, felt awful, and then went on a diet to lose weight. She lost weight and the sense of control the diet gave her made her feel powerful. She lost an absurd amount of weight and was diagnosed with anorexia. The psychiatrist also diagnosed depression and X started taking medications. [comorbidities] The treatment was not easy, but it helped a little. X returned to a healthy weight. But she still didn't feel normal. She didn't like the noise, the smell, and the crowds at parties her friends always wanted to go to. She didn't like talking on the phone because she never knew when it was her turn to talk, and also because she felt the phone interrupted important activities. She didn't like to break routine or do things when on the go. She felt she could better absorb what a person said if she didn't look into their eyes, but she learned to notice the color of people's eyes so she could make a habit of looking. She didn't like the habit of giving kisses and hugs when greeting, unless it was from a very dear person. She never learned to wear high heels or skirts. She tried several times and felt bad for not succeeding. [auditory, olfactory, tactile, visual hypersensitivity, communication problems, attachment to routine] X started a relationship and as she and her boyfriend got closer, he pointed out some flaws: "You don't understand context. Look into my eyes, not my hands. Didn't you realize that person didn't like what you said? Why do you always want to do the same things?" At work some people commented that she was laconic, had a restricted diet, always seemed calm and wore comfortable clothes that were too loose or too sporty for work. She wrote on her social network profile: "I must be an alien." [In addition to previous problems, difficulty in looking into eyes, monotone voice] Feeling so different and backwards in social situations, X began to become very discouraged. She felt that her boyfriend deserved someone better, that her parents were not proud of her, and that maybe she was too dumb, since she was an adult and unable to figure out how to relate to people. She wanted to be alone and sometimes thought of dying. [depression, suicidal thoughts]Until, in the midst of a crisis in which she isolated herself, she searched for answers on the Internet. She found a text about high functioning autism, written by an autist[1] and identified herself with the characteristics described in the text. Then she tried to meet other people on the autism spectrum and saw that many of the difficulties she had, these people also had. She didn't feel dumb, late or stupid anymore- after all, she was just different. That helped in her self-acceptance. X made an appointment with a psychologist and the doctor explained that autism is underdiagnosed in women and that not diagnosing it can lead to other disorders such as anorexia, depression, OCD, etc. So yes, high functioning autistic people are capable of accomplishing a lot in life, but their lives can be of very poor quality because without the diagnosis, it is very likely that their psychological health is jeopardized.The images are from the book The Invisible Difference, which tells a similar story of a woman diagnosed with autism when she was already an adult.[Sorry if my answer has any English mistakes, I am accepting editing suggestions]

question: Why aren't girls with autism diagnosed during the same age range that most boys are?
answer: Masking is the reason for this, where autistic people make an effort to blend in with neurotypicals and it can become unconscious. It covers any signs of autism and girls are particularly good at it because they naturally (unconsciously) try to blend with social norms and groups more than boys do because it’s ingrained in us to fit in. This is why girls/women go under the radar and tend to be diagnosed later in life (20s, 30s, 40s) where it’s a lot more difficult to get a diagnosis then, while boys are more likely to get a diagnosis in early childhood as it’s more noticeable.

question: What are some barriers between two autistic people if they want to potentially date? I know autism in women and men are different.

When I tried to feed the information through my learned circuits, I failed to understad what I read. He didn’t make sense. He didn’t fit with anything I knew about people. question: Why have diagnoses of ADHD and autism surged?
answer: For a number of reasons. First of all the disgnotic criteria for autism has changed over the years to become more inclusive. The Autism diagnosis itself has only been around since the 1980s and was primarily based on male autistic people and their social expression. Since awareness is only gradually increasing and at the time the autism diagnosis was created only cases that were very visible were considered for a diagnosis, a lot of people who are now adults went undiagnosed and have had possibly neurodivergent children. Now that there are more resources available -both information on autism for parents and doctors and screening for young children as well as clinicians that are able to diagnose autism - a lot of people are getting diagnosed these days. Also for example autism and adhd used to be mutually exclusive and how different conditions interacted and presented themselves together often meant these individuals were less likely to get diagnosed. Minorities and Women could also often not be diagnosed because they did not exibit behaviours typically shown by male autistic people, whoch the origibal diagnosis was based on. Since they could not be reliably diagnosed, a large number of autistic people were not included in any statistics on the prevalence of autism are now able to be diagnosed. 20 or even 10 years ago, I probably couldn't have been diagnosed with autism because clinicians weren't aware of how autism presents itsself for different people. My own parents didn't pay enough attention and weren't informed enough to figure out I was autistic, despite my struggles. Only because things are getting better doesn't mean everyone affected or who is a legal guardian is aware of how autism presents itsself and there is a lot of misinformation on the internet on autism - mainly written by non-autistic individuals - that gives an unrealistic stereotypical view of autism that prevents people from being recognized or supported. Also, the possibilities of getting diagnosed are getting better, but there is still a large discrepancy between the amount of people seeking a diagnosis and the number of clinician available for diagnosis. Similar to people seeking therapeutic help but therapists being overrun with patients. Depending on where you live and where you go for an autism diagnosis, a number of things can prevent you from being diagnosed. The process of being doagnosed can be very expensive, very far away from where you live or the clinicians may not be trained to diagnose you if they are not recently trained and you are part of a minority. The average time from initial research to going through the process of being diagnosed for adults is 1 - 2 for men and 2 - 3 years for women and minorities. For me it was two years. An Autism diagnosis is often very thorough and personal, involving a lot of questions about social and environmental responses and behaviors, often involuntary behaviors or understandings that are unique to autism. People who are self diagnosed are recognized among the autistic community for the most part, because of the many hoops you have to jump through to even be able to be evaluated for diagnosis if you weren't lucky enough to be diagnosed as a child. Autistic people who are self-diagnosed often show very visible autistic traits in the way they familiarize themselves with autism - often the long waiting periods leading up to a diagnosis are filled with intense research and immersing themselves and relating the experiences of autistic people. And these people may be recognized by the autistic community, but are also not present in any statistics on the prevalence of autism. So in conclusion, less people are excluded in the clinical definition of autism and clinicians are trained to be able to diagnose different groups of people that were previously excluded. Also there is more information on and awareness for autism these days, so people that were overlooked can recognize they are autistic and get diagnosed as adults or recognize ot in their kids and get themselves and their kids evaluated for autism. Also there are more clinicians trained to recognize autism and more possibilities to get diagnosed. Still, people have to wait, often for years, to get diagnosed and the clinicians are overloaded with work. Since the current state and availability of diagnostic procedures and clinicians is still not ideal, so I assume a lot more people will be getting diagnosed in the next decades. Which I think is a good thing, but I chose to be diagnosed as an adult to feel validated in my struggles and become a member of a protected class to enforce my rights on equal treatment in the workplace and receive more support with daily activities. I feel like it's sad that autistic people are often disabled by how the environment they are put is are not made for them and how they are expected to go against their wishes and cross their boundaries to avoid being targeted or harmed by neurotypicals. I personally like my autism, my meticulous perfectionist completionist hyperfocusing brain, even if it gives me meltdowns and sensory issues at times. I would prefer to be called specially abled, because I am actively bad at very basic human things but my performance compared to my peers stands out in the areas I excell at and I feel like focusing on the less or disabled parts of my autism does a disservice to autism, which can be very uniquely enabling.

question: How can Asperger's syndrome be lifelong?
answer: Aspergers, now reclassified under Autism Spectrum Disorder - Level One, is ‘lifelong’ by virtue of being a neurological condition you are born with. Despite being defined by certain diagnostic criteria, including fixed interests, social difficulties and no delay in language and cognitive development, it is complex due to nuances in each individual and the fact that there is still so much to be learnt. People are being diagnosed in different stages of their lives, from childhood to adult, and it is probably fair to say that there are individuals who could have easily been diagnosed, but have ‘slipped the net’, due to there being a lack of awareness in earlier times. I am part of this group who were diagnosed later in life. Extensive testing with much documentation from earlier years was used to confirm what I had only wondered about in recent years. Over time, it is possible that some peoples’ symptoms can fluctuate in intensity, and it is also possible some people develop strategies to help them overcome some of their characteristics, such as by adaptation as they have gotten older. This might be responsible for people thinking someone is ‘cured’ of autism. There is also some evidence now that suggests particularly in women, that a level of ‘masking’ can occur, which means that diagnosis for some females is made harder because their symptoms are somewhat disguised. It is not to say that men don’t experience some of these symptoms as well, but in a context of earlier times, it is possible that some women were not picked up in childhood, due to different socialisation experiences, and being able to more successfully observe and mimic neurotypical social behaviour. Differing stages of the life cycle, or stress may mean that certain characteristics of individuals may fluctuate in intensity. As a child and teenager, the pitch and volume of certain sounds would have me clamping my hands to my ears in agony. Over the years, I seemed to have developed less sensitivity to a lot of them. Now I am in my fifties, and my job has become much more stressful, I find myself once again, very hypersensitive to noise, and made very anxious by it. So aspergers is certainly lifelong, by virtue of what of what it is, and beyond that, how it manifests in each of us may be affected by quite a lot of variables.

question: I share all autistic traits except sensory overload, but I don't share them to the same degree autistic people do. I'm also female. Could I possibly be autistic or do I just share autistic traits?

question: What's it like to be a woman with Aspergers?
answer: The traits by which diagnosis is made are the same for both genders. However, although there are multiple presentations so no single person is the same as any other, there are distinct patterns of presentation according to gender and the diagnostic signs in both ICD10 and DSMV are biased towards the male presentation - hence the paucity of females with diagnosis compared to males. I'm hoping the update to ICD10 in the coming year will do something more to rectify this than DSM did (ICD10 is more flexible anyway). Girls tend to be better at social skills generally and, because they learn by observation in a way that males on the spectrum don't seem able to do with quite the same proficiency, they tend to stand out less as socially awkward appearing more naive than lacking in skills. They tend to be more responsive to emotion and mood than their male counterparts. Their specific interests can be very fixed and intense but they tend to be things other girls like too - like animals or make-up or art or fashion. Women on the spectrum are particularly good at masking their social inadequacies and sensitivities, only when you probe do you realise that they have learned their skills through long analysis and observation - some have remarkable analytical skills for emotionally sensitive data and they can make very good counselors and mental health workers. Recent studies have suggested that anorexia may be part of, or an alternative presentation of, autism in women. The focus on the body becomes an obsession and leads to behaviours which are very similar to those of autistic people.

question: Is it worth it to be formally diagnosed with aspergers/autism as a teenager or adult?
answer: (I am assuming this question is about the questioner being diagnosed) A diagnosis may be useful if you want an objective opinion or confirmation that you are on the spectrum. It may be useful if you want other psychological services (e.g. marriage counselling, Cognitive Behaviour Therapy, etc) as these may need to be adjusted if they are to apply to someone diagnosed on the spectrum. It may not be worth it if you lose your health insurance as a result, or lose your job (a possibility, I gather, if you are in the American armed forces). It may not be worth it if there are no specialists in your area who are familiar with autism spectrum disorders, and especially its presentation in adults (or more particularly in women if you are a woman). It may not be worth it if it will cost you a large amount of money that you cannot afford. It all depends on your circumstances whether it will be worth it.

question: Can it happen that a good expert team misdiagnose a teen with Asperger’s (observations, interviews, tests are done)?
answer: A diagnosis of Asperger’s wouldn’t happen today. Because in the DSM-V, the standard for diagnosis of mental health and psychiatric disorders, there is no Asperger’s syndrome. That diagnosis was combined with the autism spectrum disorder in the DSM-V. So the diagnosis one would receive is actually Autism Spectrum disorder level one most likely, as that is the established equivalent to Asperger’s. So, can an autism diagnosis be wrong? Studies suggest that misdiagnosis rates for autism may range from 10% to 30%, though this depends on the population studied. Misdiagnosis is more common in cases where co-occurring conditions (e.g., ADHD, anxiety, sensory processing disorders) mimic or overlap with ASD symptoms. Autism is underdiagnosed in women and minorities, and individuals with ASD1 are likely underdiagnosed as their symptoms may or may not be severe enough to prod them to even seek a diagnosis in the first place. It’s actually significantly more likely that an autism diagnosis is missed and somebody is diagnosed with a comorbid condition first! I wasn’t diagnosed autistic until I was 13 or so. Up to that point I had been diagnosed with BPD, bipolar disorder, anxiety, ADHD, ODD, OCD, and probably more that I don’t remember. Let’s break that down. The bipolar disorder, my shrink and therapist agree, was a likely misdiagnosis. The BPD? That’s a known misdiagnosis for autism, especially in women! My shrink doesn’t agree with it, but my therapist definitely sees how I could be both BPD and autistic. So for now, both are in my chart. Anxiety, ADHD, ODD, OCD? Those are all right on the money. I have a lot of symptom overlap in my life and sometimes I can explain where a specific symptom is coming from, but other times I really can’t because it is a symptom that goes with multiple conditions. I also have PTSD, which can present with symptom overlap with autism as well. Autism misdiagnosis IS possible, but it’s not highly likely. A2A

question: When someone has Asperger's syndrome, is it obvious to other people?
answer: As with everything related to autism, the autistic traits associated with Asperger’s lie on a spectrum. I believe this is probably why Asperger’s is no longer an official diagnosis; in DSM-5, it is bundled with other Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) and is often referred to as “high functioning autism (HFA)” (Aspergers & DSM-5). Some people may have more obvious autistic traits and still be high functioning while others may have less obvious traits or be better at hiding them. It also seems as if girls are often better at hiding their autistic traits than boys (Girls and women who have Asperger's). Traditionally, people don’t tend to look for autism in girls. When a girl displays traits associated with Asperger’s, people around her may assume that she is simply shy. Tony Attwood, a specialist in Asperger’s, also points out that Aspergirls (Aspergirls: Empowering Females with Asperger Syndrome - an excellent book about girls with HFA) are often better at mimicking behavior than boys, so they are able to blend in more easily. This may be why many adult women on the spectrum may not know that they have Asperger’s traits themselves, let alone it being obvious to others. When boys display these traits, it seems that it is more likely that people will notice and investigate the possibility of an autism spectrum disorder. Still, some boys are likely just as good as blending in and it will certainly not be obvious to others that they have Asperger’s.

question: Why are there more men with Asperger's than women?
answer: People with autism have always been underdiagnosed. This is not just women, this is higher functioning men as well. Many general practitioners, and even psychologists that aren’t specialized in autism, buy into the same myths as the public does, which is understandable. Autism has very many different forms, not all of which are obvious, and someone who hasn’t had specialized training won’t recognize all of them. Add to this that autism is a diagnosis which is still very much being researched and defined. Now, how does this tie into not many women being diagnosed with autism? One of the main criteria - and really the only one that will set off the alarm bells of people who don’t understand autism - is not having social skills. Not making eye contact, et cetera. Women are naturally better at this than men are, and so are women with autism. They tend to for example, make eye contact anyway, but at the end of the day they are so tired from it they might have an outburst. These women might instead be diagnosed as borderline. Others might avoid contact completely, and get a social phobia or avoidant PD diagnosis. (Yes, I had both.) In short, autism in women is less explicit - they try to hide it and get “higher level” problems instead. And doctors think it is a diagnosis for boys. I recently moved, and when I went to meet my new general practitioner for the first time I told him I was autistic. He laughed and he said he didn’t think so. Doctors buy into stereotypes as well. And I need to find a new one. Luckily, awareness of autism is increasing. After getting both of the aforementioned wrong diagnosis, I was diagnosed with autism at age 19, after spending a decade of my youth in intensive therapy for problems I did not have. Because of the recent advances in autism awareness (the good advances, not the misinformation) many girls will not have to go through what I went.

question: How do I explain to people that I have autistic traits when I'm not even sure I have autism?

We tend to hyperfocus, rather than having difficulty focusing on one thing. It sounds to me like you may have another condition, like ADHD, which would be consistent with difficulty focusing. But it’s impossible to rule out autism or reach a conclusion on the basis of a brief comment, and symptoms are often less obvious in women than they are in men. What you should do is take the AQ test, available free online. If you have a score of 28 or above, you may be on the spectrum and should seek a professional diagnosis from an expert in autism (the AQ test is just a screening instrument). The Aspie Quiz and RAADS-R can be informative as well. You might also consider the BAP test. It tests for broader autism phenotype, which is essentially very mild, sub-clinical autism and is common in the relatives of autistic people. Unfortunately, the online version isn’t very good.

question: Is there evidence that autism is a new form of intelligence for a new world?
answer: No. The problem with this idea is that it suggest that autism is new, and that it improves the chances of one’s genes being passed on to the next generations. Autism might be a new diagnosis, but there is no evidence that it is a new condition; rather, it is something that was not considered until we became wealthy enough to consider why these individuals are ‘weird’. There have been post hoc ‘diagnoses’ of many famous figures in history, from Albert Einstein to Isaac Newton to Hans Christian Anderson. In the modern world, autism diagnosis rates vary from rich to poor countries - with the rich countries accounting for the highest proportion of diagnoses. More broadly in history and pre-history, we know there have always been people who are considered eccentric, or ‘touched by God’, or indeed witches or possessed - simply because they did not understand the world around them in the same way as their peers. Of course, many probably also became priests, medicine men/women, and took other highly respected roles on the outskirts of ‘normal’ in their societies. Am I saying that these were all autistic? Absolutely not - but some of them probably were. Even in the twentieth century, before the diagnosis and management of autism spectrum disorders became common, families sometimes had the child who ‘never went out, never left home’. There are modern descendants of these families who have been diagnosed with autism and can recognise what happened to their aunt or uncle! Next to the evolutionary question, and I’ll be relatively brief. Does being on the autism spectrum mean that one is more likely to pass genes on to a new generation? Absolutely not! When you don’t even understand the rules of social behaviour, getting a date becomes extremely difficult and consummating a relationship is sometimes something that someone on the spectrum will never have an opportunity to do. So no, it is not an evolutionary advantage to be autistic. It may be an advantage in some ways in the ‘here and now’, but genes don’t care about that.

question: Can autistic people go on dates with neurotypical people?
answer: People capable of making deep human connections should take them wherever they find them. I've been married for 30+ years to a neurotypical woman and our relationship continues to grow over time. Had I believed when we met that there was some prohibition against dating an NT person I'd have overlooked the love of my life. Part of the problem is a persistent narrative that frames autism as a defect or deficiency rather than a difference. It says "take a normal person and remove social skills and empathy to get an autistic." (It's wrong both in the framing and in the traits specified, by the way.) In that context the question "Can autistic people go on dates with neurotypical people?" implies there is some particular hardship or mismatch there. It assumes all the normal relationship issues with the extra weight of autistic baggage thrown on. I prefer to frame autism as a mixed bag of gifts and deficits. Rather than assume that an autistic person is less, I start with the assumption that everyone's gifts and deficits tend to balance out. The result is a default presumption that we are all equally capable and equally handicapped on average, but with gifts and deficits distributed differently. Naturally there are people in whom the net is more positive or more negative and my model accounts for that, but by starting with the assumption that we all cluster around a median baseline we avoid the mental trap of assuming an entire class of people are automatically less than "normal." In practice my wife puts up with my annoying quirks because there are lots of other quirks that entertain or fascinate her. For example, she "gets" my offbeat and dark sense of humor. She appreciates my honesty, loyalty, and compassion. She likes that we like different things and learn from each other. For her these more than offset my obsessive compulsive traits, my lack of conversational filters, my failure to read her body language that forces her to explain things she thinks should be obvious. But doesn't that describe any relationship? For that matter, doesn't it describe every relationship?

question: What is it like being married to someone with autism?

I’ve been in a relationship with an autistic man and while I believe he can be the kindest, smartest, most generous man I know and I have very deep compassion for his struggles, I had to choose myself and walk away from the relationship before I turned into an emotional wreck. For me, biggest issue by far was communication, in two ways: 1) he didn’t maintain any connection aside from regular check-ins that became more and more generic over time which led me to feel increasingly lonely, 2) he could not handle disagreements and conflict communication in a healthy way. I understand that his brain is wired differently and we would have had to work things out, share our worlds and talk things through. But every time I would bring something up I would be met with a wall of silence and ignoring or the same frustrating pattern: telling me I was wrong, denial, trying to redirect the conversation to my flaws (that I would happily hear about but another time if they were not related to the topic), playing the victim, telling me to leave and punishing me. Once I manage to run this gauntlet and if wasn’t completely exhausted and sad, we would manage to have a constructive conversation. He would also never initiate anything - all needed to come from me. The other issue was that within days of moving in together, he stopped contributing to the day to day tasks that we decided to split. I had become the cook, the maid, the driver, the mistress, the activities planner, he even gave me all his documents to keep and carry around. He woukd walk around happy being taken care of and I would be knackered from shouldering everything. It became exhausting quite quickly as on top of giving me all responsibility he would punish me for everything that didn’t run as he planned - snarkiness, ignoring, silent treatments, verbal slams, … If I called him out on it - see above point about communication. He was increasingly forgetful and self-focused. He would promise to do activities with me only to forget we ever talked about them. He would not show up for our commitments. He would forget everything from keys, wallet, … and I felt like a mother trying to make sure we had everything we needed - because if I didn’t it would have completely destroyed our plans. Any reminders had to be done with the sweetest tone of voice and facial expression or else he would be offended and sulk or ignore me. It was a gamble mentioning anything - he could be open and accept feedback or he could scream, insult, sulk - in a few months of living together I couldn’t see a pattern to help me chose a response. He refused to talk about his autism. I read up on it all I could and wanted to talk about it. He wouldn’t. He wouldn’t educate himself on it. He said he didn’t want to give himself an alibi for what he did. But he also didn’t recognize some behaviors that were different than what is considered normal. He had his strict routines and habits and even with enough notice he would sulk if broken. We once went on a day trip we needed to start very early vs his regular getting up time. We talked about it, he agreed to it, I reminded him the night before, but he still sulked and dragged his feet in the morning. He couldn’t think of anyone but himself unless he was fed, healthy, well rested, calm, happy. So, he would be mean, self-centered, unable to look out for me, even in bed. The worst feeling was that in the beginning none of this happened. He was the man I could see myself getting old with. But with time everything changed. All in all, the time with him was a learning experience. I learned a lot about a world I never knew existed and I was with a good man. But I also became exhausted, depressed, anxious, the most lonely I’ve ever been and I didn’t feel safe, cherished or respected in the relationship. I couldn’t trust him to look out for me. So I had to do it by leaving. It still hurts to have left this smart, funny, kind man. But I couldn’t make it work with unhealthy communication and denial about our differences.

question: Are autistic kids dyslexic too?
answer: The original question: “Are Autism and Dyslexia linked?” Not really, or not as much as other neuro-developmental disorders are “linked” to each other. Neuro-developmental disorders[1] often come in packs, if you have one, you are likely to have another, and are more likely to have another one then someone in the general or complete population is likely to have even just one. But certain neuro-developmental disorders appear more often together then others appear together. Autism often causes reading problems, but the reading problems it often causes are generally different than the reading problems dyslexia causes. Both disorders often see lower reading comprehension scores, but lower decoding[2] skills, which is generally found in dyslexics and one of it’s most prominent features, isn’t typically seen in autism, or not really abnormally often, more often the opposite is seen. What is often found in Autistic people is hyperlexia. Hyperlexics are very good at decoding, though often (though not necessarily) have reading comprehension problems. So, in a nutshell, autism often has co-morbid reading problems, but those reading problems are generally not dyslexia. I am not saying you can’t have dyslexia and autism, they do appear together sometimes, but if they are “linked”, it isn’t a strong link.Explanation of a few things, such as terms and whatnot [1] Neuro-Developmental disorders are disorders in cognition or behavior that arise in the early developmental stage. In no particular order, such disorders include, but are not limited to: learning disorders, intellectual impairment, autism spectrum disorders, attention, and behavioral disorders. [2] Decoding means, essentially, sounding out words. Decoding is what the process of rapidly and accurately assigning speech sounds to printed letters is called. It is important to note that though neuro-developmental disorder s often co-occur with each other, they are separate disorders. (I understand “linked” as meaning having one increases your chances significantly for having the other, not as meaning they are the same disorder, because obviously, they aren’t)

question: Is there a correlation/connection between autism and obsessive-compulsive disorder?
answer: You may be confused because OCD and Autism are both characterized by repetitive behaviours. However, the difference is in their source. The underlying cause of OCD is usually anxiety. In fact in earlier editions of DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 5th ed) OCD was included under Anxiety disorders. The underlying cause of Autism is a neurodevelopmental abnormality with predominant language and communication impairments. OCD is not associated with any language impairment. There are biological differences too. Moreover, the onset, that is the time when the symptoms first manifest are different for both. OCD is more likely to be diagnosed in adults. Autism can be detected by 2–3 yrs i.e, it has a childhood onset. Prenatal detection is also possible, but perhaps with diminished accuracy. OCD is triggered off by a stressful event. OCD also responds to CBT (Cognitive Behaviour Therapy). Although available genetic data show a significant inheritable trend for both, OCD is more contaminated by cultural and environmental factors than Autism. I could go on but I think the difference is clear.

question: Are autistic people capable of getting feelings for other people?
answer: Absolutely! Just because many of us struggle with the finer nuances of “normal” social interaction doesn’t mean that we are wholly uninterested in it, or that we are unable to engage in and enjoy the benefits of relationships—either platonic or romantic—when desired. That many of us appear outwardly asocial or aloof is often (though not always) misleading; it has as much to do with the fact that it’s difficult to find others with similar interests and priorities as it does with the intentional avoidance of group-based social situations in favour of one-on-one or online interaction, which don’t seem to be as highly valued in terms of social status and success. Personally, I am fairly introverted, and I find group-based social situations to be draining and sometimes overwhelming. However, while I find initially making friends and forming singular relationships to be difficult and often very anxiety-inducing as well, there are a number of friendships I do my best to cultivate and maintain, and which I value as deeply as if they were my family by blood. Perhaps even more so, as I am not particularly close with a good portion of my extended family for reasons unrelated to my autism. I may not be able to easily express it, at least in the same way as other people do, but I feel things like affection, companionship, love, loneliness, and even the desire for emotional and physical intimacy very deeply and earnestly. This, which is often overlooked and yet so very important, is not an unusual thing for autistic people, especially those on the stronger side of the empathy scale. The external expression may not be the same, but how we feel inside is. One major way in which we seem to differ, in terms of how we view and approach relationships, is that Internet-based friendships are often taken every bit as seriously as face-to-face ones. Poke around autistic-friendly spaces online, and you may find that both romantic and platonic relationships that allow for text-based as well as verbal communication are much likelier to initiate and then blossom when an autistic person is involved than amongst our more socially adept neurotypical kin. Most of us, both verbal and nonverbal, generally find it much easier to communicate with the full range of expression and detail in a text-based format than with spoken-word-only communication. If you win one of us over as a friend or partner, we might be a bit more difficult to understand at first, but you will gain an unusually loyal and forgiving friend and, potentially fierce advocate after their trust has been placed in you. Lose that trust, though, and you may find it difficult or even impossible to gain back. Sometimes, the only communication might be playing a game together, or pings on a Discord server, or maybe a handful of silly memes dropped into a private message, but how is that really any different than, say, sitting on the sofa with your buddy and watching something without actually engaging in much conversation? You enjoy simply being around them, even if there’s nothing particularly exciting happening. In short—our meaningful relationships may not look quite like yours, but they are just as valued and important to us as yours are to you.

question: Do autistic people ever get married? What are relationships like with high functioning individuals with autism?
answer: Yes, they do! And it’s not that uncommon. There’s a book called Asperger’s in Love by Maxine Aston that looks specifically at this question, and will go far more into detail than I could go into here. Her work is based much more on clinical experience, so it’s not especially as data driven. But it has some very interesting insights as to the challenges and benefits that an autism/neurotypical relationship can provide. There can be real problems with differences in communication. Neurotypical partners can sometimes see their partner as being cold, aloof and overly blunt. Autistic partners can sometimes be oblivious to things they have done wrong until it’s pointed out angrily to them, at which point they can feel really guilty and confused. I heard this very touching story of a neurotypical woman who was really upset that her autistic husband didn’t take off work to pick her up from the hospital after surgery. He didn’t feel comfortable asking his boss to take off work to get the time to do it, not recognizing that it was probably the sort of thing an employer would understand. (I can relate to this part of the story in so many different ways.) So when his wife was (quite understandably) upset that her husband had done this, and she challenged him and she wasn’t getting him to talk. To her this came off as cold and unrecognizing of her pain or predicament. Later that evening, when she asked why he wasn’t talking, he broke down in tears in front of her and said that he was so sorry and he didn’t feel that words were enough to adequately express how naive and bad his mistake was. That helped them understand each other. That just about sums up the challenges, but also shows some of the characteristics these relationships can have. I have heard divorce rates are higher than neurotypical relationships, which does go to show they can be difficult. But they can also be very rewarding relationships if the two people can negotiate a balance. :) EDIT: I know Aston is controversial within the self-advocacy community in particular for her coining the term Cassandra syndrome. I don’t like this term or idea either. But despite the controversy, there are interesting insights in her work that I thought were relevant here. But she is someone who should be handled with care.

question: What is the relationship between autism and daydreaming?
answer: As a person with an ASD, you’re more likely to daydream simply for the lack of peers who you would have a great time with. Things you might dream about can either be unrealistic or very unlikely to happen. Usually those dreams are “I wish things went my way” type of thing. As a habit, it can even become worse, as you get older and discover numerous obstacles in a path you thought would be simple. A term maladaptive daydreaming might describe this well, though I wouldn’t make further assumptions since I’m not a psychologist. Nevertheless, being different has its challenges, whether they were related to having too little solitude or not finding anybody to hang out with. But one fact must always be emphasized: when you’ve met one person with an ASD, you’ve only met one person. Daydreaming, when it can be considered constant and harmful to one’s career, should be treated as a symptom.

question: As someone with autism, are you happier in a relationship with another autistic person, or with a neurotypical?
answer: I’m currently married to an NT guy but my last long term relationship was with an aspie for 5 years, but of course this is a very personal experience. NT’s are a very diverse group and so are the neurodiverse, so other experiences will vary. My relationship with my aspie boyfriend had a lot of upsides. I felt like he understood me from the very beginning, which was a nice change from the friendships and relationships I’d had my entire life. He seemed to understand my hypersensitivities, emotional reactions, meltdowns, shutdowns, and he shared my obsessive passions with similar things (the TV show Arrested Development, the music of Danny Elfman, animals and web comics). It was nice to be able to talk to him and be on the same level, both intellectually and inter-personally. The downside to dating my aspie boyfriend was that he was very rigid. It was impossible to get him out of his comfort zone. We were long distance for a lot of our relationship and he always wanted me to come to him and that was very difficult for me financially, and I too have a little difficulty getting out of my comfort zone. He would get very upset if I couldn’t talk on the phone with him every day, and that was hard for me because I had a variable schedule at times. In the end, the distance really got to us and we parted, and it turned into a rather nasty break up (unrelated to autism). My relationship with my NT husband is much better, and it is more to do with flexibility for each other’s needs, I think. He didn’t understand me immediately, but he worked really hard to get in my head and he got to know me thoroughly over the course of the years we dated. It was a fun, silly time, he always made me feel like I wasn’t strange, even though my behaviors sometimes confused him. He was very patient with me when I was upset or when I couldn’t do something that everyone else found easy. The downside is that sometimes our communication is difficult. It’s hard for him to understand the very complex, deep thoughts I have. That isn’t to say he’s unintelligent — on the contrary — but it’s hard to convey what my hypersensitivities and imagination create for NT’s to grasp. On my worst days, this is extremely frustrating, but we get it eventually because he wants to know everything about me. Really, it depends on the autistic person or the neurotypical person you are with and how passionate they are about connecting.

question: Is it hard for people with autism to form romantic relationships?
answer: My relationships up until my second marriage all lasted about two years, tops. Most were much shorter, and I tried so many times I lost count. People don't like to explain their reasons for leaving, which for an Aspie is sentencing them to repeat the same mistakes over and over. My "skills" come from my sensory sensitivities, which lend an awareness of and focus on details that plays out nicely for my partner. My neediness stems from insecurity born of constant rejection. I clung to the physical aspects of relationships because I felt like if my partner paid enough attention to my personality, I would shortly find myself alone. I believed the physical was all I really had to offer, which is terrible on the self esteem. I tended to jump into relationships helter skelter, out of a combination of the aforementioned neediness, and a lack of awareness of the danger signs. Finally, after years of suffering and a failed, short-lived marriage, I gave up. I spent a couple of years just being alone and learning to be okay with that. Then I put myself up on a dating site, spilled my guts about all my quirks and qualities, and let women come to me instead of continuing to chase the wrong ones. It wasn't long until my wife found me. This one is different. She really cares about me, and my insecurities are fading into the past. We have a family and the relationship, while sometimes rocky like any marriage, is deeply satisfying in a way none of the others ever came close to being. We have already outlasted all of my previous relationships, and I see great things for us ahead.

question: What is the relation between autism and down syndrome?
answer: I don’t think there is a connection. Down Syndrome is connected with a particular genetic mutation. Autism has not been definitively connected with any one cause. I suppose someone could have both, but my understanding is that people with Down Syndrome are actually very friendly and social, despite having an intellectual disability. Parents report that children with Down Syndrome are delightful. By way of contrast, people with Autism are not social. I found dealing with my autistic child to be nightmarish. He was totally non compliant, attacked teachers and the cleaning service personnel, actively tried to defeat child safety devices and often succeeded, threatened to electrocute his classmates or put them through a meat grinder, refused to wear clothing that we chose for him, and had major meltdowns at the slightest frustration or deviation from routine or moving of furniture or household guests. We couldn't keep child care. Differences over how to deal with his behavior were a major cause of our divorce. I don't think Down Syndrome kids behave this way.

question: Does the MMR vaccine cause autism?

This is the easiest way for those who can’t be vaccinated to benefit from vaccination. Re ‘scientific links to autism’ There are absolutely ZERO scientific links between vaccination and autism. There are a few morons that insist on publishing their ignorance of the difference between causation and correlation but we tend to just pat them on the head and hope they will go away soon. Anyone claiming that vaccines are 100% safe for everyone would equally get classed as an idiot by me too to be fair. However the incidence of serious reaction is extremely rare (far lower than my example of penicillin earlier) and the risks from contracting the illnesses they prevent against are far higher. The anti vaccination movement would like people to believe that no serious studies have been done on the safety of vaccination. This is complete, 100%, Bona fide bullshit. There have been numerous meta date studies. Global, intercontinental etc studies involving hundreds of thousands of people. They have all come to the same conclusion. Vaccination is safe. question: Autistics often are victims of abuse, what are signs of an unhealthy relationship so that people with autism can recognize them?
answer: You’re probably in an unhealthy relationship if your partner exercises control disguised as being caring/loving/protective.Wants all your passwords/wants a location tracker (your safety!)Gets upset at not being notified about small schedule/location changes (even when they’re not included in the plan - your safety!)Negative outlook towards friends of different gender (bad people will steal you to rape you - your safety!)Isolates you by mediating most interactions with others and thoroughly probes any you have on your own - sometimes by contacting the other party without your knowledge. (People will hurt your feelings/you will hurt their feelings and they won’t like you - best to let them take care of everything to maintain peace)Another sign would be attempting to fix you disguised as caring/loving/protective.Tries to “train out” your differences so they don’t “enable your autisticness”Constantly explains how you did something wrong so next time you can do it the “objectively correct” NT wayThose are all forms of abuse that shouldn’t be in a healthy relationship. Physical abuse that leaves marks seems like an obvious sign, but the forms that don’t leave marks aren’t to be tolerated either: blocking door ways, holding you down, or anything else that prevents you from having autonomy over your own body. I do want to note that psychological and emotional abuse can often go both ways due to the double empathy problem, though autistic people as a rule make far more concessions for their NT partners (not to mention the rest of the world) than the NT partner has ever begun to even consider. If you’re already in a relationship with these characteristics, you need to start reading about boundaries right now. Also, be ready for your partner to dislike your intolerance of these behaviors and for the behaviors to get much worse in an attempt to regain control and get back to stasis. Stay strong. You’re worth this. If you chooose to continue the relationship, seek out a relationship counselor that understands the autistic perspective and how to introduce that in a way your NT partner can fully grok.
