question: What do you feel is great about being in a relationship with someone with autism?
answer: My partner has high-functioning Aspergers. He has super focus - he gets the job done. I used to think he was angry when he was helping me on a project or with a task, but after talking to him I found out that he is just intensely focussed on the job at hand, and blocks out whatever else is going on till he's finished. This focus has made him a pretty good businessman. (We are both self-employed.) He thinks outside the box and is extremely creative. He thinks pretty much solely in imagery - he says his ideas are images on a 3D landscape and even words are 3D and part of that landscape - I find this so interesting as it's very different from how I process ideas and information. He's driven and is self-competitive - not competitive with other people. He's a very quick study. He's gone from someone who didn't really speak in social situations and who was intensely shy to being able to converse pretty easily and he even now is involved in doing the odd stage routine at cabaret shows. I taught him a lot about socialising. He's taught me a lot about science and problem solving - he is very literal and gets to the point quickly with things like business emails and that's something he's taught me that is useful. I struggled for a long time with with his Alexithymia, not really understanding what was going on for him and why he reacted the way he does,but after reading up on this I have found ways to help him understand what emotion he is feeling and why. He feels very deeply, but didn't used to recognise what exactly the emotion was. I adore him. He adores me. We have similar outlooks on life, even if we have different backgrounds. I come from a childhood of fairly bad emotional and physical abuse and I've survived a terminal illness, (I'm still very sick at times but he goes out of his way to make life easier for me without trying to be a knight in shining armour - something I've never wanted or needed). Even though we have vastly different backgrounds we share the same interests in subcultures like steampunk, travel, (he's travelled a lot more than me), art and making art pieces, psychology and how people tick, music, and more. I know we both complement each other's skills. We bounce ideas off each other. We are both good at problem solving in different ways. We are both autodidacts and study our areas of special interest. We teach each other. He's hilarious and funny and although we found each other later in life, which means we have only been together four and a half years, we are building our dream life together.

question: How can autism affect relationships?
answer: Autism affects relationships in every possible way. (NOTE: I have high-functioning Autism.) One of the key things that most people with Autism suffer from is the inability to read body language, voice intonation, gestures, facial expressions. Generally “reading between the lines” just doesn’t happen. It’s not something we can do anything much about - we can’t “try harder” or “learn” - there is a piece of our brain which should be doing that - but which instead has found another purpose. There is literally nothing we can really do about it. So - if you’re a “neurotypical” person - and you want a relationship with someone like me - then YOU have to do a lot of the work. People who have taken the trouble to do that (at least with me) have found the results to be rewarding…but there is effort involved. What you need to remember is that anything you do not say clearly and explicitly will probably go unnoticed. It’s not because the autistic person doesn’t care…they almost certainly do. It’s not that they don’t know how to respond…they do. They don’t “lack emotion” - quite the reverse in fact. It’s simply that something you THOUGHT they should have been able to deduce, they cannot. When my wife is upset about something that I did (or didn’t) do - then she may go storming around the house - looking angry and giving curt replies to whatever I say…but I’ll have LITERALLY NO IDEA. So she has to remember to say “Steve, you forgot to water my plants like I asked you - and now I’m really angry with you.” OK!! So now I know - I’ll be appropriately apologetic, try to recover the situation, etc. But if I’m supposed to guess and make the first move - NOT GONNA HAPPEN. The problem is that when your emotions are high - and the other person in the relationship isn’t responding appropriately - the very last thing on your mind is laying all of this out explicitly. Well…sorry…but asking me to read between the lines is like asking someone with color blindness to tell you whether something is yellow or orange. ALONE TIME: Another thing - which varies greatly from one sufferer to another - is that some of us need to be by ourselves for significant amounts of time…no reflection on the other person - it’s just a need. SPECIFIC IRRATIONAL DISLIKES: I don’t suffer too much from this - but some people are EXTREMELY sensitive to particular sounds and smells. This can be almost debilitating sometimes. I once knew a fellow software engineer who was VERY disturbed by the sound of the fan that you find in most computers. At home he had the main computer box shut in a closet with L-O-N-G cables going to where he had his keyboard and monitor. But when he started work, there was an entire office full of fans whirring away - and he simply couldn’t stand it. Eventually, they found an office far from the rest of the group where he could leave the computer outside of the door and shut out most of that sound. I’ve also heard of a guy who couldn’t stand the smell of coffee - not just a mild dislike - but a profound visceral hatred. He had to have a desk as far from the break room as possible - and fellow teammates had to be careful not to bring coffee anywhere within 20 feet of his desk! But like I said - not everyone has this…and the details are very variable. UPSIDES: Most of us are very loyal, loving, extremely smart and quick-witted - can study subjects very easily and become extremely expert on narrow subjects that take our interest. If that’s something that sounds good to you - then go love an aspie today! CONCLUSION: When two people (one of whom has the condition) have been together for long enough - this explicit laying out of emotion is kinda refreshing - charming even. But at the outset - when people are trying to form that relationship - it’s REALLY HARD.The neurotypical person has spent their entire lives with people who are like the “Deanna Troi” character on StarTrek…and suddenly they are faced with “Data”.The person with autism simply can’t tell what the hell is going on with the entire emotional mess.

question: Do people with autism want love and relationships?
answer: The majority of people on the spectrum I’ve encountered want relationships, and my experience fits with a recent study:73% indicated romantic relationship experience and only 7% had no desire to be in a romantic relationship. ASD individuals whose partner was also on the autism spectrum were significantly more satisfied with their relationship than those with neurotypical partners.[1]There are strong indicators of autism in my Father’s & Grandfather’s generations, and all but one were married, with varying levels of success. Most of the spouses I knew personally were on the quirky side themselves, so I imagine there was a bit of self-selection or quirk-centric match-making involved. My wife has full-blown, stage-3 neurotypicalism (sadly, there is no cure), but we’re a good fit (21+ years so far). In our case, we both find the other person to be mildly deranged in an amusing, but valuable fashion. She manages social obligations (making me a glorified and occasionally gloomy accessory), and I get to do the fun technical or analytical stuff she hates. My Aspie relatives who haven’t been successful romantically seem to suffer from a lack of experience & adaptability or a partner that ultimately doesn’t appreciate the different set of brain wiring. The catch-22 for autistics is you need practice to be successful at romantic relationships, but it’s harder for us to get into relationships in the first place. That makes it difficult to recognize signals from their partner, much less adapt to another person’s needs. Similarly, the significant other isn’t always able to accept or adapt to their autistic partner. If it was important to my wife for me to be bubbly and excited about parties, we never would have lasted. It isn’t possible to force myself to become a social junkie, I didn’t get that neurology. A little searching on Quora and you’ll see a lot of genuine longing for relationships, paired with what can seem like impossible barriers to entry. It’s sad because autistics have a lot of valuable traits, but the rest of the world has a hard time recognizing them.Footnotes[1] Romantic Relationships and Relationship Satisfaction Among Adults With Asperger Syndrome and High‐Functioning Autism

question: Is there a relationship between autism and histamine?
answer: It’s not just histamine itself that is possibly linked to autism, but anti-histamines are being strongly implicated. They block choline, one of the very most important neurotransmitters in the brain. Anti-histamines are being linked to dementias as well. If there is any autism or dementia in your family, you should strongly consider throwing out all anti-histamines.

question: Why do some individuals with autism seem "normal" at first, but then display symptoms later on in a relationship?
answer: As an autistic person, trying to appear “normal” is very hard. There’s this thing called “masking”- Sounds a little off, right? Like, say, a serial killer trying to fit in with the coworkers in his new, temporary workplace, or a conman trying to get to the top of his field. All relatively unflattering examples of what people think of when they imagine someone wearing a mask. Dishonesty, manipulation, deceit, danger. Many neurotypical people tend to see us that way no matter what, though. I don’t quite like the term for that reason. Here’s what masking actually is; Attempting to appear neurotypical, to fit in, to make other people comfortable. For example; Autistic people like myself feel extreme discomfort when looking someone else in the eyes, whether we’re talking with them closely or just walking on the streets. Eyes are often considered windows to the soul, and in my experience, it’s definitely true. A lot of autistic people describe either feeling vulnerable or being able to see way too much from a person’s expression, an overwhelming amount. Without looking people in the eyes, I’ve heard that we can come off as dishonest, nervous or unwilling to continue talking, even and especially when we feel the opposite. Masking is the process of training yourself to look people in the eyes while you talk- But not too much! Refusing to break eye contact is considered aggressive or obsessive, so break eye contact rarely- but not too rarely! A solid 95% percent of the time. Maybe. All the while, you’re experiencing a lot of discomfort from staring directly at someone’s eyes, but wait, you can’t express that either. Make sure your jaw’s unclenched. You don’t want them to think you’re angry with them, especially when you’re just happy to talk. Relax your shoulders. You look like a turtle. Untense your hands. Or hide them in pockets. Keep a casual and laid-back stance. Oh, and make sure to smile. What’s that? You were too distracted by perfecting your body language to listen to what they’re saying? Well, now they’ve noticed it anyway. Hide it. All of it. They won’t accept you unless you do. And all of this is only one part of masking. There’s also tone of voice, volume, facial expressions, general appearance, “sense of humor” and let’s not even get into things like fashion. Though, another autistic person may have more experience in those things than me. What I’m trying to say is, they’re beginning to trust you, deeply trust that you won’t be offended or put off by the little things like whether or not they’re looking you in the eyes. If you’re in a relationship, they’re very likely willing and happy to listen to you, and is putting all of their effort into understanding you, your intent and what you’re saying. They’re letting their shield down, letting those little things slip, letting themselves appear less, well, “normal”. Because the truth of it is, masking doesn’t serve them. They only do it to make you feel more comfortable. In the process of letting “the mask” slip, they’re choosing to show you more of themselves, unguarded and unstressed, open despite the judgment they’ve very likely received from other people. To put it to a word, they’re being vulnerable. Please be sure to treat them well.

question: What are people's thoughts on dating someone on the autism spectrum? Is it worth trying to pursue a relationship with someone on the autism spectrum?
answer: I hope so. I’ve been going out with an NT for almost a year. He’s sweet and patient and when I’m having a really hard time he always tries to help. I’ve wondered why he goes out with me. I guess at first it was because of the way I looked. But he’s found out a lot about me since then. He found out I’m trans. He’s talked to my parents about my autism so they could tell him what it would be like to date me. He’s made tons of changes and I really like being with him. I’m hoping as I get older that I will learn to show more emotion. But I write lots of notes to him so I can express what I think and feel. I write a lot better than I can show emotions. I think if the person can use critical thinking and work out social contacts in a clear way that they can learn to read your emotional cues and respond to you with empathy then there is a good chance you can work out a relationship. My weakness is with empathy. I don’t understand well why people have the feelings they have. And this is the most difficult part of our relationship. When I read an emotion on his face (I memorized emotional looks from a deck of cards my therapist worked with me on) I often have to ask him why he’s feeling the way he’s feeling. Sometimes it’s easy. If I say something funny on purpose (and it’s not too bizarre) and sometimes it’s harder. Maybe you should find someone who is easier to communicate with than me. I’m not sure I’m the best person to start a long term relationship with but I really want to keep trying cuz i like my bf a lot and we’re really good friends.

question: I've recently been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. What therapies can help me cope with sensory, relationship, and social skills issues?
answer: I have ASD and was diagnosed only this year at 42. What has helped me is talking to other ASD, such as in self help groups and web forums. Others With ASD frequently have good advice on how they have successfully dealt with any of theses issues. I also have an ASD mentor, a non-autistic mentor that has worked with ASD for considerable time and he has helped me a lot with social skills and interpersonal relationships at work. I have not found therapists to be of help in dealing with ASD, especially not psychologist because essentially they only do feelings/emotions which is what we essentially don't do so there is a considerable amount of miscommunication and many simply quickly give up on ASD clients. You don't actually require a therapist for any aspect of ASD. You may have some mental health issues that would benefit from CBT for instance, but if you do then try to seek out a therapist that is specially trained for dealing with ASD clients or is very flexible and non judgemental. It is a common story among us with ASD to be thrown out from therapists for being impossible in some manner or other. There are a number of books and websites, many are good. I found them to be a great help.

question: Do people with autism relate well to others with autism because of their similar perspectives, or do they have difficulty establishing and maintaining relationships with others on the spectrum?
answer: I personally get along much better with other “disabled” people, regardless of cause (autism, cerebral palsy, whatever), and I find that most of the non-normal people that I know are like that. It might be shared experiences with NT people, or other issues, I don’t know. I’m not a mental health professional. Three examples from my youth, 45–50 years ago. When I was 12 years old, I lived in a rural area with a physically large, population-small school district. My daily bus ride took about an hour, each way, picking-up students for both the high school and middle school, which were 5 miles apart. In addition, this bus took the two special needs children 20 miles to the nearby city, to attend the special-ed classes that our small district couldn’t afford. The first two seats were reserved for these children, so the bus driver could keep an eye on them, and prevent likely bullying. The bus driver was my mentor (I was the first pickup, last drop-off, plus we went to the same church, and we spent a lot of time talking about stuff before the next students came aboard.), so I usually sat in the front-right seat. That seat was reserved for one of the disabled girls, but I was allowed to sit there, too, as long as she didn’t mind. She liked me, eventually, because I didn’t treat her different, and let her sit next to the window, so it was OK. So, I was able to still talk a bit with the driver, when we were on country roads, and watch him drive when we were on the highway. Of course, I caught hell from my insensitive classmates, saying that she was my girlfriend, because we sat together (preposterous, she was several years younger), but I didn’t care… they were a bunch of jerks, anyway. When I was a little older, having moved to that same city, medical issues prevented me from doing any PE except for swimming. My junior high school didn’t have a swimming pool, so I was allowed go to the YMCA three times a week, where I volunteered to be the safety swimmer when the special needs children came for swimming class. Many of them were afraid of the water, but as long as they could see me treading water in the middle of the pool, watching them, they felt safe enough to swim a little. We all got along well, because none opef us were judgmental. The benefit for me was that after they quit for the day, the pool was empty for a while, and I could do whatever type of swimming, diving, etc. that I wanted. It was just me and the lifeguard. In high school, in my senior year, I sat at the table in the cafeteria, where the special-ed students sat. It was always half-empty, because “normal” students wouldn’t be caught dead, sitting at a table with “them”. We all got along well, and had some interesting discussions, mostly about the other students. I got very close to one girl, who was one year junior to me, so I asked her to go with me to the yearly Christmas school dance. I think I was her first date. She spent a lot of effort to look nice, and we had a good time. No dinner, no parking, none of that stuff. Just sitting and talking. I joined the Navy a little later, and we kept writing for several months. She listened to my advice, and I encouraged her to join the Air National Guard. She did well there, doing much better than she imagined she would. Eventually, I deployed to one place, she deployed somewhere else, and we lost touch, until Facebook a couple of years ago. During all this time, I had no idea I had Asperger’s Syndrome. I discovered it when I was 45, which explained all of my high school and early adult problems with society. It was a largely unknown mental issue back then. I met the woman I would marry when I was 23, and we’ve been married for almost 37 years.

question: What did you feel was lacking in a relationship you had with someone with autism?
answer: The kind of affection that I give and sometimes want to receive. My wife has autism and she’s wonderful, but her ways of showing affection (her love language) are different from mine, and different from the ones I sometimes want. I like hugs, cuddles, snuggles, a lot. My wife kinda hates to be touched. She likes to do the touching, and do it on her own terms. Sometimes, a good hug happens, but she usually initiates it, and she often pulls away before I’m ready. If I initiate it, sometimes it’s okay, and other times she won’t want it and will pull away quickly. That’s okay. She doesn’t like sitting on the couch and snuggling through a movie the way I do. We can snuggle some here and there. This means we snuggle up and start the movie, then we shift and take some space, then snuggle again for a bit, shift a bit. It also means, sometimes I lay in a way that makes her comfy and fulfills my snuggle needs at the same time, like laying my head in her lap, or us crossing our legs over each other while we sit mostly on opposite ends of the couch. She usually doesn’t mind cuddles in bed. (I mean platonic here. I’m not discussing sex.) An arm around each other happens frequently. This is one of the times she’s most comfortable touching. Sometimes though, she still requests hands-off for the night. Times when she doesn’t like cuddling, she sometimes still asks me to pet her hair, massage her scalp, or rub behind her ears. It’s just her comfort touches, and I often do these things to help her fall asleep whether she’s feeling cuddly or not. Daily, she shows affection in her own ways, most of which involve limited or no touching. She has a variety of ways she touches me to show love: Poking me in the ear (yes, she has a thing about ears), sticking her palm across my face (I have to endure it until she’s satisfied or she’ll make loud sad noises at me), sticking her face on my face, trying to get them to fit together best as possible (she usually lets me remove my glasses first. So considerate.), and petting/gently slapping her hand against my shoulder, arm, or back. (I have to FREQUENTLY remind her to stay off my upper arms due to my fibro, but she’s still getting used to that.) Non-touching means of expression affection include: making loud noises at me. Saying “Hey.” then waiting for me to acknowledge her at which point she waves at me and says “Hey.” again. Calling me “Squee” by saying “Squuueeee” suddenly in a cute voice. Reaching over to my desk and knocking something over. (yes, she does this daily. Usually a pill bottle or something. Once, I moved all the pill bottles to the other side of my desk and she got really sad and upset. I moved them back. I did it again one time without thinking, and she knocked over a salt shaker. I complained at her and she said “That’s what you get for moving my pill bottles.” Note, “my pill bottles”. They are my pills, but…they’re her means of expressing affection.) Sometimes she shows her love by…gosh this is going to sound wrong…picking up a candle lighter and pretending to set things on fire on my desk. She actually lights the lighter and threatens my desk objects with it. They are usually non-flammable things like my can of soda water, or a glass, etc. She is not serious, never gets the flame close enough to actually hurt anything, and is a sensible adult who isn’t going to set anything on fire. But when she does, I stop whatever I’m doing to discourage her setting it on fire, waving her away and saying “Anna no! Anna… Anna stop!” or some such, in cute voices so we are playing. This is just how she says “I love you”. By… trying to set my desk stuff on fire. ;) Sometimes she threatens to set my dog on fire. She also does this just to get me to react, and of course never ever brings a flame within two feet of him. She’s just joking to get me to react. But it’s part of our love language. Another love-language thing is our references, memes, and personal language which is really just a huge string of in-jokes between us that no one other than the two of us would ever get. Sometimes she just looks at me and says something in our personal language and it’s a way to get me to laugh, smile, or play along and finish the line. We grin, giggle, then go back to work. question: Is there any relationship between face blindness (prosopagnosia) and autism spectrum disorders such as Aspberger Syndrome?
answer: Statistically research suggests that prosopagnosia affects 2% of the general population. However, estimates for the condition within the autistic population are around 50%, possibly higher, which means that it is far more prevalent as a comorbid with the autism spectrum than as a stand alone condition. I work with university students on the spectrum and screen all of them for prosopagnosia as a matter of course because of how it impacts on social communication (if you can’t see a face properly, how would you be able to read anything in it?) - at least 50% have it at some level. In my family my father, myself and my son have it (all autistic); for my father and son it is severe- they literally cannot see faces - but for me it is in a milder form where I can see a face but cannot retain a memory, even of my own face. Can you imagine how scary a school dining room would be? Or what it’s like to never have seen the faces of those you love? Or to not be able to imagine what you look like? Edited to add: Prosopagnosia is caused by the failure of the brain to process the face, and only the face. Most visual data is processed through the visual cortex but not the face. The face is processed in the fusiform gyrus in the amygdala and is a tiny rice sized area hidden behind each ear. The amygdala is part of the network that processes for emotional salience so it is hypothesised that the fusiform gyrus is placed there to process faces because they are so important emotionally and it is more efficient to process them within that network directly, rather than as secondary to the visual network. Prosopagnosia was first studied in brain injured people who lost the ability to see faces and recognise people - one man in particular had a metal spike driven into his skull, piercing the fusiform gyrus, and consequently allowing that area to be identified as the facial processing area. It was only much later (decades) that it was realised that it could be a congenital condition - most people do not realise that they should be able to see and remember a face properly; how would anyone know they see differently from those around them when nobody would think to ask anyone else if they could see a face unless they thought the person was blind? We all assume that, if we can see at all, then we can all see the same things. As a result, nobody imagined that a sighted person might be unable to see a face and, because they never thought to question it, those of us with prosopagnosia, didn’t realise there were things (faces) we couldn’t process like everyone else.

question: Is there a relationship between head circumference and autism?
answer: Unfortunately, both previous answers are incorrect. Actually, they don't answer the question asked. The relationship between head circumference and the diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder has to do with growth acceleration. In a statistically significant portion of newborn babies who are later to be diagnosed with autistic spectrum disorder, the head circumference will begin as normal at birth but later head growth accelerates and the head circumference increases at a rate that is faster than babies that do not have autism. This does not mean that people with Autism have larger heads than people that do not have autism. It simply means that a large percentage of people diagnosed with autism reach adult size head circumference earlier than people without autism. Head circumference and growth acceleration as recorded by a pediatrician is also not an acceptable way to diagnose autistic spectrum disorder as this is not observed in every case.

question: Is there a relationship between autism (ASD) and diet?
answer: Yes, but not what many people think. Removing certain foods or additives will not “cure” autism or even improve it. It is not curable (nor is it improvable for that matter). It is genetic. That being said, if a person with autism is also allergic to, say, milk, removing milk from their diet MAY improve their autistic “symptoms” (or behaviors that upset others…). That has nothing at all to do with milk being related to autism and everything to do with the person feeling more comfortable without suffering from the symptoms of the milk allergy. If you had an upset tummy and felt awful, your actions would show it. Many autistics, especially children, can’t tell you, “When I drink milk I feel icky.” They either don’t make the connection or are simply too busy feeling “icky” to clarify that. They might not even understand how they feel icky (some autistics have trouble naming sensations and emotions). When they do not ingest milk they don’t feel icky and therefore the behaviors seen when they do feel icky go away. They are no less autistic, they just aren’t in discomfort anymore. While there is a strong link between gut and brain, and good gut health leads to better health over all, there is as of now no clear, reputable scientific evidence linking dietary changes to any changes in autistic symptoms.

question: Is there a genetic relationship between autism and aspergers?
answer: Asperger's is no longer in the diagnostic manual, DSM V. In the old manual, DSM IV, the only difference in diagnostic criteria was whether or not you had speech delay at 3 years. This proved to be an arbitrary distinction which was not sustainable in clinical practice - children diagnosed with autism because they had speech delay at 3 but who then catch up later were indistinguishable from children who did not have speech delay and were diagnosed with AS. This is because there is no difference between autism and AS, they are different presentations of the same neurological developmental condition - ASD. AS is not a milder form, nor is it a different form of autism, it is simply autism spectrum disorder, or autism. The differences on the outside, the external presentation, are not differences in the condition itself but in the impact of the condition on the person. Current research into the neurology of autism confirms this. There are, however, multiple autisms (AS is not one of these distinct forms). These probably have different genetic or epigenetic roots. The research has so far been unable to determine the specific roots of most autism but we do know that some types of autism, for example, Retts Syndrome and Fragile X, are determined genetically. Most autism seems to have a range of genes implicated and unpicking exactly what genes are involved in which presentations is going to take a lot more research and is probably not going to lead to any real furthering of knowledge or treatment - it is the neurology that is going to be the way forward in building our understanding, not the genetics.

question: Why is that not everyone with autism has a close relationship with their family?
answer: Some people on the spectrum are uncomfortable with touch and have difficulty relating to and responding to emotional expressions. Families tend to bond with infants and children through touch—cuddling, hugging, etc. If a child rejects these expressions and doesn’t like to be touched, his or her family members may feel that the child doesn’t want their company or love and grow more and more distant toward the child over time. If the child doesn’t know what his/her family members mean and feel when they say “I love you,” they don’t reciprocate and the family members feel rejected. Family members need to learn to bond on the child’s terms. If they don’t make the effort and just give up, then they may never form the kind of relationship that holds the person with autism to his or her family. It’s a sad thing when this happens because given the difficulty so many people on the spectrum have in social interactions, their family members may be among the few people they really feel close to. I hope that over time, the autism spectrum will not be so mysterious to neurotypicals and they will have a better idea of what autism is all about. Neurotypicals cannot know what it’s like to be a person on the spectrum any more that a person on the spectrum can know what it’s like to be neurotypical, but there are features of living on the spectrum that others can learn to understand.

question: Since getting rid of autism is impossible, will I ever find a relationship?
answer: The vast majority of people on the Autism spectrum have relationships. For those sufficiently high functioning to ask a question like this, the numbers are roughly similar to those of the neurotypical. This is no guarantee, of course. But in addition to being above that bar, you’ve met another: you’re interested in a relationship. And you’ve met a third bar: you’re aware that you face some difficulty related to your Autism. This means you can work on your circumstances deliberately, in ways likely to improve your chances. Work on figuring out how to read some of the basic cues people use. Both to help you read the “unspoken” things they are saying, and to allow you to use some of those cues yourself. You needn’t go full mask, but a little sugar helps the medicine go down, and a little smiling and nodding and shrugging will go a long way towards making you seem “human” at first meeting. NT’s who aren’t familiar with ASD folks often don’t even understand their initial negative reaction to us, so this helps. Second, find some hobbies and interests that get you out and among people. Volunteer for a worthy cause. This will accomplish two things. First, and most importantly, it will help you rub the rough edges off and get used to making and being friends. It’s easiest for us to isolate, stay home, heck, in today’s world, we can get a job, buy all our groceries and supplies, and never have to go out among people at all. This, as it turns out, is a bad strategy if you’re interested in a relationship with people instead of with your computer. Second, meeting and associating with people over the long terms means, in part, meeting and associating with people who might be interesting relationship partners. Now, for the most part, they WON’T be. So don’t focus on that aspect. That’s not why you’re there. It’s just… that’s where the opportunities will come from. It won’t be someone in Buenos Aires who puts a note in a bottle that you find while on an island off the coast of Scotland. It will be someone in a club, at work, another volunteer, someone you spend time with who gets to know you as a person instead of as a “wow that guy is weird.” It is statistically likely that you are a decent, kind, humble person who can be very focused on their partner, can be a very good listener and companion. Those are almost… in the symptom set. So, for a partner who can see past your oddities, who can accept them, you’re likely to be a very good partner. But it won’t fall into your lap. Also, I was lying about the humble part. I haven’t met many of us who are that.

question: What is the relationship between autism and IQ?
answer: Note: I'm not an expert on this at all; I'm just someone who's interested in the world of psychiatry. I would say that, if you look at what really is scientifically established, that very little is known about this. The diagnosis of autism, in itself, doesn't say anything about intelligence. You have highly intelligent people with autism, sometimes these people are diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome or high-functioning autism (though I think in the latest DSM, it's all part of one spectrum), but it is also true that low intelligence and autism frequently co-occur. What I've found, is that "to make comorbid diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability, social communication should be below that expected for general developmental level."[1] In other words, your social skills should be below that of what should be expected of a person of your intelligence. The relationship between IQ and autism is complicated, because it's not that easy to test for cognitive ability while completely factoring in communication difficulties: For a child to perform to their ability on a standard IQ tests such as the WISC-IV and the Stanford-Binet, they must be able to quickly respond to verbal questions and have well developed motor skills. However, these are areas that are difficult for those with autism. In effect, these IQ tests do not tap the true cognitive ability of many children on the autistic spectrum, but rather tell us more about their communication and motor difficulties. Children and teens with autism spectrum disorders are impacted by sensory processing challenges, and this as well can effect test results. A student may not be able to respond in a room with bright fluorescent lights or in an environment not conducive to someone with sensory processing issues. [...] It is important to remember that just because a person cannot talk does not mean that they are not understanding what is going on around them, what they are hearing in class, or reading in books. Conversely, just because a person sits in a class and can repeat to you what was said, does not mean he has internalized and learned it. [2] I've also heard that significant differences in IQ subscores can be a sign of autism, but I don't know how much of that is mere personal impressions of psychologists and psychiatrists and how much of that is based on scientific research. Intuitively, this would indeed makes sense, but I couldn't find any scientific research on this matter, so I think the only honest answer here is: I don't know. I don't think it's right to say that "autism makes you a genius" or "autism makes you a savant" or something like that. What's likely more accurate, is to say that autism occurs in all intelligence layers. It's hard to come up with good definitions of intelligence, and it's even harder to test for this, especially in people with autism. So testing the relationship between autism and intelligence is even harder. [1] DSM-V, Autism Spectrum Disorder, E [2] What IQ Tests Really Tell Us About Children with Autism

question: Is Tourette’s a type of autism or perhaps are autism and Tourette's subspecies of a larger group of disorders? What is, if any, the relationship between them?
answer: Tourette’s is not part of Autism. Tourette’s is one of a group neurological movement disorders under the umbrella of tic disorder. Tourette’s Syndrome has a very high comorbidity rate; 90% of those with it will have at least one other neurological or psychiatric condition. The main two often thought of with it is ADHD and OCD. Autism is a known comorbid condition with a uncommon/common occurrence. Both Autism and Tourette’s fall under the category of neurological conditions; they are not mental health conditions. In the model of disability, they are both be thought of as a neurodiverse conditions.A relationship between the two can be displayed in different ways depending on the person. Autistics can have a tendency to focus on what makes them different - their neurology - and as such can focus on tics and Tourette’s. They may re-watch documentaries on the condition over and over as part of the repetitive nature of Autism. Other conditions have a tendency to ‘fuel’ tics therefore this is expected behaviour. Autism can be a boon however. Autistics will, by nature, hyperfocus on what they are doing. By doing this there will be a dramatic temporary reduction of tics. These two conditions aren’t talked about enough as a comorbidity but there is a strong relationship between the two. However, they are not directly related. Think of it as another side to a single die - the die of neurodiversity.

question: People that have autism, what was your first relationship like?
answer: Late. My first relationship was when I went to University. Before that point I had missed signals (so many signals) and had several prospective partners turn me down and, in one case, not speak to me ever again. I was accused of stalking someone I liked (in fairness, I had sent them anonymous letters [I thought it was romantic, not creepy] in the past) because I "followed them home" - I didn't know I had, we lived closer than I realised. For the most part I was ignored and routinely topped people's lists of people who would never date. So, that background out of the way, my first relationship was at age 18 with a fellow 18 year old for whom I was also their first relationship. We held hands after three weeks, in public after ten. We kissed after five weeks, in public after eight. We shared a bed for three hours after eight months. We visited one another's parents in summer around ten months in, went for an anniversary meal and then split just before the halfway point of that term, we lasted about fourteen months. The split was amicable but I instituted it. They got married three years later, on their fourth relationship, and invited me to their wedding. We remain on good terms but life means we don't talk much or often. What was it like? Sweet, I guess. Neither of us had any clue what we were doing, so we didn't 'date'. In fact, our one 'date' was the anniversary meal a year in, after I'd resolved to end things, but it was a lovely meal. It was actually on the cusp of the thirteenth month together (scheduling issues) and thus fell about two weeks before we stopped being a couple. So, what did we do? We watched some films in the cinema together, we spent time together, we hugged and held hands and kissed. We... uh... rubbed up against one another fully clothed a bit. It was tactile, interesting, sweet. Probably looked all kinds of odd to other people. They got called 'clingfilm' by my friends back home but it was I that was the clingy one really. Around that summer, when we met one another's parents, that's when I realised we weren't going to marry and starting planning to end things. But they were really nice. I don't regret the relationship. They always said I was very kind and the least traumatic of their relationships before their last. Their current partner even went so far as to thank me for treating my ex as well as I did and being such a positive experience, in private this was, at their wedding. I did not enjoy splitting up, it was a bit akin, in my mind, to clubbing a baby seal and I was doing the clubbing. However, they said I was very good about it and, unbidden, explained that I had given all the right amounts of space and support without being weird or creepy - something they really valued in the future. They could have just been being nice, I guess I'll never really know. So... in short, it was fumbling and a bit clumsy. Nice, but directionless. Passionate in places but between people who had no idea what they were doing or how to do things. Our compliments to one another, looking back, were comically bad and uninformed. Our interactions horrendously socially immature. We were babies together, in a social sense, and both learnt a lot. I didn't know I had ASD, by the way, and they had had a very sheltered upbringing indeed. Hope this helps!

question: What does high functioning adult male autism look like in a relationship?

Yet I’ve been told by nearly all the women in my life that I’m a good boyfriend. And I stayed on friendly terms with all but a small handful. But there’s a caveat: I was not diagnosed until age 45 and so spent most of my relationships in the dark and unprepared to listen better, analyze a situation better, and engage learned work-arounds to compensate for deficits. But there is really no “typical” in this. I have friends with HFASD who have remained happily and satisfactorily married for decades. I have friends with HFASD who do not function in relationships very well at all—they are simply incapable of overcoming their socioemotional deficits sufficiently to establish good bonding behavior. And I have some HFASD friends whose lives closely parallel my own. Still, there is one common aspect among the majority of ASD persons that is worth understanding if you are about to enter into a relationship: We typically “speak a different emotional language” than do NTs, expressing emotions differently, sometimes to the point of making it seem as if we have no emotions (a common and damaging misconception about us). I’ve written before that, for many on the high end of the Spectrum, life among NTs is like living in a foreign country where, although you speak the language well enough to get around there are nuances you won’t get or be able to communicate. (Ever see an American when he or she is first trying to live in England or vice-versa?) And the same way that some people simply suck at trying to learn a new language, the HFASD person might not be able to do so either. So, the upshot is, you don’t know what you’ll get any more than anyone else going into a relationship. But constant open communication, respect, patience, understanding, choosing what to let roll off your back and what to expend your energies in conflict on when conflict does arise, and always-always-always erring on the side of kindness are the best ingredients to help establish a good relationship.

question: What is the relationship between childhood disintegrative disorder and autism?
answer: In 1907, Heller described several cases of Childhood Disintegrative Disorder, but in his paper, he called it ‘Heller’s Syndrome.’ Prior to that date, children with Childhood Disintegrative Disorder were probably classed as ‘Feebleminded’ or were classed as having what would today be called profound intellectual disability. Then it was some years more, before Autism got ‘pulled out’ of the big bucket of ‘retardation/Feeblemindedness’ and got its ‘own’ diagnostic name. That was in 1943 when Leo Kanner published his paper and dubbed it ‘Primary Infantile Autism’. The words ‘primary’ and ‘infantile’ were necessary as ‘autism’ at that time was nothing more than an adjective-like, generic word use to describe a kind of aloneness found in many conditions. As time went on the ‘Primary’ and ‘Infantile’ words dropped off and it was just called ‘Autism.’ With the DSM-5 published in 2013(I think it was 2013), Childhood Disintegrative Disorder(CDD) has been removed from the diagnostic manual. Children who used to get diagnosed with CDD are now to be diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder. And no, I don’t like that. I’ve read all the explanations. I still don’t like it. I think that CDD is different enough that it warrants its own diagnosis. For quite some time, both ‘Autism’ and ‘CDD’ were in a larger uber category called ‘Pervasive Developmental Disorders.’ This category also included Rett Syndrome and Asperger Syndrome as well. My understanding is that CDD was ‘rolled into’ Autism Spectrum Disorders because the biology of both disorders is so similar, in other words, upon examination, brains of individuals with CDD and ASD look similar, and the genetics of both are very close. To contrast CDD with autism:CDD was rarely, if ever, used as a diagnosis when symptoms were mild. There was no ‘high functioning CDD’ or ‘Asperger Syndrome’ form of CDD. In most cases, parents were told that the CDD diagnosis meant lifelong, profound disability. In fact, while diligent therapy could bring about some improvement, it was rather rare for CDD diagnosed kids to see a big, marked improvement.With CDD, children often have an ‘ostensibly normal’ period of development*, and then a very sudden, radical change in behavior skills and language and communication, around the age of two or two-and-a-half or three years**. This sudden change was usually called ‘regression.’ That can be confusing as in psychology, the term ‘regression’ was long-used for ‘babyish’ behavior that had a psychological root. That’s not what this is at all. This is a profound change in cognition and skills.Toddlers experiencing the onset of regression/severe CDD symptoms often expressed extreme anxiety and discomfort from the new more severe symptoms. Some seemed to be aware that they were undergoing a profound cognitive change.Early psychotic symptoms may be more common with CDD than with Autism. In the book ‘When Autism Strikes’, 3 and possibly as many as 5 of the 8 case studies described children with very early psychotic symptoms.In the same book, one child(one of the eight case studies) was given antipsychotic medication immediately and the psychotic symptoms, and even the CDD, were both clearly ameliorated and the child went on to attend regular school. This child had a maternal grandmother with schizophrenia.I have a suspicion that there is a closer relationship between early psychotic symptoms and CDD than there is with early psychotic symptoms and autism. We now know that there is some overlap in the gene patterns of autism and the gene patterns of schizophrenia (disorders can be quite dissimilar and still have some gene patterns in common).*In fact, children with CDD DO miss developmental milestones before their behavior undergoes its radical change/’regression.’ But generally, these missed milestones are subtle and difficult for non-experts to recognize. **Children who regress at age 5–10 do not get diagnosed with CDD, something else is going on. Children who regress at age 3–4 are even not likely to have CDD.

question: What is your opinion of the research done by Stephanie Seneff PhD on the relationship between autism and glyphosate (aka Roundup)?
answer: There is a strong correlation between autism and gut microbiota. There probably is an effect on gut microbiota by glyphosate, although this has not been tested because... i don't know why, but it hasn't. Probably because it's not mandated by any regulatory agency for approval of the chemical, and because Monsanto's interest is more about the profit and not about ensuring welfare of people, with adequate caution, as shown by the history with PCBs. The research on whether, and how, glyphosate affects the human gut microbiota is yet to be done, although it is clear that glyphosate has an inhibitory effect on microbes to different levels. It inhibits B subtilis continually and causes an energy drain to it. It inhibits some other microbes in absence of exogenous aromatic amino acids. It inhibits Pseudomonas spp. very little. Therefore, presence of glyphosate in the chyme is likely to have some effects on the gut microbiota. It is a matter of dosage and many other things, but there are indications that the levels of about 0.2 to 1 mg per day in the typical U.S. diet are relevant to this mode of action. Seneff is not a researcher with a relevant degree, as she is a computer scientist by training, but this in itself doesn't make her work invalid. Her work is quite reaching, in my opinion, more conjectural than definitive. It's interesting but it's not proof of anything, but it does generate hypotheses and present them with evidence via correlations of many kinds. However, having looked into glyphosate intensively for 8 months, and having some training and experience in microbial ecology myself, i do think it's likely that there is an effect on the gut microbiome by glyphosate. I am quite astounded that a chemical can be in the food supply and not tested for a relevant hypothesis like this one. I also think it's likely that an effect on the gut microbiota could have an effect on many things, including the possibility of causing autism, as well as immune suppression and other subtle but profound effects. I find it quite negligent that the basic research on glyphosate and the gut microbiome has not been done. I chalk it up to the profit motive being more important to Monsanto than the well-being of people exposed to their products, judging from their history with PCBs and Agent Orange.

question: What is the relationship between autism spectrum disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder? What might explain why OCD is the most common comorbidity in ASD?
answer: Q: “What is the relationship between autism spectrum disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder? What might explain why OCD is the most common comorbidity in ASD?” ASD (although I dispute the ‘spectrum idea) represents issues in the developed capacity to ‘symbolize’ - not artistic symbolization (although related), but the primary symbolic functioning - crudely the cognitive and emotional ability to allow one thing or idea to stand in place of another thing or idea (which thing may be absent or abstract). So, instead of Salvador Dali and melting clocks, think ‘mother leaves the room that baby is in and is ‘gone’; baby either has a symbolic representation of her mother in her mind, or she does not’. From this baby example you can imagine that developing the capacity to symbolize - allowing some other object or idea to stand in for an absent mother - is an emotional as well as a cognitive achievement. Although the baby is substituting a mental object so as not to be totally bereft, she is also ‘allowing’ that the mother is absent - an existential reality for her. Along the way to achieving this capacity we find the famous ‘security blanket’, or ‘transitional object’, or ‘concrete equation’, which is half symbol, half hallucination (perhaps). The development of symbolic capacity then allows the possibility of separation from the mother to be tolerated. The mother is ‘gone’, but ‘kept in mind’, and so long as she returns in time, our symbolization of her existence has protected us from the fear of her permanent absence, which is equivalent to a later fear on a par with the fear of death or annihilation. This symbolic development is probably essential in learning to communicate through speech. Language is composed of symbolic tokens - words which stand in for ‘things’ (you cannot get ‘things’ into your head to ‘think’ with) - and in a similar way to the mother example, we must trust that we can ‘let go’ of the things themselves so that the words can symbolically represent them. This is why severe autism often affects language capacity. But further, think on this. The word ‘table’ is a symbol. We use it to describe all the millions of tables in the world. We do not need to have seen all the tables in the world. When we come across a new table we have not seen before it is not a problem. But if you cannot use symbols consistently, it is not so straight forward. What you eat breakfast off in the kitchen is in almost infinite detail different from that other object with four legs in the dining room. Without being able to use the category ‘table’, how do you know that far from being what you may eat off, the one in the dining room will not rear up on two of those legs and eat you? To the extent that our autism compromises our symbolic capacity, we may need to learn ‘by rote’ every ‘object’ (things and people) quite separately in order to feel existentially safe. This is an impossible task and this is why many autistic children fly into rages of terror when routines, details and environments are changed. It is symbolization that grants us the capacity to tolerate the infinitely varied reality of our world. OCD symptoms in non-autistic people arise from a different source (unconscious fears and fantasies about the destructiveness of our thoughts), but all existential fears, whatever their source, threaten to overwhelm our capacities to contain them, and lead to concrete ritualistic behaviors, in the same way that the much more benign ‘security blanket’ solution is produced in infancy for the absent mother. In sum ASD is an effect in the area of symbolization. The capacity to symbolize contains much of the primitive anxiety we all have to experience in life and development. OCD is a more or less ‘concrete’ attempt to relieve those anxieties - in most people representing a partial and often temporary breakdown in symbolic capacity, but in severely autistic people a relative deficit or fault in such capacity.

question: Is there a relationship between mental retardation and autism?

question: What is the relationship between high IQ and autism? How does high IQ manifest in individuals with autism?
answer: Most of the people who have autism do not have a ‘high IQ.’ How do recent studies make it seem otherwise? Well, a disturbing proportion of them exclude the more severely affected autistic people. There is an unpleasant percentage of research on autism follows trends and public opinion. For example, one finds lots of studies that conclude that autistic people need job counseling and training, even though a very high percentage of autistic people are too severely affected to work. And well… for example, later in this answer I note that a study of ‘autistic males’ gave a certain result. Did I say that because I have a bias against women with autism? Nope. I said that because the only results were given for males. Especially since a few studies suggest females might in general have milder autism than males(the behavior of some of the genes involved in autism would certainly support that idea), I am hesitant to generalize from studies that only study males, or journalists that only mention results from male. Since the levels have a general tendency to follow along with IQ, about 75% of autistic people are in level 2 or 3, which means ‘needing substantial’ or ‘needing very substantial’ support day to day. Drastic changes to the diagnosis did bring in some people with higher IQs than before(before, about 57% of autistic people had an IQ below 85), but the newly qualified mostly added to the ‘average’ bucket, IQ 85–115, not the ‘high IQ’ group(120 and above, usually). High IQ ‘manifests itself’ in a difficult to assess way with autism. People are often ‘wowed’ when the autistic person shows a good recall for facts, sticks to an established routine and learns definitions to words. But the problem is this. Even among the autistic people with higher-ish IQs, there still are surprisingly serious cognitive difficulties, and a surprising number(100% in one study, 87% in others) of autistic adult males remain fully or partly financially dependent on their parents. In other words, some researchers are concluding that IQ isn’t a very accurate measure of how well autistic people can function or how independently they can live, not because of how it fails to advise in the lower IQ groups, but because of how profoundly it fails to show how disabled autistic people with higher IQs actually are.

question: What are some telltale signs that a neurotypical person was raised by a parent with an undiagnosed autism spectrum disorder? Will this affect the way people communicate in relationships?
answer: Great question. Here are some tell-tale signs, based on my own experience growing with an undiagnosed AS mother, discussions with other NT’s from an online support group and AS expert and psychologist Tony Attwood*:They have Aspie traits themselves: NT’s have basically grown up in an Aspie household. Accordingly, NTs may have problems with eye contact, find it hard to express their emotions, show empathy or make friends etc just like their parent.They are full of information, creative or unconventional: On a positive note, they may have picked up some charming traits from their AS parent too.They find it difficult to be loved or cared for: This is a tough one. NT children don’t always get the emotional reciprocity they need from an AS parent and this may create issues later on. Further to this, if the AS parent is undiagnosed, the NT child often assumes the lack of emotional reciprocity is due to something inherently wrong with them and this may get carried through into later life.They marry an Aspie: It’s what they may know and expect from relationships.They are people pleasers and conflict adverse: AS meltdowns are scary to children, particularly if it’s their parent. Children may learn to regularly read the mood of their parent and tread carefully when they sense trouble. They may take it upon themselves to try to keep their AS parent in their comfort zone by doing things that please the parent.They feel guilty about having problems and rarely ask for help: AS parents are fine when they are in their comfort zone but can really struggle when things get difficult or demanding. NT children quickly learn to not have problems.They are highly independent: Perhaps due to the generally limited social opportunities during their childhoods and the exhaustion levels of their AS parent, NT children learn to amuse themselves.They had a troubled relationship with their parent but can’t put their finger on why: If neither the parent nor the child has figured out the parent is autistic, let alone received a formal diagnosis, then imagine how confusing the NT’s childhood was. There is a generally a profound sense of relief when NT’s figure out their parent is autistic.Does all this affect the way these NT’s communicate in relationships? Yes, I imagine so, but how they communicate depends where along the healing process they find themselves. Some are still very hurt and processing their feelings. Some are coming out the other side feeling a great deal of compassion for both their AS parent and for themselves. I reckon a hug will do the trick every time. ——— EDIT: Following an interesting observation in the comments, I’ll add the following:They may have trouble expressing themselves effectively: AS parents may struggle to understand how their child is feeling a lot of the time. They may also struggle with demonstrating effective communication skills themselves or giving their NT child the right visual cues they need to feel understood. Accordingly, NT’s may develop communication habits that overcompensate for this feeling of not being understood such as “over-explaining things”.For further reading: Emma Munro's answer to What is it like to have an autistic parent? A quick note to NT adults of AS parents that may find the online forum useful, DM me for the link * The Complete Guide to Asperger’s Syndrome (Tony Attwood 2008). See also this link that summarises his views on the possible impacts of AS parenting.

question: How can you find somebody to start a relationship with when you're on the autism spectrum?
answer: That depends largely on what you mean by “start a relationship with” and on what approaches you are willing to take to “find” one. For instance, you can do what some people do and specifically seek a companion through some form of social media that is geared specifically toward coupling (sites like eHarmony, OKCupid, etc). You would be building a profile on the site to let potential prospects know about your likes, dislikes, profession/job, and personal interests. If you are fairly physically attractive and have attained a decent level of professional success, then you are likely to attract more prospects than if you have achieved nothing substantial (no degrees or job successes, for instance, obviously still dependent financially on parents, and with no solid friendships). If you are not physically well maintained (with attractive physical attributes and a clean, well kept appearance), you will be unlikely to attract anyone. Unlike many neuro typical folks, you cannot bank on being a “smooth talker”. You must present some “assets” which others will find appealing. If you take up the “mate search” approach, you will also need to prepare yourself mentally for multiple rejections before finding even one solid prospect. I know introverted people who have found lasting romantic relationships in this fashion. Please note that you are unlikely to succeed in this endeavor if you state upfront that you are autistic or mention anything about health issues. For instance, if you are heavily vested in working with marginalized communities, you would not mention anything about actually having ever been a marginalized individual youself. You are merely “an ally” at this stage of the game. You would be “selling” yourself online and would only want to present an image of self confidence, concern for others, and personal strength. That allows you to attract more potential prospects (a lot like what one might do in writing a successful resume). But this assumes you want to couple with someone in a lasting way versus merely meaning to be sexual with another human being. No matter what your intent, actually honing your social skills will make it far more likely for you to get beyond the mere “meeting/dating” stage. Even if you choose to meet women in more “organic” settings (such as by following your personal interests), you will still need to understand how to be appealing and how not to repel women. So, you will need to develop some kind of “social style”. For instance, are you a good listener who can make a woman feel special by showing a keen interest in what “makes her tick”? Are you the kind of guy who is very “gentlemanly” and is quick to open the car door, offer the lady your jacket when it is cold outside, pick up all checks, and go out of your way to make her feel comfortable (even at your own expense)? Those are two examples of “social style” when it comes to dating. Another one is that you are perfectly fine with developing a relationship over time and that you are not in a rush to “have a girlfriend”, or to get her into bed. This means conveying an attitude of being happy simply to get to know a woman “as a friend”. For many women, friendship with a male is an absolute prerequisite to even the possibility of any romantic/sexual interaction. It may not guarantee that the man will end up with her as his mate. But it will up those odds greatly over time. And it will also attract certain other females when it becomes clear that he has at least one close friendship with a woman. So, you will probably need to develop your social life beyond dating if you want to ultimately end up in any kind of sexual relationship (whether casual, or long lasting). You would be wise to focus on her instead of yourself (by asking questions) and share only a bit at a time about yourself. Revealing too much too soon forces her to mentally process that information instead of merely focusing on positives (your assets) like how easy it seems for her to talk to you, how pleasing you are to her physically, how great it is that you share similar interests, or how “safe” she feels in your presence. So, unless you are specifically hooking up with only autistic gals on some kind of “Autism dating website”, you need to nix any conversations about “the challenges of living as an Aspie” and how “neuro typical women don't understand you”. You will only be as understood as the clarity of your communications. Building lasting relationships take work. All the best to you.

answer: Yes. In fact this is written in the DSM as part of the diagnostic criteria and is very common. I've recently being doing some research on this though and I believe our struggles may not be due to a deficit, but more an overwhelming profound level of sensitivity. Highly sensitive people might have a harder time with relationships because we struggle to assert boundaries due to our compassionate nature. It can make us naive because we set high expectations of everyone. Because we are so deeply compassionate, we presume others are just the same. This can make us more vulnerable and targets for narcissists. The trauma and abuse can cause us to close up completely. Because autistic people are deeply sensitive we struggle knowing how much to give and may become overly attached and overwhelm the other person. Equally though, being so sensitive, we need our space and the other person can violate that if they do not understand. We may also become completely withdrawn due to the exhaustion and not give enough, causing the other person to get the impression we don't care. Another reason we might struggle to maintain relationships or friendships is that we tend to have quite specific interests that are deep which makes it harder to relate to others. But our interests are often much more meaningful because of how deep we go into them. They're often very authentic to us and not as popular as the things most people like. But a lot of that stuff is quite fake anyway. Because we're sensitive, we talk from the heart. We're direct and honest. This can be too much for many people to deal with and so only those with deep enough empathy and compassion tend to stick around. We might struggle to communicate our needs because of them being so different and misunderstood by most. Being so sensitive causes us to feel and experience things others might not. We might have sensory sensitivities that cause too much anxiety. We're also deeply intuitive but can become fearful of expressing that intuition in a society that does not understand. This can cause us to start bottling things up or over thinking our actions. We might get too distracted to be able to think rationally and articulate our feelings. Sometimes though, we do express ourselves very clearly, but we are misunderstood because many people just don't experience the world the same way. Communication is the sole foundation of a relationship. But it works both ways. I think maintaining relationships and friendships can be difficult for many people. But if you find the right person, there shouldn't be any complications.

question: Should I accept that I will never get married in this lifetime? I have never been in a relationship and I'm 23 and have autism.
answer: Short answer: No. And again, no. Don’t buy a lie; you’ll only hurt yourself if you do. Long answer: And just why would you accept the idea that you’ll never marry? Ask yourself what persuaded you that being single at 23—with or without autism—was in any way a guarantee that you’d remain single for your entire life? No, sir. Do not accept something that has nothing but personal doubts to support it. Do not sell yourself short. Autism is not an “eternal singles” card, even if you’re not considered “high functioning.” Autism has an unfortunate stigma to it. Don’t believe it. Most of those who stigmatize it (and I was once one of them) do so because they don’t understand it, and because they can’t/won’t see past the surface. Again, there is no guarantee that you’ll remain single, just because you’re still single at the young age of 23. Here are some examples of people I know who are autistic and married. My in-laws: both autistic (but didn’t know about it for years). They’ve been happily married for over 40 years, and the proud parents of 8 kids. My wife’s sister: married at age 26; also autistic. Her first kid is due soon. My wife: recently discovered that she’s probably autistic. She and I have 9 kids. Two, maybe three may be autistic, but that’s still 6–7 that aren’t; so even if you’re worried about passing it along to your kids, you’re not “doomed” to do so. As for “I’ve never had a relationship,” I can relate. By age 22, I’d never so much as held hands with a girl in any romantic sense. I’d been on plenty of dates, but…that was it. I began to seriously wonder what was wrong with me Twice, in about 4 months, I found myself tailspinning into depression when two different girls cold-shouldered me after I’d gone out with them just once (and my date with the first girl was great, and we were already friends, so that one really hurt). Guys all around me seemed able to get a girl at will—I never saw their struggles (though I’m sure they had them in some way I couldn’t see). But yeah—I started to feel pretty broken; and I didn’t even have the autism card to play. My luck turned around with surprising suddenness, and things happened far more quickly than I had ever imagined. I was very fortunate to meet and marry my first girl friend in the space of about 13 months. Statistically, that’s not very common in most parts of the US these days, but I say it not to brag, but to illustrate that the way things are now needn’t be a death sentence for the rest of your life. Yes, there will probably be many girls who get hung up on your autism. It’s unfortunate, but it’s best to face it head on and take control of it. It does not mean that no girl ever will see you for who you are (the whole you) and love you for you. The current average age for male marrying is about 25, 26 right now. You’re not even there yet. Don’t give up, mate. Don’t let yourself fall for a lie. Dating is hard for everyone, regardless of autism, so you’re in good company. Just keep pressing forward, and doing what you can. If you’re the religious type, pray for guidance as well. All the best, mate.

question: What is stimming in autism, and what is its relationship to sensory issues?
answer: Sensory sensitivities will frequently result in being overwhelmed daily by too much incoming “noise" that cannot be filtered out when one has ASD. Most autistics have no (or weak) filtering of incoming sensory information. “Noise" is not just sounds; all one's different senses can experience their own versions of noise stimuli. Almost anything that seems like a “nervous habit" in a neurotypical(majority) person is likely to be some kind of stimming in an autistic. Most healthy stims are or quickly become subconscious, so many autistics aren't even fully aware they're doing them. Repetetive hand and finger movements like flapping hands are more obvious versions, but far less obvious personal “habits" can also be stim oriented. Stimming is typically reassuring as well as partially self-regulating. These outward physical expressions and self-soothing mechanisms are related to the anxiety generated by all the noises. This can help keep suppressed anxiety from senses and social triggers from building up too much inside until overloading and exploding outward in negative “meltdowns”.
comment_answer: Quick comment: Recent fMRI scans have shown that the sensory issues are due to us having (way) more synapses than allistics and we therefore receive a much larger amount of information through our senses; our “filters” are probably similar but they have to filter and dampen a lot more information.

question: What is the relationship between autism and growth hormones?
answer: My autism is normal for me. I am probably flogging a dead horse when I say my autism is not a medical condition. I FEEL that there is a difference in the way neurotypical people and the autistic subsection of neurodiverse people produce hormones. By definition there is a difference in the way we experience and relate to the world we live in. Our emotional life is written differently in our very DNA. Endocrines and autism. An area of reasearch that is still in it’s infancy. The studies available are very much on-going research, rather than received wisdom. I do not know how advanced knowledge is in this area. In 2007, Writing in the journal Clinical Endocrinology, Dr. James Mills of the NICHD and colleagues said they compared the height, weight, head circumference and levels of growth-related hormones to growth and maturation in 71 boys with autism to a group of 59 healthy boys. The boys with autism had higher levels of two hormones that directly regulate growth -- insulin-like growth factor-1 and IGF-2. The boys also had higher levels of hormones that indirectly affect growth. What use is old news from nearly 2 decades ago? No corresponding study was done on girls. What does this mean? It is just a statement of fact finding. Neither good nor bad, nor cause for concern. Just a measurable difference. I question the application of such a relationship in terms of whether this is there is an opportunity to monkey around with medication. Like using a sledge hammer to crack a nut. ( No sick pun intended). Is there the whiff of discredited Eugenics? If autism is not a disorder like diabetes or epilepsy, then why try to medicate or cure it? If it aint broke, don’t fix it. Our endocrine system has over 80 different homones that interact in an amazing way, like a great big orchestra. Only a few hormones are commonly known by name. It is a delicate equilibrium. Growth hormones. It is one thing to acknowledge that there is a difference. It does not imply that one is ideal, and the other is unhealthy. JUST DIFFERENT. No causal implications that you can attribute to cause and effect. That would be bad critical thinking. No direct relationship. As yet. Is it a possible diagnostic tool? There are financial stakes when it comes to disability payments. All autistic people have some executive function weaknesses. I have a good support network including paid services that I would struggle without. If your growth hormones are out of order that is a medical condition. I do not know of any reliable statistics or studies I can refer you to. One person can have issues with both, with one or the other, or with neither. Common comorbidities include:obesity.diabetes.high blood pressure.heart disease.high blood lipid levels.arthritis.asthma.sleep apnea.Comorbidities are more than one disorder in the same person. For example, if a person is diagnosed with both social anxiety disorder (SAD) and major depressive disorder (MDD), they are said to have comorbid (meaning co-existing) anxiety and depressive disorders. My type of autism is written into my DNA. Aspergers. Also running in the family is a weak bladder, and thyroid problems, and short sightedness.
