question: Nature vs nurture. Do you think those with neurological disorder (autism, ADHD) are limited by nature?
answer: Nature vs nurture. Do you think those with neurological disorder (autism, ADHD) are limited by nature? in Memory Erasing Laboratory Great question! I know that the topics of autism and ADHD are sensitive to some, and my opinions relating to neurotypes definitely will offend some people. I have no authority on these topics despite having ASD, but this is only one “form of the autism neurotype.” I do not speak for all people with ASD or other “forms of” autism, or even for people with the other related diagnoses. I have no neurology credentials, so all information that I have taken to provide evidence to support my opinions come from my anecdotes, other people’s research, and other people’s opinions. Despite both autism and ADHD being classified as “neurological disorders,” some forms and some individuals on each spectrum (whether with just one, both, or more of these diagnoses), tend to possess their own limitations. Just like the varying physical and mental limitations of people that have a “typical” or other rewiring that is considered neurotypical (NT) by most neuroscientists, everyone has a unique range of abilities and inabilities. While I have clear and colored vision, can see, feel temperature and pain, have a functioning olfactory and gustation systems, have a high tolerance for visual and auditory stimuli, have no ticcs, can speak (although without perfect grammar), have no diagnosed cancer, can operate a motor vehicle (somewhat), have already passed sophomore year in high school at the average age, and have fast-adapting night vision within human limits, other people do not have these abilities or inabilities. I believe that the physical abilities of a person are affected by their genetics, how their enzymes interacted with their original cells during the germinal stage of pregnancy, how well the free and bound ribosomes do their work, how lucky they were not to contract cancer, and how their environments affect the expression of their genetics. These factors often overlap, as a person usually has ribosomal dysfunction if the mRNA they get fails to produce the right subunits. Additionally, I believe that they mental abilities/limits of a person are a combination of their genetic luck, fortune in the environments where their genes function to make the optimal RNA for optimal proteins, as well as a growth mindset. While people with specific neurotypes cannot (or at least cannot be bothered) to understand the biotechnological explanation of their condition if the information is readily available, other non-neurotypical people may be able to understand or even work in fields where they are able to encounter reasons why they and their diverse peers may have mental limitations. Those More Adversely Affected The earlier group need significantly more help, and to varying degrees; I feel bad for the individuals that are my age without basic academic knowledge as caused by their condition(s), because they suffer by existing. All to often I saw those children that needed help struggle within their own classes, unable to multiply single-digit natural numbers together. How can they live for themselves if they cry over the inability to understand, and how can they live for themselves if their ancestors are most entirely at fault for their strife? The growth mindset and ability to learn social thinking can only barely apply to these unfortunate people. They are limited in their awareness to the illusion around them that they suffer a series of illusions overlapping them. I am not talking about hallucination strictly, rather I mean illusions as in a distorted perspective led by the innocence and lack of understanding of the functions of the observable universe, on top of the illusions created by caretakers to comfort the not-so-well-endowed, on top of the illusion that reality is real. Some of these people who need help cannot develop object permanence even though it matters not to those with reasons by philosophy to refute even the existence of any object. Also, these people may interpret the meanings of phrases without context, and this is a common illusion suffered not only by the non-neurotypical, but by the neurotypical to a much smaller extent. I myself had to go through rigorous “retraining” where my mother and other counselors not only doubled as a therapist but also had to teach me social etiquette because I just did not understand that most polite behaviors were implied. I have since reverted back to not caring so much about the stances others take on me, but I retain awareness that every action I make and statement I write is heavily judged. I’m on Quora, after all. Those Less Adversely Affected In areas where people that are non-neurotypical still fall short of societal standards and neurological standards for neurotypicality, some deficiencies even be amplified in those that need less help. In addition to Derealization-Depersionalization “Disorder” (DDD), monopolarity, bipolarity, Cotard(‘s) Syndrome, chronic depression, and anxiety in child, adolescent, and young adults, those with any of these diagnoses as well as the more-discussed diagnoses, even while closer to the neurotypical corner of the conventional diagnoses’ spectrums, can suffer great episodes of a variety of types. They may still have the ability to pass classes and get jobs, but they will need long-term help in keeping themselves from self-harm, su1c1de, risky and/or impulsive behaviors, mood swings, drug abuse, and the like (su1c1de being the most permanent and damaging IMO). There is yet to be a cure to genetic conditions or factors that directly or indirectly result in people contracting disorders or adopting unusual delusions, but that’s a problem only to be solved by working around finding a direct solution, mostly by drastic actions—omnicide, implementation of eugenics, etc (stuff I want to happen, but stuff I shouldn’t want to happen). That’s why it is almost impossible to circumvent the problems that can only be solved, feasibly, prenatally or before conception. Not even the erasing of memory can reasonably resolve non-trauma-related problems. Forward If you would like to hear the opinions of actual neurologists on the topic, post or submit the same question on Ask a Neuroscientist. They might have more factual, or at least up-to-date, information on these diagnoses and their spectrum limits.

question: What are the pros and cons of mainstream schooling vs. homeschooling for a child with autism and ADHD?
answer: The pros and cons are personal to each one of us, but I can tell you our story in hopes of giving a little insight. I homeschooled my autistic son (and his two brothers) through 8th grade. That allowed me to hone in on his specific needs and struggles and give him time to work them through. When you're in a classroom setting, the teacher, of course, has to consider the needs of all students. By 8th grade both he and I were ready to do something different. I had introduced teaching technology the last year we were together, as he was having a hard time separating mom from teacher. Then, he went to a private school where they claimed to treat their students like family. They said he wouldn't require an I.E.P. because they knew their students personally and were able to adapt to their needs at all times. Some of the teachers did a great job, but for others adapting meant getting rid of anything the students didn't like. That's not how education works in our home, so he spent his last two years with an I.E.P. at our local high school. This was invaluable, as it allowed him to participate in a program after high school that required an I.E.P. He also found his love for videography taking that as an elective both years. So, my advice — adapt to your child’s needs as he learns and grows. Find the best learning environment and help him discover his passion and purpose. Don't underestimate him. Push gently. Allow him to be who he is. Love him. Also, if you choose to homeschool, make sure to make time for yourself. It is not for the faint of heart. There were days when I wanted to run after the yellow school bus, toss my three boys on, and run away to Tahiti. 🤔 Finding a homeschool community at my church and through a homeschool hybrid worked for me., and I'm still mostly sane. Blessings on your journey. It will pass by fast. Enjoy the ride!

question: Do people with ADHD tend to have uneven scores on components of IQ tests (eg., Verbal vs. Quantitative skills), excelling in some areas and doing poorly in others, or is that true moreso for Autism?
answer: Yes, as ADHD is a cognitive disability. The only aspect of IQ that really stood out for me was in working memory, where I scored in the 8th percentile, as opposed to 98–99th percentile overall. I haven't looked at my score results in over a decade, so I don't remember all the areas where I scored lower than on my overall score, but there were a handful. All my scores were above average, though, excepting working memory. Although not as dramatic a difference, my son performed significantly better overall than he did in a few areas of the test, but he has learning disabilities (dyscalculia and dysgraphia) in addition to ADHD. Having worked in special education, I think evaluating for and discovering cognitive disabilities is one of the few benefits of IQ testing. IQ tests are pretty much useless for telling us how smart or capable someone really is, and are highly skewed by cultural influence, but they are pretty useful at highlighting an individual person's areas of comparative weakness. I mean, 100 percentage points of difference is significant. Even if I had an especially bad day or the results of the test were influenced by my environment or internal state (tiredness, etc.), it's unlikely that on a good day I would have scored more than twice as well. Scoring in the 16th-20th percentile would still have shown profound impairment.

question: What's the difference between classic autism, Asperger’s syndrome, high-functioning autism, and ADHD?
answer: So let's start with the big ones first! Kanner's Classic Autism vs. High-Functioning Autism vs. Asperger's Syndrome. Or “why these were all combined in the DSM V.” Kanner's classic autism is “autism, with delayed speech development AND an IQ of less than 70.” HFA is “autism with delayed speech development and an IQ of 70+.” Asperger's is “autism without delayed speech development (but with the possibility of situational mutism or regression later), AND an IQ of 111+ (average or above average).” There are SOOOOO many issues with these distinctions. First, intellectual disabilities are not autism, so going based off of IQ like that would be like calling an autistic with a co-occurring anxiety disorder “flight-risk autism,” instead of “autism with a comorbid anxiety disorder.” The lack of separation led to a lot of resources being denied to “high-functioning” autistics, and aspies, while autonomy was frequently denied to “low-functioning” or “classic” autistics. Asperger's as a diagnosis was also specifically introduced as part of a Nazi eugenics program, Aktion T4 - a precursor to the Final Solution where disabled people were used to test various experiments and killing methods. The gas chamber design was first tested on disabled people, prior to being billed out for the genocide of Jewish prisoners. This is not to say that it's comparable to the Shoah, but rather that this diagnostic label was used to divide who should live and who should die among disabled people in Nazi Germany. IQ testing is poorly designed, and doesn't accommodate for disabilities to begin with. It's also racist and classist, so multiply-marginalized autistics were more likely to be labeled as “low-functioning” than white, middle-class autistics. Verbal skills are actually one part of one symptom of autism - fine motor skills development. An Autistic person may have excellent fine motor skills in the area of speech but have major developmental delays in the use of fingers for fine motor work, or have major gross motor skills issues. So this is an incredibly bad distinction to be drawn (and also ignores the possibility of a secondary issue such as damage to the throat). On top of that, it ignores the concept that an autistic person may find their own voice painful due to auditory hyper-sensitivity (which is super common for autistics). So we may understand how to talk, and still not do so because the sound is painful or overwhelming. Difference from ADHD? ADHD does not inherently come with sensory issues, and is generally caused by issues with dopamine and serotonin being metabolized in the brain. Autism involves (among other things) physical structural differences in our brains.

question: Can someone be diagnosed with both Asperger's and ADD/ADGHD simultaneously?

There are not yet definitive traits in blood or DNA that prove the existing of high-functioning autism. Instead diagnosis is relative comparison of a person’s outward behavior compared to the behavior of what is deemed as normal, at that time and in that culture. ADD has more research in the field and more methods to derive positive diagnosis. Generally, treatment for ADD should occur first, as successful behavioral therapy, addressing dysfunction in the family environment, and when necessary medication can result in positive outcomes for ADD that cause other marginal autistic behaviors now appear normal. Rarely, successful treatment for ADD will result in more obvious ASD behaviors, particularly social behaviors. Differential diagnosis through ineffective medication treatment was the strongest confirming evidence in my own diagnosis. My childhood diagnosis in the 70’s was ADD but I had never responded positively to stimulants. As an adult my therapist asks me, “Hey, you have five college degrees but don’t exhibit any hyperactive traits. I don’t think this is ADD. You said you started reading at the age of 3 and even as a child would spend hours simply writing down numbers and letters into cypher blocks?” And several conversations and years later, my diagnosis change to ASD. Today, hyperlexia and OCD regarding mental patterning are strong behavior traits suggesting ASD, that have little to do with ADD. I don’t generally recommend non-peer reviewed topics, but IMO the absolute best response I’ve seen anywhere on this question is the YouTube Video, Autism vs ADHD (The Difference between ADHD and Autism Spectrum Disorder) from Autism from the Inside”. You can have both, an ASD will focus on their favorite topics, but if they have ADD they are very easy to distract. In my case of ASD with no ADD, distractions are annoying, but noise cancelling earbuds and shaded glasses are usually enough to let me stay in a mental flow-stay, as long as I can stay on one task, for six to twelve continuous hours each day. question: ADHD and autism have some overlapping symptoms. What symptoms of autism are not also symptoms of ADHD?
answer: Both ADHD and autism are spectrums with people displaying different traits. I will not speak on the experiences of others, but I will tell you about the overlap and the different traits I recognize in myself, being both autistic and ADHD. The overlaps that I see in myself:PDA: I am a strong PDAer, this is my brain being hardwired to question authority and diverge from the path most traveled. Many autistics and ADHDers will say the same, that they do no like to be told what to do, they do not like to have others dictate their existence for them, this is something I believe as well. Being PDA means that you are most likely going to go against the grain and be more apt to want to be yourself, being rebellious, if you will. It is not a simple form of “teenage rebellion,” PDA is more of an ingrained trait that allows the PDAer to question everything expected of them. I’ve personally asked questions like, “Well, why do I have to do that if it doesn’t make me happy? I shouldn’t have to sacrifice my own well-being for the ‘greater good,’ right?”Hyperfocus: I am able to hyperfocus on things, albeit, it’s harder to hyperfocus on things that I do not find interesting (many ADHDers will relate, not all, but many). If I get into the right mindset, I can tune out everything else and may be able to focus on things I don’t find very interesting. Hyperfocusing has made it so that I have worked for hours on things without breaks. This can actually become an issue at times when I forget to take care of myself. For example, I have spent up to 9 hours at times completing art projects, I find it to be both a blessing and a curse at those times. Hyperfocusing is something that many autistic and ADHD people can both do, not everybody can do it to the capacity that others can, but many can and do hyperfocus.Empathy: It is a common misconception that autistics lack empathy, which I find to be completely untrue for many of us. The autistics that I know and am friends with are extremely empathetic and would sacrifice everything to ensure that the people around them aren’t suffering. I personally feel extremely emotional when somebody is pouring their heart out, especially when I can relate to them (the difference between sympathy and empathy). I often cry when others cry, I feel other’s emotions and it can be very draining for me. I have to sometimes close myself off from those situations so that I can preserve my own mental health, because things can be so sad that it feels like a knife to my chest. This empathy can be experienced by other autistics and ADHDers, I know a couple who have similar experiences, but it’s different for everybody. I find that those I know with ADHD also can be highly empathetic.Executive Dysfunction: For me, my executive dysfunction is extremely disabling and I need help with some tasks. I will have to do body doubling, or will have to ask for help with certain things that I do not have the capacity to complete. I know that this is common for both ADHDers and autistics alike. Executive dysfunction can impact a broad variety of brain functions like working memory and the ability to start and complete tasks. I personally believe that my PTSD pronounces my executive dysfunction and makes it much harder to maintain a certain way of life. This is why I use spoons to dictate how much I can complete in a day and try not to overdo it, or else I will experience burnout or a shutdown (even more dangerous).Masking: Masking within itself is really a survival technique, and not a “trait,” however, I find that it is prevalent in both ADHD and autism and that it should be noted. It’s highly fascinating that we develop coping mechanisms and a survival technique that we often act out subconsciously. Masking is of course detrimental for our health, it can cause extreme fatigue and increase the risk of developing mental illnesses like depression and anxiety. Masking can go so deep, that after years of doing it, you don’t even realize when you are (subconsciously, again) and it can even convince you that what you are doing is how you naturally are. This is why many ADHDers and autistics have an identity crisis when they are realizing who they truly are, I personally experienced this. I am still trying to get to know my true self because I spent approximately 18+ years suppressing who I really am to avoid bullying and torment. I was severely bullied growing up to the point that I had suicidal thoughts and that I still have extreme PTSD today. Masking only softened the blows temporarily, because I had to act like somebody I was not, so if I decided to be vulnerable and show my autistic or ADHD self, I was belittled. Masking becomes second-nature, it makes you feel like there is no other option until you finally start to convince yourself that you are just like everybody else and need to work harder, because you’re being “too lazy.” This is obviously not the case, as we often are already working as hard as we can and we can’t all meet neurotypical standards. This is why it’s important to accept neurodivergence and allow space for people to make mistakes or to be different.Having Strong Intuition: There have been many times that I have been able to predict that something was going to happen and it definitely saved my life. There have been situations where I have had to use this because I would have probably had something happen to me. I believe that this could definitely be pattern recognition, being able to guess something will happen, from similar outcomes with a similar string of events.There are many other overlapping traits and features of autism and ADHD, but I want to touch on the differences, as that’s what this question asks. Here are the differences I see:Critical vs. Creative Thinking: These are both things that I have seen in ADHDers and autistics alike, and in people who are both, but I see a separation for myself when it comes to these. I personally have both of these traits and they both allow be to think outside of the box and to analyze things from a logical perspective. I find that my autism allows me to think in a more logical manner, being more calculating about things and analyzing situations in excruciating detail. For my creative thinking, it allows me to be open-minded and to see things from the perspectives of others. Creative thinking also allows me to hone into my artistic nature. I used to paint and draw, but I have since stopped for personal reasons. However, I find myself pouring my creative side into other projects, like doing creative writing, or sewing (I loooove to sew, especially historical costumes). I don’t necessarily attribute the creative thinking to my ADHD, but I do think that it contributes to it. I strongly believe that much of my creative thinking comes from my autism.Spontaneity vs. Routine: I find that I have to accommodate my ADHD and autism by setting an open schedule for myself on a daily basis. I will allow myself to switch it up when I need to, but I still need some semblance of routine to feel comfortable. I can also be spontaneous at times, although, that is a rare occurrence for me. I have anxiety as well, so I am often thinking of every possible scenario that could happen to mentally prepare myself for situations. This also comes from a place of having to mask, trying to prepare myself to blend in as best as I can, running my conversations off of a script. I have tried not doing this as much anymore, I’ve tried to be more receptive to the volatility of this world, but I still need to go at my own pace. I could be laughing and having a good time, and then I suddenly have the need to isolate and recharge. This is a common occurrence for many autistics specifically, but I’ve also seen some ADHDers deal with it as well, for me, it’s my ADHD side wanting to have fun and be social, and then my autistic side telling me to slow down and recuperate.Being Detail-Oriented vs. Being “Careless”: I find that I can be very detail-oriented, which I attribute to my autism, but I can also make mistakes that later seem obvious to me. There are times when I rush through things and make errors and then I will have to go back at a later time when I am in a relaxed and “analytical” state to nitpick through them and correct them. These two can sometimes happen at the same time. I may be paying attention to something, mulling it over in my head, but I’ll forget one detail that would change the whole balance of whatever it is I am doing.Vulnerability vs. Caution: I have noticed that I am more vulnerable to being taken advantage of with my ADHD side. I have also noticed that I can be cautious about new situations from my autistic side, which allows me to avoid more stressful situations. Dealing with both at once is strange, I’ll be cautious about something, and then something unexpected happens, which still leaves me in a vulnerable state, even if I’m trying to protect myself.Special Interests vs. Varying Interests: I often find myself switching between special interests because of ADHD. I believe that the special interests themselves are traits that can occur with both autism and ADHD separately, but I attribute my autism to mine. I may be interested in video games one day and watching old movies another day. I went through a Jurassic Park and dinosaur phase that lasted 4 months last year, then I switched to doll faceups immediately after. I will often spend a lot of time on one interest, and then will stop halfway through and switch interests again. It has left with with many an unfinished project, but I sometimes go back to them and finish them up. I know many people who are ADHD and autistic at the same time have experienced this exact phenomenon as well.Under-Stimulation vs. Over-Stimulation: I can be either over-stimulated, or under-stimulated, but never at the same time. I believe the under-stimulation comes from my ADHD sensory-seeking side, where I may enjoy certain textures or sounds, or experience overwhelming sensory situations, like going swimming on a hot day. I believe that my over-stimulation comes from my autism and SPD. I will sometimes avoid sensory situations that I find unpleasant. For example, there are certain types of fabrics that I cannot touch because it’ll give me the chills and I’ll feel gross.No matter which traits and comorbidities we have, we all experience life as a whole, differently. Not everyone has the same overlaps or differences, some people have all, some have none. We are all diverse and view the world differently, this is what make us neurodivergent.

question: Can you explain the differences between ADD, ADHD, Asperger's Syndrome, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and learning disorders?
answer: “Learning disorders” is extremely broad and could include the above mentioned. Though I would say that personally, my issues pertain more to navigating everything else in an academic environment and getting extremely overstimulated by a number of things. Then without meds, my ADHD makes it so that my ability to focus is like a flashlight, that goes on and off randomly. Though the actual learning, when I can focus, isn’t really the issue. So it can also tie in more to things like low IQ, which can co-occur, or things, like dyslexia, which can also happen on it’s own. I knew a woman, who absolutely needed a freckle on one hand to tell left from right, but was otherwise a very bright woman. I think she became a nurse or the like via the army. ADD vs ADHD, is a question of hyperactivity. I have trouble watching anything during the day, unless I am too exhausted from sleep deprivation and/or being undernourished to be up and about. I just can’t sit still until I’m tired enough to start winding down. Some, more inattentive types, might not have hyperactivity. A lot of women on that particular spectrum (not the ASD one) tend to be that way. Hence atypical presentation and underdiagnosis. Asperger’s vs ASD is largely a question of older vs contemporary vernacular. Some people would say that folks with Asperger’s are on the higher end of the functioning scale, due to being more independent. However they also tend to get the shaft, in terms of social support and general understanding. So have a high tendency to become very dysfunctional, and potentially off themselves from mental exhaustion or to die prematurely from heart disease. So generally, the functioning labels tend to be frowned upon. What is true, is that like any population, we have our strengths and weaknesses. I hope that struck a balance between detailed and concise.

question: What is the process for getting an assessment (formal diagnosis) for an adult with ASD/Asperger’s?
answer: Find a psychologist. This one took me several tries to figure out. My recommendation would be to first find out who provides services to autistic people in your area. They probably don’t do diagnostic work but they probably know who is reputable. I called such a place thinking they might do diagnostic work but instead got an excellent recommendation. Call the aforementioned psychologist and ask for an assessment. “Hello. I would like to schedule an appointment with Dr. Cohn for an autism assessment.” The lady who answered the phone asked me a couple of questions, we discussed the costs, (my insurance didn’t cover it) then I scheduled the appointment. Go to the appointment. That probably goes without saying. The actual testing consisted of three appointments each about a month apart.Appointment #1He explained the whole process.He explained what autism is.He asked me some questions to get to know me and see if there is a good reason to think I might be autistic.He gave me a packet of roughly 100 pages to be filled out for the next appointment. These 100 pages included questions about:My interactions with other people.My school work.Memories of my youth.My relationship with my parents.All kinds of abuse from all different sources.All aspects of my mood over the years.Depression, anxiety, OCD, ADHD and every other mental health condition you could imagine.Appointment #2Mostly testing. There was an IQ test, memory testing, and all sorts of different mental tests that I’ve always found fascinating. If you’ve ever played Brain Age on the Nintendo DS, imagine that on steroids, but on paper instead of a handheld gaming console.I had to give back the completed packet of information at this appointment.Appointment #3This is where he told me exactly what he thought was wrong. In my case, Autism Spectrum Disorder and a touch of a few other little things. (He used much more official terminology but then described it all as well.)Autism vs. Asperger’s The new DSM, where doctors get their diagnoses from, doesn’t list Asperger’s Syndrome, just variations of Autism Spectrum Disorder. While Asperger’s Syndrome is a much cooler name, Dr. Cohn explained the difference to me. While people on Quora have told me it doesn’t make a difference, what Dr. Cohn said makes a lot of sense so I’ll share it. (I don’t know the requirements for an Asperger’s diagnosis nor do I remember what he used as an example so while my example might not be accurate, the concept is accurate.) He said that Asperger’s Syndrome included a lot of different things in the diagnosis that are symptoms of other conditions. For example, an Asperger’s diagnosis contains symptoms of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder. So people who had autism and OCD would get diagnosed with Asperger’s. The problem is that the treatments for OCD are only approved for OCD. Insurance companies don’t cover those treatments for Asperger’s Syndrome. Now you don’t get diagnosed with Asperger’s, you would get diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder and OCD and your insurance has to cover treatment for both. I know he mentioned a few things that conflicted with the Asperger’s diagnosis. I kind of know what he’s saying, too. I also have Multiple Sclerosis which has a lot of possible symptoms. When I go to a doctor for something and they know I have MS, I often hear, “Oh, that’s just the MS.” No tests to make sure this new symptom isn’t something else. And as long as my diagnosis is just Multiple Sclerosis, the treatments for this new symptom aren’t approved as an MS treatment so they aren’t covered. It sounds like there are cases where people with Asperger’s Syndrome can have the same problem. Is it worth it? Absolutely! Just knowing what it is that has caused all of these struggles throughout my life is such a help. Until the MS hit I was doing okay but it just seemed like I had to work so much harder to get things to work for me than everyone else. I mean so much harder. This explains why and it points me in the right direction when I’m looking for better ways to do things. And do try to get recommendations and see someone reputable and thorough. You don’t just want someone to agree with you. What you really want is to put your mind at ease and have no question in your mind that the diagnosis is correct.

question: Is Asperger's often misdiagnosed as ADHD? If so, why?
answer: Yes. I won’t go into too much detail due to time but some reasons have been expounded upon by others.there is a LOT of overlap in the more “obvious” symptoms (including the social skill deficits common in ADHD which it drives me crazy that people don’t think of when they think ADHD - stimulants aren’t the full answer to adhd because PILLS DON’T TEACH SKILLS- but I digress)the symptoms that overlap with adhd and/or anxiety are often obvious well before the social difficulties for folks with Aspergers -type ASD. so they get diagnosed first and everything that followed after is overshadowed diagnostically - people assume it’s all due to the first / original diagnosis without pausing to consider maybe it was just an early manifestation of ASD unfolding over time (when social demands get more complex and more implicit rather than explicit) at older ages - or that maybe it’s a combination of both (very common)statistically adhd is more common- and combine that with people who THINK they know autism spectrum often are working from a stereotype that does not capture the more subtle differences of aspergers / people who don’t have intellectual disability or very obvious restricted interests/repetitive behaviors for example. So to some healthcare and educational professionals they do not know / have not been trained to tease out the reasoning/thinking BEHIND the behaviors that present similarly to ADHD. So many people misdiagnose and call it ADHD. But just like a fever could mean the flu, sepsis, COVID, or Ebola… mild social and RRB oddities don’t always mean some combo of ADHD and/or anxiety and/or personality quirks. Sometimes it takes a more nuanced and specialized diagnostic approach to accurately tease apart the underlying factors and there just aren’t all that many people in education or healthcare trained to pick up on the differences in some cases- and they can’t be. Everyone can’t be a specialist in everything - and that’s not their primary role.bottom line- it’s common and people should always be willing (encouraged, even) to seek a second or third opinion for any life/sense of identity altering diagnosis of any sort if they feel like maybe it doesn’t quite fit or feel they did not really get a good understanding of why that was the result of the evaluation versus something else. I would be skeptical of any general practitioner / PCP who gave me a diagnosis of something medical that had an enormous impact on my life / sense of self and then was not supportive of me seeking further evaluation from a specialist or two. You should always feel confident in your care and the accuracy/appropriateness of it. ETA- this is literally my career - diagnostic evaluations for people with suspected ASD, especially older kids through adults. ASD vs ADHD vs anxiety or depression - or some combination thereof - is 90% of the differential questions I get. More obvious cases are diagnosed at younger ages. We get a lot of people seeking third opinions (we typically do first or third opinions for diagnostics)

question: Is it possible for autistic kids to be sociopaths or conduct disorders? Autism is linked to high IQ, but sociopathy is link to lower IQ.
answer: Ok.Autism is NOT linked to high IQ. There's a range of IQ observed among Autistic people: from very low to exceptionally high.Sociopathy is not a diagnosis per se. It is frequently used interchangeably with Psychopathy. And neither is NOT linked to low IQ. Snakes in Suits is an excellent book, describing highly successful intelligent psychopaths in white collar jobs. Just like with Autism, there's a range of IQ observed in Psychopathy.Conduct disorder could be seen as a childhood precursor of Antisocial Personality Disorder, which overlaps with Psychopathy. Traditionally, it's thought that Oppositional defiant disorder transforms into Conduct disorder which grows into ASPD. BUT! There's a different thinking, which unlinks the ODD & CD. CD doesn't have to be preceded by ODD. And ODD doesn't have to transform into CD.And now, THE ANSWER: 1) Autism — especially when accompanied by ADHD — can be complicated by development of ODD. Not Conduct disorder. 2) You know about cognitive empathy Vs emotional empathy? Autistics have (often) excessive emotional empathy, but struggle with the cognitive empathy. Psychopaths are the exact opposite: they often say they don't feel emotions and they lack emotional empathy — which is why they can coldly use people to further their agenda. But their cognitive empathy - their ability to predict people's actions & reactions — is top notch. That is why they are so successful in manipulation of others.

question: In blood pressure, there is a natural pressure in the middle and high and low pressure on the two sides. So, is there an opposite to autism such that the normal state in middle and the autistic and opposite-autistic on the sides of the normal state?
answer: Yes and no. I’ll explain, but we’ll have to back up a bit. First let me establish some terms and clarify some things. First off, autism is a natural thing and it isn’t like high/low blood pressure where someone can start off with average blood pressure and then develop high or low blood as a result of health problems. People are born autistic (probably based on their genetics) and they remain autistic their whole lives. So in that respect, the answer is definitely no. Also, there isn’t such a thing as “opposite autistic.” I’m not going to use the term “normal” or “natural” here (as discussed above), but instead I’ll use the terms “neurotypical” (meaning the range of behaviors and traits that are not pathologized medically and exist in common, average distribution among people) and the term “neurodivergent” (meaning ranges of behaviors and traits that tend to be medically pathologized and given diagnoses including autism). So…. all possible human behaviors/traits/mental states exist in their own bell curve, where most people are in the middle of the bell curve and are “neurotypical” and some people fall on the extreme sides of the bell curve and are “neurodivergent.” However, there is not just ONE bell curve for “typical” vs “divergent” but rather a separate bell curve for every set of traits. So for example, there’s a bell curve for how intensely people respond to others emotions in an empathetic way, and a minority of people have no empathetic response (a neurodivergent trait), most people have a moderate empathetic response (a neurotypical trait), and some people have an extreme or even debilitating empathetic response (a neurodivergent trait). There’s a separate bell curve for how reactive people are to sensory input. A small minority of people are “sensory seeking” and have an intense urge to seek out sensory experiences that would be unpleasant or overwhelming to most people (that’s a neurodivergent trait). Sensory seekers might enjoy sounds that would be too loud for others, or intentionally cause themselves injury in order to feel something. Meanwhile, most people have a a “typical” response to stimuli where they enjoy or tolerate most sensory experiences within a certain range of intensity (a neurotypical response to things like sounds, textures, lights, etc). There are also sensory-avoidant people who can’t handle “normal” intensity of sensory input and need sound blockers, low-sensory textures/clothes/etc, low level lights, etc. (That’s a neurodivergent trait). These bell curves exist for all kinds of traits, ranging from how social people are, how are sex drives work, how we use language, how good we are at academics, etc. If someone is in the middle of the bell curve for most traits (even if they have a couple outliers that don’t significantly impact their daily life), they are considered neurotypical. If they are at EITHER extreme of the bell curve for traits that significantly impact their daily like (such as ability to use language or the degree to which they experience delusions), they are considered neurodivergent. But depending on where they fall on each element of the bell curve, they might be diagnosed with different things (with a personality disorder vs with schizophrenia vs with autism vs adhd, etc). “Autism Spectrum” is a naturally occurring state in which an individual is an outlier on multiple loosely related bell curves — but the reason it’s called a “spectrum” is that we can be an outlier on EITHER SIDE of the bell curve. Remember where I said the answer was “yes and no”? This is the part where the answer to your question is yes, except that it’s not “autism and opposite-autism,” but rather that autistic traits are generally things that can be outside the normal distribution either due to being more or less than normal. Take sensory experience. It is a standard autistic trait to be neurodivergent in regards to sensory input. Some autistic people are sensory seeking (and as children may do things like spinning, head-banging, being obsessed with interesting textures, etc). Many autistic people are sensory avoidant and may be overwhelmed by sounds, lights, smells, textures, etc and need “sensory friendly” clothing, sound blocking headphones, etc. And a lot of us experience BOTH sensory seeking and sensory avoidant behavior at different times in our lives or in response to different input (e.g., being avoidant of sounds but sensory-seeking to the feeling of being spun around). Empathy is another area where autistic people can go either way — some of us experience hypo-empathy and have almost no empathetic response towards others, but some of us experience hyperempathy and can be so overwhelmed by empathy that we melt down when faced with the idea of other’s pain. It’s very common for autistic folks to have extreme empathy and worry about the emotions of even inanimate objects (for instance refusing to throw out a broken toy because they don’t want to make it sad) or to be unable to function socially because they are so overwhelmed by the feelings of others — and it’s also very common for some of us to have absolutely no reaction to other people’s mental states. Again, some people go one way, some go another, and some of us fluctuate back and forth. Intellectual functioning is another area where we exist on the extremes of typical distribution. Depending on the study, the IQ/intellectual functioning of autistic people tends to be 30–40% very much below average, 10–20% average, and 50–70% very much above average. We’re more likely to be highly intellectually gifted than we are to have intellectual disabilities, but we’re also way more likely to have extreme intellectual disabilities than we are to have “average” intellectual functioning. That’s because autism is defined by its divergence from the standard. (Unlike with sensory seeking, one person is unlikely to go back and forth between high and low IQ. However, what is very common is a “spikey” IQ profile, for instance having an extremely poor ability to use language and a very high ability to use math, or vis versa. Neurotypical people may have strengths and weaknesses, but are unlikely to have such an extreme difference between the two) Previously, Autism had been divided into the basic “Autistic” category and the “Aspergers” category specifically because some of us have very low language functioning and some of us have extremely advanced language functioning. So early researchers thought that people with low verbal abilities were “autistic” and those with high verbal abilities had “Aspergers.” The two categories were recombined into the single category of “Autistic Spectrum Disorder” once researchers realized that this was just another area where autistic people had either “high” or “low” settings on the bell curve distribution of a trait, but that otherwise autism and aspergers were identical. In short, autism can be hard to pin down because there are a large number of “autistic traits” in which we can go to either extreme, and a small percentage of us will also fall in the normal range for some of those. Diagnosis of autism occurs when we hit the extreme version on most of those traits (though not all of them). Common autism-related traits (in which we are likely to differ dramatically from the allistic/neurotypical average) are: — various sensory traits including reaction to stimuli, reaction to foods, and ability to use senses — various social-related traits — executive function/ability to initiate tasks and focus on them — empathy and emotion-related traits — language use and verbal comprehension — pattern recognition (which can include math ability and problem solving) — relationship to routine/organization/etc (we can be either hyper routine oriented or extremely disorganized) — probably some I’m forgetting …. so, does that make sense?

question: What do you do when your anxiety and ADHD leaves you completely restless?
answer: The link between ADHD and Anxiety If you’ve been diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), you may also have another mental health disorder. Sometimes symptoms of other conditions can be masked by the symptoms of ADHD. It’s estimated that over 60 percent of people with ADHD have a comorbid, or coexisting, condition. Anxiety is one condition that is often seen in people with ADHD. About 50 percent of adults and up to 30 percent of children with ADHD also have an anxiety disorder. Keep reading to learn more about the connection between these two conditions. ADHD vs Anxiety If you have ADHD, it may be difficult to recognize the symptoms of anxiety. ADHD is an ongoing condition that often starts in childhood and can continue into adulthood. It can affect your ability to concentrate, and may result in behavioral problems, such as:hyperactivitylack of attentionlack of impulse controlfidgeting and trouble sitting stilldifficulty organizing and completing tasksAn anxiety disorder is more than just feeling occasionally anxious. It’s a mental illness that is serious and long lasting. It can make you feel distressed, uneasy, and excessively frightened in benign, or regular, situations. If you have an anxiety disorder, your symptoms may be so severe that they affect your ability to work, study, enjoy relationships, or otherwise go about your daily activities. The symptoms of ADHD are slightly different from those of anxiety. ADHD symptoms primarily involve issues with focus and concentration. Anxiety symptoms, on the other hand, involve issues with nervousness and fear. Even though each condition has unique symptoms, sometimes the two conditions mirror each other. That can make it difficult to tell whether you have ADHD, anxiety, or both. How can you tell the difference? Though a professional evaluation is necessary, family members may be able to tell the difference between ADHD and anxiety. The key is to watch how your symptoms present over time. If you have anxiety, you may be unable to concentrate in situations that cause you to feel anxious. On the other hand, if you have ADHD, you’ll find it difficult to concentrate most of the time, in any type of situation. If you have both ADHD and anxiety, the symptoms of both conditions may seem more extreme. For example, anxiety can make it even more difficult for someone with ADHD to pay attention and follow through on tasks. Understanding Comorbidity It’s not clear why there’s a connection between ADHD and anxiety, and doctors don’t fully understand what causes either condition. Genetics may be responsible for both conditions, and may also cause comorbidity. Researchers have also observed several other conditions that are commonly seen alongside ADHD, including:anxietydepressionautismsleep disordersdyslexiasubstance abusebipolar disorderPossible causes for ADHD include genetics, environmental toxins, or premature birth. It’s possible that these causes could also contribute to anxiety. Treatment Treating ADHD and anxiety simultaneously may be challenging because some medications for ADHD can exacerbate anxiety symptoms. Both conditions need to be treated, though. Your doctor may choose to focus first on the condition that’s the most disruptive to your quality of life. They may also provide suggestions for ways to manage the other condition. The treatments your doctor may recommend for both ADHD and anxiety include:cognitive and behavioral therapyrelaxation techniquesmeditationprescription medicationIt’s important to be truthful and open with your doctor about your symptoms. This is especially true if you suspect you’re experiencing two conditions simultaneously. Your doctor will want to know if a treatment is making one or both of your conditions worse. That will help them tailor your treatment. Outlook If you have ADHD, it’s important to tell your doctor about all of your symptoms, even if you think they’re unrelated. It’s possible you could have an additional condition, such as anxiety. You should also let your doctor know about any new symptoms, as you could develop anxiety or another condition over time. Once your doctor has diagnosed you with both ADHD and anxiety, you’ll be able to begin treatment for both conditions. Managing your Anxiety Learn your triggers In some people, anxiety may be triggered by specific events, like speaking in public or calling someone on the phone. Once you’ve identified your triggers, work with your doctor, therapist, counselor or coach and/or a combination of professionals to help come up with ways to manage your anxiety in these situations. Get eight hours of sleep every night Being tired may trigger anxiety or increase your risk for feeling anxious. Try to sleep for eight hours every night. If you’re having trouble falling asleep, try meditating which is what I do to fall asleep, or taking a warm bath before bed to help quiet your mind. Also plan to go to sleep and wake up at the same time every day. Setting a sleep schedule can be an effective way to train your body to sleep when it’s time for bed. If you continue to have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, talk to your doctor. If you’re taking medication for your anxiety or ADHD, it could be interfering with your sleep. You may also need to temporarily take a sleep aid. Don’t start taking any additional medication without first discussing it with your doctor. Some medications may make your anxiety or ADHD symptoms worse. Create a schedule If you have ADHD, you may find it hard to complete tasks. This can make anxiety worse in some people. To avoid this, create a schedule and stick to it. Expect each activity to take longer than you think. You don’t want to set unrealistic goals for yourself, as this can increase anxiety. Keep a journal Writing in a journal can help clear your mind. There’s no wrong way to keep a journal. It’s only meant for you, so you should feel comfortable writing down anything that’s on your mind. I keep my journal with me all the time, and write first thing in the morning and just before I go to bed. However, during the day things happen as do they in your dreams – so have your journal next to your side table. Exercise regularly Exercise will reduce anxiety 20 minutes a day – walk or run every day. It is key to get your ‘happy chemicals’ going: D.O.S.E – Dopamine, Oxytocin, Serotonin and Endorphins. You will feel great when you finish. I will continue writing additional articles on “Anxiety.” As I have enjoyed writing over 200 articles for Quora readers to ‘Empower Yourselves,” many are related to your challenge and how the Brain (conscious and unconscious) work; be a “Follower” and you will find things that will be of interest to you (you can go back and check articles where you can get additional information for yourself on a particular subject), possibly to find “your passion” and allow you to overcome your challenges and attain your goals and thus find “peace of mind.” Have a Powerful day!Photo by Adrian Swancar
comment_answer: As there was a lot of interest in the aforementioned “Anxiety and ADHD” article, I wanted to additional information another to perhaps add value to you. Anxiety and ADHD are very different, but sometimes the symptoms can look similar. The correct diagnosis is critical to guide treatment and to make sense of things when kids seem to be struggling or when something doesn’t feel quite right. As much as the right diagnosis can heal, the wrong one can also harm. Understanding how anxiety might look like ADHD, and the telltale differences between the two, can make an important difference in avoiding a misdiagnosis, and helping kids deal with the symptoms that might be getting in their way. ADHD is one of the most diagnosed childhood conditions, and it seems to be increasing. The Center for Disease Control reports that 11% of children between 4-17 have been diagnosed with ADHD at some point in their lives. Reports suggest that about 8% currently have ADHD and about 6% are taking medication. The prescription of medications for ADHD has increased by 800% in the last 2 decades. ADHD has been the fire starter for plenty of hearty debate, with some questioning whether or not it actually exists. Let’s start by putting that argument to bed, or somewhere less cozy and far away so it won’t find its way back. ADHD absolutely does exist, and there are pictures to prove it. Brain imaging shows definite differences between a brain with ADHD and a brain without. Researchers don’t know exactly what causes ADHD, but they know for certain that it’s a neurobiological condition. It has nothing to do with bad behavior, bad parenting, too much sugar, not enough sleep, fairy dust, wearing too much yellow – or whatever other crazy theories are out there. Fortunately, these theories have been debunked, which means now researchers can get on with finding out what’s really going on, which they are. Perhaps something that has given buoyancy to the ‘does it exist or doesn’t it’ debate is the over diagnosis of ADHD, or the misdiagnosis of symptoms that look like ADHD. A major problem facing doctors and clinicians is that there is currently no widely available objective physiological assessment for the presence of ADHD. At the moment, brain imaging can’t be used for diagnosis, but researchers are working on developing a more accurate and objective diagnosis tool. In the meantime, diagnosis relies on reports of the child’s behavior from two different environments, typically school (from teachers) and home (from parents). If your child seems to struggle at school but seems fine at home, it’s not ADHD, and vice versa. Diagnosis of ADHD is based on a list of 18 possible symptoms, all of which exist on a spectrum, and all of which could apply to any child at some point in time. The 18 symptoms are divided into two clusters with nine symptoms in each cluster (‘inattentive’ and ‘hyperactivity/impulsivity’ cluster). A formal diagnosis of ADHD comes down to a question of degree. To be diagnosed, a child has to have most of the symptoms from both clusters (combined inattentive and hyperactivity/impulsivity) or one of the clusters (predominantly inattentive or predominantly hyperactive) most of the time, and they have to intrude significantly into day-to-day life. Studies that have looked at the way ADHD is assessed by clinicians have found that a large majority of practicing clinicians did not regularly follow assessment procedures that are in line with best practice guidelines. One of these guidelines is to use multiple methods to diagnose but only 15% of clinicians reported doing this. Research has also found that the youngest children in a year level are more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD and medicated than older children in the year level. Interestingly, this trend is only found with preschool and primary school (elementary) age children, not adolescents. Researchers suggest this may be because younger children, because of their age and stage of development, don’t quite yet have the neurocognitive development of their older classmates and may wrongly be diagnosed with ADHD. Without a reliable objective measure of ADHD, there will inevitably be times when a cluster of behavior’s in a child is labeled as ADHD, but isn’t. The key symptoms of ADHD – inattention, distraction, fidgeting, problems at school, problems focusing – don’t automatically mean ADHD. They can indicate several other conditions, one of which is anxiety. The problem with misdiagnosis. No parents wants their child to be diagnosed with ADHD. Understandably though, it can be a massive relief when there is finally an explanation for behavior’s that don’t seem to make sense, or which are causing problems at school, at home and with friendships. Having a correct diagnosis is vital. It can bring clarity and guide the management of symptoms in ways that see important parts of a child’s life (relationships, academics, behavior, self-esteem) improving significantly. But as much as a diagnosis can heal, it can also harm. When a child is misdiagnosed, the fallout can be immense. Not only might the child be exposed to unnecessary medication, but the wrong diagnosis can mean that the child isn’t receiving the support or treatment that actually would help their symptoms. Misdiagnosis can set a path for treatment that is unhelpful or detrimental, and it runs the risk of overlooking the true cause of any difficulties the child is having. Labeling a child with the wrong diagnosis also has the potential to shrink the expectations of teachers or other adults as to what that child is capable of. Children will live up to expectations or down to them. They’ll look to the important adults in their lives for clues about how hard they should try, and whether the reach is in them. But then there’s the overlap. The overlap between the symptoms of ADHD and other conditions can also add to the potential for misdiagnosis. As many as 75% of children with ADHD meet the criteria for another diagnosis. About a third of children who have ADHD will also have clinical levels of anxiety. The presence of anxiety seems to be related to more severe ADHD, so it’s massively important that the diagnostic process is open to this. If anxiety is present, it’s vital that it is given the attention it needs, and not overlooked or treated as part of the ADHD. When anxiety looks like ADHD. Anxiety and ADHD are very different, but the symptoms can sometimes look similar. This is because both have symptoms are driven by changes in the pre-frontal cortex BUT the nature of those changes and the processes behind those changes are different. With anxiety, the symptoms are brought about by the fight or flight response. This response can be enduring and intense, and it can happen even when there is no threat and no real need for fight or flight. With ADHD, the symptoms are brought about by structural, functional and chemical changes in the brain. When there are changes in activity in the prefrontal cortex, as happens during anxiety and ADHD, symptoms can include inattention and distraction; impulsivity and hyperactivity; and difficulty controlling emotions, impulses and habits. But if the symptoms are the same, does it matter how it’s treated? Yes. Yes. Yes. It matters. The symptoms aren’t the problem. The condition driving the symptoms is the problem. Understanding whether it’s ADHD, anxiety, or both is the first and most important step in making sure your little person is getting what he or she needs to move forward. Although both anxiety and ADHD are manageable, they need different types of support to improve. ADHD is generally treated with medication that boosts the necessary neurochemicals and stimulates the parts of the brain that need to work a little harder. This may be effective for ADHD, but if the symptoms are being driven by anxiety, the use of ADHD medication is massively heavy-handed and fails miserably to give the child the skills or resources needed to best manage the symptoms. Even if anxiety and ADHD are happening together, it’s important to also treat the anxiety as a separate condition. A growing body of highly regarded research is showing that “mindfulness and exercise” are both powerful ways to do this. If the symptoms are from ADHD, what’s driving them? An ever-increasing body of research has found that there are widespread structural and functional, electrical and neurochemical differences in the brains of children with ADHD. Researchers aren’t exactly sure what causes these changes, but there’s a lot of research happening in the area to get us closer to the answers. The changes are particularly in the areas of executive functioning (planning, organizing, concentration, impulse control, focusing attention, remembering instructions, inhibition, self-control) and sensorimotor processing (using the information that we receive through our senses, to produce an effective motor response). The frontal cortex and other parts of the brain are smaller in children with ADHD. Size makes no difference at all when it comes to intelligence, and many kids with ADHD will have above average IQ’s. What it does affect is behavior. An ADHD brain is powerful, intelligent, and very capable, but it’s not able to filter the ‘noise’ from the relevant information coming in. A brain with ADHD is like a beautiful, high-powered, high performing sports car, but without any brakes. In any brain, the different parts interact with each to form different networks that control processes such as behavior, movement and attention. These networks are like a symphony – they increase in activity or decrease in activity depending on what we are doing. For a brain to do what it needs to do effectively, the networks need to work together and increase activity or decrease activity just enough to make things happen. When we are trying to learn something, for example, the networks that process information increase in activity, while at the same time the networks involved in daydreaming decrease in activity. In a child with ADHD, some networks switch on too much and some don’t switch on enough. When this happens, they may struggle with tasks or behavior. Many people seem to grow out of ADHD, and there seems to be a good reason for this. Research suggests that with ADHD, the brain is delayed in some areas by about three years. It still develops in a normal pattern, but some areas will take a little longer. Eventually, the functioning in these areas catches up, which is when the symptoms of ADHD seem to lessen or disappear. And if the symptoms are from anxiety? Anxiety comes from a part of the brain called the amygdala. It’s a tiny almond-shaped part at the back of the brain and its job is to keep us safe by warning us when there might be danger. When the amygdala senses threat, the brain immediately switches to auto-pilot and initiates the fight or flight response. It hands the bulk of the workload to the more primitive, instinctive, impulsive lower brain (at the back of the brain). At the same time it organizes for the pre-frontal cortex to sit out for a while until the threat has passed. When this happens, behavior becomes less planned, more instinctive, and more impulsive. There’s a very good reason for sending the pre-frontal cortex offline when there’s an immediate threat. The amygdala doesn’t want the pre-frontal cortex to use valuable survival time thinking, planning, deciding – it just wants to get you safe. If there’s a wild dog with gnarly teeth running at you, there’s no time to think about whether it might be lost, angry, hungry or misunderstood, or to imagine how cute it would be if it was wearing one of those cute dog jackets that all the cool dogs are wearing. Your brain just wants you out of there – fast. It’s important to remember that the fight or flight response doesn’t only happen when there’s a threat. For kids with anxiety, it can feel constant. Sometimes, the amygdala gets a little too overprotective and initiates the fight or flight response too many times, too unnecessarily – just in case. It’s evidence of a strong, healthy brain switching into survival mode, but just a little more than it needs to. That’s evolution for you … sometimes it gives us opposing thumbs, and sometimes it gives us anxiety. Anxiety, ADHD and the look-alike symptoms. Even though the symptoms of ADHD and anxiety might look the same, they will be driven by different processes. It’s also important to remember that not all ADHD looks the same and not all anxiety looks the same, but there are versions of both that can look similar. Let’s go through the symptoms: · Difficulty in class, makes careless mistakes, distraction, inattentiveness, restless, difficulty focusing/ planning. If it’s caused by anxiety: When anxiety hits in class, it can shut down the pre-frontal cortex, the part of the brain that is important for thinking, learning and remembering. Anxiety is all about protecting you from threat, so the brain shuts down to detail. Instead, it becomes focused on staying safe. Anxiety can make kids so distracted by worrying thoughts,that they are unable to apply themselves to whatever they are working on. This can make kids appear restless, distracted and make it difficult to focus, retain information or pay attention. When kids are highly anxious, their thoughts are consumed with their worries. They might have trouble writing, sitting still, staying focused or copying from the board. They might also be reluctant to ask questions or ask for guidance. If it’s caused by ADHD: With ADHD, the symptoms are thought to be because in the prefrontal cortex, the levels of the neurotransmitters norepinephrine and dopamine, aren’t quite what they need to be. Neurotransmitters are the chemicals in the brain that help brain cells communicate with each other. Everything we do depends on the levels of these neurotransmitters being at the right levels. Even the smallest changes in norepinephrine and dopamine levels can have a big effect on the capacity of the prefrontal cortex to do its job effectively. Norepinephrine increases the signals for appropriate response. Dopamine decreases any irrelevant ‘noise’ that might get in the way. When the levels of these neurotransmitters are out, kids can have difficulty ignoring irrelevant stimuli. It’s not that they are unable to pay attention, it’s that they are paying it to different things, or too many things at once. Hyperactivity, fidgeting, squirming, talking or moving too much, extra movement when doing simple tasks. If it’s anxiety: When the brain feels there might be a threat, it surges the body with neurochemicals to ready the body for fight or flight. The idea is to get the body faster, stronger and more powerful so it can fight or flee the danger. If there is no need for fight or flight, these neurochemicals build up. The energy created has to go somewhere. Sometimes this can look like ‘too much movement’, such as fidgeting, foot tapping, wringing hands, or pacing. If it’s ADHD: The part of the brain that puts the brakes on behavior is a little slower to activate, meaning there aren’t enough messages instructing the body to stop or slow down. · Impulsive behavior. If it’s anxiety: When the sensations of fear or anxiety are strong, the surging of fight or flight chemicals sends the pre-frontal cortex (the seat of self-control) offline. The impulsive, instinctive amygdala takes charge. When this happens, the prefrontal cortex isn’t available to help calm big feelings or plan a more considered, less impulsive response. When the anxiety passes, the pre-frontal cortex will take charge again and guide healthier responses. Impulsive behavior can also look like aggression, which is the ‘fight’ part of the fight or flight response. Anxiety and big emotions come from the same part of the brain so when anxiety is on full volume, other emotions, such as anger might also be switched up to high. Something else to be mindful of is that being silly, which can sometimes look like impulsive behavior, might be used as a mask by kids to cover up their anxiety or nervousness. If it’s ADHD: Differences in the parts of the brain that manage self-control mean that behavior might be more impulsive. This isn’t because of bad behaviour, but because of a brain that’s not quite doing what it needs to. · Not able to finish schoolwork, poor time management. If it’s anxiety: Kids with anxiety might have trouble completing their schoolwork. Anxiety can cause kids to worry about making mistakes. Because of this, they might do things over and over, or take plenty of time to make sure their work is right or as close to perfect as it can be. It’s more about the need to produce perfect, mistake-free work than about ability, failure to focus or failure to plan. If it’s ADHD: Kids with ADHD are unable to keep their attention on a task, most likely because of an ability to manage impulses or to shut out irrelevant distractions. Because of the regular shifts in focus, the work doesn’t get completed. · Difficulty organizing tasks and activities and managing sequential tasks, disorganized work. If it’s anxiety: The left brain loves logic and sequences, and it helps to give structure and order to our experiences (‘this, then this, then this …’). The right brain is more concerned with emotion and the big picture of ‘what does this mean for me?’. It’s heavily directed by sensations in the body and messages from the lower brain, which is the major player in anxiety. We need both sides of the brain to work well together, but sometimes in all of us, one side will become dominant for a little while. If a child is feeling anxious in class or in relation to a specific task, the right ’emotional’ brain can take over and temporarily disconnect from the left side. While the anxiety is high, there will be higher emotion and a greater focus on ‘what does this situation mean for me’, and less concern for order or logic. If it’s ADHD: Insufficient levels of neurochemicals make it difficult for the brain to screen out irrelevant stimuli. There’s too much irrelevant information coming in and creating noise. This means that however hard kids with ADHD try to organize their work and do what’s expected, their busy brains will make organization difficult. Anxiety or ADHD? How can I tell the difference? If you suspect ADHD, it’s really important to get a proper assessment from someone who is qualified to diagnose. Be mindful that many of the symptoms we’ve discussed might always point louder to ADHD than anxiety. In some instances, it may be that both anxiety and ADHD are driving behaviour. Whatever’s happening, getting to the bottom of it is the most important step in getting your child the support they need to push forward. Because a diagnosis of ADHD depends on observation and interpretation of the behaviors, be open to the possibility that if you go to an ‘ADHD specialist’ or a doctor who specializes in ADHD, they may be more likely to read the symptoms as ADHD. Certainly they can be an important and wonderful support for kids with ADHD, but always be ready to seek a second opinion if that’s what you need for clarity. Ask as many questions as you need to ask and remember, you are the expert on your child. If something doesn’t feel right, keep chasing it down until things make sense to you. Here are some clues that the symptoms might be more indicative of anxiety (or perhaps anxiety and ADHD) than ADHD. · Kids with anxiety are generally more sensitive to social cues, and to what other people are thinking and feeling, or what they need. · Anxiety can create physical symptoms such as a racy heart, clamminess, tense muscles, tummy aches, headaches, nausea, or dizziness. This is the physiological basis of anxiety. When the neurochemicals that are there to ready you for fight or flight build up, they lead to physical symptoms. These symptoms feel awful, but if they are driven by anxiety they are all completely safe. · Children with anxiety don’t tend to have as many problems with impulsivity. Their impulsive behaviour generally happens in isolated bursts when they are anxious, and is less likely to happen when they are feeling calm and safe. · Children with anxiety will be unlikely to show problem behaviors when they are feeling calm, safe, and doing things they enjoy. Children with ADHD might struggle even when they are doing the things they want to be doing. · Children with anxiety are more likely to talk about feeling worried, even if they can’t articulate exactly what they are worried about. This is because anxiety comes from a brain that thinks there might be a threat, not necessarily because there actually is one. And finally … The importance of a correct diagnosis is so important to make sure that kids with ADHD receive the best possible support to manage the symptoms and limit the intrusion into their day-to-day lives. You will always be the expert on your child, and you’re their voice when something doesn’t feel right. There will be times when you’ll need other experts on your team, but for certain, the glue that will hold it all together will be you – your questions, your questioning, your answers, your second opinions – whatever it takes for things to make sense. All kids need a support crew, made up of the adults around them who are ready to help lift them to full flight. The support crew will look different for every child, but will likely involve family, teachers, coaches and sometimes therapists, specialists and doctors.
