question: What supplements do people with Asperger’s take?
answer: Three years ago, I held an emergency quality control conference meeting with one of our big customers. Representatives from quality assurance, engineering, manufacturing, and top level executives from both companies took part. As project manager, I kept people coordinated, answered a couple dozen questions, took some flak, corrected a couple of people’s math errors on the fly, and typed up a resolution and prioritization plan as people spoke. I even looked people in the eye for short periods of time. After the meeting ended, people seemed satisfied, and some even seemed happy. But somehow it was too easy, as I wasn’t even stressed. I was a little concerned I had missed something big… after all, people had told me about several angry exchanges before the meeting. As people left, our CEO turned to me and said, “Please come to my office in 15 minutes.” Ouch. Now I was nervous. As someone with ASD, it was always difficult for me to tell if someone was angry, unless of course they were red in the face or yelling. I went to the CEO’s office and sat down. The first question out of his mouth was, “What supplements are you taking?” The words rang in my ears. My mind raced. I knew the CEO knew that I took supplements. I wondered if he suspected I was taking drugs or high or I had said something stupid in the meeting. “I, um…” I hesitated. The CEO noted my reticence and explained, “You did an excellent job in the meeting today, and it opened up new opportunities. I’d like to discuss a strategy with you in a moment if you have time.” “But first I would like to know what supplements you are taking, if you don’t mind telling me.” “Oh”, I said, relaxing. I was taking several supplements, so I started with the most important one first. “I am taking fish oil for the omega 3s.” “How does it help you?”, he asked. “I take it because it reduces the body’s stress response. Also, the brain is made of 18% omega-3 DHA. Omega-3 is a precursor to serotonin and low serotonin can cause anxiety.” “How long have you been taking it and at what dosage?” “I started taking it 6 years ago, just after the first time we met. I was given fish oil along with digestive enzymes and probiotics because my digestion was not good.” His question spurred a point that I hadn’t really thought about. “But I doubled my omega-3 dosage to a teaspoon a day around a month ago!” “Good! Where can I get some?” Phew! I was glad to have shared the information with someone who believed supplementation can be useful, and who knew I had researched the science to back me up.I started taking supplements in mid 40’s after I told a naturopathic doctor (ND) my digestion had not been stable for 30 plus years, and that I wanted to get off Zoloft. I had been taking Zoloft to get rid of my seizures, but the side effects were terrible. Little did I know at the time that inflammatory gut issues and seizure activity were common in ASD. Nor did I even know I had ASD. The ND gave me digestive enzymes, probiotics, and omega-3 fatty acids, and told me to temporarily stop eating any foods I suspected I had an allergy to. As always, I was a skeptic that this combination could replace the Zoloft. But within a month I had lots more energy and tripled my number of work hours. Within three months I was totally off Zoloft and the seizures had not returned. But what was really odd is that over the next few years, most of my anxiety slowly disappeared. I was no longer deathly afraid of the phone. I no longer needed to sit with my back against the wall in restaurants, because I no longer cared in the slightest if people sat behind me. I was still an obsessive thinker, but I no longer spent hours thinking in a tight, stressful loop, as in OCD. And I no longer sat in the back of meetings out in another planet not saying a word. My oversensitivity to light and sound got much better too. I no longer felt like throwing up when it was too bright out. And my all-consuming addiction to video games completely went away. My CEO and others said I’m a totally different person than they knew just a few years ago. But I really wasn’t a different person inside. The difference was that life became much less stressful and anxiety-inducing, so I could become the person I had always dreamed of being. I am still a highly introverted, high dopamine deep thinker, but I am comfortable in my own skin and able to relax and joke with people without feeling like running away and hiding. My head is no longer full of just numbers, but I’ve retained my extraordinary math and estimation skills. Those were some of the unusual skills I had learned as a young autistic child, and yes, I am proud of them. Before I started the supplementation, in my early 40s, I had a highly technical but job that allowed me to work with one person at a time, because that is all that I could take without being overwhelmed. I had trouble forming words because was always blasted by jumble of thoughts. But a few years after starting supplementation, I was promoted twice, eventually to Director of Project Management., People asked to be transferred to report to me, perhaps because I understood adversity and how it feels to be relentlessly bullied, and I would always protect my team.If you’re autistic but feel like your life is okay as is without supplementation, then I totally respect that. What I’m trying to share is that some of the conditions often associated with autism, such as anxiety, poor sleep, OCD, hyper-sensory overload, meltdowns, irritability, ADHD, or issues with working memory or fine motor control, can sometimes be improved, because of the biochemical nature of how autism works. In the last couple years, I’ve researched autism genetics in depth. I was shocked to discover that there are no autism genes. This means that unlike Down’s Syndrome, there are almost no genetic polymorphisms where you could say “that person will be autistic”. Or put another way: If you are autistic and have an genetically identical twin, there is a 20% chance that they are not autistic. That is, your genes don’t guarantee you will be autistic, and definitely don’t determine your symptom severity. Instead, genes associated with autism tend to change levels, transport or metabolization of biochemicals such as dopamine[1], immune system function, or epigenetics. Each one of these genes / biochemical changes on its own is probably relatively benign, but together they affect us in a complex way. Sometimes, bringing some of these biochemicals back into balance can lessen the stressors that are associated with biochemical changes. For a moment, let’s consider oxidative stress.[2] Oxidative stress, a electron-stealing reactive chemical stress (like rusting) that breaks down biochemicals, is a primary driver in all diseases of aging. This includes cardiovascular disease, Parkinson’s Disease, etc. because oxidative stress damages cells, DNA, and can break biochemicals like dopamine down. Oxidative stress can come from the immune system (inflammation), gut dysbiosis, air pollution, toxins, and even deficiency of vitamin A, C, D, or E, or glutathione, which is manufactured in the body and brain. A good diet in theory can supply all of the biochemicals we need and help us detoxify our systems, but genetics and the toxic assault of modern living can get in the way. For an example, let’s examine vitamin D. Vitamin D is usually, but not always found to be lower in ASD:[3]We could say, indignantly, “Who cares? ASD is genetic and taking vitamin D won’t cure me, nor do I need to be cured.” But the reality is that vitamin D deficiency is associated with all sorts of negative outcomes, especially during developmental years and as we get older and risk developing systemic or neurologic diseases such as Parkinson’s Disease and Alzheimer’s.[4] In the shorter term, vitamin D deficiency is also associated with things like Restless Legs Syndrome and muscle twitching. Proper Vitamin D levels help protect against neuroinflammation[5]and modulate the dopamine system.[6] My twitching and Restless Legs Syndrome have totally gone away after I bumped my vitamin D to optimal levels a year ago. Perhaps researchers said it better than I can why people in general may want to supplement with vitamin D. Our diets are nothing like they used to be: [7]Low levels of vitamin D, considering serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D), have been recognized as a widespread health problem, affecting approximately one billion people worldwide [1]. Latitude, season, cultural norms, religious practices, limited awareness, lack of knowledge, indoor lifestyles, urban living, skin pigmentation, malnutrition, diet, co-morbidities (like tuberculosis, malnutrition, chronic inflammatory conditions, etc.), and drugs, may contribute to vitamin D deficiency, especially in the developing world, even if some genetic predispositions can interfere with it (i.e., blacks tend to have lower levels of 25(OH)D compared to whites) [2,3].In summary, ASD people usually have more biochemical differences than the average person. The differences often cluster around dopamine metabolism, serotonin production, methylation, detoxification, and immune system / inflammation. I try to improve these with a good wide-ranging balanced diet, probiotics, and exercise. Where I can’t, or where it’s low risk / high reward, I supplement. I currently take vitamin C, vitamin D, NAC (to support glutathione production), omega 3s, a variety of probiotics including spore-based, sublingual B12 adenosyl cobalamin, and a bit of magnesium threonate. Note that vitamin D needs a few blood tests and time to attain optimal levels. This all together allows me to be who I want to be, retain my autistic thinking power, and have lower stress too. Here’s some more data from 55 children with ASD versus controls:[8]The autism group had many statistically significant differences in their nutritional and metabolic status, including biomarkers indicative of vitamin insufficiency, increased oxidative stress, reduced capacity for energy transport, sulfation and detoxification. Several of the biomarker groups were significantly associated with variations in the severity of autism. These nutritional and metabolic differences are generally in agreement with other published results and are likely amenable to nutritional supplementation.Footnotes[1] Autism-linked dopamine transporter mutation alters striatal dopamine neurotransmission and dopamine-dependent behaviors[2] Oxidative Stress and Immune System Dysfunction in Autism Spectrum Disorders[3] Vitamin D Deficiency in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Cross-Sectional Study[4] Vitamin D and Neurological Diseases: An Endocrine View[5] Vitamin D protects dopaminergic neurons against neuroinflammation and oxidative stress in hemiparkinsonian rats[6] Mesolimbic dopamine system and its modulation by vitamin D in a chronic mild stress model of depression in the rat - PubMed[7] Vitamin D in Neurological Diseases: A Rationale for a Pathogenic Impact[8] Nutritional and metabolic status of children with autism vs. neurotypical children, and the association with autism severity - PubMed

question: What are the chances of passing on ADHD to children if one parent has it?
answer: First of all, ADHD is considered to be a common and highly heritable condition. Prevalence of ADHD in children is 5–8%, and among adults approximately 3–5%. It’s more common in males than females, but sex ratio in adults is much less than in school-age kids. ADHD has a very high heritability of .70 to .80. That means genetic factors account for ~75% of ADHD characteristics. So it comes as no surprise that ADHD children are likely to have at least one parent with ADHD. Studies report when kids had ADHD, 41% of mothers and 51% of fathers also had ADHD. From the opposite direction, when a parent has ADHD, the risk of a child having ADHD was between 40–57%. However, the risk stratifies according to sex of the parent and child. When fathers had ADHD the risk of children having ADHD was 2.67 times greater vs. non-ADHD fathers. Risks of children having ADHD were lower for mothers with ADHD but remained elevated at 1.5 times vs. non-ADHD mothers. And as generally the case risks of ADHD in boys was greater than for girls. But of course, it gets more complicated. Parental age is another factor and risks vary between mothers and fathers. Risks for bearing ADHD children are greatest for the youngest parents., adolescent to young adult age. Risk reaches its lowest point for parents in their early to mid-30s. Parents in the late 30’s and beyond are at increased risk of having children with ADHD. Interestingly, risk associated with older mothers (age >35) is less than older fathers. For example, for 40 year old parents, maternal odds are ~0.43, but paternal odds are greater, ~0.53. Paternal age also contributes to likelihood of offspring having other serious psychiatric conditions. Schizophrenia, autism and bipolar disorder show this pattern as well. Why that occurs is unknown but presumably has to do with aging effects on DNA “point mutations” or chromosomal “accidents”. While parental ADHD clearly matters, a lot about transmission of ADHD is unexplained. Intuitively the strong influence of genetic factors seems like it should be decisive. However, it’s well-established that effects of genes are modified by external conditions. For example, poor prenatal care can result in low birth weight and prematurity which predispose to developing ADHD. Other factors such as smoking, alcohol and other drug use may contribute. Nutrition before birth and during early childhood probably play a role. The upshot is the chances of a parent having children with ADHD depend on numerous factors. It’s clear odds are much higher when a parent has ADHD. Risks are evidently greatest when the ADHD parent is the father, particularly with fathers over 40 years old. Similarly, risks are higher for parents under 20 years old. While we can’t change risks due to genes, those caused by the environment can and should be modified. Mothers need to make sure to follow best practices re: getting good obstetrical care, nutrition, avoiding smoking, alcohol and drugs. Naturally having ADHD (as parent or child) isn’t necessarily a great tragedy. ADHD doesn’t have to be inevitably disabling. Appropriate treatment can make a major difference in outcome. Parents with ADHD benefit significantly, especially in regard to parenting. Managing childhood ADHD will have the greatest impact. Treatment doesn’t mean just medication, certainly not by itself. For kids, and adults, having useful “structure” (i.e., daily schedules), practicing expressive skills, learning to prioritize, celebrating one’s accomplishments are keys to long-term success.

question: Do a significant number of people misdiagnose themselves as having Autism Spectrum Disorder?
answer: One of the interesting things I found when I ran an ASD screening website was that people who suspected that they had ASD but were not officially diagnosed scored very high on standard screening tests for autism—with scores that were on average at or above as the people who were actually diagnosed with ASD. Mean scores on the AQ-10 test in SOASA’s sample by diagnostic group (given before people start the screening) Higher number indicates a greater number of autism symptoms. Now the questions that these tests ask are fairly specific. You wouldn’t expect someone who was introverted, or shy, or had some other disorder like ADHD to answer them the same way someone with ASD would. In other words, the people who have “suspected ASD”—and are at least serious enough about it to take some tests—probably have the core ASD traits. But that doesn’t actually mean that they would be diagnosed with ASD because a clinical diagnosis requires not only having the core features but also suffering impairment from them. Interestingly, one of the developers of the AQ test reported that students who had above-threshold scores on autism tests but no apparent “distress” were actually pretty common and claimed that the lack of distress meant they shouldn’t be diagnosed. Brains vs diagnosis What this all points to is that when people self-diagnose, they seem to be very good at identifying the core ASD features, but may not evaluate the level of impairment the same way as a clinician does (or even recognize that this factor is important) and therefore might misdiagnose themselves. Does that mean that these people “really” have ASD at a neurological level? I would argue that while the impairment criterion is useful for some things ( i.e. determining eligibility for special educational services) in a lot of other cases it doesn’t directly reflect how a person’s brain works so much as it reflects how well they’ve adapted to their environment (a well-adapted ASD person might not have any noticable impairment). So for purely descriptive purposes, well-informed self diagnosis may be good enough.

question: Is Adderall effective for autism spectrum disorder (ASD)?
answer: Depends on the particular aspects of the disorder… in my case Vyvanse (Adderall vs. Vyvanse: ADHD Medication, Difference and Similarities) helps me cope in a different way than I suspect it would for someone who is strictly ADHD. I still struggle with attention, but there is now a daily pattern to my zoned thinking, where if I take it on time consistently, my brain starts anticipating the patterns that allow it to immerse or zone in to set the tone for the day. I must admit, it is not easy to get it right, but when I manage to be steady, I can go months working very effectively, unless someone keeps throwing a wrench into the plans — usually people who are entitled to think their impulsive thinking is “normal” and I am just making up my symptoms. I was diagnosed with ADHD for 10 years before it was evident that it is ASD with strong ADHD traits. question: Why are more people on the autism spectrum getting diagnosed as adults instead of children now?
answer: First and foremost, we simply know more about autism than we used to. It’s easier to spot. But it can also get a lot more complicated than just that. As a child, I very quickly learned to mask my autistic symptoms. Then, I believe everything made sense under the ADHD diagnosis I did receive as a child. What wasn’t ADHD was the depression or anxiety. Since becoming an adult, going through therapy and dealing with my adult life, I’ve realized that I in fact have many symptoms that cannot be explained by ADHD, depression or anxiety. My ADHD symptoms were just the most prevalent, and depression/anxiety were slapped on me by a suicide rehabilitation center I went to when I was a teenager because they knew something was wrong, but did no further testing to determine if it could have been something else, and just gave me the easiest two disorders to diagnose. There’s also the matter of stereotypical autistic behavior. We’ve all seen it in that one character on TV; monotone voice, no/limited facial expressions, takes everything excruciatingly literally and doesn’t ever understand how the people around them feel. Now, these are autistic traits. Many autistic people show little to no emotion in their voice or face. I myself struggle with assuming people mean things literally, and sometimes need extra help understanding what my loved ones are feeling. However, some autistic people overemote, to give just one example of the way an autistic person may not fit into the set of behaviors commonly understood as autism. This may lead to an autistic person failing to get diagnosed, or being misdiagnosed with something else. Or as I mentioned above, some people may have ‘masked’, aka learned to cover their autistic traits. In the case of facial expressions, this would be learning to make the ‘proper’ facial expressions for the situation (when to smile, when to frown, etc.). I do that. By paying close attention to and copying the facial expressions of the people around me, I am able to pass as ‘normal’. I struggle to tell when someone is joking, and still can’t tell off tone alone, but there are certain patterns to jokes that I can recognize to tell that someone is joking, like when someone says “I sure hope x doesn’t happen” to imply sarcasm and that they actually do, vs “I hope x doesn’t happen’ to imply they actually want X to happen. This is very different from a neurotypical person, who may understand just from the tone of voice of the speaker whether or not they are joking without having to use their pattern recognition skills to see if it’s in a “joke” format or not. Stimming is another common autistic behavior I masked; I would often rub my hands together as a child when excited, but adults questioned it and other kids made fun of me for it, so I learned ‘this is a bad thing to do’ and stopped myself from doing it around others. When I began hand flapping, a well known form of autistic stimming, I very quickly cut that off for the same reason. Masking can oftentimes, as in my case, go so deep that the person masking doesn’t even know they’re doing it. Many of the ways I mask were things I picked up on subconsciously, not because I actually thought to myself, ‘Okay, we need to do X to fit in’. Once we do learn, unmasking, or behaving the way we naturally would again, is incredibly difficult. Of course, all that to say, when a person with autism goes into the psychological evaluation, they may be hiding their autism so well from even themselves that they just do not display the symptoms needed for a diagnosis. However, an adult typically has more self awareness than a child and may begin to question the things they’ve been suppressing as a child. As adults learn about autism, if they do, things may start to click for them.

question: Should I take ADHD medication?
answer: Here's the TL;DR version of what I normally tell people:Try medication asap and see how it affects you.Start with low doses, gradually increase. If it doesn't work, or has bad side effects, try a different one.Get a variety of tests to see where your real problems lie.IQ tests - is it ADHD, or a learning disability, or something else? Sleep studies - is your sleep the real problem? Can treating the sleep improve your ADHD?Blood tests for hyper/hypothyroidism, excessive inflammation, nutritional abnormalities. Checking for developmental delaysLook for longer term solutions that actually improve your brain.Medication can be extremely helpful for some, so it's worth at least seeing if it helps. But even if it does help, I tell most people to look into long term solutions in parallel - things that encourage neuroplastic change in the brain. These include but are not limited to:Improving developmental delays you may not know you haveTargeted lifestyle revamping - in short, optimizing foundational things that might be making your brain misbehave (i.e., sleep, nutrition, exercise, and cognitive habits)Trying a variety of interventions are targeted toward brain change.I've experimented with a number of neuroplastic interventions, and had a mixture of results - but overall, very good ones. A few examples of things you may have not heard of that can change your brain:Integrated Listening This method uses specially engineered music and headphones combined with targeted balance exercises, to correct some visual, auditory, balance and learning problems.Neurofeedback Involves monitoring your brain's behavior with EEG waves, and training your "attention muscles" using visual stimuli like movies.Primitive Reflex Integration Infant reflexes that don't disappear properly before you're an adult can contribute to attention and learning problems, and even conditions like Autism. Methods like Brain Gym and others can help retrain and reintegrate these overactive reflexes, and improve the brains of people that are affected by them.I've tried all of these and a number of others, and seen significant improvements over time. If you want more details, i've written a bunch of this on Quora and in various other places (see links below) So I encourage people to try both pharmaceutical and neuroplastic approaches, and see the balance that works for them. Trying both of these things will greatly increase your chances of getting the results you want. Some related info I've written on the topic, if you find it useful:Mike Cavaliere's answer to What are the remedies for Attention Deficit Disorder?Mike Cavaliere's answer to What is the best non-medication treatment for ADHD and why?Working Out My Brain With Mozart | ADHDTechiesWhy I Got My IQ Tested (And You Should Too) | ADHDTechiesBrain Hacks vs. Brain Upgrades (Compensation vs. Correction) | ADHDTechiesChanging Your Brain is Tough (But Possible) | ADHDTechiesI hope it's helpful, and good luck! You will see improvements if you keep trying.

question: What is the difference between Asperger's syndrome and high-functioning autism? How can they be distinguished from each other by laymen (non-medical professionals)?
answer: None. It’s a matter of labeling. Asperger’s was based on Austrian physician Hans Asperger’s description of “odd” behavior in children he was studying. His studies were for the purposes of identifying children who could be “molded” in “re education” camps to undertake morally repugnant tasks for the Third Reich, without having any moral compass about what they were doing, ie, their own Fascination about solving a problem / accomplishing a technically challenging task, would overcome any sense of moral questioning about what they were doing (ie, designing an extermination camp). This was a tendency that had been id’ed in these types of children for which exploitation was sought. In the 1990’s the label “Asperger’s Syndrome” became popular for folks who were intelligent but socially awkward, pretty much the standard “Idiot Savant” type person, personified in films like “Rain Man”. By the mid 2000’s, the origin of the name became more well known (this was the era I 1st read about it & realized it utterly described my whole life, circa late 2005), thus the “label” was transitioned to “High Functioning Autism”, as it was, by then, understood to be a form of Autism, as many of the traits are pretty much the same, except for the Degree of “impairment” experienced. Fast forward to the mid 2010’s, many activists in the Autistic community objected to a separate label for “High Functioning” Autism vs “Full” Autism. “Autism is Autism” they say. A new labeling system evolved, Autism Levels 1 through 3, with 1 being “milder” as you move towards 3 being “severe”, although it technically refers to “levels of support needed” rather than coping skills or intellect / IQ, as there are so many combinations of these criteria in Autistic persons. It is very common knowledge these days that every case of Autism is different & unique, with varying levels of “severity” of varying “symptoms” / criteria. But even this is controversial, & is currently considered “obsolete”. Autism is Autism is the Mantra in the Activist community. I have decidedly mixed feelings about this. I suppose it’s appropriate for children being diagnosed early, as it’s impossible to tell what criteria are mild vs severe at 3 or 4 or 5 years old, or even into the preteen years. I’m an engineer, not a psychiatrist, so am going to take the profession’s word on what the appropriate label is, even tho they’ve been “wrong” before. I, personally, was quite a “mess” as a kid (this was late 1960’s/early 1970’s, when none of this was even remotely understood). I suffered all kinds of physical & emotional abuse at the hands of pretty much everyone in my life due to my “way of being”. I did have a “high IQ” from early on, was able to learn / retain info, but was nearly impossible to integrate into society. Most likely I was highly ADHD, OCD, ODD, from hearing stories from my parents & my own personal recollections. Somehow or other, as I moved through Jr High (7th/8th grades) & into high school, many of these “coping issues” subsided & I was able to function to at least sit still & pay attention in class, get along minimally with others, complete assignments, take tests, to where I made B’s/C’s in the college track classed, went on to study Engineering at State university, gain degrees in Civil Engineering, go on to a great career with the Government. I also married twice, had several other long term relationships, established a circle of friends, got along well w/co workers, eventually moving into project management, a very people-oriented field. So yes, due to my “success” at life, I would still call myself, as a purely personal, evidence-based label, “High Functioning”. When I tell people I’m Autistic, they are usually like “you don’t seem like it”, as I’ve learned to “mask” very well, thanks in part to a lot of public speaking training as a project manager (I had to present projects to large audiences quite often). But I can still have Autistic moments - arguments can turn into meltdowns, or rants, I can get quite stressed out & dysfunctional due to outside overstimulation like over auto tuned pop music blaring too loud, a loud, rowdy, crowded bar with drunks pushing, shoving, yelling, spilling beer, strong odors like cigarettes, incense, perfumes, harsh lighting or strobe lights like in disco or edm nightclubs, stressful social situations like meeting a lot of new people at a house party & being expected to remember everyone’s names, & make “small talk” that doesn’t get into arcane subjects of intense interests to me only. Yes, indeed, I can also blather on about these arcane subjects of intense interest to only me (anything engineering / science related, history, military gear / strategy, geology, geography, music, art, etc), needing to be told “Shut Up Bob” often times. So sure, I’m Autistic, but at the same time, High Functioning. Maybe those two “labels” don’t belong together? I sure don’t want to Offend anyone who is “Woke” lol.

question: Do you still refer to yourself as having Asperger's vs. Autism Spectrum? Why or why not?
answer: I am gifted, and that term makes me feel uncomfortable because of the assumptions and biases that come along with it. I’ve been learning more about education and learning differences where an educational psychologist helped me sort through some thoughts and confusion about labels. There are overlaps and lots of labels trending right now. Highly Sensitive People (HSP), sensitivity, giftedness, ADHD, autism and Asperger’s are some of them. I have always felt off and alien, and yet was able to mask many parts of my identity through life. As I become more authentic I realize there are some things I have blind spots for. There are also some things I have heightened sensitivity and awareness of. Many articles and blogs on neurodiversity and female presentations of autism and ADHD are circulating where women are being diagnosed later in life, and they have closure. This is where I’m at. I think the giftedness label is highly misunderstood. To be called autistic also carries misunderstandings. For clarification and somewhat of a sense of the individual experience, Asperger’s seems to fit best right now. I know the term is sensitive, unique, and personal to each person. In general I would call myself autistic, but I do carry some shame and guilt for being able to mask and pass as normal. So, it’s complicated. I don’t know what I will think about this in the future, but I am highly invested in neurodiversity and acceptance. Whatever labels I own, it has been a struggle seeking to be understood and seen by others.

question: Do teachers know who the smartest kid is right when they walk in the room?
answer: No. It takes at least 5 minutes. Joking aside, we can tell who the “good” kids are almost immediately (quiet but attentive vs. distracted or surly), but the “smart” ones take some more interaction. When I worked as a substitute teacher, I was mostly concerned with the kids who were most helpful, rather than the ones who were the most capable students, however, it didn’t take long to figure those out as well. It’s not so much a categorization of behavior, like “the kids who always have the answer” or “the quiet kids”, but rather an analysis of how a student goes about doing what they do. A quiet kid not paying attention could be zoning out because they don’t understand, or because they understood days ago and are totally bored while the rest of the class slogs through it all. The kid with their hand always raised is probably trying to get on your good side, or impress a romantic interest nearby, but the depth of their questions and responses shows a difference in comprehension. The class clowns and other disruption sources are most often extremely bright but either struggling with ADHD or autism spectrum issues or some other cognitive problem OR are bored out of their minds because of how far ahead of the class they are… or both. Very VERY often it’s both. Most of those cognitive differences are strongly correlated with high intelligence. Voice cadence and intonation, as well as how many words they need to pause to pronounce, when reading out loud can sometimes be an indicator, but I suspect that has more to do with whether or not and how their parents read to them as young children. Also, as you might now suspect, dyslexia is also associated with higher than normal intelligence, especially higher spacial intelligence (“b”, “d”, “p”, “q”, and “P” ARE all the same, if your brain is running fast enough and is spatially aware enough to process them that way!). Now, if you haven’t already considered this, go back and reread that last paragraph. You’ll notice that most of the students in your class could be counted as “smart” by my definitions, especially some of those commonly called “dumb”. A lot of people who struggle with “school” are actually very bright, but ill suited for the very narrow environment of “standard western public school academics”. Some “B and C” students in high school often find themselves excelling in college, merely because of superior educational systems there, while a few “A” students flounder outside of the carefully guided paths they had before. So, I tend to largely dismiss the idea of “smart” kids. Not totally, but somewhat. It’s certainly less important to me as a teacher than personal passion for learning and growing. Properly encouraged, a kid who struggles in literally everything but honestly wants to learn is capable of achieving just as much as the kid flying along - and capable of much more than the kid who couldn’t care less about anything. Which brings me to my final comment: interest breeds understanding. When you care about something, really care about it, whether it’s football, girls, video games, or rocket science, you’ll totally geek out over it and dive in head first. You’ll read every website, book, magazine, or scholarly paper you can. You’ll join a fanpage, write fanfiction, and generally explore everything you can. And, since nothing in life is truly isolated, a careful teacher can help expand that student’s passions into just about every aspect of adult life, and hopefully into a career. I can’t tell you how many people have turned a passion for a mundane thing like football or anime into a PhD in physics, medicine, or linguistics. The passionless student is virtually unreachable by almost any teacher. But the kid with a real passion for something? I can work with that… if the school system and environment I’m working at allows me that kind of time and flexibility. Which I have not found much of in the US, depressingly. Mostly homeschooling groups. Even though most of the research that has formed my educational philosophy was done here in the States, we as a nation have largely failed to actually use any of it. Unlike some other countries, like Finland. Just like the student trying to turn a weird passion into a profitable career, it just takes the courage to just do it. I’ll step off my soap box now. Thank you for your question.

question: Are there any other AuDHD INFJs out there? Tell me about your lives.

question: Is autism intimidating?
answer: To normies, very often! Normies find lots of traits and people intimidating that do not correspond to the “norm”. Normies often have a lot of in-group thinking and do not consider people who are diverse as part of their in-group. This isn’t only true for autistic people, but also people of other races, non-binary gender, etc. What’s more normies don’t understand the mind of autistic people. They often consider them rude or even feel threatened by autistic people, when all they do is to tell their honest opinion (this is taboo among normies - you can’t always say what you think). Autistic people often tend to get angry because of that - what normies don’t understand - this never proactive aggression, but reactive aggression. Sometimes normies consider autistic people “psychos”. Nothing could be further from the truth. As Simon Barron-Cohen writes: autistic people are the opposite of psychopaths: low on cognitive empathy, but high on affective empathy. Autistic people are more likely to help a stranger than normies! Read more about the social difficulties of autistic people on my blog How neurodiverse people are like hunter-gatherers: part II social behaviour How neurodiverse people are like hunter-gatherers: part II social behaviour For two years, I have been researching how neurodiverse (ASD, ADHD, gifted, etc.), people are like ancient hunter-gatherers. It hasn’t been an easy enterprise, as the only work that has ever pointed to an origin of neurodiverse minds in ancient hunter-gatherer minds has been Thom Hartmann’s “Hunter-Hypothesis” of ADHD. Personally, I am somewhat in between neurotypical and neurodiverse, testing around 50% on online autism tests and 75% on ADHD tests. Like most neurodiverse people, I have always had a hard time fitting in and I have a gifted son who learned to read by age two (hyperlexia) and who gets similar test results as I do. I generally do include the gifted label in my use of the word “neurodiverse”, to make it clear that not only people who are considered “having disabilities” belong to this group. Here is a preliminary list of potential hunter-gatherer traits: CognitiveDistractibility and hyperfocusField-independent learnersPattern-recognizersWider field of visionSocial:Less politeness/socially awkward (learn few social rules)EgalitarianDistrust of authoritarian behaviourHigh sense of justiceSupport the underdogExceptional honestyNo-ingroupism/nepotismLess gender dimorphismPhysiological:Chronotype (tend to be night owls)Hypersensitive to physical stimuli (sound, touch, etc.)Anatomical:Ectomorph body typesLater pubertyTend to look younger than their ageFor simplicity I’ll stick here with only two types: hunter-gatherer types and farmer types. I usually include a third type (pastoralist types), but people are often mixed and, of course, reality is much more complex.Here is a comparison between hunter-gatherer vs farmer types when it comes to social behaviour: One thing almost all neurodiverse people have in common is that they are somewhat socially awkward. This is most obvious in austistic people who struggle with cognitive empathy, but less obviously so also in other types of neurodiversity, such as ADHD (e.g. blurting out seemingly irrelevant statements). As discussed in my previous post, social learning and blindly following socially transmitted knowledge were much less important in hunter-gatherer societies than farmer societies for which tradition and adherence to social rules were highly important. There is a well-known correlation between historical irrigation agriculture and tightness of culture (i.e emphasising rules and conformity). Put these two togetherAbsence of a “conformity instinct”Weak social learningAdd: extreme honestyand you get pretty much what we know from neurodiverse children with their seemingly rude behaviour when all they do is really just being honest! Hunter-gatherers do not have a lot of social rules, least of all anything nearly resembling etiquette. Words like “please” or “thank you” or even “sorry” are frequently absent. Politeness and even more so etiquette are very puzzling to people with ASD and is often perceived as “brown-nosing” even by those hunter-gatherer types who do get it. They are very straightforward and don’t understand why normies have such strange rituals when meeting. What comes seemingly naturally to NTs is often highly confusing to aspies. They would feel instantly at ease with the Pirahã hunter-gatherers of the Amazonian jungle. Daniel Everett writes about them: Expressions like hello, good-bye, how are you?, I’m sorry, you’re welcome, and thank you don’t express or elicit new information about the world so much as they maintain goodwill and mutual respect. The Pirahã culture does not require this kind of communication. Pirahã sentences are either requests for information (questions), assertions of new information (declarations), or commands, by and large. There are no words for thanks, I’m sorry, and so on. I have become used to this over the years and forget most of the time how surprising this can be to outsiders. from: Don't Sleep, There Are Snakes Now let’s add the most important ingredient of instinctive hunter-gatherer behaviour: egalitarianism. This comes with a lot of other traits, like a distrust for anybody who wants to assume authority (particularly when not being especially competent). Another aspect of egalitarianism is not forming alliances against other people and taking sides with people who are unfairly treated. Hunter-gatherer children are therefore often averse to joining groups (that often have some “alpha” type people in them) and are therefore much more likely to become the victims of bullying: they are considered weird (not conforming) and they often have no network of “allies”, which makes them easy prey. On the flip side, neurodiverse people are quick to help a bullied person themselves. For a long time I believed this to be an effect of the feeling of being an underdog, but it’s really an instinct that is part of the egalitarianism bundle. For all teachers who are annoyed by ADHD kids: watch and marvel how they will fight for a kid who is treated unfairly! If they are aggressive towards a kid they are most likely the bully’s bully. Last, but not least, what makes neurodiverse outcasts are their special interests (e.g. trains, birdwatching, evolutionary psychology - for me). Often not even other neurodiverse children are interested in endless talk about trains or insects, or whatever the current interest. There are several reasons why the interests of hunter-gatherer type children are so different from their peers’:Intrinsic motivationField independent learningMore flow experiencesHunter-gatherer people are more intrinsically motivated, i.e. money, status, grades, etc. mean very little to them. Being field-independent learners, they are also not attuned to what is socially “cool”, i.e. they couldn’t be any cooler when it comes to "cool". And finally, once hunter-gatherer types find something they are interested in (in an otherwise boring farmer world), they experience flow much more frequently than other people. Farmer-types seem to have an in-built clock (always knowing what time it is) and experience time evenly. Hunter-gatherer types experience time very differently when in flow we forget about time completely. It’s not rare that a neurodiverse person stops being occupied with his special interest only to find out it’s already sunrise - a farmer type would have felt the need to sleep 9 hours ago (and wouldn’t have missed the time). So, to summarize, it should be pretty clear by now why for so many neurodiverse children school is a nightmarish experience: getting bullied, feeling overwhelmed by WORK loads, feeling like outsiders or even aliens, and having to face angry and occasionally authoritarian teachers. Authoritarian teachers are particularly likely to have difficulties with neurodiverse children, as being stricter often only worsens the situation, which can easily spiral out of control. My hunch is that most kids with oppositional defiant disorder are hunter-gatherer type children. When dealing with neurodiverse children, the first maxim every teacher has to keep in mind is: “Be kind!”. These children are not proactively aggressive, their aggression is reactive, even if it may not seem so, but the neurodiverse child may subjectively feel that he or she is being treated unfairly. School is a recipe for social anxiety for hunter-gatherer children, and social anxiety is indeed not rare for neurodiverse people to suffer from social anxiety and depression. Have you ever heard of Hikikomori? They are hunter-gatherer type teens, bet you?

question: Why are selective mutism and autism mutually exclusive diagnoses?
answer: I don’t know why the writers of the DSM did it this way. [I’m also not certain that diagnosticians actually read it that way, since I know people with both diagnoses. ] I actually think “not better explained by autism” is a good idea, but that mutually exclusive would be a mistake. As an example, autistic people can also have ADHD. ADHD traits that are better explained by autism don’t mean we also have ADHD, but if that’s not what’s going on, we can have both diagnoses. Another consideration is whether or not the patterns of when speech is possible vs. when speech is not possible actually line up with “selective mutism.” I can tell you that in my case, it doesn’t line up. It’s not consistent within any given environment, and it’s better correlated with energy levels, my sensory environment, and whether or not I’m dealing with an illness or injury than anxiety. So, I absolutely think it’s possible for an autistic person to sometimes be able to speak, sometimes not be able to speak, and not have selective mutism. I also think it’s possible for us to have selective mutism, and that the two being mutually exclusive would be a mistake.

question: Opinion: Does the comorbidity of ADHD and autism present different symptoms than the two conditions distinct? I want to be a researcher and zone in on this topic! I feel that having both has different effects personally.
answer: Yes, they do present differently than just having either of them. Oftentimes, people who have both experience contradictory symptoms, which can be very confusing, especially if only one of the conditions was diagnosed. Here is a list of symptoms that may balance each other out a bit, or the opposite and make certain things worse: Novelty vs. routine: People who have only ADHD are typically all over the place, messy, talkative, excitement-seeking, understimulated. They are constantly looking for new experiences and go with whatever gets the dopamine kicking. People with just ASD prefer routine, predictability, are likely to not like small-talk and get easily overstimulated, which leads to them avoiding new experiences and rather sticking to routine and familiarity to cause as less discomfort as possible. When you have both, you might expose yourself to new stuff and excitement, only to get overstimulated quickly and retreat and coping with repetitive behaviors and stimming. Or you want the order and calmness, but your ADHD brain craves dopamine and feels understimulated and you get restless and uncomfortable, but you also don’t want to engage in something exciting as that would worsen the restlessness due to the autism. Hyperfixations / special interest: People with ADHD frequently experience hyperfocus with stuff that really draws them in, but those hyperfixations don’t last too long, only until the dopamine high wears off. They are likely to get into a wide varity of things and going full force with it, only to lose interest and then going with the next cool thing. When you have ASD, you typically have a very limited number of interests and stick to them in a calm and steady way. Engaging in them calms you down and helps with overstimulation and also fullfills you. With both, you might have a mix of the above. Maybe more interests, but they are long-term. Or you have 1–2 special interests and many short-term things coming and going. It really depends on the person’s presentation of either condition and how those interact. Symptoms that balance each other out: The social awkwardness of autism might be compensated by the ADHD social, talkative and energetic side. The ADHD messy ways might be compensated for by the autistic preference for order, so you might not have a cluttered thing as a home, but it being tidied up. Or you could be punctual on appointments because that being very important to your autistic brain. Dull or repetitive tasks, which might seem unbearable for someone with ADHD might be coming more easily to someone who has both. ADHD might help with the lack of spontanety in ASD and make the person more impulsive and less meticulous and rigid.There is not too much research on what the comorbidity actually looks like, but the above mentioned interrelations are what I could gather from people talking about the comorbidity.

question: I have ADHD. What are some activities that can help me focus more? (i.e. blogging, video games)?
answer: Controlling your focus is quite literally one of the most significant challenges for people with ADHD. But there are many ways to deal with it - it merely takes experimentation and persistence. There are 2 ways to approach the problem: with compensation strategies, and with methods to improve your brain. Use both. Compensation will be more straightforward to get results from, while brain changing takes more time and energy but has the potential for long-term effects.Compensation strategies There are tons upon tons of "brain hacks" that can be effective in taming your focus. I've found and tested many over the years. Here are some that I find particularly helpful. I recommend taking one or two of these at a time and trying them out. If they work for you, keep them - if not, cut them out. Either way, keep adding new methods gradually. Cutting out distractions In my experience, there are five major types of distraction at work, home, or school. Starting by controlling these while trying to get things done will make you more able to focus and be productive.Visual distraction (movement)Auditory distraction (sound)Social distraction (people)Internal distraction (thoughts)Technical distraction (computers)I'll break these down below. Controlling visual distraction If you get visually distracted often:Try to sit away from a high-traffic area (one where people are walking by a lot). A window on the second floor of the building, for example.Keep your workspace uncluttered. If there's stuff all over your desk, push it into a drawer. Visual disarray subconsciously affects your attention.Controlling auditory distraction If you get distracted by sound often:Use noise cancelling headphones. You can get some inexpensive ones from Sony ($40-50) that will help you concentrate a LOT more. Fantastic investment.Use white noise or binaural beats. These days I can't live without Music to improve focus, meditation & sleep.. Noisli is a free web app that is fantastic. Or you can get binaural audio on any streaming service. This stuff cuts out the background noise significantly, while not distracting you in the way music with lyrics does.Controlling social distraction Whereas working with people can be helpful at times, when you're trying to buckle down and get solo work done, it's detrimental. By being present, people can see you and are more inclined to tap you on the shoulder or talk to you. Each time this happens, you have to remember what you were doing and start over. To mitigate this, block off time to work alone regularly. This can be a section of each day, or a few days per week depending on your needs (and what you can work out with your employer, school schedule and so on). Even doing this at a public cafe can be better than your office or school, since nobody knows you there. People are less inclined to talk to strangers than their colleagues and classmates. Controlling internal distraction If you're often distracted by your thoughts:Use timers. There are dozens of apps for the Pomodoro technique out there or variants thereof. You can also use an egg timer app with a snooze that rings every 10 minutes, and you can use that to remind you to stay on track. I often put a text file (or post-it note) in the corner of my computer screen with my current task written on it - that way it's super easy to remind myself.Practice mindfulness meditation. There are classes for this online everywhere; it teaches you to pay attention better over time. I recommend everyone with ADHD practice mindfulness since it's useful in so many areas of one's life.Controlling technological distraction This one's a problem for everyone, ADHD or not. To prevent distraction from computers and smartphones:Put your phone on "do not disturb" mode. Make the decision that you're in work mode and commit to it.Use apps that disable other apps. This will prevent pop-ups and sound effects on your computer that are an ADHD nightmare. They can also disable use of apps that you're compelled to distract yourself with. Namely...Block social media, specifically. Facebook, Instagram and so on are highly addictive. Use one of the other many apps that lock those sites down so you can't access them while working.Brain Improvement A word on this, since I encourage everyone to look into it to get long-term improvements to your brain. There's plenty of science out there that the brain is neuroplastic; that is, your brain can change a whole lot. Focus and memory can improve. The downside is that there's no magic wand that just makes your brain better. Like the above strategies, you have to try these persistently (even more so) to get results. And sometimes spend money. But in the long run, they have the potential to actually change your brain. Also before doing these, I highly recommend doing a variety of cognitive testing to find out exactly where your problems are, and which method has the best chance of working for you. Here are a few that I have tried and gotten varying results from:Integrated Listening Systems This was among the most effective. You listen to specially engineered Mozart music while using specially made bone-conduction headphones and doing a variety of strange exercises. This significantly improved my auditory and visual processing skills which were previously more impaired. Here's an article I wrote about the experience: Working Out My Brain With Mozart | ADHDTechiesNeurofeedback A clinician puts a brainwave-reading headset on you, and has you focus on things; in my case, they were James Bond movies. When my attention was waning, the movie stopped, and I had to concentrate to get it going again. It essentially trains your brain to do what it needs to do to improve.Brain Gym Some occupational therapists use this to treat children and adults with everything from ADHD to dyslexia to developmental delays, Autism and so on. It involves yoga-like movements, pressure points and some other (sometimes strange) movements alone or in combination with things like eye movement, humming, and focusing your attention in different ways.Vipassana meditation Vipassana isn't taught casually; you have to go on a 10-day silent (no talking) meditation retreat to learn it. It's not easy, and not for everyone. But everyone I know that has done it has considered it life-changing, including myself. The Vipassana method is very much in line with mindfulness as I mentioned above - it teaches you how to persistently guide your attention to different parts of your body, over and over. And since it's all you're doing for ten days, you're guaranteed to get good at it. It's also 100% free. question: Since both autism and ADHD involve social and sensory issues, what differs the two? How can one person have one and not the other?

ADHD is specifically oriented around the lacking of dopamine while in autism the neurochemistry that is lacking or overcompensated for is less clear (some studies are pointing to lowered oxytocin or heightened serotonin levels). Autistic social difficulties are often caused by reduced emotional affect and inattention to social cues in general. ADHD also has a higher variance than it is often given credit for, but essentially causes difficulty with the reward processing center in the brain. While autistic individuals are often very structure oriented, ADHD individuals often run into difficulties with executive functioning and prioritization of tasks because of the lack of reward that comes with more tedious tasks or disliked tasks. AGAIN itâ€™s not this clear cut all the time and this doesnâ€™t cover it all, but the similarities in the conditions seem to be related to the fact that neurodivergence can be grouped together as neurodivergence and even things with differing pathology can present near identically even when the causes are different.

question: What are some tips for traveling by plane with children who have autism and sensory processing issues?

When an autistic person is having a sensory meltdown, they may find it difficult to communicate, even if their communication skills are usually average or above. An adult with autism may be aware of this and know the steps they need to take to be able to communicate their needs (though this is not always the case) but a child will likely not, meaning itâ€™s up to you to have safeguards in place. If the child is unable to speak coherently, then they will not be able to communicate what is wrong. They may not even know whatâ€™s wrong, and may respond with â€œI donâ€™t knowâ€ or â€œEverything,â€ which is only going to frustrate you. This is counterproductive. Instead, ask specific questions, such as â€œIs the seat uncomfortable?â€ â€œAre the lights too bright?â€ â€œIs the noise too loud?â€ The more specific the better. If a baby is crying and your child is covering their ears and breaking down, ask â€œIs that baby hurting your ears?â€ Donâ€™t blame the parent of course, but also donâ€™t scold your child if their discomfort leads them to shouting something rude, like â€œThat baby wonâ€™t shut up!â€ It is not the childâ€™s fault, and sensory overload can cause feelings of aggression in the face of helplessness. Solve the problem first, by providing ear coverings or something of the sort, and then casually mention (after the child has calmed down) how youâ€™re sorry the baby is so sad. Be subtle and try to instil an understanding that the baby is a person having a bad time, too, so you should care for their emotions. Just donâ€™t make them feel like they did something wrong for being overwhelmed.When solving problems, suppress your frustration, avoid vague questions, and be kind. I understand, the kidâ€™s been crying, youâ€™re getting dirty looks, you donâ€™t know what to do. But asking â€œWhat do you want from me?â€ Or saying â€œI donâ€™t know what you expect me to do about it/how to fix that/what you want or needâ€ is not helpful. Even a more gentle open-ended question, like â€œHow can I make it better?â€ Is probably not the best choice, since Iâ€™m this state of meltdown they may not be able to parse exactly whatâ€™s wrong, their brainâ€™s imagination of what â€œfixing itâ€ might be will probably be unrealistic, and they will have trouble communicating. Try not to get angry if they cry out that they want to go home, even if the plane is actively taking them home or if itâ€™s not possible. They donâ€™t want to be going home, they want to be home, because youâ€™ve established home as a safe space. The plane is a space that feels unsafe or scary, home is not scary and is safe. It might be frustrating, distressing, or even overwhelming for you yourself. This is completely valid. If the child seems overwhelmed by questions, ask â€œDo you want to be left alone?â€ Or â€œDo you want no more questions?â€ Sometimes, presenting solutions as something you want to do may help. Questions can be exhausting, especially for a child having a meltdown. If you notice your child crying and covering their ears while there are loud noises, try saying something like â€œAll these loud noises are hurting my head, so Iâ€™m going to listen to music and make the sounds go away.â€ If the child shows interest but does not ask to take part in the activity, invite them.Some autistic children are so afraid to make trouble that asking questions at all will not work and may result in forced suppression of their emotions or attempts to comfort you instead. question: How can an adult on the autism spectrum find a compatible roommate who will not trigger their meltdowns and sensory issues?
answer: Finding a compatible roommate as an autistic adult requires clear, honest, and upfront communication. It is important to be transparent about your needs and preferences from the beginning. This includes sharing information about your sensory triggers, such as noise, strong smells, or unexpected guests, as well as any routines or quiet times you follow. Being open about your communication style and desire for a calm, respectful living environment can help set expectations early. When interviewing potential roommates, it is helpful to ask about their daily habits, schedules, tolerance for house rules, and past experiences with roommates. Establishing mutual agreements regarding shared spaces, quiet hours, and guest policies can create a more structured environment that supports your needs. Although you cannot enforce a legal contract for behavior, discussing expectations openly can encourage cooperation. Using roommate matching platforms like Roomi, Roomster, and Facebook housing groups can connect you with individuals who may be more compatible. Assertive communication is essential when setting boundaries, and expressing your needs respectfully can help maintain a positive living arrangement. By taking these steps, you increase the likelihood of finding a roommate who understands and respects your sensory and emotional needs.

question: I have autism and severe sensory issues with food. How can I lose weight without changing my diet? I mostly eat things you would see on a kidsâ€™ menu.

question: What is the reason behind people with autism and/or sensory issues disliking physical touch? Is this a common experience for individuals with autism or sensory issues?
answer: I've spent some time digging into what autism is for me and other people. I'm just not happy with the absolute glut of 2 minute â€œautism is a neurodevelopmental disorderâ€¦â€ soundbites out there. And I didn't grow up knowing I had a neurodevelopmental condition, so all those â€œobviousâ€ signs of autism can be blurry to me. So I'm trying to figure it out mostly for myself, and speaking up when I think I know something. So: Touch is not just one thing. It's sensory all the way to psychological. Think about who you don't want to touch you. Some factors are whether we like the person, how we feel. What we expect. And also what we've learned about who and when to touch and not touch. Plus the evolving culture we live in, since I might now be touched in airport security, whereas we'd just walk through a metal detector when I was a child. So one physical aspect of touch is that we have nerves for pressure, heat, and pain. It seems to take me longer to perceive what I'm feeling. It's like people ask me â€œhow that feels/fitsâ€ and I need more time to think (or I just say â€œgreat.â€) It's like it takes me an extra two seconds to feel anything. That's an eternity during a conversation. Another aspect is autistic people seem to view friends and strangers the same way. I'm not sure I can explain it, but for example I feel like I have to answer any question asked of me. I don't want to ignore anyone, even if they're asking me to sign a petition to blot out the sun or something. I treat everyone with the same begrudging surlyness. So I don't touch strangers. I don't touch family. I treat people the same way. I doubt people understand it, but I'm not the only person who keeps their hands to themselves. Finally, I don't want a reputation for brushing or touching people because that's creepy. Creepy is vague and a matter of opinion, but we all know being creepy is not good. So I'm not going to be a touchy Feely hugger until I untangle all those hangups. And even then, maybe I'm just not a touchy feely person to begin with.

question: Are all autistic people sensory sensitive?
answer: I don't know about all. I would at least say most. It manifests differently, though. For me, fingernails on a chalkboard actually doesn't terribly bother me. It's not something I'd want to hear all day, but it's no more immediately bothersome than engine noise. Even a lot of NT people are bothered by that. But I do have various tics with things that don't as much bother others. Clicking fingernails together is one. I will have a very strong desire to break the fingers in question. Similarly, if you feel the need to click your pen or tap your pencil, I'll think very hard about where exactly that pen or pencil might go to stop you from that, and it probably involves somewhere you'd rather not have it. I don't generally mind being touched as much as some autistic people do. A brush past someone or pat on the shoulder is generally alright. And if I know you well, hugging or the like is no issue, nor is being much more intimate with a partner. That's actually very comforting. But I don't care how well I know you; DO NOT TOUCH MY SPINE. I don't know why but I absolutely hate that. I will pull away from that, and if for some reason I couldn't, I'd probably attack or do whatever it took. It's a very visceral reaction. So, yes, I think most autistic people, at least, have sensory tics. I've learned to carry headphones everywhere. If something someone is doing is really driving me nuts, on go the headphones, and now you can sit there and click your fucking pen all you like. I can't hear it any more.

question: Can you still be diagnosed with Autism, even though you never had trouble with social skills? For example, you can just have restricted interests and sensory issues that caused you great distress from early childhood to adulthood
answer: Whether you are diagnosed with Autism or not, you have some significant problems that are causing you distress. Look around and find a psychologist who can help you to deal with these things. Diagnosing Autism is not like diagnosing cancer where you can look at an exray and confirm that the person has it. The discovery of Autism was also not like the discovery of cancer. question: Does someone not have autism if instead of over functioning sensory issues, they have underfunctioning sensory issues?
answer: Q: Does someone not have autism if instead of over functioning sensory issues, they have under functioning sensory issues? Short answer: thatâ€™s not quite correct, and thereâ€™s a lot more to autism than just sensory issues. So, letâ€™s talk sensory sensitivities first of all. What a sensory sensitivity is not is a problem with the actual function of a sense. So, letâ€™s say youâ€™ve got an extremely under-sensitive sense of smell, which might mean you canâ€™t smell anything at all, the problem isnâ€™t with your nose, itâ€™s to do with how your brain picks up sensory information. Basically, sensory sensitivities are differences in how your brain processes information from sensory stimuli, and as a result, you have different reactions to those stimuli from other people. Sensory sensitivities can be over-sensitive [the technical term for his is hypersensitivity], or under-sensitive [hyposensitivity]. Autistic people donâ€™t exclusively have one type or the other type. In fact, for an autistic person to have such a sensory profile would be pretty rare. Itâ€™s far more common for an autistic person to have both types of sensory sensitivity. But autism is much more than just sensory processing issues - if a person just has sensory processing issues, they could have sensory processing disorders.

question: I got diagnosed with high functioning autism, but I have no sensory issues. Do you have to have it with autism?
answer: A very direct and literal answer to your question: No, you don't have to have sensory issues. Why? Well, it's part of how â€œautism" functions as a diagnostic category. It takes a while to explain how diagnoses are historically emergent, so if you have the patience for that, enjoy. Analogy: Pretend that, in the fifth century, someone comes home from a trip. Let's just say Lancelot, after coming home from a quest. He gets sick, with lots of nausea and a case of â€œthe runs.â€ Merlin has no idea what's wrong for sure, but suspects Lancelot's been cursed by this witch he says he encountered on his journey. The curse had magically removed a karge quantity of blood and bile in his system, throwing his humors out of balance. This tricked his body into disposing is of its phlegmatic and sapine liquids as quickly as possible, to bring them into balance again. Merlin just has him drink as much water as possible. Over a bit of time, Lancelot gets better. Now, let's imagine that in the early 1800s, someone revisits this story and asserts that it was not a humor imbalance at work, but that the foul stench and miasma of the witch's den was to blame. Then in the mid 1900s, someone else revisits it and says â€œNo, this was clearly a case of cholera. And thus a pathogen was to blame. Merlin was, by practical medical standards, correct. But based on the symptoms, he had an operating theory that suggested a course of treatment. This treatment addressed the symptoms, staving off dehydration, long enough that Lancelot's body could clear the disease. (Incidentally, the person in the 1800s probably would have prescribed an inadequate treatment.) However, Merlin's theory, in itself, was wrong. He did not know that there was a swarm of tiny organisms living in Lancelot's body, and thereby causing the symptoms. How is this relevant? Because, we do not know which of these three historical understandings of the illness is most analogous to our current understanding of autism. Autism is not a â€œthing.â€ There's nothing you can point to in someone's brain and say, â€œThat right there, that's the autism part.â€ All we have are diagnostic criteria. We have noticed that certain number of maladaptive traits tend to occur clustered together. Doctors isolate these traits and call them â€œsymptoms,â€ guessing that the clustering traits share an underlying cause. We then call this phenomenon â€œAutism." But Autism does not refer to the cause. It refers to the clustering of traits which are purported to be effects of the theorized cause. Similarly, cholera was not a bacterium. It was a *disease* caused by a set of related bacteria calles â€œVibrio cholerae.â€ Now, â€œSo what?â€ I hear you say. Well, what if someone has some traits but not others? How do we know that the underlying cause ALWAYS affects people such that they have that trait? How do we know that a peculiarity of how they were raised didn't compensate them in one way or another? There are no *necessary* â€œsymptomsâ€ for an autism diagnosis, but if you have enough of them, it might be deemed â€œsufficient" for a diagnosis, even if none was specifically necessary. Now, I personally have a lot of doubts that there is any underlying cause. Let's just indulge in stereotypes for a moment, and stipulate that there is a clustering between the following traits: dark skin, wide noses, thicker lips, curly hair, dark hair, height. Obviously, I am describing the schema many have for African-Americans. (A broad and sloppy one, at that.) I could then say, â€œHey, I notice these things often all happen at once. Maybe there is an underlying cause? I know these things all run in families, so perhaps they are all genetic! And perhaps there is ONE GENE that controls all of these things!â€ You'd say I was pretty silly, right? There are short people with dark skin, dark, curly hair, wide noses and thick lips. There are people who are tall, with dark, curly hair, wide noses and thick lips, yet with lighter skin (I am one such person). But plenty of people would still categorize these sorts of people as African-American. (That's, of course, because â€œrace,â€ as we understand it, is a myth based on sloppy biology and anthropology from the 17th-19th centuries.) A lot, if not all, of these traits are controlled by multiple genes, leading to an incredibly diverse human population. But you can still find clustering traits within that group of 7 billion people. Similarly, researchers claim to be looking for the genetic causes for autism often come back saying that there are some hilariously large number of genes that are more common among diagnosed autistics than among non-diagnosed ones. They'll often say this puts us closer to finding â€œthe cause,â€ but to me that looks like we are just a cluster rhat occurs naturally within large populations. If you are wondering why autism diagnoses have gone up, that is because Autism's diagnostic criteria were (and I cannot stress this hard enough) *deliberately* expanded so that more people could qualify for assitance and accommodations. They were intentionally written to apply to a larger portion of the population. Supplemental to that is increased awareness obviously leads to more people seeking diagnosis. Plus, increased mobility has led to people self-selecting partners among a broader pool than before, and people who are introverted and don't like loud noises might prefer one another to loud extroverts. And they are more likely to have children who express these traits more often.

question: What are autism sensory issues? Is it over sensitivity?
answer: Every person on the spectrum has different sensory issues. As Jennifer Christie Gudelis pointed out earlier, even â€œneurotypicalâ€ people not on the spectrum can have wide ranges of sensory issues. I'm not on the spectrum, but I'm quite sensitive to loud noises and to touch, but not to the point of being unable to attend a loud concert with no earplugs, or not wishing to receive a hug, kiss, or massage from my boyfriend. I get the sense that with a person who has ASD, it's more that certain sensory experiences are more likely to be overstimulating or overwhelming, while other senses are more likely to be understimulated. For instance, generally speaking, many women with ASD have a tendency to be clumsy, or much more so than average, probably because their sense of balance or sense of pain is not stimulated enough. But the same women might also be overstimulated by sounds or smells, touch, light, busy environments, or any number of things. My boyfriend does have Asperger's Syndrome. Unlike me, he's far less sensitive to touch or hot/cold than I am, and can 'turn off' any ticklishness. (I cannot turn off my ticklishness at all - I've always envied those who could do that). Fortunately, unlike [the stereotype of] many men who are the spectrum, he's perfectly fine being touched, or hugged. In fact a tight hug can help him calm down much faster after a meltdown than he could if he were left alone. He is also much less sensitive to high frequency sounds. (He used to play a practical joke on me by placing his phone with a frequency emitter on, under my pillow. He stopped when I told him that those high pitched sounds don't just annoy me, they hurt me). Oh, and he can tolerate maximum levels of spiciness in his food, whereas I'm almost the opposite. My boyfriend is sensitive in other ways. He's more liable to be anxious and overwhelmed in new social situations. He also gets overwhelmed and frustrated easily by complex or academic terms, or essays, or poems, or very intensive documentaries. It doesn't help that he has something like comorbid ADHD, and often zones out during such programs. He's also more sensitive to stress than I am, and partly because of that, he is more bothered by messes and clutter than I am. He's very, very sensitive to most graphic violence in media, whether it's music, movies, or tv shows - and I get the sense that this is not very typical at all for most people with Asperger's, at least based on my research on ASD, and inquiry with other people on the spectrum in online forums. For instance, he loves music of so many genres (it helps that he has a knack for remembering even obscure band names, albums, songs, and such). But suggested violence or dark scenarios that sometimes come up in some heavy metal/death metal and some gangsta rap can sometimes pose a problem. Eminem rapping about murdering his girlfriend on the Marshall Mathers LP was certainly more than he could stand. (I actually had trouble trying to listen to that song too, but the rest of the album was my jam in junior high). As for movies or shows, he can easily stand seeing a gunfight or fistfight, or people getting battered and bloodied, but someone's head being blown off or severed might be too much. Seeing someone burned by fire is too much. Slashing or spearing or slicing and dicing of people is too much. He especially cannot stand violence against animals or small children being depicted, even if it's off screen. (Which can mean his reactions and meltdowns are sometimes unpredictable. For instance, near the end of â€œThe 13th Warriorâ€, everything was good and fine, until they set up outward-facing wooden spikes, which speared the cavalry horses when they try to attack. My boyfriend just could NOT stand the killing of those horses, and we had to stop right there, 20 minutes or so from the end). I have to admit, even though sometimes his inability to handle certain violence can be annoying, it's also kind of endearing. Like, it's really sweet that he is so torn up inside when an animal or child is hurt on film, and that seeing people suffer is hard on him, even if it's fictional people and fictional animals. So, because trying to watch such violent movies or shows is such an exhausting and potentially harrowing hassle (and even seeing it on my own would just make him kind of jealous and upset), I now generally refrain from seeing [even merely potentially] gory shows and films. Also, because I've had to be so On Guard while watching a potentially violent movie with him, I have become much more sensitive to and less tolerant of gory violence than I ever used to be.

question: Is it possible to have autism without experiencing any sensory issues, such as hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity?

The severity of sensory issues can vary significantly from person to person and can change over time.
