question: Is it possible for someone with autism to be misdiagnosed with ADHD due to sensory issues, social anxiety, and meltdowns?
answer: Yes, it is possible for someone with autism to be misdiagnosed with ADHD due to overlapping symptoms, including sensory issues, social anxiety, and meltdowns. Both autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and ADHD are neurodevelopmental disorders that share some behavioral characteristics, which can sometimes lead to diagnostic confusion. Here's how the overlap in symptoms can contribute to a misdiagnosis: Sensory IssuesBoth individuals with ASD and those with ADHD can exhibit sensory processing issues, though the reasons and manifestations might differ. In ASD, sensory sensitivities are often more pronounced and can include both hypo- and hypersensitivities across a wide range of sensory experiences. In ADHD, sensory processing issues might manifest as a heightened need for stimulation or difficulty filtering out extraneous sensory input.Social AnxietySocial anxiety and difficulties with social interactions are common in individuals with autism due to challenges in understanding social cues and norms. While ADHD does not inherently include social communication challenges, individuals with ADHD may experience social anxiety as a secondary issue, often stemming from a history of social rejection or difficulties maintaining attention in social situations.MeltdownsMeltdowns or emotional dysregulation can occur in both autism and ADHD. In autism, meltdowns are often the result of overwhelming sensory environments, difficulties with communication, or changes in routine. In ADHD, emotional dysregulation might be due to impulsivity, frustration, or difficulties with executive function.Diagnostic Challenges The diagnostic process can be complicated by the fact that ASD and ADHD can co-occur; that is, an individual can have both conditions simultaneously. This co-occurrence can make it challenging to distinguish which symptoms are attributable to which condition. Additionally, diagnostic criteria and practices have evolved over time, allowing for better differentiation and recognition of the co-occurrence of these conditions. question: Can olfactory hallucinations be explained by autism spectrum disorder? I have sensory issues and I sometimes smell things that are not there.
answer: TL;DR: Probably not. To be honest, olfaction is not well understood in humans. We donâ€™t rely on it to a great extent, so most of the research on perception is weighted towards vision and hearing. We know more about gustation (taste) and touch, and more about the less well-known senses like proprioception than we do about olfaction. One issue that is not well understood is the difference between smelling things that arenâ€™t there (hallucination) and smelling things that are undetectable by others. There are super-smellers (hyperosmia) who might be considered to be having olfactory hallucinations, but who really are capable of detecting subliminal odours. Adding to the confusion, super-smellers are not necessarily capable of smelling all subliminal odours: some are sensitive to sweet odours, some to unpleasant odours, some are sensitive only under certain circumstances (having a migraine, being pregnant, etc.). Olfaction has been linked to the KAL1 gene and its variants. If this gene does not function normally, the olfactory bulbs fail to develop, and there can be further developmental repercussions, e.g., Kallmann syndrome. There is some evidence that duplication of KAL1 can cause hyperosmia, but, thus far, no evidence that KAL1 duplication is found in ASD. There is one report of a boy with Kallmann Syndrome who also has ASD, but in his case, the KAL1 gene was a mutation - not a duplication - and related to his Kallmann Syndrome, not his ASD. So, if KAL1 is implicated in ASD, itâ€™s probably only involved in a tiny number of cases - and itâ€™s more likely to be KAL1 deletions or mutations which also cause Kallmann Syndrome than it is to be duplications that cause hyperosmia. But, wandering off into the handy-wavy depths of hypothesis snorkelling, since ASD can involve gene duplication, itâ€™s at least theoretically possible that someone with autism could have KAL1 duplication, leading to hyperosmia, which - as noted in my second paragraph above - can be unpredictable. On balance, though, you may be autistic AND a super-smeller, but itâ€™s a coincidence - in the same way that you can be autistic AND red-haired. Neither is a feature of the other, and neither is caused by the other. If you are concerned about these odd smells you detect - whether hyperosmic or hallucinatory - see your doctor. There are neurological conditions which can sometimes cause olfactory hallucination, and you should get them ruled out.

This means that a dose which would cause sunburn in a skin which has not been exposed to sun for a long time, may have no noticeable effect on â€˜practicedâ€™, tanned skin. Sunscreen was invented at the beginning of WWII, and was not on the market until the 1950s. Many people survived before that! Before the 1920s, in the whole world, tanning was not seen as good, pale skin was better. This is because a tan suggested the you had to work out of doors, suggesting that you were a labourer. Pale skin meant that you were wealthy enough not to have to go out of doors much! As an aside, there was an interesting Quora question recently, about Minoans being dark skinned, and it was pointed out that the meant were painted with brown skin, but the women with white skin. In the late 1950s and the early 1960s, It was noticed that tan enthusiastsâ€™ skin was aging far more quickly, and skin malignancies were becoming far more common, than previously. question: What is the difference between autism and social anxiety disorder?
answer: Autism and social anxiety disorder (SAD) are distinct conditions with some overlapping symptoms but fundamentally different in their nature. Autism is a lifelong developmental disorder that affects social interaction, communication, and behavior. Individuals with autism often have difficulty with social cues, nonverbal communication, and may engage in repetitive behaviors. Social anxiety disorder, on the other hand, is an anxiety disorder characterized by an intense and irrational fear of social situations or scrutiny. People with SAD are typically very self-conscious and worry about being judged or embarrassed in social settings, leading to avoidance of social interactions. While both conditions can involve social difficulties, autism is primarily a developmental and neurological condition, whereas social anxiety disorder is a mental health disorder driven by anxiety and excessive fear of social situations. question: If people on the autism spectrum and people with social anxiety disorder both hate eye contact, how can we discern the difference?
answer: Avoidance of eye contact is common in ASD and SAD/GSAD, but is not a defining feature of either.There are other, more pertinent criteria for diagnosis of both (see below).DSM Criteria for ASD: A. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, as manifested by the following, currently or by history (examples are illustrative, not exhaustive, see text):Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, ranging, for example, from abnormal social approach and failure of normal back-and-forth conversation; to reduced sharing of interests, emotions, or affect; to failure to initiate or respond to social interactions.Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction, ranging, for example, from poorly integrated verbal and nonverbal communication; to abnormalities in eye contact and body language or deficits in understanding and use of gestures; to a total lack of facial expressions and nonverbal communication.Deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships, ranging, for example, from difficulties adjusting behavior to suit various social contexts; to difficulties in sharing imaginative play or in making friends; to absence of interest in peers.Specify current severity: Severity is based on social communication impairments and restricted repetitive patterns of behavior. B. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities, as manifested by at least two of the following, currently or by history (examples are illustrative, not exhaustive; see text):Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech (e.g., simple motor stereotypies, lining up toys or flipping objects, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases).Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, or ritualized patterns or verbal nonverbal behavior (e.g., extreme distress at small changes, difficulties with transitions, rigid thinking patterns, greeting rituals, need to take same route or eat food every day).Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus (e.g, strong attachment to or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessively circumscribed or perseverative interest).Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interests in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement).Specify current severity: Severity is based on social communication impairments and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior. C. Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life). D. Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning. E. These disturbances are not better explained by intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder) or global developmental delay. Intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder frequently co-occur; to make comorbid diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability, social communication should be below that expected for general developmental level. Note: Individuals with a well-established DSM-IV diagnosis of autistic disorder, Aspergerâ€™s disorder, or pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified should be given the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. Individuals who have marked deficits in social communication, but whose symptoms do not otherwise meet criteria for autism spectrum disorder, should be evaluated for social (pragmatic) communication disorder. Specify if: With or without accompanying intellectual impairment With or without accompanying language impairment Associated with a known medical or genetic condition or environmental factor With catatoniaDSM Criteria for SAD: A. A persistent fear of one or more social or performance situations in which the person is exposed to unfamiliar people or to possible scrutiny by others. The individual fears that he or she will act in a way (or show anxiety symptoms) that will be embarrassing and humiliating. B. Exposure to the feared situation almost invariably provokes anxiety, which may take the form of a situationally bound or situationally pre-disposed Panic Attack. C. The person recognizes that this fear is unreasonable or excessive. D. The feared situations are avoided or else are endured with intense anxiety and distress. E. The avoidance, anxious anticipation, or distress in the feared social or performance situation(s) interferes significantly with the person's normal routine, occupational (academic) functioning, or social activities or relationships, or there is marked distress about having the phobia. F. The fear, anxiety, or avoidance is persistent, typically lasting 6 or more months. G. The fear or avoidance is not due to direct physiological effects of a substance (e.g., drugs, medications) or a general medical condition not better accounted for by another mental disorder.

question: Is an autism diagnosis helpful?
answer: I want to expand on this original question because a diagnosis is only a fraction of the broader topic of “knowing yourself”. As children, we are tasked with knowing ourselves. Learning how to move our bodies. How to process our sensory stimulation. Develop cognitive skills and so on. We are also learning our environment and about others too, but this, in my opinion, is all built on our knowledge and control of ourselves. I write this from my experience of being an adult that was late diagnosed with ASD at age 59. I had been diagnosed about age 11 with ADHD/ Dyslexia. But “in those days” there was little knowledge or support available. About the only thing it changed was what my parents and teachers expected from me… I became the learning disabled kid. The slow-learner etc… So… in a situation where there is no follow-up services, a diagnosis is of little use. This does not mean the diagnosis was of little use. But it is only a first step in a critically important process. This is true for adults who are given a late diagnosis… We’re given this shiny new diagnosis, but after the door closes behind us and we stand in the real world… there are no real services or support still. ( Cue - wisp of wind, tumble weeds and crickets) … So, a diagnosis IS important and is a necessary first step. Especially if the child/adult is struggling with challenges they cannot understand or define. It is a “road map” that gives us a point of reference and possible destinations.. It helps defines roads that others have already built that we can follow. Or that will lead us to places where we can learn to blaze new trails to fulfilling our needs and goals. For me at least, I was tying to be “like everyone else” which was trying to be NT (neurotypical). Trying to NOT be ADHD and teaching myself to read in a way I could cope with the dyslexia. These were survival skill. Coping behaviors I needed to feel even a hint of self worth and sense of belonging. I gave it my all… I learned to deny my most natural instincts because I had learned from the social pressure, (and an abusive father), that I was “not acceptable” as I was. So it was more complex than just the ASD/ADHD/Dyslexia. What I learned after 59 years of trying to be NT was that I was only fooling myself. I was not just denying my disorders, but was denying the development of my true self. Denying my wants and needs. You end up being what T. S. Elliot called “the hollow men - The stuffed men”. It is hard to describe how I feel now… looking back and wondering HOW I lived like that. I’m amazed I did not develop other more serious disorders from it all. But, am also starting to realize how destructive that life was. And I am also understanding there are dysfunctional behaviors I must learn to recognize and try and change. I’ve come this far. And so have so many late diagnosed adults I’ve met. Many do have other comorbid disorders that are more serious and difficult to manage. To be honest with myself, I realize I’m struggling still.. But as I said above, most of us get our shiny new diagnosis, and its tumble weeds and crickets once that door closes behind us. But, all this emphasizes the importance of the diagnosis. We NEED these maps. We cannot navigate our lives thinking we should be going left when we need to go right. It is very often a relief to know the truth about ourselves. So we can start to understand that there is a reason we are different and have different needs. So we can know and ACCEPT our TRUE self. Not a self we feel obligated to project for the benefit of others. The sad truth about the diagnosis is that we lack the support we need to benefit from that diagnosis. Be it a young person or old, we’re behind in many ways. We are struggling with behaviors we’ve developed as “band-aids” to cover gaping wounds in our developmental needs. We’ve been taking left turns all our lives when we have needed to turn right. This can mean, at many levels we need help finding our orientation and even knowing what we need or where we need to go. We often don’t even understand what we were just diagnosed with. We’re so used to suppressing our real-self, we barely even know ourselves. This varies for each person depending on multiple factors. But we all are healing from a very stressful and challenging past. I believe it is crucial that children find “their way” as soon as possible. So they do not start off on the wrong path. This of course also assumes they have the supports they need. What those needed supports are and providing them, is they key to really making a diagnosis “helpful”.

question: How can I get over my autism diagnosis?
answer: My entire life was filled with trying to fit in and attempting to be “normal” when I knew I wasn’t. I was always told I was “weird” and socially awkward, but that nothing was actually wrong with me. So, I spent my teen years wishing someone could tell me what was going on and why I felt like I didn’t fit in with anyone. It wasn’t until I was 23 years old that I finally went to see a psychologist and was diagnosed with Asperger’s Syndrome, which falls on the Autism Spectrum. As she described the criteria laid out in the DSM-IV for diagnosis, I realized I had more than the minimum requirements for the diagnosis. She set a plan in place to assist me in relearning normal social cues and other social skills, which helped me tremendously. I will admit, that going into the whole situation was terrifying, especially knowing there was going to be some sort of diagnosis at the end of the initial intake visits, but I found myself relieved to finally have an explanation for everything that I had felt throughout my life. After 23 years, I could start moving forward with more confidence and self-awareness. Telling my family and friends was a bit difficult, but they were very supportive and understanding. If you truly feel your Autism diagnosis is incorrect, then I would seek a second evaluation. Don’t - I repeat - Don’t continue to seek opinion after opinion until you get the answer you want to hear. If a new doctor evaluates you and confirms the initial Autism diagnosis, you will need to come to terms with this and move forward. You are NOT defined by a diagnosis, regardless of what it is. We are ALL normal in our own unique ways. No two people are exactly alike, which is what makes this world such a diverse and interesting place. Give yourself a chance to actually be YOU. Not the person you think everyone else will like, but your true self. It won’t be easy, but it will definitely be worth it. You will never know which of your “friends” like you for who you are if they have never gotten to know the REAL you in the first place. You NEVER have to tell anyone that you are Autistic if you don’t feel comfortable enough to do so. If you do tell someone and they start treating you in a way that makes you uncomfortable, let them know. Don’t be afraid to remind them that you are a human being, just like they are, and that you deserve to be treated with respect and dignity regardless of what their preconceived idea of what a person with Autism is like. As the saying goes, “If you’ve met one person with Autism, you’ve met one person with Autism.” It is called a Spectrum for a reason. At the end of the day, you are the one that has to accept yourself for who you are, regardless of what the world around you says. You are in control of your life, and I truly hope you find the peace you need to continue moving forward.

question: How do I get my autism diagnosis removed? I was diagnosed when I was about 6 and I know for sure that I don’t have it.
answer: OK, so you might have been misdiagnosed. Here are some of the core symptoms of an autism spectrum disorder, just so you can double check you don’t have any of them, or not a significant amount of them. I would break down autism into four main areas - social/communication, behavioural, emotional and sensory. In the social/communication area, things you’d want to be crossing off [if you don’t have them] are:Misinterpreting and/or not reading social cues from non-autistic/neurotypical peopleHaving significant difficulties establishing and maintaining friendships and relationships - a worst case scenario of this would be that a person is unable to make friends their entire lives. But as I said, that’s worst case scenario. It’s not completely impossible for autistic people to make friends or have relationships - just very difficult in most cases.Varying degrees of echolalia - this just means repeating words and phrases they’ve heard. All autistic people have it to some degree, but the most obvious and severest this can be is in the case of a person with classic autism [what is now called level 3 ASD], where the only speech the person has might be echolalia.Literal use and interpretation of language. Here’s an example scenario from my own childhood - I was in junior school [I’m in the UK, so that’s age 7–11], and I’d done a good piece of work. My support worker said that my teacher would be “over the moon” [which means that they’d be very happy or delighted]. I didn’t know that at the time, and took it to mean that my teacher would literally go up into space and over the moon.Having a one-track mind - you may find it very difficult to stop doing something that isn’t finished.Obsessive special interests - some people call them obsessions, some people call them special interests. I personally don’t mind either term, but others will prefer the term special interests. These can be any subject, or even more than one subject, which the person can research and talk about at length, and they will enjoy their special interests and might even make a career out of them - i.e. if a woman with autism has an interest in people, or in psychological matters, they might study psychology and get a job as a psychologist.BehaviouralStereotypical and repetitive behaviours, i.e. hand-flapping, toe-walking, etc.Restricted and rigid routines and not liking changes to those routines [however, it should be noticed that there are some autistic people, myself being one of them, that don’t have routines and don’t mind change].EmotionalHaving intense emotions - think of the range of emotions a person can have as being like a thermometer labelled from 0–10. Neurotypicals have every point on their thermometer, whereas autistic people have 0, 1 and 2, then 8, 9, and 10. The middle of the thermometer isn’t there for autistic people.Alexithymia - also called emotional blindness, this is basically that autistic people have great difficulty putting their emotions into speech. Ask an autistic person how they feel, most likely you will get “I don’t know”. That is short for “I don’t know how to grasp one of the many thoughts and feelings inside my head, identify it and explain it in words so you’ll understand.”SensoryAutistic people are often hypersensitive [over-sensitive] or hyposensitive [under-sensitive] to sensory stimuli. Hypersensitivity is also accompanied by sensory avoidant behaviours, i.e. wearing dark sunglasses, or hoods to avoid bright lights, and hyposensitivity is accompanied by sensory seeking behaviours.That’s not a comprehensive list - I’ve written fuller answers on this topic in other questions [you can see those if you wish]. But just to give you some idea of things you could cross off if you don’t have. I’d say the social/communication area is the biggest and most noticeable area of an autism spectrum disorder though - so, if you have little or none of the social side of autism, or what you do have doesn’t affect your ability to function normally, then the chances are you don’t have autism. Everyone has one or two autistic traits, so there might be a couple of things you identify with, but what makes a person have the condition is not that they have autistic traits at all, but how prominent they are and how do they affect the person’s abilities to function.

It was not easy to convince myself to live, even when divine providence seemed to me, the only thing that kept me alive. That is what lead me to gain a diagnosis in adulthood - refusal to be a suicide statistic
comment_answer: My heart is with you, Emma Skinner. I am so, so very glad you did not become a statistic.

question: What has caused the huge increase in diagnosed cases of autism?
answer: Great question. Unfortunately the answer is probably not the one you want. Autism has always been with us. Just until 100 years ago, most kids died in their first few years, now all kids pretty much survive. Everyone has stories about quirky uncle who always ate the same thing, someone who always read the newspaper before breakfast, always with no exceptions. Quirky people who had peculiar habits. That weird scientist, engineers and mathematicians who rocked back and forth when they were thinking. Went for long walks and walked in a peculiar way. History is full of these people. But until around 50 some years ago. There was no word for this. Doctors called kids with severe autism lazy, weird and idiots. There were also words like retarded and few others that are less pleasant. Especially around the time my grandparents and even parents were in school, left handed kids were often punished for writing with their left hand, even got their left hand tied or something so they would use their right hand. Many of them had been through this at home, so they just used their right hand even if they did not like it. They did not want the attention and punishments. Autism is a spectrum, you almost can’t say you have a lot of autism or you have little autism, but people do understand what you mean. Often called functioning autism even though that is condesending. My mom and grand mother often talked about some relatives as they had read so much they became weird, some were called “know to much” (doesn’t translate that well from Icelandic). But none of this was meant negatively. But just as you could claim that there was a huge increase of left handed people in the 1980s, there wasn’t. It leveled quite quickly once people could use their main hand without negativity. Autism is a spectrum. Scientists are simply diagnosing this, which no one did 50 years ago. And the time between now and 50–80 years ago has shown drastic increase in diagnoses, because there were none before. People are writing more about this, and this is much more known now by people. There are stories about autistic people in the old Icelandic sagas, stories from around the year 900 and were written down ca year 1200 of people who were for example tied to a pole, not for show and tell, so they would not wander about and get hurt. There are others about kids being removed from parents and basically made to live in barns like animals. Often they died. This has always been with us. We are simply writing it down and doing research on this. Understanding it more. This is quite universal, it happens in far away tribes and in every soceity. Just some places hide these people or simply get rid of them. Fortunately that is happening less and less today. Just as people died from cancer all through our millions of years of being on earth, long before anyone knew what cancer was. When doctors started doing autopsies, they figured out why people died and wrote down cancer. When the first doctor wrote it down, did not mean there were no cancer before that time. Just that we did not have a name for it. Now we do.
comment_answer: One thing I would quibble with. While cancer may be more easily diagnosed today, it is also more prevalent. It is more prevalent because it is a disease associated with age. A child that dies of measles will not live long enough to get cancer. A woman who dies in childbirth will never get cancer. As we eliminate causes of death, others step up to the plate.

question: Have you ever questioned your autism diagnosis?
answer: It is interesting to read responses to this question. Since that moment, a part of me realized I was autistic, I started going through the process of acceptance. Those who have not gone through this must find it hard to understand what I and many of us have gone through to get to the start of this realization. I’m speaking for myself, but have found that many of the late diagnosed adults I’ve met and talked to, have very similar experiences in this process. First off - autism as an etiology of this undefined “influence” over our lives, is not obvious to even us. There is no little voice in us saying.. “ Yea… these things are happening because you are neurologically autistic”. We realize this difference VERY early in our lives. I read that studies show that autistic children begin to mask as early as 6 months of age. So, we not only struggle to adapt and accommodate to our world, but we do it alone and with barely a clue to what it is, or how to cope with it. We struggle within ourselves, and with the world around us. The stress level is high enough that 1 in 3 autistic people will attempt suicide. 3 in 4 will have suicidal ideation. So this is not a simple challenge we face from almost birth. I now that I learned to cope through denial and avoidance of my autistic/ADHD/dyslexic challenges. My ADHD and dyslexia were diagnosed about age11. But, from lack of support, personal understanding, the shame and anxiety of being “exposed” as “disabled” - you learn quickly that you’re on your own. The Calvary is not coming. And if you just ‘fake it’ people tend to leave you alone. I did that for 59 years, until I started losing the stamina and will to deny such intense physical and emotional hardships. I built walls for 59 years…. Then it all started crashing down… finally knew I had to get real because I was in a dark place that was getting close to midnight. It was a life of experiences and searching that all came together at a moment of personal/professional crisis. It was obvious at that moment WHY the crisis was happening. I had suspected Asperger Syndrome very strongly after talking with a coworker about here aspie son. But I dismissed it then… Now, I knew I had to follow that suspicion. When I finally realized all the stories I was reading, all the questions I’ve read from other aspies were the same questions I had been asking all my life, it literally HIT me physically and emotionally. I had an adrenalin dump that lasted almost 3 months causing my heart to go bonkers. That is when I told my Doctor what I found about autism and it is what had my adrenaline so high. He got a diagnosis scheduled and 6 weeks later I was diagnosed. But that is only the first few steps on the ASD journey. I had to learn about autism. What it means and how it might apply to my life. I had to tear down the walls of denial and am still working on that. I had to realize and accept ALL the autistic/ADHD/dyslexic traits I’ve been denying and covering up. I’ve had to go back through all the childhood emotions and start there again… learning about and understanding what I really do struggle with. But also what my gifts are too. It will be a life long journey of tearing down my false self-concepts and building/ nurturing the person I really am. This is not an easy process and effects every past memory and self-concept to the deepest and most private and protected facets of my life. I still have times I find it hard to believe “ I’m Autistic” and all the other comorbid and related things that come with being neurologically different. I DO accept it now. But it is still hard to believe in some ways. Its a lot better life now, because these are struggles I doing FOR me… not struggles I run away from and only prevent me from being my autistic/ADHD/dyslexic best.

question: How do you accept your autism diagnosis?
answer: Everyone brings their own constellation of thoughts, feelings, biases, etc. to the process of accepting their diagnosis. It's a very personal, individualized experience. I was thrilled to get diagnosed, because after decades of not understanding why I was "different," learning that I have Asperger's answered so many questions for me (and my loved ones). It made me feel coherent instead of a senseless mess of contradictions and quirks. Before my diagnosis, I thought I was a poor excuse for a neurotypical. Afterwards, I realized I'm a damn good Aspie. This outlook helped me embrace my Asperger's and immediately focus on the strengths that come with being on the Spectrum, as opposed to the challenges. That said, I've known a few people — male autistics in particular — who struggled mightily with the idea that they had a condition that is so pervasive across the brain. It made them feel like they had less control over their own thinking, behavior, destinies. I do understand that. A major reason the autism community rejects person-first language is that there's no separating our autism from our identities, the way one can with a physical or mental illness. It's not all of who we are but it's fundamental. That can be intimidating, if you're distressed by the idea that you're not "normal" (whatever that means). If I were to suggest one thing to newly self-discovered or diagnosed autistics, it would be that all knowledge is power, but self-knowledge can be a superpower. You've just been handed a very valuable key to who you are, in some ways a more profound insight than many neurotypicals will ever have about themselves. How you choose to frame your autism is going to decide your future far more than your autism itself.
comment_answer: When 1st tested way late in life and found out I was autistic would not except it seemed like a low blow.

question: Is there anything I should do after my autism diagnosis?
answer: Method 1 of 4:Understanding Autism 1. Forget everything that you thought you knew about autism.Television, books, documentaries, and other media rarely depict autistic people correctly. Even so, autistic people vary widely. Each person is impacted, gifted, or impaired by being autistic in a unique way. If you've met one person on the autism spectrum, you've met just one person on the autism spectrum. There are a lot of very negative stereotypes about autism, which can be scary, especially to people who don't understand autism well. Remember that lots of the things you have heard are worst-case scenarios, things that can be helped and improved over time, or blatant lies. Stay away from Autism Speaks and other groups that use scare tactics as a fundraising technique. They tend to exaggerate the negatives and often don't have your best interests at heart. 2. Now that you know nothing about autism, research it.Read books and articles written by autistic people. Learn about what makes them different, what misconceptions people have, and what therapies are helpful. Autistic people can paint accurate pictures of what life is like for them. Look for autism-friendly communities online. Remember, autistic people are a very diverse group (just like non-autistics). You will read from people with a variety of abilities, needs, and traits. Don't only read from non-autistic people's descriptions of autism. Go directly to the source. Focus on things written by autistics, and use things written by loved ones and professionals as supplementary material. (Emma's Hope Book has a list of blogs and books written by autistic people, which is a good starting point.) Try starting with wikiHow's autism articles. 3. Stay away from negativity.There are some toxic anti-autism groups that paint autism as a defect or a demon, and say horrible things about autistic people. This isn't kind, and isn't true of you or your loved one. Avoid the traps of pity or blame, and walk away from anything that treats autistic people like they are inferior. There's a growing community of people who believe that autism is a form of diversity—not a disorder. 4. Keep in mind that autistic people can be successful.Autistic people write novels, run organizations, create art, compose music, become athletes, and make contributions to science and mathematics. Being autistic does not mean being incapable, and many autistic people are able to make positive contributions to the world. Many autistic people can, now or someday... Learn many new skills they don't have yet Develop career skills Live partially or completely independently Make friends Enjoy hobbies and passions Find a lifestyle and routine that suits them Lead happy lives, even if they can't do all or any of the above things 5. Keep in mind that every autistic person is unique.Autistic people, as a group, are extremely diverse. One family's story may look dramatically different from another's. No two autistic people are alike in terms of abilities, needs, or personality. It's great to learn from a diverse group of people, without assuming that your or your family's future will be exactly like one source. What is helpful for one person may be unhelpful for another. What's true about one autistic person may be untrue about another. There is no one-size-fits-all way to help yourself or a loved one. You just need to try things, use common sense, and figure out what works. Around 1 in 59 people are autistic. Thus, you've probably met quite a few autistic people, without necessarily knowing it. They were all probably very different from each other, too. Method 2 of 4:Adjusting Your Attitude 1. Give yourself time to process.Especially if the diagnosis came as a surprise to you, it may take you a while to sort out your feelings. Don't expect to understand everything right away, or to know how to react right now. You're allowed to be confused. Give yourself time and space to work through your feelings. After a diagnosis, people may feel... Relieved to finally have an answer Scared due to lack of knowledge, lack of support, or negative stereotypes Sad because some past goals may be unrealistic Happy to let go of self-blame, because autism is no one's fault Excited by the possibility of finally getting support Worried about the future Confused about what this means A mix of some or all of these 2. Avoid making or believing scary predictions about the future.Stereotypes and misunderstandings abound. If you or your loved one is deemed "low-functioning," you may be told that a dim future is certain. That's just not true. Nobody knows what the future holds, and many good things could happen. Autistic people usually are late bloomers. They'll keep learning and growing throughout life. They may start making big strides, especially once they are given proper means of communication, put in a comfortable environment, and surrounded by people who presume their competence. Even professionals may jump to worst-case scenarios. Take their words with a grain of salt. Scammers tend to target frightened people (especially parents) and say "use my treatment or your loved one is doomed." That isn't realistic. Don't make fear-based decisions, and stay far away from any "treatment" that seems cruel or isn't scientifically validated. 3. Take autism-related challenges seriously.People will misunderstand. Things other people find simple might be terribly difficult for you or your loved one. Your life won't be like the picture-perfect "inspirational" photos of disabled people doing exceptional things. Sometimes, it's difficult to be autistic. It is okay to feel confused or unhappy about the diagnosis, and to recognize that disability makes life harder in some ways. You or your loved one is not suddenly a new or different person because of a diagnosis; autism is thought to be inborn. An autism diagnosis does not change who someone is; the person was always autistic. A diagnosis just clarifies things, explaining quirks and offering ideas on how to meet a person's needs. 4. Appreciate the strengths that accompany autism.Autism isn't 100% negative. An autistic person will also enjoy certain strengths that can improve their lives. It's important to appreciate and build upon these strengths. An autistic person will likely experience many or all of these: Intense, passionate interests Out-of-the-box thinking A strong desire to help others Systems thinking Observational skills A strong sense of morality Kindness towards people who are different 5. AcceptNeurological differences don't make you or your loved one any less of a person. They don't change a person's strength, skill, dedication, or compassion. People can be wonderful and autistic at the same time. Acceptance is a process. It'll take effort and practice to adjust your expectations and remember not to stress too much over the little things. Autism acceptance is correlated with less stress in autistic people and their parents. Method 3 of 4:Reaching Out 1. Talk to supportive people in your life.You may be experiencing a lot of different emotions, and it's normal to be confused or overwhelmed, especially if you're not very familiar with autism. Talk to a good listener about what you are going through. If you're talking about a loved one, be mindful of whether the person is within earshot. You don't want to confess your darkest feelings only for the autistic person in the next room to hear everything. Try leaving the house to talk in private. 2. Make autistic friends.Autistic friends, along with being cool and fun-loving people in general, are crucial to your coping skills. You can find them in person, through autism advocacy groups, or autistic spaces online. Here are a few ways in which autistic friends are helpful. Autistic people find it easier to communicate with each other than with non-autistics. It's nice to have like-minded friends. Autistic people have firsthand experience with what works and what doesn't. If you don't know what's going wrong, they may have some good insights. Tackling difficulties in a neurotypical world feels a lot less overwhelming when you have someone else who knows what it's like. With all the negative discourse on autism, it's easy to forget this. There's no judgment. 3. Check out the autistic community online.The autistic community is a welcoming place that provides a positive space to discuss autism. Many autistic people congregate under the hashtags #askanautistic and #actuallyautistic (since ableist family members have mostly taken over the autism tag). If you're having a rough day or are feeling down about autism-related problems, go to the autistic community. They write many things that help. Consider getting involved in advocacy groups. Some autistic and other disabled people dedicate their time to fighting stigma and shame. Find a group that is run partially or completely by autistic people. Non-autistics are welcome to ask questions under #askanautistic, and read from #actuallyautistic (although it is rude to post in it if you are not actually autistic). 4. Consider counseling if you're struggling to cope.If you're doing your best but you still can't manage what's going on, or you're dealing with a lot of negative people and you are struggling to handle it, you might need a little extra guidance. Look for someone who is understanding, and autism-friendly. If you are feeling a lot of negativity about a loved one's diagnosis, and you think that your struggles might be affecting your loved one, get help now. You owe it to both yourself and your loved one. Sadly, not all counselors are understanding about autism. Some buy into the pity narrative and act like families are victims of the autistic person. Stay away from any counselor who treats you or your loved one like a burden. Method 4 of 4:Handling a Family Member's Diagnosis 1. Take a deep breath.It's natural to be worried, confused, and uncertain. A diagnosis is big news. Keep in mind that many negative things you have heard about autism are only one piece of the picture, and big groups tend to use scare tactics to raise money. It may be difficult at times, but it's going to be okay. Your child can have a happy life. Autistic children, while different, are still children who have their own gifts and skills. These will become clearer and clearer as they grow up. Your child has a lot to offer. Remember that most of the bad things you have heard about autism are negative stereotypes. These have carried over from past negative perceptions, when autistic people were institutionalized, tortured, bullied, and treated very terribly. While some of this continues, society come a long way, and knowledge and understanding have greatly improved the lives of autistic people. 2. Find a few resources for parents and caregivers of newly-diagnosed autistic kids.Much has been written about adjusting to the news and making the first steps afterwards. Welcome to Holland and Fido's New Kitten are two short pieces for parents about unexpected diagnoses. Read them both. Multiple people and organizations have put together resource lists for parents of newly-diagnosed kids. Try starting with The Thinking Person's Guide to Autism's "13 Necessary Next Steps for Parents" or Miss Luna Rose's Autism Resource List. 3. Keep in mind that your loved one can see your reaction.If you act like the diagnosis is the end of the world, they will see this and blame themselves. Save your most vulnerable moments for when your loved one is not around, and make it clear to them that you love and appreciate them (autism and all). Don't pass a negative view of autism onto your loved one. Autistic people with more accepting environments tend to have better mental health outcomes. A caregiver's job is to help them be their best. That means you need to learn how to get past emotional hang-ups, readjust your expectations, educate yourself on autism, and advocate for your child. 4. Support your loved one.They may be feeling lost and confused too, and a little extra support will help them understand that your love for them hasn't changed. How you decide to do so will depend on the person: hugging them, telling them how much you love them, talking about their special interests together, enjoying quality time, or something else. 5. Seek and accept help.Parenting is an exhausting job already, and it can be especially difficult when you are trying to find resources for a disabled child. You don't need to do this alone. Find appropriate resources as early as possible, to help your child learn how to communicate well and have a fulfilling life. Having supports in the community will greatly enhance your child's capabilities, as well as your own well-being and happiness. Look for therapies that will increase your child's coping abilities, and give them new skills. Avoid compliance-based therapies and fad "treatments," as these can harm your child. Don't forget your own needs! See if there's a support group for parents that you can join, or a group that provides parenting advice catering to special needs. Your mental and emotional health are important both to your child and to yourself. 6. Choose support groups mindfully.Some support groups seek to help loved ones of autistic people and teach them about autism. Yet others are toxic communities full of complaining, negativity, and blame. Stay away from groups that might encourage a downward spiral, and find something with a positive focus. Here are a few things to consider: Do autistic adults (such as autistic parents of autistic kids) attend? Do they seem happy and comfortable to be here? Do group members routinely blame and shame themselves or their loved ones? Are group members interested in helping their kids, or do they just want to play the victim? Do conspiracy theories about vaccines, modern medicine, or other things get passed around? Is the focus on fighting autism, or do they make peace with autism while seeking to help? Do they hate autism? Would you be okay with people talking about non-autistic children this way? 7. Talk to autistic adults for advice and support.Along with being good friends, autistic adults can help you imagine what an autistic child's future could look like. They will also help your child's self-esteem by showing that autistic adults exist and are good people. They may also be able to offer insights into autism that no non-autistic therapist could. 8. Accept that your loved one is going to be different.They may flap their hands in grocery stores. They may use sign language instead of speaking. They may speak in an idiosyncratic way, and you might have to try harder to understand them. However, this does not mean that they will be incapable of loving you, finding fulfillment, and making a meaningful contribution to the world. Recognize that "different" is no lesser than "normal", and that it's okay if your loved one is unique. Autistic people who don't hide their autistic traits have better mental health. 9. about autism.Teach your loved one Explain how autism makes some things harder for them and tell them about the positive aspects of autism too. Look for books written by and about autistic people. If your loved one feels positively about autism, this is a sign of healthy self-esteem. Tell a child that they're autistic before they enter school. Autistic kids may figure out quickly that they're different. If you tell them about it first, you can set the tone and help them understand that there's nothing "wrong" with them. Since accurate and accepting media about autism is hard to find, you can also point out characters who seem to display some characteristics (without an official diagnosis). For example, "Do you see how she loves computers and asks her friends to understand how others are feeling? I think she's kind of autistic, just like you!" Say this with a positive tone of voice, so your child knows that it's okay to be autistic. A few autistic role models (official or not) may greatly improve your child's self-esteem. Older kids, teens, and adults may benefit from reading articles on autism. You can direct them towards wikiHow articles such as How to Accept Your Autism or towards the autistic community online. 10. Work together with your loved one to make their life easier.Talk with them about which things are hard for them and why. Brainstorm solutions together. Let them be an active participant in the process, not the object of a project. You can work together to make life better. Brainstorm coping strategies together. 11. Give yourself and your loved one a break.You do not need to put them through 40 hours of therapy per week. You don't need to spend every minute hovering over them or micromanaging what they do. No one will die if they meet a few milestones late. Autistic people need time to relax, do things they enjoy, and have fun without an adult giving them directions. Give yourself time to rest, relax, and stop obsessing over developmental timelines and "should"s and "shouldn't"s. It isn't good for your child, and it certainly isn't good for you. You don't need to hover. It's okay to sit quietly or do a chore in the next room while your loved one lines up objects nearby. It's okay to let them watch a little parent-approved TV. Enjoy quality time that isn't focused on a lesson. Be willing to just explore, chat, hang out, and have fun. Take a break if you're overwhelmed. Behave the way you'd want your loved one to do: Say you need a break, step out, breathe deeply, and do a relaxation exercise or two. Don't try to meet unrealistic expectations. It's normal for autistic kids not to meet their milestones at the average times. Some milestones might come early, and some might come late. Throw out the standardized calendar, and instead focus on what the child can do, and on what they are ready to learn to do. Don't worry about what the next-door neighbor's kid is doing. 12. Learn about best practices for raising an autistic child.If your loved one is still a kid, then now is a good time to start learning about the best parenting techniques for autistic kids. In general, autistic children do best in a structured, empathetic, and gentle environment. Tailor your parenting style to their unique needs. You won't always be a perfect caregiver, but showing that you care goes a long way. Reduce stress for your child as much as possible. Create a stable routine. Predictability can reduce anxiety. Presume competence. Assume that they're capable and focus on letting their abilities shine. Listen carefully to them. Autistic brains work differently, so if you're non-autistic, you'll have to try harder to understand. Making the effort is important. Focus on empathy, not control. If they're behaving imperfectly, try to figure out what's bothering or stopping them, instead of trying to make them behave. Focus on positive feedback for positive discipline. Be forgiving. When they make a mistake, talk to them about how to handle it (now or next time). Encourage them to express wants and needs, from "I'm scared" to "I need a break" to "I want to do this more often with you." 13. Put your loved one's happiness first.It doesn't matter if your child spins in public. It doesn't matter if your child doesn't talk. It does not matter if your child has a ridiculously focused interest in bridges. What makes us human isn't just what's "normal". It's our kindness and love that matters most of all.

question: What are the biggest benefits in getting an autism diagnosis?
answer: I haven’t read any other responses, but I’m sure the first thing everyone will mention is getting assistance. One that others might not mention was oddly presented to us by our school as an argument AGAINST getting an official diagnosis: they would not be eligible for military service. When that argument was presented to my wife and I at an IEP we looked at each other like we could not believe this woman thought we should actually avoid an autism lable so that our children could later serve in the armed services. Don’t get me wrong, I’m a vet, but what was she thinking? Getting assistance depends a great deal on in which state you reside. Florida is among the worst. We’ve been on the MedWaiver wait list for over eight years now, and even recently got a letter in the mail from the state agency saying that we were going to be dropped from the list because they could not contact us. Yet there was that letter. They claimed they’d tried to call (believable since we screen our calls and they can’t legally leave messages), sent mail (we got THAT mail!) and even attempted to contact us in person at home (there’s ALWAYS somebody here at home). Calling them back only gets voice mail and unreturned calls. All this is with an official diagnosis. Imagine trying to get help without one. On the bright side, we were able to get medical coverage because of the diagnosis, which allowed for several non-autism related surgeries that we could never have otherwise afforded, plus mental health care and dental care, including braces. Technically, you’d be able to apply for social security benefits, but they are very difficult to get, even with the diagnosis. Your child/children will need to learn to interact with society and again, that likely will not be available to you without the diagnosis. The bottom line for me is that there is no downside to getting a diagnosis. Your child is exactly the same child he/she was before the diagnosis (or “label” as the school system wanted to say). Nothing negative has ever happened as a result of our getting our children’s diagnoses. If you live in a state that is autism-friendly, and a little research will tell you which states are the best, then do not hesitate. I’ve heard of families moving to autism-friendly states JUST for the benefits and services available.
comment_answer: I have been battling for my son for years here in the UK and it is very similar here. It depends where you live, what resources your child's school has, etc. It shouldn't be like that but with such a lack of funding in social care across the board, no-one wants you to get a diagnosis in their back-yard in case it costs them money!

question: As an adult, is it worth getting an autism diagnosis?
answer: I can only speak for myself. I was diagnosed at age 61. It explained my entire life. It explained why I couldn't make friends. It explained 90% of my arguments with my NT wife. The diagnosis was a godsend for me. I am an attorney and self employed so I didn't have to worry about what my boss thinks because I don’t have one. I am in a unique position to educate attorneys and Judges about autism. I have done so. My purpose in life from a career perspective is to remove the stigma from any type of mental health diagnosis. Attorneys have come to me privately to tell my what their mental health issue is. The stigma must end! ##autismnonstigma By the way, I am now making friends, something that was very difficult before my diagnosis. My self esteem is sky high. The NTs that kept telling me to change to “fit in” have been silenced. For me, the diagnosis was invaluable. I just wish that folks that are in denial that they are autisic be tested so they can know. The American with Disabilities Act helps you. You are not rude, wierd, obnoxious, or “social moron”. You are just NOT NT, you are autisic. (NT = neuro-typical).
comment_answer: Thank you for sharing this, you have no idea how uplifting this was for me to read

question: Why do adults need an easier path to autism diagnosis?
answer: I was on the fence about seeking diagnosis until my GP looked at me one day and asked if I was autistic, said he would give me a referral to get evaluated. Okay, I figured, with my GP making the suggestion, and referring me to a psych he knew, I’d have an easier time than if I just showed up on my own. Why not give it a shot and see how it went. First road block was the psychiatrist. He wouldn’t even discuss whether or not I might have autism until I’d given him a reason why a diagnosis would benefit me. Now, it is perfectly valid for a shrink to say, ‘look, if insurance doesn’t pay for it, this assessment is going to be expensive. I understand you think you have autism, but maybe do a cost benefit analysis first okay?’ What is not valid is to refuse to discuss symptoms, experiences, needs, or problems (which might, ya know, give him a basis for evaluating how a diagnosis might help me himself. He might even, as a professional in the field, know resources I don’t know that might help me. What a thought!) The ironic thing is if that had been one of my bad functioning days, I wouldn’t have been able to come up with an answer that would satisfy and never would have even been able to explain why i thought I was autistic. Okay, so psychiatrist signed off on it and sent me to psychologist for assessment. First session, the psychologist is leafing through a stack of paper and says she isn’t quite sure how to go about this, she’s used to assessing children, and I don’t have any teachers or parents she can send the evaluation paperwork to. We muddled through, my caseworker was willing to fill out the papers as was (unsurprisingly) my nesting partner. I probably could have asked my neighbor and a few other people as well. But let’s cover the high points here: Even with a recommendation from my GP, who he had worked with before, the psychiatrist tried to play gatekeeper and could have kept me from getting evaluated. The psychologist didn’t have a plan for how to evaluate an adult presenting with symptoms of autism. She had no assessments available to her which were intended and designed to be used for adult patients.I had insurance that paid for the eval and a recommendation by a GP. And I’m still lucky I managed to get the diagnosis. Why do adults need an easier path to diagnosis? question: How can I get an ASD or autism diagnosis?

question: Is an autism diagnosis subjective or objective?
answer: It’s pretty objective, but no two autistic people are the same. To help this make sense, let me explain. The autism spectrum isn’t linear, you don’t have “normal” on one end and “profoundly autistic” on the other. Rather, the diagnosis is very specific. You either are autistic, or you’re not. But the reason autism is a spectrum disorder is because each individual is unique, the way their autism presents is unique, and thus, their support needs will differ. As the saying goes, if you know one autistic person, then you’ve met one autistic person. Add on top of this, most people don’t even know what autism even is, which I think is the reason people are saying in other answers that it’s subjective. It isn’t. Autism is a specific diagnosis. It is a specific thing. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disability that affects social communication, restricted interests, and repetitive behavior. By social communication issues, I really mean the person is socially awkward, they don’t understand social cues, they’re often misunderstood when they communicate, because they have a strange way of interacting with people, like their tone of voice seemingly doesn’t match what they say, they might have a flat affect or “resting bitch face,” or their body language might not match how they feel, and they tend to come off a bit too logical and literal minded when it comes to communication. Social issues are the core of autism, so much so, that the DSM-5 says that a person must meet all of the Criterion A symptoms, all of which are the social issues, as part of the official diagnosis. Don’t confuse this with a person who’s introverted, introverted people don’t have the same issues with social communication that us autistic people do. By restricted interests I mean inflexibility of behavior, extreme difficulty coping with change, being overly focused on niche subjects to the exclusion of others, expecting others to be equally interested in those subjects, and difficulty tolerating changes in routine and new experiences. This covers our love of rules and routines, and our inflexible and rigid thinking patterns. We do the same thing every day, we eat the same food every day, we take the same routes every day, and when those are disrupted, we don’t handle it well. It also covers what we like to call special interests, which are subjects or interests that are perseverative, that is our focus on that subject is extreme, like a laser. We think about these all the time, we want to talk about them all the time, and we foolishly think others share the same level of interest in that niche subject. In fact, this type of laser-like focus on a niche subject can leave us with an uneven skill set. And finally, by repetitive behavior, I mean sensory hypersensitivity, stereotypical movements such as hand flapping, rocking, spinning, and arranging things in a very particular manner. This covers our sensory issues. We’re either extremely sensitive to sensory stimuli, or we’re not as sensitive as a normal person, there’s no happy middle ground, though, the former is usually more common. This also covers all manners of stimming behavior. Now, stimming behaviors are repetitive motor movements that we do, and everyone does them, just for us autistic people, they’re notable enough to be odd or quirky. The classic ones are hand-flapping, finger flicking, rocking back and forth, but it could be anything. Stimming actually regulates us and prevents us from getting too overwhelmed by the environment and situation. Some of us we can’t hide it well, and others, like myself, are subtle in how it presents, but if you observe us long enough, you’ll see it. And finally, this covers how we like to arrange things in a very particular way that makes perfect sense for us, but makes no sense to anyone else. A classic way I like to tell people is think of Sherlock Holmes in the Sherlock Holmes movie with Robert Downey Jr.These are covered under the Criterion B symptoms, and the DSM-5 states that you must have two in addition to the social issues mentioned earlier. Finally, for these to be considered symptoms, they have to be actual problems. They get in the way of normal life, and they impair the person in a very real way. For example, I can’t enter grocery stories unless I have my noise-cancelling headphones and a fidget toy in my pocket to stim with. Otherwise, I get sensory overload. Now, when it comes to actual diagnosis, that’s determined by an experienced clinician who understands autism, and they use a lot of screening tests. Tests for autism are more like a weighted score, where if we assume 100 questions, and 10, maybe 20 things apply to you, you might not have autism. However, if 60 or 70 of them apply to you, then there’s strong evidence for autism. The most popular screening tests for autism are:The AQ Test. This is a simple screening for autism. It’s 50 questions, and the threshold score is 26, meaning if you score 26 or above, there’s some evidence that you might be autistic. A higher score means you might be, lower scores mean you might not be. As a reference, most autistic people, around 80% of them, score around 32 or higher, and neurotypical people score around 16. I myself scored 40 on the AQ Test. Anything above a 32 is significant for this test.The CAT-Q Test. This is a test for if you mask your autistic traits or camouflage them. A high score here can explain why you score lower on other tests, because you’re actually masking your autistic traits. It has 25 questions, and it has a scoring range of 25–175, with the threshold being 100, meaning if you score above 100, this means you camouflage or mask your autism. As a reference, autistic people score around 109.64 for males, and 124.35 for females, with non-binary autistic people scoring around 122. Neurotypical people tend to score between 90–96. I myself scored 134. Meaning I mask my autism, and I mask in social situations. The hard part is unlearning the masking process, because I just found out I was autistic as an adult, so I have a whole life of masking my autism to unlearn, and replace with more healthy and productive things.The RBQ-2A. This is a test for restricted and repetitive interests and behaviors. There’s 20 questions, the scoring range is between 20–60, with the threshold being 26. Meaning, if you score 26 or higher, you definitely have restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior, and restricted and repetitive interests. As a reference, most autistic people score around 36, and neurotypical people score around 25 on average. I myself, scored 50, which means I have quite a lot of restricted and repetitive interests and behaviors.The Aspie Quiz. This one is a little different than the others as it doesn’t just measure for autism, but other things too like ADHD or OCD. The Aspie Quiz doesn’t just measure whether you have autism, it also measures how typical you are, and screens outliers, people that maybe have escaped a diagnosis. It measures atypical vs. typical talent, atypical vs. typical perception, atypical vs. typical communication, atypical vs. typical relationships, and atypical vs. typical sociability. In other words, it outputs a neurodiverse and neurotypical score and compares them, leading to you being neurodivergent, neurotypical, or mixed. It has 119 questions, measured 0–200, and it gives you a specific percentage, and there’s four control questions to ensure you answer consistently and honestly. Higher scores and percentages indicates a higher probability that you are neurodivergent. I can’t give you direct results that most autistic people get with the Aspie Quiz, I can say that a score of 140 results in a 100% chance that you’re neurodivergent, a score of 100 indicates a 50% chance that you’re neurodivergent, and a score of 95 indicates a 63% probability that you’re normal. I myself, just to give reference, scored 117 of 200, indicating an 87% chance that I’m neurodivergent. Which, if you read my answers on autism or ADHD, that shouldn’t be shocking, as I’m diagnosed with both.In other words, I am autistic. That was figured out from my AQ and CAT-Q results from the psychologist who tested me, and the other two I took out of interest, and it just seemed to reaffirm my diagnosis, just, a little more specifically. Funny part is, he was testing for my ADHD, and the possibility of me being autistic just sort of… came up during the screenings for ADHD, leading to him screening for autism too. Now I think the reason people might be saying it’s subjective is because of the confusion that autism is a spectrum disorder by definition. They confuse that to mean that the diagnosis itself is subjective, not the fact that no two autistic people are going to be alike. They’ll differ in their support needs and symptoms. So, really, autism is a specific diagnosis. It has an objective definition. You’re either autistic or you’re not. However, because everyone is unique, no two autistic people are alike. The way their symptoms present is different, their support needs will differ, and that’s why autism is a spectrum. I hope this helps!Originally answered: Is an autism diagnosis subjective or objective?

question: Can a toddler outgrow autism diagnosis?
answer: An autism diagnosis? Yes. Which in that case would mean it was a misdiagnosis. But autism itself a person cannot outgrow. It’s a neurodevelopmental disorder, which means the brains have developed differently. That doesn’t change during life. Autism does not improve during life, it doesn’t go away, but it also doesn’t get worse. How a person deals with his or her autism can obviously change during life and in most cases that means the autism affects a person less and less as they grow older because they learn how to live with autism and because they learn about the neurotypical (non-autistic) world around them. That being said: a lot of people on the autism spectrum run into trouble in their 30s somewhere. Often because at that point they finally start figuring out how the world works and realise all the things they’ve missed before that point. That can lead to some serious depressions, existential crises, panic attacks, you name it. It’s some form of (early) mid-life crisis, just worse. And it can be prevented when taking good care of yourself where it also helps a LOT of people close to the person with autism keep an eye out and offer support when needed.

I still feel I am a good dad and a good life partner for my wonderful wife. I am just being very open that “mental health” is a process not a goal and getting a diagnosis can be freeing … and very confusing. I was only assessed a year ago, so I’m still processing and adapting. I am *grateful* to know I am autistic. In that sense my mental health is *much* better in that I’m finally able to stop asking “Why do I always feel not normal?” “Because I am autistic.” Knowing *why* I’m Different is *huge* and well worth the “extra” mental health struggles I am going through as I learn how to embrace my autism and work with it … not against it.

question: Has receiving an autism diagnosis in adulthood improved your mental health?
answer: For any autist such as myself, suffering with co-morbid conditions such as anxiety and depression, this is the million dollar question. The answer is an unqualified yes. Autism has given me a framework with which to understand myself better than I ever have before. With the help of a sensitive therapist I have been able to unpick the threads of my existence and expose those that are discoloured or worn. I used to think, for example, that I was uncomfortable in my own skin, that underneath the mask I wear in public, I was a broken eight-year-old boy, traumatised by events outside of my control, and always confused by other people and situations I found inexplicable and often downright surreal. But with a combination of therapy, reading, my own hard work, and a lot of very close analysis, I have realised that a great many of my issues are caused not by outside events or other people, but by myself, by the thoughts, ideas and beliefs I hold about myself and my world. I'll give you an example of my thinking… “In reality, I am a broken little boy traumatised by people and events. I carry the scars of that trauma and those scars dictate my future. It is achingly, catastrophically sad that this has happened to me, and I will NEVER get over it. I will ALWAYS be BROKEN.” This kind of thinking causes my depression and maintains my anxiety. So I challenged it. I challenged it intellectually first, examining the truth content of the statements, and then I challenged it emotionally. I challenged it deep down inside myself where it really counts, where I can really begin to believe it, all the while testing reality as I went along. It isn't easy. It's not simply a question of reframing it and your new beliefs just falling into place with instant emotional change. You have to work at it, constantly challenging yourself, which involves being mindful of your thoughts, and quick to notice when things change. It is often the feeling first: anxiety kicks in. Why? What was I thinking just then? Track back, work out what image, word, statement, thought led to this. “I'm USELESS and I'm BOUND to FAIL.” Ah, that's what it was… Practise, practise, practise, until challenging these thoughts becomes second nature, until the thoughts and beliefs you hold have changed and, more importantly, are emotionally grounded. That is the key - emotionally grounded. In other words, you have to trust in the truth of it, and trust is nowhere better developed than in places where the trusted thing WORKS. “Bad things happened to me, things I didn't always understand. It isn't great they happened, but it clearly wasn't the end of the world, and I learned a lot about myself, my ability to cope and be resilient. There is no direct causation between what happened then and what I do now. Now, I am free to do things differently.” And that is what I do - I do things differently. I know autism effects my executive function, so I ask people to give me visual lists instead of verbal. I know I can be prone to sensory overload, so I'm sensitive to my body's needs. I know I don't always understand people, so I ask for patience. I know I need to mask sometimes, to survive in society, so I mask consciously and deliberately. I know that I'm nowhere happier or more comfortable than in my own head, so I take time for myself to be there. In short, I think and behave differently to the way I used to, always sensitive to my needs, which thanks to my diagnosis, I understand so much better. And it works. Believe me, it works. If you put the time in, and practise, if you make your self your special interest, and devote your powers of attention and rational analysis to the workings of your mind, you will make it. This world is full of suffering and misery and sadness. I know this only too well. But it doesn't mean we HAVE TO suffer and be sad. We can be sensitive and compassionate to ourselves, always mindful of how our minds work. If we are, consistently and appropriately, we can achieve great things - and the greatest thing of all is acceptance of ourselves as we are and as we can be.

question: How do you get an autism diagnosis?
answer: To begin with, a point of clarity: autism isn't a diagnosis. You don't diagnose autism. One may make efforts to identify autism, but it is not a diagnostic label on its own. The diagnostic label is Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), which encapsulates the support needs someone might experience because of their autism. Not everyone with autistic neuroarchitecture can, or should, qualify for an ASD diagnosis; those who do not we may sometimes label as ‘clinically subsyndromal'. The process of evaluation for ASD varies significantly based on presentation and potentially with other comorbid factors that may be involved. It is generally a multi-step process involving multiple specialists; generally at a minimum your primary care physician and a mental health specialist. Other specialists may be involved and have their own evaluation methods as well. One can expect, at a minimum, some sort of file review and either an extensive structured interview or observations (dependent on the ability of the individual to participate in the interview process). Interviews with parents, caregivers, educators, and other such individuals is common; for both children and adults being assessed. Formal diagnostic and screening tests are common, though it is not uncommon for the materials to remain in the hands of the mental health professional and to be filled out during the interview process rather than the person being evaluated actually filling out the assessments. For individuals with less (or less obvious) support needs, it isn't uncommon to need to repeat this process more than once; seeking out specialists to reevaluate after initial diagnosis was rejected.

question: Are autism diagnosis accurate?
answer: It depends on what defines accuracy, and perhaps more importantly, who defines accuracy. Mental diagnoses will rarely not reflect one’s behaviours. If you have an autism diagnosis, that is because your behaviour was analysed and dissected by a psychiatrist who aligned your traits with the criteria of autism. The same can be said for any other mental diagnosis; if you have an ADHD diagnosis, then you will likely exhibit the traits associated with ADHD. To that extent, yes; autism diagnoses are generally accurate, so much as they do reflect out behaviours. However, many would say that there is no logic behind the classification of autism as a mental disorder in the first place. After all, if it wasn’t for the fact that the term “autism” was invented only a little over a century ago, we would simply have people who are different, just as there are many traits that can make somebody seem different but not necessarily constitute a diagnostic category. This is to be expected in a society as a result of the natural variations between human minds. So, if that is your philosophy, then in fact all autism diagnoses are inaccurate. This is why it depends on what we mean when we talk about accurate diagnoses. Do they accurately reflect one’s behaviours? Generally, they do. But is it accurate to claim that such behaviours necessitate the creation of a diagnostic criterion? Let’s just say that that is certainly more difficult to justify.
