question: Can you object to an autism diagnosis?
answer: If you don’t feel that an autism diagnosis is warranted for you, or for your child, don’t present yourself for one in the first place. People get diagnosed with autism because they feel that they are not functioning well, so they see a psychiatrist, psychologist, or neurologist, or some other person qualified to make such a diagnosis, and the diagnosis is made— sometimes it is a parent presenting a child, because the child is not progressing developmentally like he or she should be. If you were diagnosed as a child, but you feel that as an adult, you are functioning without the need of any special interventions, completely independently, and the diagnosis was not warranted— maybe you had some other problem that was misdiagnosed, or maybe you were successfully remediated*, and no longer warrant the diagnosis, you can see a doctor, and ask if you would still get the diagnosis if you were presented for the first time now. The answer might be “No,” and then you can consider yourself no longer autistic. It does happen that occasionally therapy is extremely successful, or someone was misdiagnosed, although it is rare. If you are a parent who has a school system telling you that you need to have your child examined, and you don’t want to, you should probably look closely at your reasons. If you think you don’t want your child labeled, your child is going to get labeled no matter what, if he or she is struggling in school, and not fitting in socially. The label may be “weirdo,” “problem child,” “trouble-maker,” or “retard,” but the child’s peers and teachers will label him somehow. It is much better to have a clinical label that correctly describes the situation, than a pejorative label like “weirdo.” If you just aren’t prepared to have a child with autism, consider that nothing changes about your child because you get this label. Your child is the same little girl or boy before and after acquiring this diagnosis. But to answer the question directly: you can object to anything you want, but the truth is the truth. A child will be autistic whether you object or acquiesce. Albeit, getting a second opinion is never a bad idea— but getting a third, fourth and fifth, searching for one doctor who will tell you what you want to hear, in the face of a platoon of doctors who agree on something else, is. However, and this bears repeating, if you are the person in question, part of the definition of autism is how well you function. You can be as quirky as you please, but if it doesn’t interfere with your day-to-day living, then you will very unlikely receive a diagnosis of autism. If lay people, and not professionals, are telling you you should get tested because you seem like an internet article they read, or a character in a movie they saw, you can safely ignore them. *NOTE: “remediated” is not a synonym for “cured,” and that’s not how I’m using it. I’m just saying that one part of the constellation that produces a diagnosis of autism is how well one copes with day-to-day tasks of living. Someone who experiences no distress during an ordinary day may no longer warrant a diagnosis of autism. There are people who may be on the far right of the spectrum where it fades to “neurotypical” who don’t need accommodations, but are still fairly described as “on the spectrum.”

question: Have you, or anyone you know, had to handle a late autism diagnosis?
answer: I was diagnosed with Asperger’s syndrome (now part of autism spectrum disorder) in my mid-fifties. Was it too late to get help? I actually got help in my twenties, long before anyone knew about Asperger’s syndrome except Asperger himself and a few other German-speaking clinicians. But I still needed help with a co-morbid condition (misophonia) in my mid-fifties and such help often needs to be adapted for people on the autism spectrum. So, no, it wasn’t too late for that. And growing up is a lifelong process - at least for me. Why did it take so long? Asperger’s was not officially recognised as a diagnosis until I was about forty years old. I was never going to be diagnosed with it in my teens or twenties - that was back in the late 1960s, the 1970s, and the early 1980s. Asperger’s syndrome first appeared in diagnostic manuals in the early 1990s. Back in those days - the 1960s and 1970s - you did not get psychiatric help unless there was something drastically wrong: a suicide attempt, juvenile delinquency, a “breakdown”. If you were quietly struggling (as I was) you were left to sink or swim. If you could fake normal, people didn’t notice that your coping mechanisms were wearing very thin. So I was one of the “hidden Aspies” - not having big, noticeable meltdowns, not coming to the attention of responsible adults, just not growing up as fast as the world around me … until I couldn’t cope. I burnt out. I was struggling. Do you think it helped? I think it was worth it, because you cannot be yourself when you don’t know who you are. Think of the story of the ugly duckling: as long as it was trying to be a duck it was going to fail. It needed to recognise that it was something different - a swan. Then it could begin living realistically. Aspies don’t need to become (second rate) neurotypicals, we need to become the best Aspies we can be. We cannot do that while we are desperately trying to “fake normal”. When I was in my twenties, I tried to complete a social work degree. I wanted to do something that helped people, but I realised (the hard way) that I was unsuited for working with other people (at least, I was unsuited for working with neurotypical people). Since getting diagnosed I have taken up working with people again - but this time with people on the autism spectrum … my people, so to speak. I discovered that my original motivation was not impossible after all, but I needed the right “other people” to work with. I can work with teenagers on the spectrum. Diagnosis can have its own problems: internalised stigma can hit you unexpectedly; you now need to start learning how to be your autistic self while working out ways of getting along in the non-autistic wider world; and then there is disclosure (Do you tell others? Who? When? How?). Hopefully, though, it will be a step towards being a more realistic version of you. And you shouldn’t stop learning how to be that.

question: How long does it take to get an autism diagnosis?
answer: This would of course depend on the system and the actual procedures. These seem to be quite various around the world and even between different institutions. But where I work, it seems like a year would be a realistic time frame. And most of this is basically waiting time. Our procedure for the diagnostics if pretty extensive in my opinion and I cannot see how much more you could do and also out waiting times are long due to the lack of resources (meaning we don’t have enough people doing the evaluations) so I would assume this time frame of a year would be longer that it usually takes. I’ve heard of cases where they have had the diagnosis on the first visit to the psychiatrist. That’s quick, but I would have some doubts about that diagnosis. I mean it might be correct but it probably would have been a good idea to take some time to really look into it since it’s a permanent diagnosis. In my opinion, allowing a reasonable waiting times, I would expect maybe 6 months from the first contact to the diagnosis. Without waiting times, more like 4 months. For example (this is according to our health care system): First contact with a psychiatric nurse and 4 more visits for evaluation (including blood tests and several psychometric tests). One appointment per week = 5 weeks. Ends with referral to the ADHD-evaluation team. ADHD-evaluation: 4 meetings with a psychologist, 4 meetings with a psych nurse, 4 meetings with an occupational therapist and 2 meetings with a psychiatrists (I picked a random but realistic sounding amounts of meetings, could also be a lot less). One appointment per week = 14 weeks + 5 weeks with the previous nurse = 19 weeks. Just something to give you an idea but could also be different.

question: Why do some autistics go through a period of grief following their autism diagnosis?
answer: I am self-diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (Asperger’s). My journey began in a classroom where I was subbing for the special education aide (Autism Unit). The lightbulb moment was one of the students getting up from their chair, pacing the floor, speaking a language only she could understand, and at times, leaping with excitement. The staff had seen her do it plenty of times and wondered what was going on inside that child's mind. Her behavior was "normal" to me because I did the pacing and make-believing too. I still do. I just do it when I’m least likely to be caught doing it. Although I couldn't know what was going in the student’s mind, if she was like me when I did the pacing and self-talk, she was in her own world with a cast of characters and dialogue unfolding in her mind. This moment was the beginning of my journey to self-diagnosis through research and talking to my doctor and special education teachers and behavior therapists. My immediate reaction was one of relief. A big chunk of the mystery of “myself” had been solved. I still felt like an outsider with my family and peers, but at least, I knew why I did. I recall, though, after it had been about two months, the newness of it was wearing thin and the sinking of it was settling in. It has started hitting me that I was not a tourist on the Spectrum. This diagnosis didn't just drop in and pay me a visit. Instead, it had been with me all my life and it wasn’t going anywhere. For instance, on my job, my companion is constantly raising its head. I'm in the gym subbing for the P.E. aide. The sound of the children trying to raise their voices over another is sensory overload. I need to stim and I find a way to do that without attracting attention. The coach plays music while the kids play the games. The coach remarked I must like Michael Jackson's music because I was swaying and stepping to it. I nodded "yes", but the truth was, I was secretly "stimming". Michael's music just provided me cover. The diagnosis provided the explanation of why I had moments where I felt like a cat with its tail on fire. They are called meltdowns. I didn’t know what caused them for many years. I thought it was just me acting crazy. I wouldn't have known my rocking and pacing was "stimming" and how such is essential during and after meltdowns. Such repetitive behavior is the insulation from a meltdown's cold and cruel wind that sometimes blows in from seemingly out of nowhere. I felt some grief for a time knowing that meltdowns were not only in my past, but in my future too. My diagnosis helped to explain some of why I missed some experiences such as walking down the aisle, hearing someone call me Mom, or getting a valentine card from a grandchild. I have shed some grief over this, but I am better about it now. ASD has given me compensation as it has others with ASD. A special talent of my own - writing. It's something I don't have to struggle with doing as I do with social interaction or any activity heavy on motor skills. The mystery used to be why I was not in step with my peers. Now that I know why I have a different drummer to listen to, I have another mystery. What's it like to live off the Spectrum? To be a neurotypical? I’ll never know since the only exit off the Spectrum is in the life beyond.

question: Are meltdowns and/or shutdowns necessary for an autism diagnosis?
answer: Are meltdowns and/or shutdowns necessary for an autism diagnosis? Neither meltdowns nor shutdowns are explicitly listed among the diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder. They are not required for a diagnosis. However, a diagnosis of ASD is given to people who have experienced “significant impairment” of some kind associated with their autistic characteristics:D. Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning (Diagnostic Criteria | Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) | NCBDDD | CDC)Meltdowns and shutdowns would certainly be evidence of “significant impairment” in the life of someone who had autistic characteristics. But other things — e.g. persistent unemployment, difficulties in forming significant relationships when desired, etc — might also count as significant impairment. So meltdowns and shutdowns count towards a diagnosis, as one type of evidence of “significant impairment”, but they are not requirements for a diagnosis.

question: How long is the process of getting an autism diagnosis?

question: How "sticky" is an autism diagnosis?
answer: I would submit that the diagnosis is secondary to your son's actual ability to acquire skills for functioning independently. That of course is what you really want. These autism-related diagnoses tend not to be very helpful, in my opinion, because they don't identify what is really causing the problem. When you connect with other families working with developmentally disabled kids, you hear their stories about how this or that intervention accomplished wonderful things, which naturally makes you want to explore the same treatments. I explored everything, and absolutely would not discourage you from doing likewise. I also don't want to discourage hope. The trouble is that, despite sharing similar diagnoses and symptoms, kids can have different underlying conditions, which means there is no one universally helpful therapy. My son is 29 and I still have a very poor understanding of his issues. Consequently, my efforts on his behalf succeeded only to a certain point. This is not to suggest that your son will follow a similar trajectory. But based on what we know there's no way to gauge the likelihood of success. All I can suggest is to find resources you trust, learn as much as you can, stay open to new ideas, and stay positive.

question: Has receiving an autism diagnosis in adulthood improved your mental health?
answer: Absolutely yes. I grew up feeling very much that I was like an alien growing up in the human world. I wasn’t like the other kids my age- I was smart, but I wasn’t allowed to be in the gifted programs because of how disorganized I was, so I was bored and unmotivated at school— and yes, I was literally tested into the G&T program in 3rd grade, pulled out of class with three other kids to do enrichment work in the SpEd department, only to have my teacher call and have me sent back to class because my grades weren’t high enough and have to do a walk of shame by myself out of the room and back into my classroom after everyone hearing her make that call. I was 8 years old. Continue for the next 5 years of constantly being told that I wasn’t working hard enough. That I was to smart to have this many bad grades— my test scores proved it! I needed to back up and do what I was told. I was frequently punished for things that weren’t my fault. I remember when my Dad asked me if there was anything I wanted to tell him, already aware that I had been given a progress report and failed to have it signed and returned to school on time. He knew it was because my grades weren’t good since they had already called when. When I told him “no, there isn’t anything that I want to tell you” I wasn’t lying, I had taken his question literally and answered honestly— because I didn’t want him to know that I was failing again and I didn’t want to get punished for it, so I just didn’t do anything about it. I got punished extra for lying to my dad, even though I was and still am incapable of telling a lie without having a meltdown. Things got a little better when I was diagnosed with ADHD and given medication. But I still felt like I was always stumbling through social interactions and I was acutely aware that my “friends” weren’t very close to me but were kids that were in my orbit and too nice to be anything but kind to me. They were good kids, but it was painfully clear to me that they didn’t seek out my companionship on their own. After moving up to middle school I suddenly didn’t see any of my friends outside of school or swim team unless my parents were friends with their parents. So I became even more isolated. And eventually I just accepted that it was my fate to not have any friends that I was truly close to, just people who I was friendly with. I got along better with the adults I knew through my parents and later through my job than I did with youths my own age. When I was 22 I asked my therapist about being assessed for autism but I was told that I couldn’t have both an adhd diagnosis and have autism. It was technically true when this occurred, but the DSM changed the next year. As an adult, social interactions became more difficult. I no longer had a natural peer group. I had almost nothing in common with the people I knew except for sharing a workplace. I didn’t like to go out to clubs, or drink and party. I would rather stay home and read. I was usually the youngest person in the workplace wherever I went even into my mid twenties. I was praised for my knowledge and expertise and quickly raised from menial caregiving work to mid-level worker, and eventually given an upper management and administrative position. And here is where my autism and special interests had launched me into a job because of the technical knowledge I had, but also failed me because I didn’t have the soft skills to do the job of managing employees and selling my company to people. I was lucky enough to have a boss who had seen the things that were beneficial to her as my employer and who was willing to take the time and invest the effort in training me in how to handle people. Because training it certainly was, and people are something I don’t understand. Over the course of years she would literally coach me and help me script interactions with clients and employees until I had a base knowledge big enough that I could come up with the appropriate words and tone well enough, but I still needed to have her approval for me to be able to do any of them. When she was forced to sell the company and I started working for another boss, things started to fall apart. A job I had successfully done with help for over four years, ended in four months. I got a similar job, was quickly promoted, and fired again within 6 months because I couldn’t keep up with the amount of hours I was being required to work between direct care, administrative duties, and sales went to the wayside. And I had my first autistic burnout. I didn’t know it, but had brownouts before, but that was usually remedied by switching jobs. This burnout was epic in comparison. I barely managed to get out of bed for 8 months. I slept 13 hours a day. I got up just to take my dogs outside to potty and feed them and got back in bed. It was hell. My parents convinced me to change careers and enroll in school again. So I needed to go back on my ADHD meds. My doc ended up refusing to prescribe me the meds I was used to getting and referred me in to psychiatry. Fine with me. 7 months later I had my ADHD meds and an autism diagnosis. It took 8 years from the first time I questioned it to actually get the diagnosis, despite being under the care of psychiatrists for most of that time. I still struggle, but knowing why helps a lot. I can now figure out what I am feeling or doing and why. I don’t hold back my stims anymore just because I am a grownup. I am more forgiving with myself when I had bad days because I am more symptomatic. Life is getting better.

question: Are there a lot of people with an autism diagnosis, who probably do not have autism?

What were parents like? Siblings? Family hx. Family Psy Hx. Drugs, alcohol, forensic hx. question: Is it possible to get an autism diagnosis removed or any mental diagnosis removed?
answer: No, it’s not like having a criminal record expunged. We have to keep medical records, fully intact, for periods of time set by regulations, laws, and ethical standards. We also have to keep them private, and there are complicated laws in the USA like HIPAA to make sure we do. The only way to get a diagnosis “removed” is with a new, more recent diagnosis, preferably based on better data and more thorough examination. The evaluation will review past records, and might include a line like this: Mr. Smith was diagnosed with autism (date, place, time, provider given), based one (xyz). It seems that diagnosis was likely incorrect for the following reasons (xys). Mr. Smith shows no such symptoms currently, nor does he meet criteria for any DSM 5 diagnosis at this time. You’re not going to get that old diagnosis removed (though those old records could be legally destroyed at some point, according to established regulations). But getting a new eval that specifically address that old diagnosis is the next best thing.

question: How likely is it to get a false positive asperger or autism diagnosis from a psychiatrist?
answer: That depends on the psychiatrist. To my knowledge, it’s unlikely. Really, it’s more likely that they will be missed for high-functioning autism. With low-functioning autism, a diagnosistic criterion is having an IQ lower than 70 so it’s hard to miss. With high-functioning autism, depending on their experience, they may have worn a mask for so long that they act like a neurotypical. The autistic criteria was originally developed for males so more men than women were diagnosed with autism. It has been getting better but still to this day, women are being diagnosed differently with disorders like ADHD. Part of the autistic diagnosis is typically having someone who knows your history personally, like a parent. The psychiatrist or psychologist will ask questions regarding you in your formative years, since children with autism are quite different than neurotypical children. In this regard, a mask wouldn’t be in effect and there wouldn’t be a need to lie about their autism so it’s unlikely to provide a false positive here. In regards to asking an autistic person questions about themselves, they are unlikely to lie if autistic. Media portrays autism, and to a lesser extent Asperger’s, as a negative disorder, something you don’t want to have as it can be seen as a disability. A neurotypical wouldn’t want to be diagnosed with autism and so wouldn’t say things which would indicate autism. With someone who’s autistic, they’re unlikely to lie as lying isn’t as prevalent in people with autism. Anything they say that indicates autism is likely to be true. The only people who can diagnose you with autism are those who are specicially qualified to and they know a lot about autism so they’re unlikely to give a diagnosis unless they’re really confident. In general, the problem isn’t being diagnosed with autism, it’s not being diagnosed if you have it.

question: Who should I tell about my autism diagnosis?
answer: First start by changing what you say. You have been given a diagnosis of “autism” but that does not define you, describe your strengths or your areas of weakness, make you better or worse than everybody else. You likely would not ask what you should tell about your reading ability or your bath routine or other personal information. The diagnosis does likely suggest you have some difficulty with communication, social interactions and have some obsessive or repetitive behaviours. You could also have numerous other “co-morbid” (co-existing) diagnoses such as ADHD, learning disorder, gifted intellect, strong visual perceptual abilities, musical talent and many other characteristics that make you unique. So, first ask why you would tell and what difference it would make? Then, choose wisely and share only when you are confident the individual knows enough about autism to be understanding and supportive and cares enough about you to protect your privacy. Everyone has their own temperament and personality, as I am sure you do. If you have not established a trusting relationship with someone, you might just let people think it is your personality to be whatever way you are.

question: Is it worth getting a second opinion for autism diagnosis?

question: Is it possible to lose your autism diagnosis as an adult?
answer: No. If you “lose” it, it wasn’t autism from begin on or you discovered a masking/coping strategy that helps you get along with ease. As you can probably guess the first variant is probably the one that is rare, but more frequent, than the latter. The usual way - by my estimate, no data - is that you gather some coping and masking strategies throughout your life, making it easier to pass as a neurotypical. Or, best case, that you find the perfect fit job and relationship wise. From what we know at this point, autism is rooted in bodily development. While scientists do develop some option to try and ease the symptoms through medication and while there might be some “high functioning” people that are passing easily as neurotypical, they will still be autistic. And while for example borderline can “learn” structures and therefore shape their brain into something more neurotypical over the course of decades(!), we havn’t yet found any way to do that with autism.

question: Can someone get an autism diagnosis in their 50s?

question: How do I process my autism diagnosis?

question: Is there a correlation between vaccination rates and autism diagnosis?

question: What are the pros and cons of getting an autism diagnosis as an adult?
answer: The cons: you need to be realistic that getting a diagnosis won’t alter your autism per se, it’s not suddenly cured or becomes milder. People who are biased towards you will continue to do so, they may even now use the diagnosis as a “valid” reason to exclude you. To pros: for yourself, you no longer need to play guessing games that rob you nights of sleep as to why you’re different or why you suddenly get so frustrated and angry when you’re the kindest person of all 99% of the time. You stop thinking that something must be “wrong” with you. You begin to fully accept yourself for who you are and feel more empowered and entitled to make alterations to your life without having to justify yourself or think that you’re just being lazy or not trying hard enough. Your internal blame game comes to an end. For others, those who accept your diagnosis will support you in making adjustments to your life, your place of work, and your environment. They will understand why you cannot cope with certain situations and will constructively look for compromises wherever they can. They will stop telling you what to do (take a short break, go for a walk, see a therapist) and start asking themselves what they can do (make space, allow you to work from home, allow you to work at staggered times, give you more flexibility, understand why you don’t like Xmas parties, understand why you’re awkward in social settings and coffee breaks).

question: Is it hard to get an autism diagnosis as an adult? I was diagnosed 3 months ago and I am trying to come to terms with it.
answer: I can only say how it is for us in the UK, but the first autist specific piece of legislation we got, only came into effect just over ten years ago. What it did was to ensure that local authorities made provisions for adults with suspected autism to be tested as well as offering post-diagnosis support. Before that it was incredibly difficult for adults to gain access to services and receive a diagnosis. Its still not “easy” to get listened to. Doctors are still reluctant to send adults for screening unless they can see that the person in front of them is having real struggles with dealing with potentially autism. I feel that throughout the screening process, one of the biggest questions asked was “if you are autistic how the hell did you reach this age without it being picked up on? “ My answer to that wasnt a simple one, or a single incident that I got away with and evaded capture from. But I had to support how I had managed to fall under the radar whilst living with some severe impairments that very much effect my daily life. All of that was analysed and. I had to give an explanation for it all, throughout school, college and how it affected my work, my interactions, my position in life - truancy, conduct disorder, failures to attend.. How I've managed to have friends when I am socially impaired and missing a big chunk of social perception. My whole life was scrutinised in a way that was absoulutely necessary for them to be able to help me continue wanting to live. I know how dramatic that sounds and it was very difficult to suddenly be very open about something that I've tried my best to hide. Whereas for children, the process involves observations made by school teachers who see your child interact everyday. Children aren't expected to explain if and why they feel different and how exactly… What can make the diagnosis for children much more longwinded is that when there is no family history of autism, no relative who has it, then more often than not professionals will always look at the child's home life and i have known of quite a lot of families who have found that harrowing and its left them feeling like their parenting skills are under question - because they are. Its not necessarily a bad thing that this is the process because autism isn't a light diagnosis, it's not something that just pops up every now then or a maladaptive coping mechanism that's been learnt… for a diagnosis for autism to be given in the UK, there has to proof of impairment and signs of this impairment has been present throughout your life. To get a diagnosis wrong is dangerous. To give a child a label for a neurological condition is a serious matter, it can change their lives. So I'm sorry to be an argumentative git, but it's only just got easier for adults with autism to get access to screening services, a lot of organisations that have sprung up since the 2009 act are still fledgling organisations - the adult autism Centre in my area was literally only established a couple of years ago. So nationally speaking, we probably have a larger backlog of adults waiting for screening than we do children. Well that was until covid struck us down, a lot of these services aren't open right now, they have a skeleton crew running the building and everyone else is working from home. Its easier to see autism in children than it is with adults because we've often been forced to repress who we are to learn camouflaging techniques, ways of masking by using social skills so that we seem to conform to social expectations and children haven't had as much time to learn how to do that. I do recommend reading Thomas's answer - I entirely agree that getting a diagnosis for autism in adulthood means it's sort of like being born again - uncovering who we really are, behind years of trying to confirm and hiding nuances like the need to gently rock when i am in standing position and talking to people. Its just what works for me, I find it easier to talk if I'm stood up and rocking seems to help me concentrate. Sheesh, I used to get told off for doing that when I worked in offices - I was basically told to sit down at my desk and that looking like I am working is more important that attaining results and meeting targets. And now, I am fine with it, people generally don't care and most probably don't notice. But before diagnosis, I was so caught up with trying to hide such little things that are insignificant to other people anyway, but I couldn't accept it myself before I was diagnosed because I didn't understand the function that stimning can play in just helping us to feel calm and more content. So essentially, I think it is easier in some ways to see autism in children because their reactions are authentic and haven't been groomed by society to act in a certain way, stand in a certain way and so on… In order to not stand out as “different. “

question: Are high IQ and autism diagnosis mutually exclusive?
answer: The Distribution of IQ for autistics is about the same as neuro-topicals. We take the same test; we end up on the same bell curve. There are approximately 50% of us that are average, 25% above, and 25% below. There are however differences in how our brains process information. Many of us are very logical thinking making certain occupations easier for us. Computer programming and certain types of local based occupations. I myself worked as quality control for a company. I would visually inspect objects under a microscope. The job was boring, repetitive and I loved it! My brain was designed in a way that made pattern recognition a snap. question: Has anyone regretted obtaining an adult autism diagnosis? I'm thinking of seeking one but bit nervous it might draw unwanted attention to myself.
answer: Sometimes, but the feeling is most often simply unwarranted or just misplaced anxiety. Most of the personal benefit of diagnosis is in KNOWING for certain yourself. If autistic, it can often deeply increase self-awareness and self-acceptance. Over time it leads to far more overall knowledge of why we experience certain feelings, habits, strengths, and weaknesses that others don't. It also explains why we often cannot seem to change certain skills or compulsions in the ways that society allistic people(the human majority) would prefer. There's also a mental social benefit if joining into autistic social media groups. Realizing finally 100% for sure, that we/you are not actually alone! Others ARE out there that ARE so very much like the real unmasked you! Proof of diagnosis is not usually required to join such groups because getting diagnosed is often so terribly difficult in many places. Too many healthcare professionals were trained about autism with badly wrong information, and many have never corrected their misunderstandings. So, self-identified is usually ok in such groups assuming you took the time to really research deeply & confirmed via multiple sources. It might help you with doubts about your resolve to go through a diagnosis if you join social groups sooner. You may find that the others there really do reflect just like your true self. Growing up in allistic modeled society, most of us didn't know there were others like us because most of us were socially “closeted" through childhood intolerance and persecution of our natural traits. The same ways non-heterosexuals were socially closeted by society for centuries, neurologically different and many other invisibly disabled folks have & do still experience many of the same kinds of hate based abuses when not masking their true nature. That knowing we're autistic, and then interacting with other autistic people & “comparing notes”, often leads to FAR better self-care! Until we know, we often aren't usually very good at giving ourselves a break. Being hard on ourselves develops from being raised as if we were allistic, even though we're not. They made us feel defective or wrong because we were born with perception differences and we often treat ourselves like they treated us. We might have had loads of evidence that we are just different, but have only had their doubts shoved down our throat for years. Blatant allistic invalidation of our perception like that occured/occurs daily or nearly daily. The other use for having a diagnosis for now would be to provide “proof” with a specific request for a work or education accommodation or for other public assistance. Those processes don't always go well anyway(in the US) because of huge prejudices even when one has it in writing. It's typically a wise thing to get & have an official diagnosis of ASD, so when proof is needed later it's already done. Many of us can only mask while working so many years before autistic burnout costs us that career. Recovery from autistic burnout just takes too long. Less masked autistics may more easily avoid burnout, but often will find staying employed difficult because of social presumptions, ableism, persecution, and abuse. Human allistic society ableism/intolerance tendencies frequently lead to allistics expressing active disrespect and skepticism instead of accepting diagnosis of the disorder(ASD) - but ironically they CREATE the disorder in the first place! If persecution wasn't so widespread and harsh, and tolerance and acceptance were there instead, identifying autistic neurology wouldn't be a “diagnosis" at all. In the most basic form, autistic is just a natural neurology pattern. Social persecution causes all the ASD criteria symptoms except the (only recently added) presence of physical neural sensitivities.

question: I got my autism diagnosis a few months ago, am I broken and is there something wrong with me?

It only means your nervous system is different and this effects what you can and cannot do in different ways than NTs. How you do things, what you like to do, what you do well… can and often is be different than NTs. Different does not mean “wrong” or “broken”. It means you walk a different path than NTs. But because I kept telling myself… “ I’m broken.. my life was a mistake (wrong)”… instead of using my incredibly deep, strong sense of passion and joy… I did not fully develop my gifts… You may not see them now… you may not understand what your gifts are until you explore your abilities. I created a T-shirt for a group of kids going to camp that said “ You only reach your limits, when you limit your reach”. Life is a journey of self-exploration and growth. Using your gifts to do good in this world… You will find that being autistic only means “broken and wrong” if you are now saying “because I’m autistic there is nothing I can do or do right. It is called “making a self-fulfilled prophy”: Quitting before you even try. Saying you cannot, then doing ever thing you can to prove yourself right. That is what I did and want you to see before you do it to yourself. I also want add, I know there can be very difficult challenges being autistic. This is true too, for NTs… Some have very difficult lives. If this is the path you have been given. Do your best. Know your limits But don’t define yourself by comparing these limits with the limitations of others - even those who are autistic. You will do well… believe it.. make it so…

question: Can a person's autism symptoms worsen after receiving an autism diagnosis?
answer: It may be that they are no longer keeping up the facade they felt they had to before their diagnosis, or it may be imitation. Folks on the spectrum often imitate those around them, as a way to solidify an identity. My spouse, who absolutely refused to wear sunglasses and let himself get repeatedly severely sunburned on his outdoor job for decades, started wearing sunglasses in the house after he read about light sensitivity in ASD persons, post diagnosis. He developed a lisp after working with a co-worker with one, and collected and pretended to love to read books to impresses a former girlfriend. Spouses in my support groups report similar things. We all fear them becoming friends with a terrible person, for the traits they may pick up. This is likely why high functioning autistic people are often excellent actors. They thrive with the attention, and easily imagine themselves in other roles and personas. It is natural to want to do lots of research on a diagnosis you've received, and that may provide fodder for imprinting.

question: How can you tell if an autism diagnosis was wrong?

My personal diagnosis remained in doubt until an EEG scan showed a clear picture of someone with an autistic perspective that isn’t standard for ADHD, OCD, or depression (though I had all of those too). Autism more than some other diagnosis is neurological hardcode that results in behavioral issues. It is rather rare for someone to “grow into” autism, or it developing as a result of something happening to them. Alas while technology is improving all the time, most tests still strictly focus on measuring the behavior so errors can be made. question: What happens during an adult autism diagnosis assessment?
answer: What Happens During an Adult Autism Diagnosis Assessment? Getting an autism assessment as an adult can be a detailed process, as symptoms may be masked or misunderstood. The evaluation is typically conducted by a clinical psychologist, psychiatrist, or neurodevelopmental specialist and involves multiple steps: 1. Initial Consultation & History-TakingThe psychologist will ask about your developmental history, including childhood behavior, social interactions, and any past diagnoses.If possible, input from parents or close family members is helpful.You will discuss current challenges in areas such as social communication, routines, sensory sensitivities, and emotional regulation.2. Standardized Autism Screening & Questionnaires You may be asked to complete tests such as: ✔ Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) Test – Measures autistic traits. ✔ Cambridge Behaviour Scale – Assesses empathy and social cognition. ✔ Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS-2) – Evaluates social skills. ✔ RAADS-R (Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale) – Identifies autism in adults. 3. In-Depth Behavioral Observations & InterviewsThe psychologist may assess how you respond to social cues, eye contact, conversation, and emotional expression.They might ask about special interests, sensory sensitivities, or repetitive behaviors.Common questions include: Do you find social situations exhausting? Do you have strong preferences for routines? Do you struggle with understanding sarcasm or body language?4. Ruling Out Other Conditions Autism symptoms can overlap with ADHD, anxiety, OCD, and personality disorders. A thorough assessment ensures the right diagnosis. 5. Diagnosis & Discussion of Next StepsIf autism is confirmed, the psychologist will explain how it affects you.They may suggest therapy, coping strategies, workplace accommodations, or support groups.Many adults find relief and clarity after a diagnosis, as it helps them understand lifelong challenges.

question: How long did it take to receive an autism diagnosis as an adult?

My mom and I went to the appointment. The specialist told me that it normally takes her 1–2 hours of interviewing to determine if someone has Asperger’s. After about 20 minutes of interviews, she said that I had the the most textbook, classic, severe case of Asperger’s she had ever seen. Nonetheless, I got rejected for SSD because I did not have enough work credits. In October of 2018, I re-filed for SSD, with my mom as representative payee. Again, I got a letter from the Department of Social Security saying that had an appointment with a Disability Determinations Specialist (different specialist this time), for January 11, 2019. My mom and I went to the appointment. After about 45 minutes, the specialist said that I was definitely on the spectrum. This time around I won my disability case (and without having to go through the courts I might add). The things is this: The specialist I saw recently told me that half of those who would’ve qualified as Asperger’s years ago no longer qualify. In addition to eliminating/lumping the autism subsets together and replacing them with “Autism on a Severity Scale” or “Autism Spectrum Disorder level _,” the American Psychiatric Association added a new disorder to the DSM-5: Social Communication Disorder, a disorder very similar to Asperger’s. question: Did kids that lose the autism diagnosis really lose autism?
answer: Yes and no. The brain of recovered autistics remains autistic. What has happened is that it has rewired at a time when neuroplasticity is high so that other brain centers compensate for the dysfunctional ones. I’ll give you an example from personal experience. I was mute until I was three or four years old. At that point, I started talking, and thought the whole business (“selective mutism”) was done with. Then, when I was in my forties, a psychologist asked me if I could tell her “what the child would have said.” I found myself unable to speak to her! This lasted until the next day. Since then, psychologist have triggered both muteness and a full shutdown in me. So — my brain had found strategies that circumvented these phenomena. Neurotypical people do not understand what they are like, or how, in some of us, they can be avoided unconsciously because we learned the strategies when we were little children. Again returning to selective mutism as an example, neurotypicals often muteness for an inability to form words, when it is not; we know how to speak, we want to speak, but we can’t get the words out. Some of us are fortunate enough to find ways around this, and those who are very physiologically oriented will attribute that to the rewiring of brain centers — which of course occurs at a time when, as I said, the brain is still highly plastic.

question: What are some changes in the first year of an autism diagnosis?
answer: This was my experience: For me to say it was a relief receiving my diagnosis would be an over simplification. Prediagnosis I had been living in a state of self-loathing — I was so aware of being out of sync with the world around me, and I was constantly being told that I just wasn’t trying hard enough or that I wasn’t paying attention. In other words, everything that I struggled with was my fault, something that I should have been in control of but I wasn’t. A failure. With diagnosis, finally, came an acceptance of who and how I was. I gradually became much more comfortable in my own skin. My struggles didn’t lessen but now the knowledge of why I struggled empowered me to attempt to modify my behavior or my approach to challenging situations. I started to give myself permission to opt out of some situations that were overwhelmingly difficult for me, or if I couldn’t opt out, to give myself a time limit for having to be in that difficult situation. I learned to laugh at my faux pas and try to learn from them instead of being overwhelmed with shame. The diagnosis gave me a sense of empowerment in general. It also let me look back at my many accomplishments, prediagnosis, and commend myself for those accomplishments despite my ASD. My first year following my ASD diagnosis turned out to be a period of tremendous growth.

question: What are the benefits that children receive from an autism diagnosis in school?
answer: There were many benefits to having the official “autism” diagnosis. The support services available contribute greatly to the success of the autistic student. Having the diagnosis immediately requires the school to include the parent(s) as part of the IEP (individualized education program) team. The team meets several times a year, as needed, to discuss and outline the provisions and accommodations the child will need in order to succeed in the classroom. The IEP can also include a behavioral component which addresses how the child will be disciplined and by whom. For my son, there were accommodations in place for fire drills, testing environment, break time, lunch time, changing classrooms. etc. The actual test themselves had to follow a certain format — no open questions that required written sentences for answers. All questions had to be multiple choice answers, or fill in the blank from an answer bank, for example. He had a teacher’s aide in all of the core classes. He received speech and occupational therapy during school hours for as long as he needed them. In high school, there were a few social skills classes that he attended. He was allowed to attend physical education classes during the summer with a small group of students, as he could not tolerate the loud, boisterous PE classes during the school year. Having the diagnosis, and educating the other students about autism, helped my son avoid much of the bullying behavior of the immature students. In high school, the girls were very “maternal” and protective of my son, and the vast majority of the students were encouraging and supportive.

question: How long does an autism diagnosis take when diagnosing adults over 25?
answer: Short answer: About six months due to misdiagnosis and lack of knowledge on my part about autism. I was diagnosed at age 36 by a neuropsychologist. The process included 8 hours of various tests to measure abilities such as working and long-term memory, spatial and visual memory, verbal skills, facial recognition (I did very poorly on that one), and attention span. A lot of the tests were quite fun, such as trying to put together a puzzle while blindfolded. But, I was initially diagnosed with ADHD as a result of the tests. It wasn’t until I read some studies on the similarities between ADHD and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) that I realized I identified a lot more with the description of ASD. At that point I’d probably been working with the neuropsychologist for about six months to learn some tricks to improve my attention span. I decided to discuss what I’d read with him and ask his opinion on whether I might have ASD. Initially he was very surprised and said I was too high-functioning to have ASD, but when I began telling him about issues I’d had from childhood with learning social skills and stimming, he started to take me more seriously. He gave me a questionnaire which was designed for parents of children with suspected ASD and asked me to answer it the way I thought my parents would. He changed my diagnosis to ASD based on that. I do believe there are questionnaires specifically designed for adults but I didn’t take one. My advice to an adult who suspects they may have ASD is to read as much as you can about it and don’t be shy about discussing your experiences in childhood and as an adult which may support an ASD diagnosis. It’s easy to overlook in adulthood because by that time many of us have learned to blend in with neurotypical peers, but that doesn’t mean we no longer have ASD. In truth, not much changed for me after receiving a formal diagnosis but it helped me to understand why I’ve struggled with certain things throughout my life. It was comforting to know that I’m not the only one out there. I have a better appreciation of my unique brain now. I hope you find the answers you are looking for!

question: Why has autism diagnosis in USA gone from 1 in 3000 back in 1960's to 1 in 36 today?
answer: Aaliceinw in her well summarized answer presents a good summary of reasons for greater numbers of diagnosed cases—raised awareness, referrals, recognition in family lines, and a realization that it also occurs in women and various ethnic groups. Along with these reasons that are tied to the research and diagnostic advantages of modernity, we would also suspect that mild or somehow formerly masked ADD is exacerbated in recent times because of the pace of life. It’s not that what’s been labeled as an “ADD world” causes ADD, but that more of us experience the downside traits of ADD whether we have it or not, and for those of us who do have it, the condition becomes so evidently stressful. I wasn’t diagnosed until I was in my fifties. A friend and coworker who had been diagnosed with ADD recognized the traits and patterns in me and encouraged me to get tested. When I was very young, I showed fidgeting traits, but these weren’t interfering with others. Teachers were frustrated by my disruptive behavior in class, but also saw that I was genuinely interested in learning and would even go the extra yard to do so. Reading was still popular before the electronic age, so when we had free time in class after finishing our assignments, we’d gladly grab a book and that kept us engaged. The greatest ADD nightmare was adolescence. The sleep disorders became chronic; the mental and physical underperformance became manifest; and the social alienation became torturous. However, in the seventies, most of us had never heard of ADD. In the years that followed, I found some techniques of what one psychologist explained to me were self-treatments. Chronic exercise was the most effective. It was also considered laudable. And I liked the results of better performance, better appearance, and a certain extent of calming (although never enough). I believe that in very recent times, ADD had actually become far less acceptable, and this is a factor in greater diagnosis. In earlier times, we were credited as long as we got the job done, and the job was defined as furthering the mission. In modern times, the criteria becomes more did you do the job according to prescribed methods. The importance of doing it “our way” became more important than fulfilling the eye on the prize sense of mission. This may be a jaundiced explanation from personal experience, of course. I’d welcome any further discussion of this point.

question: How can I convince my psychologist to take back my autism diagnosis and remove it from my records?
answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorders can be very mild, or quite serious. That’s why its a “spectrum.” That’s also why if it’s mild, one professional might diagnose and another not. If you’ve still got the same psychologist, you can make a case for a new look, and get it, but they’re not going to just erase an existing medical record and replace it. Instead, there could be a new note providing a new or modified diagnosis, based on changes in symptoms or other factors to justify the change. You could also hire a new ASD expert to assess and diagnose you, and then you’ll have records in two separate places, and they might be different, or the same. If the issue is your ability to do a certain job, or the like, it may easier to have a professional assess your functional capacities in relation to the job, whatever past spectrum diagnosis was made at one point. I have a number of friends who are on the spectrum with mild symptoms, and they are successful in a wide variety of careers. One of them is a medical doctor in a very challenging speciality, another manages a large company’s operations, and two, are fine psychotherapists.

question: Could an autism diagnosis harm me in any way?
answer: Sarah, you ask what is surely one of the more difficult questions to answer honestly about Autism; can getting this diagnosis harm you? My first response may be hard to hear. In many ways, it can. Our world sees this diagnosis as indicating something is broken in the person. This is not true in my theories. In my theories, Classic Autism and AS are two of the four minority personalities. Sadly, currently, the medical model rules and difference is often seen as brokenness. This can lead even close friends to treat you differently (as if you’re broken, fragile, or socially dumb). If this happens, then being diagnosed can seriously undermine your self-worth for a time. Just know, in time, it will pass. For example, in my case, I am autistic (AS variation). And many years ago, when I first learned this, I felt broken inside. I also felt the need to apologize to every person I’d inadvertently snubbed or insulted. Talk about putting a hole in my self worth. Today, most of those feelings are gone. And I have no problem telling people I have AS. But I only do it if and when I think it may help the other person (like right now.) The plus side? Getting this diagnosis can help you get services. It can help you to know yourself better. It can also, in some cases, entitle you to considerations which might make things like school easier. The thing is, if you then let this diagnosis define who you are as a person, then in the world’s eyes, you’re defining yourself as a broken person, rather than as a beautiful, but different, human being. Speaking of which, Sarah, I don’t know you. But from the fact that you were brave enough to ask this question, I’m sure that if I got to know you, I would find that you are a beautiful person. Did I just make you squirm? If so, I understand. If you’re autistic, then intimacy can be terribly hard. If so, just try to allow for the possibility that what I’ve just said is true, even if my saying it does make you squirm. As for services, if you need them, such as the help of a knowledgeable therapist or counselor, then take your time and choose this person wisely. Then please do what you need to do to get this help. Just know that like all “coming-out” experiences, coming out as autistic can be hard. And great. And exciting. And done with kind gentle support from others, in time, it can change your life in such wonderful ways, you may come to ask yourself why you waited. Know that coming out changed my life in this way. And after many years of being “out,” I haven’t a shred of regret. And to be honest, if you see this as who you think you are, then hiding it will only undermine your self-worth even more. To be happy, you must learn to be yourself, warts and all. Above all, whatever you decide to call yourself, do your best to see yourself as a beautiful, but different, human being.

question: Are false/reckless allegations of Autism diagnosis considered defamation per se?
answer: You mean autism jokes? Like where someone acts a certain way, and someone notices that it fits a stereotype of autism and calls the person autistic? Nah, that’s not particularly harmful. People know the difference between a joke and real life. I haven’t seen anyone treat autistic individuals poorly over a joke. What it does ensure is that people know at least:What autism is- a disabilitySome commonly held stereotypes about autism- intelligence, obsession, stimming, and social deficitAre some of those stereotypes incorrect? You bet. But professionals get them wrong too. Those professionals need to listen to people who actually have autism. The fact that they don’t is the most damaging to people who have autism. If someone calls autism a “loathsome disease”, well, that’s an opinion. And it’s an opinion they share with many individuals who have autism and would do anything to change that reality. They can’t, and that makes the condition even more loathsome.

question: Should I find another therapist if mine doesn't believe my autism diagnosis?
answer: Should I find another therapist if mine doesn't believe my autism diagnosis? The critical thing to know in this situation is whether your therapist is an expert at diagnosing autism. Diagnosing autism requires people with specialist knowledge of autism. Unless your therapist has had such training then assume they do not know enough to diagnoise autism. If your therapist is saying that your diagnosis of autism is wrong then they think they have enough expertise to diagnose autism. Without proper training they will not have this expertise. The American psychiatric association has a diagnosis manual called the DSM5. This lists the criteria for diagnosing autism. Diagnosing autism is pretty complex compared to most other conditions because autism traits can exist in so many different ways, which is why diagnosis needs greater skills. Unless psychologists or psychiatrists have been taught by experts in autism then their attempts at diagnosis will at best be amateurish. One of the biggest barriers to profesional understanding of autism, is that the way people with autism think and communicate is too different to be understood easily by people outside the spectrum unless they put the effort into understanding it. Knowledge of autism among health professionals has been focused for many years on male autism in a fairly obvious form. Our daughter went through years of working with doctors, psyhciatrists, cousnsellors and psychologists who all pooh poohed the idea that she could have autism. Now in her mid thirties she finally obtained a diagnosis this year form a clinic which specialises in assessing autism. One of the problems with getting a diagnosis for women, is that awareness of how differently women present from males with autism has only recently been recognised. This is particularly because of a tendency for women to mask or camouflage their social dificulties because they have learned to adapt in social situations even though this takes a lot of energy. I hope my assumption that you are a woman is OK. Our doctor who knows our daughter says that it is only in the last few years that journals for doctors in general practice have been providing information on female autism. Before this she had said that she did not think our daughter had autism. Having recived her diagnosis which came complete with a report about which specific autism traits our daughter was struggling with, she has continued with her psychologist and psychiatrist who were open minded enough to do further research to help understand her issues. Both said they would never try to diagnose autism. Now both are able to help her with issues she needs to work on. Unless this was happening she would be wasting her money. I have outlined some things to think about in deciding whether to continue with your therapist. I would start by talking to your therapist about their expertise in diagnosis of autism bearing in mind the possibility of misconceptions by professionals about autism. Compare their response with the approach taken by our daughter’s psychiatrist and psychologist. Also think about the expertise of the professional who assessed you for autism. How thorough was your assessment. Our daughter’s assessment took 6 sessions though many of these were taken up with intelligence type assessments which were important in assesssing her strengths and difficulties. The assessment process took account of information about autism provided by both our daughter and her mother. The final report highlighted areas of difficulty and strengths so she can learn how to manage getting into a job, keeping it and more importantly managing her life in things like emotional reglation, getting enough sleep to cope with exhaustion from social interaction and too much sensory input and putting in place supports like her counsellors and employment mentoring. The report also identified where she might need some changes in the work environment to help her function and contribute her best. Good therapy is about working on your immediate identifible issues. Make sure this is what you are getting.
comment_answer: Yes, I am a woman. I was diagnosed a year ago just before my 50th birthday! 50! Before getting tested I talked with my therapist about my concerns. He said, “I don’t see it.” Meaning he didn’t think I was autistic. So I had to go out on my own and find someone who would test me. I was a lengthy process and came with a 22 page report. I gave a copy to my therapist. He looked over it but didn’t say anything. After a few more sessions, I asked him if he now ‘saw it’. He started shaking his head, and when I seemed surprised he said, “well, it’s subtle”. When I asked him point blank if he believed I had autism, he said, “well, I have that report you gave me.” Pssshh. Later when he accused me of having an attitude about something I said, “I think you forget that I’m autistic.” He nodded and said, “Yes, I do forget that you struggle in that area.” So I think that he refuses to admit it outloud that I am autistic and he forgets about it when we’re discussing things. Thinking about all this, I guess I probably should find someone else.

question: How long does it take to get an autism diagnosis? Is it lifelong?
answer: There is an old staying about autism: if you’ve met one person with autism, you’ve met one person with autism. Meaning: they are all different. It’s a spectrum situaiton and thus can vary significantly. My own son was so severe he was (accurately) diagnosed at the age of 9 months and some experts at six months saw the problem. On the other hand, I have a friend who is a psychologist who believes that her son is on the spectrum now that he is in his early twenties, yet for years he was diagnosed simply with ADD. Ultimately, the words are not as important as the issues that you are experiencing and I recommend addressing any issues and don’t worry about what a doctor wants to call it, because they can often miss the big picture, unfortunately. If someone has problems interacting socially, I would read this as an issue worth addressing regardless of what doctors are willing to diagnose it as. (Parents and teachers can often have a clear beat on the whole picture, so I would listen to them). A child or even adult who is self-isolating a lot may need sensory integration therapy, or may need more help learning one-one-one imaginative play or more group interactions and more opportunity to socialize. The more practice the individual has the better. Think of it as clocking in the hours. Often it may seem that finding opportunities to socialize for an individual who is awkward with peers is harder than it seems, and it is hard, but there are creative ways of making sure that the individual stays in the community such as group classes, being with groups of individuals with a variety of disabilities, improv. classes, group therapy, social skills classes, individual therapy. Opportunities for one-on-one are important and this can happen with any family member. Keep imaginative play in the forefront if possible and keep it interactive. This combination is a must for developing the flexibility and imagination and empathy that are a must for proper social and psychological development.

question: As a veteran, can you get autism diagnosis from the VA?
answer: Speaking as an autistic disabled vet and former employee, no. The VA healthcare system is designed to treat and diagnose a lot of issues with veterans. The patients are all adults. Most autism diagnostics are focused on children, there’s simply no reason to have a person on staff to diagnose adult autism. Plus, qualified clinicians are pretty rare in the US, the chances of enough being available to hire are extremely slim. I’m also a VA psychological/psychiatric patient. I was diagnosed while a VA patient. But, they couldn’t diagnose me, there was no one available who could. I was able to self diagnose well enough to convince both my therapist and psychiatrist that I’m autistic. However, I had to go outside the VA for a formal diagnosis; luckily, my personal health insurance covered most of the expense.

question: Why are autism diagnosis rates leveling off after years of increases?
answer: Because the increase was not due to more autistic people having been born, but rather that the medical knowledge of us have increased by leaps and bounds the last 30 or so years. This means we've simply been found by the medical community. We were always here. And autistic adults have been saying this for decades, but been largely ignored since the medical community or society at large for that matter haven't realized yet that autistic kids grow into autistic adults, and we know many many things about autism that's been ignored until now. The increasing voices of autistic adults combined with modern research will likely bring more changes in how we are viewed.

question: What are the most misunderstood criteria in autism diagnosis?
answer: Difficult question. Do you mean “misunderstood by the autist” or “misunderstood by the diagnostician”? I was diagnosed at the age of 75. Many of the criteria on the DSM list are phrased as though diagnosing a young person. For example, I can’t really be said to have “highly restricted, fixated interests”, because I have added a variety of special interests over my lifetime. Also, because I wasn’t diagnosed at a young age, I was always expected to conform to “normal” behaviors, and a lot of these have become habitual for me over many years. It would probably require more conscious effort to “unmask,” than it does to continue my habitual behaviors.
comment_answer: Congratulations. You were even older than I was when diagnosed. I was 69 years old.

question: What are some reasons why someone would want proof from their doctor/psychiatrist about their autism diagnosis?
answer: It seems standard issue, here in the UK, that all patients have a right to know what is information is held in medical records. Infact, every time I see a psychiatrist or psychologist, I can guarantee that I will receive hard copies of everything that is sent to my doctor (GP) I need to know that information because its about me, it affects who I am and I need to be aware of that, as much as anyone else. Obviously there is no cure for autism - that makes it especially important to us, to be aware of whether (objectively) we have hyper or hypo sensitivity to stimuli. And when you receive a diagnosis, these factors are identified and knowing can make life a whole lot easier, because it enables a means to “identify” problem areas, in view of developing strategies that will help reduce problems which might commonly manifest and it's difficult to understand how it affects you, without somebody else (who is qualified and experienced) picking key points out. One example is that I was convinced that I had hypersensitive auditory awareness; I get really distracted when I hear people talking, it stops me being able to carry on doing stuff in a flow. Because I was provided a full breakdown of all my sensory sensitivity levels, I read “hyposensitive” auditory processing!! I felt indignation for this, but seeing it in writing made me think and realise that “yes I can hear noises from far away BUT I need people to repeat themselves often, because I can't process the exact words or even what they mean!” They were right (of course were, my mental health team has decades of experience with being objective over people like me and clinical and qualified experience, that I do not.) My diagnosis was about ten pages long! Very detailed and it contained some helpful advice on something that I could do to reduce specific sensitivities - visual for example; I'm hypersensitive, I get dazzled by the sun and I turn brain dead around bright colours that are man made. In fine in gardens that a bright and colourful - not so good in certain lights. Ideally I belong in a woodland environment with a light canopy of 70% foliage, to create dapples of light, full on bright light, especially torches in my face, cause a physical reaction that renders me angry or makes me want to run. And just knowing that, really helps me - on bright days or in cluttered environments, I effectively need blinkers - but instead wear I wide brimmed hat and that's it - I used to blame it on the weather, the fact that I preferred to leave my house at night or in cloudy conditions. Now, I wear a hat and feel like I can access a whole portion of my life again! Too many people think “I don't like socialise or it makes me nervous and so I'm autistic” and it's not just that, I used to be great at public speaking, I have a certain ammount of charisma that helps in those scenarios and I know there is no reason for me to feel fearful about my ability to blend in or stand out in the way I want to. My problem isnt with eye contact, or dealing with confrontation and that's why it took me so long to grasp the fact that I am impaired and in so many subtle ways it all lead me to a big frozen standstill… and I didn't understand why I needed to rock, or stand up when I talk. I can't talk sat down and it was problematic in office work because it makes others uneasy. I have nuances that I needed for someone else to explain, so that I could understand. Seeing my paperwork from an objective panel of experts, it was a massive relief. I genuinely feared that I was unveiling myself as a sociopath and I thought that my paperwork would say “not autistic and will be referred for further testing” I thought that because I told them I suspect I had a conduct disorder as a teen and they nodded in understanding (looked like agreement to me!) And so on. I was open minded about what I'd see in my diagnosis paperwork - I figured I just needed to know, come what may - personality disorders or not, I told them as much as I could splirt, in the time I had. When I had the meeting about their findings, and they declared “yes, you are definitely autistic" - it didn't sink in at all until I received my own copy of what they'd observed in clinical settings. It didn't feel real at all, until I read it because I'd disassociated my way through the whole process and I couldn't remember what I'd actually said, I just remembered a few sentences and how I'd spluttered it out sporadically. I couldn't even remember the questions they were asking, so I'd start talking and then ask them to repeat the question, five minutes later! So I remembered very little about what I said, I knew I' was honest and forthright. But that was all I could remember really and so seeing it written out, felt like a missing puzzle piece was found and knowing about my diagnosis is a massive help to me, I think it is for all of us adults, our lives and the condition raise questions and when we look at our lives and don't fully understand why we are, the way we are - it's worse than frustrating, it's dangerous because autists can start hating themselves for the things they can't do easily, for reasons they can't even explain. That's the type of situation that leads to suicide and early deaths, for many of us. Because feeling like a part of some of other puzzle, one you don't know and can't understand - can be so overwhelming and cause a massive load of despair that can be avoided somewhat, by understanding ASD and understanding ways to deal with it. Those are some of the reasons that illustrate why someone would want a full breakdown of previous findings. The whole point of the mental health professional is to help us live our lives the best we can, how can we do that if we aren't allowed to see our own paperwork?? So, not being allowed access to this stuff is really unfair. People have a right to know about themselves and those professionals, their very purpose is to help!! How can a label help, if we aren't sure how it was even applied!?!? The short answer is - because they have a right to understand so that they can help themselves too.
comment_answer: What about other doctors not believing you even with your shrink's letter? I wasn't happy at first to accept that autism Dx but as time went on I surrendered to it. It's the best way to understand myself. I still have problems with my other doctors accepting that and some flat out deny it. My dentist thinks I'm infantile, my gastro doesn't want to acknowledge that obsessiveness is how I can be in decent shape with my dietary routines, etc. Gee, isn't that a hallmark of autism, obsessive need for routines?

question: Is it worth getting an autism diagnosis for a child?
answer: Absolutely yes. You will get access to services and be able to explain to teachers and others why your child has certain problems. As your child gets older it may also help them to understand who they are and explain this to close friends, or link up with others on the spectrum.
