question: How does your life change after getting an autism diagnosis as an adult woman?
answer: It must always be remembered that autism is unique for every person who has it. That means there is no one way that women act when they are assessed as autistic.I can talk about what happened for me. At first, I was in denial. I kept reading my autism assessment report, and it allowed me to look back over my life, and see more, and more things that were due to my autism. It has allowed me to understand meltdowns, and stop blaming myself for them. Just because you know what a meltdown is, and what is most likely to cause one, that doesn’t mean they can all be avoided. Not everything has been easier. I can feel certain things happen to me that I now know are due to autism, and they hurt a bit more. Getting bullied in public is frustrating. I am 57, and am still getting bullied. Fallouts with friends can be very painful. Misunderstanding situations is horrible. I have found that I am no longer willing to put up with certain things from friends. One of them is lying. If I found out someone has lied to me, I will end that relationship. I have become more willing to hurt other people, if they hurt me. I must admit that I kind of enjoy it. It makes me feel more powerful. I have allowed myself not to always play by the rules.I spend at least an hour each day answering questions on Quora. It is an interesting exercise, because you get to see how a lot of people view those with autism. I hope that I am doing a little bit to educate people about the disorder.My guess is that you have set up an autism assessment for yourself. I commend you, if that is the case. I wish that more people would get an autistic assessment done. Don’t be too afraid. It will teach you a lot about yourself. ♥️

question: What do you think of this statement, "vaccines do not cause autism. However, vaccines may result in an autism diagnosis"?
answer: Original question: What do you think of this statement, "vaccines do not cause autism. However, vaccines may result in an autism diagnosis"? The first part of the statement is true; that vaccines do not cause autism. The Second.. is essentially false. The main reason more children are diagnosed is because just around the time they’re given one vaccine or another (12–15 months in the UK.. which is just around the time a child starts talking and walking) it becomes more obvious that the child is not following the expected pattern. But that in no way means that vaccines ensured they were diagnosed. Just because a child is due for a checkup and a vaccine (and a lot goes on developmentally which makes it more obvious when a child falls behind) doesn’t mean that the vaccine part is related to the doctor or parent noticing the child is not developing as they should in one way or another.

question: My little boy is awaiting Autism diagnosis and is non-verbal. He is 4. Can anyone share their experience of a non-verbal child at this age that progressed to speak? When and how, etc?
answer: Yes, yes, yes. my daughter was non verbal at 4, (and diagnosed at 2 yrs). I put her in special education in CA. (I rejected the first placement offered though). I did a lot of outside work with her. The school offered OT for 30 minutes a week. I took her to private OT for 2 hours a week. We did a huge amount of cross body work, which builds new pathways in the brain. They gave her speech therapy. Until about 4th grade. We did brainwave biofeedback. Which we believe was a huge part of her success. Look at EEG focus and the work of the Othmers What is Neurofeedback? We did it intensively ( few time a week early on, then monthly) in elementary school, and then when she asked for a "tune up" in middle school. When she did start talking it came slowly, and long before she could formulate her own phrases she could repeat them in context from movies. Please look up the recent article in the NYTimes about autistic kids and Disney movies. For years we all communicated in movies quotes, probably 7 years of it. and then years of it because it was a habit... We never quit looking for improvement. We worked for 2 years on having her look us in the eye. It took years, but it worked. Everyone in the family worked with her. We taught the extended family the things we were working on so everyone was consistent. We worked on language for so long she fell behind in other subjects in school. It was not until fourth grade that we were confident in her language skills. Then she had to catch up on other subjects. We were not sure she would ever catch up in math but she did, and finished calculus in high school. Middle school was hard. We hired outside tutors when she got behind. she had a hard time making friends her own age, she usually had a few friends but they were typically older. Mid high school she was pretty typical and now in college she is very typical, happy, social. a real joy to be around! She is 20 now and people do not believe that she was ever autistic. Even one of her current physicians did not believe it, but we provided pictures, movies and other information. She could not believe it. We get a lot of "she must have been high functioning", but she wasn't. We were asked to leave a lot of places including church... she acted out. She wore us out, everything took a lot of time. There is a lot of work in your future, but there is hope!! I am sorry to be anonymous, but I need to protect my daughter. My daughter remembers those years, she calls it "locked in her mind" It is painful to remember. When my mother sent me the link for the NYTimes article it was hard to read because it took me right back there, but I did not know that other families were doing the same things... Good luck to you.
comment_answer: Thank you for sharing your story this gives me hope for mine. 🙏

question: My therapist invalidated my autism diagnosis (given from a specialist) because she says I am too empathetic? Can't we be empathetic and autistic?
answer: What an ignorant thing for a therapist to think. But I’m not surprised given how many similar stories I’ve heard from people trying to get diagnosed but getting turned down for the most stupid and silly reasons ever. And most of these stupid times it’s because of the therapists believing in one or more autism stereotypes, like the eye contact thing for example. Anyway, to answer your question, not all people on the autism spectrum have Alexithymia (emotional blindness, limited or monotone emotional expression, and I guess some people associate it with reduced empathy too). In fact, many (or perhaps even most) people on the spectrum has the opposite problem when it comes to empathy: We have way too much! Sure a lot of autistic people can probably more easily turn off their empathy at will, especially those of us who has suffered a lot of trauma and had/has to do this as a defense mechanism. But we can also be a lot more thoughtful and understanding than allistic people. We really care about other people, just not in the same way as allistics might do. Allistic people might see us as these selfish, egotistical, ignorant beings who lives inside our own bubble. And maybe that’s partially true. We do like to indulge a lot in our own thoughts, fantasies and interests. And we might not care enough to try to remember important information about other people, such as what their profession is, or when is their birthday. But when we really care about someone, we will in fact remember even the smallest details about them which they don’t expect us to remember. We will give them presents (penguin pebbling), we will really enjoy their company even when we’re not directly engaging with one another (parallel play), and we can talk to them for hours! Check here if you’re interested to read more about the love languages of autistic people:The Five Neurodivergent Love LocutionsThe 5 neurodivergent love locutions: infodumping, parallel play, support swapping, Please Crush My Soul Back Into My Body, Penguin Pebblinghttps://stimpunks.org/2022/01/22/the-five-neurodivergent-love-languages-2/In other words, many autistic individuals are extremely empathetic! We simply might not be able to show it as easily as allistic individuals! And the ways we show our love can easily be overseen and/or misunderstood. This is why we might come off as assholes to people who doesn’t know us well. Anyone who thinks that all autistic people are assholes either only knows like one autistic person who just so happens to be very mean (at least towards them), OR they’ve never gotten emotionally close to an autistic person. Could also be both. Most likely it’s the latter. Autistic people are indeed very much capable of learning to have empathy. However, we might not have it in the appropriate situation when it’s actually expected to show some sympathy. Not only that, but many of us don’t like wasting time and energy on showing sympathy to just anyone and everyone. We instead choose to commit to the people we already know and love so much. But of course, there are always many exceptions to everything as Autism is a whole spectrum. I’m only talking from my own experiences and from some of my own research. Make of it what you will.

question: How can I get my autism diagnosis purged from my medical records? I read that you can't adopt kids and can be refused certain medical treatment if you have an autism diagnosis in your records.
answer: If you live in the US you can take heart that there is no centralized database of medical records. No one will know your autism diagnosis unless you tell them. As to the medical records themselves, just don't give your providers permission to share your records with your current professionals. HIPPA gives me you total control of your medical information and you should take it. As long as irrational stigma exists the decision to disclose is a difficult and deeply personal decision. It would be nice for all the rest of us if you would come out of the autism closet. Ultimately that is what actually weakens and maybe even ends the stigma. But it isn't anyone's business but your own and if you need to remain hidden then hide. None of the non-autistic people here have any business trying to pressure you to disclose. Those of us who are autistic have an interest in your decision, but if you make a choice I wouldn't make it is up to me to exercise some empathy and accept your decision with compassion and understanding.

question: Which are the decisive points in the DSM-5 for an Autism diagnosis in a short, concise bullet point list form?
answer: First, let me point out that there IS no such thing as an Autism diagnosis in the DSM-5. There is only Autism Spectrum Disorder. Former diagnoses such as Autism, Asperger’s Syndrome, and Pervasive Development Disorder have been discarded and former diagnoses of those are now considered part of ASD. Some people use “autism” as a shorthand for ASD, some for “people who were formerly diagnosed with Autism,” and some who don’t adhere to the new DSM edition’s definition continue to hold it as a separate diagnosis. But it’s not “in” From the DSM-5: Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Criteria A. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, as manifested by the following, currently or by history (examples are illustrative, not exhaustive, see text): 1. Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, ranging, for example, from abnormal social approach and failure of normal back-and-forth conversation; to reduced sharing of interests, emotions, or affect; to failure to initiate or respond to social interactions. 2. Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction, ranging, for example, from poorly integrated verbal and nonverbal communication; to abnormalities in eye contact and body language or deficits in understanding and use of gestures; to a total lack of facial expressions and nonverbal communication. 3. Deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships, ranging, for example, from difficulties adjusting behavior to suit various social contexts; to difficulties in sharing imaginative play or in making friends; to absence of interest in peers. Specify current severity: Severity is based on social communication impairments and restricted repetitive patterns of behavior. (See table below.) B. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities, as manifested by at least two of the following, currently or by history (examples are illustrative, not exhaustive; see text): 1. Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech (e.g., simple motor stereotypies, lining up toys or flipping objects, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases). 2. Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, or ritualized patterns or verbal nonverbal behavior (e.g., extreme distress at small changes, difficulties with transitions, rigid thinking patterns, greeting rituals, need to take same route or eat food every day). 3. Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus (e.g, strong attachment to or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessively circumscribed or perseverative interest). 4. Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interests in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement). Specify current severity: Severity is based on social communication impairments and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior. (See table below.) C. Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities or may be masked by learned strategies in later life). D. Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning. E. These disturbances are not better explained by intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder) or global developmental delay. Intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder frequently co-occur; to make comorbid diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability, social communication should be below that expected for general developmental level. Note: Individuals with a well-established DSM-IV diagnosis of autistic disorder, Asperger’s disorder, or pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified should be given the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. Individuals who have marked deficits in social communication, but whose symptoms do not otherwise meet criteria for autism spectrum disorder, should be evaluated for social (pragmatic) communication disorder. Specify if: - With or without accompanying intellectual impairment - With or without accompanying language impairment - Associated with a known medical or genetic condition or environmental factor (Coding note: Use additional code to identify the associated medical or genetic condition.) - Associated with another neurodevelopmental, mental, or behavioral disorder (Coding note: Use additional code[s] to identify the associated neurodevelopmental, mental, or behavioral disorder[s].) - With catatonia Table: Severity levels for autism spectrum disorder Level 3 "Requiring very substantial support” Severe deficits in verbal and nonverbal social communication skills cause severe impairments in functioning, very limited initiation of social interactions, and minimal response to social overtures from others. For example, a person with few words of intelligible speech who rarely initiates interaction and, when he or she does, makes unusual approaches to meet needs only and responds to only very direct social approaches Inflexibility of behavior, extreme difficulty coping with change, or other restricted/repetitive behaviors markedly interfere with functioning in all spheres. Great distress/difficulty changing focus or action. Level 2 "Requiring substantial support” Marked deficits in verbal and nonverbal social communication skills; social impairments apparent even with supports in place; limited initiation of social interactions; and reduced or abnormal responses to social overtures from others. For example, a person who speaks simple sentences, whose interaction is limited to narrow special interests, and who has markedly odd nonverbal communication. Inflexibility of behavior, difficulty coping with change, or other restricted/repetitive behaviors appear frequently enough to be obvious to the casual observer and interfere with functioning in a variety of contexts. Distress and/or difficulty changing focus or action. Level 1 "Requiring support” Without supports in place, deficits in social communication cause noticeable impairments. Difficulty initiating social interactions, and clear examples of atypical or unsuccessful response to social overtures of others. May appear to have decreased interest in social interactions. For example, a person who is able to speak in full sentences and engages in communication but whose to- and-fro conversation with others fails, and whose attempts to make friends are odd and typically unsuccessful. question: Is it possible to have an autism diagnosis if you never had any speech problems?
answer: Communication skills are extraordinarily complex. Communication encompasses five broad areas: using appropriate rhythm/intonation patterns, pronouncing sounds correctly (articulation), knowing what words mean (semantics), putting words into sentences in the right order (syntax). The fifth area is combining all of the above to appropriately and effectively communicate feelings, ideas and experiences. This is called pragmatics. Good pragmatic skills involve being able to answer and ask questions appropriately, being able to follow directives, maintaining topic of conversation, understanding the give-and-take of conversation, and knowing when to change the topic of conversation. It also includes noticing, understanding, and responding to body language, facial expressions and tone of voice. It means being able to pick up on subtle inferences that are not specifically spoken. Many people with autism who are high functioning have “communication problems" in the area of pragmatics. They may have difficultly with understanding sarcasm. They may take things very literally. They may blurt out comments that are not appropriate to the situation. They may monopolize a conversation with some topic they love totally unaware that others in the conversation are no longer interested. Many speech-language pathologists who work with people with autism focus on helping them develop appropriate pragmatic skills. Since I have never met you, I have no idea whether or not any of what I described pertains to you. However it may give you an idea of how a person with autism may not have what is typically though of as a “speech problem,” but still has problems in the area of communication.

question: Is Speech Therapy considered an "alternative therapy" for a person with Autism diagnosis?
answer: Anon to protect the identity of our teenage son on the spectrum. Her comments refreshed our memory of the way insurance claims were handled back in the Dark Ages --- in 2000, when our son was first diagnosed as a toddler and few professionals other than SLPs knew what the heck to do with him---and remains to the present day. Our son's program (which has yielded spectacular progress for our guy) was an amalgam of Speech/Langauge Therapy, Behavioral/ABA and Play Therapy (Greenspan). I know that some folks have a visceral antipathy to Behavioral therapy (we disagree, but concede it may not be for every kid or family). If all those options were not available, we would say that SLP evaluations and treatment were the single irreplaceable element. We certainly had plenty of Speech Therapy bills covered by insurance, but the insurance claims where always tied to a particular Speech or Language deficit (Teaching Sign language, specific speech deficits, etc.) and specific diagnostic codes. Even before ABA or behavioral Therapy was widely accepted as a treatment, I recall that Insurance companies never paid for Speech Language therapy for Autism, per se. Here's language I copied verbatim from an SLP evaluation: "DIAGNOSIS: Language disorder characterized by lexical/semantic and supralinguistic deficits, resulting in deficits in language comprehension and reading comprehension secondary to diagnosis of autism with hyperlexia." [emphasis mine] I suspect you might need to---and really should--- discuss this with your SLP. You really can't do without it. Good Luck.

question: What are the three levels attached to an autism diagnosis. e.g. Autism level III?
answer: It's a scale used to approximate living assistance needs for support purposes. The rating is ONLY really made for that purpose! Please try NOT to read anything more into it! Most descriptive adjectives or ratings used about autistic people cause them harm from a plethora of unjustified assumptions that non-autistic people make upon hearing. The rating idea behind this particular scale unfortunately wasn't made with much or any autistic input, and it ignores aspects that should really be considered if any decent ability rating scale were to be developed. There are certainly a significant portion of autistics that may find themselves seemingly at different of these levels at different points in their life, depending very heavily on multiple varying factors. It's usually just more complicated than most people will fathom. Level 1 is typically defined as everyone that is able to live & function in society either fully independently, or with only very limited assistance really needed (usually includes but is not only all those in the former Asperger's category). Level 2 is someone that unquestionably needs significantly more help & support with daily living tasks, but still may not be fully dependent on others in every situation. Level 3 has the most living support needs by far including but not necessarily limited to anyone requiring full 24/7 care.

question: Can you get an autism diagnosis reversed? My daughter and I both think her diagnosis is faulty and she is scared this diagnosis will ruin her law enforcement career plans.
answer: An autism diagnosis is not going to impact your daughter’s aspirations to be a law enforcement officer. Realize that autism is not a singular developmental disability. People are said to be “on the spectrum” when their behaviors and social interactions are consistent, to varying degrees, with the criteria for diagnosis. It’s not the diagnosis that’s an obstacle. It’s only the potential obstacles that come from aberrant behaviors and skill deficits associated with autism spectrum disorder. Full-blown autism is quite serious. It is highly doubtful that your daughter would be hoping to become a law enforcement officer if she had full-blown autism. If she did have what is sometimes referred to simply as “autism” (meaning, the most serious form of the spectrum disorder), she would have great difficulty talking to people (even you), difficulty understanding “social interactions” and body language, she would not be able to learn in a regular school classroom. It’s not the diagnosis that is a problem any more than a diagnosis of diabetes or dyslexia would be a problem. It’s the behavioral and social skills patterns your daughter has (those used to determine the diagnosis) that your daughter should be considering. As a law enforcement officer, excellent “people skills” can be the difference between life and death. Does she have keen observation skills when it comes to other people? Does she recognize the parts of communication that go beyond the words someone says (e.g., the way the words are said, body language)? Can she comfortably pay attention to numerous factors simultaneously (what’s going on to her left, right, and straight ahead, for example)? Is she comfortable being around other people throughout the day? Asperger’s Syndrome is one type of autism spectrum disorder that is more common than most people realize. A person with Asperger’s may be able to hold down a job quite successfully, graduate from college, and have a family. But they are handicapped when it comes to successful social interactions— often missing nonverbal cues or saying socially awkward things. For these reasons, they may have difficulty maintaining friendships. Such people might shy away from careers that require strong social skills, including strong communication skills— both verbal and nonverbal. They may become exhausted if they have to be around other people for more hours than is their “limit.” However, those with Asperger’s can benefit from specific therapy that helps them learn strategies and techniques that will improve their functioning in social situations, such as on the job and at home. I recommend that you meet with the physician who conducted the interviews with your daughter and you and who developed the diagnosis. You can ask which of your daughter’s characteristics he/she felt were indicative of an autism spectrum disorder. You should also ask “where on the spectrum” the doctor believes your daughter fits and what, if any, therapy could help her function better in social situations. I understand your daughter’s fear. My daughter struggled with basic math, which meant she struggled even more as she progressed through high school. I finally decided we needed to know how to help her. She was evaluated by a specialist in learning disabilities who concluded that my daughter has dyscalculia. For some reason, this diagnosis frightened her and embarrassed her. Yet, all it was doing was putting a name to what had been true for her since she was very young. Her reaction was puzzling to me until I understood that putting a name to something— a diagnosis of something “abnormal”— affected her self-image in a more profound way than her lifelong experience of not being able to comprehend most aspects of mathematics. An analogous thing might be going on with your daughter.

question: What is having an autism diagnosis like in countries other than the US?
answer: A whole lot better than in the US as far as I can tell…. For starters we don’t have any benefits (unless low on the spectrum and incapable of working all together). That may sound like something bad but I think it’s really good! It’s also a signal to society there’s nothing wrong with autism and that people with autism are usually capable of working for their money like anyone else. This also means people with level 1 autism (needing only little support) usually have a job and are able to keep that job. There are hardly any limitations to people with autism. You can go to regular schools, university, etcetera. No problem, no questions asked and only special treatment when you yourself ask for it (or if a mentor notices you’re struggling with something). This means most people with level 1 autism have had education (which again helps in finding and keeping a job). We have universal healthcare. So whenever you’re struggling with something and can use some support it’s available. And it doesn’t cost you a lot of extra money. Psychological healthcare is rather easy to get (though there are waiting lists now, mainly due to Corona) and is of high quality. Nearly all people working with people on the spectrum really understand what autism is and how it works. In America there are unfortunately a LOT of professionals who have absolutely no clue what autism really is. The things I read here on Quora alone from American professionals working with kids or adults on the spectrum? Utterly ridiculous! For instance Amelia Gray claims to hold a degree in psychology and run her own practice. And honestly, I believe her!. She however claims things like autism being an intellectual disorder (wrong), it being a learning disability (definitely not!), people with autism always being incapable of taking care of themselves or getting any education (extremely wrong!), she downright refuses to accept Asperger’s is also autism and when given literal quotes of DSM-5 which inform that Asperger’s IS now actually part of Autism Spectrum Disorder she just claims those quotes are from a random online magazine and not DSM-5… She also claims autism is always caused by family incest (wtf??) and frequently advises people here on Quora struggling with mental issues to just kill themselves because no-one would care… Reported her many times, but to no avail. That’s part of American professionals ‘helping’ people with autism! You may by now have noticed I speak of having autism or people with autism. That’s very, very common here! Nearly everyone I met who’s on the spectrum here spoke like that about their autism. You hardly ever hear someone say they are autistic. In America (and many other countries) it’s not very much accepted to speak person-first language. Many even consider it insulting. It’s not.Saying you are autistic is letting your autism define yourself. Everything about you is autism. That’s not how most people here think about it. It’s just something you have, but you’re still a unique human being first. Your condition may be an important part of you, but it only comes second. It just isn’t that big a deal… Which is also because by far most people here understand what autism is more or less. In America there’s a LOT of ignorance on autism. If you tell someone here you have autism it’s likely they’ll just respond with “Oh, ok.” or maybe “Ok, good to know”. And that’s it. And they will take it in account when working or speaking with you, but they won’t start treating you like some sort of alien. It’s also not likely to get remarks like “But you don’t look autistic to me??” and such. We also have a lot of things where people with autism can get help if needed. For instance in many amusement parks we can get a card which allows us to skip waiting lines and which can be used if these cause sensory overload. You do need to have some proof you actually have autism, but besides that: no questions asked. And most people with autism don’t actually use that option because they can handle the waiting lines (me included). I don’t abuse the existence of this possibility. It’s there for people who really need it and which allows them to also have a fun day at an amusement park. There are companies tat specifically hire people with autism because of their special abilities. Also people somewhat lower on the spectrum. And they offer extra support and custom schooling on the job. All pretty normal here. With my autism I would never ever want to live in America. The things I heard from people with autism living in America: just horrible. And quite often they don’t even realise it themselves. They don’t know any better! And the insults I got from Americans, sometimes in conversations that weren’t even about autism are just ridiculous, but still hurtful. Some even claiming I wouldn’t survive long in America because I’m supposedly so proud of my autism (I’m not at all! I even quite frequently tell in answers I’m not proud of my autism, but I’m also not ashamed of it and I like many aspects of my autism…). Or people claiming I must be loud, obnoxious, lacking empathy and in general just be a terrible person to be around with because of my autism. Or people claiming I shouldn’t be having children because of my autism (or actually: I was told ‘autistic people shouldn’t breed’). And when I told I already have two very talented children who actually don’t have autism they started insulting my children…. And except an occasional other person with autism there isn’t a single American stepping up and saying it isn’t normal. It is even quite common other people join. And reporting it to Quora (American company) is also useless… They hardly ever take any action. I consider America to be one of the very worst places to live when having autism.

question: What do you attribute the dramatic rise in autism numbers to?
answer: I see many possibilities:That the DSM criteria for “autism” changed with version 5 of that book. Most diagnosticians use that manual as their “bible” for deciding who has what mental issues. So, for example, people who were formerly diagnosed with PPD-NOS are now ‘officially’ autistic. That same change in the DSM also recognised that things like OCD, ADD and ADHD (which are NOT autism) frequently occur alongside autism. (These are called ‘co-morbid conditions’.) So it’s more likely that someone who presents as an ADD sufferer will cause the diagnostician to also wonder whether they have autism - and that adds to the number of people diagnosed that way.Greatly increased awareness of the higher-functioning forms of autism may result in people being more likely to seek a diagnosis - and (in the case of children), being diagnosed earlier than they were before. People who were merely socially inept and perhaps “geeky” or “nerdy” are now able to understand that this is an actual mental disability and not just merely a matter of personality. They’ll now seek a formal diagnosis rather than going through life misunderstanding their own condition.It might be evolution in action! In the past, those with Aspergers (high functioning autism) found it hard to make their way in society because of their poor communication and social interaction skills. This undoubtedly meant that they were less likely to marry and have children. But with the rapid rise of information technology - computers and the internet - people with high-functioning autism are, in a sense, less disabled. Our poor ability to discern emotion from facial expression, body language, verbal intonation and such is no worse than neurotypical people when communicating via email, text messaging, etc. As more and more human interaction happens online, people who do not expect to recognize another person’s emotions do better than people who have suddenly had their empathic abilities ripped from them. With that barrier to social interaction removed - we’re on a much more level playing field - and so we have a better chance of being understood by the opposite sex. Since autism has a strong genetic component - evolution will, for 100% certain, grab this shift and adapt accordingly.Because high functioning autistic people tend to be much better at computer skills than the general public, they tend to gravitate towards places like Silicon Valley where the best computer jobs are. This concentration of autistic genes in particular geographical areas may well dramatically increase the probability of two extremely mildly autistic people getting together and having more intensely autistic children. Since we know that autism is a spectrum condition and isn’t linked to any particular SINGLE gene - this would be the expected result. This could easily have a dramatic effect on the number of more noticeably autistic children appearing in the gene-pool. This too would be “evolution in action”.My bet is that the increase is due to all four of these effects acting in harmony.

question: How should I go about bringing up an autism diagnosis to my new therapist?
answer: I'm not a professional, just a patient of therapy for 40 years. These are suggestions. I've looked up some of your questions, they are familiar. I'm using them to base this answer. You want to find someone comfortable or experienced first with people on the spectrum, who also has knowledge of CPTSD and PTSD due to family dynamics. Don't select a therapist without having a consultation first. When you meet them the first time, they'll ask you why you're there. (I received my diagnosis late, thanks to an astute new therapist who sent me to be tested because the extent of my anxiety was so high, I could only ramble for 45 minutes during my first visit.) When I meet a new therapist (or doctor), I explain I am Autistic, I have a history of trauma, and that if I'm asked a question that illicit an answer they aren't expecting, they should rephrase it because I may have misunderstood. Then, I let the visit continue on their lead, and during the visit I'm silently checking out their books on the shelf, answering their questions, judging if the appear to be satisfied that I'm cooperating with their answers, while still being allowed to explain myself. If they appear hesitant, uncomfortable, dismissive, or otherwise unacceptable to me, I decide to keep looking. I also understand I am not looking for a friend. I am looking for someone to listen to me, explain if my concerns are real or can be viewed in a more positive light. I am paying them to answer questions about myself (or how to find the answer), to have someone to listen while I vent, or just to have someone smarter than me to talk to, about who I am and how I see or view the world. Of course, I'm leaving a lot of personal stuff out of this post. View a therapist as a teacher, but not a friend. You are not entitled to know anything about them they don't want to share. I don't ask, some patients do. I don't want a friend or a personally friendly relationship. I just want someone who can help me redirect my constant anxiety or assure me I'm not crazy when I feel like I am.

question: How can I support my roommate as they seek an autism diagnosis?

They're going to be “all over the place” with “preoccupations”. Roll your eyes & smirk. That's what they're going to do when they look back upon it later. Just let them know that if they want to “talk through” any of their concerns or fears here, that you've got an ear to spare? Because they're probably internalising a LOT of doubts & turmoils, presently. Not the least of which will probably be a bit of “impostor syndrome”. Just “hold the fort” & “leave your door ajar”. And if you see anything “going on” in their facial expressions, then pester them about it in a way that you can either both get a giggle out of it or so that it'll take their mind off it a while. As there's nothing that they can do about it right now. They might be feeling a sense of “waiting for the executioner”. Not knowing that when the executioner comes, they will be carrying a tray of fresh baked cookies. It's not necessarily going to be as bad as they fear. But they don't know that yet. Because their analytics will be in "overdrive”, scanning all of the potential permutations, without sufficient data to fulfil the task. Hence the “processing program” in their head won't cease, until the Diagnosis is Formally given. Their brain will be a “whirlwind” right now. Just help them “maintain normality”. Best of luck… 😊🙃

question: Can I get an autism diagnosis removed from my medical records if I have been misdiagnosed?
answer: Medical records are covered by regulations and laws that govern exactly how they are created, what goes in them and how they are taken care of. First of all, let me make it very clear: it is not “your” medical record. It is a record about you, and contains the experiences of many individuals who are providing care for you. If you disagree with a diagnosis, and you have every right to see and examine the record and its diagnosis. Then, the proper protocol is for you to verbalize your frustration with your caregivers. Then, they have one of two choices: 1). They realize the mistaken diagnosis, and make a record of such…without “removing” the one that is in error. Or, 2). They still feel that their diagnosis is correct, and state such, with your protestation. In either case, the original diagnosis will not be removed; it will simply be changed along with the reason why.

question: During an autism diagnosis, would autistic adult females cry when they are overwhelmed or would they not show this emotion?
answer: Autistic adult females likely vary greatly in response to overwhelming situations, as do non-autistic females, and “camouflaging” comes into this issue as well. Humans all get different socializing and have different capabilities and preferences. Some of us autistics have “meltdowns” when overwhelmed, some of us have what are called “shutdowns” — and those two things can each look very different in different people. Non-autistic people, female or male, get overwhelmed too, and can cry or not cry depending upon all sorts of things. Males in general are strongly socialized not to cry in my society at a pretty young age, yet many females are too. I myself rarely cry, especially in public; it was very much not safe to do so when I was a kid. For females and males of any neurotype, I think crying can be healthy sometimes! Sometimes people judge others for crying, or not crying, in circumstances where they think that person should or shouldn’t cry… us females are considered “weak” often if/when we cry, in my experience, but then empathy is often not extended to us if we simply verbalize our feelings without crying; it’s assumed if the situation were “really bad”, we’d be crying. It can feel like a lose-lose to me… so I learned to sort of “override” my strong emotions with logical thinking while around others, in an effort to stay safe. This, for me, is one of my “camouflaging” skills that I developed for survival; it can use a ton of energy and leave me exhausted and numb, yet I am still employed and alive, on the plus side. I let the feelings out more in private, but then one doesn’t get support either; years of therapy pre-diagnosis were not nearly as helpful as they “should” have been as a result since I camouflaged there too. Crying is hard now for some of us. I’m sure things are also complicated for men who are feeling strongly, for nonbinary folks, for humans in general! I was not diagnosed as autistic until a few years ago, and I know relatively few autistic folks. But most autistics are likely undiagnosed still; most are adults; most females in particular may be still going undiagnosed at any age — so which subset of us does the OP mean? A ton of us with “camouflaging” skills will not cry in the situation the OP specifies, I bet (you can google “autistic women camouflage” for instance)! Others would. Who is the tester, too? Do we feel safe with them? But camouflaging autistics might be less likely to get diagnosed in the first place; I had to realize I was autistic myself, before any professionals did; but then the ADOS confirmed it when I sought answers. So this is all very complicated to answer; we can just speculate really and give some anecdotes. Why I Fake Being ‘Normal’ — and Other Women with Autism Do, Too

question: After much research, we decided not to pursue an Autism diagnosis for our son. However, he still presents many autistic behaviors. How do we best support him?
answer: “After much research, we decided not to pursue an Autism diagnosis for our son. However, he still presents many autistic behaviors. How do we best support him?” That’s a big subject but I’ll start with the things that come to mind first. The “special interests” that people make so much of in the context of autism are commonly the autistic person’s way of learning broadly in a connected and coordinated way. It can be much more efficient for them than the normal school mode of teaching. You may be able to help your son to see how other subjects connect into their special interest but do it very lightly. Their special interests can feel very close to an autistic person’s individual identity and self-directed learning is an important part of it. My approach is to learn alongside the autistic child. To be drawing, for instance, and ready to share paper and pencils with the child when they ask. Another point is to treat their achievements as those of a person, not just a child. For the child who loves drawing, not to indulge them with lots of cheap children’s pencils and paper but occasionally to give them real artist-quality media that will reward the work they put into what they do. Not the most-expensive quality, but what real artists use for everyday practise and sketching, for instance. Autistic people often hate excessive praise. I aim to give a sense of recognition of their achievement but to engender the sense that the best they can do is the best preparation for doing better. Not to praise work so much that they child fears going further for fear of not being able to maintain that standard. Because a child’s special interests can be a path to diverse but well-connected learning, a diversity of modes of learning can contribute a lot. Being able to learn by pulling things apart and by building things related to their interests can help greatly. Another vital point is that, although most talk about neurodiversity focuses on the individual, neurodivergent people can be excellent in collaborative settings. Their social skills are commonly in the area of working and thinking together effectively, rather than simply socialising. Such things as triggering questioning in a public meeting or a schoolroom. By being the person who dares to ask the first question, the neurodivergent commonly lowers the inhibitions others feel about asking questions. Even once the questioning is happening, it may be the neurodivergent person who asks the questions others dare not ask for fear of social censure. They are often also the person to suggest ideas that others have overlooked, that may lead to really productive discussion towards resolution of problems. So don’t accept the simplistic idea that autistic people “lack social skills”. I hope that is of help, at least in provoking your thinking in extra directions.

question: What are some early signs of autism in toddlers?
answer: Baby may seem confused at times and cry when there doesn't seem to be anything wrong. Baby may not use as much eye contact as he should. Baby might get upset at unusual things: seeing a dog, hearing a song, the tone of someone's voice, a certain sound. Baby's facial expressions might seem unusual and when you look back at photos, you'll notice it more. You'll notice this more if you have experience with other babies or have had other children. Baby may be unusually undemanding at times (such as during the night and make noises rather than cry) but become demanding and unsettled during other parts of the day, (ie crying after he's been fed, changed and cuddled). Sometimes he just won't settle. As he grows there may be increasing differences in baby compared to his peers, ie: he might be slightly delayed in some or all of his milestones. He may not go past the chewing and banging toys stage without a lot of help. He may play in the same way with toys over and over - especially favourite toys. He may be fixed on certain things such as cars. He may be prone to temper outbursts over unlikely issues such as you buying a new sofa or moving his cot. He may seem confused when others outside his immediate family visit or when people make a fuss over him. He may do funny little movements with his hands, get excited and make sounds either for no reason or by seeing something although this usually develops as they grow. Some babies do not develop speech although they might use sounds. Others may have overall speech and language development delays. They may be slower to speak their first speech sounds (Dada, baba etc) and pick up words more slowly. These are all mostly things I noticed with my son who has ASD and some of these points may be exclusive to his development and not another child who goes on to have ASD as they are all different.

question: What is the process of diagnosing autism in toddlers?

question: Is mental age of a toddler a stereotype in terms of autism?
answer: The concept of "mental age" is generally considered outdated and not a useful way to describe the cognitive abilities of individuals with autism or any other developmental condition. This concept is based on the assumption that all individuals follow a linear developmental trajectory, and that a person's level of cognitive ability can be assessed based on their chronological age. However, this view has been challenged by research that shows that individuals with autism can have a wide range of strengths and challenges, and that their development may not follow a typical trajectory. Moreover, using mental age to describe the abilities of individuals with autism can be problematic because it can reinforce negative stereotypes and stigmatize individuals with the condition. For example, describing a person with autism as having a "mental age" of a toddler can be dismissive of their abilities and potential, and can lead to underestimating their abilities and not providing appropriate support and opportunities for them to develop and learn. Instead of relying on mental age as a way to describe individuals with autism, it is important to focus on their individual strengths, needs, and potential. This approach can help to promote a more inclusive and respectful society that values diversity and supports all individuals to reach their full potential.

question: Why shouldn't I use "high-functioning" when describing autism? That is the term written on my toddler's diagnosis.
answer: It's a misnomer that causes harm and is considered offensive by many. It also isn't a formal diagnosis anywhere, so I have no clue why someone decided to write it on the diagnosis of your kid, but it shouldn't be there. Autism is a spectrum disorder. That means it affects every single person who has it differently. There are many different aspects to autism, and they will all have their own challenges and advantages to each individual person on the autism spectrum. It's something like this:Nowâ€¦. With the functioning terminology you try and divide this broad spectrum in just two categories and judge who are functioning and who aren't. Who's to decide that? What makes someone function well and someone else not so much? Does high-functioning mean a person is â€˜normalâ€™ and needs no support? The term seems to suggest exactly thatâ€¦. But, spoiler alert: that's a completely false assumption. A person with â€˜High-Functioning autism â€˜ will face certain challenges due to his or her autism and they will need support. Now, someone low-functioning, does that mean they're basically â€˜retardsâ€™ sitting in a corner, unable of speaking, throwing around their own faeces? The term seems to suggest something like that. While in fact someone with â€˜low-functioning autism â€˜ may be very gifted in certain areasâ€¦. So, the functioning terms make no sense, cause misunderstandings and misconceptions which can be harmful to people with autism. And the terms are also very subjective and judgemental and therefore potentially offensive. There fortunately are better alternatives, like the levels of severity in DSM-5, which tell how much support a person needs in certain areas where level 1 means little support is needed and level 3 means very substantial support is required. These levels can change over time, are no subjective, judgemental misnomers but just numbers that say something that's factual and measurable. So better in any possible way, except maybe needing a bit more explanation when talking to someone who doesn't know autism (which I personally consider a good thing. I rather explain things often, than have people make false assumptions all the time).

question: What are the best parenting strategies for toddlers with high functioning autism?
answer: No one strategy is going to fit every child on the autism spectrum because each child is individual and so are their needs but there are a few basics that will work for almost any child if implemented persisistently. Bonding Taking as much time as possible to bond with your child and allowing them to let you into their world will make it easier for them to bond with you and feel comfortable, meaning they may better be able to express their needs to you. Part of the problem a lot of us face with communication is due to feeling isolated or unsafe to do so. We much prefer the simpler things in life but society promotes cutting corners and hiding from true intentions and emotions. If we are not given that bonding time from an early age, we may become too detached from emotion and struggle to make relationships. On the flip side, just like any child, if we are pampered or spoiled we will grow up ungrateful. Having lower tolerance to too much stimuli is actually useful for maintaining gratitude as long as the child isn't made to feel left out or pitied. Love Your Child You may have heard the saying â€˜There is in fact a cure for autism - unconditional love.â€™ The autistic mind cannot tolerate needless distractions from societal expectations because many of them are rather unhealthy anyway and not natural. These expectations can make us resentful if we are pressured too much and that will make us less likely to cooperate. We like things simple and direct. Instead of being angry or upset with us when we get something wrong, focus on our achievements and praise us for our effort. Appreciate the work we put in and how difficult it is and offer encouragement when needed. Be Patient This one is highly important. Autistic people need more time to process things because we are highly sensitive to our environments and have to work a lot harder to filter out stimuli and distractions that a lot of people take for granted. The more impatient you become, the more stressed we become and the less productive we are. Let us go at a comfortable pace and learn in the way that is best for us, then we will likely enjoy it more and produce better outcomes. Implement Routine and Structure Autistic individuals typically love routine and structure. We can be quite poor at thinking on our feet because we can feel pressured and overwhelmed in environments where we can't take the time to think about our options. On the contrary, having too much time to think sends us into overload because we have heaps of creative energy and this can send us spiralling into a whirlwind of decisions. Having structure distracts us from that overwhelm because it's repetitive and we don't have to spend too much energy thinking about it once it becomes a habit. It is important though that you don't create routine and structure that is too tightly time based because this can cause more overload than what no structure might. It's best to introduce something new into a routine gradually as well. Make it fun. Autistic people are highly creative but a lot of us feel fearful of stigma and suppress much of our creative energy. We have a strong distaste for anything mundane but tend to resort to it as a coping strategy for anxiety. Encourage us to use that creative energy when performing mundane tasks and introduce a special interest into that task to make it more enjoyable. We also love problem solving but hate time pressure or interruption. Let us figure out a creative solution to a problem in our own time. We love to challenge ourselves but tend to avoid doing so socially because of the attitude of others. These are the main ones I can think of. Some of them will be useful for all children but patience and routine are highly important for those in the spectrum.

question: What type of speech therapy is used for verbal toddlers with autism?
answer: Assuming the child is verbal and mostly intelligible, then language is targeted. Speech sound disorders ( articulation) are way down the list of priorities. In the school setting we worked with toddlers starting at age three. Here is a very well written article that guides best practices with autistic students as a guideline for SLPs, but is written at a level that parents and teachers can understand. 5 Principles of Speech Therapy for Children with Autism As the saying goes, if youâ€™ve met one child with autism, youâ€™ve met one child with autism. Each child with this diagnosis is completely different and will have different communicative strengths and needs. For that reason, itâ€™s impossible to set forth a single plan of action in speech therapy that will work for every child with autism. Instead, I like to use these 5 principles as a framework when decided what to work on in speech therapy with a child who has autism. 1. Establish Functional, Spontaneous Communication Your first goal with any child who has autism is to make sure that he or she can communicate functionally, and spontaneously. This means that the child needs to be able to communicate his basic wants and needs to those around him without needing to be prompted through it (the adult shouldnâ€™t have to say â€œwhat do you want?â€ or â€œuse your wordsâ€). If the child already has that down, awesome! You can move on. If not, stop here! DO NOT PASS GO, DO NOT COLLECT $200! This step is a MUST! 2. Provide Social Instruction in Various Settings throughout the Day The next thing that all children with autism will need to some degree is social instruction. Children with autism have a problem with understanding socially acceptable behavior. They donâ€™t always know how to act or behave in various social situations. Since school is basically just one big social situation, that can make learning environments especially hard for them. Direct Instruction of Socially Acceptable Behaviors: It is important to teach children what behavior is socially acceptable in various environments. This includes what the child should do and say in social situations as well as how he should listen and attend. For young children, you will target basic skills like listening to a teacher, answering questions, and following directions. For older children, you will include things like group conversations and being a good friend. Here are several strategies that have been proven effective methods of social instruction for children with autism: Visual Supports: Visual reminders placed in the room or presented by adults help the child remember the expectations for that situation. Social Stories: Books designed to teach a child the expected behavior in various situations Video Modeling: The student watches videos that demonstrate the expected behaviors 3. Target Peer Interactions Finally, since children with autism have such a difficult time with peer interactions, these must also be directly taught. All children with autism struggle with this to some extent as part of the nature of autism. However, you will target significantly different skills depending on the age and developmental level of the child you are working with. Peer Interaction Skills for Younger Children: Here are some skills for children who are just beginning their peer interaction training: Play skills: Teach the child how to play with other children and get along during play. Responding to Name: Teach the child to respond when someone says his name. Establish Joint Attention: Help children tune into those around them. Peer Interaction Skills for Older Children: These activities are better for older children who are struggling with peer interactions: Target Conversational Skills: Look at social skills that the child is lacking during normal interactions with other students and adults. Teach Perspective-Taking: Help these children understand how to see things from another perspective 4. Provide Training and Support to Other Adults, Not Just More Speech Minutes One of the most common requests I hear from parents of children with autism is â€œMy child needs more time with the speech therapistâ€. I completely understand why they want this! The speech therapist is the person who is helping their child communicate better so more time with that person should equal better communication, right? Unfortunately, thatâ€™s not exactly how it works. The Trouble with Generalizing: Children with autism tend to have trouble generalizing skills. For example, if you teach a child with autism to count to 5 using the same 5 yellow cups at the kitchen table and you never practice counting anywhere else, the child will do great at counting to 5 in that exact situation but may not be able to transfer that to counting anything else. The same goes for communication. If a speech therapist teaches a child with autism to communicate with her in the speech therapy room, it doesnâ€™t necessarily mean that the child will then start communicating with other people and in other settings. Instead, the child must practice the same communication skills with a variety of different people and in a variety of different settings. For that reason, it is vital that the child does not spend every waking moment with the speech therapist. We want the child to communicate in any situation, not just when the speech therapist is present. When the speech therapist trains the other adults, the child will make faster progress with his communication skills because he will be getting the same instruction from multiple sources and heâ€™ll be able to practice those skills in the natural environment (at home and in the classroom as opposed to just in the therapy room). How Does This Training and Support Look? Speech therapy services for children with autism can look very different depending on a lot of factors. Each speech therapist will need to determine which services will be best for each child. Here are some different ways that speech therapy services may be assigned to help the child make optimal progress: As you can see, there are many different ways to serve children with autism and you cannot just add more direct therapy minutes and expect it to help the student. Each student needs an individualized plan including a combination of different services. 5. Fine Tune Communication Skills as Other Areas Improve Finally, we look at other communication skills that may be impacting the child with autism. Once the child begins to make progress on these larger items, we can begin to address some of the smaller issues that may also be impacting the childâ€™s communication. Here are a few areas that may need to be addressed: Speech Sound Errors Errors in Grammar Problems Asking and Answering Questions Difficulty with Figurative Language THIS HAS BEEN ABRIDGED FOR THE QUORA AUDIENCE: The full article can be found here. Again, it is excellent and contains the best practices in my professional opinion. 5 Principles of Speech Therapy for Children with Autism

question: What are some signs that a toddler may be on the autism spectrum? Are there any other disorders that can mimic symptoms of ASD?

Distressed, I immediately contacted the school and arranged to meet with his teacher the following day. According to her report, she had briefly stepped out of the room to change another baby. His younger sister, who is about four and a half years younger, is also on the spectrum, but with different capabilities and nuances. Every child is unique, after all. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is indeed a specific condition with its own unique characteristics and challenges. It is important for individuals to be properly diagnosed and for professionals to accurately observe and assess the symptoms and behaviors associated with ASD. Misdiagnosis can occur when there is a lack of understanding or awareness of the condition, leading to other conditions or situations being mistaken for ASD. question: Would a toddler with autism sleep in bed with a parent or do they want to sleep alone?

question: On the autism scale, what level of functioning is an autistic toddler who rocks back and forth and bops up and down in the fetal position to sleep?

This evaluation will involve assessing the child's language and communication abilities, social interactions, cognitive skills, and adaptive functioning, as well as the presence of any repetitive or restrictive behaviors. If you are concerned about a toddler's development or behavior, it is essential to consult with a healthcare professional who can provide guidance, support, and appropriate referrals for further evaluation and intervention if needed. question: My toddler has autism and often has temper tantrums, what can I do to help him?
answer: They might not be temper tantrums. Many autistic children (and adults) have meltdowns, where they have been overloaded by too much sensory or social input, and need to dispel a massive buildup of emotions. Meltdowns are involuntary â€” the child is overwhelmed. A tantrum is a voluntary behaviour used to manipulate other people. Autistic children can have tantrums, but often their emotional outbursts reflect problems that you are not noticing. The main culprits are likely to be unexpected changes in routine or their environment, sensory stimuli that they are unusually sensitive to, or social interaction, especially with strangers. An autistic child has a brain wired differently to yours. They will experience things more intensely than you, especially loud or sudden or high pitched sounds, smells, light touch to the skin, clothing labels, the texture of certain foods, and many other things. Learning what is triggering your child may take time, but it will improve their life and your life if you can reduce their meltdown triggers.

question: What are some tips for pottytraining an autistic child?
answer: If you can identify when the child is likely on the verge of a bowel movementâ€” actually a pretty easy thing in a toddler or young child, get him to a toilet ASAP, and provide a stool his feet reach, along with a seat insert. It may make bowel movements so much more comfortable, that the child may decide always to poop in the potty after the first experience. This happened with the autistic son of a friend of mine. Peeing was a bigger struggle, but pooping was a snap. If the child does not have a lot of language, let him or her observe the same-gendered parent using the potty. That might be a little uncomfortable for the parent, but the child needs to learn what behavior is expected, and if it canâ€™t be explained verbally, this may be the only way. Whatever reward that is used, whether is it food, or five minutes of a favorite video, it must NEVER be available EXCEPT as a reward for pottying. Something that is a little controversial, but that I have seen work with older children on whom other methods have failed, is to spend a whole day not more than about 15 feet from the potty, and give the kid A LOT to drink that day, then putting the kid on the toilet every ten or fifteen minutes until he pees a little bit, and IMMEDIATELY rewarding the behavior. I have seen children who were still in diapers at 5 be nearly completely trained at the end of a day like this. It it grueling, and probably other methods should be attempted first, but if they have failed, this does work. Some children, especially boys, respond to having a target in the toilet. I know someone who got a urine specimen collection bucket (a â€œpilgrimâ€™s hat,â€ as hospital employees call it), and put it in the toilet. Her son loved peeing in it, and was thrilled to do so. He was completely trained once she got it. He also was happy to use urinals in public restrooms. The only remaining â€œproblemâ€ was bathrooms at other peopleâ€™s houses. He would try to hold his pee until he got home and could pee in his pilgrimâ€™s hat. I donâ€™t remember if she started carrying around some kind of target for him, or how she solved that, unfortunately. Night training can be a long time coming. I know parents whose children wet the bed up until age 11 or 12 unless they were gotten up at night and taken to the bathroom, but eventually they started getting up on their own, because a full bladder woke them up. Using nighttime incontinence underwear is usually not a good solution, because they donâ€™t wake up to feeling wet. If they do have accidents at night, note the time, and wake them up about 1/2 hour before their typical accident time, and then try to push the time a little closer, say 20 minutes before accident time. The idea is to wake them when their bladder is full, so they experience the feeling of waking up with a full bladder. Limiting liquids after supper may help, but might not be healthy if they have been playing outside when it is hot.

question: Is "late-onset" autism spectrum disorder/Asperger's possible?
answer: How late? I am very, very sure that lay persons quite often mistake a great many other conditions for Autism. In fact these days you can go online to almost any mom’s website, describe almost any behavior of your child, and you will immediately have a whole chorus of people insisting to you that he has Autism. Of course today the online trend is shifting so that NOW, almost any behavior will result in people insisting your child is a ‘psychopath’ or ‘sociopath’. Anyway, I have seen people insist a child had Autism when he actually had:a habit of flapping his handsspecial interestsa curiosity about dead birdsan interest in math and scienceability to draw well from an early ageshynesssocial anxietyvarious personality disordersdepressionADD/ADHDTourette Syndrome or other tic disordersOCD(Obsessive Compulsive Disorder)difficulty making friends due to mild social awkwardnesstrouble empathizing (a learned skill for all, but hard to learn when one has learning/language/communication problems)what some people call ‘attachment disorder’, when a previously neglected child is put in a healthy adoptive or foster situation and has a great deal of difficulty with relationships, emotional regulation and anxietyselective mutismintellectual disability(what we used to call ‘mental retardation’)global delay (intellectual disability with physical disability)just about any language or speech disordermental illnessblindness, deafness and other disabilitiesAutism is a developmental disorder of very early childhood. There are signs very early in life. It used to be called ‘Primary Infantile Autism’ because it was so obviously present, so early in life. If a child started having trouble at age 4, 5 years old, and had absolutely no symptoms before that, and before that was on target neurodevelopmentally and language-wise, he or she would not get diagnosed with Autism. It occasionally happens that a child is in a situation where there is no access to medical care, and thus, Autism is not diagnosed until later in life. What matters is when the symptoms emerged, not when the diagnosis was received. For a diagnosis of Autism, those symptoms must commence very, very early in life. Children can develop severe mental illness like schizophrenia at a young age(my brother in law was diagnosed with childhood schizophrenia at age 3 1/2 or 4), kids can have intellectual disabilities, and they can develop neurological disorders that affect the brain as well. In some people, symptoms of Autism are obvious from birth or very shortly after. We do know that it is present long before birth. That much is very clear. Some people have what used to be called ‘Regressive Autism’ or ‘Childhood Disintegrative Disorder’ that will start after “a period of normal development.” This was formally described in a paper by Heller in 1907. That very early period is not actually “normal,” developmentally, though, research has shown that these kids are not neurotypical during that first early period. Their developmental milestones are actually not on target. For example they will pick up a few words, but not as many as a neurotypical child would. The trouble is that the differences at that age between neurotypical and not simply are not very obvious. And then, these kids go through a period at around 2 or possibly even as late as 2 1/2 or 3, during which more severe Autism symptoms seem to hit them very hard. They lose skills, both language and social, they may have effects on their physical coordination, they quite often become very anxious, distraught and very disrupted. They often develop seizures. They often experience very severe psychotic symptoms like hallucinations (read Catalano’s book). Some have suggested a connection with familial schizophrenia or bipolar disorder since psychotic symptoms are not unusual. Clearly, their symptoms change at that key age. They seem at 2 or 2 1/2 to be more severely affected than they were at age 1 or 1 1/2. Parents are often utterly blindsided and shocked by this type of Autism. There is also Rett Syndrome, which starts to show itself at around six months, and affects mostly girls. It is a genetic ‘misspelling’ but generally not inherited from parents(that area of the same genes are not ‘misspelled’ in the parents). It has a very strong physical component as kids with Rett Syndrome tend to lose physical skills. I also believe there are children who have more severe intellectual disability, who develop seizure disorders and/or mental illness at a very early age. There are also kids who have a combination of Autism and Psychosis, from a very early age. I’ve taken care of some kids who had both Autism and Psychosis. Some of them were initially diagnosed with Autism and then diagnosis was later changed to ‘Psychosis with Intellectual Disability.’ For some years after Kanner insisted Autistic kids never had any psychotic symptoms and that the illness never overlapped with other disorders(despite some of his own patients having high rates of psychosis in their immediate family members….), the practice of rediagnosing any Autistic kids who showed psychotic symptoms, continued. At some point people realized this deprived them of programs they needed and was very detrimental to them. But also, research on the brain and genetics made such a switch demonstrably wrong and illogical. There are other conditions, other than Autism, that involve loss of skill, coordination, language skills, and these can emerge later in childhood. Some of them are:LeukodystrophySubacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (subsequent to a measles infection)Lipid Storage DiseasesTuberous SclerosisVarious mental illnesses, drugs, syndromes like FAS (Fetal Alcohol Syndrome), infections, tumors, seizure disorders, endocrine disorders and malnutrition can cause a child to develop serious symptoms that some lay people may mistake for Autism. From Dyken: subacute sclerosing panencephalitis; neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis; tuberous sclerosis with degeneration; West disease, or idiopathic degenerative encephalopathy associated with infantile spasms; Werdnig-Hoffmann disease, and hereditary spastic paraplegia. A classification is offered grouping the neurodegenerative disorders into five major categories: polioencephalopathies, leukoencephalopathies, corencephalopathies, spinocerebellopathies, and diffuse encephalopathies. Disorders in each subgroup may be either genetic or nongenetic. Neurodegenerative diseases have multiple causes, including metabolic, viral, immunopathic, environmental, and epileptogenic. The cause of many remains unknown. PMID: 6301358

question: Can parrots have autism spectrum disorders?
answer: I have long considered (and often said) that having a parrot is like living with a child who has ASD. What I mean by that is not that parrots have ASD, but that it's useful to apply the same insights about interacting with parrots to interactions with kids with ASD and vice versa. Both the kids and the parrots are behaving in ways that can seem “wrong” to neurotypicals. The “Theory of Mind” that neurotypicals rely on to explain interactions with other neurotypicals fails miserably in dealing with both parrots and autistic kids. Theory of Mind takes observations about someone else's observed behavior, expressions, etc. and uses a person's own patterns of thought and behavior to explain what's going on in the observed person's mind. If the thought patterns are similar, this is a useful shortcut for predicting behavior and knowing what other people are thinking. When a neurotypical person applies his or her own thought patterns to explain a parrot's behavior, it just leads to trouble. There are similarities to the way that neurotypical people misinterpret lack of eye contact, outbursts of “inexplicable” rage, negative reactions to touch, etc in autistic children. Theory of Mind makes people believe that their parrots or kids with autism don't love them, are deliberately disobedient, and are “not paying attention” It also predicts that certain reactions from the neurotypical person will be understood by the parrot or the kid: a reprimand, a scowl, a yell, a time-out that would have been effective for the neurotypical person is assumed to work the same way for a bird or child with very different mental “wiring,” and Theory of Mind offers the neurotypical person a reason for the miscommunication that puts the blame on the parrot or the child. It can be easier to think about a parrot's mind and how to suppress one's own Theory of Mind about bird behavior than to do the same for interactions with autistic children. But in both cases, realizing that Theory of Mind can be a handicap and learning to ignore it in favor of other ways of interacting can produce great results.
