question: What are autism, Asperger's, and Autism Spectrum Disorder?
answer: Over the past 70 years, the medical community’s understanding of autism has evolved in both definition and implication. The public’s understanding of autism has changed as well, and though misconceptions persist, it’s now widely known that autism disorders exist along a wide spectrum of ability. Autism was most recently redefined in 2013, when the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) folded all subcategories of autism into one umbrella diagnosis called Autism Spectrum Disorder. It’s defined by two categories:impaired social communication and/or interactionrestricted or repetitive behaviorsThe autism spectrum can be a difficult one to interpret given its breadth and complexity. Rather than being limited to set characteristics and behavior, disorders along the spectrum can vary infinitely in combination and presentation, like colors on a prism. Though individuals share core symptoms, those with ASD range from severely challenged to extremely gifted and everywhere in between. The spectrum: a history Though autism by name is over a century old, the spectrum it encompasses is a very modern understanding of the diagnosis. The word autism was first used in 1908 to describe a certain subset of patients deemed schizophrenic, who were characterized by withdrawn and self-absorbed behavior. Then, in 1943 American child psychiatrist Leo Kanner published research describing highly intelligent children that displayed “a powerful desire for aloneness” and “an obsessive insistence on persistent sameness.” Kanner would call these traits early infantile autism; just a year later in 1944, Hans Asperger described the milder form of autism now known as Asperger’s Syndrome. In the 60s, misinformation prevailed when the “refrigerator mother” theory emerged, spreading claims that autism was caused by unloving parents. In 1977, scientists determined the cause to be a largely genetic one, and it wasn’t until 1980 that “infantile autism” was listed in the DSM. In 1987, the DSM replaced “infantile autism” with “autism disorder,” a more expansive definition closer resembling Autism Spectrum Disorder in function. Improved diagnosis capability and new types of behavioral therapy gave hope to parents, as did the emergence of special education in schools for children on the spectrum. After more progress (expansion of diagnosis) and missteps (a now-discredited 1998 study blaming vaccines for autism), 2013 brought about the current ASD definition and the spectrum as we know it today. ASD: What it encompasses Everyone along the autism spectrum embodies, to some level, core traits associated with autism. These include difficulty with social skills, empathy, flexible behavior and communication. Along the spectrum exist disorders that have more specific definitions. These are:Classic Autism: Also simply called “Autistic Disorder,” individuals with classic autism closely characterize traits associated with the disease such as language delays, trouble with communication, and unusual behaviors and interests.Asperger’s Syndrome: Individuals with Asperger’s display milder side effects of autism. They may have some social challenges as well as unusual behaviors and interests, but lack any impairment in language or intellectual development.Pervasive Developmental Disorder (Not Otherwise Specified): Also called “atypical autism,” individuals with PDD-NOS may meet some but not all of the traits associated with autism and Asperger’s. They typically display fewer or milder symptoms, causing challenges in one area rather than several.Individuals on the spectrum also range from low to high functioning. Those with Asperger’s or PDD are more likely to be high-functioning, and may even display extreme intellect or above average IQs. Low-functioning individuals may have severe to moderate learning disabilities that may or may not be overcome with therapy. Not under the spectrum but related to it are two rare but severe conditions: Rett syndrome and childhood disintegrative disorder. Is your loved one on the spectrum? If your child or family member exhibits difficulty with social interaction or communication, or displays abnormal behaviors and interests, there is a chance they are on the autism spectrum. Early signs include a lack of language skills or unusually obsessive behaviors. Children exhibiting these characteristics should be examined by a professional team with experience diagnosing autism. It may not be immediately apparent where on the spectrum they fall (if at all), but the sooner the diagnosis the closer you will be to providing the best possible emotional and physical support. To learn more, visit the SAILS Group online at http://sailsgroup.org/blog

question: What would you rather have, autism spectrum disorder or psychopathy?
answer: Neurotypical individuals have default empathy. They normally have a feeling echoing what they think others are feeling. ASD people have cognitive empathy. We can, if we learn cues and work on relating cues to our own experiences, have a vague understanding of what other people are feeling, when we think about it. Psychopathic people have default non-empathy. Normally they do not feel what other people are feeling. NT’s can turn off their empathy, which is what allows them to engage in fights, warfare, cutting in line and other “anti social” behavior (air quotes because often those behaviors are very social indeed) Psycopaths can turn on their empathy, which is what allows them to “con” and “charm” people. They can, if they want, understand perfectly well what other people are feeling. So on the emotional/empathic front, psychopaths are closer to NTs than ASD are to either. It’s like NT’s have good hearing, but carry around safety earphones which can muffle the noise, and psychopaths have good hearing but wear their safety earphones unless they really want to hear… and ASD have terrible hearing, but carry around a hearing aid which only works if they constantly crank a hand held generator. On the empathy front, and that alone, I think I’d rather be a psychopath. It’s sort of the goal of learning to decipher all your hidden signals, if I ever learned to decode and to emulate your combination of body language, eye contact, and tone of voice, and had a lifetime of experience figuring out how to relate it to my own emotions, I’d be where they are now, able to ignore all that when I want, but to tune in when I really wanted to pay attention to it, and also able to show you my own feelings at will, rather than having to flail around vaguely hoping I’m doing something clear enough that you can get what I mean… but not having to spend every second of every day broadcasting all my emotions unless I pay attention enough to try and hide it. Learning to be NT, to be tuned in to all that all the time, would be… alien to me. I can’t relate to that. I don’t think a person who was there would be “me” any more. Even though I understand you can turn it off when it’s convenient. I’ve also spent a lifetime awash in sensations the NT aren’t even aware of, and I really don’t need one more “constantly on” input stream. There’s more to ASD than this one aspect, though, and I don’t see what psychopathy has to do with that. I would not want (although I complain about it) to lose my hypersensitivity, to go to living my life in a cocoon that stops almost all sounds, almost all sights, almost all touch, from getting in to me? Sounds like a nightmare, although of course the NT don’t know any different so they wouldn’t miss it. Losing the ability to focus on what I’m doing, being forced to pay attention to a hundred other things when I’m trying to do just one? Never again to be “obsessed” with anything, to experience all the great joys of learning and discovering and exploring something intensely? Yeah, you can keep your intuitive empathy, whether it’s default on or default off, I’m not interested in sacrificing what I have to be better at this. I’ll just stick with the cognitive empathy I’ve been working on all my life. I do OK with it. And like you with the ‘plus’ side of ASD, I don’t miss what I’ve never had. But I’m “high functioning”. I imagine there are people who fit so poorly into the principally NT world that this might really be a boon to them, for whom it might be worth any sacrifice. It can be lonely stuck in your own head, no matter how much better the acoustics are in here. I imagine. (I mean, I’m trying hard to think about how it might be for them. To relate it to my own experiences. It… doesn’t come naturally. Which is… the point.)

question: Can autism spectrum disorder cause death?
answer: Not directly. If everything is done right and the child is well looked after and supported, autism will not kill them. However, autism can come with certain risks, such as their issues with perceiving danger. An autistic child might go into the street or go with a stranger because some of them aren’t that good at telling what’s dangerous. They can be victims of police violence. If not supported (for example, if you put them in ABA, you are not supporting them and their needs,) they can try to kill themselves. Comorbid conditions such as epilepsy can also kill them. Some autistics will also tend to downplay or try to ignore issues, usually dismissing them as “just a toothache” or “a headache that will be gone with an aspirin,” which can lead to some issues not being discovered and treated until it’s too late. Or, horribly, they can be murdered by parents or guardians. Autism doesn’t cause death directly, but other issues can.

question: What is the differenec between Autism and Autism Spectrum?
answer: What is the difference between autism and ASD? Nuance and understanding, really. Consider that "autism" is a singular noun. It names "a thing" and by doing so asserts that the named thing can be specifically described. Given the nature of what it is the name purports to describe, assigning a singular noun to it required a heady mix of hubris, anxiety, bureaucracy, and probably a lot more I haven't credited. Hubris because there is no definitive test nor any definitive collection of symptomatic markers. No singular noun can possibly encompass the scope and variety of symptoms, nor can it describe when the fuzzy boundaries are crossed from autism into something similar but not autism. That we once thought we could do so belies a certain amount of arrogance and naiveté that we have hopefully outgrown. Anxiety because by giving it the name of "a thing" it is less intimidating. "Autism" sounds curable. "Autism Spectrum Disorder" sounds nebulous and hard to pin down. Collectively we act against our interest all the time because the action itself is reassuring. This is no different. We feel better trying to understand "autism" than an "autism spectrum" and to the extent that we depend on donors to fund research that matters a lot. To the extent that our research is shaped by bad terminology we act against our own interest. (Autism Speaks is the most visible example of irresponsible spin doctoring in this field. Many autistics will tell you "Autism Speaks doesn't speak for me" and I count myself among them.) Bureaucracy because everything that happens in a doctor's office is distilled down to discrete diagnostic codes. The system STRONGLY favors things that can be definitively diagnosed and described as a code. Not only is this easier for the caregivers, the office staff, the insurers, the clearing and settlement houses, the plan managers, and anyone else who handles the paperwork, but the more specific the coding, the less chance for fraud. Provide stringent criteria for "autism" and more caregivers will be in agreement about who has it and who does not. To define it as a spectrum covers a lot more territory and therefore reduces accountability. The term "autism" was always of limited use. This is obvious when we look at the plethora of alternative terms and qualifiers that sprung up around it. There's Asperger's and high functioning autism, mild autism, severe autism, profound autism, pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified (PDD-NOS), Childhood Disintegrative Disorder, Rett Syndrome, and a ton of even more informal descriptive terms. The official adoption of the term Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) seems to me to indicate that we are advancing in our understanding. Clearly it was never a single thing and apparently we are prepared to admit that now. Officially, and with enough humility to admit that we have barely scratched the surface in our understanding. But we at least now know enough to not let the scope and breadth of the autism spectrum intimidate us into picking a friendlier name for it. We can now look it in the eye and see it for the kaleidoscope that it really is. In the autism community we have a saying that if you've met one autistic you've met *one* autistic. It seems we are now better prepared to deal with autism on its own terms. As for the bureaucracy, it hasn't changed and there's still a massive incentive to distill any human being down to a collection of discrete diagnostic codes. That we are now willing to broaden the scope of the diagnostic code to better fit the condition rather than make a diverse population of humans fit into the old narrow code seems to me to be progress. Thanks for the A2A. This is all conjecture of course but as an autistic with amped up pattern recognition it all seems so obvious to me. :-) I hope you had fun reading it.

question: Could future brain surgery permanently reverse autism spectrum disorder?
answer: What we are talking about is culling autism. The book The Speed of Darkness is based on this question. Many of us that are functioning well would not wish to be culled from society. In the same way that neurotypicals think that it must be awful to be us, many of us think that it must be awful to be a neurotypical. For one thing you could kiss a lot of Quora content goodbye. Oh the silly and socially entertaining questions would all be there. As would questions such as What's the most overrated food item?; Gordon Ramsay will come to your house. You have 2 hours and $50. What will you make to impress him? The friends I have here with ASD continuously answer questions every day, day in and day out, because they get to write about their special interests. A blog like The Educational Blog would be unlikely to exist as most of the owners are on the spectrum. Then there are autistic traits I really really like such as honesty, open mindedness, hardworking, loyal. To us things like cheating on your partner are utterly unappealing as we like and love our partners and have zero interest in someone else. We just have zero interest. Our partner becomes our special interest and so we get continuous pleasure from our partner. Neurotypicals get dopamine from exposure to new people etc. But your question is whether future brain surgery could reverse autism. I would say that it is unlikely. Autism is genetic and is throughout the brain and every autistic brain is unique in its connectomes (as opposed to similarities in neurptypical brains). This would make surgery in my opinion virtually impossible as some areas are over pruned and others under pruned. In addition the brain is plastic and thus you would alter a person completely as you would need to base the brain on the neurotypical connectome schema. Autism could very likely be culled from the gene pool, however, but I think one should be wary of removing a gene that is responsible for half of Silicon Valley and many many brilliant advancements of humanity. The more optimum idea may be to prevent the occurrence of the low-functioning issues while still allowing the ‘superpowers’. However, I think that many of my skills come from my extreme sensitivity, so I am not even sure if that is an optimum solution. Ultimately genetic advancements will allow us to be able to choose the genes of our offspring. That said, without humanity beginning to understand the gifts each difference brings to society, we may end up with a society worse off than the one we currently have.

question: Can an autism spectrum disorder be so mild as to go undetected?
answer: Conditions don't have to be "mild" to go undetected. Back in the 1970s and 80s there was a major research project into Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD), and the possibility of treating it with various drugs and with Cognitive Behaviour Therapy. Before this time OCD was considered a fairly rare type of anxiety disorder. As part of the research, the team went into a number of high schools and carried out diagnostic interviews on every student to get a better idea of the incidence of OCD. They found quite a lot of students who were suffering from OCD in silence and in private, thinking they were the only ones on the planet with this weird set of symptoms. Following that time, OCD was recognised as a very common form of anxiety disorder. And OCD is not the only example. I have had misophonia ever since the 1960s, and it caused me serious problems during my teen years (and on up to the present). I even tried sneaking earplugs to the dinner table in the early 1970s so that I could block out the trigger sounds. I really thought I was the only person on the planet with this weird problem. Then in 2009 I discovered that there were thousands of people online who complained of similar or identical problems to mine - and I finally had a name for my condition. But this condition has only been named since the 1990s ("selective sound sensitivity syndrome" or "4s") and early 2000s ("misophonia"). And it is only in the last couple of years that mainstream research about misophonia has been published in journals. It has gone undetected for decades, mild and moderate and severe cases alike. So it is not surprising that I went for more than fifty years without realising I was also on the autism spectrum. But that doesn't mean that it was exceptionally mild ("so mild"), it just means that no one thought my particular issues had a name. Back when I was growing up, unless you were a "delinquent" (got in trouble with police), were caught in attempted suicide, or had a "nervous breakdown" (e.g. a very obvious meltdown before other people), or some similar dramatic problem, you were left to struggle on by yourself. You could be depressed, anxious, even suicidal for quite some time - and no one would notice.

question: Is there a link between autism spectrum disorders and ADD/ADHD?
answer: There is not yet a direct, causal, proven link. What is known is that in many children with ASD, the pruning phase of development (when neurons are said to transition from having many connections to retaining just the few necessary connections) does not unfold in a typical fashion, i.e. there are unexplained flaws in it. The theory is that a flaw in the synaptic connection pruning phase of development causes more than the desired amount of neural connections to be retained. Neuroscientists have confirmed this in autopsies of about a dozen or more children varying from 2-12. The over connected brain of these toddlers causes them to have issues with their senses,e.g. light sensitivities, sounds etc. In the case of ADHD/ADD, the exceptionally connected neurons of a toddler, for example, can be caused by the same underlying flaw that leads to sensory issues in ASD. Hope this helps establish the theorized underlying connection between the two disorders.

question: Are there any upsides to autism spectrum disorder?
answer: There are quite a number of up-sides to having autism!Heightened sensory sensitivities are often a pathway to work we love (wine-tasting, cheese-making, fragrance-blending, colour-matching, tuning instruments...)Because we have to get very good at pattern-recognition in order to manage all of the extra sensory information we receive, we tend to be very good at deciphering patterns in other complex information, mostly according to our interests.Systems thinking is a way of perceiving and interacting with the world which is highly valuable... and it's a natural for those of us in the autistic spectrum not to be able to see an item outside of its context in one inter-related whole.Outside the box creativity comes naturally when you don't read between the lines, or see the boxes that keep other people from linking disparate information into useful models and strategies.Change management capacity is highly honed by autism challenges; we have to plan our changes to make them successfully, and other non-autistics benefit tremendously from our insights into how to make changes more smoothly.Most of us autistics have a very powerful drive to make the world nicer/ better/ healthier/ cleaner/ safer, etc. My theory is that our heightened senses combine with modern global economic ugliness on all sensory levels (including emotional), and the pain of that ugliness either overwhelms us and turns us off, or inflames our stubbornness in fighting back the ugliness in whatever small corner we're most interested in.Heightened intelligence is the norm in the spectrum. Even those autistics considered "low-functioning" show up with heightened intelligence in certain areas, areas not visible in tests like the IQ, which demands verbal and written competence, as well as social awareness we often lack. And "low-functioning" is increasingly showing up as those autistics with the highest degrees of health challenge. And when health is repaired to whatever degree possible, marvelous further high-functioning abilities appear (fancy that).Most of us autistics have incredible long-term memory -- if only in the things we care most about. Fortunately, the things we develop encyclopedic knowledge about tend to grow in complexity (and in relevance to others) as we gain health and function. Agelessness, culturelessness and less-gender-defined behaviour often mean that we can effectively cross social boundaries where others cannot, or would not, thereby missing on useful connection, information, and capacity-building.Our intensely productive focus -- called monotropism -- can allow us to shut out everything except the single thing we are paying attention to. question: Why is Autism Spectrum disorder controversial?
answer: That’s a good question. Since I only learned I was living on the Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) nearly a year ago at 58 years of age, I have wondered that question myself. Before my diagnosis, I only knew about ASD through my job as a substitute teacher’s aide where I sometimes am assigned to autism units. According to what I learned on Wikipedia, diagnoses of autism have become more frequent since the 1980s, which has led to various controversies about both the cause of autism and the nature of the diagnoses themselves. Is the cause of autism genetic or developmental? Is the a degree of coincidence between autism and intellectual disability? There is the controversial theory that vaccines cause autism. However, scientific consensus holds firm that vaccines don’t cause autism and I am on their side on this issue. I’m more inclined to think the cause is genetic. There are other members of my extended family who have been diagnosed or who I suspect are on the autism spectrum. According to the Wikipedia article, genetics is viewed as an underlying factor because there is a statistical pattern for a significantly high risk to have another autistic child in families with an already affected child. I know personally of a family with triples, 2 boys and 1 girl, who are all on the autism spectrum. One of the 2 boys is nonverbal but his siblings are verbal. However, while some parents of autistic children are progressively also being diagnosed on the autism spectrum, at least some autistic children have apparently NT parents. This suggests to some that genetics are either not a necessary cause or that they don't play a part in all cases of ASD. The spectrum of autistic disorders is notable for its significant gender disparity, with the incidence of autism in males greatly exceeding the incidence in females. Whilst this could be evidence for a genetic theory, it has also been argued that male brains may be more vulnerable during early development. I think there’s more females who are on the Spectrum but just aren’t diagnosed. I think it is harder to detect than it is in males. I hope this helps to answer your question.

question: Do people with autism spectrum disorders experience the uncanny Valley?
answer: That’s a really good question. The important thing to understand about the uncanny valley is that it’s a concept that has never really been tested. It’s just generally accepted because it “feels about right.” A lot of questions haven’t been answered.Does everyone have it?Is the “geography” of the valley the same for everyone?Can it change over time for a given person?I’m going to guess that everyone on the spectrum has at least a bit of uncanny valley. It’s going to vary a lot from person to person, but it does seem to be much much smaller (perhaps an uncanny ditch) for autistic folks on average. I think we’re also more prone to normalizing the things that other people find uncanny. What we find uncanny at first just becomes a quirky feature later. I think this partly explains the observation that certain fandoms contain a higher than average percentage of people on the spectrum. These are fandoms with anthropomorphized or exaggerated human characters, like anime, furry, brony, etc. The fact that these characters “look weird” is much less likely to bother us.

question: What autism spectrum disorder do you have?

question: What are some extreme misconceptions about people with autism spectrum disorders?
answer: I am the first neurotypical person so far to answer this question, and a parent of a low-functioning autistic child. The most extreme misconception about autism, as far as I am concerned, is the belief that high-functioning autism is the only kind of autism there is. Most of the general public imagines autistic individuals as uniformly intellectually typical, but with certain mild sensitivities and “personality quirks”, usually in the vein of sphinx-like aloofness. Low-functioning autistics, most of whom cannot speak for themselves, might as well not exist. Most literature aimed at “raising awareness” of autism either omits low-functioning autism, or mentions it only in passing. This creates the impression that autism is a mild condition, and perhaps should not be regarded as a disability at all. Also, that parents who pursue treatments for their autistic children are sadists and abusers who do not care for their children’s well-being and are only serving their own ego. Here is a particularly egregious example of what I’m talking about:Applied behavior analysisABA (Applied Behavior Analysis) is a controversial and pseudoscientific therapy that uses an aversion and/or reward system on autistic children, in which a desired behaviour is rewarded, while the disapproved behaviour is harshly punished.[1] Some ABA therapists refuse to participate in the aversion side of ABA, instead focusing on reward and praise to improve the behavior of autistic children.[2]https://rationalwiki.org/wiki/Applied_behavior_analysisa “rational” article that falsely suggests that ABA, one of the most prevalent therapies for autism, involves deliberately subjecting autistic individuals to harmful and unpleasant stimuli as punishment, and torturing them with hot peppers and bleach. It condescendingly advises parents that they should reconcile themselves to the fact that autism is incurable (thanks for the info! I had no idea!), that the only legitimate therapy for autism is consultation with a psychologist (no explanation as to how a psychologist is supposed to help someone who is non-verbal and has very limited receptive speech), and that perhaps the best course of action is to just let autistic children be autistic. I cannot even begin to discuss how wrong this is. ASD is a large spectrum, and there are tremendous variations among autistic individuals. I have no doubt there are some who can function independently, experience only mild limitations, and as a result, do not accept the label of ASD and do not believe they ever needed therapy. However, along these high-functioning individuals, low-functioning autistic individuals also exist. For the latter, autism is a pervasive developmental disorder that creates severe neurological and cognitive limitations in addition to emotional and social ones. Many low-functioning individuals are non-verbal or have severe speech limitations. Many have an array of neuropsychological problems, including poor sleep, aggression and food sensitivities so severe, it is hard for them to maintain a healthy diet. Stiffness, poor coordination and poor balance are often present. Simply training a low-functioning autistic individual to use the toilet is a colossal undertaking that can take years. To simply “let them be autistic” is not an option when it comes to low-functioning individuals; helping them improve their functioning is absolutely necessary to give them greater independence and improve their quality of life. To ignore the existence of these people on the ASD, or to trivialize the seriousness of their condition, is insensitive and cruel. Frankly, from my perspective as a mother of a low-functioning child with autism, minimizing the disorder as just its highest-functioning subset is like describing cancer as a skin tag.

question: Should autism spectrum disorder be removed from the DSM? I am curious because I know that several people on the autism spectrum certainly have no need to be cured.
answer: As long as people with ASD need treatment and support to thrive and even survive, a diagnosis will be needed. Children getting support in schools, adults getting placement in assisted living or a full-time carer, employment placement, disability accommodations at work, and disability financial support such as SSI all require a diagnosis. A diagnosis is also helpful in getting therapies that help with ASD’s particular issues — a diagnosis is a tool for professionals to fine-tune their approach, not a mark of shame. Disability is not a bad thing, it just indicates what one can and cannot do. It helps people know what they are dealing with. I was diagnosed at age 49. A doctor once told me that I could not be autistic because I had a spouse, a job, and didn’t have that “weird way of talking.” (this was after the diagnosis) He was not there for the years of speech therapy, anger management therapy, and cognitive therapy. He didn’t see me getting bullied in school, teachers telling my Mom I was retarded, failed relationships, people yelling at me for reasons I didn’t understand, long periods of unemployment or minimum wage jobs, bankruptcy, and getting passed over for promotions because of unspoken rules and disorganization. Every lesson I learned was at the cost of pain and often failure. A diagnosis back then would have been so much help, even if it was just to know what the issue was. I can understand some people on the spectrum not wanting a cure, but that is not does not mean there are not other ways to be helped. It also doesn’t take into consideration the much more profoundly disabled autistics who can never live independently, have intellectual disabilities, may be nonverbal, and even do basic self-care. I know of some people with ASD who WOULD take a cure if they could — I figure, if someone doesn’t want it, they don’t have to take it. Usually for those who want it, they want to get rid of more troubling symptoms: sensory overload, unable to read nonverbal communication, or executive functioning issues, without getting rid of more positive aspects, like the way they think and perceive the world.
comment_answer: You can’t cure ASD. You can only support the people with it. For every person with high functioning Autism there are people who have low verbal ability and intellectual disabilities and are unable to live independentantly.

question: What social cues do people with Autism spectrum disorder miss?
answer: Subtle interpersonal cues Into adulthood I didn’t get how wrong it is to just sit down with a group of strangers and introduce myself. I’d learned the lesson a few times. But every once in awhile I’d fool myself this time I can be natural and they’ll accept me. Nerp. I often held people in a too-idealistic light. I am a bit intuitive, but didn’t understand. So I’d be unaware I’d be tuning into the one topic they didn’t want to discuss. Whatever was really bugging them at the time, I’d blather on about it. I was terribly needy and people-pleasing. It didn’t occur to me how annoying that might be. Too many times to count I missed some known cues that this information is secret. If I wasn’t told directly to shut up about something, I’d miss cryptic references or gestures. Was this neurodiversity or the result of minimal healthy human contact? Most of this behavior is in the past. It’s likely it’s trauma healed. But it’s also likely neurodiverse people experience a far higher rate of abuse and trauma than others. I was unable to really read the room and understand it. Or how the real world worked. Like, everyone who lives in the same apartment building must all be pals. There’s a disconnect I can’t seem to totally fix. Logically I’m on top of it now. But I still have to fight this uber-naive nature they tell me is from being neurodiverse.

question: What symptoms are present in an "autism spectrum disorder" diagnosis?
answer: In plain English, autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disability that can affect the ways a person interacts, communicates, and behaves. As I understand it, the spectrum itself exists on two axes:Deficits in social interaction and social communication. Known as Criterion A symptoms.Restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. Known as Criterion B symptoms.So, really, the autism spectrum itself looks like this:Less of a linear spectrum, and more like a pie chart. In all forms of ASD, the symptoms one is experiencing is rated by levels numbering 1–3. Level 3 requires very substantial support, level 2 requires substantial support, and level 1 requires support. This is where people get the idea of “low” and “high functioning” labels from, but that’s misleading. These merely just describe the levels of support this person might need with how they experience ASD. There is no low or high-functioning autism. There is just autism, and it’s important to understand that ASD requires support. Some only need a little, some need a lot. Remember, if you know someone that’s autistic, then you’ve met only one person that’s autistic. Everyone’s unique. The DSM-V describes the Criterion A symptoms as:Socially Awkward. Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, ranging, for example, from abnormal social approach and failure of normal back-and-forth conversation; to reduced sharing of interests, emotions, or affect; to failure to initiate or respond to social interactions.Strange Way of Interacting With People. Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction, ranging, for example, from poorly integrated verbal and nonverbal communication; to abnormalities in eye contact and body language or deficits in understanding and use of gestures; to a total lack of facial expressions and nonverbal communication.Overly Logical. Deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships, ranging, for example, from difficulties adjusting behavior to suit various social contexts; to difficulties in sharing imaginative play or in making friends; to absence of interest in peers.The DSM-V describes the Criterion B symptoms as:Stimming. Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech (e.g., simple motor stereotypes, lining up toys or flipping objects, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases).Love of Rules and Routines. Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, or ritualized patterns of verbal or nonverbal behavior (e.g., extreme distress at small changes, difficulties with transitions, rigid thinking patterns, greeting rituals, need to take same route or eat same food every day).Hyper-fixated Interests. Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus (e.g., strong attachment to or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessively circumscribed or perseverative interests).Sensitivity to Sensory Stimuli. Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g. apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement).The bold parts are a more simplified and practical view of the rather overly clinical way of describing the symptoms. So when observing someone you think might be autistic, you’re looking for someone that’s a bit socially awkward, has a strange way of interacting with people when they’re being social, they come off as a bit too literal and logical minded, leading to misunderstandings and issues, they engage in stimming behavior a lot, they crave schedules, routines, and rules, and changing them suddenly causes them distress, they have what we call special interests, or very laser focused interests that can sometimes lead to an uneven skill set, and finally, look for sensory issues. Not every autistic person is going to experience all of these symptoms, and some will be more intense than others. Think of the first three symptoms as how they interact with other people, and the final four symptoms as how they act when they’re by themselves. To meet the diagnostic criteria, the DSM-V requires that you meet all three Criterion A symptoms, and you meet two of the Criterion B symptoms. Also, for these to be classified as symptoms, they must be pervasive, the symptoms were present from early childhood, and they limit or impair everyday functioning. Those are the additional criteria for this to be considered Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). It’s up to the clinician to describe the severity of the symptoms, and every person is going to be unique, thus, that’s why autism is a spectrum disorder. Everyone experiences it a bit differently, and as a result, they’ll require different levels and kinds of support. Some will need a little support, some will need a lot. I know this was a bit more of a clinical way of looking at ASD, but the plain English way of looking at it is that an autistic person is:Socially awkward.They have a strange way of interacting with people.They come off as too logical or literal minded, leading to misunderstandings and issues.They engage in stimming behavior a lot.They love rules, routines, and structure, and any change causes distress.They have special interests that are very intense, sometimes to the point of them having an uneven skill set.They have sensory processing issues. They’re either really sensitive to sensory stimuli, or not sensitive at all to sensory stimuli.I hope that gives a very straightforward way of looking at autism. I know clinicians and us autistics tend to use clinical and precise language to describe the condition, but sometimes such language goes over people’s heads. Hope this helps!Originally answered: What symptoms are present in an "autism spectrum disorder" diagnosis?

question: How much does it typically cost to get a formal diagnosis of an autism spectrum "disorder"?
answer: There is no need to spend thousands. First of all, you can look at the diagnostic criteria yourself, making sure there are symptoms in both the social communication area AND the second area: repetitive behaviors/restricted interests and sensory issues. I can't find the correct version of the criteria online (everyone is using the draft criteria) so I just now posted them here for you: Diagnostic Criteria for ASD (now officially including Asperger's). There are screening instruments that do cost money for an agency to implement; but the ones that are the most valid are the ones that stick most closely to the criteria. You don't need to use a psychiatrist or even a psychologist: I'm a clinical social worker, and there are speech and language pathologists and others with expertise in ASD. They can help not only diagnose but understand how the symptoms reveal something about the mind, which is a start of being helpful. There is no need for a brain scan or any fancy equipment, though there are some screening activities that are helpful. Someone should interview the parents and get information from teachers (or day care providers or employers), and then interact with the person with possible ASD. Two sessions are a solid start, which means under $250 total, although that's just the beginning if you then are going to get help guiding development and making improvements in coping and interacting. If no improvements are needed, if there are no problems to be solved, then it is not a "disorder", even if all the behaviors and differences are there: Diagnosing a disorder requires that there be some level of distress or impact on functioning (getting a job, getting along with people) that needs to be addressed in treatment. I mention this last point only because you've put quotes around "disorder;" you may be referring to the idea that autistic ways of thinking and behaving do not need to be thought of as a DISorder, only a different order, if the person is getting along happily in life.

question: What is it like to have an autistic parent?
answer: I spent the first half my life living with a very confusing woman. As a child, I took some pride in the fact that my mum was not like other mums. I don't recall her ever picking me up from school, turning up to parent teacher interviews or chatting with my friends parents. Instead, she got involved in her own way, making giant crepe paper butterfly wings for a Book Week costume or sewing her old diamante necklaces onto my shoes for the end of year play. She was great like that. But for those first twenty years living under her roof, I could have done without the extreme states of panic that I'd often find myself in, wondering why I had dared disagree with her or messed with the routine. Those transgressions would send her into a monster rage from which she would eventually withdraw for the rest of the evening. My dad and my sister would give me furtive looks for setting her off again. I'd hide in the bedroom and pick nits off the cat. The thing is, no one knew she was autistic. She didn’t know herself. And no one got help. Only now, with a greater level of understanding about autism, through forums like this, I can finally make sense of my childhood and put her delightful, unconventional, confusing and upsetting behaviour into context. Obviously, some of what follows can possibly be attributed more to her personality than to autism per se – it is impossible to separate the two, but here is my take on living with an undiagnosed autistic parent. It can be:Brutally honest – she once told my little sister she would never win a beauty pageant. She blurted out she didn’t like dogs when an old uncle tried to give us a book on them.Structured and stable – the house ran like clockwork. Everything was tidy and in its place. Heaven help you though if you left for school 2 minutes late or didn’t set the table on time.Full of mild disasters – she cut her fingers while cooking more often than I can count and her clumsiness was the stuff of legend.Embarrassing – she had no fear in loudly voicing how much she detested cigarette smokers, for example.Isolating – she struggled to make friends or get along with my dad’s family, so I didn’t get to play with my cousins or participate in broader family events very much.Magical – she was far more creative and a bit goofy compared to other mums, setting up themed birthday parties for instance (although she always seemed to get the flu at the last moment and hide in her bedroom when my friends arrived).Lacking in social norms – my sister and I would eat at a table in the bedroom because she couldn’t cope with the chaos and noise we made at the dinner table.Like walking on eggshells - to avoid meltdowns, which were scary.Lacking in cuddles – I can’t sugar coat this one either. I reckon I have had to work through my fair share of attachment issues as an adult. She used to brush my hair though, which I craved.Aspiefying – is that a word? It was easier for my dad, sister and I to adopt her routines and opinions for the sake of harmony. If you had an emotional, teenage problem, you had to ‘get over it’ on your own.Inspiring – watching her defy all her fears, enroll in university, spend months studying at her desk and graduate inspired me to do the same. She also had an innate sense of fairness and took jobs fighting for social equity.Quite poignant – I watched her weep as she listened to a bunch of kids sing like angels at Carnegie Hall once. Her emotions would just bubble up in beautiful ways sometimes.Full of cats – cats kept her calm.As a result of such a childhood, I became a highly autonomous, over achiever. I have an uncanny ability to read peoples moods and I obsessively seek out cuddles from my own kids these days. But I have also had to teach myself certain social norms and progressively drop some of the unhelpful Aspie traits that I had acquired. I genuinely hope it is easier for the next generation of parents and kids. I imagine it will be, given there is a lot more help at hand.

question: Do a significant number of people misdiagnose themselves as having Autism Spectrum Disorder?
answer: ASDs are common and are being talked about a lot, so yes, people do mistakenly self-diagnose. First let’s look at the reasons behind self-diagnosis. Self-diagnosis is what happens when someone who cannot, or does not want to, get a professional diagnosis does the best they can with the information they can get. Self-diagnosis is not uncommon; consider what happens if you wake up with a sore throat, runny nose, and headache—you probably self-diagnose a cold, and you’re probably right. Even if it turns out you actually have allergies, your symptoms are mild enough that you really didn’t need to see a doctor. That’s the ideal situation. But self-diagnosis is also something people resort to when they cannot get a doctor. Maybe they don’t have medical care, or they can’t get in to see a specialist. In some cases, they are working in fields where anti-disability prejudice is significant to the point that if people knew you had autism, you might lose your job. These cases are more like being lost in the woods, falling, feeling pain in your arm and seeing that it’s bent the wrong way; you self-diagnose a broken arm, and you might have to splint it yourself because you can’t get to a doctor and you don’t know when you’ll be able to. If you actually have a dislocated joint, but self-diagnose a broken arm, you may be in for a world of hurt. If someone has self-diagnosed an autism spectrum disorder, they’ve done it because something is causing them enough distress that they have motivation to try to put a label on it, understand it, and address it. So if someone self-diagnoses autism, they have something… it may be autism; it may not be. They may be the equivalent of the person with the cold—they have autism, but it’s quite mild, and they’re coping well because of a good support system or good coping skills. In some environments, people with mild autism can get along rather well—for example, academia, engineering, computer science. These are orderly, information-focused environments, and if a person happens to be autistic and has a talent for these fields, they might just be seen as unusually nerdy and never really need much help. Or they could be like the person who thinks they have a cold, but actually have allergies. These are people who have problems that are relatively mild, but aren’t actually autism. The milder varieties of social anxiety are in this category. Some people who are really just introverts, but who live in an environment where introversion is stigmatized, might wonder if they are autistic not because they have an actual disability but because people expect them to be extroverts; so they’re suffering not from a mental condition but from the way they are treated by others. Some people who are habitually targeted by bullying and harassment may begin to withdraw socially and end up in the same boat. So in these situations, there’s a real problem, but it isn’t severe, and it isn’t autism. But luckily, since the problem is mild, they may have so much in common with people who really are mildly autistic that a lot of the same strategies will work for them. The person with the broken arm, who self-diagnoses a broken arm, is in a worse situation, and so is the person who has autism and self-diagnoses autism but can’t get an official diagnosis. This is a person whose autism is significantly disabling, but who can’t get treatment for it. They may be desperate to keep their job, or they may be poor and unable to get medical care, or they may have (ironically) been misdiagnosed by a professional as having some other disorder and been stereotyped by the mental health system as having this disorder. I once met a man who was in his late 30s, newly diagnosed with autism. He had gone for over ten years diagnosed with “schizophrenia”, even though he had never had psychosis. His atypical communication style made his doctor think “schizophrenia”, and once that was on his record, nobody questioned it. He self-diagnosed autism and basically had to go on a quest to get a proper evaluation—which he eventually did, with a child psychiatrist. Not everybody is as lucky as he is. People in this situation have to do the best they can with the resources they have. Without access to mental health care or therapy, they may end up homeless; the lucky ones get the help they need from friends and family. Some stay independent for some time, but because they’ve had to work so hard at it, they burn out and “crash” and are often diagnosed with depression. The situation of the person who thinks they have a broken arm but actually have a dislocated joint is probably worst of all, and a person who has a severe problem that isn’t autism, but self-diagnoses autism, can be in a lot of trouble. The big problem for these folks is that they have a serious issue, but they can’t get help for it, so they’ve done their best and come up with autism even though it isn’t actually autism. They might have OCD, ADHD, learning disabilities, speech/language disorders; it could be schizophrenia or a personality disorder masquerading as autism. It’s a tough situation to be in, without a correct label for the problem you’re trying to deal with. It’s marginally better than pretending the problem doesn’t exist, because at least if you self-diagnose autism incorrectly, you will still apply strategies that work for most mental illnesses and neurological disabilities—things like maintaining a support network, using reminders and checklists to supplement poor executive function, and connecting with other people who are also disabled to benefit from mutual support and share strategies. In a perfect world, anybody with a serious problem would get treatment for it, but that doesn’t always happen. When people who are “neurotypical with autistic traits” self-diagnose as autistic despite not being disabled, all you get is somebody who’s got a lot in common with autistic people identifying with autistic culture. That hurts nobody. Nor does it hurt anybody if somebody with mild autism self-diagnoses. But when people with serious problems can’t get medical care, they can end up homeless or even dead. Self-diagnosis isn’t the problem; it’s only a person doing their best to deal with the real problem—that is, the lack of access to care and the stigma involved in getting help.

question: Is it normal for people with ASD (Autism Spectrum Disorder) to have days-long headaches? Why?
answer: Along with being high-functional autistic, I suffer with what my GP and I have always felt are migraines, which have lasted up to a week at a time before now, and cause significant problems for me beyond the issue of pain - they can cause blindness, hypersensitivity, and various what are termed "halo" effects (sensory hallucinations) Over the course of several years we've done a lot of work to try and establish what causes them and how to effectively manage the issue as he actually specialised in Migraines when studying for his MD way back when, and so he's enjoyed being able to study it with a willing and I hope reasonably competant guinea pig. What I do find interesting, and had never really considered prior to spotting this question a few minutes ago, is that a lot of the triggers I have for migraines are the same as the ones that would normally stress me out and see me in need of retreat. Bright lights are a bad thing for me (summer is essentially "migraine season" for me) lack of/too much sleep and an interrupted routine are great ways to put me at risk, and dealing with complicated social situations doesn't just mess me up in terms of being ASD, a few hrs later I can find myself clutching the sides of my head as a new migraine threatens to take the top of my head off. I guess it makes sense really - a lot of headaches and migraines are caused by things which cause our bodies physical or emotional stress, and can be mitigated against by using the same management techniques to control stress that we would use in managing ASD. The honest answer is, "I don't know"... but there does seem to have been a lot of study into the issues being co-morbid which is suggestive that people seem to think the problems going hand in hand, and from personal experience, I can certainly see how that would work.

question: Is autism spectrum disorder a personality disorder?

The biggest issue with ODD as a diagnosis at all is that once you get it, you can’t question it, or you just look like a person with ODD being defiant for the sake of being defiant. ADD/ADHD Stimming can look like fidgeting. Being distracted by talkative classmates or a loud fly can look like an inability to focus on schoolwork. A headache from fluorescent lighting can look like work was just too overwhelming. There are so many things that we notice that others don’t, and when we focus on those things instead of a piece of paper with math equations, someone says we have ADHD. Psychosis: I was 17 years old, speaking to a psychiatrist in the hospital about a rape that had happened to me a few months back. The nurse had just given me a blood test a few minutes ago, something that still had me shaken. Everything about this particular unit was terrifying to me- there were horrible things scribbled on the walls in Sharpie, and everyone else in the unit had slashes across their wrists. I wasn’t in a good place when the psychiatrist, who had barely glanced at my file, scribbled down “psychosis?” in the notes on her lap. “Psychosis” is marked by a deep disconnection from reality that results in anxiety and depressive disorders. There are several symptoms associated with ASD that can be mistaken for symptoms of psychosis, including:HallucinationsIf other people don’t notice the things that make you sensitive, they may not think there’s anything there in the first place.Some people with autism, including myself, have had a history of talking to ourselves. I did it almost every day as a child, until someone bullied me for it. I still have mental “conversations” but have learned not to let it show- other people don’t respond to it well. It’s not a hallucination because we know there isn’t another person/thing there.Disorganized SpeechMany of us on the spectrum find it hard to articulate our thoughts. This can include an inability to verbalize a connection from one topic to another. If a thought is organized, and you present it wrong, it can look disorganized, and that’s what’s happening with some of us with ASD.SuspiciousnessIt’s not a secret that people with ASD are treated worse than the average person. We’re more likely to be bullied, abused, assaulted, raped, you name it. Anyone with a history of being the victim of criminal behaviour is going to have their guard up around new people. Anyone who went through such things would be just as suspicious.Anxiety and/or DepressionCo-morbid anxiety and depression are far more common in people with ASD than in the general population. Having, say, generalized anxiety disorder is not psychosis, but having it can stockpile a psychiatrist’s suspicion that one has psychosis if undiagnosed and combined with too many other misunderstood symptoms.That said, I hold some skepticism when it comes to a depression diagnosis. Depression as a diagnosis suggests a chemical imbalance, but it’s always good to check outside factors before medicating what could be a response to a set of unhappy circumstances.I fit almost all the checklist symptoms for depression from the ages of 12–18, and then 100% of those symptoms vanished when I moved out of my parents’ house. I guarantee that the air in my boyfriend’s house is not any different from what I breathed in my parents’ house.If one person can face that much confusion in the eyes of professionals, you bet almost every psychiatric condition in the book is being placed wrongly onto someone with ASD somewhere.

question: What are the key differences between autism spectrum disorder and Asperger syndrome?
answer: It differs in onset, intelligence and presence of developmental delays from other autism spectrum disorders. Asperger typically has an onset around the toddler-age, while other ASDs can be observed in infants as early as one year and prior. What distinguishes Asperger from other forms of autism is the absence of language delays, as well as no intellectual handicaps. If you’d look at HFA for example, there is the language delay, but no intellectual impairement. Kanner’s syndrome or “classic, infantile autism” shows both, language delays and intellectual retardation or borderline-retardation (IQs <70). That does not mean that those with Asperger don’t face similar issues in terms of social behavior and communication. Given the intelligence and lack of speech delays, they may come off as normal or neurotypical at first, but their autism may become visible exactly due to this assumption that they are NT. Coming off as normal at first glance attracts social attention, but this focus on the person only reveals their autism to others. This in turn oftentimes causes social exclusion or ostracism, and the person with the condition to start masking their symptoms, which can be very draining and not fulfilling.

question: What percent of people with high Autism-Spectrum Quotients have Autism Spectrum disorders?
answer: Among adults, my guess is that many, many people with high ASD quotients have never been diagnosed with ASD. Among children, I think it would be the opposite. ASD is being over-diagnosed in schools and pediatrics now, as the pendulum has swung strongly to erring on the side of treating all children who could possibly have ASD rather than risk missing one child with ASD, especially at the level of early intervention (age 1-5). It's very similar to what happened with learning disabilities in the 1980's and ADHD in the 1990's. Eventually the pendulum will swing back to the middle and we will manage to more correctly diagnose children who actually do have an ASD, and the ASD quotients will more closely match people with the diagnosis. Of course, then there's the question of how accurate the ASQ rating scale is..... And then there's the question of what defines ASD, where the line is drawn, whether ASD is a disability or an ability, and where the line that causes it to be a "disorder" should be drawn. Is it a disorder to be socially awkward but intellectually gifted? Is it a disorder to be hypersensitive to ambient sensory stimuli but have a photographic or instant-replay memory? More questions than answers still exjst with the autism spectrum, but at least people are looking at and thinking about the issue.

question: Is autism spectrum disorder, a disability, or a gift?

question: What mental disorders are on the autism spectrum?
answer: First of all, autism spectrum disorder is NOT a disease. It is a collection of behaviors. The way we determine if a person is on the autism spectrum is to assess the degree to which these behaviors occur and the severity to which they impede a person’s ability to function. The three broad areas in which we see functional difficulties are: 1. Repetitive/restrictive patterns of behavior in which change/transitions to different activities are very difficult. Repetitive behaviors can include head-banging, rocking, spinning. It is thought that the person doing this is on sensory-overload and these behaviors mask the overwhelming sensory input and help the person self-sooth. The need for organization and structure (such as lining up toys in a certain, deliberate way is also felt to be a way to organize a world that the person with autism feels is chaotic. Transitions from one activity to another can also be difficult. 2. Social interaction - This can range from having very little interest in interacting with other people to not understanding how to read social signals. People with autism often make conversation about their interests and are completely unaware that their listeners have stopped being interested or are trying to change subjects. 3. Verbal/non verbal communication skills- This can range from totally non-verbal and relying on gestures to request what is wanted (which is very inefficient and ineffective) to being able to make sentences, but being unable to answer basic questions or maintain the topic of conversation. There is a lot of overlap in these areas. Let me make it clear that just because a person loves to talk about his interests or loves to keep all her cans of vegetables in a certain order, it does not mean that that person is on the spectrum. It takes observation and assessment (there are tests and checklists) to see if there is a preponderance of behaviors and to see to what degree the presence of those behaviors impede a person’s ability to function in the “real world” that helps make a determination of whether or not a person is on the spectrum. And in some “mild” cases it may be a professional judgement call. I feel that as we study the genome we discover a variety genetic/metabolic disorders that result in people exhibiting characteristics of autism. There is already some evidence of this in on-going research.

question: Can kids with autism spectrum disorder not ride a bike?
answer: Q: “Can kids with autism spectrum disorder not ride a bike?” There is no specific disorder called ‘autism spectrum disorder’. I think that is the point. The mainstream colludes in pretending that there is a ‘spectrum’ (of what? Autism? What’s that?) on which one can locate various diagnoses. Childhood autism is often a very severe disability, which can extend to delayed or absent speech development, and several other difficult symptoms like intense anxiety and paranoia. So called ‘high functioning autism’ is supposed to occupy a milder end of this spectrum - although it might be hard to explain why - and need not produce noticeable symptoms or difficulties at all, although when there are, they tend to include negative effects on social interaction. A young child with typical childhood autism might struggle with some aspects of riding a bike - the letting go required in a two-wheeler perhaps - but not necessarily. Nothing is cut and dried; but the idea of a ‘spectrum’ was meant to tidy this all up.

question: Why is autism spectrum disorder very diverse?
answer: Autism diverse because autistic people can be affected by many other diagnoses in addition to autism. People forget about co-occurring diagnoses and speak of autism as if it were the only diagnosis that can affect a person with it. They see it as a standalone diagnosis. It isn’t. There are many comorbid or co-occurring conditions. My adult son is autistic. He also has several “bonus” diagnoses. That’s my way of referring to the comorbid diagnoses with a bit of levity. In addition to being autistic, he has verbal apraxia of speech; he is nonverbal. He also has epilepsy. Did you know up to 30% of autistic people also have a seizure disorder? Of course that also means that 70% of autistic people do not. However, it is so much higher than in the general population that it’s considered “comorbidity“. Imagine how having any comorbidity could affect your life. You can’t drive if you have frequent breakthrough seizures due to your epilepsy. And epilepsy is just as stigmatized as autism, if not more so. Think about what it would be like if you couldn’t physically speak, you would have to learn a new way to communicate. Think about if you were affected by intellectual disability. There in lies the diversity of autism. It is the other neurological conditions that bring about diversity on the spectrum. Intellectual disability, speech disorders, anxiety, headaches, OCD, epilepsy, learning disabilities, intellectual disability, the list of co-occurring conditions goes on and on. Now ifyou’re autistic, people will look at your neurology as if it were all one thing: the autism. They will attribute everything to the autism when it is much more complex than that. Before everybody gets their panties in a bunch, this does not mean that an autistic person is necessarily affected by any of these. Many autistic people are not. It’s that interplay between autism and other conditions that makes the spectrum diverse. These just happen to be diagnosed more often in autistic people. When they are, those characteristics are often attributed solely to autism. People are far more complex than just autism. question: Do people with autism spectrum disorders tend to be impractical?

question: Why are individuals with very high functioning autism spectrum disorder said to have an "invisible disability?" What are some examples?

I graduated from University with honors, I have a stable job and a family, and would appear to most people as a fairly ordinary person. question: Do most INTPs have autism spectrum disorder?
answer: All INTPs I’ve known in person exhibit some form of ASD, mostly symptoms of ADHD. Online polls also associate the introverted iNtuitives to autism, up to a point that being in the spectrum seems to be more of a rule than an exception for the introverted NT-NF types. But here is the thing: if most INTP’s can be observed to exhibit ADHD or autism, then wouldn’t it make sense to consider it a phenotypic trait of the INTP’s, instead of a disorder? A phenotype is an individual's observable traits, such as height, eye color, or blood type. Autism should be considered a trait of an INTP phenotype, because it is frequently and systematically exhibited by the INTP’s worldwide. Autism may be even be hereditary and caused by genetics, It certainly is not an developmental disorder as it is commonly referred to. I personally do not think that ADHD or autism are disorders (as it has been painted by the psychiatric literature), in a sense that the common usage for the word “disorder” implies that a person is “out of order”. This leads to a culturally widely adopted notion that a person that exhibits a “disorder” differs from others and their behaviour is therefore abnormal. But one autistic person might not even know another is autistic, because the manifestations are quite different and it isn’t obvious to them. Psychological diagnosis is doing it partly based on people matching some subset of symptoms.. it may be that technically there are different conditions, and they just happen to sometimes occur together. Neuro-science could provide more answers in the future.

question: In what ways is interacting with animals similar to interacting with those who have autism spectrum disorders/Asperger's?
answer: When I was a kid, I wanted a pet parrot. Then I heard that keeping a parrot as a pet required trimming their wing feathers so that they could not fly. I already had pets that couldn't fly, so that really diminished my enthusiasm for the idea. Plus it just didn't seem humane to reduce a bird to a pedestrian creature. But about ten years ago I learned that you can keep parrots as pets without clipping their wings, you just have to train them. This doubled my enthusiasm for the idea. Not only could I have a flying pet, I could - would need to - learn to communicate with my flying pet. One of the problems with flying pets is that if they don't like you, you can't get near them. So you have to stay on very good terms with them, and that can be a challenge when they're chewing on your furniture. So I started doing my homework on animal training, in preparation for introducing a flying animal into my home. Curiously, one of the leading figures in the field of parrot training also happens to be a leaning figure in the field of people training (http://www.psychologytoday.com/experts/susan-friedman-phd). Dr. Susan Friedman ran (maybe still runs?) an email discussion list about Applied Behavior Analysis, or ABA. This is a set of ideas and practices that were originally developed for use with humans, which also happen to be a fantastic set of tools for understanding and modifying animal behavior (which is a fancy way of saying "training, via communication"). And ABA is also widely used by people who work with (or are parents of) children with autistic spectrum disorders. When explaining the concepts of ABA, Dr. Friedman would occasionally illustrate the ideas using examples from her work with autistic children. One of the fundamental ideas in ABA, perhaps the fundamental idea, is that you should not even try to guess what your bird or child is thinking. Don't try to reverse-engineer their thoughts from their actions. You're very likely to guess wrong, because they don't think in quite the same way that you do. They notice things you don't, and they ignore things that you think are important. So don't even try. That doesn't mean you have to give up on training or teaching, it just means that you have to do it without attempting to read their minds. Instead, you should look very closely at just three things: 1. What are the antecedents of the behavior - what happens right before the behavior in question? 2. What is the behavior itself? Exactly what is it that you'd like to reduce, or amplify? 3. What are the consequences of the behavior? What happens afterward? If the behavior is happening frequently, or with increasing frequency, then there is almost certainly going to be something about the post-behavior environment that your bird or child prefers, relative to the pre-behavior environment. You can figure those things out without mind-reading. When you do, you're halfway to changing the behavior. The next step is to figure out what you can do to suppress the antecedents or change the consequences. If you can prevent the triggers, or suppress the rewards, you can reduce the frequency of a problematic behavior. Conversely, if there's a behavior that you want to increase, reward it as soon as you see it - you'll get more of it. Or reward something that resembles the behavior that you want (even if just vaguely) and gradually shape that behavior into what it is that you really want, by judiciously rewarding variations in the behaviors that are offered to you. Or if there's a behavior that you want to decrease, look for an incompatible behavior that you can increase instead. Find cues for that behavior, and reward it when you see it. It is also critical to shape behavior with rewards. If you find yourself contemplating punishment or force, you're doing it wrong. The following is from from the PsychologyToday link that I posted above, with some emphasis added by yours truly: The guiding principle of this approach is a hierarchy of teaching interventions starting with the most positive, least intrusive, effective behaviour solutions. Friedman is a steadfast proponent of changing behaviour through facilitation rather than force [...] The fundamentals are pretty simple, but the implementation can get tricky. It takes some creativity, and it helps to talk with people who have experience. And it takes discipline to avoid assuming that you know what they're thinking. Your default assumption always needs to be that you don't know, and that doesn't matter. Because all you really need to do is observe. When you get into the habit observing what you see, rather than assuming what they're thinking, this approach works amazingly well. Incidentally, this way of thinking has also informed my interactions with all animals, human or not, autistic or not. The better you treat someone - anyone - the more likely it is that they will work with you rather than against you at any given moment. The parrot you see in my profile picture had a personality that, in people, would probably have been considered bipolar. She oscillated between sweet and vicious. She mostly liked me, but I still got bit every day for the first few weeks. But I think it's been over a year now since she's tried to kill me.

question: Is it helpful for an adult to learn they have autism spectrum disorder? If so, how?
answer: Is it helpful for an adult to learn they have autistic spectrum disorder? If so, how? Yes, for me personally, it was a great relief to finally figure out that I was autistic and that there was nothing "wrong" with me. I am a perfectly normal autistic woman. I have always been different and this difference got given many labels, I was called shy, an introvert, a nerd, a bookworm, clumsy, quiet and yet none of these labels felt like they were the perfect fit. I never could understand why I didn't have any friends, I would think that I had made a new friend and then these people would disappear and I would never see them again. When I did make a friend it seemed to be when they had stopped speaking to other in the group and often meant that these new friends would resign their job or leave the town within weeks of me thinking I have finally managed to find a friend. I couldn't understand why I felt exhausted after attending a party and started making excuses not to go to any. I thought everyone struggled to hear when multiple conversations were going on, or when the TV competed in the background. I thought everyone just pretended to hear what the others said when they were in the pub. I thought everyone hated scratchy clothes and would cut out the labels and test the seams to feel if the thread it was sewn with will bother you. I always wondered how other managed to respond to questions so quickly. Why I could never spot the gap in the conversation where I can start talking. Why no one else seemed to talk over others and blamed me for not getting it right. I had to study how to have conversations and for years I had to keep reminding myself to ask questions in return and not just answer questions and leave. I accepted that I was a bit strange and eccentric and worried that I could be a psychopath. I would have told you that I don't stim, doesn't everyone wiggle their toes, rub their finger, play with their hair, ... For even more years I ignored the possibility of being autistic and only started reading about female autism after realising that my son was autistic. I finally understood my dad's behaviours, I knew why my grandmother was never without her crotchet and knitting, I realised that most of my family of teachers, preachers, housewives and artists are on the autism spectrum even though none of them have officially been diagnosed. The ones who committed suicide at an early age probably were too. So why is it helpful to know? Because I now finally know who I am. I spent hours reviewing, re-interpreting, and integrating the events that happened through my life into the person I now know I am and I feel that it has made me a lot stronger and given me a new freedom. I no longer have to worry about what is wrong with me. I no longer have to mask when I don't want to mask. I finally recognise my behaviours for what they are and I have become kinder to myself and allowing myself alone time when I need it. I no longer feel silly for planning trips to the minute and using GS to drive to places I've been dozens of times. Doing that allows me to relax and feel in control. I am more honest with others when asking them to notify me of changes in advance and I know that when I panic due to an unexpected change I can sit down, plan it out and mostly deal with it. I don't feel guilty anymore when declining invitations when I have reached my limit for the day or week. Life still isn't perfect. I don't tell everyone I meet that I am autistic for fear of how they would respond. Some of the people I have told now treat me differently and not in a good way while others seem to avoid me. Still, to me it is worth knowing who I am and why I struggled so much growing up and fitting into teams at work. Would it have been better to know earlier? Maybe, maybe not, What is past is past and I am happy with what I know now.

question: How effective is MDMA at treating autism spectrum disorders?
answer: If you’re only interested in the drug itself, scroll down to the How-To Portion. I just readEva Silvertant's answer to How effective is MDMA at treating autism spectrum disorders? and it’s blowing my mind, while simultaneously shrieking a deafening DUH! in my ear — Ecstasy (MDMA) and Autism are a match made in heaven!
