This man — no longer with us — wanted nothing more than to share the magic of a drug whose effects he was certain could soothe and heal the world. But no, spreading Love and Peace is not something our government will allow, and so zap, this magnificent invention was illegalized, which not only led to increasingly “dirty” versions of it, but to the loss of the knowledge of how best to benefit by it. And the MDMA-wasting Rave culture was born. My year and a half on Quora has taught me enough about ASD to realize I’m on the spectrum. (Which I’ve written an answer about: Emily Fisher's answer to How did Quora change your life?). Quora has taught me a lot not only about ASD, but about spectra in general. When first learning of Asperger’s, decades ago, I recognized who in my life probably fit the bill, folks I’d always found extra interesting. It made me giggle to think of all my childhood self-soothing activities that sounded so Aspie, when I so clearly was not, for so many other reasons. But my conviction that Autism didn’t apply to me was only because I (we) did not yet understand about the spectrum. Since my discoveries, I’ve analyzed my teenage progression away from the private Aspie activities I needed to comfort myself as a child. I deducted that I was a beneficiary of the 60s, that by leaving home young as a little hippie, and moving to a distant, isolated, small town hippie community where hugs were a form of multiple types of communication, eventually I overcame my lifelong aversion to being touched. Although MDMA had not yet been invented, there was plenty of access to psychedelics, and these, too — LSD, psilocybin mushrooms, peyote — have the capacity to break down walls and form bridges between humans. Small group and solo usage of psychedelics as a teenager helped me overcome my lifelong inability to speak in certain situations. I hold the decade and its still clean drugs responsible for the personality changes that led to far greater comfort in my own skin which soon caused me to shed all those Aspielike childhood actions of mine, as I developed my own sense of security in the world. But that took a number of years. Whereas I suspect a few MDMA trips would have had the same effect a hell of a lot faster. MDMA was developed as a theraputic drug and it's sad as fuck that it's been banished, that the magical beauty of it is mostly lost. THE HOW-TO PORTION: If you really want to experience what MDMA is, you need to seek out the opposite of rave-like atmosphere in every way. The more lights/sounds/people/noise/distraction/movement, the more you are diminishing the effects of the drug. Ecstasy is for deep connection and euphoria. To experience this you should be with either one other person to whom you are close, or a small group of very close friends and/or lovers, people with whom you have no qualms about being naked (both physically and mentally), people you trust. Or maybe with one new person with whom you're looking to connect. You'd do best to be in a safe quiet space, undisturbed. The degree of connection, deep love, and spiritual bliss you can achieve in this fashion puts the rave scenario to shame. It saddens me that Ecstasy turned into a rave drug, a loud dancing party drug. It's not cheap, so why throw it down the toilet by diminishing 90% of its effects? It’s a very delicate high, and can be wiped out in an instant if something comes up for which you suddenly have to have your wits together. That's related to why all the loud and bright distractions of raving with it diminishes it so much. Also important: ALWAYS MAKE SURE YOU HAVE PLENTY OF DRINKING WATER NEAR BY. ----------------------------------------------- In the decades since MDMA was illegalized, the quality of the drug has gone to shit. These days it seems more speedy and teeth-grindy. Though even with the good old stuff, it was pretty common to get at least a little teeth-grindy when coming down. If you're a weed smoker, do that to combat the grind; it also mellows the descent. In fact, my only issue with the drug back in the day with the good stuff was with the descent, which can be abrupt. Feeling yourself slipping away from the bliss can be sad, and weed definitely helps with that. It also extends the trip, brings you back up a bit. My true favorite way to do MDMA is to take 1/2 a hit of LSD, then when I begin to feel it, I take a full hit of Ecstasy. It still feels like an Ecstasy trip, not an acid trip, but a longer one, with a much more gradual descent. I haven't done Ecstasy or LSD in years now, because I no longer know where to get any good clean stuff...

question: How would someone with autism spectrum disorder use "repetitive questioning"?
answer: Note: I’m anonymous because these details are personal (obviously). That’s also why I use only familial titles, not names. Both me (a professionally diagnosed autistic) and my self-diagnosed autistic mom use “repetitive questioning” when we don’t think my dad heard what we were asking. And yes, my mom is a baby boomer who learned to fake normality (sort of) and diagnosed herself because when she saw m growing up she realized she had to be autistic because of the ways she resembled me in spite of her upbringing being different from mine, but she still does “repetitive questioning” nonetheless and does it with the same exact tonality I use; then again, her dad, my maternal grandpa, was autistic too; we know this because he was like her and me in the same fundamental way. I did not get to know my maternal grandpa very well because he died when I was a kid in elementary school and we did not see him very often because he lived a long way away, but I bet he did the same thing, and probably for the same reason; he just didn’t have a reason to use it with me. Basically, my mom and I use this in the same way neurotypicals do when we aren’t heard; the only difference is me and my mom both repeat the question in the exact same tone until somebody answers.

question: Should I tell my child he has Autism Spectrum disorder?
answer: It’s heartening to read all of these thoughtful answers — especially from the autistic adults on this thread. So much time, attention, and emotional labor freely given to help a child they don’t even know. (Yet the stereotype about autistic people lacking empathy persists!) My only suggestion is that you work on unlearning the stereotypes and biases we have all been taught about autism and autistic people. Learn about neurodiversity and healthy models of ability and disability. Give extra consideration to the perspectives of autistic writers and thinkers.* Their expertise and perspectives are extremely valuable in and of themselves, but it is also important for your child that you practice thinking of and relating to autistic adults as competent, respect-worthy, whole human beings. The fact is, most of us who are not autistic have been socialized to think of autistic people (and to some extent, disabled people in general) as “others.” Just take a look at the language of the DSM-5, to see how the medical establishment pathologizes this neurological minority. Most of us have had too few opportunities to connect with autistic people as equals. So it’s not your fault if you have some work to do, but every bit of insight you gain in this area will pay off for your child many times over. If you were parenting a child of a different race than yourself, you’d do some work to develop your cultural competence so you could help your child form a positive, realistic identity that included their race. Developing our own cultural competence around autism, disability, and disability justice is an ongoing personal development project for many of us parents. If you haven’t yet shared your son’s autism with him yet, you have a nice opportunity to get a jump-start on this so his first impressions (from you) of his neurology are well informed and balanced. *Judy Endow MSW, Amythest Schaber, Rabbi Ruti Regan, Sara Luterman, Dr. Stephen Shore, Shannon Rosa (not autistic but still good), Sparrow Rose Jones, and Michelle Sutton are a few to get you started.

question: What is the comorbidity rate between borderline personality disorder and autism spectrum disorders/Asperger's?

question: Why are IQ test scores unstable in autism spectrum disorder?
answer: My (autistic) son’s IQ is unstable. This means the variation between testings has significant change, depending how the tests are administered. His range varies between low 30s and upper 60s. If he were to attempt a standard written IQ test, his score would be even lower than 30. question: Is there a relation between schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders?
answer: Yes, there is a ‘relationship’ between schizophrenia and autism. Several of the other answers here are very concerning as they are not accurate and much information is disregarded or misinterpreted. So here are some facts. 1.) Both disorders, schizophrenia and autism, are genetic in origin. No one has to do anything ‘wrong’ for these types of genetic errors to occur. 2.) Both disorders, schizophrenia and autism, involve a type of gene error common to a great many disorders. In other words, there are errors in gene locations all of us have. 3.) Both disorders, schizophrenia and autism, involve multiple gene locations. The inheritance of these disorders is not a simple ‘100%, 75%, 50%,’ etc. You can forget the grade school lesson with the Punnet Squares. Think of how you flip a coin. Over many throws, a 50% chance of getting one side, a 50% chance of getting the other side. If you add two more coins, the chances of flipping all 3 to the same side are less than 50%. Each time you add another coin, your chance of flipping all the coins to the same side goes down. Let’s say instead of coins you have gene locations. Then you can understand that if 100 children had one parent with schizophrenia, only around 14 of those children would develop schizophrenia. It is simply ‘more and more difficult’(unlikely) to get more and more gene locations to wind up with a specific pattern of spelling errors. 4.) Further, both autism and schizophrenia do not ‘have to be’ inherited. They can occur due to gene misspellings (‘mutations’ if you must call them that) that only occur in the individual, not his parents. They can occur due to a small mutation from a parent being ‘amplified,’ or more altered, in the child. Further, gene location misspellings can occur in cells copied from the genetic material of the parent, even when the misspelling does not occur in the genetic material from the parent. 5.) People with autism are at a higher risk for schizophrenia, solely based on genetics. That does not mean that everyone with autism will get schizophrenia. In the general population, the risk of schizophrenia is very small, around 1%. Studies vary in what they find the risk for people with autism to be, because studies vary in how they recruit or exclude participants. Some studies find a risk as high as 30%, others find a risk about 6%. 6.)Some gene locations that are involved in schizophrenia are also involved in some cases of autism. 7.) In most cases, the type of gene error is very small ‘spelling errors’ (coding differences, usually of the ‘CNV’ - copy number variation type). In other words, these errors occur on gene locations, not the entire gene or chromosome. One gene location generally produces one protein(a simple chemical the body needs for growth, repair or development). Originally it was not recognized that these small errors were significant or that they interacted with each other or potentiated each other. Until gene locations were more fully mapped, and they were studied more carefully in so far as what they code for and what the effects of miscoding are in each location, what was going on was not entirely obvious. So early statements (and articles based on that earlier research, even if written much later) are not accurate representations of the facts. 8.) As a very general rule, the coding errors in schizophrenia are ‘scrambled letters’ where as in autism, they are ‘deleted letters.’ So while they may even be on the same gene locations, the spelling errors in autism do often look different from the spelling errors in schizophrenia. 9.) There are gene location errors that carry a ‘share-able risk.’ This means that some gene location errors can contribute to multiple different conditions - and this is the case with certain gene locations conferring a share-able risk to autism, schizophrenia, bipolar and intellectual disability and severe depression. 10.) There are about eight patterns(maybe even more since I last checked) of gene location misspellings recognized as ‘common’ in autism. There are also individual variations to those patterns. Because of this we say autism can ‘vary from one person to another.’ 11.) More gene locations misspelled, and bigger misspellings, result in more severe autism. Fewer gene locations misspelled, and smaller misspellings, result in milder autism. Some observations and comments — I have known several people who had both autism and schizophrenia. Prior to the DSM-5, in the 80s, 90s and for a very few diagnosticians, part of the 2000s, some of those people would have been re-diagnosed with ‘mental retardation and psychosis’ and the autism diagnosis dropped, when they developed psychotic symptoms. There is no biological, genetic or observational information that suggests that is a sensible approach. It was done more due to Kanner’s insistence of how separate the two disorders are, despite his own data showing the opposite. In the 1940s when he published it was important to his professional career to insist the two disorders had nothing to do with each other. A person with autism could develop psychotic symptoms at any age(as is true for the general population). My husband’s brother showed psychotic symptoms at age 3. But others with autism have not shown psychotic symptoms until 7 or 8(like a friend’s son), or more around the usual time psychosis/schizophrenia shows, 18–21. I have no doubt that a few people diagnosed with autism do not have autism, but rather, have schizophrenia. A very small group of children never speak or develop any communication but have complex symptoms suggesting both disorders, and they represent a diagnostic challenge. Another very small group of adults has schizophrenia but ‘diagnosis shops’ until a doctor diagnoses them with autism. In the cases I have seen, it was clear the person had schizophrenia but could not accept that. What used to be called Childhood Disintegrative Disorder(CDD) but is now rolled into the ‘Autism Spectrum Disorder’ diagnosis, may blur the lines between autism and psychotic disorders or psychotic symptoms. Read Robert Catalano’s excellent book ‘When Autism Strikes’ for a very thorough treatment of this subject. In his book at least two of the eight children he gave case histories for, had psychotic symptoms. In CDD children experience what appears to be normal development initially*, then typically at 2 or 3 undergo an acute period of extraordinary upheaval and distress due to no outside stressors, after which they show a loss of skills, vocabulary, and autism symptoms. So what does any of this tell us? How should the person with mild autism regard all this? What should parents do?All of us need to be aware that a person with autism could develop a mental illness. This could be mild depression or anxiety, or something more serious. Untreated mental illness causes much suffering and distress, and that suffering need not occur as these are treatable illnesses.A person who has mild autism and develops symptoms like despair, paranoia, rage(not anger, rage), self-injury or hallucinations, is not at all likely to have these symptoms ‘because of autism.’ These are signs of mental illness. question: How do you teach piano to a child with Autism Spectrum Disorder?
answer: A2A, thanks for the request Barbara Johnson ! I am a piano teacher who also has Asperger’s/ASD. I think a lot of these suggestions are good and there are a lot of good points that have already been made. I’m a piano teacher with 10+ years experience, I have taught 6 students with special needs (ADD, ADHD, ASD) and I have taught maybe 3–4 students who I suspected might be on the spectrum and let me say, every child has their difficulties. When you work one on one with a kid, no matter what their learning style or neurology is, you have to able to adapt on the fly to their moods, their attention span, their interests and their innate abilities. I usually use the same approach on my neurotypical students as I would my ASD students. I try to get to know them; their likes and dislikes, what their basic schedule is, what their parent’s involvement is, what their favorite songs are, so I can tailor the lessons to the child rather than trying to force the child into the same method as everyone else. For instance, I have a 5 year old student who comes from a musical family. She is NT (neurotypical) but she hates piano and she also hates me sometimes! I found out she loves horses and drawing, so now we do a lot of note-drawing games and she gets horse stickers when she plays a song correctly. She has started to really look forward to her lessons and actually practices now that she has a good incentive. I would do the same thing for a child on the spectrum. Do they only have a 10 minute attention span for playing? Well, then 20 minutes of the lesson is going to be music and note learning games. Do they have a special interests like dinosaurs? Then we are going to be learning songs about dinosaurs and I will let them info dump about dinosaurs when they complete a musical task like drawing notes or playing a song from start to finish. Teaching children is always about being creative. Teaching them one on one is about constantly changing pace so that they don’t lose their patience and momentum. I know there are a few suggestions to say that you shouldn’t even try to teach something an autistic child isn’t interested in because they may have a meltdown or become difficult. I think this is an unfair assessment. I’m a firm believer that early childhood music lessons can and should be fun, rewarding and bring out the natural gifts your child has. Not every child has an ear for music and some of them will quit after a few years, but music education can help with language development, proprioceptive senses, spatial awareness, time keeping, and focus, which are just a few of the many long-term benefits of learning an instrument.

question: Why is autism considered a spectrum disorder?
answer: Autism is also known as a “spectrum” disorder because there's wide variation within the type and severity of symptoms people experience. Autism Spectrum disorder may occur in ethnic, racial, and economic groups. treatments and services can improve an individual's symptoms and skill to function. A diagnosis of Autism spectrum disorder now includes several conditions that wont to be diagnosed separately: Autistic disorder, Pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified (PDD-NOS), and Asperger syndrome. Children or adults with Autism spectrum disorder might: 1. Not point at objects to point out interest 2. Not check out objects when another person points at them 3. Avoid eye contact 4. Want to be alone. 5. Social interaction affected 6. Poor attention span 7. Poor concentration 8. Repeat or echo words or phrases said to them. 9. Have trouble expressing their needs using typical words or motions 10. Repeat actions over and over again 11. Have trouble adapting when a routine changes 12. Have unusual reactions to the way things smell, taste, look, feel, or sound Asperger's syndrome may be a condition on the autism spectrum, with generally higher functioning. Asperger syndrome (AS), also referred to as Asperger's, maybe a developmental disorder characterised by significant difficulties in social interaction and nonverbal communication, alongside restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests. As a milder autism spectrum disorder (ASD), it differs from other ASDs by relatively normal language and intelligence. Although not required for diagnosis, physical clumsiness and unusual use of language are common. Signs usually begin before two years aged and typically last for an individual's entire life. The syndrome is known as after the Austrian paediatrician Hans Asperger, who, in 1944, described children in his care who were clumsy, and lacking in nonverbal communication skills and understanding of others' feelings. The modern conception of Asperger syndrome came into existence in 1981 and went through a period of popularization. It became a standardized diagnosis in the early 1990s. Symptoms : Problems with social interactions, restricted and repetitive behaviour. PDD-NOS or pervasive developmental disorder-not otherwise specified, was one of the categories of an autism diagnosis.In the past, a diagnosis of PDD-NOS was given if an individual decided to possess some symptoms of autism but didn’t meet the complete diagnostic criteria for conditions like autistic disorder and Asperger’s syndrome. PDD-NOS was diagnosed when an individual had impairment in social skills, the inability to successfully interact with other people, problems with verbal or nonverbal communication, or stereotyped behaviour, interests, and activities. PDD-NOS only applied to people who didn’t have any of the following diagnoses: 1. Specific pervasive developmental disorder 2. Schizophrenia 3. Schizotypal personality disorder 4. question: Do people with autism spectrum disorder feel normal sometimes?
answer: A lot of us feel normal when we are by ourselves or in the company of other neuroatypical folks, or the occasional neurotypical person who accepts us. Because we are feeling what is normal for us. Most of feeling out of sorts comes from realizing that society assumes the default is what an average neurotypical person is capable of and finds comforting, and that is harder for us. Thinking back to my school days, I felt the most uncomfortable when I was isolated from my peers and I didn’t understand why I was the only one having those problems (aka before my diagnosis). When I was playing alone or with my sister and cousins, I felt normal. When I started to understand myself better and met people with shared interests, I felt normal. High school was like the sun coming out from behind the clouds as I finally had a circle of friends (again, several of whom were also on the autism spectrum). To, say, my mother, we were weird as heck, but I felt normal to have them. Our ability to feel normal is related to the extent we feel like we fit into society — either because society is expansive enough to accept many sorts of normal, or because we have chosen our own pocket of society to live in.

answer: (updated 2017) I have known of others in this situation, feeling mis-diagnosed, sometimes to their detriment, so I have an especially strong opinion about patient empowerment here. Behavioral issues may arise from physical properties such as genes and anatomy, but these conditions are not binary states like diabetes, where your pancreas is or isn't working. Every clinician has his own particular combination of training, belief and bias affecting which DSM labels they choose. The whole DSM itself is a consensus document compiled by committee and then applied in practice by people who come from many different traditions. For you to decide based on this patchwork system and the opinion of one clinician that you do or don't "really" have X condition would be unfortunate, especially if you have lots of evidence that something other than the diagnosis chosen could be true. I spend a lot of time these days helping people become self-advocates, and I hope you have increasing success in taking a stand on your own behalf. question: Do people with autism spectrum disorder fear being touched?
answer: Many people with ASD fear being touched UNEXPECTEDLY. There’s nothing quite as awful as an unseen hand coming out of nowhere and lightly touching my arm. As with many things, however, this varies from person to person. If I know the touch is coming from a trusted person, I am much more likely to be receptive of it (providing I’m already in a good headspace). The best thing you can do for someone with ASD in regards to touch is — simply — ask them! “You look like you’ve had a really hard day, can I give you a hug?” “Can I lean into you as you read a book?” “Can I rest my head on your lap?” The above sentences can and SHOULD be used to ask anybody (regardless of if they’re on The Spectrum) if close physical contact is okay. When you’re in the presence of someone who has Autism (or you suspect they have Autism) it’s always better to air on the side of caution first. If you think you should ask if they want to be touched, chances are your gut instincts are right.

question: What do people with autism spectrum disorder want to mask?
answer: “Masking” is an informal and imprecise term to describe what autistic people are doing. Sometimes it’s called “social camouflaging”, but even then I don’t think it captures the real essence, which is more like “simulating”. It’s not about hiding anything, or pretending to be invisible. It’s presenting a communication-interface to the world that matches everyone else’s interface. Imagine if instead of a 4G phone, you had this imaginary thing called a “7F” phone. It would work reasonably well with other “7F” phones, on a “’7F” network, except that the whole world is made up of 4G networks instead. So if you want to talk to other phones, you need your 7F phone to pretend to be a 4G phone. It needs to mask. Why would you want to do this? Because it’s pretty lonely and frustrating if everyone else can communicate with each other, but you can’t talk to them. I’m over-simplifying a little, because autism is still poorly understood by the general public, and so autistic people may often want to hide the fact that they are autistic. The effect is the same, though. It’s about pretending to be neurotypical, to avoid difficulties with neurotypical people.

question: As a person with autism spectrum disorder, are you particularly interested in trains?
answer: I’ve also observed the odd connection between autism and trains. I was mildly interested in trains growing up but I suppose no more than any other little boy that age. My theory on why autistic people are so frequently fascinated by trains is that trains appeal to the autistic tendency (not a universal one but a common one) to seek organization within a system. Laying out a big train set is a neat little engineering puzzle, and also a way for a child to impose a little order on his little corner of the universe. “MY train set goes here, and here, and then over there, and then comes back here, and it has this car, and that one, and this other one, and they all do stuff.” It’s a very stimulating thing for a small child to see a train set rumble around and do all the gimmicks like tip the logs and deliver the mail and so on. And switching cars? Good night. I once knew a little autistic boy who would happily spend hours switching his train cars around (the real trick is doing it without picking any of them up). EDIT: And another thing. It also occurs to me that unlike some other obsessive activities that autistic children may develop, an obsession with trains is unlikely to be suppressed by parents. Being fascinated by trains is seen as “normal” especially for young boys, and it’s a hobby that can be scaled up as the child ages. There are more complicated train sets that can be bought for older boys who are still really into trains. Even as an adult, if you have a really fancy train set in your home people are more likely to think it’s really cool. At worst, they’ll just laugh and treat it as a charmingly child-like personality quirk. All of this is less true of many other obsessions that autistic people have had. A little boy obsessed with, say, cameras will be seen as “weird”. His parents may try to push him into other activities when all he really wants to do is read camera magazines.

question: Why do autism spectrum disorders affect coordination?
answer: Coordination for running and many types of fast physical activities involves the nervous system working in what is perceived as “normal harmony". It's what most would call allistic or “normal" neurology. Neurology is all about the nervous system regardless of who we're describing. The overall difference between autistic and everyone else is considered to be in our consistently differing neurology. We're talking about natural variation in human development (autism is NOT a disease nor a defect). The harmony required to run or do certain tasks just seems to be replaced by other substantial potentials in us autistics. There is at least one identified difference in the natural childhood brain “synaptic pruning” process. Autistic brains don't lose as many of the supposedly “unneeded” synapses as allistics, and a more obvious consequence is usually sensory enhanced perceptions(often considered both a gift and a major challenge). Physical nervous system sensitivities and difficulties just seem to come along as part of that same package. With most natural gifts there's a hidden cost to any advantage. In my own case, no matter how big or small I was or how strong, some tasks have just never worked. Running more than maybe 40 yards, pull ups, climbing a rope, and a handful of similar common activities always have been impossible for me. On the other hand, I've carried, poured, and at times even tossed around 80 pound bags for a day or two at a time (cement) without trouble. I've also been able to swim or do some other types of strenuous activity continuously for an hour or more fairly regularly. So although I was gifted with reasonable stamina and strength, there is a real muscle coordination challenge mixed in too. My balance while walking can falter randomly, although usually not enough that I fall and no one has ever really noticed thanks to masking. Banquet hall set up and teardowns were also never a problem. In case you were going to ask, YES a few odd and sometimes unpleasant pain issues can also be included.

This does not significantly affect how disabled a person is (sign language and adaptive communication devices are both utilized just fine, thanks). Nor does it reflect how significant other symptoms are. A person who's diagnosed with Asperger's may need to utilize assisted living and so on because their other symptoms are so disabling that they can't live on their own. A nonverbal “classic” autistic person may be able to function perfectly well on their own and simply…. Not be verbal. Even the concept of functioning labels is based less on how severe our symptoms actually are, and more on how much other people feel inconvenienced by our symptoms. For example, a person could have severe hypersensitivity to textures due to autism. But they may still be considered high functioning because other people can comfortably ignore the autistic person's pain in that instance. An autistic person who visibly stims a lot may be considered low functioning because stimming bothers neurotypicals and they can't just ignore it. An autistic person might be labeled high-functioning if they have a special interest (or “obsession”) with something useful, like dentistry. Another autistic person will be marked low-functioning for having a special interest in, say, horror movies. Why? One special interest is seen as useful, and the other isn't. So the one that isn't useful is labeled as “worse” autism than the one deemed useful.

question: Is it correct that autism spectrum disorder is not an intellectual disability?
answer: “Is it correct that autism spectrum disorder is not an intellectual disability?” It's a bit more complicated than that. Overall, yes it is correct that ASD is not an intellectual disability. The problem with that statement comes when examining the wide range of abilities & disabilities in ASD patients, where at one extreme there is no intellectual disabilities in the patients at all & at the opposite extreme there's clear & obvious intellectual disabilities. For many people it can be difficult to separate the intellectual disabilities from the Autism in the “lowest-functioning” of cases, although frequently in those cases the intellectual disabilities are the result of the person having other diagnoses in addition to ASD. The ASD mantra is “If you've met one person who has Autism… you've met ONE PERSON who has Autism.”, & when a person has ASD along with other diagnoses… WELL let's just say that the similarities, opposites, overlaps, contrasts, & interconnectivities between the symptoms of ASD paired with the symptoms of other diagnoses tend to have some fascinatingly unexpected results.

question: Is there any relationship between face blindness (prosopagnosia) and autism spectrum disorders such as Aspberger Syndrome?
answer: Statistically research suggests that prosopagnosia affects 2% of the general population. However, estimates for the condition within the autistic population are around 50%, possibly higher, which means that it is far more prevalent as a comorbid with the autism spectrum than as a stand alone condition. I work with university students on the spectrum and screen all of them for prosopagnosia as a matter of course because of how it impacts on social communication (if you can’t see a face properly, how would you be able to read anything in it?) - at least 50% have it at some level. In my family my father, myself and my son have it (all autistic); for my father and son it is severe- they literally cannot see faces - but for me it is in a milder form where I can see a face but cannot retain a memory, even of my own face. Can you imagine how scary a school dining room would be? Or what it’s like to never have seen the faces of those you love? Or to not be able to imagine what you look like? Edited to add: Prosopagnosia is caused by the failure of the brain to process the face, and only the face. Most visual data is processed through the visual cortex but not the face. The face is processed in the fusiform gyrus in the amygdala and is a tiny rice sized area hidden behind each ear. The amygdala is part of the network that processes for emotional salience so it is hypothesised that the fusiform gyrus is placed there to process faces because they are so important emotionally and it is more efficient to process them within that network directly, rather than as secondary to the visual network. Prosopagnosia was first studied in brain injured people who lost the ability to see faces and recognise people - one man in particular had a metal spike driven into his skull, piercing the fusiform gyrus, and consequently allowing that area to be identified as the facial processing area. It was only much later (decades) that it was realised that it could be a congenital condition - most people do not realise that they should be able to see and remember a face properly; how would anyone know they see differently from those around them when nobody would think to ask anyone else if they could see a face unless they thought the person was blind? We all assume that, if we can see at all, then we can all see the same things. As a result, nobody imagined that a sighted person might be unable to see a face and, because they never thought to question it, those of us with prosopagnosia, didn’t realise there were things (faces) we couldn’t process like everyone else.

question: What are some recommended books about autism spectrum disorder in adults?
answer: You've heard the saying? “If you've met one person with autism, you've met one person with autism”. Because every person with autism is different. Unfortunately, this also means you're unlikely to find what you're looking for in any one book or from anyone else's experience on the subject. The sheer size of the spectrum of symptoms, skills and levels of ability and presentation of autism from one person to another makes it impossible for any book - medical, dietary, guide or memoir to really feel relevant to your specific needs or situation. I would say that 99% of the books on the subject of autism are written for and purchased by people who are in the very early stages of having autism enter their lives. Which is to say the confused, the desperate, the scared and the gullible. I certainly bought my fair share of books the first six months after my son was diagnosed with autism. Before his diagnoses I was only very peripherally aware of autism. I Had maybe (knowingly) met two or three autistic people and I had a very specific and narrow definition of what autism must be. No eye contact, a lot of hand flapping, not necessarily verbal, not affectionate. That's what I thought autism was. My son who spoke quite a few words definitely made eye contact, loved to hug and laugh and kiss and did not flap his hands at all…could not possibly be autistic?? So, off I headed to the bookstore to read up on the subject and get me some answers! Holy hell! I read everything I could find on the subject and it was voluminous. From assessments and diagnosis to coexisting sensitivities and conditions and stimming and triggers and floortime and then the acronyms!! ASD,SPD,DSM,PDNOS!!!! The acronyms! It was overwhelming and terrifying and disheartening. What I took away from all the reading I did was that I would have to homeschool my child with a drill sergeant like approach of repetition where he would be rewarded with an m&m when he did it ‘right’, become a dietitian and master chef now that I would be making my own bone broth and learning how to incorporate enzymes and supplements into our new gluten and dairy free diet, and prepare to document, file and retrieve every piece of information and every observation on my son because I would be juggling therapists and specialists and providers and services and rather than parenting I would now be ADVOCATING. I spent a lot of time, in those early days, crying and/or hyperventilating. Because no matter how many different books I read, I would have an A-HA! moment because ‘Yes!..that!..right there! That's just like like my son’ only to turn the page and ‘wait? What?…nooooo, that's nothing like him at all’. So, my suggestion based on my experience with the search for information? Don't buy any books... yet. The Internet is your best friend and worst enemy. There is a lot of outdated, unsubstantiated and just plain ridiculous information out there. So, start with a FACTUAL search on the internet, take note of the date and the source!(information from a major medical journal written in 2016 is probably more reliable than something by Jane Doe in 2004) just sayin'. Look up the definition of autism and autism Spectrum disorder. Familiarize yourself with the basics of neurology and neurodevelopment. Understand the complexities of communication both verbal and non verbal and how it affects behaviors and relationships. I know that sounds really clinical and daunting but in order to have any understanding of autism you need to dissect something so basic that you take for granted. Communication. We communicate millions of things millions of ways all day every day without even thinking about it. So to understand autism is first to understand the typically developing (non autistic) brain and how it sends communication signals through the body and then how needs are met by communication with the world. Once you have a good solid understanding of that you can go to a bookstore and not waste your money or your time. Rather than buying a book on autism you can look for specific areas of interest with in autism, you'll better be able to understand what you're reading and most importantly you won't fall victim to a lot of the drivel out there that only exists to separate you from your money and maybe a little of your sanity. Good Luck on your quest, Shawn (single mom of 2. One autistic, One sarcastic ;) Side note* My personal favorite autism related book ....because while reading it I felt all the pieces of information come together in my head and I finally began to understand what it was I was trying to grasp about my son. Ido in Autismland

question: Can encephalitis lead to autism spectrum disorder?
answer: In recent years, many studies indicate that children with an autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis have brain pathology suggestive of ongoing neuroinflammation or encephalitis in different regions of their brains. According to the Encephalitis Society, encephalitis is inflammation of the brain, and this inflammation is caused by either an infection invading the brain (Infectious Encephalitis) or the immune system attacking the brain in error. Autoimmune Encephalitis usually follows a viral infection (such as those that cause rashes in childhood) or immunizations. However, it has been recognized recently that there are other types of Autoimmune Encephalitis resulting from the brain being attacked by the body’s immune system. question: What is autistic masking?
answer: The term ‘masking’ refers to an ability to be able to hide or cover up how one is truly feeling and appear to be functioning in a ‘normal’ manner. Everyone wears a mask to some degree, because we have to abide by specific social expectations, but autistic people may mask a lot more of themselves than a neurotypical might in an attempt to avoid unwanted stigma and judgement. Masking is more common in Asperger's or late diagnosis because those more ‘high functioning’ have higher expectations socially and so we tend to mask better for longer periods of time. But at some point this mask causes burnout due to the stress it entails; then you might notice more autistic traits being portrayed. Some autistic people cannot mask and this immediately gives off the impression that they are ‘lower functioning’ or ‘more severely autistic’, when actually what you might be seeing is more of that person's comorbid illnesses or a learning disability that might accompany their autism. They may even be completely fine and fully embracing who they are - not having to mask will certainly lower stress levels. Many people dislike the functioning labels used in autism because they can be misleading. Just because some of us function more socially than others does not mean our autism is less of an issue. We have to work hard to reach that point and mask an awful lot of who we are. It also disregards the gifts and strengths of those less socially capable and overlooks - or takes for granted - the struggles of those more capable. How ‘well' someone functions is often a result of either some degree of masking, and/or the environment at that particular time and how it caters to one's sensory needs.

question: Is it possible that being transgender is caused by autism spectrum disorders (ASD)?
answer: Caused by, no, not exclusively. But research does find that a higher number of transgender people have ASD than would be expected by chance, and that a higher percentage of ASD people are transgender than would be expected either. (Martin Silvertant, who also answered your question, has an excellent post on that on his ASD blog here.) The reason for this isn’t known but it may have to do with the fact that those of us with ASD are neurodiverse and frequently have other neurodevelopmental oddities like ADHD or seizures. In this case, our neurodiversity would extend to some of the circuitry that determines gender-specific behavior. It’s also been noted that ASD seems to mess with gender differentiation. We guys often have more feminine faces and a feminine gentleness, but also exhibit unusually male characteristics in systematization and localized processing. Women with ASD also frequently have some stereotypically male characteristics. Finally, ASD may predispose us to certain paths of psychological development. We may be less influenced by society’s strictures regarding gender roles, and more sensitive to emotional trauma. It really isn’t understood well enough at this point. But I can attest to the fact that like Martin, my gender identity isn’t conventional. It’s played out differently in me than it has in him, but I can identify with a lot of what he says (and made the same decision he did re transitioning).

Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 68, 101-110.Co-Morbidity of Autism and Gender Dysphoria In Layman's Terms: Co-morbidity means having two conditions at the same time. In this context, it means someone might experience both autism and gender dysphoria simultaneously. Detailed Explanation: Autism and gender dysphoria can co-occur, which means an individual can experience both conditions simultaneously. This overlap can influence how they perceive and understand their gender identity. It’s important to consider how each condition affects their experience and to provide appropriate support. Understanding these connections provides insight into why autistic individuals might recognize gender dysphoria in unique ways. Further research is needed to explore these intersections more deeply.

question: People who have dated someone on the autism spectrum, what is it like?
answer: I have been in a long-term cohabiting relationship with an autistic partner for almost four years. When we started dating, he didn’t yet know he was autistic, but once we started living together, I began to suspect that this was the case. I helped him connect with a neuropsychologist to get the diagnosis, and it’s really helped him contextualize things. What we found was that meeting online allowed him to begin a relationship in a way that was non-threatening for him. We met on OKCupid. I will say that we only connected because I messaged him. (He told me later that he’d been on OKCupid for awhile, but he’d never managed to get past his anxiety over messaging someone himself.) We corresponded in long, long messages for about three months. Once he felt like he’d gotten to know me through text, we moved on to chatting on the phone. This, too, inspired some serious anxiety, as I found out later. He was apparently drinking wine the entire time we were on the phone the first time. After that, we made plans to meet for the first time, and I drove up to the city in which he lived. It was a fairly awkward first date in some ways, but because we’d talked for so long online, it wasn’t as difficult for him to talk with me in person. We went to a book store, a restaurant, and a karaoke bar, and we had a lot of fun. He wasn’t certain what to do with physical touch, but I kind of guided him through what was appropriate. In general, I’ve taken the lead on most physical aspects of our relationship, because I’ve found he doesn’t pick up on those cues otherwise. After nine months of a long-distance relationship, we moved in together, and we’ve been very happy. Sometimes it’s difficult for me to relate to his extreme anxieties, and it negatively impacts our social life together in a big way. I have a very active social life on my own, though, but I feel bad that he can’t often participate in it. So I do think that it’s perfectly possible for an autistic human to have a great romantic relationship, but there are a few particular things about me that I think have helped me deal with his various difficulties more effectively.I have bipolar disorder. It’s not in any way the same as being autistic, but because I’ve gone through a lot of periods of severe anxiety and depression in my life, I understand the anxiety itself, even if I don’t always understand his particular triggers. Because of my experiences with the unsuccessful ways that others have tried to deal with my anxiety, I already had a roadmap in place to know how to deal with a very anxious person in a supportive way.We share a lot of interests, so I’m perfectly happy to listen to him ramble on about Metal Gear Solid or whatever other video game he’s super into at the time.Having navigated our society’s labyrinthine healthcare system for many years, I’m capable and willing to navigate it for him and advocate for him as necessary. This is sometimes very stressful, as my executive functioning isn’t always the best, either, but we’ve managed. I’ve found and vetted mental health professionals for him, and helped him find new ones when the ones he was seeing weren’t good fits. I go with him to see our primary care practitioner and usually sit in the examination room with him so that I can sort of “translate” between him and the doctor, because he’s not very good at communicating his problems and his needs.I don’t get too hung up over it if we make plans and then he’s too anxious or depressed to go out. We play video games or watch a movie instead, and I know I can go hang out with my friends while he’s at work or something.I accept that sometimes I’m going to have to serve as his caretaker in some ways. We do our best to communicate and set good boundaries so that this doesn’t become a burden, and because I have a very active social life and good outside connections, I can seek emotional support elsewhere if things get hard, which they do sometimes.I directly tell him when I want to have sex. This took a little time for me to figure out, but eventually I realized that he didn’t understand the nonverbal cues to initiate intimacy, and he didn’t want to feel like he was violating my boundaries in any way. So now I just straight-up ask. It took some getting used to, because I think women are social conditioned to assume that the man will initiate sex and seduce her or whatever, but it works out for us pretty well now.I think it’s some extra work to make this relationship function, but we’re so happy with one another that we deal with it. He doesn’t think he would have ever been able to start a relationship like this unless it was online, because “meeting” me through text and then essentially being my penpal for a few months allowed him to get over the hurdle of initial conversation, which is incredibly difficult for him to do. I’m not sure if online dating is the solution for everyone, but it might help others in a similar situation.

question: Does a person with autism spectrum disorder have a learning disability?
answer: I’d say yes, ASD can be considered a learning disability. A learning disability has quite a broad definition - it’s basically defined as any condition that affects someone’s ability to learn in a traditional classroom setting. With ASD, you have sensory sensitivities that can definitely hamper their ability to cope in a classroom, you also have the differences in social and communication skills that would make group tasks challenging, just to name a few things autistic people would find difficult in a classroom.

question: Autism: How is the prefrontal cortex affected by autism spectrum disorders?
answer: Actually, it's probably the other way around: a problem with the prefrontal cortex effects (which is to say, causes) autism. In some people with autism, usually the types with fairly good language, but poor social skills, anxiety disorders, and problems like "face blindness" appear to have either damage to or minor atrophy of the prefrontal cortex. What causes the problems is unknown, though: it could be bloodflow disruption during pregnancy, or it could be genetic, or it could be birth injuries. People who have other kinds of autism don't necessarily have prefrontal problems, but will have problems with other parts of the brain, like the parts that process language. Not having good language development can then disrupt development of other parts of the brain that depend on social stimulation. In some people that can be the prefrontal cortex. It really depends on what sort of environment they have, and what sort of compensatory skills they have. It's also important to note that many of the autopsy studies of the prefrontal cortices of autistic people, which noted things like undersizing, were done on people between 10 and 30 years ago, and that means those people had probably spent significant amounts of time institutionalized (people who were aged 40 to 75, 10 to 30 years ago, so born anywhere between and 1901 and 1954). Many of the differences in their brains may not have come from autism itself, but from being institutionalized. It's well known that absolutely neuro-typical people who undergo POW or concentration camp-type experiences have brain changes and behavior changes, so we could hardly expect less from autistic people who don't understand why they are confined, and are confined sometimes for decades. Fortunately, it doesn't happen anymore, but the generation who has grown up at home, and lives in home environments, is still young, and we don't have autopsy data. We have some data from imaging, which is where I get what I wrote above. There are lots of articles on this in journals if you want to read more.

question: I've recently been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. What therapies can help me cope with sensory, relationship, and social skills issues?
answer: I have ASD and was diagnosed only this year at 42. What has helped me is talking to other ASD, such as in self help groups and web forums. question: What is the comorbidity rate between autism spectrum disorders and sociopathy?
answer: I would argue "no", but go further and argue that they are practically the opposite ends of a spectrum of which neurotypicality is in the middle. In the most superficial and lazily glib interpretation, autism and psychopathy are similar: "they don't care". But when you break down the parts of empathy, the specifics are entirely opposite each other. There's cognitive empathy: does the person understand your subtle signals to read your mood? With autists, the answer is "usually, no". A deeper sense of this is "do they understand that you have a different mood from them?" And this too can be a problem. We can learn this through practice and training, but it is always a conscious skill, and a second language. We don't just "get it". Psychopaths can look at a person and know them. The difference is in what they do with it. There's expressive empathy: can you see a person's mood expressed? With autists, the answer is "usually no". Indeed, with Alexithymia, we often don't know our own moods. Until we're in a meltdown or rage or deep depression or something, when there's no hiding it, and even then our moods can be easily misinterpreted. Psychopaths are famously good at displaying a mood. Whether or not they feel it. This, combined with their ability to read other's moods, can make them fabulous manipulators. As the saying goes; the key to life is sincerity. Once you can fake that, you've got it made. Then there's affective empathy. Does the person feel bad if [they know that] another feels bad? Do they feel happy if another feels happy? With autists, the answer is "yes". Almost too much. Once you get past the problem of reading another, when we are made aware of another's feelings, they affect us deeply. Many of us have had the experience of recalling, sometimes years or decades after the event, something we did or said, and realised that it was hurtful, and we will take the pain of having caused pain to the grave. I can't watch comedies based on humiliation, I just can't. It's almost physically painful to me. (TV, at the least, is unsubtle enough to be emotionally comprehensible. This is not always a feature.) I feel every humiliation personally in the pit of my stomach. Other autists have described walking into a room, and drowning in emotion. Psychopaths, on the other hand, don't care. There's the difference. They know what you feel, they can expertly manipulate how you feel, but they don't care how you feel. And without some intellectually imposed system of morals, they don't have that inherent crawling feeling of wrongness telling them not to do something. As well, autists tend to be painfully and reflexively truthful, lying being somatically uncomfortable. Psychopaths can lie easily and freely. By my reckoning, on every measure, psychopathy and autism are not just not comorbid, they are for all purposes the opposite of each other.

question: Autism Spectrum Disorders: What is your favorite stimming method?

question: Can someone without Autism Spectrum Disorders have poor gross motor skills?
answer: Sure. You could have dyspraxia, or developmental coordination disorder (DCD), which is a brain-based condition that makes it hard to plan and coordinate physical movement. Motor neurone disease (MND) causes a progressive weakness of many of the muscles in the body. You may find yourself having trouble walking, picking things up, even breathing. You might have carpal tunnel syndrome from repetitive movements such as using a mouse. A major nerve in your hand becomes compressed and you become prone to dropping things as well as experiencing tingling, burning and sometimes pain. Poor motor skills could be a sign of many disorders, often neurologically based. Or you could just be clumsy. Join the club.

question: How and Why is Autism Spectrum disorder Misdiagnosed in Adult Patients?
answer: I agree with Rodney’s answer and have a bit to add, as I have a family member who is on the Autistic Spectrum (diagnosed at age 47) and also holds a Ph.D. in psychology. There is no physiological text for autism. Diagnosis is by symptoms only. As most or all Autistic Spectrum Disorders (ASD) begin in childhood, diagnosis is focused there. There are several challenges in diagnosing adults:The current definition of ASD came out in 2013, and so is only 5 years old, and it is a major change from prior definitions of autism, and much broader. As a result, there are now many adults who might be ASD per the current definition who were not autistic according to the definitions present during their childhood.Definition and diagnosis and funding for diagnosis and treatment are biased toward children.Differential diagnosis in psychiatry is a very challenging skill. Even most psychiatric Ph.D.s are not well trained in it. Anyone who is not a specialist in differential diagnosis is likely to create some false positive diagnoses (diagnosed ASD but not) and some false negative diagnoses (ASD spectrum but not diagnosed.The definition of ASD is still, I think, fluid, subject to change, and in need of clarification.ASD is a physical brain structure issue which manifests with behavioral symptoms, but there is no test on a living person that is available to assist in diagnosis. Thus diagnosis cuts across the brain/body (psychiatry/medicine) divide. Things that fall into this category are partly outside the training of both psychiatrists and medical doctors.Each person is very gifted in handling functional limitations and in doing so in a creative way. Adults, in particular, may develop coping mechanisms that mask symptoms, making specific diagnosis difficult.In addition to the above reasons, all of which are a natural result of the time it takes for our definitions to be refined and put into use, there are also personal, political, and financial biases that can make it more difficult. Some individuals face fears of the diagnosis or desire it as justification for their challenges. Some families and friends may fear the diagnosis and the person diagnosed. ASD is currently in some ways a political and financial football when it comes to funding for research and care.

question: Are hypermobility syndromes more common in people with Autism spectrum disorders?
answer: The other two answers made assumptions, but their intuitions were right. There is indeed a CORRELATION between hypermobility/Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and autism, but also a CAUSATION, as this study published on December 1st, 2020 shows: The Relationship between Autism and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes/Hypermobility Spectrum Disorders EDS = Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes / HSD = Hypermobility Spectrum Disorders Preliminary work from Casanova et al. [16] also suggests that autism and EDS/HSD co-occur within the same families. The researchers found that more than 20% of mothers with EDS/HSD reported having autistic children—a rate not significantly different from those reported by mothers who themselves are on the autism spectrum. In addition, the rates of autism in the children shared a significant positive relationship with the severity of maternal immune disorders in EDS/HSD, suggesting that the mother’s immune system may play an additional role in autism susceptibility in these connective tissue disorders. [...] In consideration of the materials presented in this review, we (along with previous authors) have proposed that hereditary connective tissue disorders represent a subtype of autism whose prevalence is currently unknown, although the common nature of HSDs (and likely hEDS) suggests it may comprise a significant minority of autism cases. This relationship indicates that connective tissue impairment may influence brain development, either through direct and/or indirect means. Future studies will ideally involve in vitro and in vivo research to address these possibilities and further define the causative factors in autism susceptibility. So the causation goes this way: EDS/HSD affects the development of the brain, making it become autistic. This might not be uncommon (‘a significant minority of autism cases’).

question: Is left-right muscle imbalance commonly associated with autism spectrum disorders?
answer: A lack of muscle tone is common symptom in those who fall into the spectrum. question: Wikipedia says that OCD is commonly comorbid with Autism Spectrum Disorders; is this true?
answer: OCD is a very common symptom for people in the autistic spectrum, and a highly common diagnosis for women in the spectrum who have been missed or misdiagnosed by the medical system. Some people include it in the spectrum, and I do sometimes. However, the key here is that, just like autism and over 80 different chronic mental, emotional, and physical challenges that are skyrocketing in incidence, OCD is caused by inflammation. The same interventions that reduce or eliminate autism challenges also reduce cancer challenges, heart disease challenges, diabetes challenges, dementia challenges in seniors, depression, anxiety, and all those other non-communicable, inflammatory diseases… and these also reduce or eliminate OCD. Before the 1970s, health determinants (things that indicated whether you’d have vibrant health or suffer from various health issues) were almost all active lifestyle choices: nutrition, food, sleep, exercise, and most of all (by far), love. However, we’ve been incorporating more and more challenging — and outright toxic — substances into daily life since, well, really the beginning of the industrial revolution, but most rapidly since the end of the first world war, when the governments of allied countries got strong-armed (by industrial moguls who had profited from the war) into finding peace-time uses for the gases which killed soldiers in the trenches, and for the factories which produced war weaponry. This was the beginning of three stealth wars which are still building:A war on insectsA war on microbes (germs?!)A war on smells (body odour, anyone?)Post WW1, many toxin-related diseases began to first creep up in incidence, and then emerge as exponentially-rising problems. During the 1970s, all of a sudden active and healthy lifestyle choices weren’t enough to keep people healthy, and it became environmental exposures at home, in learning and other institutions, at work, and at leisure which determined whether or how sick people would become. 50 years later, we’re beginning to reach the tipping point, where there are so few working-aged adults who are fully healthy that it’s getting difficult to afford to support the continually-rising number of children, already-vulnerable adults, and seniors with serious illnesses. So is OCD on the autism spectrum? Is the autism spectrum on the inflammatory, non-communicable disease spectrum? These are questions that are hard to answer. Early in the days of CGI, one of the projects was to make an “aging algorithm” for children. Of course, human faces stop developing at some point and you settle into your adult face, but the researchers thought it would be fun to pull out the stops and see what it would look like if you kept “maturing” beyond adulthood. The result stopped looking like a model of aging and started looking like a model of human evolution, but running backward. They saw what looked like early hominid reconstructions, even something akin to modern chimpanzees. The reason is that recent human evolution has used a process known as neotony: the preservation of adolescent characteristics into adulthood [1]. Among the neotenic characteristics you see in humans are: * flatter foreheads * larger and wider set eyes * compressed middle faces (nose and cheeks)smaller mouths * larger heads relative to body size * less hair * more rounded head * eyes set lower * less sexual dimorphism The development of human intelligence was probably closely related neotony, letting us produce larger brain cases. question: Are Autism spectrum disorder and eating disorders interconnected?
answer: Neurodiversity and eating disorders go hand in hand, more often than most people are aware of. I have just written a blog post about it: Eating habits and eating disorders in neurodiverse peopleEating habits and eating disorders in neurodiverse peopleMichael McCreary, a comedian on the spectrum wrote in his 2019 book  Funny, You Don't Look Autistic  that as a kid he used to explain to oth...http://the-big-ger-picture.blogspot.com/2021/06/eating-habits-and-eating-disorders-in.htmlMichael McCreary, a comedian on the spectrum wrote in his 2019 book Funny, You Don't Look Autistic that as a kid he used to explain to other people that autism means you can’t drink milk. He made fun of himself, as obviously there is no connection between autism and lactose intolerance, as everyone knows. Or was he wrong about joking? Considering how many comorbidities are common in neurodiverse people I have come to the conclusion that neurodiverse (despite all it’s good intentions) is a misnomer. If eating disorders and unusual eating habits are an integral part of neurodiversity it becomes kind of hard to see “neurodiversity” as a neurological only condition. We are in need of a term that includes body and mind. I have been arguing that most neurodiverse people are evolutionary forager types as opposed to farmer-herder types and that not only cognitive and social differences are to be expected, but also physiological differences. To begin with it is recommended for neurodiverse people to cut down on gluten and dairy - farmer/herder nutrition. Children with neurodiverse conditions (ASD, ADHD, gifted) tend to be very picky eaters and are five times more likely to throw tantrums when it comes to mealtimes. For severe cases of picking eating researchers concluded that selective eating that results in impairment of function should now be diagnosed as avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) – a new diagnosis that has been included in the latest Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. ARFID is another label in the alphabet soup of diagnoses that neurodiverse children are given. We may think that these are the tantrums signs of a spoiled child or of an underlying psychological problem, but it doesn’t seem unreasonable that many of the foods or at least some ingredients really do hurt the neurodiverse child. It’s not a psychological phenomenon, it’s a physiological one. A coping strategy to avoid harmful foods that may easily backfire and worsen health like in the case of Greta Thunberg whose refusal to eat anything except tiny amounts of rice, avocado and gnocchi almost got her hospitalized. The trouble with food may start much earlier: many mothers of neurodiverse children report that their child had been a colicky baby. Even though by far not all colicky babies are neurodiverse (in the strict sense) the condition may be an indication of struggling with certain nutrients in baby formula or the mother’s breast milk. Colicky as babies, picky as toddlers, that isn’t the end of struggles with food intake for neurodiverse people. Come puberty come eating disorders. In recent years it has more and more crystallized that neurodiverse people are at much higher risk for eating disorders than neurotypicals. This is true for both ASD (especially anorexia nervosa) and ADHD (especially bulimia). The typical onset for anorexia and bulimia is around 17 years and therefore most likely tied to sexual reproduction and psychological in origin. These eating disorders are also often accompanied by self-harm (40%). Even if neurodiverse people have been spared all these troubles by the time they are grown-ups there is still a high chance of developing gastrointestinal problems.Crohn's DiseaseInflammatory bowel diseaseIrritable bowel syndromeCyclical vomitingGastritisLactose intoleranceFood intolerance may be a lifelong problem for many neurodiverse people. It is what we would expect to happen if their (relatively) recent ancestors were foragers rather than farmers or herders. If this is really the case, it is time to think of neurodiverse people differently. For more information on the “forager” view of neurodiverse people check out my book Beautiful minds - a new view of neurodiversity

These findings indicate that alleles for autism overlap broadly with alleles for high intelligence, which appears paradoxical given that autism is characterized, overall, by below-average IQ. question: Are there any treatments or cures for autism spectrum disorder?
answer: Exploring Effective Treatment Options for Autism Spectrum Disorder Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses a diverse range of conditions affecting individuals differently. While there is no one-size-fits-all solution, several effective treatment options exist to enhance the lives of those with ASD. 1. Early Intervention Programs Early diagnosis and intervention play a crucial role in managing ASD. Targeted programs, often involving speech therapy, occupational therapy, and behavioral interventions, can significantly improve developmental outcomes. 2. Behavioral Therapies a. Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA)Focus: ABA aims to reinforce positive behaviors and diminish undesirable ones.Effectiveness: Widely recognized for its effectiveness, particularly in improving communication and social skills.b. Social Skills TrainingObjective: Helps individuals with ASD navigate social interactions.Implementation: Sessions often involve role-playing and real-life scenarios.3. Communication Therapies a. Speech-Language TherapyTarget: Addresses challenges in speech, language, and communication.Benefits: Enhances expressive and receptive language skills.b. Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC)Usage: Utilizes tools like pictures, gestures, or technology to support communication.Adaptability: Tailored to the individual's communication preferences.4. Pharmacological InterventionsMedications: In some cases, medication may be prescribed to manage specific symptoms such as anxiety, aggression, or hyperactivity. Consultation with a healthcare professional is crucial for proper guidance.5. Educational SupportIndividualized Education Program (IEP): Tailored educational plans cater to the unique needs of children with ASD.Inclusion Programs: Integrating children with ASD into mainstream classrooms can foster social development.6. Sensory Integration TherapyObjective: Addresses sensory sensitivities common in individuals with ASD.Approach: Utilizes activities to help regulate responses to sensory input.7. Parental Training and SupportEducation: Equipping parents with strategies to support their child's development.Community Engagement: Connecting with support groups and other families facing similar challenges.Conclusion The effectiveness of treatment options for ASD varies among individuals, and a combination of therapies often yields the best results. Tailoring interventions to the unique strengths and challenges of each person with ASD is essential. Collaborating with a multidisciplinary team, including therapists, educators, and healthcare professionals, can provide comprehensive support.

question: How can I prevent myself from having an autistic meltdown during a test?
answer: I’ll first talk about dealing with an autistic meltdown as the one having it. Train yourself not to speak at all, at those moments we tend to lash out at people. If you were interacting with someone, excuse yourself. Breath focus on breathing and find your way to an outdoor area where you can see at the sky, breath fresh air into your lungs, feel it and smell it. If you have any calming tools use them here, earphones, sunglasses, cellphone, etc. If you don’t have access to the outdoors, find a private silent room like the restroom. In here we can use our coping maneuvers like rocking, pacing, etc. Find peace and keep breathing till you can calm down. These episodes are what we want to avoid and to help ourselves cope, we need to do our homework and write down every event that triggered a meltdown. Start figuring out your triggers and try to avoid them or keeping them to the minimum. Also, we must train our minds to go to a good place, for this we use meditation. Sitting down in a quiet place and visualizing good things that calms us and makes us happy, while holding a finger or a hand position. That way with time you just have to breath and hold your finger or hand position to make your mind calm more easily. Now, dealing with another person’s meltdown is a different scenario. This is for the family or friends around the person with a meltdown. Don’t scream or use a low calming voice if possible, right now the person needs calm and quiet. If there was any arguing, do your best to interrupt it and save it for a better time. Don’t touch, try to pull or move the person with the episode. They are probably having a sensory overload, and touch can be very bad at this moment. In this part I must add that for some kids or older autistic persons a tight hug from someone they trust like a parent or friend helps them calm down. But they must have previous practice, in many cases is good to let them know they are going to be hugged. Help them get to a quiet private room without too many stimuli, where they can deal with the episode calmly.
