question: Can you describe an autistic meltdown?
answer: I love the other answers that are being given - but only another neurodivergent individual can truly understand an autistic meltdown: so I'm going to describe it from an outside perspective. Here is a serious of texts I've sent to my fiance at the beginning of a mild meltdown - in a larger meltdown, I do not have the capability to text, and only gibberish will come out due to my racing heart, foggy brain, and shaky hands. This is a REAL EXAMPLE. Real texts, real situation, and it has my fiance in a leading role of continuing to be the best man out there. Take a look at the timestamps - this meltdown lasted a little less than an hour. They can be short. They can be long. And they are emotional rollercoasters. Like an actual rollercoaster, autistic meltdowns usually start out by going from 0 to 100 real quick. Things then go up and down from there, depending on stimulation, emotional maturity, and self-regulation. In the very first text, there's no signs of distress, barring an accidental typo - but the next text takes it to 100. “I'm losing my mind” is a much more aggressive, bold statement than “I'm upset”, and it told my fiance right away that I was MORE than “just upset” - hence why he smartly decided not to joke at the moment. Though it is the most LOGICAL idea, this doesn't work: my husband then begins trying to come up with solutions to my problems. This is normally helpful, but an autistic meltdown is about emotions - so… logic doesn't help. What really helps is listening to the frustration and letting them express why they're upset. I'm able to do this throughout more texts, and my fiance realizes that his logical solutions aren't working, hence his frustration and loss of confidence in exactly what to do. This is totally normal for someone who is not autistic to experience - this feeling of helplessness because you really can't fix them in the moment. And of course, he can only interpret my distress through text, because he was at work and I was home sick. So at home, I'm almost in a fetal position, trying to hold back sobs while tears stream down my face. I'm angry - not at the cats for annoying me, but at myself for not being able to handle it. It becomes a vicious cycle of self degradation and kicks to my own self-esteem. This makes it particularly hard to recognize I am in a meltdown, because it feels like the entire sky is falling down and I'm not strong enough to hold it up. I'm quite lucky - I have caring roommates that heard my tussle with trying to deal with my cats. They've decided to check in and remove the stimulation, aka my cats, taking them out of my room and allowing me time and space to cool down. This is one of the best moves you can make when someone is having an autistic meltdown: remove the stimulation, because 99% of the time, that's the reason why we're having a meltdown in the first place. By removing the cats from my room, my roommates effectively made it so I could just lay down and think by myself for 5 minutes - and that's all I needed to calm down and start talking through my feelings, eventually coming to the conclusion I had a mild meltdown. This is a mild meltdown for me, as I've exhibited much more harmful behaviors in the midst of a meltdown - specifically self-harm, the most common of which has become slamming my head into hard objects, otherwise known as self-injurious behavior (SIB). Why do I do this? Why does any autistic do this? I can't speak for all of us, butn speak for many - I've found a majority of autistics feel the exact same way as I do. It's because we have to match our physical pain with our mental pain - because no one can see the pain of mental anguish, but one can visualize the pain of a bruise or a bloody wound - because pain is what grounds some of these people. This is not an excuse for the behavior, because it's absolutely unhealthy and needs to be worked on in any struggling autistic, but it is an explanation as to why someone may do it. Meltdowns come in all forms, from shutting down completely - not talking or moving for a long time - or even property or bodily damage. People run away, people get in fights, people make impulsive decisions. And a meltdown is never really a simple moment of anger - it's often fluctuating feelings that go numb and then come back even worse than before. Imagine it's as if their brain has hit a fire alarm, and now all the braincells are screaming and running through the hallways, all logic gone. Something to keep in mind - brains are a complex thing, and behaviors are coping skills. When an autistic begins to have a meltdown, they move from the executive functioning part of the brain to the emotional. This is why logic DOES NOT WORK. It RARELY does. And for some autistics who have been traumatized or victimized too many times, they automatically slip down into the survival state of the brain. Depending on the situation, either or is quite possible. Here's a little model to help explain these states:This chart actually helps understand what an autistic then needs in their moment of meltdown. In an emotional state, they need to feel VALIDATED. They need to feel like the room is listening to them and they are SEEN. This is what it means to feel loved and connected. Your listening ears need to be on and your mouth should be mostly shut - let an autistic get the feelings out and vent, this is not the time to shame them, reprimand them, or reason with them. They need to return to a calm “executive state” for that to be possible. Their emotional state is shown through EMOTIONS. These will mostly be verbal indicators, as the chart has mentioned. This includes crying/wailing for children - it's how they communicate! In a survival state, they need to feel SAFE. This is when it's more important to take action because it will be much harder for them to calm down on their own, as well as much more harmful and destructive to themselves or others. Actions taken could be things like: removing stimulation as mentioned earlier, allowing the person space and time to themselves (people can be a trigger), walking an autistic through breathing or grounding techniques, or helping provide a distraction. The goal of this is to focus LESS on the situation that upset them. No matter how important it is, it can be discussed when they are feeling more calm - someone in panic won't retain information. The survival state usually causes fight, flight, or freeze to kick in, and it's usually the first two. Keeping this in mind, it's best to handle an autistic in this state almost like a wounded animal. They WILL lash out, it WILL be hurtful and 99.9% of the time, it's not actually personal, they're just in pain. As a neurotypical, you can choose to take it personally or you can stick it out and see what the root of the problem is. I hope this makes it easy to understand that meltdowns are FAR from tantrums (especially a temper tantrum), and they are actually an emotional overload for someone who's already struggling with big feelings™. As others have mentioned, these meltdowns start with small things stacking up before something finally breaks that emotional dam. And whether it's just a crack or a big hole, the whole thing is coming down.

question: What is a meltdown in autism?
answer: Meltdowns can be rage or tears (mine are almost never rages), but it always means the brain has reached its capacity for coping with emotions, sensory input, demands and so forth. A flood of flight/fight chemicals hit the brain and nervous system and the person having a meltdown is not in control of their behaviour at this point. They are not having a tantrum, trying to be manipulative or trying get their own way - they are gripped with emotions like sheer terror and powerlessness to avoid the onslaught on their nervous system. The best way to deal with meltdowns will vary for each person. Often deep pressure can be very helpful as it kind of acts as a pressure release valve via proprioceptive input. Often an autistic person hitting themselves, rocking, headbanging or throwing themselves around is an attempt to gain strong proprioceptive input for relief from what feels like your body and mind completely fritzing out. Some autistic people may need to be left alone completely until the meltdown passes because all sensory input can become painful and frightening. Some may have other ways in which they can be helped through such as quietly talking in a positive and loving manner and so forth. Care should be taken to avoid placing any demands on an autistic person in mid-meltdown as they are not processing anything at this point and it can increase or prolong the duration and severity to do so. Help them feel supported and loved and try not to place emotional values on the meltdown such as "terrifying, tragic, stressful, harmful, burdensome" as autistic people can often feel deep shame at their lack of control during them. Mental health issues are a large problem for many autistic people and, aside from the social issues, can stem from feeling like a burden and being unsupported or even punished for meltdowns. Very violent and destructive behaviour can be a part of meltdowns for some autistic people and this needs addressing with professional help. As I don't have experience with these I don't have any specific advice for this. My own meltdowns tend to be full of confusion, floods of tears and stimming. The worst of mine may involve shouting or self harm but I've never been violent towards people, pets or property. Meltdowns shouldn't be confused with shutdowns. Shutdowns are the brain's way of trying to head off a meltdown. It can look like total withdrawal from interaction, sleepiness, unresponsiveness, staring off into space etc and it may involve stimming (repetitive movements, sounds etc) which is another proprioceptive input that autistic people use to help regulate their bodies and emotions.

question: Why are Autistic meltdowns normal?
answer: Meltdowns are not part of the diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder (ASD). They are common for quite a few people with ASD, especially children who have not learned to recognise and manage their sensory, social, and emotional stress loads. But they are not a mandatory feature of ASD, and a lack of meltdowns does not exclude a person from a diagnosis. Some people with ASD suffer “shutdowns” rather than meltdowns - they turn inwards rather than outwards, and disengage from their environment and stop responding. They don’t look like they are having a tantrum, as many people mistake meltdowns for. They are more likely to look motionless and unresponsive. Many people just withdraw from overloading situations, perhaps giving rise to negative comments from “typical” people who do not understand how an autistic person might be feeling at that point. Rather than melting down, they might come across as rude or abrupt, as they brush aside any social interaction that increases their emotional load, and try to withdraw as far as practicable (that’s me). If you are just trying to hang back and stay quiet and recharge, it may be annoying to have someone persistently trying to draw you into a social group. Even non-autistic introverts have this experience a lot. I am not aware of having actual meltdowns, although I am aware of being overloaded and having difficulty coping with particular situations - and I am aware of the need to spend a lot of time alone recharging. While adults are more mature and able to recognise and manage their own emotional state, I also think that adults are less likely to be coerced into situations they cannot handle. Children are often forced to endure situations that - as adults - they can avoid. For example, as a child I had to sit at the family table, even though I was suffering misophonia there and found it very stressful and tried smuggling in earplugs to cope. As an adult, I can sit somewhere else without having to ask permission; I can put in earplugs if necessary; I am allowed to make my own choices. So I suspect that some meltdowns reflect the lack of choices given to children - the expectation that they will cope with situations that the adult does not understand from an autistic perspective. Dictatorial adults must be the bane of some autistic children’s lives. No wonder they melt down when forced, yet again, into autistic-unfriendly situations by an unthinking adult. My sympathies are with the child.

question: How do we eliminate autistic meltdowns?
answer: When someone (child or adult) is emotionally dysregulated, the “thinking” part of their brain is completely shut off. Don't try to rationalise. Don't scold. Don't apply logic. Don't threaten. Don't say anything that requires any level of processing. Don't expect anything you say to register. Depending on the dysregulated person's comfort level with the following: You can be present. You can comfort. You can use a soothing voice (the words don't matter, song or hum if you want). You can locate and offer a comfort item. You can distract with the right stimulation (maybe an activity, maybe a favourite song). You can have a calm conversation with someone else about something else. Once the moment has passed (often longer than the person appears calm), you can gently find out the causes or triggers for the episode. Help the person find ways to manage their emotions more constructively - if you have access to professional help, use it, if not, look up calming strategies online. Be kind and compassionate.

question: Why are autistic meltdowns sometimes cute?
answer: An autistic meltdown is anything but cute. Being on either side of it is distressing- you either suffer, or watch a loved one suffer, and nothing can stop it. Only time will allow that. That being said, my brother and I were only diagnosed with autism spectrum disorders after childhood. We were too old to be considered “cute” if we lost our cool in public. I was 12, and my brother was 10 (he’s always been tall, and we’ve been mistaken for twins for much of our childhood, since he looked older than he actually was until a few years ago when height stopped defining perceived age). My brother’s meltdowns are much worse than mine because he lashes out at his environment in panic, and his size makes that very risky. Surprisingly, he’s managed to stop lashing out in the past year, but he still gets in your space and it’s incredibly scary. Sometimes, I forget what he’s going through because I worry for other people. But even my meltdowns aren’t cute. Unless you think that a 19 year old girl crying and screaming is cute. I don’t. There are a lot of tears. If anything, my thoughts after a meltdown go to “I should drink a glass of water”. But it’s just a mess. I suppose it calms down once I isolate myself to just tears. Lots and lots of tears. Think the sad part of any chick flick where the female protagonist lost something important to her and cries. But imagine that scene lasted an hour or two. That’s what it gets like on the way down. Sometimes, that’s as bad as it gets. The screaming only comes into play when someone is making it worse. Like if my dad decides to blame me for being upset, or doesn’t give any space when I go to my room to get away. That’s the only time that the screaming comes into play. And none of it is cute. Even though I’d say I’m pretty cute otherwise, my meltdowns are not. For the time that I’m crying in my room, I’ll allow myself to wallow in self-pity. Poor me, poor me, poor me. Nothing bad that happened to me could have possibly have been my fault (it usually isn’t in these cases, but that’s not to say that I’m always blameless. Only most of the time). These thoughts would be unacceptable for me any other time, but I let them come when I’m having a meltdown because I’m not really “there” to think rationally. I’m not anywhere where those thoughts should get out, and I can collect them a little later, but not when I’m like that. It’s not a time for thinking, I suppose. It’s a time for feeling just a little bit more than way too much.

question: Why is the cause of an autistic meltdown so cryptic?
answer: It isn't. Not to me. I know what I'm upset about. I can identify it. (Usually. I can't account for every trigger, but neither can most people.) I can explain it. I can show what was behind every moment. But…"Everything was smooth and calm, I did my best to be kind to you, and you lashed out at me for no reason at all." No: it was for no reason that occurred to you. For me, it was the last straw in a string of provocations I'd tried to be nice about. [My customary disclaimer: "You" is a rhetorical device, I have no quarrel with the original poster.] You insisted on meeting in an acoustically-active space where (even though not painful) I couldn't pick your voice out; you rapid-fired topics (e.g. gossip) off-point for our relationship, leaving me no space to contribute. (I need time to parse and assimilate — which is not a deficit, socially it's quite constructive). You interrupted. You talked over me. (You're not a boor, you have habits that kill communication with the neurodiverse.) But you don't know anyone else with those needs; therefore I don't; therefore my requests for relief are frivolous, not sincere attempts to make a pleasant moment work for us.Your side of the looking-glass? You'd coaxed me out of my shell so I could enjoy 90 minutes at an exciting new venue; you shared generously in the face of my shy disengagement; just as sweet as apple pie. And despite your kindness, for no reason at all, I blew up at you. See what you have to put up with? If we're lucky, I'll just slam my hands on the table. Or shout you down. These aren't deliberate, I can't help it. This is the leading edge of a meltdown. I'll have mortally offended you, but at least I'd saved us both from the maelstrom.Please don't deprecate us for being cryptic; I guarantee every autistic here knows exactly what I'm talking about.(I had a marvelous theory of the topology of autistic cognition, but it was too lengthy to fit in this margin.)

question: Can you explain what an autistic shutdown and meltdown is?
answer: I only have those types of episodes at work, where I get the most stressed and over stimulated. Meltdowns were angry tantrums. I would come in and find things not being done the way I would have done them or expected them to be done and I’d yell and act a fool. That’s one example of something that would trigger a meltdown. It’s very rare that I have meltdowns anymore because I taught myself an important lesson: to not judge people against myself. I’m not suggesting that I’m so much better, rather I’m rigid and unyielding and do things in a specific way. When I saw things being done a different way, not even a bad way, I would get overwhelmed and angry. I can “talk myself away from the edge” now and avoid a meltdown because I remind myself that it’s just my perception when I see things being done differently, but with the same results. It takes work but I don’t lose my mind. Shutdowns are rare, unless I have a really bad day. A really bad day is multiple people calling out and I’m running around trying to do my job as well as get as much of their work done as I can. That situation is rare these days but in early post Covid times, it was almost the daily norm. I would have periods where I couldn’t talk and just hyper focused on one task, working at it until completion, moving to the next task, banging it out and muscling my way through the rest of the day. It was brutal and painful. When I got home I would just pass out, sleep like 10 hours and usually feel better when I awoke. Again, I passed out as soon as I finished my dinner and felt a little better the following day. I wasn’t really normal until the day afterwards though. My wife and I have caused each other to meltdown when we would argue and fight but that’s not something we do anymore, thankfully.

question: Is electroconvulsive therapy good to prevent autistic meltdowns?
answer: No. It is deeply misrepresentative of what AS fundamentally deals with, in terms of meltdowns, processing and stimulation. Autistic meltdowns, derives, oftenly, from overstimulation, high levels of angst, high levels of anxiety or other issues, such as OCD related things. But, the point is, that by virtue of these small tricks - you, as a AS person, learn to adapt and integrate in a constructive way, comparatively to “breaking down”, as that is what AS meltdowns are - Just, NOT being able to cope, with said overstimulation.

question: Do you hurt yourself during autistic meltdowns?
answer: Physically, no. When I have a meltdown, I feel physically weak. I might collapse in my room and cry it out. What hurts most during a meltdown is all in my head. Irrational thoughts play on loop, and I convince myself that those thoughts are true. Usually it’s some shit about how I will never be able to do ____, or that other people are pure evil. It usually depends on whether I feel I was the problem or not in events leading up to my meltdown. It's the best I can make of my thoughts with all that adrenaline shooting straight into my heart and brain and nowhere else. Convincing myself of something so horrible hurts me in its own way. But once I calm down, and I recollect my thoughts, the pain can go away so much more easily. I don't think there are scars left behind. I consider myself very lucky that I am not in any physical danger during a meltdown. If there is one thing I don't need around while distressed, it's someone watching and grabbing at me.

question: What can I do in an autistic meltdown?
answer: What can I do in an autistic meltdown? I copied and pasted this from my other answer. I hope it can help you. I take Risperidone (Risperdal): It helps the irritability and lessons the sensory overload. I think it dulls out some of the bodily annoyances, helps my headaches too…It helps a lot but I’m not saying this is the answer. Once you are in the meltdown, it’s going to be hell on earth sensation wise, irritation, emotionality, body pains, and you just have to have a place to go meltdown that is safe until you can ride it out. As you probably are well aware of. Then you have to deal with the aftermath of the pain it left on your body. Have medication and Tylenol ready for that. The best thing is to prevent it from happening but that is not always too easy in this world, is it? If there are frustrations that detract from your well-being, trying to hit those head on and get plenty of rest, sleep, and eat right. That sounds totally cliche but when you are lacking in bodily comfort and tired and have your senses off kilter, it can and usually will lead to a meltdown. You are trying to cope with too much sensory overload as it is, and you have to take good care of yourself so you can handle each task at a time. Sensory Triggers Pay attention to what your sensation triggers are and try to avoid them. For me, working under fluorescent lights for 8 hours, was a no GO! Pay attention to heat and cold triggers and avoid noisy environments or wear noise cancelling ear plugs. The fabrics on your clothes, wear mesh fabrics in the summer, and soft fleece in the winter. Don’t wear constricting clothes, cut tags off, anything scratchy, or ill fitting. If your body temperature has trouble regulating, wear layers that you can take off and put back on instead of being stuck being too cold or too hot. Certain sounds are triggering, and they range from various things. Sometimes people and their irritating sounds are the trigger, get away or take a break because you can’t really tell them that they are getting on your nerves. ;) People are stupidly rude with perfumes and irritating sounds, so always be prepared to combat that with tools you keep on you. If you have too much sensory overload, you are going to have a meltdown. It doesn’t change when you get older, you just know how to manage it better. If you are in a meltdown you can try to listen to music or wrap yourself in a weighted blanket if you can. Try to listen to something uplifting and hang in there. Skin You might have skin issues and get rashes easy so keep your skin hydrated and use sensitive products to protect your skin. Use non harsh laundry detergents and have a good skin regime and also lots of fruits and veggies. Your skin will give you clues to your health if you pay attention to it. Food Avoid gluten at all costs. Autistic people do well eliminating gluten. A lot people on the spectrum do not know to do this and it is proven time and time again they either have Celiac disease or gluten intolerances or sensitivities. Eat properly for you and avoid food triggers or allergies at all costs even if you have to turn down people’s potluck dinners because you feeling unwell is not worth the risk. I have Celiac and I will not EAT someone’s food they offer to me even if it hurts their feelings. Never compromise your health. Exercise You have to do it! Cardio will help you with energy metabolism. If you can do some weights do them, stretch, etc…just do something. Yoga is always good. Relaxation Whether it is taking time out BEFORE you fatigue yourself, or feel like you might be getting overwhelmed, do not push yourself. You do not have to apologize to anyone or be pressured into going beyond your limits. There are too many situations where we feel we have to be strong for people and do “too much” which compromises our well-being. Do not go past your limits. You are in control of you, and YOU set YOUR limits and don’t tolerate for one second people pushing your boundaries. :)…because they will if you let them. Sometimes I have these “mini” meltdowns that are not full blown, that are preemptive signals. Ut oh, I feel weird, I need to chill and eat and do some ASMR and or binaural beats before shit hits the fan. ASMR is like a life preserver for me. Put that on with some calming oil and a candle and go into deep relaxation as this will help regenerate you. If you need medication or a green herbal type of medication, that’s ok. Whatever you find that helps you. I have had 30-hour meltdowns and that is because I had trouble with boundaries. Do not do that and you will find that actively preventing them, will lesson them.

question: Why are Autistic Meltdowns rarely happy?

question: Does closing your eyes help prevent autistic meltdowns?
answer: Maybe - it depends on what’s causing the meltdown, and how early you catch it. For me, there comes a point where nothing will stop the meltdown. It’s inevitable. However, if I catch it early enough, removing any stressful stimuli can help “free up resources” for me to process and deal with the remaining ones. So - if it’s loud and bright, closing my eyes might help me deal with the noise. Or putting on sunglasses, headphones, or ear defenders. Closing your eyes is sensory avoiding behaviour. Sensory seeking behaviour - such as rocking, cuddling, or stroking something soft - can also help soothe and prevent meltdowns.

question: What is the difference between an autistic meltdown and a borderline personality disorder meltdown?
answer: The shorthand answer is that one is environmental, the other is interpersonal. The longer answer is that the core of each is different and you have to understand that to understand that the sameness you think you see is just not there with meltdowns. Autistic people have to deal with A LOT that most neurotypical people don’t have to put up with. Imagine if every single social skill you have ever learned from the age of five upward, you’ve had to learn by rote. And when I say every single skill, I mean ALL of them. Even very basic stuff like, “I must not take up all the seats on the subway with my crap because others may want to sit down.” “I must wait my turn in line.” “I must remember to smile and say hello to the doorman so he is not rude to me later.” “I must say please and thank you; I must not do repetitive stims at work because that freaks others out….Not everyone automatically has the same point of view that I do and I must never assume ANYTHING where other people are concerned.” It is EXHAUSTING. This is what comes to the neurotypical naturally; those on the Autistic Spectrum are born without it and it is life long. Socially interacting isn’t always happy and stimulating, but rather draining. It isn’t that those on the spectrum don’t like other people or are misanthropic. It might appear that way, but remember, most on the Spectrum even if there was a cure would probably remain naturally introverted. It is just that the world is not built for them. Everything is always upside down. Everything caters to the neurotypical. They do not like surprises because for them, that openness to a new experience could mean danger. Remember the words of Chuckie Finster: “I don’t know, Tommy. That could put us in a heap of trouble. What if?…..” Sometimes the aloofness people detect is actually the autistic guy being overwhelmed or needing to recharge his batteries-give him time, he shall return. It isn’t that he does not find your adventures with your pal Mabel in Pacoima fascinating. He actually might think they are funny and he is not leaving because he didn’t like the tale. It is that he is trying to communicate to you what he is thinking and feeling and interpreting what you are thinking and feeling all at once and has been at it for weeks with the whole dang world and now he is running on empty and if he does not go lie down or do something stimmy (goes to his computer to read knitting patterns and knit til the cows come home) he cannot soothe himself and recharge. You were blessed with a limitless power, whereas his kryptonite is that he cannot function for periods that are as long. He is sorry he has to go upstairs and lie down. He may even curse himself for having to do it and wish you could have better, but if he does not go lie down, he is going to melt down. So much smiling. So much putting others at ease. So much tired. So many rules to remember and so hard trying to fit in. He wants you to have the best friend you could hope for, as good as any of your other friends, including Mabel. But curses! Curses! He is at the end!! On top of that, if you are on the spectrum and have sensory issues, sweet Jesus, it is hell. Your five senses are more sensitive than anyone else’s. A simple sound like the sound of a heater vent can sound like a heavy metal concert that you cannot escape. Certain foods you just can’t eat without gagging; this is more common in children and adolescents, but it can continue into adulthood. People think you are crazy when you can’t wear things made out of wool because you react to the sensation of every single teeny fiber against your skin scratching, scratching, scratching. If it gets bad enough, people may catch you writhing on the ground in agony, but you are too far gone into the episode that you can’t verbalize “get this goddamn thing off me!!!” and you are trying so hard not to hurt the feelings of the person who knitted it for you (you don’t always know which social rule or custom to prioritize; it isn’t like there is a handbook or manual assigned to you at birth since for 99% of humanity the rules are intuitive.) in summation, it is an environmental reaction. Outwardly it looks similar, but it is not. And the higher you go up the spectrum, the less frequent they become: that is a mistake a lot of people who are normal make. Higher functioning autistics can go YEARS without a true meltdown. And simply removing the stimulus is enough to avoid a meltdown, as is being a little flexible and understanding the autistic guy. He may come off as aloof, but to him, in a relationship, you are his most precious pearl. He won’t even know if you feel neglected unless you verbally TELL him so and then he will curse himself for not seeing it coming. You may have to accept he is not always up to snuff socially, he is Egon Spengler in a lesser form, but let him have his little collection of rubik’s cubes, his little hobbies and quirks, and know that the answer is actually no-they can never replace your love. His obsession with washing machines cannot kiss him. He just needs that stuff to stim on so he can calm down and keep himself regulated. BPD is a different beast. Meltdowns are usually triggered by interpersonal problems. It is always emotional in nature. BPD is a very, very painful mental illness to have. Most with the condition do not intend to hurt the people they care about, but unless they are in treatment and stick to it long term, they inevitably do. A pwBPD does not have the outer skin most folks do to deal with even the slightest negative criticism, even a tiny bump of negative feedback can send them in a tailspin. They are hypersensitive to EVERYTHING. They deal in extremes-they are not just sad, they are anguished, depressed, and maudlin. They aren’t just angry-they are a volcano of rage. They aren’t just happy-they are euphoric. And their thinking is often all or nothing at all. (Sorry BPD folks, ’tis true. Pause. Breaaathe. Now, remember a time where you thought, “it is a gray area.” Not many of those, are there? I am not being a critic. I am trying to ask you to think, clear your head, and use logic, use math. Count.) Unlike autism, BPD is not present from the time one is a baby. question: What is the physiology of an autistic meltdown and its after effects?
answer: A meltdown for an autistic individual (ASD) is the singular, ultimate escape from an overwhelming situation or conditions that exceed neurological coping ability. Unlike a child's classic tantrum that derives from emotional escalation and consciously chosen behavior, the ASD meltdown is a neurological shutdown that short-circuits the individual's ability to reason or self-regulate. Internally, it is a state of abject terror and helplessness. There is no ability for conscious self-control, and self-injury or injury of others can occur. Compassion, care and soothing are the appropriate responses from caregivers. Attempts at reasoning or problem-solving will simply be ineffective. The primary model describing the physiological and neurological cascade of events: Executive Function Shutdown: Under the cumulative stress of sensory overload, the brain's limbic system activates the fight or flight response . The amygdala in this fear state, triggers a flood of stress hormones and chemicals (adrenaline, norepinephrine, cortisol). The sensory processors in chaotic communication with the neural circuits of frontal cortex reach a 'tipping point' in which the ' system crashes.' This includes a shutdown of the synaptic chaos of the prefrontal cortex (pFC) and its executive functions. Reasoning, problem-solving, and self-regulation are inactivated. The meltdown may be overt in a physical outburst of fight-or-flight, or sometimes the meltdown may be covert, with a 'freeze' response and general lack of responsiveness. In either case there is conscious control of behavior. Note: The comorbidity of ASD presenting with epilepsy (30%), and conversely, epilepsy presenting with ASD (46%) leads to speculation that similar synaptic overactivity seen in both disorders may help explain the nature of Austism and the seizure-like properties of a meltdown. The similar irregularity of EEG brain wave activity in both ASD and epilepsy may shed light on the neural short-circuiting that accompanies a meltdown. The Neurology of Autism Spectrum Disorders Once the meltdown has run its course, exhaustion follows for hours or even days. A recovery period of hours, days or even weeks may include reduced cognitive and language engagement. This may reflect the time needed to restore former connectivity and synaptic activity in the frontal lobe and and pFC. ANATOMY OF A MELTDOWN:https://hes-extraordinary.com/executive-functions/ It is always urged that intervention during the early signs of a meltdown is critical in avoiding full escalation. Noting the triggers, reducing the sensory load, changing the environment, removing the individual to a 'cool down' place, etc. are all urgent. This early time is also when problem-solving and coping strategies (that have previously been taught) should be modeled and guided.

question: Why do autistic meltdowns resemble tantrums?
answer: In both cases children (and adults, a lot less fun to watch) are being loud and noticeable, something our culture doesn’t generally approve of outside of being on a stage. However, in a tantrum, the person acting out (and it is an act, which can start or stop on a dime) is carefully watching for any sign of relenting on the part of their company regarding whatever it is that they do or do not want to happen. Tantrums are, at their base, one of the least pretty ways of manipulating other people to do as we wish, and there are far too many bosses who never grew out of this pre-schooler behaviour. On the other hand, meltdowns occur when any human being reaches a state of overwhelm that feels so hopeless and helpless, the only response is to express the pain in the hopes that someone who has power (God? Teachers? Parents?) will change the circumstances that are causing the physical or emotional pain. An example of a meltdown would be someone screaming and crying after an earthquake, so upset that the only way to stop is to wind down, and so consumed by their own pain that they have little-to-no awareness of the world around them. If you are near an autistic child — or adult — having a meltdown, the best thing you can possibly do is to notice what might be in that environment causing physical or emotional pain, and do what you can to reduce it. Sometimes that means moving the person out of a sensory-overwhelm location, sometimes it means providing health support (most often for gut pain, or headaches related thereto), sometimes it means just staying nearby and being loving.

question: What are the types of autistic meltdowns?

question: What is an autistic meltdown and how should it be handled? Has anyone experienced an autistic meltdown before?

question: What is the best way to handle an autistic meltdown? I would prefer someone who is autistic answer this if possible.
answer: Validate, validate, validate. Many times people react to our meltdowns with frustration and annoyance. They try to fix our behavior instead of helping us cope with the cause of our meltdown. Things like, “That's not that big a deal", “why can't you just calm down", and “You're an adult (or big kid) act like one"; is not helpful. Things like, “Hey, you seem overwhelmed! Do you want to go somewhere quiet?”, “Hey, is something going on? Do you want to talk to me about it?” And “That was really rough for many of us, is there anything I can do to help you cope?”; Are much more validating. The behavior we are exhibiting in those moments is not the problem. As long as we're not hurting anyone, its usually us trying to cope with how something feels. That's not necessarily emotional either. That high pitched ringing sound or flickering light or smell that you can tune out…we can't because it genuinely causes physical pain. We aren't being overdramatic or difficult. We are in excruciating and debilitating pain and us flapping our arms, rocking or crying is us trying to communicate that we are in pain and need help to fix it. We can't just calm down. It's not bothering you but its a red hot iron against our skin, which is a big deal. Start with identifying what's causing us to meltdown. If that takes more than a minute or can't be eliminated, get us away from the potential stimulus immediately. Then validate how we are feeling. You may not experience it the same or understand why we feel that way but giving us the space we need and understanding we need to feel safe in that moment can make all the difference. Stim toys, grounding techniques, talking it out or just letting us express our meltdown in a safe environment is a game changer once we escape the situation. Then when we are calmer, talk through it with us. Ask us what you can do to help. Things that help me: Stim toys Deep breathing Grounding techniques Hugs Food/water/sleep Someone to talk to Turning off lights/sound till my body stops panicking Everyone is different, so what helps me may not help others.

question: Why do some autistic people suffer from hard to predict "autistic meltdowns" while others appear not to?
answer: Everyone has a different threshold for meltdowns. Some are very good at identifying when they’re going to hit their limit and take steps to decompress and emotionally recharge. Others aren’t so good at self-monitoring, or a single situation was more overwhelming than they expected and a meltdown was unavoidable. I’m reasonably good at knowing when I need a mental health day away from people, or when I just need to step away from the crowds and get me head back into a good space. In the middle of a London street, the same spot we’d been three times because Mum refused to ask for directions, after the fifth time in an hour that someone had walked into me, after two weeks in the same jeans and alternating between two shirts and sets of underwear because the airline lost my bags, with no opportunity to have some time to myself… I couldn’t help it. I stamped my feet, refused to move, and was on the verge of bursting into frustrated tears, because I’d tried to tell my mother that I needed a break, but no one would listen! I’d managed two weeks of chasing the airline, in the company of near-strangers and in extremely stressful circumstances (The clothes and shoes that I wear for comfort on an aeroplane is NOT what I wear hiking around Scotland), and I’d hit the wall. Mum apologised for not listening, and we found a quiet restaurant to have dinner and get away from noisy crowds. I apologised, too, and we managed another hour or so of sightseeing before heading back to the hotel. Meltdowns are not tantrums, and having one doesn’t indicate a fault or a lack of self-control. If a Meltdown seems random, unpredictable or spur-of-the-moment, then you missed the dozen or so signals leading up to the straw that broke the camel’s back.

question: What is the best way to avoid autistic meltdowns? What are the best ways to calm down when it's on?
answer: Some of the Ways to Help autestics with AnxietyPinpoint what triggers anxiety. Identifying what causes the child's anxiety can be helpful in identifying ways to help them. If the anxiety trigger is known, you can help him cope with and possibly overcome their fears. Parents and teachers may encourage the child to engage in situations that are anxiety provoking (but safe), and praise or reward the child when they do so.Visual Schedules and Transitions. Children with anxiety and autism often struggle to transition between activities at school and during daily life. The struggle to transition between activities can often be intensified if children are transitioning between a high-preference activity and an activity they do not enjoy. To help with this, many children can benefit from a visual schedule, which may include a picture of the activity and a time that the activity will occur. These schedules can help children know what to expect and in turn reduce anxiety levels. It may also be helpful to show the child a picture or video of transitioning smoothly to the next activity before doing so. The video or picture can provide a positive example of a smooth transition, but can also help the child know what is coming up next.Safe spaces. For children who have anxiety, providing a safe space for them when they are feeling anxious or overwhelmed can be helpful. However, it is important to keep in mind that a safe space should not be used as a regular solution to anxiety. Rather, it should be used only when needed during extreme situations. If a safe space is overused they could become a way to escape daily life and activities in fear of anxiety triggers, which is not the intention. Often, a child who is experiencing social anxiety at school will become overwhelmed while interacting with peers in group settings, walking down a busy hallway, or eating in a noisy lunchroom. If a child is experiencing extreme anxiety from these things, a teacher may create a safe space that can include beanbags, calming games such as some puzzles, stress balls, or relaxing music. Different things will relax different children, so it’s important to keep the child’s individual needs in mind while creating a safe space.Relaxation techniques. There’s a lot of recent research coming into schools about relaxation techniques such as meditation. Meditation has been shown to help many students reduce their anxiety levels, from test-taking anxiety to anxiety in daily life. However, meditation may not be the right fit for every student who is experiencing anxiety, which is important to keep in mind while searching for anxiety reducing techniques.Social Stories. Social stories can be a great way for teachers and parents to show children situations before they happen. A social story can be as simple as a story about walking to the cafeteria or going to a grocery store, but the story should model what events will likely occur during the situation. By reading the social story before the event happens, children may feel less anxious about what is going to happen. It’s also an option to create a social story that shows something anxiety provoking, and modeling a way to overcome this. By modeling this through a social story, children may be more likely to handle the situation in a calm manner. Because children with autism are frequently visual learners it can help children understand a social story by providing a set of cards indicating next steps.

question: How does an “autistic meltdown” look on an “high functioning” adult? Can it look like a borderline or narcissistic rage?
answer: An autistic meltdown on a high functioning adult may appear that way. It may present as a tantrum when in fact it isn't related to not getting what you want but more sensory related. For example they might be complaining of the light flickering and it being distracting and become increasingly agitated with it to a point of a meltdown. We also have a hard time learning to regulate our emotions because of how intense we feel things. The difference between an autistic person wanting control and a narcissist wanting control is that a narcissist will try and manipulate others to get what they want and make them feel guilty if they don't deliver. An autistic person just wants control of the situation to relieve anxiety and avoid sensory overload but won't manipulate other people in the process. We don't use others to our advantage. If someone is making it difficult, we tend to just leave the situation rather than try to persuade anyone to meet our needs. Also if we get what we need we will be grateful and be able to function much better, whereas a narcissist won't show gratitude. So I think an autistic meltdown can indeed look like a narcissistic rage, but the motive behind it differs greatly.

question: How can I anticipate an autistic meltdown in someone I care for?
answer: The more you get to know the person, the more you can openly discuss it with them (assuming they are verbal), the more trust develops and the easier it will be. Basically, ask them, check in with them. Alternatively, keep a discrete eye on them and watch for build-up signs and make a mental note of what was going on when the meltdown happened. Slowly you'll build up a map and learn how to head the meltdown off before it starts in many cases. As a recently late-diagnosed ASD person, I am learning the anatomy of my own meltdowns. Obviously everyone is different, but here are some triggers of mine…Too much simultaneous input. E.g. trying to understand what is being said to me while multiple people are talking at once, trying to decipher speech while music, machinery, traffic is in the background. Also, music, TV too loud — especially if I am trying to think, write or perform a task.Being in a loud bright unenclosed environment — stadiums, wide open spaces, crowds, busy streets, airports, motorway or train stations. This is worse when the sky is overcast yet bright, winter low sun or there is noisy wind or rain as well.Loud aggressive speech and behaviour can set me off as well as being around drunk people or near excited crowds. Male aggression or machismo really sets me off.Unexpected changes to my planned activity. Also people letting me down or making unexpected demands.Stress and pressure, particularly when I am not allowed time to think about what I actually want to do or say.Any kind of confrontation or conflict, especially when it's with people I don't know.Long term build up of too many unresolved issues.“loop conversations” where there is no conclusion, where each contribution is met with “yes but” — people being deliberately argumentative or obstructive. Also people lying to my face and assuming I am stupid.Unfamiliar situations and unknown itineraries.Being in a fast moving vehicle or up high.Life itself. Sometimes there is no specific external or obvious trigger — it's just overwhelming being me.Lastly, I am developing a personal theory around the phenomenon often described as “catastrophizing emotions”. I have noticed in myself and other HF Autistic people I have worked with, that a single negative or stressor can quickly expand in our thinking and become our whole world. Our whole identity rapidly collapses into a pit of self-destruction and suicidal desolation from one initial point. Similarly, if we become absorbed in a single task or subject the opposite happens — we globalise our joy instead of our catastrophe. If we can learn strategies to utilise this globalizing feature, we can perhaps manage and reduce the tendency to meltdown.Hope that's helpful.

question: What are some tips for dealing with an adult autistic meltdown?
answer: Focus on de-escalating the situation. Don’t react intensely or negatively. You will only escalate their meltdown. Don’t scold or shame the autistic person. The focus should not be solely on containing the situation and shutting them down. This is harmful. This can lead to emotional suppression (i.e. bottling it up), masking, and autistic burnout if the autistic individual is forced to internalize all their pain and struggles. The focus should not be on trying to make them behave “normally” and “appropriately”. Normal is different for those on the spectrum than it is for neurotypicals. You may not understand why the autistic child/adult is having a meltdown, but you don’t have to. Remember that whatever they’re freaking out about is real to them. Don’t trivialize or invalidate their emotions and experience. Use calm, positive language when speaking to them and about them.Let them express their frustration, anger, hysteria, sadness, etc. Don’t invalidate their emotions and make them feel like they’re bad or deviant for having strong negative emotions. Of course, you can teach healthy coping mechanisms and responses to those on the spectrum, but this shouldn’t be done just to make the autistic person conform. Coping mechanisms should benefit the person’s emotional and mental health. NOTE: What is actually healthy for someone on spectrum is often different than what neurotypicals think that they need. Autistic individuals primarily need emotional and social support when they’re having meltdowns. That can be in the form of talking to them and comforting them or giving them the space they need.

question: How can I distinguish between an autistic meltdown and a temper tantrum?
answer: While they may look similar, meltdowns and tantrums are totally different things:Causes: Tantrums often occur because a child wants something they can't have and consequently gets frustrated. Meltdowns may be caused by this as well, but they also have other causes such as sensory overload or extreme emotions that a person can't control.Control levels: A tantrum is a controlled outburst. The child knows what he/she wants, and once he/she gets it, he/she will stop. On the other hand, meltdowns are often uncontrolled. A person having a meltdown often cannot control the course of it the same way a child having a tantrum can.How they stop: Like I said, a child having a tantrum often wants something and will stop once he/she has it. Unlike tantrums, meltdowns often do not end once the needed thing is provided to the person and only go away with time.Awareness of danger: Since tantrums are more controlled, a child having a tantrum is aware of his/her surroundings and danger. A person having a meltdown, however, may lose this sense due to the lack of control.

question: Are there any ways of dealing with an autistic meltdown that don't involve just waiting it out?
answer: Nothing fast that I have ever come across or heard of. There are however clear potential ways to shorten the time.More substantially reducing the stimuli like loud noise and bright or flashing lights or excessive heat or other people that are affecting the person (or just moving them away from source may be preferable). question: What is an autistic meltdown? What are some ways to stop an autistic meltdown?
answer: The way to stop a meltdown is to prevent the meltdown. As has already been said, a meltdown comes from being overwhelmed by the situation we are in. If you know the autistic person and want to help them, help them by making accommodations that help prevent the overwhelm. So, if there are routinely loud noises where the meltdown occurs eliminate them or let the autistic person work in a quieter place. If there are bright fluorescent lights turn them off and let the autistic person use a lamp with a warmer hue. Ask the autistic person what you could do to head off meltdowns before they happen. There could be any number of triggers but cutting down on the triggers is all anyone can do to help. Don't ask the autistic person during or after the meltdown. Wait until the next day, but early, before the triggers have a chance to begin the overwhelm. Any changes you need to make to the environment will probably make it more comfortable for other people who have to spend time there.

question: Can an autistic meltdown be caused by dealing with difficult and toxic people?
answer: Oh, HELL yes. For me, that is the worst thing, by far. Intent is all important. A difficult child or animal is not a problem for me. But an otherwise competent adult that chooses to be irrational or illogical and/or unreasonable is unacceptable. It makes my head explode. I try to reason with them. I point out the illogic of what they are doing. But you can’t reason with such a person. They only want to bolster their ego or attack or be extremely selfish. The worst are people that choose a path that is even detrimental for themselves, but they don’t care as long as they can harm me. A neurotypical person with good social skills is much better able to deal with such people because such people are mostly driven by emotions, not logic or reasonableness. Not being able to deal with them makes it worse for autistic people. Indeed, just being autistic is more likely to trigger unreasonable or toxic behavior from them. Plus, being autistic means I’m less likely to identify such people prior to their irrational behavior, so they catch me off-guard. Finally, I’m generally expecting people to be logical and reasonable because I am. A neurotypical person can better relate to such people and understand them, or at least has the skills to defuse or avoid them.

question: What are the signs of an autistic meltdown? How can a non-autistic person tell if they are witnessing an autistic meltdown?
answer: Autistic meltdowns are often mistaken for temper tantrums and then mostly in children. It is very hard for an outsider to just see the difference. One thing that we can use to come to understanding is that a temper tantrum is ultimately a performance. It is still a way to get what we want, like that particular sort of candy that our parent refuses to buy for us. If you pay real close attention, you will notice that a person/child in the tantrum is checking what happens. An autistic person in a meltdown is not performing. They are (almost) entirely closed off from the world and are just processing the inertia of the meltdown. It is a fully automated process that will run its course. The reason is that the person concerned has been pushed far beyond what they can bear or tolerate and now the brain shuts down in an ultimate attempt to be safe. A meltdown is a very much externalizing way to shut down and shut out. Some people internalize in such moment and the result is a shutdown. Much less embarrassing for all concerned but basically it is the same thing. Meltdowns can be rather violent and look like anger or rage. It is not anger but, again, the difference is very hard to see. The best thing we can do is learn to know what triggers meltdowns and then try to stay away from those triggers. One note for parents of autistic kids: exposure therapy doesn’t work! It will only traumatize the kid further and put them on a hair trigger. So just forcing it to go to that busy place that is so hurtful for them will make matters worse. Far better then to work with the child to get some insight into their own emotional life and empower them in that way. Perhaps, later on, they will choose to go somewhere they found difficult before.

question: What are additional autistic meltdowns?
answer: In the spirit of the meltdown confession. I know someone who would like to remain anonymous but also has a neurodivergent moment. They were between the ages of five and eight, beginning in school, and experiencing difficulty. They had begun the intervention process between home and school, and it was overwhelming them. The child had come home from another stressful day at school where they were not understanding much. They had homework to do. The parent was helping the child with their homework, but there were gaps so the parent was basically doing the homework for the child. When the two of them were done, the parent stood up and got off the bed. There happened to be a hair brush on the bed. The child was so frustrated with the homework and their inability to understand it that they suddenly and impulsively picked up the brush. When the parent was not looking, they jerked their arm quickly and released the brush at the parent’s head. The parent wasn’t facing the child and didn’t know the brush was flying towards their head. It whizzed past and smashed the bedroom window, crashing right through it. The sound startled the child, and the child started to cry. They had shocked themselves by causing a big accident. The parent took the child out of the room, away from the glass. The parent helped the child to bed and didn’t concern the child with the window late at night; they only reassured them things would be better, and school would be easier. They would fix the window, and they would talk about what the consequence would be for breaking it. The child apologized to the parent and went to bed crying. The person had forgotten this happened for decades and was mortified to remember it. They said it would have been so much worse if their parent was freaking out too. They were afraid.

question: What are common misconceptions about autistic meltdowns?
answer: Meltdowns are meltdowns. A melt down happens when you have reached the end of your tether. When someone who isn’t autistic has a meltdown, what do you call it? It’s the terrible 2’s when you are a toddler. It’s hormones when you are a teenager. Maybe it is called going off the rails when you are a bit older. Don’t tell anyone to “snap out of it”. A meltdown releases strong hormones into your body. After a meltdown ANYONE needs a period of time to settle down. A physical fact of biology. Never mind ‘Mind over Matter’. Time out. Time without stimulating more emotional responses. Pre-empt the melt down. Get a formal procedure together, a drill so that you and the autistic person agree what to do next. A drill to cope with a melt down BEFORE IT HAS HAPPENED. The Domino Effect. In September 2024 I visited a friend near London. One thing after another set me off. I ended up on Victoria Station just sitting and watching, and being in my own autistic safe place. A nightmare for me. I was so on edge I could hardly make myself breath sensibly. My safe place? My mobile phone. Just sitting. Sips of water. Throwing my timetable away, and getting rid of hopes to achieve targets that day. Watching the world go by. Getting used to all the sensory overload so that I knew all the sources. Singing to myself. Visualising favourite places, like a walk by the river or in the park with trees around. Feeling my lucky stone in my pocket. Playing with the toy car in my other pocket. Rooting through my handbag with out knowing why. Just seeing my familiar things and touching them. My pen. My cotton handkerchief. My diary. The receipt for my train ticket. My keys. Grounding myself. Sitting on the bench swinging my legs. Soothing behaviour that some people call ‘stimming’ or comforting yourself. Don’t push your luck if someone (in my case, me) is showing signs of being emotionally overwhelmed. It usually has a build up. The warning signs should not be ignored. They need to be recognised and accommodated. I need to be still. I am quelling the hormone-driven reflex to ‘fight or run off’. I need a mentor and companion to go through airports. Someone to lead the way. Lots of us autistic people find those things too much on our own. I can follow and blank out the oppressiive busyness if my companion is taking responsibility for both of us. I look around and see lots of people travelling in twos. Autistic people are not unusual in that respect. It is more unusual to be confident and self contained and have the social skills to eat out on your own, or go on holiday on your own. An agreed procedure on what will happen if you have a meltdown. How to look after yourself after a melt down. Psychological abuse. Recognise that there is a big difference between the heat of the moment, and the cold light of day. Save meaningful discussions and negotiations about boundaries fo another day. I am pleasant, well-meaning, and frequently don’t consider the same things that other people do. Inconsiderate. Inconsiderate means I have not taken things into account. An error of omission is totally diferent compared with the same error driven by meaness of spirit or spitefullness. Try giving the benfit of the doubt, and ask direct questions if you think someone has a grievance. BE KIND. Break the vicious circle while you can. Change your attitude. STOP the old fashioned ways of disciplining people. Shouting. Telling them off. Pointing out what they have done wrong. Threatening them. Giving them bans, and grounding them. creating unnecessary anxiety and distress. Boundaries. Discuss and agree boundaries in the cold light of day. Don’t rub anyone’s nose in their mistakes and short comings unless you are deliberately trying to goad them. If that is the case, ask yourself what sort of person you are. See how you like it! Controlling yourself only works so far. Who ever you are.You might get sent on an anger management course. Why are you supposed to have the insight to deal with these intense emotons. Environmental factors can make a huge difference. The more alien the surroundings, the more likely you want to break out, or give up, and curl up and die. There are many people who take a pleasure in tormenting and controlling other people. Who likes being bullied and controlled? Really? Do you like being talked down to? How about being bossed around as if you don’t have a mind of your own? Autistic people are capable of taking responsibility for themselves. A temper tamtrum is a sort of meltdown. A large amount of emotional energy is stored up and released. People who bottle things up are more likely to have a meltdown. Bottled up emotions are a concentration of highly charged emotions. They are neither good nor bad. A meltdown is a release of those emotions. People cry when they are overjoyed. It is all too much for them. People cry when it is all too much, one way or another. Learning to control and monitor and vent your emotions of all sorts is the key to avoiding meltdowns. Anyone can have one. Whether that person is autistic or not. Meltdowns are not inevitable. There are anger management courses, assertiveness courses. Grief councelling, parenting courses. Non-autistic people have emotions too. And mental health statistic show that 1 in 4 people have some sort of breakdown in their life time. Inclusive Policies matter. Most measures benefit everyone at one time or another. A quiet bench, a small amount of public space in a busy area, a tree of two, colour coded route guides to signpost the way. All these things enhance everyones life by upgrading the physical surroundings. It can be difficult to do in retrospect. So EASY TO INCLUDE inclusivness at the architectural inception and planning stages. Autistic people can live better lives if anxiety , stress, and depression are dealt with. Living conditions are important.

question: What should a spouse do to assist a partner who has an autistic meltdown?
answer: Help them escape the situation and bring them water. Try to create a sensory environment according to their needs, which will vary for each individual. Meltdowns are supremely draining.

question: What are the symptoms of an autistic meltdown and shutdown?
answer: When I am heading into a meltdown I first feel like I need to cry. I feel overwhelmed and full of anxiety. If I am in situation triggering a meltdown the anxiety gets worse and worse and the need to cry gets worse. If I’m doing tasks I become less coordinated and less in control of my body. I’m more likely to drop something, fall, or injure myself because I’m not as coordinated. My mind starts ruminating about whatever is bothering me. If I retreat to my room and rest I can stop a meltdown before it’s full fledged crying. In the worse meltdowns I actually cry like you would if someone died, get physically ill, sometimes get fevers, have body aches, and other physical symptoms. Shutdowns are when I feel so incredibly exhausted all I can do is lay in bed and stare at the wall. My mind ruminates and won’t stop thinking so I can’t actually sleep much. I would say it’s like having the flu in terms of body exhaustion. I have to lay there for days off and off (I still do some daily activities) until my body has recovered. I know I’m feeling better when I can watch TV again. In full shutdown TV makes me stressed out. I have to be in silence with my fan on.

question: How is an autistic meltdown/shutdown different from an anxiety/panic attack?
answer: I have only had one panic attack in my life. I’m not even sure I can put the difference into words, but the fact that I recognised it as a different thing suggests that there are noticeable differences between that and a meltdown. I think for me, the panic attack felt more like my heart was racing, like I might collapse maybe? There was a definite difference, but interestingly I describe my meltdowns as a feeling of panic. To me, a meltdown is much more fight or flight. I describe it as feeling like I’m a scared mouse trapped in a small cage, and there’s a hand reaching in to grab me and I can’t get away from it. How would you feel if you had a hand reaching for you, grabbing at you, and you couldn’t escape from it? It manifests as a cross between panic and rage, a desperate need to ‘bite the hand’ to escape, so I’m usually so panicked and upset that I will shout in a way that sounds angry, or cry through the feeling of panic, and flap my hands a bit to try and cope with some of what I’m feeling. It isn’t anger, it’s fear, but it can come across as anger to the outsider. Even my husband, to this day, often believes that I’m angry before he realises I’m having a meltdown. It takes him some time to work it out. Despite the fact that he has seen me genuinely angry I think twice in the time we’ve been together, and both times he said “you’re never angry like that”, because then it has been actual, genuine anger. In fact, when I’m angry I’m coherent - my words come out clear, and determined, and meaningful. When I’m in a meltdown, the best you’ll get out of me is desperate shouting and stammering. If I try to ‘hold in’ a meltdown, it sends me into shutdown. This is entirely different. When I go into shutdown, all energy disappears from my body. I can barely move, I don’t have the energy to speak and can go non-verbal because it just takes too much effort to force words out, I’m so incredibly tired, I can’t process what’s going on around me so I feel almost like I’m underwater - like I can see and hear things, but everything is distorted. My brain just doesn’t have the energy to process information any more.

question: Could I have autism even if I don't remember having an autistic meltdown?
answer: Meltdowns are not mentioned anywhere in the diagnostic criteria for autism. Think about that. Having a meltdown does not make you autistic, and not having a meltdown does not rule out autism. It doesn't rate a mention. Meltdowns are one form of evidence that a person is impaired by their autistic traits. But a lack of friends, difficulty finding employment, having shutdowns, avoiding “normal” places because of sensory stimuli, and various other experiences would also count towards a finding that the person was impaired in their daily life. A single characteristic does not make or break an autism diagnosis. Autism depends on a whole set of characteristics, in the context of your whole life. Meltdowns, or the lack of them, are just part of a bigger picture. It is the total picture —- your life as a whole — that makes you autistic or not. If you meet the criteria for autism, you are autistic. And the criteria don't mention meltdowns. But you do need evidence of past or present difficulties resulting from your autistic traits, and meltdowns would certainly be one example of such difficulties.

question: Do autistic meltdowns justify physical or chemical restraints?
answer: An Autistic Meltdown as described by the National Autistic Society UK is 'an intense response to overwhelming situations. It happens when someone becomes completely overwhelmed by their current situation and temporarily loses behavioural control.’ So it entirely depends on the person, what triggered the meltdown and the behaviour they are exhibiting. The only circumstances physical or chemical restraints are justified being used is if the person is violent toward others who haven’t caused an issue by touching them or trying to make them respond, they are being destructive i.e. throwing / breaking things, or they need immediate medical attention whether it’s because they are having a medical episode or have severely hurt themselves and are fighting help. Physical restraint though can be a family member or friend who knows how to hug or hold them properly to give them the pressure they need to feel safe and help them desensitise from the environment. Most of the time physical and chemical restraints aren’t ever needed. The best thing is to let them process it and deal with it themselves and then when they are back to being ‘present’ ask if they need anything and support them with what they need. question: Can you explain what an autist meltdown is and how to identify if a child has autism?
answer: An autistic meltdown looks similar to a temper tantrum, but is the outward manifestation of a brain system that is overwhelmed. Autistic brain only means different brain, not disabled brain.
