question: Why do autistic meltdowns resemble tantrums?
answer: I’m noticing a trend in my answers. To emphasize that Autism is not a disease you catch that makes our neurotypical (NT) brain and body suddenly autistic. It is a developmental difference… Or the way the autistic nervous system forms compared to the NT’s. nervous system. So, to understand why meltdowns are different than tantrums, you have to understand that you cannot use NT child behavior to understand autistic child behavior. There is also so much variation between the traits and the degree of influence between each autistic person that trying to state “general traits” becomes so basic it is stated as the big three - Social + Communication differences and restrictive repetitive behaviors. These are so general they do not begin to describe how these can manifest in individuals. I feel confident in saying that physical and psychological sensitivity and regulation are two important factors that are common among many if not all autistic people. It gets complicated because the smallest neurological changes can have vastly different effects from person to person. Then you have to factor in billions of variables in location and degree. What devastates one person may be manageable to another. Depending on the intensity of the neurological stimulus and ability of the person to cope… the most simple stimuli can be either bothersome for one person, or send another person’s system into fight/flight/freeze survival mode where the instinct overrides conscious self-control. At the most extreme case, the child/adult has been so neurologically overloaded, the survival instincts take over. This is a subconscious act like going into shock after an injury. It is not a consciously controllable event. And like it says… the person will FIGHT(physically or psychologically) to stop the current OR accumulated past stressors. FLIGHT or run away from (physically or psychologically).. or FREEZE or shut down physically and/or psychologically. This is not a process a child and even some adults are aware is happening. Both to the events that lead up to this level of crisis, or during… It is not as if there is a meltdown meter in our brains like a fuel gauge. There may be overt indications another person may understand in context. Over time, an understanding between stimulus and response can be learned by the autistic person. Remember that being autistic does not mean you “FEEL AUTISTIC”. Meltdowns can be a puzzling and frightening as a seizure. We cannot perceive our own perception and look into why we do things. These traits we experience are often interpreted by NTs as“typical” behaviors… such as “tantrums”. When they are really behaviors of s person trying to cope with extreme physical/emotional traumas. Again, it may be simple sound to an NT, but to the autistic child/adult, its a neurological trigger. I look back and realize I’ve had possible meltdowns. I don’t consider myself as extremely sensitive senses… but light can be blinding from dark to light areas. The most quiet and unexpected noise can make my entire nervous system fire the same way we feel when you hit your elbo’s “funny bone”. That simple noise and my response, would be all it takes to take an already stressed system over the edge to Fight/flight/freeze. I searched for 59 years for “something” until circumstances led me to research Asperger Syndrome. When I read what other late diagnosed adults were experiencing since childhood, it was an life-changing realization that THIS is what I had always been trying to understand and explain about my own life. So, autistic children will know they are different, but why and even how can remain a mystery until adulthood. It is so complex we never totally understand even our own system. So, please resist interpreting an autistic child's behaviors with the same criterion you would use for an NT child. They often cannot be compared because in the most fundamental way, they are different.

question: How do I handle my autistic meltdown so that I don't accidentally hurt people physically or emotionally?
answer: I feel the biggest issue with people being hurt by an autistic meltdown isn’t related to the person in question having a meltdown, but their own uncertainty of how to handle the situation. One example I can think of in my life was when someone came over to babysit my brother who’s further on the autism spectrum than me. He had a meltdown, screamed at the babysitter how much he hated her (he didn’t even know her) and she couldn’t handle it. She burst into tears, called her parents who came by and sat around until my parents got home. They questioned me, but I was rather unresponsive engrossed in my video games. For me I just told her and them to ignore him and let him stew in his room. Even the parents of the girl seemed a little taken aback by this idea. If you know your going to have a meltdown around people and you can’t detach yourself in such a way to take care of it privately then you need to just inform people that you do have meltdowns, what your meltdowns look like, and what the best reaction is when your having one. This allows others around you to be/feel safe and not have what amounts to a neurotypical meltdown at your meltdown.

question: Why does my mother not understand my autistic meltdowns and just gets angry?
answer: This got crazy long but it really is a subject with more and more details the further you go. Here, however, is the oversimplified version : It’s likely either, 1. because your mom has never experienced a meltdown, and doesn’t know what it’s like. She doesn’t understand it as something happening to you (on the inside), she only experiences it as actions and behaviours you are doing (on the outside). Because she’s never had a meltdown, the only way she would ever act ‘that way’ would be deliberately - and because meltdown behaviours are so extreme, the only reason to do them deliberately would be to be an a**hole. So, with that perspective, anger is the reasonable response. 2. because whenever your mom had similar experiences at your age, people responded to her with anger. This ‘generational trauma’ means that she’s now making the same mistake, but she’s not even aware that she’s doing it. She’s just ‘playing out the role’ she was given. Below is the longer, more in-depth answer I initially wrote <3 Along with some ‘just my thoughts’ suggestions.It’s really important that I start by saying this : I can’t give you a ‘definite’ answer, because I don’t know your mother. She’s an individual. All I can give you is some common reasons why this happens. I’ll try to give some advice as well, at the end - ways you might try to start discussing this with your mother. Possibility 1. She’s never had a meltdown, so she literally can’t imagine what it’s like. Instead, she likens it to the only comparison she has. If your mum isn’t autistic, and has never had a meltdown… it’s possible she’s never even been ‘out of control’. The closest she might have gotten is being too drunk, but even that experience is quite different. Instead, she only knows that the only reason she would ever do the things you’re doing would be if she actively chose to do those things. So, to her, it’s not an experience happening to you. She has no context to imagine that. Rather, it must be a set of behaviors you are choosing to do ‘at’ her. It’s easy for us, as autistic folks, to see someone in meltdown and think ‘that person needs help’. But that’s because we know that those behaviors are tied to someone not being okay. To non-autistic folks, the only time they’d do those things would be if they wanted to be an a**hole. So, they see someone in meltdown, and make the connection that is natural for them. (It’s important to note, here, that many neurotypicals don’t ‘think’ things like we do. They’re not always aware of having their thoughts. So your mum may not even be aware that she’s making this assumption, which is why she doesn’t even have a chance to think ‘but wait - my child isn’t an a***hole’.) Suggestion: Try to have a ‘neutral’ conversation with your mum. Make a time when you both have time talk about it, then tell her. Tell her that you never mean to cause her pain, but you know that your meltdowns do and you want to try and fix that. Tell her that you’ve been researching, and you’ve learned that it can really help non-autistic family members if the autistic person explains what meltdowns are like, and why you act the way you do. Then explain it to her. Explain that you aren’t in control of your body, or your expressions. Explain that you can’t think. Heck, you can even say that someone on the internet told you it’s a bit like being incredibly drunk and out of control in a really noisy club (so she has a point of comparison.) Keep the tone of the conversation aimed at “understanding and compassion.” You can apologize for the effect your meltdowns have without having to apologize for having meltdowns. But, do not expect apologies from her just yet. She may well need time to digest what she’s learned. Apologies, if they come, will come later <3 It’s not an easy conversation. You have to ‘put aside’ a lot of your own hurt to have it. But it’s worth it, if you can. Possibility 2. Your mum was treated this way by her mum (or her teachers/her authority figures etc) The wider term for this is ‘generational trauma’. It may be that when your mum had meltdowns, she would get shouted at… or even hit. As a result, whenever she experiences your meltdowns, she ‘relives’ some of the trauma she experienced back then - reliving what happened to her when she acted that. Reliving trauma shuts down your ‘logical’ brain (a bit like a meltdown itself) and puts you in a state of pure fear. This means that she isn’t even realising that she’s repeating the same mistakes. She’s in a state of pure emotion, and her response to that emotion is anger. That anger might not actually be aimed at you - it might be aimed at way back in her past, at the people who did that to her. But… they’re not there to be angry at. You are there, and so her brain irrationally attaches the anger to the person who is there. Suggestion: This one is much harder, because it’s a bit like two people having meltdowns at the same time. I would still recommend chatting at your mum, a bit like above. But instead of purely aiming at ‘understanding’, try to think of some things that will help you during a meltdown. For example, explain that you need to be alone in order to ‘destimulate’ - and ask her to please just let you stomp away if that’s what you need to do. Then, next time you have a meltdown, take extra care to come to her (after you’re feeling more settled) and thank her for doing it. If she doesn’t do it, take some time after you’re recovered to discuss it with her again, and ask her (with ‘please’) again. These ‘thanks and pleases’ are really important. It’s a bit like you’re ‘training’ each other.This got crazy long but it really is a subject with more and more details the further you go. I’ve written a simplified version at the top. I hope this helps. It’s a long journey towards understanding each other, if she’s not autistic. It’s like speaking two different languages, when you both thought you were speaking the same one. Good luck, and if this does help you - I’d love to know.

question: How does one de-escalate an autistic meltdown with attempts of self-injury?
answer: There’s no de-escalating something that’s already out of balance/control. Let it play out according to the person’s body regulation needs, so they can find their balance again, unless they are causing very serious damage to themselves (and by that I mean hospital-grade, very-hard-healing damage). What you can do is try and lead them (without touching them, simply and gently, with your voice and body language) away from any potential noise and commotion into a quiet and familiar/safe space, and/or to minimise any potential triggers around them. This will in turn reduce the need for self-harming levels of stimming. Such a meltdown is a sign that the person is going through serious sensory/emotional abuse or stress. The best course of action is a preventive one — make sure that their body needs are addressed and that their body is not under such enormous amounts of stress. Here is a very basic guide to get you started — consider each point in itself:But the best thing you can do is ask the person what is hurting them, what feels unwelcoming/bad in the before- or aftermath — make dire adjustments to their body’s comfort. We may not be the most articulate when it comes to expressing our needs, but we do know our body best, and intuitively we know what’s wrong and what’s wearing our body down to the point of shutdown/meltdown. Most often this involves being socially pushed into (to our neurotype) unwelcoming/inhospitable/painful environments and sensory experiences for a prolonged period of time, to the point that our body/brain can’t take it anymore. A meltdown is an accumulation of harm on the person’s body/brain, keep that in mind. Try to be more considerate to our different bodies (basic human needs) and more unconditionally loving/gentle with us. Respect us as our own person, and our autonomy over our bodies. Even as a parent, you do not know your child’s body better than they do themselves. Nor does the doctor know the patient’s body and experiences better than they know it themselves.

question: What is the difference between an autistic meltdown and a psychotic episode?
answer: These are two totally unrelated things. A psychotic episode is a break from reality. It involves visual or audio hallucinations, distorted thinking, delusions and/or paranoia. A person experiencing a psychotic episode cannot distinguish what it real from what is not real. It cannot be stopped immediately. With medication, symptoms are improved, but it will still just run its course. A meltdown is nothing like that. A meltdown is a reaction to a high degree of stress, usually, but not always, triggered by too much sensory input. It may involve crying, kicking, and/or self-harm, to cope with the stress. In adults, sometimes a meltdown is in the form of a panic attack, or often may be difficult to distinguish from a panic attack. The autistic individual experiencing a meltdown usually needs to merely get to a place or situation in which they feel safe or removed from the source of stress and it will then end. In a meltdown, there is no hallucination or delusion. The autistic person may feel as if what is going on around them is more intense or threatening than it is, but that’s a case of personal perception, not delusion. Other than being a difficult time for both the individual, and those who love them, they have nothing else in common.

question: Can someone have such a severe autistic meltdown they cannot ever snap out of it?
answer: No. There can certainly be cases of people with very severe autism who find themselves perpetually at odds with their environment due to aspects of their condition, and very prone to angry outbursts. I am part of a team dealing with such a person at the moment, a lady who has adpated to supported living arrangments after her family could no longer care for her pretty well, but we still have some issues. But everyone has to go to sleep sometime, anger will make you tired and though people might be agitated for quite a number of hours eventually they will sleep. You might need shifts of carers, you might need to get special legal permission for deprivation of liberty if the person is a risk to themselves or others, you might even need to section someone under the Mental Health Act (only ever had to do this once thankfully), but eventually they will sleep. And when they wake it will be a new day and hopefully the care team has some idea of what the triggers are and how to avoid them this time round. Long term this kind of thing will lead to a cycle of mental health issues though, the continual stress will cause harm, it needs to be resolved as fast as possible. I did do a training course from a professor of psychology who himself had Asperger’s who said he once had to lay in a darkened room for thirty-six hours getting his head back together after a particularly furious argument with his boss. This is the longest I have heard of, and he did isolate himself deliberately to avoid snapping at his family and pissing them off.

question: What's the best thing to do when you see the early warning signs of an autistic meltdown coming on?
answer: Remain Calm! Put aside any anger or embarrassment you may feel. Those will only make the situation worse. A lot depends on what your position in the situation is, but if you can exercise any authority, use it. You need to get other people away from the overwhelmed individual or vice versa, and you need to keep the person from hurting self, others or property. If you are large enough or strong enough to physically control the person, do so. Wrap your arms around him or her and just hold them, strongly and firmly but gently. If you are not that large or strong, try to get someone to help you. But try to be sure that that person is calm and controlled. Talk calmly and quietly to the person, asking or telling them to calm down. Even if you have to escalate to saying something like “If you can’t calm down, I’m going to have to ask the police officer who is standing here to carry you to the car,” stay calm and keep your voice gentle. I once watched a mother of a highschool student who was having a meltdown control her son by holding on to the lanyard that held his ID. She remained calm even when he threw her glasses across the hall, even as students were changing classes and staring at the spectacle, even as more and more of the highschool staff gathered around the two of them; she just kept holding onto the lanyard and talking quietly. Eventually her voice and words got through, the young man did calm down and dissolve into remorse, and they were able to leave the school peacefully.
comment_answer: Thanks for the tips

question: What happens in my brain while I'm having an autistic "meltdown"? There are always parts of it that I forget and I've hurt myself rather badly before.
answer: I don’t know, but I know that a meltdown is a result of over-stimulation and stress. If the autistic brain was a computer then a meltdown would be the equivalent of the computer crashing, the over-stimulation can cause the brain to crash in a similar fashion since negative emotions can spread like wildfire in the brain considering the fact that autistic brains are less-effective at switching back to a calmer state. Self-harm resulting from meltdowns is usually an act of distracting oneself from the internal pain caused by the emotional wildfire, it can also be an act of punishing oneself due to negative emotions. Some autistic people even self-harm to calm themselves which is basically stimming, some feel better because they feel like that they deserved the pain and others do it because of a lack of stimuli. To sum up my answer, meltdowns happen because autistic people usually have extreme emotional reactions to certain things and they find it very hard to calm down. I’ve been here, its not nice but identifying what causes me to overreact really helps with managing it.

question: Why do some people think that an autistic meltdown is the same as a toddler having a tantrum?
answer: It looks very similar. And it’s usually triggered by something seemingly small, so it can look very unreasonable to outsiders. As a parent all you can do really is try to prevent it, not for those outsiders but for the children themselves because that state of overstimulation is just really uncomfortable for them. Once you know the signs that precede a meltdown, it gets easier to navigate. With small children, the meltdowns usually happen faster, the signs are less clear and parents are still learning to recognise them so it’ll look like a toddler having a lot of tantrums over nothing.

question: Why do tantrums have obvious goals (e.g., I want a cookie) whilst autistic meltdowns often are so mysterious in their cause?
answer: Tantrums are an “I want” response. get the thing, and the tantrum stops. Sometimes, what is ‘wanted’ can be mysterious (even the child doesn’t necessarily know). Meltdowns are a ‘make it stop’ response. That seems like it should be similar - locate the distress, and make it go away, and the meltdown will stop (Gradually, maybe, but it’ll stop). That’s not wrong, but the problem is that so many of the causes of meltdowns are due to sensitivities that those around us do not have. In addition, we have often been brought up to ignore those sensitivities in ourselves. How can you remove a noise you cannot hear? How can you prevent overstimulation from painful clothing you’ve just told your child they are being oversensitive about? Unless you know what the cause is - and very often, you won’t, if you don’t both ask us and encourage us to consider it - meltdowns will obviously appear mysterious. You can’t always percieve what causes a meltdown - and while we can, we are actively discouraged from self-awareness, because people tell us we can’t possibly have it. How, then, could they be anything other than mysteries? No one that can understand them is being listened to.
comment_answer: Ok thanks the sensitivities that others do not have and “make it stop” help get my head around this mystery.

question: Should you let an adult having an Asperger’s meltdown run away?
answer: This depends on the situation, but generally “let” is not in question. If the person is a ward of the state or of some guardian then you may be able to stop them though most likely by calling the police not through manhandling them yourself (check the laws in your area), but since you say “Asperger’s” I assume the person is not that low in functioning. If the person is not a ward of the state or of some guardian then ultimately it’s their freedom to “run away” (odd phrasing since they’re an adult) so you will have no choice but to “let” them. The most you can do is try to calm them down and talk them out of it, but cannot use force, and will get nowhere if you try to call the police. “He’s an adult, he may not be making the wisest decision, but there’s nothing we can do” is what you will hear if you try. If it’s really because of a meltdown then they will calm down soon and will probably come back and even be very apologetic. If they don’t come back then there’s more reason to why they left than just a “meltdown”, and maybe they are even making the right decision. It’s important not to dismiss the validity of someone’s feelings just because they have Asperger’s or any other condition. And a person with mild Asperger’s can often still make good decisions. They may leave and be very happy and productive in their new life, though that depends on a lot of things. One more note, if you think the person will drive angry and they are trying to drive away try to talk them out of getting behind the wheel, but even then unless you observe them breaking traffic rules you can’t call the police on them, and assuming you’re trying to maintain a relationship with them you’ll need to decide how risky their driving behavior is before calling the police even if you have grounds for doing so.

question: I had an autistic meltdown in my clinic and was escorted out into the street by the staff. It was hard. Should I complain?
answer: Hi Sam, Without knowing the details of the situation, I risk proposing an answer that is totally irrelevant. But… here goes! :) There are two sides to this…. The clinic’s side and yours. I’m not sure what your melt-down entailed but I’m assuming the people there did not know you or that this was an autistic melt-down, and that they reacted on what information they had. So if the safety of the clinic was thought to be threatened, then they did act in what they thought was the best way given the information they had to work with. It depends on the situation whether your complaint will be taken seriously. I’m not saying you do not have a legitimate complaint, but if you do and they are still defensive instead of receptive, you’ll have to decide if “this is the hill you are willing fight and die for”. You know what happened and why… It could be a great way to turn this into a win-win for the clinic and you. Call them up or even arrange to meet someone in person… ask to speak to a person in charge… Tell them who you are, what happened,.. ( the condensed version) and that you want them to know how this happened and why… You’re not complaining but want to know how you can work together to prevent this from happening again with you and possibly any other autistic patients they may see. If they see you as trying to help everyone and not just complaining.. your efforts may be a lot more effective. If you are comfortable, even offer to come in to do an inservice presentation so other staff can learn from this incident. If they are not open to this offer and you do not feel it is worth getting them to understand YOUR experience and perspective, then it may be best to find a clinic that is more accommodating to your needs. Those are my thought! Sorry about the situation… Best wishes!
comment_answer: Great advocacy suggestions, Thomas! Thank you.

question: Why is there not more research into autistic meltdowns and shutdowns? They can be so crippling and prevent normal life.
answer: Having dealt with some epic autistic meltdowns in the past few decades, I'd postulate that there might not be a lot of researchers who want to get anywhere near one.
comment_answer: My 26 year old nephew with aspergers still has meltdowns. They seem to occur when he can’t get his message across and seem to be from frustration. I think there should be more counselling available to autistic people to help them learn coping mechanisms and then this may be more manageable. But when he has his meltdowns everyone suffers and can be very stressful.

question: Why are autistic meltdowns so mysterious and hard to predict when or where it will occur?
answer: To/ Reader I would say that to the outsider, meltdowns could be unpredictable because you can not see what happens inside an autistic person’s mind. It’s almost like water building up behind a dam, anyone on the other side would only know anything is wrong when the dam breaks. For the autistics, like myself, we may know what things can trigger meltdowns through months or years of experience behind the scenes. However, we will not know when the trigger will occur, so we may get blindsided by the timing. Back to the dam analogy, imagine the water keeps building up behind it at a constant rate. You could calculate approximately when the pressure will become too much and think of countermeasures to limit the damage, but if the rate suddenly changes, it throws off all of your carefully made calculations in a matter of seconds, causing chaos. Michael
comment_answer: Does that mean you could predict an autistic meltdown, within a few hours, but not any more accurate than that?

question: How do autistic meltdowns or shutdowns happen and go? How will the autistic person perform intellectually, socially, and environmentally?
answer: How will all cars perform? How strong are all hydraulic cylinders? How much money is enough? Sorry/not sorry.. As an autistic person with some autistic friends I’m amazed that anyone can think of autism as a monolithic issue. I think if you examined 2000 autistic shutdowns or meltdowns you would have 2000 sets of data to answer your questions. We are all so different. When you think of fingerprints you think that of 7 billion people it is unlikely that two people will match all of their fingerprints with another human. The brain if far more complex than the fingerprint and each autistic person has a slightly different reaction to something slightly different. One autistic person might see a purple stuffed bear and have a meltdown because bears aren’t purple while another sees the same thing and loves purple but is sure that bears should not be stuffed animals…then the third person sees it and hugs it for comfort. If the stress levels are controlled in the specific ways that are needed by the autistic person in their environment then they will be able to function at the level that they are capable of functioning. Some have high intellectual capacity and some do not (like anyone) and some have high intellectual capacity but can’t express it and it’s locked inside them. I have problem with people who are inconsistent. If a person is happy one day and angry the next or sad then I may not be comfortable around that person. Being around them makes my own sense of well-being off center so I’m not sure how to respond or feel. When I am not balanced it’s hard for me to concentrate. This is one of the reasons that autistic people melt down. Inconsistencies in our environment. Sometimes it’s noise or lights and sometimes it’s the people being inconsistent. I’m probably very much like what my uncle describes me as, “a cat in a room full of rocking chairs”. he doesn’t think autism is real so he thinks of me as “too nervous”. But his description is perhaps not inaccurate when it comes to being in an environment that is uncontrolled. I think you need to start a question with the premise of describing a type or level of autism first and then asking how they handle stress or perform under different conditions. And I guess that’s all I know about that.
comment_answer: Great explanation 👍 I especially agree about the people being inconsistent part. That’s why I try to fit a very specific role in helping clients with autism, and then be consistent at it.

question: Wouldn't a term like " (sensory) overstimulation crisis" be more appropriate and perhaps also less pejorative than " (autistic) meltdown"?
answer: Maybe, but people don’t like big words. I used to call a shutdown a “parasympathetic overcompensation” because that’s exactly what it felt and looked like. That was before I knew I was autistic. People would laugh at me for using big words they didn’t understand. Even medical professionals derided me and asked me, mockingly, where I went to medical school. I don’t generally think in words. So when words are needed I have to come up with something accurate, then think it over to translate it into smaller words that others can understand. Otherwise, they get upset and say I’m trying to make them feel stupid. Why would I want to do that? I’m just trying to express my experiences as accurately as possible.

question: How can I best handle the after effects of a casual acquaintance and work peer witnessing an autistic meltdown?
answer: Purely from my perspective here. The first thing to do is apologize for your behavior. Then I recommend you explain what triggered the melt down. Tell them what haing an ASD means to you as an individual. Possibly, depending on the colleague, let them know of other things that have triggered you. Emphasize you mean them no harm. You would not do anything to them. In a sense you are venting. It will also help to let them know what they can do in the event something like this happens again. Finally apologize again and make some form of recompense. I’ve used flowers and cards with female peers. And with a male I’ve bought them a nice bottle of malt scotch because that’s what he liked. Although in his case he did say, jokingly, I might have to trigger you again. Or words to that effect. Helping them with something they are doing or bringing them a drink is a good idea as well. I’ve been in situations where they’ve actually apologized to me. It’s rare but there are some wonderful forgiving people out there. Do your best not to let it happen again. A meltdown gets old very quickly.

question: I filmed my autistic 9-year-old daughter having a temper tantrum and posted it on TikTok. Why is she upset? Some people are calling this an "autistic meltdown", but I don't believe in those.
answer: Why would you shame a child with a disability? I have taught autistic students for about 15 years. Autistic children have sensory overload episodes for different reasons. There are times when an autistic child can show volitional “naughty” behavior. But as a parent you should be able to differentiate “naughty” from sensory overload. If not you need to talk to someone about your child’s behavior. When this happens make note of what the time is, what was happening in the 30 minutes before the incident started. Figure out what could be triggering the behavior—Is the environment too loud? Is the child hungry? Are you breaking a routine they depend on for self regulation? Was there something promised but not delivered? Can the child ask for what they want? Non-verbal children are VERY easily frustrated! Make sure that any communication devices that you child uses are available to them in all situations. Denying that “autistic meltdowns” are real will not help your child.
comment_answer: My autistic child DOES ask for what he wants, and when he doesn't get it, EVERY time he doesn't get it, he does throw temper tantrums. It is not a meltdown. It's a daily struggle.

question: Can a specialist still detect the severity of someone's autism even if they see them on a "good day" when autistic meltdowns are not presenting?
answer: Firstly, the diagnostic criteria for autism encompass a lot more than meltdowns. In fact, meltdowns are not themselves one of the criteria - they are a response to being overwhelmed, and are an indirect indication of a couple of the actual criteria. So it’s hard to imagine a competent specialist diagnosing autism based on either the presence or absence of meltdowns. Secondly, developmental disorders such as autism are diagnosed based on a pattern of interior experience and external behavior that is “enduring” and “inflexible and pervasive across a broad range of personal and social situations” (this is from the DSM V, but there are similar definitions in other diagnostic texts). What this means is that someone isn’t diagnosed just by observing them for a short while. The specialist giving the diagnosis will either collect information from a range of sources, including records and interviews with family members, or will spend an extended amount of time with the client across multiple sessions. So no, a specialist cannot detect the severity of someone’s autism on a good day or on a bad day. A quick note though, because other answers have said that autism doesn’t have “severity”. This is a position held by the the autistic community, but for the purpose of diagnosis, there are “levels” of autism. These are based on the overall extent to which the symptoms currently interfere with functioning in different areas of life (social, employment, education etc). Again, these can’t be judged just from short observation - the specialist needs to investigate how the person’s life outside of the consultation is affected.

question: What are the symptoms of autism in girls?
answer: I'm “the obsessive fan girl.” I'm “the quiet girl in the corner.” I'm the girl who helps others with their homework. I'm the girl who's seen as a mom-friend to people a few years younger than me, but who doesn't have many friends my own age. I'm the “artsy” girl. I'm the girl who *always* wears leggings. I'm the girl who has snacks in her backpack. I'm the one who daydreams. The one who does quiz bowl. The one who reads all the books in the school library. The one who is clumsy. Autism in boys is often affectionately called “Little Professor Syndrome.” In girls, it is sometimes called “Little Philosopher Syndrome.” In reality, we have the same symptoms. It's just that society perceives them differently because of our genders. I am artsy and am picky about clothes, which was perceived by most outside folks as just a girl being a girl. My autistic brothers are also artistic and picky about clothes. That's seen as weird, because guys aren't “supposed” to care about those things. I've had special interests, and essentially have obsessed over things like Batman, animal healthcare, horses, plants, and various fictional worlds from books. However the voracious interest I demonstrate in such topics is labelled as “fan-girling” because girls are often stereotyped as obsessive fans anyhow. If a boy has a similar level of interest in topics (for example, one of my autistic brothers has a special interest in Minecraft) then it's seen as abnormal, because he expressed his excitement for it THE EXACT SAME WAY I express excitement about Stephanie Brown in the Batman Comics finally being put back into the canon where she belongs or things like that. So if you're looking for signs of autism in a girl, just ask yourself if you'd think a boy acting that way might be autistic. If the answer is yes, odds are good that the girl is also autistic.
comment_answer: “we have the same symptoms. It's just that society perceives them differently”. Precisely.

question: Why does it seem to be more difficult to diagnose autism in girls?
answer: Thanks for the A2A. There are lots of flaws in the way autism was diagnosed from the moment it was discovered. Although it was discovered by two different men, neither thought to consider how the condition would affect females. It was pretty common back in the early nineteenth century for females to be diagnosed with hysteria and sent to live the rest of their lives away in institutions, regardless of the symptoms they showed. Simply not wanting to have sex with your husband could be seen as a sign of insanity back then. Things have improved a lot since then, but old habits stick hard. With the belief from the early nineteenth century leading people to believe that only males exhibited traits consistent with an autism diagnosis, pushing our way in as females and saying, “Hey, I’m autistic, too!” has been difficult. Another reason that explains the difficulty in diagnosing autistic females is the fact that there hasn’t been as much research into how the condition affects us. We have a lot of catching up to do before our symptoms are understood in the same way men’s symptoms have been acknowledged for years. Autistic females are receiving late diagnosis’ at record rates, though, helped in part because of female-dedicated research studies. People are trying to gain an equal understanding, and it’s working, but it’s going to take time. A lot of it. And it’s unfair—it sucks. Some people suggest autism diagnostic rates are a feminist issue, and to be honest, I don’t completely disagree. It isn’t helped by the fact that doctors are still struggling to see past the medical misjudgement from years past. Even though we know more about it now, many doctors are reluctant to believe that girls could be autistic. We are far more likely to be misdiagnosed with conditions like borderline personality disorder before going on, later, to receive an autism diagnosis that fits better. And, while this doesn’t necessarily fit with the consensus I’ve been discussing above, girls are also harder to diagnose because we commonly hide our symptoms from an early age. Autistic females are far more likely than our males counterparts to overcompensate for what we don’t understand. We often look towards our peers, at how they interact in social situations—from what they’re interested in, to the way they fidget when they speak—and try to emulate it to come off as ‘normal’ as possible. It’s suggested that autistic females struggle to keep up with their peers socially when puberty begins, lagging behind and becoming obviously developmentally delayed. This could also be why a lot of autistic females receive a late diagnosis: because, while autism is there from birth, the mask we use to disguise our symptoms falls off when puberty begins. (Sorry for writing such a long post—if it’s not obvious, I could sit here and write all day about the inequality in diagnostic rates).
comment_answer: Also many of the symptoms of autism overlap woth certain gender roles ie oh shes just shy, quiet, introverted and such and as a result some girls remain undiagnosed. Same goes for boys and personality disorders

question: What are some lesser known symptoms of autism in girls/women?
answer: I would say probably the passivity. Because it’s also a stereotype of being female, it often gets overlooked. It shouldn’t be overlooked though, because it can cause problems.

question: What are the symptoms of autism in girls?
answer: My personal experience was that I did not experience a “typical" adolescence. When the other girls were suddenly preoccupied with boys, fitting in, what others thought of them, and what they looked like, I couldn't wrap my head around it. It all seemed so trivial to me. I've also never been the type to be in any hurry to grow up, and I've never cared much for change, as far as my personality goes. When I'd watch my friends change seemingly overnight, my OCD had a field day. I'd constantly worry that they'd leave me in the dust, and I would overanalyze their behavior, wondering WHY they liked certain things one day, and then the next, seemed “over" them. Why were they changing so much? That never happened to me. I've always been pretty static in my personality and my likes/dislikes, etc. Why suddenly disrupt the equilibrium? I like familiarity. My early 20s were kind of similar. I watched some of my peers, albeit early, get engaged and even married. I couldn't understand WHY on earth they'd want to jump into adulthood just like that, when they still had so much time to be young. It baffled me, and I didn't think of myself as anywhere NEAR old enough for that life. Over the next few years, and by the time I was in my mid 20s or so, I learned to let go and not worry so much about what others were doing. It didn't impact me, it didn't cause people to have those same expectations of me, and it didn't mean I had to do those things! :) I figure, “better them than me,” and I've learned to live and let live. It took me a while to get there, but I got there. At the same time, I've retained my personality and tastes. I've never been swayed by the crowd. I'm 37 and still “different.” I've never been on a date, much less have ever had any desire to be in a relationship or married. I learned I'm aromantic and asexual. I still like the same things I always have, like video games, technology, plushies, and just having fun! I'm still a big kid :D Again, this is just my own autistic experience; others may have gone through some of the things I mentioned that I haven't. We're all different! Tell me about your experiences!
comment_answer: I can completely relate to your experience and I’m happy that you put it out here on the internet. Big thank you to you!

question: Since autism in girls is different than it is in boys, what are the early signs in girls?
answer: Early signs of autism in girls can be extremely hard to see, and many woman take years to be diagnosed, some reaching adulthood or even older. The amount of diagnosed boys compared to girls is 3:1, but it is expected that girls make up half of those with autism, meaning that the signs stand out much less, and they may not even be aware of the strategies they use to fit it and go unnoticed. I like this information below as it looks into the behaviours of autistic girls who don’t really stand out or have particularly odd behaviours that would be warning signs to some.If you are talking about a girl below school age then the signs will be even more obscure and hard to spot. I can only speak from experience, but as a young girl with autism I would cover my ears when I didn’t like sounds (such as the bath draining) which my parents decided to wait for me to grow out of. All this being said, it may not be in a child’s best interest to be diagnosed with autism. This is a personal choice for all families, but I personally feel extremely lucky to have been diagnosed at 15. Having something about me that everyone knew was different would have isolated me from the kids that I got along with fine, and I would have been very insecure. Being older, I had the emotional maturity to embrace the diagnosis and decide what I told people and what kind of support I received. If a young girl is not struggling, it may be best to wait until she is mature to talk to her about a diagnosis. Girls with autism can be very social and fit in with those around them, and in some cases a diagnosis could hurt their social life. Autistic girls have every ability to thrive under personalised support and love. Hope that helps :)

I deliberately did not bring my second daughter for a diagnosis, although it was quite obvious to me that she is autistic, for the very reasons you mentioned. Also, I did not want her teachers to treat her differently, when she had no issues academically. I did wish that I knew that my older daughter was autistic. It was not until I learned that autistic girls are more susceptible to eating disorders and self-medicating that I was able to put it all together. By then it was too late to do anything about it. question: What are some signs of autism in girls?
answer: Based solely on observations, the following is a short list.High IQ and creative “genius.”Lack of empathy or the opposite—enhanced ability to empathize (HSP).Truthful and a justice-seeker and supporter (to the degree of what a neurotypical would call, “to a fault”).Thrives in imaginative play, fantasy books, and music.Difficulty understanding social cues, nuance, innuendo, sarcasm and jokes.No need nor desire to make or engage in conversation.Happy being alone or with a pet; especially a cat.Challenged by fashion trends (matching clothing or accessories).Greater or sole interest in scientific research over sociology, history and/or politics.Childlike or infantile views and behavior (no matter the age).

question: What are the main differences between autism in girls and ADHD in girls? A lot of the symptoms seem similar.
answer: They are similar but different. Symptoms of ADHD in girls typically include daydreaming and inattentiveness more so than hyperactivity and impulsiveness. Girls with both conditions can be quiet and shy but this occurs a lot in girls with ADHD since their daydreaming and difficulty focusing is missed a lot. These girls aren’t being disruptive, thus, they are not viewed as having any initial issues. Girls on the autism spectrum, on the other hand, struggle with social cues and can be literal-minded. They may be more social and want friends more than their autistic male peers, but struggle to form such connections and understand certain types of societal norms that associate with girls. They may not want to talk about makeup or boys like their neurotypical peers. Since girls mature faster than boys and are inherently more adept at social interactions, it makes sense why autistic girls are more self-aware and are better at masking their symptoms. They are also repetitive with their interests and behaviors just like autistic boys are, but they may have interests geared towards animals, social sciences or art and music instead of mathematics and science. Ironically, I have more male ADHD symptoms and more female ASD symptoms. I am hyper and impulsive, not as much inattentive. For autism, I am able to understand certain social cues and mask my symptoms a lot but I still qualify for a diagnosis. My interests are in psychology but like boys with the same diagnosis, I love numbers and am quite obsessive with them. Personally, I think more research needs to be done in this field. Ultimately, it’s different for each person

I make friends easily and I'm really good at reading emotions. Social-cues, I'm not so sure how I am with them although according to my mother I'm terrible at communicating, and I'm also really bad at expressing my emotions, or handling other people expressing their emotions. Especially if it's my mum. With friends I'm better at helping them, and opening up myself but it's still a weakness of mine. But all in all, I'm fairly confident I don't have autism, but I like scheduling (although schoolwork-wise I'm terrible at sticking to it) and when it's disturbed by someone or something even slightly I get infuriated. question: Is there a correlation between shyness, social awkwardness, and the development of autism in girls?
answer: There isn’t a direct correlation between shyness, social awkwardness, and the development of autism in girls, but there can be overlapping characteristics. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by challenges with social interaction, communication, and repetitive behaviors. It can manifest differently in girls compared to boys, often presenting in more subtle ways or being masked by social coping mechanisms. Shyness and social awkwardness can be common experiences for individuals with or without autism. However, in autism, these traits might be more pronounced and pervasive due to difficulties in understanding social cues, navigating social situations, and expressing oneself effectively. Girls with autism may also develop coping mechanisms to camouflage their difficulties, leading to a later or missed diagnosis compared to boys. They might mimic social behaviors they observe or withdraw from social situations altogether, which can contribute to feelings of shyness or social awkwardness. It’s essential to consider the broader context and individual differences when examining these traits. While shyness and social awkwardness are not direct indicators of autism, they can be part of a complex interplay of factors that influence social interaction and development. If there are concerns about autism or any developmental issues, seeking guidance from healthcare professionals experienced in autism assessment is advisable.

question: How do you get a diagnosis of high functioning autism in a girl?
answer: There is a lot of information online written by autistic women about how difficult it is to get an ASD diagnosis. Many mothers realize they are autistic when their children are diagnosed. Bright, highly verbal, older girls and women present differently than boys. The DSM standards were written for non-verbal, intellectually challenged young boys. A huge number of kids, boys and girls, get diagnosed ADHD before eventually getting an autism diagnosis because it is harder to recognize the subtleties of autism in kids who seem more "high-functioning." For more information on females with ASD, check out descriptions by Tony Attwood, Tania Marshall, and Liane Holliday Willey. There are also lists of female Asperger's traits on the blogs Everyday Asperger's and help4aspergers.com - Home As for getting a diagnosis for your autistic daughter, keep trying! Find someone who is very bright and able to look beyond the standard diagnosis, preferably someone who has experience with teenagers and bright girls. If your daughter was already assessed and the diagnosis was missed, go through the findings line by line so that next time you give them the "right" answers during the parent interview and the surveys. Focus on meltdowns -- the times when she becomes "low functioning" due to stress, anxiety, and being overwhelmed. Focus on her social and communication difficulties and sensory issues (not part of the official criteria, but virtually all autistics have sensory issues), not her intellectual strengths. "Significant impairment" is what gets the diagnosis. Be very aware beforehand of how girls present differently (often they internalize rather than externalize, they cry or melt down rather than become aggressive). My daughter was also missed because she is exceptionally gifted, but she had lots of difficulties in school when the social demands became too great and she was overwhelmed with sensory issues. She self-diagnosed as autistic and got provisional accommodations in college, and she feels much better. (She is also off meds, which did not help with her anxiety.) She needs the formal diagnosis in December so I am looking right now for the right person/ team to assess her. Good luck!

question: What are the signs of high functioning autism in a preteen girl?
answer: The signs of “high-functioning” autism in many females tend to be quite different than those in many males, though the research is still mostly early on females. Most research, “general knowledge’ and official diagnostic guidelines on autism have come from studies on predominantly male subjects. Traits different in females then got missed by people looking for (actually) male criteria but who assumed all autistics were like the males; the missed females were not included in the next set of studies, and so on, repeated for decades. Circular… Girls vary greatly though, like boys, and no one will have all the possible associated traits. People often learn to modify expressions of their traits to, as many autistics value social interactions and want those to work out as well as possible. Some possibilities for girls: the girl may be aware of working hard to fit in, but this may not be obvious to other people. Autistic females apparently “camouflage”, i.e. work to “act normal” and fit in, more often than boys. Camouflaging requires careful observation of others over time to figure out aspects of behavior, what to mimic, what works when, etc. It’s a long-term process to learn this way, since the innate brain parts that many non-autistics use to do some of this social stuff isn’t working the same in such autistics, but the non-autistics don’t discuss the social behavior in ways the autistics need to learn it… more cognitively or rule-based, than automatically/intuitively. Strong interests of autistic girls can match “normal” girl interests, though sometimes their interests are relatively strong and play can have some differences, according to a couple articles I’ve read, and videos by Dr. Tony Attwood. Dr. Attwood has done many wonderful videos on autistic girls and women, imho. http://www.tonyattwood.com.au/215-what-is-aspergers/girls-and-women They might be having sensory sensitivity difficulties but react differently than some autistic boys, going inward, being quiet, and developing emotional problems rather than acting out like many autistic boys. (internalizing” vs. “externalizing”). However some girls do externalize too. Some read the same books over and over… Some great videos with content by and about autistic women: female autism - YouTube Magazine article: Autism--It's Different in Girls More actual research seems to be coming out all the time. question: How is autism different in young girls vs boys?
answer: In my case I’d say it presented the same, but as a girl, no one paid attention in the 1970s/1980s. Looking back, after all my reading on childhood diagnoses and what made some parents question if their kid was autistic, I see it as a glaringly obvious. But no one noticed, and I was initially shocked at 47 to learn this applies to me. But, it does. I know by age 3 I liked tools, drawbridges and tugboats. I had a lot of boats in the bathtub, and would get excited any time we’d cross a bridge or see a tugboat (we lived near water). I also liked my dolls and other toys, hated water on my face, certain things about clothes, and I recall sleepless nights as young as 2. But, I also spoke and read ahead of time, and by school tested as gifted, so all my weirdness and awkwardness was chalked up to simply being smarter than kids my age. I had the little professor’ issue, where I wanted to talk to the grown ups, they had more interesting things to say, and kids were often mean, or would not let me play with their toys. Little girls were often quite mean. In preK, during playtime the girls took all the dolls, and the boys would not let me join, but there was a real (early 80s, safety was different) workbench of sorts with a real saw and some scrap wood and bottle caps and glue. So while the other kids played, I sawed wood and glued bottle caps to the pieces, alone. I memorized movies I liked. I reread my favorite books, partly to manage not always having someone to talk to at lunch. And I got time out for recess a lot, not knowing when it was ok to talk in class and not. I changed schools a lot, went to 9 total, and each school was a chance to reset and try not to be the weird girl. It failed, I always ended up saying or doing something odd. I hated homework. Until high school I believed it did not matter and no adult ever gave me a good reason to do it, so I didn’t. I passed all my tests anyway. By high school grades were ‘real’ and counted for scholarships so I did all my homework, and was an honor student/grad. But, as a girl, people ignore you lining up your My Little Ponies, or stuffed toys. In boys, lining up your matchbox cars is noticed. As a boy, wandering off alone and not trying to play sports with the other boys is odd. As a girl, you usually end up hovering NEAR the other girls, but may not speak much, may not get a turn at the swings or jump rope. Adults don’t notice this, they just see little Angie with the others girls, all is fine. Or, she’s ‘shy’. Because boys are expected to be rowdy and roughhouse and rambunctious, if they are solitary, bookish, easily absorbed for hours, it stands out. If a girl reads for hours, it’s just seen as normal. Now, the fact she’s reading the encyclopedia may be strange, but that’s what it was purchased, right? If a girl isn’t very social as a teen, she’s just a shy ‘good girl’ who isn’t running off to party. Not a social outcast who’s afraid to try to be around people and mess up and be teased. The signs are the same. Whether that are noticed is what is different.

question: Is autism hard to detect in girls? Could I be autistic and not know it?
answer: Is autism hard to detect in girls? Could I be autistic and not know it? Yes and yes. The problem is, when they wrote the old manuals for detecting autism, they had only boy patients, and they wrote about what autism in boys looks like. What autism looks like in adults or girls was omitted. And the thing is, autism is mostly known from behavior. And different genders and age categories of people are expected to behave differently. Girls are more likely to be formally taught about the right way to be polite and otherwise get along with people. So it’s easier for them to “pass” for neurotypicals who have some other kind of problem. Likewise, with age comes experience and skill at managing your limitations. And also freedom to manage your limitations. So autistic adults seem a lot more ordinary than autistic children. Because we can avoid having a meltdown. As scientists’ understanding of autism grows and is distributed to doctors, girls will have an easier time getting diagnosed properly. But for now, doctors operating on very outdated assumptions is a valid concern.

question: Since autism shows up differently in girls, what are the signs, especially on the lower side of the spectrum?
answer: Okay so I technically has “high functioning” autism and my sister has “low functioning” autism, although I try to refrain from functioning labels as much as possible. However, my sister shows very stereotypical signs of autism, such as constant stimming, echolalia, limited verbal abilities, no eye contact, etc. while I don’t show as obvious difficulties outwards but internalize them greatly. My sister lives in a group home and needs 24/7 supervision while I graduated with a bachelors degree from college and work a part-time job that pays decently. I am quirky and socially awkward but am able to hide my symptoms, or mask, fairly well until you get to know me. I despise change in routine for the most part and am rigid and sometimes black and white in my thinking. I do stim but I don’t typically outward rock or hand flap; my stims are more subtle such as pacing, finger flicking/flapping, and deep pressure compressions. I hate certain noises with a passion, like hand dryers, and can get overstimulated and overwhelmed easily. Yet again, you wouldn’t know this from meeting me. I also engage in perseveration and hyper focus on topics of great interest to me and am keenly focused on attention to details. I am okay with small talk but I sometimes get bored or don’t know what to say typically prefer more meaningful or intellectual conversations. Therefore, to answer your question, girls tend to internalize their autism symptoms and they might not become apparent until adolescent. As a kid, I presented more like a child with ADHD (hyper, inattentive, impulsive) when in fact, I was just not understanding people and social cues surrounding me. I feel like the presentation of other mental health disparities is more common to see, I.e. anorexia nervosa, depression, anxiety, than autistic symptoms in girls. But those with “classic” autism as to say presents similarly to boys.

question: What are the signs of autism in a 20-year-old girl?
answer: The signs of autism in adult women are really just the same sort of symptoms you normally see within autism. These can include: • Problems with direct eye contact • Preferring to be alone at times • Struggles with starting a conversation, or keeping one going • Sensory symptoms (Touch, Smell, hearing) • Having reserved/particular interests As you can see, autism in girls isn’t a whole lot different than autism in a boy for example; however, for years there has been a sort of social perception that autism in females is a lot rarer than in males. This may have very well been the case within data from around 10 to 20 years ago, and even findings from recent years have shown a ratio of 4:1 male to female autism diagnosis. However, current diagnostic methods have been found to misdiagnose many females with separate conditions such as ADHD and Bipolar disorder when, in actuality, they are autistic. It isn’t completely ludicrous as a disorder such as ADHD shares many mirroring symptoms with autism, however it is unfortunately a reason for why many adult women do not receive a correct diagnosis. In general, I’d say that the signs I’ve mentioned above prove that autism may be just as prevalent in females as it is in males, it’s just the historical studies that have falsely painted autism as a male-dominated condition. Hopefully, modern research can soon help to dispel this belief and provide some support to the autistic girls in our community.

question: Why is it said that Asperger 's syndrome and autism in general is different in women and girls?
answer: This topic gets fairly deep and controversial. However, I CAN tell you one reason that boys are diagnosed at a much higher rate (5X higher in fact!). Facts about Autism The debate really is about WHY? Are there actually 5X more boys WITH autism than girls? If so why? Or are there just 5X more DIAGNOSED than girls, and if so why? So I can give you some anecdotal experience after working in the field for over 15 years. Autism often expresses itself differently in boys vs girls. The boys I have worked with are MUCH more likely to hit/scratch/bite/run way/disrupt a group verbally. Girls are much more likely to turn inward, become uncommunicative. This means that in school districts who do not have a wide spread culture or education of supporting children with special needs, that the disruptive/dangerous child is seen, the quiet uncommunicative one is ignored. If your child hit the teacher every day for a year, or ran away from class every time there was story time, you would be motivated to seek out a solution because the teacher would be telling you about every time it happened. To the lesser trained teacher a quiet child is a “good kid.” So, because of the TYPE of behavior that the genders display, it becomes a case of “the squeaky wheel gets the grease.” I cant tell you WHY the genders behave differently. And this is not to say that ALL members of a gender display the same behaviors. Its just a trend I have anecdotally noticed. One of the reasons for the increase in diagnosis of autism is the ever increasing awareness of the signs of autism and the further education and training of teachers/parents. The first to get diagnosed would be the ones that act out in ways that are dangerous. Now we are getting to a point that people are recognizing the more subtle signs as well. I would not be surprised to find over the next ten years you begin to see an increase in the diagnosis of autism among girls.

question: Is there any cure for autism? What are the best medicines that could be easily available for combating autism in a 14-year-old girl?
answer: Autism is something one is born with. There is no cure, there is no ‘combating’ it. The best thing you can do is to provide the necessary support to the autistic child. This may include special educational programs, training for her carers, and other ways to ensure she gets the life skills she needs. It is possible that an autistic person requires certain medications, for instance to assist them in dealing with anxiety. This is something that you and she would need to discuss with her doctor, if and when she identifies certain life problems. To repeat, autism is not something to be cured - it is something we live with for our entire lives. Many but not all autistic people live valuable, productive lives. Finally, teenage years are especially difficult for people with autism. This is the time when people really start forming bonds with others, and those of us on the autism spectrum have difficulty understanding how to form those bonds. A fourteen year old girl will have special challenges and needs, and is at high risk of depression and similar problems. She needs a lot of support, and she needs to know that things do get better. I hope this helps. I also recommend that you read up on autism, to understand a little what this young lady is going through and to help her through it. Here is a list of some suggested reading.

question: A large overlap is found between autism and transgender. Autism is severely misdiagnosed/undiagnosed in girls. Is it ethical to transition young girls?
answer: It is not ethical to permanently alter the body of any young child based on some arbitrary position that child is holding for a while. Let’s look at the figures for a second. About 0.3% of the general population identifies as being transgender. But how many children go through a phase of “I wish I were born into a body of the opposite sex” for whatever reason? Almost all children. Is it ethical to pump hormones into kids based on something that almost all kids go through, but under 1% of kids will actually continue to go through by the time their brains are fully developed? Hell no! But let’s talk about the specific issue at hand- kids with autism being “transgender”. I doubt that the rates of transgenderism are as high as the figures say they are. Here’s a list of reasons why an autistic person is more likely to be encouraged to be transgender:They are already seen and treated as “different” by classmates. This eventually drives many girls on the high functioning end of the spectrum to assert their differences in an attempt to embrace oneself. This can take the form of adopting further “special identities”.Girls on the autism spectrum are more likely to have male friends, because their social impediment may repel them from the bitchy things that are more normal among girls, and less common among boys. They might identify with their male friends, even though they do not physically believe that they are a boy trapped in a girl’s body. The girl’s parents, being eager to jump on a trendy bandwagon of “look how much I love my weird kid”, push this idea on a child who would have just said “I like male friends better than female friends” 10 years ago.Mental illness is more prominent in people on the autism spectrum. Gender dysphoria can be classified as a mental illness because it:Is a blatant rejection of reality by the individualOften results in self-harm (look at the heightened suicide rates in the transgender community, that don’t improve whether a person has transitioned physically or not)People on the autism spectrum are used to being put in neat little labeled boxes, rather than being acknowledged as complex people with complex personalities. Unfortunately, a lot of today’s “genders” (especially the 70 something recognized ones ones that are not male or female) are just personality traits, not genders.I think it’s even worse that this whole situation is being pushed into the autism community. A lot of young girls with autism have identity crises, and are now being pushed into another box that sets them yet another step away from a functional life in society. It’s another unnecessary hurdle for these people. What high functioning girls on the autism spectrum usually need most to succeed is support towards learning social skills, coping mechanisms for sensitivities presented by the disorder, and encouragement. Not “are you happy with your genitals?”. No child should be presented with that question, but especially not a child who is facing enough challenges as it is.

question: What are some early signs of autism in toddlers?
answer: Baby may seem confused at times and cry when there doesn't seem to be anything wrong. Baby may not use as much eye contact as he should. Baby's facial expressions might seem unusual and when you look back at photos, you'll notice it more. You'll notice this more if you have experience with other babies or have had other children. Baby may be unusually undemanding at times (such as during the night and make noises rather than cry) but become demanding and unsettled during other parts of the day, (ie crying after he's been fed, changed and cuddled). Sometimes he just won't settle. As he grows there may be increasing differences in baby compared to his peers, ie: he might be slightly delayed in some or all of his milestones. He may not go past the chewing and banging toys stage without a lot of help. He may play in the same way with toys over and over - especially favourite toys. He may be fixed on certain things such as cars. He may be prone to temper outbursts over unlikely issues such as you buying a new sofa or moving his cot. He may seem confused when others outside his immediate family visit or when people make a fuss over him. He may do funny little movements with his hands, get excited and make sounds either for no reason or by seeing something although this usually develops as they grow. Some babies do not develop speech although they might use sounds. Others may have overall speech and language development delays. They may be slower to speak their first speech sounds (Dada, baba etc) and pick up words more slowly. These are all mostly things I noticed with my son who has ASD and some of these points may be exclusive to his development and not another child who goes on to have ASD as they are all different.
