question: How do I recognize the signs of autism in a child?
answer: Method 1 of 4:Recognizing Social Differences 1. Interact with your baby.A typical infant is a social creature by nature and loves to make eye contact. An autistic infant may appear like they are not interacting with parents, or may look "inattentive" to non-autistic parents. Make eye contact. A typically developing baby can return eye contact by six to eight weeks of age. An autistic child may not look at you, or may avoid looking at your eyes. Smile at your baby. A non-autistic baby can smile and offer warm and happy expressions by six weeks of age or earlier. An autistic baby may not smile, even to a parent. Make faces at your baby. See if they mimic you. An autistic child may not participate in playing copycat. 2. Call your babyâ€™s name.A typical baby will respond to it by nine months of age. Typically developing babies will be able to call you Mama or Dada in return by 12 months of age. 3. Play with your toddler.By ages two to three, a typical child will be very interested in playing games with you and others. An autistic toddler may appear disconnected from the world, or deep in thought. A non-autistic toddler will be involving you in their world by pointing, showing, reaching, or waving by 12 months of age. A typical child engages in parallel play until they are about three years old. When your toddler engages in parallel play, this means they play alongside other children and enjoy their company but do not necessarily engage in cooperative play. Donâ€™t confuse parallel play with an autistic child not being socially engaged. 4. Examine differences of opinion.By around age five, a typical child can understand that you have a different opinion about things. An autistic child tends to have great difficulty in understanding that others have different points of view, thoughts, and feelings than their own. They often appear to lack empathy for others. If your child loves strawberry ice cream, tell your child that chocolate ice cream is your favourite, and see if they argue or get upset that you do not share the same opinion as them. Many autistic people understand this better in theory than in praxis. An autistic girl might understand that you like the color blue, but have no idea that it would upset you if she wandered off to check out the balloons across the street. An autistic child may experience meltdowns, or outbursts of extreme emotion that often resemble a temper tantrum. However, these are not voluntary and are extremely upsetting to the child. An autistic child experiences many challenges, and may attempt to "bottle up" emotions to please caregivers. Emotions may spiral out of control, and the child can become so frustrated that they engage in self-injury, such as banging their head against a wall or biting themselves. Autistic children may experience more pain due to sensory issues, mistreatment, and other problems. They may lash out more often in self-defense. Method 2 of 4:Watching for Communication Difficulties Listen for increasing sounds and babbling as they grow. Children usually become fully verbal by 16 to 24 months of age. A typical baby will be able to share sounds back-and-forth with you like sharing a conversation by nine months of age. An autistic baby may not be verbal at all or may have been verbal but then lost the skill. A typical child will be babbling by about 12 months of age. 2. Have a conversation.Talk together about your childâ€™s favourite toy and listen to their sentence structure and conversation skills. Typically developing children will have many words by 16 months of age, can create their own meaningful, two-word phrases by 24 months of age, and have coherent sentences by age five. An autistic child tends to misplace words in sentence structure or simply repeat othersâ€™ phrases or sentences, called parroting or echolalia. They might mix up pronouns, saying "Do you want pancakes?" when they are trying to say that they want pancakes. Some autistic children pass over the "kid-speak" phase and have superior language skills. They may learn to speak early, and/or grow large vocabularies. They may converse differently than their peers do. 3. Try some expressions.Determine if your child takes phrases literally. An autistic child tends to misinterpret body language, tone of voice, and expressions. If you have a moment of sarcastic frustration and claim, "How wonderful!" when you find your autistic child has used his red marker all over the living room walls, they may think you literally mean their art is wonderful. 4. Check their facial expressions, tone of voice, and body language.Method 3 of 4:Identifying Repetitive Behaviours While all kids enjoy repetitive play to some degree, autistic children will exhibit strong repetitive behaviours such as rocking, hand-flapping, rearranging objects, or repeating sounds over and over again, called echolalia. These can be essential for self-calming and relaxation. All children partake in some verbal mimicry until the age of three. An autistic child may do this more often, and beyond the age of three Some repetitive behaviours are called self-stimulation or "stimming," meaning that they stimulate the childâ€™s senses. An example of this is if your son wiggles his fingers in front of his eyes to stimulate his vision and amuse himself. Another example of stimming happens when the child hums to the exact or near-exact pitch of an external noise (also known as auditory stimulus or stimuli) of something that buzzes or hums that the child can hear, like a bumble bee, a lawn mower, a chainsaw, or even a vibrating cell phone. 2. Notice how your child plays.Autistic children may not engage in visible imaginative play, preferring to organize objects (e.g. organizing toys or building a city for their dolls instead of playing house). The imagination is occurring inside their head. Try breaking the pattern: rearranging the dolls they are lining up or passing in front of them while they are trying to walk in a circle. An autistic child will be noticeably bothered by you interfering. Autistic children may be able to engage in imaginative play with another child, especially if that child takes the lead; however, these children will usually not do it on their own. 3. Recognize special interests and favorite objects.Intense and unusual obsessions with everyday household objects (such as a broom or string) or, later, facts, may be a sign of autism. An autistic child may develop a special interest about a topic, and gain an extraordinary depth of knowledge. Examples include cats, baseball statistics, The Wizard of Oz, logic puzzles, and checkers. A child may "light up" or open up when asked about these subjects. A child may have one special interest at a time, or a few. They can change as the child learns and grows. 4. Notice a need for routine.Many autistic children have a strong need for routines and consistency, and may show exaggerated reactions or protests to changes in routines. For instance, if you always walk with your child to school taking the same route, try changing it up. An autistic child may become very resistant and upset by this change of routine. Routines may have to do with the order of daily tasks, but they may also be verbal (such as asking the same questions repeatedly), have to do with food (only eating foods of a certain color), clothing (only wearing clothes of a specific fabric or color), the location of furniture, and so on. Routines can be very comforting for an autistic person. The world can seem unpredictable, confusing, and scary to this person, and a routine can give them some sense of control and stability. 5. Look for heightened and diminished sensitivity to sensations.If your child shows unusual discomfort to light, textures, sounds, tastes, or temperatures, talk to your doctor. Autistic children may "overreact" to new sounds (e.g. a sudden loud noise or a vacuum cleaner), textures (e.g. an itchy sweater or sock), et cetera. This is because the particular sense is magnified, so it causes real discomfort or pain. Method 4 of 4:Assessing Autism Across the Ages 1. Know when autism may be noticed.Some symptoms are clear around two to three years of age. Beyond that, a child may be diagnosed at any age, especially during a transition (e.g. going to high school or moving house) or other stressful periods. Excessive life demands may cause an autistic person to "regress" in order to cope, causing concerned loved ones to seek a diagnosis. In some children, signs may be noticed in the first one to two years of life. Some are not diagnosed until college, when their developmental differences become especially obvious. 2. Know your childhood milestones.With some variation, most children meet developmental milestones following a specific pattern. Autistic children may meet these milestones later. Some may be precocious, and their parents may consider them a struggling or introverted gifted child. By age three, children are often able to walk stairs, work with simple dexterity toys, and play make-believe. By age four, a child can retell their favourite stories, scribble, and follow simple directions. By age five, a child can generally draw pictures, talk about their day, wash their hands, and focus on a task. Older autistic children and teens may exhibit strict adherence to patterns and rituals, engage passionately in special interests, enjoy things that are not typical of their age group, avoid eye contact, and be highly sensitive to touch. 3. Watch for loss of skills.Speak to your family doctor if you have concerns at any point in your childâ€™s development. Do not delay if your child experiences a loss of speech, self-care skills, or social skills at any age. Most skills that are lost are still "there" and can be regained.

question: If you recognize early signs of autism in a child before his/her parents do, should you inform the parents?
answer: If you are a professional in the field and spend a lot of time with the child, and if you have a good relationship with the parents, it might be worth mentioning to them that you've noticed certain things that might indicate a developmental difference. Obviously you cannot diagnose autism based simply on casual observation, so you wouldn't say 'I think your kid is autistic'. But if you have a very high level of knowledge about neurodiversity and various developmental differences, and if you spend enough time with the child to make this possible judgment (note: this is a lot of time with the kid. If you only ever see it playing in the garden over the fence, you have no idea if it is autistic), then MAYBE mention it to the parents. But you need to be really sure there's something that needs investigating and you need to be making this observation with absolutely pure motives. Because if you're wrong, you will have caused the parents a degree of worry you cannot even imagine, not to mention trouble and expense to get the child checked out.

question: What are the signs of autism or Asperger's in children? Are there any indicators to look for during their early years?
answer: It's extremely variable. My immediate family includes 7 cases of autism--none are non-verbal, two are in guardianship, and the rest are doing darned well as adults (a pilot, Ph.D. in Physics, accountant, and two computer scientists, three military officers, 10 college degrees, and a National Merit Scholar--some people fit into more than one of those categories). And yet, all 7 members face challenges due to their autism. Two need significant help in adulthood, all seven had significant behavioral issues as children (three were in Special Ed and five have needed a lot of mental health support which, in a couple of cases is ongoing). To answer your question, only one person showed very early issues. My second child was noticeably different from neurotypical babies on his first day of life. He had a very hard time learning how to breastfeed. It took me 27 tries on his first evening before he figured it out--even though I was experienced and knew what he needed to do and how I could help him. Then he lacked the ability to transition to accepting a bottle after I had to go back to work and never did figure it out--which was absolutely awful. He rolled over very late, couldnâ€™t support his weight on his legs at all for months longer than most babies, and avoided touching things with his palms and, particularly, his index fingers. We didn't figure out for years that his skin was hypersensitive and that he has several issues with muscle control. He also has a lot of autistic need for routine and predictability and struggles whenever there's a need to problem solve and be flexible. He's also face blind and can't reliably recognize even his siblings just based on their facial features. But, at 5yo, his verbal IQ tested at just shy of 200 and, just after he turned 3yo he picked up a 250 page hardcover book and started reading it to me fluently despite the fact that I hadn't started teaching him anything at all in the way of reading skills, and actually told him, â€œYou don't know how to readâ€ when he asked me to let him read the book to me. He's an interesting mix of amazing skills and troublesome deficits. The deficits caused more and more problems as he moved into preschool and grade school, but his skills masked how much trouble he was having and caused most of the people in his life to think he was choosing to be difficult. (For example, he couldn't recognize any classmates or teachers, so he'd look for one girl in his class who had really long, bright blonde hair, and join that line when it was time to come in from recess. If she wasn't at school that day, he'd wind up with the wrong class and teachers would think he thought he was being funny and punish him.) He wasn't formally diagnosed until he was 9yo, and it took several more years before I understood most of the ways that autism affects him. The rest of us were diagnosed anywhere between the age of 5 and on into adulthood. My husband and I both behaved exactly like kids on the spectrum in childhood, but no one knew that people could have autism and still be smart and verbal when we were kids, and Special Ed was extremely limited in the â€™60s when we were in school, so we all just muddled through as best we could. (To be honest, in some ways that worked out in our favor. We were both Air Force officers which couldn't have happened if we had had autism diagnoses, and, we got great educations which can be hard to achieve if you get shunted into Special Ed classes.) Meanwhile, my sister has a grandson who was just diagnosed a few months ago. He's 5yo. I was suspicious because he was showing the same behavioral rigidity that my whole family has. Also, autism is a developmental delay. If you see a child who can't handle the behavioral expectations that his chronological peers handle with ease, be suspicious. And if you do discover that you're dealing with a child on the spectrum, try adjusting your behavioral expectations to something that would be appropriate for a child who's 1â€“3 years younger. There's a good chance that the developmental delay means that the child is incapable of being more mature yet. Pushing for chronologically appropriate behavior is certain to result in a meltdown, frustration for everyone, and sometimes long-lasting psychological damage. Whereas, often, the maturity will arrive eventually. Kindness and understanding are almost always the best.

question: What causes Asperger's syndrome or high functioning autism? Are there any early signs that can be recognized by parents or teachers?
answer: Nobody knows, though based on its prevalence within families it is most likely a genetic conditionâ€¦which does not rule out the possibility that environmental factors could be involved. The interesting thing about autism is that the pathology behind it that makes sense involves something that hasnâ€™t actually been proven to exist yet, though it is strongly suspected: mirror neurons. Mirror being the neural function that allows members of a species to integrate the witnessed experience of other members of the species into their own consciousness, just as empathy allows members of the same species to experience emotional transference. Of course, thereâ€™s no proof of a pathology behind empathy, either, but itâ€™s widely accepted that it exists. It goes a long way to explain the difference between the autistic and allistic mind, no matter where on the Spectrum an autistic person might be. Non-autistic people, whatever their nature, have two components of their awareness: the individual awareness of their own life experience, and a mirrored awarenessâ€¦a social consciousness. For many of us, the social consciousness, with its constant input and expansion from every other person we interact with, may eventually overwhelm our individual identity, which can be a problem for Neuros. Autistic people do not have this mirrored awareness, or a highly diminished one. They remain individual entities throughout their lives. And letâ€™s not forgetâ€¦the brain is not a passive receptor. It actively seeks input. So non-autistic people have a literal hunger for contact with others. This goes beyond the easily-recognized social issues associated with autism. It also is a possible explanation to the sensory issues: we are ALL born with heightened senses, easily overstimulated, and only begin to filter sensations over time, most likely through the development of a mirrored awareness of what to pay attention to and what to ignore. Iâ€™m also suspicious it plays a role in why many autistic people become non-verbal. Take away the social reinforcement of speaking, and itâ€™s a pretty unpleasant physical sensation. Put that together with heightened sensitivity to physical sensations and a strong dislike of unpleasant ones (letâ€™s not forgetâ€¦we learn to tolerate the things we donâ€™t like through the intercession of others), and you can understand why some folks just stop doing it. The tendency to perseverate can also be seen as a simple extension of the disinclination to put themselves in unpleasant situations. Stick to the tried and true. Soâ€¦what to look for? Unfortunately, there are no tried and true rulesâ€¦more like a collection of individual signs to add up. And also, needless to say, all open to interpretation. Being unusually picky when it comes to taste and touch. Not outgrowing the tendency towards tantrums. Not being comfortable with facial contact. An infatuation with lightbulbs (curious, but common). Poor impulse control that does not improve with age. Highly risk averse. A general sense that they do not â€œneedâ€ other people other than to meet immediate needs. These are just a few.

question: Are high-functioning autism and Asperger’s the same diagnoses, or are they different?
answer: Asperger syndrome and high-functioning autism (HFA) are often referred to as the same diagnosis, although before the introduction of the DSM-V they existed as two separate diagnoses. The DSM-V combined all the ASD diagnoses and generalized them to the same autism spectrum. Prior to the new diagnostic criteria, both individuals with Asperger syndrome and high-functioning autism were defined as having average or above average intelligence, but may struggle with issues related to social interaction and communication. The primary difference was that a diagnosis of high-functioning autism required delayed language development in childhood, whereas in Asperger syndrome, there were no significant delays in language development. Below is a Venn diagram of the old situation:Image: Copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All Rights Reserved. And below is a Venn diagram of the new situation, after the introduction of the DSM-V:Image: Copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All Rights Reserved.There are two domains where people with ASD must show persistent deficits. They include:Persistent social communication and social interaction.Restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior.People with ASD must demonstrate or have at one point demonstrated deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors (used for social interaction), and deficits in developing maintaining and understanding relationships. Additionally, they must show at least two types of repetitive patterns of behavior including stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, insistence on sameness or inflexible adherence to routines, highly restricted and fixated interests, and hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment[1].For more information on (high-functioning) ASD, have a look at: Embrace AutismA blog about quantitative- and qualitative research on autism, by Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht ND RP and Eva Silvertant.Footnotes[1] Answers to Frequently Asked Questions about DSM-5

question: What's it like to live with a person with high functioning autism?
answer: It's awesome! Maybe I'm well-suited to it, I don't know, but having my friend with high functioning autism as a roommate for the past year has worked better for me than anyone I've lived with in the almost 50 years I've been on this planet. The Good: -- My job involves a *LOT* of interacting with people so a roomate that doesn't need or want constant interaction gives me much needed downtime. -- While my sensitivity to noise is to a lesser extent, I do get stressed by too much noise so a quiet home keeps us both on an even keel. -- We have opposite strong suits. While he has no patience for forms, online purchases, or waiting in lines and cannot load the dishwasher in any kind of logical way, he is amazing with my dogs and cats, keeps the plants alive, decorates, and does a variety of household tasks that I have limited patience for. -- He has an amazing amount of knowledge on so many topics and we can have thoughtful, intelligent conversations daily. -- In a world where people often use words to hurt, it's beyond refreshing to be around someone who only says what they mean and doesn't even have the ability to TRY and be hurtful. I'm not sure I can say enough about the value of that, especially when you can't go on FB anymore without seeing post after post spewing hatred. On the flip side, *occasionally* honesty isn't flattering, but at least it's REAL. -- The genuine gratitude for anything I do for him, no matter how minor. What I've Learned: -- To speak clearly and directly. If he's going to the store, saying "I want something chocolate...cookies, cake, donuts, something" will result in a lot of stress for him trying to work out what I want most and may result in getting all three. Now I say, "Oreos - Mega Stuffs". :) -- Not to assume and more importantly, not to be upset about something I assumed he *should* do but didn't say that I would like for him to do. Because if I do say it, he will move heaven and earth to do it. -- Not to sweat the small stuff. If it's important to him that all furniture is at angles instead of flush against the wall like I would do it, does it really matter? No. Nor does it matter if dishes are in different cabinets than I would put them. I'm now grateful that I didn't have to unload the dishwasher. -- Not to take offense and what sometimes feels indifference. I value this person as a friend very, very much and sometimes, I feel like he could take or leave me. But then I hear from his family how much of a friend he considers me and I think about HIS version of showing friendship...getting something he knows I like while he's out, bringing one of the flowers he bought for my vase in my room, pretending to be interested in something I'm going on about when I'm pretty sure he really isn't. -- How to accept responsibility for my part in things that irritate me. The only time I got really annoyed with him was when on the way home from somewhere, I said, "We need to change the air filter." To him, that meant it was the very next thing we should do. But we got home and a toilet had run and caused a small flood. He turned off the water while I figured out the problem but then while I'm still trying to sop up water to prevent water damage, I hear, "Can you help me with this?" He had started the air filter project (in an old system, getting it back in place is challenging and often takes us both.) My instinct was to scream, "Are you kidding me? We're drowning in water, I don't care about the air filter!" But I took a breath, realized he was still following the plan I set, got the HVAC back together and returned to the water. At the end of the day, I am a better person for having my friend here. I'm calmer, I'm more careful not to say hurtful things out of frustration, I'm more patient, and things that I would have nagged at the last person I lived with about (who I was in a relationship with), I shrug off. People are way more important than anything else and I am grateful for all I've learned from my friend and for all he does around the house to make my life easier.

question: What are the telltale signs of high-functioning autism in adults?
answer: I’ve read a lot of the answers here- I have Autism, ASC1, (used to be called High Functioning or Aspergers)… and perhaps it’s just that my experience is different, but…I don’t visibly stim. I stim in my head with repetitive thoughts or scraps of songs that I like, or sayings- I’m a visual thinker and can kind of watch “memories” in my head if I’m stressed.I can make eye contact.My voice, albeit loud, is very expressive.Why are these things so different than what others have said? Because of a couple common key features of people with ASC 1, people at my end of the spectrum…We learn to “mask” and “camouflage”. We don’t want to be outcasts, we want to get along, and as there is a correlation between ASC1 and intelligence, we figure out what the “script” is for the “character” or “situation” we want to emulate “normality” in, and we learn to fake it, usually very effectively. That masking is absolutely characteristic of this end of the Autistic Spectrum. So, I don’t stim because I mask it.Not everyone with Autism struggles to make eye contact.As with masking, you can learn to control at least some elements of your voice- and as I was taught considerably through story telling (in the Native American part of my childhood) we were taught how to tell stories… so I learned more about how to use my voice.As with everyone who is not autistic, people with Autism are all individuals. How they learn to survive amongst the unkindnesses and intolerances of the NT world is as dynamic, diverse and individual as they are. Intelligence and verbal skills are variable amongst people with ASC 1 but they tend to be better than ASC 2 and 3 and the better they are, the easier many autistic people find it to cope and adapt. Culture, upbringing, personal choice and tastes, physical health, family dynamics, experiences, education, etc all make a huge difference to how an individual will manifest, and cope with, their autism. For me, I would sayA degree of dyspraxia or clumsiness is common amongst adults at the ASC 1 end of the spectrum.Extreme ability to know a *lot* about certain topics, and to exhibit a deep and thorough understanding to the degree that people say things like “Is there anything you don’t know about ‘Topic x’ ?”Anxiety about uncertainty and changeTendency to be visual thinkers and to express/ explain things in what are often seen as quite unique and original waysNoticing things that other people don’t, especially when those things are related to an area of interest.Social discomfort or inability to handle social interactions when under stressA black and white view of the world, and difficulty shifting to a new interpretation once one is set (clinging to a first impression).To many, rules and following rules is very important even when the rules might not make sense. You might even know the rule doesn’t make sense… but it’s a *rule*. Lots of times, the world and the people in it don’t make sense, and the closest thing we’re got to instructions are the “rules”. It causes me personally a lot of anxiety when others break simple rules- like- don’t cut the queue in front of me, trust me, it’s just not worth it.A unique way of relating things that others wouldn’t necessarily relate…Intolerances for certain types of fabric, sounds, lightings, sometimes even colours. I once had a lovely office chair but it was orange and had “squinchy” fabric… it was comfortable but I despised it. Orange is not a good colour (I told you, weird relationships…. a friend had a girlfriend who was nasty to me, and she always wore orange nail varnish; when I see orange, I see those nails, and feel the emotional destruction she did… so orange is not on my ‘favourite colours’ list).An odd way of organising things… one of my (autistic) friends organised her record collection (remember those?) first by type of music, and then… by the name of her favourite song on each album. Made sense to no one but her but it was her collection.Some people with Autism struggle to speak up. I struggle to shup up.I often struggle to get jokes. I have a good sense of humour, but in that my initial reaction with anything is to take it at face value, I need to get in a certain mindset to get jokes. For example - My hubby said “I bet they could take that to the bank” when someone on a TV show bought a vaulting horse. I was like “why do they need that in the bank?” and he said “Vault? Bank?” and I groaned. If I know to expect jokes, I do a bit better… like if we went to see a comedian. If Hubby had said “Hey, got a joke for you… “ and told me, I probably would have got the joke.I have superb spatial reasoning. You know these test questions? I love them, they are so easy I don’t even need to think about them. I love logic problems and find them easy to solve as I can “see” them in my mind. I have an excellent sense of direction. It’s all part of thinking visually. edit- For those who have asked … It cannot be A, as the two small squares and the large orange square cannot be side by side. B- the orange circle is on the opposite face as the three small spots, so they cannot be as this cube shows. In C, the three small dots are still on the opposite face as the large orange circle… so it can’t be C. D is then true, not only by exclusion but because the shown sides do relate to the flat image.If I am not interested in something I can get bored and distracted very eas… oh look! Something over there is SHINY!I don’t really have close friends. Everyone always seems to know me, but, I just don’t ‘get’ how relationships work. I don’t feel confident, I get nervous, and I don’t have a script to use for 1–1 relationships so I can’t mask. I have people who love me, and I love them, but I might not speak to them for ages- sometimes years- unless there is a reason to speak to them. “Hi Joan, thought I’d call, Im making a cake and need your icing recipe”. It might sound like I am using them, since I only call if there is a reason but … oh well. It’s very lonely sometimes, but I sincerely don’t know how it works. I know my “eccentricity” drives other people crazy, and I feel ashamed, so… that’s why we have QUora, right? So you have something else to do?Games. I love games. I not only play minecraft (for like 12+ years) I admin a minecraft server… so I can make people follow the rules! Muhahahaha cough cough cough So… the point of this is… you can’t tell (unless you are exceptionally skilled and know the person pretty well) if someone is Autistic based on ‘tells’ as we as individuals are usually quite good at being one of these…I’ve had people who on one hand have told me “You are so eccentric!” who will then say “Autistic? You can’t be autistic… you’re just…. really really you…” What they can’t see is how it’s *their* perception of my behaviour and nature that chalk me up as “eccentric” in their minds.

question: What are the misconceptions about high functioning Autism?

Some of us do have more sense enhancement than others.Bluntness, common with ASD, is not usually intended to be an insult. Taking it that way presumptuously makes the listener an asshole, not the speaker.Slow seeming functional response should not be seen as indicative of an impairment in intelligence. Enhanced senses mean those with ASD have far more information coming in that needs to be sorted through. It's for life, and it never goes away.Masking skills cannot allow those with ASD to want, feel, and need the exact same things as an allistic no matter how much other allistics want them to. The pretending is not really for the autistic's benefit and will cause us harm in the long term.Masking is a survival mechanism that protects us against dangerously toxic and widespread allistic ignorance. Most of our friends and family are inherently clueless about ASD as much as strangers are, so the masking is most definitely not “personal” nor is it about “tricking" people.Adults with ASD are more common and more capable than anyone realizes, but their intelligence and needs are still rarely taken seriously. question: Is high functioning autism hereditary?
answer: Genetics play a role in autism. But it is by no means hereditary in the sense that if the parent has it, the child will have it. DNA is a complicated thing. Every person has a unique DNA structure made of four unique compounds. When two people reproduce, the child gets half of each parent’s DNA. There are so many possible combinations that every person’s DNA is unique (save twins, I believe). My mom and dad are both NT, or neurotypical. They had 4 kids. I was the only one born with autism. My sister, who is as neurotypical as they come (and I mean that in a good way) and her boyfriend, also NT, have an autistic daughter. Now I, on the other hand, have a higher probability of having an autistic child because I am on the spectrum. That means that somewhere in the coding of my DNA created the different brain development that leads to autism. I don’t know which coding it is. But there’s a 50% chance that I will pass that coding down to my child someday. But there’s a 50% chance I won’t. It depends on my partner as well. Now, that only applies if it’s one particular DNA mutation that causes autism. But most research either hasn’t found the single DNA mutation or has research indicating that it is a unique combination of mutations in the DNA. It still leaves me with a higher chance, but it’s no longer a simple probability where I can say 50% chance. Let’s say it’s 4 specific mutations. I have a 1/2 chance for each mutation, so it becomes a 1/16 chance. And then we would have to take the father’s DNA coding into consideration. long story short: yes, it is Hereditary, but it’s not so simple as NT parent = NT child or Autistic parent = autistic child. DNA mutations happen, and they may or may not always be passed on.

question: Does having high-functioning autism make one ineligible for military service?
answer: Unless things have changed since my time, I would say that NO you cannot join the army with Asperger’s. I first tried getting into the Canadian reserves ten years ago (July 2008) when I was told to come back in one year when I would be closer to graduating from high school. A year later, I came back to the recruiting office, and this time they accepted me for the hiring process, despite still being two semesters away from graduating. I went through the same process as everyone else: I had an interview; provided references and a resume with a cover letter; did a background check; and then I had to go through an interview process which was then followed a week later with an aptitude test. When I had applied, I was trying to join as a non-commissioned soldier in either the infantry or the artillery. Apparently I scored fairly well on the aptitude test, which was why one of the people that interviewed me later asked if I would be willing to do other types of work that were more “specialised” if the offer came up. I agreed to it, so they had me go through the medical checkup. I was deemed to have normal health and was told I would soon be able to go through the final process — physical training. However, it was at this point in the recruiting process that I came face to face with an obstacle that I could NOT get around: my medical diagnosis. The Canadian Army cannot legally turn somebody away just for having Asperger’s and High-Functioning Autism (more on that later) but they are allowed to make it nearly impossible for someone with the diagnosis to get in. Upon finding out from my school and medical records that I had Asperger’s, their tone about me joining went from optimistic to sombre very quickly. Despite having spent four months at this point going to the recruiting office at least ten times during this period in order to get accepted, I suddenly found myself being turned away at a time when I was only a few days away from finishing the application process. At the time I had tried getting into the reserves, there was a war going on in Afghanistan, and when a recruiter had mentioned that if I join the reserves there is a good chance I would be sent there, I told him that wars were one of the reasons why a military exists in the first place. I don’t know what he thought of that answer, as this recruiter was not known for commenting on people’s answers, but I was able to get through the next several stages and get interviewed by other officers and recruiters without a hitch. It was only upon finding out about my medical diagnosis that they took a sudden 180 degree turn on me. One of the requirements I suddenly found myself being forced to do was to pay out of my own pocket a psychiatrist that was deemed qualified by the military to judge whether or not a particular person with Asperger’s was fit for service. The recruiter went further and reminded me that it would cost up to $1,000 to see someone like that, and that there was a good chance they would say I am not eligible for military service. Having next to no money at the time meant that there was no way I could afford to pay the $1,000 — especially when there was no guarantee I was even going to get accepted. I was forced to essentially withdraw my application by ceasing to return to the recruiting office to update myself. Three months after my last visit, I got a letter from a reserve officer saying something to the effect of: “We are sorry to hear that you have not been following up on the recruiting process. We therefore take it that you are no longer interested in joining the Canadian Forces and we will therefore be closing your application file.” Needless to say, the Canadian Army did not OFFICIALLY deny me from joining the military based solely on my Asperger diagnosis, but they did see to it that my chances of getting in were very small by forcing me to pay exorbitant fees to see a specialised psychiatrist that none of the other recruiting applicants were being subjected to with the intention I would drop out altogether. It would therefore allow the Canadian Army to disqualify those with Asperger’s while also being able to claim that they don’t discriminate against people with Asperger’s/Autism. A few years before I tried joining, however, the story was much different. People that were being diagnosed with Asperger’s after joining the army — including one person that was known to somebody else that I knew — were being kicked out of the military, despite the fact that some of them had already been in the military for decades up until their diagnosis got them disqualified. Eventually, this practice got some negative reactions on social media by pundits and their supporters who were outraged by the way the Canadian military was purging recruiters and veterans alike solely based on a medical disability. To get around this, the Canadian military simply responded by making it harder for future applicants to get in by putting up the type of loopholes they put me through. Those that get into the military have reportedly been harassed by having officers and other soldiers alike be extra harsh on those with the diagnosis in hopes that they either quit the forces, or they do something that can get them discharged. The military has become a bit more accepting of people with disabilities in recent years — thanks largely to social media making it harder for military officers and recruiters alike to be able to openly discriminate against those deemed less “desirable.” However, in practice, the military is still not the friendliest place to be if you are someone diagnosed with Asperger’s or Autism.

question: How was your childhood with high functioning Autism?
answer: Difficult. I was undiagnosed until I was 21. I was bullied in different ways by different people. My teacher labelled me a drama queen when I was 6 years old (probably thanks to my meltdowns and sensitivities) and the label stuck, other kids loved calling me a drama queen whenever I expressed my emotions, or when something that seemed small and insignificant to other people would really bother me. It didn’t help that I was so academically intelligent, because it meant that people thought that I was socially intelligent too. When I failed at social intelligence, they thought I was doing it deliberately. Certain girls would find immense pleasure in tricking me by pretending to be my friend and then being really nasty in front of everyone. It was hilarious to them. I was very easy to manipulate and I trusted people inherently. I didn’t learn from my mistakes. They would be awful to me, and then afterwards they would tell me that they were sorry and wanted us to be friends. I believed them, time and time again. People took advantage of me in many different ways. I was sexually assaulted by an older child due to being so easily manipulated and tricked. I was literally dragged by my arms around the playground, tearing up my knees. On the first day of a summer school when I was about 8, I was tricked into going into a toilet cubicle and then I was locked inside for hours. As unbelievable as it sounds, the teachers knew, and they were watching and laughing too. I was only taken out when my mum came to pick me up and she saw dozens of kids sitting down outside the bathrooms, with teachers at the sides, all laughing. She had to push through everyone and physically unlock me and carry me out of the school. I changed school around that age, and I found much better friends. This school did not tolerate bullying, at all. I found other intelligent weirdos who were fantastic, we played cards and debated and made up games to play. I think that school and the friends I made there saved me from being completely destroyed by the effects of the bullying. In secondary school, things got hard again. I didn’t know anyone and lost contact with my primary school friends. Once again I was manipulated by deceptive girls, but in a much more subtle way. Thankfully, I met another bunch of intelligent, creative weirdos who are still my best friends and have allowed me to be myself. My meltdowns were not understood and I was labelled a drama queen once again. I remember feeling very overwhelmed in one lesson and I literally hid under the table. I went into shutdown and wouldn’t respond to anyone, covering my ears and shutting my eyes. My teacher thought I was attention seeking and told everyone to ignore me (I did want everyone to ignore me, I wanted to disappear, but attention-seeking is the furthest thing from the truth - I wanted to be completely alone and away from the situation, which was impossible, and of course hiding under the table only brought more attention to me. But in a meltdown/shutdown, I go into autopilot and fight or flight mode, there’s no logic there). I had a difficult time as a teenager. I went through a lot of personal and family issues that I won’t go into here, but by the time I was 11 years old, I was depressed, self-harming, and I’d starting drinking and smoking. I started trying drugs soon after that, and by the age of 14 I was regularly taking Class As. I was a messy wild child with a reputation and I didn’t know how to cope. This confused people. I was so intelligent but I was behaving so irresponsibly. I would argue with teachers without a second thought, because if they’re wrong, they’re wrong. One (male) teacher tried to make us believe that women bleed a bucket of blood every month. I didn’t stand for that shit and earned myself a week’s detention (I mean, really? You would die after your first period, as a young girl. No one would survive long enough to reproduce. It doesn’t even make sense). I always challenged poor teaching, which pissed off other students and the teachers, but I couldn’t let teachers teach us bullshit! I had no fear in that sense, and logic and truth overrode any desire to just get out of the class, or not piss off my teachers, or keep out of trouble, or not come across as a know-it-all. As a teenager I had the worst fights with my (undiagnosed) mother. We would both meltdown and hurt ourselves and each other. I can’t count the number of phones I’ve smashed (I’ve never had a smartphone for this reason). The neighbours called the police on us several times. I nearly lost everything by the time I was 17 as my meltdowns were so frequent that people didn’t want anything to do with me anymore. I nearly lost my partner and all my friends. I was in the deepest depression I’d ever been, and there was no support available for me (it was all for under 16s or over 18s). I made a lot of changes to help myself. The biggest thing which has changed my life and saved me was discovering autism at age 18, and self-diagnosing myself and my mum. Everything made sense. The first three days after I realised, I went over my entire life with these new autism glasses, and understood it all. It finally made sense. I made so many changes with my life and it pretty much saved me. I could explain to my partner and my friends why my behaviour was so extreme and erratic, and I understood that I experienced meltdowns, and I figured out how best to avoid them. It took another three years to get a formal diagnosis, but that was just a formality, so that my university would recognise my support needs. The benefits came from finally understanding myself. This is one of those times that I feel very exposed and I don’t know if I’ll regret writing all this later, but people need to unlearn their stereotypes about autistic people. We are just as varied and messy as everyone else.

question: Do females with high functioning autism present (symptoms, behaviours) differently than males with high functioning autism?
answer: Every autistic presents differently, as does every allistic! This is a question about averages or tendencies, and there is just so little research comparing autistic men to women. Most autistic adult women may be undiagnosed; the tests to detect autism are being studied and may be revised to better detect autistic women. So if the actual official tests that detect autism have trouble finding all the females, that could be a good indication that autistic women present differently. So, what does “present” mean, if an autistic person has spent decades learning to watch others and focus on “passing” almost 100% of the time during interactions? This is being called “camouflaging” in some research and other writings. “Camouflaging” I’ll define as learning to build mental models of allistic behavior in various situations (it started as mimicking, but is way beyond that now for me) and also use other techniques to be accepted as (allistic) by (allistics); to pass. It takes a lot of cognitive effort for me personally. This is pretty necessary in order to attain a better quality of life in many ways, sometimes even just to survive. It seems to be done somewhat more and/or thoroughly, maybe better? — by female adult autistics, according to a study or two. The research is very sparse and new. A study of South Korean kids that came close to randomly testing a full population for autism, found that 2/3 of the autistic kids were in mainstream classes, undiagnosed. Many were female. A bit on this study here: South Korean Study Uncovers Higher Rate of Autism As an undiagnosed adult, one has had lots of years and experiences to dwell on, study, theorize about, generally with no appropriate help and no coaching by anyone with a clue what is going on with you. So what does “present” mean if you are forced to act like a different neurotype, do it well enough that no clinicians identify that as the source of challenges you may have, and do it so long that you forget even learning to do that? What if you then discover your autism at a later age and start trying to unwind all that; what does “present” mean then…? Camouflaging is very stressful, though; it takes a lot of brain CPU time; I don’t have a built-in “social app” the OP may have been born with. :-) So female autistics may be also very stressed but totally hide it. Or not. There are loads of mental health problems associated with prolonged camouflaging… yet there are also ways to try to be resilient, and autistics can be quite self-aware imho. Human behavior is very complicated, whatever your neurotype, and the variance among autistics’ behaviors is so great in many ways that the utility of an “average” is really questionable… Human brains rely upon categorization way too much for some situations.

question: What is the difference between high and low functioning autism?
answer: Quite specifically, until 12/2013 (DSM-V) the term “High-Functioning Autism” was a label given to a child when the child’s “tested” IQ was 70 or more. Although, an MR label (IQ less than 70) was never considered a core symptom of autism, MR was often a separate, co-morbid label—meaning that both autism and separately, mental retardation were both diagnoses that the child received. Asperger’s Syndrome, which is now considered an ASD along with all of the other diagnostic distinctions thru the DSM-IV-TR, was never the same as HFA. Finally (as I have seen that when I offer too many specifics, my answers do not get read), to give a child who does not relate to anyone a neuropsych evaluation and expect that he/she will respond with appropriate answers can only lead to the expert conclusion that the child’s intelligence (not a core symptom of autism) is low. This kind of testing, if given at all, could only result in a true determination once the child is relating to others and able to follow simple directions—at the very least! We do these children a grave injustice when testing their intellectual abilities before this. There has never been an actual label of “low-functioning autism.” Severe/profound—though even these do not describe the child’s future, unless those who can be of greatest help choose to believe that there is nothing they can do! Further, with these labels educators and others assume that the child is less capable or incapable of learning—a terrible self-fulfilling prophesy. The children that I have had the privilege and joy of working with over a 25+ year period—once the underlying causes of their core autism symptoms were resolved—were quite bright and a few had near genius IQ’s. It’s time to change the way children with autism have been viewed. It’s time to recognize that this was thinking from decades past. Would you want current procedures if you had specific needs, or would you choose those that were all they had to offer decades ago?? Answers and interventions based on each child’s unique needs have changed this paradigm, all based on solid research. And the best experts about each child’s true abilities are that child’s parents—when empowered with understandable education and collaborative professional-partnerships, as needed.

answer: This is a really tough question. If you are autistic, it's a bit easier, because you can say, "You are like me, there are many of us". If you are not autistic, and nobody else in your group is autistic, you're essentially saying, "you are disabled and you are not like us". That's a hard sell. There are other details you need to figure out, such as his attitude towards disabled people in general, what his beliefs are about autism, etc. I have confronted this choice before: 1. A young man. He actually said he suspected he was autistic. I posted some general information, implied that I was too and suggested talking to autistic people. He did not respond and never talked to me again. I left some specific hints... think he picked it up. Plus I was promoting autism acceptance in general. At some point after that he mentioned some things about Dr. Asperger... so he was at least that aware.

question: Is high functioning autism considered autism?

question: Why is "High-Functioning Autism" also otherwise known as "Mild Autism"?
answer: Generally, it means autism that doesn’t get in the way as much. You can talk, hold a job, live independently, and so forth, whereas someone with severe autism might not be able to do those things. However, the distinction is not actually very useful, because how autism manifests varies so much, and not just person to person but day by day or hour by hour. There are people who can talk most of the time, for example, and then suddenly lose their ability to speak temporarily. On any given day, who is high-functioning and who is not might be different. More importantly, defining “function” is difficult. Autism is not a straight line. For example, Dr. Temple Grandin is obviously autistic, whereas I might not be autistic at all—I only have some autistic-like traits. You might assume, from meeting us (not that I’ve ever met Dr. Grandin—I’ve only seen her in interviews) that I have a very mild case while hers is much more severe. However, I struggle to accomplish goals and have trouble earning a living, while Dr. Grandin has been very effective at making things happen for herself. So which of us is higher functioning? A person can function well in some ways and not others, and not everybody has the same pattern. Finally, while autism is officially defined as a disorder, it really isn’t—or at least it isn’t simply a disorder. Among other issues, there are abilities as well as disabilities associated with autism. The famous cases are people with savant abilities (picture Rain Man counting cards) and those are quite rare, but even autistic people who are not savants are often good at things not in spite of autism but because of it. It’s simply a different way of thinking, one that carries both advantages and disadvantages. Personally, I’d like to see the term changed from “autism spectrum disorder” to “autism-related disorders,” in recognition of the fact that “autism” describes who a person is on a very deep level (it’s how you think, what you feel, what you like and dislike, want and don’t want—all of that) and that it is possible to help a person live better—resolve the disorders, at least partially—without the person losing their distinctiveness. The important thing is for autistic people to live well, not for them to become normal. Society needs those who are different. So if, as I and many other autistic people contend, autism isn’t really a disease, then it doesn’t make sense to talk about having a mild case, does it? Personally, I think phrases like “high functioning” are really about stigma. They are ways for autistics, or their parents, to disavow a connection with “those people,” the obviously autistic, the ones whom society really has a big problem with. And the thing is that’s not a very good response to stigma. I might be different, in some ways, from some more obviously autistic people, but at the end of the day we’re both human. At the end of the day what matters is not “how severe is your autism” but “are you OK? Do you need anything?” I don’t think the concept “high functioning autism” helps anyone.

question: Are meltdowns only with high functioning autism?
answer: No, meltdowns are not only with types of autism typically referred to as “high-functioning”. Meltdowns are one of the big things people use to talk about how severe their child’s autism is, no matter how severe, or otherwise, their collection of autistic traits is overall. In those who are referred to as “high-functioning”, meltdowns filmed without the child’s consent can be one of the things parents will use sometimes that lower the child’s “functioning level” in the eyes of society. Children, that is. If an adult displays meltdowns for educational purposes but can talk, however, either people express appreciation of the insight and sympathy, or they accuse the adult of being attention-seeking. Never mind that the adult who does this type of thing is not doing it for attention, but is doing these meltdown videos because they can safely put up those videos without wrecking a career, and they know that since it is relatively safe for them to do that because they do not risk losing a job or getting an immediate and unwelcome psychological evaluation from the wrong people (the kind that can get people committed - that is not the same thing as psychotherapy, do not confuse the two), they can put up those meltdown videos so people wanting to know what meltdowns look like can be able to view videos of meltdowns that were not obtained from a child without that child’s consent during their most embarrassing moments. For those labeled “low-functioning”, sadly, they are likely to be portrayed as if the meltdown is a large part of what and even who they are, basically, because they are incredibly vulnerable and put under a lot of stress by the environment and, often, authority figures including parents as well. Autism is a major part of who we are. Meltdowns are not. To express this in autistic language:It’s as if Te Ka is the autistic in meltdown mode, and Te Fiti is the autistic who is not raging due to a meltdown. As Moana sings, Te Ka is not really who that creature is, her real name is Te Fiti, and her true self is the big green lady who is essentially nonverbal, very powerful and full of life magic, and sort of carries herself the way I imagine Elsa from Frozen (another character I head canon as autistic) would as an old grandmother. Of course, no real autistics have life magic, but, then again, even those who have the worst meltdowns don’t literally turn to lava either - it’s more like a metaphor, really. When people think of “low-functioning” autistics having meltdowns to the point of naming the meltdown, it’s like the way people label “Te Ka” as being the nature goddess’ identity, but in truth, the identity of an autistic is more like the “Te Fiti” side, the side that feels connected to whatever they get into, and also the side that absolutely depends on things that may seem small and insignificant to onlookers yet are vitally important, so important that if those tiny things are ripped away from them, metaphorically, they are likely to be highly prone to meltdowns and have trouble stopping them so long as they are not able to engage with the things they need and care about (i.e. it is metaphorically as if their hearts are ripped out). In real life, every autistic needs a different set of accommodations that they care about and need to be able to feel okay and not have meltdowns. that variance is why people usually give broad advice when talking about autistics in general - if you blanketly recommend accommodations for one set of interests, sensory needs, and stims, you are very likely to have recommended a set of accommodations that is right for some autistics, partially right for others, and completely wrong for yet more autistics.

question: What would you like neurotypicals to know about high-functioning autism?
answer: I’d like people to understand that high functioning autism is frequently subtle enough so that only an expert would recognize it. Certainly no one ever recognized mine, not even psychologists whom I saw regularly for years. Autism has no unique symptoms and as an adult, I don’t have obvious signs like stimming, serious meltdowns (as in they can be distinguished from an occasional outburst of temper), or mechanical speech. An expert who met me would say “Aspie” in no time flat, but not anyone else, because there are lots of people who tend to avert their gaze or have poor posture or have gentle dispositions or don’t like small talk, etc. An expert would recognize the entire constellation of signs but to most, I’m just shy and a bit anxious and socially awkward. I’d also like people to recognize that we really do suffer and struggle. Because we’re high functioning and sometime supremely capable in certain areas and adept at emulating neurotypical behavior to the point at which some of us can actually become better at aspects of it than they are, it’s hard for some people to understand that life is a battle for us. I struggle to change my clothes, brush my teeth, make a phone call. I can design a loudspeaker or dash off a sonnet, and then be unable to buy a pair of shoes. I wish people understood that our difficulties are often imposed by society. We wouldn’t suffer sensory overload if we hadn’t created a world that is bright, noisy, and crowded. We’re intrinsically motivated and have powerful special interests, but society expects us to work for grades or a salary and to do a bit of this and a bit of that. I wish people understood that we care and paid real attention to what we do. We’re in the paradoxical situation of being more honest, moral, and, according to studies, hard working than others, but of being perceived as deficient because we don’t push the right emotional buttons. Neurotypicals go for fakes, people with great personalities who lack competence or cheat. Again and again, I’ve done the right thing, and been mistreated, sometimes because I insisted on doing the right thing. The situation began when I had my first summer job and it never really stopped. Eventually, it became so demoralizing that I just dropped out of the workforce. I wish that people would lose some myths. Yes, we are creative. Yes, we have a sense of humor. Yes, we have emotions. No, we aren’t violent psychopaths, unless we *also* happen to be violent psychopaths. And no, not all of us are unable to read facial expressions. And finally, I wish people would understand that I can’t always make contact. The personal pronoun is intentional, but it applies to others as well. If I’m out of contact with you, it doesn’t mean that I don’t like or care about or value you, or that I don’t want to make contact with you. It just means that I can’t.

question: High Functioning Autistics: Is your IQ higher than average?
answer: A high functioning autistic, is, statistically speaking, more intelligent than average, perhaps even significantly so, but while it is essential to be able to function, being afflicted with autism, that is to say the ability to learn that which does not come naturally, it is not, in it of itself, what makes the big difference, I think. What exactly does make the difference, is not entirely clear of course, but I do believe that upbringing play the biggest part, and I also believe what makes the difference is really very simple. I do not believe for a moment that the significant raise in these sorts of diagnosis's over several decades comes down to pollution, vaccinations, nutrition or any such thing, as some will claim. It is true to say that we’ve become better at identifying these things, and that is part of it, no doubt, but more than anything, it comes down to how we raise our children. It has become the norm to shield them against the world, and to teach them that they do not have to conform, and when raised with that mentality, it is easy to see how this might result in an inability to handle the real world, once this is required. Of course severe autism cannot simply be cured by essentially torturing these children, but I do believe that challenging them, in moderation, uncomfortably though it may be, will be a benefit to all such children. And yes, I am talking from personal experience, though I’ve had very little help, so in my case, my relatively high intelligence has no doubt helped identifying the issues, and ways to deal with them, on my own. On the other hand, had I had, let’s say, a suitable upbringing, which it is safe to say I didn’t, for reasons I shan’t get into here, I dare say my life would’ve been an entirely different and a whole lot more positive experience.

question: Is it safe to say that people with high-functioning autism have few to no problems?
answer: I would say I have very high functioning autism and I have had a lifetime of social misery and career challenges. In grade school and high school I was considered odd by classmates and in high school I was a constant target of bullies. I was called “gay” but I wasn’t even that. I would endure school, go home eat a lot and watch tv or read. My parents had some psychological quirks. I would try to do homework on the bus on the way to school or in class before it was collected. Somehow I found it my calling to be as big a slacker as I could without getting in trouble. I too uncoordinated for sports and never around children outside of school. I did not get invited to things. I liked to do science experiments and I read all sorts of books. In grade school, I would sit at recess reading from an encyclopedia. Some educator mentioned to my mother that in 8th grade I got the highest IQ score in the county. I put little work into academics, but still got pretty good grades. I did band but not sports. I always tested very well. I got some amazing high scores on a variety of standardized tests throughout high school and college. When I was 18 and getting a physical from the doctor who had cared for me since I was a toddler, I overheard him in another room talking to the nurse about me having “(some German name) Syndrome.” I remember it was kind of like Klinefelter, but that clearly was not it. Nothing like that went onto the written form for the college. In college the main way I had a social life was by tagging along with my roommate and his friends. At least there were no hallway bullies. I was less shy with girls and had some good times. As a junior I moved off campus with some science geeks and had a social life with their friends. I spent a lot of years in college in a couple of fields before I got a marketable degree. I got married and became a parent. I would say that social relationships were via people who went to the same church or played in the same band, or were friends of my wife. In a crowd I would not be the person others flock to to have a conversation. I read a book in which a character had Asperger Syndrome and everything clicked. That must be the name the doctor used 30 years earlier, long before it became well known. As a child I would be a “little professor,” reading everything about some subject and being slow to notice that others glazed over when I wanted to tell them about it. I am sure that I have too often said “Did you know that….” to someone who was not interested in the least. Then I would move on to another subject and feel compelled to read all about it. I was not an extreme case of autism or Aspergers, with aversion to sounds or lights and flapping my hands, or having everything be just so, or with food aversions. And my difficulty recognizing faces or remembering routes is not something I hear about in Asperger Syndrome people. I had trouble predicting how others would take something I said; my casual observation would be taken as a calculated insult, or others might ridicule something I said, even though it was accurate. My efforts at humor tended to be very dry and obscure jokes or puns. In my career I seemed to be appreciated more by my bosses than by my coworkers. When I retired there was no retirement party. I’ve had no phone call from a coworker to hang out or have lunch. Now I’m retired, still married, financially secure, and come home from a part time job to be in various musical groups, do Quora, watch movies or read books, or just drink a bottle of wine to self-medicate. I have a few friends from church or musical groups, and am friendly with coworkers and several customers, who say they enjoy my take on the news and politics. I socialize with my wife’s relatives, but my own relatives are stand-offish. When I was seeing a psychiatrist for depression many years ago, I raised the subject of Aspergers and he said there was little to be accomplished by doing an assessment for it, since there is no treatment.

question: How did you realise that you might have high functioning autism?
answer: When I did more research into the symptoms, I realized that I am autistic.* It was easier for me to understand and accept that I have ADHD because I have always had stereotypical hyperactive and inattentive traits. Can't sit still, can't stand being bored, change conversation topics, change the TV channel, change hyperfixations. My autism was not as obvious to me because I hate having a rigid schedule. It prevents me from finding novelty and stimulation to assuage my ADHD. However, I learned that autistic routines can manifest as habits and rituals. I have things I do every day, just not necessarily at the same time or in the same sequence. I also thought that autistic people tend to have a flat affect and speak in a monotone. However, I have learned that there are many autists on the other end of the spectrum, who are extremely animated and loud. It isn't that autists look or sound like robots. It's that we have a hard time adjusting our expressions and speech to meet neurotypical expectations. So I either get too excited and talk too loud in formal settings where I am expected to stay quiet and serious, or I try to repress my reactions completely so that I become flat and monotone to avoid doing too much. I have also learned how trauma intensifies my autistic traits. I did not have an issue with eye contact from childhood through young adulthood. However, after some difficult and traumatic years in my mid- to late 20s, I avoid eye contact as an autist in my 30s. I have had many meltdowns and shutdowns during times of stress and trauma as well. I did not have any self-awareness about these incidents when I was younger, I only knew that I was so upset that I could no longer think or function. Understanding my autism means that I better understood my unhealthy coping mechanisms as well. When I tried to be extroverted and work in a job with lots of social interaction (college instructor), I drank alcohol daily to weekly. Autists who are very social are at significantly increased risk for alcohol abuse. I also became a daily cannabis user. Now I work as a personal assistant and only provide care for one person who I already know and trust. I do not seek out social interactions with large groups of people. I am sober, including no caffeine. I try to control my environment to keep my nervous system and emotions regulated, rather than ping-ponging between highs and lows. I am unmasked and much more obviously autistic now, and I am the happiest and most stable I have ever been. *NOTE: I don't use functioning labels because my ability to “function” in neurotypical society changes depending on the amount of external stress I experience. Functioning labels are sometimes used to differentiate between “good autists” and “bad autists” in a way that is harmful for the “bad” ones. I am autistic, and I am just as autistic as a non-speaking autist or an autist who is unable to work or manage their own finances.

question: How are mild autism, high functioning autism, and Asperger’s syndrome different?
answer: They are all the same in the sense that they don’t exist (anymore)…. Mild autism makes no sense since autism isn’t a disease. Autism can affect a person mildly, it can’t be mild (or moderate or severe) by itself. It’s just a condition you either have or you don’t. Just like you can’t be mildly pregnant. “High-functioning autism” is a term used to accommodate people who don’t really understand autism. It is an attempt to divide the broad spectrum autism is into just two categories using misnomers. They talk about something subjective and judgemental like ‘functioning’. All people with autism function well in certain areas and function less in other areas. There’s no way to tell if someone is therefore high- or low-functioning. These terms are also known to be harmful (ableist). So they fortunately aren’t used anymore that often. But they do keep showing up and people need to be reminded how these terms are outdated and harmful and not to be used anymore And finally Asperger’s syndrome also doesn’t exist. At least: not anymore! (with the exception of very few places in the world where it’s still in use). It was fortunately taken out of the two main diagnostic tools (DSM-5 in 2013, ICD-11 in 2022). Just like with the functioning terminology the different sub-labels that previously existed within the autism spectrum were all about trying to divide the spectrum into certain parts to make it easier to talk about autism, especially with people who don’t really know autism. But any division of the spectrum you make will be flawed. There will always be people who match with multiple of those sub-labels, or people falling in between sub-labels. Nowadays we just talk about Autism Spectrum Disorder. Not about mild autism, high-functioning autism or Asperger’s Syndrome (anymore).

question: Are people with high-functioning autism and Asperger syndrome ever gifted?

Someone with Ni as their dominant function will use it as the lens through which they think and feel. This mostly means that a person with Ni will mainly try to analyze and think through intensely on everything that crosses their mind. Sudden interests and curiosity seems to also be common in autism, which suggests the presence of this function. Lastly - Extroverted Sensing (Se). Oh, man, Se. Keep in mind this is our inferior function and is unbalanced, clumsy and uncontrolled. This is someone's ability to feel, analyze and incorporate the world around them in a concrete way. question: Can someone with high functioning autism/Asperger’s learn to be "normal" socially?
answer: “Can someone with high functioning autism/Asperger’s learn to be "normal" socially?” Of course. Anyone can learn anything, short of brain death, anyway. The difference is how fast certain individuals can learn something in a certain area of study. Your speed of learning can be affected by your overall intelligence level, your natural talents or lack thereof in that area, and how educated or studied you are in the area or in areas with similar/parallel concepts. For example, astronauts are often recruited from Air Force pilots, because those pilots already have a good grounding in the physics and control measures necessary to operate space craft. NASA could recruit from the plumbers union, and some of those plumbers could do very well as astronauts, but NASA would have to spend more time training them in the basics before they could start training in actual space flight. The same is true for people with Asperger's/Austism. These people don't naturally use the language of social cues and subtext that most people use and learn growing up. So for the neuro-diverse, it's like learning a second language. It takes time and intentional study, and won't be as easy as learning it natively, but it can absolutely be done, and the Autistic/Aspie can become just as good at it as anyone else, given enough time and effort. It's just that the time and effort required will be more for them than for someone who was born neuro-typical. By the way, your phrase “high functioning” autism basically only has one meaning that makes any sense - that of someone who has successfully done what you're asking. They've learned to act in the way others expect them to. That's not a better way to act. It's just more common, and they've learned to act like everyone else because it's easier than explaining themselves to everyone they meet.

question: Can someone with high-functioning autism be non-verbal?
answer: That would be very unusual. In fact, a lot of health care providers would tell you that is not possible, because if someone was nonverbal, they cannot be high functioning, because being verbal - being able to speak and use language - is part of being high functioning. If that sounds arbitrary or unfair, think about this. First, with most people with Autism, their functioning is fairly ‘even’- IF you think like the difference between very severe and very mild and don’t get too fussy(it’s common for a person to have one area of Autism be ‘mild’ and one area to be ‘moderate’, and another to be moderate, for example. If they have very severe problems with language, they usually have very severe problems with social rules and repetitive behavior. And if language is very skilled usually the other areas of Autism also are quite good. So, if I meet a person with Autism who is nonverbal, I will usually find that his other 2 areas of Autism also give him considerable challenge. I have, for sure, met people with very GOOD language skills who have a great deal of trouble with social rules and repetitive behavior. But the opposite is not common. Never say never, for sure, but not common(that said it’s wise to assume nothing when you meet someone with Autism, just get to know the person as they are). The term ‘high functioning’ isn’t formally defined anywhere (I don’t think, LOL). Well, there are a number of fairly similar definitions, all have something like ‘how you are doing overall.’ And most health care providers take that to mean, for Autism, ‘in all 3 areas of Autism.’ And while health care providers generally do not use terms like ‘high functioning’ and ‘low functioning,’ and they aren’t a formal part of a diagnosis, they will usually tell the parent something additional about the diagnosis, though the terms ‘mild and ‘moderate’ and ‘severe’ and ‘profound’ might be more informative. If any sort of swag at severity were included in the diagnosis, we’d have to consider all 3 areas, then we’d have to debate if we mean ‘language’ as in speaking only, or any type of communication. Most health care providers would probably say ‘language as in speaking,’ not out of prejudice (as most of them teach total communication and are very gung ho on it), but because that’s often the only available method of communication, day to day, in our world. Most people don’t understand sign language, and most people don’t understand or use easily, the more high tech communication devices, or the person may not even have that device with him always. Thus it stands to reason that a person would need to be high functioning in all 3 areas of Autism (language, social rules, repetitive behavior) to be considered ‘high functioning.’ The global assessment scale might be helpful to be familiar with: What Is the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) Scale?

question: Do people with high functioning autism always develop into low functioning adults?
answer: Yes. The stress of living as a high functioning autist is unbelievable. Many of the same problems as “low functioning”. But almost no support of any kind.
