Living in a world where your very wiring is at odds with the “norm” leaves most burned out at young age, despite any talents they might have. Always being the target for sociopaths and narcissists is extremely traumatizing. Feeling like there is literally no place for you in the world causes hopelessness. Never being able to read social cues effectively enough, never getting it “right”, being incredibly talented but not knowing how to please the boss, often not even being able to tell when neurotypicals are lying to you or not…all of this will slowly drive a person nuts and make it impossible to trust. question: Is high-functioning autism part of the autism spectrum?
answer: “High-functioning” autism is actually not an autism diagnosis, but people who are considered by others to be “high-functioning autistic” are on the autism spectrum. Generally, a person is diagnosed with ASD1, ASD2, or ASD3. Many people diagnosed with ASD1 are referred to as “high-functioning” or described as having “mild” autism, but this description isn’t really fair or medically correct, which is why it’s not used in diagnosis. Many people in the autism community don’t like labels like “high-functioning” or “mild” because not only does it imply that they experience autism less than others, but it also implies that others within the autism spectrum are less mentally capable, which isn’t always the case. We’ve found many non-verbal autistic people (who generally are diagnosed with ASD2 or ASD3) are actually quite intelligent and make brilliant writers, so calling them “low-functioning” or stating that someone else is “higher-functioning” than them isn’t very accurate and unfairly compares the way they experience being on the spectrum.

question: How do people with Asperger’s/high functioning autism come across to non autistic folks?
answer: My son has autism and some might call him high-functioning. (I say might because high or low functioning are not official or measurable terms, so they're quite subjective.) The usual reaction I get from people who have just met him: I didn't know he had autism. Some even seem apologetic about it, though I’m not sure why. It doesn't offend me that people don't recognize it right away. Sometime the lack of recognition stems from a misunderstanding of autism. Some people seem to think that a particular characteristic (what you could call a symptom) is true of all people with autism or is true all the time. Autistic people are a lot more diverse than that. An example would be eye contact. My son is capable of making eye contact and he sometimes will spontaneously, but he doesn't prefer it. He has now been in social skills classes in school for years and they focus on that skill a lot so I’m sure that has helped. People's surprise at finding out his diagnosis makes me feel they have an outdated view of autism—that of a child sitting in the corner, rocking and not interacting with anyone. That can happen but it doesn't represent every case. I often wonder if people think he has an intellectual disability (he doesn't) because his stimming (self-stimulatory behavior) and lack of focus make him seem kind of out of it. He definitely looks odd. Why odd? Well, he talks and giggles to himself often. He spends a few seconds rubbing his food against his lips and intensely smelling it before eating a bite. Even his intense humming looks strange if you're not familiar with it. Of course there's also his lunging behavior—the standing up version of rocking. He definitely stands out. The other reason I think he might appear intellectually disabled is because he has a sweet and rather innocent personality. (Presumably an extension of his lack of understanding of social situations.) He also makes unusual comments that are just not factual, which you wouldn't expect from a nine year old. Interestingly, he’s pretty social, however, he still likes a lot of alone time. He certainly doesn't necessarily engage in long conversations. His responses tend to be rather short. My friends who are also parents of kids with autism remind me that it's better that my son is so verbal (which he really is) but there are still plenty of times when I get nothing out of him. I guess the ultimate answer to this question is, in many ways—I don't know. It's very hard to know since most people probably wouldn't tell me the truth about how he appears. Or they get to know him and the oddness isn't as important anymore. One final note (a little off-topic)—I’m not really fair to people with regards to how they view him. If they don't compliment his progress enough, I feel they don't appreciate him enough. If they gloss over his issues, I feel they're not taking his autism seriously. It's hard for people to “win” with me on that issue. I’m working on it.

question: How do you help high functioning autism?
answer: The first thing to understand is that the label “high-functioning Autism" is a transient state that can fluctuate dramatically throughout a day. An Autistic person's level of functionality is directly related to mental, emotional and physical stress levels in an inverse relationship to the Neural Overload or Sensory Overload they're currently experiencing. So… LOW level of Overload = HIGH functioning (in terms of neurological and sensory processing and decision-making ability/capacity). HIGH level of Overload = LOW functioning (in terms of neurological and sensory processing and decision-making ability/capacity). This is directly related to our levels of failure of Synaptic Pruning which typically begins during the second or third trimester a of gestation. To help an Autistic person who is experiencing little or no Neural or Sensory Overload (currently high-functioning), try to prevent any raising of the volume of sensory signals being sent to their brain's Sensory Processing Centres. This will help free up their capacity for executive decisio-making and reasoning — and memory retrieval. If, however, they're already Overloaded — and therefore lower-functioning — focus on practical help by either lowering the ambient light, sound and visual signals, adjusting temperature, noise, number of voices, etc in the immediate vicinity — or remove the overloaded/lower-functioning Autistic person to a quiet room or area where the environment is less over-stimulating. Many shopping centres, sports and entertainment venues have such facilities these days. Parents of Autistic children often plan for possible Overloads — but adults with Autism often fail to plan ahead.Chart illustrates the different levels of stress and Neural/Sensory Overload experienced by Autistic and NT people.

question: How likely is it that Einstein had high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome?
answer: This isn’t really known. The term “Einstein Syndrome” applies to bright kids from mathematical and musical families who had delayed speech. Famous examples include not only Einstein himself, but Richard Feynman and Edward Teller. Sowell’s thesis is that in such children, brain regions involved in logic and mathematics prosper at the expense of adjacent regions that are involved in speech. He states that such children aren’t autistic, but are not infrequently misdiagnosed as such. However, speaking as a classical Einstein Syndrome kid myself (delayed speech, stubborn as hell, intellectually gifted, musical and mathematical family) and someone with high functioning autism I am not at all certain that the conditions are distinct. Many have, in fact, suggested that Einstein was autistic, and certainly he had many of the characteristics that we associate with autism. Increasingly, it seems to me that there is a larger category, neurodiversity, with multiple genetic and environmental influences and that the boxes we draw around conditions such as giftedness, ASD, broader autism phenotype, schizophrenia, Bipolar disorder and clinical depression, ADHD, and so forth are somewhat arbitrary. I see these neurodevelopmental conditions running through the same gifted families. Sometimes one rears its head, sometimes another, in varying degrees and in varying combinations. Often, it seems, one condition is actually a collection of disparate conditions involving different genes or alleles. That’s increasingly the consensus view of schizophrenia — that it isn’t actually one single disorder. I’m not sure that autism is any different — see for example the paper that found a correlation between the physiognomy of the face and the nature of autistic symptoms and intellect. One thing that seems clear — a disproportionate percentage of highly gifted people are HFA or broader autism phenotype. Cf. my answer the other day to the question of whether autistic people here had any autistic gifts. Autism is peculiar among disorders in that it doesn’t just rob us of ability, it confers it. And then there’s the research that shows that people with genes that predispose towards these conditions are smarter, even if they don’t manifest the conditions themselves. Our understanding of neurodiversity is increasing, but it’s still woefully incomplete. We need a better understanding of the genetics, physiological changes, and environmental factors before we’ll really know the answer to this question.

question: If someone didn’t have help in dealing with high functioning autism, what would life look like for them?
answer: I am self-diagnosed and would be considered extremely high functioning. I am intelligent, had no developmental delays, reasonably attractive, multiple university degrees, married 20 years. I have done well by most measures. Even my sensory issues are minimal — my hearing is very sensitive but I live in a very quiet way. And yet, even with all of that, life is extremely hard for me in ways that are simply invisible to everyone but my husband. And even he doesn’t fully understand. In my opinion, Neurotypicals are essentially blind to how much the modern world is optimized for their preferences, and how alien, even painful, that world is for the neurodiverse. They also have no idea how aggressively and shockingly badly an NT will act when you transgress an invisible rule that you have no hope of ever understanding. What’s worse, NTs pretty much excuse each other’s appalling behaviour by believing that you “provoked” or “deserved” it somehow. The crazy, totally-off-base, whacked-out things people have felt the need to tell me about myself would knock your socks off (yes Aspies understand figurative language, but we still take things literally all the time, I don't actually understand it myself). I’ve been told e.g. that I have deep-seated rage issues stemming from unresolved childhood trauma, and that I’m not welcome until I fix myself with therapy first. What kind of person thinks it’s ok to talk to others like this? From the POV of an Aspie — and here, I think the more rational neurotypicals like my husband are actually on our side — these social rules are stupid, petty, arbitrary, and constantly shifting in ways that benefit the people engineering the shift. It is obviously a power game. But we are caught it in regardless, even though we don’t know how to play, and have no interest in the game whatsoever. I have worked much of my life in sectors filled with highly educated, compassionate people, with a genuine interest in diversity and inclusion. And yet, they have NO CLUE that the workplaces they create in these sectors are pretty much toxic to the neurodiverse. They are too gregarious, too social, too loud, too open concept, and too filled with subtext for Aspies like me. It’s all groupwork and collaboration, facilitated conversations and feedback (often with zero clarity on what we are expected to do with the feedback). Meetings galore. And no real clarity on who is in charge either. Modern workplaces like to present a veneer of egalitarianism, while still cleaving to traditional hierarchies, but invisibly. This is extremely challenging for people like me, this casual doublespeak that comes naturally to NTs. Some of the challenges are so bizarre that you’d hardly believe it, if you didn’t witness it yourself. I’ll see that a problem is arising, and will say something. It will be dismissed. I persist in raising it, no dice. Months later someone else says it, and boom! everyone suddenly gets it, and realizes what they need to do. But when YOU say it, they disagree and insist that it’s YOU who doesn’t get it! I've been gaslit so much at work. It’s so exhausting. Then there are the mental health challenges. I am mentally a tough person, and I’m happy and even keeled most of the time. I’ve always been like this. But what I have after a lifetime of simply being who I am is a constant hyper-vigilance that I will offend by saying the wrong thing, OR that I'll say the right thing in the WRONG way (ie, too soon, too forcefully, not forcefully enough) OR to the wrong people. There are just so many ways to transgress, it’s not even funny. It’s just shitty. So yeah, this is what it’s like. What supports? Dream on. There is no way for me to be supported, other than NTs reorganize their workplaces to allow for people who prefer more solitary work, without constant meetings and emails, and stop with the politics and social posturing. As if that’s going to happen. From what I can tell, right now, people seem to think that accepting diversity is just accepting that we exist, a few workarounds and accommodations, but changing how they do things, to actually include our way of being in the world? I’m not seeing that yet. Having said all this, it’s nice to have Quora to discharge some of my frustration, which is bubbling over this weekend but I'm normally more chill. I love NTs and am happily married to one. And I am super impressed with my current colleagues. But it’s very hard sometimes to live in your world. I would like you to know that.

question: Do people with high-functioning autism spin themselves around and around?

When I was a kid, I jumped up and down, shuffling from one foot to the other, on my toes, flicking my wrists, which looked like a weird happy dance. I did this when I was happy or excited, it was my body expressing positive emotions. Nowadays, I still occasionally do this, only when I am alone and really, really happy about something. I guess the neurotypical equivalent of this would be yelling cheerfully. But no spinning. One thing I liked to do as a kid was rolling down a hillside, I would do it over and over again. I would still do it if there were a clean hillside nearby, but I live in a large North American city and I wouldn’t take the risk of stabbing myself with a dirty syringe. And no, I wouldn’t care that people are staring at me. I occasionally do use the slide and the swing in parks if I have a little bit of time, I climb up into play structures, I hook my knees around a horizontal bar and dangle myself head down. Then I have to sit down for a moment because I get dizzy. I also like to jump off of swings in midflight and the impact gives me a really nice sensation under the skin of my legs. I don’t think there is anything childlike about any of this. I think this is just a way for a person who has vestibular issues like most people on the spectrum to propriocept, or orient oneself in three-dimensional space, which I wouldn’t be surprised if it were why people on the spectrum stim. This might be the equivalent of grabbing something or someone, or sitting/lying down, in neurotypicals as a reaction to certain emotions, a way to anchor oneself to the physical environment.

question: What is the reason that people with high-functioning autism have a lower quality of life than neurotypicals or those with low-functioning autism?
answer: Thanks for the A2A Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht ND RPI can name a few reasons why someone with HFA would have a lower quality of life. I will focus mainly on work life, home life, and interpersonal relations. Also, I will focus on how someone with HFA compares against a neurotypical, as I believe that quality of life for someone on the low-functioning end is mostly lower than for those on the high end. 1: Poor executive function People with HFA commonly deal with something called “poor executive function.” This, in layman terms, means that we have trouble taking care of ourselves. For me, the main issue with it is that, while I know I SHOULD brush my teeth/do the dishes/take a shower/etc, it isn't as high on my priority list as it would be for neurotypicals, so I tend to procrastinate doing it. I am also quite apathetic about my physical appearance unless I am attending a formal event or something like an interview, so most of the time I have clashing clothes and rat-nest hair. People who haven't developed coping skills as well as I have may completely avoid doing necessary hygiene tasks and cleaning, making them and their living space a total mess. This will affect their job outlook tremendously (basically making things much harder and even impossible in some cases), and will drive many people away from them. This makes it even tougher to create relationships with other people, which most people with HFA already struggle with. 2: Lack of social skills The defining feature of the autism spectrum is a lack of the social skills that NTs seem to be born with. For us, the social laws that govern interpersonal relations might as well be written in hieroglyphics. And even when we do decipher some of them, I find them incredibly arbitrary and tedious. Unfortunately, not following these rules puts strain on interactions and a lot of people will choose to just end them altogether, especially if it's the first time they've met. This usually kills whatever chance there is of a friendship forming or a romantic relationship sparking. For those who can't figure out/couldn't give a shit about these rules, they face a reality of social ostracization, which can lead to isolationism and depression. Even those with very good learned skills are still at a disadvantage compared to the NT population; much like someone learning a foreign language may never reach the level of a full-native speaker. We may get close, but never 100%. This also affects their chances of landing good jobs, as interpersonal skills are necessary for obtaining and keeping a job. Try going into an interview with a wrinkly suit, never making eye contact, and mumbling your responses to questions. You'll never find a decent job, no matter how good your resume is. That's the unfortunate reality we must live in. Either we learn to speak the “NT language” or we are perpetually the odd men/women out. 3: Overstimulation Work environments can be highly stressful for those sensitive to sensory stimulation. Fast food kitchens are frenzied and chaotic during dinner rush. Offices are full of printers printing, computers beeping, keyboards clicking, etc. There’s always a social hierarchy and a quasi-political element to the workplace unless you work independently. All of these things may hinder someone with HFA, as we are prone to being hypersensitive to certain stimuli. Imagine that someone turning on a light was as bright as staring directly at the sun. Imagine that the normal volume music in a room is actually as loud as a rock concert. Imagine the smell of your less-than-ideal gas station sushi actually smells like very strong and fresh diarrhea. That's what some of us feel on a daily basis. If we get overloaded, it culminates into something colloquially known as a meltdown. If the brain is our internal computer, a meltdown is what happens when the CPU gets overworked, overheats, and the whole thing crashes. Basically, we go catatonic and retreat into ourselves, violently lashing out at anything that gets near. Not exactly a good thing if your in the middle of an important task or talking to your boss about some important meeting or promotion. It is necessary for someone who is hypersensitive to be in an environment that won't trigger a meltdown. However, many companies, rather than making those accommodations, would rather just hire the next guy who doesn't need them. This also plays a part in home life. Living in a city would be impossible for some people based sorely on how much noise and how many smells there are. Diet can be massively affected as some people literally cannot eat certain foods without gagging: either the texture of the food triggers something or the taste is simply too overpowering. Living with another person can be very stressful unless that person knows how to give space when required. Finally 4: Hyper-focus and Obsession Another archetypical autistic trait is hyper-focus/obsession with a narrow field. Basically, rather than being a “jack of all trades, master of none,” someone with autism will tend to narrow their focus to one subject and block most everything else. Now, this can be great if that focus is towards something that is valued by society, such as mathematical savants and musical virtuosos. There won't be that much pressure to do anything else as these fields can both be rewarding financially and socially. However, if your obsession just happens to be something like underwater basket weaving, there will be a lot of struggling trying to balance out the obsession with stuff that can make you a living. From my experience, it feels like there's a magnet pulling my focus away from whatever I'm doing towards whatever my hyper-focus wants to focus on at the moment (right now it's chess and piano music), and the magnet gets stronger the longer I resist it. This adds to the stress of everyday life, and can even catalyze a meltdown. TL;DR, People with HFA may experience a lower quality of life simply because we struggle to cope with the everyday occurrences that happen in life, while NTs can simply go with the flow.

question: Does high functioning autism get better with age?
answer: Let's first clarify the terms used in the question: High functioning autism — is an old, misleading and confusing term from the 1980s and earlier, when it was thought that Autism was able to be quantified like a one-dimensional, less/more slider control, like this:It's actually a multi-faceted, multi-hued, multi-dimensional, highly-nuanced SPECTRUM, more like this:Get better with age — the nature of Autism is genetic and neurological. It's passed from generation to generation at the moment of conception and it's central characteristic is failure of Synaptic Pruning along the neutrons that commences in the second or third trimester of gestation and continues into maturity. This can also be complicated by a Neurological condition called Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) which results in internal and external tumours called neurofibromas that are composed of excess growth of unpruned synapses in other parts of the body. External neurofibromas — often in the form of benign, fleshy skin tags, moles and larger growths, are usually able to be surgically removed. Internal neurofibromas — which can grow along nerves in the body and limbs, are typically benign, but are often risky to remove because of the high risk of loss of the underlying nerve function. If the become inflamed, they can be extremely painful. The complication appears to be that while there appears to be evidence that excess growth of synapses subsides in nature autistic adults, those with NF1 can experience continual growth of both internal and external NF1 tumours into old age. I have both Asperger's Syndrome and NF1. I'm currently 75 yo, and growth of both internal and external neurofibromas is still evident, but seems to have slowed in the last couple of years. What made the most noticeable difference for me in learning to manage the effects and impact on my life and those around me, has been the following:Diagnosis of NF1 in mid-2000.Diagnosis of Asperger's Syndrome in December 2002.My decision to disclose both conditions, openly.Education and research around both Neurological Conditions.Active public involvement in ongoing awareness, acceptance, education and research into both conditions for the past 20 years.Engagement with other interested, including researchers, educators, advocacy and support organisations, etc.

question: How can you tell if someone with high functioning autism likes you?
answer: I don’t know how to flirt. People have tried to teach me, but it’s just useless. One of the reasons is that I may not be able to learn to flirt is that I don’t like how it looks. I notice when people flirt and there’s something repulsive about it. Maybe it’s because it looks so fake? We don’t like fakery. We don’t like things to be implied. My suggestion is that you don’t flirt with him. An up-front question is something we appreciate. If you make him have to guess that you like him, he’s not going to like it. People with autism tend to stare at people they like, but only when they’re not looking back. And it’s likely to be from a distance. We like to be in the proximity of the people we fancy, but not too close. Since I couldn’t really flirt, if I fancied someone I’d muster the courage and eventually just go up and tell them. If you do decide to go to him and tell him upfront, don’t be too worried about feeling rejected. I mean, he might say that he doesn’t like you back, but he’ll be very sorry to hurt your feelings. He won’t want to make you feel bad. You could also try to brush your hand by his, as if by accident. We are very sensitive and a skin-on-skin touch REALLY gets his attention. When I was a teen, if someone I fancied touched me, the whole world would freeze for a few seconds. Nothing else mattered. I would day-dream about that single accidental touch for days and days.

question: Can high-functioning autism be an advantage?
answer: I participate in a very fast group ride every Wednesday night. It’s basically a bike race, with some neutral areas here and there, to keep things fun and not overly competitive. One section of the ride, from Sandy Beach to the Makapu’u Lookout, and back, is marred by really poorly maintained roads. If we’ve got a really large group, or new riders, we skip that part because it’s small kine dangerous. Bumps, rocks and pot holes jump out in front of you unexpectedly and they can take you down immediately. It’s been a couple of years since we’ve experienced an accident on one of our rides, but the possibility is always there, especially along that route. While riding full speed, my front wheel inches from the back wheel of the rider in front of me, I can’t see the road coming up and have to trust the guys in front of me to guide the group around dangers and keep us safe. This can give me lots of anxiety and pushes me into fight or flight mode. Flight being falling off the back of the group, to fight the head wind alone, or fight, step out of the pace line and put in an attack, passing everyone and going off the front, where I can see the road and release my feelings of anxiety. I often choose plan B and take off up hill like a bat out of hell. That seems like it would be cool but in cycling, when someone attacks, others have to respond and counter your move. This means everyone has to work harder to keep the group together, to maintain the aerodynamic advantage of the group vs a lone rider, and they too have to tear ass up the hill to get me. Moans and groans ensue. The ride back, though downhill, is the same story. I hit it hard, to get out front so I can see the road and not fear dying, which forces everyone to chase my ass at high speed. They kinda know why I’m doing this but it isn’t really appreciated, since those are typically neutral sections on the ride. You aren’t supposed to put in an attack but I’m fired up in fight or flight mode and take off like a rocket. There really isn’t much I can do about this either. My mind is screaming at me to get out front, so I can see the road and reduce the danger, and I have to obey. In a way, that’s an advantage, a speed advantage anyhow.

question: Do people with high-functioning autism/Asperger syndrome have difficulty talking on the phone?
answer: Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All rights reserved. I’m not sure if this is a feature that is present in all autistics, and research on this topic seems to be more or less absent—but if you search something along the lines of “ASD phone calls”, you will be met with a myriad of links[1][2][3][4][5] to forums, blog posts and videos of people with ASD talking about issues with telecommunication. I generally have a great dislike for talking on the phone myself, and will often make sure I do not have to. You would think that the extent of issues with telecommunication is inversely correlated with how high-functioning the person is, but based on experience I would say even the very high-functioning autistics may have a great dislike for talking on the phone, and may even refrain from talking on the phone mostly or completely. As for the underlying issues with talking on the phone, here are a few:Lacking those visual cues — People with ASD have problems intuitively understanding what to say, and rely on visual cues to inform them about the proper way to respond. In absence of visual input, a large part of visual communication is missing, and thus there is an absence of information. This can cause anxiety and social friction.Visual-reliant — People with ASD process an extensive amount of sensory information[6], and thus experience hypervision as well[7]. This in combination with reduced intuitive and greater reflective processing means that people with ASD are going to rely more on what they observe in order to internalize proper conventions than that they intuitively know what to do or say, and with a greater sensory ability they are going to acquire more sensory input through observation, too. As such, it could be said that they rely more on visual input than neurotypicals, which would thus be a larger aspect missing during telecommunication.So not only do people with ASD lack visual cues during telecommunication which they rely on to inform them about what to say, but they rely on visual input on a cognitive and purely visual level more so than neurotypicals would.Expectations — Where is the conversation headed? If you don’t trust the other person, or if you don’t talk with a great conversationalist, then an uncertainty of where the conversation is headed can cause anxiety and awkwardness, which creates more uncertainty, and so on in a downwards spiral. For people with ASD, not knowing what they can expect can feel like there is nothing or too little they can rely on for comfort and have a smooth interaction.Also, being called by a stranger, being called at an unexpected time, or being called at the wrong time can dysregulate a person with ASD, which is a bad start for any conversation. Even a ringing phone alone can feel like an invasion[8].Also, not knowing what to expect from a conversation can cause enough anxiety for someone with ASD that they refrain from calling altogether, or keep postponing obligatory phone calls they have to make. This can potentially lead to larger problems, depending on who you are supposed to call, or who is trying to get a hold of you.Anticipation — Missing visual cues, it can be difficult for people with ASD to know when it is their turn to talk, which can greatly disrupt proper communication. This, too, can cause anxiety and social friction, which is going to undermine communication or the will to sustain or initiate it further.Hyperfocus — You would think that without the need to maintain eye contact, communication on the phone could be easier. But without visual input to rely on, the focus comes heavily on what is said, and so communication may become overwhelming. Snagglebox blogger Bec Oakley writes[9]:It feels […] overwhelming for me, and leaves me […] vulnerable. And that’s because on the phone I feel trapped—someone wants something from me and there is nowhere to hide. Their full attention is directed my way, as if there’s a big fat spotlight shining directly at my head. This focus can be extremely exhausting, and I can only keep it up for short periods at a time.Overstimulation — As communication on the phone can be an intense experience for someone with ASD, problems with social conventions can potentially greatly undermine communication as one becomes overstimulated. As such, the need to disengage from the phone call may emerge.Social conventions — Another big problem is adherence to social conventions, as people with ASD won’t understand all of them or otherwise have difficulty following them. For me at least, phone calls like having to call a family member to congratulate them on their birthday are some of the worst, as the phone call is made purely out of a social convention and no purpose beyond that. What I wish the conversation would be like was this:Hello, Bob speaking.Hello, Bob. Martin here. Congratulations on your birthday!Thank you, Martin. Goodbye.Goodbye, Bob. You are the ideal family member. But alas, it is not to be. Instead, I have to go through the motions of asking the same old questions, just to make the phone call sufficiently long for an indication that I am disengaging from the phone call not to sound awkward.Unnatural — For some[10], the absence of the visual presence of the person they are talking to, the person with ASD can have the feeling they are talking to a machine or to themselves, which can be uncomfortable or unsettling.Sensory issues — Lastly, some people with ASD[11] experience sensory issues, such as:Pain from holding the phone next to their ear.Challenges with keeping their hands still when they talkThe volume, pitch, and frequencies of the sound as well as inconsistent volumes, crackling, distortions or a bad connection can be overwhelming after only a few minutes.Although there are a great many potential problems when it comes to talking on the phone, a lot of the issues—though not all—can be improved upon with practice, and people with ASD also report finding comfort with talking to a selected few people on the phone only, which emphasizes the importance of trust, and knowing what to expect in terms of communicating with someone you cannot see.For more information on (high-functioning) ASD, have a look at: Embrace AutismA blog about quantitative- and qualitative research on autism, by Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht ND RP and Eva Silvertant.Footnotes[1] Wrong Planet Autism Community Forum[2] Autism & Difficulties with Phone Conversations - Remrov's World of Autism #21[3] Really bad at phone calls[4] How Asperger’s Taught Me to Hate the Phone[5] High-Functioning Autism and Phone Use: Likely Reasons People With Asperger's Aren't Calling You[6] The Complete Guide to Asperger's Syndrome[7] New research explains autistic's exceptional visual abilities[8] Why I Hate Talking On The Phone[9] Why I Hate Talking On The Phone[10] Why I Hate Talking On The Phone[11] Why I Hate Talking On The Phone

question: Is Asperger's/"high-functioning autism" a disability?
answer: If it's bad enough to be disabling, yes. If it's not bad enough to impair your ability to function then it's legally not a disability. Calling something a disability has more to do with how it impacts your life rather than what it is. This is to the point that two people can have the same condition and it's possible one wouldn't be considered disabled because of it yet the other one may be impacted enough because of it that they are unquestionably disabled. That said, Asperger's is an outdated diagnosis and the person it was named after worked with Nazis. He helped set up a system to decide which autistic people should be kept alive and made use of and which ones (the “lower functioning” ones) should be offed outright. Also, high vs low functioning labels for autism aren't ideal since it's a spectrum with multiple areas it can affect and it's possible for someone with autism to not be greatly impacted in some regards, mildly impacted in others, and greatly impacted in others. Meaning someone with autism can be “high functioning” in some areas and “low functioning” in others.

question: If there is such thing as high-functioning autism and low-functioning autism, then why isn’t there a mid-functioning autism?
answer: No, there isn’t really such thing as these. These labels and categories are not clinically based. At least, they’re not officially defined in this way, so anytime you see “high-funtioning” or “low-funtioning” it’s an arbitrary label based only on that person’s perceptions. The reason being is that every autistic person is both “high” and “low” funtioning in different areas. The autism spectrum is not a linear one dimensional spectrum labeled “high funtioning” or “mild” on one end and “low functioning” or “severe” on the other end. It’s a three dimensional spectrum in which people have different needs and talents in different areas, and these may fluctuate based on circumstance and time. You can’t put an autistic person on one point on a line and say this is where they “funtion.” It doesn’t make sense. That’s not how autism works. I have seen people use the term “mid-funtioning” before, but it’s no more accurate than any of the other funtioning labels. Again, these aren’t officially defined anywhere other than in the minds of he people assigning these labels. I wish people would stop using funtioning labels like this. They’re innacurate, and only hurt autistic people who are labeled to them. (“What’s your problem? You’re high funtioning after all, so just high funtion your way through your disability like a normal person!” or “oh that person is so low funtioning so I’m going to talk to them like a child, and assume they don’t have any actual talents or skills. Maybe I’ll call them broken and a burden too.”) It’s B.S. The only difference between high funtioning and low funtioning is that high funtioning means your deficits are ignored and low funtioning means your assets are ignored. So, OP, please don’t use these labels. If you have questions feel free to ask me, but I think I’ve pretty clearly explained why we should stop using these labels. Now, some autistic people are definitely more disabled in some areas than others, but rather than attach some arbitrary label why don’t you discuss them in terms of their actual problems instead of a useless label. For example, “non-verbal” instead of “low funtioning.” Some of the smartest people I’ve ever talked to were non-verbal autistics (well, we were both typing, but you get the gist). And, don’t assume that just because someone isn’t obviously autistic doesn’t mean they aren’t disabled and need support (often what “high funtioning” is taken to mean”). Every autistic person is severely affected by their disability. Funtioning isn’t linear, and autistic people don’t fit into two or three categories. Thanks for reading.

question: Why do people insist that women with high-functioning autism are not autistic?
answer: High-functioning autism in women is difficult to diagnose because it’s more obvious in men than women. The average female learns to adapt to society’s standards and act accordingly to fit in. We’re pressured to do so or we’re outcasts. And women with autism are no different. We are good at blending in because we’re observers and learn from watching the world around us so we learn how to act so our autism is harder to detect. This is called masking and it is the main reason most women with high-functioning autism don’t get diagnosed until adulthood, or sometimes never. We adapt to survive basically. We show the world what we know it wants to see because our true selves usually aren’t accepted. Thankfully though female autism is becoming more and more accepted so women with autism are starting to be more themselves than their mask counterpart. I know from personal experience that the more stressed I get, the more my mask slips because so much of my energy goes into maintaining a facade and stress just depletes that energy. I work at a library where I have to be happy and sociable to people all day so when I get home at the end of the day I’m just mentally drained and want to be alone in my room. Just the prospect of walking in the house and someone saying hello and asking me how my day was can be tiresome and irritating, even though that’s just a regular social convention. My family sees it as rude because they just don’t understand how draining it all is for me. So, believe me, high-functioning autism in women is very real and we struggle with the label of not being “autistic enough” for society to accept our diagnosis.

question: What's it like being an adult with aspergers or high functioning autism?
answer: What's it like being an adult with Asperger’s or high functioning autism? It is impossible to really describe what it is like to have autism, as we have no “normal” reference point. I had a college friend who was born blind, but in her late teens was given sight in one eye. We spoke at length about the experience. How do you understand that you are or are not seeing the world as others do? She said if she stood on the edge of a curb looking down, she had no idea how far the step down might be. It could have been two inches or ten feet. That is similar to having Autism. I may believe that I can be the life of the party, funny and gregarious, but my view of the world is skewed. I liken this to a plane’s altimeter and compass that tells you if you are flying straight and how high up. Ours is effectively broken giving us false readings. We may think we are flying straight and level, but to others we appear to be wandering all over the sky. Finding out later in life (I was 50) that you cannot trust your idea of level is rather distressing. Most of us go through grieving, denial and anger. Some feel relief as it explains so many awkward social situations. Each of us are all so different (it’s a wide and deep spectrum), but for me, I can feel like an alien in a human’s body dropped here at birth to try to figure out this odd species. It can be exhilarating and pure hell. I have been lucky to walk among you for over fifty years watching and listening. A helpful hint: We didn’t choose this, we don’t usually enjoy it and you cannot make it go away by yelling at us or demanding that we, “Stop it!” Hopefully you wouldn’t try this caring and sensitive approach with someone with cancer, Alzheimer’s or depression, either. We are not trying to be obstinate, overly sensitive or irritating. We are sometimes doing the best we know how to survive what seems like a minor incident to you. If you are in this situation, DON’T GIVE UP. These “humans” are not all bad and you can learn coping skills to deal with the intense moments. It gets better with work. My childhood experience was filled with awful jerks who were cruel to any one that was different. These creeps searched us out to humiliate and bully us, and others say nothing to avoid being targets or as a way to socially bond with them. We want those types to leave us alone. I learned to fight really well. Many bullies regretted messing with me once I got to the breaking point. How I see the world. My head is filled with constant stream of movies being played at the same time over my normal vision and hearing. This is my first language. I use this to condense and translate ideas from those streams into English. Ever see the Marvel opening where a myriad of comic pages are flipping past like a book? That is often what is going on in my mind. You may say, “I couldn’t see the trees for the forest.” Some of us may take that literally and that may start us on a mental adventure where we are walking in the woods looking at the all the different types of trees and there we meet a raccoon merrily strumming a small, dark brown rosewood guitar. The story goes on to have us on a canoe trip (aluminum boat with riveted seams, caramel colored wicker seats and a blue and white plastic cooler set between the seats) with the raccoon, who is raucously singing about his love of pretzels. We are feeling the wind and the choppy waves, maybe smelling the pretzel, when you ask a question that requires a response. Oops. Our internal world is often far more fascinating and engaging than the external world. For survival, some of us have learned to be chameleons playing back what we hope are the proper social cues. We don’t fully understand these copied acts, but they may have worked satisfactorily in the past, so we reuse them. Minimally, we come off as a bit (or very) weird, as we miss some of the important subtle social cues. We are often blind to other’s irritation when we have to state some arcane fact to correct a misnomer or when we feel that we must definitively prove our case. We find joy in knowing weird things and expect that you will appreciate that as well, but you probably don’t. We are honest to a fault and don’t always get when it is socially appropriate to lie. Many of us are extremely trusting, and that can be with the wrong people. We may share inappropriate intimate personal information with unsavory people as we don’t always get their intent or that they are slyly mocking us to amuse others. I feel weird making blanket statements such as, “No one would ever do ___.” I know that there are always outliers that will do something that no one else would rationally think of doing. I would feel the stupid need to point this detail out in a caveat. Some of us are absolutely brilliant or fanatical in our interests, but we really don’t care about anything about what does not interest us. We often don’t get your expression based hints that you don’t find British passenger trains from 1920-1937 as wholeheartedly enthralling as we might. Contrary to belief, autistic people don’t all love trains. I have a genius level IQ and see patterns in everything. I talk in spirals, where to many, my conversation is a confusing tornado of unrelated points, but at the end, if you are still trying to follow it, they meet back up to form a circle when viewed from the top. Again, maybe this is only to me. Most of us have the problem of over-stimulation. Rough clothing tags become little thorns being jabbed into our flesh that scream incessantly for our attention. We may make a ton of noise or a mess, but if we cannot control it or someone else is doing it, the stimulus may be far too much for us. Social statement: Regardless of autism, most of us need a quiet work-space free of distraction to work at our best. Open floor plans look good in cinema, but studies show that productivity drops in such environments. Everything may feel overly magnified to us. A crowded venue full of laughter, talking and loud music is a morass of pummeling noise and light that we cannot block or filter. Imagine each person as there broadcasting as a different radio station, set to the highest level possible, with prison grade spotlights stabbing you in the eyes. This may sound dramatic, but it is a war on our senses for many of us. Some cover their ears and close their eyes tightly trying to slink back in their heads to hide. If it gets to be far too much and we cannot retreat, we may have a fit, wanting to destroy the irritant until there is nothing left. I mean, going completely nuclear leaving not even DNA behind. Of course we cannot. We sometimes miss social cues, and even if we have become good at masquerading as normal humans, we may come off as odd, emotionless or volatile. We are tolerated by some as they can see reasonable financial returns. Some hate being touched as it is too invasive or there are too many stimuli. Some love being touched up to a point, then it can become too much for them and they may shut down. People love to read and see stories of great minds, thinkers, visionaries, engineers and artists, lauding their great skills and achievements, but in reality they wouldn’t want to be around them. That makes sense as many of us are irritating, full of our own strict special coping rules and strange ideas of how a process should have gone. Few overly driven people are fun to be around and their families suffer, but we need them. Many of us are brilliant, but we are chronically unemployed or underemployed as the world doesn’t know they need us or how to use our giftings. Automated HR processes weed us out before human eyes see us. Then if we do get noticed, our resume may not fit a pattern that HR understands. We may not have a degree or certification in a field, but we can know it better than those that do if it is our passion. We can be great assets as we are wired differently and we can see unique ways to approach highly complex problems that others may not. A recent study says 1 in 63 boys are on the autism spectrum. Girls present differently, so there could be as many of them that fit that diagnosis but we miss it. We are everywhere. I have been to engineering firms, software companies and art schools, where the majority are spectrum. Most of them don’t even know that they are autistic. I didn’t. Society must embrace those that think and who are wired differently, those who are not just engineers or software developers. They are the minds that will move us all forward.

question: Is mild autism very similar to high functioning autism and Asperger syndrome?
answer: Ish. Let me explain. People who use those terms use them interchangeably to mean the same thing. However, I and many autistics fundamentally disagree with using any of those terms. The thing is, autism isn’t a linear scale. It’s not like height - you’re either short or tall or somewhere in between. It’s more like size: you might be tall, or short, or in the middle; you might be skinny or large; if you’re large it might be fat or muscle or both. You might be big in some areas and small in others. Unlike physical size though, how much a person is or isn’t affected by their autistic traits depends on a number of things: how much that trait typically affects them, yes, but also how tired they are, how social they’ve had to be recently, how hungry they are, how loud it is, etc. For example, I’m okay with loud shops, unless I’m also hungry and tired, in which case I become extremely irritable very quickly. If those things all continue, and perhaps someone is rude to me or bumps into me, I’ll have a meltdown. This is partly why autistics like to be in control: we’re constantly making sure our “base level” is high enough that we can cope with what life throws at us. That said, we mess up a lot, because many of us have issues with interoception (being aware of what we’re feeling) so we might not notice that we’re hungry or tired until it’s also loud and suddenly all too much. This diagram explains the idea of the “full spectrum” nicely.

question: What do people with high functioning autism think of people with low functioning autism?
answer: Many autistics, and even some few enlightened allistics, simply wish for greater communication and equal acceptance with fairness for ALL neurologies. Most autistics don't have very much direct interaction with other autistics at all (that's starting to change, but very slowly) Many among autistics would wish medical science to be focus on relief & correct identification of real co-conditions or co-morbities as they're sometimes called, and finally stop making the mistake of calling those other rare & secondary physical affecations part of autism itself. Some of us believe that our own autistic neurology has never really been a “mental health condition”. We know it has been considered as such and many of us were raised to think the same, but if self-awareness comes far enough along, there can be major “awakenings” that show something else instead. The differences we know seem to actually be expressions of a natural physical trait, and there are one or two known studies with clues as to where and how. The major difference resulting comes out in perceptions, and unfortunately because of horrific stigma, only visible outward behaviors are honestly considered at all by medical professionals. Motivations rarely are even discussed with patients, even though honest consideration employed consistently COULD conceivably change the entire world. Autistic neurology seems to simply be neurodiverse people manifesting in our global population, as is a fairly commonplace process in Earth's vertebrate life forms at least. Humans specifically have more complex brains than most other species, so perhaps more neurology variations as an effect aren't really any surprise. Natural evolution is trying to occur, as it always has. The allistic majority seem to often reject even that idea, because they tend to see conformity as the only moral right viewpoint. Unrealistically that socially & over-emotionally perceives all differences as threats. Of course, the time frame of evolutionary changes doesn't ever actually “rush forward" as is postulated in marvel's x-men fiction stories. The irrational allistic fear of thus, is magnified often simply because the time-frame isn't perceived honestly due to allistic delusion projection habits. Only the more self aware humans seem honest enough to be willing to accept the world just as it is without projecting any major lenses of emotion laden subtext onto everything that occurs. Recognition and acceptance of actual real autistic & other neurodiverse human natures would be a huge step in a better direction. Many humans still don't realize quite how much biased infirmation and fiction has been preached among the medical & science establishments for too many decades about all sorts of natural human differences. Both concepts of high/low & mild/severe are misunderstood far too much to discuss meaningfully. Those labeled as “low" & “high" are typically perceiving the world in far more alike ways than is currently recognized. There actually is vast variety in the combinations of neuro-traits expressed within natural autistic biology, so it's not unusual that it is difficult to recognize. Natural personal needs can vary greatly, and so does ability to conform to allistic unreasonable social expectations. The adjectives of high or low functioning are false concepts, because these consistently lead to assumptions that presume allistic majority social standards have some kind of inherent morality above other neurotypes. Nothing could be further from actual truth. Being a majority may create literal “might" among allistics, but it does NOT make allistic presumptions “right” nor even resembling anything at all akin to wisdom. The vast majority of allistics and a significant portion of autistics have been convinced to presume that neurology is homogenous & people are super alike. Allistics typically presume many things socially as is often their nature, but autistics are usually more literal and more diverse because they perceive directly and observe directly & then trust their perceptions far more than other people. That one pattern specifically makes autistic forms much more alike. Unfortunately, most are not able to recognize another like themself quickly or at all in public because they mask so much of their real nature due to social pressures. Face it, most autistics are really very consistently ill-defined by any added adjective labels. That doesn't mean there's any devious or conformity based agendas among autistics. Most with our traits seperate themselves naturally from everyone else, and would not have any ill conception of other autistics except when it occurs at the behest of allistic demand or social conditioning.

question: What are some challenges for people with high functioning autism?
answer: Some people assume that because I can communicate verbally and don't require daily care that I am somehow incapable of struggling with other autistic traits. Many use the label “high-functioning” as a cop-out to tell me my issues are irrelevant, and that I don't need extra help or resources. But that's not true. I struggle with sensory problems. I can't wear socks with seams, I can't handle riding the bus or falling asleep without my headphones, and I constantly crave deep pressure, which makes it difficult to concentrate at times. The only thing that seperates me from a low-functioning person is that just one of these things at a time is unlikely to cause a meltdown, and I know how to speak to tell people I'm distressed. I suffer coordination issues. My sense of rhythm is nonexistent, I can't throw a ball to any noticeable degree of strength, and watching me play sports is almost tragic. But because I don't suffer as badly with these issues as another autistic person, I've just been left to deal. I am never not lost in any conversation. I have difficulty paying attention, I cannot carry a conversation, and I can't keep the thousands of rules neurotypicals enforce with much success. But because I have been forced to adapt and find social crutches (for example, hiding behind an eccentric persona and non-sequiturs,) instead of others who need more help to understand more basic rules, I have never gotten assistance with socialization or conversation. My crutches are barely sufficient, and I often find myself stressed out and bewildered by social interaction. Autistic people labelled as high-functioning suffer from many of the same issues that other autistics struggle with. Our traits don't go away because we know how to talk pretty and suppress stims. However, since we present in different/less noticeable ways, our concerns and problems are often ignored. My biggest challenge has always been a lack of resources and a lack of understanding.

question: What was your immediate feeling when you were diagnosed with Aspergers/high-functioning autism?
answer: All these answers are kind of making me jealous. I’ll give my story, but first, a bit of background. I received my diagnosis with the results of an IQ test. It seemed utterly foreign to me. In hind sight, this is likely due to the book being written for parents, from the perspective of an outsider looking in. It wasn't misinformation, but was still rather different than my own experiences. Anyways, I was fairly sure this test would give something different than neurotypical results. And that was my mindset going in. So, fast forward to the days directly after receiving my diagnosis. For a short while I was very confused. I had yet to figure out if autism was something I must fight against, or if I could turn it to my own advantage. Worse, I had this nagging question. I’ve made many decisions in my life based on the belief that my choices would make me a better person, someone I wished to be. How much of that was based off me, and how much was skewed due to autism? Was the person I strive to be not really a good goal? For a while, this was a serious problem for me. Then it clicked (and I include this part because it's far more important than how I felt immediately after my diagnosis). This autism thing isn't some force changing who I am. I’ve always been me, and I’ve always been autistic. Better yet, I enjoy being myself and it's far more important that I approve of who I am than others. As I learned more about autism, I realized just how important it was to how I’d grown (not as a label, but my characteristics and values). I learned that it is indeed something I can use to improve myself. And since then I’ve done my best to learn what I can about autism to better understand myself. I am not autism, but autism is a part of my life. Random gibberish note to further add to this mess and replicate my mental state: I always worry about these long drawn out answers. question: Do people with high functioning autism need help?
answer: Yup. Sure do. I am currently trying to find someone to help me understand a little better what to say or not to say and why. Unfortunately, I need to understand the “why” before I will remember in any meaningful way. I am usually blindsided when people get hurt by something I have said. Obviously, I know not to call people names unless I am trying to be hurtful, or point out their flaws in public, etc. I get that. But for some reason, I still end up hurting/pissing people off and I just don’t understand. Other people, NT’s will say pretty mean stuff to me, and somehow, their mean stuff is okay, but stuff I say is not, and I need help understanding the subtle differences. I believe there are professionals who help mostly younger people learn NT communication, and although I am older, I want some help too. Aspie’s really unfairly get branded as mean or jerks or even a-holes, and maybe some are. I have been and can be if I am really pissed off. But MOST of the time, I have no Earthly idea why someone gets upset over something I say. This is what is called “lack of empathy” I believe, but I am extremely empathetic. I can look at someone and see how they are likely feeling better than most NTs can. But what I cannot seem to do, is predict how someone is going to feel if I say something. I am very factually oriented, and to me, it is just a fact. Facts do not particularly bother me, even facts which would bother others. You could tell me I have gained weight, or have some grey, or whatever. I have a mirror. It will not surprise or shock me that you can see me. And I know not to say things of that nature to others. I understand that people do want to pretend no one can see things they do not want seen. Whatever I do, it is more subtle than that, so I am hoping to find someone who will communicate with me, and, in the moment, catch me doing whatever it is I do, and help me understand the hows and whys that is not okay socially. So yes. High functioning people on the spectrum do need some help. I will never be able to naturally interpret some of the unspoken social stuff. But I can learn rules and apply them. I actually do very well in short professional types of communication. But if the communication drags on, I will invariably “out” myself as insensitive. Since I have no desire to hurt people by mistake, I am hoping I can finally get a better understanding of what NTs want and need in their communication.

question: Do people with high functioning autism elope?
answer: Yes, some do. But as we are all different, others may not. There is research that supports anxiety as a problem for many autistics. We will go into fight, flight, or freeze mode when stressors or triggers occur. Flight was my main defensive in my school years. For example….there was a group of kids who would tease me until I melted down. I dont understand to this day why they enjoyed doing this. My instinct was always to run. Many, many times my mom or police were called because I left school premises. I've also found research that shows we release increased amounts of adrenaline which would explain this instinct as well as the increase in my strength and endurance. At home I would elope as well. Looking back I can tie it to meltdowns that were met with restraint. When my mom was just home she would let me just meltdown and recover. My dad would intercede the meltdown which stimulated my fight response and I would pace or throw stuff and he would restrain me. Then I would fight and elope. As I've gotten older I've learned how to better supress my instinct but it causes me a LOT of anxiety to do that. Like many other autistics, my protection response kicks in all the time. Because of so many incidences of how I was treated as a child, I've become hypersensitive to perceived pain. For instance…..if someone even seems to react as if they are not believing me my instincts kick in…..which ironically makes it more difficult to verbally convey myself and I often ended up panicking internally fighting my instincts and say something totally wrong from what It was in my head and actually cause a problem. Anyways, I would say as an adult that I dont utilize elopement as much. My home is autistic friendly so meltdowns are fewer as well (when I was working this wasnt true as I melted down almost daily when I returned from work…anything with the kids triggered me because I gave all I has to give dealing with discomforts of work.) So while I still feel the instinct to escape…I need only go as far as my rocking chair….then I rock it out :) nowadays because I dont leave home often, my main stressors typically are caused by people outside of my home (for example a big one is when one of my autistic daughters goes through something that was painful for me or I feel that there is a perceived threat of them having to) or financial. I also find as I age that I opt more for the freeze than fight or flight. this is my personal experience but I am only one “high functioning" autistic.. God, I hate that term, high functioning. Basically for a good amount of my life I was able to mostly supress my instincts and mimic neurotypical behavior In social setting as well as fight through sensory discomforts without showing response. however I'm burned out from it and having some identity issues. I guess if that's what makes me high functioning, then so be it.

question: Is there a link between high-functioning autism and insomnia?
answer: Yes, there seems to be. In one study, a majority of adults with Asperger’s were found to have sleep disorders: Compared with controls and with normative values of good sleep, AS adults had frequent insomnia. In sleep questionnaire 90% (18/20), in sleep diary 75% (15/20) and in free description 85% (17/20) displayed insomnia. There was a substantial psychiatric comorbidity with only 4 AS subject devoid of other axis-I or axis-II disorders besides AS. Also these persons displayed insomnia. It can be noted that the distribution of psychiatric diagnoses in AS subjects was virtually similar to that found among patient with chronic insomnia. Insomnia is a frequent finding in adults with Asperger syndrome In addition, there is some evidence that autistic children suffer from dysregulation of the melatonin pathways: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4478596/

question: Why are individuals with very high functioning autism spectrum disorder said to have an "invisible disability?" What are some examples?
answer: I’m 40 years old. As a child, I was initially diagnosed with a learning disability in kindergarten, and it was only as an adult that I realized that what I actually had was Asperger’s syndrome. Despite having a “learning disability” in kindergarten, I enjoyed moderate academic success throughout my education. I graduated from University with honors, I have a stable job and a family, and would appear to most people as a fairly ordinary person. However, I never was able to learn many basic motor skills that other children learned quickly. Motor delays are very common among those with A.S.D. I was 8 years old before i learned to ride a bike or tie my shoes. I never learned basic skills needed for normal athletic activities in school: I can’t dribble a ball, I can’t catch, I can’t throw, etc. While this may seem insignificant for an adult who works in an office, consider how extremely important such skills are for the development of social structures in a person’s teenage years. Frankly, if you’re a 15 year old male in the rural U.S. South and you can’t catch, throw, or dribble a ball, your life is going to be hell. Lack of social skills is also pretty limiting, and goes hand in hand with the lack of motor skills. Why is this a “hidden” disability? Because if you look like an ordinary person and are clearly intelligent, people simply don’t accept that you lack these skills, which virtually every one around you takes for granted. The social mine field of an office party or the coordination required for minor home repairs projects may be daunting to you, but no one else would ever even think about it. And good luck explaining this to others, too.

question: Can someone have low and high functioning autism?
answer: The question that needs to be asked ( or at least one of the important questions) is “High or low functioning doing what? Is it a question the ability to cognitively understand and do certain tasks or the energy/ stamina to perform enough tasks to maintain one’s independence? I have a dear autistic friend who is intelligent, intellectually capable, has been independent most of her life, but easily becomes exhausted with very basic daily living tasks. She was given the ASD Level 2 in her diagnosis at age 49 about 4 years ago…. She reached a point of “autistic burnout” and lost the mental will and physical stamina to push past the constant exhaustion. I was also diagnosed about the same time. I feel I’ve burned out too but I was 10 years older (59) when I was diagnosed. My neuropsychologist said I was “high functioning”. But, at what? Socially I can mask well.. I pushed myself to function while failing to live for anything else but “learning how to function” I think this is why there are so many suicides in our community. To answer the question… I think these “level of function” are terribly misleading and limited in usefulness and meaning… They try to oversimplify the staggering complexity of autism and how it affects autistic people.

question: Do you think "high-functioning" autism and ADHD are linked?
answer: I think they are sometimes misdiagnosed. I have a son with severe ADHD and through three different schools in the past 4 years I have had several teachers say they think it’s autism. He was literally just reevaluated for autism at the beginning of the year and his new school is already asking he be evaluated again through the school. At least this time they are asking it be done on their dime. I have severe ADD and everyone with autism thinks it’s autism. I think that when you have “atypical” behaviors you can’t control, people always assume it’s autism. I also think that a lot of coping mechanisms for ADHD look like autistic behaviors. For example, I find most “extra” sensory things like loud music, flashing lights, arrhythmic noise, etc distracting. They frustrate me because I have gotten really good at ignoring/blocking out normal stuff. So when I am presented with something I am not experienced with blocking out, I get really frustrated because I can’t think straight and usually end up with a migraine. My son tends to self stimulate a lot to meet his hyperactive needs. Both of us can be said to have Sensory Processing Disorders. Having ADHD also usually causes social problems. We cut people off and often speak before thinking. And I often tune people out when I need to focus. Plus we perseverate on topics, A LOT. I also think that people think autism is ADHD because they can look similar. My son with autism has an ADHD diagnosis. Stimulants do help a little with his stimming behaviors and impulses, but his lack of focus is an autism thing for sure. He is highly focused when motivated without medication. Which is why he rarely takes it… only when he’s in stressful situations. The problem is he doesn’t do “shared attention” well. If he isn’t personally invested in the conversation, he stops listening and returns to HIS world. But that’s not ADHD, that is social problems.

question: In your opinion, what is the greatest similarity and difference between psychopathy and (high-functioning) autism?
answer: There’s the obvious difference of psychopaths lack emotional empathy but have cognitive empathy, to varying degrees depending on their level of functioning, while high-functioning autistic people lack cognitive empathy, but can be improved, but tend to have normal to better than normal emotional empathy. While this is a difference, it’s not the largest one in my opinion. On a side note, you can have someone with autism who has other disorders which are comorbid with autism which may impact their emotional empathy. If they have these disorders but also intelligent, they may, in fact, have impaired emotional empathy but superior cognitive empathy. However, this would be a rare case and is not representaive of general differences and similarities.‘High-functioning’ is in brackets so I’m not sure if you mean exclusively high-functioning autism or you have a preference that the answers would be centered around HFA. However, if we’re allowing answers containing low-functioning autism, the largest difference, in my opinion, is how both disorders interact with intelligence. With psychopathy, no relationship between intelligence has been found. There’s a suggestion that those with psychopathy have an average IQ lower than 100 but there aren’t many studies finding this and one problem is that many psychopaths are diagnosed in prison — and there’s arguments that the criteria being used to diagnosed them has it’s problems — and a study done found that the average IQ of prison inmates was below 100, about 90. However, what can be said is that psychopaths have an average IQ within the range of average, within 1SD of 100. However, with low-functioning autism, it’s been found that even though many have below average IQs and learning disabilities, many seem to be quantiatively gifted, being superior in their non-verbal reasoning abilities than the average person. For example, since Mensa uses a culture fair test that is matrix reasoning and therefore non-verbal reasoning, someone with low-functioning autism may be able to get into Mensa. The difference I’m pointing out here is that psychopathy doesn’t seem to affect general intelligence and people tend to have relatively even cognitive profiles, as people tend to do near the mean IQ. With low-functioning autism, it seems to confer quantiative skills, at least to some, and ends up with the individual having quite an uneven cognitive profile.If we must talk specifically about high-functioning autism then, while it does seem to also confer non-verbal reasoning skills, it doesn’t seem to be to the same degree and the cognitive profile seems to be more towards being even than uneven. The main similarity that’s more specific to them, rather than just towards disorders with a neurological basis in general, is hard to decide upon. There’s many between the context and environment around the disorders, like their apparent popularity and the quanty of research behind them, but actually finding similarity in the characteristics instead is difficult, since they’re both very different. If I had to say, which I must for this question, I’ll say that certain ways they both act without their masks is similar. If a psychopathy and someone with HFA had a conversation, both would tend to be more logical than the average person, both would ignore small talk, both would want a stimulating conversation, and both would be more blunt and direct in what they say. The lack of care for other people has a similar effect in this respect as the different dopamine system for conversations and lack of awareness about other people has the effect on people with HFA.The main similarity, to me, between psychopathy and high-functioning autism, if we’re talking about the DSM-5, is that I disagree with how they are both categorised in the DSM-5. With psychopathy, that now comes under ASPD, which houses sociopathy as well. Someone can be a psychopath and be diagnosed with ASPD but someone does not need to be a psychopath to be diagnosed with ASPD. Psychopathy is a variant brain structure and so someone needs their brain to be a certain way to be a psychopath, though their pyschopathic traits can be influenced based on their childhood. My issue is that ASPD as a diagnosis doesn’t take into account the brain and so treats psychopathy, sociopathy, and general ASPD as the same thing. At least an fMRI scan can be used with a diagnosis of ASPD to find out if someone has the brain structure of a psychopath. With high-functioning autism, I disagree with how it’s been grouped into the same diganosis as low-functioning autism, coming under autism spectrum disorder. If autism was a spectrum, which I believe it’s more complex and so a spectrum is inaccurate, then there be varying levels of functioning I find fine. With psychopathy, low-functioning and high-functioning psychopaths aren’t diagnosed that way but may identify that well based upon how they function within society. With autism, I believe that there’s too large a difference between the two types of autism in how they work that there should be a larger separation than merely low-functioning and high-functioning — similar to how the ICD-10 has Asperger’s Syndrome separate from Classical autism.If we’re talking differences between people with the disorders themselves that’s a very different question. I’d say it’s how both disorders interact with their emotions. With psychopathy, they lack certain emotions but the emotions they do have are muted and generally fleeting. In general, they lead very unemotional lives and are much more logical, ignoring their emotions — boredom is perhaps the most intense emotion for them and is one they may listen to the most and so may be considered as an exception to the point stated above. With HFA, the majority of people, according to a study it was around 80%, experience alexithymia. They’re unable to identify or understand their emotions easily. People with HFA are still emotional people and so they act on their emotions as well, whether they fully understand or not. The difference here is that those with psychopathy know their emotions and what they feel but ignore them or the emotions play little roles in their lives. However, those with HFA have difficulty knowing their emotions and what they feel and their emotions play a larger role in their life.I must say, it’s a rather interesting question but quite difficult as the similarities aren’t immediately obvious while those that are may not run very deep.
