question: Are people with high functioning autism more like neurotypical people than like people with low functioning autism?
answer: There is no formal definition of “high functioning.” The DSM does have some formal definitions that describe, essentially, how much support an autistic person needs. But “high functioning” is a very vague term that can encompass both the degree and nature of autistic symptoms and the intellectual abilities of the autistic person. High intellect can go far in helping an autistic person make a successful life. For example, I know a prominent therapist who is an Aspie. She was bright enough to obtain her PhD and become a widely-known expert in her field. And because she has a good income, she has been able to create a world in which she can function well — a home and office on a parcel of land in the country, where she isn’t at risk of sensory overload. And it can compensate in many others as well, e.g., by allowing someone to figure out social conventions intellectually when an intuitive sense is absent. That said, autism is referred to as a “spectrum” for a reason — some autistic people are more neurotypical than others. For example, 1/3 of Aspies can make out facial expressions (I’m one of them, which is one reason it took me many years for me to suspect that I was autistic). Recent research has found that familial autism (as opposed to di novo mutations) is a consequence of numerous genes that confer one or another autistic trait. When someone has enough of the autistic genes, one is diagnosed as autistic. That means that there really is no fix line between autistic and neurotypical, and in fact, people with relatively few autistic traits — often the close relatives of people with autism — are said to be broader autism phenotype, and aren’t considered to have a disorder. So yes, in that regard, people with high functioning autism can be more neurotypical than others. But it isn’t the only factor.

question: If high-functioning autism was diagnosed by its advantages instead of deficits, what would that look like?
answer: It’s currently called Mild Autism Spectrum Disorder. I want to start by adding here a full listing of what the deficits of Autism are just as a reminder as it helps in explaining my answer. Autism Spectrum Disorder 299.00 (F84.0) (DSM-V, American Psychiatric Association, 2013; https://www.autismspectrum.org.au/sites/default/files/Vic/The%20DSM%205%20Autism%20Spectrum%20Disorder%20criteria.pdf Diagnostic CriteriaA. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, as manifested by the following, currently or by history : 1. Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, ranging, for example, from abnormal social approach and failure of normal back-and-forth conversation; to reduced sharing of interests, emotions, or affect; to failure to initiate or respond to social interactions. 2. Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviours used for social interaction, ranging, for example, from poorly integrated verbal and nonverbal communication; to abnormalities in eye contact and body language or deficits in understanding and use of gestures; to a total lack of facial expressions and nonverbal communication. 3. Deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships, ranging, for example, from difficulties adjusting behaviour to suit various social contexts; to difficulties in sharing imaginative play or in making friends; to absence of interest in peers. B. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities, as manifested by at least two of the following, currently or by history: 1. Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech (e.g., simple motor stereotypies, lining up toys or flipping objects, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases). 2. Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, or ritualised patterns or verbal nonverbal behaviour (e.g., extreme distress at small changes, difficulties with transitions, rigid thinking patterns, greeting rituals, need to take same route or eat food every day). 3. Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus (e.g, strong attachment to or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessively circumscribed or perseverative interest). 4. Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interests in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement).There is no authoritative listing of benefits as far as I know. That does not necessarily mean that there are none, but and this is a rather large but, it also means that it is not necessarily the case that one could be created. That is not a list that would capture the same population as the criteria for deficits Many are keen to list things like honesty, meticulousness, eye for details, routine and punctuality, to name a few as ‘clear’ examples of benefits. Alas we just are not all like that and quite many who do not have the deficits are like that. I for example am rather honest and punctual I guess but very disorganised, I do not have an eye for detail, I have difficulty with planning and and I talk a lot and sometimes to much and too loudly such that I’m complained about. ADHD a common comorbity with ASD really strips of the image of the quiet careful detail oriented hyper-focused computer programmer which appear to be the stereotype of Autistics. Essentially if the above criteria was turned around and each element was instead used as a positive somehow then I’m afraid it would simply become too deluded and it would effectively diagnose most everyone as Autistic. I therefore agree with Nicholas Stone in this that this criteria is diagnosing deficits that determine whether and to what extent individuals need assistance in daily lives. I understand that many want or need to see Autism in a more positive light and that is fine but loosing job after job or not being able to find a partner or not managing to gain friends, and other similar basic elements of the lives that others have, because you can’t maintain the expected eye contact or just don’t know how to appropriately reply to greetings, small talk, a direct order from your manager are not benefits. People do need help for this and most seek it very hard.

question: Why is Asperger’s an ableist way to say high-functioning autism?

The trouble is, using function labels often leads to people who are capable of working and caring for themselves for the most part not receiving help that they actually need with the areas where they’re struggling due to their condition. Just as an example, I’m autistic. Until becoming disabled by ME/CFS (unrelated), I was able to work full time, pay my bills, cook and care for myself… but… I filed my taxes late. Every year. I couldn’t make myself do them on time. I wound up with a pile of late fees and had to pay off my taxes on a payment plan. And this is something absolutely would not have happened if I were not autistic, because it was the result of executive dysfunction. Dishes would pile up in the sink into a mountain. Dusting? That’s a laugh. Persons who are autistic usually need extra help with something. A little help, or a lot, but something. And people have this idea that ‘high functioning’ autism just looks like a person who has sloppy social skills and acts like Mr. Spock. They assume that person doesn’t need help or any special accommodations, and won’t be prone to melt downs or shut downs, or struggle with any basic tasks. question: As a female with high functioning autism, what are some general symptoms that males don’t have?
answer: First of all, I’d like to categorically state my hatred of the term “high-functioning”. It implies I don’t need help, that I’m not really disabled, and so on. Yes, I can wipe my own bottom; that doesn’t mean I’m not really autistic or that I have nothing in common with those who can’t. I highly dislike the term “low-functioning”, too, since it overlooks skills and talents in people with obvious autism, or who need a lot of help—talents and skills that people like me, who live semi-independently, may not have. Dividing us up into functioning labels by whether we seem autistic, or live independently, or talk out loud, is worse than useless. We are all autistic, and autism simply has a very wide range of expression. To the actual question: I really haven’t encountered any symptoms in females that don’t exist in males. There are some general tendencies, mostly due to the different ways children are raised based on whether they’re assigned female or assigned male at birth. Females (and assigned females) are encouraged to communicate more and to talk more, so we often end up able to talk more easily. That doesn’t necessarily mean we can communicate more easily; some of us learn to just talk whether or not it has any meaning, so we learn to match our words to the conversation rather than expressing what we are thinking and feeling. Females are also socially allowed to be more shy, so many of us will become quiet and learn to mask our symptoms by simply being the “good little girl” who doesn’t make waves. Social anxiety and a desire to “fit in” are very common. There are also artifacts of diagnosis. Females with autism tend to have more severe autism, but this is because autism in females is underdiagnosed; only when our autism is extremely obvious can we be sure of a diagnosis. As a result, we are more often diagnosed later in life, and those of us who are diagnosed as children often have the sort of extreme, stereotypical autism that is obvious even to the casual observer. But I need to strongly emphasize that these are general trends, not hard-and-fast rules. I did learn to talk more easily than assigned-males, but primarily because my mother read to me constantly when I was a baby and I figured out language and reading just about simultaneously. And yes, I have the problem of just saying things that fit into the conversation (not while writing, thankfully). But I’ve never been a “good little girl”; in fact, I’ve always been outspoken and assertive, with no significant social anxiety, despite my introverted personality. My diagnosis in my early 20s doesn’t come from female stereotyping, but from medical neglect in my childhood (my mother, an occupational therapist, knew I was autistic, and did not get me evaluated). Autistic people are individuals. I have reason to believe that we are even less defined by gender than most people are—I for one identify as androgynous—because we don’t soak up gender norms as easily. That doesn’t mean that the way we’re treated based on perceived gender isn’t different, but it does mean we internalize less of it. And that means that, when social influences are damped down by autism, we tend to stick closer to our genetic tendencies than most people do, independent of what others say we should be. (That’s also why masking can be so painful for autistic girls: They learn to pretend, but they never quite learn to change into the people society says they should be. It’s hard to pretend to be someone you’re not.)

question: Why is high functioning autism diagnosed in people that function like the average population?
answer: Autism is a spectrum condition, which means it affects each individual differently. Those more high functioning have learned to function that way from their upbringing and environmental experiences. It hasn't come naturally like it would to a neurotypical. Some of us on the autism spectrum can learn to pass as neurotypical, but we never lose our autism and it is hard work to reach that point. The problem with high functioning autism is that we can mask it which makes us appear to be coping fine from the outside, but we are still consuming huge amounts of mental energy from trying to accommodate to society. Because we can learn to cope, people assume we are capable of competing with neurotypicals and we often feel pressured to keep up. We might be able to keep going for a short while and seem fine, but we end up getting burned out from being so forceful and engaging so heavily in what is unnatural to us. We feel conflicted between our autism and social expectation and if we pass of as too social it may be that we are fighting against our autism and what's natural to us and we can end up losing touch with our inner self because of it. This can and often is seriously unhealthy long-term and can affect an individual in many ways both physically and mentally. No matter how high or low functioning someone autistic is, they are still autistic and will have some level of social difficulty, otherwise autism wouldn't be a diagnosable condition.

question: Do all people with Asperger Syndrome have high-functioning autism, but all people with high-functioning autism don't necessarily have Asperger’s Syndrome?
answer: Ian MacKinnell provided an excellent answer! I see so many people misunderstand that Aspergers = high IQ and/or high functioning = no significant disability. Not true at all. Aspergers= no communication or intellectual impairment and high functioning = no intellectual impairment. The only thing I would add is that Aspergers indicates no communication impairment, not necessarily just lack of a speech delay. Autism has the follwing criteria under DSM IV which is missing in Asperger’s: Qualitative impairments in communication as manifested by at least one of the following:Delay in, or total lack of, the development of spoken language (not accompanied by an attempt to compensate through alternative modes of communication such as gestures or mime)In individuals with adequate speech, marked impairment in the ability to initiate or sustain a conversation with othersStereotyped and repetitive use of language or idiosyncratic languageLack of varied, spontaneous make-believe play or social imitative play appropriate to developmental levelAnd as Ian pointed out… If you meet that criteria for Autism… you do not have Aspergers. My son was an articulate “little professor” who was reading at 3. He has a high (Mensa level) IQ, never received any IEP academic services because he often had the highest scores in the district for standardized testing and still has classic autism because he has “marked impairment in the ability to initiate or sustain a conversation with others” He has a lot of issues with figurative/abstract language,(at 9 he was still learning how to use “yes” and “no” appropriately), verbal expression (writing/speaking to meet the needs and expectations of the audience) and a slight impairment in processing oral speech . He frequently has communication breakdowns because he does not clarify, will not ask for clarification on things he doesn’t understand, and rarely asks follow up questions or attempts to keep a conversation going. He got a 730 verbal score on his SAT (99th percentile), but only a 4 on the essay portion (roughly the bottom 10%) because his essay showed no understanding or analysis of the topic and lacked clear organization. (He also had some idiosyncratic language and lack of varied, spontaneous make-believe play or social imitative play appropriate to developmental level). However, when he was diagnosed at 9, the therapist actually asked if I would like him to have the Asperger’s diagnosis instead, given his intelligence and the social/educational stigmas surrounding a autism diagnosis. He was given the Asperger’s label because his school did not allow children with autism (we have a public school for Developmental and Behavioral disabilities). Two years later, when I chose to enroll him in online education, he was rediagnosed as having “autism” so that his SLP could address his communication issues. He is labeled as “high functioning” due to his lack of intellectual impairment. His intellectual prowess and ability to learn new skills quickly in therapy do make him function “typically” in the school setting… but at 17 he still needs me to check and make sure his clothes are on correctly each day, that his homework is complete with appropriate (though not necessarily correct) answers and manage plans for anything in the future (i.e. which classes he needs to graduate, does he have clean clothes for school tomorrow, what time he needs to leave the house to arrive on time for an appointment). Although he started taking online college classes at 14 and started getting full scholarship offers at 16, he still does not have the executive functioning or communication skills necessary to go to an actual college when he graduates this year and likely could not independently successfully interview for a job commensurate with his intellectual ability. However I am often told he is a very responsible big brother, well mannered and mature by people who do not know how much micromanaging and planning goes into creating his social scripts, agendas and routines. My ex-husband has Asperger’s but never qualified for gifted classes, however he rarely has “communication breakdowns”. He failed two grades because he never did homework and would not do any reading and had to take Algebra 3 times because he slept through classes. He dropped out of college twice and did not have a “career” until his late thirties (working in factories, grocery stores and restaurants at entry level). At 40 he still needs someone else to manage his business affairs and handle all his finances for him because he is so forgetful and bad at prioritizing. When I met him at 21 he had literally only read 2 books in his whole life… not because he had problems reading but because he was highly unmotivated and would rather fail a book report than read (he reads a lot now). He has never lived independently. He often says our son is “smarter” and will probably be more successful because he has better coping strategies and support systems in place (my ex-husband was diagnosed in his thirties when my son was diagnosed). I for one am really glad that the DSM V got rid of these labels, because I think they just perpetuated stereotypes and division in the autism community. Autism with/without language impairment, with/without intellectual impairment, included related co-morbidity and a corresponding severity level is the best way to categorize in my opinion. Having Aspergers does not mean you manifest milder traits or are intellectually superior to those with High functioning autism… it means that you do not have any impairment in language use/ability, and developed communication skills normally. Oddly I often see people on these boards say that they have Aspergers, but then go on to say they have significant issues with expressive or receptive language. According to the DMS 4 a communication or language impairment means you have Autism, not Aspergers.

question: Which is worse, high functioning or low functioning autism?
answer: I would say that high-functioning autism is actually “worse” if you are talking about the challenges in life. Somebody who is low-functioning may not be able to speak or socially interact, but when it comes to living, it is sometimes much easier to be on the lower end of the spectrum for several reasons:Low-functioning autism is much closer to the stereotype of a person with “disabilities”, so people will take pity on them and be less critical of their actions, and offer the types of social and economic support that those on the higher end do not getThose with low-functioning autism are less likely to know they are “different”, so they do not feel the same social pressures that those with higher-functioning autism feelSince those with low-functioning autism are generally more laid back in terms of life goals, they are less likely to burn out if their work is allocated to something menial, such as shelving books at a library — by contrast, people with high-functioning autism are far more energised, and far more determined to do work with a higher stimulus; the problem, is that either they are legally barred from such work, and/or the employer does not want to hire them, due to their socialising skills not meeting “cultural norms”Many countries, such as Canada and the United States, give employers financial benefits for hiring somebody with low-functioning autism, because they are so “apparent” — no such motive is given for those with higher-functioning autism, who are expected to keep up with the general population, despite severe legal restrictions on where those with the condition can workTruth be told, at the end of the day, the only main difference between somebody with low-functioning and high-functioning autism, is that the latter has difficulty speaking, and may experience sound delay, whereas the other does not. It is not uncommon for children who start off as low-functioning autists early in life to become a socially interactive high-functioning autist — the latter being known as Asperger’s Syndrome by many of those in the community. There is also some debate as to whether there is an intellectual difference — at one time, low-functioning autism was believed to be limited to those with an intellectual quotient of 70–100, whereas those with high-functioning autism had an intellectual quotient of 100 (or higher), but this may be flawed, since results may be a matter of interpreting information differently, as opposed to inferior intelligence. Studies have also shown that once a person with autism reached an intellectual quotient that was above 120 they became six times more likely to commit suicide. [1] Why is that? For many generations, the consensus had been that those with any medical diagnosis were “dangerous” and so should be generally kept out of the public work sector — this effectively meant subjecting such people to a lifetime of unemployment and destitution. When newer research showed how those with such a condition were far more likely to be victimised than to perpetrate — the latter often being followed only by the former — the new mindset was to say that people with a medical diagnosis were “incompetent”. In other words, they were no longer classified as “dangerous”, but would still be relegated to the same limited career settings. As it turned out, even obtaining a college or university degree did not change the circumstances for the overwhelming majority of these people, and some research suggests that, if anything, it made their employability worse, because in addition to racking up post-secondary debt, they were now too “overqualified” for many jobs, yet the field they now had a degree in would simply turn them away as soon as their autistic traits became apparent. Rarely, some of these graduates would find work, and it was mostly limited to sorting out books at a local library, despite having an advanced degree in library research. One mother of a twenty-six-year-old autistic son by the name of Maria Scheiner said in 2019, in regards to the limited support and opportunities even graduates have: “The problem is, most vocational placement services are in low-skill jobs. They’re behind in helping individuals with autism get introduced to professional, entry-level positions. If you get out of college with a science degree, your dream job is not coming out and working in food service, or stocking shelves for minimum wage.” [2] In the end, those who do graduate from college or university — more than a third — have an 85% unemployment rate… one that is approximately the same as those who never attended. Suffice it to say, the situation that many people on the spectrum face is little different than in the old days, when one’s gender or skin colour could be grounds for rejection by an employer. Those who do find a stable job that pays more than minimum wage have to simply win two marathons in order to win one gold medal. Here is a list of jobs that people with autism are typically disqualified from having, regardless of their individual personalities:They cannot serve in the militaryThey cannot work in jobs involving physical “security”They cannot work in any sort of emergency servicesThey cannot work in healthcareI remember applying for the first category in my youth, only to be turned away after months of interviews, aptitude tests, character references, and medical exams because they carried out some sort of background check from the local police that revealed I had been diagnosed with Asperger’s Syndrome at thirteen. Since the Canadian military was not legally allowed to reject me outright on the basis of my diagnosis alone, they proceeded to tell me that I would have to pay $600–700 out of my own pocket to meet a military-approved speech therapist before I could continue any further. At eighteen years old, I did not even have $700 in my pocket — never mind the fact that nobody else was being made to go through this process — and because I am a far better writer than speaker, I knew there was a high chance that I would spend nearly a thousand dollars, fail the session, and be left in financial debt, in addition to a legal disqualification. Mind you, until they saw my diagnosis in a background check, they raised absolutely no concerns about my “communication” skills. A few months later, I even got a letter from the military expressing their “sadness” that I had become disinterested, and that they would now be closing my file. What a joke. The types of jobs I mentioned above, are also the ones that young people trying to move from minimum-wage to career-level employment seek, especially if they have not yet graduated from college or university. In the end, many of those who are high-functioning simply “burn out” and end up committing suicide — I have known quite a few in my life who did this, some of whom were in their twenties, while others ended up becoming chronically hospitalised because the discriminatory practices of rejecting those on the spectrum for a “socially normal” candidate drove many into resignation. One friend of mine who later killed himself had a previous suicide attempt that was largely a result of being left at the bottom of the economic barrel. Even years after the fact, this incident showed up on every background check of his — making it even harder than previously to find stable employment — and he had to pay monthly to see a “specialist” regarding his suicidality, which included taking electro-shock therapy, and he was not allowed to move out of any home address he was staying in without notifying the police, or he risked being sent back for another term at an institution. Seriously, what kind of life were the authorities leaving him at that point? It started off with him hacking two of his fingers with an ax during a mental breakdown, followed by his death less than three years later. And because we are regarded as “normal” on the outside, despite all these legal limitations that are imposed, we are also looked down on as “lazy” and “entitled” if we find ourselves unable to make it through the employment sector as easily as everybody else, who are not restricted in their career choices on a diagnostic term alone. As a result of these limitations, most people with Asperger’s, and even those with low-functioning autism begin taking a career plan in the art field more seriously — writing, painting, drawing, inventions, filmmaking, game programming etc.. This field not only allows for independent work — something that those on the spectrum typically do far better than your average worker — it also allows them to express themselves in ways that cannot be done in the private sector, and it has the benefit of allowing those who still find traditional employment to make a side income, and therefore earn more than minimum wage. It is therefore a stereotype that everybody with autism automatically prefers to do artistic work for a living. They get into this field because it is one of the few areas that legal regulations do not prohibit, it does not require approval from an employer, and it allows them to have a work setting that at least permits them to express themselves while also earning long-term income that will go much further than the types of part-time work that the traditional employment sector usually provides. Many of those with low-functioning autism also get into the artistic field, but because they are more likely to be employed by an employer, due to receiving government grants that those with high-functioning autism do not qualify for, they are less likely to turn a serious hobby into a career choice. In conclusion, while those with “low-functioning autism” may be more likely to stand out in a crowd, and thus be perceived as “worse”, the easier time they get in finding employment, as well as their presence more likely to garner sympathy than apprehension more than makes up for it when it comes to independent living.Footnotes[1] Autism combined with high IQ increases risk of suicidal thoughts[2] Most college grads with autism can't find jobs. This group is fixing that.

question: Do people with high-functioning autism engage in any repetitive movements? If yes, then such as?
answer: I don’t use functioning labels to describe myself because they aren’t accurate and my ability to function changes on a daily basis, but I’m probably what you would refer to as such most of the time. I have limited verbal communication skills—I rely on scripted communication, but I can still talk most of the time—and I’ll never be independent. I can’t succeed in proper employment, but I can work my way around the internet, and I’m of pretty average intelligence. I excel in written communication skills because I rely on them to get my message across when I can’t do it verbally. Now we’ve got that out of the way… Yes, I do engage in repetitive movements. It’s called stimming—self-stimulatory behaviour, and we all do it to some degree. Like fidgeting with your pen, or fiddling with a bit of blu-tac—both of which are signs of ‘stimming’. However, autistic people usually engage in more obvious signs of repetitive movements that are more of a necessity than something they do to cure boredom/for fun. My favourite repetitive movements are rocking back and forth and flapping my hands. It feels so good. I’m not very good at identifying my emotions, but if I’m being totally honest, I don’t always need one. Sometimes I just do it for fun. I also squeeze my hands into fists a lot, especially when I’m thinking about something (I’ve done it a lot in answering this question). I also click my fingers a lot, which is kinda obvious as it’s kinda noisy. Some less-obvious stims are shaking my leg. I do that often, and it might not be obvious to people who don’t know what it is, but damn does it annoy people who does. My friends think I do it to piss them off, no matter how many times I tell them I can’t help it and don’t notice until they point it out. My mum’s the same, though, as far as telling me off is concerned. I’m also constantly fiddling with my glasses, even though they don’t need adjusting nearly as much as I adjust them. If I’m nervous, it’s every two seconds, touching the bridge of them to pull them up. I try and stop myself because I know it looks unprofessional and makes how I’m feeling obvious, which prompts people to ask how I’m feeling (hate it), but it’s just one of those things I can’t help. I know this isn’t necessarily the question you asked, but I also have a lot of verbal stims—or vocal stims, more accurately. Something I do a lot is say ‘Mow’ like a cat would. I can’t help it. Seriously, it’s like a tic, an urge that starts in my throat and doesn’t disappear until I say it. I also make a clicking sound with my tongue. That’s something I only started recently, and though repetitive, I’m sure it’s more a habit than anything. I have been watching a lot of Shane Dawson lately. EDIT: I’ve just sat down at my desk to do some work, and started making this noise at the back of my throat. Completely forgot about that one. I also rub my thumb and fingers together, and rub fabric against my lips to test the feel of it, and if it’s nice, I’ll keep doing it. In truth, there are so many things that I do that could be considered stimming that I’ll never remember to write them all here, but these are just a few of the ones I can remember off the top of my hear.

question: Can you self-diagnose high-functioning autism with an online test?
answer: Short answer - a definite maybe! Long answer … I discovered my autism after many years of “searching” and a combination of the right circumstances… It really was the perfect storm for me and I will always be grateful things came together as they did or I may have never known.. There are so many variable in the diagnostic process that there really is no “ANSWER” to this question. By nature, people with autism tend to be very honest, thorough, truth-seeking people.. so those I have known who discovered they are on the spectrum are very careful about jumping to a false conclusion.. This is almost in spite of the fact that we also tend to “KNOW” we have found our answer to a life time of questions about circumstances in our lives.. Literally all the dots connect and we realize we have found something profound! For me.. I was afraid of coming to the wrong conclusion.. but not in the way you are probably thinking. I had searched so long and hard for this answer I was afraid something that felt so right, was wrong.. that I would have to go back to that state of searching and wondering what was wrong with me. Let me be very clear. Being in this state of UNKNOWN - is a type of living hell. The stress, confusion, mixed messages from everyone… conflicts of feelings… and the total feeling of being absolutely alone in this world is horrible. It is why the suicide rate is almost 1 in 3…. ONE IN THREE people on the spectrum will attempt suicide. You can count me in this group too! A diagnosis for an adult is a extremely significant finding. We are tired of living life the way we have been living it.. At some level, we have known we are not being true to our nature.. but can never define why. We are close to autistic burn-out where we literally become tired of the fatigue of living… Suicidal Ideation starts to become a more active thought… Things start to fall apart because we can not keep up with this act of being neurotypical… yet we don’t understand still what is happening in our lives.. Everyone has a story of how they check into Asperger Syndrome or ASD or autism…. Many have taken that on line test as I did. It gives you a VERY questionable result because of your bias. It is very hard to be truly neutral in your answers - if your test results are borderline.. it probably has little affect. For me, it said “ VERY LIKELY NEURODIVERSE” - but still I just thought “Hummm?”. It was not what really convinced me.. That happened when I was on the forums and reading blogs.. and these people were talking in my language about my experiences that I had never shared or even understood.. But they knew… exactly! That is when I realized I found my key… but it took about 9 or 10 months after diagnosis, till I finally could say without doubt -” I am autistic” The problem with these tests is that many questions require you to know what your autistic traits or tendencies are… I was in denial or so used to masking these traits that I did not have a clue. My dear aspie friend told me I would be shocked what I will find the next 2 years.. and this has been so true.. At the time I took the test I did not think I had any stims… or perseverations… dependency on routines… hyper focusing, special interests, let alone things like alexithymia, echolalia or echologia.. etc… My friend would laugh at me and say “ You are so autistic! “… and I would just wonder what she was talking about… My best friend’s wife, A teacher for 30+ years.. told me after my diagnosis.. “I’ve known you are on the spectrum for a LONG time”.. So you see.. we have to go through a process of “learning to be autistic - again”. This ties into trying to diagnose the autism.. whether self-diagnosis or a professional diagnosis. Because we have hidden our traits so completely that all but the best clinicians can miss the tell-tale signs. Sadly, some adults who desperately NEED to know they are autistic… can get a false negative diagnosis. This is why the self tests for Autism, are very general indications of whether a person is or is not autistic. Plus there are other disorders that may have similar traits… An individual can self-diagnose, but it takes a long time and a lot of research to come to this conclusion.. There is usually a stage where we “know” BUT still harbor doubts… It is too important of an issue to get wrong because finding you are autistic, is a life changing moment in a extremely profound way.

question: How did you learn that you had high-functioning autism?
answer: Growing up, I was often being brought into paediatrician appointments about my development, and my parents were often warned that although nothing could be diagnosed so young, they should not get their hopes up for a normally functioning and well-adjusted child. The term ‘autism’ was thrown about very often as I grew up, so I learnt to accommodate the idea that I may not be the same as everybody else. The first time I really felt different from my peers was when I was six. My father is a very intelligent man, and he enjoyed history greatly. One morning, he and I watched a documentary (I struggled to watch cartoons and much preferred calm and quiet documentaries, which helped to expand my vocabulary) about dinosaurs. Immediately, I was awed. After re-watching the same episode with me for months, my father bought me a book about dinosaurs, mega fauna and early humans, and my first special interest was established. Even today, pre-history is a special interest of mine. I always took my book into school. Every day, I would sit on a bench just outside of my classroom, and read the chapters while I ate my lunch. When I finished the book, I just read it all over again. My peers had already dubbed me as a bad playmate - I dominated conversations with information about dinosaurs, and couldn’t handle normal imaginative play - so I was never once bothered. That was, until a new staff member came to my school. Despite the fact that I cannot remember her name, I do remember how much distress she sent me into. She perceived me as a child who was being rejected by her peers, rather than a child who was enjoying her solitude, and confiscated my dinosaur book in an attempt to encourage me to speak with the other children. I was still not a good playmate, so between being kicked from games, I spent my lunch breaks alone. Eventually, I received my book back, and I returned back to my routine. In class, I was also different. During primary school, lots of work is done in groups, and I was never able to work as a team. I either did the whole groups’ work for them, or I did not participate. My ‘fidgeting’ (stimming) caused irritation, and a few meltdowns had disrupted lessons. By December, my teachers had had quite enough of me. After months of struggling to socialise with the other children, my teachers called my parents into the school to inform them of my difficulties. They sent me to a speech and language therapist, who could not diagnose me as they were unable to figure out whether I was being deliberately evasive of the tasks laid out before me, or if I genuinely ‘needed’ a diagnosis. The thing about primary school, is that many children are too young to notice social differences between them and their peers. If explained to me now, I can observe my alternate behaviours, but previously I was unable to do so. All I knew was that no one wanted to play with me, and I wanted to play with no one. (In Year Six, I gained my second special interest - the Korean music industry. Again, that interest is still present.) And so life moved on. It wasn’t until secondary school that I felt more separate. Attending an all-girls secondary school is competitive, and I struggled to manage under so much pressure. In Year Eight, I went on my first residential trip with my school. We drove from England to Germany, and spent three days in Aachen, enjoying the Christmas market. We were given plenty of freedom, and I migrated into a large group of around ten girls, and together we toured the shops. As we browsed, I came upon a store selling fossils. From a kind German man, I purchased an Ammonite fossil. One of the girls, (we’ll call her Rachel) noticed my excitement. My ‘fidgeting’ was more rapid, I could barely contain my excitement, and I was constantly looking at the bag that I had it in, to check that it was there. She had smiled, and asked me, “What did you buy?” So I told her about ammonites, and I didn’t stop telling her for the good part of an hour, when she bounced off to another girl to chat about Snapchat. Later, when I returned to my room in the youth hostel we were staying in, I heard another girl from the group complaining about me to my other roommates. But Rachel stuck up for me, and told her that she thought it was interesting. I got diagnosed with autism last academic year. After everything intensified at school, I went for a final speech and language therapist appointment, and received my diagnosis. I was in the grey area between being high-functioning and not being high-functioning, but I thought that my life was pretty much over. You see, girls in my class make jokes about autism. If someone says something not particularly intelligent, they say, “You’re autistic.” and tell each other to go to a special school because of it. Not a single soul in my entire year group knows, because I am already an outsider. The last thing I want to do, is make myself more of someone who is only able to perch on the edge of friendships. I suppose that I knew it all along, it was just a case of being told.

question: Can toddlers with high functioning autism/aspergers have speech delays?
answer: My suspicion is yes, but only insofar as everyone is different and all ASD people I know present in different ways. At least, different to NTs, I suspect the same root to all the differences that I have seen. I digress, I have little scientific backing here (and the other people who have answered this have a much better scientific handle on things than I), the answer is in all likelihood a yes. Like others though, I wonder at the reasoning for the question. I interpret simply as a diagnostic question as in "my toddler has speech delays, does this mean they are HFA/Aspie?" but others suggest differently. Without knowing that I'm uncertain what answer, beyond a simple 'yes/no' you were looking for. All the ASD people I know are lovely people, some experienced speech delays, some did not. My own child with confirmed ASD had a huge speech delay and is still working on bridging that, but they will and by the time they are my age I suspect no one will ever know they had any such delay. My eldest, who may have ASD but it is unconfirmed, seemed to display no speech delays. I, unconfirmed ASD, may or may not have had speech delays depending on who in my family you speak to and at what time (my mother and father have both claimed I showed speech delays and told me that I never had speech delays as a child at different points, so I don't know). In that sense, speech delays may be connected to HFA/Aspie traits or may not be. All people, and ASD people are people, are different. If your toddler has speech delays they may have ASD, but if they don't that doesn't mean they don't. Or, if they are already diagnosed, they may show speech delay or they may not. Indeed, if they have speech delays they may not have anything connected with ASD. It may just be, in the law of averages, they are developing at a different pace. In short, don't worry about it. I know of no 35 year olds who still crawl because they learned to walk later than their peers or who still soil themselves because they toilet trained later than their peers. In that sense, anyone with speech delays is likely to be indistinguishable from others as they grow up. Not to disrespect or ignore mutism, but that strikes me as less a speech *delay* so much as a mode of communication in its own right.

question: My new flat-mate said she can't work because she has Asperger's Syndrome. She said she has difficulty interacting with people at a workplace. Why can't some people with Asperger's Syndrome (or high-functioning Autism) work?
answer: I once knew a chap, at the time we were friends, but because of this and a number of other reasons, we’re no longer speaking. He and I both received diagnoses for Asperger’s (which still existed then) - mine being marginally more severe - but we responded in different ways. He went into the testing almost determined to get diagnosed with something. I went in wondering what would happen, and whether the results would give me any answers to questions I’ve had about myself since I was a toddler. As it turned out, I was relieved that I now understood why I felt the way I did. The diagnosis helped me get in touch with myself a little better - understand my limitations, and my strengths. Just to have something logical “This happens because of X” was, in many ways, the beginning of the rest of my life. I explained it to my boss, assured him that I didn’t require anything but just wanted them to be aware - I asked for one small allowance - a tiny thing that they could do, which would make my life easier; a desk with a wall behind it, and which faced the door. They accommodated me, and said that they would do anything else they could to help me, and in fifteen years I have never taken up the offer him up on his offer. I became a better person, and I continue that struggle even now. I am proud of my achievements, both because they’re good achievements and because I fought for every single one. I am driven to make new ones, and to never stop challenging myself. That’s not how he reacted. He got what he “wanted” - his first act upon receiving the diagnosis was to research how much free stuff and special exemptions he could get himself. He didn’t want to know what was wrong and find ways to help himself; he wanted something he could use to turn his problems into everybody else’s problems. He fought for a disabled badge, parking spaces, free laptops, benefits, exam extensions, free transport, special treatment at work, and got them all. He took his Asperger’s and wielded it against the world, using it as a mallet to bash at anybody who ever expected him to take any kind of responsibility for his life. He was very open and honest that he was doing this. He openly mocked the system that looked out for him, because he was going to make “the man” work for him. He didn’t need a disabled badge; he simply realised that with it he could park where he wanted and save himself the effort of walking or using public transport. He didn’t need the free laptop - he already had a better one than what they were offering; but he fought tooth and nail for the free laptop, paid for by the taxpayer, sold it, and spent the money taking himself and his friends to the Download Festival. He didn’t need exam extensions; he was just lazy and didn’t want to study. He didn’t need special treatment at work; he resented going to work because he considered himself “too intelligent to abide the daily grind so beloved of other, average people” (his verbatim words) and because his colleagues were “knobs” - he found a way to leverage his Asperger’s to make his life easier. He objected to shift work, but was asked to attend to help cover a night shift for somebody who was critically ill (they had been hit by a car) in hospital, refused to do it, threatened to take his manager to HR because he was “discriminating against somebody because they’re disabled”, and then promptly resigned. “But, my Asperger’s!” became a mantra. He didn’t get another job - he searched for a little while but couldn’t understand why, as a man with no experience and no qualifications, he had to start in an entry level position. He considered himself a genius and thought they he should begin at the top. After evading “get a job” pressure from me and from other friends, he took out a large student loan because he said he wanted to get a degree in engineering (in actuality, he just wanted to move to Brighton to get drunk and have sex) so off he went, and he attended one class, told his professor that she was an imbecile and that the classes were “beneath him”, and never went back. He squandered the loan money on beer and kitting out his pathetic rusty Ford Fiesta with a floor-shaking sound system. Then, it was discovered that he never attended University, and the Student Loan Company started proceedings to get the money back - which he’d spent. “But, my Asperger’s, I have a disability!” he said at the age of 29, and his father paid off all his debt. Now his father is almost bankrupt and his mother is descending into depression. Meanwhile, he sleeps in until midday, watches Star Trek, and yells at his mother when she asks him to contribute some money towards the rent - which he still doesn’t, aged 32. (His mother is still friends with mine, so there is some news throughput - but not direct.) It was an utter disgrace - and far from being ashamed, or feeling guilty - he was overjoyed - he’d found a way to beat the system, and to get more in exchange for less. I worked - HARD - to get what I’ve got today. I’m not rich, but I’m comfortable. Every single posession (with the exception of the obvious things; Christmas and Birthday gifts, etc) I have, I bought with my own money which I earned through hard work, or I crafted by my own hand. I have never made my diagnosis somebody else’s problem, and I have never abused it to get an easier life. As a matter of fact, I have made a conscious effort to under-exploit it, and voluntarily take on the additional stress that it causes me. I am almost certainly dealing with more than I have to; but I would rather do that. Following my stroke, all sorts of benefits, freebies, additional time off work, and special treatment was offered; and I refused them all because I didn’t need them and I didn’t want them. I took the time I needed to recover, squared everything with my doctor, and I went back to work. It took me a little time to get back up to “full strength” but I did, and it was worth the effort. I wanted to get there on my own. I have always had to fight for everything, and I’ve got so good at fighting that people don’t realise that I’m fighting at all. I am the living embodiment of the famous Swan Metaphor; gliding gracefully over the water, but propelled by desperate flailing under the surface. I’m terrified of making a telephone call, but I present to a group of 80 executives, and I get applause. I’m terrified of travelling, but my company has an office in Switzerland, so I go to the airport, fly to Geneva, take a train and then a funicular and walk up a mountain to get to work, and everybody asks me how I’m doing and I tell them I’m doing just fine. Then I go and hide in the toilet for half an hour and cry. I’m terrible at interpreting body language and tone of voice. I’m crappy at conversation and I die a thousand deaths a minute in any social gathering. I’m bad at showing empathy. I’m obsessed with routines, and the prospect of change - any change - scares me to death. I speak the way I write, and people think I’m arrogant because of it - they don’t realise that it’s because I actually write out every sentence I’m about to say inside my head, edit it a thousand times, play it back in my head to make sure I’m getting the words and the tone correct, and then read it from my mental “script” - because the thought of speaking “off the cuff” paralyses me with fear. I am overly sensitive to light, noise, and heat, but I share an office with someone who keeps playing with the lights, banging and crashing around, and won’t open the window because they’re too cold. I’m physically clumsy - both as a result of the Asperger’s and worsened by a cerebellar stroke in 2015 - and have poor hand-eye coordination. Sometimes all the sensation just disappears in my right leg and is replaced with stabbing pains that run all the way up to my neck. I have sleep apnea, and on the rare occasions I can sleep, I have nightmares. Life isn’t easy. Especially the parts of life that look easy. But I shut up and I get on with it. And, when I realise just how well I’m doing, it makes it all a little easier. I feel like I can do it - because I am doing it, and if I can do what I’m doing now, maybe I can do a little more. I’m not saying people with Asperger’s shouldn’t seek help where they need it. Not for one moment. But I am very aware that, as with all disabilities, there is a number of people who will try to milk it for whatever they can - at the expense of the genuine people who really do need support and understanding. I don’t need help, I need an absence of hindrance. That’s a subtle but significant difference which many people don’t seem to appreciate.
comment_answer: “An absence of hindrance” would be a true gift to many of us, whether “neuro-typical” or not. Kudos to you for choosing to define yourself on your own terms, and for sharing your wonderful writing.

question: What are the causes of high functioning autism?
answer: Nothing. We in the autistic community have long been advocating for people to stop using the term “high functioning”. First of all, it’s derogatory towards those you wouldn’t consider “high functioning”, because the existence of high functioning autism suggests other autism is “low functioning”. Whether or not an autistic person is labeled high or low functioning is entirely up to the assessment others have of our abilities just based on the way we look. It also very much reads as “here are the Valuable Autistics that can be like us, and here are those… other guys..”. The language treats those you’d deem as “low functioning” as inherently less valuable. It’s also simply not accurate. Many children labelled ‘low functioning’ autistics are actually just not having necessary needs met, and could perform much better with them, so to imply that it’s something inherently wrong with them when that’s often not the case just isn’t fair. When we say autism is a spectrum, we don’t mean there is a high end and a low end. We mean that there are a number of symptoms people might have more or less of, and that those symptoms are on a bunch of little spectrums. If you’d like to hear other perspectives on the matter, there are arguments that can sum it up far better than I can. Here is one such article;https://www.psycom.net/autism-single-spectrum-mythTo answer the question of what causes autism period, our current best answer is genetics.

question: If you have high functioning autism, did you have trouble with hand writing?
answer: The question:”If you have high functioning autism, did you have trouble with hand writing?”Yes. My handwriting is considered illegible and like a child's. I recently wrote a note to my son’s teacher and the teacher thought my 14-year-old son had written it and was trying to make it look like an adults handwriting. Neither the teacher not my son could make out what I had written. When I was in school I kept getting complaints about my handwriting and lack of neatness. I took a course in Anatomy in high school and the teacher had only multiple answer questions. I got the highest mark in a class of 30 students. When he showed us the results and grading, he asked me if I knew why he had only had multiple answer questions. I replied that he was making it easier to go over everyones answers. He said, yes that was part of it but it was mainly so he didn't need to read my handwriting. I hate filling in forms. I can't fit my answers into the little boxes and they always look as if a child filled it in. I also have difficulty keeping rhythm with everyone else. For example, when I do exercise classes like Body Pump or similar I can't manage to keep in rhythm with everyone else. Even after multiple sessions I'm still falling out of rhythm. I'm either too fast or too slow and I keep losing track and remembering what to do next etc. Also when I walk with others I find it difficult to match their speed, I would usually walk faster than others. People complain that I walk too fast despite me having tried to match their speed. I have a terrible sense of direction. If I enter a shop then when I exit I often can't make out which direction I came from and which direction I'm heading. Even in quite familiar setting it can take me a while to reorient if I have been away for a while. My self organisation and planning is terrible. I keep under and overestimating time needed. Managers soon learn that they need to assist me in that more than others. This is all related to mild Developmental co-ordination disorder (dyspraxia)[1] which is frequently comorbid with Autism.Footnotes[1] Dyspraxia (developmental co-ordination disorder) in adults

question: How do people with high functioning autism/Asperger's syndrome cope with workplace politics?
answer: Sadly I don’t think I ever coped. My method pre diagnosis I may add-was I would suddenly quit much to everyone’s confusion, or try my best to be fired to remove the situation if they did not let me quit. It was draining enough to engage with clients and colleagues while doing the work and dealing with meetings interruptions -the second workplace drama or politics was added to the mix, I was done for. Watercooler talk: I could never understand why people don’t just do the job they were supposed to do and why they sat around talking versus solving the problem they complained about ( black and white thinking ) On that same note, I Balked at the concept of going to dinners at the bosses house or any additional social activities outside hours I did not get paid for. To me, it was illogical to spend my limited energy on things that had nothing to do with performing the actual job. Especially because it needed to be conserved for tasks I could do well. This lack of understanding really hurt me later , and it took me a long time to realize playing politics was often more important to bosses than doing the job well. Any workplace drama directed at me was extra confusing. I would react poorly to the sensory confusion (example crying in bathrooms and later meltdowns at home.) I didn’t even know why or what I was feeling, just “bad.” It always confused me as to why too, my coworkers would constantly tell me to “stop working” or go home when I was hyper focused, or say outright “hey you’re making me look bad just go home.” All I could see is I got a poor reaction from somebody and they don’t like Something so I’m “bad.” Jealously and competition wasnt wasn’t something I could process as I never felt this way. When faced with all this extra stuff, My brain internalized it as another clue I was on the wrong track and should leave or try another role entirely. Sometimes the hyper focus can be a threat, complicating work relationships even more. I found many insecure ambitious climbers took that as an assumption that you’re a “company person who drank the koolaid” and made it their mission to convince me it was wrong and being me down to their standards. Not at all, i just couldn’t connect office politics to success at work or how I could even affect others that way in a work context. Those things were separate and totally unrelated In my mind. I just wanted to do my work uninterrupted. Sadly , nobody needed to try very hard to get rid of me if they saw a nuisance, because the second politics took over or a bad apple was hired, Work would become so painfully intrusive and unbearable I would just leave. There was no coping.

Also I began to care less about my coworkers. I just imagine that it’s just a game, like a video game. Missions need to be completed, rewards to gain and try to level up. I try to less involve with people. I constantly remind myself that my coworkers are not my friends. There are a few things I do.

question: What is the problem with the term high functioning autism?
answer: High-functioning suggests that an autistic person needs minimal support, and can behave within neurotypical standards. They may be able to live alone, have stable finances, or seem as though they don’t need accommodations at all. You will get the odd person that uses it due to internalized ableism, feeling a need to be superior, not knowing the controversy, personal reasons, or simply refusing to believe it is a problem at all. However. High-functioning is ridiculous (sorry not sorry to the “HFA” reading this!) because not even a neurotypical person ‘functions’ well throughout their entire life. Autistic people are not robots: We do not feel the same 24/7, we do not act the same 24/7, and we do not function the same 24/7. Diagnosing someone with HFA is like labeling a person's gender based on what their outfit is for the day. It simply does not work like that and is rude to assume. Sometimes, I sit up straight, look others in the eye, and buy things at the store with confidence. I behave accordingly around my family and at times experience no pain from sensory input. Other times, I hear every noise around me to the extreme, suppress tears, speak way too loud and shut off conversations. I cry and try my hardest not to scream, sometimes even hitting myself or behaving like a toddler. So, you tell me, am I high-functioning or low-functioning? Here are two results from a spectrum quotient. Which person is high-functioning, and which is low functioning? Figured it out? Actually, It’s the same person, three months apart. Autistic traits fluctuate. They change, they can be masked, and they can be exposed depending on the environment and stimuli. I guarantee every autistic person you’ve spoken to has at one point behaved in a way that qualifies them as low-functioning or vise-versa. Autistic people need different levels of support at different times. We feel different things at different times. We are energetic in some places while exhausted in others because we are human too and do not fit a simple line graph or “functioning” category.
comment_answer: Thank you! Great answer, and couldn't agree more. It is unfortunate there are still people with autism (or their partners) indisting they do have HFA and insisting it isn't wrong, or harmful or offensive….

question: Why is high functioning autism hard to diagnose in adults?
answer: Hello Laura! It can never be overstated that every autistic person is unique. So our experiences of being autistic are as unique as snow flakes. This is not true of those who are not autistic. Their neurological systems are very similar and so is their life experiences. It is part of the reason they have such a hard time understanding what autism is. Because our autistic life experience is unique for each of us, so is our story of how we discovered our autism or how someone else discovered it for us. How we lived with autism, without knowing why our lives were different. This pre-diagnosis period was affected by so many things from family dynamics, our own personality, our abilities to manage our autistic traits or cope with what we could not manage. I had a father who was very narcissistic. He gas lighted his family, was unfaithful, and always blamed us for his woes. That got my life off a terrible start as an autistic child. Because I believed I was to blame for my father’s discontent. Then I started to see this “discontent” in everything I did to the point I felt cursed. Life was a punishment. A debt to pay. The level of shame, and even self-hatred was something I don’t know how I endured. I felt that alienation so common with people who are autistic. I struggled in school… at the age of 11 I was diagnosed ADHD, Dyslexic, and brain-damaged from hypoxia at birth. This was about 1969.. so only “classic” cases of autism were being discovered. I had already learned to mask by that age and “be a good boy”. This meant suppressing all I felt emotionally and physically: Especially life’s pain. It all came at a cost. By chance at age 20 I had a doctor order an Upper GI exam that turned up 11 years of stomach ulcers. That was also my first suicide attempt when realized the level of stress I had denied existed in my life. I looked for answers. I was told it was depression but that never answered this question.. this reason why I felt so distant from everyone else. By this time, I did not understand that I as masking. Better stated I was not acknowledging I was masking because I still felt there was something wrong with me and it was necessary to not be that person. The more the years went on, the more I accepted who I was as a masked person. That question of why…. became a more distant voice as the years rolled on… Then about 6 years ago… that voice was given a glimpse of reason. A coworker was talking about her aspie son and it all resonated… a connection I was baffled to feel so deeply. I even asked her if it was possible I could have Asperger Syndrome. But I disregarded it thinking I as not like him as a child. True I was not the same, but no two autistic people are the same… It was not until circumstances at work forced me to realize that a communication breakdown that threatened my employment was liked to this feeling of having Asperger Syndrome, that I finally started to research what it truly was. There, at the age 59, the voice had found it’s answer. A life time of confusion, fear, misunderstanding and self-avoidance (masking) would suddenly lose its force. It was a rebirth - My first real chance to live and discover who I am. I was extremely fortunate to have a clinician who was able to see in me what, at that time, I could barely see in myself. I was still in denial of my true self. I did not know my behaviors could be seen by others.. My social and communication awkwardness. My dependence on repetition and so on… About a year later, my friend’s wife who had taught autistic children for over 25 years shocked me when we talked about my diagnosis and said “ I’ve know this for a LONG time”. She has known me since I was in my teens though she was not a teacher then. Especially those of us who are older, autism was not even suspected so part of our coping was to mask. Many of us thought masking was just part of who we were yet did not understand why we did. In a sense we were hiding from ourselves. Some did find it was autism by exhausting other possibilities. Some were told by others it was a possibility. Some never do find their reason. More kids are diagnosed now because it has become a social issue people are aware of. But still, kids slip through undetected for various reasons. It is a shame because we need to know ourselves and be ourselves to have full productive lives as autistic people.

I used weed as a coping mechanism to fit in. It still helps me from having “Aspie Meltdowns”. My diagnosis has however made my life make sense. I understand me now.

question: Are people in the autism community offended by the terms "high functioning autism" and "low functioning autism"?
answer: Some are, and some aren’t. Just as there are varieties of ability to function as neurotypical people, there are varieties of abilities to function amongst autistic people. I personally think levels are better than functioning labels. I know quite a few level 1 neurotypical people. They are reasonably capable of dealing with folks on the autism spectrum without major social gaffs, and mostly seem to cope provided they are given a little support and assistance. There are level 2 neurotypical people. They need a bit more support as they blunder around completely oblivious that others have different sensitivities. However, level 3 neurotypical people are seriously unable to function in the presence of autistic people, and should be kept separated from them and given constant assistance at all times, as at this level of functional difficulty they present a risk of harm to themselves and others. In contrast, the labels don’t really tell us much, do they? Some folks find difficulty in tying their own shoelaces, some struggle with wiping their backsides, whilst others appear incapable of using their own name when asking a question.

question: How do adult people who have high functioning autism see others?
answer: Usually with eyes. Most often in colour. 😉🙃 Seriously, I'm on the spectrum. The reason I so often ask to clarify questions is because I simply cannot answer them. Too broad, too vague, too subject to interpretation. I'm not blaming you. Or anyone. I get it. This is how you think. Just don't be offended by an occasional joke, or the endless stream of, “Could you clarify this, please?” And take pity on other AUTISTICS in your life. Especially, the intelligent ones. B/c so often when we ask to clarify or say we don't understand, we are thought to be assholes,. Or “they're taking a piss”. Or “they just don't want to do it”. If some asks you to be more specific, please help them. Because this is how we think: How do I see others? The most obvious jumps to mind, “with eyes”. I know to eliminate that possibility: some people might struggle. How do I see others physically? Like, how do I see their faces? (See prosopagnosia). How do I see them because it's assumed I have poor eye contact (I don't), so how do I manage to capture anything but their shoes? How do I see them in terms of sensory difficulties (is, too bright, too loud, too colourful)? Or how do I see them as a group? As in me vs them? Just as a bunch individuals; some friendly, some hateful, some indifferent. How do I expect them to treat me? I have no idea. question: Is Asperger's the same thing as high functioning autism? If not, what is it exactly?
answer: Autism is and always has been a very difficult sort of thing to describe. It covers a wide range of behaviors and characteristics, some of them viewable as deficits and some of them just differences (and some even viewable as enhancements). “High-functioning autism” isn’t a real classification in the clinical sense, but there are many people who have autism and are able to function and thrive within society, and they are often referred to as “high-functioning.” Asperger Syndrome (AS) is no longer used as a diagnosis, as of the DSM-V (some other measures still include it as a subdivision of autism). What was called AS is now grouped under autism. It was thought of by many as a particular kind of “high-functioning” autism, mainly because of the lack of verbal and intellectual deficit associated with it, although people who were diagnosed with it certainly varied in their ability to interact with the world. A significant number of people who were given the diagnosis have taken it on as part of their identity. Some call themselves “aspies.” If you look around online, you’ll come across numerous communities of “aspies.” Others dislike this and see it as self-segregation. There is also controversy, both within and outside of the community, about whether to consider it a “disorder” of any kind at all rather than just a different way of thinking/interacting with the world. The world of autism can be difficult to navigate because of the seemingly vague definitions around everything. The diagnosis covers such a range of characteristics that it can seem like a catchall for anyone who is a bit (or more than a bit) quirky. I’ve struggled with it as a parent. My son was initially called PDD-NOS (pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified), which sounds more like a meaningless jumble of words than a disorder. He has big verbal deficits but no real intellectual ones, and some big strengths, so he would be considered “high-functioning” but not AS. Now he is simply categorized as having “autism.” One of the reasons for grouping everything under the wide banner of “autism” is that the lines between AS, PDD-NOS, and other subclassifications are very fuzzy. It starts to feel a bit artificial or contrived to put people in neat little boxes. A few points one way or another on an IQ test or a verbal assessment don’t make much of a difference when everything else is the same. When it comes to AS, there are a few key items. One is a very specific and detailed focus on specific topics. I met an Aspergers kid who knew every station on every line of the NYC subway, for instance. He otherwise knew nothing about trains or how they worked, and he wasn’t particularly interested in them. He just devoured information about the routes and stations. Importantly, in AS, this is not coupled with verbal or intellectual impairment. People with AS can come across as extremely intelligent, even genius level, when they are talking about their area of interest. They usually have distinct ways of speaking and moving, sometimes coming across as clumsy. They often aren’t particularly attuned to other people’s reactions and won’t realize it when they’re committing a social faux pas or going on too long about a topic.

question: How can high functioning autism/ Asperger’s syndrome be distinguished from introversion?
answer: How can high functioning Asperger syndrome be distinguished from introversion? The first few autistic people I knew personally happened to be extroverts. It was very easy to tell them apart from introverts. It actually made it harder to recognise myself as having Asperger’s syndrome, because I am not an extrovert — I didn’t “look like them”. Some people with Asperger’s withdraw from social interaction. Some engage with other people quite happily, but come across as “odd” or “quirky”. Asperger’s is not a dislike of social interaction, it is (among other things) a difficulty in understanding non-autistic people. For some autistic people, the way to manage this difficulty is to withdraw from non-autistic people. Others, however, will engage with non-autistic people but find them difficult to understand and perhaps find the other people withdrawing from them. It takes a professional to decide whether a person is autistic. Autism consists of a variety of impairments in social interaction (at least, impairments in social interaction with non-autistic people) — not a preference for solitude — and also a range of repetitive or restricted behaviours and interests (including possibly sensory sensitivity, “stimming”, special interests, a preference for routine or sameness). Most introverts do not have these characteristics, only autistic introverts ... and autistic extroverts … have these characteristics.

question: How do people with high-functioning autism repair themselves after a social event?

During this quiet down-time my system will "normalize" itself again. It goes through a process of resetting itself. Honesty there isn't much I can do to speed up the process… it just takes my mind and body however long it takes to "cool down" to a normal "operating temperature" again. I have noticed with my son and partner, they both gravitate toward "watching things" to help during the normalizing phase, rather then game playing. Like movies, YouTube, or TV shows on the iPad or iPhone. (A smaller hand held device seems to work better then a TV or computer.) I don't know if it's because they are male, or if it's just a coincidence that they have the same sorts of things they use to normalize with. I just know if I'm overstimulated watching something will just keep me in a hightend state and not allow me to relax. Then slowly I will be able to start adding activities to my day again. It's basically waiting for the burn of over-stimulation to wear off. Depending on the stress involved it may take only a few hours or… when it's really bad, I come away from the event and begin to feel like I've been beaten all over with a baseball bat. I ach worse then any flu I've ever had and EVERYTHING hurts to move it… when this happens it may take up to a week to recover… a week of laying on my bed in the dark just zoning out until my body and mind begin to work properly again. It feels so powerless… there doesn't seem to be anything I can do to speed up the process… it's sort of like being sick… I can take measure to help myself heal (drinking plenty of fluids, getting enough rest) but I cannot MAKE myself heal any faster. So for me it's just a waiting game. I'm sorry I don't have anything more helpful. It feels really bad to be at the mercy of the stress of one's environment… it feels unfair.

question: Can someone with high-functioning autism get autism benefits?
answer: There is no HFA. We are autistic. Mildly autistic. Secondly, there are no autism “specific” benefits, at least in the US. However, there is assistance for people who qualify with a disability if your doctor believes you can benefit. For adults, who need work, you can contact your state’s vocational rehabilitation office. Each state has offices in cities near you or near the biggest city in your area. They can assist with job training or retraining, career testing, resume writing and interview preparation and sometimes, job placement. If you are not able to work, you may be able to receive general assistance (rent), medicaid and food stamps, but some places have welfare-to-work programs. you will have to provide proof you are not able to work or you were working and lost your job through no fault of your own. If you were fired, they may penalize you and you may not get assistance or get a reduction in assistance (this happened to me). You may qualify for SSI (social security income), so you can contact your local Social Security Administration office for more information. There may be local organizations that assist autistic people with things like finding an apartment, furniture and clothing, etc. The best thing to do is to call 2–1–1 or 3–1–1 depending on your state and find out if there are agencies who have resources available, but you’d be competing with people who are not autistic as well as people who are more severely afflicted than you are. GRASP is an organization that may have information on where you can go to find help, but I only know them as a support group. For people between 0 and 21 years of age, there is assistance via early intervention, public schools, and so on. However there is a process that starts with a parent or guardian reaching out to a pediatrician, teacher or the department of education for an evaluation and it sounds you are well past that. Good luck!
