question: What is it like for you to have high-functioning autism or Asperger's? How would you explain to a neurotypical that high-function doesn't always mean "normal"?
answer: I know there are many people who are not autistic ( neurotypical) who want to better understand autism. Its in the news, on television, in books and movies. You know someone who knows someone, or you have a child, or sibling… a brother or sister, parent or grand parent… coworker, classmate.. and so on. You want to know why they do what they do. What they are thinking. What does it feel like? You think of something they’ve done, or have not done. Something they say or do not say. And either out of curiosity or love and concern you want to know. You want to relate. Maybe help some how… or at the very least better understand… “What is Autism?”. If I ask you from my autistic perspective… What is it like to be like you? Why do you do what you do, or not do. Say what you say or not say? How would you respond? What could you say that would tell me what it is like being neurotypical? Could you do it in a hour? A day? Knowing you would take a long time - and in that time I would only know bits and pieces of your life. I would not know how you experience life or what it is to be YOU. We are all very unique. We each have our own life experience. The more our life experiences are the same, the easier it is to understand how each other thinks, feels and so on. But less we are alike, we can only image each other’s experience. What you experience as “normal” is not what I experience as “normal” - If you are a very skilled musician - I can only “imagine” what your experience is being a musician. Music is a normal part of your life but not mine. Autistic and non-autitstic people are very different because our nervous system (NS) is different than your NS. This is why many autistic people have heightened senses, the ability to focus all our attention to a task and hold it there for very long periods of time. These differences changes how we think, how we feel physically and emotionally. And when you changes so many fundamental experiences of life, what is normal to our autistic life experience will become very hard for you to understand because it is so different from your normal “neurotypical” life experiences. But do understand this - We are living OUR normal like you are living yours. Our experience are not “abnormal’ - they are only different normal life experiences. The best you may ever understand is that we experience the world differently than you. To make this even more complicated - every autistic person has a different nervous system. People who are not autistic have a NS that are almost identical. So, every autistic person experiences their world a bit different than others who are autistic. Here is a good article that shows three different types of ways autistic people think. Research Shows Three Distinct Thought Styles In People With Autism The differences are often subtle in comparison ( autistic vs not autistic) but have a profound affect on how each one experiences life. When you add different intensity of traits, genetic factors, nurture and so on… it creates differences that even autistic people cannot not imagine. But there is a common “core” to each neurotype - and these commonalities are what bind us in our neurological “tribe”. I as with 4 adult, college educated “aspies” about a month ago for a weekend. It was there for the FIRST time in my life I experienced socializing with others that shared my normal autistic perspective of life. We ALL felt it and I think it was a first for us all as well! Trying to understand Autistic people by understanding autistic traits is like trying to understand music by listening to individual notes. Every person is a unique song. We may not be YOUR NORMAL type of music, but we are still beautiful songs. If you take the time to listen… not compare our song with your song, then you will start to understand Autism the only way possible. That is person by person!

question: How can someone with high functioning autism be better in conversation?
answer: I do better with the conversations with myself, but that’s not your question. Conversations with others is a necessity and sometimes I do well on my end and sometimes I don’t. The thing I suppose helps most in having better conversations is “active listening”. I’m working on that but there’s plenty of room for improvement. Here’s an example where I actually did better than usual at listening. I was subbing for an elementary school P.E. coach's sidekick. The first half of class was walking laps outside around the baseball diamond. While the coach watched sitting on an upside down bucket with his speaker phone, I walked the laps. I thought my walking might inspire the kids to walk or run and not hide behind a tree to get out of the exercise. With my gray hair, the kids think I'm the same age as Old Father Time. A 1st-grade girl came up and took my hand. Unlike me, the girl didn't have a problem starting and carrying on a conversation. We had an unspoken deal. She did most of the talking and I did most of the listening. She had a good reason for wanting to talk. Her Grandpa passed away just 2 days earlier. It wasn't so much sadness I heard in her voice but curiosity. Perhaps it was her first encounter with the death of a loved one. He had strokes and as she put it, "he just died". She didn't even know he was in the hospital until after he had passed away. She had observed that her Grandma still had his clothes. Other than telling her I was sorry about his passing, I just listened. She just needed someone to talk to and that someone that day was me. She didn't want to go off and play in the playground as the other kids did when finishing their last lap. She couldn't hold up as long as some of the other kids because of her asthma. It does get in her way sometimes. It is routine for her to use the asthma inhaler as soon as she gets home from school. She said pretty much her whole family had asthma. I told her I had Asperger's. The word wasn't familiar to her and I didn't go into details about it. She said she can't run as much as her friends without wearing out. I told her sometimes I am not up to being with people. She said sometimes asthma gets her out of doing stuff she doesn't want to do such as strenuous activities. I told her Asperger's sometimes gets me out of going to parties.

question: How is it that some people can be diagnosed with high-functioning autism but interact with others and display no visible signs of autism to the casual observer?
answer: A lifetime of practice (it's called autistic masking). This masking does come at a VERY high life cost for most of us. Most of us learned to “live” normally, but in near-constant misery as adults with depression, chronic fatigue, and bouts of extreme exhaustion. Acceptance and success in the neurotypical world we all live in often comes at a rather obscene price. There may be mild outward signs too, but just not the kind most people would recognize. Often, the person might be accused of having a temper/“short fuse" or be rather uncomfortable around loud or crowded places. Frequent migraines are often common too. Many of us “middle-age” folks that grew up unaware of our ASD will eventually build up a long-term condition known as “autistic burnout” or “autistic regression” after living too many years of unknowingly increasingly masking. The eventual crash known as Autistic Burnout seems to involuntarily (instantaneously) erase many of our masking abilities that we didn't even “know” we were engaging in. It can happen out of the blue, and result in EXTREME confusion and “brain fog". Recovery can be very slow if autistic burnout gets that far, as it requires learning to deprioritize most masking behaviors and also learning how to be one's true self for the first time ever at a relatively old age. Brilliant careers are often cut rather painfully short by this phenomenon. Masking skills can return in time, but are rarely at the high level they were before. *** Children with ASD can often begin masking/socially camouflaging their own real needs and preferences long before they're even potty trained. Anyone ever knowing that they have ASD is not required! Learning to avoid invalidating and negative consequences as kids can begin to occur even at an insanely young age. Many born with with ASD learn from personal observation far better than they are able to communicate with others (even from their youngest age). Intellectual ability on the high end just further increases one's ability to mask. Being told by parents and other adults that their natural instinctive behaviors are “bad behavior”and that they must “behave" properly around others or be punished may sink in very early. That unknowingly triggers more and more masking and efforts trying to “cope” with unnatural demands at any cost. Masking sensitivity to sensory stimulation(real physical pain/agony/anxiety) is much harder, but may be learned and can be done the same way by many of us. It also can be learned long before puberty.

question: What sports would a child with high functioning autism excel in?
answer: Team sports could be difficult or stressful. Lots of highly intense and irrational social impulses tend to surround them, and socialization can be straining or challenging even if you aren't busy trying to do well athletically and strategically at the same event. Additionally team sports mean there is a lot more going on and often an audience cheering and such. It could lead to sensory overload easier as well, and if your sensory progcessing can handle it it may still feel like chaos if you aren't used to it. Solo sports, or team sports done in turns, are a safer bet. And then there are things that arguably aren't sports because you don't necessarily compete but which can provide the same level of exercise and a comparable level of socialization anyway. Personally I like miniature golf, bowling, skating, walking, swimming, and jumping on a trampoline. I can enjoy such things as football, baseball, and basketball but it requires a group of people I feel comfortable with and who don't take it too seriously or talk a lot of smack. I'm not a very competitive person and prefer that it stay friendly.

question: How prevalent is synesthesia in individuals with high-functioning autism?
answer: I will address this question in three parts:Prevalence of ASD and synesthesia comorbidity.Prevalence of Asperger syndrome (now called high-functioning autism) and synesthesia comorbidity.Addressing the limitations of the study.Prevalence of PDD-NOS (now called high-functioning autism) and synesthesia comorbidity (speculative, due to missing data).ASD and synesthesia comorbidity Synesthesia occurs in 4% of the population[1], and ASD has a prevalence of 1%[2]. If there were no correlation between the two conditions, then synesthesia and ASD should co-occur in only 4 in 10,000 people (0.04%)[3].Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All rights reserved. However, a study by Simon Baron-Cohen from 2013 indicated that synesthesia occurs in 18.9% of people with ASD (31 out of 164 participant), which is almost three times greater than in controls (7.22%, 7 out of 97 participants)[4]. As such, the prevalence of ASD and synesthesia comorbidity is not the expected 0.04%, but 0.189% (18.9% × 1%).Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All rights reserved. This makes the prevalence of ASD and synesthesia comorbidity 7.75 times greater than expected.Limitations of the study Note however that the control group is not actually matched to the ASD group, as can be seen in Table 1 below; there are 164 ASD participants compared to only 97 participants in the control group, and the gender ratio between the two groups is not matched either. Also, the cut-off point for the AQ for controls was 25, while the cut-off for the people with ASD was 26. As such, there are several factors that potentially skewing the results. That said, the estimate for the rate of synesthesia in ASD is unlikely to be an overestimate, and could even be an underestimate. The authors of the study state:Because they [the participants with ASD] reported not having synesthesia, we conservatively considered them to be non-synesthetes. These participants with autism declared that they did not have synesthesia because they said they were uncertain whether their experiences counted.[5]Asperger syndrome and synesthesia comorbidity The prevalence of Asperger syndrome is 3 per 10,000, or 0.0003%[6]. As such, the expected comorbidity rate of Asperger syndrome and synesthesia among the general population is 1.2 × 10−7−7% (0.0003% × 4%).Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All rights reserved. However, a later study from 2013 based on Simon Baron-Cohen’s research indicated an occurrence rate of synesthesia among people with Asperger syndrome of 23.8% (based on 21 participants)[7]. This puts the prevalence of Asperger syndrome and synesthesia comorbidity at 7.14 × 10−7−7% (23.8% × 0.0003%).Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All rights reserved. This makes the prevalence of Asperger syndrome and synesthesia comorbidity 5.92 times greater than expected.Asperger syndrome and synesthesia comorbidity Furthermore, the study above indicated that synesthesia occurs in 1.1% of a general population of museum goers. As museum goers tend to be people of a particular sort who spend their time in museums rather other recreational activities, so this proves an interesting study in its own right in terms of a possible correlation between synesthesia and the group of people that tend to frequent museums. The finding of 1.1% is not necessarily contextualized in the same manner as the prevalence of synesthesia among the general population found by Julia Simner’s figure of 4%. Either way, the expected prevalence of Asperger syndrome and synesthesia comorbidity among museum goers according to this study is —assuming the occurrence of Asperger syndrome among museum goers is at the same ratio as the occurrence of Asperger syndrome among the general population—3.3 × 10−8−8% (0.0003% × 1.1%).Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All rights reserved. Given this assumption, the comorbidity of Asperger syndrome and synesthesia among the general population is, as stated earlier, 7.14 × 10−7−7% (23.8% × 0.0003%).Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All rights reserved. This makes the prevalence of Asperger syndrome and synesthesia comorbidity based on museum goers as the general population 23.7 times greater than expected.PDD-NOS and synesthesia comorbidity (speculative) Also, the prevalence of PDD-NOS (now superseded by high-functioning autism or ASD, but should be counted as high-functioning autism) is much higher than Asperger syndrome, at 20 in 10,000 people (0.002%)[8]. Assuming the occurrence of synesthesia among people with PDD-NOS to be the same as with Asperger syndrome (this is not a scientifically valid assumption, but is purely meant to illustrate the possible different comorbidity rates based on the prevalence of the autistic disorders), we get a prevalence of PDD-NOS and synesthesia comorbidity of 8 × 10−7−7% (0.002% × 4%).Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All rights reserved. This is compared to the actual prevalence of PDD-NOS and synesthesia comorbidity among the general population which based on the same occurrence as with Asperger syndrome is 4.76 × 10−6−6% (23.8% × 0.002%).Image: copyright © 2017 Martin Silvertant. All rights reserved. This makes the prevalence of ASD and synesthesia comorbidity 7.75 times greater than expected. This makes the prevalence of Asperger syndrome and synesthesia comorbidity 5.95 times greater than expected.Read about the connection between ASD and synesthesia here:Natalie Engelbrecht’s answer to What has the research demonstrated in terms of the connection between synesthesia and ASD?For more information on (high-functioning) ASD, have a look at: Embrace AutismA blog about quantitative- and qualitative research on autism, by Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht ND RP and Eva Silvertant.Footnotes[1] Synaesthesia: The Prevalence of Atypical Cross-Modal Experiences[2] Prevalence of autism-spectrum conditions: UK school-based population study[3] Is synaesthesia more common in autism?[4] Is synaesthesia more common in autism?[5] Is synaesthesia more common in autism?[6] Epidemiology of autistic disorder and other pervasive developmental disorders.[7] https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259457031_Is_synesthesia_more_common_in_patients_with_Asperger_syndrome[8] Epidemiology of Pervasive Developmental Disorders

question: Why do some people with ASD get offended by the term high-functioning autism?
answer: There are multiple reasons for this, but I’m only going to go over a few.It’s an incredibly ill-defined category. Even in the research literature, there’s no agreement on what it actually means[1]. Do you use an IQ cutoff? A functional skills cutoff? What should the cutoff be, anyway? “You know it when you see it?” What do you do with someone who has a genius-level IQ but no functional skills to speak of? How about if they can’t speak or follow an IQ test, but produce stunning works of art[2] or bestselling literature[3]? What if they can’t complete a verbal IQ test, but ace a non-verbal one[4]?It tends to have the function of segregating autistics into two categories: the ones we consider people, and the ones we don’t. The former may get a good deal out of this, and may even insist on it (particularly if they’re a fan of throwing ‘low-functioning’ people under the bus to get better consideration from the general population[5]….sorry, but I’m uncharitable). Of course, now any profound difficulties they have, up to virtually starving themselves to death[6], will be ignored, or chalked up to laziness/a ‘bad’ character, since they’re “high functioning.” The latter may benefit by having easier access to services that they may or may not need…at the expense of being considered fully human. Any strengths they have, and which could serve them in building a meaningful and useful life[7], will be pathologized (‘idiot savant’) or simply ignored altogether, as nothing good or ‘functioning’ can be expected of them. People will defend the uselessness of people labeled low-functioning to the death, citing “Kanner autism”…ignoring those ‘low-functioning’ children originally diagnosed by Kanner[8] who had very good outcomes as adults with no interventions to speak of (and no, Donald T. is not the only one). By the way, those that were institutionalized, and thus written off, did not turn out nearly so well. Ability does not emerge unless you let it (and no, talent is not rare[9]).If you don’t know them closely and personally, you don’t know their strengths and difficulties. You don’t get to label them, implicitly dismissing either one or the other. Knock it off, and check how they identify first.Footnotes[1] Are you high or low functioning? question: Can people distinguish people who have autism or high-functioning autism?
answer: People with autism are often described as being “high functioning” or “low functioning”. But you won’t find these diagnoses in the manual. The difference between high and low functioning autism can, in many cases, be based on the personal perspectives of a practitioner or teacher. The terms high and low functioning are simply confusing. Is a person high functioning if he's verbal and bright but has such severe sensory challenges that he can't stay in school or hold down a job? Is a person low functioning if they can't use spoken language but is a successful visual artist? I hesitate to use the words “low” and “high”. Low can discourage or overlook a so-called low functioning’s potential talents or strengths; whereas, high can overlook a high-functioning’s struggles. Some have told me that they are surprised I have high-functioning because I behave so “normal”. If they could see me when I’m alone, or feel what’s going on inside of me, they wouldn’t be so surprised. In answer to your question, I guess those who are or appear to be closer to "normal" are considered to be high functioning. Thus, for example:High functioning people use spoken language to communicate. Low functioning people are more likely to use technology or picture boards and may have limited or no spoken language.High functioning people are more likely to be able to manage the expectations of a classroom setting. They have a better handle on spoken language and an awareness of the expectations of others.Low functioning people generally look and sound very different from their typical peers. In other words, their disability is more visual to the casual observer. High functioning people are more likely to appear typical (until some event or conversation makes their autism more obvious).Low functioning people are less likely to be included in typical classes or activities and are more likely to be in a special education classroom. High functioning people are more likely to be included -- with or without support -- in general classrooms and out-of-school programs.All of these distinctions, however, are by no means absolute. That's because autistic people behave differently in different situations -- and every individual has a range of strengths and challenges.

question: Do people with high-functioning autism have a special interest in the feel of different surfaces?
answer: Honestly, it's up to the individual. A theory that is had on sensory issues is that in some way in the individual's past they experienced something that they, we, considered either good or bad and then the internal rule was that we either wanted or hated that thing. A great example for me is sweet pickles. My entire life I had only had dill pickles. So when someone gave me a pickle at the age of 11 without telling me it was sweet, my response was visceral, including gagging and vomiting. My expectation was a sour flavor but I received a sickly sweet sensation instead. It wasn't until I was 31 that I was able to eat and somewhat enjoy a sweet pickle. Even then, I still dislike them. I know that example isn't so much a surface thing, but I hope that conveys the idea. The reality is that unless there is an allergy, most sensory issues can be addressed through ABA (Applied Behavior Analysis) and some expose therapy. Building up tolerances is important, but must be done in the right way and take into consideration the physical and mental needs of the individual. It is the rarest case where anything good happens for the sensory equivalent of being thrown in the deep end. Conversely, we need pushback. Allow any child or adult to get his or her way all the time will result in bad things. Giving an autistic individual a set schedule with no variation or external stimulus all the time to prevent melt downs is just as detrimental in the long term of functionality. Even if it's a little change here or there, there needs to be challenges made so that he or she can grow and be independent. This applies to all ability levels.

question: Are there any conditions that are sometimes misdiagnosed as Asperger's (high functioning autism)?
answer: There are conditions that can be misdiagnosed as Asperger's Disorder. There are actually several groups of mental conditions that can appear similar to one another. Asperger's Disorder in the past, has been primarily understood as non severe Autism. After working with many children with the Asperger's diagnosis, I felt it was an unfair distinction. Asperger's Disorder was diagnosed in children and adolescents who demonstrated serious social deficits, including problems with communication, lack of understanding of social milieu, and cognitive, developmental and emotional difficulties. Often, emotional difficulties seemed more pronounced in children with Asperger's, due to the perception of defiance and or oppositional behaviors. Over the years, certainly, there have been many children diagnosed inaccurately, due to confusion over the fine distinctions of Asperger's Disorder. The inclusion of Asperger's into the Autism Spectrum made sense too me as a practitioner. I believe the criteria are more clearly spelled out for the diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder. I'm even beginning to understand, and even see and diagnose children who are more appropriately diagnosed under the new diagnosis, Pragmatic Communication Disorder. Diagnosing children is not an easy task, and should not be tackled lightly. The diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder can have life long implications. Pilots; Military; Law Enforcement, and some legal and professional callings, carry out very thorough background checks to screen individuals with debilitating conditions. Asperger's and Autism Spectrum Disorder, Oppostional Defiant Disorder, Conduct Disorder, as well as depression and anxiety are a concern to some hiring agencies. So accurate diagnosis is critical. I would recommend going through a new diagnostic manual at http://www.dsm5.org to see how closely some of the childhood mental disorders can resemble one another. Pay close attention to autism spectrum distinctions, especially the developmental glitches, beginning at or around age two. This is critical since many of the other symptoms can be found in childhood anxiety, severe depression in children, and oppositional defiant disorders. It is the disruption in an otherwise normal developmental trajectory, beginning some time around the second year of life, that distinguishes autism spectrum disorders. In adults, Schizoid Personality Disorder, and Schizotypal Disorder, if one isn't aware of someone's developmental history, can have the flavor of the autism spectrum. Always refer to the developmental history. And finally, its a long road through college/university, graduate school, internships, fellowships, national licensing exams, and continuing professional education. MDs, PhDs and related doctorates, and Masters Degrees are required, in most cases, to manage the very fine distinctions made in diagnostic work. Don't self diagnose, or give one to someone close to you. Consult a pro. We diagnose, only so we can understand, and treat more effectively. Peace.

question: Is it possible for someone with high functioning autism/Asperger's syndrome to have a special interest which revolves mainly around understanding him/herself to the furthest extent?
answer: Oh yes. Absolutely. I’ve never really heard it put that way, but it most certainly applies for me. I have routinized existential crises which require me to dig into my past, my attitudes, etc. in order to come out of it with some sense of stability. These involve exactly the kinds of rumination, perseveration, obsession/compulsion, research, graphomania, etc. which apply to my other special interests. The funny thing is, much of what necessitates these crises is also probably a factor of autism. Poor and inconsistent memory, taking a long time to process traumatic events, not always being aware of some feature of my behavior – it means that I’ll sometimes be struck much later by a sense that I might have really gotten something wrong along the way. Not only in my behaviors toward others, but in my evaluation of others, of myself, events, etc. Sometimes it feels like I’m swimming through my own history, and I have to find an anchor by focusing and working to develop a body of knowledge. Just like sometimes it feels like I’m swimming through the world in general, and have to find an anchor in those external things which aren’t confusing or alienating. And also, as many are saying, other interests are often rooted in some form of identity-processing. I started as a psych major, ended up a philosophy major – both of those things are related. My creative and/or academic work is always in some sense tied into articulations of or questions about identity which reflect my experiences and speculations.

question: What are the most common problems people with high-functioning autism face after growing up?
answer: For me the biggest single problem was applying for jobs/college places. The whole process seemed so chaotic and random that it still makes little sense to me today. Looking back on interviews that I have managed to get invited to they seem to be structured to specifically stress an ASD applicant, and are designed to make sure they can’t get the job (or college place). At one interview I went to, I did so badly, that out of two candidates being interviewed, they chose the one who two weeks later turned up drunk for work and assaulted a customer, even knowing he had past issues with alcohol!! For that one, I actually cried when I was told after the interview, so much so they took pity on me, and asked me back for a post interview briefing with the VP. He asked what I thought went wrong, and I then proceeded to spend 30 minutes showing him how the whole process, from application form to interview, was so loaded against applicants with Autism. He was genuinely shocked, and probably for the first time in his life realised that something needed to change within his organisation. So much so that he then sat down and worked out how I could ace the process next time. The following day I applied for another (very similar) job, and got it over 40 candidates. What he did was to explain to me the expected programmed response to each part of the process. I held that job down for many years, before a new boss sacked me for being autistic and being too difficult to manage (despite the previous year’s review that ranked me the top employee). I have worked from home since in the gig economy, getting work through word of mouth, as I fail at every formal job application I make (again). Discrimination? What discrimination? Wait, there’s a law prohibiting it? Then how come the many government jobs that there are ALL use the same job application process that excludes us?

question: Can people with Asperger's syndrome or high functioning autism be funny?

I’m doing a ‘knock-knock’ joke. SITUATON COMEDY. I love the sit coms where you have visual and spacial jokes that rely on perfect timing. I love musical jokes, where there is a pause, then something unexpected happens. JUST DESERTS. The slap-stick jokes have gone out of fashion and used to rely on accidents waiting to happen. Too much Health and Safety at Work training has spoiled that a bit. (Sigh) Now it looks more like evidence for a law suit. THE FALL GUY. There’s something satisfying about a fall-guy. Not very politically correct. (sigh). However every good fable has a moral ending. Orphans get saved, kittens don’t drown. There is something satisfying about the triumph of good over evil. A few good twists on the way, to create the tension. A couple of near misses. The three little pigs live happily ever after. The baddie comes to a sticky end. (Are wolves baddies, or endangered species?) PUTTING A BRAVE FACE ON IT. You would rather have a good laugh even if you really need a good cry. A well developed sence of humour helps us keep our inner selves private from the eyes of the world. It takes the sting out of sensory overload, and not being too disappointed when we are misunderstood. No one likes to lose face and become a laughing stock MEETING AND GREETING. I like to get a smile and give everyone a bit of limelight and use their name, when I am going around the room at Bridge club collecting subs. “Hello Sylvia, another £20 note? It would be a nice bit of change to get some silver from you. (get it?) “LITTLE THINGS PLEASE LITTLE MINDS”. Most of us are on the serious side of the spectrum . I make the same corny jokes and get a groan and a smile, or someone comes up with a mildly witty quip so that the standing joke moves on very slowly one week at a time. The others nod and smile at each other and say. “Mary Jane is attention-seeking again” 🤗 SOME autistic high IQ people are so pedantic they cannot see the funny side of anything. When you have to explain that something is funny, it falls flat, and usually loses something in the translation. PROFESSIONAL PEOPLE ON SHOW. We can also entertain other people. MASKING, acting, playing a role, making jokes, and keeping a good face on things. Lecturers, CEOs, News presenters, Weather presenters. You only get the shop window view. THE REST OF US HAVE A SENCE OF HUMOUR. We need it as an essential form of MASKING. It helps to get by if you can put a spin on things. You don’t need to be clever to make jokes, and see the funny side of things. It is much more fun to lighten up and have a laugh. Even dying is more pleasant if you can grin about it. DARK HUMOUR IS LIKE FOOD.Not everyone gets it The LAST WORD. question: I got diagnosed with high functioning autism, but I have no sensory issues. Do you have to have it with autism?
answer: A very direct and literal answer to your question: No, you don't have to have sensory issues. Why? Well, it's part of how “autism" functions as a diagnostic category. It takes a while to explain how diagnoses are historically emergent, so if you have the patience for that, enjoy. Analogy: Pretend that, in the fifth century, someone comes home from a trip. Let's just say Lancelot, after coming home from a quest. He gets sick, with lots of nausea and a case of “the runs.” Merlin has no idea what's wrong for sure, but suspects Lancelot's been cursed by this witch he says he encountered on his journey. The curse had magically removed a karge quantity of blood and bile in his system, throwing his humors out of balance. This tricked his body into disposing is of its phlegmatic and sapine liquids as quickly as possible, to bring them into balance again. Merlin just has him drink as much water as possible. Over a bit of time, Lancelot gets better. Now, let's imagine that in the early 1800s, someone revisits this story and asserts that it was not a humor imbalance at work, but that the foul stench and miasma of the witch's den was to blame. Then in the mid 1900s, someone else revisits it and says “No, this was clearly a case of cholera. And thus a pathogen was to blame. Merlin was, by practical medical standards, correct. But based on the symptoms, he had an operating theory that suggested a course of treatment. This treatment addressed the symptoms, staving off dehydration, long enough that Lancelot's body could clear the disease. (Incidentally, the person in the 1800s probably would have prescribed an inadequate treatment.) However, Merlin's theory, in itself, was wrong. He did not know that there was a swarm of tiny organisms living in Lancelot's body, and thereby causing the symptoms. How is this relevant? Because, we do not know which of these three historical understandings of the illness is most analogous to our current understanding of autism. Autism is not a “thing.” There's nothing you can point to in someone's brain and say, “That right there, that's the autism part.” All we have are diagnostic criteria. We have noticed that certain number of maladaptive traits tend to occur clustered together. Doctors isolate these traits and call them “symptoms,” guessing that the clustering traits share an underlying cause. We then call this phenomenon “Autism." But Autism does not refer to the cause. It refers to the clustering of traits which are purported to be effects of the theorized cause. Similarly, cholera was not a bacterium. It was a *disease* caused by a set of related bacteria calles “Vibrio cholerae.” Now, “So what?” I hear you say. Well, what if someone has some traits but not others? How do we know that the underlying cause ALWAYS affects people such that they have that trait? How do we know that a peculiarity of how they were raised didn't compensate them in one way or another? There are no *necessary* “symptoms” for an autism diagnosis, but if you have enough of them, it might be deemed “sufficient" for a diagnosis, even if none was specifically necessary. Now, I personally have a lot of doubts that there is any underlying cause. Let's just indulge in stereotypes for a moment, and stipulate that there is a clustering between the following traits: dark skin, wide noses, thicker lips, curly hair, dark hair, height. Obviously, I am describing the schema many have for African-Americans. (A broad and sloppy one, at that.) I could then say, “Hey, I notice these things often all happen at once. Maybe there is an underlying cause? I know these things all run in families, so perhaps they are all genetic! And perhaps there is ONE GENE that controls all of these things!” You'd say I was pretty silly, right? There are short people with dark skin, dark, curly hair, wide noses and thick lips. There are people who are tall, with dark, curly hair, wide noses and thick lips, yet with lighter skin (I am one such person). But plenty of people would still categorize these sorts of people as African-American. (That's, of course, because “race,” as we understand it, is a myth based on sloppy biology and anthropology from the 17th-19th centuries.) A lot, if not all, of these traits are controlled by multiple genes, leading to an incredibly diverse human population. But you can still find clustering traits within that group of 7 billion people. Similarly, researchers claim to be looking for the genetic causes for autism often come back saying that there are some hilariously large number of genes that are more common among diagnosed autistics than among non-diagnosed ones. They'll often say this puts us closer to finding “the cause,” but to me that looks like we are just a cluster rhat occurs naturally within large populations. If you are wondering why autism diagnoses have gone up, that is because Autism's diagnostic criteria were (and I cannot stress this hard enough) *deliberately* expanded so that more people could qualify for assitance and accommodations. They were intentionally written to apply to a larger portion of the population. Supplemental to that is increased awareness obviously leads to more people seeking diagnosis. Plus, increased mobility has led to people self-selecting partners among a broader pool than before, and people who are introverted and don't like loud noises might prefer one another to loud extroverts. And they are more likely to have children who express these traits more often.

question: Are people with high-functioning autism considered mentally disabled?
answer: No, because almost by definition, we are not. Autism, in and of itself, doesn’t mean intellectual impairment. Which is to say that while someone with autism may be intellectually impaired, one can be diagnosed with autism while having no intellectual impairment at all. Indeed, high-functioning autism seems to be unusually common among the intellectually gifted. People like Newton, Einstein, and Bill Gates appear to have autistic traits. Some of the genes that predispose towards autism are now known to increase IQ, and that may have something to do with the connection. It doesn’t help that “autism” really refers to a number of similar conditions with different causes, e.g., different genes are known to be involved. Autistics whose condition is a result of a de novo mutation seem in general to be lower functioning than those who come from families in which there is a lot of neurodiversity.

question: What does the research show regarding thinking styles of people with high-functioning autism/Asperger syndrome?
answer: I recommend you go to youtube and look at lectures/presentations by Simon Baron-Cohen, as he is an expert on this subject (possibly the best). To summarize, men and women are different in their thinking in that women are better at empathy-related skills, such as language, while men are better at spatial thinking and systemizing, such as understanding the rules of a system and to know how to throw a spear at a moving target. Autism appears to be an “extreme version” of the male brain, in this sense, where tests show that autistic people are even better at the things that men are good at, while being even worse at the things that men are bad at, compared to women. So autistic brains are great systemizers and visio-spatial thinkers, but poor empathizers. (Lacking some cognitive empathy, while still having very strong affective empathy.) But I do recommend that you go check those lectures/presentations out, since I don’t think it should be over-simplified, and you should also see the evidence behind this.

question: Is high functioning autism considered Asperger’s?
answer: Asperger's is an old name for a range of symptoms that were rolled into the ASD envelope when DSM5 was released. Asperger's does not exist as a diagnosis any more. There is literally a question a week on Quora about why Asperger's was rolled into ASD. Since it's the obvious follow-up question to my answer I'll give an abbreviated answer to “why was Asperger's consolidated into ASD?” Historically, when Dr Asperger was working with autistic kids, he identified a group of the “high functioning" kids as exceptionally gifted. By identifying them as valuable resources, he was able to save their lives from the eugenics of the nazi party. The total history is of course more complex, but this is the gist. When DSM5 was being drafted, it was known that the border between autism and Asperger's was so blurry that the same patient could visit the same practitioner at different times on the same day and receive either diagnosis. So Asperger’s and some other formerly recognized issues were dropped and rolled into the broader envelope of ASD.

question: As someone with high-functioning autism, what are your personal most liked sensory stimuli?

Touching my stuffed toys is great too. I have this stuffed polar bear and he has the softest fur - I love just petting him, since the fur feels so silky in my hands. I love the sound of acrylic paint on paper. The slight squelching you can hear when you layer too much pain up is just so gripping for me - it's the one of the biggest reasons that I like painting with acrylic from time to time. I don't like to over do it with this one though. The sound is almost precious and shivery. I'm pretty enthralled with the sound of the Japanese language too. I figure that how the language is spoken just really connects to me in a pleasant sensory way. Other than that, I really love touching nice tissues. I've spent a lot of time finding the perfect brand of tissue, since some are really nice and almost silky. I like running these over my skin because they just feel nice and gentle. I'm pretty fond of the taste of a certain brand of gingerbread too, especially if it's all soft and malleable.

question: Is it possible for someone to have high functioning autism without being aware of it? Can someone with high functioning autism still function normally in society?
answer: Yes, it's possible for someone to have high-functioning autism (HFA) without being aware of it. HFA, also known as Level 1 Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), can be subtle and not immediately apparent. _Reasons for unawareness:_ 1. Lack of obvious symptoms 2. Compensatory mechanisms (e.g., social masking) 3. Limited understanding of autism spectrum 4. No formal diagnosis or evaluation 5. Co-occurring conditions (e.g., ADHD, anxiety) masking autism traits _High-functioning autism characteristics:_ 1. Intellectual ability within normal range 2. Verbal communication skills 3. Ability to adapt to social situations 4. Special interests or talents 5. Sensory sensitivities or difficulties _Functioning normally in society:_ 1. Many individuals with HFA lead successful, independent lives. 2. They may excel in fields leveraging their strengths (e.g., technology, art). 3. Social challenges can be overcome with strategies and support. 4. Self-awareness and acceptance can improve relationships and overall well-being. _Challenges:_ 1. Social interactions and relationships 2. Executive function and organization 3. Sensory integration and regulation 4. Emotional regulation and mental health 5. Masking or camouflaging autism traits _Getting diagnosed:_ 1. Consult a psychologist, psychiatrist, or neurologist. 2. Comprehensive diagnostic evaluation (e.g., ADOS, Autism Quotient). 3. Self-assessment and reflection. _Resources:_ 1. Autism Society of America (ASA) 2. Autism Self-Advocacy Network (ASAN) 3. National Autism Association (NAA) 4. "The Autistic Brain" by Temple Grandin and Richard Panek 5. "Thinking in Pictures" by Temple Grandin _Key takeaways:_ 1. High-functioning autism can be subtle and overlooked. 2. Self-awareness and acceptance are crucial for success. 3. Strategies and support can improve social and emotional functioning. 4. Diagnosis and understanding can bring relief and empowerment. 5. Autism is a spectrum, and each individual's experience is unique.

question: Have you had high-functioning autism?
answer: More or less. I have a diagnosis of “Asperger’s syndrome”. The assessment took place in 2010, before DSM-5 came out with its newfangled “autism spectrum disorder”. Under DSM-IV, the classic difference between Asperger’s syndrome (AS) and “high functioning autism” (HFA) was delay in learning to speak. Both AS and HFA require broadly average or above average intelligence. But AS requires no clinically significant delay in learning to speak, while speech delays are common in HFA. However, many clinicians used to diagnose a person with AS even if they had speech delays, provided their speech had caught up and they had no intellectual disability. In effect, AS is more or less the same as HFA but without speech delay in childhood, and HFA is more or less the same as AS but with speech delay in childhood. So if someone asked me if I had HFA I would reply “More or less”. The usage of the terms was very fuzzy, which is why the distinction between AS and autism was abolished. It’s all “autism spectrum disorder” now.

question: Do most people with high functioning autism wish they weren’t autistic, or are they happy the way they are?
answer: Do most people with high functioning autism wish they weren’t autistic, or are they happy the way they are? — Some folks say autistics shouldn't mask or have to mask as this hides who they are. I'm only now finding out that I am on the spectrum and have learned in great detail how to mask and I am very good at it. Folks still have a sense I'm different but they think I am just smart-quirky and a bit unusual. The thing is … most neurotypicals mask on some level, too! Very few people are fully comfortable in their own skin. “Not me! I don't have multiple faces I put on for different people!” Hah! Anyone with adult siblings who finds their family back at home with parents will find themselves regressing back to the patterns and habits of childhood. We all have different faces we wear in different situations. I had no clue I might be autistic so I thought everyone masked as much as I do. Well, almost as much. I've always felt odd. So much so that I once asked a girlfriend “do you ever feel normal?” “Yeah. All the time.” “I almost never do.” It can be stressful to mask much of my day and I need to decompress after work with something repetitive like “playing guitar without purpose.” I think that is one of my subtle “stimming" responses because I play the same chord or picking patterns over and over and over and again for weeks or months. It is my way of rocking back and forth in the music, not with my whole body. But I choose to continue to mask because it helps me navigate certain work situations and I have a successful career in a highly complex write environment. I am not ashamed to mask. But even if I choose to mask I wouldn't give up my autistic traits for anything in the world. I see things differently than anyone else at work. It can take me a long time to learn all the ins and outs of a complex system but when I do I have a sense of the entire system from the viewpoints of people with different roles skills. I can then tell if small changes will disrupt it. I am valued because of who I am. I have had to work my ass off to find my place in the world. More accurately, I have had to create new places in the workforce where my skills fit. When I do that I express my strengths and earn respect. In that way I am not masking. I also had a lot of trouble with liars and manipulators. I'd get angry and kinda freak out. Okay. I'd drop f-bombs and yell. I need accurate information otherwise my head hurts! question: Do you believe high-functioning autism to be a neurological difference or a disorder?
answer: Both; they are not in necessary conflict. If a high functionning person has problems understanding other minds’ desires and emotions to the extent it imperils their relationships, their advancement at work or getting a job, or other significant life needs it is an impairment. If it can be overcome with learning it may be a temporary type of mental illness; if it cannot be overcome due to organic brain organization and the like then it is a brain disorder. No reason you can’t say “vive la difference” for the upsides and recognize your impairment on the downside at the same time.

question: How do you get a diagnosis of high functioning autism in a girl?
answer: There is a lot of information online written by autistic women about how difficult it is to get an ASD diagnosis. Many mothers realize they are autistic when their children are diagnosed. Bright, highly verbal, older girls and women present differently than boys. The DSM standards were written for non-verbal, intellectually challenged young boys. A huge number of kids, boys and girls, get diagnosed ADHD before eventually getting an autism diagnosis because it is harder to recognize the subtleties of autism in kids who seem more "high-functioning." For more information on females with ASD, check out descriptions by Tony Attwood, Tania Marshall, and Liane Holliday Willey. There are also lists of female Asperger's traits on the blogs Everyday Asperger's and help4aspergers.com - Home As for getting a diagnosis for your autistic daughter, keep trying! Find someone who is very bright and able to look beyond the standard diagnosis, preferably someone who has experience with teenagers and bright girls. If your daughter was already assessed and the diagnosis was missed, go through the findings line by line so that next time you give them the "right" answers during the parent interview and the surveys. Focus on meltdowns -- the times when she becomes "low functioning" due to stress, anxiety, and being overwhelmed. Focus on her social and communication difficulties and sensory issues (not part of the official criteria, but virtually all autistics have sensory issues), not her intellectual strengths. "Significant impairment" is what gets the diagnosis. Be very aware beforehand of how girls present differently (often they internalize rather than externalize, they cry or melt down rather than become aggressive). My daughter was also missed because she is exceptionally gifted, but she had lots of difficulties in school when the social demands became too great and she was overwhelmed with sensory issues. She self-diagnosed as autistic and got provisional accommodations in college, and she feels much better. (She is also off meds, which did not help with her anxiety.) She needs the formal diagnosis in December so I am looking right now for the right person/ team to assess her. Good luck!

question: What are some indications a toddler may be on the autistic spectrum/ have high functioning autism?

At age 5 and a half, he has recently started to control his own upset when his baby brother cries (he can't stand the noise), and instead will sometimes try and comfort him. He likes people, but doesn't have friends he talks to. He also doesn't copy other children, so struggles with learning mechanical tasks, as he has to figure them out by trial and error himself. So how did this express itself when he was a toddler?As a baby, he would sleep through anything, including discosHe walked late (20 months). He did crawl.He couldn't pedal a bike till he was 5. He can't be shown how to do mechanical tasks. He is not toilet trained and cannot dress or undress himself, even nowHe was fearlessHe talked late (about 3 and a half). His speech is still stilted and about 2 years behind.He played around other children, but never with other childrenHe never indulged in any imaginative play. Unlike some with autism, he wasn't bothered by colour or size order.He struggled with instructions, to the point that he was tested to see if he was deaf. He isn't, he just wasn't interested in what people were saying.He struggled with anything that involved deferring gratification, or sharing. So queueing up, taking turns, etc. Think typical 2 year old on steroids.Poor eye contact, though he will do it with people he knows.Forget any kind of team or group activity. question: Why do people assume those who have high functioning autism are idiots?
answer: For a long time the myth that AS people had subnormal intelligence was parroted by researchers, simply because they had read it somewhere. Unscientifically, they took it as established fact, and prefaced a lot of studies with this. Then the did all they could to get media attention for their studies. So the media picked up the myth unquestionably (“if a scientist says it, it must be true”) - which is about as unscientific as science can get. AS science is based on theorising, and is thus particularly contaminated by myth and assumption. A second reason -not unlinked to the first - is that boys with Fragile X Syndrome were wrongly identified by professionals as autistic. They are intellectually handicapped, so this reinforced the myth propagated by the researchers. The psychiatrists followed suit, not questioning the “facts” nor the methodologies in use. So AS people suffered because of widespread incompetence and ignorance from professionals who were not helping AS people, as they claimed, but cruelly labelling them with a disability that is not part of HFA at all. You are more likely to find very high intellectual power in the HFA population, terrific memory and analytical ability, but the researchers continue to ignore this, partly because catastrophising “how bad” it is helps their personal interest of getting research funds.

question: How can high functioning autism be identified in a teenager?
answer: Identifying high-functioning autism (HFA) in a teenager can be challenging, as the symptoms may be subtle and varied. Here are some signs and behaviors that may indicate high-functioning autism in a teenager: 1. **Social Challenges:** - Difficulty with peer relationships and making friends. - Limited interest in socializing or engaging in social activities. - Challenges understanding non-verbal cues, such as body language and facial expressions. 2. **Communication Differences:** - Formal or repetitive speech patterns. - Difficulty understanding sarcasm, humor, or implied meanings. - Limited use of gestures or facial expressions while communicating. 3. **Rigidity and Repetitive Behaviors:** - Strong preference for routines and rituals. - Resistance to change, becoming upset if plans deviate from the expected. - Engaging in repetitive behaviors or having specific interests that are pursued intensely. 4. **Sensory Sensitivities:** - Heightened sensitivities to sensory stimuli (e.g., light, sound, touch, taste, or smell). - Unusual reactions to sensory input, such as covering ears in response to loud noises. 5. **Specialized Interests:** - Intense focus on specific topics or hobbies. - Difficulty shifting attention away from areas of interest to engage in other activities. 6. **Executive Functioning Challenges:** - Difficulty with organization, time management, and planning. - Struggles with transitions between tasks or activities. - Challenges with initiating and completing tasks independently. 7. **Emotional Regulation:** - Difficulty expressing emotions appropriately or understanding the emotions of others. - Heightened anxiety or stress in social situations. 8. **Academic Performance:** - Inconsistencies in academic performance, with strengths in certain areas and challenges in others. - May excel in subjects related to their specific interests. 9. **Literal Thinking:** - Difficulty with understanding metaphors, idioms, or figurative language. - Tendency to interpret information in a literal manner. 10. **Difficulty Empathizing:** - Challenges understanding the perspectives and feelings of others. - Difficulty forming and maintaining close friendships. It's important to note that every individual is unique, and the presence of some of these traits does not necessarily indicate high-functioning autism. A comprehensive evaluation by a healthcare professional, such as a developmental pediatrician or a clinical psychologist specializing in autism spectrum disorders, is essential for an accurate diagnosis. If you suspect high-functioning autism in a teenager, seeking professional guidance is crucial for appropriate support and intervention.

question: Isn’t high functioning autism an actual condition?
answer: What most people are referring to when they say “high-functioning” autism is ASD1 or Asperger’s Syndrome (AS), and yes they are diagnosable, identifiable forms of autism. However, terms like “high-functioning” or “mild” are not actual classifications of autism. They’re commonly used, mostly by neurotypicals to describe those with a form of ASD who do not have learning disabilities and live relatively independent lives. There’s a good reason why “high-functioning” on its own is not a diagnosis though. It’s not an accurate way of describing autism to say that some are “high” or “low” -functioning, at least not as often as we think. Firstly, it leads many to believe that those labeled “high-functioning” deal with fewer symptoms or struggle less so than others on the spectrum, which is not always true. Secondly, we have seen case after case of those who may be viewed as “low-functioning” due to factors like being non-verbal or more socially awkward being brilliant individuals sometimes with talents and skills that most people don’t have. So ASD1 or AS is a condition that is legitimate, but “high-functioning” autism is merely a descriptor that, for various reasons, is not official and is a mostly colloquial (and often inaccurate) observation. That being said, the term “high-functioning autism” is commonly used to describe certain autistic people, even by professionals.

question: What is it like to be a therapist with high functioning autism?
answer: —I’ve updated the answer. The main challenges come from people who know I'm autistic and my sole existence breaks their expectations of what I should be doing. “You're teaching kids social skills? How? You are autistic, you don't have any!” But the thing is, as anybody else in this world, I can learn, but what most people learnt from instinct I did by reading and having someone point out when I was off the mark. There’s many things I didn’t learn by just living and going out with friends. Many of them had to be learned as long algorithms, like polite talk or chit chat. Or getting stopped by a police officer. I’m consciously aware of the way most of these interactions are supposed to go, so when I talk with clients I can often pin point where and how things could improve. I have a lot of personal experience thinking in other people’s shoes and then taking into account the other’s personal life experience, personal views and so on and so forth to try and think like them, one is called empathy and the other is the process of mentalisation. Being consciously aware of the kind of questions you need to ask yourself to empathise and mentalise helps me help others do the same. The therapy environment is a lot more manageable then say a trip to the mall to buy clothes, or dinner with 5 more people. In therapy people expect you and wants you to ask questions, to clarify intent, as long as it serves the purpose of allowing them to know themselves better and the objectives of their treatment. And they also want you to give them your own point of view, in a way is a lending of the mind, I lend them my mind and my observations so they can make connections and observations about their own lives. Because I’m autistic I have exceptional observational skills and can account for very minute changes in people. Also, in a way, people and specially children are my special interest. I’m just constantly in awe with humanity and humanity’s endeavours. I’m an avid reader and film watcher, and I often fall back on metaphors learnt through the appreciation of these arts to relate to the children I work with, and their parents. I also do a lot of work with late-teenagers. Who need a lot of help learning self-control and planning skills and I happen to excel at breaking down problems and problematic situations in more manageable bits. I still have blind spots, and I try to be very aware of them. Some things whizz way over my head and it isn't until I'm being supervised that I notice them, but it happens to my fellow therapists as well. I'm still in training so we're bound to make a few blunders, the important thing is to learn from them. Other than that, I guess my experience varies on a sensory level, as many other people with autism I have a sensory processing disorder that sometimes makes it really hard to be able to stay calm and calm down a screeching 11 year old having a meltdown. Those are really hard. Luckily I used to be a screeching 11yo having a meltdown, so I know what to offer to help and it allows for a unique perspective that I also offer to parents in order to help translate what's going on with their kid. I also have a lot of knowledge on sensory integration and the many uses and makings of fidget toys and how to use those moments of creation for kids and parents to bond together. My hearing is kinda screwy too at times, and it leads to funny tension-breaking moments. 6 to 9-year-olds are the often the most curious on the inner workings of hearing processing gone wrong. They like to test my hearing and some come up with really clever ways to do it in therapy (I do play therapy by the way; which I also thinks stems from my autism, my fascinations with play, with creating and appreciating every creation no matter how small). Because I get tired more easily than most, it takes me longer to achieve the same quantity of hours as my peers. I take longer breaks. I work less hours. But you know what? I'm happy and 100% confident I'm doing well and my clients think so too, and even most importantly, they're getting better themselves. PS: I was diagnosed by a professor at uni when I was 21, so my journey may vary a lot from other therapists with ASD. But I'm glad it happened, even if I struggled with my expectations and prejudices for a long while, in the end it was the best gift I could've gotten. PPS: I went anon on this answer because of those still lingering prejudices and it turns out this answer has more upvotes than any of my other answers. I had a humbling laugh at that. Thank you!

question: How does having Asperger Syndrome (High Functioning Autism) affect academic performance in High School and College?
answer: When I was diagnosed in my fifties, the psychologist pointed out that the “worst” stage of life for many people with Asperger’s syndrome was the teenage years and early twenties - which happen to coincide with high school and university (in Australia “high school” means grades 7–12, and “university” rather than “college” is the usual term for higher academic study after high school). In any event, those ages were the most difficult in my life, so how did it affect academic performance? In high school, I was sort of aware that I was academically one of the top students in my year, but emotionally and socially I was falling behind. There was a big gap between my academic performance and my social and emotional performance. I had friends, and even briefly one girlfriend, but I wasn’t coping well emotionally. I was anxious and depressed. However, high school was a relatively enclosed and structured life, and that gave me just enough support to keep performing academically. I was part of the nerdy “music group” who hung about with the young music teacher and went to concerts and other cultural activities together outside school hours. I used to have long philosophical arguments with my music teacher (a devout Catholic) over the existence of God. The structure of high school kept me together - barely - and I succeeded academically: I did the top levels in all my subjects, and got high marks. I was told by the school that I had come 40th in the state in mathematics, so whatever my emotional state it hadn’t interfered too much with my academic performance. My end of high school marks were the same as a friend at another school who was accepted into medicine, commonly considered back then as the hardest course to get into. I chose to do a social work degree (oblivious to my lack of social skills!). I started to run out of emotional strength towards the end of first year. University was more adult, less structured, much larger than high school - and I didn’t cope. I had some supports, but they were not enough, unlike high school. In second year I burned out and collapsed academically. I spent an entire week obsessively reading Lord of the Rings every waking moment, missing all my lectures and tutorials, and sleeping all day and staying awake all night. I retreated into my special interests (medieval Germanic languages) and did poorly in my academic work. I attended lectures, but failed to complete some key essays. By the end of the year, I failed two major subjects and scraped through one because I had lasted the year and their quota for failures had been filled by drop outs. I had to leave full time university for two years in order to catch up. I worked full time, which gave my life some structure and support. I repeated subjects at night and got my first Distinction (my first and second year results had all been straight passes or fails). I was now ready for third year … or so I thought. I returned for my professional subjects in social work and soon learned my limitations in social interaction. Actually I enjoyed interacting with a twelve year old boy (maybe we were on the same emotional and social level) but couldn’t really manage social interaction with adult clients (such as his mother). I failed the professional subjects, and ended up switching to a plain Arts degree. I moved out of my family home into a rehabilitative community, where I stayed for five years before getting married. In this structured and supportive environment I completed two remaining Arts subjects and got Distinctions in both, finally getting somewhere closer to my high school achievements. I now had a pass Arts degree, with three Distinctions, six passes, and five Fails - not quite reflecting the academic ability I showed in high school. Some years later, I undertook a Masters of Letters degree in philosophy, which I completed with Distinction. I also attempted master of Arts (Honours)and PhD courses, and enjoyed learning post-graduate philosophy, but could not get through the research thesis part of those degrees. I can handle the structured coursework, but a thesis requires more executive functions than I possess, I think. All up, I was able to perform academically in high school, despite lagging socially and emotionally. I burnt out at university and struggled with the greater demands for executive function (self-management), and the less structured and more adult social environment. I never really understood how to interact with an academic supervisor during post-grad studies as well - that remains a mystery to me.

question: Is it common for someone with high functioning autism to wear diapers even though they don’t have any medical issues?
answer: Yeah, I was diagnosed later on in my early adulthood with autism after they began to know the signs in women. After potty training, I would diaper myself with the cloth and disposables left over. I would often sleep in them and pee and poop them as I played in the morning. My mom finally discovered me in a soaked stinky diaper one day and I tried to explain how it was comforting to me to sleep in them as well as how normal it felt to use them like I had most of my life. I was allowed another pack of tape up diapers since my Dr thought I needed to get sick of diapers on my own. Given access to them whenever I wanted but having to change myself (except poop until she taught me how to clean myself), I wore them every night. Some days I got out of them and went to the potty. Some mornings I spent until after my morning wetting in them. Some days, I wet and messed them and wouldn't change until I leaked. My mom invited lots of friends over for sleepovers to dissuade me but I'd tell them about my diapers and often wear and wet one while we played, for bed and long into the morning. After months of this, I still didn't want to let go. My dr said I probably wouldn't until school from peer pressure. I was already wearing them to daycare after she suggested I show the kids there to cause humiliation and I happily used them and got changed with the younger kids there. I got cut off. Everything seemed normal except me spending any morning my mom slept in to pee and poop my pajamas or panties. I stopped by high school and got two years in before buying diapers myself. When I moved out, I got very into them because I was denied my comfort object and sense of control for so long. I wore adult baby ones a lot and wore them constantly. I went through times of guilt where I would stop but would go back. My therapist now thinks my eating disorder came from a way to gain control when I stopped going in my panties and became self destructive. Now I wear baby style diapers mostly 3–10 days a month and I do usually use them for every thing but will wear cloth training pants instead of underwear and not use them most days. Its a pretty normal thing to develop a comfort object relationship with and if my mom had actually let me get sick of them, I'd likely rarely or never use them but having it be taken from me, I clung to it very hard. My therapist says as long as it causes me no issues, wear and use them when you want to and even as a way to deal with my sensory disorder and anxiety. Tolieting issues are common in kids with adhd and autism and diapers used to be a way to go when I couldn't make it due to procrastinating the urges or missing them. I wanted my comfort object back because my autism made it a special object. My fixation makes sense and I'm stuck on it since it felt like safety and control over things for me. I know lots of other autistic people who admit they had this and grew out of it. My friends almost all know and it is mostly accepted by everyone. I face a little mocking for it but I usually am the one who makes the jokes, I can't deny its good joke material. Don't let the world tell you how to cope. Seek actual mental health professionals if it causes distress. Otherwise, it hurts no one and gives you deep comfort

question: Why does adult high functioning autism get mistaken for personality disorders like NPD & BPD?
answer: This is a broad view, generalising generalisations.. This is how you get a wrong-diagnosis, so let’s run with it. An apparent lack of empathy. (Cognitive empathy: Being able to discern/predict emotional reactions in others. Not a strong feature in autistim. Affective empathy: I feel for you/ I care, can be very strong in autistim). Affective and cognitive empathy are not always differentiated by professionals. Indeed, expressing the inner mechanisms takes a lot of self-reflection…which can only be done well when the mechanism has already been identified. Dispassionate. Being able to differentiate someone else’s feelings from one’s own is, in psychology terms, a high prize indeed. But while this can make for the person you want with you in a crisis… to a superficial regard, it appears uncaring. True “Haute Couture” Friend/ knock-off Primark friend. No Schroedinger’s livedeadcatfriend hiding in a box. “True friend”/”acquaintance” divide can appear manipulative. Friends stay friends even if they join a colony on Mars, and you never see or hear from them again. Acquaintances come and go, but aren’t cut from the same cloth. A hindrance to understanding, or even timetabling, can make the game not worth the candle. It looks selfish, but that view doesn’t account for the sheer amount of effort involved in social communication… Or the platinated-gold-quality stuff invested in True Friends. The True Friend may be the life partner, cos who else do you need… and that can look needy. (It isn’t, of course; there are plenty of other people providing company. It’s just they’re in books.) Black/white thinking. I think this is a myth, or at best a misunderstanding. Autistic people (of my acquaintance) will change their stance on something more readily than “normal” people, as they aren’t emotionally invested in their own opinions in the same way. If better information comes along, they will reassess their position. (If you find trouble getting an autistic person to change their mind, it’s probably because they already know more than you do.) Black/white thinking is a hallmark of certain personality disorders, ie another person is regarded as first all-good, THEN all-bad, on the whim of a perceieved slight. This can be confounded with the above (apparant) “easy-discard” of acquaintances. It isn’t an “easy-discard” process in autism, as much as “not having picked it up in the first place”. You can’t treat people as “objects” if they are autonomous individuals seperate from oneself. It’s just that “normal” people are socially-motivated, and require emotional validation in ways which don’t always occur to autistic people, who tend not to need it (or in such quantities) in the same way. Rigid thinking, which can very much be a hallmark of autism, can look like black/white thinking. It isn’t. It’s more akin to an internal Cochrane Review deciding on a best course of action, then sticking to it. Rigid patterns of behaviour feed into misdiagnoses (I am so, so telling you, you do..even if you’ve done it all your life, and haven’t noticed). ‘Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht ND RP posted a marvellous question about the three forms of social reciprocity in autism: Introverted; overbearing - (she had a better word, but it’s what you do when you spoil your hippy friend’s eager faith in the Annunaki, by explaining everything that’s wrong with Ancient Aliens…can’t just be me…?); and ..imitation. Get this; they each look a bit iffy already, on their own; but quite a few autistic people can change from one to another like they change gears. It looks fantastically unstable, as with many personality disorders “lacking a sense of self”. There is a stable internal self; it’s just the internal self doesn’t get out much. (Even worse, without a correct diagnosis, it can get so boxed-in that it’s hard to define.) This is different from PD people who live the shifts in personality. But it can look the same… The “imitation” strategy can be particularly damaging, as it necessarily requires a degree of submission to others, which means relinquishing autonomy, which…looks like something it isn’t. Special interests “obsessional”…special interests being more entertaining than people “narcissistic”. A person can also at times be a special interest (don’t do this, it looks well-creepy). Social interaction can be an interest as well. It’s a fascination for an autistic friend, who studies human behaviour with an enthusiasm I’d rather invest in slime mould (mind you, I do like slime mould.) Social interaction is, only very occasionally, an interest for me: “So…why’d you do it all, if you don’t want to make friends?” It’s like going on Safari. It’s all very engaging, from inside the bubble of the LandRover in my mind, but I don’t fancy my chances amongst the baboons. Add in… wariness, naiveté, all the generalised PTSD crap from struggling socially for decades. Face it; you look like a basketcase. Thing is, for all that people jump up and down, and declaim “every autistic person is different”, that’s not entirely true. There is a kind of Haynes Manual for Autism, in all the information available. Special tools may be required to fit the pieces together, but; being a well-running autistic person, is shed-loads better than being a miserable, angst-ridden, misdiagnosed, unknowing autistic. Imagine someone trying to correct engine problems by re-chipping your car’s fuel management system…when what your car actually has is a mechanical carburetor. Get the model right, the trouble-shooting flows much better.
