question: Is it possible for people with high functioning autism to grow up without realizing they have autism?
answer: Yes, highly possible.I hadn’t a clue that I was on the spectrum until about 8 years ago when I was over 50. I, our 2 adult children and my husband were never diagnosed as children. My son was a married man, suffering depression following a bad break up with his wife. He was referred for psychotherapy and it was his psychiatrist who informed him that he was “quite possibly autistic, if you want to check, take this online test”. He scored 33 - “probably”. My daughter took the test - she scored 35 (highly probably). I took the test - I scored 28 (possibly) which surprised me. I knew I was a bit weird, but I never thought that I was autistic. As the 3 of us studied autism, we all came to realise that my husbands male family line is dominated by HFA’s. There was only one girl born before my daughters generation - she shows no obvious signs, but her grandfather, his three sons, their 4 sons (and the aforementioned girl), the following generation (my adult children) and now the newest generation all have a high proportion of autistic traits. Luckily high IQs went with them. No one needed help in school, and some of them were involved in the development of helicopters and hold patents and one was a nuclear scientist who decided to become a homehelp for the elderly after he retired. Three months ago my husband suddenly said “I think I may be on the autistic spectrum”. Errr… yeah? Neither I, nor our children had ever raised our suspicions that he was with him. If he took the test I suspect he would score 33–35similarly to our children. I suspect my siblings are also on the spectrum, as well as one of my nephews. The other one seems NT. I know that both of my parents were atypical for their generation - my mother was a “wild child” that I put down to her being an “army brat” farmed out to relatives while her father was posted abroad (her father was a very senior officer in the British Army) and his wife went with him. Now I wonder if she was also on the spectrum, and my father, well he was his “own man”, never one of the gang.

question: Is inattentive type ADHD the same as high functioning autism?
answer: Is inattentive type ADHD the same as high functioning autism? No. The only thing they really have in common is difficulties with executive functions (e.g. planning, starting, switching, finishing tasks). Also, about half the people with ADHD have sensory sensitivity, and the vast majority of people with ASD (autism spectrum disorder) do too. I’ll mention one other common link below. People with ADHD may have poor social relationships, but that will be due to their impulsiveness, etc. A person with ADHD — unless they also have ASD — will be able to read body language and non-verbal cues, which are classic areas of difficulty for autistic people. People with only ADHD don’t have the characteristic autistic issues with communication either: e.g. unusual “prosody” (loud and soft) or an odd accent (apparently I have both). And while a person with ADHD may be fixated on something which is intrinsically rewarding (e.g. playing a computer game) they don’t generally have autistic “special interests” or stimming, or a need for “sameness” (in fact, they get bored easily). Autism and ADHD have distinct diagnostic criteria, and meeting one set of criteria does not at all guarantee that you will meet the other. However, there are some common genes — genes that increase the likelihood of both ADHD and ASD in the same person — and consequently many people with ASD also have ADHD. But ADHD is rather more common than ASD, and so a large majority of people with ADHD do not have ASD. They are distinct conditions with distinct diagnostic criteria, but a few traits are similar and there are some genes that can make it more likely to have both conditions.

question: Do you think of high-functioning autism as a deficit or a difference?
answer: Let me tell you a story. Imagine that a strange man walks up to you and says, “Où suis-je?” You ask him what he said, and he responds, “Je ne comprends pas!” You decide he must be crazy, so you call the cops. They drag him away. The shrinks examine him and conclude he has a communication deficit. See, nobody else can understand him, and he can’t understand anyone else. They let him out of jail. He acts kind of funny, so people yell at him a lot. Over time, he learns a few rudimentary words and gets a basic job. He soon is able to communicate basic things. Eventually, he can hold entire conversations. He still talks funny, though. You sigh and say, “Poor guy. He must be retarded or something.” One day, lo and behold, you see him talking excitedly with another person who acts just like him. They sound like this: “Oh, Dieu merci ! T'es Français, toi aussi.” “Toi, le pauvre, comment t'as fini ici?” “J'ai été kidnappé ! Ils pensent tous que je suis débile!” You can’t believe what you’re seeing. They’re spouting gibberish at each other! It’s ridiculous! You ask what’s going on. The one you knew from before turns to you. He tells you that he is not, in fact, retarded. In reality, he speaks a language called “French”. You shake your head sadly and say, “I don’t think you understand. You have a deficit. You can’t talk right. If you’re not retarded, then how come you can’t pronounce ‘this’? You say ‘zis’ instead.” He expostulates. He argues that other Frenchmen can understand him just fine. Therefore, he doesn’t have a deficit. He just talks differently from you. If it’s a deficit, then how come other French people can understand him? You laugh warmly and say, “That doesn’t count! You can only talk to other French people because they’re all retarded, too!” Let me tell you another story. Imagine a world where 98% of people are autistic. In this scenario, autistic behavior is normal. Imagine that you grew up in such a world. Nobody else makes eye contact. They just stand at right-angles to the person they’re talking to. As a child, you looked people in the eye too much. That’s abnormal behavior. You must be crazy or something. Everyone else is very detail-oriented. You don’t care about detail too much. Why can’t you retain details? Are you even awake? Everyone else has a special interest that absorbs their attention. You don’t have anything like that. What’s wrong with you? Don’t you have an interest in anything? Everyone else soothes themselves with repetitive motions, like rocking back and forth. It’s called “stimming”. But you, you never stim. You must have issues with stress management. If you don’t stim, then how do you calm down? Are you dangerous? You never talk to yourself, either, and that’s just weird. Don’t you ever think about things? If you don’t talk to yourself, that means you never think. Clearly, your head is totally empty. Is anybody in there? Are you even a real person? Eventually, someone has you examined by a doctor. Rocking back and forth, he tells you (while looking at the wall) that the signs are all there. Too much eye contact. Insufficient attention to detail. No special interests. No stimming. No self-talk. The diagnosis is clear: you’re crazy. You object that you’re not retarded. You’re just different. You’ve met one other person like you, who is your good friend. You and that person get along fine. The doctor laughs warmly and says, “That’s because you’re both crazy!”

question: Are people with high functioning autism known to be speech impaired?
answer: Are people with high functioning autism known to be speech impaired? A person with high functioning autism may or may not have a speech impediment. The two sets of difficulties may occur together, but neither has to arise from the other. It’s important to distinguish speech from language. A tape recorder can exhibit speech, but the recorder itself lacks language. A native ASL signer has plenty of language, but uses motions of the limbs, torso, and face to communicate rather than speech. Language form (e.g. grammar and diction) and language content (meanings of words, phrases, and sentences) can be intact in high functioning autistic people. However, people with high functioning autism often have difficulties with the social use of language. For example, many of them have difficulty understanding and using figures of speech and other non-literal language. Many find it hard to follow basic conversational rules such as taking turns, making plausible assumptions about what the listener does or doesn’t know, and interrupting others in an appropriate way.

question: What is your personal definition (not the scientific definition) of high-functioning autism or Asperger's?
answer: Asperger’s or high functioning autism is the physical manifestation of randomness with an ironic cherry on top. We’re at the mercy of (truly) unique brains, an eclectic mix of traits, varying strength of those traits, our environment, personalities, and more. It’s all pretty strange… Non-Boring Brains - While we have a great deal in common, autism is bizarrely individualized. My favorite studies are those that involve fMRI: actually scanning the brain to get hard data on autism. Among those, are studies that show the autistic brain is much more varied and unique compared to the NT brain.[1] So all brains are unique, but some brains are more unique than others. I find the idea of owning a truly unique brain profoundly beautiful. (See Martin Silvertant's answer to How is autistic brain connectivity different from typical brain connectivity? for a wonderful synopsis) Trait Trail Mix - Take some random people, remove the social obsession, impair cognitive empathy, and then fill the available space with obsessive interests, compulsive behavior, repetitive whatever, repetitive whatever, sensory changes, synesthesia, alexithymia, raisins (trail mix always needs raisins for some reason), sensory issues, and god knows what else. Voila! Autism! But wait, there’s more… Game of Traits - It would be pretty boring if the Starks prevailed in the first Ice & Fire book, just like autism would be boring if only one trait prevailed. I have some of the items on that list above, but not all. Same is likely true for autistics reading this (if one of you got them all, please comment so we can anoint you the winner). I have hearing and light sensitivity, with some touch/texture issues, but it’s fairly manageable. I hate raisins but have some challenges around compulsive/repetitive behaviors. If every possible trait has a slider from zero (the lowest) to one-hundred, it’s likely your autism is unique too! My Environment is Trying to Kill Me - I’ve noted this elsewhere, but with autism, quality of life can vary based on where you live. My son was hugely sensitive to wet clothes, which drove him crazy. He (relatively speaking), hit the autistic lottery since we live in a desert, where we get 12 inches of rain per year. I can’t even imagine how horrible his life would have been if he’d been born in Waialeale, Hawaii (rainiest place in the US at 460 inches of rain per year). With any sensitivity, you can conjure a place where it would be either easy to manage, unbearable, or somewhere in between. Personality Blues - While there are only two of us formally diagnosed, there are strong signs of autism across four generations in my family. The quality of life across generations and individuals has varied hugely. One person was never able to maintain employment (from their 20s to retirement age). His sibling was fascinated by mechanical things, married, had a large family, stable income, and seemed genuinely happy. Another is a tireless worker, but always has strong personality conflicts with their managers. Some are pleasant, others jerks, there are optimists and pessimists, hard and lazy workers, you name it. Some have been able to parlay their autism into advantages, others have been oppressed by it. Special and Not-So-Special Interests - If an autistic is really lucky, they may be able to translate their interests into a career. That can be a huge advantage, so a girl fascinated by fish grows up to be a marine biologist. Somewhere else, a guy is mesmerized by birthdates and can name the five most famous people born on a given day of the year. He’s popular for about half a party… We all live with this surreal mix. In some cases, the mix delivers unambiguous gifts. Other times the delivery is very clearly a curse. Some days are mostly a gift, some mostly curse. Now the ironic part: despite autism being considered a ‘disorder’, with all of the normal (average) people horrified at the thought, some of us believe we are better off as autistic. question: Why have many people with high-functioning autism thought they might be psychopathic before they got diagnosed with ASD?
answer: I’m one of those autistics who thought he was a psychopath. Watching Dexter and then subsequently reading the novels, I felt a vague connection - here was a neurological condition that seemed to partially explain why I felt so emotionally distanced from things. The counterpoint was that I also sometimes experience a much greater emotional impact than a situation warrants, and psychopathy did not offer an explanation for that. I even went so far as to take a few of those online “are you a psychopath” tests and while I scored technical positives on a very select few points, the results were pretty conclusively “no”. Then one day about a year ago, an ASD quiz hit my Facebook feed and I decided on a whim to take it even though I had no suspicions in that direction. I scored as “on the spectrum” and when I shared my surprise with my wife, she said “I thought you knew”. So that’s where I am today - I’ve taken a couple different online tests a handful of times each over the past year and the results are fairly consistent despite my efforts to always answer “in the moment” instead of just repeating my answers from previous tries. I have not actually sought a professional diagnosis, but feel comfortable with the ‘fit’ of my self-diagnosis and with how that has affected the way I view and manage my social interactions. On Quora, I have just recently started seeing answers posted by Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht ND RP and Athena Walker, which have given me further insights into the two conditions, how they differ, and why they might be confused by someone not familiar enough with them to see those differences.

question: Can someone have high-functioning autism without showing any signs of it when they were a child?
answer: High functioning autism is just a term (now going out of favour) which merely describes the level of independence an individual has: it does not describe the symptoms. What you are potentially referring to is what is typically named Aspergers which is part of the Autism Spectrum. A defining feature of Aspergers is that there is an absence of language delays as a young child. Additionally, a child with Aspergers may not display ‘symptoms’ of autism in a noticeable way. This, of course, is not the same as saying the traits do not exist. An Aspergers child finds it easier to copy behaviours for example and this might give the impression that there are no problems. However, as a person goes through life they experience different challenges and certain autistic traits may start to become more obvious. Additionally, many autistic people who have tried to adapt their behaviours to societal norms may reach a point of exhaustion or burn out and be no longer able or willing to mask their behaviours. In answer to your question, if you are looking at someone else and thinking that they didn't display autistic traits when they were younger so they can't be autistic, it is entirely possible that they were just adept at masking their behaviours. However, if you are thinking about this in terms of yourself, you will absolutely know if you struggled with certain things when you were younger even if you managed to convince everyone else that everything was fine.

question: Why do people with high functioning autism have difficulty understanding and following through basic concepts?

Depression and anxiety both cause issues with everyday (which I think is probably more appropriate than ‘simple’, since cooking and driving aren’t ‘simple’ tasks) tasking. question: Which school districts in the Bay Area provide inclusion for kids with high-functioning autism?
answer: So the decision to include a student in a “regular” classroom is made by the IEP team, which includes district representatives, parents, and any doctors, therapists, or psychiatrists that serve the child. Full inclusion is NOT recommended by the LDA (Learning Disabilities of America). Full Inclusion of All Students with Learning Disabilities in the Regular Education Classroom They support the IDEA which is the Individual with Disabilities Education Act. This act which mandates…A free and appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment appropriate for the students’ specific learning needs.A team approved Individualized Education Program (IEP) that includes current functioning levels, instructional goals and objectives, placement and services decisions, and procedures for evaluation of program effectiveness.A placement decision must be made on an individual basis and considered only after the development of the IEP.A continuum of alternative placements to meet the needs of students with disabilities for special education and related services.A system for the continuing education of regular and special education and related services personnel to enable these personnel to meet the needs of children with disabilities.In many cases, having a child in a regular education classroom is beneficial for socialization or academics, sometimes it is not. It depends on the child and the severity of their disabilities. Many districts are attempting to move to this model as it is cheaper, regardless of the impact on the child. It is up to the parent to demand the services that IDEA mandates for their child. Many students can be quite successful with a 1:1 instructional aide in a general education classroom. In some ways this can be the most beneficial, as the child receives specialized instruction by a professional trained in their disability, while at the same time avoiding the “stigma” of either a special day class or special education school. Other students require a special education school that focus’ on their particular disability in order to have access to all of the services that they need. Full inclusion is a money saving method used by school districts that CAN benefit some. However some students are NOT served by this model.

question: Is it possible for people with high functioning autism to have sensory overload?
answer: Functioning labels aren’t helpful. Take it from me, as an actually autistic person. Let me tell you about two autistic people I know. One (let’s call him A) has a good job as a teacher. His IQ is higher than that of over 98% of the population. He speaks two languages fluently. He plays bass in a rock band, he’s happily married, he has a social life. He’s been active in several community groups and has done plenty of charity work. He’d be regarded by most people as high functioning. The other (let’s call him B) gets overwhelmed very easily by flickering lights or discordant noises. He has meltdowns and shutdowns brought on by sensory overload, and at such times he becomes completely non-verbal and non-functional, and struggles to understand basic spoken instructions. He rocks back and forth and flaps his hands. He hides away in a darkened room under a weighted blanket to avoid interacting with other people. He’d be regarded by most people as low functioning. A and B seem like very different people, even though they are both autistic. But here’s the thing: they are actually the same person. They are both me. A is the ‘me’ that I allow others to see most often. ‘B’ is the other side of me, that others see far less often, but he’s no less real despite that. The same person can be ‘high functioning’ and ‘low functioning’ at different times. That’s why functioning labels are unhelpful. ‘High functioning’ is a label that is often used as an excuse to deny autistic people the help that they need, just because they don’t need it when that side of them is visible.

question: Is high functioning autism considered Asperger syndrome?
answer: High-functioning Autism is NOT a classified diagnosis — and NEVER has been. Some well-meaning diagnosticians took to adding it as an informal explanation of Asperger's Syndrome, which often had little or no real meaning to those diagnosed with it. But the two are NOT the same things, and widespread misunderstanding and misinterpretation soon followed. Asperger’s Syndrome — a distinctive profile of Autism — has NOT been a classified diagnosis since mid-2022 — when it was declassified by the World Health Organisation in the ICD-11 Confirmed Edition of its diagnostic manual

question: How does risperidone help for people with high-functioning autism?
answer: I recently answered a similar question. We started giving our son Risperidone when he was 8, because his “autistic rage” was making it difficult and sometimes dangerous to be around him. Most of the time he was a very sweet person, although “high strung” and anxious. The Risperidone was a life-changer. He’s taken it for 17 years now, and it, plus Focalin for severe ADHD, have given him a life. He graduated from a good college and is now in grad school. He has friends, but he still has difficulty with a lot of practical things and social skills. He’ll sometimes say, “Let me know if I’m doing something annoying, because I have Asperger’s, and I can’t always tell.” A few years ago he tried taking a lower dose, with a thought to getting off of it, but on a half dose he found himself chewing our leather couch, beside himself with anger because his baseball team lost when the umpire blew a call, and he said, “Well, that experiment didn’t work.” He takes it at night, and it helps him sleep and not get so “worked up” about things that make him nervous or upset him. For our son’s ADHD, it took several tries to find the right medication. After he “maxed out” on Focalin, adding Wellbutrin to the mix was pretty helpful. As he gets older, impulsivity is less of a problem (although he’s still high energy and slender) but dealing with his day-to-day limitations in focus is a never-ending struggle. He also takes a little Clonidine for anxiety: that was the final piece of the puzzle. We’re thankful that his meds haven’t had to change much over the years and hope any long-term consequences will be minimal. For us, and now for him as an adult, taking meds is a “no-brainer.” He was risking institutionalization at age 8 but now lives fairly independently in a school-furnished apartment. He doesn’t yet feel safe to learn how to drive, and it’s unclear if he ever will. He sets multiple alarms and reminders to help remember to do necessary tasks, everything from taking out the trash and paying bills to everyday hygiene. He still needs extended time on tests in a distraction-free room. How and if that will work in the “real world” remains to be seen.

question: How do you communicate with high functioning autistic adults?
answer: In general, I find that words will do. I mean, come on, it isn’t as if we’re Martians or something. You can hold a conversation with us, just as you can with anybody else. Be aware that: We don’t much cotton to small talk, and we don’t always know what to say, unless it impinges on an interest of ours, in which case we are apt to speak at excessive length. Our faces and voices aren’t emotionally expressive, but inside, our emotions are unusually intense. We can be insensitive and frank, like a child. We don’t mean any harm. We’re just very straightforward, and we often don’t have a sense of how the other person is feeling. Many of us can’t even make out facial expressions — imagine what it’s like if you don’t know the difference between someone who is smiling, and someone who is enraged. We may have difficulty catching on to sarcasm, irony, and metaphor. This can make us vulnerable. I’ll borrow this from another answer, because it’s so good: Don’t assume we have an ulterior motive. We generally don’t. That kind of falsity is basically a neurotypical thing. We may not make eye contact. This isn’t because we have anything to hide, but because we find eye contact too emotionally taxing. And — we don’t take hints. “Gee, I like that dress” doesn’t mean “I want you to get me that dress for my birthday” to us. It means that you like the dress. You have to be direct with us. But, you know, while all of this is true, it’s probably subtler than you think. Typically, you’ll just find us a little bit odd. Most people don’t even recognize that someone is an Aspie.

question: How do I communicate with non-verbal autistic adults?
answer: I’m by no means an expert in this subject, but have worked with many adults, from young to not so young… that have been not expressed themselves vocally. Autism is a neuro-developmental difference. When the nervous system is altered from what is “typical”, there can be changes along any part of the communication coding and decoding process that can attribute to not being able to speak. This can be physical or cognitive causes.. and there can be more than one change in the process and not just ONE cause. Depending on what change or changes have happened to affect this person’s ability to speak, and what capabilities for language are present still, will determine what alternative forms of communication will most likely be successful. So you have to find the abilities to communicate. Carly Fleischmann is a great example of an autistic adult who only needed an alternative means of expression - in her case - typing. What she lacked was not the ability to process an spoken language, but the means to express. Her inability could have been caused by many things along the language process.. This will not be true with all autistic people. There could be audio processing issues so that the sounds of language cannot be interpreted by the brain. It could be something as deep as not making sense of what is seen… no continuity cause and effect… object permanence… things that are very basic to making sense of our senses. I’m sure you can find information about how the brain processes language.. how we make sense of our world… You have to find a way to evaluate the person’s capabilities… indications of other forms of how the person relates to all things around them. Eye movement, gestures, patterns of behavior, actions and reactions etc. Every person will be different in how complex of a language they can process. How long it will take to develop and so on. I worked for a year teaching a young autistic lady to use American Sign Language. Her expressive abilities were only basic.. I’m not sure how much her language developed later in life. This was back in the early 90s… so there were not the electronic options we have today. I’ve worked with deaf-blind adults, born deaf-blind who were taught basic sign language for communication. I worked with a man who grew up in a very small town and was the only deaf person there… was there all his life and the sign language he learned was what “home signs” he developed with family… I believe there is a human need to communicate in some form. If you can find this person’s abilities, you may be able to develop a form of communication with them too.

question: What are some ways to communicate with an autistic child or adult who does not speak much or at all? How can you teach them things like social skills, manners, etc.?
answer: Here’s a list of things that can help:Have a box or bag of sensory items that they can bring with them everywhere in case they become overstimulated. Some good things to have in the sensory box/bag are sunglasses, noise cancelling headphones, scented squishies, something they can chew on, something soft like a puffball, and something rough and textured like a plastic buckeye.Take them clothes shopping with you if they’re up for it and have them feel the different clothes to see what textures they’re okay with wearing. They’re also more likely to wear things that are soft, stretchy, or loose. Hoodies, T shirts, leggings, jeggings, sweatpants and basketball shorts are usually a good place to start.Sometimes you have to talk to them like you’re directing a toddler away from the candy aisle, calm, direct, and focused.When they’re starting to have a meltdown you NEED to stay calm and ask them yes or no questions, occasionally if they’re younger you should gradually change the subject and that usually helps a lot. Sometimes you just have to ask them if they would like some alone time to breathe and calm down, sometimes you have to show them how to take deep breaths in order to keep themselves from getting too worked up, which is especially important if they’re younger. Just breathe in and out slowly and tell them to repeat after you and that everything is going to be okay.If they’re acting inappropriately in public do NOT under ANY circumstances get onto them in front of everyone, they might not understand that what they’re doing is inappropriate for the situation, even if it’s obvious to you, even if they’re screaming or cussing. What you need to do is take them somewhere private and explain to them why that’s inappropriate behavior and how they should communicate their needs next time, CALMLY.If you’re having trouble agreeing on something, be a good example and show them how to compromise. If they want to go to the park but you want to go shopping, agree to go to the park for an hour and then go shopping for an hour.A big part of teaching someone who is neurodivergent is remaining calm and educating them instead of degrading them. Degradation and confrontation will only make them not want anything to do with you and not want to talk. Hope this helped someone out there! 😊

question: How do people interpret the facial expressions of autistic adults who cannot communicate verbally? Do you have any personal experience with this?

It has to do with understanding why an autistic person would be in distress and the motivations behind their behavior. I'm able to do that because I have similar reactions myself to the same types of situations. For example, I remember being in a classroom with a child who was making sounds of distress. It was obvious to me that he was overstimulated and perhaps the music in the classroom was making him unhappy. Nonautistic people seem to interpret such things to mean that we are trying to be uncooperative out of aggressiveness, as they would likely be doing if they did such a thing. question: How can an NT person effectively communicate with an adult autistic person to ensure a smooth and natural conversation flow?
answer: Do not expect smooth and natural conversation flow. We may need time to process information and/or more time to verbalise our answers. Communicate precisely and avoid any subtext or additional non-verbal comunicates. There’s no place for guessing games. In the same vein - do not try to read subtext or non-verbal communicates of autistic people. Even those who are good at masking may sometimes feel off. Process just words that were said. Questions are good! If you have doubts, you can ask what we ment. Maybe we used wrong word or something got “lost in translation”. Ask before you got angry or deffensive. Allow us ask clarifying questions too. We sometimes need more data to start the process or need to know how exactly you want something made. It’s not attack on you, we are not being rude, defiant or mean. We need to know. Do not yell. That's surefire way to overload us with stimuli and push us into meltdown or shutdown.

question: My 9-year-old son was diagnosed recently with Asperger’s Syndrome and I feel powerless to help him. Where do I start and what do I do?
answer: Heya! I'm an autistic adult. I have two brothers who are also autistic. I was diagnosed at twelve, my older brother was diagnosed at fourteen, and our younger brother was diagnosed at two. Suffice it to say, I have a good bit of personal experience on the subject! First thing's first! Autism spectrum disorders are not strictly things that we need “help with,” anymore than, say, you need help to learn a foreign language, or you need help to participate in your own hobbies. There's a lot of information out there which suggests that autism is essentially as terrible and bad as a death sentence, or cancer, or other world-ending things. I would like to reassure you that these versions of our lives are patently false (yes, even for autistics who are considered very low-functioning. Yes even for nonverbal autistics. Yes even for autistics who live in assisted living). Start by talking with him honestly. Autistic kids (and kids in general) tend towards understanding a lot more than us adults give them credit for. Explain to him that there's a name for why he has some of his issues, and why some of his strengths are so good. Let him ask questions. If you don't know the answer, offer to research it with him. This gives you both the opportunity to learn more about how autism affects him specifically. After all, if you've met one autistic person, you've met ONE autistic person. I'd suggest that you explore the ASAN website as well - this is an organization devoted to autistic self-advocacy, education, and information. There are also online forums for autistic people, and usually we're okay with parents asking us questions about how best to help with individual issues, such as hypersensitivity to sounds or lights, or over-stimulation. Don't use ABA therapy. Most autistic adults who have been through it consider it to have been a major traumatic incident in their lives. It's also based off of inherently abusive, dehumanising practices back when it was thought that autistic people had deficient theory of mind abilities. A lot of having an autistic kid is just listening and learning. We develop at our own pace and may go in surprising directions, but if you give us the chance to communicate with you in our own ways, you'll find that we're pretty straightforward, and don't view our spectrum disorder as being a bad thing or something that needs “fixing.” Sometimes we need changes to the environment we're in (like if there's too much light or sound or colors), but in and of itself that stuff is just us having a different threshold for handling it than neurotypicals.

question: Why are autistic adults not taken seriously in discussions on autism?
answer: It all depends on who is listening. If you are having a discussion with someone like me, I will probably be taking notes. My son is profoundly autistic and non verbal. I’ve learned in time to understand even the slightest gestures as communication. It’s still not much. I might sometimes understand what he needs, but not what he feels. He can’t tell. But other autistic people can. So, I listen carefully. I am like a sponge, absorbing information. Sometimes, the knowledge I get is priceless. My most recent example, would be a post of an autistic adult here, on Quora. My son is almost 7, so despite his condition, I try to apply rules that would go for most children. As a teacher and parent I know how important it is to give a choice to children. So asking something like What shall we do first, garden or playground?, shouldn’t be the cause of an absolute meltdown. Wrong, my son’s brain doesn’t work like that. An autistic adult on here, shared his struggles with choice. The anxiety it brings, the unnecessary pressure it puts on him. So I tried the new approach. Simplify the options and offer one at a time. For the first time ever, my son started to follow simple instructions. The same might not apply to everybody, as the spectrum is so wide. But you know what? If it helps one autistic person, if it helps one mother, one family, it’s still good enough. There is always someone listening, so please don’t stop talking.

Autistic often try to accommodate for both sides, but it fails frequently because it isn't realistic.

question: Any advice for someone who works with autistic adults?
answer: Honestly, your best bet is to read a lot of stuff by autistic people. Most of the stuff written by researchers is stuff that never tries to understand us or learn how we experience the world. Simon Baron-Cohen is notorious in the autistic community for his many comments indicating he has no fucking clue what we are like or how we experience the world. You’ll find some great resources here: Autism Self Education Resources The more you understand how we think and experience the world, the better you will be able understand, communicate with, and help your clients. If you are working with non-verbal autistic adults, definitely take some time to learn about AAC and the types other non-verbal autistics have found most helpful.

question: Why do we hear a lot about children with autism and not much about adults with autism?
answer: The answer to this is likely complicated… Here are some of my guesses, and they are likely to be United States -centric… In the U.S., there is more help for kids than adults in many ways, and (lucky) kids have the advantage of fierce parental advocacy. It’s possible that allistics don’t listen to autistic adults as well as they do to allistic adults, due to communication differences. So allistic parents advocating for kids may be heard better than autistic adults self-advocating. Autistic adults seem to become invisible to some allistic parents as soon as they find some way to have a voice. “You’re not like my autistic child” seems to be the gist of statements that are thrown at autistic self-advocates by some allistic parents of autistic children… Even though those autistic adults may have had the same issues as kids. (Yes many autistics learn coping skills and behave much differently in public as adults.) Advocating for kids is considered generally a great thing! Kids are cute, they are the future, etc. etc. etc. There is a huge social construct of helping kids; adults “should” be self-sufficient. Self-advocating is hard to do sometimes without some people thinking you selfish. (True more of some sub-groups, like females, than others. Imho.) There’s not much of a safety net for adults with all sorts of problems in many ways in the U.S., but kids have the whole schooling system surrounding them, so researching how to help autistic adults isn’t connected to as large a network of providers etc. Historical reasons — “Autism Speaks”, one of the best-funded autism nonprofits in the U.S., was founded by wealthy allistic adults with autistic child relatives. They’ve partly used this funding head start to maintain a primary position in the public eye and garner a lion’s share of donations, and they continue to be mostly child-focused…not necessarily in ways that actual autistics agree with, either. Many autistic adults are “camouflaging”, i.e. passing, and didn’t even know they were autistic until very recently. So the population of diagnosed kids is much higher, population percentage-wise. This may be particularly true of autistic women. Autistic adults who are recently diagnosed and have been “passing” know they’d have to potentially face stigma and maybe have careers damaged by prejudice, if they “come out”; this at least slows down the process for many… there is a lot to deal with. I bet there are more!
comment_answer: I agree with basically all of this — but I think there’s one more important reason. Widespread knowledge about Autism is a pretty new thing — even in the medical community. Going back just a few decades there were a lot less people diagnosed than is the case today, and many adults who today would’ve been diagnosed might not even know that they’re on the spectrum. You can’t be visible as an adult autist unless you actually know (or at the very least suspect) that you’re autistic. I dunno how old the average diagnosed autist is today, but I’d not be surprised if the answer is under 25. Not because there’s not also a lot of people who are 40, 60 or 80 and on the spectrum, but quite simply because so few of the latter have a diagnosis and/or knowledge about autism.

question: How open are autistic adults about being autistic?
answer: I just ended a three-year contract at a school whose population of kids with special needs hovers around 25%, which is higher than the national average. I built the inclusion program from the ground up and really enjoyed the impact I had on the students and their families. One of my students, Adam*, came to us three years ago. He is on the autism spectrum, and he had been receiving ABA services at his preschool. His parents wanted him to experience a more flexible environment that utilized a different therapeutic approach so they enrolled him at our school. When I met his parents, it was clear that his father had many similar characteristics to his son. This man was clearly highly intelligent, accomplished and rigid. In the first couple of years of knowing him, Adam’s father and I did not interact much outside of annual IEP meetings but I always appreciated his direct communication and dry sense of humor. He was quite pleasant to deal with. Fast forward and Adam has significant struggles in the program. It turns out that being flexible with boundaries and expectations is NOT what he needs. As a flexible program, it was difficult for us to adapt or change our methods without intervention from a behavior specialist. The woman we hired is a miracle worker. When I say she is the Mary Poppins of working with autistic people, she really is. She’s just incredible. Every time I see her and talk to her, I am in awe of her expertise and her ability to clearly communicate, and figure out what autistic people need to reach their full potential. When she came into the picture and started attending meetings with the family, it was like she knew who Adam’s father was from the moment he opened his mouth. Anytime we discussed Adam’s behavior, Adam’s father openly shared that his challenges were the same when he was Adam’s age and he “turned out fine.” Now, Adam’s father had a mother who took no shit. She raised Adam’s father to be a successful professional, so she also knew how to manage Adam (since he was just like his father). It was fantastic to see Grandma in action. Adam’s father was open about his quirks and did not see any problem with who he was. I loved this about him. From my experience, autistic adults are quite self-aware and open about their challenges. In fact, once autistic kids become self-aware, it’s even more beautiful to see how perceive themselves. Take a look at this letter that one of my students wrote to me this year. question: How can I make sure an autistic child reaches their potential, without undermining the wellbeing of the child?
answer: I cannot answer this question out of the personal experience of raising a child that is autistic. I answer it, from my own memories growing up, and what I’ve learned from others who are autistic. What is wellbeing? A quick search of the definition says… “the state of being comfortable, healthy, or happy.” I was a child that was raised in a very stressful / abusive family. - I think it is important to consider wellbeing in the immediate and long term for a child. Immediate term - What is there current life experience? Internally what are they thinking and feeling? Is there constant fear and anxiety in their lives? Is there so much confusion that they cannot figure out how to cope in their interactions with people and processing how to communicate? Is there a chance for them to rest mentally and physically? Are they constantly in a fight/flight/freeze mode or can they just let go of control and the struggle for understanding and just BE? Are they being encourage to be themselves or what others expect them to be? Are they learning that being autistic is a bad thing? That they are broken and need to be fixed? When they face an overwhelming autistic challenge, are they given an autistic solution that works or neurotypical solution that may make things worse? When they are crying for help, how are their autitic needs being met? Are they learning how to be their autistic best? Or do the give in and give up trying to be autistic, and settle for a dysfunctional neurotypical life in order to fit in and please others? “the state of being comfortable, healthy, or happy.” Long term - Our childhood is the stage of development we must go through, to become adults. We start totally dependent and hopefully reach adulthood as independent beings. For adults to maintain their sense of wellbeing, they need to have learned how to control themselves mentally and physically. This means, as children they needed to develop who they are. And they are autistic children. Let me rephrase the question - and see if the answer is not obvious… “How can I make sure a neurotypical child reaches their potential, without undermining the wellbeing of the child?” Allow and support this child to develop according to their biological needs. What would happen to a NT child if you forced them to be autistic? Gave them only autistic solutions to their neurotypical needs? What would it do to their wellbeing? Remember too - that the environment these autistic children are in, has evolved to support the NT biological needs. Some of these supports will work for autitic children/adults too, but many do not. The biological/neurological needs of an autitic child are different. If you fulfill these autitic needs, they will be able to develop the knowledge and skills to maintain their balance as autistic adults. When we know ourselves, know our skills and limitations, and how to keep our lives in balance, we will thrive as adults. Can there be any better source of wellbeing than being self aware and in self control? Providing autistic solutions to the autistic needs of children, will take a cooperative effort between autitic and non-autistic adults. Just as autistic people do not know what it is like to be neurotypical, the opposite holds true. Working together to better understand what autitic children are experiencing and need, may best be understood by those autistic adults who had the same experiences and needs. Children need to know and see autistic adults. This will ground them in normality, give context to their lives and give them a place in society. It will show them they are NOT alone. Not some freak of nature, just a different “normal”. Its ok, to be who you were born to be. These are some of the fundamental needs autistic children have that are so easy to overlook because they taken for granted in the neurotypical world.
comment_answer: Great answer. So many parents think about their own needs and not the needs of their child. When I think back to my childhood I can only remember the things I were told NOT to do. Don't talk like that. Don't play like that. Don't run like that. Don't look like that. Don't move like that. I cannot think of a single time when I was praised for doing something. I also did my best to give them choices (would you like broccioli or carrots?)and not spring surprises on them (we are going to the shops this afternoon).

question: Why does applied behavior for analysis for children with autism spectrum disorders lead to PTSD in autistic adults?
answer: Because even under the best circumstances, ABA is aimed at training children to act as if they were somebody else. The priority isn’t on how to function or how to stay safe or how to communicate well, it’s how to act normal—the first problem with that is that it’s degrading. The second problem with it is that autistic people have reasons to act the way they do. They avoid eye contact because eye contact is uncomfortable for them. They get anxious around certain noises because those noises hurt. Etc. ABA does nothing to teach these kids how to be comfortable with these things, it trains them to act as though they’re comfortable. Imagine being told that treats and affection are conditional upon your pretending that you’re not in pain, not scared, not grossed out. Imagine being a kid in pain and knowing you can’t tell an adult, you can’t ask for help, you can’t even express the fact that you’re in pain (or afraid, or angry, or anything else) or you’ll get in trouble because pretending to be normal is more important than being happy or safe. And that’s under ideal circumstances. When ABA was invented, it involved a lot of “aversives,” that is punishments for kids who didn’t get it right, like being sprayed in the face with vinegar for not acting normal enough. Officially, it’s supposed to be all about rewards now, not punishments, but a lot of places still use aversives anyway. And a lot of programs are gruelling—like little kids putting in 40 hours a week of training. I have heard that some therapists call what they do “ABA” so that insurance will cover it but they actually do something else, so it might be complicated, but basically ABA is about training little kids to ignore their wants and needs because the experts think who they are is bad and wrong.

question: Autism: If a child who can't communicate well displays frustration by hitting and pinching people and pets, how do you teach them to stop?
answer: Something I have heard from several parents of autistic children who don't have verbal fluency is that if the child has a way to communicate without words (sign language and/or iPad apps) this lowers frustration and reduces hitting/biting. Something I've heard from autistic adults is that it was very stressful to them to have people tell them to "use their words" when they wanted to, but couldn't. They still flinch if they hear someone use that phrase.

question: Why is my ASD level 1 kid able to sustain play with his sibling but can't do the same with other kids?
answer: Due to Autism’s genetic components it is possible this sibling may also be autistic, but even if that is not the case they are both much more familiar with each other and thus know how to communicate with one another. I am autistic, but my brother is not, though we still got along fairly well for the most part, though our relationship got a bit strained during our teen years due to me becoming violent during that time due to anger issues (thankfully both problems have been addressed). Autistic children and in many cases even autistic adults often struggle to communicate with their peers and most people don’t know how to communicate with autistic people which creates a double empathy problem. His communication skills might improve as he gets older, but he will struggle for a while. This isn’t entirely linear though as I had far more trouble relating to my peers during my teen years that at any other time in my life aside from when I was under the age of 6. Everyone was so much nicer to me in elementary school than in middle school and high school. The adult world is also far harsher, and autistic burnout is an unfortunate reality for many autistic adults that can sometimes cause regression via executive dysfunction. I bring this up not to scare you or make you lose hope as there are successful autistic adults even with these challenges, but it takes a lot of struggle to get there.

question: Does autism symptoms get worse with age? Or is that just part of the spectrum?
answer: This is a very important question because it addresses the phenomenon of how autistic expressions evolve with age. I feel it is very important to correct the use of the word “symptoms” as if Autism is a disease… Our behaviors are expressions of our neurology for both autistic and neurotypical people. Autism is OUR normal - it is who we are and what we do and is no more a symptom of autism than what YOU do is symptom of being neurotypical. Autism is our normal as neurotypical behaviors are your normal… This is so important to understand - especially if you are not autistic and a parent, sibling or spouse.. I see two general shifts as one ages… 1) coping mechanisms evolve, get refined , more habitual, and more adaptable to changing situations… A good example is “eye contact” - Remember as kids we are still becoming self-aware so may not even recognize there is a problem with eye contact. There are so many reactions we get that are confusing, it is overwhelming until you start “studying” situations and actively try to address them. This is what masking refers to - we cover up our autistic traits with behaviors we hope will make us appear to behave like everyone else. I was doing this not knowing I was autistic. Its an attempt to be more acceptable or less noticeable. This “masking” comes a great expense to us on a physical and psychological / emotional level. Some people who know they are autistic, can consciously mask and the benefits outweigh the expense ( example is how you act to secure your job) . I felt ashamed, less-than, broken and ostracized. It is reinforced, by not only people’s reactions, but by the social/communication challenges that seem to happen for no reason other than it is who WE are… Almost a feeling of bad fortune or even some cosmic punishment we are fated to endure. I’m being literal here and not exaggerating! I remember the thought of my life being a “mistake” . I believe this ties into the high suicide rate in our community. Remember, what we are experiencing feels normal… and as far as we know it is the same experience everyone else has.. So knowing we are autistic or not, we spend our lives “ fine-tuning” our appearance to be what we need to be - to be accepted or at least tolerated. As I said above masking comes at a great expense… this includes the energy it takes to mentally process and monitor our actions and everyone’s reactions. Eventually, we become exhausted. I think at some level we think we will some day not have to “mask” any more… that we will just become what we hope is “normal”. It never happens… :( This is why I tell parents with autistic children - that your child will become an autistic adult. Don’t try to make them neurotypical - help them to be THEIR best as an autistic person. They have to master being true to themselves, before they can be their best at anything. This does not mean they should not be learning how neurotypicals do things… But what is critically important is that they are not being told, intentionally or unintentionally, that being autistic is being bad or doing something wrong and THAT is why the are learning neurotypical behaviors. It is a very subtle difference from the neurotypical perspective but can be devastating from the autistic child/adult perspective. From the neurotypical perspective, as we age, they might say our “symptoms” have gotten better or we are less “autistic”. But the truth is autism is not a disease that can be cured. Our neurological system is as hardwired in us as our genetics. The behaviors can be altered, but not the underlying neurological autistic tendencies will always remain. So… eventually - “the juice is not worth the squeeze” and we get tired of or even unable to continue masking. I’ve seen this called Autistic-Burnout. I’ve lived a life of trying to be neurotypical. Now that I know who I am… I’m dropping the masking… and letting my natural tendencies emerge. This includes self stimming, using routines to my advantage, appreciating my abilities to focus and learn in depth all that my mind wants to know, appreciating my heightened senses… Giving myself permission to rest… and recharge… and NOT expect myself to function like a neurotypical person can. I’m experiencing a joy and freedom I’ve never known before! Overall, I’m embracing my autism, appreciating my autism, and being TRUE to myself. I AM AUTISITC!

question: Do Asperger /autistic people learn (from experience) to become less ‘open and trusting’ over time, or will they always be vulnerable?
answer: Hi Barbara, Everyone is different ESPECIALY us Auties! So this is just MY experience. The foundations of our personalities are reflections of our neurological construct just like our needs and motivations are also “hard wired” into us.. We are not “open and trusting” people because of high moral standards or virtues.. it is because this is how our minds process information… We try to deal in truths and absolutes.. We ARE very moral people with high standards, but that is our true nature… not something we’ve learned to become through self-discipline. We “assume” everyone else is like this because, after all, WE are just being our selves and of course this is how ALL people think and feel.. Right? To our minds this is the “only” way to logically live. It is too much effort and has no purpose to deal in anything but absolutes and truths… Ironically, these characteristics are over looked and the focus in put on what is “unusual or offensive” etc. Our lives are transparent. We communicate with the intention of clearly and accurately conveying information for everyone’s benefit. Our socialization is the same.. we are a “live and let live” people. We socialize with those we want to be around. There are no ulterior motivations… We understand power and hierarchy differently.. it is a natural order not a “man made” order. It will “naturally” establish itself based on who is best at what they do or what is needed for the community. I’m not saying we have achieved a utopian level of coexistence but our “system” is based on much more organic foundations than in the neurotypical community. In time, we learn everyone is NOT the same as we are… usually after being taken advantage of, or finding a person’s word or actions could NOT be trusted after repeated attempts… etc. Its the “school of hard knocks” and most of us are graduates! How autistic people react will be different. Some WANT to “master” socialization in the NT world and do so… I tended to isolate myself. I did not know WHY these things happened or what to do about them. After a while it only made sense to stop trying since it was just an exercise in frustration and personal pain. I had an abusive childhood and withdrew into myself in many ways. So it was natural reaction to withdraw from the socialization part of life. I think this issues emphasizes why I tell parents to raise their autistic child to be a well rounded, stable, self-aware and self- accepting AUTISTIC adult. Learning the necessary skills to navigate the NT world should be secondary to the primary needs of developing from an autistic child to an autistic adult. If they do not have a firm foundation that is true to who they are ( autistic) and they try to build a neurotypical structure on a weak autistic foundation, it is the recipe for disaster both personally and socially for that child. Off on a tangent… ( autistic trait) Anytime we act contrary to our nature - it creates stress and tension between who we really are and the way we feel me must act. In the case of being open and trusting: It is our nature - we do learn from our experiences and approach unknown people with caution and skepticism. but it is not who we are and that natural tendency does leave us vulnerable. question: As an autistic person, can you work? Is your life stable? Do you have any friends? My child just got diagnosed a few weeks ago, I can't stop crying, I'm so worried for him.
answer: NB: As well as being parent to an autistic child, I am autistic myself. My child was diagnosed as autistic in pre-school. Shortly after, in my 30’s, we realised that I am also autistic. I did extremely well at school - selective secondary school, 13.5 GCSE’s, 4 A-Levels, 2:1 BSc at Uni. I have worked in IT / Investment Banking (working on the software traders use to trade on the stock market) for over 10 years. I’ve been a team leader, a technical lead, and I’ve run big projects. I’m fine talking to clients, giving presentations, writing documentation, training newbies. I stopped working when my child started school, as they needed me to be available more than my career allowed. I now keep busy with vegetable gardening, knitting, sewing, and writing. I run a knitting group that meets every other week. My child is doing wonderfully, too: with the right school placement and private speech therapy, they have made phenomenal progress. They are academically ahead of the curve across the board. I have friends. Not as many as an allistic (non-autistic) person might, but I have as many as I need. I’m friendly with everyone at the knitting group and have no problem being social with strangers in daily life (unless I’m burning out - but that’s not often, because I manage myself well). We both struggle with certain things: transitioning, sensory overload. We both need time alone to recharge, familiarity, and knowing what to expect in any given situation. What’s really important for you to do now is to realise that you have a big hand in shaping how your child’s life pans out from this point on. You know they’re autistic, and that’s GREAT! The most important thing any parent can do for their child is to know them, really know them, and do everything they can to meet their needs. That’s doubly true for autistic kids, because their needs can be different from others. It’s going to be a learning curve for you for a while as you identify which autistic traits your child has (and doesn’t have). Once you identify a trait, you can work out how to make life easier for them. For example, my child is easily spooked by loud road noises, so they wear ear defenders. They also have a speech delay, so we use visual forms of communication to support that. I strongly suggest that you reach out to autistic adults, as you have done here, but more privately. Get to know them and understand their struggles and strengths - you’ll see some of them in your child. If you make some autistic friends, you can speak specifically about the struggles your child is having, and they probably already know how you can help and support them. After all, we’ve been living with it all our lives - we’ve worked out what works and what doesn’t. Don’t be sad. Your child is who they are, and autism just happens to be a part of that. It might not be what you expected, and you might not know what to do right now, but that’s okay, and that’s part of parenting. The important thing is that you move forward and learn how best to support your child, just as they are.
comment_answer: Don’t be sad. Be glad that you are aware. I am on the spectrum (Asperger’s). I would never have met him at something like a football game. The strange thing is — when I was a little girl, in the early 1960s, autism was much more poorly understood than it is today. Asperger’s was sort of “new” and thought only to occur in boys. Anyway, here’s a true story: when I was about three or four, my pediatrician said that I had “autistic tendencies.” My mother thought he said “ARTistic,” so she gave me paints and crayons and sketchpads. And I did do well in art. How do I know this? When I was in my 30s, I was painting a mural on consignment. One day, I told my mother about it. That led me to see a neuropsychologist, who confirmed that I was an adult with Asperger’s. It explained my WHOLE LIFE: extreme introvert, great difficulty sustaining eye contact, social awkwardness, panic when called upon in school, poor vocal volume control, complete loss of focus around sudden or sustained noise, hypersensitivity to tastes and textures, clumsiness in sports and dance, obsessive interests in certain topics, etc. etc. Now you know what to expect. Hopefully your child is at a point on the spectrum where they can function fairly well. Don’t worry about success in sports. Don’t expect them to be the prom king, or even want to go to prom. Understand when they can’t explain why certain foods feel weird in their mouth. question: If an autistic person seems very high-functioning or “normal,” does it mean they’re masking a lot or very good at masking?
answer: We autistic people do mature just as non-autistic people also mature. We are not adolescents all our lives, coping with high school cliques, bodily changes, emotional changes, etc. We learn, to varying degrees, how to be autistic adults, how to cope with a non-autistic adult world. So an autistic adult will not present the same as an autistic adolescent, and especially not as an autistic child presents. But we are still autistic — we still have sensory sensitivities, special interests, stimming, difficulties with unexpected change, problems communicating with and relating to non-autistic people, etc. We do, however, manage those problems in a more adult way. Not all of this is “masking”, but rather it also includes “maturity”. We shouldn’t lump all adult autistic behaviour into the “masking” bundle. Some of it is learning how to be an adult, and how to negotiate the adult world, something that all human beings need to learn. Teenage years are more turbulent than adult life. Being autistic complicates that process. Growing up does not mean that you are now “masking” whatever you felt and did as an adolescent — as though the adolescent you was the “real you” and the adult you is a “fake you”. It can mean that you have outgrown some of the drama of adolescence. So separating “masking” from “maturity” is an art. I coped a lot better as a thirty year old than I did as a twenty year old. I had help and I grew up emotionally, having greater strength and resilience. Instead of struggling, I was able to finish a degree, start a good career, and begin a lifelong relationship, resulting in marriage and children. At twenty, all this seemed impossibly remote. The difference is not that I learned to mask, but that I matured. PS: None of this means that masking isn’t a real issue, it just means that coping isn’t a simple function of “masking more” — there is also maturity to consider. The story is more complex than a single factor.

question: How do I deal with my students on the autism spectrum?
answer: Hello Efrayim, You must truly understand that we are very different from NT people in the most fundamental way - we are neurologically different. I cannot emphasize this enough. We are as different from you as a foreign language is from your native language. You must immerse yourself in the autistic community. To learn the “language” of autism, and see how autistic adults interact. What challenges we face. How we think and learn. How we maintain our physical and cognitive balance. The social/educational structure that meets neurotypical (NT) needs, does not accommodate the autistic child’s needs. There will be many accommodations that are needed for that child to thrive as an NT child would. Every “traditional” method must be reassessed to see if it fits the autistic child’s needs. This means how the child is prepared for preschool, their stages of development as well as what they need to develop at that stage of their autistic life. The introduction of concepts, the pace, the duration. The amount of environmental stimulation, such as lighting, sound, smells, how “busy” the room is, how the school clocks “alert” students, the bus ride in… All of it… Autistic people live intense lives because we filter out very little of our environmental stimulation. We also regulate and process this information very differently. We can be affected by a stimulation for weeks as it processes.. This is how deeply we consume all information. A depth of emotions and cognition rarely seen in NT children. In a sense even our concept of time is different than NT time. There will be other comorbid disorders along with the autism. Understand what these can be. I’m ASD, ADHD, dyslexic. have alexithymia, possible PTSD, theory of mind issues, I was hypoxic at birth… So Autism maybe just the tip of the iceberg. Develop, open, clear, concise communication with this child. Be as “matter of fact” about them being autistic as you are with the other students being neurotypical. It is part of your task to help them be autistic not neurotypical. If you hide or shelter them because they are autistic, you lay the foundations of guilt and shame. They must feel totally safe and comfortable expressing their needs. This may be through behavior or other means as well as through spoken language. This is a future autistic adult. They must learn autistic life skills as the other children learn NT life skills. These skills will be different because they are managing different neurological systems. If possible, find autistic peers and adults that can be models of HOW to be autistic. When age appropriate, online connections with other autistic peers and adults is a good substitute. This normalizes this child’s concept and self image of being autistic. Autistic and Neurotypical children are different. The way to teach both groups social interaction is to normalize the differences by letting everyone be true to their nature, not making the autistic child conform to the NT standards. Autistic and NT children need exposure to each other’s differences. Develop your network with autistic adults as advisors. You will see many behaviors you will not understand. Autistic people are all different but there is a common experience we all relate to.. We will not always have “THE” answer for every question, but we can give you a genuine autistic perspective. You can develop this network locally or through on-line groups, forums etc… I hope this gives you some important things to consider and integrate into your class. Best to you all…

question: How much overlap is there with ASD and c-PTSD? I have two independent diagnoses of Asperger's. Two psychiatrists have since said I only have c-PTSD and not ASD. I've had sensory issues since childhood and trauma from 18 months.

If they can give you specific reasons they think you are not… they can still be wrong if they have not worked with adults. If you do have doubts about your ASD, or if they offer other possibilities that seem to make sense too, it is possible the first diagnosis was a false positive. They are people and make mistakes. I’ve heard of older adults getting a false negative just because they could make eye contact. question: What are some examples of how people with autism have it rough?
answer: Job hunting, job hunting, job hunting. Most of what it takes to successfully land a decent job doesn’t rely on knowledge or actual practical skill (things autistic people are most likely to be strong in), but social skills and resources like a broad social network, the ability to give adequate eye contact, and the ability to decode and communicate in heavily coded social language (things many autistic people struggle with). As a result, the modern job hunting process, from resumes and cover letters to interviewing, can not only be stressful and confusing, but also often leads to long-term unemployment or underemployment due to neurotypical H.R. managers and recruiters dismissing or misjudging autistic candidates. The autistic person may be the perfect fit for the job, but if they don’t have a broad enough reference pool or are too direct in their cover letter, or come off as too socially awkward in an interview, or even just give an unexpected answer to one of those opaque and heavily coded interview questions, they will be passed over for someone less technically qualified but more socially adept. It’s not that we don’t try, we try very, very hard. It’s just that not everyone is a skilled masker or has access to the “proper” social resources. Some of us need a secret decoder ring to know when a question is asking exactly what it sounds like it is or if there is a hidden meaning that we must uncover and answer to properly in the same highly coded language. Some of us are just bright and talented but socially awkward. If neurotypicals could learn to accept the presence of bright-but-awkward people in their spaces, maybe we wouldn’t be seeing unemployment and underemployment rates for employable autistic adults ranging between 70% and 90%. We’re basically being cringed into poverty…

question: Is it even true that all autistics can understand all other autistics? That doesnt seem realistic since everyone is different.
answer: The idea you are referencing here is called the “double empathy” theory. Successful communication requires “role-taking”, or imagining how the other person will receive and understand the communication. Early theories of autism suggested that role-taking is something that autistic people are bad at. The double-empathy theory suggests that autistic people aren’t intrinsically bad at role-taking, they just have a mismatch with non-autistic people. Non-autistic people good at role-taking with other non-autistic people, and autistic people are good at role-taking with other autistic people. There’s a small amount of empirical evidence that backs this up, suggesting that autistic people do indeed communicate better with other autistic people than they do with non-autistic people. But neither the theory nor the evidence suggests that the communication difficulties faced by autistic people magically go away when they are in community with other autistic people. There are many more challenges autistic people face than just role-taking. However, from my own experience, it’s certainly easier to communicate with some autistic adults, because people with a lifetime of communication difficulties themselves can become very patient and considerate communicators. This isn’t universal, it’s just one of the reasons why autistic people can be more comfortable around other autistic people.

question: How is it that some people can be diagnosed with high-functioning autism but interact with others and display no visible signs of autism to the casual observer?
answer: A lifetime of practice (it's called autistic masking). This masking does come at a VERY high life cost for most of us. Most of us learned to “live” normally, but in near-constant misery as adults with depression, chronic fatigue, and bouts of extreme exhaustion. Acceptance and success in the neurotypical world we all live in often comes at a rather obscene price. There may be mild outward signs too, but just not the kind most people would recognize. Often, the person might be accused of having a temper/“short fuse" or be rather uncomfortable around loud or crowded places. Frequent migraines are often common too. Many of us “middle-age” folks that grew up unaware of our ASD will eventually build up a long-term condition known as “autistic burnout” or “autistic regression” after living too many years of unknowingly increasingly masking. The eventual crash known as Autistic Burnout seems to involuntarily (instantaneously) erase many of our masking abilities that we didn't even “know” we were engaging in. It can happen out of the blue, and result in EXTREME confusion and “brain fog". Recovery can be very slow if autistic burnout gets that far, as it requires learning to deprioritize most masking behaviors and also learning how to be one's true self for the first time ever at a relatively old age. Brilliant careers are often cut rather painfully short by this phenomenon. Masking skills can return in time, but are rarely at the high level they were before. *** Children with ASD can often begin masking/socially camouflaging their own real needs and preferences long before they're even potty trained. Anyone ever knowing that they have ASD is not required! Learning to avoid invalidating and negative consequences as kids can begin to occur even at an insanely young age. Many born with with ASD learn from personal observation far better than they are able to communicate with others (even from their youngest age). Intellectual ability on the high end just further increases one's ability to mask. Being told by parents and other adults that their natural instinctive behaviors are “bad behavior”and that they must “behave" properly around others or be punished may sink in very early. That unknowingly triggers more and more masking and efforts trying to “cope” with unnatural demands at any cost. Masking sensitivity to sensory stimulation(real physical pain/agony/anxiety) is much harder, but may be learned and can be done the same way by many of us. It also can be learned long before puberty.
