question: As a person who is high functioning ASD, what suggestions do you have to help families with low functioning ASD?
answer: Hello Marrianne! Every person is unique in what they need and how they fulfill these needs. This is even more true with autistic people because neurologically we are very unique. More so than people who are not autistic: Its just one of the characteristics of autism that our nervous system develops much more unique. Our bodies and minds are autistic and not neurotypical. Just as you would not expect a neurotypical child to grow up autistic, you cannot expect an autistic child to grow up neurotypical. Autistic children become autistic adults. Just as neurotypical children need to develop their neurotypical life skills, the same is true for autistic children. Then, as autistic adults, they will have the needed skills for their neurotype. Autistic children, who face difficult or dysfunctional levels of challenge, need to learn how to manage these challenges to the best of their ability. Let them develop autistic solutions to these challenges. If they need to stim let them stim. If they need isolation or feelings of enclosure etc. , let them satisfy these needs in non-injurious ways. Learn from them how they are fulfilling these needs. Help them achieve what they seek by providing the tools and environment they need. Behavior is communication. Seek the advice from autistic adults who faced similar challenges and learn how they managed. These skills take priority over skills that help them socialize/communicate in more “acceptable” (ie neurotypical) ways. If you cannot manage your basic neurological needs, social/communication etiquette will be useless. Stages of development are important times and are building blocks that later stages build upon. It is important to let the autistic minds develop at the time and rate they naturally develop. This means the environment needs to be supportive of these stages. If sensory over stimulation is an issue, the environment needs to be less stimulating. If isolation is needed there needs to be the place / means to isolate. So those who are there to support these needs must use autistic solutions, not neurotypical solutions that will only work for a neurotypical child. Know your own limitations. Understand that you see the world through a neurotypical perspective and not an autistic perspective. This will be your biggest challenge: To realizing what you needed as a child/adult is different for a child who is autistic. You will need to be very aware of this so you are not trying to raise your child in a way that is against their true nature. This means you will be constantly thinking in ways contrary to your natural thoughts, much as your child must think. You will have one foot in your world and one in theirs. This is because you are each neurologically different. Just as you cannot function at your best trying to be autistic, they cannot function at their best, trying to be neurotypical. If you can understand and embrace this fact, you will be a gift to your child's life. Don’t try to do this all alone - seek the support of other parents with autistic children both locally and online. As important if not more is to seek support from autistic adults for an insight you cannot understand from the same perspective. Its not a sign of weakness, its the difference in neurology. finally - let your children see and be with other autistic people of different ages and abilities. This grounds us and gives us a connection with others who are like us. It will give them a level of comfort that can be achieved in no other way. They will not be as isolated and alone in the world. I hope this gives you some important insights.. I wish you all the best!

question: Why don't autistic people realize that ABA therapy is actually good for them?
answer: Applied Behavior Analysis therapy, as the name suggests, modifies behavior. Autism can create behavior that seems cold, callous, or cruel to neurotypicals. It can also produce behavior neurotypicals see as disruptive, dismissive, or disengaged. That is, there’s a disconnect between how we behave, what our behavior stems from, and how neurotypicals judge us when they see us acting strange. Which we do. Often. ABA aims to correct this disconnect by changing our behavior. This can improve certain things about our lives. It can teach us what behaviors elicit positive and negative responses from neurotypicals. Being able to communicate our actual feelings and intentions through our behavior is useful, even essential. None of us are islands, though autists are happier in isolation than most. I say it’s important for autists to learn about neurotypical expectations and thought processes; we are a minority and that’s never going to change. If certain things prejudice people against us, it’s useful to be aware of that. We can’t manipulate people into tolerating us unless we know how people think and how to change their assumptions.I Colori di Arlecchino by Giovanni Domenico Ferretti. Public domain.If that’s all ABA did, I’d support it. Blending in is a useful skill. Learning to communicate and interact in a way that the majority of the population will interpret correctly is helpful. But ABA teaches other lessons along with these useful skills. It teaches us that our behavior, our manner of perceiving the world, our desires and our pleasures are incorrect and inappropriate. It teaches us that acting in ways that are unnatural and deeply unpleasant for us is an indispensable prerequisite to being loved or accepted. The prevalence of suicidal behaviors and attempts in the autistic population is 24%, suicidal ideation is seen in 34% of us.[1] Suicidal behaviors occur in only 4% of the general population, while ideation sits around 13%.[2][3] Research into why we kill ourselves at such high rates is invariably new. Decades of time and millions of dollars have been spent figuring out how to make us look and act normal, but research into how we feel and how these treatments and tendencies impact our health, mentally and physically alike, only gained traction in the 2020s. We don’t know a whole lot yet, not for certain. But a leading theory? Masking, particularly spending a lot of time masking, leads to mental illness and, in quite a few cases, suicide.[4][5]I Colori di Arlecchino by Giovanni Domenico Ferretti. Public domain.It’s generally acknowledged that masking allows us to function and meet societal goals better in the world we share; that, in its turn, can create some sense of belonging and fulfillment. We shouldn’t underestimate that. Exclusion subsequent to obvious autistic traits damages us. Masking, however, doesn’t fix these problems without an attendant cost. Heavy and frequent masking are especially associated with exhaustion, poor mental and physical health, and a poor or unhealthy sense of self. ABA teaches children to mask. It teaches children to mask and informs them in no uncertain terms that masking is essential to their survival. It alters observable behavior and instills the necessity of not acting naturally without addressing any of the cognitive or emotional causes of our abnormal behavior. It teaches young children to ignore their needs and their inner lives for the sake of everyone who meets them. When neurotypicals encounter similar treatment, we call it coercive control and label it abuse. question: What are some common misconceptions people have about living as an adult on the spectrum?
answer: That we don’t exist. It may sound stupid, but so many people think that autism only affects children. Some doctors are unwilling to diagnose adults with autism because they don’t think it will do them any good. It does. I was diagnosed as a teenager and suddenly my life made sense: I understood why I had always felt like an alien and made so many mistakes when socialising. I cannot imagine how my life would have turned out had I received my diagnosis later. Documentaries have always been about autistic children and how their parents deal with it. Thanks to pushback from the autistic community, were has been an increase in autistic adults getting to speak for themselves but progress has been slow and many people have grown up associating autism with children. People carry these misconceptions their whole lives. “But I thought only children had autism. I heard about this mother who put her child on a gluten-free diet and their child grew out of their autism.” This response is depressingly common, but I think it’s just a result of a lack of education. People cannot grow out of their autism, they can just become better at masking it which is physically and emotionally exhausting. We hear about how severe emotional repression leads to burnout and depression - masking your autism all day every day is just like that. Many therapies which are supposed to help autistic people are focussed around getting us to mask our symptoms. ABA (applied behavioural analysis) is a popular therapy used against young autistic people, and many autistic people consider it to be abuse. It involves rewarding desirable behaviour (holding eye contact - which I find incredibly painful) and punishing undesirable behaviour. Unfortunately the ‘undesirable’ behaviour includes stimming, which for many autistic people is a method of communication or calming oneself down. The aim of ABA is to make a child appear normal to make the parent feel better (I’m not disposed to be charitable about this), at the cost of the autistic individual’s right to self determination and expression. If you are considering ABA for an autistic child in your life, please read the testimonies of autistic people who have undergone ABA and consider whether you really want to do that for your loved one. “Your autism is not an excuse for being weird. It’s time to start taking some responsibility.” This misconception kind of stems from the other one. People thing that when you are an adult you have complete control over your behaviour. I get this when I explain that I struggle to work in groups or need to sit in a dark room for a while. Unfortunately, when you tell people you can’t go to the supermarket and have to hide in bed they assume it’s because you’re lazy. They don’t consider that your brain is fried from a short period of time in a loud and hot room when your headphones weren’t enough to stop the sensory bombardment, and you cannot face the flickering lights or extreme temperatures. Finally, when you become an adult you often lose access to services and support. I don’t know what the situation is like elsewhere, but in the UK demand for assistance for ASD far outstrips supply. Even if you are unable to live independently, there is no guarantee you will get support. There is no magic change when someone turns 18 which stops them from being autistic. Autistic children grow into autistic adults, even if we are better at hiding it.

question: What are some possible explanations for why some autistic adults seem immature?
answer: I’m going to go out on a limb here and assume that you mean autistic adults who are also verbally articulate on a more-or-less age-appropriate level and similarly academically capable, with relatively light support needs. In the case of autistic people who hover in that region of the spectrum, there are a number of factors that can cause neurotypicals to assume our immaturity:We tend to be more true to ourselves and not just drop our hobbies, prized possessions, and special interests just because society has arbitrarily decided that they no longer match what we should like or value based on our chronological age. For example, I not only collect dolls and My Little Pony figurines as a grown woman, but I also still own the majority of my dolls and stuffed animals from childhood. I still watch cartoons (American and international, and not just the ones made explicitly for grownups), read manga, and play video games. I have no interest in following celebrities and fashion, or having kids, or reality T.V., or scripted dramas about back-biting adults who haven’t mentally matured past 14 but swear up-and-down that they’re grown. Because my interests and hobbies appear to be those of a 12–15-year-old and I feel no compulsion to hide them, people assume my immaturity based on that.Our sensitivities can cause us to shy away from activities or environments that “people our age” are supposed to endure or enjoy. Take working in a retail store, for instance. Most people in our modern society see that as basically “baby’s first job.” The tasks are generally regarded as relatively simplistic and no special training is required to qualify. But, the environment! AC on year-round to compensate for customers wearing winter coats, constant music that never ends in the background all day long, the beeps and buzzes of check-out equipment, not to mention the florescent lights and (if you’re especially unlucky) lots of extra smells. Most adults and teens can tolerate such an environment for long periods of time with little trouble because NT people are better at filtering sensory information and aren’t as sensitive to it as autistic people often are. Not having this filtering ability makes us seem immature when we complain about noises or smells or physical sensations that others aren’t bothered by or barely even notice, and even more so when we refuse to go to an event or work in a certain field because that environment is Hell on our senses.We communicate differently than what is considered “normal.” We tend to make less use of body language, especially subtle body language, when we communicate, preferring our words to do the talking. When we do use body language, we may use it a bit differently or only deliberately communicate in broader or more obvious poses and expressions. We also tend to miss subtle cues of body language and vocal tone given off by NT people and interpret certain messages quite literally, especially if we aren’t familiar with the idioms or shorthand being used. This can make us look distant and under-emotional, overly emotional, naive, and immature, and especially works against us in job interviews and professional settings.We tend not to play or buy into the social games NT people play. Why does it matter what a good conversationalist you are when your work should speak for itself? Why does it matter what you wear to work so long as it’s clean, especially if you’re doing a good job? What’s with all the ring-kissing, hoop-jumping, and networking? That’s so inefficient! We often openly question superiors, point out flaws in plans and company policies, and give suggestions and ideas on how to improve when invited…without realizing the invitation to do so is an empty platitude to make people feel acknowledged and valued without actually acknowledging or valuing them, not an actual invitation to help improve the status quo. We don’t pick up on silent hierarchies as easily or quickly as NT people, and we’re often very honest with people. All of that can make us look immature or childish just because we’re not playing by the unspoken “rules” of the adult world.We’re highly intrinsically motivated. Instead of being motivated mostly by someone dangling a physical or social reward in front of us to do a thing, we’re motivated to do a thing because it makes us happy and aligns with our interests or personal goals. This can look childish and sometimes lazy, when what we are or would prefer to focus on might actually be a lot more productive than what the NT people around us are trying to force us to do. In fact, left to our own devices we can be quite industrious just because we can and we want to be. But, because our productivity does not always align with what the NT people around us want to accomplish or what they want us to do (for them) with our time, we get labeled immature and lazy.Constant rejection from jobs, especially decent-paying ones, which often leaves us stuck living with our parents much longer than either we or they want us to. When potential employers constantly misread you on interviews, when you don’t have the references or work history for a great job even though you have the credentials, when you either can’t land any job at all or the only thing you can get is a low-wage grunt job that doesn’t allow you to be able to afford to put a roof over your own head, when all of your own independent business ventures fail due to a lack of social resources…Well, if you don’t end up homeless or on welfare, you end up stuck at home with Mom and Dad. In our society, Failure to Launch is a failure to be an adult, and thus, a failure of maturity.However, under my Eeveelution T-shirt, behind the shelves full of toys and comics, in spite of the fact that my social aptitude is definitely below what a “grown woman” should have…I am a mature and intelligent adult. I can cook for myself, I can do highly-skilled work, I hate being in a position where I need to depend on or ask help from others for things that I should be able to do on my own, I know myself well and understand when to stop before I hurt my fool self and when to keep going, I can analyze and evaluate a situation and decide for myself if I should stay or go, I can make solid plans based on prior observations and current knowledge to get things done well and on time, and I’m darn good at making and keeping to schedules! I’m responsible, honest, hardworking, passionate about the things I do and darn good at them. I don’t need someone else to tell me to be productive or what to spend my productive energies on, I can do that myself and I have two 400+ page novels to my name to prove it! I think more deeply and seriously about life, my feelings and needs, the world we live in and how to improve it, and big stuff like the nature and concept of “God” than most people I know. I recognize the rights of people to live their own lives on their terms so long as they aren’t infringing on another living person’s right to a happy, peaceful, and free life. We’re not immature, just misunderstood.

question: Do people with Asperger’s show less affection towards their spouse and children than most people?
answer: No. But I understand why some people might think so. The problem is that you’re judging a minority by the eyes of the majority. The “expected” types, amounts and intensity of affection are defined by, and judged by, neurotypical people, and then they (often) conclude that Autistic people come up short. The same would happen in reverse though. If you had a society made up 98% of people with Asperger’s and a few NTs thrown in, and then these NTs had their emotional response, communication-styles and attention judged by the standards of the majority in that society — then almost all of them would end up being judged severely deficient. In fact, if you behaved the way you are in this world, you’d struggle even more. Because the autistic person you’re seeing with a spouse and children is an adult who has literally spent a lifetime learning how to interact with and cooperate with NTs. AFTER you have spent 3–4 decades practicing how to interact with and cooperate with autistic people — in a society dominated by them — you’d be equally skilled. But you don’t have that experience today. In short: Measured that way, yes, many on the autism-spectrum come up short. That’s an artifact of the fact that the judgements are created by and for nts.

question: How are companion caregivers for autistic adults trained in dealing with behavioral and mental health challenges?
answer: I work with Alzheimer's and Dementia patients who experience a lot of the same kinds of frustrations and anxiety as autistic adults. I've also met with many caregivers who work with autistic adults. It was interesting to find out just how similar the training was for both. So, some of the training involves something called redirecting. When a person gets frustrated or angry about something, the best thing to do is redirect them to something else. Giving them something that is very enjoyable to them, like their favorite snacks, or favorite music, or even taking a walk…anything to relive them of the frustration. The key for the caregiver is to remember that they don't have full control over their thoughts, but you do. Most of the time, the frustration is the result of trying to communicate or get something done, but not being able to express how they feel about it. With autism, things like art, music, games and puzzles, or even drawing can be very calming. It's important for the caregiver to not stop redirecting until the client is calm and content. The biggest difference between Dementia care and Autistic adult care is the physical ability of the client. While a senior citizen may not have much strength, an adult with autism may have a huge amount of strength. Therefore, it's important for the caregiver to get the autistic adult as calm as possible as quickly as possible. Unlike autistic children, autistic adults cannot be picked up and held or offered a cookie. They are adults and should be given the choice of what activity they choose from several options. They often don't know exactly what they want right away, but if you list some things, they can choose what they want from the list. It takes lots of patience and a very calm tone of voice to get the answers from them as to what they want. Thanks for the question 💜

question: What challenges do therapists face when working with autistic clients?
answer: I think that the challenges that therapists face working with autistic clients probably varies with the therapist’s own familiarity with the autism spectrum disorders (ASD). As a person who is probably somewhere on that spectrum myself, although I have not been formally diagnosed, I view working with clients on the spectrum in a different way than I view working with neurotypical clients, but do not necessarily view it as more challenging. So, rather than discuss the challenges that I face when working with autistic clients, I’ll discuss things that I simply try to be sensitive to and aware of when working with the high functioning autistic adolescent and adults who come to see me.First, the practice office’s environment is set up to assist someone with autism to be able to focus more effectively. I do not use fluorescent lights, noise is kept to a minimum, and air filters are used to reduce any distracting odors, and I myself do not wear “loud” perfumes. Notepads and pens are provided to either allow clients to doodle and not have to maintain consistent eye contact, or to take notes when that is helpful.I do not use neurotypical behavior as the yardstick to measure my autistic clients against. I try not to make assumptions that symptoms being displayed or discussed should be eliminated or reduced. I do not assume that a person with autism should function the way that a neurotypical should and I do not use a neurotypical’s behavior as the example of the end goal to be achieved in therapy. If my client with autism wants to work on improving their comfort level going to parties, for example, or work on managing their anxiety levels which increase with unplanned changes to their schedule, then we will set that as a goal and work toward it. We can discuss ways that behaviors may be causing difficulties in their lives and if they want to address them. But, I do not make the assumption that they should be doing those things or want to do those things or end up doing things the way a neurotypical person would.I am aware that OCD, ADHD, and Eating Disorders along with anxiety and depressive symptoms are often co-morbid with Autism and that they express themselves differently sometimes than the way they do in neurotypical clients. I try to be careful and not go too far to dismiss symptoms that need separate attention, but also not assume everything is just another manifestation of autism.Related to this, I try not to pathologize behaviors or symptoms without extreme vetting. For example, I avoid making the assumption that having difficulty with emotional regulation, which is often seen with clients with autism, is a sign of a mood disorder like Bipolar Disorder or a personality disorder such as Borderline Personality Disorder. Similarly, other behaviors such as social isolation, a preference to work alone, obsessions about a particular topic, or unusual routines or self-soothing behaviors are not immediately put into categories which would suggest anti-social, obsessive-compulsive, or self-harming tendencies.I try not to make common assumptions when communicating with my client and vice-versa. I avoid the use of sarcasm, for example, as that is an indirect form of communication that can be misinterpreted or misunderstood easily by my client. And I do not infer intention from the statements that my autistic clients make, but rather check them out first. For example, very blunt (honest) statements are not usually meant to be offensive. I also do not assume that they will pay attention to our “time” on the clock on the wall or notice any of the non-verbals that neurotypicals will often notice to be aware that our session is ending.I do not interpret my autistic client’s need to ask me questions or direct the flow of a session as a “control issue” that needs to be addressed.Many high functioning clients on the autism spectrum have many adaptive behaviors that sometimes have obscured even getting a diagnosis of ASD. Females in particular are good at “camouflaging” in order to fit in with neurotypicals. I try hard to create a safe space in my therapy office so that an autistic client does not have to camouflage with me. Many of the conditions I attempt to achieve in therapy regarding exhibiting unconditional positive regard, avoiding being judgemental, and avoiding making assumptions are helpful to most clients, but they are essential for those with autism. Creating a safe environment to simply be one’s self not only increases the likelihood of a good therapeutic outcome, autistic clients have told me that coming to therapy is not as tiring an experience as maintaining conversation usually is for them. One client who said that she thought it would be tedious, boring, and unproductive to talk to someone for an hour (eventually) told me that she began to look forward to our sessions.I will often end up helping my clients to reassess the ways they perceive themselves, focusing on their strengths first which often include excellent problem solving skills, admirable work ethic when interested in a project or task, the ability to intently focus and work for long periods of time on difficult tasks, the ability to be alone without feeling anxious, and valuing honesty. All of these strengths can be brought to the task of working on any issue the client decides they want to work on in therapy, and they will often achieve success quickly due to their diligence, discipline, and ability to focus once they are interested in learning something.Usually, although not always, I will help clients with high functioning autism to discover ways to navigate social and work-environment complexities in ways that work with their already established internal decision-making systems to reduce stress, help them to learn how to manage overwhelming affective states and cope with change more effectively, learn ways to overcome challenges related to motor skills deficits, and find or create social-support networks that accept and value them for who they are.

question: What is it like to be a high-functioning autistic?
answer: Since diagnosis, I’ve thought about this far too much. There’s no sensation, feeling, or pain that accompanies autism. Or at least not my case. In fact for years, I was unaware that I had autism spectrum disorder. Before diagnosis, I knew something was amiss. So what’s it like? I know something is missing, but I don’t know what it is. Prior to diagnosis, I used to call it my emotional blindspot. An emotional blindess that prevents me from reading other people’s feelings; where the colour of verbal communications is absent and where intimacy is not appreciated. I see other people engage in social skills or enjoy a romantic relationship or explore each other’s personalities. I see the evidence of this social enlightenment, but I will never intuitively experience this. I miss all this but I’ll never know what it’s like to miss it. My world is one of observation, learning, and copying. And I assumed others viewed the world as I do. But then I discovered that I have autism. My world view and the incorrect assumption that others see the world as I do, is because of autism. That’s all I know and all I will ever know. But at least it has a medical name now. But I do know how to make myself happy. And I do know how to replace anxiety with calm. For me, this means following self-imposed rules or indulging in the rituals of a special interest. And always striking the right balance between social interaction and periods of isolation. I hear things equally, making it difficult to follow one conversation in a noisy environment. Well practised coping strategies do help. I used to think it was my hearing: a hardware fault with my ears. Now I realise it’s a software issue caused by my autism. Autism robs me of emotional sight but gives me insight elsewhere. I also have ADHD, which can complicate things. But that’s for another Quora question and answer.

question: Can children and teens with Asperger’s disorder be taught feelings?
answer: When I see this question, I think of my life as a child and a teen. Nobody knew much about Autism in “those days”… but looking back on those times with the understanding that I was just as autistic then as I am now. So many things that seemed unrelated, can now be understood in a new way. I look at this question with concern because of what I experienced then and what I am trying to do to finally be who I was born to be. Not what society expected, or family… or even myself.. I was born autistic and I thank God, I will die autistic. Not some confused half of a person who tried to be something he was not. I’m not neurotypical: I’m Autistic. Can we be taught feelings? Autism is not the “lack of” anything. It is the extreme of almost everything, including feelings. Feelings that cut so deep and wide as to touch the soul itself. What you are seeing is not the inability to feel or relate to others. Its being connected so deeply to everything that our energy goes into managing this massive input of almost every physical and emotional feeling a person can have. And all at the same time. Just because you do not see familiar neurotypical responses, does not mean there are not feelings there. These children are still learning to manage more basic developmental priorities than “proper social responses”. These will come in time and in their own autistic ways. Many autistic children grow up alone in a terrible wilderness. The world YOU know and experience is not the world they live in. The world has evolved to support the needs of neurotypical people but not autistic people. Neurotypical children have the social supports and people around them, who understand them and cater to their needs. Autistic children must find their own ways to cope and manage with a mind and body that feel SO much all the time. There are few autistic social supports and rarely any autistic adults or peers around to learn from and share their autistic life. Autistic children don’t need to be taught about feelings. They need to develop naturally as autistic children, not neurotypical children. Just like NT children can not develop normally trying to be autistic, autistic children cannot develop normally trying to be neurotypical. Autistic children have autistic needs and providing these needed supports must be available for then to naturally develop their needed life skills. We ARE different because we ARE autistic. If we do not socialize or communicate just like neurotypical people it does not mean we can not socialize and communicate. We do so OUR way… our AUTISTIC way. If you want to see any child thrive and become their best. Let them be THEIR best. Let Autistic children be autistic and neurotypical children be neurotypical. It takes us longer to learn how to manage this complex, and high energy life that is Autism. Let us develop and grow in our way, at our pace to become what we need to be and want to be. Everyone just wants to be themselves… Let autistic children be autistic.

question: How does trauma affect the autistic mind?
answer: I personally suspect that many autistics learn to dissociate in very creative ways mentally, in order to survive and function. I believe that autistic shutdowns and dissociation might be equivalent in many cases. Allistics dissociate too of course, but other allistics believe them more, there is a shared emotional communication style. Maybe? The fact that many allistics disbelieve the experiences and terrible sensory-related pain of autistics could be a big source of trauma, but the autistics likely have to hide the effects of the trauma too… so no social support, no relief from continuing trauma, often… huge risk for PTSD. Therapies for trauma can need adjustment for autistics… that is barely studied too. Of course, undiagnosed traumatised adult autistics can hardly be helped by the little knowledge out there on how to treat traumatized autistics. On the plus side, I just saw a video in which Dr. Baron Cohen appears to be listening about the differences and higher numbers of autistic women, imho, so maybe things are changing. In the mean time though… There is evidence that a heck of a lot of autistics get traumatized. There is also evidence that one of the most common “therapies” for autism, ABA, frequently results in PTSD in autistics. Lots of folks using ABA will resist believing autistics reporting trauma from ABA and studies supporting such …humans do that. Trouble figuring out one's emotions is common among autistics; needing some things stated more literally; trouble verbalizing… all these things can make healing from trauma need adjustments in therapy… but there are solutions. I noticed that folks at Portland State are doing great work in Oregon on related things. I hope more therapists will learn about and work with autistic clients in the future!

question: How do autistic parents deal with having children, in terms of sensory processing, need for order, etc.?
answer: With significant (but rewarding) difficulty, lots of love, and a very supportive (NT) spouse. At least, that’s how it works for me—I can’t speak for other autistic parents.My daughter, Miriam, has been very inconsiderate of my need for order and calm ever since she was conceived… about four months before my wife and I had agreed we were going to start “actively trying” for a child. My reaction to the news was something along the lines of, “Oh no… but yay! But still kind of oh no?” She then had the unmitigated temerity to insist on being born a full two weeks early. That’s when my superpowers decided to make themselves useful. Don’t get me wrong—it was a pretty routine birth with no complications other than being unexpected. But my wife woke me up at around 4 AM, all in a tizzy, and after about two minutes of groggy panic, I shifted right into, “OK, just grab the bag we packed and get in the car. I’ll be right there… I assume the hospital will appreciate pants.” By all rights, I should have been freaking out through the whole process, especially once Elizabeth went into active labor, and especially because it was the heart of the pandemic, so there was no family present and everyone had to wear masks (especially unfun for autistics, but that’s a topic for another time). But for whatever reason, I was almost completely calm the entire time, even when they asked me to cut the cord. I don’t know if that’s something all fathers experience, but it certainly felt a lot like an instance of autistic detachment—the ability to simply decide that things are Not Important and therefore Not Worth My Notice and instead focus in only on whatever thing I’ve decided matters in that moment. (This is not a thing that can be fine-tuned, unfortunately—or else meltdowns and the like wouldn’t be a thing. It’s all-or-nothing: either I’m processing everything or I’m tuning out everything except the one thing I’m focused on. So, sure, I can just Not Notice all the overwhelming stimulus at the grocery store… but I also won’t notice that someone’s trying to pass me in the aisle, or that I’m about to bump into someone with my cart.)After that, the next few weeks were similar (though I wrote about one particular experience before*). Similar, at least, in that I was in full-blown, “This is what must be done, and I’ll bill myself later” mode. Like most new parents, my wife and I were both up multiple times each night. I learned to deal with feeding, with diapers, and with spit-up (still can’t handle actual vomit… but I can handle spit-up). I still had all the other responsibilities of my life to handle. I knew I was basically redlining my brain without an oil change for weeks on end, and the bill would eventually come due. I don’t actually remember when it did, though—I know it wasn’t catastrophic, but I’m fairly certain I spent several days straight being basically useless to anyone.From there, things settled down into more of a routine. We worked out feeding schedules, and I learned to do one-handed feeding so I could have my phone or a book in the other hand. We set up a bassinette in my office so that I could watch over Miriam while I worked or reach in to stroke her cheek while typing one-handed (I knew a lifetime of hunt-and-peck typing would pay off…). And the autism-related challenges began to be more normal, too. Things like, “No thanks, I’ve already seen her giggle at the stuffed animal three dozen times today—I really don’t need to stop what I’m doing to come and see her do it again…” Or, “Small child, most of your noises are very cute, but could you please stop making that noise, because it’s like you’re taking a cheese grater to my brain. No? That noise is your new favorite noise and you intend to make it nonstop for the next hour? Oh well… I guess sanity is a luxury I can do without…” Or, “No, Elizabeth, I do not want to read the picture book to her. How would I even do that?” Or, “You’ve learned your first words! That’s great! I have a hard time communicating with people who speak English, so I’m going to love trying to communicate with someone who speaks Groot!”Really, predictability and order go out the window with a baby or young child. Even now (or especially now), at three and a half, I can never tell when Miriam is going to suddenly discover some new way to disrupt and complicate my day. (I also can never tell when she’s going to suddenly come up with some way to delight me—so that helps!) What gets me through are three things:Love is a superpower. When Miriam needs me, I always find that I can manage whatever she needs. I’ll pay for it later—but that’s not what matters now.If I can’t have predictability and order in parenting, I need to make it somewhere else. Specifically, for me at least, I know that the hours of roughly 9 PM to 1 AM are my time to be alone and decompress.My wife, Elizabeth, knows I have some unique needs and struggles, and she picks up the slack when I need her to (I do the same for her, of course, at other times and in different ways).Parenting as an autistic parent is most certainly a challenge. But it’s an exceptionally rewarding one. Some achievements only unlock on Hard Mode.Original Question: “How do autistic parents deal with having children, in terms of sensory processing, need for order, etc.?” *[The linked answer is flagged as “Adult” for some incomprehensible reason. I promise you, it’s 100% G-rated.]

question: Why are all level 2 autistics under guardianship for the rest of their life?
answer: First, “level 2 autistic” isn’t really a thing. (How many XP would that take, though? Just in case…) Even though you’ll hear the term used—even by people who really ought to know better—and even though it’s in the DSM-5,* it’s actually shorthand at best. There aren’t “levels of autism” but there are levels of support needs that an autistic person may have in various categories. Why isn’t this “to-may-to, to-mah-to”? Because a given autistic person might have “level 2 support needs” in communication, but only “level 1 support needs” in executive function (just as a random example)—meaning they struggle to communicate, but have only mild difficulty in taking care of ordinary tasks and organizing their lives. Also, support needs fluctuate. I probably have “level 1” support needs or less across the board on most days. But if I’m overwhelmed and exhausted from a full week of unrelenting chaos, I might spike into “level 2” in many categories that weekend.Second, it is simply not true that all autistics with “level 2” support needs in any category or even all categories are universally under guardianship. If an autistic person cannot “navigate” the adult world in a way that enables them to make and effectuate meaningful decisions on their own behalf, they might be under a guardianship—if a court has ordered it. But if they can handle their own affairs (even if they require significant assistance to do so), then they have a right to do so. A guardianship is not for anyone who cannot live independently—to the best of my knowledge, Stephen Hawking was never the ward of any guardian, and he couldn’t have survived one day on his own. Guardianship is for those who lack the capacity to make important choices for themselves. Most autistics do not fall into that category.Original Question: “Why are all level 2 autistics under guardianship for the rest of their life?” *[No, I’m most certainly not implying that I know autism better than the people who wrote that section of the DSM. I’m expressly stating that I know autism better than the neurotypical people who wrote that section of the DSM.]
comment_answer: My wife and I both have similar levels of support needs, but we managed to mostly have them in different aspects of life. This usually works out fairly well. But neither of us would do well alone at all.

question: Can children with autism be cured?
answer: No, because autism is an entirely different neurotype from allism and affects an entire person's way of functioning. There is no "cure" and in fact many autistic self-advocates like myself *do not want a cure.* There is nothing wrong with autistic people. The problem is the way that autistic people are mistreated, misunderstood, abused, and refused a voice. Just because an autistic person is nonverbal and not comfortable with eye contact, doesn't mean there is anything wrong with them. They may need alternative methods of communicating, but this does not mean that they cannot communicate or have anything wrong with them. You do not have to be sad to see him like that. What you should be doing is giving him other methods of communication. This page has a huge list of resources on autism written by autistic adults about autism, neurodiversity and acceptance, sensory issues, stimming, disability rights, and the problems with things like ABA therapy, Autism Speaks, and functioning labels. Please, for the well being of your cousin's son, read them and educate yourself and share them with your cousin. I know it helped me as an autistic person to feel more accepted and learn how to better cope with and feel pride in my autism after many years of being mocked and abused for it. question: I’m dating a guy who has an autistic son and he doesn’t speak. I’m meeting him for the first time for his birthday party. Does anyone have any advice on how I should interact with his son? Do you have any advice in general?
answer: Don’t treat him like a baby. Don’t get sing-songy, or simplify your language. He’s… whatever age he actually is. Not younger. So, if he’s 10, don’t treat him like he’s five and do the whole, “Mmmm, isn’t daddy’s cooking really yummy?!” sort of thing. He’s 10. Treat him like a 10-year-old. He’s no less intelligent than another kid his age.* He just doesn’t have the same practical skills in interpersonal interaction. But you wouldn’t infantilize an otherwise-intelligent kid who hadn’t learned to swim or ride a bike, right? *[Not due to his autism, anyway—autism can sometimes be comorbid with intellectual disabilities, but they are completely separate conditions.]Do not expect or demand eye contact or physical contact. He may be fine with eye contact. He probably isn’t. He may love to give hugs. He may hate to be touched. Even neurotypical kids don’t “owe” any adult a hug or anything. But even simple things like shaking hands or the aforementioned eye contact, that we typically consider “common courtesy”—if he doesn’t want to, he’s not being rude, he’s trying to avoid severe psychological or physical discomfort.Probably avoid jokes. He may have a great sense of humor, but you won’t understand whether that’s the case on a first meeting. And if he either doesn’t have much sense of humor, or simply has a very unique sense of humor, then trying to make jokes towards him will make him confused and frustrated at best—no one likes to feel like they’re the only one who doesn’t “get it”. Or he may possibly even feel hurt, if he reads actual meanness when you were trying, in all good faith, to just “give him a hard time” in a humorous way.Don’t try to force a relationship—especially on the first meeting, but even afterwards. Let him become comfortable with you, and until then, keep your attempts at interaction low-key. If he perceives you as “that woman who’s always loud and tries to pull my attention away from the things I actually like,” he’s not going to want you around.Above all, observe. If this is a family you ever want to be a part of, you need to learn to understand this boy (though, don’t get me wrong—the fact that you bothered to ask this question already speaks very highly of your good will in that regard). Watch how he reacts to things, how he plays, what upsets him, what makes him calm down, what makes him smile… And try to figure out the pattern in your head. You might get it wrong, and that’s OK. He might very well not understand that you were genuinely trying your best, and that’s OK too. Just update your mental assessment, and try again next time. In a weird way, the best way you might try to get to know an autistic boy is to think like one. Not in the sense of “put yourself in his shoes”—that will be worse than useless, because it will be you in his shoes, imagining how you would feel in a given scenario, and his reactions will only overlap with yours by coincidence. No, I mean literally think in the manner that he does. To him, lacking in the “social instincts” that neurotypicals possess, each person he meets is a puzzle to be solved by observation and experimentation. As he gets older, he’ll realize that many of the “rules” can be generalized to most people. This isn’t “cold” or “clinical”—you’re not a puzzle to him because he doesn’t see you as a person. Rather, it’s the only way he knows to learn about you—because the part of your mind that makes intuitive assumptions about other people is diminished or absent in his mind. In fact, the more effort he’s putting in to understand you (not that you’ll necessarily be able to tell), the more he cares. Try doing the same. Your social instincts and intuitions will not work on him—he thinks differently, reacts differently, and even emotes differently (I, for instance, tend to smirk when I’m either very embarrassed or dealing with situations where others’ emotions are too deep to easily process… which works fine at weddings, not so much at funerals). So approach him as a “research subject”. Study him. Again, not in a cold, detached way—but in terms of gathering and collating datapoints until you reach a usable conclusion. He may or may not realize you’re doing it, but unless you’re doing it very ham-handedly, he’s unlikely to mind. He may even be pleased that you’re making a concerted effort to get to know him. Or he may not care. And once you’ve worked out how to communicate with him, at least a bit, do your best to learn about him from him. But remember that he may simply not want to interact at any given time, and you should always respect that.None of this is a magic formula. Getting to know this boy will be hard work. But it could be very rewarding, and I’m sure his dad will greatly appreciate it too. (Of course, it should go without saying that you should also be talking to your boyfriend about this—and that whatever he tells you is best for his son supersedes what Anthony RandomInternetGuy Zarrella tells you.)Original Question: “I’m dating a guy who has an autistic son and he doesn’t speak. I’m meeting him for the first time for his birthday party. Does anyone have any advice on how I should interact with his son? Do you have any advice in general?”

question: Should teens with autism receive full consequences when they fly into a rage and break things? Please parents of kids with autism and professionals only in this response.
answer: I am both a parent of an autistic adult son and formerly worked as an academic coach and behavioural therapist (note: not ABA) with autistic teens. I have been there when autistic teens became overwhelmed and broke things, sometimes even injuring themselves and (slightly) hurting others. In every case I can think of, that young person was overwhelmed by sensory overload, unrealistic expectations, lack of choice, exhaustion, extreme anxiety, or being unable to express themselves in another way in that moment - or a combination of two or more of the above. Whether the teen in question had strong verbal skills or mostly communicated nonverbally, it was always obvious they were not in control at that particular point. Every time, once that young person was calmer, they expressed shame, regret, sorrow and a wish it had never happened. Even those who didn’t use spoken language would demonstrate those emotions. Sometimes they would say they hated themselves. Sometimes they would smash their fists into their heads. Sometimes they cried, or tried to hide. They were always apologetic. I honestly felt they gave themselves more severe consequences than I would ever have dreamed of meting out. Often, my role was to comfort them afterwards, and reassure them. Once the dust had settled, we always worked together to learn from the event. There were always - ALWAYS - warning signs that they had missed and I had missed. So it was an opportunity to figure out how to prevent or interrupt those triggers in the future. Depending on the teen’s levels of independent self-management and communication, I could help them figure out their own escalation pattern and we could develop coping strategies together.

question: If you are autistic, can you give some good examples of neurotypical privilege you have encountered?
answer: Mental Health. Now I’m not saying that NTs don’t suffer from mental health issues. They do. But they tend to suffer from less mental health issues (like they ONLY have depression, or ONLY anxiety, or only one or two issues…whereas autistics tend to have more than one co-morbid issue) and their privilege comes into play with how it’s treated. Both drugs and therapies are designed for NT systems and NT minds. Many autistics are sensitive to drugs. So when they prescribe a specific dose, we’re prone to being TOO affected by the drug or suffering very unpleasant side effects. Our bodies are already sensitive, so side effects are hard to manage. For example, I’ve tried Xanax before and the recommended dosage completely knocked me out and the headache that came as it wore off was unpleasant. I had to cut the pill in fourths and ultimately stopped using it since it can be addictive and result in dependency. So NTs are privileged because drugs are designed for them, as most are tested on them. Therapy is also NT centered. Therapists are largely NT, so they offer NT advice. They might suggest things like, “just get some friends. That will help with depression.” That’s easy for an NT, but not so much for us. There are actually VERY FEW therapists that are trained to help autistic adults. Just try doing a search for therapy only for an autistic adult. You’ll get a huge list of child doctors and therapists, but not for adults. What’s worse…if you’re an autistic who is having relationship issues with your NT partner, you get to choose from maybe 20 therapists trained in neurodiverse couples therapy IN THE ENTIRE UNITED STATES. NTs have privilege when it comes to medical care and therapies and they don’t even realize it. They are offered so much support as adults. Autistic adults are left to fend for themselves. We experience the world differently and communicate differently and have different needs. There’s almost no support for us. And people wonder why we commit suicide at a higher rate…

question: As an autistic woman, I find relationships and social situations very tiring. It's like I have to learn everything (including communication) from scratch. Why is it so hard to be an autistic adult (diagnosed at 22 years old)?
answer: I am a 37 year old autistic man, there are many reasons why being an autistic adult is often difficult. More is expected of adults in general, more responsibilities, and with that often comes significantly less patience and understanding even for minor mistakes. Autism is an invisible condition, there is no distinctive look for an autistic person like there is for Downs Syndrome. Autistic adults just so happen to sometimes behave in ways people may find odd, or even abhorrent, even if said tics may be minor. When we do open up and explain that we are autistic people may not always be understanding or receptive to that due to preconcieved notions they may have about autism and autistic people despite how far we have come. Misunderstandings can often occcur on both sides due to Double Empathy Problem being caused by the vastly different communication styles between autistic people and most others. Autistic people tend to be much more direct and to the point, while many other people are often less so and can sometimes assume hidden meanings that autistic people usually don’t intend. Some people may be put off by the direct nature many autistic communicate. Speaking of hidden meanings there are often hidden meanings in many ways people often communicate that autistic people will sometimes miss. This can offend people that may forget or perhaps not even care that these cues just aren’t as obvious to us as they are most others. One common criticism I and many other autistic people have expressed is “why can’t people be more honest with each other?” It is an age old question and the answer is not getting any clearer even as I get older. Discrimination is also unfortunately common, some of it can be subtle and some of it a bit more blatant. Things have gotten better than they were in many respects, but discrimination is one of the main reasons why the unemployment rate among autistic adults is so appalingly high. Many employers are hostile to simple accomodations, and HR departments tend to unfortunately be full of a bunch of karens that are willing to sell their own mothers down the river to protect their corporate overlords from having to treat their employees like actual human beings. And for what purpose? To fulfill their life dream of makings peoples lives miserable? To pretend they have actual power? I honestly don’t understand what the appeal is of HR as a career path.
