question: What is life like as an adult with autism?
answer: Personally, it is an extremely lonely existence. It feels like no matter what I do I feel “off” or “out of place” in any environment. It’s like I don’t belong anywhere and it can get very frustrating. It never seems like I can communicate my thoughts vocally in a way that other people can understand leading to misunderstandings. I frequently misread other people and they frequently do the same with me. Sometimes I get accused of rolling my eyes when I’m actually just feeling uncomfortable with eye contact sometimes. Based on my life so far and my experience with people, I’ve become quite a misanthrope and isolationist. My brother (also autistic) and I frequently say that we “hate people.” I feel like a different species, often talking about people by referring to them as humans as if they were indeed a separate entity because my life experience has been quite different from theirs. Another thing I tend to say is “cats make more sense than humans, humans suck” and “if Earth was a living, breathing entity, then humans would be its cancer.” Hopefully you get the point. Much of my life I lacked any real friendships or just plain didn’t have any. In Elementary School I was bullied and traumatized by peers and some teachers. I had quite a coordination problem and students would trip me frequently. I also didn’t learn to tie my shoelaces until the 4th grade so some students managed to tie my shoelaces together so I’d fall on the floor when I stood up. Oftentimes I couldn’t undo the knot so a teacher had to do it. When my method of tucking in my shoelaces failed, especially during the mile run, I’d end up tripping myself. I had a minimal reaction to physical pain so some students would purposely step on my feet and try to get a reaction out of me. One day in school, during recess, I noticed a toad in harms way, hopping between the stomping feet of dozens of eager students that were ready for their break from the school day. I managed to catch him and when I was just about to get him on the other side of the fence, another student purposely bumped into me and I dropped the toad. He caught up to the fleeing toad and smashed it with his shoe right in front of me as I lay motionless on the ground. He laughed and then spat on my face after he finished killing the poor creature. I had a resource teacher that strongly disliked my lacking of eye contact. Sometimes she’d force my body into the positioning she wanted by grabbing me by my arms, sometimes bruising me, especially one time when I ended up falling out of my chair and on to the floor. The worst experience by far with her was when she singled me out, I still have nightmares about the experience I’m about to tell. One day she told me stay after my resource time had ended. She grabbed a chair from underneath the table and put it in the middle of the room, underneath one of the fluorescent lights that I hated. She told me to sit there and she yelled at me next to my face about how she was sick and tired of how disrespectful my lacking of eye contact was. Towards the end she physically grabbed my face and forced me to give her the eye contact she wanted. Tears started rolling down my cheeks as soon as our eyes met. In middle school I was mocked because I was terrible at sports and couldn’t catch anything thrown at me. I was never picked for teams and I was usually assigned to teams. In high school, when my depression started some teacher would practically announce to the class that I was failing their class or they’d mock me usually in a way that related to a missing assignment. Oftentimes so-called friends of mine would betray me. I had one that abandoned me because I wasn’t popular enough for their liking and hanging out with me impacted his social standing in school. I had two others that didn’t seem to understand why I had “unfriended” them because I caught them mocking my weight. When I depressed close to none of my friends attempted to help or comfort me. Only about 1 of 5 did. The other four basically stopped being friends with me after I told them about my depression. I have thoughts of dying just about every day of my life. I’m so afraid of making mistakes that I’ve become quite a perfectionist. Any mistakes I do make hit me hard. I try to limit my weirdness in public, but sometimes I can’t and I beat myself up. I remember going to a concert and I just couldn’t handle the lights and the noise so I sat alone in isolation in pain that the majority of people had never experienced, wishing I was normal in the moment. This trend remains unchanged into adulthood. The distrust of people, the feeling of being “out of place” etc.
comment_answer: Its like my life story with different examples of the abuse I and so many others suffer every day. I myself am battling very hard with suicidal thought at the moment. You’re not alone.

question: Can autistic adults have friends?
answer: Yes with work at social skills. We have friends of both Nuerotypical and Autistic people. But, we’d have even more neurotypical friends if more neurotypical peole try having empathy and patience with us and also learn how to communicate with us rather than make snap judgements about us and then shun us based on those snap judgements.

question: Is autism more common now?
answer: It isn’t. I was diagnosed for the first time about ten years ago, but had spent my life wondering why I was ‘different’. I went through school being tormented and bullied, and continue to have nightmares 30+ years later. I didn’t know how to communicate with other people. I found that alcohol made me feel better, so I self-medicated… not a good thing, but what else was there? Finally, I heard about Asperger’s. I read an article about it, and realised “that’s talking about me!” With the help of my doctor, I found someone who specialised in diagnosing adults on the autism spectrum - and she confirmed that yes, there are other people just like me. Hans Asperger did his research on children in the thirties and forties, in Austria. Unfortunately, it was in German and very few people read it. It was only in 1981 that Asperger Syndrome was first defined, and 1991 when Asperger’s work was fully translated into English. Since the recognition of Asperger’s, and a more clearly defined idea of autism more generally, many times more people than before have been classified as on the (very broad) autistic spectrum. A lot of people like me learn how to hide most of the signs in adulthood - we seem normal to most people, and so there was no reason from the scientific community perspective to even see a problem. Unfortunately, hiding it doesn’t make it go away - and many people have suffered lives of misunderstanding and miscommunication, as well as being consigned to ‘mental hospitals’ before we got to this point. So autism is not more prevalent now than it was ten, twenty or even fifty years ago. We simply have a better understanding of what it is and how to diagnose someone on the autism spectrum.
comment_answer: Thank you, that was really informative!

question: How can we support autistic adults?
answer: Just by recognizing that autistic adults need support, you are helping. Be patient. Learn the signs of an aspie and help us communicate, and understand when we can’t. Those things seem to be hard enough for NT’s.

question: How can the public education system be improved for children with autism/ASD?
answer: There is the “ideal” answer and the more practical answer… Of course I want the ideal but that is the goal we should strive to achieve, to guide us as we improve all aspects of life for people with autism. I’ll try to keep this short.. ( under 2 volumes :)) The ideal is that every autistic child has the same quality of environment and guardianship ( parents, teachers etc) as neurotypical children have. This is not happening and I believe I know why. There is a terrible “invisible” prejudice against autistic people. It happens when the assumption is made that neurotypical standards are what are best for autistic people to “live up to”. That what is best for neurotypical people is also best for autistic people. I call this an “invisible prejudice” because most neurotypical people are not aware of how their standard of measure was established and why it is not a universal standard that works when determining what is best for an Autistic person. This standard is set by our neurology. It is what some will call their “survival” instinct. Its purpose is keep the mind and body safe and in a steady state of homeostasis. All personal and social functions are established in some way to maintain this needed balance. Autistic people share some of these basic needs - food, water, shelter, security creature comforts, self-control, predictability and so on. Pretty much what every organism shares as base-line needs to survive. This is where the similarity between Neurotypical and Neurodiverse should be greatly scrutinized. Because even though the basic needs are the same, the things that are being kept in balance are different. Autistics experience a different reality. Our minds are constantly processing, We absorb all our sensory input and process it. Examining interrelationships, developing elaborate ways to store and process vast amounts of information. Our senses are heightened. Our nervous system is stressed at a higher level. Our minds and bodies are being pushed to their limits. Our highs are much higher and lows much lower. A system like this develops differently, at different stages and rates of progress, emphasizing different types of development of different cognitive centers being developed for different purposes. THIS is why our social and communication behaviors are different. This is why our minds use repetition. We, as autistic children ( and adults) must learn to control OUR neurological system. How we do that will, of course, be different than what someone neurotypical does to control theirs. But this is where the “invisible” prejudice happens. Most if not ALL autitic are painfully aware of this invisible prejudice because we’ve had to live with one foot in our autistic world and one in the neurotypical world. The more fortunate ones have been able to develop enough of their true autistic self that they can learn “neurotypical” as a second language. I was not that fortunate or was on the edge. I am trying to recover who I am and that person is autistic. Neurotypical people will have trouble with this concept because they have not had to examine this level of awareness before. It is like learning our native language. We did not learn it by examining the rules of grammar but by using it and learning by trail and error. Its a subconscious process. The same is true for this issue: Seeing beyond our own neurologically set standards of survival and seeing someone else’s standards. Seeing our AUTISTIC standards. What is missing in the educational systems, home life and society in general for many autistic children is an environment that supports their unique autitic needs. The instinctual ways neurotypical adults raise neurotypical children are based on the neurotypical neurology. Autistic neurology is different and has different needs. These needs are provided for neurotypical children because these are already part of the neurotypical social structure where autistic needs are not. These needs are very foreign to neurotypicals because they are not part of the NT life experience and instinctually known and understood. NT supports and accommodations are often provided instead of autistic support and accommodations. I worked with deaf children for a number of years. I will use the analogy of language development to emphasize my point. It was believed that for a deaf child to have the best chance in the “hearing world” that they MUST learn to use and speak the English language. It was often policy that sign language was forbidden to be used because no body understood what it meant, it made them look weird, and kept them from learning how to communicate the “right way”. So, “speech therapy” and endless hours of learning to produce sounds that could only be felt and not heard were practiced.. They were praised for any intelligible sounds! But the fact is that few hearing people outside the therapy environment could really understand them. :( It took a few generations before it was realized while they were being taught to live up to “hearing” standards, they were not allowed to develop their natural abilities. Deaf people are by fault naturally VERY gifted in the sense of vision. They excel in every way over “hearing” people. Sign language was the means they instinctually knew to develop the language centers of their brains. Those who had deaf parents, naturally learned to develop their language skills. This is more than how to communicate. It is developing depth of thought, how to categorize, how to remember, and control information. It was THESE children who had well develop use of language and thrived as adults. Those who missed these critical stages of development never would be able to develop them later and would struggle with this for the rest of their lives. Do you see the parallel I see happening with Autistic children? Can you see beyond your own life experiences and understand the needs of autistic children are different and just as valid and crucial as yours? We instinctually know what we need as children. Our neurological needs lead us to find our path of proper development. And with our extremely sensitive neurological systems, special care needs to be given that those needs are fulfilled and developed in their natural autistic ways. I’m one of those autitic people who missed many important stages of developing my autistic self. I get by on my lame neurotypical life skills and what autitic skills I did develop in spite of tremendous pressure to abandon them. But I have vowed to myself and to my community that this critical and over looked truth that is destroying autitic lives must be known! Must be exposed. This is not a condemnation of neurotypicals. You are doing your best with what you know how to do.. That is raising neurotypical children. But the time has come to honestly and truly address this critical issue! HOW? It will require both NT and ND community participation. Autistics adults of all ages need to take an active role in helping our children through their stages of development in the time and manner which they need. We need to advise and support the parents / guardians of these children to help then understand what these Autitic needs are and how to support them. Neurotypical parents, guardians: Know your limits. This is not a condemnation or declaration of inadequacy but is in fact the means to how you can be the best parent for an autitic child. This is a new frontier for everyone and we are all learning how to provide this for all autitic people, not just children. Autistic parents are in a similar situation when raising neurotypical children except NT children are surrounded by other means to learn neurotypical ways.. Autitic children don’t have this same opportunity. This is why we need to make a special effort to provide for their autistic needs. This is why it is crucial for autistic children to see and interact with other autistic children and adults. THIS is how we connect with our autistic sense of “normal”. I did not feel I belonged anywhere socially, until about 17 months ago when I found my autistic community. I finally have a home in this world and am no longer totally alone. I know this is a new concept. I also know that NT parents with autistic children know there is truth in what I say. YOU had to learn how to see beyond YOUR normal and into your child’s autistic normal. Your children have different needs. We must advance this concept. We must provide what these children need to be their autistic best. THEN, they can learn the language of the NT world. I’m NOT suggesting segregation into autitic exclusive classes. BUT, if the needs warrant special conditions, such as safe/quiet spaces, flexible schedules, changes in developmental priorities, rethinking timing and durations of developmental phases. Giving that child what then need NOW to keep their neurological system in homeostasis. Anything short of this can be an act of negligence and even cruelty to deny such needs. This is a VERY heavy answer and is not proposed as THE answer but only the right direction we need to go for autistic children and adults. I hope this stirs people’s thoughts and opens up discussions about this topic. I hope this has not been offensive in any way. It is not my intent to blame but to emphasize a situation that has not been properly addressed. Change is needed and I believe this is ground zero.. where it all must begin.
comment_answer: This is a very detailed and thoughtful comment. I think we take for granted what you have mentioned here. Thank you for your comment.

question: Should children on the autism spectrum be specially marked by color blue so that they can be identified on Halloween night at trick and treating doors?
answer: Nice try. Nobody has said or suggested that all autistic children should wear blue costumes to mark themselves. The question is about whether or not autistic children should carry the blue jack-o’-lantern candy buckets that have gone viral on the Internet. A lot of people feel that’s humiliating. Some parents feel it’s helpful to explain their children’s behavior, particularly if their are older, nonverbal, or have trouble with direction. What might look intentionally naughty to some might not be. The question is how should it be handled? My son is an autistic adult. He is nonverbal and doesn’t type. He uses an ACC device or PECs cards to communicate. I can see why some parents might feel the need to ask for additional patience. I never did, but in some areas, or with some children it might be helpful. If my son comes to your front door with his ACC device that I’ve programmed to say trick-or-treat for him, I hope you’ll be understanding. I hope anybody would be. He may look a little too old or too big to be out trick-or-treating. And at this age he is, but let’s face it, a lot of adult sized typically developing teenagers go out trick-or-treating. And while people whine about it, they are rarely rude to them. People feel they can get away with attacking a child verbally they feel is weaker, the autistic child. “Aren’t you gonna say trick-or-treat? Or what!?!”, so I understand why some parents might inform others. Is this the right way to go about doing it? I don’t know. I don’t have a problem with parents asking for a patience for the children. I think of it as a very personal decision. Some people, including autistic people themselves perceive the disclosure as something to be ashamed of. Of course they shouldn’t be required to tell anyone, but sometimes when a behavior appears out of the ordinary, it’s helpful just to say it. And if autistic people are not less, then the disclosure doesn’t make them less either. Should parents be the ones to disclose? With a young child they make the decisions. Just as all parents do. That’s what parents are for, autism or not. I’ll leave it to the parents to decide whether to tell others of their child’s neurology. I hope they consider their children’s wishes. I’ll leave it to adults to decide whether they should. That’s their call. This isn’t about me or you. Because what’s right for one individual may not be for another, and only that individual has a right to speak for himself. Nobody speaks for anyone else without explicit permission. Nobody speaks for me, and anybody who speaks for my son needs his permission. I don’t speak for him.

question: Autism runs in my family and many of my close relatives have it. I show many symptoms of it. One of the symptoms of autism is a speech delay, though I had no problems learning to speak. Is there a chance of me having a form of autism like Asperger's?
answer: Hi Parker - I can tell you from my experience, that when we are questioning if it is possible that we ourselves are autistic, we can be misled by comparing ourselves to others who are autistic. This happens for a number of reasons.We don’t really understand how vast a spectrum autism is. Each autistic person’s brain is unique. No two people experience or express autism the same - Neurotypical brains do not have this degree of variation.We do not know ourselves or understand our own autistic traits. When I was first diagnosed, I would have said “I do not stim”. That I do not have repetitive behaviors or reliance on routines. That I do not have Alexithymia or possibly Echolalia. and so on… This, and more I have learned to see in myself.Many late diagnosed adults have either compensated for differences in communication or socialization methods ( masking ) , or are in denial they even exist. It has taken me 15+ months of constant self evaluation, research and interaction with others on the spectrum discussing our differences and similarities etc.. and I STILL feel I’m just beginning to understand my autistic traits, and heal from a lifetime of self-denial.With your family history, it increases the chance you are on the spectrum. Especially if you are now seeing signs of this from the past and in the present. Talk with your family members who are autistic about what you feel. You may be surprised to hear them say… What took you so long, Ive know this for YEARS!!” - This happened to me - A friend and his wife that have known me since I was in my late teens… told me after diagnosis “ Oh.. I’ve know that a LONG time! “ She has not only known me all my life, but is a teacher who works with autistic students… My mouth literally fell open…. If you can be honest with yourself… I mean if you can look at the facts without a bias of wanting to be or not be autistic… and are open to other possibilities other than Autism.. you should be able to at least determine if it is possible. Look at family history, look at school performance issues, or experiences with socialization or communication that you have not been able to truly understand. Talk with others who are autistic… ask questions.. tell them you suspect you might be but dont’ know…etc.. There are many out there who suspect this maybe the key to understanding a very confusing life. It is a common experience that if a person IS autistic, they will “know” it is true. I wish you well in your pursuit of the truth!
comment_answer: All my children have a diagnosis, I recently joined them. It allowed me to reconcile many things that happened in my life and understand that despite having a hi IQ I was extremely vulnerable and needed to be on guard. It is important people get properly diagnosed. Just be aware there is a lot of bias out there. Eventually we got genetic testing as my son is severely effected and was rapidly degenerating. We share a gene mutation with so far only one other family in the world. No surprise to find out they are also Autistic! The gene testing also led me to research, an understanding that our Autism results from an Autophagy deficit and a low protein diet. Everyone has improved dramatically. Many people told me over the years that the only things that help Autism is things like behaviour intervention etc. I think many will end up with egg on their face. I have read much research and spoken to others with conditions under the DSM. The common factor is Autophagy deficit. When you have Autism in the family you should be pushing for full genome genetic testing. We are in early stages, very little data and more needed. Everyone is in a sharp learning curve, but there is a hell of a lot you can do to improve everyone's lives.

question: If a high-functioning autistic person (Aspie) is able to live independently, work, get married, etc., how important is the diagnosis?
answer: Based on a true story. Once upon a time there was a girl, X. X was a seemingly ordinary girl but she had few friends. X's parents watched her behavior when she was with other children and said: “You have to play more with the other kids! Why are you so shy? Why are you so quiet? Talk more with your classmates! ” So X felt like she was a weird girl. [communication issues] X didn't eat all types of food. When she went to parties she didn’t care about sweets, and she didn't eat cake because of the icing. X's parents said that she was silly because she never enjoyed the sweets, so once she forced herself to eat sweets and became sick. [food selectivity] After watching gymnastics videos at the Olympics, X fell in love with the sport and started practicing. She wasn’t good at it, but she just talked about it all day, watched the same videos dozens of times, turned her dolls into gymnasts, dreamed of traveling to meet the best gymnasts in the world. People called her a little fanatic. [highly restricted interests] As a teenager, X observed the behaviour of her popular peers and began to imitate them by copying the hairstyles, the clothes and accessories, the slang, the jokes, the small talk... But X did not understand context and did all of this out of time, until her peers began to move away from X. They said she was boring and it made her feel a weirdo again. At this age, she began to be interested in boys, but didn’t know how to flirt. Sometimes she kept staring at them. She also didn't know when she was being flirted with. If no one spoke, no matter what clues the boy gave, she didn't realise he was interested. So X was the only one in her class who hadn't kissed a boy. She felt that something was wrong, thought she must be ugly, but she wasn't. [issues interpreting nonverbal communication] X felt lonely, ugly and like a weirdo. She didn't understand how a fast learner who got good grades at school and was called smart could not know how to behave in social situations. Feeling so out of place, she began to change each of her characteristics, including how she ate. Before, she always ate little, but now she forced herself to eat a lot. She gained weight, felt awful, and then went on a diet to lose weight. She lost weight and the sense of control the diet gave her made her feel powerful. She lost an absurd amount of weight and was diagnosed with anorexia. The psychiatrist also diagnosed depression and X started taking medications. [comorbidities] The treatment was not easy, but it helped a little. X returned to a healthy weight. But she still didn't feel normal. She didn't like the noise, the smell, and the crowds at parties her friends always wanted to go to. She didn't like talking on the phone because she never knew when it was her turn to talk, and also because she felt the phone interrupted important activities. She didn't like to break routine or do things when on the go. She felt she could better absorb what a person said if she didn't look into their eyes, but she learned to notice the color of people's eyes so she could make a habit of looking. She didn't like the habit of giving kisses and hugs when greeting, unless it was from a very dear person. She never learned to wear high heels or skirts. She tried several times and felt bad for not succeeding. [auditory, olfactory, tactile, visual hypersensitivity, communication problems, attachment to routine] X started a relationship and as she and her boyfriend got closer, he pointed out some flaws: "You don't understand context. Look into my eyes, not my hands. Didn't you realize that person didn't like what you said? Why do you always want to do the same things?" At work some people commented that she was laconic, had a restricted diet, always seemed calm and wore comfortable clothes that were too loose or too sporty for work. She wrote on her social network profile: "I must be an alien." [In addition to previous problems, difficulty in looking into eyes, monotone voice] Feeling so different and backwards in social situations, X began to become very discouraged. She felt that her boyfriend deserved someone better, that her parents were not proud of her, and that maybe she was too dumb, since she was an adult and unable to figure out how to relate to people. She wanted to be alone and sometimes thought of dying. [depression, suicidal thoughts]Until, in the midst of a crisis in which she isolated herself, she searched for answers on the Internet. She found a text about high functioning autism, written by an autist[1] and identified herself with the characteristics described in the text. Then she tried to meet other people on the autism spectrum and saw that many of the difficulties she had, these people also had. She didn't feel dumb, late or stupid anymore- after all, she was just different. That helped in her self-acceptance. X made an appointment with a psychologist and the doctor explained that autism is underdiagnosed in women and that not diagnosing it can lead to other disorders such as anorexia, depression, OCD, etc. So yes, high functioning autistic people are capable of accomplishing a lot in life, but their lives can be of very poor quality because without the diagnosis, it is very likely that their psychological health is jeopardized.The images are from the book The Invisible Difference, which tells a similar story of a woman diagnosed with autism when she was already an adult.[Sorry if my answer has any English mistakes, I am accepting editing suggestions]
comment_answer: People do not seem to understand how isolating it is to feel like an alien. It is devastating. And the more you are around others, the lonelier you feel……………… until you find other aliens.

question: Should I still have a baby if I don’t think I can ever handle a typically developing teenage girl? I’d do better with a boy or with a special needs girl who deals with a different set of problems. I am an autistic woman who went to a special school.
answer: People tell me I’m a good mother. I don’t always feel like a good mother, but people tell me that I am. I write answers about parenting here on Quora, and people tell me I’m a good mother. Even when I’m writing about times I feel like I failed as a parent. I work with homeschooled kids every week, and other parents tell me I’m a good mother — and that they’re amazed by how well I understand and connect with their kids. Even when I'm feeling overwhelmed and strung out. Even my own children tell me I’m a good mother. And, being that my eldest child is 11, ensconced in puberty, and suffering through pre-teen angst right now, I take that as a prettty big compliment. But I have a secret. See, before I had children, I was sure I’d be terrible at motherhood. I’ve never felt particularly maternal. I generally find children to be too loud, too emotional, and too overwhelming. Oh, and I’m also on the spectrum. Both times I found myself pregnant, I hoped against hope that I would have boys. Because I knew — just knew — that I wouldn’t be able to handle raising a teenage girl. I didn’t even understand teenage girls when I was one. I certainly didn’t like teenage girls. In my experience, teenage girls were spiteful bullies who made my life hell for years. I couldn’t bear the idea of actually having to parent one of them. As it happens, I had boys. I celebrated. For a while. But over time I came to realise that all the things I was worried about having to deal with if I had a daughter, I’ve still had to deal with now that I’ve got sons. Sure, sometimes I’m approaching the issue from a slightly different direction — and there’s a hell of a lot more fart jokes and conversations about penises than I expected! — but the issues are still there. I’ve still had to teach them about clothes, and body image, and bullying, and friendship, and sex, and consent, and safety, and personal responsibility, and trauma, and emotions, and hormonal changes, and interpersonal relationships, and being bullied, and power dynamics, and critical thinking, and eating disorders, and peer pressure, and courage, and that they can do anything they want to do with their lives — as long as they’re kind to others while they’re doing it. These days, I regularly teach creative writing to teenage girls, and do you know what? They’re great. They’re really no different than the teenage boys I teach. Some of them are more challenging than others. Some of them have self-esteem issues, or anxiety, or have been bullied, or have excluded others. All of them are kids — young adults — looking for guidance and leadership as they flail and struggle towards adulthood. Sometimes I have to approach issues from a slightly different direction, but the issues are the same. If you were to go straight from the point of thinking about having a baby to suddenly having a teenage girl — a teenage girl whom you didn’t raise — it would be nigh on impossible. (I have so much respect for foster and adopted parents who do exactly that!) But that’s not what happens when you have a baby. You have a baby. You learn how to parent your newborn. Then you learn how to parent a 1 year old. Then a 2 year old. And so on. And eventually you’re the parent of a teenager. But they’re not some strange and incomprehensible creature that sprung out of nowhere. (Even if some days it might feel that way.) No, that teenager is still the same little person you’ve known for over a decade. And that makes all the difference. Regardless of gender. And, don’t tell anyone, but I’ve discovered that having ASD actually gives me parenting superpowers. It came as quite a shock, let me tell you. But there you have it. So, let me tell you about them.Special interests. When my children are interested in a subject, I’ve often ended up (accidentally) adopting that subject as a special interest myself. Want to know about dinosaurs? Or the solar system? Or trucks? Or the French Revolution? I’m totally your girl. (At least, up to a point.) When my children want to know something, I’m like: “Oh my goodness! I want to know about that, too! Let’s learn all the things!” Even more importantly, for the last 11 years, I’ve had the same primary special interest: My children. I’m fascinated by them. I’m interested in them. I want to learn all the things — not just about them, but about how and why and what they’re doing, so I can understand and help them. That’s a super power right there. (It also explains why I spend so much time writing answers about them on Quora!)I take things at face value. I don’t tend to get wrapped up in the emotional melodrama of things. I can hear my children, validate them, and then help them work towards a solution. I’m also able to rationalise and understand their emotional outburst (once they’re over), process them, and move on. I can let things go if they don’t need to be held on to. This also means that when I learn that something I’ve been doing isn’t beneficial for my children, or that there’s a better way to do something, I can take that on board and make a change without going through too much personal melodrama about it. (That doesn’t mean it’s always easy, but I seem to be able to move forward easier than the neurotypical parents I know.)I’ve learned social interaction and social cues the hard way. I’m one of those people with ASD who “passes” as neurotypical 95% of the time. That’s not something that came naturally to me — it’s something I’ve learned. The hard way. I’ve learned how to read body language and social cues. I’ve learned how to use body language and social cues. I’ve learned how to change my tone of voice to something appropriate to express my feelings. I’ve learned when to stop talking (even when I really want to keep explaining the awesome thing that’s going around and around in my head) based on non-verbal clues. I’ve learned how to respond to overwhelming outpourings of emotion from others. I’ve learned how to communicate in a way that NT people understand. I’ve learned how to advocate for my own needs. What that means, in parenting terms, is that I’m much more self-aware in regards to social situations than even most neurotypical people, who do all these things naturally, without giving them a second thought. That means I can consciously use those skills. I can consciously modulate my voice to ensure my children understand when I’m happy vs angry, without changing the words I use. I can consciously use body language and facial expressions to communicate to them without words. (I know this is a standard NT thing to do, but in my experience, many NT parents are subconsciously sending out slightly different messages than they intend.) And, even better, I can teach my children how to moderate their own body language when they’re having difficulties in a group. (This has obviously been a particularly useful skill for my ASD son, since I’ve been able to teach him these things since he was a toddler, and he’s been able to “pass” about 70% of the time since he was about five.)I’m naturally inclined towards rules and routine. All children thrive in routine-heavy environments. At least for the first few years of their lives. And — yay! — that’s a thing that’s completely natural for me. Not only is it natural, I can articulate our daily routine. And I can do it every day for a year if necessary. It’s not even something I have to work at. I also like rules. I like to know where the boundaries are. So it comes naturally to me to discuss expectations and house rules, and to understand and utilise natural consequences. My children have grown up knowing what the rules of the house are, and what happens if they push those boundaries. No one is surprised by consequences. Everything is transparent and clear. And, again, children thrive in this type of environment — regardless of whether they’re autistic.There you go. Four super powers for ASD parents. Now, there are extra challenges as well. Babies (and children) like to be held. And so much physical contact can be really, really hard. They’re also loud, unpredictable, potentially explosive, and have trouble managing their emotions. All of those things add extra pressure, particularly for parents on the spectrum. But they can be managed (largely by managing yourself and your own needs). All of these things are true, regardless of a baby’s gender. So, should you have a baby? No one can tell you but you. If everything I’ve said makes you feel overwhelmed and slightly unhinged, then no. At least, not right now. But that’s true of every woman. Being on the spectrum doesn’t, in itself, make you unable to be a good parent. It adds challenges that NT parents don’t have. It gives you super powers that NT parents don’t have. It’s not easier or harder. It’s just different. And, at the end of the day, isn’t that true for everything in our lives?

question: Do many adults with autism not realize they are on the spectrum? What are the reasons for this?
answer: Growing up with a mother and sister who I much later in life realized were Autistic, and a father who probably was too, I knew we were somewhat ‘dysfunctional’ but accepted that we were just ‘eccentric’ as many who knew us described us, individually or as a family. I always knew I was strange and different, but despite working in education and CBT, at one time specializing in working with Autistic adults in groups, I still did not twig that I was Autistic ! I am intelligent, self-aware and well read, so how come I did not recognize Autism up close and personal? After diagnosis I’ve obviously given this some thought (a lot actually!) and come to realize that most of my intimate relationships and my only close friendships have also been with Autistic people, who were the only ones I felt had any understanding of me and I of them, though mostly the latter. As being Autistic is just being me, normal, all I know, how was I to know any different. As so many others have said, most examples of Autism in mainstream films etc have been men and/or at the more extreme end. Know I know what to look for I remember that I was a very fussy eater as a child (slightly better now); terrified of loud noises, bright lights, large gatherings of people (unlucky for me, as my birthday is November 5th; Bonfire Night; and always ‘celebrated’ with all those things and ending in me having meltdowns !) Only felt soothed when rocking and/or sucking my thumb; sensitive to rough surfaces/itchy clothes and bedding; huge affinity with animals, from mice to horses, I communicated well with them all and could build a telepathic relationship with those I knew well. I learned to copy others to get by and masked well most of my life, but still always felt alien. Now I know why I feel much more content in myself, but life is obviously still a struggle, and always will be I guess, but I’m glad to know the reason for this and am relieved that I’m not mad !!

question: How do autistic adults feel about their disabilities? Do they wish they were neurotypical instead?
answer: The idea of me being neurotypical fills me with dread. When I over hear conversations between people, the gossip, the posturing, the complaining, I think to myself, ‘This is who you are? This is what you value?!’ What part of this am I suppose to envy? I view my neurology as part of who I am. Is it just pure happiness all the time? No it is not, but it’s not pure tragedy either. It’s life, plain and simple. Now I say this and I’m sure there will be people that’ll say something along the lines of, “Well you’re high functioning, so you can’t speak for people who are low functioning” and they’d be right, but I’m not inclined to believe that the caretakers of high-support needs autistic adults know what their wards/clients are thinking or feeling. Neurotypicals see the most harmless behaviour an autistic person does and make it into a tragedy because they don’t understand it. I’ve heard people describe stimming as seizures and as a child, my grandmother made the comment that my siblings and I, “You guys move around like robots, you move around like demons”. I am more than happy to hear a high support needs autistic adult, when they’re the ones communicating about their experiences. I’m mistrustful of other people talking for them.

question: How would you encourage a 20 year old high functioning autistic man to start thinking like an adult?
answer: I’ve chosen to answer this question because it raises an even more important question about the differences between what I call the Autitic Normal and the NT Normal. Our Neurology ( brain, nervous system) defines and manages what we call “NORMAL” - Our normal is our own perception of life.. It is what we sense, how we sense it, and how we interpret it into something of meaning. Our neurology holds the memories and present experience of life that we base our opinions on. What people fail to realize is that what they call normal is not the same for everyone. And just because a person has a normal that is different does not make their normal less valid than your own. There are subtle variations in the neurotypical neurology that change perceptions of normal. Take the thin built 98 lb adult and the 300+ lb line-backer and put them in a pro game. Is their perception of that event the same? Is one’s perception more valid than the other? NO: They both have different and valid perceptions of what is normal. Now - lets talk about two VASTLY different neurological structures - Autistic and Neurotypical. Two VERY different normals. My autistic normal is that when I eat something my senses are heightened to the point I can detect what each ingredient is in what I’m eating. I know the NT normal is different - That is not an NT normal. My autistic normal is that I can hyper focus on a task for hours and even days. That is not an NT normal. My autistic normal is that I have music I’ve listened to and memorized in such detain I can hear it as if it is being played. This music plays every waking moment of my life - That is not an NT normal My autistic normal constantly is processing information from current experiences to thoughts and memories. This information loops around as I take that new information and connect it to previous knowledge. I interconnect all this information into greater depths of understanding and meaning - Everything from the simplest daily activity to a new life endevor is processed in this way and the process is never ending - even in sleep. That is not an NT normal. To manage this constant flow of information, I develop routines so that the information I have to process is familiar. It is a way I can relax or rest from the processing of NEW information. This is why disrupting my routine is sort of like being waken from a state of rest… NEEDED rest.. It forces me to start processing NEW information again. That is not an NT normal The way I socialize is very different than the NT’s way. We have different personal needs and therefore social needs as well. This changes how I interact with people. My socialization world is very practical - it is a way to meet people and develop different levels of relationships. A relationship with a person fits into my way of managing information. It is taken at face value and no deeper meaning is intended or interpreted from this process. That is not an NT normal This constant high level of sensory input and cognitive processing can create high stress and fatigue. We expend a lot of energy in this process and need rest from this process. This is why we seek solitude - to minimize the input of sensory and cognitive processing. This is not an NT normal. If I cannot regulate this stress and fatigue, my system will start to become inefficient or even shut down. They refer to these as shut-downs and melt-downs. They can take minutes to days and even months to recover from depending on the person. This is not an NT normal OK - off the top of my head I made this list of things that are normal to us but not to NTs. This does not mean NTs are NOT normal or that they should be more like OUR normal… it is just that we are very different. From our perspective - we could call your behaviors “abnormal” - that you have a “disorder” or “disability” - But that does not take into account your neurology - that defines your normal. There is nothing wrong with you.. you are just “different” We can both live well within our own normal. Where it creates problems is when I have to “live up to” YOUR standards of normal and if you have to “live up to” mine. It will not work because what you body and mind NEED and how it needs to do it will not fit into OUR normal ways of doing things. And we cannot fit into yours! WE CANNOT FIT INTO YOURS! Your 20 year old is an autistic adult. Not a 20 year old neurotypical adult. Has your child been allowed to develop his autistic normal all his life? To BE autistic and learn how to solve autistic problems with autistic solutions the same as NT children do in their lives? To explore and understand what it is to be autistic? Or has he been expected to live YOUR normal? A normal that does not fit his neurology any more than our autitic normal would fit you. Your child is probably being perfectly autistic for his age and considering his lack of autistic developmental supports. Autistic people tend always hold onto what we call our “child’s perspective” of the world. It is a sense of wonder and awe that is one of our NORMAL gifts that NTs do not understand. What are you basing your definition of “…start thinking like an adult” on? Is it your perception of a “normal” adult? An NT adult? When will your young autistic adult, be allowed to be true to himself? To be himself? To be autistic? I went 59 years - not knowing I was autistic. Trying to ignore, deny or cover up ( mask) that evil dirty side of me that I now know was “THE AUTISTIC SIDE”! I thank God that even with my best efforts, I could not extinguish who I was ( am). We are already very isolated from society because of our neurological differences: Our different Normal. It’s literally killing us to have to deny who we are in public. With family and in other social situations. I did not feel part of this world, until I found I was autistic. I was able to stop lying to myself and be autistic. I found my community that can relate to MY normal. We socialize and communicate in the same basic way because we share the same neurology - the same normal. Think about your son. Think about who he is and who he will always be. He is autistic. That is not bad.. that is not broken. That is a different normal than yours. He will always be autistic. He cannot have a fulfilling and NORMAL life if he cannot be true to himself. Acknowledge his TRUE needs and these are AUTISTIC needs. You cannot understand these needs as normal because they are not YOUR normal. You are very different that we are. And that is ok! We’re ok and you are ok… We’re both normal! What is happening to your son is what is happening to almost everyone who is autistic. We are struggling between our normal and society’s expectation that we live up to their normal. It will be an amazing day for our community when society understand this simple change in perspective: We have a different normal. That we have different needs and when these are not met we struggle in our personal and professional lives. So much talent and knowledge is being wasted in coping instead of living. I hope this gives you a new perspective of autism to think about! P.S.- An important thing I forgot to include in this answer is that fact that autistic people need to be around others who are autistic. We cannot feel NORMAL till we see we are not alone and there are others that share this normal. Children especially need the models and mentors to help them learn HOW to be autistic just like NT children are learning how to be NT. This is a critical factor in the NORMAL process of development of children and adults who are autistic. We need this validation to achieve our best. To learn who we are and how to be autistic.
comment_answer: It’s one of the most important lessons people need to learn. Neurotypicals to a greater extent, neurodiverse/neuroatypical to a lesser extent. Not being neurotypical does not mean you’re “broken” and need to be fixed to function like a neurotypical person. Odds are you’re going to require some tools or tricks to function within a NT-dominant society, but for far too long it seems that the goal of society has been to “fix” anyone who doesn’t fit their narrow definition of ‘normal’. Luckily we’re slowly getting to a point where that perspective is shifting. Where understanding and tolerance to differences is growing, albeit slowly. Someone who is different doesn’t need to be “fixed”. They’re not broken.

question: My 2-year-old daughter was diagnosed with autism yesterday. I feel heartbroken. What should I expect?
answer: Hello. I’m Jaime, a late-diagnosed autistic woman. I was diagnosed at 35, and I’m 41 now. I’m sorry to hear that you’re heartbroken. I’m sure a lot of that heartbreak comes from the stereotypes and misconceptions about autistic people. It can be very scary to hear you “have an autistic child” when there are hate groups out there like Autism Speaks who would like nothing more than to scare you to death. Let’s take a deep breath together. You and your daughter are going to be just fine. Seriously, just fine. Will it be challenging? Yes. You and your daughter (assuming you are neurotypical) are going to speak two different social and neurological languages, which can be very confusing and frustrating for both people. Having said this, the best thing you can do is read books from the perspective of autistic adults. Really immerse yourself in understanding how your child’s brain works, so you can understand her feelings, needs, wants, motivations, and intentions. This will help improve your communication with each other ten-fold. Also, as she gets older, follow her lead when it comes to communicating. Don’t automatically think that if she’s not talking by a certain age that she will never talk, but don’t force the issue. Offer her alternative methods to communicate with you such as an AAC device. Let go of the concept of embarrassment. Your little one is probably going to make a lot of social missteps and mistakes, and that’s because, again, we speak a different language. I think it’s much more important to focus on protecting your child than openly correcting her behavior in front of others because you feel they are judging YOU as a parent. We’re just being ourselves. When we’re children, we don’t know it’s considered inappropriate by neurotypical standards to stim in public, have a meltdown in public (which is often misinterpreted as a tantrum when it is anything but), point out someone’s big nose, or answer with direct honestly if someone asks us if their butt looks big in a pair of pants. You can repeatedly unintentionally gaslight and traumatize your autistic child if you continue to react to these natural behaviors of ours as though we are purposefully trying to be rude, get attention, avoid doing something, or embarrass you. That’s simply not the case. That’s why it’s so important to explain WHAT it is your child did that is deemed inappropriate by society before you explain WHY and what to do instead. There’s often a disconnect here that causes frustration on the part of the neurotypical person and trauma on the part of the autistic person. Since our intention was one thing but our behavior seemed to indicate some other intention, we don’t understand why people are reacting to us the way they are. So, don’t say, “Don’t do that!” or “Why did you do that?” What’s ‘that’? What does that mean? Say your child knocks over a glass bowl in the middle of a meltdown: “Why did you do that??” is just distressing and confusing. We often don’t even realize what’s happening outside our own bodies and brains during a meltdown. Say, when your daughter is calm, comfortable, and receptive again, “During your meltdown, you swept your arm across the table and knocked over a glass bowl. I know you didn’t do it on purpose. It’s OK. I just wanted you to be aware of it. I didn’t want you to get hurt by stepping on the bowl. How about next time, if you feel upset, will you come to me so we can go someplace quiet and safe?” It’s that type of specificity that’s SO important. Always be specific when making a request of an autistic. Always. Even if you feel like you’re over-explaining, do it anyway. Example: Specific - YES “Krista, I need you to go into the other room and get me the yellow-handled scissors on the desk where my computer is. It’s right by the coffee mug I left there from this morning. You know, the one with the platypus on it?” General - NO “Krista, go get my scissors out of the office.” Oh, the panic I felt in my gut just writing that last one. Last, but not least, please come check out my website. It’s got a ton of information I think you’ll find very, very useful. Don’t be discouraged. You’ve got this.Jaime A. question: I'm in love with a guy who has Aspergers, and he tells me he can't feel love. How would I go about going further in life with him?
answer: The belief that autistic people lack emotions like empathy and love was propagated by some of the world's most famous autism researchers. Many of the experts who work with us learned those myths during their training. Many autistic people have been told those myths and believe them because they trust the experts. Then they spend their life living down to those expectations. If your lover can be convinced to study more recent experts and the autobiographys of autistic adults that have been published recently there is a chance the two of you can make it work. You will also need to do the same research as your lover. You will need to learn the way your lover communicates emotions and you will need to adopt some of the same techniques to communicate with him. It will be a lot of work but if you love each other you can have a long and happy life together. And of course, it all depends on his ability to unlearn what the experts have told him about himself.

question: What should you know before meeting a non-verbal autistic adult?
answer: My adult son is autistic and non-speaking. Here’s what you should know about him. Most importantly, his receptive language, (what he understands), is excellent. Please do not talk about him in front of him. Speak to him like you would any other person. If someone has a question about him, I ask that they ask me when he is not around. Imagine being talked about when you are unable to respond. It’s rude. Understand that he does communicate, even though he cannot speak. He either uses an AAC device, PECS, or word approximations. You can ask him a question and he will say to “yes” or “no” as an answer. Don’t expect him to hold a conversation with you. He cannot. Be patient with the methods that he uses to communicate. Please understand whether a person is intellectually disabled or not is not important with regards to all of the above. It doesn’t make the person that can’t speak less if he/she is intellectually disabled. You wouldn’t think that if a person with Down’s Syndrome or another intellectual disability. People who are autistic and intellectually disabled deserve the same respect as others. Finally, try to get to know this adult you’re speaking of. What does he like to do? What are some activities he enjoys? How does the individual communicate? find out if this person has any other medical issues that you should be aware of. My son also has epilepsy. His seizures are in frequent, but not fully controlled with medication. If he should have a seizure, don’t freak out. Follow the protocol. Be patient with communication. It’ll take more effort on your part to understand, and probably more time for that person to communicate. Look at the person as an individual just as you would anyone else, disabled or not. Anything I’ve said here applies to my son, and not to all autistic, non-speaking people. Everyone is an individual.

question: How did you realize you were autistic as an adult?
answer: For me it was the culmination of many circumstances… I was at work… I admit I was frustrated with a number of things and I now realize I do not filter my emotions well to make them “NT acceptable”. I was in a conversation with my boss on the phone when, what felt like out of nowhere, I hear.. “ Well I guess then you really don’t want to work here any more….. “. It was so out of proportion to where I thought the conversation was… that I said to myself.. “Shut up Tom.. say nothing more… just shut up!”… and I did…. I nicely ended the conversation and at that point knew something was “wrong”. I still do not know why my first instinct was to check out Asperger Syndrome. About 4 years prior to this, my co-worker had talked about her son who was an aspie. She talked about what they were doing at school to address social / communication issues. At times his traits seemed very foreign to me.. but most of the time there was a very strong connection. Strong enough to ask her if it is possible I can be an aspie.. But I dismissed it thinking ‘ I’m really not like her son’… Well. I think it was that week… I was having trouble sleeping so was up at 4am… I started to research Asperger Syndrome. There was an “Aspie Quiz” on youtube by an aspie Carol Bird. I scored 149 out of 200 with the added text “ Very likely neurodiverse”. That did raise my curiosity to look further but was not convincing to me.. That day or the next, I found blogs and forums by and for adults who are autistic. It was surreal… it was as if I had found a portal to another dimension. At some point it hit me… these people were talking about everything I had or was experiencing in my life… When I say it was a profound experience… let me qualify this… My adrenaline level shot up so high that it started to cause atrial fibrillations. To the point that 2 weeks later, I went to my doctor. I was going to tell him about my very strong suspicion I was autistic but was half embarrassed and uncertain myself.. Until.. he said.. “humm…. these arrhythmias are symmetrical… this means it is from a high adrenaline level! “ That is when I said “ Dr.. I think I know what is causing this…” and I just broke down and cried…. I have an amazing doctor. He did not hesitate or doubt me in any way… He just said.. “Ok…. we have to figure out the best way to get you diagnosed”.. About a month later it was official! Now… My report says “ASD” in accordance with the DSM-5, but the clinician said “ I’d say you are mild Aspergers”… It was all so fast that I continued till today to learn and apply this to my life… I still held a shadow of doubt until just 2 days ago… My best friend’s wife is deaf. She’s also a teacher at the deaf school ( for the last 35 years)… and has worked with many autistic students.. I ran into her at a autistic function Saturday… It came up .. “Jon says you found you are on the spectrum?” I of course said yes… and she said “ I’ve know that for a LONG time!”… My mouth literally dropped… She has known me for over 40 years! I took this as the best “diagnosis” I could ever had gotten! Strangely.. I think that doubt I kept was a way to protect myself from the truth… A truth I wanted to believe but was afraid to… Well… now I’m entering a new stage of acceptance… Call it “absolute”… Now, begins my full life as an autistic adult. It’s sort of triggered a new wave of grief. Of fear. But also relief… and joy as I can now drop the doubts… keep learning how to drop the masks.. and be Autistic! Be Myself. Be at peace.

question: I speak to my adult autistic daughter similarly to how I speak to typically developing six-year-olds. She complains but I don't think she understands adult speech. Am I wrong?
answer: You are very much wrong. Autistic individuals are capable of understanding adult conversation and can carry it out themselves. Although social interaction can be challenging, they do typically have an average or large vocabulary and understand concepts necessary to hear you. She’s an adult. Disabled or not, she deserves to be treated like one. When you treat her as if she is six years old, you are disrespecting her based on her disability. This is unfair to her because she is a human being. All human beings deserve the amount of respect appropriate for their age group and lifestyle. Imagine that you, a fully functional adult, went to work and all your coworkers treated you like an actual child. They talked to you in a baby voice, looked condescendingly at you, and told you what to do all day. You would walk home feeling furious, hurt, and disrespected. That’s EXACTLY how your daughter is feeling right now. You are doing that to her. If she is intelligent enough to communicate taking offense to your treatment of her, she is intelligent enough to be talked to like the adult she is. She deserves it. As her mother, it is your job to respect her. She will never want to be around you if you always disrespect her. Treat her like a HUMAN. Also, please look into learning more about autism :). I mean no disrespect, but I’m trying to communicate how frustrating this must be for her. Try to understand where she is coming from and how you can help her without disrespecting her.

question: Is ABA recommended for Asperger's?
answer: NO. As an autistic person, I could never endorse ABA in its current form, as marketed to parents - not under any circumstance. There are several better options. Many forms of ABA basically amount to torture, or at least severely degrading mechanical behavior alteration, for reasons that become obvious if you put yourself in the shoes of the person at the receiving end. And, on top of all of that, it’s expensive and, in many cases, just flat-out doesn’t work. My Thoughts on ABA - Autism Women's Network Would You Accept This Behavior Towards a Non-Autistic Child? - Speak For Yourself AAC ABA teaches kids how NOT to communicate - stimmyabby on Tumblr I’m admittedly taking the hard line on this because this is not the kind of thing you’re going to hear from most neurotypical “experts”, who may at best gloss over all of this. This is something that you’re going to have to make reasoned decisions about as a parent. … As far as whether or not it’s typical… sadly, it’s prevalent enough that a good portion of autistic adults have gone through it and have had bad experiences. I managed to avoid being subjected to it first-hand because there are a fair number of autistic people in my extended family and because my parents had a pretty hands-off, permissive, “we’re telling you not to do this because you’ll hurt yourself” attitude to parenting. That said, I’ve almost certainly run into artifacts from it in the families of friends from school.
