question: If you're autistic, have other autistic people accused you of being bad, mean, wrong, stupid, ignorant and/or arrogant for different reasons?
answer: The first incident I had was when, at the age of 5, I interrupted my parents' conversation by saying: Why do you speak ill of our neighbors? Do you like it when others talk bad about you? My father turned red with rage and shouted at me, as he had never shouted at anyone, not even at The earliest incident I had was when, at age 5, I interrupted my parents' conversation saing: Are you an idiot or what? You, you stop now to get involved in the affairs of elders, do you understand? How scared I have been, very scared. It was when I started masking, and despite knowing after 51 years that I am autistic it took me another 8 years to take it off. Or rather, it fell on the day of my son David's death. Within society, until I became a survival expert I risked my life many times working from job to job, to avoid being called inept, crazy, or guilty of something I never committed. Same in my family environment; when I was able to make decisions for myself I have been to them great at times, and bad for not being full-time that genius, so, as a consequence, I also had to accept the bad treatment, and to avoid it I became submissive. The lack of authority in front of my family members, and transparent communication negatively impacted my neurodivergent son’s life. When things in our lives got complicated, we accused each other of everything you mentioned because we had been led against who we really are, and I mistakenly considered it fair because not fiting in it prevented us from moving forward in this competitive world but not our tribe. The life of an autistic adult surrounded by neurotypicals is like Einstein's fish.
comment_answer: I hear you on how that lack hurts our ND kids.

question: How do the parents of autistic children think the way they are raising them is affecting their autism?
answer: I don't think my parenting (or anyone’s parenting/therapy/intervention) has any impact on autism at all. Autism is innate, like being left handed. It's the canvas, not the paints. What we can and do work toward is decreasing anxiety, increasing communication ability, increasing self-care skills, managing sensory issues and so on. The goal is to eventually produce an autistic adult with as little childhood trauma as possible, as another answer says, who is as happy and as independent as possible. Some of the things we do are:Protect his downtime. We do not overschedule. We make sure that he has plenty of downtime so that when we do have something to do, he's able to fully engage with it so it can be a successful and enjoyable outing.Ensure his schooling is right for him. Last year, we moved him from mainstream to a special needs school, and it's made all the difference. He's so much happier and more relaxed, his anxiety levels have plummeted, and their curriculum is so much more appropriate.Respect his sensory needs. There is one stim we have to limit because of practical considerations, but for the most part home is where he can avoid sensory input he dislikes and access sensory input he needs. Again, this helps to fortify him for the outside world.Listen to him. His communication may not be typical, but it's very much there if you pay attention. And conversely, we do our best to explain things to him in a way he can understand and make sure he knows what's going to happen so that he has time to adapt and prepare.On that note, we've ditched certain expectations and practices that just aren't relevant to our child. For instance, surprise events. They suck. What works is to let him anticipate and mentally get set for what we’re going to do. Birthday parties are also the total opposite of what he actually enjoys, so we don't do them any more.None of this affects his autism. All of it (hopefully) supports his development along naturally autistic lines towards being a healthy and happy autistic adult.
comment_answer: Your child is very lucky to have you as his mother.

question: Anyone with non-verbal autism willing to provide feedback on how well they think they communicate with animals (pets)?
answer: I don’t usually answer from my son’s perspective, but I will for your question. He is a nonverbal autistic adult but he also doesn’t type well, so he can’t answer your question. He does not have a special way to communicate with animals. Or at least he doesn’t appear to. He likes animals. He’s gentle with them. He takes care of our dog. Every dog we’ve had seems to recognize that he is different. Been very gentle with him. When he was very young and walked out of the house without us knowing, our golden retriever alarm barked. She never would have done that for his sister. They have been very gentle with him. When he was very young and walked out of the house without us knowing, our golden retriever puppy alarm barked. She never would have done that for his sister. The cats annoy him sometimes. They annoy me sometimes with their meowing about the food dish being empty. However, my son doesn’t seem different in how he communicates with animals than some people who are not autistic. I know some autistic people do have a different communication with them, like Temple Grandin, but certainly not all. And she is verbal.
comment_answer: Thanks. I am on the spectrum (and verbal) but I am trying to write a book with a character that is non-verbal. I don’t want to go too far afield with non-human communication. So i was looking for inspiration.

question: Why do autistic children cry without tears?
answer: How are these kids’ meltdowns reacted to by people around them, I wonder? This is a hypothesis on my part — but I wonder if the kids don’t feel safe enough at a deep level to cry with people. Those levels of safety are not really consciously controlled I think. I don’t know if this generalizes to other autistics, but crying at all was hard for me if in public, except when I lost a loved one. Then in a couple cases (out of 50 years of life), the grief was overwhelming to me and I did cry in public. I also can cry at some movies in the dark… But for myself, at least some of it is that I’d learned that not being “in control of myself” was quite unsafe around many people. I think now that this may be a trust issue; I could cry alone. That isn’t conducive to long-term mental health... I would hypothesize that perhaps if allistic people around an autistic kid have been pushing that kid to “act normal” very strongly while not helping the kid with the kid’s internal issues, like sensory overload, and other pain that those allistics may not understand, to some of us at a deep level, means you have shown many many instances of not caring about our pain. I understand that this may not be intentional, but kids may not understand that. For evidence, I only have some personal anecdotes, and snippets from other autistic adults… the experience of autistic kids does not seem to be a major topic of study, just their behavior. Adults (autistic, or allistic!) can often verbalize better than kids, and we learn over time to communicate with other adults — which could include researchers — and have memories of our childhoods, but researchers are not using us much at all in setting up treatments or generating explanations of behavior of autistic kids. So… a lot of “therapies” for autistic kids seem to ignore the internal experience of the autistic; behaviorism in general ignores internal experience, and ABA is behaviorism-based. I did not go through ABA personally, but “being normal” felt like a survival requirement, in my vague memories… harsh discipline at times. No one mirrored my own experience back to me and helped me understand myself. Relaxing enough to really express emotion is something we cannot then do. We are too wary at a deep level; we may not have the concepts to communicate this. (But it’s not like the adults have a clue either, in much of ABA and similar “treatments” — from my perspective.) Setup for the very frequent ptsd in the autistic in a few years, imho. I’ve camouflaged for decades and was diagnosed 3 years ago at age 52. Acting the same as others on the outside means a lot of deep squashing of personal feelings for some of us with different neurologies. I’m not saying autistic kids don’t need to learn skills, but autistics also need to be able to trust and connect in our own ways.

question: What specific advice would you give a neurotypical parent in terms of conversing to connect with their Aspie child?
answer: Lots of good answers about explaining stuff to Autistics, not that many that actually talk about connecting with us. There’s a lot of information about how to talk to us in a way that we’ll understand, but not a lot about how to get us to communicate back. Connection is a two-way street, after all. So there are two facets here: How to get a verbal Autistic child to talk with you more, and how to connect with an Autistic person by doing things that don’t involve talking. Because sometimes talking is hard but you want to connect anyway. The most obvious way to get almost any Autistic person to talk (or type/etc.) your ear off is to ask and show genuine interest in our special interests. You won’t just be learning about whatever subject interests your child, you’ll also learn about what parts of that interest are important to that child. Ask questions, get involved (presuming that they’re comfortable sharing their interests. Not everyone is.) If you can, find things about the interest that you also like, so you’ll both have something to gush about and discuss. For example, I got my dad to start watching Steven Universe with me a year ago. By talking with him about our favourite characters, I can learn more about him by knowing who he likes, and how facets of that character reflect in his own personality, his values, or even what he admires in others. (As of the end of 3rd season, his favourite is Amethyst! He hasn’t caught up to the madness of 5th season yet.) I don’t know if he’s using the same technique to learn more about me, but the option is certainly open to him. More importantly, the option is open to do the same with your child. Heck, this isn’t limited to children and I’d venture to say it’s not limited to Autistics either. The second facet ties into the first: Instead of discussing the interest, just partake in it. Sit down and watch the show with your kid, read the book they’re raving about, go swimming with them and try to do that awesome underwater barrel roll they keep doing. You might not get the same joy that they get from partaking in their interest, but you’ll understand their experience a little more than before you tried. More importantly, your child will see you trying to communicate in ways that are more comfortable to them, they’ll see you making an effort to be part of their world, instead of trying to acclimate them to yours. And seeing that effort is huge. I know my dad is a busy guy who would rather be doing all sorts of stuff than watching an animated kid’s show with his adult child. But while we’re watching those episodes, for those ten minute stretches we experience the same stimuli. We hear the same lines, we watch the same scenes, and we’re part of the same experience. For a brief stretch of time, the pressure is off: I don’t have to worry about communicating like an NT, or in a way that he’ll understand. I can just let my interests do the talking for a time, and share an awesome experience that way.

question: Should parents force their autistic kids to socialize?
answer: (Edited to correct grammar.) I am so torn on how to answer this question. Emotional Autistic James wants to say no, never force her to be something she is not. Her social skills operate differently, and will never function the same way as the other children. She will not learn the social skills you want her to, she must learn them in a different way. Forcing her to socialize will cause her discomfort at the least, anxiety and pain at the extremes. It can reinforce feelings of alienation and failure. It can cause an Overload. Realistic Autistic James wants to say yes, not to push, but gently direct her into situations where she can practice social skills. She will grow up and become an Autistic adult. Her challenges and strengths will never leave her, she will only learn how to manage them better. She needs to learn how to live in a world that she is not made for. She needs to be taught the unwritten social rules first. In explicit detailed language. She will fail in socializing because she cannot recognize and interpret body language and non verbal communication. She needs to know about them, and the correct reaction to them. Be direct. For example; “James, when you talk with a person never stand closer than an arms length from them. People have what’s called personal space, and unless the person is a family member, they will get uncomfortable when you stand in that space and speak to them. Always stand an arms distance from people when you speak to them. Do you understand this and do you have any questions.?” (Real life example btw, I tend to stand too close so that is a rule I learnt.) She will then need to practice her skills. Never push, gently direct. That means if she does not want to interact, then let her sit on the periphery instead. She will be watching and listening even from there. CBT calls these “exposure exercises,” and the child needs to be allowed to advance at a rate that is almost what they want, with just a small bit of nudging. Annoying, but not stressful. ”Social skills,” are really just the ritualistic steps during an interaction that NT people use to communicate information. Focus on strengthening your daughter’s communication skills. Social skills are a means of communicating information to NT people. Needs, wants, dreams, whatever, all information transmission. She can make it in the world with good communication skills and poor social skills. She will not do as well with good social skills, but a poor ability to communicate her needs. I am in this latter category, I studied how to move, speak and behave like the other children, at the cost of learning how to effectively communicate. I got pushed into group activities to socialize, and it only made me feel more alien, different and alone. It did not work for me, and it is taking a long time to unlearn the damage. No one’s fault really, nobody knew better at the time. My experience and opinion, nothing more, nothing less. I am just one Autistic dude on the internet. I hope there is something in there that helps. be well.

question: What do I do if an autistic person has a sensory overload, they start hitting themselves and crying?
answer: A general factor that common with many autistic people is regulation of physical and emotional feelings both on a conscious and subconscious level. The degree this affects us varies greatly from person to person. Also, what feelings are most prone to imbalance, the frequency of imbalance, and the cause of imbalance also varies greatly. This is why each autistic person is so unique and one solution that works for one person may not work for another. When we are young, our bodies and minds are mysteries. This is what we do as children: We learn about ourselves and how to keep everything in balance. Children with a typical neurology, have the advantage of having models of behavior, and supporting people who know how to keep the NT nervous system in balance. This is why childhood for autistic people is so difficult. We’re sort of on our own trying to figure out our mind and body. The models we do see may be showing us ineffective ways of maintaining balance or may be totally unaware of our imbalance and helping us regain it. There are communication factors too. How does a child find the words to describe extreme sensory issues when the adults around them cannot relate to what they feel? How would they even know if they have synesthesia? They may already have developed alexithymia and don’t understand what is causing the way they feel. Their attempts to communicate may have already been discounted so often for trying to express their feelings they don’t try any more. So, the parents or guardians of this child needs to address this child’s needs without assumptions. Question everything. You have to establish understanding of this child’s world because it is totally foreign to your life experience. This holds true for autistic adults too. The term “melt-down” is an extremely general word when it comes to autistic people. The cause, the degree, the duration, the form it takes, the remedy, the prevention, are different for every autistic individual. In general terms, a melt-down is where the instinctive “fight/flight/freeze responses have taken control and the person maybe conscious of their behavior but not in full control. Its like being charged by a tiger… You may think, “ Oh s..t, that tiger is trying to kill me!” .. But the body/mind has involuntarily assessed the situation and reacts beyond conscious control. This is why you will see melt-downs as protective (fight), evasive ( flight ), Immobilizing ( freeze) or a combination of these. So what is this “Tiger” that is causing this reaction (melt-down)? This can be difficult even for the autistic person to fully understand because it is a mostly a subconscious response. The “tiger” can be a combination of physical and psychological stresses. They can be stresses that combine over time and build like the pressure building in a volcano. Or that volcano can blow without warning. There is usually a trigger or stress that pushes the person beyond conscious control and the subconscious takes over. There is also a good possibility that CPTSD is a factor from a permanent and unresolved stress. And like the frog in the pot of heated water, we try to manage the rising temperature (stress) but this does not mean we have relieved the stress it may just become the new normal temperature, until we reach critical mass and the volcano blows… So consciously we think we have it under control… but then comes the unseen trigger and boom! So stress management is so important to all autistic people’s lives. This is why you let children stim, or take breaks, zone out, not make eye contact, leave the room, try to control sensory stimulation, seek isolation and so on… These are management tools not “ Restrictive/ repetitive behaviors” that should be discouraged or prevented. Self-abusive behaviors can also be preventative or stress relieving behaviors… Self-inflicted pain can lessen other stressors by overriding or anaesthetizing high stress issues. Understand that high stress and pain can be synonymous. A physical pain may help relieve a psychological pain. I’m not saying self-abusive behaviors should be allowed to continue, but you need to have a substitute way to relieve the stress the person is targeting. If not the stress and the problem remain. Do you understand better why a person would hit themselves and cry? Can you see that this is an instinctive reaction to the need to relieve or release of a perceived life threatening level of stress that has gone beyond their means to control? Their instinct takes over as a means of self preservation.
comment_answer: Thank you Thomas. We need to invent new words for sensory overload and find ways to process them The best thing is to acknowledge that their senses aren't bad or wrong and to give it a name. They need to be able to develop positively without trying to just block it all out.

question: What strategies can an autistic adult use to improve communication with non-autistic individuals?
answer: Honestly, having a social educator helps: those people are literally paid to teach us autistic folks how to make our part to break the neurological language barrier. Of course, non-autistic people also have their own part of the job to bridge the gap.

question: What are some tips for communicating with an autistic adult?
answer: Say what you mean and mean what you say. Be specific in your requests. Don’t think we don’t like you because small chat is difficult. At times it’s difficult to talk at all. We’re not really socially motivated. We still wish to be included and appreciate being so even if we decline often or always. We may interrupt you, this is not out of disrespect or disregard for what you have to say. We love honesty and authenticity. If you want us to talk all you have to do is ask us about our interests 😉 we might forget to ask you about what’s going on in your life and it may seem like conversations always go back to being about us but we’re just trying to show you how we relate to your story. Hope this helps! 🙂

question: Should I force a toddler who might have Asperger’s to go to daycare if after a month he still hates it?
answer: I agree with Estelle; figuring out why he hates it is pretty crucial. I think that trying to help with that might help build trust between you. Lots of autistic adults have a lot of trauma from childhoods in which some adults forced them to “adapt” to all sorts of painful things — sensory overloads of different sorts, in many cases. But what are this kid’s sensory issues? That is so critical to figure out imho… Forcing the kid to go, without helping him with his sensory issues, communicates on multiple levels to him… that adapting is important. Fine… true. But how about… That his actual pain is unimportant, that others don’t care about his pain, that his issues cannot be talked about ever, there are no words for them… If his caregivers won’t help him, how can he expect anyone else to care about what, to him, is a truly basic need — lack of pain? The latter are some of what autistic adults have learned by forced adaptation. Sometimes in “normal families”, sometimes in “therapies” like ABA that are now getting massive funding... (Terrifying to me to read that.) You can read about autism and camouflaging if you wish, it is finally being studied; autistics have a different neurology, and learning self-care as well as stretching one’s own limits, are both crucial for us to learn. Imo.
comment_answer: So true.

question: I found out my coworker has autism. We work with children and I am uncomfortable with the idea of an autistic person being around children. Should I tell our supervisor?
answer: I’m sorry people here are being mean and insulting you. I’m autistic, and I spent many years working with children. I worked as a kindergarten teacher, I co-taught a summer program for first through third-graders; and I spent some time teaching two, three, and four-year-olds in a daycare center. I cringe at this lack of humility, but being as objective as I can be, I’ll say I was a really good teacher: I was praised and loved by kids, parents, other teachers, and administrators. I’ve since worked as a writer, a teacher of adults, a computer programmer, and a theatre director, but I was better at working with kids than any of those things. I miss it. I would have kept doing it, but I was tired of being poor. As I’m sure you know only too well, teacher salaries suck. When I worked with kids, my autism didn’t create any obstacles. And it helped me work empathically with the autistic kids I sometimes had in my classroom, though I saw plenty of non-autistic teachers work well with them, too. What I recommend you do is learn a bit more about autism. Autistic adults can be a good teacher. Maybe the one you know one who was a terrible teacher, and that’s what’s making you nervous. That would make me nervous, too. But if he or she is a bad teacher, it probably isn’t the autism that’s caused it. Both autistic and non-autistic people can be bad teachers. One interesting trait of autistic people is they tend to be very patient—sometimes freakishly patient. This can be a useful skill for a teacher. I remember parents (and sometimes other theaters) asking me—on days when kids were particularly unruly—”How do you cope with it without getting upset?” It was easy for me. They were kids. They needed a patient teacher. So I was a patient teacher … Autism can make people so bad at understanding social cues, they can’t communicate easily with others—including children. But there are lots of autistic people who aren’t that debilitated, and it’s worth noting that kids tend to be easier to read than adults. They haven’t yet grown all the complicated layers they’ll one day have. Adults tend to hid their feelings. Kids usually wear their hearts on their sleeves. If grownups regularly cried when they were sad and danced for joy when they were happy, autistic people would have an easier time understanding them. Worrying that an autistic person won’t be able to understand your kid is like worrying that a French person won’t be able to understand her. It really depends on the French person. Some folks from France don’t understand English at all; some understand it a little; some understand it as well as native Americans. There’s a similar range when it comes to folks with autism. I have no trouble understanding social cues. I did when I was a kid and a teenager. Autism delayed me in that regard. But I caught up. Eventually, I became so interested in people that I spent years studying psychology, character-based novels, films, and plays, and I became attracted to social fields like teaching. I’ve reached a point where non-autistic friends often come to me for social advice. The ways autism most affects me as a grownup include a hyper-sensitivity to things like bright lights and loud noises, and a tendency to get nervous during fast transitions (e.g. a sudden, freak thunderstorm) and deviations from a schedule (e.g. a meeting that runs overtime). Sometimes these issues did challenges me when I worked with kids (kids can be super-loud, parents can be late picking them up, etc.), but that’s all they were: challenges. A non-autistic person teacher might be challenged because she has a headache, a cold, or because she’s in the middle of a messy divorce. Autistic or not, as grownups we often face challenges at work. And, as grownups, we deal with it. We behave responsibly and do our jobs, challenges or no challenges. If you have specific worries about your autistic coworker—who may indeed by a bad teacher—feel free to ask me questions. I’m happy to help if I can.
comment_answer: As the father of two very high-functioning adults who have both been diagnosed with Asperger’s Syndrome, I whole-heartedly agree with this answer. The questioner shows a very old-fashioned misunderstanding of autism.

question: People get angry about the phrase "cure for Autism" but what about helping low functioning autistic individuals who struggle and suffer trying to express themselves? Are we abandoning that group?
answer: My wife is a life skills instructor at a non-profit college for Autistic adults. The staff of the school works incredibly hard to help non-verbal (we don’t use the term low-functioning; its pejorative) Autistic individuals. Most of the students are in their early twenties. Many have additional issues with seizures. But, thanks to RPM (Rapid Prompting Method), a non-verbal communication technique pioneered by Soma Mukhopadhyah*, we can now communicate with these people…and most importantly, that means we can listen to them. They have much to teach us. I’ve “spoken” with a number of non-verbal Autistic students (through RPM) at my wife’s school. And my observations might surprise you: 1: Non-verbal Autistics possess advanced vocabularies and concepts. They possess humor, sarcasm and snark. They are far, far more complicated and sophisticated than we realized. 2: The #1 frustration most of the students have is how the world judges them. They’re fully aware of the world’s judgement. Since they were small children, they’ve been listening…and comprehending…what people think of them. This includes the whispers from their own family members. Many of these comments became internalized when they were very, very young. Perhaps, it was a visiting grandparent who obtusely said “You are so brave to endure the hardships of raising Lisa all these years.” And seven-year old Lisa heard that, understood that and internalized that. Perhaps, it was a parent who, in a moment of frustration, whispered under their breath “I have no friends because I’m stuck here in this house with you.” That whisper became internalized. Or, perhaps it was a simple phone call to a cousin “Oh, I can’t leave the house. I can’t leave Jason alone.” And Jason was fifteen (and if you read the points below, you’ll see how foolish this point of view can be; perhaps Jason can’t drive a car but Jason can most certainly be trusted to be alone in his own home) so Jason fully understood…Jason fully internalized that he can’t be left alone…not even for a moment…and that he has imprisoned his parents while he, too is a prisoner. People are way too glib in front of non-verbal Autistic people. They simply assume that because they cannot speak they cannot hear, see or think. 3: The second-greatest struggle non-verbal Autistics have is with parents who gave up on them when they were young and have infantilized them even as they enter adulthood. The parents have no expectations of them. None. Even though the state pays for their tuition, the parents don’t treat the school as a real school; it is, from the parent’s point of view, a daycare and a respite from having to constantly care for their children (even though the constant care isn’t actually necessary). Ironically, the parents often go ballistic when the instructors introduce new life skills that are intended to help the students progress towards true independence. Many of the students are more than capable of living in a group home environment. Some could live semi-autonomously in their own apartment, only needing someone to check in on them once a day…or once a week. But, their parents can’t see (or don’t want to see) this as an option for their adult children. 4: Most of the students are on wacky diets, usually lacking protein, because the parents bought into the “Cure Fad” of the 1990’s and 2000’s. Because of this, the students have (what I believe; it isn’t scientifically proven) underdeveloped muscles and a lack of energy due to consistently being undernourished. They become exhausted easily. They struggle to type for extended periods of time. And so would you if you had no protein in your diet! NO PROTEIN! The students sensitivity to texture limits their palettes, to be certain, but the parents have overlaid a non-scientific diet culled from various fads over the past two decades all with the intent to “cure Autism through diet.” Tidbits of chillation and some stupid statement from Jenny McCarthy become the foundation of what is forcefed to these adult children. No one can eat their way to being non-Autistic, but that hasn’t stopped these parents from trying. One of my wife’s responsibilities is teaching the students to cook for themselves. She’s also teaching them about eating well. Some students’ parents find the concept of eating enough protein “highly controversial.” (Personally, I think the parents are anti-science whack-jobs and the greatest source of frustration for these autistic adults.) 5: Many non-verbal Autistics use scripts to communicate. Often (not always!) the scripts are quotes from Disney films or other childhood entertainment. We often assume this reflects the “state of maturity” of the student. They may be 22 years old, but because they are quoting a line from The Lion King, they must have the maturity of an 8 year old… …RPM has revealed we have this so very, very wrong. Often, the adult Autistic is not allowed to watch anything other than children’s programming, so it is the only metaphor they know how to use. Often, it is the only thing they watch with their parents and so it is their attempt to come down to their parents level and use a reference they think their parents will understand. I want you to think about that again; from the adult child’s mind, they are trying to relate to their parents. Their parent has spoken to them in a high-pitched, kiddie-voice for two decades. They speak about “You need a pottie break, son?” It is the parent who seems like a child. It is the parent who has created no additional context for the adult child. So, the adult child is communicating with the only context provided to them…the context of children’s entertainment! 6: Surprisingly, many of the students have areas of arrogance. One of the non-verbal students describes himself as a genius and finds almost everything he is tasked with to be beneath him. More than likely, he has an extremely high IQ. But, this is not uncommon amongst Autistic people and my wife has taught him a phrase that is common in our household; “Genius is a verb, not a noun.” What we mean by this is “You think you’re bright? Show me. Do something. Don’t just brag. Don’t think you’re above loading a dishwasher or cleaning a toilet because you’re clever. Show your genius by doing something. Don’t use it as an excuse to be lazy.” My son, who is a fellow Aspie, would use his intelligence as an excuse to avoid hard work and we began using “Genius is a verb, not a noun” to make it clear to him that if he wanted to prove to the world he was special he’d need to do special things. You’re great at math? Then, earn your A in Advanced Algebra. Don’t talk about it. Show me. You want to be a professional writer? Then, write. Don’t talk about it. Do it. We do this with love. We do this with kindness and compassion. But, there is absolutely nothing wrong to holding people to a high standard, particularly if they themselves claim they can be. You tell me your special, then you’re telling me I have the right to hold you to a higher standard than you’re holding yourself to right now. And personally, I don’t care if you’re non-verbal, I’m not going to feed into the myth that “disability equals no agency.” You have agency. You’re alive. You have value. You can contribute. I love you. I believe in you. Now, lets get to work. Genius is a verb. My wife is introducing a significantly watered-down version of this at school. But, not because the students can’t handle it…it’s the parents. The parents can’t handle it. Which leads to my last point… 7: Because the parents gave up on their children when they were young, these adult students have never had any expectations placed upon them. Most (not all!) simultaneously resent “adulting” but do not want to be infantilized. This is to be expected; they have the intellect of an adult and want to be seen as an adult but they don’t understand that adults do dishes, laundry, close the bathroom door, don’t touch themselves in public…it isn’t their disability that causes these outward and unexpected signs of asocial behavior, it is a support network that has absolutely no expectations of the individual. As usual, we humans struggle with cause and effect. The parents low expectations result in low results… …and they expect the school to do 100% of the work to make up for their poor parenting… …and they become fearful when the school makes progress with the students. What would solve this? It’s not more drugs or a different diet or another fad-program for the students. The solution is both simple and impossible. The parents need therapy. At the very least, the parents should be in a group counseling program lead by a qualified psychologist with a deep understanding of how quickly our knowledge of Autism is changing. Most of these parents studied a few books fifteen years ago, decided those books were the Ten Commandments and that became their dogma. They do not understand that science changes and our theories are a moving target. The worst parents (and that’s a fair phrase if you met some of these people!) are the ones that were highly social and popular in their own youth. They have little empathy for and no expectations of their children. They feel trapped in a prison, eternally burdened, unable to have a social circle as large as they did when they didn’t have children. I struggle to have empathy for these people. As an Aspie, I find “hyper-socials” to be the ones with the disability. They seem to have no autonomy and their need for the approval of others is…unhealthy. I judge them as much as their kind has judged us. Almost all of these nonverbal Autistic adults would be doing far, far better and far, far more if they simply had parents who had higher expectations of them and treated them like full human beings. It is not their parents “fault” that their children are Autistic. It is entirely their parents fault that they have been infantilized, that they resist enabling these Autistic adults to live semi-autonomous lives. If you are a parent of a non-verbal Autistic person, your child is capable of far, far more than you realize. It might take them longer to learn something, but that doesn’t mean they can’t learn it. If they learn to properly use a bathroom at 15 instead of 3, that’s still massive progress. If they learn to help with chores around the house, even if it takes them years to master that chore, they’ll feel like a true member of your family. Its your job to have patience and hope…yes, 500% more than the typical family…but that’s what being atypical means! When you give up, you make that your child’s permanent reality. If you’re struggling with teaching your seven-year-old Autistic child to use a toilet don’t give up. Yes, it takes far, far longer with Autistic people…but when I hear someone say “my child is 15 and he still struggles to use the bathroom” I have yet to meet a parent who didn’t give up when the child was young. You, the parent, made the reality…not “the autism.” And certainly, not your child. Obviously, non-verbal Autism is a serious disability. It often comes with co-morbid issues like severe seizures. We are starting to understand the biological differences in the non-verbal Autistic brain; it is wired differently and so no one is denying that the struggle to communicate is difficult and demanding… …but, what you see and hear is not all there is to your children. You assume permanence. You assume an inability to learn. You assume they aren’t listening. You assume they don’t understand. You assume…you assume. Your assumptions are the second-greatest challenge your child has. “Are we abandoning this group?” That’s an excellent question. From my point of view, there are social workers, scientists and volunteers working very hard to help these people become as autonomous and self-actualized as possible. So, I turn the question back to you…are YOU abandoning this group? One of my wife’s students recently “said” to several instructors “Is there any hope for me?” The subtle fear and desperation was plain on her face. Yes, she has serious physical challenges. But, the lack of hope could very well be the greatest disability she faces. And that’s why my wife goes to work everyday. She’s trying to help these students have hope. She’s raising their standards, expecting more of them than they expect of themselves and she’s showing them they can do more and be more than anyone every though they could be. *Please note, the scientific community has not independently verified the validity of RPM yet. This is an area of ongoing debate and learning. However, my personal observation and experience is that it is an effective method of communication. If the science proves the technique is ineffective or flawed, I’ll readily change my point of view. However, I have interacted with more than a dozen non-verbal autistic students who use RPM through the same instructor and their approach to sentence construction is completely different. They have a “voice.” One student is sarcastic and snarky. Another student is timid and shy. Another student makes grammar errors unique to himself. Another is commenting on science. Now, how on earth would a single translator be capable of introducing that level of variation into each person’s speech? How is it not self-generated? That being said, I readily admit that until a theory has been independently tested and validated under rigorous standards to isolate any vectors, it isn’t (yet) scientifically proven. So, I remain open-minded, despite the overwhelmingly positive results I’ve seen from RPM.

question: My 21 months old son is showing autistic traits. Apart from prescribed therapies, what can I do as a father to help him become normal?
answer: ‘Becoming normal’ should not and can not be the goal for your child, if he does turn out to be autistic. Autism is classified as a Pervasive Developmental Disorder. The word ‘pervasive' is related to the word pervade, meaning to be perceived in every part of. An individual that is autistic will always be autistic, in every way. The goal you are setting has many problems. For starter's, it is totally unreachable. Constantly pushing a child toward something that is unattainable, such as changing the way their brain processes information, is setting them up for failure, which often results in low self-esteem and feelings of inadequacy. Second of all, autism itself is not a bad thing. It is a manner of brain function that has pros and cons, just like being neurotypical. The only part that makes it any harder is that the world has been built with the neurotypical person in mind. You likely think of the more ‘problematic' symptoms of autism: difficulty with communication, sensory problems, rigid thinking, etc. What you fail to realize is that good comes with that: an easier time with introspection, the ability to perceive and understand details others miss, the ability to be systematic and thorough, and much more. The most important part of this, however, is that your child is an individual. He is one unique child, and your goal should not be to ‘make him like the others,’ it should be to help him grow to be himself; a parent should be teaching their child how to be a good person and how to pursue their dreams and talents, as opposed to how to fit in. As for doing that, as your child gets older, see what he likes and what he excels in. Encourage him. Praise him when he does well. Find the way to communicate with your child that he understands best. Is your child highly verbal? Speak with him, often and using literal language. Words aren't his strong suit? Learn ASL, modified signs, PECS, typing, see a speech therapist, whatever seems to fit the best. Help your child with what he struggles in. Praise him for small victories and advances in skills he finds difficult. Seek early intervention, although I would avoid ABA, as it tends to be unnecessarily painful and often relies on punishing the child for unintentional mistakes. Talk to autistic adults; we have a lot to tell you. Remember that autistic kids aren't all the same; your son is going to grow at a different rate, just like every other child on the planet. Most of all, don't try to change your son. It will hurt him more than you know.

question: Can autistic children live a normal life?
answer: Children? Children!?!!! Do you have no concept that there are tons of autistic adults already existing and roaming on this earth? Sorry, that was dramatic. Now that this is out of the way, I will go through the post question by question. “can they learn to take care of themselves?” it depends on what their support needs are. Some autistics have more executive functioning than other autistics and may need less help. Others with more support needs need more help. But do realize a core feature of being autistic is impaired executive functioning (the part of the brain that has to do with planning, executing tasks, keeping track of things, maintaining them). If they have ADHD (as many as 1/4ths of autistics do also have ADHD and I am one of them), then their executive functioning will be even more impaired. It’s not about JUST teaching them how to do something and that's it and if they can't maintain it then “you’re not trying hard enough”— it may be that they are really impaired in this area. Don't dismiss it as a possibility. “what other normal kids do” while autistic people will get much farther in life with people presuming competence or them, it seems you are still harboring an expectation that they will one day be NT and have not found a way to accept their neurology yet. May I ask this? Is your kid receiving any kind of behaviorism (like aba)? If so, run the other way. If a therapy is designed to break a person by trying to get them to comply with the impossible (and being told to become the neurotypical you never were meant to be, it IS impossible), you're telling that kid that it’s not okay to be who they are. Growth and learning should be goals for autistic people. Not being “"indistinguishable from peers”. The latter will just result in a broken sense of self, no self-esteem, eating disorders (my personal experience), being groomed for abuse (many of my friends’ personal experiences— because if you can't say no or have the option to say no and be taken seriously, what’s to say they will say no to someone who seriously harms them? And will they seek support and help in another person if all day long they are inundated with the fact that their needs, their wellbeing, and their security don't matter. And being told their body doesn't belong to them?) and then, on top of that, they will funnel all energy they have into passing or trying to remain indistinguishable, to where either a) their support needs aren't taken seriously when then they hit a wall of burnout or b) they don't have any energy left in the tank for legitimate things like advocacy or executive functioning. Then at age 24 they find themselves right where I was, in autistic burnout and so shut down (like all systems for thinking go offline shutdown, when it’s no longer a temporary “let’s just kick the can down the road”) I could barely speak for 6 months. It took me years to fully recover from burnout. “can they have a good future not depending on anyone or anything” i don't know. It depends on how disabled they are, whether or not people are working with them, how accepted they are, versus how much stigma they are against. It seems you are putting a lot of weight on independence. So, what if your kid struggles to find independence, are you going to judge them? I'm only pretty sure they are trying hard enough. But society isn't set up for us and workplace discrimination for autistic people is very prevalent, real, and existing (extremely rampant), and if they get stuck in a sheltered workshop they are even more screwed because of a loophole in law they get paid sub-minimum wage. But, here is the thing; most people in life are actually interdependent than independent. It sounds like you have a bucket of ableism to sort through. Please don't be like my mom back in the day though, harping over and over anxiously about my future and “whatever will you do with your life”— I was all of 6–7–8 years old when she did that. my whole childhood I had the “"whatever will you do” anxiety doomcloud hanging over my head. It stagnated my progress because I would freeze in horror, not grow as a person. That’s anxiety though. Things may change though. They may learn coping skills. Assistive tech might come a long way, they already have here one earbuds that filter sensory noise out. Those have been amazing for me and i’ve only had mine 3 Weeks so far. And afaik I have way more skills at 33 than I ever did at 5. Remember that. And you only see a text representation of me over the internet (a lot less overstimulating than talking in a busy environment). You're seeing the 33 year old working autistic who is supported by dad’s business, lives in grandma’s other house, has a boyfriend who helps tremendously, and this autistic who has gotten farther in the last 3 years than the last 20. I couldn't do it without support, so honestly i dont think this dichotomy (black and white) style thinking where one has to do it with no support is feasble for a lot of autistics. It’s also not feasible to not presume competence of autistic people (infantilization). Believe it or not, there is a giant swath of gray area in between the two that is far more healthy (I find it weird when people say that autistic people are all about black and white thinking when the see-saw of flawed expectations that people ram down our throats from day one to all throughout childhood is all about black and white thinking. It’s almost like, we learned it from them! Sorry, that was a little snarky) “will they be able to take care of themselves?” What if I told you that even if they can't, there are people called PCAs (primary care assistants), that if they have trouble cleaning house that maid services are pretty hopping these days? And there is no shame in seeking out services if they need them. it seems that you are not terribly keen on services, but for some people that’s the way to go. I just hope that people can sort out the carnage this government is doing because I am legitimately scared for a lot of people I love that they are going to die under this new administration, from poverty, lack of healthcare, and lack of services. I hate to get political but congress and trump are gutting the social safety net stuff that already was on shaky ground and not getting enough money to begin with. Disabled people stand to lose a lot. Unfortunately, there is very real danger in the capitalistic view of viewing autistic people as burdens (that goes for “"every man for himself” type liberatarianism as well). I have seen a lot of parents rationalize that they don't want their kids to live one more breath than them because they are so-called worried for their kid’s future and “"what about the services” but those statements have been repeatedly used to defend filicide against autistics (and other disabled folk) so I draw the line obviously. well, looks like your work is cut out for you. In the meantime perhaps visit one of the many autistic blogs (yes that too, real social skills, invisible strings, radical neurodivergence speaking/time to listen, emma’s hopebook, olliebean (both Amy sequenzia and Judy endow’s blogs are great), and perhaps hop over to parenting autistic children with love and acceptance, and we are like your child. I'm only pretty sure I forgot 12 blogs and groups though (literally there is no shortage of material, people just need to look for it, instead of going to that one fear-mongering “"charity” fundraising scheme that I call “bewareness”— you probably know which org I am talking about— yes, they are that terrible). I'm also a member of ASAN (autistic self advocacy network). Either way, see if you can find spaces that are autistic-run or support autistics. If you have questions on autistics it’s better to ask autistic adults directly (we have been there, in those kids shoes!) instead of going to allistic (non autistic) parents (who are likely clueless or coming to the wrong conclusions) or “professional” for bungled answers that go wrong (double bonus negative points if those “professionals” have something to sell you— like if they are peddling some kind of aba, books of anti-science, or snake oil supplements— either way, a lot of people come to the wrong conclusions.) i hope this helps you understand autistics more from an adult perspective. and if your kid hasn't been through even half the shit I’ve been through they are lucky. Even more so if it’s even 1/8th of the shit my friends have been through (they've had some really terrible traumatic experiences, and unfortunately there is only one — out of hundreds of autistic adults I know who doesn't have any ptsd from their life experiences, all of the rest of us I have meet in the autistic community do— that includes me). We’ve come out on the other side, and what you may see with autistic adults talking to parents is that we may come off rough around the edges, (after all, communication isn't exactly our strong suit, especially with a topic that evokes very traumatic memories) but with the altruistic intention that we really do truly want the best for your kids. Don't make the same mistakes our parents did if you can help it. Even with the best intentions, a person can be harmed (you know the phrase, “the road to hell is paved with good intentions”?). I (as well as many autistic adults) want to minimize that from happening. Here is a pretty good post that K did. You, yes you, need Autistic friends.

question: Why do autistic, non-verbal kids cover their ears?
answer: Many of us autistics feel that sounds that don’t bother most non-autistics, are in fact painful. It is not the same feeling for me as the pain from a physical injury, exactly, but it can be truly aversive. The refusal of people around us to validate our discomfort can also create enormous problems for us; for me, it led me to not tend to disclose other sorts of discomfort, to not trust people in certain positions of power, as a kid and older. Trust is a tricky thing! Non-verbal kids have fewer tools available than a 58-year-old autistic with degrees and such like myself, but for all the good my communication with adults of different neurotypes did me as a kid, or as an adult trying to communicate with “autism experts” omg… anyhow! No wonder they cover their ears, basic communication like that is where we all start. Eye contact felt like electric shocks to me the whole way through college, but only in certain contexts where I felt at risk, btw! My experience. No studies to “prove” it. I hope that the OP will (begin?) reading writings by adult autistics — including non-verbal autistics who have been taught typing! — about their experiences esp. before learning how to communicate with very different people. It’s pretty hard to communicate across neurotypes, there are often misunderstandings. Before getting diagnosed, I took classes in psychology, animal behavior, all sorts of stuff trying to figure out those weird human creatures. :-) A diagnosis helped me understand NT perceptions of autistics better, because that’s really what most of the research seems about, rather than our (autistic) inner worlds. However, covering one’s ears seems really clear to me! Whether the adults will support the kid and help the kid limit the aversive stimuli - that’s a different question! No, we autistics cannot hide from NT society completely, but trusting ourselves, learning to control our environment as best we can so we can also contribute what we want to society instead of being stuck having meltdowns/shutdowns in awful cycles… Adults around autistic kids can totally help with that. (I personally learned to do what is called partial “shutdowns” to cope, and have held a job my whole life. But I’ve had other issues that fit in with what I read about “dissociation” well before I got diagnosed autistic. I suspect the brain can use those powerful tune-out tools to survive, brains are amazing, but I really don’t recommend forcing kids to learn to dissociate so they can “act normal”. Too long a story!) question: What are some breakthrough treatments for autistic children?
answer: Acceptance is the best treatment for autistic children. Autistic people of all ages, actually. In all seriousness, I know what you mean, but I’m here to tell you that those treatments only suppress what an autistic person’s brain naturally tells them to do. Do you really want your child to experience high anxiety because you’ve made them stop stimming, or doing something that is so against their natural impulses that they completely meltdown when they’re around others, or shutdown to deal with the pain if they’ve been trained out of expressing themselves in meltdowns? These treatments often come under the umbrella of ABA—applied behaviour analysis. Otherwise known as puppy training, or abuse, it’s left many autistic adults with severe post-traumatic-stress disorder and a lifetime of internalised ableism. It also hasn’t had many long-term, proven effects, either. There are some treatments you can use to make sure an autistic person lives the best version of themselves, though. These include:Speech therapy—I had this myself, to treat a lisp and my ‘shyness’ (I had limited verbal abilities when I was a child, but because I was a female they were never picked up on as an autism trait—I still struggle with this now). It’s highly effective in some autistic children.Talking Therapy—This helps some autistic people to process and deal with strong emotions in a positive, productive way, stopping them from reaching a point where they feel like the only way they can communicate with others is by melting down.Play therapy—play therapy, like using dolls to help people understand social rules, can help autistic people understand social norms in a friendly way without insisting they do something ‘right’ (aka, non-autistically) to receive a reward. This should be fun, and probably not listed under ABA. Some people use ABA to describe other therapies in America for insurance purposes, but I’d still be weary.Social books—I’m not sure of their official name, but these basically provide people with an understanding of how a certain social situation will work. Like going to the hospital, or to the cinema, for example. It’ll help the autistic person prepare themselves for a situation before it occurs.I hope these help!

question: Would two friends with autism struggle to communicate or get along more than two without?
answer: Most of my favourite people are autistic and that's not to say we don't miscommunicate or misunderstand each from time to time, just the same as everyone else but it's the way react to each others social blunders or “statements that could easily be construed as offensive" — that makes it easier to be friends with other autistic people. I've found we tend to be forgiving of that sort of thing, with each other because we've had lifetimes of not just feeling mis-understood, but actually being mis-understood, no matter how verbally explicit we try to be with our neurotypical counterparts. Whereas with autistic friends, we all know we are prone to other people not liking us, it starts in school and can affect our work, it can affect everything and amongst autistic adults, many of us havent reached our potential whatsoever, despite being bright and hard working, just because of how we come across to other people. Most autistic adults that I know have had to deal with lots of shit from other people, because we think differently and it can come across badly to others in so many little ways, it's difficult to keep count. When autistic people I know, including myself, feel annoyed with someone — in our community what seems to happen is it comes to a head pretty quickly and gets resolves quickly but best of all, we don't hold grudges towards each other 1) because that's not how teams work well and 2) we don't lack object constancy whatsoever. A lot of people are fickle, one moment they love someone, next moment they hate them — I think it's nigh on impossible for some of us to do that, even when somebody has abused our trust, we don't suddenly hate them and don't lose track of the fact that people are complex and that there are some things we might not necessarily like or agree with — hell, it's possible to disagree with most of what a person says and still like them. Sometimes it doesn't feel that other people get that and a lot of autistic people have been on the harsh end of people hating on them for relatively minor things, like single statements that cause people to devalue them forevermore. A lot of us have had to deal with the same shit, ongoing throughout our lives, insinuations that we are boring and not fun to be around — the lack of invituations to birthday parties when you are literally the only one who wasn't invited and everyone else was and talks about it for weeks afterwards. There are always reminders that we don't belong, which starts when we are so young we don't know anything else, but feeling like a constant spare part. Or if you do manage to fit in, you know it's only a matter of time before you say something that causes you to be ostracised AGAIN. Im not saying that all autistic people feel this or that all groups for autistic people are welcoming — cos they aren't — but it's worth ploughing through all them (if needs must) in order to find people/fellow autists that you can strike up a genuine friendship with. It is definitely worth it because we can understand things that only people who have experienced similar things firsthand, can understand. A lot of people have the narrow mindset of believing they can only be friends with people who share similar beliefs to them, some autistic people are like that too, very fixated on sticking people into polarised categories of “good" and “bad" — it's difficult for people with that mentality to have friends because they are looking for a carbon copy of themselves and raising the bar higher than my bar. So as ever, the answer is that it depends on the individuals, but yes, it can aid communication in friendships, to have a lot of shared experience that has come about from being autistic in a world dominated by a different neurotype, it's not an insignificant commonality to share.

question: Do people with autism give up easily?
answer: Its not as simple as that. On one hand autistic people can be extremely focused and driven when able to pursue a passion or interest that is important to them. They are very unlikely to give up here. Autistic people learn differently - it has to be by interest, for the motivation to occur and they will often want to pursue it exclusively. This means that if they forced to pursue other things they do not enjoy - such as in schools, universities, jobs, other expectations or commitment, their momentum dries up. Or if they have to pursue a wide range of tasks and are not able to pursue they interest enough, again motivation and internal momentum will dry up and the autistic individual will appear to â€˜give upâ€™ or â€˜not be tryingâ€™. This is also partly due to autistic inertia. Autistic people are like a heavy boulder - they can take a bit to warm up and get into a task, once they get going they can stick to it well - even focus better than most people for longer periods (hyperfocus), but it makes task-switching difficult, because there is momentum behind the current task. They may need space, a break to unwind from the previous task, and time to warm up into the new one to effectively task switch. A standard education on one hour subject changes is not appropriate for an autistic person. They may seem to do well on the first task, but be unable to engage with further, different tasks or subjects, but this is not due to giving up or not trying - its just how their neurological system functions. There is also autistic burnout - this is more for autistic people who can mask in order to pass as neurotypical. They have studied their peers, perhaps through TV, books and observation and mimic neurotypical voice inflection, conversation patterns, copied speech, body language - all the things that neurotypicals do intuitively and fairly naturally, autistic people are orchestrating - and juggling with intense effort, all while holding in their coping mechanisms like stimming and difficult reactions to sensory and social information. This can lead to a complete burnout - on smaller and larger scales. This often occurs in higher-functioning individuals and those who have gone undiagnosed into adulthood and had to learn to appear normal to survive. Autism is a completely invisible disability, so those who can pass as normal often dont recieve the support they need, them trying to continuously compensate for their disability alone - and meet expectations unsuited to them as a person, can lead to complete exhaustion, burnout and a reduction in level of functioning. A person may find they are no longer able to handle a work or school environment, when previously they seemed to be coping just fine from the outside, they may need to withdraw completely to recharge their batteries deeply, and adjust to a different way of doing things that doesnt lead to the same result of burnout. Iit is not the same as a meltdown which is just sensory overload and the individual may need decomprension time alone, without sensory input or with a particular stim to soothe them. Burnout can last weeks, months, or even years depending on its severity. It is not for lack of trying - it is from too much trying in a world that doesnt fit or acknowledge them.

question: If you are diagnosed with high-functioning autism as an adult, is it easier or harder to admit you have some deficiencies in your social competencies?
answer: This is a very complicated topic. Let me start with late diagnosed adultsâ€¦ The reason some autistic adults do not discover they are autistic until later in life is because we have been able to develop coping strategies to function in a manner that is â€œacceptableâ€ to the standards of behavior as established by the general society. This starts as very young children and we do not question why we have to develop these strategies. We assume this is what everyone is doing and so we are just as normal as everyone else. That is, until we are still corrected, rejected, ridiculed, or ostracized for our behaviors. We are then faced with the dilemma. Why are these things happening to us if we are normal? What makes our behaviors different than other people? We do not automatically assume this is because we are physically (neurologically) different than other people. We cannot understand that we are fundamentally different people. Unfortunately, nor can NTs understand this either. So we are expected to behave the same way. It seems to be part of some NTs nature to reject people who are different. Autistic people do not understand this behavior. Is it rooted in the fear of the unknown? Is it the need to associate only with those behave predictably according to their own familiar ways of behaving? NT behavior is as much a mystery to us as our autistic behavior is to them. The behaviors of people, autistic or not, are compelled by their true nature. I believe most of this is set by our genetics and our genetics form the development of our nervous system. We know that the nervous systems of autistic people are very different than non-autistic (neurotypical/NT) people. Though they are different systems, they are normal for each group. Autistic behaviors are as normal to us as NT behaviors are to them. These groups perceive and process life experiences very differently. Autistic people think in concrete terms, and process the details and how these details connect in more general ways. Where NTs tend to think in more abstract ways, seeing general categories and symbolic concepts. Neither way is right or wrong, but both do have advantages in certain situations. Autistic people, because of our analytical nature, and the constant pressure to conform to NTâ€™s standards of behavior, are more aware of this double standard that exists between the two groups. NTs are not held to a different standard than their true nature. They are free to be NTs. We become aware of this double standard as very young children. Unless our behaviors are recognized as autistic by adults around us, and we are diagnosed as autistic, we never understand WHY there is this double standard we have to live by. Undiagnosed autistic adults are always aware of this double standard and constantly feel this in every part of our lives. At some level we keep searching for why this double standard existsâ€¦ Until one dayâ€¦ we discover that we are autistic. This was to me and most late diagnosed adults Iâ€™ve met, the most profound realization of our lives. I want to address the second part of the question: â€œâ€¦is it easier or harder to admit you have some deficiencies in your social competencies?â€. â€œ Once we understand that we are neurologically different. That THIS is why this double standard exists, this dilemma becomes clearer. What we start to realize is that the problems are not because of our differences in behavior. It is because we have been expected to behave the same as NTs. In ways contrary to our natural behaviors. Autistic people do not pressure NTs to behave autistic. So it is very confusing, frustrating, upsetting, and inappropriate, we are expected to conform to NTâ€™s standards of behavior. Do we have â€œdeficiencies in our social competenciesâ€? Or are our standards and means of socializing just different than NTs? To say they are deficiencies, is to say one standard is superior or correct. Is this true? Or are they different standards that support the true nature of each group? There is a terrible effect that this double standard has on autistic people. I hope that those who are autistic understand that there is nothing wrong with being autistic. There is nothing wrong about being different. That this terrible stress this has caused in our lives is not cause by being autistic, it is caused by societies expectations that we become NT. I would hope that NTs would understand that their standards of behavior are not universal standards. That different is not bad or threatening to the standards they need to function well and be comfortable with who they are. That those with different standards have the same right to be true to their nature. To function well and be comfortable with who they are too. This realization would help not only autistic people, but all people just trying to live true to their nature. Trying to be their best in the only way they canâ€¦ and that is to be themselves. So many of our worldâ€™s problems come from these multiple standards and the false assumptions that any one of them is superior to the rest. We can all learn and be better people if we open our minds to different standards. Not that we have to adopt them, but to be accepting that they are all equally valid and necessary.

question: As an autistic person, do you sometimes have the feeling that living in a non-autistic world is slowly warping your thoughts and your personality in a non desirable manner, so that you become alien to yourself?

question: If autism is just a difference, then what are the problems that neurotypicals face as individuals that autistic people do not struggle with, and not how they act towards autistic people?

Like, new and better evidence makes them actually double down on a discredited idea, instead of assimilating the new data and coming to an updated conclusion. It's apparently a developmental delay in the ability to invest mental energy in comprehension and critical thinking. Once the neurotypical person decides what they think is correct, they're unable to assimilate any new information on the subject. The idea becomes fixed, to a pathological degree. I suspect that their strong social instincts are at the root of this problem, because of a co-morbid condition: the instinct to divide into loyalty tribes. They appear to believe their identities are predicated upon the things they perceive to be true, and any evidence that their beliefs are incorrect triggers a strong defensive mechanism; the data are rejected as a threat to the individual's actual identity as a person. Hence the neurotypical tendency to band together in groups of people who share similar beliefs, and to launch coordinated attacks on others who do not share their particular set of beliefs. These attacks give the group, and the individuals in it, a sense of righteous purpose, and deliver a significant emotional boost. If seen as a statistical minority, these tendencies would rightfully be viewed as developmental delays, since they're evidence of a stunted ability to analyze, assimilate, and apply new information. But since neurotypical people are a majority, this is largely seen as â€œnormalâ€ behaviour, and is condoned if not encouraged by the larger society at hand. It's why bullying exists, and it's why nothing can or will ever be done to stop or prevent bullying. Bullying is just neurotypical people exercising their inherent neurotypical skills, but just a little bit harder than necessary. But take a moment to imagine what the world would look like if tribalistic thought had never been prominent. Imagine all the advances we'd have made already, if not for all the time, resources, and lives consumed by the need to dominate and attack others who don't share the same belief sets. If information had never been suppressed because it threatened somebody's sense of identity or social standing. If people found it easy to acknowledge when something they believed was incorrect, and to change their minds instead of working harder to support something that has been discredited or found to be factually incorrect. But since sanity is statistical, with the majority dictating what is â€œnormalâ€ and what is â€œabnormalâ€, autism has been pathologized as â€œdevelopmental delayâ€. I guess hand flapping and item sorting is much more dysfunctional than grouping together to hurt others for a rush. *Edit: Not ALL neurotypical people, of course. But that's another neurotypical delay, thinking that observing a tendency in the majority automatically means the observation must apply to all individuals in the majority, instead of just a majority within the majority. *eyeroll*
