But for most of us the mirror reaction leaves a rather hollow, empty version of the feeling which we just portrayed. It is not yet real. We first have to think about the issue at hand, understand it somewhat, wrap our minds around it and accept it: then it is ours. I am not happy just because you smiled and then I mirror smiled. I'm happy because I like your smile. Your smile is beaming and radiant and real, and it makes me wonder about the beautiful thing that must have occurred for you to have a beautiful smile such as that one. And this is empathy. I have emotionally put myself in your shoes. I have shared in your emotion not by merely mirroring it, but rather by embracing it as my own. The mirroring reflex is often misconstrued as empathy. The mirroring reflex is capable of triggering the beginning of empathy in some people, but it is not at all required for empathy. Someone who is perceived to be lacking in empathy would often be perceived as a jerk. You donâ€™t care about me? While perhaps selfish, this very human trait is shared amongst both autistic and neurotypical people. An autistic person wants you to care just as much as a neurotypical person would. Although neither will show it in those ways the other intuitively understands. Autistic people are known to be sensitive, and are particularly susceptible to stress. An autist will not mirror automatically or correctly. This subconscious neurotypical trait is sacrificed along the way to gaining filmographic memory and other such autistic traits. Through intense practice (and many, many fails), this can become a learned trait in order to appease neurotypical peers; very similar to learning the parts in a play. However then it would be acting rather than reflexive. And most neurotypicals, so well-versed in their subconscious social cues, are perceptive enough to receive this as fake or as lying. It is! No more or less than the mirroring reflex, but it is indeed a conscious lie, rather than a subconscious lie. Fake is also often perceived as â€˜a jerkâ€™. So is dishonesty. Autists are perfectly capable of empathy. Autism in fact encourages hyper-empathy. It takes longer for many autistic people to learn to talk or engage with others, yet the mind is racing; ever, ever racing. A very few autistic people never do learn to engage with others, but, most do! Imagine being around others and never learning their language for many long years. Not just deficit in their verbal language, but in their body language too. Your mind, active and engaging, cannot communicate properly with any other human being readily accessible to you. But you can tell when they are happy and when they are sad. And you can tell when they are frustrated. Or angry. Or excited. Or scared. And you probably care about them too, especially if they are kind to you. You don't know how to show it in the body language that they understand, but with this lack of language comes a grasp of empathy which is raw, and unfiltered, and real. For as we know, true empathy goes much deeper than any language. The autistic person will not mirror your sadness, but the autistic person who cares for you will study the cause of your sadness and set about trying to correct this so that you can feel better. The autistic person is worried about you when you are sad. The autistic person is sad, and frustrated, and perhaps angry at other things, when you are sad. To know that you feel better again, would make the autist feel relieved. This is empathy. Mirroring is outdated, anyway. But I should note that if you try to hide your emotions, as is another subconscious trait developed for group survival, you will succeed with an autistic person. That stuff between your lines is not going to get read. The driving force is to understand; and so, autistic people do not naturally hide their emotions amongst the subconscious from which they can be so hard to analyze. Doing so is inefficient and an autist is hardwired to want to be anything but. However the powerful subconscious does not go to waste: it is rather essential as sort of an extra RAM to support the highly intensive processing of a naturally filmographic memory. Because hiding the emotions in the subconscious is unnatural to autistic people, autists are also not well-suited to reading the emotions which are hidden by others. For fear of appearing weak, group cohesion drives neurotypicals to hide that which is angry, or sad, or hurt, or dare I say itâ€¦ bored. The habit of hiding the emotions can be forcibly trained, however it is extremely unhealthy for the psyche to process both autistic and neurotypical tendencies at once. Doing so is more likely to cause overload, which is not a complicated thing: it is very much the body or the mind shutting down and being unable to go on until it has recovered. When the body overloads, someone panics and takes you to a hospital. When the mind overloads, the body appears bored and disengaged. Rude, amirite? Autistic people will overload from time to time when presented with stress. Autistic people will appear bored, and disengaged, and therefore rude. The autist, conversely, feels that being told to hide oneâ€™s emotions is rude. Remember that to one with autism it must be a conscious decision, rather than a subconscious decision, to copy someone else's emotions (to mirror) or to cover up one's own emotions. A conscious decision to pretend, which the autist will consciously view as a lie. And it is a very human trait to feel that lying is rude. Lying is disrespectful. Lying is dishonorable. When a neurotypical asks an autist to hide the emotions, to play the social game, the neurotypical is unknowingly asking the autist to be disrespectful. Who, then, is the autist being asked to â€˜be politeâ€™ (or to lie) to? â€œYou need to be polite to me! Donâ€™t show me how you really feel!â€You need to respect me.â€œYou need to lie to me! Donâ€™t show me how you really feel!â€You need to disrespect me.Tell someone to disrespect you often enough, and he just might do it. Autistic people prefer to use a very direct, informational, and honest form of speech. An autist will not lie to you if you have his full respect. If you need things hidden from you, you will lose respect. If you need credit for an idea falsely attributed to some higher source in order to entertain the idea, you will lose respect. If you require what may be viewed as 'social fluff' before allowing the telling of information, then you will annoy, although you will probably retain respect if you are not dismissive in your request. The reason this request will annoy is because it is inefficient: by the time a teller has spent extra effort in buddying up to be worthwhile to listen to, and a listener has spent extra effort in judging whether or not the teller is worthwhile to listen to, the teller has lost time and the listener has lost energy for the ability to pass on what may be a large sum of detailed information. Which requires more time, and more energy, in order to both deliver and digest. It is possible to annoy someone enough to care less about you.

question: How do adults on the autistic spectrum get diagnosed?
answer: Well, how I found out is a bit of a process, but let me just say an experience thatâ€™s pretty much universal for all autistic people, and other neurodivergent people. The feeling is is that weâ€™re somehow different than other people. We communicate slightly differently, we think in ways that arenâ€™t the typical way of thinking, we notice and see things that others donâ€™t at first, and it creates experiences and problems that others donâ€™t experience, to the point it actually causes issues in educational settings, occupational settings, or problems in our relationships. So hereâ€™s how I found out I was autistic, and some things I would do if this resonates with you.JUST A BIT DIFFERENT:As I alluded to beforehand, this is where many of us autistic people started our journey. Many of us knew as early as 2â€“4 years old that weâ€™re not like other people. I knew that I was different a long time ago, around when I was finishing pre-school and going into kindergarten. So, around 3 or 4 years old. I learned to read at 3 years old, technically 3.5 years old. This is known as hyperlexia, where a child learns to read far earlier than expected, and at a level much higher than that of their peers. As an example, when I was in kindergarten, I was reading college science textbooks and books on all types of science ever since I first learned how to read. My family would joke that I didn't have stuffed animals, but books instead. I also always had divergent senses. I always was a synesthete, and have been for a long time, just I kept it to myself because of a social consequence when a kid said, â€œYou canâ€™t see sounds, that's impossible.â€ On top of this, I remember I always was treated as the â€œweird oneâ€ I never truly fit in to any clique or friend group, and I was bullied a lot as a kid, clear up to high school. All of these experiences (and trust me on this) do not go away. They just only become more ingrained as you get older, to where itâ€™s not a big deal if a child gets overwhelmed in a crowded shopping center, but if I do, it is a major problem. Everyone calls you a gigantic baby, or overdramatic, or tries to downplay what youâ€™re feeling in that moment because youâ€™re an adult, you should have grown out of this by now. But you donâ€™t. Instead of growing out of being autistic, I grew up to become an autistic adult, and guess what? I still have sensory sensitivities, I still stim, I still have issues not fitting in or feeling like I donâ€™t fit in or belong anywhere, and I have to externalize so many little things that neurotypical people take for granted. In other words, it costs me actual brainpower to do my morning routine, it costs me actual brainpower to will myself into doing chores, errands, and boring, menial work, bright lights and loud noises interfere with my trains of thought, and can get easily derailed, and when focusing on special interests (like anything science or music for me) it costs me actual brainpower to pull myself away from it. Most normal people donâ€™t have to do that. They donâ€™t have to consciously think about these things. But I do. All the time. This is how I first suspected Iâ€™m autistic, and my therapist urged me to seek all this out, including my suspicions that I have ADHD too. In fact, for me, I first suspected I was ADHD, because my brother at the time recently got diagnosed with ADHD, and his experiences sounded oddly familiar to mine, and they both sounded oddly familiar or reminiscent of our dad. So I then made an appointment with my doctor, who then referred me to a clinic that diagnoses people, and I had to wait 6 months for the psychologist to call me.SCREENING FOR AUTISM:So my psychologist suggested I take a few screenings for autism in addition to the general screenings for ADHD. He set up to get general screenings, as well as set a date to get a full psychological evaluation. Part of that included an IQ test. I actually scored 128 there, so that was a bit of an ego boost, and a confirmation that instead of being considered â€œgiftedâ€ in elementary school, I should have been considered Twice Exceptional. All of this was taped with my consent so he could observe my general behavior. The tests most relevant to my diagnoses were:Brown Adult Executive Function/Attention Rating Scale. A rating scale directly screening for all types of ADHD.AQ Test. A simple autism screening.CAT-Q Test. Another autism screening that determines if you mask or camouflage your autism.The ADHD scale correctly figured out I have ADHD, specifically, ADHD-Combined Type. I took the AQ Test. I scored 40. Just so youâ€™re aware, anything above a 26 on the AQ Test is considered above the threshold in which youâ€™re likely to be autistic, and autistic people average around 32 for this test. Normal people score around 16. I also took the CAT-Q test, and I scored 134. Just so youâ€™re aware, anything above 100 means you mask or camouflage your autism. As a comparison, normal people score between 90â€“96. Those results were enough for my psychologist to diagnose me as autistic, in addition to ADHD. As for reference, hereâ€™s my scores on various autism screening tests that you can find on Embrace Autism:AQ Test: 40.CAT-Q Test: 134.RBQ-2A: 50.The Aspie Quiz: 118/200, 87% chance of being neurodivergent.RAADS-R Test: 181.Online Alexithymia Quiz: 114.Monotropism Quiz: 199.The Synesthesia Battery (Auditory-Visual): 0.43. Anything below 1.00 on the Synesthesia Battery is a synesthetic experience.All of these screening tests can be found online at Embrace Autism. If you have a similar sort of feeling that I do, and want to rule out autism or find out for yourself, seriously, take these screening tests. Unlike what those that arenâ€™t autistic say, these arenâ€™t BuzzFeed level quizzes, but actual scientific screening tests to screen for autism. The more you take, the more their accumulated accuracy grows, and each is around 80% accurate for screening for autism. So say you take these screening tests, and all of them point to the fact you might be autistic, because you consistently score the average score autistic people have, you pass the threshold for the test in the scientific literature, or you score significantly higher than normal, that very strongly suggests you might be autistic. But this doesnâ€™t necessarily mean youâ€™re autistic. At best these tests test if you experience typical autistic traits, and like with ADHD, since autistic traits are human traits, we have to go a step further. So what's the official diagnostic criteria say?AUTISM DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA:The greatest challenge with figuring out if you are autistic is that the DSM makes it difficult to understand and interpret the language. So let's reframe what's being stated in the DSM-5-TR in a different way. A. Persistent Difficulties in the Social Use of Verbal and Non-Verbal Communication: Basically, if you find that:Social communication and following social conventions are things you do, but prefer not to do.You use more formal language, or use words that people donâ€™t understand.You have a tendency to take things literally.You are not great at following the (proper) social signals for interaction, so that you:Speak out of turn.Interrupt people.Talk too much.Donâ€™t talk.Talk about your own topic of interest when it doesnâ€™t connect to anything said in a group.Sometimes/often miss sarcasm as you donâ€™t understand with what intention a statement is made (you may use sarcasm with ease yourself, while not understanding when others are being sarcastic).If any of this describes you, then congratulations! You pass Criteria A for autism. B. Restricted, Repetitive Patterns of Behavior, Interests, or Activities: Basically, do you do better with a routine or have special interests (things that you kind of get obsessive about?); do you stim (repeat a movement such as fiddling with keys, flap your hands, move your fingers in a particular way, headbang, etc. to alleviate anxiety); and finally do you have sensory challenges (find wool itchy/scratchy, get overheated, donâ€™t do well in crowds, sensitivity to light or sound, etc.)? If so, then congratulations! You pass Criteria B for autism. C. Symptoms Must Be Present in the Early Developmental Period (But May Not Fully Manifest Until Social Demands Exceed Limited Capacities, or May Be Masked By Learned Strategies Later in Life): Basically, were these symptoms present when you were a kid? Have the negative symptoms intensified as you got older and had to take on more responsibilities and navigate the social world? Have you masked certain symptoms later in life because you found it makes people accept you more? If so, then congratulations! You pass Criteria C for autism. D. Symptoms Cause Clinically Significant Impairment in Social, Occupational, or Other Important Areas of Functioning: Basically, do these symptoms cause you problems in your life? If so, then congratulations! You pass Criteria D for autism. E. These Disturbances are Not Better Explained by Intellectual Disability: Pretty self-explanatory, these symptoms are not better explained by ID, or something else. If so, then congratulations! You pass Criteria E for autism. If you pass 5 or 4 of these diagnostic criteria, I strongly urge you to take the screening tests I mentioned above, as they can directly test what your symptoms are, how intense they are, and any other traits you may not have been aware of.COMMON STATEMENTS FROM AUTISTIC PEOPLE:Another way some of us have found out is that someone we love, know, or trust said something that really resonated with them and their lived experience. So hereâ€™s some common things Iâ€™ve said about my autism, and what other autistic people have said.â€œI feel different in some way.â€â€œI feel like an alien.â€â€œPeople don't understand or know me.â€â€œI feel isolated/lonely.â€â€œI fake being normal to be seen as someone more socially acceptable,â€ or, â€œI hide who I really am.â€â€œI don't know who I am (anymore).â€â€œI have sensory issues/challenges.â€â€œI have panic attacks/meltdowns/shutdowns when I get overwhelmed.â€â€œIâ€™m often seen as blunt or rude.â€â€œI often overlook sarcasm in others, even though I use sarcasm myself.â€â€œIâ€™m seen as obsessive.â€â€œI have special interests.â€â€œI need a lot of alone time.â€â€œI hate social events/crowds/parties/gatherings.â€â€œI can be naive.â€â€œIâ€™ve gotten taken advantage of.â€â€œI got bullied a lot.â€ [1]A lot of us have said something similar, so if you feel these, or these resonate with you, maybe start learning about autism, maybe take a few of the screening tests I mentioned earlier, and read the diagnostic criteria for autism from the DSM-5-TR, and after all that, begin the process of getting an official diagnosis, if youâ€™re able to. We autistic people are also loyal to a fault, honest to a fault, and kind, though we often overlook our positive traits. And yes, there are positives with being autistic.STRENGTHS OF AUTISM:As autistic people, we have certain strengths, part of the spiky skill sets we tend to have. We may not be the best in social situations, understanding social cues, or may be socially awkward, but everyone knows at least one autistic person who is an expert on a subject, and is like a walking encyclopedia on it. Autistic people are like this to an extreme. Our strengths are based on our unusual talents, skills, qualities, and advantages that are often beyond the normal range of human experience. Everyoneâ€™s good at a few things, but us autistic people seem to pick up on things insanely quickly, weâ€™re really knowledgeable on areas that are part of our special interests, and because of how our brains are wired, some of us have a unique way of experiencing the world, and thus, offer valuable insight. And this is not just me talking, a lot of these strengths are born out in scientific data and research, so while not every autistic person will have these strengths, this is born out in evidence. Sensory Strengths:Visual hypersensitivity. Some of us have extraordinary vision, with better visual hypersensitivity, pattern recognition, attention to detail, and some of us have sharp visual attention to small details.Tunnel vision/sharp focus of attention. Our focus of attention has been found to be sharper, with a sharper spatial gradient of attention.Color intensity. Some autistic people have changes in the rods and cones of our retinas, researchers found. This results in some of us experiencing color more vibrantly and intensely, with some reporting that some colors were so vibrant, they appeared almost florescent.Synesthesia. Synesthesia is found to be three times more common in autistic people, than neurotypical people. I myself have auditory-visual synesthesia, and since for me, the concurrent involves color, I have chromesthesia, specifically.Acute hearing. Some autistic people have been shown to have an increased auditory perceptual capacity relative to neurotypicals. This increased capacity may offer an explanation for why some have better pitch detection.Superior auditory discrimination. Autistic people tend to be better at detecting a target sound within a group of sounds, and notice (irrelevant) background information more readily. About 1 in 5 autistic individuals show exceptional frequency discrimination skills.Heightened pitch detection. Some autistic people show superiority in memorizing picture-pitch associations and in detecting pitch changes in melodies. A subset of autistic individualsâ€”known as â€œmusical savantsâ€â€”are also known to possess absolute pitch, or perfect pitch.Enhanced olfactory detection. Autistic people show enhanced connectivity between the thalamus (a brain area responsible for relaying sensory information) and insula, which is thought to be the cause of heightened sensitivity to smell, sound, and taste.Cognitive Strengths:Correlation with giftedness. Estimated rates of intellectual giftedness and autistic children is 0.7â€“2%, compared to up to 1% in the general population. This shows a correlation with autism and giftedness. [2].Savant syndrome. Savant syndrome is characterized by a stark contrast between disability and profound abilities (in music, art, mathematics or mechanical domains) and occurs in 10â€“28.5% of autistic people, compared to 1% in the general population.Powerful memory. Autistic people can have enhanced or even savant-like memory. This is due to our greater declarative memory. It is this memory that allows us to memorize many things, including thousands of social scripts.Encyclopedic knowledge. When it comes to our special interests, and many of us autistic people have science, math, music, and history as our special interests, weâ€™re basically walking encyclopedias. For me, music, guitars, science (namely astrophysics, astronomy, quantum physics, paleontology, and biology), history, and mythology I can go on for hours about.Great problem solvers. Autistic people are up to 40% faster at problem-solving, and appear to use perceptual regions of the brain to accelerate problem-solving. Weâ€™re also great at picking up on complex patterns.Rational decision makers. Weâ€™re less likely to make gut decisions. Our consistency in the choices we make and our attention to detail helps us avoid being swayed by our emotions.Hyperfocus. Autistic people are able to exert an intense form of mental concentration or visualization (called hyperfocus) that focuses consciousness on a subject, topic, or task; and are significantly more able to focus for extended periods of times. Also a trait of ADHD.Hyper-systemizing. Weâ€™re really good at analyzing and constructing systems.Heightened pattern-recognition. The autistic brain excels at recognizing patterns. In fact, brain regions associated with recognizing patterns (temporal and occipital areas) light up more in autistic people than in the general population.Lateral thinking. Or â€œthinking outside the box.â€ Research shows a link between autistic traits and unusual & novel ideas, which occurs due to their strong ability to think outside the box. In studies autistic people were far more likely to generate creative ideas than non-autistic people.Strong work ethic. We strictly adhere to routines, schedules, and rules, and on top of that, some of us love doing boring, menial tasks for fun.Sure these do apply to many people, and for all of these, remember Iâ€™m comparing a normal person to an autistic person in that situation and looking for whatâ€™s different. So if you find these apply to you, just know that these arenâ€™t necessarily autistic traits, but if you find your experience in these areas is different from normal, then it could be something to look into.SO WHAT NOW?:So all of this points to you being autistic. The next question for most people is, â€œOkay, what now?â€ And, honestly, I canâ€™t make that decision for you. Itâ€™s time to actually start advocating for yourself and taking charge and making your own decisions about what to do. Iâ€™d suggest talking to a friend or loved one first, someone that you can trust. Theyâ€™re going to help you through this process of self-discovery. If any of these apply to you at all, I urge you to take the screening tests I mentioned earlier, quickly compare yourself to the diagnostic criteria, and if all of this points to the same thing, that this all strongly relates to you, or very strongly suggests you might be autistic, I would urge you, if you can, to actually get diagnosed. Why do I suggest that? Because you now have rights and legal protections for supports and accommodations that you canâ€™t get otherwise, and such accommodations and supports can be game-changers in making living life just a little easier. But ultimately, knowledge is power. Knowing that you have real explanations for your neurological experience, that itâ€™s not because you're a failure, or you lack discipline or motivation. That alone is powerful, but whatâ€™s more powerful is that now you can account for it. You can plan, strategize, and work with the brain you have, instead of holding yourself to a standard you cannot possibly achieve with the neurological makeup you were born with. And if you happen to be one of those that a psychological evaluation is just inaccessible, or wonâ€™t be covered by insurance, or you just donâ€™t live in an area that has enough knowledgeable or experienced clinicians, I strongly urge you to do everything in your power to advocate for yourself to get the supports and accommodations you need. Because, a piece of paper isnâ€™t why you're autistic. Undiagnosed autism is still autism. Autism is a genetically determined wiring of the nervous system, itâ€™s a literal difference in the brain. That therefore means you perceive the world differently and think differently than a normal person. And thatâ€™s okay. Thatâ€™s what neurodiversity is all about. I can assure you, it wasnâ€™t a neurotypical caveman that made the knife, the spear, or came up with writing and did cave art. It was one of us.FOOTNOTES: [1]: Unfortunately, a lot of autistic people experience bullying/peer abuse, around 94% of all autistic people, which is sharply contrasted with only 30% of neurotypical people experiencing bullying/peer abuse. That means out of 50 autistic people, all but 3 of them will have experienced bullying/peer abuse. Contrast that with out of 50 neurotypical people, only 15 of them will have experienced bullying/peer abuse. [2]: If youâ€™re reading this and were considered a gifted child in school, so was I. The â€œgifted child to adult ADHD/autism diagnosisâ€ is a real pipeline. I was considered gifted as a child in school, and now Iâ€™m diagnosed with both autism and ADHD.Originally answered: How do adults on the autistic spectrum get diagnosed?

question: Can a mild autistic child be treated?
answer: I am answering as a parent of an adult autistic daughter. Based on my experiences parenting her when we did not know she was autistic (from birth to late teens) and when we knew, but were in a long term learning process, which will probably continue indefinitely. I would say that this isnâ€™t a very clear question to ask. When you say â€œbe treatedâ€ what end result do you envision? What I know is autism is a part of who a person is. It cannot be undone. However, autistic persons can be helped to cope with the society around them, and people who work with or live with autistic persons can learn to understand how to support and help them, and how not to undermine or harm them. The good news is there is a great deal more that we know now about autism than we did 40 years ago. Early diagnosis can help to create a positive support environment. However there are many ways people can make wrong turns, get bad advice and do more harm than good, with the best of intentions. Thinking that the end result of the journey you will take with an autistic child is that you will create a person who is not autistic is not a realistic premise. AUtism is a part of who a person is and cannot be erased. An autistic person can be helped to understand their responses to society and develop coping skills for living in the cultural environment that confronts them. They can be given skills and support services that will help them prosper. That is my idea of effective treatment. The best way to equip yourself as a parent or helper of an autistic person is to listen to what autistic people can tell you about what it means to be autistic and why they behave as they do. Every autistic person is different. They will exhibit a unique constellation of behaviors. These may change over time, for better or worse depending on how the world treats them. Good treatment will help an individual thrive. Bad treatment will bring bad results. No different from non autistic people! Autistic people and skilled and knowledgeable teachers, doctors and social service providers can help. But there are pitfalls. The first and biggest are starting with the wrong assumptions about what autism is and not accepting autistic children for who they are.

question: If a child has a subtle form of autism, is it usually picked up through a public school system? Or do many on the spectrum slip through the cracks?
answer: When I saw this, I knew I had to answer it. A lot of people who have no understanding of how the system around diagnosing and supporting autistic people works. The truth is that so many people fall through the cracks. Itâ€™s quite common for autistic girls to slip through the cracks when theyâ€™re younger. Weâ€™re more likely to observe social skills from our peers, and while they arenâ€™t complicated, itâ€™s quite easy to go undiscovered. For me, the problems started when I hit puberty, at eleven years old. From what Iâ€™ve read from other autistic peopleâ€”girls in particularâ€”this is not uncommon. In the UK, this coincides with when girls go into secondary school. But wherever you live, the beginning of puberty is when social rules from your childhood go out of the window and things become far more complicated. You need to know how to discuss more complex subject matters. How do you feel about that boy? What that girl did was so stupid, right? What happened to the girl code? But weâ€™re not judgemental, at all. Itâ€™s hard to understand the right way to answer that. A lot of it is about context, but I still got it wrong. As teenagers, autistic peopleâ€™s fixations also become more obvious, because neurotypical people quickly move from one thing to the next because they want to fit in and follow the latest crazes. Guess what, though? I still fell under the cracks. Even after I left mainstream education because of my mental health, they didnâ€™t detect that there might be something else at play, too. But I was luckyâ€¦ I received my autism diagnosis when I was seventeen. In fact, it was three days after my seventeenth birthday. Thatâ€™s a fact I like to tell people a lot. I donâ€™t know if youâ€™re asking this question because youâ€™re curious whether you could have fallen through the cracks, or because you suspect a loved one might have, but thereâ€™s every chance this is the case. Thereâ€™s stories of people who are many decades older than I am (Iâ€™m currently 20) receiving diagnosisâ€™ after going through life knowing there was something wrong with them but not knowing what. Itâ€™s something thatâ€™s been prevalent in both genders in recent years, but females especially. In fact, some people have dubbed us â€˜The Lost Generation of Womenâ€™ because we have been all but forgotten about in autism research for so long. If this is you, or someone you care about, I wrote this piece about whether getting an autism diagnosis is worth it. Iâ€™m sharing this in the hopes that it could help you, a loved one, or even a stranger who just so happens to come across this post. With that being said, I just wanted to add one more thing: If you feel like you could have grounds for an autism diagnosisâ€”and you want to go for itâ€”donâ€™t be put off. You are perfectly entitled to find out as much, or as little, about your neurology as you desire, regardless of anything else going on in your life.

question: What are some things that neurotypical people find difficult to understand about people with Aspergerâ€™s or autism?

Taking away the â€œchildish thingsâ€ of an autistic adult who is struggling to become independent because you think itâ€™ll shock them into suddenly â€œbeing a proper adultâ€ only causes trauma and emotional distress in a situation that is already stressful and difficult.Just because an autistic person is intelligent and educated but still struggling to find decent work doesnâ€™t mean theyâ€™re lazy and not trying hard enough. Because a lot of employers looking to hire people for higher-paying office jobs are more interested in hiring people with a certain personality profile (gregarious, outgoing, highly socially-adept), instead of people who can and want to do the job and do it well, highly-qualified autistic candidates often get overlooked or rejected. This leads to most college-educated autistic people being unemployed or underemployed simply because we donâ€™t interview well enough to satisfy the social desires of prospective employers. Trying to fake those skills and personality traits that these employers prefer is often difficult, and an autistic person can fail miserably even when trying their hardest to â€œplay normal.â€ Itâ€™s not laziness or not trying thatâ€™s the problem, itâ€™s employers not being willing to give a skilled and qualified person a chance just because they come of as quiet, introverted, and socially awkward thatâ€™s the real problem here.Just because someone is â€œlow support needsâ€ doesnâ€™t mean they have no support needs. Even autistic people with low support needs still need some accommodations both in family life and in their professional lives. Things like a regular work schedule instead of one that constantly fluctuates, being allowed to wear sunglasses or noise-canceling headphones to avoid sensory overload, speaking plainly and directly instead of using a lot of hints and implications, being clear about team structures and everyoneâ€™s place in them, etc. These things can go a long way to help an autistic person live productively and harmoniously within society. Also, the lack of services meant to directly help autistic adults with low support needs is just plain appalling. Someone with low support needs who is academically capable on an age-appropriate level and may even have specialized skills does not need to be placed in a group home, they donâ€™t need to be saddled with some low-wage pity job just to get them employed as fast as possible. You know what they need? With the focus on help for autistic people being so firmly on children and individuals with high support needs, though, the needs of those who are adults with low support needs often get overshadowed and ignored.Just because an autistic person is not looking you dead in the face when youâ€™re talking doesnâ€™t mean they arenâ€™t listening to you/arenâ€™t interested in the conversation. We listen with our ears, we donâ€™t pay much attention to body language and donâ€™t read subtle facial expressions well, we express ourselves in conversation with words first and foremost. If we want to talk with you (casually or professionally), the very fact that we are listening to your words and making an effort to reciprocate with our own is proof enough that weâ€™re listening to you and paying attention to the conversation. If we donâ€™t make a lot of eye contact, or fidget, or are doodling or whatever while involved in a conversation, that doesnâ€™t mean we arenâ€™t listening or interested. If an autistic person isnâ€™t listening or isnâ€™t interested in a conversation, theyâ€™ll usually just try to find a way to end the conversation and leave.Autistic people do not make inferior employees as a result of being socially awkward. Do we not always parse the double-meanings of interview questions, especially the most innocuous-seeming ones (like those dumb desert island scenarios)? Absolutely. Does that affect our ability to do amazing work when weâ€™re in our element? Hell no. We know our s#!+ and donâ€™t mess around when it comes to getting the job done. Give us a chance to work with/for you and youâ€™ll be amazed at what we can accomplish.

question: What are some common misconceptions people have about living as an adult on the spectrum?
answer: That we donâ€™t exist. It may sound stupid, but so many people think that autism only affects children. I was diagnosed as a teenager and suddenly my life made sense: I understood why I had always felt like an alien and made so many mistakes when socialising. I cannot imagine how my life would have turned out had I received my diagnosis later. Documentaries have always been about autistic children and how their parents deal with it. Thanks to pushback from the autistic community, were has been an increase in autistic adults getting to speak for themselves but progress has been slow and many people have grown up associating autism with children. People carry these misconceptions their whole lives. â€œBut I thought only children had autism. I heard about this mother who put her child on a gluten-free diet and their child grew out of their autism.â€ This response is depressingly common, but I think itâ€™s just a result of a lack of education. People cannot grow out of their autism, they can just become better at masking it which is physically and emotionally exhausting. We hear about how severe emotional repression leads to burnout and depression - masking your autism all day every day is just like that. Many therapies which are supposed to help autistic people are focussed around getting us to mask our symptoms. ABA (applied behavioural analysis) is a popular therapy used against young autistic people, and many autistic people consider it to be abuse. It involves rewarding desirable behaviour (holding eye contact - which I find incredibly painful) and punishing undesirable behaviour. Unfortunately the â€˜undesirableâ€™ behaviour includes stimming, which for many autistic people is a method of communication or calming oneself down. The aim of ABA is to make a child appear normal to make the parent feel better (Iâ€™m not disposed to be charitable about this), at the cost of the autistic individualâ€™s right to self determination and expression. If you are considering ABA for an autistic child in your life, please read the testimonies of autistic people who have undergone ABA and consider whether you really want to do that for your loved one. â€œYour autism is not an excuse for being weird. Itâ€™s time to start taking some responsibility.â€ This misconception kind of stems from the other one. People thing that when you are an adult you have complete control over your behaviour. I get this when I explain that I struggle to work in groups or need to sit in a dark room for a while. Unfortunately, when you tell people you canâ€™t go to the supermarket and have to hide in bed they assume itâ€™s because youâ€™re lazy. They donâ€™t consider that your brain is fried from a short period of time in a loud and hot room when your headphones werenâ€™t enough to stop the sensory bombardment, and you cannot face the flickering lights or extreme temperatures. question: Autism manifests itself in many different ways, but at its core, what is missing in an autistic person that a non-autistic person has?
answer: Autism manifests differently in different people, but from what I can tell, every autistic person lacks this common thing: the relentless need for social validation and status that neurotypical people have. Beginning in childhood, neurotypical children excel at things to which adults guffaw and say â€œYouâ€™re so good at that!â€ Autistic children just do what interests them; it doesnâ€™t matter whether or not other people are pleased by it. In adolescence, when children become sensitized to social cues and hierarchy, autistic teens may either not-care about those things and appear â€œchild-likeâ€ (clinging to My Little Pony and drawing when their peers consider these things childish) or they may develop an outward distaste for social demands and hierarchy and seem non-conformist/rebellious dying their hair interesting colors outside of fashion norms. Either way, they will focus on things they like while their neurotypical peers spend the next decade obsessing over the art of fitting-in. As a result some autistic people, often the ones with a supportive environment, will become very good or knowledgable about something entering adulthood, while being socially inept or antisocial. As adults, autistic people may find it difficult to have deep conversations about subjects with neurotypicals because (with neurotypicals) there is a constant meta-narrative in place: people are always assessing statements on the basis of â€œdoes this elevate me?â€ or â€œis this putting me down?â€ Neurotypical people can take any subject (that has nothing to do with them) and take a particular opinion or position as a personal vote of solidarity or a personal attack. You canâ€™t ever just talk baseball, you are always arguing for or against your team so to speak. But autistic people just talk about what they are talking about without this meta-narrative of power and status. The best analogy I can think of is: If you are a neurotypical person and have contact with someone who has Narcissistic Personality Disorder, you know that NPD people can be charming and lovely, but you get close to them their ego needs (need for narcissistic supply) are strangely large and burdensome. Still, they may be a family member and you have to manage by establishing boundaries and giving yourself space. That is roughly how autistic people feel around neurotypical peopleâ€¦ they seem obsessed with social â€œsupplyâ€, rudely self-involved in their socializing, and prone to lying in such a way that it is socially desirable/acceptable (like kissing a boss/professorâ€™s butt rather than engaging them as equals). On the one hand, the survival and strength of our species (as well as many animal species) has been linked to working together in community/tribe/pack, and so fitting-in is a reasonably good instinct to have. But at the same time this desire to fit-in and belong is at the root of some of the worst in humanity... There must be a reason why the genes that make autism possible have been able to survive and multiply these centuries..

question: Is Jungkook autistic? I am, and I think he might be too.

Iâ€™ll break this answer into parts to make it easier to navigate. SOCIAL SKILLS/EMOTIONAL REGULATION One of the most predominant traits of autism is a difference in social skills. He joins conversations by staring at people or hovering near them, which could potentially demonstrate a lack of innate social skills. Jungkook also engages in echolalia - which is the repetition of sounds or phrases. EXECUTIVE FUNCTION Flexible Thinking: Jungkook can be very, very rigid in his thinking. He likes clear guidelines, and he has very firm opinions on â€˜goodâ€™ and â€˜badâ€™, just to name one example. His rigid thinking can also manifest as overwhelming perfectionism. Organisation: Jungkook has been noted as the member with the messiest bedroom. INTENSE AND FOCUSED INTERESTS His interests read a lot to me like special interests. During the 200507 YouTube live, Taehyung said that Jungkookâ€™s skill for filmaking would make him the best candidate for the album photoshoot making video, but Namjoon and Hoseok worried that he would become so absorbed in the task that he could be hard to photograph or otherwise involve. He has often been described as going through â€˜phasesâ€™, but to me they seem even too repetitive to be simply a style. Later, he went on to wear the same pair of cargo pants for an excessive amount of time. He has also been known to buy the same item of clothing several times over, or buy the same item in every available colour. SENSORY SENSITIVITY Jungkook is very, very sensory. JK: Soap.As he is sensitive to light, Jungkook can often be seen wearing a low hat to shield his eyes. Stimming is something almost everyone does, not just autistic people, but autistic people use it a lot more to self-regulate, manage emotions, and cope with sensory input. Jungkookâ€™s stimming suggests those reasons as the cause. One example is drumming his fists, often when very excited. He also frequently touches his face, moves his head from side to side, picks at his skin (particularly on his neck). He also oral stims a lot, which looks like chewing on his lips, mouth, chewing on things, putting things in his mouth. question: What are signs of autism in non diagnosed adults?
answer: Iâ€™m autistic, and hereâ€™s some subtle ones I notice in most autistic people Iâ€™ve talked with and encounter online, and in my neurodivergent support group. Now, of course, there is the caveat that autism is a spectrum, meaning every autistic person is a unique individual with a unique experience, but, these are the most common things Iâ€™ve noticed and experienced myself, and the other autistic people in my life noticed and experienced too. So, while they arenâ€™t 100% universal, theyâ€™re ubiquitously common.Having a hard time intuitively grasping what others are thinking or feeling. Us autistics are commonly accused of lacking empathy, which we donâ€™t, we just show our empathy differently, and are commonly accused of being heartless, because we show our emotions differently. Part of this is alexithymia, which around 1 in 5 autistic people have, and alexithymia is a co-occurring condition wherein the individual has a hard time intuitively describing felt emotions in themselves and others. Not that they donâ€™t have emotions or empathy, just that they have a hard time describing them intuitively. Most people donâ€™t have this difficulty, because each emotion feels different. The best way I can describe alexithymia is confusion. A lot of the emotions feel the same, so describing them and naming them is a common therapeutic practice for us autistics that are also alexithymic, like myself. Again, I want to stress that the problem is not in not experiencing emotions or empathy, itâ€™s just that we have a hard time describing them intuitively like others can. For lack of a better phrase, youâ€™re â€œin your headâ€ too much about your emotions. Thus, we show our emotions and empathy in ways people donâ€™t expect. The other part of this is the fact that literally nobody tells you what their emotional state is. They just â€œsignalâ€ it with body language or subtle cues that us autistic people struggle with in different ways. Neurotypicals seemingly can easily pick up on these cues, but us autistics struggle with this. Others just expect you to get this, but autistic people donâ€™t intuitively get it. Weâ€™re â€œin our headâ€ too much about it. Think about it, if I throw you a baseball, you donâ€™t think about it, you just catch it. You donâ€™t do calculus to accurately predict where the ball will be so you can catch it, because by the time youâ€™re done, youâ€™ll have missed catching the ball. Itâ€™s the same sort of thing here with autistic people. Others donâ€™t think about it, but we do, and as a result, many of us feel like others were given a manual for this and we didnâ€™t.You find it difficult to function in a group. Taking what I mentioned previously, it seems natural that autistic people find difficulty functioning in a group. How can you function when thereâ€™s no clear procedure of how to address everyone or what to do with them? How can you cooperate when others are constantly speaking over you because you find it hard to insert yourself in a conversation, because you donâ€™t know when itâ€™s appropriate to do so? How can you keep track of multiple conversations at once? In short, how can you cooperate or follow the rules of a game when the rules are not clearly written down or explained?You feel like you have no real friends. Taking the previous two signs, it seems natural then that many autistic people find difficulty making friends. Since thereâ€™s no procedure for socializing, and thus, making friends, you naturally struggle trying to make friends, despite you wanting to make friends. You get frustrated that the friend-making procedure isnâ€™t documented or written down anywhere. In frustration, youâ€™ve then tried observing how other people do it, either in movies, shows, or in reality, and tried to copy what theyâ€™re doing. But it doesnâ€™t land. Thus, others find you weird, awkward, that somethingâ€™sâ€¦ off with you. You wish you knew why, and you feel lonely, and thus, others having core childhood memories with friends is something you get robbed of.You have your own unique way of speaking. Whether itâ€™s a flat affect, or your vocabulary, or simply the way you speak, others find itâ€¦ peculiar, odd, quirky, too formal. Youâ€™ve been accused of being a professor or robot when you talk, or, you might make up your own words because you find language itself to be too limiting to express yourself. Your tone sounds too formal and sophisticated for the situation, or your vocabulary is too sophisticated for the situation. This is most noticeable in children, because it makes them sound precocious and like an adult.You canâ€™t tell when itâ€™s your turn to speak. Again, seems strange to point out, but most people donâ€™t struggle with the normal back-and-forth of having a conversation. On the surface, conversations are simple. One person speaks, stops, then the other responds, and on it goes, right? Well, what about when someone pauses because theyâ€™re thinking, and you misread that as if theyâ€™re done? What about when someone asks a rhetorical question? This is even more pronounced in group settings with multiple conversations, because everyone inserts themselves into the conversation, while youâ€™re either speaking over them, interrupting them, or, youâ€™re spoken over because youâ€™re struggling to insert yourself into the conversation, because you donâ€™t know when itâ€™s your turn.You donâ€™t know what to talk about when having a conversation. Maybe you struggle with small talk and find it agonizing or pointless, or you just have a loss of words when you do finally get your moment to talk. Conversations just donâ€™t come naturally, and when you do speak, others find your remarks rude, naive, or embarrassing. They might feel that youâ€™re always talking about a subject that only you find interesting. They might feel youâ€™re talking about people, events, places, and topics without sufficiently explaining what they are, and when you do try to explain, even those very same people find you condescending when explaining things.Youâ€™re bothered by things that others donâ€™t notice. When you say youâ€™re uncomfortable with these things, others accuse you of being overly dramatic because they literally donâ€™t notice what youâ€™re noticing.Youâ€™re really good at noticing and memorizing details. The autistic and neurodivergent brain excels at bottom-up thinking, or inductive reasoning, which is noticing details, recognizing patterns, and connecting them to form a cohesive view of whatever it is youâ€™re noticing. Most people donâ€™t think this way. Most people are top-down thinkers, or, they use deductive reasoning, which is noticing the bigger picture first, then looking at the details after. What this means then is, as an autistic person, you might notice details and things that others donâ€™t, like catalogue numbers, how an animal is acting and how theyâ€™re feeling before they act, the timbre of a specific instrument, and so on.You understand language literally. As a kid, you took sayings and turn of phrases literally, but as you grew up to an adult, you still have a certainâ€¦ literalist or naivety in how you understand language. For example, you might answer literally when someone asks, â€œHow are you?â€ You might take rhetorical questions as actual, legitimate questions to be answered. Or, you constantly wish that people would just bluntly say what they mean. Youâ€™re not a mind-reader. No one is. The core of this issue lies with words having specific meanings, and when others use words in a different way to mean something different, we autistic people have a hard time picking up on that.You HATE changes in routine. You have a specific way of doing things, every day, or when it comes to that activity, it must be done in a specific way. As a kid, your play might have been highly structured, and thus, had to line up things or organize them before you played with them. But, the rub is, itâ€™s your way of organizing them. As a fun aside, this is why I occasionally check the Wikipedia page on autism to make sure the kid lining up cans is still representing our culture. But now, as an adult, this applied to your daily routine. You have a specific way of doing your hair, your dental hygiene, your shower time, laundry, clothes, and so on. We all have routines, but hereâ€™s the important questionâ€¦ How do you feel when things disrupt your routine? Distressed? Annoyed? Frustrated? Overwhelmed?All of these are rather subtle signs that are more noticeable in adulthood, in my experience. Children do exhibit these things too, but theyâ€™re more noticeable and pronounced then. As they grow up to be autistic adults, these signs become more subtle and harder to pick out. That could be due to masking, could be simple maturity, but whatever it is, something about that individual feelsâ€¦ off. Thatâ€™s because theyâ€™re autistic, and thereâ€™s nothing wrong with that. In short, autism can be hard to spot for neurotypical people, because most people donâ€™t know what to look for, because theyâ€™re not autistic. They donâ€™t know what to look for, and everything theyâ€™ve learned puts a certain view and stereotype of what an autistic person is in their head. Thatâ€™s why I pointed out the fact that, while every autistic person is unique, these are common things that many of us autistic people feel, or have experienced. Hope this helps!Originally answered: What are signs of autism in non diagnosed adults?

question: What are the signs of autism that nobody talks about?
answer: So many people have already answered, but I would like to add some common things that are usually passed off as â€œquirksâ€, but are very real signs as autism. Not all these things are individual signs of autism, but combined with other symptoms can be very telling.Systems for things. I want to give some examples of this that people may not immediately recognize as a â€œsystemâ€. Keeping in mind, in this sense, a system is a mode of organization that causes distress if deviated from.Washing dishes in a particular order (cups first, then bowls, then plates, etc.)Showering in a particular order (never use body wash before washing hair, or the other way around.)Gaming â€œquirksâ€ (that person who fills up all the resources before moving on? Who does the work for fun? Who automates stuff to make things satisfying? Who organizes every inventory religiously? That type of stuff. Also some of the people who will build those crazy maps on Minecraft ðŸ’€)Keeping items filled or â€œlevelâ€ (always got the same amount of hand soap in the container? Cereal containers always level? There's a certain satisfaction autistics derive from having things â€œlined upâ€).Lining up toys, items, etc. For a young kid, this can be very obvious. It can be a bit harder to spot as an adult, but sometimes you'll see it in how a person organizes their desk, their dishes, maybe even their icons on their desktop.Sorting candy/food by color/size/shape and/or eating it in a certain order. (Skittles or M&Ms work very well with this: do you compulsively sort them into colors and then eat each color individually? Do you eat them in a pattern? Is there a color you refuse to touch simply because it's that color?)Only feeling comfortable eating meals in order (breakfast - then lunch - then dinner).Echolalia: this is the repetition of words and phrases, or even noises. It's been mentioned, but it comes in many forms. Sometimes this can be a person randomly saying something they've heard that their brain decides to echo, or sometimes it can be something stuck in their head that they say repeatedly. This can happen with song lyrics, conversations, and viewing media.Harsh reactions to sudden changes in ANYTHING. I will say it a million times: autism is a highly transitionary disability, meaning people with autism need extra â€œpaddingâ€ if something changes. New plans? Try to warn them a few days in advance. Hours is not enough. Unexpected weather? That can put them in a bad mood. New people? That can cause anxiety and run their social battery dry quick. Even being late can make a difference, as that gives them less time to transition between places. Anything that breaks routine is going to be some cause for anxiety and anger.Picky eaters: for children, this is a bit harder to distinguish. Is this a child that simply likes junk food? Or do they like that all chips have the same crunch, but if they eat something like blueberries, every one could taste different? The key is: consistency. Texture is a big trigger for many autistic people. Maybe guacamole makes them want to puke, or beans make them gag? Maybe the difference in sour and sweet berries is too jarring to allow them enjoyment in eating them? I've also found many autistic people that say spice is an easy trigger. Then again, I've found others that can't get enough spice.Pain tolerance: due to autismâ€™s effect on interoception, a lot of autistic people have a high pain tolerance. Because communication can be an issue, this is often overlooked, since the person's normal perception of pain is skewed. How is an autistic person supposed to tell you that they SHOULD be in more pain than they are? The opposite can also be true, causing some autistic people to be labeled as hypochondriacs, as they genuinely feel MORE pain than the average person.Neglecting needs: as mentioned before, interoception can often be affected by autism, which causes a person to not be in tune with their bodily needs. This means they can't feel hunger correctly, the need to go to the bathroom, to sleep, to socialize, etc. With hunger, it can be easier to spot: someone becoming a bottomless pit because they just DONT FEEL SATISFIED. (An extreme example would be Tarrare, and if you don't know this manâ€™s story, you should look it up. I've always theorized this man to have autism because of this, but autism wasn't diagnosed back then.) Alteratively, you might have someone who can't seem to keep on weight. This is also why many autistic kids are known to wet the bed much later into their childhood than neurotypicals, as they really can't feel when they need to use the restroom (along with sleep problems and sometimes their vestibular and proprioception). Even as adults, some autistic people struggle to feel when they need to use the restroom, often until it becomes an emergency (me, ouchie).Obsessions: this is also a symptom of OCD and ADHD, so these alone REALLY CAN'T BE INDICATORS, but, again, when clustered with other symptoms, can be signs of autism. These obsessions can come in forms of hobbies, interests, people, or even ideas. That person that's been listening to the same song on repeat for two weeks in a row? Might be autistic. That avid scrap-booker that has a whole basement full of supplies, and they make crafts for everything? Again, might be autistic. Everything is foxes (lol, me)? In my case, autism. The extreme comes in the form of hyperfixation (which can be a symptom of other things, once again), where a person can neglect their needs and focus solely on one goal for an extended period of time. I can do this with video games: I've spent up to 16 hours gaming without leaving my computer for anything. Very unhealthy, but when fixated, nothing could pry me away, not even extreme hunger.There are a bunch of others, but I feel these ones are either neglected or extremely important indicators of a person's mental health. I want to say AGAIN that one of these symptoms does NOT mean someone has autism, but many of these collected together can be a good hint. Edit: Thank you for almost 10k views! I wanted to add some more since this post is so popular, and these signs are sometimes overlooked!Stimulation issues:People with autism can become overstimulated easily. Whether it's lights, sounds, or people, too much of a thing can be directly why an autistic person may be upset or have a meltdown in public. Multiple conversations at once can make an autistic person extremely agitated.People with autism are also frequently UNDERstimulated, and they make up for it with little "quirks", or "tics", depending on how people speak about it. There are many ways for adults and children to stimulate - some safer and more preferable than others:hitting, tapping, or kicking things repeatedlyecholalia: already mentioned, but making noise can be a form of stimming (like humming, tongue clicking, or even narrating what they're doing).watching multiple things at once/participating in multiple activities, like studying while watching videos. Sometimes a lack of stimulation can make an activity harder, which is why background noise or having a body double (someone just in the room to be with you while you do something) can help a lot.watching something on repeat endlesslybiting/sucking on clothing seams. This is very common in young children and ABSOLUTELY a sign they need to stim.stim toys (poppers, fidget spinners, infinity cubes, etc.)rubbing fabrics together.eating certain foods (for me - ones that go CRUNCH, like crackers)oral fixations (toothpicks, suckers, cigarettes, etc.)hitting, biting, or hurting oneself (also known self injurious behavior (SIB))Speaking of self-injury, suicidal ideation is not uncommon among autistic people: living in this world is inherently traumatic for any autistic person. We live in a world full of "No!" and "How do you not know that?" Most of us have learned we are not and possibly never will be fully accepted by society.On that note: PTSD. Basically all autistic people have PTSD, even the young ones. When you struggle to communicate, those around you become frustrated and often take it out on you, citing it as a fault of yours, when you simply haven't been taught how. That's why so much of ABA is centered around communication, and is overall one of the largest areas we target. And sometimes you get lucky: you get amazing parents who love you no matter what and do anything they can to further your education, and you come out the other end a little less worse for wear than the rest of us. And sometimes you get a parent who becomes irate whenever your autism makes an appearance - and those of us suffer the most. Just like NT people, autistic people generally have a group of people supporting them: and unfortunately, for a lot of us, that group is MUCH smaller, or sometimes non-existent. If you as a neurotypical somehow fear autistic people, trust me, we fear you far more.Lack of spatial awareness. For a lot of people, they're already overstimulated and trying to focus on masking or just simply trying to exist in this harsh world. This makes us a bit more clumsy than the average person.Reaction times: like other skills, autistics can sometimes be lacking in reaction time. Others may be hyper-alert and have faster reaction times than normal people.Impulse control: with everything going on in our heads, it's sometimes hard to tell ourselves â€œnoâ€ too. And since depression and anxiety often come with autism, that lack of impulse control can even be a coping mechanism.I hope with this addition, more people can spot these behaviors! Edit 2: Thank you for 20k views! I think it's only fitting I add more to help further your autism education. These issues are more obvious and can be quite common among autistics:Co-occuring diagnoses/disorders: many autistics will be also diagnosed with PTSD (as previously mentioned), anxiety, and possibly mania/depression. Some may be MISDIAGNOSED as ADHD or bipolar. Some may ALSO have ADHD(AuDHD) (ðŸ˜­ me) that exaggerates or minimizes a symptom. Some may be diagnosed with IBS. Some may have insomnia. Some may have ODD. Every diagnoses, physical or mental, is affected by or will affect their autism. This is why it's just so hard to define by symptoms, alone. We can say stimming is a good indication, but that's also an ADHD symptom. As is obsessing. There isn't a symptom you can point at and just go "THAT! That is AUTISM!"Temperature sensitivity. Many autistic people feel too warm to too cold. As such, they respond to changes in temperature much differently. I, myself, struggle with heat, and it actually makes me feel nauseous and anxious. This is controlled by your mechanoreception senses.Light sensitivity: it's been mentioned before but light can be very overstimulating, to the point that it can become PAINFUL. A lot of autistic people like myself and many of my kids at work prefer the dark and stay away from "the big light". Natural light sources tend to be easier for autistic people, as LED or other lights also add an element of sound stimulation.Sound stimulation? From what? The lights! Many autistic people report being able to hear the transfer of electricity through wire (myself included). I describe it sounding almost like tinnitus, and this can change somtimes in pitch rhythmically or just ring. Sometimes it hums or buzzes. I've also found older technology seems to be the worst with these sounds, while some of the newer technology can be quiet. Charger cords in power strips can often cause these noises to get worse (especially if it is older (micro-usb seems to do it the most, and old iPhone cords too)). LED lights are also extremely harsh on the eyes, as they emit blue light, which is what makes light so overstimulating for so many. It's like looking at a phone screen all day long: damaging, I would dare say. Incandescent are a bit easier on the eyes, but they also still produce blue light. Any artificial light source potentially could. The only thing worse are fluorescent lights. You know, these guys? The ones that are basically everywhere commercial or educational? Like nails on a chalkboard: I swear these are the loudest lights on the planet, and I'm so certain that some of you NTs MUST hear it, because how can't you? It's impossible NOT to hear. These lights also play a part in light sensitivity as 1) they strain your eyes, making headaches and fatigue more likely, and 2) autistic senses can sometimes be incredibly different from what the NT can expect. It is 100% possible for a bright room to cause an autistic person to become PHYSICALLY ILL. I know light can make me nauseous. Please keep in mind that if your autistic child attends a public school, their senses likely being assaulted by these harsh lights all day, which can decrease their comfort and therefore increase behaviors. Consider buying your child blue light glasses if they do not already have them. This may also help them with their sleep issues.Sleep issues (insomnia/parasomnia)! I swear almost every autistic person on this planet will have some kind of issue with sleep, whether it's falling asleep, staying asleep, waking up, or even actually GETTING sleep. Stress really messes with a person's sleep, and autistic people are gonna be like 10x more stressed than the average NT.Speaking of stress, you know which parts of your body get affected the most by stress? Let's start with our stomach and bowels! (Your cardiovascular, nervous, endocrine, and reproductive systems are also affected, but those symptoms are usually NOT overlooked.) Most autistic people have some struggle with their stomach, whether certain foods make them sick, they can't feel they need to use the restroom, or aversions to texture may limit what they can eat. Many different struggles come with food - and using the restroom afterwards.Social distress with double meanings. People say autistics "take things literally", and many of them do. Some autistics understand when you say "it's raining cats and dogs" that it's not ACTUALLY raining cats and dogs; a young autistic (and sometimes older autistics) might mistake this for something else entirely (ie: it's literally raining live cats and dogs outside). Most of us learn with age what many of these sayings ACTUALLY mean, but oftentimes, we can still get tripped up by everyday conversation or jokes. Another example of something an older/more experienced autistic person might miss (I did) is a bumper sticker on a car that says "honk if you like pizzaâ€. The NeuroTypical Secret Â© is that whenever someone honks, the driver will just dismiss it as liking pizza instead of their bad driving. An autistic person (ME) might look at that sticker and LITERALLY honk because I like pizza (I don't but for this case). I include myself in this example because I was 24 when I figured that out ðŸ’€ AutismConveniently, that actually circles around to our sense of justice. Most people believe that if you do something bad, you should be punished, and if you do something good, you should be rewarded. With autistics, this is different: autistic people tend believe that if you do something bad, you MUST be punished. This causes many autistics to be labeled as "tattle-tales" because they are constantly trying to manage others' behavior as well. It feels WRONG to see some people punished (or even be punished, yourself) for something while others get away with it. We are an EVEN-MINDED people. There is a lot of belief in "an eye for an eye" with autistics. This can be where some autistics can become dangerous: due to revenge or sometimes grudges that are taken out on the wrong people (or sometimes the right people) in the wrong way.This is where we come to SIZE OF THE PROBLEM. If you trip and drop your food on the floor, it is a large irritant, but a small problem: you can generally clean it up and get yourself more food, perhaps a little more bitter than before. If you lock your keys in the car, that's a bigger problem - one that affects people, maybe more than just you - and a larger irritant, but this is still a solvable, medium-sized problem. You can wait around for a locksmith to come unlock your car or get a ride. Now our child breaks their arm. This is a BIG problem, and generally a cause for HIGH anxiety for ANYONE. This takes specialized help and can have lasting consequences if it isn't treated. This generally requires immediate and DIFINITIVE action.For an autistic person, it can very difficult to judge the size of a problem, as sometimes they can factor in their own feelings instead of remaining unbiased (this is much harder to do for some autistic people). Sometimes, when an autistic drops their food on their floor, due to their stress, feelings, and perception of the situation, they can quickly judge this as a BIG problem, which may result in many "unwanted" and harmful behaviors. In an autistic's mind, it truly is a big problem, and you should NEVER tell an autistic person they are "overreacting". Instead, ask the person to take some deep breaths. Ask them if they need to leave the area to collect themselves, or if they need anything to help comfort them. You can even HELP them clean up. This is an act of love that a lot of autistics can recognize. The issue isn't their reaction, it's how they feel: if you just focus on their reaction, it will become worse. If you help regulate their feelings, they are more likely to calm down. (Note: This is how ABA changed their treatment for the better: actually looking at how an autistic feels instead of JUST suppressing a reaction.)Underreacting: a lot of autistics are seen as "unemotional". This is generally not the case - that person just has issues COMMUNICATING their emotions. Sometimes, they may even have trouble understanding them (I did as a child/teen), and the most you can do is be there for support. Try not to put a lack of reaction down to "they don't care". Often, we do.Missed social cues. Autistics sometimes struggle to read the room (and sometimes they're hyper-aware), and when the mood changes, they might not change with it. For example: A couple hosts a party, and they begin to fight, causing everyone to become quiet and focus on them. There is TENSION and ANTICIPATION in the room. But an autistic person continues to laugh and talk, perhaps even becoming a bit upset that the hosts have deviated from the comfortable atmosphere of the party. Alternatively, people may be having a wonderful time while an autistic may be having a panic attack in the corner from misinterpreting a look or a conversation. This also falls in line with jokes, as sometimes autistics may not understand a joke is being told. As awkward as it is for you, trust me, we feel so much worse. I definitely know the pain of taking a joke literally and having a group of people stare at me quietly, suddenly not comfortable talking around me. It's not pleasant for anyone. This can also lead to improper body language. And some autistics struggle to line up their body language with their emotions, so it can be even more difficult.Mutism. Many autistics communicate nonverbally (waving, taking things, gesturing, mimicking etc.), as do you! Reading body language and trying to understand why someone is doing what they're doing is important. Some autistics can ONLY communicate nonverbally - sometimes they don't make noise at all, and sometimes they simply can't/won't speak, but can still hum, grunt, etc. Mutism is sometimes a coping mechanism (selective mutism), and it can come in temporary periods, especially those of high stress. This can happen to children AND adults. Sometimes being mute means an autistic can only speak to ONE person (that they are usually comfortable with), and that person relays their message. Sometimes they can't communicate at all, due to high stress, and they completely shut down, nonverbally and verbally.I'll continue to add more as this post gets more popular. There are countless symptoms I could list, common or not. Thank you for reading! Edit 3: Wow, almost 60k views- this I didn't expect. And I love all the comments! Let's talk about some more symptoms! And at the end, I'd like to clear up some misconceptions. This may be my last addition - not that there aren't more symptoms, but other symptoms I can mention can also be symptoms of many other developmental disorders or mental illnesses.I've mentioned it before, but consistency is very important with autism. For some, it's because of the comfort of routine, and for others, it's to avoid burnout or mental overload. Consistency is necessary in almost every aspect of life: food, plans, interests, and people. As mentioned before, texture and taste can become an issue regarding food with some autistics, and it's very important to be understanding. It's not a learned pickiness - it's stimulation issues. Routine is also very important for autistics, as previously mentioned. Most autistics like to adhere to a particular routine and may become upset if plans change. Hyperfixation was previously mentioned: but the depth of hyperfixation was not. Hyperfixations can last for MONTHS or YEARS. Some autistics spend half their life dedicating themselves to a hyperfixation. Many people may like something for many years, but to talk about it and/or participate in an activity relating to it happens almost every day with an autistic. It's more common for NTs to take a break and return to an interest over time. It can also be difficult for people with autism to consume new media, as that means having to absorb information - sometimes we're just too damn tired to do or see anything new. Many of us are happy to explain how we feel and what is going on in our heads, but to do so with almost everyone gets tiring. It takes time to get used to new people - longer for people with autism, generally, unless that person is also on the spectrum or has ADHD.Which leads to my next point: people with these disorders tend to group together. People on the spectrum tend to do better being friends with animals than people. Animals don't bully or judge. Many are naturally loving unconditionally (cats and dogs), which makes autistics more comfortable just focusing on being happy instead of hiding themselves. Animals also communicate via body language, and many of us can read that body language more naturally. That doesn't mean an autistic can't hate or hurt animals, but they are less inclined to.Inappropriate speech. Understanding when it is and is not appropriate to say something can be a little more difficult for autistics, leading to inappropriate jokes, possible slurs/swearing, and insensitive comments. It's a bit harder for autistics to filter before they speak. Sometimes this is why autistics have different speech patterns, as they speak very fast, just saying what's on their mind, or sometimes they have to take extra time to formulate their sentences and thoughts.Time blindness/over consciousness. Time feels different for autistics and ADHDers. This can cause them to lose track of time or even be TOO aware of the time. This can also fall in-line with consistency, as mentioned before: many autistics don't like to be late.Lack of personal space. This goes a long with lack of spatial awareness.
