Most of the smartest people in the world have autism (once diagnosed *Asperger's, as it's more known for being more "low interference" than what people think of when they hear "autism"(or incorrectly known as "high-functioning")) [YES, ASPERGER'S IS AND ALWAYS WILL BE AUTISM] or some kind of developmental disorder.(If you want to know more about why "high-functioning" is a bad term, look at my post here: Cynicality's answer to If an autistic person seems very high-functioning or â€œnormal,â€ does it mean theyâ€™re masking a lot or very good at masking?)Unexplainable symptoms/illnesses. Stress does a LOT to the body, as does HOW we perceive physical sensations. I mention in the linked post that we are taught we have 5 senses, but we actually have 9, and these other 4 senses are also affected by autism. Let's learn about the other 4. I will include the formal definitions, but they do not go into depth with how autism affects them. The first two are very similar and I actually got them mixed up previously, so any errors have been corrected (I'd rather be accurate than self-proclaimed "correct").Interoception: this sense is literally "how you feel inside". Not everyone feels their body in the same way. For some, a hunger pain is a minor irritance, but one you can take care of soon. For an autistic person, this can be painful and even make them nauseous. For some women, a period is an inconvenience - for some autistic women, they may dread this time of month due to longer/heavier periods, and they can be especially painful, even moreso if they have something like endometriosis (for the men out there, this is one of the most painful conditions in the world. Be patient with your endometriosis-diagnosed women.) or POCS. Now all the opposite could also be true: for hunger, pain, or sensitivity - they don't feel it as much. This is known as hypointeroception, while the former is hyperinteroception.Proprioception is the sense "physical" self. Where you are, the feeling of movement, and force. This and mechanoreception control how someone moves, and, similarly to the previous term, hyperproprioception can make this over-sensitive, cause clumsiness and accidents to happen. Sometimes they are under-sensitive, and a person may have a hard time telling how hard they may be squeezing, holding, hitting, or pushing something - which also causes accidents. This is hypoproprioception.Mechanoreception: this is the sense that controls how your body reacts to outside stimuli, and if it even senses it. Similar to interoception, but instead of perceiving oneself, it's the perception of others.It was mentioned some autistics may be more clumsy: this can also be because of hyper or hypo sensitivity to the vestibular sense. This sense controls - can you guess it? Balance! Balance is a sense of its own, and you have organs and bones (in your ears specifically) that control that sense. This can make it hard for an autistic to balance, walk, or even stop shaking. And again, the opposite may be true, where you have someone with remarkable balance. This also affects motion sickness - along with your interoception and proprioception senses. This also controls how delicate your movements are. Sometimes people need to move quickly, and your vestibular senses help you achieve that - sometimes you're doing delicate work that might shatter under the tiniest mistake - it's the vestibular sense. Autistic people are known for having a strong grip, moving jerkily or clumsily, and sometimes being exceptionally fast. This is when the vestibular sense is too insensitive and causes less precision with movements, causing explosive and quick movements instead. These people may have trouble with heat or cold, as goosebumps are easier to get and they're more prone to overheating and possibly even sweating with both the vestibular and mechanoreceptive senses. It's also not unheard of for the opposite to be true as well. Some autistics can be a bit weaker - they may not feel the cold or heat as much and may need prompting to realize their body needs attention (again, mechanoreception) - they may move more slowly and carefully than others.Literally all these senses are usually HIGHLY affected by autism, but because these senses are not common knowledge, a lot of people ignore autistics' feelings because they don't believe they could actually feel them. Temperature and touch can be particularly sensitive (or in some cases, insensitive) for some.Smell: some autistics have a more deep and perhaps "picky" sense of smell. This is called hyperosmia, and can make some autistics sick, as they can LITERALLY taste smells. As always, the opposite could also be true (but I think is less common.)Taste: texture (touch) and flavor are a big deal: autistics like them to be consistent and sometimes stay away from foods like blueberries, bananas, and other foods that are not always sold at their ripe point (usually a lot of products are received under-ripe so they can not only last longer in the store but on your counters too). There is a stigma surrounding there term â€œAsperger'sâ€ and it's no longer accurate. When speaking of â€œAsperger'sâ€ or â€œhigh-functioning autismâ€ (also an archaic term), you ACTUALLY mean â€œlevel 1â€ ASD. Some misconceptions:Autistic people are not stupid, there is just a lot going on in the brain. Like recessive and dominant traits/genes, the right combination of these genes can create a child with autism where neither parent has autism (as both parents would have the autism gene in their family, but it's not active in themselves). If someone seems to develop autism symptoms where there weren't before, it's likely they've been either masking all along or in survival mode, hiding their autism. I will not lie to you: autism isn't GOOD either. It's hard to live with, both as the person who has autism and as the people around them.Autism is commonly misdiagnosed as OCD, bipolar, or ADHD. Much of these behaviors and perceptions are instinctual to neurotypical people. They instinctively project their emotions and perceptions onto others, they instinctually imagine how they appear from what they believe is others perspective, they instinctively categorize people into in-groups, out-groups, and use a kind of hierarchical ranking of relationships, and know where they fit in and how it affects others and why it's important. Their communication includes social constructs being validated and manipulated and respected. This helps prevent â€œbluntnessâ€. Autistic people may not do this. Many do learn to, but many do not. They also may have a sense that they are different from others, and that others do not perceive as they do. So this may prevent them from making assumptions about what others feel or think. Autistics donâ€™t generally try to seize power by sharing information. But neurotypical people may see it as a power grab because they donâ€™t solely share information while speaking, they also manipulate others socially. question: What are the pros and cons of having a child tested for autism?
answer: It is vitally important that autistic children and of course adults, are diagnosed. I write this based on my own experiences and what Iâ€™ve learned by NOT being diagnosed as a child. question: How do people with autism think differently than neurotypical people?
answer: Recent studies have shown that autistic people take in significantly more sensory information which is a double edged sword. On the one hand this can result in a higher attention to detail which can in some circumstances grant an ability to â€œhyperfocusâ€. This most commonly manifests in intense â€œspecial interestsâ€ where autistic people can gain a large amount of knowledge of certain, often niche topics. If properly focused this can lead to rewarding hobbies and even careers with the right supports. On the other hand this can result in sensory challenges such as sensitivities to sound, taste, touch, certain lights and other sensations which can make various public interactions much more difficult and can result in energy balancing issues due to autistic people expending larger amounts of energy for public interaction. This larger energy expenditure can often require more down time and can unfortunately often result in autistic burnout, especially in work settings which is one of the main reasons why unemployment rates among autistic adults are so appalingly high. Linguistic delays are common among autistic people due to autism having effects on the speech and language portions of the brain. This can result in some autistic people like myself taking longer to learn to talk, but can also result in some remaining non verbal for the rest of their lives. Even in these cases though it can be possible in many cases for an autistic person to catch up or even surpass their peers in this regard. Recognizing social cues is more difficult for autistic people meaning they will often need certain therapies to help them acquire social skills that are more intuitive to neurotypicals. This commonly results in misunderstandings between autistic people and the general public as well as autistic people, their employers and fellow employees in a workplace setting. With Double Empathy Problem it is often not just other people misunderstanding autistic people, it is autistic people having difficulty understanding others as well. This is why it is common for autistic people to prefer a more direct, often blunt style of communication which can come off as tactless to some people. Though not universal many autistic people highly value logical thinking which in stark contrast to the intuition based thinking common among many in the general public. In some cases this can be tied to a black and white thinking, though the relationship to this is quite complex and varied. An autistic people can depending on the individual and their circumstances either hold tightly to their own narrow set of rules, or actively rebel against various societal rules and norms that they deem unjust or nonsensical. During my childhood years I tended toward the former, the latter in my teen years and a more refined â€œpick your battlesâ€ approach to the latter in adulthood. There are of course many more, but these are the most important ones that come to mind for me.

question: Is oxytocin likely to help profoundly autistic people?
answer: No, it isn't. The studies of oxytocin sprays for autistic children were based on the flawed hypothesis that autistics can't bond emotionally. This is demonstrably not true. Later studies that took the experiences of actual autistic people in mind showed that the sensory and communication issues are the core of autism--which can manifest in ways that are perceived by others as not showing empathy or emotional bonding. If someone is overwhelmed by their environment, that will interfere with social behavior. If someone can't talk, it's not fair to complain that they don't say "I love you" even if they're showing affection in other ways. If eye contact feels threatening, why insist on it? There are also problems when children undergo abusive types of autism therapies or are treated as subhuman by their parents; this type of abuse would impair bonding in any child. Also, oxytocin's reputation as the "love hormone" is oversimplified. Administering oxytocin to non-autistic people not only increases bonding and camaraderie but hostility towards outsiders of the group. Adjusting the emotional responses of "profoundly autistic" people is not going to address sensory hyper/hyposensitivity, the mechanics of communication, sleep/wake cycle issues, or executive functioning. These are the difficulties faced by high-support autistic people, not their social ability.

question: Why don't autistic people try to behave and talk normally? Are they just faking to be authists?
answer: â€œWhy don't autistic people try to behave and talk normally?â€Thatâ€™s what masking is. If youâ€™ve never heard of it, autistic masking is hiding or suppressing your autistic traits in order to try and pass off as normal, or as someone more socially acceptable. So you ask why donâ€™t we? Well, we do. Thereâ€™s even a screening test called the CAT-Q. Itâ€™s called the CAT-Q, because it stands for: Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire.The Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q)The CAT-Q is a self-report measure of social camouflaging behaviors in adults, used to identify camouflaging behaviors in autistic people.https://embrace-autism.com/cat-q/The CAT-Q Test can determine if you do mask or camouflage your autism, and this is why many clinicians donâ€™t consider an autism diagnosis, because the masking of autistic traits can cause clinicians to miss it entirely. This is why autism requires a skilled clinician to spot. A good clinician often screens for autism by the CAT-Q Test, alongside the AQ Test, which is a simple autism screening. So we autistic people do try to just talk and behave normally. Itâ€™s called masking. So whatâ€™s the issue? The issue is is that masking actually leads to worse mental health outcomes overall for autistic people. Studies are now beginning to find how detrimental to our mental health masking can be (Bradley et al., 2021; Hull et al., 2019). Autistic people who mask more show more signs of anxiety and depression, and the strategy may even been linked to an increase in suicidal behaviors (Cassidy et al. 2018). Masking uses up vital resources that we canâ€™t use in other areas of our lives. To put it simply, it is exhausting. This increases stress, meltdowns/shutdowns/withdrawal become far more common, and increases the risk of autistic burnout, a state of extreme stress where the person is so stressed and exhausted, they start to lose skills. It also stops us from developing our true identities, who we really are. The pressure to fit in means we rarely have time or energy to do the things we want to do, or to behave like our true selves. This also means, dangerously, that weâ€™re very vulnerable, because we donâ€™t learn how to set healthy boundaries and advocate for what we need. This makes us more prone to being taken advantage of. If weâ€™re trying to be like other people, we forget about who we are. Think about it, if all youâ€™re doing is pretending to be someone youâ€™re not, your whole identity, who you are, is tied to the mask youâ€™re wearing. How do you know what you like? What your interests are? What you like or dislike? Everything becomes connected to what you think you should be, instead of who you really are.The picture is a quote from my second favorite video game of all time, The Legend of Zelda: Majoraâ€™s Mask. The quote says:Can I ask a question? Your true faceâ€¦ What kind of face is it? I wonderâ€¦ the face under the maskâ€¦ Is that your true face?That cuts right to the heart of the matter. If all you do is pretend to be someone youâ€™re not, you lose yourself in the process. Ironically, a study done by researchers found that masking didnâ€™t change the judgements that neurotypical peers made towards autistic peopleâ€™s social behaviors. Even when the autistic person was masking, neurotypical people still rated them more harshly than their neurotypical peers. So weâ€™re ineffectively trying to appear as normal, and neurotypical people see right through it. Even when an autistic person is masking, neurotypical people will still rate them more harshly than neurotypical peers if they donâ€™t know they are autistic. This unconscious bias is evident throughout society for anyone deemed to behave or think atypically by neurotypical standards.Are they just faking to be authists?No, they arenâ€™t, most of the time, theyâ€™re trying to fake being normal. Look, just because someone doesnâ€™t behave the way you think an autistic person should behave doesnâ€™t mean theyâ€™re not autistic. People think itâ€™s so easy to fake being autistic or ADHD, so much so that they think people can fake these for clout and attention. These same people are woefully misinformed about autism and ADHD, are unaware of how the diagnostic process works, and are unaware of how deeply it affects your life. Autism and ADHD affect me so deeply, that every thought I have, every sensory experience I have, is colored by ADHD and autism. They in almost a very literal way, affect how I think, affect how I perceive the world, and thus, how I feel emotionally, and the resulting behaviors I do. Ever since autism was first described in the medical literature, itâ€™s always been judged by how it appears on the outside instead of how it feels from the inside. So what can we do? First, this is for neurotypical people. The best solution to reducing the need for autistic people to mask is to spread awareness to neurotypical people of different neurodivergent behaviors and thinking patterns. When neurotypical people know someone is autistic, they seem to judge them less harshly. However, this strategy is not an easy one and will take years of effort before itâ€™s fully ingrained in our society. Second, for us autistic people, we need to prioritize ourselves by protecting ourselves and improve our mental health and well-being. That means undoing all of the stigma and ableism that we have internalized. We have to accept that we are autistic. No matter how much we fake trying to blend in, no matter if we hold ourselves to an unfair standard we can never attain, we will always be autistic. And there is nothing wrong with that. Weâ€™re only taught that thereâ€™s something wrong with being autistic because of unfair, unhealthy, and unfounded stigmas and ableism from other people and society. Masking is a vicious cycle. The worse we feel about ourselves, the more we feel a need to mask, which the more we mask, the worse we feel. We need to let it go. The type of masking weâ€™re doing is just harming ourselves. When youâ€™re a circle born in a hexagonal world, thereâ€™s nowhere where you fit in, because a circle takes up more area than an equivalent sized hexagon. By forcing yourself to fit in this world, youâ€™re damaging yourself and your circularity. You are not a hexagon, youâ€™re a circle. Embrace being circular. In other words, embrace being autistic. Masking, in so many words, is an inherent denial of who you really are. Denial of yourself is believing a lie about yourself. Be honest with yourself and embrace who you really are. Are you going to run into challenges being autistic? Sure, and thereâ€™s ways you can begin to start working with the brain you have, instead of trying to pretend to be someone youâ€™re not. But no good comes from masking, so peel them off, realize why you wore that particular mask, and by coming to terms with it, you can begin to let it go, as it no longer is useful to you.We originally masked to protect ourselves. In the short term, it worked, but over the long haul, we suffered. Now thereâ€™s better ways and you can begin to start slowly removing them and letting them go. Once you come to learn youâ€™re autistic, your problems and issues you experienced wonâ€™t just magically disappear, you now have to learn how to strategize with the brain you have instead of pretending to be someone youâ€™re not. This is why autism requires support, no matter how â€œsevereâ€ it appears to the outsider. You simply do not know how much the person is going through even if they donâ€™t have many support needs, or what many well-meaning but ill-informed neurotypicals call â€œhigh-functioning.â€ So, really, for neurotypical people, you have to exercise more compassion and understanding. Learn about autism from the perspective of the real experts: autistic people. So, to answer the question. No. Autistic people arenâ€™t faking being autistic. Just because they donâ€™t conform to what you expect autistic people to be like doesnâ€™t mean theyâ€™re not autistic. Thatâ€™s not even how autism is defined by any meaningful metric, scientific, personal, clinical, or otherwise. Everyone agrees autism is a literal difference in the brain. And thereâ€™s nothing wrong with being neurodivergent. Hope that helps!Originally answered: Why don't autistic people try to behave and talk normally? Are they just faking to be authists?

question: Does the theory of mind develop better in autistic individuals if they are raised as neurotypicals/forced to understand, and by how much?
answer: I can speak on this topic because I was only diagnosed last year at age 59. So there are many of us who were â€œforcedâ€ to understand theory of mind - Iâ€™ve kept this response as a draft because the original was very harsh - and possibly unfair. But I felt the person asking this question would be in favor of â€œforcing someone to understandâ€ theory of mind. If not, I apologize. I can force a square peg into a round hole - but it will usually damage both the peg and the hole. My point here is that you have two different things - that share a lot of similar attributes but fundamentally are different - This is what neurotypicals do not seem to understand - An autistic person is NEUROLOGICALLY DIFFERENT than a person who is neurotypical. question: What do people with autism understand that most people don't?
answer: that people can be extremely harmful with even the best intentions. I can't count how many times I have had this conversation where I have had to explain to neurotypicals that a "therapy" can be inappropriate at best and harmful at worst to autistic people and still be done with the best of intentions. The road to hell is paved with good intentions. A person can suffer tremendous abuse even when it is under the guise of "good intentions." We are not that naive as NT people when it comes to thatâ€” even if it bucks the non-inclusive "mommy knows best" ideology. I am tired of having this conversation with NTs who want a cookie for sending their kid to ABA without legitimately listening to autistic people explaining to them that anything behaviorism gave us ptsd. Even trying to rationalize it with cost/benefit analysis doesn't tell you the whole story because some problems don't surface right away, but becoming catastrophic over time decades later.That indistinguishability is not in fact functioning. It comes at the expense of resources used for actual functioning (especially executive functioning). Teaching someone indistinguishability doesn't teach people self-advocacy at all, it doesn't teach consent. It goes against learning and employing advocacy skills and consent. Compliance training teaches you to disregard boundaries, not advocate for your needs.Adding to that, indistinguishability also lauds inauthentic connections done in an NT way, because it is so draining that it leaves us depleted and then requires tons of time to recover from. So I just end up making connections that are shallow and unsustainable because I can't maintain them in my downtime. It is just better to make authentic autistic connections where someone understands my needs from the get-go and is less draining for me.We usually have a "cut the bullshit" shrewd attitude about life. We don't have all day to hang around a store or restaurant and getting overstimulated. We don't have a lot of social spoons to waste. Like what's been said, we are more utilitarian at maximizing our resourcesâ€” we have to be. So when someone is out to sell me something, they aren't just irritating, they are also overstimulating. I just want them to cut to the chase and explain upfront why they are engaging me in conversation because I am overstimulated and I also have the attention span of a fly (a large percentage of autistics are like me and have ADHD too). Like if a guy follows me in a supermarket talking about how "blessed" I am and something about Jesus, it is one of two things: 1) come to my church and 2) I want money or oh yeah 3) I want money and come to my church and give more money. I just want him to drop the other shoe and tell me what he's after. Door to door salesmen too, but they are less rare nowadays. In some ways that is even worse than how sales clerks at Best Buy used to be where you would just buy a DVD and they'd try to upsell you on a $600 thing you can't afford while wasting time overstimulating the autistic person.Functioning isn't static or even linear. I need downtime to recover. It is also contextual. I will function a lot better in a quiet office than I ever will in a loud department store. This in of itself makes functioning labels useless. One functioning label is used to dehumanized people and not presume competence of them. The other is used to deny supports entirely.Not all labels are badâ€” they can even be rooted in power when they are used by the person with said condition to claim power over their own existence and find ways of connect with other people who also have the condition. Don't deny a person a sense of community. And definitely tell your kids they are autistic so they can learn to not hate themselves. With that saidâ€” it is worth more for the person to identify themselves than to let other people pick identifying language for them. I know you mean well, OP, but much of the autistic community prefers identity-first language (autistic) over person first language (person with autism). The way I see itâ€” if people insist on PFL to remind themselves constantly that I am in fact, a person, they have already failed at seeing me as such (it plays right into that dehumanization, as well as recentering the narrative on autism on everyone but the actually autistic people, which needs to change, and no, I know it is not what they taught you in medical/psych schoolâ€” they are behind the times tremendously and they never listen to us at all).Sensory issues aren't preferences. God I wish they were. That would make it so much easier. And that our existence isn't wrong just because we don't experience the world the same way you do.We are masters at understanding what alienation consists of. My life is a never-ending stream of alienation, between people who won't meet me halfway (and yet expect endless social burden and emotional labor out of me), people who have the audacity to tell me that I didn't come with a manual, or rationalize that I am "in my own world" without bothering to even include me in anything. I am forever counted as "other" even in the narrative that is my own existence (thanks to parents who make it all about themselves, and thanks autism speaks), which is unacceptable and even infantilizing (autism "charities" I am talking youâ€” especially the mega marketing campaign ones). I don't need "awareness" (aka fear-mongering BewarenessTM) I need acceptance. And unlike what I have seen last April where people talk about inclusion and awarenessâ€” you can't actually get that inclusion without actual acceptance being involved. Awareness won't touch me with a 50 yard pole. Awareness doesn't even want to be in the same room with me. Acceptance is where it is at.I hope that explains a few things. :)

question: I honestly believe autism is a severe anxiety disorder and not an intellectual or psychological disorder. We get so overwhelmed by the environment and social ethics that we shut off. Why doesn't society get it?
answer: Hi Micah, It all gets so complicatedâ€¦ Autism is not like the common cold where everyone has the same symptoms and it all goes through the same progression.. Its more like trying to track a wild animal after a hard rain. Thereâ€™s nothing to see directlyâ€¦ just a lot of indications that something was there. What makes it so elusive to understand is that it is a very complicated neurodevelopmental difference. Its not a system with hundreds or even thousands of parts that are affect, its in the billions. It a nervous system (NS) that has developed without a specific â€œblueprintâ€. Where the typical nervous system (neurotypical /NT) develops very consistently, the autistic NS is unique to each person. This is so important to understandâ€¦ No two autistic people have the same autistic experience because we are neurologically unique. It is no â€œcoincidenceâ€ that other neurological disorders are commonly part of being autistic. Iâ€™m ADHD /dyslexic, and other body perceptual issues such as disorientation of left/right.. what I call â€œmissing wordsâ€ that you know but cannot remember how they are pronounced or spelled and some things I donâ€™t know how to define and some Iâ€™m still discovering. These traits are not obvious because they are normal from our perspective. And we cannot know any other experience but our own. The differences are not out there for direct comparison. We only have the tracks that are left behind to try and make sense of. When I was in college, I remember a class where we talked about a student who could read if it was on a vertical plane like the chalk board but when it was flat or horizontal, their mind could not interpret the letters in that orientation. I worked with a woman with a traumatic brain injury to the vision center of the brain. She was totally blind though her eyes were not injured. The only thing she could sense was the color red - no shape, no contrast, no depth nothing but the â€œfeelingâ€ of red. We donâ€™t realize that our awareness is not a single thing, but the combination of millions of bits of information. Change one thing and sometimes you affect everything. Autism can be like trying to juggle 50 balls of different sizes, in the dark with welderâ€™s gloves on, in the windâ€¦ on a unicycle while intoxicatedâ€¦ Ok.. that might be a bit much but it feels that way sometimes. Some people manage their traits better than others, have traits of different types and degrees and so on. Weâ€™re a community that ranges from totally dependent on others to total independent. But level of independence is no indication of the degree of challenges a autistic person manages. Only an indication of how well they can manage them. We not only have to learn our own unique neurological system, how it works, how to manage it and keep it stable, we also have to do this in a society of people that have a homogeneous neurological system that function in very different ways than ours. There is tremendous pressure on us that we DO function like everyone else as well. And we face this as children, without models to learn from or supports to help us learn how to be autistic. Is it any wonder that we are stressed out? That anxiety â€œdisordersâ€ are common with autistic people? That we get so fatigued and worn down that rates of attempted and successful suicide are as high as 1 in every 3 autistic people. That 3 of 4 autistic people consider suicide as a way to find relief from the stress. And who do we have to turn to for support and understanding? Who can relate to our autistic lives that are not autistic? NTs experience a totally different life challenge than we do. The general society developed to support the NT challenges not the autistic challenges. In fact some of the ways society has developed are destabilizing to autistic people. I started counseling recently, and its so frustrating trying to glean bits of help or hope from someone who barely speaks our languageâ€¦ So - to answer your question - I say .. no doubt anxiety, stress, fatigue and the energy we expend constantly, is a major component of being autistic. But it is more a result of managing our autistic lives than a cause. The autism does affect us intellectually and psychologically too. I know that I process slower than most, but its not because I have lower intelligence. Its the exact opposite. I process so MUCH information that it takes longer. I also have audio processing difficulties. The ADHD - the dyslexiaâ€¦ Its those countless neurons that function differently than the NT neurology that Iâ€™ll never know or understand. Its a complicated difference so foreign to those on the â€œoutsideâ€ that it really cannot be understood or defined. I think many of the psychological problems associated with autism are not caused by the neurological difference directly. Its that we are like a very complex computer and this means we are affected by more things than a system with a less complicated function. Psychologically we are more sensitive to fatigue and overload too. We start our lives without the support systems that NT children have and have to create our own coping strategies to survive. This psychological pressure is constant throughout our lives. If we had a society that supported our needs as well as the typical nervous system, there we be a lot less problems than we have now.

question: Why don't autistic people realize that ABA therapy is actually good for them?
answer: Applied Behavior Analysis therapy, as the name suggests, modifies behavior. Autism can create behavior that seems cold, callous, or cruel to neurotypicals. It can also produce behavior neurotypicals see as disruptive, dismissive, or disengaged. That is, thereâ€™s a disconnect between how we behave, what our behavior stems from, and how neurotypicals judge us when they see us acting strange. Which we do. Often. ABA aims to correct this disconnect by changing our behavior. This can improve certain things about our lives. It can teach us what behaviors elicit positive and negative responses from neurotypicals. Being able to communicate our actual feelings and intentions through our behavior is useful, even essential. None of us are islands, though autists are happier in isolation than most. I say itâ€™s important for autists to learn about neurotypical expectations and thought processes; we are a minority and thatâ€™s never going to change. If certain things prejudice people against us, itâ€™s useful to be aware of that. We canâ€™t manipulate people into tolerating us unless we know how people think and how to change their assumptions.I Colori di Arlecchino by Giovanni Domenico Ferretti. Public domain.If thatâ€™s all ABA did, Iâ€™d support it. Blending in is a useful skill. Learning to communicate and interact in a way that the majority of the population will interpret correctly is helpful. But ABA teaches other lessons along with these useful skills. It teaches us that our behavior, our manner of perceiving the world, our desires and our pleasures are incorrect and inappropriate. It teaches us that acting in ways that are unnatural and deeply unpleasant for us is an indispensable prerequisite to being loved or accepted. The prevalence of suicidal behaviors and attempts in the autistic population is 24%, suicidal ideation is seen in 34% of us.[1] Suicidal behaviors occur in only 4% of the general population, while ideation sits around 13%.[2][3] Research into why we kill ourselves at such high rates is invariably new. Decades of time and millions of dollars have been spent figuring out how to make us look and act normal, but research into how we feel and how these treatments and tendencies impact our health, mentally and physically alike, only gained traction in the 2020s. We donâ€™t know a whole lot yet, not for certain. But a leading theory? Masking, particularly spending a lot of time masking, leads to mental illness and, in quite a few cases, suicide.[4][5]I Colori di Arlecchino by Giovanni Domenico Ferretti. Public domain.Itâ€™s generally acknowledged that masking allows us to function and meet societal goals better in the world we share; that, in its turn, can create some sense of belonging and fulfillment. We shouldnâ€™t underestimate that. Exclusion subsequent to obvious autistic traits damages us. Masking, however, doesnâ€™t fix these problems without an attendant cost. Heavy and frequent masking are especially associated with exhaustion, poor mental and physical health, and a poor or unhealthy sense of self. ABA teaches children to mask. It teaches children to mask and informs them in no uncertain terms that masking is essential to their survival. question: How do autistic children get their emotional needs fulfilled?
answer: I think that you might really be asking â€œhow does a person who doesnâ€™t like touch get their emotional needs fulfilled?â€ Itâ€™s important first to note that lots of autistic people love touch. The stereotype of an autistic person who canâ€™t bear anyone to touch him is true of a small part of the autistic population. Many autistic people, on the other hand, need regular deep pressure physical contact in order to help them regulate and feel grounded in their body. (Temple Grandin famously has a hug machine that provides that deep pressure without the unpredictability of other people.) And of course, plenty of autistic people like touch as a way of connecting with others, and each person will have their unique preferences. My son loves hugs, although heâ€™s less keen on kisses. Then again, you may have been asking â€œhow does a person who canâ€™t interact with others get their emotional needs met?â€ This is a fatally flawed idea of autism. Pretty much every autistic person can and does interact with others when given the tools to do so. Some people need alternative communication methods or a supported interactive environment, but that doesnâ€™t negate the fact that theyâ€™re interacting on a level that is adequate to their needs. And to be fair, some people just have much less interest in other people than average. There have always been hermits and aesthetes who preferred to live alone and avoid other people - itâ€™s a natural variant on human nature. Some autistic people are extremely social and extroverted, and others arenâ€™t. (Note that the triad of impairments is more about picking up social skills rather than a lack of desire to use them. Autism is not a synonym for introversion.) There is one emotional need that I think autistic people find harder to get met, and that is the need to be accepted for who you are. There are sadly still a lot of parents who think they must Fix Their Kid!! and put the child through all sorts of exhausting or even abusive treatments in order to try to drive the autism out. Weâ€™re increasingly seeing with the autistic adult population that people who have supportive, understanding parents who gave them room to develop according to their nature become happier and more able to deal with the neurotypical world in later life. People whose childhood was full of people relentlessly trying to make them neurotypical end up traumatised and much worse off in adulthood. Many have PTSD or C-PTSD, as well as an array of anxiety disorders. And this shouldnâ€™t surprise us, because we already knew it. We know that early rejection is traumatic, and that being forced to meet unreasonable expectations has long term impacts for mental health. Why should we have imagined that this wouldnâ€™t be the case for children with a developmental difference? So to sum up: autistic people are people, with individual needs and preferences. They get their emotional needs met in many of the same ways you do, although it might look a little different than youâ€™re used to. (I increasingly think that the great failure of the neurotypical mind is a lack of imagination. If a child always wants you in the same room with them but doesnâ€™t like hugs, theyâ€™re clearly getting their need for closeness met by being in the same room as you.)

question: What is life like as an adult with autism?
answer: As an autistic adult myself, I feel that I can answer this question. My sister, who is 18, is also autistic but very different from myself. I’m was people consider “high functioning” meaning I have lower support needs, typically. My sister is in a residential facility covered by the state, she needs 24/7 supervision and care. However, she will be attending school until she is 21 and afterwards, will have to move to an adult residency. Which my parents and I are extremely apprehensive about. To give you some background on my childhood, I was diagnosed with pervasive developmental disorder, not otherwise specified. This occurred in 2010. That’s essentially mumbo jumbo for the ICD-10 condition, “Atypical Autism”. What is atypical autism you might ask? Similar to HFA, atypical autism means I did not have enough traits to belong to a specific DSM-4 category because my autism presents uniquely. However, I still had enough social difficulties to fall under the spectrum. Now with the DSM-5, ASD is one disorder featuring 3 levels of severity. When I was retested in 2018, I was diagnosed with ASD level 1. The reason I’m providing this background is because my experience with autism will differ vary from many as I present differently than the stereotypes. Now, what’s it like living as a 22- year old autistic adult. Well, some days it’s great, some days it’s pure hell and some days it’s ehh. Let’s just balance that out to neutral. On the days that I work full-time, I’m typically exhausted from subconsciously masking my symptoms. I will either go home and stim, which is usually pacing/self talk for me, or watch TV and go to bed early. I do like having a job because it provides me a set schedule and certainty, which I greatly thrive off of. Im concerned for when I live on my home because after working 7–8 hours, I don’t have the energy to cook, clean or do any chores. Im just fatigued. Where the atypicality of my autism comes in is in the realm of socialization. Unlike most adults on the spectrum, I thrive off of social interactions, specially with my close family and friends. A lot, if not all, of my friends are neurodivergent so this makes sense in the great scheme of thinks; I can just be myself. I love going on adventures, trying new things, and being with people. However, my autism doesn’t always agree. There are times in which I struggle to say the appropriate thing at the right time, or modulate my voice, or argue with a joke because I took it literally. Other times, something external or internal will trigger me and my sensory world becomes a nightmare, I will stare blankly, shutdown, scream, cry and sometimes run away. As an adolescent, any change to my plans or schedule would ruin nearly my whole day. Now as an adult, I have been able to deal with transitions and change better but that doesn’t mean I’m perfect. And due to my comorbid dyspraxia and ADHD, my life and executive functioning skills suffer. On top of that, I deal with anxiety and depression so that’s always fun. Nevertheless, I find that some of my autistic traits help me in my adulthood. I’m extremely conscientious and meticulous when it comes to my work, which makes me a great employee. I am willing to help people whenever they need out which makes me a great friend. And my detailed oriented mindset and superb memory, specially with numbers, can be very beneficial in a lot of situations. It’s fun to be quirky in some ways because no one views me as boring! Now, for my sister, I don’t live inside her world but can only imagine what she experiences. My sister is primarily non-verbal and highly aggressive. Unlike me, she hates being told what to do, structure makes her angry. She also isn’t as obsequious me and is obstinate to basic tasks. All she cares about is her tablet, her radio, her boots and her father and me. Everything else is irrelevant in her world. In some ways I feel that she wants more autonomy over herself but right now, that’s not feasible. I get extremely stressed when I shutdown and become non speaking for 30 minutes so I cannot imagine what my sister feels like. Please note, this is just my experience. Everyone’s life is different. However, autistic people tend to struggle more than allistics in adulthood due to the lack of structure, predictability and support. So if you are an autistic or know one out there and you are reading this, my best advice is to make sure you accommodate yourself first!

Then I read it some more.I have trouble remembering things I don’t particularly care about or things that seem trivial. Lessons in school? Bingo. Names of people I’ve met? Right on. Face of the girl that broke up with me because reasons? I don’t even care to memorize her face. Not out of spite, but because my brain thinks, “Why should you remember this?” I guess it’s the reason I remember every line uttered by Darth Vader but I still can’t remember what I had for lunch today.I have two brains. One part of my brain is all the emotions I can feel, and the other brain contains everything else. Sometimes contact between the two is weird, random and sparse. It’s like couple who broke up, but since they live in a small town they see each other every time they go to the grocery store. I think this is the reason I like fictional robot characters more than living people characters.I adore organization. I organize legos, my schedule, my desk. Chaos is an enemy. Change and randomness are not overtly treated with hostility, but they’re rarely welcome.I wouldn’t be caught dead with a desk like this.PerfectionI’m quiet. If I have something to say, I’ll say it, but don’t expect me to be the next Martin Luther King.When I hear the song “Wait for It”, I’m rooting for Aaron Burr.I eat my foods one at a time. Eating is a game of war. Destroy the food plate piecemeal (pun intended).I’ve often contemplated the meaning of life. I’ve wondered of the point of my existence. I’ve thought about the time I have and what I’ve done with it. I’ve stood on the precipice of wondering if my entire existence is meaningless. Then I realize the next episode of Game of Thrones was premiering. Or that i’ve got an assignment due in a couple days. Or I’ve got a new book I’ve been meaning to read. Then I think, “Meh, this existentialism stuff isn’t going anywhere. I’ll think about it some other time.”Other than all that, I’m just another person, living his life and trying to be a stable human being.

question: Can you explain what it’s like to live with autism to someone that doesn’t have it?
answer: It is very difficult to explain how exhausting, terrifying, and demoralizing it is to be picked apart on a daily basis for subtle infractions of social rules. What I have observed is that instead of being more tolerant, neurotypicals watch for things to criticize when they know one is on the autism spectrum that they don't even notice or excuse when it is a neurotypical person doing them. It is a life of constant stress. Most of us suffer comorbid disorders, both as a consequence of our wiring and the effects of stress. The most common comorbids are anxiety disorders, both social and general, and mood disorders, depression or bipolar disorder, and difficulties in executive function. ADHD, learning disorders, and deficits in motor coordination are not unusual, but are not universal. Sensory processing problems and sensitivities are pretty much universal, but vary widely in their intensity and manifestation. I will come back to this. It is hard to put you in the head of a person on the autism spectrum, because we are wired so differently not only from neurotypicals but from each other. Some of us think in pictures, some in words, and some in patterns. Some of us are classical autistics with severe behavioral manifestations, while others of us are high-functioning people that you may think of as quirky when you meet us. Some of us end up living in a bubble, while others are doing our best to survive and excel in the workplace, academics, and daily life. We're at our best and happiest when we are given free reign to utilize and develop our talents and abilities. Our brains are constantly active. Though we are missing much social information, we're always taking in other information that the neurotypical brain may discard and processing it in ways that enable us to make associations that the neurotypical brain may miss. I may have come down in the world since my days as a head reference librarian, but in my second career, with I've developed a peculiar degree of accuracy in screening mail in a prison for drugs and security threats, because my brain takes in so much detail and picks up on aberrations, before I am even conscious of them. Words fall short of conveying a complex thought life. However, computer and audiovisual technology is making it possible to finally get an idea of the overwhelming amount of information that is coming through our senses. Imagine how it is to have everything turned up “loud", not just sound, but often fragrances, colors, movement, and sunlight itself. One can't focus. When we are overstimulated, the world takes on a nightmarish quality. We may need to escape, but there is nowhere to go. Then people wonder why we meltdown. Some persons on the spectrum have done simulations of how it is to navigate “adult" environments, such as store and street environments, but one of the best I've come across is the Auto-Sim simulation of the school playground.http://www.gamesforchange.org/game/auti-sim/

question: Is there anybody who lives with autism who is able to ride a motorcycle?
answer: Sure. I’m a 28 year old 5.1 ft male living in Belgium who has autism, and is currently on his sixth motorcycle. I love motorcycles, I love to work on them, restoring them, upgrading them and of course talking about them on and on. So far I have owned five Honda’s and one Suzuki. My current bike is a 2003 Honda deauville 650 which is referred to as big fat Willy . He comes in at 550 pounds and has only little over 50 horsepower. He may not be fast but he has an indestructible engine which was first developed to be used in the Dakar races and then won six of them consecutively. By now I’m probably boring you with these facts. So I’ll stop. I have both sensory issues and poor gross motor skills. But whenever I’m riding this all goes away. All sounds are drowned out by the exhaust note and the wind. And when I’m at speed it feels as if I’m weightless. There is no pressure on my back and shoulders, which allows me to really breathe. I have never gotten a speeding ticket or traffic ticket and I have never been in an accident. Not even after 180 000 miles! Over the years, riding has become a coping mechanism, a reward for a day’s work or a job well done, sometimes I take a ride to think about stuff or to cheer myself up which it never fails to do. If you are thinking about riding but you are worried about your autism, stop worrying! You’ll probably be a great and considerate rider! Never let anyone tell you that you can’t ride because you are short! A motorcycle is meant to be ridden not walked. On a more practical note it is worth mentioning that motorcycles, parts and gear can be expensive. Even more so than owning a car. Never cheap out on maintenance and parts! Research gear before buying, expensive does not always mean better. Have a good one!

question: How can I survive with autism?
answer: To be quite blunt, the way to survive with autism is to do the exact same things as you were doing before you received your diagnosis. You know, eat, drink, sleep, etc. Autism is not a terminal condition. It is not an autoimmune disease like AIDS or HIV which will seriously undermine your ability to withstand illnesses. It can seem quite surprising that someone could come to the conclusion that autism could lead to them suffering a premature death, unless they read the statistics on the life expectancy of the average autistic person. Unfortunately, autistic people on average do tend to die at an earlier age than is standard for the neurotypical population; however this figure is mostly due to the horrific fact that many autistic people chose to end their lives prematurely after a long period of loneliness and depression. However, since each person is an individual and statistics are not determinant of one’s own destiny, you can go on to lead a happy and long life. I would recommend contacting a psychiatrist or a psychologist if you have the means to do so, or to join an autism support group. Being autisitc can be lonely, so if you can you should try to make a few friends. You may be able to use your special interest(s) to find new friends, as not only will you be knowledgeable about the subject, but having the focus be on the interest itself and not so much on interpersonal communication can ease social anxiety and lead to more fluid conversations. I would also recommend studying body language and non-verbal cues, as this can benefit greatly your ability to socialize with others. Due to the high rate of unemployment among autistic people, I would advise getting in contact with a social welfare program or some form of apprenticeship or scholarship so that you can enter the job market. Being employed will provide you with both your own financial independence and the general sense of self-worth and meaning that often comes from pursuing a career you enjoy. I would also recommend that you use a diary or a notebook to help organize you schedule and to provide some emphasis on what tasks you have to complete, as the world can be very disordered and may overwhelm us if we are not careful. I wish you the best of luck out there in the world. Don’t be afraid to ask for help if you feel you need it. Good luck!

question: How is it to live with autism level 1?
answer: I can not speak for everyone - but for me it can feel like I have been sentenced to prison for a crime I did not commit. I suffer with incredible bouts of overwhelm in many capacities, I have co-morbid disorders that accompany autism like POTS, EDS, etc… so there are those ailments to deal with on a daily basis. Managing day to day tasks is dreadful because if I have anything on the calendar that I must do the next day - I will not sleep the night before. Relationships are nearly impossible for me as I am significantly impaired in my ability to attach to humans and animals - so I live a very isolated life. I rarely leave my bedroom… and when I have to it takes me a day or more to recover. A tiny change in plans or routine can send me into a deep meltdown and depression - even if it was a tiny insignificant thing. I suffer with both alexithymia and synesthesia - further complicating matters, for example - a room with artificial light “FEELS” like a lie touching me - making winters dreadful for me as we use artificial light most hours of the day inside and it’s too cold to go outside. I can not listen to music because I “SEE” it and it is far too overwhelming of an experience. For the most part I feel like an alien that was accidentally dropped off on the wrong planet and I want to go home… but that is just how it feels for me.

question: How do adults living with autism 'mask' their symptoms?
answer: GOOD MANNERS. I had to learn how to conduct myself in an acceptable manner. When I walk into a room I may be bursting to tell some one something. I have to BEHAVE MY SELF by masking my spontaniousness. I assess the room, I modify my emotional energy. I resist to temptation to butt into an existing conversation. I wait for a gap, “ Excuse me please, I want to change the subject”. I don’t fidget about, or hop from foot to foot, or pick things up and put them down again. I collect my thoughts together in an orderly manner instead of just letting them burst out of me. I don’t scratch itches, or play with my hair, or get distracted by something else. I wear clean tidy clothes like a uniform, so that I am not odd man out visually. Even though I am an adult, I feel like a well-behaved child when I am masking. I can change hats in an instant. If the cap fits, put it on. I have a professional aspect to me that I never deviate from during working hours. At home I am a different person. I dance, I twirl, I vault off the newel post at the bottom of the stairs. I talk and sing to myself, and prompt my self out loud. I laugh at nothing in particular, and grin like a simpleton. I wear hippy boho clothes, or my biker jacket, and an over the top quantity of jewellery. Not showing off. I just love the light scintillating and reflecting and splitting light. I sprawl on the settee, sit of the floor and lose track of time, happy in my home zone. Children remind me not to speak with my mouth full, and prompt me not to burn the cooking by wandering off in the middle. I am the adult, they are the responsible ones. No one gets into trouble. I listen when they speak, and reinforce the clear boundaries that we have agreed. We are kind and understanding. We can all be ourselves and dovetail in with one another. FEAR IS THE ENEMY. I am no longer afraid. I mask out of respect to other people. I used to mask in order to hide from plain sight. Now I mask less and less, according to time and place. MY NATURAL SELF IS INFORMAL. I speak to strangers. I may be slightly eccentric; a bit of a charactor. I AM ON THE SPECTRUM. It seems to me that that is a lot more learned behaviour about than you might suppose. I am off duty right now. No masking. I drive myself mad. I am still trying to have a shower before I get dressed. I have an archaic fright of the shower.. There is a lot of physical sensory experience having a shower. Today I had to undress to have a shower. . . then I used my mobile. Back on automatic pilot. . I started getting dressed again. This cycle has only started since I have had to live on my own. No one to prompt me now. It happens at home. I am “Behaving myself” at the swimming pool. I would not forget myself there. I am ‘on duty’ and it still does not come easily to me.

question: Can palilalia come and go in children living with autism?
answer: Can palilalia come and go in children living with autism? The repetition of words or phrases seems to be a form of stimming. Our guy repeats things related to his current thought process. When he is looking forward to something, he scripts (quotes sections of a dialog) from Oh, The Places You’ll Go. When he is getting upset, he scripts the scarier passages of Tangled. When he starts repeating, “Your MAAJ-ist-y,” (Lion King) he is getting angry at someone, usually his younger twin sisters. I think that when he is having trouble finding original words of his own, he relies on repeating things from memory. He understands that we are not always able to follow his original thoughts and reaches around for something in his mind that relates to his message. I would think that in the same way that most of us sometimes sing a song periodically throughout a day without realizing it, palilalia will come and go. It might be stress related, and it might not. I have talked to a lot of parents, and most report that when their child starts ramping up with a particular phrase or passage, they raise the DEFCON level and try to head off an impending meltdown. There is so much that nobody knows about this disorder. Fact-finding is slowed by the truth that every person is completely individual, exhibiting his or her coping mechanisms. Sometimes they stop with behaviors, and sometimes they add something new and exciting. (Note - exciting does not always mean something great and wonderful. I like to keep things positive, though, and it is what it is. Applying negative labels to elements does nothing to make things better.) I hope that my answers help someone. It is helping me because I have started to focus and clarify some of my observations and working theories in my own mind. -ALR

question: Does living with autism improve with age?
answer: No. Life with autism, just like life without autism i think keeps getting more complicated with age. I just had a birthday. The recruiter told me they can help with a lot of key special needs but there are things I have to do and to be ready for when I get there. People around you are watching you to see how well you do at things. If you do well they don’t say “oh great! What an accomplishment!” They say, “Okay, you go that, now do this (more)!” And sometimes inside your quiet mind you are thinking, ‘okay, what if I just don’t try as hard? Will they expect less?’ But I know that’s dishonest and I can’t do less than my best. It never feels right. But my father says our life is less like a hamsters wheel and more like a tall mountain with impossible paths and transitions that we just have to figure out. We don’t have a choice of not climbing. So to make my life simpler I make my lists for every next day and i follow my list and never leave anything undone. Everything I do everyday is on my list from waking up to sweeping and moping my room and washing my sheets and pillow cases (daily, blankets once per week cuz mom says they don’t need to be washed daily…i disagree cuz, gross!) and every task during the day including classes and homework. This is what helps me. You hve to find what helps you. Sometimes a therapist can help.

question: What are the most disturbing facts about living with autism that most people do not know?
answer: Autism is a neurotype which comes with differences that can be neutral, positive, or negative. I’ll talk about the negatives—many of which come from the outside world. When you have autism, every moment of your life has the potential to be incredibly stressful. Lights, sounds, images, sensations, and movement can all cause you pain. Often, these things are preventable, but other people refuse to turn the lights off or be quiet because they think it doesn’t matter. Your access to support and education is limited. Every day, society‘s strict rules and customs confuse you. All of this, along with many other factors, makes you more vulnerable to illness, suicide, bullying, and rape. Here are some potentially disturbing statistics relating to autism:14% of autistic children have considered suicide, compared to 0.5% of non-autistic children.30–50% of autistic adults have considered suicide, compared to roughly 6% of non-autistic adults.People with autism typically die 12–30 years younger than the average person, not from their autism, but from other issues which you’re more vulnerable to if you’re autistic.This statistic is not specific to autism, but 83% of women and 32% of men with developmental disabilities have experienced sexual assault.

question: What is your experience living with a parent with autism?
answer: Spent a lot of time getting ignored in favor of neat and complicated hobbies like weather observation and playing musical instruments, as well as getting ignored for news sports and weather. A lot of chaos, moved to a lot of different cities chasing various sensory issues. Had an Aspie specialty job rotating shifts, brutal on all involved. A lot of unique religious and parenting ideas and “new traditions.” The usual ups and downs of being an autodidact trying to make it in the real world affected all of us. Work disappointments, false starts of the RTFM vatiety on topics that weren't as interesting. People taking advantage of naivety and good nature shaped several key moments of our childhood. On the plus side:Conversations with grown ups on grown up topics like feelings, work, the details of complicated hobbiesAble to ignore kid's superficial objections to story time, etc. We eventually warmed up to it and had a blast.Able to tell me “XYZ thing all your school chums care about but does not register for you at all…does not register for me either…and Doesn't matter as an adult.In general the parent child divide seemed weaker. We could be more collegial.At this point, our relationship is distant and it is possible that we are both sad about it. I've done too many hurtful things over the years and his new wife used to think our relationship was unacceptably close. I think she asked him to stop talking about feelings, and we already read all the same religion, news, sports and weather. On balance, I am in favor of autistic parents, but I wish I knew how to improve my individual situation. My advice to autistic parents, partner with your children instead of ignoring them. If you feel like you spend 90 percent of your time with your child, that might be about enough. As teenagers, that lets up, less time but it is more valuable, long conversations, rescues from bad situations, etc.

question: How do I act normal with autism?
answer: Do not. This is called masking. It is when you pretend to be neurotypical to fit in. It is EXTREMELY, EXTREMELY harmful to your mental health. Masking increases the risk of autistics committing suicide, and you will not be able to keep it up. Let me tell you what happens. You put on a mask every morning and go out into the world. You keep your arms clamped tightly to your sides when you feel happiness or stress building up, so you don't stim. You mimic the conversations of others to 'look normal'. You force yourself to stop whatever you have a special interest in, and force yourself to do things or watch things that you're not interested in, so you can keep up with the trends and keep seeming normal. Every day, you arrive home from work or school and you CRY AND SCREAM. You curl up into yourself because everything was just so stressful. Forcing yourself to suppress stimming only made you more stressed, and it built up and up until your exploded. You want to gush about your favourite show so badly, but everyone will think you're a weirdo. Everyone will think you're crazy if you let your true self shine through. Right? Wrong. There are idiots out there, reader. There are people who don't understand. But do they really matter? The people who really matter are those who accept you for who you are. If your boss doesn't understand, he can't fire you just for being autistic, that's disability discrimination which is illegal. If your teachers don't understand, they're required to learn. What I'm trying to say is that you can be yourself, and people will still love you and accept you. For every bigot, there is someone who might not understand, but who will accept and help you. If you continue with the masking, you will burn yourself out, and there might come a time where you think 'is this really worth going on for?' It's not. Cast off the mask. You can be who you really are. I know. I did.

question: Do individuals with autism prefer being referred to as "Aspie" or "person living with ASD"?

question: Can you explain what it feels like for someone with autism and/or Asperger's syndrome to live with their condition?
answer: "Condition" sounds like I'll fall over flailing at any moment. Sheesh. "Aspergers" is an obsolete term, to start with. Its history is particularly ugly:If you're autistic, you're autistic. I just found out a week ago. I've been this way all my life, it's not a disease, it's a variation in neurobiology. I was married to an undiagnosed autistic guy, for three decades. My middle son is also autistic. Of the three of us, his is most pronounced. When he was little, I wanted to have him evaluated but his father didn't want it. In hindsight, I should have persevered because he could have used help, all the way to his adulthood. But probably his father didn't want the stigma because people hear "autistic" and think idiot, or tactless clod. So my main thing appears to be, I *really* don't like socializing. It used to be rare for females to be diagnosed and that's largely because they're forced to be more sociable so they learn "masking" survival skills better. Masking means you suppress your autistic traits. You make whatever physical tics (stims) less obvious. You learn to mimic appropriate social cues. You try to engage in the usual social banter in order to fit in. I actually sucked at social interactions. I deplore small talk. Oh I can *make* myself do it, but ugggggghhhh. I'd rather clean a toilet. My stims are covert ones. I bite my nails, I pick at myself. Lately, since buzzing off my hair since it was approaching balding status, I find running my hand on my velour-like hair has become a stim. I found out during the mega cold winters I spent outside, that rocking to warm up at night before sleep also felt pretty mellowing. For space reasons, my chairs here are hammock chairs which can be taken down. Rocking in a hammock chair became reflexive after a while. When I'm away from home too long I feel very tired, from contending with the activity of people. I really feel the stress of it now; for years when I had a young family, we were constantly doing field trips and meeting other families so I got good at dealing. But now? If I can talk myself OUT of a social event I will, even if it's one I had looked forward to for weeks. I'm constantly auditing myself in a social situation. Meeting new people is horribly anxiety-provoking for me and I hate it. I hate parties, hate social functions, hate receptions or dances. Events like fireworks, live concerts, nightclubs, shows—-are absolutely NOT happening, ever, period. Surprises are a good way to get me very uncomfortable and angry. I will leave. From November til January is the worst time of the year and I avoid going anyplace if I can, for as long as I can. I don't go anywhere for holidays and if friends try to invite me, I decline. I was what's called "hyperlexic" or very verbally gifted. I used to be harassed a lot for having and using a large vocabulary. I used to literally READ dictionaries, and to this day, Scrabble is one of my favorite games. Yet if there's any public speaking to be done, I'm like a fucking deer in the headlights. I can go happily for weeks without seeing a soul. Give me my books and my dogs and I'm extremely content. Covid lockdown, meh, big deal. I've learned *never* to discuss my areas of interest, as they bore people to tears. Which is a shame, but if anyone ever wants to know about training a horse or Norse pre christian beliefs or how to survive outdoors in northern New England, I'm the one to ask. When I'm walking to town, I can tell you where edible plants can be found all along the route, even ones that won't be out for months. I have absolutely horrid Executive Function, that is, planning time and allocating my energy in an effective way. I have notebooks of lists, lists for everything. I get lost horribly easily especially if I try to alter course in a place I've never been before. Being lost is nerve wracking. I experienced autistic shutdown in college and had no idea what the hell it was. In hindsight it's super obvious but back then? Not a clue. It factored into my leaving college for good in my junior year. There's lots more but those are the high points. I know for a fact, my way of being is considered very eccentric but I also know my ability to hyperfocus has been an amazing tool. It gives me incredible tenacity. Autism is not a disease or a tragic flaw. It's just one of the variations humans come in. Even a non-verbal autistic person has a lively mind at work under the muteness. I've done childcare for nonverbal autistic kids, and they were amazing.

question: Who hold the record for the oldest living person with autism?
answer: We don’t know. There are probably some pretty old people who have autism, but many of them were never diagnosed because autism wasn’t used as a diagnosis until the 1960s and even then it had very narrow criteria until they were expanded in the 1990s. There are many people who were born before 1990 who weren’t diagnosed, and may never be diagnosed, simply because nobody expects to see autism in an adult. The oldest autistic person I know of is Richard Meredith. He died at the age of 82.Mr. Meredith was born in the early 1930s, during the era of eugenics, lobotomies, and forced sterilization. Digging through old medical records, Mr. Meredith's family gathered that if he had been born today, he would have been diagnosed with "a moderate case of autism... [a] relatively mild disability." He was a quirky, shy young man who did not look people in the eye and tended to fidget. He liked to spend his free time listening to radio programs, and he wanted to work on a truck. He had a few close friends; he loved to read, and he loved sports. He would spend hours shooting baskets or tossing a football. At age 15, Richard Meredith was admitted to a state institution. He would spend the rest of his long life in such residential placements. When he was about 17 years old, without his family's permission, officials at the institution had a doctor perform a lobotomy on him. During the interview with the doctor, asked what he wanted most of all, Richard said that he wanted to develop his thinking, and that he wanted to go home. Instead, he got a lobotomy that made it impossible for him to ever live on his own. This now-infamous procedure, used on more than forty thousand people in the United States alone, severely damaged Richard's brain as doctors intentionally severed the connections between the prefrontal lobe and the rest of the brain. The prefrontal lobe is approximately the front one-third of the brain, involved in planning, personality, and self-regulation. Brain damage from the lobotomy "...left [Mr. Meredith] a virtual toddler, unable to ever again carry on a coherent conversation." Mr. Meredith spent 48 years in institutions; some were good, some bad. He found happiness visiting with his family and participating in the Special Olympics. He loved music and chocolate. At 82, Mr. Meredith died in the same institution that had ordered the lobotomy, now modern and much changed. His family says he was happy there. The institution told Mr. Meredith's family that he had died from a heart attack. His sister only found out that they had lied when, months later, she read a newspaper article about the institution having been fined for giving Mr. Meredith a peanut butter sandwich when he had been prescribed a pureed-food diet. Mr. Meredith, who had a swallowing problem and, because of the lobotomy, could not communicate well enough to inform anyone that he had been given the wrong food, tried to eat the sandwich, choked, and died. Staff found him slumped over a table, unresponsive, and could not revive him. The worker who gave Mr. Meredith the sandwich has been dismissed for negligence. Taken from my Web site: Autism Memorial— Richard Meredith.
