question: What's it like to live with a person with high functioning autism?
answer: It's awesome! Maybe I'm well-suited to it, I don't know, but having my friend with high functioning autism as a roommate for the past year has worked better for me than anyone I've lived with in the almost 50 years I've been on this planet. The Good: -- My job involves a *LOT* of interacting with people so a roomate that doesn't need or want constant interaction gives me much needed downtime. -- While my sensitivity to noise is to a lesser extent, I do get stressed by too much noise so a quiet home keeps us both on an even keel. -- We have opposite strong suits. While he has no patience for forms, online purchases, or waiting in lines and cannot load the dishwasher in any kind of logical way, he is amazing with my dogs and cats, keeps the plants alive, decorates, and does a variety of household tasks that I have limited patience for. -- He has an amazing amount of knowledge on so many topics and we can have thoughtful, intelligent conversations daily. -- In a world where people often use words to hurt, it's beyond refreshing to be around someone who only says what they mean and doesn't even have the ability to TRY and be hurtful. I'm not sure I can say enough about the value of that, especially when you can't go on FB anymore without seeing post after post spewing hatred. On the flip side, *occasionally* honesty isn't flattering, but at least it's REAL. -- The genuine gratitude for anything I do for him, no matter how minor. What I've Learned: -- To speak clearly and directly. If he's going to the store, saying "I want something chocolate...cookies, cake, donuts, something" will result in a lot of stress for him trying to work out what I want most and may result in getting all three. Now I say, "Oreos - Mega Stuffs". :) -- Not to assume and more importantly, not to be upset about something I assumed he *should* do but didn't say that I would like for him to do. Because if I do say it, he will move heaven and earth to do it. -- Not to sweat the small stuff. If it's important to him that all furniture is at angles instead of flush against the wall like I would do it, does it really matter? No. Nor does it matter if dishes are in different cabinets than I would put them. I'm now grateful that I didn't have to unload the dishwasher. -- Not to take offense and what sometimes feels indifference. I value this person as a friend very, very much and sometimes, I feel like he could take or leave me. But then I hear from his family how much of a friend he considers me and I think about HIS version of showing friendship...getting something he knows I like while he's out, bringing one of the flowers he bought for my vase in my room, pretending to be interested in something I'm going on about when I'm pretty sure he really isn't. -- How to accept responsibility for my part in things that irritate me. The only time I got really annoyed with him was when on the way home from somewhere, I said, "We need to change the air filter." To him, that meant it was the very next thing we should do. But we got home and a toilet had run and caused a small flood. He turned off the water while I figured out the problem but then while I'm still trying to sop up water to prevent water damage, I hear, "Can you help me with this?" He had started the air filter project (in an old system, getting it back in place is challenging and often takes us both.) My instinct was to scream, "Are you kidding me? We're drowning in water, I don't care about the air filter!" But I took a breath, realized he was still following the plan I set, got the HVAC back together and returned to the water. At the end of the day, I am a better person for having my friend here. I'm calmer, I'm more careful not to say hurtful things out of frustration, I'm more patient, and things that I would have nagged at the last person I lived with about (who I was in a relationship with), I shrug off. People are way more important than anything else and I am grateful for all I've learned from my friend and for all he does around the house to make my life easier.
comment_answer: Sounds like someone most of us would appreciate. Happy life

question: Is it normal that my parents still let my 23-year-old sister live with them even though she does absolutely nothing in life? She has autism but other people with autism manage to get a job too so that shouldn't be an excuse.
answer: It’s difficult to decipher whether or not this poster a troll; the use of anon suggests they might be. However, I’ll give them the benefit of the doubt and respond anyway, at the risk of yelling into the wind. This is going to be long, though, and I hope they have the inclination to stick around. Let’s look at it this way: For the sake of argument only, I’m going to presume you are a 20-year-old NT (neurotypical) / allistic (aka someone with no cognitive differences) female, studying at college for a bachelor’s. Why are you not doing a double majors? If other students of your demographic can, what’s your excuse? How about this: Some 20-year-old NT/allistic females studying at college also manage to be A list celebrities, so what’s your excuse? This, too: There are plenty of double amputees in the world. If some other double amputees can compete in Olympic sports, why aren’t they all doing it? Why aren’t you competing in the Olympics, for that matter? What’s your excuse? Some other 20-year-old NT/allistic, college-going females are. Or is that why you’re on anon? ;) Why are you deliberately choosing to be a slacker and only study for a bachelor’s, when you could—nay, should—be like so many other young women your age and read a double major, or competing in the Olympics, or acting in blockbuster movies; etc? Does any of that sound unfair to you? Judgemental? I would hope so. Because, whether you intended it or not, that’s the sentiment of your question. To put it even more harshly, essentially you are saying your sister has an obligation to be a particular way and she’s opting out of it because she’s nothing more than a freeloading loser, so shame on her! Imagine if someone said the same thing about you because you’re not an overachiever? You’d feel more than slightly pissed off, right? The key word that you could have included in your question is: some. Some people with autism get jobs, in the same way as some 20-year-old NT/allistic females take double majors, or compete in the Olympics, or are A list celebrities. The fact that some can, and do, means nothing more than that. Autism is a vast, vast spectrum. What some are capable of, others may not be. Everyone, whether they be NT/allistic, autistic, visually or audibly impaired, bipolar etc, has their own set of strengths, weaknesses, abilities and lack of abilities, none of which are purposely selected by the person. I think it's safe to say very few people want to be social omegas. Who would actually welcome the social stigma of being jobless and living at home past college age? I highly doubt this is what your sister genuinely wants in her life—it's far likelier that she stays this way because she feels there is no alternative. Maybe she has depression, too, or even PTSD? A significant amount of people with autism have both, because all they know of the world is that it's a hostile place which rejects them—often violently, too—regardless of their attempts to succeed in it. If you've always been surrounded by friends, and have never experienced long term bullying, you may not be able to understand. Maybe her view of the world is that she always tries her level best to get along with people, but they keep rejecting her for reasons she cannot fathom, and has ultimately concluded that trying to be a part of that world is pointless? Autism, depression and PTSD are not simply things you can just suck up and get on with, nor do they make someone pathetic or weak, and they most certainly are not excuses. Imagine you want to leave the house, but the walk from your door to your car is awash with scorching hot coals and red hot razor blades? Every time you try to make it to the car, the coals end up burning through your shoes, and you end up in the hospital due to severe injuries? Now imagine yourself attempting that over, and over, and over, and over. You keep trying, and you keep getting burned and cut up, and have to endure weeks or months of sheer agony due to your injuries. Maybe you slip and injure yourself in other areas? What if you nearly die? Sooner or later you're going to realise it's neither viable nor sane to leave the house that way. Those hot coals are the people—virtually everyone, it seems—who deliberately taunt, harrass, and ostracize you, and those razor blades are the resulting mental trauma. This is akin to what having autism, depression and PTSD feel like, and they are no less debilitating or real simply for the fact that they are invisible. True, plenty of people with autism get jobs, ranging from the menial to the decent to the elite. Some succeed in those jobs, and go on to become wealthy. A significant number work “regular”, middle income jobs, get married, mortgage a house, have children, and live what amounts to a “normal” life by the standards of NTs/allistics. Those are the lucky ones, a significant proportion of whom have started out with advantages such as early diagnosis, a strong support network, and an understanding and caring educational environment. There are of course some who are naturally more resilient than others, and others who are able to grow a thicker skin; they too are the lucky ones. Being "weak" as society sees it is, for most people, not a conscious choice. I doubt many people would choose emotional vulnerability, “weakness”, or happily volunteer to be bottom of the social pile. In the same way as you don't choose to be "weak", neither do you choose to be "strong". It's not as simple as snapping your fingers and saying "hey, I'm going to change from a weak person into a strong person". With sufficient support, some people can make a lot of progress, but it takes considerable time and energy, especially if the damage done to that person is extensive. However, consider that for every one of the people on the spectrum diagnosed early there is someone who goes undiagnosed until chronological adulthood; for every one who breezes through the social aspect of school and college there is another who has to endure often merciless bullying and social exclusion by their peers, and even sometimes teachers and their own family; for every one who is fortunate enough to have a robust support network, there is another who has no-one to turn to. For every socially “capable” person on the autism spectrum, there is someone who, for whatever reason, is not afforded the opportunities to be capable. Interviews aren’t geared to people with autism. It’s been proven that people with autism are much greater predisposed to stress and anxiety than NTs/allistics—if a job interview is nerve-wracking for someone without any form of cognitive difference, can you imagine how it would feel for someone who, through no fault or deliberation of their own, feels negative emotions far more intensely? Many fail interviews simply because the stress of the event brings their autistic traits to the fore, causing them to behave in ways they have little or no control over, and which are in fact far more extreme than their usual behaviour. Interviewers are quick to discriminate, and so they reject potentially brilliant employees simply because those candidates might be fidgeting relentlessly, unable to make eye contact, or whose speech might sound a little stilted. They see only what NT/allistic society perceives as weaknesses and flaws, but overlook the strengths that person may have to offer. Disability discrimination is very real and very present, and the mere disclosure of autism on a candidate’s resume can make the difference between being hired or dismissed. Perhaps a person with autism has sensory issues, gets a job, but the workplace refuses to make the very simple accomodations for them, resulting in the sensory issues becoming too much for that person to be able to concentrate on their work, and so they are fired? If you were trying to work and someone was playing a song you absolutely hated on repeat and at ear-splitting levels, don't you think that would take its toll on your psychologcial wellbeing? What about if someone kept poking and prodding at you with the sharp end of a syringe, and wouldn't stop even when you were reduced to begging them to? How about if someone kept shining a bright light in your eyes, or you were made to inhale the worst smell you've ever known, and you couldn't escape from it? Can you not imagine how that might drive someone to act out just to get the offending sensation to stop? That's what can happen when very simple, very basic alterations are not met, but it's mostly always the person with autism who gets the blame. Furthermore—and this is crucial to understanding autism—people on the spectrum tend to be a little or a lot younger mentally than their chronological years. Even those with jobs, although you might not notice it. Your sister is chronologically 23, but mentally she could be around 11 in some neurological areas, and even younger in others. This is neither her fault nor her choice, and there is nothing she or anyone can do to "get her up to speed" with NT's/allistics of her own age. This doesn't mean she should be treated like a child, or as if she has learning difficulties; but that you should accept and acknowledge the fact that she simply cannot be expected to behave like her peers. People with autism are not defective. Autism is not a choice, and people with the condition do not choose to be "socially inept" because "heeeyyyy, it's like, fun, guyssss!". Most of them want more than anything to integrate and thrive; they simply do not have the luxuries NT's/allistics take for granted. When given the chance, some fly to great heights—these might be the ones you are thinking of. But in a neurotypical world, an equal amount simply have the door shut on them time and time again. I don't know your situation, or your sister's, other than her having autism. I don't know what your relationship is like with her. But maybe if you choose not to be one of the people who joins in with the door shutting, she might have a shot at a positive future.

question: Why don’t we have many independent housing options for those living with autism?
answer: I’m a community advisor to The Kelsey, which is piloting an integrated housing complex that will reserve 25% of units for tenants with developmental disabilities (including cerebral palsy etc. not just autism) and provide services in conjunction with the local branch of the state DD agency. There’s another complex that already does something similar. The staff of The Kelsey are consulting actual disabled people and are familiar with the neurodiversity movement, so this isn’t just an institution made to look like an apartment building. They’re also trying to incorporate features such as having connecting doors between some apartments so that a caregiver can live in a separate unit but still enter when needed. People who are already in the developmental disability system can qualify for supports if they can find suitable affordable housing. People who don’t need much support just need to worry about the affordable housing… and that is the sticking point. There’s a shortage of housing that is affordable to people with extremely low incomes (such as autistic people who haven’t worked and are on SSI, or those who can only work part time at a minimum wage job). Most affordable housing rents are indexed to the Area Median Income. So if you live in a major metro area with high AMI (such as the Bay Area or anywhere non-rural in California), even “affordable housing” will be too expensive. (Rents for new tenants in the 50% AMI building where I live start at $1100/mo for studios.) Rural areas would be cheaper, but probably lack supports or specialty medical care, and definitely lack public transit. It’s difficult to live in rural areas without being able to drive, whereas The Kelsey is located next to a Lightrail (trolley) station and stops for several buses, with transfers nearby to the rest of the county bus system and beyond. Most of the units subsidized for 20% AMI or below are earmarked for Housing First, to get people housed who are living on the street or in shelters. It just isn’t a priority to get autistic people out of their family home or group home into independent living. (Though some of the unhoused are probably autistic, if the results of a study from the UK apply here too. A substantial proportion of supposedly mentally ill unhoused people actually have undiagnosed autism—and they’re not going to cope well with homeless shelters or street life.) If you’re wondering why there aren’t more privately funded independent living options, it seems to be that parents in a position to fund things privately aren’t interested in “independent living.” All the rich parent plans seem to be so-called “intentional communities” in rural areas where they believe their children will be protected from the dangers of city life. (If past history is any predictor, this just makes it easier for staff to abuse them without being caught or without them escaping successfully.) So the main reason there aren’t more independent living options for autistic people are the housing crisis and perceived higher priorities. Unless you’re autistic (about 2% of the population) or family of an autistic person, you probably don’t notice that autistic people need appropriate housing. But everyone knows there are unhoused people camping in creek channels and sleeping in doorways, so guess who complains the loudest at community meetings? Yeah, the people tired of encampments and human waste in their neighborhoods.

question: What are some things that can help people with autism transition from living with their parents to living on their own?
answer: This seems like a tricky and complex question. There are many aspects to living independently. This includes areas like understanding the world, earning for a living, understanding the daily schedules well, understanding finances, even things like buying groceries, understanding monetary transactions, healthy living, and many more. The list can be long! Generally, neuro-typical children start understanding these concepts early in their lives, however, on a case to case situation, and also on the levels of severity, these skills are taught to children on the autistic spectrum band. Some things that come to my mind regarding a successful transition (in the long run) are:Making the children understand day to day living. Try to make them independent as early as possible. For example, small things like making sandwiches for themselves, using a micro wave, understanding what to do when they are sick, how to dial somebody’s phone number in case of emergencyMaking them understand health and safety aspects - what is considered safe and what is unsafeMaking them learn how to clean the room, this includes keeping their belongings nicely (toys in toy box, clothes in cupboard, etc.), using a hoover to clean their roomMaking them learn how to see time, and gradually move them into looking at their time tables and figure out what to do next, and at what timeMaking them understand the currency, the value of money (eg. adding how to add £5+£5 - it is not ‘2’ notes, but the value ‘£10’)Take them to grocery stores right from the childhood, and make them pay money for chocolates (to start with), and then increasing the number of items so that they can add the money together and make the payment independently.Making them understand who are the important people in the society and what are their roles. eg. what does a police officer do, what does a doctor do, etc. so that they start learning when to reach out to which person.Looking at their interests and trying to channelise the same so that once they grow up, they can start working in the area of their interest.I think the list is endless, however, if we start working and partnering with them through their early stages, we can see them doing wonderfully well. Early intervention really helps in all areas - let it be social skills, communication skills, or independent living!

question: What are some tips for living with autism?
answer: Understand yourself. Accept yourself. Change what you can about yourself if it impacts you negatively. Strive to be the best you can be and do the best you can do. Seek help with your problem areas.

question: What sensory tools may be useful to a child living with autism who has high oral sensory needs?
answer: While food items can be used, they pose a problem. Crunchy crackers and pretzels, sour gummy candies, juice sucked through a narrow straw, and the like create the need for more brushing and oral hygeine which is often a problem for kids with oral sensory issues. Xylitol or other sugarless gum is one option but it has to be disposed of properly and some parents aren’t happy with all the artificial ingredients. Better choices are chewable items that are nontoxic, whether it’s a pendant worn as a necklace, a bracelet, a pencil topper (a tube that slips over the end of a pencil), or a hand-held item. Then the issue is how to keep it sanitary. Having several acceptable chewies that are sterilized regularly and kept in, say, a plastic tub (like the kind spreadable butter comes in) or a resealable plastic bag is often the best way to go. Then too, consider getting a nutritional evaluation. Common nutritional deficiencies in kids with sensory issues can cause extra oral sensory seeking. Kelly Dorfman’s book Cure Your Child with Food has a lot of good information on why certain deficiencies are common and what can happen when they’re addressed.

question: How can someone overcome their problems associated with autism to live a normal life?
answer: Ahhhhh! - here I go again… on my SOAP BOX!!! Those who have followed me know that I have a strong belief in why Autism is perceived as it is.. First off - I want to clarify that my comments are taken from my perspective of being autistic and that I have not had to struggle with the very extreme traits that some with autism do. This is deeper than differences in personalities. A neurological difference is THE foundation of our life experience and defines every aspect of our biological being. How our bodies and mind respond chemically to stimulus. How our minds retain and manage information, our physical and psychological needs, and even perception itself. THIS is the profound difference we need to acknowledge when we talk about two groups that are neurologically different. So, what does this all have to do with the question? I’m not sure if the person asking this question is ND or NT. This does change the intent of the question. What is a “normal life”? What are we using to measure or compare a life to, so we can determine if it is “normal”? If you are NT and using your life, then all autistic people are “abnormal”. Because as I stated on my soap-box, we are PROFOUNDLY different. So different there is a Neurotypical “normal” and an autistic “normal”. They are not the same normal, but they both are normal for each type neurology. So will autstic people ever be “normal “ in the eyes of neurotypical people? Only when they realize their measurement of normal only applies to them.

question: What percentage of adults with autism live with their parents?

question: As someone on the autism spectrum, I find myself not wanting to live with any of my neurotypical family members. Why do family households have to be toxic for those with autism spectrum disorders?
answer: I'm going to assume you are young enough that you have to live under adult supervision.If you're on The Spectrum [TM, patent pending], the one utility-grade thing you need every day is a place that's safe from judgment. You don't have to be "normal." You don't have to stop fidgeting. You don't have to put up with sensory and affective pressures that feel like you're staring into the sun. You don't have to like runny eggs or things with gills. And now you're stuck in a house for 12 hours a day with people who feel it's their business to "help you get along better." No refuge, no decompression. Do I have that right? What you're feeling isn't discomfort, it's self-preservation.In a perfect world, living with just one person who is imaginative and kind, you'd sit down with her, say you'd get by a little better if she'd just ease off on you for a few hours a day, and so long as you're not hurting anyone, let you be strange. Maybe watch some YouTube clips together. (Huh. I should ask about that.) Not many households with room for another member are comprised of a single kindly person. One member may be fine, but now there's a network of people with different ideas of what they're entitled to for themselves, and what's fair for you to have that they don't. They don't want to share the attention and love of that kindly Mom (especially Dad). They all have to be on the same page, they all must have enough imagination, they all have to take the trouble to exercise it, and not one of them can be an asshole on general principles. Honestly, that sort of household is rare, I wish I could say otherwise, but it's always been hard and I fear it's getting harder.I think I've answered your "why." I wish I had a good answer to "what next." There can be strength snd comfort in trying, even if it you don't expect a big payoff: Find that one kindly person. Have that talk. Ask how you and she can carry the lesson over to the others. You might not bring the whole family along, but when the tension gets high, maybe she'll be there to bail you out.

question: Should mild autism be diagnosed if someone can live with it?
answer: I have autism that would have been labeled Asperger’s back before they changed the terms. I am married with children. I have worked jobs all my life and have attended college. I am living with it. But I didn’t really live as well as I could have, had I known I had autism. It effected so many areas of my life, but I didn’t know why. Instead of getting jobs in the fields of my expertise, I ended up working in fast food or as a receptionist because I could not pass job interviews. I found that friends often became angry with me, but I could not understand why. I couldn’t fit in. I had trouble making friends because I struggled terribly in social situations. I lost jobs because of angry bosses or co-workers because I said something they didn’t want to hear, no matter how carefully I tried to choose my words. At night, I lay awake wondering why, and I could never make sense of it. I knew I was different, and I felt like no one liked me, but I just couldn’t understand what I was doing to make it happen, or, more importantly, how to change it. No matter what I tried, I just couldn’t fix the problems. I found out I had autism very late in life. And, finally, all the pieces made sense. And, I know beyond any doubt that had I known when I was much younger, things would have been very different, because I would have understood what was happening instead of blaming myself for being a “failure”. I have three daughters who also have Asperger’s. And, although one of them functions so well that most people don’t know she has autism, I made the decision to get her diagnosed, simply because I knew there were areas in which she struggled as well, and that she was masking them. And I wanted her to know why she is the way she is, so when she struggles, she won’t blame herself the way I did all those years. The day we had her diagnosed, she was so happy. (We did it when she was a teen). The neuropsychiatrist who diagnosed her has a wife who is autistic, and he explained autism to her very well. But, more importantly, he gave her “permission” to just be herself and to acknowledge her need to do things like stimming, instead of trying to pretend to be neurotypical. That validation meant so much. Even though we knew she was autistic, having the diagnosis seemed to take this weight off her shoulders. It was a reassurance. And it allowed her to know who she is and embrace it.

I am glad I wasn’t diagnosed when very young as it might have got me stuck in a special needs class which would have been torture for my brain. But I would have benefitted from a diagnosis at high school age or early adulthood.

question: Why do people with autism, who need assistance with daily living, live with their parents instead of specialized housing?
answer: You can't always trust specialized housing. One YouTube person has a profoundly autistic son with self injurious behaviors and seizures and they tried specialized housing but the staffing was insufficient and when the young man had a self abusive episode he punched his ear so hard that it got a hematoma. Needed surgery to fix it and now his ear is permanently disfigured. No staff were around to protect him. At other group homes the staff will physically or emotionally abuse the residents. Those with serious disabilities often have no way of reporting what has happened to them because they cannot communicate effectively and so may regress severely, show marked changes in behavior or show signs of neglect or abuse (bruises, emaciation, other unexplained injuries or clinical signs). To top it all off, abusers often are not properly punished for mistreatment of the disabled. They can just get a slap on the wrist and continue their abuse. With all the bad things that can happen in specialized housing it isn't at all surprising that many parents would want to keep their severely disabled child home. At least they can say that though it will be very hard at least their child can be cared for in a safe, loving and familiar environment.

question: How do adults living with autism 'mask' their symptoms?
answer: Nearly everyone masks to a certain degree, the difference is autistic people have to mask considerably more than most others to achieve the same result. This is because autistic people can’t read social cues as easily as most other people and have difficulty filtering out sensory information most others can much more easily. This means that no matter how high functioning an individual autistic person might be, even if they can mostly pass, there will come some occasions where that mask may slip off a bit. Autistic people employ various social scripts to suit situations they find themselves in by mimicking the behavior they see in others, they don’t always get it right and it can take years to be able to do this effectively and some autistic people can’t mask no matter how hard they try. Stimming behaviors are minimized, talk about special interests are reigned in a bit. As a retail worker I have a few go to phrases I use to cover my ass. I despise having to use them because it all feels so fake and pointless to me, but it is a necessary evil until I can exit that dehumanizing industry once and for all. Unfortunately excessive masking often leads to autistic burnout which can come with all kinds of negative mental health outcomes which can include increased mentldowns/shutdowns, depression, regression or loss or certain skills. When I am in autistic burnout some negative symptoms such as sensory difficulties and executive functioning difficulties can sometimes get worse. My social skills can also sometimes take a nose dive as certain social cues I normally spot can sometimes get missed. It is disturbing to me how ubiquitous masking in general is, I think society would be far better off if everyone autistic or not would mask considerably less. We are supposed to be thinking, feeling, human beings not soulless automotons pleasing people that don’t give a damn about us. I understand tact is necessary in some cases, but this is so bad that many people honestly don’t have enough time and space just to be themselves. This is one of the main reasons why there is such an identity crisis going on in the west.

question: Are living with autism and having Asperger's Syndrome the same thing?
answer: Good question. Autism, is the more politically correct term nowadays. Personally, I dont care what it is called. Autism, Aspergers, same thing to me. There’s a common misconception that anyone who uses the word Aspergers thinks they have something different from autism, which is not the case. I always knew they were interchangeable and I was diagnosed with Aspergers. Yes, I’m sure there are some people who think this, but this is not always the case. Another thing to remember is that not every country runs on the same system. Aspergers is still used here in Ireland by doctors. Autism can often be a more general term. Again, this is not very politically correct, but there are levels of functioning. I’m moderately high, as is my girlfriend and my friends who have it, but our disabilities are still quite disabling in life. There are people who are higher functioning than me, who are fine, and there are people who are lower functioning than me, and (I am going to be beheaded with the axe of public opinion on the block of political correctness of for saying this) have no concept of language. Sure, there are people who can think fine and for some reason can’t talk but can type, but this is often assumed to be always the case, and it really isn’t. Facilitated communication is a pseudoscience. And it’s harmful. If you think there’s someone in there who is just like you, you are not going to pay attention to the needs of the actual person, who is quite real and feels pleasure and pain. That’s quite a terrifying idea.

question: Is it easy to live with autism? My brother has it and I don't know if it can be put aside.

Meltdowns will happen, it about being ready for them, knowing how to deal with them, shortening the recovery time and extending the distance between them. Autims is part of who you are, now all but part. You bother is still a brother, Son, and most importantly a human being. Being autistic in a nero tipical world is hard. I often see that I see stuff other people completely miss and miss things other people find ovious. I find the processing and sensory processing disorder the hardest part of my autism. And skills will help to a certain degree. It's about carving your own path. Finding what makes you happy. Giving back to other people and living your life, not 'the fullest life you can have' no, YOUR life. People will judge you. People may stare but at the end of the day sometimes you just have to prioritize your needs. You may have a disability, and it will stop you, frustrated the living daylights out of your and make you angry. It is also part of you. Go live you.

question: How can someone living with autism learn to overcome social limitations?
answer: As an 11-yr-old with autism, I was given a month at a wilderness summer camp by my parents. My health — and the cognitive function and emotional awareness that rides on that health — improved so much during that month that I was able to figure out social patterns I’d never been able to spot, before. Although my health and function crashed after returning to my usual inner-city environment, I didn’t unlearn those skills, but kept adding to them as I figured out which kinds of environments crippled me with autism challenges, and which environments enabled me to thrive. My experience since then has been that we autistics figure out social skills just fine when our improving health stops making enough noise to drown out other signals. That said, I’m all for teaching communication coping skills. My later community-building experience with theatre training and non-profit training (mediation, facilitation, and consensus-building skills), as well as the collective experiences of other autistics in gaining communication skills, has convinced me that this training would be profoundly useful to any and all members of the autistic spectrum — if not for all humans altogether. However, social skills come much more easily when brain fog, short-term memory challenges, emotional volatility (or numbness from thyroid issues), and various inflammatory issues (including the brain inflammation that’s a hallmark of ASDs) caused by intestinal permeability aren’t dragging down functional capacity. In other words, physical health has a very profound impact on social capacity…

question: As an autistic adult, what kind of support do you wish your parents had given you as a child?
answer: I’m in my late 20’s right now, and when I was a kid, we just didn’t have any education on this at all. It wasn’t popular in the media, and it definitely wasn’t educated for even a second when I went through grade school. Both of my parents have been very isolated from the rest of society: one due to chronic illness that limited ability to leave the house at all, one due to overworking in order to provide a family of four on a single income. There are a lot of ways I am glad things turned out the way they did, because I think I’m in the right place in life now. But looking back, I wish I could have had more help understanding how to do things collaboratively, since even among our family unit, most things that are essential for independent living — cooking, cleaning, the most BASIC things about How To Take Care Of Yourself — these are all skills I lack because I grew up in a home environment where if you can’t, depend on somebody to participate, you shouldn’t depend on them at all, and the pain of not being able to participate when you want to but are too ill too not only worsens bad health but it isolates you further by saying “don’t bother asking, I hate disappointing you.” Also the joke my folks used to throw around about “we actually wanted to have three kids in case one of you turned out wrong, but just two kids is already too tiring” was uhhhhhhh extraordinarily traumatizing to me because it fueled the concept that if I wasn’t perfect then I wasn’t worth shit and that I should be replaced and that they wanted to be able to replace me if they had had the choice, and I understand now that it was humor as a coping mechanism, but holy MOLY I thought that I couldn’t come out for YEARS because of that, grouped with the fact that my parents’ only lasting social outlet is church…….. which has quite the bad reputation, given the horror stories of religious families casting out LGBT kids on the daily. Yeah so basically not knowing I was ASD or what that even meant ended up with me hearing jokes like that, seeing all the horrible stories in the world of actual excommunication with people just for being who they are, and because I couldn’t sense their actual intentions and didn’t know how to both ask AND trust them… messed me up real good, I gotta say. This got real long, but it boils down to this: I wish we had established open and honest communication, and established an ability to be able to Know what times jokes were actually reflecting the truth and what times they were really just meant to be funny. And I wish that we had done more stuff like walks together instead of all my exercise being at school or on sports teams where I was laughed at for doing shit wrong. AND I wish that they hadn’t depended on me picking up other essential life knowledge at school because I Didn’t Fit In At School and also the education system at the time was (and still is) a garbage fire. Grateful, however, because I was encouraged to do whatever it was that I took an interest in! Which was cool, because it means I got a lot of valuable experiences and ended up with a lot of interests. And was given a loving home, enough to eat, and was allowed and encouraged to express my mind and share what I love. And nobody minded when I would watch the same stuff I liked many times and listened to the same CDs until I had them all memorized. And they funded the new hobbies I took interest in whenever I showed I was super into it. I was really really really lucky because they showed me how being generous — with your time and your money both — is showing care, and it inspires me to put that same kind of energy back out into the world. Show people who need attention that they deserve it… show people who need money that their lives are valuable… show people who who need help that everybody deserves help. That’s the kind of person I was taught to be, and even if there were a lot of things I need to learn how to do now rather than later… I’m glad that they showed me a lot of the principles for being a good person through their actions, even if they didn’t necessarily understand the harm of their words. tl;dr, wouldn’t go back and change anything, but if I were to give advice to others to not make similar mistakes, I have it in spades: show that you care, but also SAY that you care, and don’t tell people to “learn to take a joke” — explain why something is funny to you when they’re still learning what a sense of humor IS, and don’t tell people to “get a life” — it proves that you completely have no sense of value of their life and are undermining what they’re going through, and don’t teach kids that other people’s needs are of higher and lower value than anybody else’s. Everybody’s needs are important, and what really matters is understanding that everybody needs to communicate what their needs are: and that communication of needs is not to change people’s feelings, but their behaviors. Adapting to other people’s needs is very much a strong suit especially for “high functioning” (a misnomer) ASD folks, so saying what you need but also expressing care in what they need… these things are of equal importance and finding a balance is the ultimate reason for living, at the end of the day.

question: I am 19 and live with autism, depression, and anxiety. I am finding it extremely difficult to get through life and overcome its struggles. Is it possible for me to live a normal life?
answer: “I am 19 and live with autism, depression, and anxiety. I am finding it extremely difficult to get through life and overcome its struggles. Is it possible for me to live a normal life?” You are exceptional but are destroying yourself through trying to be normal. First of all, don’t accept the idea that anxiety and depression are “co-morbid” with autism. They result from bullying and harassment from people afraid of anything they see as not normal. Don’t let their prejudices and fears dominate your life. Normal people think normal thoughts that they absorb from other normal people. Autistic people are generally more able to think for themselves and to judge ideas on their quality and validity, rather than only their orthodoxy. A sprinkling of autistic people is essential to the health of any community because they are the people who ask the questions others don’t dare ask and provoke others to think. A vital thing to realise is that autistic people commonly don’t lack social skills, they just have different social skills. Instead of just hanging around with friends, they commonly find meaning and true companionship through achieving things together. If you were to get involved in getting things done in your community you are very likely to find a lot of the other autistic people in the community also involved, and you are likely to find people you get along well with. (By way of translation, in North America people say “hanging out” instead of “hanging around with”. However that sounds to us in Australia as if they are in a dishevelled or even obscene state, so we avoid that usage).

question: Are there online classes to learn how to live with autism?
answer: I don’t know about online classes, but I’ve developed a few things to help with keeping up with tasks I tend to forget. Google Calendar has features to create recurring reminders for tasks and events. The tasks can be marked off as completed, which helps with things such as medications where I sometimes can’t remember if I’ve taken them or not. Events help with things such as doctor’s appointments and upcoming bills, because they can be set up to stretch across several days to give a ‘heads-up’ when something is due or upcoming. You can also set up a task separately from an event, so that the event serves as an upcoming reminder, while the task allows you to mark it completed. I’ve found that this helps greatly. I also use cell phone alarms with custom MP3 ringtones using snippets of “Yakety Yak” by The Coasters to help remind me of cleaning tasks such as dishes, laundry, bathroom, kitchen, etc. There is also a website I’ve been told about called Goblin Tools. It provides tools for toning down potentially wordy or offensive statements, breaking down large tasks into steps that are more easily processed. For instance, it’s common for those with autism to let a mess get out of control and then get overwhelmed when trying to catch it up, because we often wind up sorting the mess rather than cleaning it. So I’ve found that spending 10 minutes a day on some aspect of cleaning my quarters tends to help.

question: Can people with autism live to 100?
answer: I know of no reason why not. You’ll see statistics around the internet that autistic people have a much shorter average lifespan. This is technically true. But many people don’t realize that “average lifespan” statistics don’t differentiate between people who died of natural causes and people who didn’t. Autistic people are prone to suicide, due to lack of acceptance and due to the stresses of coping with a world that was quite literally designed to accommodate not us. That drives average lifespan down. People with less-well-adapted forms of autism are less likely to get prompt and sufficient medical care, because they don’t clearly communicate (or sometimes don’t correctly identify) physical distress that would ordinarily be a warning of illness or injury. That drives average lifespan down. People with very severe forms of autism may have difficulty caring for themselves or identifying and avoiding hazards in their environments. That drives average lifespan down. But if an autistic person doesn’t die of suicide or accident, and maintains good overall health, I’m unaware of any data that says we’re less likely to live into extreme old age than anyone else. My grandparents are only fairly recently starting to decline, and they’re 95. I’m 34 and in good health (other than being obese). I have no reason to think I won’t live into my 90’s or maybe to 100.Original Question: “Can people with autism live to 100?”

question: Can you write a step-by-step instructions to conquer autism?
answer: Interesting question you are asking. I am autistic and I am 20-years-old and I personally don’t believe that you can actually qonquer autism, you just gradually learn how to live with the fact that you are different compared to neurotypicals, and in time you learn how to work around the differences even though you know that they are still there. I know lots of other people with autism and they all live completely normal lives with little to no problems. Even though social interaction sometimes can be a hazzle for them and sometimes for me too. People with autism faces a lot of issues, but most of them learns how to overcome them. There is no recipe for perfect social interaction but most people with autism gradually learn how to interact with people properly, and in time it is almost no longer a problem. There is of course lots of issues that a person with autism can face but it is mainly the social part. Most autistic people that I know have pretty good social lives, they just had to overcome some obstacles when they where kids. But if I should make a list about how to overcome the most common obstacles that autistic people are facing, it would probably look like this:Try to get out of your own comfort zone. Try to do something that makes you uncomfortable from time to time, it does not have to be something big, and you don’t have to do it all the time, but try something new once a week, for example if there is a certain grocery store that you are used to then try and shop at another grocery store nearby. Autistic people often have trouble trying something new, and it is important to learn that “new” is not the same as harmful.Don’t be afraid to ask for help. I remember a time when I had to visit a friend, but I didn’t know how to get to her house and I wasn’t comfortable taking the bus, so I asked her to text me a complete guide on how to take the bus to her place, and now taking the bus isn’t as intimidating as it used to be. It is not healthy to hide the fact that you are autistic and need help from time to time, just ask a friend or a family member if you feel lost doing something.Build up self esteem. Way to many people with autism suffer from low self esteem and that is not healthy at all. Do something that you are good at, and ask for feedback. If you are good at drawing then show of your drawings to your friends or family, or if you are good at sport then go to sport events and invite your friends and family to come and cheer for you.Do stuff that you like. plain and simple just do something you enjoy, make the best out of life. Just because you are different doesn’t mean that your life has to be bad.I hope that I answered the question properly. I am not a native english speaker so I hope it wasn’t too painful to read through :)

question: Is Living With the Land, an Epcot ride, a great ride for someone with autism?
answer: Yes, absolutely. As an autistic person, I always found Epcot to be the most pleasant park as a whole, and the Land is full of the wonders of botany and science with none of the sensory assaults some other experiences have that can be challenging. It is a gentle boat ride (the boat glides on a track in a few inches of water, shallow and clear like a shopping mall fountain) through a futurist's garden. The plants are being cultivated in new and exciting ways, such as being frown upside-down, or sharing a tree, or different in size and shape from what we usually see, but nothing is alien or upsetting. You can see real people working through windows at a couple of points, and it really is like a big garden and greenhouse with gentle narration. It is quiet, the boat does not rock, it is cool in temperature, it feels peaceful and isolated. For me, it is actually like a rest. You or your child may not like having to exit back into the busy atrium, which I have found echoes loudly because of all of the people dining and talking in the space. But that's the end of the ride.I think it is wonderful for autistic people. I have not done the private behind-the-scenes tour, but if someone is really into botany, that could be a fun follow-up if you have the time and wish to spend a little extra.

question: What is the most useful advice you have received about living with autism, Asperger's Syndrome, or other neurodiversity?
answer: MAKE LISTS! FOLLOW YOUR LISTS! Lists are really important to me. If you see me without a list you can assume I have lost my mind. It’s just comfortable not having to make any decisions or to be told what to do and try to figure out if I’m doing it right. I can get up before everyone and just start following my list and know everything is okay. I know that when I get to #22 and start making tea that mom and father will start making noise back in their room and will be out soon. So I go to #23 and put 4 saucers, 4 cups and 12 apple slices out on the table with one cube of sugar on grandmother’s saucer and a small spoon (the kind you stir tea with). After I get to #28 I take that list back to my bedroom and put it on my desk neatly next to my tablet and pencils and pick up my school stuff which has my school day list inside. Then when I get home from school I have another list but that one changes three times during the week because I get some shots on Monday that used to be at the doctor’s office but we’re doing them at home now, a therapist for personal stuff on Tuesday, and then on Thursday is my autistic group therapy and learning/coping skills. I have to go to those before I can start my evening list. They are part of my responsibilities. If you organize your life and just let your list run your day you can relax and not worry about what comes next. These are all things that my father and mom have shown me and then there’s tons of coping skills that I’m still learning from my therapist. One of things that has been the best is grandmother’s advice. She says “always be grateful for what you have and never worry about what you don’t have.” She kind of taps me on the back when she says this and I think she knows that’s not my favorite thing but it’s also weirdly comforting so that’s okay. She has really been strong in teaching me the ma philosophy. My whole family lives by this and for my autism it’s REALLY super helpful. No clutter and no “things”. That we don’t really use everyday. Just a few pieces of furniture to clutter a room and our walls are always clear and bright without distractions hanging all over them like my bf’s house. I wanted to clean up his room but i learned thaat sometimes that’s not helpful and can actually be rude. So he always makes his bed and straightens where I’m going to sit before I come over now. I think that’s nice. Well I think that’s all I know about that.

question: What are some things to expect when you live with someone with autism?
answer: You are asking the wrong people in the wrong place. The reason is because autism is on a “spectrum”. This means that the best way to understand their “disability” is that it is:DIAGNOSED on a spectrum of valuesOnly diagnosed - there is no “cure” and there is no ABSOLUTE IDENTIFYING MARKERNo one knows what “causes” it.Most children affected will grow up, given the right SCHOOLING and PARENTING, to be able to HIDE and COMPENSATE FOR their “disability”.Best understood in most children by only two phrases - DIFFERENT and ON THE SPECTRUM.You are asking the wrong people in the wrong place, because each child diagnosed is DIFFERENT in their own way, it is better to not consider it just as a “disability”, and because the only two people you need to consult are the:child psychologist - who will diagnose and recommend “strategies” for the homeschool specialist - who will prescribe the special educational support that child will receivePlease understand what is meant by a SPECTRUM.your child is different in some wayyour child’s difference is on a scale of valuesthese values are calculated in the specific context they appearso there is no possible way that you can get the right prescription for your child “in general”Now since I know that you are not happy with my answer, how about if I give you an example? Me. I was never diagnosed on the spectrum, but that is because I was “low level on the spectrum” and “highly functional” at school - in fact I was at the top of my class. And because I can only know this about myself after having to teach “autistic” children and having a son who was diagnosed as “low level”.So yes I would sometimes appear to be not “focused” on the school work in the classroom. Yet I would always do very well in school.Always performing some sort of “tension release activity” - like pacing and muttering to myself.Not being able to look someone in the eye when talking to them.Not picking up on “contextual clues” when communicating with other children.Too much time reading books and not enough time socialising with other children.Very vivid “imagined events” that I knew were not “real” but still believed they were - note the problem in being able to keep “imagined” and “real events” separate.Often shouting out and being agressive to adults - and not for the usual reasons.Getting bullied because I was “different” - but then when I had enough, being extremely violent and physical - almost to the extent that the police would have to be called in.And that is just me - the highly functioing low level autistic, who could grow up and learn to hide it and compensate for it so well no one would ever suspect - unless they were very perceptive and knew me very very well. So you are asking the wrong people in the wrong place. In most places you should be able to get advice specific to your child, and school support specific to your child. What you should expect as a parent is a lot of time being spent learning how to “work around” the higher up on the spectrum children’s interaction with both you and with the other children in school.

question: Can you share any personal experiences or insights about living with autism? What are some common misconceptions about autism or individuals with autism?
answer: This is a big question with lots of different answers. Autism is very individual. There are core symptoms that most of us share, but how we react, how we cope, what skills we learn? That’s very individual and is influenced by so many factors. Did we get diagnosed young, midlife or later in life? Did we have a good solid support system? Did we experience trauma at any point? What do we struggle with most? For some it’s processing information, others could be social interactions and communication. What is the degree of challenge for those symptoms? Because it will be different for everyone. I was diagnosed later in life, and I find it challenging to adjust my way of thinking. I spent my whole life thinking and feeling something was very wrong with me, very different. But for reasons I don’t entirely understand, I never told one single person how it felt, how I felt. Being a girl in the late 70’s and 80’s, girls weren’t diagnosed very often with autism. So just about everyone attributed my behaviors to something else. I also learned very young that some of my behaviors were unacceptable, and had this sort of knowledge that I had to hide them. From what I’ve read, girls with autism are better at this than boys. Instead of a visible reaction to stress and anxiety, I would internalize it. I would wait until I was alone to get it out. In my case, I was the youngest of three kids being raised by a single mom in the era of latchkey kids. My older brother and sister were quite difficult, so I think my mom was just grateful I was so quiet. I don’t think she ever thought it was odd. She did take me to the doctor when I was four years old because of a stimming habit I had. That was the first time I knew I was doing something wrong or inappropriate. Her and the doctor kind of whispered about it, and I just remembered thinking this is something I’m not supposed to do. So I tried very hard only to do it when I was alone. Not always successfully, but I hid it enough to not be “weird”. I had terrible nightmares when I was young. Horrible vivid dreams that woke me up. I never told anyone. I just went to the bathroom and read a book until I could sleep again. I often had trouble sleeping- going to sleep, waking up. My mom thought I was lazy and didn’t want to go to school. I was just tired. I’m not sure if going to school was a big issue for me in grade school. Middle school and high school were definitely harder for me. Grade school I was very different from the other kids, but that young it didn’t seem to be as noticeable. I didn’t really have friends- the kind you have sleepovers with, but I played with them at recess. I was so quiet and got very upset if people fought in front of me. I would hide from confrontations. I didn’t get into many as a young girl, but hated it when my siblings fought. I had a very one minded obsession with horses. It’s the only thing I talked incessantly about. You couldn’t shut me up about horses! It is literally what everyone from grade school remembers about me today. The horses! I still love them too. I had a lot of fears and anxieties that other kids my age either didn’t have, or they didn’t have them with the same severity I did. I was molested by a boy one year older than me. Often- he would visit his grandmother who was our landlord. And every time he would “play” with me, locking us in a closet, a storeroom, and then touching me. He was very young too, and I didn’t like it, but I think I was confused by it. I didn’t know if it was wrong for sure. I thought it was but he was my age, and I guess it didn’t make sense. I also would freeze when I became very uncomfortable. An unfortunate habit that would carry through my life. This inability to stand up for myself, to defend myself. I hate to admit this, but I remember being afraid that if I told on him he wouldn’t want to be my friend anymore. Even though I didn’t like the touching, we did play regularly and I didn’t have many friends to play with. That fear of not being wanted, not being loved if I ever admitted my feelings or thoughts or defended myself against things was a big problem for me. I allowed so much awful treatment of myself because I didn’t know what to do, or how to express myself. I still have trouble to this day. In everyday situations and conversations I may feel very conflicted, but stay silent. In my teens and early twenties I was no longer able to internalize everything as successfully as I did when I was younger. I had emotional outbursts, and a pretty bad anger issue. The anger only came out when I had been internalizing things for too long and I was like a tea kettle. Once I was boiling hard, my top would blow. And it was scary because I couldn’t control myself, couldn’t stop words that came out of my mouth. I would have this tiny voice in my head saying STOP! Don’t say that! You don’t want to say these things! But I couldn’t stop. I sought help, and was eventually diagnosed with ADHD. I wasn’t given much information about ADHD, just out on meds. Why didn’t I do my own research? I don’t know. I was great at research. I had developed some coping mechanisms that made me very successful in college. But I never questioned the therapist about ADHD. I could never stay at a job. Still can’t. It wasn’t lack of work ethic, it wasn’t that it was too hard. I always actually excelled at any job. But I would begin to get very anxious and stressed. The two main reasons I’ve been able to isolate are interpersonal relationships with coworkers and supervisors, or a kind of strange one. I would start a job, learn my position, and become very proficient at it. Things would go well for a while, but I would begin to get bored of what I was doing. I wanted to learn more, be able to do different positions and tasks. I would outgrow the position pretty quickly and as I kept doing it I would start to feel claustrophobic, panicky. Like I was trapped. I still don’t understand why this happens, or how to cope with it. I earned a college degree in Exercise Physiology, and graduated with a 3.94 GPA. Yet, my extremely poor interview skills became a factor in finding work. This was when I fully realized that I avoid eye contact when uncomfortable or nervous. Pretty sure I was always like that, I was so shy and quiet when I was younger that I didn’t look at people much. But interviewing for a job was when I realized how bad it was. My eyes darting everywhere, looking at them and quickly away. I’d leave the interview thinking to myself how shifty I must have looked to them. I kept feeling different. I looked at other adults and felt such a loneliness. I was so confused and sad- I couldn’t understand why I had such a hard time doing things that people do everyday. Why some less appealing thing's that normal people seemed to deal with were so huge and overwhelming to me. My husband always said how smart I was, smarter than he realized. But he also said I was irresponsible, lazy, flighty, flaky. I wasn’t lazy. Every day I was busy and worked tirelessly raising my kids, taking care of our animals including a horse by myself. No matter the weather (in Iowa) it was me that took care of them. I was going to college full time, home by the time my kids were home from school, baking their class party treats, making craft gifts for my family, drawing (also an artist), handling volleyball games, band practice, kids homework , college homework, cleaning the house, etc. I wasn’t lazy, but he wanted me to have a job. And I struggled. I also dealt with severe headaches after brain surgery. I’ve had a few head injuries from car accidents, I have vasovagal syncope and had issues having seizures and hit my head a lot. I felt very bad about myself. Being diagnosed at 44 didn’t help as much as I thought it would. Before, I was blissfully ignorant of many behaviors. But once I was diagnosed everyone began to point out things they noticed all along. And as I learned more about autism, how it affects me and those around me, I became very hyper aware of my behaviors. I feel a constant anxiety now that I didn’t before. I’m always measuring what I say now, worried I’ll be misunderstood and possibly offend someone or hurt feelings. I’m still unable to keep a job. Never been fired, always quit. It took a long time for my family to accept the diagnosis. I was having more trouble than usual masking for some time before the diagnosis. But after? It became impossible to mask. It was like my brain was saying “We finally know why you are this way and I’m too exhausted to keep hiding”. it was difficult for my family to get to know the real me. Hell, I was getting to know the real me! But they were used to 44 years of the Brandy I presented to others. The one who hid so much. The one who struggled with so many things and never said anything to anyone. They were used to thinking I was lazy, or irresponsible. Not meeting my potential. My son was the first and only one to research autism himself, to try to understand and learn to communicate better with me. It took years for others. And most of them still think it’s a choice. I can just decide to change or be different. I’m on my own now. My kids are grown, I’m divorced. I struggle a lot with executive functioning, decision making, sensory overload. I don’t know if it’s the autism or the head traumas. I’ve been referred to a TBI clinic so maybe I’ll find out. Autism has had a profound impact on my life. I often wonder if I had told my mom all the things I wanted to tell her but didn’t, would it have been more apparent that I needed to be tested for something? If I had known younger, would I have had better skills? Would I have been able to avoid some pretty awful situations that resulted in trauma? Would I have been a better mother? A better wife? Now my biggest concern is learning to live with my weaknesses, my limitations. Putting more effort into my strengths to improve both myself and my chances of living successfully independent. I still feel confused a lot, anxious, and for a while very depressed. My dog Kane died 5 months ago. When I lost him, I lost my only friend in the world. I’ve had a terrible time adjusting to being without him. So I’m focusing on my well being, focusing on my art. And hoping and praying I can be of use again. Helping animals, helping people. I’m trying to have a better outlook, but it’s hard. I didn’t start this answer intending it to be so long!! But I was trying to be very truthful, even with things that are uncomfortable.

question: What happens when children with autism live in an environment that isn't aware of autism?
answer: I’ve interpreted your question to mean: What happens when a child who has undiagnosed autism lives with people who have not heard of the condition? So, onto the scenario. What happens to the child really depends on the context of the family. If the child attends preschool or daycare, it is highly likely that the teachers/ carers would notice red flags in your child’s behaviour, which would cause them to suggest an appointment with a pediatrician. When my son was diagnosed, I was aware of ASD (my niece had been diagnosed five years earlier), but I didn’t spend much time around young children, and all the signs I was noticing, seemed, to my uninformed perspective, to be caused by his giftedness. The report from the preschool was critical in getting a diagnosis from the pediatrician, and from that, support swiftly followed. If the parents send the child to preschool, the teachers are on the ball, and the parents are willing to listen and see a doctor, the outcome for this hypothetical child can be really positive. However, if the child doesn’t attend preschool, or the parents refuse to admit that there’s a problem, the future for the child becomes a little bit more difficult. This means that the child is unable to access any early intervention, or support until they reach school. They will certainly start school behind in social and communication schools. Because children with ASD often have sensory processing issues, it’s also likely that this child has poor gross and fine motor skills, and potentially an undiagnosed learning difficulty. Because there is no diagnosis, the teacher has no allocated funding for a classroom aide, and may even be unaware of the problems until the child sits in his or her classroom for the first time. From there, things can go a few different ways. In scenario one, the teacher is switched on, and personable. By the end of the first or second week, she has a meeting with you, the parents and arranges for an appointment with the school counselor to discuss different options. You see the light, see a doctor, and your child is diagnosed. He begins weekly appointments with various therapists, funding is secured for a teacher’s aide, and, within a year or two, much of the gap has closed between him and his peers. That’s the best case scenario. In scenario two, the teacher is overworked and underpaid. She has thirty kids in her classroom, and she hasn’t even managed to learn all their names by the end of the first week, let alone figured out who has learning difficulties. She knows your child’s name, though, because he’s the one who pushed Sarah when she was singing too loudly. He’s also the one who went and hid under the desk in the back of the classroom and refused to come out for three hours on the day when recess was switched with assembly. On his third day, he had an accident in his pants because the teacher didn’t let him go to the toilet when immediately when he asked. And then he exposed himself to the class because he couldn’t manage his clothing by himself. He’s the one who likes to make a loud, low-pitched droning noise when he’s colouring, and he never makes eye contact. She’s been meaning to speak with you about it, but she doesn’t have time this week. Maybe you can make an appointment next week? But by next week, your son is suspended, because he bit another boy who was standing too close to him. Your son is singled out as a trouble-maker, and he goes through the revolving door of suspension, after suspension. He never really seems to get it, but you blame the school. His teacher is clearly picking on him. Someone suggests, somewhere down the track that you see a doctor, but you know there’s nothing wrong with your kid, so you take him to a new school, but the change of routine just sets off a whole slew of problems you hadn’t anticipated. By the time he finishes primary school, he’s spent more time out of school than in. When he’s at home he pursues solitary pursuits like lining up dinosaurs, or counting, or playing the computer. He hates school, has no friends and thinks of himself as “dumb” and “naughty.” This is, of course, the worst case scenario. Most situations would fall somewhere between the two, hopefully closer to the first than the second.

question: Has anybody lived with a partner with autism, who withdraws suddenly for days or weeks? It’s like living with 2 different men. One is so loving and then the next minute hardly talks.
answer: Some with autism get overloaded and shut down. Too much noise and light, or too many demands they feel they cannot meet, or even severe depression. Autistic people are six times more likely to commit suicide. Ups are great, downs are crushing and they feel as if they will never get better or the problems only get worse. It could be that you were disappointed in him and yelled at him. To him, he failed completely. I liken autism to having a broken altimeter in a plane. The pilot with autism thinks they are flying along on a steady straight course. To everyone else, they are up and down, all over the sky. Some with autism are funnels for other peoples’ powerful emotions, and they take them in not even knowing why they are now upset or angry. Imagine they can tell that everyone (to their thinking) finds them irritating, but they have no way to process how to stop being irritating or get people to stop being mean. If he is unready to talk, you cannot drag it out of him. That will make it worse. If he is in a phase of frustration, words may seem difficult and the right words just out of reach. We all have had moments where we are looking at something and our brains keep giving us the wrong word. “Would you hand me the—” The brains says, “Cabbage.” No. “The——” “Cabbage.” Ideas: Depending on his willingness for touch or companionship, you may say, “You seem upset/unhappy. What would you like to do? Be held? Watch a movie? Have some tea/coffee/brownies. All of the above.” If he is hypersensitive, touch may be too much, or it may tell him that he is still loved and accepted. Sometimes getting them to laugh helps. Just like all of us, that takes discernment to know if you need to stop or go farther. I get it that the rest of the world doesn’t get to have fits and shut down and it is not fair to those around them. Autism is not a set of bad decisions that they can just will themselves to stop doing. Many autistic people are kind, but they can be locked into their own personal world that is frustrating to those that have to be around those moments (weeks/years). I hope that you can find ways to help him blossom for both of your sakes. Autistic people tend to be very loyal and loving, sometimes in their own way.

question: Does a child with autism engage in echolalia throughout their lives?

question: How can someone with autism be happy with his or her life?
answer: Everyone so far has given really good answers to this question. So, to recap:Manage your stress. Find good, safe hobbies; be careful with stuff like woodworking and metalworking if you have poor motor coordination. These hobbies will most likely be your go-to when you need to recharge and “work off” your anxiety levels.Figure out how to monetize your special interests. If you enjoy woodworking, build some birdhouses and sell them. If you like rebuilding cars, go into auto mechanics. Find something you enjoy that will get you out of bed in the morning.Do your best to be sociable. This one may be the toughest. Using the other two items in this list, it’s doable. If you like reading, join a book club. If you like woodworking, join a woodworking club or take a class to learn how to do something with wood in a different way. If you like chess, join a chess club. The list goes on and on. This way, you won’t isolate yourself completely and you are doing something that you know helps you with anxiety. It may not completely cancel it out, but it may help lessen the problem for you.Find a suitable romantic companion. Much harder than the other three, but still doable. I found my fiance through an online dating site I signed up with that was for people with a specific interest. You could also pick up some info in books or online on how to begin and maintain conversations, which would help. Statistics show that married men tend to live longer than unmarried men - something to consider. This item isn’t really a necessity to living a happy life, but it can help if it’s done right.You don’t have to advertise your issues. What I mean by this is that you don’t go flying out the gate with, “Hi, my name is XYZ, and I have autism spectrum disorder. What’s your name?” This is sort of a restatement of Nicholas Stone's answer; don’t focus on being autistic. This isn’t about you being autistic; this is about you living a happy life. Of course, if the subject comes up in natural conversation, you could pursue it. I always do - and it has a tendency to weed out folks I wouldn’t care to continue to associate with anyway.And my own addition to this advice: Don’t sweat the small stuff. If you make a mistake, don’t beat yourself up about it. This may be the hardest thing of all, to not go back home after a “bad encounter” socially, and continue to ask yourself, “What did I do wrong?” Focus instead on what you did right. If, somehow, you turned someone away from you because of something you said or did, I’m sure you’ll eventually make a friend who doesn’t. I mean, there were, at the time of this writing, over 325 million people in the US, and nearly 7.4 billion people in the world (see Population Clock). Don’t stress yourself over one person. Go out and meet the rest of them.

question: What are some effective ways for people living with autism or Asperger's syndrome to navigate social situations?
answer: “What are some effective ways for people living with autism or Asperger's syndrome to navigate social situations?” One useful technique is simple bluntness. question: How many people with autism can live independently with little assistance?
answer: It really depends where they are on the autism spectrum, and whether they are fully conscious of their condition. I was told in my thirties that I should not try to live an independent life, although I was told very little why. This is when autism did not make much sense to people with this condition, until you added the label Asperger’s syndrome, with a list of the features that made up this clinical profile, which did not come until decades later. If I had been given this information at the time, I would have immediately seen the sense of this advice. Information is all important with autism, and our ability to conceptualise our problems within the framework of what they are. Without it we are lost. I would also suggest that anxiety is one factor that has to be taken into account, even when we have reached a degree of understanding. Very few of us will ever be clear of anxiety. It is written into our condition. Our brain simply processes anxiety all the time, and it matters very little what the content of that anxiety happens to be at any particular time. This means that if living alone is how we manage it, then living alone is the answer. If living with safe secure people is the answer, then that is the answer. What is not acceptable is living with people who are full of toxic stuff, or some institutional arrangement where this danger is possible. It is essential we have control over our own self regulation. We should not go for security by giving up our freedom. It is the same rule for everybody. Lastly, there is no general rule whether we should or not live independent life. Each autist is an unique person, with unique needs, more so than the rest of the NT population. We require special services, whether we are dealing with doctors and hospitals, or dealing with our domestic needs. When these special services have been established, our needs will be met, and our undoubted creative gifts will be fully available to the rest of the population. At the moment we are wasted by the lack of proper focus. Thank you for the question Ellen.

question: Is it possible for someone with autism to live alone?
