question: What is the impact of adults with autism living with their parents indefinitely? Can it become a burden for the family?
answer: Adults with autism living with parents long-term can offer emotional bonds and stability, particularly if structured home environments support their needs. However, challenges often arise as caregiving demands increase over time. Financial strain from therapy, medical costs, or limited income contributions may stress family resources. Aging parents may face physical or emotional exhaustion, compounded by uncertainty about future care once they can no longer provide support. Social isolation for both the individual and family members, restricted career opportunities for caregivers, and potential sibling resentment can deepen tension. Cultural norms and access to external support (e.g., respite care, community programs) influence outcomes. While dependency may hinder skill development in some cases, proactive planning and resources can mitigate burdens. The impact varies widely based on autism severity, family dynamics, and available systems—highlighting a balance between compassionate care and sustainable solutions.

Itâ€™s a phenomena in which the autistic person copies other peopleâ€™s behaviors in order to pretend to be normal. By doing this, they are able to hide that they are autistic temporarily. Some people get so good at masking that they can mask for days, weeks, months, or years. Thatâ€™s why many people, especially women, go undiagnosed with autism. Now, thereâ€™s something called autistic burnout. Autistic burnout happens when an individual is exhausted from a long period of masking and cannot mask anymore. This happened to me in 8th grade (13 years old). Basically, you are finally letting people see what you have been hiding for so long. You arenâ€™t really any worse, youâ€™re just not able to hide how you are. This could be along the lines of what happened to the adult in the question- they are autistic but suffered a burnout induced by additional stress in their life and were unable to continue masking. question: Do people with autism wear masks like psychopaths and sociopaths?

In addition it creates an identity crises because we have to alter our own fundamental identity, which results in shame, because we are so stressed about presenting something that we are notâ€”it creates a moral crises. For the psychopath there is no shame, no moral crises, and thus a potential to be all of those things. There is no cost, only gain to their mask. For us the cost is enormous. Societal standards are based on neurotypical perspectives, and anyone who deviates from the neurotypical normative standards has to mask. We the â€˜outsidersâ€™ have to conform to the neurotypical standards, or we donâ€™t get partners, jobs, our very survival depends on it. By the way, I think a strong ground of my personality is based on a form of devils advocate personality. Which would and does show the more I take my mask offâ€”a kind of joker devils advocate. question: Does autism masking become easier with time?
answer: People often have to mask for survival reasons. It's not just something that can be easily turned on and off at will, especially when you have no other choice. People who have to work in spaces that are intolerant of autistic behaviors have to mask heavily to thrive or are barely scraping by (I'm one of the latter group). It's not as simple as not wanting to be ourselves, masking is ingrained from a young age, especially when it has to do with social rejection due to natural autistic behaviors. I personally started to learn to mask from before the age of 10 and it has taken so much effort to unmask. Unmasking can be a very painful and messy process when you have an extensive trauma history attached to it. Autistic people aren't just accepted by the rest of the world, we are still very much ostracized and treated poorly. Until autistic people don't have to mask for our physical or financial safety, there will always be a need to mask. Until social repercussions for unmasking are diminished and people become more accepting and tolerant of autistics and the behaviors that are inherent to our ways of being, there will always be a need to mask. What it all boils down to is bigotry and the oppression of autistics within neurotypical-dominated environments. When the majority actually wants to accommodate us and create safe spaces for autistics to be ourselves, that's when people may feel safe enough to unmask to some capacity, but I suspect it may never fully happen, at least not in my lifetime (I'm 22). Your experience doesn't align with all other autistic people, sadly. I wish we all felt safe enough to be our autistic selves, but that is very difficult to even fathom when we are at such a great risk of being traumatized when we don't mask. As for whether masking gets easier, I have to say that it doesn't. Masking already requires so much energy from autistic people and constantly being hypervigilant about everything you do can become very stressful. I have masked my whole life and I find that even though I'm young, I am exhausted from doing it, I can't imagine what 20 or 30 more years of that would be like. The biggest piece of advice I can give is that if you have any control over how much masking you have to do and you have the rare privilege to reduce it, do that, as it can take a serious toll on your mental health and even your identity (many autistics have an identity crisis after unmasking). Self-care is so important, but not everybody can practice it, so please do that whenever you get a moment to, because I know how much this world can wear you down when you have to constantly mask. Just know that you're valid in every part of this, wanting to mask is okay and your choice, having to mask is a burden, and refusing to mask is a privilege not many of us get. So I hope you someday get that option, because I know it greatly improves the quality of life for an autistic when we have that option. I wish you the best of luck.

question: How is autism diagnosed in people old enough that they habitually use masking techniques?

question: Can an autistic person improve his/her social skills without masking their autism?
answer: Yes, and no. Depends what you put behind the words â€œsocial skillsâ€. If you mean by that gaining a satisfying social life, yes. But if you mean by that socially presenting as non autistic then no, it is by definition masking. What needs to be understood by both autistic individuals for their own happiness, and by neurotypical individuals for an inclusive society, is that autistic individuals do not lack social skills, instead they have different expectations of social interactions and communication. Autistic individuals will have to mask to make small talk and to use implicit (â€œlet's have lunch sometimeâ€ meaning â€œI don't want to see you again but I want to sound politeâ€), and the reason for that is that they don't feel comfortable being dishonest. Autistic individuals can have very satisfying social lives, it would just look very different from a neurotypical individualâ€™s satisfying social life. They don't necessarily know less people, they just consider anyone who is not a close friend an â€œacquaintanceâ€ instead.â›” Fewer social events as their social needs are inferior to neurotypical individuals. They value their â€œalone timeâ€.âž• More intimate social events (small gatherings, hobby clubs..) of longer time enabling deep connections or deep conversations.â›” Less crowded, noisy or active social events (parties, large meet-upsâ€¦) which are sensorily overwhelming for them to the point of not being able to enjoy the social interaction.âž• More remote/online interactions as autistic individuals are more comfortable interacting in written (keep in mind it's a social and communication neurodivergence) and from the comfort of their home.â›” Less of quick face-to-face meet-ups (e.g. have a drink) or quick phone calls. Autistic individuals do not feel much of a need to frequently â€œcheck-upâ€ on each other.âž• More lengthy quality time with each other on the phone or face-to-face. Autistic individuals don't overcome their dislike of phone calls for staying 2 seconds with you. If they call or answer a call, it's for spending at least the next hour with you. Similarly, autistic individuals don't get out of their comfort zone (home) to chat 2 mins with someone or just pick up bread. They need a stronger motivation.Now, from a neurotypical point of view, if they have a friend who goes out to social events only twice a month at best, have only 3 friends, and decline all invitation to social events involving a noisy/busy environnement, and won't do any chitchat with them when waiting with them but rather open a book or observe the world around, that person very likely cannot help but think their friend lack of a social life and social skills. That's because they do not take into consideration the differences between their social lives, and the extra layer of social interactions the autistic person has. Autistic individuals as a whole do not lack social skills, they have different social skills. It is to be noted that being more difficult for an autistic individual to meet individuals valuing the same social interactions as them, it is not unusual that they would grow lacking a social life and social skills. However, that lack definitely would hamper their mental well-being and no amount of trying to push neurotypical views of social skills on them will help them build a satisfying social life. As a side note, individuals with superior intelligence (gifted individuals) have similar social preferences and functioning, reasons for which autistic individuals will often find it easier to build friendships with them than other neurotypical individuals, but the difference is that neurotypical individuals with superior intelligence have a preference for those more authentic social interactions but are not inflexible (rigid) like autistic individuals are and they are also happy to join other types of social gatherings and can do small talk without it being a strain on their mental health (masking). Hope this helps bridging the social gap between neurodivergent and neurotypical individuals as well as comforting autistic individuals in their own social competence.

question: Why is there such a huge difference in the criteria for autism, with autistic people claiming the main symptoms are sensory overload and masking, and scientists claiming interaction abnormalities and ritualistic behavior to be main symptoms?
answer: Why is there such a huge difference between the criteria for autism, with autistic people claiming the main symptoms are sensory overload and masking, and scientists claiming interaction abnormalities and ritualistic behavior to be main symptoms? I have to laugh about the â€œritualistic behaviorâ€ thing. Hah. Interacting with many NTs on a casual basis feels like Iâ€™m in a spy movie from the â€˜60s. â€œHello, how are you? â€œI am fine, how are you?â€ â€œFine.â€ â€œGood morning!â€ â€œWhatâ€™s good about it?â€ â€œDid you see that ludicrous display last night?â€ â€œWhatâ€™s Wenger doing sending Walcott on that early?â€ â€œThe thing about Arsenal is, they always try to walk it in.â€ â€œNice weather weâ€™ve having today.â€ â€œYes, but the weather in Switzerland is blowing.â€ â€œOK, agent 99, here is the secret document on microfiche.â€ It feels like a challenge-response between undercover individuals attempting to identify members of the in-group. I have had people I know make sports-related comments, usually something about a televised game the night before. When I respond that I donâ€™t watch sports, they lose all interest in talking to me =at= =all=. Some of them, from that point on will act as if I were invisible. It is VERY ritualistic. Think about handshakes. Iâ€™ve run into many NTs who have very definite ideas about what makes a good handshake. Hard, just firm, grasp the wrist with the left hand, gentle, crushing, extended shake and hold with very close eye contact, one quick hard shake and release, barely grasp and let go, etc. â€¦ Many will say that they base their opinion of a person on the first handshake. But they donâ€™t all agree on what makes a â€œcorrectâ€ handshake. Get the ritual wrong, you are out forever. Some will use it as a power play; shove hands together, then suddenly drop their hand a couple of inches so they have your fingers, not your palm, and squeeze hard. My inclination is that when I interact with someone, especially at work, I walk up and just ask the question I need to ask, or pass on the information I need to impart. People would often look offended or upset, and I would go over and over in my head what I might have said to upset them. Sometimes people would angrily say â€œYou could at least say hello!â€ What? Weâ€™re at work. It isnâ€™t a social event. Weâ€™ve been at work for hours. Weâ€™re not friends, you arenâ€™t interested in even talking to me except for work purposes. What is there to get angry about? Iâ€™d call =that= an â€œinteraction abnormalityâ€.If someone says â€œdonâ€™t talk to me until Iâ€™ve had my first cup of coffeeâ€, everyone nods with understanding. If someone says â€œI have to check every door to make sure it is locked before I go to bedâ€, most people will indicate they get it, but think it is a bit extreme. If someone says â€œI always pause reading a book halfway down the right-hand pageâ€, most people will think that is weird, ritualistic behavior. I do this. I have a very good reason for doing this - I am regularly in the process of reading a dozen or more books concurrently. I pause my reading halfway down the right-hand page and put a bookmark in. Then when I come back to any book, I take up reading again halfway down the left-hand page. This reminds me where I am in the book, kind of like when a show comes back from commercial and they reiterate a bit of what happened before the commercial. This is not ritualistic behavior. It is a well thought out behavior with a purpose.As to masking: because of the seeming inability of many NTs to handle differences in behavior and preferences, to get along I must learn those greeting rituals, avoid being â€œoutedâ€ as not a ball game watcher, and somehow suss out exactly what kind of handshake this person I just met requires to accept me. This is masking. It is exhausting. If you donâ€™t think it is, think about some time when you were faced with a person speaking to you at great length about something you have no interest in, in a social situation you cannot avoid (perhaps an event at work). Iâ€™ll bet within 30 seconds, you were ready to chew your leg off to escape. Now imagine doing that for 12 hours every day. Add to that, many on the spectrum tend to have sharper senses; better hearing, more sensitive sense of taste and smell, more sensitive sense of touch, more vivid sense of vision. And often have difficulty, compared to NTs, in filtering out unwanted/uninteresting sounds, smells, and visual stimuli. So now imagine that person boring you, is doing so at high volume in a subway station at rush hour. Do that for hours at a time, every day. Got the picture?Perhaps an illustration of why a person and someone diagnosing them may view different aspects as more or less important. Your doctor cannot feel pain. When a Dr sticks you with a needle, the Dr does not feel any pain. You feel the pain. But people stick you with needles all of the time, so you have become rather stoic about it. The Dr can, however, see a rash. The Dr will see the rash as more important than your pain, and so wants to give you a series of painful injections to help hide, but not cure, the rash. Meanwhile, you know that the rash will still itch. It wonâ€™t be as visible, but only at the cost of an ongoing series of painful injections. So naturally, to =you=, the rash is less important.A British sitcom called â€œThe IT Crowdâ€ covered ritualistic behavior in NTs quite well in an episode about â€œproper menâ€ and football. I took some of the above quotes from that episode.Now where is that much vaunted, supposedly-superior â€˜Theory of Mindâ€ that NTs are always telling me they have?

question: My best friend got diagnosed with autism and would like to slowly unlearn masking behaviors. Is there a way I can support and help him do that as an NT?
answer: Iâ€™m f-ing shocked at the level of internalized ableism in some of these responses. For OP, the book â€œUnmasking Autismâ€ by Devon Price is a good place to start. It explains the affects of masking really well, and some of the problems from the autistic personâ€™s perspective, so it can help to build empathy for your friend as they go into this. And to counteract the other anecdotal claims with my own story (scroll to the last paragraph if you don't want to read about me ðŸ¤·ðŸ¼): I didn't find out I was autistic until my kid was diagnosed. Iâ€™m high masking, but did start out nonverbal and visibly autistic. My parents were antivax and I was beat if I had meltdowns, so I wound up having shutdowns far more often. People still saw me as weird, and their relationships with me WERE tied to my mask rather than who I really am. Eight years ago, when the Navy left me with a brain injury and memory loss, my mask slipped. I didn't know what it was at the time, just that I couldn't act â€œnormalâ€ anymore and friends abandoned me. Shortly after that I found new friends, though, and they liked me for who I was. They enjoyed my info dumping, and genuinely liked my oddities. When I had rough days they were forgiving and let me make rain checks. They didn't judge my food choices or make *the face* that people make when they see you as lower on the social ladder. Importantly, a lot of the new friends and found family are also neurodivergent, because there are a lot of us. Now my brainâ€™s recovered, and I can mask again, but Iâ€™ve implemented healthier habits. My husband really loves me when Iâ€™m being myself, as well as my friends, even though they arenâ€™t autistic (as in, they scored single digits on every screening test). They like seeing my excitement with stimming, or being able to get straightforward answers. They enjoy parallel play styles (e.g. playing games on laptops around each other) as well as things like DnD where we can all get really into rules and technicalities while laughing. My current friendships and relationships are so much healthier and happier than the ones I lost. Iâ€™m also less stressed at home, and have fewer shutdowns now that Iâ€™m recognizing my limits, and I can teach my kid better as well. I still mask for certain things, like going to a business meeting or meeting new people, but itâ€™s still more relaxed and far less focused on what others think. Because even when I masked full time, it was never really enough. Awkward moments and miscommunications still happened, and I was still â€œweirdâ€ and â€œupsettingâ€. Itâ€™s important to know that unmasking can be very unpleasant at first. We barely know ourselves when weâ€™ve masked our whole lives, so that's terrifying, and then there is usually some backlash from people whose love turned out conditional. Having even a single person accepting you through that makes all of the difference, so OP is already on the right track. Itâ€™s not like a mental illness like some of these comments claim, because unmasking isn't abusive to others. Itâ€™s literally just us existing and making allowances. Letting ourselves stim safely (I always stimmed, but it was harmful before, like picking at skin or biting my thumb, grinding teeth, stabbing a pencil into my palm, etc. I don't do any of that anymore, like night and day). Choosing to keep our safe foods on hand and not force ourselves to eat something that we hate. Yeah, that means I eat a lot more â€œkidsâ€ foods than before, but I make them for my kid anyway. Itâ€™s a win-win. It also looks like making â€œglimmerâ€ playlists to listen to before events (music that makes my brain sort of tingle and feel good. Surprisingly a lot of indigenous throat singing metal bands for me). Picking clothes based on texture and not forcing myself to wear stuff for looks alone. Allowing myself quiet recouping days after get togethers or events, because I realized that my â€œtired stutteringâ€ and forgetting words was actually me going partially nonverbal. Most importantly, just letting myself be â€œweirdâ€ and goofy around my husband and kid. Dancing how I want, making random noises (echolalia is huge between my daughter and me), using â€œCalmerâ€ earbuds to cut out background sounds like AC and electricity, etc. Iâ€™m not going to pretend like I didn't lose friends. But I will say that the friends I lost were the people that I didn't look forward to being around. They were all people who exhausted me, because they reacted poorly when my mask slipped before. They berated me for acting weird when I got excited or happy. They literally tore me down whenever I felt slightly comfortable. Looking back, Iâ€™m so fucking glad theyâ€™re gone from my life. My husband has gotten so used to me and our kid that he feels weird around other neurotypical people now. Our relationship has grown to be so much stronger than before. If you love your friend (yes, platonically included) then absolutely take the time to read up on it. Most importantly, accept them for who they are. If youâ€™re into computers: remind yourself that the mask was essentially them running a glitchy emulator of being allistic, and when they can just run things on their own operating system everything can be smoother and less stressful for them. question: How can I mask my autism symptoms and seem normal? I have high functioning autism. How can I mask and hide my autism symptoms and make it seem less obvious?
answer: The best way to learn is to observe and memorize. Every time I make a social blunder, I go over all the elements in my head and I memorize them so that I can recognize a similar event in the future. Then I test out and adjust my behavior until I get it right. Observe what people are doing, how they are talking, their tone inflection, their body language, how people hold themselves, how people express humor. Observe even the smallest nuances in people's expressions. Practice what you observe. Pay more attention to your tone, and how people react to different inflections. Don't fall into the monotone trap. Practice sarcasm, but don't overuse it. Keep humor special for certain occasions. Use humor when you are trying to get someone to like you upon first meeting them, or when you are at a social gathering. Otherwise if it is close friends, be yourself. Don't spend the conversation talking about your interests. As good as it feels to talk about something you are passionate about, remember that people also like to have a day in the conversation. Stop yourself and let the other person talk. Only mention your passions, and if the other person wants to know more, that's when you go into it. Pay attention to slang and jargon. Adjust your tone and the way you speak to match the kind of crowd you are in. It's inappropriate to use slang and casual speak at a business meeting, but it is also inappropriate to use formal sounding words with a group of people that seem very casual. People like eye contact. To get past this problem, lol between their eyes, not at them. Don't stare too long. Generally, people that are more comfortable with each other will maintain eye contact longer. If it's too difficult, make eye contact and then glance away periodically, while using some active body language while you are talking. Think abstractly. question: What does autism and ADHD masking look like?
answer: Autism and ADHD masking is a phenomena in which people with these problems learn to hide their symptoms in order to conform to social norms and prevent unfavourable outcomes. question: How do you detect an autistic person who is using a social mask to hide their autism?

question: How can someone on the autism spectrum learn to mask their symptoms? What are some common signs of masking in individuals with autism?

To answer your first question, someone who is autistic learns to mask their symptoms thanks to their keen observation, as well with a good ability to imitate and copy others characters. As a short term way (such in work settings) but not in a long-term as it may impact negatively our mental states. Indeed masking is something deeply rooted in us,, within our education , that we may not recognise consciously at the beginning but we still still use and depend of it , a lot, in our lives. Masking can show in a lot of ways, conventional and unconventional ones. Some autistic persons might act nervous or always, use a low or high pitched voice (in regard to their imitation to neurotypicals) ask atypical questions they might think are common (as a vain attempt to copy small talk ) while gesturing (touching their hands for example) .they might look away nervously, or stare openly in their interlocutorsâ€™s eyes in opposite. Others might look distant or too straightforward, joke a bit too much or react bad in social interactions (when they miss clues) they might become embarrassed and desperately search for a way to get themselves out of the situation. Despite being autistic persons it's important to reminder we are still persons regardless, and our way of reacting and masking is closely linked to our inner selves. question: What's the difference between a person with quiet BPD and a person with autism masking?

In mostly contrast, Allistics (the human majority) seem to have inherent ability to ignore much more of their physical perception than autistics, and that ability influences a lot. Masking isn't required because society ONLY caters to their perceptions & needs.

question: What does autism and ADHD masking look like?
answer: Autism and ADHD masking refer to behaviors that individuals with these conditions may exhibit in order to hide or camouflage their symptoms. Autism masking can take many forms, depending on the individual and their specific symptoms. Some common behaviors that may be associated with autism masking include:Mimicking social behavior: Individuals with autism may learn to mimic social behavior that comes naturally to others in order to fit in and be accepted. This can involve learning to make eye contact, smile, and use appropriate body language and gestures, even if it doesn't come naturally to them.Avoiding stimming: Stimming, or self-stimulatory behavior, is a common symptom of autism that involves repetitive movements or actions, such as hand-flapping, rocking, or spinning. Individuals with autism may learn to suppress their stimming behavior in order to appear more "normal" or avoid drawing attention to themselves.Overcompensating: Some individuals with autism may go to great lengths to overcompensate for their social difficulties or other symptoms. For example, they may become obsessive about following social rules, or they may develop highly structured routines and schedules to help them cope with changes in their environment.ADHD masking, similarly, can take many different forms depending on the individual and their symptoms. Some common behaviors that may be associated with ADHD masking include:Hyperfocusing: Individuals with ADHD may hyperfocus on certain tasks or activities in order to compensate for their distractibility or impulsivity. This can make it appear as though they are highly productive and engaged, but in reality, they may be struggling with other aspects of their life or work.Avoiding tasks that require sustained attention: People with ADHD may avoid tasks that require sustained attention or long periods of focus, because they know they will struggle with them. This can make it appear as though they are lazy or unmotivated, when in fact they are simply struggling with their symptoms.Impulsivity control: Impulsivity is a common symptom of ADHD, but individuals may learn to mask it by suppressing their impulses in certain situations, such as in the workplace or in social situations. This can require a great deal of effort and energy, and may lead to feelings of frustration and exhaustion.Overall, masking can be a useful coping mechanism for individuals with autism or ADHD in certain situations, but it can also be a source of stress and anxiety. It's important for individuals with these conditions to receive proper support and accommodations, so that they can thrive and be successful without having to constantly mask their symptoms.

There have been studies of genetic correlates of clinical autism, and while there are some correlates there are no major dominant or recessive genes involved but rather a number of small variations in at a number pf particular loci in DNA sequences (single nuclear polymorphisms). However, their functions in producing Autism are unknown and made more complicated by the problems with the underlying problems in defining the syndrome precisely. Thus there are some genetic correlates of the disorder, but they are weak, and one cannot make reliable predictions or diagnoses of the disorder from knowledge of the genes alone. While there may be some tendency for autism to run in families, we do not know to the specific roles genetic factors or, for that matter, non-genetic, epigenetic or environmental factors. While there may be some evolutionary effects (which by definition would be genetic in nature) they may be very weak. I should mention that many individuals who are diagnosed with autism in childhood seem to function better socially as they mature, and many may have and rear children, in which case there would be no (or very weak) evolutionary pressures which would affect the gene pool of the population.

question: Does anyone here understand their ADHD as a form of neurodivergence? If so, how did you come to this understanding? What does neurodiversity mean to you? Please share your story!
answer: I have ADHD (combined type), as well as bipolar I disorder and borderline personality disorder. I don't use the term neurodivergent in connection with my diagnoses. I find the term alienating because it focuses on the neurological side of my condition, rather than the psychological and interpersonal sides. I feel that the relation between body (i.e., the brain, the nervous system) and the psyche is still not determined. In general, I reject paradigms that perceive the mind as a second-order phenomena relative to the body, and usually seek a point-of-view that balances materialism/physicalism and idealism. Neutral monism appeals to me for that reason. There's also the issue of context. The neurodivergent paradigm seems to imply that because the brain is implicated in ADHD and other conditions, a person would definitely have a neuropsychological profile that could be broadly likened to others in different times and environments. I tend to take the opinion that ADHD qua ADHD would not be a fitting term for someone who lived in the Iron Age or the Middle Ages, for example, even if their brain-based differences were precisely like what modern pwADHD deal with. The psychology of other times and places would be sufficiently distinct for ADHD to be an improper idea when applied to humans of the past (and maybe even the future). But because the human brain must have been relatively consistent across history for our species, the neurodivergence concept implies having similar neuropsychological differences would be sufficient for a broad comparative categorization irrespective of context. I tend to privilege the mind over the body, to counter physicalist assumptions we all make. For me, the psyche is primary (and so too is the body). I tend to be suspicious of the ideologies linked to subordinating mental phenomena to the body. I feel like the appeal of the neurodivergence paradigm is how it reifies the psyche as an embodied idea. Perhaps this helps reduce stigma, since people are generally more ready to look beyond the psychosocial struggles of people with these conditions if the cause can be attributed to the body, which is seen as more immutable/determinate than the mind. But then, are we really reducing psychological stigma in that case, or are we merely reducing stigma only on the basis of physical imperfection? Indirectly, the neurodivergent construct communicates to society that we are acceptable in our psychological otherness only insofar as the condition is based in a very rigid notion of the body as discrete causes and effects. This is a problemata in the history of ideas, because a common argument about the body is that mental phenomena can be rooted within it (i.e., embodied cognition) without a corresponding sense that the body can be embedded within the psyche, or even that physicality can be partly or wholly determined by mental phenomena. I also feel suspicious of neurodivergent labeling in my conditions because I actually do see them as syndromes or illnesses. The idea that neurodivergence is partly a failure of society to adapt to psychophysical diversity often leads to the conclusion that conditions like ADHD are not illnesses, but adaptations. It doesn't have to be so either/or: ADHD could simultaneously be a health problem and an adaptation. I feel like denying that these conditions involve symptoms in the manner of a syndrome or illness is comforting on a certain level, but not accurate. I would find it more heartening and impactful for stigma to be overcome/released in relation to illness, than for stigma to be denied and channeled into alternative forms of language that do little to address the actual problem: systems that have yet to develop maximally adequate supports for people whose lives are meaningfully impaired by these symptoms. It seems like the neurodivergent term allows us to hedge our bets by totally attributing a psychophysical experience (ADHD) to the biological element yet also denying the condition is an illness in the same manner that any other biologically based maladaptation would be. Last, neurodivergent feels like a defensive use of language to me, which tells me that there are underlying intrapsychic and interpersonal motivations involved. Rather than transpose my concerns onto a new vocabulary, I would favor understanding my representations of and resistance to everything the neurodivergent term seeks to address: a personal and social phobic reaction to illness resulting in stigma, a misattunement between psyche and context, a personal narrative of struggle in communicating the subjective experience of ADHD (i.e., alexithymia), and so forth.

question: Some people with ASD say they're just "not neurotypical." What does this mean?
answer: It is referring to the neurodiversity model. It was pioneered by a woman named Judy Singer in the late 90s to promote awareness and acceptance of everyone’s unique brains. There are various different ways that a brain can be “wired” and no brains are wired correctly or incorrectly, there isn’t a good or a bad way to think, there are just differences that should all be respected and embraced. There is a “neurotypical” brain wiring which refers to most people, and then there are a variety of other “neurodivergent” conditions. Autism is the most common diagnosis that people are talking about when referring to neurodivergent vs neurotypical, but there are others that are generally considered to be neurodivergent as well, such as ADHD, dyslexia, and dyscalculia. There are other diagnoses as well that are debated as to whether or not they “qualify” as neurodivergent (for example, I have heard people say that schizophrenia, Tourette’s, and bipolar disorder may also be considered neurodivergent). So when someone says they are “not neurotypical” they mean they are neurodivergent in some way. But what it comes down to is that just because someone’s brain may process things differently from the average/typical person doesn’t mean they have something WRONG with them. Embracing neurodiversity means celebrating all the different ways people think.

question: Is autism intimidating?
answer: To normies, very often! Normies find lots of traits and people intimidating that do not correspond to the “norm”. Normies often have a lot of in-group thinking and do not consider people who are diverse as part of their in-group. This isn’t only true for autistic people, but also people of other races, non-binary gender, etc. What’s more normies don’t understand the mind of autistic people. They often consider them rude or even feel threatened by autistic people, when all they do is to tell their honest opinion (this is taboo among normies - you can’t always say what you think). Autistic people often tend to get angry because of that - what normies don’t understand - this never proactive aggression, but reactive aggression. Sometimes normies consider autistic people “psychos”. Nothing could be further from the truth. As Simon Barron-Cohen writes: autistic people are the opposite of psychopaths: low on cognitive empathy, but high on affective empathy. Autistic people are more likely to help a stranger than normies! Read more about the social difficulties of autistic people on my blog How neurodiverse people are like hunter-gatherers: part II social behaviour How neurodiverse people are like hunter-gatherers: part II social behaviour For two years, I have been researching how neurodiverse (ASD, ADHD, gifted, etc.), people are like ancient hunter-gatherers. It hasn’t been an easy enterprise, as the only work that has ever pointed to an origin of neurodiverse minds in ancient hunter-gatherer minds has been Thom Hartmann’s “Hunter-Hypothesis” of ADHD. Personally, I am somewhat in between neurotypical and neurodiverse, testing around 50% on online autism tests and 75% on ADHD tests. Like most neurodiverse people, I have always had a hard time fitting in and I have a gifted son who learned to read by age two (hyperlexia) and who gets similar test results as I do. I generally do include the gifted label in my use of the word “neurodiverse”, to make it clear that not only people who are considered “having disabilities” belong to this group. Here is a preliminary list of potential hunter-gatherer traits: CognitiveDistractibility and hyperfocusField-independent learnersPattern-recognizersWider field of visionSocial:Less politeness/socially awkward (learn few social rules)EgalitarianDistrust of authoritarian behaviourHigh sense of justiceSupport the underdogExceptional honestyNo-ingroupism/nepotismLess gender dimorphismPhysiological:Chronotype (tend to be night owls)Hypersensitive to physical stimuli (sound, touch, etc.)Anatomical:Ectomorph body typesLater pubertyTend to look younger than their ageFor simplicity I’ll stick here with only two types: hunter-gatherer types and farmer types. I usually include a third type (pastoralist types), but people are often mixed and, of course, reality is much more complex.Here is a comparison between hunter-gatherer vs farmer types when it comes to social behaviour: One thing almost all neurodiverse people have in common is that they are somewhat socially awkward. This is most obvious in austistic people who struggle with cognitive empathy, but less obviously so also in other types of neurodiversity, such as ADHD (e.g. blurting out seemingly irrelevant statements). As discussed in my previous post, social learning and blindly following socially transmitted knowledge were much less important in hunter-gatherer societies than farmer societies for which tradition and adherence to social rules were highly important. There is a well-known correlation between historical irrigation agriculture and tightness of culture (i.e emphasising rules and conformity). Put these two togetherAbsence of a “conformity instinct”Weak social learningAdd: extreme honestyand you get pretty much what we know from neurodiverse children with their seemingly rude behaviour when all they do is really just being honest! Hunter-gatherers do not have a lot of social rules, least of all anything nearly resembling etiquette. Words like “please” or “thank you” or even “sorry” are frequently absent. Politeness and even more so etiquette are very puzzling to people with ASD and is often perceived as “brown-nosing” even by those hunter-gatherer types who do get it. They are very straightforward and don’t understand why normies have such strange rituals when meeting. What comes seemingly naturally to NTs is often highly confusing to aspies. They would feel instantly at ease with the Pirahã hunter-gatherers of the Amazonian jungle. Daniel Everett writes about them: Expressions like hello, good-bye, how are you?, I’m sorry, you’re welcome, and thank you don’t express or elicit new information about the world so much as they maintain goodwill and mutual respect. The Pirahã culture does not require this kind of communication. Pirahã sentences are either requests for information (questions), assertions of new information (declarations), or commands, by and large. There are no words for thanks, I’m sorry, and so on. I have become used to this over the years and forget most of the time how surprising this can be to outsiders. from: Don't Sleep, There Are Snakes Now let’s add the most important ingredient of instinctive hunter-gatherer behaviour: egalitarianism. This comes with a lot of other traits, like a distrust for anybody who wants to assume authority (particularly when not being especially competent). Another aspect of egalitarianism is not forming alliances against other people and taking sides with people who are unfairly treated. Hunter-gatherer children are therefore often averse to joining groups (that often have some “alpha” type people in them) and are therefore much more likely to become the victims of bullying: they are considered weird (not conforming) and they often have no network of “allies”, which makes them easy prey. On the flip side, neurodiverse people are quick to help a bullied person themselves. For a long time I believed this to be an effect of the feeling of being an underdog, but it’s really an instinct that is part of the egalitarianism bundle. For all teachers who are annoyed by ADHD kids: watch and marvel how they will fight for a kid who is treated unfairly! If they are aggressive towards a kid they are most likely the bully’s bully. Last, but not least, what makes neurodiverse outcasts are their special interests (e.g. trains, birdwatching, evolutionary psychology - for me). Often not even other neurodiverse children are interested in endless talk about trains or insects, or whatever the current interest. There are several reasons why the interests of hunter-gatherer type children are so different from their peers’:Intrinsic motivationField independent learningMore flow experiencesHunter-gatherer people are more intrinsically motivated, i.e. money, status, grades, etc. mean very little to them. Being field-independent learners, they are also not attuned to what is socially “cool”, i.e. they couldn’t be any cooler when it comes to "cool". And finally, once hunter-gatherer types find something they are interested in (in an otherwise boring farmer world), they experience flow much more frequently than other people. Farmer-types seem to have an in-built clock (always knowing what time it is) and experience time evenly. Hunter-gatherer types experience time very differently when in flow we forget about time completely. It’s not rare that a neurodiverse person stops being occupied with his special interest only to find out it’s already sunrise - a farmer type would have felt the need to sleep 9 hours ago (and wouldn’t have missed the time). So, to summarize, it should be pretty clear by now why for so many neurodiverse children school is a nightmarish experience: getting bullied, feeling overwhelmed by WORK loads, feeling like outsiders or even aliens, and having to face angry and occasionally authoritarian teachers. Authoritarian teachers are particularly likely to have difficulties with neurodiverse children, as being stricter often only worsens the situation, which can easily spiral out of control. My hunch is that most kids with oppositional defiant disorder are hunter-gatherer type children. When dealing with neurodiverse children, the first maxim every teacher has to keep in mind is: “Be kind!”. These children are not proactively aggressive, their aggression is reactive, even if it may not seem so, but the neurodiverse child may subjectively feel that he or she is being treated unfairly. School is a recipe for social anxiety for hunter-gatherer children, and social anxiety is indeed not rare for neurodiverse people to suffer from social anxiety and depression. Have you ever heard of Hikikomori? They are hunter-gatherer type teens, bet you?

question: Are gifted, highly gifted, exceptionally gifted and profoundly gifted people considered neurodiverse or neurotypical?
answer: When people talk about neurodiversity, they generally do not have gifted people in mind. You will come across different definitions. Many people think of ASD only, but others include ADHD, dyslexia, and other learning difficulties. Others like me also include gifted people and generally tend to think of neurodiverse as hunter-gatherer types and neurotypicals and farmer types. Here is why: How neurodiverse people are like hunter-gatherers: part I cognition January 01, 2021 For two years I have been researching how neurodiverse (ASD, ADHD, gifted, etc.) people are like ancient hunter-gatherers. It hasn’t been an easy enterprise, as the only work that has ever pointed to an origin of neurodiverse minds in ancient hunter-gatherer minds has been Thom Hartmann’s “Hunter-Hypothesis” of ADHD. Personally, I am somewhat in between neurotypical and neurodiverse, testing around 50% on online autism tests and 75% on ADHD tests. Like most neurodiverse people I have always had a hard time fitting in and I have a gifted son who learned to read by age two (hyperlexia) and who gets similar test results as I do. I generally do include the gifted label in my use of the word “neurodiverse”, to make it clear that not only people who are considered “having disabilities” belong to this group.Here is a preliminary list: CognitiveDistractibility and hyperfocusField-independent learnersPattern-recognizersWider field of visionSocial:Less politeness/socially awkward (learn few social rules)EgalitarianDistrust of authoritarian behaviourHigh sense of justiceSupport the underdogExceptional honestyNo-ingroupism/nepotismLess gender dimorphismPhysiological:Chronotype (tend to be night owls)Hypersensitive to physical stimuli (sound, touch, etc.)Anatomical:Ectomorph body typesLater pubertyTend to look younger than their ageFor simplicity, I’ll stick here with only two types: hunter-gatherer types and farmer types. I usually include a third type (pastoralist types), but people are often mixed and of course, the reality is much more complex.Here is a comparison between hunter-gatherer vs farmer types when it comes to cognition: Foraging and farming required different cognitive skills. One huge difference is that farming requires a sustained focus on long and boring tasks, whereas hunters are more easily distracted by all kinds of stimuli that may or may not be relevant. Once a stimulus is perceived as relevant (e.g. a track of a potential prey) the hunter keeps (hyper)focusing on it until the task is finished. Also, hunting skills are very different from farming skills. The latter requires tradition and much more social learning. Once a young grown up a farmer basically kept repeating the same tasks over and over. Hunting is very different, it can’t be learned by tradition and social learning is much less relevant. It’s not young grown-up hunters who are the best hunters (even though they might have a fitness advantage), but the older and more experienced hunters. Hunting requires therefore much more self-directed learning. Being high pattern-recognizers is another advantage. A hunter will perceive patterns leading to the prey that are imperceptible to, like recognizing from the patterns on the surface of the water where fish can be found. Neurodiverse people are therefore much more likely to recognize patterns that neurotypicals (farmer types) miss. As farmer-types were more dependent on social learning their cognition is more dependent on other people’s (e.g. teacher’s) opinions. Neurodiverse people are often independent of collective truth and tend to perceive patterns others don’t. Children with ASD and ADHD are also notorious for pointing out logical flaws in a teacher’s arguments, which may often get them into trouble with their teachers. All the more so, that hunter-gatherer minds don’t accept authority without competence and they may become straightforwardly rebellious if they perceive the teacher to treat them unjustly. Finally, I have come across a wider field of vision for hunter-gatherer types several times in my research. Scanning their environment for danger, prey and food sources foragers are more likely to have a wider field of vision than farmer types who have to focus long on routine work. This wider field of vision in hunter-gatherer types may interfere with learning to read as the learner may be more distracted by neighbouring letters or images. In combination with pattern-seeking a wide field of vision would not only allow a hunter to spot prey more easily, but also make a hunter a great astronomer. I estimate that about 90% of astronomers are hunter types and usually hunter type children can become obsessed with astronomy very early on (before schooling) from my experience with my own children. Most of the great geniuses and pattern-seekers in history (e.g. Edison and Einstein) had difficulties adapting to school and most Nobel Prize winners have few fond recollections of their time in school. Our different minds make it harder for us to go through the traditional school system. Hunter-gatherer type children are often among the gifted, but also among the twice-exceptional (2e) and more frequently among special ed children than farmer-type children. Even for those who are gifted, you often get the “brilliant but lazy” type of student. By now it should be clear that these brilliant students are not lazy but that their minds find it incredibly hard to focus on rote tasks and crave for more interesting stimulation. Instead of being able to show that they are super-learners, their boring school work turns them into super-procrastinators. Hunter-gatherer type children are often much better at self-directed learning (autodidacts) than learning in a classroom setting. I have met many neurodiverse children who had amazing skills to show off: knowing everything about insects or the solar system. And yet these children found it hard to learn telling the time when taught in school. Very often these self-directed hunter-gatherer type children are great at learning with computers, especially when they get to control their own learning. As a teacher, I have noticed that there are two types of students who love learning with computers, whereas the majority of children aren’t too happy about it or often even hate it. These two types are special-ed children and gifted children. They are really one type: hunter-gatherer types. Learning for hunter-gatherer type children is PLAY, learning for farmer type children is WORK. If learning turns into WORK for hunter-gatherer type children, they start to do poorly, if it remains PLAY they start to excel. The very same cognitive skills that helped our ancestors hunt prey often turn hunter-gatherer type children into super-gamers nowadays: hyper-focus, pattern-recognition, wide field of vision, and a sense of completing the mission and perfecting your hunting skills (a love for life-long learning).

question: How big is the "Autism Spectrum"?
answer: Its larger than he galaxy of disparate ideas that have spawned it, and which subsequently stood idly by while the nosological offspring have taken on mass exponentially. Any construct whose netting/catch-basin grows unimpeded, and which, subsequently, takes up more and more space over time—and in doing so, crowds out and forecloses on other explanatory paradigms—should be viewed through a more skeptical lens. This is especially true when that construct begins to adopt the trapping of a form of identity politics, at which point, it moves from the realm of pathology-meme to lifestyle choice. I am sure that people will react angrily to this missive; but before rendering judgment they might want to more carefully parse out some of the more loaded language and unexamined assumptions which often take refuge within those taxonomic baskets used to contain such promiscuously evaluative categories and typologies. A Pinata—in this case a theoretical one— can only grow so large until it bursts open. I believe Hanna Arndt had once written about the knowledge problem that occurs when a particular category gets so large that it begins to transform into a default explanation for all manner of phenomenon. At that point, the category itself begins to determine and shape what goes into it, much like a Procrustean bed, which adjusts the body sleeping upon it to neatly fit within its own specific and rigid contours. This usually signifies a growing epistemological issue with that system of knowledge; one which may raise important questions concerning criterion, diagnoses, the expertise of those doing the diagnosing (how they purport to know what they know, and what methodological complexities and distortions loom behind the accumulation of such knowledge) and liminality. This isn't to say that there is no truth in the diagnoses, only that the way such differences are now being defined says a lot about the requisite structures of those institutions which necessitate and create the need for the taxonomic growth-industry that accompanies their redefinition (IE, discovery), and the various technologies used to identify, diagnose and situate them as viable DSM entities. If the language I am using sounds convoluted it is not because my thinking is manipulative, but because the process I am describing is also convoluted. I expect that this post will either be ignored, or that it will prompt a lot of very angry answers from people who are, maybe, apt to cherry pick certain statements in it while ignoring the larger context. I do not block people or delete answers, but others have often done that after I have responded. I can’t do anything about the ad hominem that may ensue; all I can say is that it wouldn’t be the first time that I have gotten someone really angry. Usually, they are misreading me. I do not say that the phenomenon is imaginary, only that the borders separating it from other neatly defined states, as part of a binary (IE neurodiverse vs, neurotypical) are far too simplistic and ignore liminal overlap, as well as the existential questions that exist outside of such neatly divided categories of being. It is the larger cultural conversation that creates the boundaries upon which such categories rest; different contexts often lead to differing interpretations. In an age of Utilitarian science, which seeks consensus within a larger and very messy human cultural maelstrom, everything is automatically redefined as a question requiring a, scientific, or quantifiable interpretation. It is this tendency which I would take issue with., as it frames everything within a reductionist and misleading paradigm.

question: Is "fat acceptance" a good thing or bad thing?
answer: This is another one of those nasty either/or situations, that makes for a potentially untenable position, no matter which side is chosen. If you say it’s a good thing, howls of protest will erupt in the form of health advisories, the prevalence of diabetes, and how the attitude is undermining acceptable standards. If you say it’s a bad thing, the roof will come down and you’ll be condemned for shaming, for being judgmental, and valuing people only for their physical appearance. No matter which camp you decide commit to, it’s a losing proposition. It’s a debate that’s set up for failure. When facing this sort of topic, I try to step back and anchor things like this into a larger context, and avoid absolute commitments to a single side. For example, in our contemporary society, there is an axiom at work which goes something like, “my ignorance is as valid as your knowledge.” This creates all sorts of scenarios where people pit themselves against each other, in defense of their “territory,” their truth: Science vs. pseudo science, Atheists vs. Theists, Conspiracy Theory vs. the Narrative, Neurodiverse vs. Neurotypical. That I do enjoy the challenge of writing answers that address those topics, among others, is due, I believe to the freedom I’ve given myself to not make a 100% commitment to anything intellectual. I’m not the final source, so I don’t need to pretend to be. Likewise, in our contemporary society, “__________ is beautiful” now carries with it a certain prestige, and endorses an end all/be all justification. Body positivity is the buzzword associated with this phenomenon. My opinion? It’s probably two parts insecurity, one part delusion, mixed together with some wishful thinking. My educated guess is that it is a handy way to avoid the hard work and effort that would be required to make a change. I think the “acceptance” phenomenon provides temporary relief, but is probably an unsatisfactory substitute for being a little more honest and facing squarely the issue at hand.

question: Do autistic people have a more objective perception of reality than neurotypical people?
answer: I think the answer has to inevitably be a yes, from, to use the turn of phrase from the Matrix and very much in that context, a Red Pill vs Blue Pill dichotomy. We know from the discovery of Milton’s Double Empathy problem, that those of us who are neurodiverse and those who are neurotypical have profoundly different ways of not only seeing the world, but incredibly difficulty with having how the other sees the world, resonate with us.. However when it comes to social engineering, the profound difference is that this is very much a neurotypical’s world. Being in the majority, it is neurotypicals rather than those of us who are neurodiverse, who have decided on the rules, customs and acceptable range of behaviour of society. This is also a critical difference between how both groups perceive and interact with not only society, but the world as a whole. The sad truth about human nature is that when humans are comfortable, we cease to question, to explore and to discover. Why rock the boat when everything is “all roses and sunshine”, right? In this regard, the lived experience of neurotypicals might indeed be compared to the Matrix, as in both cases, you are talking about accepted reality, which compels all too readily given conformity and compliance - to the point where most neurotypicals might as well be in a permanent living dream. It’s the inverse for those of us who are neurodiverse. We are the lepers, the “social deviants”, the “outcasts”, the “freaks”. We do not fit in, because the very social contract itself was designed in a manner where it is impossible for us to fit in. We can never get comfortable or complacent, because this neurotypical world, simply doesn’t allow us that luxury. More to the point, the very nature of our masking requires to observe and consciously adapt as best we can. In the analogy of the Matrix, this is very much a red pill reality. In such a state, people who are the perpetual outsider can only observe what is there from a forced- 50,000 ft overview and see things for how they are. Ironically, doing so, simply further results in those of us who are neurodiverse being ostracised. We are naturally more accurately able to perceive the world, because we are free of the constraints of neurotypical societal norms. In fact this even reminds me of Morpheus’ monologue during the scene with the woman in the red dress:“The Matrix is a system, Neo. That system is our enemy. But when you're inside, you look around, what do you see? Businessmen, teachers, lawyers, carpenters. The very minds of the people we are trying to save. But until we do, these people are still a part of that system and that makes them our enemy. You have to understand, most of these people are not ready to be unplugged. And many of them are so inured, so hopelessly dependent on the system, that they will fight to protect it.”Sadly, that perspective is both the curse and the blessing of Milton’s Double Empathy Problem, when you are neurodiverse.

On the other hand, neurodiverse individuals display higher rates of fluid intelligence, which indicates novel, outside-the-box, approaches to learning. A neurodiverse person may not approach a task in the same way, even if they have already learned a successful method, because the fluidity of their intelligence, in context, is non habit-forming. question: Can you explain what a neuro type is and how it can be determined? What are the differences between each type?
answer: Sure Bro! Here is the Explanation : What is a Neurotype? A neurotype refers to the inherent wiring of an individual's brain, encompassing their neurological make-up, which influences how they think, behave, and interact with the world. Neurotypes can be considered as variations in brain function and cognitive processes that contribute to an individual's personality, preferences, and behavioral tendencies. The concept of neurotyping is often used in discussions about neurodiversity, which recognizes and respects the different ways in which brains can function and develop. Determining Neurotypes Neurotypes are typically identified through a combination of self-assessment, psychological evaluation, and sometimes neuropsychological testing. Factors considered include:Behavioral Patterns: Observations of how individuals respond to various situations, their social interactions, and coping mechanisms.Cognitive Assessments: Tests that measure different aspects of cognitive functioning, such as memory, attention, problem-solving skills, and sensory processing.Personality Assessments: Tools like the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) or Big Five personality traits can provide insights into an individual’s typical responses and preferences.Medical and Psychological Evaluations: Professional evaluations by psychologists, psychiatrists, or neurologists may involve clinical interviews and diagnostic tests to understand neurological and psychological conditions.Differences Between Neurotypes The term "neurotype" is broad and can encompass various categorizations. Some common frameworks include: 1. Neurodivergent vs. NeurotypicalNeurotypical: Refers to individuals whose neurological development and functioning are typical or average, as per societal standards. They usually don't experience significant cognitive or behavioral differences.Neurodivergent: Refers to individuals whose neurological development and functioning are significantly different from the average. This includes conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, dyslexia, and others. Neurodivergent individuals often have unique strengths and challenges in their cognitive and behavioral patterns.2. Personality-Based Neurotypes Some frameworks, like those used in neurotyping for fitness and coaching (e.g., Christian Thibaudeau’s Neurotyping System), classify people based on neurotransmitter dominance and personality traits:Type 1A: Dominant in dopamine, characterized by high confidence, risk-taking, and competitive nature. They prefer short, intense training sessions.Type 1B: Also dopamine-dominant but more coordinated and explosive. They are often seen in roles requiring precision and quick reactions.Type 2A: Balanced between dopamine and adrenaline. They are adaptable, thrive on variety, and can handle both high-intensity and endurance training.Type 2B: Adrenaline-dominant, sensitive to stimuli, emotional, and empathetic. They excel in activities requiring mind-muscle connection and aesthetic-focused training.Type 3: Dominant in serotonin, characterized by high anxiety, methodical and detail-oriented behavior. They prefer routine, structured training with gradual progression.Key Differences Between NeurotypesCognitive Processing: Differences in how information is processed, stored, and retrieved.Behavioral Responses: Variations in how individuals respond to stimuli, stress, and social interactions.Sensory Perception: Differences in sensory sensitivity or sensory processing.Emotional Regulation: Variations in emotional responses and coping mechanisms.Social Interaction: Differences in social skills, preferences for social interaction, and communication styles.Conclusion Neurotypes highlight the diversity in human brain function and behavior. Recognizing and understanding neurotypes can foster better self-awareness, improve interpersonal relationships, and encourage inclusive practices that respect and accommodate different ways of thinking and functioning.

question: Has being diagnosed with autism as an adult been of any help to you?

The longer I travel down this path of self-discovery,,, of rewriting my entire life with an autistic perspective, and understanding, the more I begin to realize how unique of an experience this has been and will continue to be. Autism is not a neurotypical neurological system with Autism added. It is a Autistic Neurological System. The reason people with autism struggle like they do is in part , because we are trying to fit into a neurotypically evolved society. Our neurological system wants to be in an environment that compliments how that system functions. Lets take language for example. What I’m seeing as the difference in the use of NT vs ND language is that because of the NT’s needs to reinforce social cohesion, language rituals are used to check and maintain the integrity of these social connections - We call it “small talk”. It is not intended ( as IS within the autistic community) to exchange vital information, or to teach/ learn new information, or clarify misunderstandings etc etc… It is basically to affirm that social relationships are maintaining a status quo. Neurodiverse people have other ways to judge within OUR community what social status is.. and we then use communication as stated above. We have different emotional and physical needs - This is why some self stim. We are more comfortable forming routines for repetitive tasks. If I could have my perfect work environment, I’d be able to sleep when needed and be on an 8 - 5 work cycle. You asked has knowing I’m autistic helped me? Yes - it has unlocked an understanding I was literally searching for all my life. This is the first step needed to being and living my best. Unfortunately, society is still woefully ignorant and unaccommodating to the needs of people with autism. Because people with autism have been so misunderstood we are still exploring and learning our own needs. Neurotypical people can learn about themselves from the system they live in that supports THIER needs. We don’t have that advantage and in a sense have to create our own system in each of our lives. This will change as our communities grow and we share OUR systems with each other. I hope this explanation gives people without autism, a better understanding of how important it is that our autism is identified, and we are allowed to be what our minds and bodies need us to be. We have so much to offer to the world. Unfortunately, we are struggling just trying to survive in an often hostile society where our differences are dismissed as unimportant and strange.

question: Why do some people with autism not realize that they have it?
answer: When you think of a person with autism, what image springs to mind? (Your very first thought.) Likely, this person is:CaucasianChildMaleAnd if not, probably it's a specific person who comes to mind — your niece, a television character, your coworker's brother, your own child, etc. Most of us have limited exposure to what autism looks like, both in the media and in our own personal lives. So it's easy to think, “I'm different from that person, who is the face of autism to me, and therefore I must not have autism myself.” For me as a 40-year-old female, homeschooled, who came of age before the golden age of autism diagnosis, it's no wonder that I didn't connect the dots until the age of 34. I had been reading up autism for the sake of a family member who was potentially autistic, and saw myself in the research more than I saw them. It was a shock to say the least — yet it ended up being the greatest gift because it explained sooooo much of my past life that I'd written off as confusing and unknowable! Things finally made sense. And now that I've joined various autism communities, I see how diverse we really are. Lately I've been likening it to an iOS vs. Android comparison — if allistics/neurotypicals are iPhones and autists/neurodiverse are Androids, there's still a whole lot of variety in betweenst individual phones, from the manufacturer, to the apps one has chosen to install, and more. (Yes, similarities are present, but they’re at the operating system level.)Why did it take so long to discover my autism? I knew I wasn't an iPhone, but neither was I a purple Samsung. I didn't fit the only model I knew. I suspect this is the case for many.

question: What do neurodiverse and neurotypical mean?
answer: You will come across different definitions. Many people think of ASD only, but others include ADHD, dyslexia, and other learning difficulties etc. I also include gifted people and generally tend to think of neurodiverse as hunter-gatherer types and neurotypicals and farmer types. Here is why: How neurodiverse people are like hunter-gatherers: part I cognition January 01, 2021 For two years I have been researching how neurodiverse (ASD, ADHD, gifted, etc.) people are like ancient hunter-gatherers. It hasn’t been an easy enterprise, as the only work that has ever pointed to an origin of neurodiverse minds in ancient hunter-gatherer minds has been Thom Hartmann’s “Hunter-Hypothesis” of ADHD. Personally, I am somewhat in between neurotypical and neurodiverse, testing around 50% on online autism tests and 75% on ADHD tests. Like most neurodiverse people I have always had a hard time fitting in and I have a gifted son who learned to read by age two (hyperlexia) and who gets similar test results as I do. I generally do include the gifted label in my use of the word “neurodiverse”, to make it clear that not only people who are considered “having disabilities” belong to this group.Here is a preliminary list: CognitiveDistractibility and hyperfocusField-independent learnersPattern-recognizersWider field of visionSocial:Less politeness/socially awkward (learn few social rules)EgalitarianDistrust of authoritarian behaviourHigh sense of justiceSupport the underdogExceptional honestyNo-ingroupism/nepotismLess gender dimorphismPhysiological:Chronotype (tend to be night owls)Hypersensitive to physical stimuli (sound, touch, etc.)Anatomical:Ectomorph body typesLater pubertyTend to look younger than their ageFor simplicity, I’ll stick here with only two types: hunter-gatherer types and farmer types. I usually include a third type (pastoralist types), but people are often mixed and of course, the reality is much more complex.Here is a comparison between hunter-gatherer vs farmer types when it comes to cognition: Foraging and farming required different cognitive skills. One huge difference is that farming requires a sustained focus on long and boring tasks, whereas hunters are more easily distracted by all kinds of stimuli that may or may not be relevant. Once a stimulus is perceived as relevant (e.g. a track of a potential prey) the hunter keeps (hyper)focusing on it until the task is finished. Also, hunting skills are very different from farming skills. The latter requires tradition and much more social learning. Once a young grown up a farmer basically kept repeating the same tasks over and over. Hunting is very different, it can’t be learned by tradition and social learning is much less relevant. It’s not young grown-up hunters who are the best hunters (even though they might have a fitness advantage), but the older and more experienced hunters. Hunting requires therefore much more self-directed learning. Being high pattern-recognizers is another advantage. A hunter will perceive patterns leading to the prey that are imperceptible to, like recognizing from the patterns on the surface of the water where fish can be found. Neurodiverse people are therefore much more likely to recognize patterns that neurotypicals (farmer types) miss. As farmer-types were more dependent on social learning their cognition is more dependent on other people’s (e.g. teacher’s) opinions. Neurodiverse people are often independent of collective truth and tend to perceive patterns others don’t. Children with ASD and ADHD are also notorious for pointing out logical flaws in a teacher’s arguments, which may often get them into trouble with their teachers. All the more so, that hunter-gatherer minds don’t accept authority without competence and they may become straightforwardly rebellious if they perceive the teacher to treat them unjustly. Finally, I have come across a wider field of vision for hunter-gatherer types several times in my research. Scanning their environment for danger, prey and food sources foragers are more likely to have a wider field of vision than farmer types who have to focus long on routine work. This wider field of vision in hunter-gatherer types may interfere with learning to read as the learner may be more distracted by neighbouring letters or images. In combination with pattern-seeking a wide field of vision would not only allow a hunter to spot prey more easily, but also make a hunter a great astronomer. I estimate that about 90% of astronomers are hunter types and usually hunter type children can become obsessed with astronomy very early on (before schooling) from my experience with my own children. Most of the great geniuses and pattern-seekers in history (e.g. Edison and Einstein) had difficulties adapting to school and most Nobel Prize winners have few fond recollections of their time in school. Our different minds make it harder for us to go through the traditional school system. Hunter-gatherer type children are often among the gifted, but also among the twice-exceptional (2e) and more frequently among special ed children than farmer-type children. Even for those who are gifted, you often get the “brilliant but lazy” type of student. By now it should be clear that these brilliant students are not lazy but that their minds find it incredibly hard to focus on rote tasks and crave for more interesting stimulation. Instead of being able to show that they are super-learners, their boring school work turns them into super-procrastinators. Hunter-gatherer type children are often much better at self-directed learning (autodidacts) than learning in a classroom setting. I have met many neurodiverse children who had amazing skills to show off: knowing everything about insects or the solar system. And yet these children found it hard to learn telling the time when taught in school. Very often these self-directed hunter-gatherer type children are great at learning with computers, especially when they get to control their own learning. As a teacher, I have noticed that there are two types of students who love learning with computers, whereas the majority of children aren’t too happy about it or often even hate it. These two types are special-ed children and gifted children. They are really one type: hunter-gatherer types. Learning for hunter-gatherer type children is PLAY, learning for farmer type children is WORK. If learning turns into WORK for hunter-gatherer type children, they start to do poorly, if it remains PLAY they start to excel. The very same cognitive skills that helped our ancestors hunt prey often turn hunter-gatherer type children into super-gamers nowadays: hyper-focus, pattern-recognition, wide field of vision, and a sense of completing the mission and perfecting your hunting skills (a love for life-long learning).

question: How do non-autistic people know they're allistic/neurotypical/not on the autism spectrum?
answer: I interpreted the question not as the universal definition of normalcy but simply as turning around the usual question "How do you know you're autistic?" Considering the broader definition of neurodiversity, this could be stated "How do you know you lack neurological differences?" Under either definition, I find this a very valuable question. It is part of human nature to create ways to identify the Other but not necessarily to think of how they know they aren't in the same category, or realize that the dividing line can be like the edge of a fogbank instead of a brick wall. The people on the other side of the wall are clearly separated from you, and it's easy to tell Us from Them. They're not like Us, and we can keep Them over there because They don't belong in Our Society. They're different, after all. But if there are people distributed between the clear air and the thickest part of the fog, which ones are Us and which are Them? Obviously we could think of the ones who have disappeared into the fog as Them, but what about the people whose outlines you can see, but not the details? The people whose features are slightly blurred by the fog? The people who are barely touched by misty edges of the fog? Should we look at this as Us vs. Them and argue over the dividing line, or simply acknowledge that a binary separation is unproductive? Should we perhaps focus instead on helping people lost in the fog find their way back, with flashlights or even ropes to hold? The traits associated with autism and other neurological differences exist along a continuum. Some people express these traits so strongly that they appear obviously different and may have difficulty navigating a society designed by and for the general population, so much so that they may be treated like an inferior species. Others have lesser degrees of difference along these scales and blend accordingly into the general population. Because these traits are expressed at varied levels, people assume they have no neurological differences unless they've received a diagnosis. Very frequently, parents whose children are diagnosed with autism spectrum disorders recognize the signs in themselves after these have been pointed out to them. Some go on to get a formal diagnosis, but many do not if they seem to be getting along well enough. Instead of worrying about Us vs. Them to exclude autistics and people with other neurological differences, we could focus on providing supports so that they can participate in society.
