question: Do people with autism tend to struggle more with gender identity issues? If so, why?
answer: Q > Do people with autism tend to struggle more with gender identity issues? If so, why?Short answer: It’s not that simple. Long answer: The majority of people deal with their identity through affirmation. The most common example, that is subsequently enforced through a gender bias is going to be boy vs girl. With both being treated quite differently yet both finding plenty of recognition within their respective groups. But these things extend beyond that. It’s not strange that most people will have some identity struggles as they go through puberty as their body is quite literally changing on them. Even if you were to ignore the purely physical changes there are neurological/chemical changes that affect internal workings and perception. So as you grow up, you form a certain image of yourself. Your identity. And as you go through puberty this identity is challenged. Some people struggle more with this than others. But on the whole most end up figuring it out eventually.Now we look at someone on the autistic spectrum - or really anyone with some form of neurodiversity. Their perception of themselves and the world around them is inherently different from most neurotypical people. Yet all aspects of identity end up being enforced and affirmed from a neurotypical perspective. To make matters worse? Even now, as more and more people become familiar with autism and neurodiversity. More often than not if someone were to relay their perception as someone with autism a large part of society will not respond in a positive manner. So when everyone around you tells you one thing, but you experience another? What do you think happens? One of the major underlying problems is that there is no one ‘template’ for autism. While colloquially we say autism, there’s a reason why it’s defined as Autism Spectrum Disorder. The key part being spectrum, not disorder. This gets even more complicated for those on the spectrum who are also affected when it comes to communication. It’s one thing to experience things differently but at least be able to relay (or try to) those differences to others. It’s a completely different story when you can’t really do so. Ergo:Not everyone with autism or other forms of neurodiversity will deal with (gender) identity issues per se, but plenty of them will at one point or another and in one form or another.Of those that do, the nature of the identity issues will very much be related to the nature of how they differ from the people around them and how willing those around them are to accept those differences.Finally the ability to communicate these differences is also going to play a major role.Finally it’s important to understand - both for people who are dealing with these kinds of issues and those who have someone who is dealing with an identity problem around them. You won’t always get a clean resolution. Sometimes the best you can hope for is find a sort-of neutral balancing point where the issue no longer (negatively) affects your daily life. But don’t assume that because you can’t *see* the problem that it’s gone. That might well be one of the major contributors. People who assume that there is no problem because the person doesn’t seem like they have one. “You don’t seem *blank* at all?” Just because they no longer visibly deal with the issue, doesn’t mean that they aren’t still dealing with it internally.
comment_answer: Many struggle with the concept of gender because of their autism. Many others don't. A lot of us are in some way gender non-conforming as a result of being autistic because we often don't conform to societal norms in general. Our brains are wired different. Many who appear to conform are just masking but by no means all.

question: Is it easier/better to raise a kid in Europe vs the US?
answer: I'm in the UK. Like Cheryl Koevoet I'm the mother of an autistic child. My experience could hardly be more different to hers, which goes to the point many people have already made about the folly of lumping all of Europe together. I've told this story elsewhere, but to briefly recap - my son’s preschool key worker was the first person to suggest that we have some assessments done. The assessment process was very thorough, and took a year all told. Following the diagnosis, we were offered access to training courses for parents of autistic children. These sessions were aimed at educating us about autism, and helping us understand our children. Nine months after diagnosis, my son entered mainstream education with an IEP and support already in place. He had seen various professionals already, and the school were fully aware of his needs. Within a month, he had 30 hours of one-to-one support. This continued for three years. I am writing this on 20 September 2016. My son has been going to the county special school for just over two weeks. It became apparent last year that mainstream was no longer a viable option for him. We visited a lot of special schools, autism schools and units in our area, and were accepted to our first choice. He's doing very well - his anxiety has reduced enormously, and he's happy to go to school again. Yay!! Here's a really big difference between our experience and the experience of some parents in other countries - the special school isn't offering a ‘cure’. They aren't doing 30 hours of therapy a week to ‘fix’ him. They ARE working on life skills, social interaction, and sensory management in a way that respects and is sensitive to the individual unique needs of each child. Their goal is to enable the child to be independent, if possible. Or if not, then to be able to access and engage with as much of life as they can. They could not care less about making them appear neurotypical. Our main autism charity, the National Autistic Society, very much takes the neurodiversity perspective. Indeed, all the autism professionals I've come into contact with seem to have this view. The Autism Speaks approach that autism is a disease which has stolen our children just doesn't seem to be a mainstream opinion over here. I think it's much better to be the parent of an autistic child in my part of the UK than in many other places. The support isn't perfect (we badly need more speech therapists in this area), but it's pretty good. We have been very lucky.

question: Does the term “neurodiversity” do more harm than good?
answer: No, I don’t think think it does. For background, my son is an autistic mostly nonverbal adult. He has intractable epilepsy. I am not autistic. I believe I would fit a diagnosis for sensory processing disorder. I don’t seek a diagnosis because it would be expensive and would not change much. I adjust my life to be comfortable. I think as intended the neurodiversity movement is positive. The idea that it is the human experience to have neurological differences and disability is good for all people. Those should be accommodated and accepted. Individuals should be valued. Disability is not a slur. It is human. My son is no less than any other person. Yet he has experienced ableism from medical professionals, educators, proponents of neurodiversity, and the public. Medical professionals find treating a difficult condition in a disabled patient not worthwhile. Educators may assume he cannot learn. Neurodiverse individuals may marginalize him by not accepting that he has a different viewpoint than they do. He wants treatment for his medical conditions; they may not have comorbid conditions that affect their functioning as he does. The public may view him as tragic and me as heroic for accepting and loving him. That’s bullshit at its best. It’s not just about differences vs. disability. He accepts himself as an individual. They need to as well. In my opinion neurodiversity only becomes an issue when individuals co-opt it and make it only about themselves and their experiences and traits. All autistic people do not fit an Asperger’s diagnosis. The range of support needs is a part of neurodiversity. Nobody speaks for others without express consent. Yet some purport to speak for others within the neurodiverse community. It isn’t a competition or a linear spectrum. It’s the range of possibilities and those require different approaches. All voices need to be heard. It’s easy to lump all people into two rigid groups, autistic and not. People who are not autistic are no more alike than autistic people are. Yet it’s cool to talk about people who are not autistic as if they are all identical. We need to check ourselves every time we say, “Neurotypicals…” Which neurotypical are we talking about? The one who is an introvert, the one who doesn’t enjoy small talk? Because some people who are not autistic are introverted. Basically it boils down to one thing. Stereotypes don’t work. We need to accept that individuals have different needs and not make it about the group as a whole having the same opinions and needs.

question: Is Donald Trump an excellent example of what a neurotypical is like?
answer: Characteristics The terms “neurotypical” and “neurodiverse” originated as a more comprehensive way to describe autism. Currently, these terms aren’t recognized in the medical community, but are used by some in the autism community. Instead of seeing autism as a disorder, it’s a way to recognize the rich differences, abilities, and strengths individuals with autism have. According to some theorists, autism can be describedTrusted Source as a human variant with extreme advantages. Instead of seeing autism as a disorder that needs fixing, they see autism as a characteristic of an individual, like having brown hair or being left-handed. Being neurodiverse simply means having a brain that’s wired differently. Some individuals who support the use of neurotypical and neurodiverse believe that autism doesn’t need a cure. They believe the differences it presents in people should be respected, not feared or belittled. A group of people within the autism community sometimes use the term “neurotypical” in a way that says individuals who aren’t on the spectrum can be lacking in strengths that those on the spectrum have. For example, they may be too focused on material things or go along with social norms that can be hurtful or destructive to themselves or others. Not everyone in the autism community agrees that autism isn’t a disorder, so the terms are still somewhat controversial. Some believe that autism is a disorder, so it deserves research and funding to help find a cure. Studies of autism have found that there are certain brain structure and neurotransmitter abnormalities in individuals with autism. What characterizes neurotypical? Neurotypical individuals are often described in relation to individuals with autism, so they may have: no problem interacting with peers or having a conversation no noticeable speech delays as children no sensory issues, such as not being able to tolerate crowds, loud noises, or being too hot or too cold the ability to adapt to change What characterizes the neurodiverse? The signs of autism can vary and may be different for older individuals vs. children, for example. The National Institute of Stroke and Neurological Disorders lists the following as typical signs of someone who is neurodiverse: a lack of babbling or pointing by the age of 12 months poor eye contact no smiling or social responsiveness not responding to their name fixation on lining up toys or objects that appears more than typical no single words by the age of 16 months no two-word phrases by age of 2 years In older individuals, signs can include: low social interaction inability to initiate or hold a conversation lack of social play repetitive language intense, focused interest, usually on an object or subject fixation on certain routines or rituals

question: Is anyone really neurotypical?
answer: This is honestly one of the most subjective questions I haver ever came across. Neurotypical implies normality, in the sense that everything a person says, does, believes in, and senses are within what is considered both culturally and socially acceptable. Take Chinese culture for example: we tend to be relatively humble compared to Western societies, where confidence and power are seen as socially desirable traits. Asian cultures in general also depend less on indirect communication such as body language, facial expressions, etc. We tend to say wat we mean and interpret their words at face value. Being a Chinese immigrant ever since coming to Canada I’ve learned that there is quite some “reading between the lines” in Western styles of communication. Also being on the spectrum I can either “blame” my lack of social awareness on my cultural difference or my ASD… (you get the point). Then there is the topic of character. Different personalities usually present with varying characters and morals . For example someone who is achievement driven and conscientious might appreciate hard work over creativity, whereas it’s the other way around for an open-minded person. Someone high in agreeableness might easily sympathize with a neurodiverse person despite speaking a different “social language”. A very neurotic person is not as likely as an emotionally stable person to call someone mentally ill. As for autistics, we tend to be accepted by NT introverts far more than NT extroverts. At the end of the day there isn’t a distinct line between neurotypical vs neuro-atypical. It all depends on the specific criteria you are measuring someone up against.

question: Can a parent raise their child to be more neurotypical than they were raised themselves, especially if said parent was on the autism spectrum themselves?
answer: To act more neurotypical? Probably. question: What are your thoughts on neurodiversity and its importance/side effects in the society?
answer: I’ve seen the term “neurodiversity” used in different ways. I originally thought of it as just a medical term ND vs NT. That there is not a right/wrong or good/bad type of neurology - they are different and normal unto themselves. They are only unusual or abnormal from one’s own neurological point of reference. question: I'm autistic & say I wanted to have a child with a neurotypical man. What are the chances of autism passing down to our child?
answer: There's a strong chance the child of a NT and ND individual will have traits -- if not a full-blown presentation -- of neurodiversity. Twin studies have shown that ASD is roughly 80% genetically linked, the rest environmental (nature vs nurture). Now, this isn't to say there's a 100% chance your child will be autistic, but will have a strong disposition towards autism or asd-like traits. An “advanced maternal age" (above roughly 38) increases the risk of developmental disabilities (due to lower quality eggs), which compounds with the predisposition to heightened chance of autism.

question: Could extreme autistic overloads or meltdowns actually be mild Exited Catatonia or even schizophrenia? Is the resistance to these labels due to denial?
answer: The problem you’re running into here is that there is a limited number of human behaviours (neurotypical, neurodiverse, and psychiatric), so there is bound to be some cross-over of behaviour among NT, ND, and Ps. For example, autistic meltdowns are really not that different to NT toddler tantrums. The difference is that autistic meltdowns can happen at all ages, and are often completely irrational - even compared with toddler tantrums. A toddler will throw a tantrum when thwarted - being refused a large bar of chocolate, having to go to bed, etc., etc. Reasons that make a certain kind of sense, as trying as it can be for the unfortunate parent dealing with it. Autistic meltdowns … don’t make sense, unless you can get into the autistic headspace. My cousin, who appears on the surface to be NT - very sociable, only slightly nerdy (which is mostly overset by the fact that he is tall, dark and handsome, and gets away with a lot because of that) - goes into violent meltdown if a single thing is out of place in his room in sheltered accommodation, or in his childhood bedroom at home. That absolutely is NOT reasonable or rational, except through the lens of the autistic need for environmental control. He’s the same age as me - 55 - and his bedroom at home is still full of cuddly toys and Legos, ffs. I’m autistic too, and I barely understand it. Similarly, autistic overload is not that different to NT stress. The difference is that autistic overload is more frequent, and triggered by different (and often irrational) things. I have zero reaction to NT stress. Overwork, bereavement, house moving, all the things that cause NTs to collapse, don’t bother me - I can cope with them, because I can think/plan ways out of the impact. But present me with a situation that I can’t think my way out of, an obstacle I can’t get over, and I’m foetal and sobbing in a corner, complete with stereotypy, shaking, repetitive speech and motor restlessness. It’s like exCited catatonia, but it isn’t. Just leave me alone, and I’ll calm down. I’m not going to hurt myself or anyone else.You need to think of autistic behaviours in the same way as symptoms of illness. For example, a cough can be a symptom of the common cold, the flu, COVID-19, bronchitis, bronchiolitis, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, asthma, pharyngitis, costochondritis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, choking, cystic fibrosis, sarcoidosis, lung cancer… It can even be caused by some drugs, like ACE inhibitors. Similarly, you’re going to find that autistic “symptoms” are common to other neurodivergent conditions, psychiatric disorders, and neurotypical behaviour. The differences are in theaetiology (causative event - e.g., common cold vs cancer),in schizophrenia, the aetiology of a behaviour is often in a skewed understanding of reality;in autism, it’s mainly something in the environment that the autist can’t control, e.g., someone moved their Legos.frequency (e.g., frequent infection vs rare cell mutations resulting in tumour),in schizophrenia, the skewed perceptions are of extended duration, though actual episodes may be relatively infrequent;in autism, the episodes may be quite frequent, but of relatively short durationprognosis (disease course - e.g., recovery in days vs death/recovery after treatment)in schizophrenia, the behaviour may occur once and never reappear, or it may be recurrent. Medication may control or eradicate the behaviour;in autism, the behaviour will probably reappear throughout life. Medications, and other treatments, have only a limited effect, if at all.Hope this helps!

question: What is the definition of neurotypical and autism?
answer: I prefer the framework of “autistic” vs. “non-autistic”. The reason is, there is no real “typical” brain, and there are many forms of neurodiversity. Being Gifted is a form of neurodiversity, as is Bipolar, Schizophrenia, and various language and learning impairments. A better question is “How is Autism Unique to other Neurodiverse Conditions?” Autism is different than any other form of neurodiversity in the following ways: 1) Memory encoding is different because the autistic baby does not look at faces and eyes. Blindness to social information, a lack of the sense of “We” (vs. Me) in experiences, and a focus on objects will impact the developing child’s schemas about the world, and how to create meaning from experiences. Non-autistic babies use their parents as a critical reference point in the world as they begin to interact with object. The autistic baby does not. 2) There is abundant research discussing differences in static vs. dynamic functioning and information processing, from visual processing (differences in perception of biological motion for example). These are the things that will hold an autistic adult back in life. The intact ability to follow rules and scripts and black and white problem-solving, but difficulty adapting to changing, dynamic circumstances and information (which yes ,much of that is also social nonverbal information). Episodic memory, self-awareness, experience-sharing communication, creative problem-solving and flexibility are the main areas that research shows a consensus on core features of autism, regardless of language and IQ. 3) IQ does not compensate for autism in terms of quality of life. In general populations quality of life improves as IQ increases. This is not true for autism. As long as the individual has an IQ that does not fall in the extremely low end (which would indicate co-occurring conditions, not just autism), there is not a significant difference in highly verbal vs minimally verbal or average IQ vs. higher IQ for autistic people. This is because the areas impacted by autism are so pervasive they create significant barriers to functioning on many levels. (And this is why if your child’s “autism program” is mostly school skills and academically oriented, you are likely not addressing root causes.)

question: Are you an honest person or is it just your autism?
answer: People generally do not consider me autistic, but like people on the spectrum, I have always had difficulties not telling the truth. Honesty is one of the most important traits I value in other people too. Billy Joel’s song “Honesty” one of my all-time favourites. Just wrote a blog post about it: Beautiful minds - the egalitarian side of autism January 24, 2021 The movie “A Beautiful Mind” is among my favourite movies, featuring one of my favourite scientists, John Nash, who received the Nobel Prize in economics for his contributions to Game Theory. The movie focuses on his paranoid schizophrenia, but it’s hard not to notice how he was also on the spectrum and even though it’s impossible to give a diagnosis posthumously, many scholars have convincingly argued that Nash had Asperger’s. The beauty of Nash’s theories is beyond doubt, however, the movie has also been criticized for beautifying his personality. People on the spectrum aren’t exactly known for being the “nicest” people, on the contrary, they are often perceived as extremely rude, due to their “ruthless” and “blunt” honesty. How can honesty be a bad thing? I have argued for a hunter-gatherer (vs farmer) origin of neurodiverse minds. Hunter-gatherers usually do not have all the politeness and etiquette we know from our societies, which grew out of farmer societies. Expressions like hello, goodbye, how are you?, I’m sorry, you’re welcome, and thank you don’t express or elicit new information about the world so much as they maintain goodwill and mutual respect. The Pirahã culture does not require this kind of communication. Pirahã sentences are either requests for information (questions), assertions of new information (declarations), or commands, by and large. There are no words for thanks, I’m sorry, and so on. I have become used to this over the years and forget most of the time how surprising this can be to outsiders. Daniel Everett: Don't Sleep, There Are Snakes In my most recent book, I argue that people with ASD have ancient egalitarian hunter-gatherer minds, that aren’t in need of many social rules and conventions. A lot of politeness phenomena most likely grew out of showing deference or obedience to authority - something that does not exist in hunter-gatherer societies as they are completely void of hierarchy. question: Are the brains of psychopaths neurotypical or neurodiverse?

Simon Baron-Cohen writes in his book Pattern-Seekers: His [autistic person] challenges with cognitive empathy are typical of many autistic people. 10 But while he struggles with this, people who know Jonah describe him as very caring. For example, if he hears that someone is unwell, he tries to think what he could do for them, to help them. If he hears that someone has been treated unfairly or is suffering, it upsets him, and he wants to do something about it. So as with many autistic people, his “affective” empathy is intact. 11 In this sense, an autistic person is the mirror image of a psychopath, whose cognitive empathy is often highly practiced (to exploit others) while their affective empathy is blunted. Psychopaths, unlike autistic people, just don’t care how others feel. It hasn’t been an easy enterprise, as the only work that has ever pointed to an origin of neurodiverse minds in ancient hunter-gatherer minds has been Thom Hartmann’s “Hunter-Hypothesis” of ADHD. Personally, I am somewhat in between neurotypical and neurodiverse, testing around 50% on online autism tests and 75% on ADHD tests. Like most neurodiverse people I have always had a hard time fitting in and I have a gifted son who learned to read by age two (hyperlexia) and who gets similar test results as I do. I generally do include the gifted label in my use of the word “neurodiverse”, to make it clear that not only people who are considered “having disabilities” belong to this group.Here is a preliminary list: CognitiveDistractibility and hyperfocusField-independent learnersPattern-recognizersWider field of visionSocial:Less politeness/socially awkward (learn few social rules)EgalitarianDistrust of authoritarian behaviourHigh sense of justiceSupport the underdogExceptional honestyNo-ingroupism/nepotismLess gender dimorphismPhysiological:Chronotype (tend to be night owls)Hypersensitive to physical stimuli (sound, touch, etc.)Anatomical:Ectomorph body typesLater pubertyTend to look younger than their ageFor simplicity, I’ll stick here with only two types: hunter-gatherer types and farmer types. I usually include a third type (pastoralist types), but people are often mixed and of course, the reality is much more complex.Here is a comparison between hunter-gatherer vs farmer types when it comes to cognition: Foraging and farming required different cognitive skills. One huge difference is that farming requires a sustained focus on long and boring tasks, whereas hunters are more easily distracted by all kinds of stimuli that may or may not be relevant. Once a stimulus is perceived as relevant (e.g. a track of a potential prey) the hunter keeps (hyper)focusing on it until the task is finished. Also, hunting skills are very different from farming skills. The latter requires tradition and much more social learning. Once a young grown up a farmer basically kept repeating the same tasks over and over. Hunting is very different, it can’t be learned by tradition and social learning is much less relevant. It’s not young grown-up hunters who are the best hunters (even though they might have a fitness advantage), but the older and more experienced hunters. Hunting requires therefore much more self-directed learning. Being high pattern-recognizers is another advantage. A hunter will perceive patterns leading to the prey that are imperceptible to, like recognizing from the patterns on the surface of the water where fish can be found. Neurodiverse people are therefore much more likely to recognize patterns that neurotypicals (farmer types) miss. As farmer-types were more dependent on social learning their cognition is more dependent on other people’s (e.g. teacher’s) opinions. Neurodiverse people are often independent of collective truth and tend to perceive patterns others don’t. Children with ASD and ADHD are also notorious for pointing out logical flaws in a teacher’s arguments, which may often get them into trouble with their teachers. All the more so, that hunter-gatherer minds don’t accept authority without competence and they may become straightforwardly rebellious if they perceive the teacher to treat them unjustly. Finally, I have come across a wider field of vision for hunter-gatherer types several times in my research. Scanning their environment for danger, prey and food sources foragers are more likely to have a wider field of vision than farmer types who have to focus long on routine work. This wider field of vision in hunter-gatherer types may interfere with learning to read as the learner may be more distracted by neighbouring letters or images. In combination with pattern-seeking a wide field of vision would not only allow a hunter to spot prey more easily, but also make a hunter a great astronomer. I estimate that about 90% of astronomers are hunter types and usually hunter type children can become obsessed with astronomy very early on (before schooling) from my experience with my own children. Most of the great geniuses and pattern-seekers in history (e.g. Edison and Einstein) had difficulties adapting to school and most Nobel Prize winners have few fond recollections of their time in school. Our different minds make it harder for us to go through the traditional school system. Hunter-gatherer type children are often among the gifted, but also among the twice-exceptional (2e) and more frequently among special ed children than farmer-type children. Even for those who are gifted, you often get the “brilliant but lazy” type of student. By now it should be clear that these brilliant students are not lazy but that their minds find it incredibly hard to focus on rote tasks and crave for more interesting stimulation. Instead of being able to show that they are super-learners, their boring school work turns them into super-procrastinators. Hunter-gatherer type children are often much better at self-directed learning (autodidacts) than learning in a classroom setting. I have met many neurodiverse children who had amazing skills to show off: knowing everything about insects or the solar system. And yet these children found it hard to learn telling the time when taught in school. Very often these self-directed hunter-gatherer type children are great at learning with computers, especially when they get to control their own learning. As a teacher, I have noticed that there are two types of students who love learning with computers, whereas the majority of children aren’t too happy about it or often even hate it. These two types are special-ed children and gifted children. They are really one type: hunter-gatherer types. Learning for hunter-gatherer type children is PLAY, learning for farmer type children is WORK. If learning turns into WORK for hunter-gatherer type children, they start to do poorly, if it remains PLAY they start to excel. question: Do folks with long term mental health issues sometimes act a kind of 'stereotypically crazy'? I.e., ‘acceptably atypical’ as a kind of ego defense to avoid being stigmatized on the basis of genuine (but perhaps less socially understandable) symptoms?
answer: Perhaps this would be better described as “Doing what one can do to present acceptably in some social context in spite of certain limitations introduced by mental health issues.” I think everyone frames themselves to some extent for an audience. Some do it so much they aren’t aware that there is any other way of being. Some do it so much they would never admit to doing it because their persona depends on their being a “straight shooter.” Some are so aware of any discrepancy between their inner condition and outer representation that they have imposter syndrome, always believing they are falsely misrepresenting themselves—perhaps more concerned than in justified. So lets say you have some kind of Mental Health abnormality. Call it what you like I don’t care. Maybe it’s a developmental disorder like a cluster of characteristics that could get you or has gotten you diagnosed with an autistic spectrum disorder or ADHD; maybe it’s depression. Maybe it’s a personality disorder—borderline, narcissism, whatever. Maybe it’s Bipolar. Maybe it’s just anxiety or depression. In the first place, the very labels become useful for helping to normalize the cluster of behaviors. I can tell you I’m on the autistic spectrum as an alternative to describing my tendency to mumble sounds to myself when I am alone or in deep focus. “Oh, he’s on the autistic spectrum.” That’s more socially acceptable in 2018 than “Oh, he makes alien type noises to himself while working alone.” “I have anxiety and tend to pace while thinking,” I can tell someone who wonders why I might prefer to live on the bottom rather than the top floor. The truth is I like to pace and talk to myself to think through things. It’s not necessarily an anxious response, but I’m describing a behavior in the context of a mental health issues that is like, more acceptable probably to most who hear about it. Then I don’t have to explain why I think better when I’m walking. I have of late realized it would be a good idea to do this “stereotypically crazy” thing any time I am considering explaining in more specific detail my various quirks. “I sometimes have social anxiety” might be a better, though less true, way of describing why I didn’t do something. The real reason is more complicated than that but could be perhaps more strategically described that way. “Have you ever had a friend who was diagnosed with Aspergers, and s/he would sometimes get overly excited about interests and go on and on? Sometimes I do that, so just interrupt me if I do it too much, it won’t offend me.” That might be a better way of explaining that “I suck at figuring out how to summarize complex information and expect people want all the details.” In some ways really what I am talking about, I guess, is just the difference between what is going on for the person with the mental illness vs how it is understood by their audience, and the distinct advantage one gains by framing oneself in comprehensible and relatable ways for the audience that exists among, for example, two conversing neurotypicals, still exists between neurodiverse and neurotypical conversation partners.

question: What causes autism in adults?
answer: My views on this subject are not mainstream - let’s start there. The answer is found in rephrasing the question. First of all, the neurological wiring of an autistics’ central nervous system / brain is diverse from that of a neurotypical… we are far more sensitive and susceptible to neurological assaults (such as mercury poisoning for example). Upon investigation, through the study of epigentics (epigenetics: the study of heritable {phenotype} changes {which do not involve alterations in the DNA sequence}), one could easily identify the familial pattern of neurodiversity most often in an adult presenting with ASD symptoms. As the adult’s expression of these symptoms intensifies or persists - the diagnosis of autism can be made later in life vs. in childhood. This however does not mean that the autism was not there previously, but for whatever reason (and there are many), the symptoms were either missed or not severe enough for the diagnosis to be made or possibly even sought. Several factors can be at play here - from an assault on the already overly sensitive brain (bacterial, viral, hypoxia, brain injuries, a vast range of nutrient deficiencies, environmental exposures, and even emotional factors), to simply a downward trajectory in ones ability to self-regulate and mask as ones ages. The operating system did not change - but the factors over time likely did - therefore leading to the late diagnosis of autism.

question: How can I tell if my cat is neurotypical, psychopathic, or autistic? What are some tests I can do to find out?
answer: As far as I know, there aren’t any tests for this… I’m pretty sure animal mental health is only examined in cases of depression/anxiety/trauma. However, there is a book out there called “All Cats are on the Autism Spectrum.” And as a neurodivergent cat-mom, I would agree. My cat shows affection the way I do, quietly and with small gestures. We are the best of friends, we can tell when each other is upset and respond accordingly, and no human or dog has ever vibed with me on this level. I’d say cats are more similar to neurodivergent humans, while dogs are more similar to neurotypicals. My cat doesn’t walk up and tell me he loves me, he shows me he loves me by always being around me, sitting beside me, and sharing small moments of cuddles with loving gestures like the slow-blink eye contact and rubbing our noses together. When I’m upset, he comes to calm me down by softly licking my forehead. Cats are naturally solitary creatures and they have great focus for stalking/hunting their prey. So while the concept of neurodiversity is a human concept, I feel like it could be used as a metaphor for dogs vs cats, since being different species their brains would work differently. I don’t think psychopathy would fit for them, since it has some basis on morality/empathy, and animal morality wouldn’t be as easily measurable. Also, (some) animals do have empathy, you may notice that your dog yawns when it sees you yawning. If you were thinking that about cats because of their love of hunting, it wouldn’t apply because it’s their instincts (and do we call people who love hunting psychopaths?). Overall though, as long as your cat is happy and healthy, it doesn’t matter if they’re neurotypical or neurodivergent. Cats show their love quite obviously when you learn their love language and learn what their actions/behaviours are communicating.

question: Why do autistic people seem to lose "energy" when too long in close contact with neurotypical people? Is this due to sensory overload, or is this another effect?
answer: Um. *Googles “analogy” for the 800th time* A particular analogy popped into my head after reading this question, so I’m just going to run with it despite the obvious problems- Have you ever spent time with one or more small children? Like, under the age of 6 especially? And not crappy random small children, but ones you are fond of? A child or children that you cared for and made an effort to spend time with and talk to in a meaningful way, because you wanted them to like you as well as feel important and seen? Were you tired afterwards? Was it at all challenging trying to figure out wtf they were talking about, or why they suddenly changed subjects from nice kitties to how much they hate pants and then started crying for no apparent reason? Was it exhausting trying to keep your face attentive and smiling so they would stay in a good mood, because they don’t yet know how to care about your feelings or personal issues, and you didn’t want to scare them or have them misinterpret your behaviour negatively? Did you find yourself doing things you don’t necessarily enjoy, for their sake? Alternatively, did you sometimes find that you DID enjoy spending time with them overall, but were still glad when a particular interaction was over and you could have some time to yourself again? (I don’t know why everything had to be in question form, sorry. It just happened.) Looking over what I wrote, it seems to me that it doesn’t have to be a comparison to being around children, so much as spending time doing anything with anyone that you don’t want to offend or hurt but whom you know doesn’t think or understand things the way you do. I’m sure this must be how a neurotypical person feels when they make a big effort to connect with a neurodiverse person as well. I suppose the biggest difference is the level of sensory stimulation that an autistic person experiences during these interactions vs a neurotypical. I guess you could think of it like the neurotypical person is being talked to by another person, while the autistic person is being talked to by another person, and being talked to by the lights, and the background sounds, and the textures of everything touching them, and their own minds, and their biological processes, and nearby smells…this slows down the ability to successfully process and respond to other people in a meaningful way, so if you are having what seems like a “normal-ish” conversation with an autistic, perhaps try to keep in mind that they are processing much more incoming data at a conscious level than you are, which is very tiring. And that’s not even touching on the difficulties of relating to the subject matter being discussed by many neurotypicals. Acting like most of that stuff matters is exhausting on its own. If you are having a successful conversation about clothes shopping or sports with an autistic person, and their special interest isn’t clothes or sports…they probably love you. A lot. *shrugs. stares off into space. eats another cookie. seriously wonders why they bothered writing this many words when others did it better*

question: What do you believe? Does Autism Spectrum disorder cause disability? Or does the Neurotypicals society disable us?
answer: I think autism expression is highly variable, in a way that makes the answer to this question complex and individualized. Many autistic individuals experience little to no support needs (though, to be pedantic to your question, such individuals would not qualify for an ASD diagnostic label, being clinically subsyndromal). Some experience challenges that could disappear or be negligible if they lived in a different setting that better fit their experience (though that is not necessarily the same setting that would be easily navigable for a different autistic person with a different presentation of their autism; this is rarely an ‘autistic’ vs ‘non-autistic’ variable, let alone any other factors of neurodiversity that may be involved). Some people have significant effects from their autism that would likely create support needs regardless of the setting. Some people have such enmeshed combination of autism, other comorbidities that may or may not be associated with their autism, environmental factors, societal factors, and other unknown variables that it is impossible to meaningfully ‘point the finger’ at any single significant causative factor as being central to the support needs of the individual. No single model is going to adequately encapsulate the entirety of autism, or of the experience of all autistic individuals, or even the experiences of the same autistic person across their lifespan and the different contexts of their life.

question: Has anyone's child recovered from Autism Spectrum disorder (ASD)?
answer: I think there’s a fundamental misconception in this question, so let’s clear that up right away: Autism is NOT an Illness. Autism is NOT a Disease. Therefore, Autism is NOT something people can “recover” from. Autism is a neurodevelopmental difference—a different way the brain is wired. It’s not a flaw, a sickness, or something that needs to be cured. It simply means that an autistic person’s brain and a neurotypical person’s brain fundamentally differ in how they process information, perceive the world, and interact with their environment. That’s all. Theoretically, that’s all there is to it. If we lived in a world that perfectly accommodated all ways of thinking and processing, autism wouldn’t be seen as a “disorder” at all. It would simply be a different way of being. Then Why Do People Talk About “Recovery” or “Improvement”? The confusion often comes from the co-occurring conditions (called co-morbidities) that are commonly associated with autism. These are not autism itself but are often seen alongside it. They can include:Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) – Differences in receiving and processing sensory information.Anxiety and Depression – Often due to social pressures and sensory overload.ADHD – Difficulty with attention regulation and hyperactivity.Learning Disabilities (Dyslexia, Dyspraxia, etc.) – Specific challenges in reading, writing, or maths.Speech and Language Delays – Differences in communication style or speed.These co-morbid conditions are often the source of the struggles people see, not autism itself. And this is where the misconception of “recovery” comes from. People don’t recover from autism, but they can learn to manage the symptoms of these co-occurring conditions and develop coping strategies to navigate a world that isn’t designed for them. Managing Symptoms vs “Recovery” This is a crucial distinction. Autism doesn’t go away, but with the right support and strategies, autistic people can learn to adapt, thrive, and live fulfilling lives. Here’s how:Self-Awareness and Self-Acceptance – Learning to understand and accept their own neurodivergence.Coping Strategies – Developing personalized strategies to handle sensory overload, anxiety, or executive functioning challenges.Accommodations and Adjustments—Making environmental changes, such as reducing sensory stimuli, using noise-cancelling headphones, or having structured routines.Therapies and Support – Occupational therapy, speech therapy, and other supportive interventions that help with specific challenges.Education and Advocacy – Empowering autistic individuals to advocate for their needs and educate others about neurodiversity.None of this is about “curing” autism. It’s about empowerment and quality of life. A Personal Example: Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) One of the most common co-morbidities associated with autism is Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD). My child, for example, is a sensory seeker, which means he craves sensory input and constantly seeks stimulation. When he was younger, this meant crashing into the sofa repeatedly or even trying to eat stones because of his intense need for sensory feedback. He also struggles with sensory filtering. I’m not an expert, so I might not have the exact technical terminology, but essentially, he doesn’t have the neurological filter that most neurotypical people have to block out background stimuli. To give you an example: Suppose I’m having a conversation with you in a room with background music, children playing, pictures on the wall, and colourful decorations. In that case, I can tune out all of those distractions and focus on our conversation. My son can’t. It’s as if his brain is trying to process every sound, every image, every movement, all at once. Imagine trying to read a book at a busy train station with constant noise and movement. Reading even a few pages would take ages because you’d constantly be distracted. That’s how it is for him—all the time. His brain is constantly overloaded, affecting his learning speed, social interactions, and emotional regulation. This isn’t because his brain is “broken” or “deficient.” It’s just wired differently. He experiences the world more intensely. He can’t recover from this, but he can learn strategies to manage his environment and reduce sensory overload. For example:Studying in a quiet room with minimal decorations helps him focus better.Noise-cancelling headphones allow him to regulate auditory input.Structured routines reduce the anxiety of unpredictability.These are coping strategies. They don’t change his sensory processing but empower him to live comfortably and thrive. Bottom Line Autism is a neurodevelopmental difference, not an illness or disease. There is no “recovery” because there is nothing to cure. I cannot stress enough this last detail. THERE. IS. NOTHING. TO. CURE. I could underline this sentence not just once but twice, thrice… even more. There really is NOTHING to cure. The challenges often associated with autism come from co-morbid conditions like Sensory Processing Disorder, Anxiety, ADHD, or Learning Disabilities. These co-morbidities can be managed through coping strategies, accommodations, and supportive therapies, allowing autistic individuals to thrive in their own unique way. Autistic people don’t “grow out of” autism, but they can learn to navigate a world that wasn’t designed for them, often with remarkable resilience and creativity. My child is still autistic, and he always will be. But with understanding, acceptance, and the right support, he can live a happy, fulfilling life. And that’s not “recovery”—that’s just living. Final Thought I hope this helps clear up the misconception about autism and recovery. If you have more questions about autism, neurodiversity, or parenting a neurodivergent child, feel free to ask. I’m not an expert, but I’ve learned a lot from my journey as a parent. I believe in open dialogue and learning from each other. 😊

question: What does a person with Asperger's syndrome usually think about other normal people?
answer: I can’t speak for other Aspies (or autists as manyt of us presently call ourselves). But I can speak for myself. When I was younger and certainly before my relatively recent diagnosis, I thought I *was* one of those other normal people. In short, I wore a mask. Anything that I felt bad about myself projected onto them and they, onto me. But now I know about the double empathy problem. And relatively recently I have come to appreciate the incredible beauty of this vast neurodiversity which encompasses all beings with a nervous system. We all resonate with eachother, learning and supporting each other. These are the lessons of autists like Temple Grandin and Albert Einstein, to name a couple of famous ones. And a similar lesson can be appreciated from a “neurotypical” point of view in the teachings of the historical prophets (Jesus, Buddha, Gandhi, etc.) as well as more recent masters like Richard Rohr, Tara Brach and Michael “Mickey” Singer. These messages all ring true to me now, saying, “We are all equal and worthy of respect.” “It is a friendly universe.” “This existence is sacred, whether we recognize it or not.” So the young undiagnosed Aspie I was didn’t understand the friendly universe, and yet he did. When I was a child, I always believed in fundamental human goodness. I just didn’t know how to share the good news. Now I do. To more directly answer your question, then, I still carry certain social fears into any conversation, whether with someone I consider neurotypical or someone I consider autistic and whether they are a stranger or a childhood friend. There is a way that I am still stuck at Eric Erickson’s first stage of psychosocial development (Trust vs. Mistrust). I haven’t mastered a quick reading on who I can and cannot trust, and that holds me back. I see this as an ongoing challenge. A part of me can’t possibly trust neurotypical people, because I have not lived the same experience as them. But those that I do choose to trust and stay intimate with continue to teach me more, so that I can learn what it is like to be them and treat them with the same sort of respect that I so much long for, myself. Namaste

question: Does the term ‘cisgender’ reinforce othering of the trans community?
answer: No, although some trans people can use the term in a way that does. The original idea or intent behind the term “cisgender” or just “cis” for short, is a term to refer to people who are not trans, a lot like how asexuals use the term “allosexual” to refer to people who are not asexual, or autistic people use the term “neurotypical” to refer to people who are not autistic or otherwise neurodiverse. As such, the term has the effect of facilitating dialogue about issues that affect trans people, and drawing attention to cisnormativity in society. The hope might be that if people are able to see their “cisness” as part of their identity, they might be able to see cis privilege and thus start breaking down cisnormativity and making life a bit easier for trans people. Sometimes things go wrong though. Left-wing ideology can sometimes go down the toxic path of bashing members of “privileged” groups, and in this case this includes “cis people”. This plays out in things like the whole “down with cis” rhetoric you see on Tumblr, and with people ranting about or verbally bashing cis people, trying to exclude cis people from groups or spaces, etc. I don’t find this constructive. And I do think this ends up reinforcing the “othering” of the trans community…it seems to send the message that trans people somehow need to isolate ourselves from the rest of society, and I think that’s a really damaging message. I really wish people would target transphobia, and not cis people, when discussing issues that affect trans people. I’ve had countless cis people help me and support me in my path through and struggles with gender, and I’ve also experienced transphobia and binarism from other trans people. So, while I support the use of the terms “cisgender” and “cis”, I think it’s important that we use them only as neutral descriptive terms. I vehemently oppose using these terms as insults or put-downs, or using them to frame an “us-vs-them” between cis and trans people, or using them to exclude cis people from spaces, activism, groups, or dialogue. I think it’s critically important for us all to work together, both cis and trans people, on issues that affect trans people.

question: What is a good place to start researching if you suspect you might have ASD?
answer: You can look at various websites and look at lists of symptoms, but there are also a few tests you can take. If the tests give an indication of possible ASD, you might want to consider going to your doctor for referral to a specialist who can diagnose you.Autism Spectrum Quotient The best place to start is probably to take the Asperger’s AQ test, which is a measure of the extent of autistic traits in adults. The average score in the control group was 16.4, while 80% of those diagnosed with ASD scored 32 or higher. It is not meant as a diagnostic tool, but it can give an indication of possible autism.The distributions of Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) scores by the four groups: males and females with and without autism spectrum conditions. (Image source: Attenuation of Typical Sex Differences in 800 Adults with Autism vs. 3,900 Controls) Do the test here:Autism Spectrum QuotientAnd have a look at what (other) people with ASD on Quora scored:What scores do various Quora members get on the 50-item Autism-Spectrum Quotient Index test?The RAADS-R The RAADS-R is a modified version of the Ritvo Autism Asperger’s Diagnostic Scale, which is useful in identifying autistic traits and as a screening instrument (but not as a diagnostic tool). Do the test here:The Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale-Revised (RAADS-R)And have a look at the results of other Quorans:What do various Quora users score on the Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale-Revised (RAADS-R)?Aspie Quiz The goal of this test is to check for neurodiverse and neurotypical traits in adults. The neurodiversity classification can be used to give a reliable indication of autism spectrum traits prior to eventual diagnosis. Do the test here:Aspie QuizAnd have a look at the results of other Quorans:What is your score on the Aspie Quiz?Alexithymia Alexithymia is present in 50% of individuals with ASD compared to the general public at 10%.[1] Since empathy deficits common in ASD have been linked to alexithymia[2], as well as poor recognition of facial expressions[3], testing for alexithymia can actually give a strong indication of possible ASD. Do the test here:Online Alexithymia QuestionnaireAnd have a look at the results of other Quorans:What were your results from the alexithymia test?Empathy Quotient The Empathy Quotient (EQ) is a 60-item questionnaire (there is also a shorter, 40-item version) designed to measure empathy in adults. The test was developed by Simon Baron-Cohen at ARC (the Autism Research Centre) at the University of Cambridge. Clinically, the empathy measurements provided by the EQ are used by mental health professionals in assessing the level of social impairment in certain disorders like Autism. Do the test here:Empathy QuotientAnd have a look at what (other) people with ASD on Quora scored:What is your score on the Empathy Quotient test, and how accurately do you think your results reflect your behavior?VIA Character Strengths Something else you could test are your VIA Character Strengths through the VIA Character Survey, which is a simple self-assessment which provides a wealth of information to help you understand your core characteristics. The interesting thing is that certain core characteristics often come up for people with ASD. Do the test here:Free VIA Character SurveyAnd have a look at what (other) people with ASD on Quora scored:What are Aspies’ and people on the autism spectrum’s top and bottom 5 character strengths on the VIA?Embracing ASD You might also want to have a look at Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht ND RP and my blog Embrace Autism, which can be a great source of information if you want to know more about what high-functioning autism entails.For more information on (high-functioning) ASD, have a look at: Embrace AutismA blog about quantitative- and qualitative research on autism, by Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht ND RP and Eva Silvertant.Footnotes[1] Alexithymia, not autism, is associated with impaired interoception[2] Empathic brain responses in insula are modulated by levels of alexithymia but not autism | Brain | Oxford Academic[3] Alexithymia, Not Autism, Predicts Poor Recognition of Emotional Facial Expressions

question: How can I change? I have autism and maybe narcissism. I don't think what I say and do things without thinking. I am lazy, stupid, ignorant, arrogant, weird, immature and depress with schizo. I am a nuisance to others. What can I do?
answer: It sounds like you’re really hurting. Autism can make life difficult sometimes, and the biggest difficulties are often about being misunderstood. I have autism and ADHD diagnoses, and I count “weird” as a strength, not a weakness. Being “normal” is very simply not that important, though I have tried hard to conform to expectations at many times in my life. I like to be liked by people, but I’m not willing to suffer stress overwhelm just for the sake of being liked. I have definitely been seen as “lazy, stupid, ignorant, arrogant and weird”. That’s all to do with autism, with ADHD providing an extra dose of “lazy”. I’m intelligent in some ways, and “stupid” in other ways, so people might just see my stupid moments as awkward and selfish. No, I’m not selfish or arrogant. These things are misunderstandings. I’m actually kind and gentle, but people who judge me quickly may not see that.I’m guessing you’re having trouble with similar misunderstandings. I know this in part, simply because misunderstandings are so common for those of us who are neurodiverse, but also because some of these words you’ve used do not go together! Someone who is narcissistic, really does not describe themselves as “lazy, stupid, ignorant, arrogant, weird, immature and depressed”. I’ve spent a bit too much time with a few people who have levels of narcissism that probably qualifies them for a diagnosis, and self-confidence is a defining characteristic of narcissism, typically with an exaggerated belief in their own abilities, talents, and accomplishments. Where I’ve been seen as “arrogant”, it’s usually with regard to the self-confidence I have in my special interest areas, and my inclination to tell facts and discoveries about my special interest areas to anyone who looks even remotely interested. :-) This is normal for those of us with autism.You might find your depression is simply chronic stress. Stress avoidance and stress management techniques can bring huge benefits to us. For both depression and schizophrenia, it’s better to get a diagnosis than to just guess. Ask your doctor or counsellor about chronic stress, too, because it’s actually very, very easy for anyone to mix up depression, anxiety, and stress. All three feel rather similar in many ways, and it’s valuable to understand what is really happening. It’s also worthwhile getting assessed to see if you might have ADHD. Having both autism and ADHD together increases the likelihood of being labelled as “lazy”, and ADHD can be mistaken for schizophrenia, depending on the circumstances. It’s important to get an accurate diagnosis, because the medications and therapies to treat ADHD vs schizophrenia are very different.While there is no medication to treat autism, there are medications and therapies for other conditions you might have, and that could make a huge difference for you. Stress avoidance, stress management, and quiet time in your special interests can also make a big difference for how well we handle autism. Most of all, maybe you just need some time with other autistic people? These “lazy, stupid, ignorant, arrogant and weird” misunderstandings tend to come from neurotypical people, whereas neurodiverse people are far more likely to understand each other. In the clinical literature, the fact that autistic people typically understand each other is called the double empathy problem, so it’s definitely a thing.Naomi Lauren · 5yHow do you separate somebody’s autism from their core character? For example, how can you tell if they are just selfish?Thinking that somebody’s autism makes them “selfish”, is generally about issues of perception, communication, needs assessment, or self-care. If you’re asking about narcissism, that shows itself in patterns of behaviour. I’m yet to meet a narcissist who is on the autism spectrum, and that’s probably because ASD tends to make us painfully honest and blunt. Narcissists are devious manipulators, so that’s kinda opposite to ASD. Here’s a post on narcissism if you’d like to know more. Naomi Lauren's answer to What should I know about a time when you were gaslighted? If you’re expecting us to read your mind, and then calling us “selfish” when we don’t, that’s not selfishness … that’s unrealistic expectations. If you have a need, that you want us to fill for you, then you will need to explain that need, and explain what it means for you. This is an issue of communication, and good communication skills are vital for all relationships, whether family, friends, romantic, or business relationships. Many of us simply cannot read your mind at all … you must communicate explicitly, and say what you’re really thinking in a way that we can relate to. Learning those communication skills is an asset to all relationships, not just your relationships with neurodiverse people. For me, I can understand most of these unstated neurotypical expectations and needs, if I’m looking for them. That’s a big IF sometimes! I’ve learned to read those things, but it was a very deliberate acquisition of skills on my part, and it takes a very specific effort. I’ve spent a lifetime working to understand neurotypical psychology, so that I can compensate for all the things that neurotypical people don’t tend to explicitly communicate. It takes an effort to read your mind, and I’m not really reading your mind. I’m cataloguing your behaviour, and facial expressions, and tone, and consciously comparing that with your history … and then guessing about what it all means. It would be much better, if you have a clear need, to express it clearly. Most people on the autism spectrum are very kind and generous, when we see a need, but we might not see it. We might also be balancing your needs, with what we perceive as being the needs of others. Our perception of that might be different to yours. We might also be balancing your needs with our needs. Some of our needs are vitally important to our self-care and ability to function, even though it might not look like that to you.

question: What is the term "neurodiversity" and is it necessary to explain that people have different brains?
answer: neurodiversity attempts to highlight that people can be functioning members of society even if you do not understand why a person doesn’t behave the same way as other people. unfortunately, most people who grow up exposed only to people who act like they do, don't realize there are others out there who are different. and tensions occur when they finally meet a neuro divergent person. one such tension is that for those who have ADHD they literally cannot stop fidgeting; neurotypical thought goes like “I can choose to stop so you can stop too.” another tension is that for those who have depression, ae often faced with things like “have you tried just not being sad.” we see similar issues with growing up in white only neighborhoods. the lack of exposure to others reduces the ability to relate to those who are different, as well as creating an us vs them mentality

question: What are some common challenges that neurodivergent workers face at work that neurotypical employers may not consider?
answer: Teamwork: many autists (and some others, too) don't work well in a team. It's not just that they may not enjoy it, or that they don't have the right personality type or set of skills, it's also that many neurotypicals aren't happy with autistics in their group. They feel uncomfortable, they resent making allowances or accommodations, they don't know how to communicate effectively with them, they can be biased, unkind, and even abusive as they attempt to exclude or drive away the neurodivergents among them. Sensory sensitivities: Many neurodivergent people, especially autists, are hypersensitive or hyposensitive, or a combination of the two, in one or more of the seven senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch,[1] vestibular,[2] and proprioception.[3] These can be problematic in many different work environments, but especially when workers must share one, large space, such as a cubicle farm, where it is very easy to become stressed, be unable to focus or concentrate because we can't filter out unwanted stimuli, have meltdowns when we're overwhelmed, and even burnout. Each neurodivergent person may have different sensory needs, so ideally each worker might have their own office, room, or area set up with their specific needs in mind. That is often not possible or applicable, but it is possible to create an environment that is more sensory-friendly by reducing common irritants, and/or to have a room or space set aside where those feeling overwhelmed can take a break and self-regulate. Communication: Neurodivergent workers may be able to complete tasks more quickly and effectively, respond to feedback or questions, follow instructions, and have fewer miscommunications if they are able to use specific methods of communication that best suit them. For example, written communication may be preferred, where the worker can be given (and refer to at need) written instructions that detail their responsibilities, what's expected of them, who to go to if there is a question or if more information is needed, and what procedures to take when things go wrong. A nominated member of staff that they can go to if they have questions, need more information or feedback on something can also be very helpful. Someone who is approachable, patient, and who can communicate well with the neurodivergent, acting as a liaison of sorts between neurotypical and neurodiverse workers. Staff training is another possibility that may help improve communication. Differences between the communication styles of the neurodiverse and neurotypicals might be explored and explained to the benefit of all. Some examples:Knowing that autists or ADHDers may struggle with eye contact, making too much or too little, not because they're lying or deceiving you, but because it's overwhelming for them.Autists who fidget or doodle in a staff meeting are not being rude or ignoring the speaker(s) - many of us find it easier to focus or concentrate when we fidget/doodle, but if forced to look up, sit still, watch the speaker (pay attention as neurotypicals see it) we often cannot focus or concentrate at all. We spend the whole time repeating to ourselves “sit still, look at her, don't fidget" over and over instead of actually listening and paying attention.Or the difficulty many autists have with reading and interpreting body language, facial expression, and vocal tone - and our tendency to be literal. So, in general, don't expect an autist to ‘read the room', know how you feel about something, read between the lines, and don't rely on hints, inference, subtext, or the mystical ‘everyone knows this' to get your message across. Use your words, clearly and directly, and with precision.Stereotypes: Don't rely on them. While some traits, challenges, and strengths may hold true for some autists, they don't always do so. Neurodivergent workers, like neurotypical ones, are individuals. We aren't all the same. Not every autist is white, male, and good at mathematics. We're not all good with computers. We're not all trainspotters. We're not all introverts, either. Just as, despite the name, ADHDers are not all hyperactive. Put the stereotypes aside and learn about each individual. That may be enough to be going on with. I hope it's helpful.Footnotes[1] http://not just things we touch with our hands and fingers, but anything that touches us or our skin anywhere on our bodies.[2] http://movement and balance; the sense of where our body is in space; it helps us stand, walk and sit up without falling over.[3] http://body awareness; it helps us understand where our body parts are in relation to each other; it helps us calculate how much force to use in different actions, such as picking up a fragile glass vs a carton of milk.

question: Why are high-functioning female autistics more likely to be abused?
answer: This is a topic I’ve thought about a lot, moreso over the last couple of years, and have been attempting to figure out and resolve in therapy. I recall one session in particular in which I was almost in tears from frustration saying, “It’s like everybody else got some sort of rule book and I didn’t. Things that seem to come intuitively to other people don’t even occur to me.” My ex-husband was also fond of saying I was book smart and street dumb. While hurtful, his words have truth in them. I recently read a book written by a woman on the spectrum, “The Aspie Girl’s Guide to Being Safe with Men- The Unwritten Safety Rules No-One is Telling You” by Debi Brown in which she states, “a lot of what we really need to know are “unwritten rules,” which non-spectrum people may find intuitively obvious without there ever being told to them, but which we do need to be taught.” The author doesn’t assume the reader knows certain things but instead spells everything out and while I already knew most of what was contained because it’s more geared towards younger girls and those inexperienced with sex and relationships, I still learned a couple of things. I recently just learned from the previously mentioned book that your mind and thoughts are included in your boundaries. I knew I was entitled to my own thoughts but I didn’t know it was a boundary violation when someone is trying to impose their thoughts, or more specifically, version of reality, on me. Or even my sense of self. My ex-husband used to help me with this by saying (pardon his crudeness), “Put a dick on her.” It may sound ridiculous but it worked. Thus, we’re not walking around paranoid or ever expecting ill-intent from others because that isn’t our internal experience. It does not come naturally to us to think otherwise. When we first meet someone and they seem nice, nice = good. Our brain categorizes them so when they do something ‘not nice’ there has to be some other explanation. Cognitive Dissonance. Since I have abuse in my history I don’t know what or how much to attribute to that vs. just normal Aspie thinking. There can also be the tendency to dissociate if you have substantial abuse in your history. My ex-husbands (I have two) used to perplex me by the things they would suspect or accuse others of doing and I’d say, “How could you think that?!” It was precisely because they themselves had thought of it. Once I implemented that quote and observed people with that knowledge it became a useful tool at times to gain insight into others and most people don’t even know they are giving themselves away by doing this. (I have quit sharing when this happens. I also question whether it’s ethical because it seems like an invasion of privacy.) I believe this has to do with both hyperfocus and sensing with high levels of empathy but I am talking out of my ass on this one (not literally you guys but that’s a funny visual) I’m not sure but it’s cool and useful when it works. I think the problem is if I am hyperfocusing on our conversation, that’s the only thing I’m focusing on. I have the same problem with foreign films. I can either watch the movie or read the subtitles, not really both. I can’t process everything that fast and simultaneously. Another factor is feelings. I know NT’s have a problem with this as well but I believe it’s in a different way. While NT’s can and do let their feelings drive their car sometimes, and I’ve done it as well, I think there’s something additional at play in Aspie’s which can be observed during meltdowns and shutdowns. When feelings get past a certain level it affects my brain in weird ways. I do not have a special interest in the brain and neuroscience. As Tina Mulhall mentioned in her comment this makes us much more likely to stay with and tolerate abuse. The law of scarcity is in play. It is much more devastating to lose one person when all you have is that one person. Aspies, in particular, are an extra vulnerable group as a whole for many of the reasons I mentioned. This is not a comprehensive list but are my thoughts alone on the topic thus far.
