question: Is an autism diagnosis subjective or objective?
answer: It’s pretty objective, but no two autistic people are the same. To help this make sense, let me explain. The autism spectrum isn’t linear, you don’t have “normal” on one end and “profoundly autistic” on the other. Rather, the diagnosis is very specific. You either are autistic, or you’re not. But the reason autism is a spectrum disorder is because each individual is unique, the way their autism presents is unique, and thus, their support needs will differ. As the saying goes, if you know one autistic person, then you’ve met one autistic person. Add on top of this, most people don’t even know what autism even is, which I think is the reason people are saying in other answers that it’s subjective. It isn’t. Autism is a specific diagnosis. It is a specific thing. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disability that affects social communication, restricted interests, and repetitive behavior. By social communication issues, I really mean the person is socially awkward, they don’t understand social cues, they’re often misunderstood when they communicate, because they have a strange way of interacting with people, like their tone of voice seemingly doesn’t match what they say, they might have a flat affect or “resting bitch face,” or their body language might not match how they feel, and they tend to come off a bit too logical and literal minded when it comes to communication. Social issues are the core of autism, so much so, that the DSM-5 says that a person must meet all of the Criterion A symptoms, all of which are the social issues, as part of the official diagnosis. Don’t confuse this with a person who’s introverted, introverted people don’t have the same issues with social communication that us autistic people do. By restricted interests I mean inflexibility of behavior, extreme difficulty coping with change, being overly focused on niche subjects to the exclusion of others, expecting others to be equally interested in those subjects, and difficulty tolerating changes in routine and new experiences. This covers our love of rules and routines, and our inflexible and rigid thinking patterns. We do the same thing every day, we eat the same food every day, we take the same routes every day, and when those are disrupted, we don’t handle it well. It also covers what we like to call special interests, which are subjects or interests that are perseverative, that is our focus on that subject is extreme, like a laser. We think about these all the time, we want to talk about them all the time, and we foolishly think others share the same level of interest in that niche subject. In fact, this type of laser-like focus on a niche subject can leave us with an uneven skill set. And finally, by repetitive behavior, I mean sensory hypersensitivity, stereotypical movements such as hand flapping, rocking, spinning, and arranging things in a very particular manner. This covers our sensory issues. We’re either extremely sensitive to sensory stimuli, or we’re not as sensitive as a normal person, there’s no happy middle ground, though, the former is usually more common. This also covers all manners of stimming behavior. Now, stimming behaviors are repetitive motor movements that we do, and everyone does them, just for us autistic people, they’re notable enough to be odd or quirky. The classic ones are hand-flapping, finger flicking, rocking back and forth, but it could be anything. Stimming actually regulates us and prevents us from getting too overwhelmed by the environment and situation. Some of us we can’t hide it well, and others, like myself, are subtle in how it presents, but if you observe us long enough, you’ll see it. And finally, this covers how we like to arrange things in a very particular way that makes perfect sense for us, but makes no sense to anyone else. A classic way I like to tell people is think of Sherlock Holmes in the Sherlock Holmes movie with Robert Downey Jr.These are covered under the Criterion B symptoms, and the DSM-5 states that you must have two in addition to the social issues mentioned earlier. Finally, for these to be considered symptoms, they have to be actual problems. They get in the way of normal life, and they impair the person in a very real way. For example, I can’t enter grocery stories unless I have my noise-cancelling headphones and a fidget toy in my pocket to stim with. Otherwise, I get sensory overload. Now, when it comes to actual diagnosis, that’s determined by an experienced clinician who understands autism, and they use a lot of screening tests. Tests for autism are more like a weighted score, where if we assume 100 questions, and 10, maybe 20 things apply to you, you might not have autism. However, if 60 or 70 of them apply to you, then there’s strong evidence for autism. The most popular screening tests for autism are:The AQ Test. This is a simple screening for autism. It’s 50 questions, and the threshold score is 26, meaning if you score 26 or above, there’s some evidence that you might be autistic. A higher score means you might be, lower scores mean you might not be. As a reference, most autistic people, around 80% of them, score around 32 or higher, and neurotypical people score around 16. I myself scored 40 on the AQ Test. Anything above a 32 is significant for this test.The CAT-Q Test. This is a test for if you mask your autistic traits or camouflage them. A high score here can explain why you score lower on other tests, because you’re actually masking your autistic traits. It has 25 questions, and it has a scoring range of 25–175, with the threshold being 100, meaning if you score above 100, this means you camouflage or mask your autism. As a reference, autistic people score around 109.64 for males, and 124.35 for females, with non-binary autistic people scoring around 122. Neurotypical people tend to score between 90–96. I myself scored 134. Meaning I mask my autism, and I mask in social situations. The hard part is unlearning the masking process, because I just found out I was autistic as an adult, so I have a whole life of masking my autism to unlearn, and replace with more healthy and productive things.The RBQ-2A. This is a test for restricted and repetitive interests and behaviors. There’s 20 questions, the scoring range is between 20–60, with the threshold being 26. Meaning, if you score 26 or higher, you definitely have restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior, and restricted and repetitive interests. As a reference, most autistic people score around 36, and neurotypical people score around 25 on average. I myself, scored 50, which means I have quite a lot of restricted and repetitive interests and behaviors.The Aspie Quiz. This one is a little different than the others as it doesn’t just measure for autism, but other things too like ADHD or OCD. The Aspie Quiz doesn’t just measure whether you have autism, it also measures how typical you are, and screens outliers, people that maybe have escaped a diagnosis. It measures atypical vs. typical talent, atypical vs. typical perception, atypical vs. typical communication, atypical vs. typical relationships, and atypical vs. typical sociability. In other words, it outputs a neurodiverse and neurotypical score and compares them, leading to you being neurodivergent, neurotypical, or mixed. It has 119 questions, measured 0–200, and it gives you a specific percentage, and there’s four control questions to ensure you answer consistently and honestly. Higher scores and percentages indicates a higher probability that you are neurodivergent. I can’t give you direct results that most autistic people get with the Aspie Quiz, I can say that a score of 140 results in a 100% chance that you’re neurodivergent, a score of 100 indicates a 50% chance that you’re neurodivergent, and a score of 95 indicates a 63% probability that you’re normal. I myself, just to give reference, scored 117 of 200, indicating an 87% chance that I’m neurodivergent. Which, if you read my answers on autism or ADHD, that shouldn’t be shocking, as I’m diagnosed with both.In other words, I am autistic. That was figured out from my AQ and CAT-Q results from the psychologist who tested me, and the other two I took out of interest, and it just seemed to reaffirm my diagnosis, just, a little more specifically. Funny part is, he was testing for my ADHD, and the possibility of me being autistic just sort of… came up during the screenings for ADHD, leading to him screening for autism too. Now I think the reason people might be saying it’s subjective is because of the confusion that autism is a spectrum disorder by definition. They confuse that to mean that the diagnosis itself is subjective, not the fact that no two autistic people are going to be alike. They’ll differ in their support needs and symptoms. So, really, autism is a specific diagnosis. It has an objective definition. You’re either autistic or you’re not. However, because everyone is unique, no two autistic people are alike. The way their symptoms present is different, their support needs will differ, and that’s why autism is a spectrum. I hope this helps!Originally answered: Is an autism diagnosis subjective or objective?

question: Is it possible to have a mild form of Asperger's syndrome? How can one determine if they are on the autism spectrum?
answer: Asperger’s Syndrome is now classed as part of Autistic Spectrum Disorder rather than as a separate diagnosis. Autism is a spectrum, and autistic people vary - some have very high support needs, and some can “pass” as neurotypical a lot of the time, a process known as “masking”. At other times they can experience difficulties or distress. Sensitivity to noise or light can be a problem, or individuals may experience stress in social situations. The way autism affects people, and what their “triggers” are varies from one individual to another. These days we tend not to use terms like mild vs severe or high vs low functioning, but to say that a person has high or low support needs. There are checklists available online which someone can use to check the probability that they are autistic. For some people a self-diagnosis provides an explanation and they go with that. If you think you may need special accommodations or support at work or college you will probably need a formal diagnosis; this has to be made by a clinician, either a clinical psychologist or a psychiatrist, preferably one who specialises in neurodiversity. This a detailed clinical interview, and often a questionnaire to fill in. Usually the clinician will want to speak to friends or relatives who know you, or ask for other “evidence” such as school records. They will also ask if there is a family history of neurodivergence. There is research evidence to show that there is often an overlap between autism and other neurodivergent conditions such as ADHD.

question: How has ADHD affected academic performance and social relationships in school, and what strategies have been most effective in managing its challenges?
answer: For me, subjects and teachers that interested me were terrific, others not so good. Teachers that didn’t mind rambling answers, or writing that went off topic were great (and few), others not good. I constantly had a fear that my inability to determine what I should be remembering in class would hurt me and I’d fail. Frankly looking back after a few years on adult ADHD meds, I wish I had the meds, it would have been much easier to get through. Social relationships had the same problem - people who said interesting things interested me, and few were interested in what I had to say… so I tended to have a short list of friends, but good ones. Constantly picked on for being “different” and perhaps a more advanced vocabulary than most kids my age. Strategies that helped ?Mindmapping helped me think about organizing and how to do itswitching from “to do” lists to “I want to see this happen lists”Deciding on a “prize” should I complete a difficult project successfully. ( Over the years this has amassed into an amusing collection of books and gadgets)living with people who could help me spatially organize thingsthinking about projects in reverse order from “deliverable” back to “what do I need to do to get there”Finding my own “tribe” of kids with similar interests or ways of thinking - finding mentors of the same mind bent helpedIf social issues are a real problem , note that ADHD and autism spectrums often live together. Some kids benefit from behavioural therapies that take a reward vs pain approach, some kids are the opposite - they benefit from “radical acceptance” Personally I would have preferred the latter. There are different traits with ADHD - some kids are going to be more kinesthetic, some more intellectual. The basic advice I’d give as a starting point is - honour the neurodiversity. ADHD has many wonderful elements to it. We see things that neurotypical people don’t catch, our hyper focus allows us to achieve things others cannot and often we are the best people to have in an emergency situation because we think spontaneously.

question: As an autistic or potential autistic person, did you embrace that you feel like an alien in the world around neurotypicals? If so, how do you accept it and yourself?
answer: The short answer is a simple yes, the slightly longer answer is yes, but I also experience similar feelings with some other autistic people as well. I was diagnosed young, so I always knew I was different, though this sense of feeling alien became more intense in some ways and lessened in others in a very counterintuitive way. Since my early 20s I have felt as I have one foot in the neurotypical world and one in the autistic world due being able to pass to the point where most people can’t tell I am autistic, yet still suffering the negative effects of autistic burnout from prolonged masking. Until a few years ago I have always felt a sense of belonging in the autism community, though this has changed due to the cultural war happening within the Autism community making the online community a toxic dumpster fire. This culture war is over things like self diagnosis, neurodiversity theory, the medical model vs the social model that has often pitted high support needs autistic people vs low support needs autistic people in a self destructive way. Though I often feel a sense of alienation and confusion regarding mainstream society, there is this bizarre phenomenon now whereby I have very little middle ground in regard to other autistic people. I either get along so well with other autistic people that it is almost as if we are a band of brothers/sisters, or I have to resist the urge to strangle them with almost no in between. In regard to the general public there is far more grey in terms of how well or poorly I get along with them in addition to the two extremes I mentioned. I have learned through trial and error that we only present parts of ourselves to people, and not our whole being. Those who are unable to mask or whose mask inadvertently slips off may reveal more than they intend, or those we trust get more of ourselves, but society itself is based on elaborate deceptions and pretenses that go far beyond what is simply reasonable tact. question: Has anyone thought that it might be the 10.5 grams of microplastics that are in your brain that could be the cause of all the neurodiversity? I dont think it is a very good electrical condictor for brain activity.
answer: The idea that microplastics in the brain could be linked to neurodiversity is an interesting thought, and it's understandable to wonder about the potential impact of these foreign substances on brain function. However, it's important to approach this idea with a critical and evidence-based perspective. Here's what we know so far:Microplastics are ubiquitous: Microplastics are indeed widespread in the environment and have been found in various parts of the human body, including the brain. Studies have confirmed the presence of microplastics in human brain tissue.Potential for harm: Research suggests that microplastics can have toxic effects on cells and tissues. They can cause inflammation, oxidative stress, and disrupt cellular processes.Neurodiversity is complex: Neurodiversity encompasses a wide range of neurological differences, including autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and others. These conditions are believed to have complex genetic and environmental causes.Why a direct link is unlikely (based on current evidence):Causation vs. Correlation: Even if microplastics are found in the brains of neurodivergent individuals, it doesn't necessarily mean they are the cause of their neurodiversity. Correlation does not equal causation. There could be other factors at play, or the presence of microplastics could be a consequence of other underlying conditions.Timing: Neurodevelopmental conditions typically arise during early brain development. While exposure to microplastics is a growing concern, it's not clear whether exposure levels are high enough during critical developmental periods to cause significant neurological changes.Specificity: Neurodiversity encompasses a wide range of conditions, each with its own unique characteristics and underlying mechanisms. It's unlikely that a single factor like microplastics would be responsible for such a diverse range of neurological differences.Lack of Direct Evidence: There is currently no direct scientific evidence linking microplastic exposure to the development of neurodevelopmental conditions. More research is needed to investigate this potential link.Alternative Explanations: Genetic factors, prenatal exposures (e.g., infections, toxins), and early childhood experiences are all known to play a role in neurodevelopmental conditions. These factors are more likely to be the primary drivers of neurodiversity than microplastic exposure.Electrical Conductivity: While it's true that plastics are generally not good electrical conductors, the impact of microplastics on brain activity is more likely to be related to their toxic effects on cells and tissues rather than their direct interference with electrical signals. The brain is a complex system, and even subtle disruptions to cellular function can have significant consequences.What research is needed: To determine whether there is a link between microplastics and neurodiversity, researchers would need to conduct studies that:Measure microplastic levels in the brains of neurodivergent individuals.Compare these levels to those in neurotypical individuals.Investigate the effects of microplastic exposure on brain development in animal models.Examine the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which microplastics might affect brain function.Control for other potential confounding factors.While the idea that microplastics could contribute to neurodiversity is intriguing, there is currently no scientific evidence to support this claim. Neurodiversity is a complex phenomenon with multiple contributing factors, and it's unlikely that a single environmental toxin like microplastics would be the sole cause. More research is needed to investigate the potential effects of microplastics on brain function and development, but it's important to avoid jumping to conclusions based on limited evidence.

question: In Robert Sapolsky's latest book, "Determined: A Science of Life Without Free Will," he argues that "a huge amount of humanity's misery is due to myths of free will." Do you agree?
answer: I will be up front about the fact that I have not read THIS particular book by Robert Sapolsky, though I have read his earlier book “Behave” which I found to be excellent. That book doesn’t address the consequences of belief in free will vs. not having the belief, but it does lay out a scientific case for free will being unlikely as he has accounted for pretty much all of the relevant variables that lead to a behavior/decision at a point in time starting with what’s going on neurologically at that moment to all of the various intervals of time prior all the way back to the influences resulting from the evolutionary history of our species. I have, however, read other philosophers who address free will and societal consequences such as Gregg Caruso who has written quite a lot on that and I would anticipate is probably going to find a great deal to agree with Sapolsky on. So just a quick answer — I do think quite a lot of human misery does result from beliefs in free will, for example, how people are ostracized for being who they (for example, LGBTQ) are even though who they are isn’t a choice they have freely made. Our criminal justice system is punitive/retributive in nature (as opposed to rehabilitative) which is an abhorrent idea if behaviors are not a result of free will. Those advocates for free will unfortunately assume that the alternative is to allow crimes to go unaddressed if free will is not assumed, but that too is another mistake. While we should not punish for reasons of wishing retribution or to be merely punitive, in a “no free will” reality there are potential deterrent effects to be weighed, as well as removing a person whose prior life history and neurological wiring is apt to have them harming others (whether they freely choose to or not) from circulation in the interest of protecting others. Or most importantly, if there is an opportunity to rehabilitate a person so that they might return to society as a more productive individual who can co-exist peacefully with others without doing harm, that’s worth pursuing. It also bears mentioning that people who take a “free will” approach also try to understand motives more in terms of someone just being “evil” and then CHOOSING to do harmful things rather than understanding that the person might either have some kind of earlier trauma which can be addressed through cognitive behavioral therapy, or might have a neurological disorder which can be addressed in one way or another, or might just have the neurological makeup which predisposes for psychopathy which may or may not be treatable, and if not, that would be a case for incarceration for the protection of others. Seeing those actions as just being “evil” and “willful” does lead to entirely the wrong perspective on it, an unwillingness to look for a productive solution, a likelihood of punishing the individual in ways that are unnecessarily cruel just because it makes the one advocating for the punishment feel better and get some satisfaction out of hurting an “evil person”, and takes a potentially reformable productive person from society (after some rehabilitation, that is). Even on other matters, as someone who is on the autism spectrum, who has a child on the autism spectrum, and who has had an abundance of awareness and interaction with others on the autism spectrum, people who don’t accept the reality of behaviors and interactions being heavily influenced by how one’s neurological wiring happens to exist will make moral judgements about others. There are social norms and cues that are pretty obvious to neurotypical people that are absolutely NOT clear to neurodiverse people who will react to a situation in the only way they know, as the standard rulebook is not embedded in their brains. Others will be quite uncomfortable and stricken by how utterly strange the neurodiverse person is, and it will never occur to them that the person’s fundamental brain wiring has directly caused the interaction to go this way just as much as the neurotypical person just naturally knows how to “read” other neurotypical people and to do “normal” things such as engage in small talk, so they will judge the neurodiverse person as if he or she is just willfully being annoying or responding in uncomfortable ways, when the person is really completely unaware they have done this and might never realize it or might come to realize it hours or days later. I’ve heard some pretty cruel things said by people who assume the other person is just being an ass. This same moral judgement can be directed to many other scenarios, such as someone who happened to have been born with whatever advantages (socioeconomic background and/or a neurological makeup that allows for resilience, ingenuity, drive/motivation, etc) would get them to a position of repute who morally judges someone who can’t ever seem to make good decisions who lives a life of complete poverty, struggle, hardship, and misery. Why don’t they just decide to do X, Y, and Z and then have a great life? It seems so obvious… but go deeper into why they don’t just do those things and there are usually reasons that are much more fundamental than “using their free will to consciously make bad decisions” — because this is really pretty much never the case, and it’s always a lot more complicated. Moral judgements can be directed at people in different cultures, different beliefs, different circumstances of all sorts. Easy to imagine that if you had been born a starving impoverished lowest-caste Indian that you’d have the moral fortitude and ingenuity to go get yourself a job and follow some clever path to a successful life, but that smuggles in the unrealized assumption that you’d take the background you REALLY had along with the neurological wiring you actually do have into that situation. So yeah, from what I know of Sapolsky’s views and what I presume he’s written based on what I’ve read in others who also do not believe in free will and from what bits I can glean from what I have read from him, I’d say I would likely agree with that book, and I should make a point of reading it sometime.

question: Why is it crucial to understand that neurodiversity encompasses a broad spectrum of cognitive and neurological differences beyond specific diagnoses?
answer: Living with uncontrolled ADHD for more than 70 of my 82 years my approach to life has been governed by trying to understand and respect every person’s individuality.(Respect being the hardest part of that during my untreated years.) Different “normal” people without any neurodiversity would be pretty dull cardboard cutouts of each other living in a society much like a colony of ants or bees guided only by the way they were raised in the colony’s culture. Thanks to evolution the human brain is different in each individual - and the social societies of nations, communities and families are much more diverse than other species. But, evolution also depends upon change and mutation to adapt to survived in ever changing environments and competition. Making those changes over millennia using DNA exchanges between sexes and individuals provides an imperfect system of procreation. As a species we have only begun to understand and measure how these natural mechanisms work. It is only in the last 150–200 years humans have been scientifically learning and better understanding how the brain works and how our neurology affects our cognitive abilities and expressions. In many parts of the globe it has been only 125 years since real work has been done in categorizing and working with behavioral disorders or variations as other than criminal or anti-social choices of individuals deserving isolation or punishment — or as demon possession requiring exorcism or death. Still in its infancy this developing body knowledge is imperfect - with both truth and error being rejected by some traditional and/or ignorant societies, religions and individuals. Too often this means any variation from their perception of “normal” is considered sin or curse and is shunned. When it comes to diversity of behavior being rejected because of biological causes, not visible or obvious from birth or wound, little knowledge or therapeutic corrective measures have, or will be developed or easily advanced for use in those societies or by individuals. Variations of individual behavior within normal bounds are tolerated - but the spectrum of variation that oversteps the rules is an item for discipline, not research and amelioration. WIth medical science’s early tries at diagnosis and treatment during the last 150 years, clumsy and sometime abhorrent research and treatment methods, the growing body of data alongside the development of new technological instruments that can measure brain activity, see and record biological variations or problems in the brain (fMRI). By looking at nervous system and correlating the information and data, science has shown that each individual is wired differently. We are not motor cars with exactly the same wiring installed on an assembly line. By looking at this accumulation work and research, over time science has shown that there are variations inside the general diagnostics sets early work had categorized. Severity of problem vs. normality has been found to have a range (or spectrum) of symptoms or behaviors within the defined diagnosis. In a growing number of cases different approaches and medications could be seen or measured as effective (and in the US considered acceptably affordable). These can be widely used to control or cure various degrees of each different level or category of diagnosis. At the same time certain procedures and drugs and procedures have found to be ineffective or even dangerous for use in individuals at various points along a specific spectrum. Professional assessment and measurement today goes well beyond former guess and “try this”diagnostic techniques of the early past 150 years. With education, continuing research (both woefully underfunded) world-wide) I hope previous malodorous refusals to recognize or use the knowledge of how each individuals’ brain varies via biology, not sin or choice, can be corrected. More directly on the question, top me it becomes critical that we recognize that not only is there a range or spectrum of individual behaviors showing their neurotypical activity, but that there is developing science applied to those who fall outside that spectrum. It is important they understand that in any specific diagnostic category there can be many congruences of how of a neurotypical person lives and reacts found in the diagnosed individual. How well the neurodivergent person functions in daily life and how any disfunction is treated by professionals depends on where the individual falls on that diagnostic label’s spectrum.

question: What is the cause of ADHD? Is it due to the brain's inability to produce enough dopamine or is it related to the brain's utilization of dopamine?
answer: It's a very interesting question, one I can't answer. But let's remember that not only do ADHD brains have some different neurochemistry in the brain vs NT’s, the ADHD brain also has different neural circuitry than NT’s. Our brains are lacking certain sophisticated signal processing circuits that NT brains have. When I was doing some deep research about 2 years ago, I thought deeply about potential reasons why we're overflooded by too many signals and signal distractions clogging our minds and hogging up our more limited processing slots. Our working memory is smaller and more limited in size than that of NT’s, causing certain processes and focus connections to overload and jam the signal board, I suppose very similar to the way computers with older and more limited RAM can't keep open 40 or 50 tabs, whereas the larger RAM in computers today can do that easily. But when our memory slots get flooded or overwhelmed by “just one more sound” competing for our ears attention, or too many extraneous visual signals that hog the processor slots, this is when too many brain inputs overflow the available signal processing circuits, forcing one or more to drop — which we experience as those signal-loss glitches when something was just in our head then suddenly igone and we can't remember what it is we were focused on. (This is still my theory of what's going on. ) … And I began focusing on music mix boards at performance venues. Band members signal to the sound crew mixing the board when there’s sudden feedback sound, or electronic noise from a bad cable connection. Or singer can't hear his guitar outputs… Many of these issues can be handled by dialing down certain sliders, dialing up others, or switching off certain input voice, EFX, instrument sliders entirely closing the circuit, preventing signal travel or pollution of “the mix”. It was after thinking about guitar players and keyboard players’ switchers at their feet controlling EFX, that I thought about signal rejection circuitry, and thresholds activating or turning off certain sounds under certain conditions. That's when I theorized “No! There's no way that these family members who are too smart for doing any research, think they're right just because their gut tells them so. No! there's no way these people who go around gaslighting people with ADHD that their problem is that they're not focusing enough or have no discipline and other ridiculous pseudo reasons for an ADHD person claiming distractibility, or “can't filter out that damn noise from that motorcycle!” There's no way these arrogant NT’s can account for their alleged greater concentration or ability to complete tasks coming down to more commitment, harder work, self-discipline, willpower to shut out distractions vs the “Not trying hard enough” Neuro diverse people with ADHD. I next theorized that NT’s could only really reduce or turn off distracting signals in their world if they had built-in circuitry in their brains that ADHD people do not have. So I went to the journals and searched for “signal gating” and “signal rejection circuitry” in brains. And sure enough, I found at least one reference to signal-gating between the path of the neuron entering a neural pathway and the synapse (which opens and closes a gate that either lets in neuron signals or rejects them, at which point they can't get through the synapse, they can't get into the neural pathway, they can't get into the brain, so those neural signals are filtered by some unknown formula. And lastly I theorize that this signal rejection circuitry found in neurotypicals but not in neurodiverse brains, would have to be some kind of sophisticated algorithm that can sense what your cognitive intention really is, ( what you're really trying to do, vs. the signal from the eye showing what your eye is looking at, and NOT equating that automatically as = your cognitive intention.) …. Closing: Even if any of my theories turn out to be true in some form, none of this at all explains WHY? Why are the two brain types wired differently?

question: Why hasn't natural selection eliminated autism?
answer: Despite ableist views many have about autistic folks, their neurodiversity continues to be a valuable enough trait to the human species that we continue to mate with our autistic brethren and pass the genes on. Natural selection has not eliminated autism because autism as a form of neurodiversity has proven to be an integral part of the success of many many folks in modern society. Autistic special interests can lead to a persistent drive for knowledge and a tenacious work ethic because of how much joy it brings that person to engage with their special interests. As society grows to value and appreciate the things some autistic folks excel at, we tend to value and appreciate the autistic traits that have led to that excellence. This is currently especially apparent in fields that require engineering, programming, and research. Without their autism, many successful contributors to society would likely not have had the drive and focus to develop the same level of expertise in their field. But because of their persistence in studying a topic and because of the fact that they think differently, they can end up being great problem solvers in that realm of knowledge and implement novel solutions to those problems. This combination of dedication, work ethic, expertise, focus, and novel problem solving has come to be highly valued in a lot of occupations. Similar to neurotypical folks, autistic adults who find the right environment and field to work in end up being successful, happy, and interesting to talk to. And this can make other folks value them and potentially find them attractive as a sexual partner. Then bam, the autistic genes continue to be passed on. Additionally, with technological progress in things like the internet and digital communication, the world has become a much easier place for a lot of autistics to be able to find folks to connect with and find employment in environments where sensory differences and differences in communication aren’t as debilitating. The internet, in particular, is a wonderful place for neurodivergent folks to find like minded people to connect with, so there’s a greater chance for autistics to find people they relate to, and who relate to them. Having the ability to contribute in their own way and in an environment that they can control so they can focus has opened up many doors to socialization for autistic folks and more socialization means folks who want to have children are more likely to find a partner and have children. Also, with women gaining more rights and a voice, getting educated, and joining the workforce, autistic folks have become more and more likely to find partners. The structure and regularity of school and work as social environments can make it a lot easier for autistic folks (and people in general) to make a connection with a potential partner because one doesn’t have to be as socially extroverted to meet people in those social environments vs other social environments. Plus, things like seeking specialized degrees and careers tends to naturally group folks with similar values and interests together, so it gives everyone in those fields a baseline of things to talk about, which helps autistic folks socially. The addition of women to these spaces has meant that autistic folks are much more likely to find each other, potentially like each other’s often more direct style of communication, partner up, and pass their genes on.

question: What is the relation of MBTI types and human evolution?
answer: Andreas Hofer writes a lot about thishttps://www.quora.com/profile/Andreas-Hofer-5?q=andreas%20hHis%20hypothesis%20is%20that%20there%20are%20three%20types%3A%20farmer%20types%2C%20hunter-gatherer%20types%2C%20and%20pastoralist%20types.https://www.quora.com/profile/Andreas-Hofer-5?q=andreas%20hHis%20hypothesis%20is%20that%20there%20are%20three%20types%3A%20farmer%20types%2C%20hunter-gatherer%20types%2C%20and%20pastoralist%20types.You may wish to read the previous answer to get full context:Aaron Matthews · 2yCan the frequency of MBTI types change over time as a part of evolution?To understand the types better, check out this answer: The genetic traits of populations can change due to changing circumstances. What I mean is that a previously harmful mutation can become beneficial. An example would be with peppered moths in Britain. In the preindustrial era, 98% of peppered moths were white while 2% were black. This was because white moths were more difficult for birds to see. When the industrial revolution rolled around, the pollution made the tree barks darker, causing the white moths to get eaten and the black moths to survive. By the end of the 19th century, black moths dominated the population, making up as much as 98% in the most polluted areas. As you can see here, white peppered moths are more difficult to see against the light bark And here, the black moth is much harder to spot while the white one sticks out like a sore thumb As I explained in this answer, sexual reproduction means that the genes of both parents are thrown into a blender with a few genetic mutations resulting. Some mutations are harmful while others are beneficial. The only thing that really determines whether parents pass on certain genes to their children is whether they’re dominant or recessive. When people with different genes have children, the dominant genes will be passed on while the recessive genes don’t. Inbreeding increases the probability that recessive genes pass on, most of which are harmful. This is why people tend not to fall for their family members. This also explains why men, even as they get older, tend to prefer younger women because the odds of recessive traits passing drastically increase as a woman gets older. With that said, it makes sense that over the course of human history, certain traits may have emerged. When we look at other primates as well as many other animals, we see that males compete over mates while females are more selective. The reason for this asymmetry is quite simple. Females have to carry their offspring to term and in K species, have to raise them as well, incentivizing them to be very picky about their partners. Males in most cases merely mate, making them not very selective. As a consequence of this asymmetry, males have to put on a show while the females don’t. The result is that with particularly social animals like primates and lions, you see polygamy in which the best male mates with all of the females. This explains why male gorillas are so much larger than females. Considering that males will happily murder offspring which isn’t theirs, one would wonder why the lesser males didn’t just gang up on the bigger one. After man began to develop language due to increased intelligence, that began to happen. As a result, things became much more equal with the average man not being much taller than the average woman. Overall, foraging groups were fairly egalitarian. Any hierarchy which formed was purely based on merit and if anything, furthered egalitarianism by distributing resources equitably. Anyone who didn’t like their tribe could simply move to a neighboring one. Although homo sapiens date back 315,000 years, the cognitive revolution was around 70,000 years ago which is also how long ago Mt. Toba erupted. This eruption, the equivalent of a full eruption by Yellowstone, caused dramatic global cooling, making the current global warming look rather puny by comparison. The world as a whole cooled by 4 degrees with the hardest hit regions cooling 10 degrees. The archaic humans in temperate and arctic zones were doomed. Those in desert and tropical climates had a chance of survival but even then, the eruption reduced humanity’s population down to 15,000 (mostly in Subsaharan Africa since the southern hemisphere and tropical regions were hit less hard). Funny enough, that actually didn’t cause the neanderthals to go extinct, they would last until 40,000 BCE. The humans which survived benefitted from greater intelligence. The humans who survived did so by fishing since aquatic ecosystems weren’t as negatively affected. The increase in intelligence had previously been a slow and steady process but the eruption placed increased pressure on mankind to think outside the box. Although man had previously left Africa, the eruption set them back to square one. From then on, the earth would be populated by modern humans. The earth slowly began to cool again until 20,000 BC when it hit the glacial maximum. From then on, the world began to slowly warm up again, allowing the population to increase. In 10,000 BC, the levant region and north africa were actually green. In fact, the levant region was the fertile crescent. It stood out from other parts of the world because the climate and geography enabled a sedentary population. Thus, the Natufian who resided in present-day Syria would have likely discovered agriculture at some point. However, hunting and gathering remained preferable to agriculture for a few reasons. The first was that farming actually required more work than hunting and gathering. When adding up all of the work that hunter-gatherers did in a week, the total added up to 40 hours at most. The second was that foraging provided a varied diet while the diets of farming societies was oftentimes restricted. Hunter-gatherers were the same size as modern men but farmers were a few inches shorter because of less nutrition. All of this makes you wonder why farming was adopted at all. The main virtue of agriculture is that it comes with higher food density, increasing the population ceiling. This was particularly useful when the younger dryas hit, lowering global temperatures. Agriculture was likely something that the Mesopotamians fell on to make up for lost food. Another thing worth touching on is that according to some, our neurobiology was a bit different back then. Most people back then were high in openness, not so much in conscientiousness. The N function’s main virtue is that it enables people to think outside the box. That doesn’t mean that S people are dumb but rather that they tend to learn through experience rather than inductive reasoning. The J function deals with conscientiousness which mainly concerns the fixation on getting something achieved. This has been very useful since society formed because it mainly centers around delayed gratification. Those who had more pronounced J traits made for better farmers and were more likely to survive the famine. Farmers were also dominant in the S function rather than the N function. This meant that farmers preferred gaining information through experience and pay less attention to their inner selves and looking for deeper meaning. Agriculture first emerged in the river valley civilizations of Mesopotamia, Egypt, Indus valley, and China. The rivers there were highly unpredictable, requiring intense coordination from the top down. This placed a particularly downward pressure on NPs from those societies. People who weren’t conscientious enough were ostracized. Those who were open enough to dissent got killed. The 7R gene basically describes openness to experience. It’s likely less common amongst Chinese for that reason and has much higher frequency in the Americas, likely due to settlers and immigrants open to moving to the US as well as indigenous people who were previously hunter gatherers (obviously, not all of them were but when Europeans arrived, they were certainly more common there than in Europe). Then there were pastoralist societies. Like foragers, they were nomadic and held hierarchy in disdain. Like farmers, pastoralists were less focused on intuition than foragers, making pastoralists SP types. However, pastoralist societies differed from both farmer and forager societies in an important way. You see, natural selection favors neurobiology which does the best job in securing offspring. This means that whether the dark traits of sociopathy (lack of regard for others) and narcissism (care for oneself rather than others) become dominant depend on whether the social environment encourages cooperation or competition. In a cooperative environment like with the foragers, such a person would have likely been kicked out of the tribe. In a cooperative environment, nobody wants freeriders or people who will cause trouble for the group. Farming societies were internally cooperative and externally competitive, encouraging an in group mentality. Pastoralist societies were both internally and externally competitive. As such pastoralists were very materialistic and sometimes caused problems for the farming societies. Other times, they traded with farmers in the form of goods like food, weapons, and slaves. This internal competition helps explain why SP types are at an increased risk of sociopathic traits. ASPD, the most well known manifestation of dark traits, is basically the dark version of an ESTP. This leaves us with NJs. As intuitive judgers, they rank well in openness and conscientiousness. One would think that these people would thrive in civilization. However, openness and conscientiousness in a sense seem to be at odds with one another. Although people with the J function excel in a structured environment (like modern day society), they tend to struggle when something doesn’t go according to plan. On the hunt, everything could go wrong, meaning that hunters had to keep their options open. Radio host Thom Hartmann came up with the hypothesis that ADHD was a beneficial trait during the hunter-gatherer days, making it a beneficial trait throughout most of mankind’s (as well as its ancestor’s) history. Then with the circumstances in the world of farming, ADHD became a negative trait. It’s not particularly known why NJs didn’t outcompete SJs but perhaps it had to do with SJs being more prone to conformity and a bit more materialistic, showing off for potential mates. This below chart tells us a lot. One thing I noticed is that the most common personality types for both men and women were introverted even though extroverts seem to have an easier time getting ahead. This may have to do with how violent our past was. An introvert is more likely to sit on the sidelines while extroverts get in on the action. This typically comes with more wealth and glory for the extroverts, increasing the chance for a mate if successful but it also icnreases the liklihood of getting killed. Perhaps fittingly, ESTP is the least common of the S types, being the most glory seeking of all. SJs are the most common group, making up 43.2% of men and 49.6% of women. SPs are the second most common, likely because pastoralists were less common than farmers but more common than hunter-gatherers. SPs make up 28.6% of men and 25.3% of women. One interesting thing worth noting is the vast disparity in prevalence for ISTP’s in men vs women. ISTP is the third most common type for men but the fourth least common for women. I’m not exactly sure why there’s such a huge disparity. Then there’s NPs which consist 19.3% of men and 18.4% of women. No surprises here since hunter-gatherers were less common than pastoralists or farmers. That leaves us with NJs which make up 8.8% of men and 6.9% of women, making it the smallest group. In fact, all four of the rarest types for men (and 3 of the 4 for women) are NJs. This is likely because they never had their own societies, always living in the shadow of other types. This, however, is beginning to change. As mentioned in the previous answer, the tables are turning in favor of NJ types. An increasing number of well paying jobs require openess. In the age of automation, conscietiousness is no longer sufficient because no matter how conscietious a person is, a robot will always be more conscietious. Just as the neolithic revolution did not end well for NPs, the age of automation will likely lead to mass unemployment, disproportionately affecting S types. With tech companies such as Google offering flexible work schedules and progress beginning on neurodiversity, it may very well be the case that conscietiousness will be displaced by openess as the main trait which affects income. Another trait worth looking at is agreeableness which is not part of the MBTI. Agreabbleness is the willingness to put up with stuff that you don’t want to do. So far, agreabbleness is inversely correlated with wages for a few reasons. 1. People low in agreableness are more likely to stand up to their bosses in confrontational ways such as joining a union or asking for a raise. 2. People higher in agreableness tend to take jobs which pay less. 3. People high in agreableness are less likely to change jobs for a higher wage. 4. Some of the wealthiest people are those who went against the grain. People who are high in agreableness (especially SJs), tend to just go with the flow. Those type of people typically end up average. In the past there has been an inverse correlation between education and fertility due to the demographic transition model. However, this inverse correlation has been decreasing for the past few decades. The reason for this may simply be that more well educated women have less time to raise kids due to their careers. This inverse correlation was fueled by the fact that female non college graduates were more likely to stay home to raise the kids. However, it doesn’t have to be that way. With third wave feminism challenging basic gender roles and a push for paid maternity leave, all of that may no longer be the case. There has always been a direct correlation between education and income. As people consider their means before having kids, we may start to see a direct correlation between education and fertility. With that, the demographic composition of personalities may start to change. Although plenty of smart people find it immoral to have kids, there are those like Elon Musk who have 9. Once that starts to happen, you will see the N types replace the S types.The reason why different MBTI types exist is because each offer beneficial strategies. NP types were hunter gatherers. They were well suited to keeping their options open. SJ types were farmers. They excelled in conscientiousness which is important for farming. SP types were pastoralists. It’s not quite clear why the N function would have been detrimental but it seems that it has to do with S types being more grounded in reality, making them more prone to materialism. Hunter gatherers weren’t materialistic because they couldn’t afford to be. As nomadic people, their property was what they could carry on their backs. Agriculture changed all of that. We tend to think that farming enabled division of labor since less work was required to find food but that wasn’t really the case because if anything, it required more work. The reason comes down to the fact that agricultural civilizations were stationary, enabling the accumulation of wealth. Pastoralists societies were limited in wealth accumulation, like the hunter-gatherers, but enough of them wanted what developed societies had to gain reproductive success. Thus, anti social traits are the most likely to manifest in SP types because their societies were internally competitive. SJ types tend to be in groupish because while developed societies were externally competitive, they were very much internally cooperative. Hunter-getherer societies were both externally and itnernally cooperative. The different traits can mainfest themselves in neurobiology in different ways. Extraversion and introversion are based on how much internal stimulation the brain has. Introverts already have plenty of internal stimulation and may resent active scenes due to overstimulation. Extraverts don’t have a lot of internal stimulation and seek it from the outside world. The N trait T vs F governs whether someone views the world through logic or emotion. T people prefer to look at the facts before making a decision while F people go based on their feelings. This is probably the hardest one to pin down because it has no big five equivalent. However, one of the distinctions of those on the autism spectrum is that they tend to be super logical. Because they grow up in a world which is not so logical, they tend to struggle in developing social skills. J vs P governs conscientiousness. The 7R-DRD4 gene may increase the likelihood of P traits emerging. It has been linked with ADHD, addictive behaviors, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and anorexia. This gene has a 20% prevalence in North America and is much less common in Eastern Asia, likely owing to the latter region’s high level of conscientiousness.Dopamine receptor D4 (DRD4) gene in Han Chinese children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): increased prevalence of the 2-repeat allele - PubMedThere is an increased prevalence of the 7-repeat (7R) allele of the dopamine receptor D4 (DRD4) gene in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, the population prevalence of the 7R allele varies considerably across ethnicity and is very low in Asians. To test whether this 7R allele/ …https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15578612/#:~:text=There%20is%20an%20increased%20prevalence,is%20very%20low%20in%20Asians.The 2 repeat allele (2R) also correlates with ADHD and essentially makes up for the lack of prevalence of the 7R in Asia. It also correlates with antisocial behaviors. Bearing in mind that evolution is really just natural selection on a large timescale, it would make sense that there are certain benefits and drawbacks to each. For example, the J trait would be highly advantageous in civilization since it involves focusing on a specific goal and not getting sidetracked. This is important because the success of civilization is largely based around investment. People with the J trait tend to have specific interests which fits well in an advanced economy, largely cetnered around specialization. However, the J trait may not be so useful when things don’t go according to plan. In hunter-gatherer groups, this happened all the time, making the P trait beneficial. Perhaps the reason why some of us long for the apocalypse is because that would actually make the P trait beneficial rather than a nuisance. The ADHD hunter-gather hypothesis is that prehistoric hunters had two modes: radar mode and hyperfocus mode. Radar mode is very peripheral in its focus, keeping an eye on its surroundings. Hyperfocus mode kicks in as soon as the hunter spots potential prey. This would be considered an example of evolution at work. Just as white moths did well when the tree bark was its natural white, those with ADHD thrived and were considered neurotypical in prehistoric society, not so much when civilization began. The biggest shortcomings of ADHD has to do with a lack of conscientiousness. Those with the farmer mindset became mainstream, likely because they were better with time management and delayed gratification. Natural selection also occurred in pastoralist societies but instead of becoming more conscientious, pastoralists became more materialistic and with some sociopathic and narcissistic tendencies. Every single personality type exists due to genetic mutation. The ones which are the most common are such because they’ve had the most success. The metric of success always remains the same: passing on your genes. SJ types are the most common today because they did the best job passing down their genes. But as explained in the previous answer, the way success is achieved is subject to change. The traits which make a good hunter-gatherer are not the same as the traits which make a good farmer. For most of history, doing better was directly correlated with reproductive success. However, since the dawn of the industrial age, this has no longer been true because education is directly correlated with income but inversely so with fertility. The type of person who is super smart but doesn’t want children will be selected against. There is evidence to suggest that narcissistic sociopaths have a better chance at succeeding at capitalism because it means making as much money as possible at any cost (no pun intended). However, that doesn’t necessarily mean they have better odds of passing down their genes. As time goes on, this will likely be less so as women become more empowered, making them less likely to settle for an abusive husband. I also pointed out in the previous answer that the inverse correlation between education and income is getting weaker. The reason why NJ types had trouble passing on their genes may have less to do with so innate resentment of children and more to do with the difficulty in finding one another. Since NJ types value both openness and conscientiousness and since they’re so rare, they’ve likely had a difficult time finding a partner who values the same things that they do and some decided to remain single. There’s also the historical inverse correlation between education and fertility. Even though NJs did a better job in SJ society than NPs, they often focused on studies rather than starting a family. In some societies, this was because of certain factors selecting against them. NJs in medieval europe were more likely to become monks, causing them to remain celibate and be selected against (this didn’t happen with Ashkenazi Jews which is why they have the highest average IQ). In today’s society, this is less true. Types who don’t feel like they belong can find one another on the internet. In the future, there may also be better paid family leave, enabling high skill workers to balance their jobs with their family lives. Meanwhile, those not well suited to high skill jobs will be making significantly less, probably resulting in them having fewer children. If human history with the MBTI tells us a story, it’s one of neurodiversity. Obviously, it wasn’t intentional, offspring have a random chance of being born with genetic mutations. However, by not leaving all of mankind’s eggs in one basket, it gave the neurodivergent SJs the chance to thrive following the neolithic revolution, eventually becoming neurotypical, just as the black moths replaced the white moths during the 1800s. This explains a potential finding that genetic mutation for humans has sped up. It would seem that since SJ and SP types were a deviation from the NPs which had dominated humanity for all of prior history, they were types more prone to genetic mutations. This was additionally aided by the mutation which made us lactose tolerant. It appears that we are once again approaching a genetic replacement. I would also like to give a special mention to autism which is caused by a recessive gene. As of 2020, around 2% of children in America have this diagnosis. This percentage is increasing rapidly but mainly because of expanding standards for what makes someone autistic and better detection methods (i.e. better diagnosis). Currently, people with this condition are big losers when it comes to natural selection because they’re terrible at socializing which happens to be very important when it comes to selecting a romantic partner and having children. People on the spectrum also have difficulty learning in the conventional way. That doesn’t necessarily mean that they are intellectually substandard but rather that they think differently. It seems like they display extreme T traits, being hyperlogical. In a world more attuned to people in the middle, it makes sense why people on the spectrum struggle in social settings, not merely because they’re often introverted but because they often struggle with knowing what’s appropriate to say. It seems like changing society to make it more livable for them would increase their odds of reproducing. Neurodiversity may actually be abenefit in of itself rather than merely be putting eggs in different baskets. Take the wisdom of crowds which was illustrated in a 1906 country fair in which 800 people guessed the weight of a slaughtered ox. The median guess of 1207 was within the 1% margin of the correct answer which was 1198. By putting our intellectual opinions together, we come closer to the right answer than any one of us could have done on our own. In order for the crowd to be wiser than the idividual, three things must hold true.No member should hold a disproportionate opinion on the whole. Othwerwise, the group will be biased towards the influencers.Nobody should be emotionally attached to any answer. Peer pressure and other biases can undermine the wisedom of the crowd.There must be heterogenity so that different opinions may converge on the right answer.The third requirement is where neurodiversity comes in. Most people are fairly close to the center regarding each of the personality traits. This gives plenty of room for those along the extremes to share their insights. People on the spectrum tend to be less subject to social pressure, giving them an edge on 1 and possible also 2 to some extent. The jobs which will exist in the future will largely have to do with critical thinking, making it beneficial to have multiple viewpoints. Each of the four MBTI groups are ideal for a specific society. NP: forager SJ: farmer SP: pastoralist NJ: scientist

question: How do I help a daughter see she has BPD like myself?
answer: There’s a thing that (in caps for emphasis) EVERYONE does, called projection. It gets a bad rap because folks who have experience of relationships with BPD folks think BPD folks are doing defensive projection to/at them, sometimes —basically misinterpreting those thoughts that are a product of abandonment/rejection fears as defensive projections of someone with an inherently untrustworthy disposition (but that ain’t necessarily how it goes). Literally everyone projects that others are similar to themselves in some way —it’s the basis of empathy. If we assume that others are more similar to ourselves than not, it allows us to call up imaginings in our own mind of ‘what it’s like to be them’ in the moment, and empathize effectively. Easier with some more than others, for some more than others, and in some situations more than others. When BPD is involved… I mean, I’m sure this question is borne of genuine concern for your daughter’s well-being, and if you have BPD you probably know a thing or three about it, and what the signs and symptoms are, but nevertheless because you have BPD there’s still a chance you’re seeing things through the lens of BPD. This doesn’t mean you’re wrong, just that you might be seeing some things that aren’t BPD as indicative BPD, because just like anyone and everyone else you only have your own experience and perception to go on. So whilst your daughter might be having some genuine difficulties, they might not be full-on BPD difficulties. Considerations of biopsychosocial inheretance might justifiably lend weight to the idea that your daughter has either the genes for it, or has developed it from her upbringing, or at least ‘knows the emotional langauge’ of BPD —having grown up on the borders of BPD-land. But speaking the language of a place doesn’t mean you’re necessarily from that place, and whilst she may have learned the emotional language of BPD, her underlying cognitions might be fairly neurotypical —there’s no way to know for sure how another person thinks, and if she doesn’t agree with you, then she doesn’t agree with you, and you kind of just have to take her word for that (otherwise, you risk getting into a big invalidation-fest that puts strain on your relationship). BUT, also, your intuition on the matter is still worthy of serious consideration. The above paragraphs are not to say you are wrong, just that there’s some sifting to be done to get to any nuggets of truth, generally speaking —but this goes for all of us, BPD or no BPD. Everyone is prone to subjective bias, it’s everywhere on the internet, subjective bias is like ‘the wallpaper’ of the internet, lol. I agree that the best ways to approach it would be those described in Rachel Ernst’s answer herein. However, depending upon the nature of your relationship… …I dunno, I talked to someone recently where they descibed a BPD-ish person being confronted by their family ‘intervention-style’, and this led to the creation of a big defensive wall that proved to be a barrier to recovery. But if you’re a person with BPD, and you’re taking responsibility for that, and you want to take responsibility for any BPD-ish-ness you might have passed on to your daughter, then I’m guessing this is likely to create less of a ‘her vs. you’ scenario than if you were to outright blame her for stuff without taking responsibility. But at the same time, recovery from BPD generally requires each of us coming to our own realizations about BPD, about ourselves, and about our thought patterns and life patterns. So it can take time, before a person is ready to be honestly and whole-heartedly open to beginning the process of recovery. So perhaps the best thing you can do for her is to keep it in mind, and be there if and when she needs you to be there, but don’t push it for fear of putting strain on the relationship, if that makes sense. If she trusts you she’s more likely to take your recovery-based advice if and when she needs it, basically, but if you invalidate her by treating her like she’s BPD-ish before she herself has come to her own realizations about that, then even if you’re right you’d still be creating a barrier between you and her, and as this question is borne of concern I’m guessing that is the last thing you want. As a final consideration/complication (sorry) —there are many different forms of BPD. 9 diagnostic traits, 5 of those needed for diagnosis, equals (I think) 256 different potential manifestations of the disorder. So, for example… say you’re right, and you can see from how she treats herself and listening to how she thinks about things that she has underlying BPD-ish cognitions and behavioral patterns:Because there are many different types of BPD, her BPD might manifest differently than yours, and she might not need help with that same aspects of the disorder as you do/did —so you could be right and wrong about her at the same time, if that makes sense.Also, if her type of BPD is different from yours she could very easily say ‘No, wait, my mom is what BPD is like, I’m different from my mom, therefore I don’t have BPD’ —when in reality she might have a different type of BPD that goes untreated and un-helped for want of proper identification.There are risks involved, basically. This is a person’s personality that’s under consideration —and on whatever basis we question or critique that there is huge potential for defensiveness when we do. Goes right to the core of things. So whilst you might have genuine concerns, based in reality, that you might feel you have to do something about, urgently… …Perhaps a less direct approach is your best bet in helping your daughter with any difficulties that either: a) she does have, or b) you perceive her to have. So maybe just keep it in mind, but towards the back of your mind so as not to invalidate her, and be there as and when she needs you to be there for her, I guess. Walk the middle path. Wise mind FTW. I mean, with the right understanding you can facilitate a recovery, definitely, but you can’t force one. You can’t change a person who doesn’t want to change, even if it’s your judgement that they might need to change, because you want the best for them. BPD is a big complex ‘thing’, and realizations of underlying neurodiversity can kind of be analogous to getting hit with a psychological brick. It’s a lot to wrap one’s head around, in other words, and can’t be understood all at once, and the finer details have to be understood before we approach helping another person with it. Long post, hope this helps with some of those finer details —but, also, it’s important to remember that this is the internet, and most folks aren’t professionals, and whilst we might share info to try to help one-another these things are best diagnosed and helped by professionals, really. Even so, as I say, hope this helps :)

question: I have an 11-year-old son with Asperger's. He gets very angry at times. What can I do to help him?
answer: I was late diagnosed. Spontaneous anger, uncontrollable rage from LITERALLY NOTHING, is a symptom of ASD. One of the realizations I had that I must be ASD. As a kid, oh, I beat up a scout leader, threw a kid through a wall at hs, and broke a kids arm at military camp… I was kicked out of the scouts, he got a suspension while i had a detention, and i had no punishment for breaking the arm. You see, 2 of those 3 were basically ruled “I was pushed enough”. Kid made a holocaust joke… so I threw him through a wall (barely dry wall, not like cement). Kid was throwing rocks at me, so I broke his arm. He was expelled, I had no issue. I still stand by that scout leader had it coming too, but, kid vs adult, adults sided with adult… The point of these stories is that the violent rage is unfortunately there. Those unfortunate individuals, decided to push me past it, and got the results. If you kick a bear, the bear will maul you. That isnt really the bears fault. I've learned meditation, and through medication and therapy i can control it more… I can feel the rage just randomly show up, and I can realize, now, that it actually isn't because of something someone else is doing, it is a part of me i need to deal with. I haven't physically assaulted anyone in probably 15+ years (the last was a roommate who stole from me, and then his mouth wrote a check he couldn't cash… so again, I'd argue, deserved, I mostly threw him to the ground and sat on him… i outweighed him by 70-100 pound). My ex would push me, and I'd scream and run. That is my response to my rage now. With that said, therapy. You need therapy, he needs therapy. You are not neurodiverse (I assume) and you will need to do research. There is a difference between a 37 year old adult (arguably… growing old is mandatory, growing up is optional), who actually enjoys studying, learning about the diagnosis, and working through it, and an 11 year old child. He will need help, and guidance, both from professionals on a regular basis, and parents and family on a continuing basis. You will learn about the triggers, things that likely trigger rage. You may find that is just means you can't wear a certain color, or perfume. Maybe that you can't listen your favorite music on speakers with him around. Maybe it means yoh just need to carry a little stuffed animal, that if you see a certain facial expression, you pull him aside and let him squeeze the toy for 5 minutes. (Fidget spinners in a corner of a stressful environment? Oh i love those things… the pitch of the hum, and vibration of the spinning… so relaxing, at least to me… Lets me be in crowds a lot longer) There could be a lot of little things, that may seem weird, that would drastically improve his disposition. For example; dont chew gum with your mouth open near me. That clicking will drive me up a wall. Certain styles of music, “dance”, and certain forms of hip hop, will force me out of a moving car… think about your feelings about someone taking a nail and scraping it on a chalkboard. Triggers, are things like that, that neurotypicals may not even notice, but ASD and other neurodivergent, can't see or hear anything else if that is present. You, and he, REALLY need to learn his triggers. THAT is what you're looking for, and that likely, will need professional assistance. At least for a time. I truly love my therapist. Without her, I have no idea where I'd be. Hope that helps.

question: How can an Aspie like me handle being misunderstood by others?
answer: A life of being misunderstood and not knowing why. I am quirky and I’ve made dozens of “naive” statements that became running jokes … jokes retold for *years* after I said whatever it was that seemed so comical. Some of these jokes were about things I *never* figured out why they were funny and the times that I asked for clarification only lead to more laughter. My group of friends growing up were relentless ball-busters. The thing that allowed me to fit in? Everyone picked on everyone! This was not a neurotypical vs aspie environment. In the 1970’s and 80’s when the worst of the ball-busting happened a lot of my friends were strange, odd, different. At the time, though, there were no words for aspie or autistic known to small town folks. A good friend had a nickname “Johnny Brain Damage” and another was in a band called “Johnny Prick and the Virgins.” but they were probably neurotypicals. Subtlety was not something my friends understood! I was picked on but I mostly felt at home because everyone got a ton of ball busting. Everyone. Even the girls and they gave it right back. Being different was relatively easy in a big school (600+ kids in my graduating high-school class) and in a working and middle class small city. I mean it kinda sucked being different but there were so many people that everyone somehow screwed up on a rotating basis. I also consciously chose to act crazy and do crazy things so I could fit in more easily. This wasn’t a truly wise decision in hindsight but it did allow me to ‘fit in.’ I found I had a knack for trying outrageous, sometimes illegal or immoral things. (The 1980s were as unhinged as movies portray.) Being small, dorky, dweeby and apparently a bit insane helped me develop a reputation as someone unpredictable. That helped cement me as “entertaining enough to keep around” and “not a pussy about trying new things.” It also earned me a place on “The Top 10 Kids I’d Like to Kick the Shit Out Of" made by a local bully. Ah, the glory! And I even managed to date a few girls before I got out of high school. I was dorky but persistent! Unfortunately, almost everything I did to be crazy in 1980 is now a reason for Homeland Security to get involved and/or can get you 10 years in prison. Law Enforcement has *no* sense of humor anymore so high-speed chases, setting things on fire, explosive rockets, smoke bombs in schools, drunk driving**, property damage and other idiocies are for some reason actually enforced as illegal. Rats! I suggest you don’t follow my lead on being crazy. BUT, being different and being yourself — even if that makes you odd — is not always a bad thing. I’m finding that — while there are still mean girls and asshole guys — my daughter’s good friends are very interesting and quirky kids. Some are aspies, some are trans, some are gay, goth or (horrors) relatively normal! Find people who are good people, treat them well and … still keep a sense of humor about yourself! Learning to laugh at yourself is actually a really good trait. How I am perceived when I do something stupid still hurts but *most* social failings fall out of the memories of others before the end of the day. YOU will probably remember them and rehash them but try to let them go. I’m in my 50’s and am still bothered by the stupid mistakes I make … and I still make them. Laughing at yourself and learning why other people think what you say is funny can be healing. A few of the things I said I eventually figured out why they were funny. The most common theme was I was too trusting of what other people said. I don’t like to feel like I’ve been ripped off so when a salesperson told me something I believed what they told me. When I got taken advantage of my friends would laugh and say “they told you that those holes were suppose to be there? Hahahaha!” Sigh. They were still good friends. Sensitivity training was not a strong point, though! My aspie side can only understand neurotypical lies by experiencing them firsthand. It rarely occurs to me to not trust people I meet. There are exceptions. When untrustworthy people — people who have screwed me over multiple times — introduce me to new people I am often wary. Otherwise, my default mode is trust. Don’t fuck with me, though. I have an incredibly bad temper when people lie directly to my face or accuse me of not doing my job, etc. And don’t fuck with my peeps. I get equally upset when I see someone who can’t necessarily stand up for themselves at work get wrongly accused of something. I can’t always intervene. I need to have knowledge-or-a-lever of some kind to help them but if I have that lever I will either go publicly ballistic or risk a private conversation that my put me at risk, just so I can try to set the record straight. The hardest lesson from that is that some people can not be trusted, will not listen to reason or logic, are lying, self-serving delusional fucks. Ahem. Yes. That kind of person should just be avoided. Smile. Be polite. Do your job. Stay the fuck out of their way and warn your allies and friends not to trust them either. I used to try to fix people like that. Dumbass thing to do. I put myself in a world of hurt by taking on a few bosses. Even if I can be … stubborn … I am liked and respected. I’m sure I’d be labeled “high-functioning” and I have a job with a lot of responsibility and a high level of technical understanding required. I’m good at what I do.
