I’ve earned the trust and respect of the rational people I work with. When I say something aspie-naive or am certain of something I heard or thought … but I’m totally, insanely wrong … I still feel embarrassed. I still get That Look from others and I can see in their eyes something akin to “Dang! He’s usually so on target. How can he have said something that stupid?” “Because I am me. And I say stupid things. I can’t stop it. They seem okay to say when I say them.” I’ve had to get used to it because there are still few social events that last longer than 10 minutes where I don’t say something odd or ridiculous. I kinda “game” social events, trying to get through them with dignity, but am often just trying not to screw up. I don’t come off as weird as I think I am. No one ever told me I might be aspie. I considered it a few times when someone mentioned that children of older parents may more frequently be autistic but wrote that off as unlikely. (“I’m different but not that different.”) A lot of neurotypical people come off as stranger than I do but I’m also a master at masking, I had a huge advantage in that I was raised upper-middle-class and spent tons of time at adult-social functions when I was very young, under 10 years old. I basically learned that all social constructs are pretend and based on largely arbitrary and made-up rules. If we are given opportunities observe, learn or be trained in The Rules, and if the rules are clear and consistent, aspies can often perform admirably in social situations. Invisibly even. When the rules go sideways? Fug. All bets are off. “Hip” social functions make me nuts! The rules are too new. All of the inside jokes people have picked up from TV shows or YouTube stars are meaningless to me. Everyone laughs … and I laugh, too, but only so I don’t stand out. Just a friendly warning In the past — and I don’t recommend this — I’d deal with social events by drinking a fair (or ridiculous) amount of alcohol. Alcohol allowed me to relax enough to be social to the point of being downright chatty. Later in life I realized I became “Loud and Brilliant” which meant I’d pick a subject of interest to me and start spouting off long incomprehensible speeches. My wife finally figured a way to get me to stop: “Honey, I love you dearly but you are making my head hurt.” Alcohol also ‘helped’ in that I’d generally not remember the stupid things I said the night before. I eventually learned to say to myself “Alcohol is not my friend” because I had too many ‘threshold moments’ where I’d lose count of how much I’d been drinking. I came to say, “Yeah … when I drink I tend to have 1 beer, 2 beers, 3 beers, Twelve!” I still have a beer at some social gatherings but mostly I stick to cranberry juice or ginger ale. They look like alcohol and I don’t get a hangover! I miss the “loose” feeling I used to have at social gatherings but I do not miss being doing drunk-stupid things in addition to aspie-stupid things. Being misunderstood is a real challenge. I don’t have any great solutions to being different and saying things oddly. Being different in a crowd takes a ton of practice and the learning curve never ends. I will always be awkward and I will probably say something stupid in any complex social situation. Or I won’t and I will come off as charming and witty. I can never tell. I will probably also continue to say things that are hurtful to my wonderful and loving wife when all I think I’m doing is “telling the truth.” I have to run conversations I want to have with her over and over and over and over in my head. Quite often … I just don’t say anything for months at a time until I can really, really, really understand if something is truly important to me. (We’ve been together for 20 years, so a few months is a lot shorter to us than it sounds!) I’ve learned that just because I feel something doesn’t mean I have to say something about my feelings. Feelings that persist for days, weeks or months … are usually important but I may need even more time to understand for myself what is the core of what is bothering me. And then it takes forever for me to find the proper words and the proper time to say the words. Being certain you need to say something exactly when your wife just came in soaking wet after 5 hours in the rain trying to save rotting plants … means you have to undo your aspie sense of certainty … and shut … the … fuck … up. And then tell her how wonderful she is and take care of her … even if your insides are all aspie-tangle and full of “ouch” and “fuck this busts my routine” and “I’m still upset” and all that other wonderfully confusing ungoodness! Patience. Fug. Good news? Neurodiverse is becoming more normal. The number of 50 year old folks who are discovering they are autistic/aspie/ASD or just freaking neurodifferent is astonishing. What that means is that — even if it has been painful, confusing, full of depression and anxiety — tons of 50+ year old people have survived in NT society for 50+ years or more through practicing and failing and practicing and failing. AND they had no clue they were “officially” challenged. You can do this. You have gifts and things to contribute to society. Our perspective and honesty are needed. Our deeply held empathy for others — even if often not visible — is incredibly important for society. Dare to be different. Reach out to the support communities that are now available. If you need help do not be afraid to accept help. (I just came out as aspie to my wife and I’m asking for her help in creating and prioritizing lists for our life. That has been hard for me to do. I’m not great at accepting help … or listening to my own advice!) And don’t be afraid to make (aspie) mistakes. People will forget. You will learn. Be Well. — ** Seriously, though … I feel bad about the drunk driving. Driving drunk was so absurdly common with both adults and teens that cops would tell a slurring drunk “just drive slowly, okay.” It is a different and *better* world for intoxicated driving no longer being acceptable. I feel very, very, very lucky I never hurt anyone. — P.S. I’m undiagnosed but I am not neurotypical. Adult diagnosis is a challenge and I’m still not sure I’m up for the search for good doctors in my area and/or the expense and time to prove I’m aspie. I may eventually get a diagnosis … in part so I can write with more authority … but I’ve only suspected I might be autistic for less than a year and I’m still coming to terms with my own feelings and my wife’s feelings about my aspie-side so I’m very, very early on my journey. — Question originally asked: How can an Aspie like me handle being misunderstood by others?

question: What should I make sure not to do while dating someone with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)?
answer: Because the human brain frequently follows the train of thought better if it is in a positive form, first, I am going to give a “to do" list, despite the wording of the question. Then after, if there are any left, I will pick on the don'ts. There are some things better left undone, yes, but I also believe that most of them can be expressed as “dos" rather than “don'ts”. So, without further ado: TO DO LIST FOR WHEN YOU ARE DATING SOMEONE WHO IS AUTISTIC (not necessarily in this order):DO: Ask for their preferences on how to refer to their being autistic. Many don't like being talked about as having autism, as it's not an illness (not that having an illness would somehow be less acceptable, just so as to give the more correct picture of the sitch). Many have a preference to being referred to as autistic, because how we see the world is influenced so profoundly by how our brains are structured and we would be completely different people if not autistic. But not, like, unnecessarily outed, if being outed is a relevant concept to the situation, if you get me? As for the situations where it is a necessity, circle back to your partner about that, because I am unable to know that for them. We're individuals, same as y'all, despite having some things in common, and prefer to be considered as such. So get to know them well I guess?DO: See other language matters through. Also worthy talking points regarding this matter: functioning labels, yay or nay (it's usually nay, they have a lot of ableist package many are eager to shed via using terms that work for them, so a point of consideration there) and the pros and cons of identity first language vs. person first language (if you personally can find fault in the latter, I completely understand, we know we are people, folks should remind themselves if they need a reminder so bad, preferably in silence, as this is pushed on us by educators, therapists, etc., which, yuck). This is a basic courtesy which costs you exactly 0 of whatever currency you use. But obviously discuss these with them and find out what they prefer.DO: Listen and be supportive. If you are unsure of what they meant by something, ask about it. Usually we're assholes by accident rather than choice, and tend to avoid putting stuff in between the lines, so putting things there for them seems a bit… premature, as even if they did mean to implicate something, it's probably different from what you thought. We appreciate people being straightforward if they have a problem with us, as long as they also take responsibility of their own feelings towards something not inherently harmful, such as stimming. That’s by definition still different from “being deliberately insulting” though.DO: Say what you mean and mean what you say. Try to use tact in a manner that is honest but reassuring, as too much of dressing up and obfuscating the issue can feel a lot like pretension, ie. one form of lying for many of us. Try to learn to only put stuff into your lines instead of between them.DO: Follow up on promises and other commitments unless the reason us that they're being kind of a dick about the whole thing somehow, even after you talked it through. Honesty really means a lot in a context of any close relationship, so making promises you are unable to keep isn't a good look to that end.DO: Study up on autism spectrum conditions and specifically the sort of experiences people who are most like your significant other have. Understand that we're not all alike, and look into ableism while at it so as to recognise it and throw rebuttals as needed, as this is safer for you to do than ourselves. You make an even better partner by being a true ally.DO: See their interests as good things that make them happy, instead of something taking up your time with them. And take at least some interest in what they say too, but do butt in if you want to talk about your stuff too - all gentle-like but clearly. After all, if you love someone, you want their happiness, even if there are more reasons for happiness than simply your existence. I mean, do try to read this in the nicest possible way, because that's my intent here, but their life would be otherwise incredibly bleak if you were the only sunshine, no matter how bright. You want other good shit to happen for them too, right? People need a bunch of stuff – not always necessarily material stuff though – to be happy, and personal time doing what you love is most often one of them, in this, we don't really differ from neurotypicals. It's just good for people in general to take the time and interedt to get to know themselves, what they like, what they need, what they do well, and what they want from life, and while that can be a realisation triggered by other people, it's good to take stock and reflect in solitude once in a while, too. On that note, make the most of your personal time while at it. You can thank me later, if you didn't do that before this. 🙃🙂 Good for you and good for your relationship if done by considering both partie's needs equally.DO: In the same vein, do keep up your friendships even when you date. That's just smart and also being a good friend. :) I'd be surprised if anyone in their right mind can fault you for that!DO: discuss a lot about everything, including your personal boundaries in a relationship and what each of you is looking for in a relationship and your other feelings too, because honestly, that's important and it makes the other person feel like they can share feels and insecurities with you and state their boundaries, like if they have any touch sensory hyper/hyposensitivities which affect how they like to be touched. If this doesn't happen unprompted, you can just say this is what you also mean to do by telling all that stuff, besides that they know the literal stuff you told, and ask about the things I mentioned when they are becoming topical in your relationship. It can be hard for some of us sometimes to offer up even that information unprompted, because many of us have been deeply hurt by our families by always being given an earful when expressing an opinion or a need or a boundary or a feeling they didn't approve of. I know I have and I am working to be more open about my feelings, both to myself and others. That can be a lot of work but having a loving, caring, supportive partner can help. It has helped me at least.DO: Honor their trust by being a trustworthy person in general. Stand up for them as needed and wanted.DO: Only share their personal info and neurodiversity status after obtaining a permission for doing so from them, and only if necessary unless otherwise agreed by you both.DO: Be mindful of their personal needs and express yours clearly so as to help them be mindful of yours. You can help by telling what being mindful to you looks like, and in the interests of having a truly reciprocal partnership we're usually more than willing to help in whatever way we can, provided we actually can and that it's not an unreasonable to us. Explain to the best to your ability why it's important to you in the interests of understanding each other. Help them help you by understanding you better. I get it that you can't just produce a manual of dealing with you, but every little bit of info on you generally helps to fathom how to treat you right like you like it. Compromise when in opposition to each other if you can, unless a deal breaker happens, then what's left is to mitigate the damage.DO: Communicate frustrations with your mouthwords and try to avoid taking out on them what isn't on them. And even if it unavoidably sometimes is on them, a little mutual patience and understanding can go a long way.DO: Be fair and understanding, but decline from taking any shit either. Unless that's your specific kink that you do together with mutual consent. In which there is absolutely zero shame whatsoever.Okay, now for the DON'TS list.Don't be an asshole.Really, that's it.

question: It’s said every sociopath and psychopath is a narcissist but not all narcissists are psychopaths or sociopaths. However, if psychopaths are born, (neurodiverse) where does the narcissism enter?
answer: I thought this article was interesting… CRIME TRAVELLER Home » Psychology of Murder » Psychopaths – Born Or Made? Psychopaths – Born Or Made?Are Psychopaths Born Or Made? - Crime TravellerThe truth is, whether it be an old boss, co-worker, friend, or partner, most people have known a psychopath.https://www.crimetraveller.org/2020/03/psychopaths-born-or-made/Written by Mildred DelgadoThe term psychopath or sociopath is not listed in the DSM or other medical reference resources. Instead, the terms are referred to as ‘Antisocial Personality Disorder (ASPD)’ which is generally defined as a long term disregard, violation, or abuse of the rights of others. People diagnosed with antisocial personality disorder also show a low sense of morals or ethics and often lack the level of conscience that most people possess. This condition is usually accompanied by criminal or violent behavior. The most common archetype of manifestation of psychopaths is in the serial killer. During the 60s and 70s, serial killers were at the forefront of the public mind. Shortly thereafter names like the Zodiac Killer, John Wayne Gacy, Ted Bundy, and The Son Of Sam killer became household names. In the early 2000s and beyond, serial killers became the focus of many popular TV series and documentaries. Numerous books have been written on the subject, both academic and for popular consumption and the interest does not seem to be waning. The truth is, whether it be an old boss, co-worker, friend, or partner, most people have known a psychopath. Not all psychopaths or sociopaths turn out to be murderers and criminals, some people are able to harness their complete disregard for others to their advantage and achieve success in certain environments. Still, one of the most commonly asked questions in regards to this topic is whether psychopaths are created or born. It’s the classic nature vs nurture debate which becomes even more interesting when applied to this subject. Here we will examine this question and hopefully add some clarity to the issue. The Genetic Aspect: A true psychopath is rare, only about 1% of the population can be confidently diagnosed with ASPD. From this 1% scientists have been able to perform brain scansand determine there are some striking differences between the brains of those with ASPD and neurotypical individuals. The scans concluded that two main regions of the brain which control behavior and aggression are markedly different in psychopaths. There also seems to be something of a genetic component to psychopathy as well. While the child of someone with antisocial personality disorder is not guaranteed to develop the condition they are statistically much more likely than average. Throughout human evolution, certain traits have been selected for because they are useful. Having a level, or at least being capable of, narcissism, aggression, and a “me first” attitude do have its advantages at times. Resources were often scarce and the ancient man needed to defend himself when required. That being said, humans are by nature social creatures so a level of cooperation and concern for the well being of others was also required. The standard neurotypical individual possesses the ability to draw on both classes of personality traits. In fact, standard societal norms afford certain allowances for these types of behaviors. The issue arises when an individual cannot control their aggressive, narcissistic traits. They end up operating outside the societal norms and thus are considered to have an antisocial personality. Another interesting aspect of a psychopath’s brain is their inability to perceive or register the emotions of other people. The human brain is acutely aware of minor changes in an individual’s face. Things we cannot consciously pick up on are noticed by the brain. Many studies have shown that people engage in a small form of mimic to help the brain better understand the emotional state of the person they are viewing. People with ASPD seem to lack the ability to draw any information from minor facial mimicking. They can understand mood, state, and emotion on an intellectual level and often use this understanding to manipulate people for their benefit. An interesting observation made some decades ago is that when people with ASPD are asked to draw cartoon face representations of emotional states such as joy, sadness, fear, anxiety, guilt, and pleasure they often draw identical or minutely different faces. There seems to be something fundamentally wrong with a psychopath’s ability to interpret the feelings of other people. It is also unclear to what level psychopaths experience these emotions. The Nurture Aspect: Having the genetic disposition to psychopathy or ASPD is a necessary but not sufficient condition to becoming a sociopath. There appears to be an environmental component that triggers this mindset in many of those afflicted with ASPD. The most common of these environmental triggers is trauma. The vast majority of those with ASPD also have had some sort of trauma occur in their life. The most common, and the strongest, form of trauma to trigger psychopathy in those with a disposition is childhood abuse. The number of psychopaths who also suffered some form of childhood abuse, usually violent or sexual in nature is the norm and not the exception. Conclusion: As with most things in life the answer is not a simple yes or no. The same platitude can be applied to the psychopath question. It appears that there is a requirement for a genetic, physical, and social combination to result in antisocial personality disorder. Those born with the genes, and perhaps associated brain structures, of a psychopath are not guaranteed to become one. Likewise, those who suffer some form of childhood trauma or abuse are also not likely to become psychopaths. It is when both these conditions are met that psychopathy occurs. ReferencesAkaike, H. question: Who decided that not missing people is a disorder? How is someone needing to be missed anybody else's problem to fix?
answer: Not Missing People: Mental Health Quirk or Valid Emotional State? Most of us expect to miss our loved ones when we’re apart – it’s seen as a sign of caring. So if you’re someone who doesn’t really miss people, you might wonder: “Is there something wrong with me? 🤔 Could this be a disorder?” On the flip side, plenty of folks argue that not pining for others is perfectly fine – just a different way of feeling. Let’s explore both angles in depth, blending psychological insights with cultural context and a dash of neurodivergent and philosophical perspectives. When Not Missing Someone Feels “Not Normal” Human bonding & expectations: From a young age, we learn that missing someone is linked with love and attachment. Psychology expert Jeremy Sherman notes that *“to miss people means to love them, to be partial to them, incomplete without them”*. In other words, longing for someone’s presence is often viewed as proof that they matter to us. Society reinforces this – telling a friend or partner “I didn’t miss you” can raise eyebrows or even hurt feelings. One person with alexithymia (difficulty recognizing emotions) put it bluntly: *“I never miss people. Of course, I can’t say this, as it often offends them.”*. There’s an unspoken cultural script that if you care, you’ll miss them – so not missing anyone can make you feel like an outlier. Is it a disorder? There’s no official diagnosis of “won’t miss people syndrome,” but certain mental health conditions do involve low attachment or limited emotional expression. The DSM-5 (the diagnostic manual) doesn’t list “not missing people” as a symptom, yet it describes some related traits in specific disorders. For example, Schizoid Personality Disorder is characterized by a long-term pattern of detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of emotions in interpersonal settings. People with schizoid personality may have “limited or no enjoyment in close relationships,” prefer solitude, and appear emotionally cold or indifferent. Such individuals often don’t yearn for others’ company – so they likely don’t experience “missing” people in the typical way. However, this is a rare and extreme case; it’s only considered a disorder if it’s pervasive and causes dysfunction. Other conditions can also dampen the feeling of missing someone. Childhood emotional neglect or trauma might lead a person to shut down longing as a coping mechanism. If you grew up learning that emotional needs won’t be met, you might stop acknowledging them. One commenter, reflecting on an abusive parent, said: *“My father lived to 97 and I felt almost nothing when he died... I never shed a tear and I don’t miss him at all.”* Years of abuse and neglect had essentially numbed any sense of loss. In cases of PTSD or depression, people sometimes report feeling “empty” or unable to muster strong emotions like longing or excitement – this is often called emotional numbness. And in the concept of alexithymia (difficulty identifying and expressing feelings), a person might literally not register the internal cues of missing someone.Note: None of these mean that not missing people = you have a mental illness. Mental health professionals would look at the bigger picture – a cluster of symptoms and whether it causes you or others significant problems. Not feeling one particular emotion (like longing) isn’t pathological by itself if you’re otherwise doing okay.Social Norms: “You Should Miss Them… Right?” Our reactions to absence are shaped by culture and context. In many societies, openly expressing affection and longing is encouraged. Saying “I miss you” is often seen as sweet or loving, while not saying it can seem cold. There’s even an expectation that if a relationship is important, of course you’ll miss each other when apart – anything else might be interpreted as a lack of love. These norms can make the non-misser feel guilty or pressured to perform missing. (Ever caught yourself sending a “Miss you!” text because it felt like the right thing to do, even if you weren’t feeling it strongly? 🙋‍♀️) However, social expectations aren’t monolithic. As Sherman points out, there’s a contrasting cultural value of independence: *“Miss (ignore) whatever you want to miss: To each his own. You do your thing; I do mine... And whatever sinks your boat because you find it uninteresting, just miss it.”* In other words, not being overly attached can be seen as a sign of autonomy and personal choice. Western societies especially celebrate self-sufficiency – being okay on your own – even as they simultaneously romanticize deep emotional bonds. It’s a bit of a double standard: we’re supposed to form close connections but also stand on our own two feet. No wonder there’s confusion! Context matters too: In some cultures or families, emotional restraint is valued. Not everyone says “I miss you” freely. Some languages even frame “missing” differently (for example, in certain languages the phrasing is more like “you are missing from me,” emphasizing the absence rather than the speaker’s emotion). So before slapping a disorder label, we should ask: Is the person truly unable to connect, or are they just more reserved or self-contained due to their upbringing or values? Neurodivergent Perspectives: Wired Differently, Feel Differently It’s crucial to recognize that not everyone’s brain processes relationships and emotions in the same way. Many neurodivergent individuals (people with atypical neurodevelopment, like ADHD or autism) report experiences that could explain low instances of “missing” others – and it’s not due to lack of love or sociopathy, but simply how their minds work.ADHD – “Out of sight, out of mind”: You might have heard that phrase as a simple proverb, but for folks with ADHD it can be almost literal. One ADHD advocate, Vicky Ashley, explains that many people with ADHD struggle with “object permanence” or “object constancy” when it comes to people. She says, *“If it’s out of sight, it’s out of mind... If it’s not in front of you it doesn’t actually exist.”* This means an ADHD brain can forget to feel the presence of someone who isn’t there right now. It’s not intentional neglect – it’s that their attention is consumed by whatever (or whoever) is in front of them. They might go long stretches without contacting friends or family and genuinely not experience that ache of missing, simply because their brain isn’t firing reminders of those absent people. As Ashley puts it, an ADHD person may love their friends dearly, but *“when something is out of sight, it often slips from their mind until they are reminded.”* Importantly, this isn’t considered a disorder in itself; it’s seen as part of ADHD’s impact on memory and attention. In fact, medical sources note that while the term “object permanence” is borrowed from infant development, many use it informally to describe this ADHD tendency. The takeaway? If your ADHD friend doesn’t text “I miss you,” it likely has more to do with brain wiring than lack of affection – as one article reassures, it doesn’t mean they don’t love you.Autism Spectrum – different emotional rhythms: Autistic individuals often describe their relationships in terms of consistency rather than constant emotional highs and lows. Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht, an autistic psychotherapist, shared that *“One thing I find very different about my neurology is that I do not miss people that I stop interacting with. I mean absolutely no one.”* Her feelings for people are like a light switch – on when she’s with you (intense, present caring), and off when you’re gone. She loves deeply and is attentive in the moment, but when someone is absent, she feels “just no feelings” until they reconnect. This might sound stark to neurotypical folks, but for her it actually eases the pain of separation. It’s a bit like emotional object permanence again: once a person isn’t actively in her life, her brain sort of stores away that attachment. Many autistic people in online communities echo this experience – they might only “miss” someone when prompted by a memory or a scheduled catch-up, rather than a continuous longing. It doesn’t mean they don’t value their friends or family; they often show care in different ways (like intense focus when together, or practical help).Other neurodivergent or cognitive differences: Even having aphantasia (an inability to visualize images in your mind) could influence this. Some individuals with aphantasia report that because they can’t picture their loved one’s face or recall vivid memories, they don’t feel the pang of missing them in their absence – the emotion doesn’t get triggered. Again, this isn’t well-researched in literature yet, but it’s a fascinating example of how our mind’s eye (or lack of) can affect feelings.In all these cases, the lack of “missing” is not pathological per se – it’s a reflection of a different operating system of the brain. Neurodivergent voices often emphasize that they still care; they just don’t experience the sentimental longing that society expects. Recognizing these differences is part of accepting neurodiversity. 🌈🤗 Philosophy: Stoic Strength or Buddhist Non-Attachment? Beyond psychology, some philosophical or spiritual traditions actually see not clinging to others as an ideal (or at least a virtue). This can flip the script: rather than viewing “not missing people” as a cold dysfunction, it becomes a sign of emotional maturity or wisdom in certain contexts.Stoicism: The Stoic philosophers (like Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, Seneca) taught that we should cultivate an attitude of acceptance toward things we cannot control – and that includes the comings and goings of people in our lives. A modern Stoic writer summarizes one core tenet: *“Do not be concerned with the presence or absence of others in your life. ... People can leave you through any number of ways, none of which are in your control. Loss is not in your control; therefore, we must be indifferent to loss.”* This isn’t about not loving people; it’s about not agonizing over their absence. Stoicism encourages *“mastery of emotional response”* – meaning you can acknowledge missing someone but not let it wreck your peace. In practice, a Stoic-influenced person might deliberately train themselves not to miss others so intensely, viewing that pang as an unhelpful attachment. They might say, “I prefer my friend’s company, but if they’re away, I’m content and focused on what’s here now.” This echoes the idea of self-sufficiency – a kind of emotional resilience that some would admire rather than pathologize.Buddhist perspective: Buddhism speaks of attachment as a source of suffering – tanhā, the clinging or craving, is what makes us miserable when things inevitably change. A classic Buddhist reflection is to remember that separation from loved ones is unavoidable in life. The aim is not to stop loving, but to love without clinging. So, a Buddhist practitioner might strive to feel compassion and love for others, yet accept periods of solitude calmly, perhaps even enjoying the solitude as a time for inner growth. If you told a Buddhist monk that you don’t really miss people, they might gently smile as long as you’re treating those people with kindness when together. Non-attachment can look a lot like not missing people – it means you aren’t yearning and longing in a way that causes you distress. (Of course, Buddhism also emphasizes compassion, so it doesn’t mean “feel nothing ever”; it means equanimity – a balanced mind.)Existential and individualist takes: Some philosophical viewpoints simply celebrate individuality. The idea is that each person has a unique emotional landscape. For some, that landscape has towering peaks of longing; for others, it’s a flat, stable plain. Neither is “right” or “wrong.” An existentialist might say, “Hey, if not missing people is authentic to your experience, then that’s your truth to make meaning of.” Some people channel their emotional energy into activities or creativity rather than pining for others, seeing solitude as a productive or sacred state.In these frames of reference, not missing someone isn’t a disorder at all – it might even be seen as enlightened or empowered. It’s interesting how much the interpretation can change depending on our mindset! 🧘‍♂️💪 When Not Missing Is Just Fine (and Even Healthy) Now for the counterargument: that not missing people can be a valid, non-pathological emotional state. There are several points in favor of this view:Individual differences in attachment: People have different attachment styles. Some are very anxious and feel upset when apart (they might miss others intensely), while others are more avoidant or secure and can function independently without constant contact. A securely attached person, for example, might love their partner but not miss them painfully during a short trip because they have trust and confidence in the relationship. This isn’t a lack of love – it’s a form of stability. On the other hand, someone with an avoidant style might deliberately not allow themselves to miss others as a way to maintain autonomy. In either case, these are variations in personality and attachment, not illnesses. As long as you are capable of forming relationships and you treat people well, not frequently missing them is just a personal trait. 🤷‍♀️Emotion versus action: You might not feel the ache of missing, yet still deeply value someone. Some people show care by being present when it counts, even if they’re not texting “I miss you” every day. What matters more? The internal feeling of longing, or the way you behave toward the person? One could argue it’s more important how you act. If you’re loyal, considerate, and engaged when together, the fact that you don’t lose sleep missing them in between might be a sign of emotional resilience, not deficiency.Focus on the present: Not missing people could mean you have a great ability to live in the here and now. You might be so absorbed in your current activities and surroundings that you simply don’t dwell on who’s absent. This mindful presence can actually be a strength. Instead of ruminating on missing friends, you might pour energy into hobbies, work, or self-care. As long as you reconnect eventually and maintain the relationship, this can be quite healthy. In contrast, someone who constantly misses others might struggle to enjoy the present moment – which can increase sadness or anxiety. So there’s a bit of a silver lining: not missing people might spare you some emotional pain and let you be more grounded day-to-day. One writer even suggested that we should stop romanticizing the pain of missing someone, noting *“there should be an end to romanticising and glorifying pain... missing someone is extremely painful.”* From that perspective, not experiencing this pain could be seen as fortunate, not pathological.Coping mechanism, not pathology: In cases where not missing anyone is related to past hurt (like the trauma example earlier), it can be understood as a coping mechanism. People who have lost loved ones or had unstable relationships might emotionally “wall off” to survive. For instance, a child who was sent to many different foster homes might learn not to attach or miss caregivers, because it hurt too much each time they were moved. As an adult, that person might still have a habit of “I don’t miss anyone, I just move on.” This could be viewed as a scar of trauma, yes, but also as a form of emotional resilience – a way they learned to keep going. Instead of immediately labeling it a disorder, therapists would likely approach it with understanding: it made sense as a survival strategy. Over time, if the person wants to open up more, they can – but if they are content with their level of attachment, that’s okay too. In the mental health field there’s a growing awareness that we shouldn’t pathologize every trauma response; sometimes it’s about gently adapting it, not “fixing” a person who isn’t broken.“If it ain’t broke…” A key question professionals ask is whether a trait is causing distress or impairment. If you generally do not miss people and it doesn’t bother you or harm your relationships, then it wouldn’t meet the criteria for any mental disorder. As the DSM-5 notes in its introduction, it’s not a disorder unless it leads to significant distress or dysfunction in life. So if you’re totally fine and your friends/family have adjusted to your style (maybe they know you care even if you don’t say I miss you 100 times), then there’s no problem to diagnose. It’s just part of your personality or neurological make-up.Embracing Different Ways of Feeling In a world of diverse emotional experiences, there’s room for both the yearning hearts and the stoic souls. 💖🤝 Some people tear up after a week apart from their BFF; others can go months, even years, without a reunion and feel perfectly content – picking up right where they left off when they do meet again. Human attachment exists on a spectrum. Rather than rushing to label the absence of “missing” as a mental health disorder, many experts would urge a more compassionate and nuanced view. Psychologist Jeremy Sherman highlights that in negotiating our connections, we have to decide *“Who should you love so strongly that you’ll miss them... Who should you just miss altogether (ignore)?”*. It’s normal to not deeply miss every person; we all prioritize whom we truly can’t imagine life without versus those we’re fine not seeing often. And even for those closest, not everyone experiences a void when apart – sometimes it’s secure attachment or confidence in the bond that fills that space. On the other hand, if someone finds their lack of “missing” corresponds with other issues – say, difficulty forming any close relationships, feeling emotionally numb in many aspects of life, or others consistently feeling hurt by their detachment – then it could be useful to gently explore that with a professional. It doesn’t mean they’re disordered, but if they are unhappy with the status quo (or a partner is), therapy can help uncover if there’s suppressed hurt or teach ways to communicate affection that don’t feel unnatural. question: Why do some neurotypical people see autistic people as selfish?
answer: “Neurotypical” people (read, anyone who considers themselves to be part of a majority group that is considered normal - not just exclusive to the specific neurotypical mental wiring) tend to see anyone who is different as selfish because they’ve conditioned themselves that they are “normal”. In large part it’s an echochamber effect. And it’s not just neurotypical versus neurodiverse. Just look at extroverts vs introverts. From a young are these people tend to congregate together. They’re naturally drawn to a certain style of behaviour that they share with the people around them. And while they may have minor differences from one another? They typically share major overlap. Extroverts are (due to their mental wiring) drawn to socialization. There are a number of variables that go into this, but a big one is that they are more responsive to dopamine. Whereas introverts tend to be more responsive to acetylcholine. It creates a feedback loop where extroverts become more likely to want to socialize whereas introverts are more likely to be drawn to solitary activities and introspection rather than looking for confirmation outside of themselves.So we have this group of people who from a young age naturally socialize together - and in doing so tend to create an image of what “normal” is. They share notes with the other people in the group and this image gets reinforced in their nice little echochamber. Then, when this group of social kids sees the awkward goth kid or nerd walking alone. Always alone or with one or two other people. Never socializing like they do? Well clearly he’s weird… And they start making fun of him for it. Why doesn’t he try harder to fit in like they do!! Selfish weirdo. Always hanging out by themselves… Now I’ll ask you this. Out of these two? Who is selfish? The person who just wants to be left alone? Or the group that goes after anyone that isn’t like them? This typically progresses as people grow up and even in professional settings you often still see these groups form. You’ll have the social people who are naturally drawn to each other and the less social ones who stick to themselves or remain on the edge.There’s a secondary variable here. Which is that a lot of (western) society has a major tolerance problem. You don’t have to look far in news reports to come across hatecrimes, racial disparity and worse. Anyone who is different tends to get the short end of the stick. While people like to believe this only goes skindeep? Sadly the same judgement is often directed at things that aren’t necessarily visual. (Though in some cases mental impairment does lead to visual distinction - but that’s another matter.) And so here too… Why don’t the neuroatypical/autistic/etc person try harder to be “normal”? Here’s the thing. They ARE normal. Their normal just differs from your normal.

question: Is it wrong to be bothered by the neurodiversity movement? For the record I'm autistic and I have PTSD and depression, but all this preachy neurodiversity stuff just feels like an excuse for bad or childish behavior to me more often than not.
answer: It depends what the movement wants to achieve. Diversity: OK. Justifying bad behaviour: Not so much. It raises the question of receiving treatment to cure vs to normalise. I dont like the a suggestion that no help or treatment is needed or that managing bad behaviour necessarily will take away individuality-it arguably gives more individuality if we are selective. But i also like that it challenges the efficacy of present day treatment, to consider that it implies factors of situationism, sociology and phenomenology as approaches often naively voided by professionals. So its maybe about challenging the definition of mentally abnormal. If people act outside of social norms they are not necessarily bad, and still can distinguish between bad and good behaviour. One example of this was a study that revealed that social interaction between aspergers and neurotypicals was considered awkward because of the neurotypical’s flaws and not the aspergers. It takes two to tango. Neurotypical socially functioning people have a narrow mode of communication, sometimes even ritually repetitive with little actual content. Mentally ill people are forced to have a wider view outside of arbitrary norms, but do not necessarily lack intrinsic skills… …its just, they are ‘weird’ to many, and a lot of the time that is just it. it takes two to tango, and a neurotypical often won’t change their narrow mode of communication to accept a ‘diverse’ person. Yet the weird mode is not necessarily flawed, just unusual, and might require a bit more effort, like the reward of reading a more complex novel. This also leads to reasoning that those with similar disorders will potentially share more emapthy for eachother, and associate more with eachother, but then this is a barrier to a lot of things if most are neurotypical. In the case of stigma, we might want to recognise gifts of those who sometimes display bad behaviour. This is not so much excusing the behaviour but not devaluing the person’s other traits, like potential intelligence of Aspergers, or creativity of BPD or something. But not just to apply to bad behaviours. These disorders limit people. People are outcast from certain positions, and doubted about their skill level because they might fail in a basic task. They might be unsuited to particular environments…yet they might be a great asset, or even a genius. So one solution is I know software companies are giving autistic progrmmers an isolated room to work in, rather than then failing by being in the shared office environment: problem solved and the company gets new products and profits from the savant. Its like the wheelchair access a paraplegic requires to get into work. That’s one example, bad behaviour is not the only factor in these people. Bad behaviour is not necessarily excused, however we could mitigate it without outcasting sometimes. If a reactive person reacts, maybe keep them out of the reactive environment, etc. But things like: if an aspergers person sucks at interviews, so can’t get a job, yet possesses amazing skills that will save your company, what would you do? Would you maybe change the interview process and parts of the job that require people skills, for this one person, since it seems in the interest of everybody?

question: Do high functioning autistics understand consequences?
answer: Is this question for the science folks or for us who are just ASD (not in the aforementioned crowd)? In short, I do observe that a relationship has changed. However, I have no clue why and how to influence or fix it. For me, it is difficult to fathom how someone else is feeling without getting visual cues from their face and body, or without them stating it. It is best if the person just says it, because visual cues only tell me that something has changed, not exactly how. I also really do try hard to avoid generating negative feelings, which ultimately feels like a bull chased by a wasp swarm, trying to get out of a tight tiny glass goods store without breaking anything. I can immediately perceive that something has changed in a person’s attitude towards me. Three problems tho:I don’t know what has changed.I don’t know how I caused it, and can spend months worrying and years thinking about it.I don’t know how to influence or fix it. It would seem that neurotypicals generally won’t settle for less than me having the same social abilities as them when it comes to those matters.And if I add that every day brings new potential situations of the sort, that should illustrate the size of the problem. This gets more complex if you belong to a minority group, e.g. women in tech / stem, because [unconscious] bias combined with social clumsiness spells out even worse for a person than just social clumsiness. It is difficult to separate what comes from a toxic work environment vs. what comes from neurodiverse-neurotypical differences.

question: Are not neurotypical parents, those with mild autistic disorders, ADHD, and similar conditions, better parents, for children similar conditions, ADHD, Asperger, Tourette, than neurotypical people? Some people frown upon non-NT as parents.
answer: For Autism / Aspergers, I would say that it probably depends. Autism doesn’t effect everyone the same way. I can clash with others who have autism - same as NT people can clash. I suppose someone with Autism might be more understanding of a child who has autism in general. I don’t show too many facial expressions compared to other people. I also don’t really “get” symbolism / single-leadership which can be upsetting to some people. I also don’t enjoy it when people hide their emotions. Reading gestures - hidden meanings between words - facial expressions (I have gotten better at some of this, but it doesn’t come naturally) and such don’t come work well with me. Just say what you are feeling / thinking. Pushing excess feelings onto me is also annoying. I have different ways of coping with things than others. I do try the approach of “treat others how you want to be treated” - doesn’t work well with the whole logical brain vs emotional brain thing. Some people with autism are fine with all of this - it depends on the person. A NT parent may not understand why a neurodiverse child doesn’t act the same as them, immediately think the same way as them - may try forcing them to act “normal”. Putting an Autistic child into a high stress area could cause the child to get overloaded and shut down - usually called “outbursts / tantrums” by a lot of people. Acceptance in general seems to be changing for the better though. A neurodiverse parent might not understand certain emotional outbursts from a NT child - or what they did wrong in a situation. It could be better or worse depending on specifics about the parent / child.

question: Why is non-verbal autism associated with severe autism?
answer: Being unable to speak is often found in severe autism because severe autism affects connections between, and development of, parts of the brain involved in language. They also were able to predict symptom severity by looking at the connectivity in the brain. Atypical functional connectome hierarchy in autism A quote: â€œOne paradox of autism is the co-occurrence of deficits in sensory and higher-order socio-cognitive processing. Here, we examined whether these phenotypical patterns may relate to an overarching system-level imbalanceâ€”specifically a disruption in macroscale hierarchy affecting integration and segregation of unimodal and transmodal networks. Combining connectome gradient and stepwise connectivity analysis based on task-free functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we demonstrated atypical connectivity transitions between sensory and higher-order default mode regions in a large cohort of individuals with autism relative to typically-developing controls. question: Can someone with high-functioning autism be non-verbal?
answer: That would be very unusual. In fact, a lot of health care providers would tell you that is not possible, because if someone was nonverbal, they cannot be high functioning, because being verbal - being able to speak and use language - is part of being high functioning. If that sounds arbitrary or unfair, think about this. First, with most people with Autism, their functioning is fairly â€˜evenâ€™- IF you think like the difference between very severe and very mild and donâ€™t get too fussy(itâ€™s common for a person to have one area of Autism be â€˜mildâ€™ and one area to be â€˜moderateâ€™, and another to be moderate, for example. If they have very severe problems with language, they usually have very severe problems with social rules and repetitive behavior. And if language is very skilled usually the other areas of Autism also are quite good. So, if I meet a person with Autism who is nonverbal, I will usually find that his other 2 areas of Autism also give him considerable challenge. I have, for sure, met people with very GOOD language skills who have a great deal of trouble with social rules and repetitive behavior. But the opposite is not common. Never say never, for sure, but not common(that said itâ€™s wise to assume nothing when you meet someone with Autism, just get to know the person as they are). The term â€˜high functioningâ€™ isnâ€™t formally defined anywhere (I donâ€™t think, LOL). Well, there are a number of fairly similar definitions, all have something like â€˜how you are doing overall.â€™ And most health care providers take that to mean, for Autism, â€˜in all 3 areas of Autism.â€™ And while health care providers generally do not use terms like â€˜high functioningâ€™ and â€˜low functioning,â€™ and they arenâ€™t a formal part of a diagnosis, they will usually tell the parent something additional about the diagnosis, though the terms â€˜mild and â€˜moderateâ€™ and â€˜severeâ€™ and â€˜profoundâ€™ might be more informative. If any sort of swag at severity were included in the diagnosis, weâ€™d have to consider all 3 areas, then weâ€™d have to debate if we mean â€˜languageâ€™ as in speaking only, or any type of communication. Most health care providers would probably say â€˜language as in speaking,â€™ not out of prejudice (as most of them teach total communication and are very gung ho on it), but because thatâ€™s often the only available method of communication, day to day, in our world. Most people donâ€™t understand sign language, and most people donâ€™t understand or use easily, the more high tech communication devices, or the person may not even have that device with him always. Thus it stands to reason that a person would need to be high functioning in all 3 areas of Autism (language, social rules, repetitive behavior) to be considered â€˜high functioning.â€™ The global assessment scale might be helpful to be familiar with: What Is the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) Scale?

question: What are these "non-verbal cues" that people with autism are missing?
answer: Humans (and many other species) communicate their feelings using a complex combination of tone of voice, facial expressions, and sounds. In the NT, and most forms of neurodiversity, thereâ€™s an instinctive core in the brain that connects up a basic language of those elements to the empathy centers in the brain, allowing people to learn to translate what they see and hear into feelings analogous with feelings they themselves have. Right alongside learning a language, infants learn more and more of those social cues, learn to make them themselves, and learn to interpret the ones others make more and more clearly and with more and more layers of complexity and subtlety. Different cultures have different sets of cues at the higher levels, so itâ€™s not an innate languageâ€¦. but it is an innate ability to make this specific sort of cross connection. People on the ASD ballpark lack that ability, from birth. We donâ€™t innately see the signals, or they donâ€™t connect to anything, itâ€™s really hard to say where exactly the difficulty lies, and it may lie in different places for different people. When I grew up, I was taught that pen (the writing impliment) and pen (a sort of holding cell, usually for animals) and pin (a small needle-like thing with a broad blunt back end) were homonyms; three words that sound the same but have different meanings, and in one case are even spelled differently. However, for most of the English speaking word, pen and pin are not homonyms, but rather have two distinct sounds. I can hear them differently if Iâ€™m paying attention, I can even deliberately SAY them differently. But itâ€™s like putting on a British accent. Normally they sound the same to me, and I say them the same, and imagine that everyone figures out which is which via context, like I do. This, then, is much like that. If I look carefully and think about it, I can see a smile, a wink, a glare, a grimace. I can make those same expressions, and do so deliberately trying to communicate a feeling I have. I actually have acquired a fair number of combinations of expression and tone and can do a decent job of passing for NT under some circumstances. But if I donâ€™t pay close attention, itâ€™s pen/pin all over again. And the subtle shades and nuances? No, sorry, not in a million years. The best I can do is fake a dry sense of humor, and sarcasm, because both of those involve being expressionless and ironically not looking like you mean what you say. I have emotions. I can care about your emotions. But it helps an awful lot if you listen to me when I tell you how I feel, and if you tell me straight outâ€¦ because I donâ€™t really get what you mean when you say it the way a gorilla might, by puffing out your chest and drooping your eyelids.

Even if the kid doesnâ€™t get what they want, theyâ€™re still getting something. That reinforces the bad behavior.The rule of thumb should be bad behavior should never lead to an improving situation. question: Can children who are non-verbal but can communicate through sign language be diagnosed with autism?

Children raised by deaf parents communicate very well in this complex culture which is quite different from the verbal culture. If parents have been able to teach elementary signs to their child by fear that verbal communication would not happen, or that signs can be complementary, understand that this child who eventually does not develop speech at all has issues which are not specific to verbal communication. When those parents bring their child to the expert they also speak about sleep problems, feeding issues, mood and learning difficulties, repetitive movements which canâ€™t be interrupted, and other signs indicating an atypical development. The expert will run tests, observations, possibly brain biochemistry evaluations, and run questionnaires with the parents to assess the history of the child, the daily concerns as much as the achieved milestones. question: Are there different forms of autism that affect communication differently, such as being non-verbal but using sign language or pointing?
answer: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) encompasses a wide range of communication styles and abilities, reflecting the diversity of the condition. Others might experience challenges in processing language or organizing thoughts coherently, even if they speak fluently. Non-speaking individuals, who represent a subgroup within the spectrum, often communicate through alternative methods like sign language, gestures, picture boards, or augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices. Importantly, being non-verbal doesnâ€™t equate to a lack of understanding; many comprehend language well and simply need different tools to express themselves. Communication differences in autism can also include atypical speech patterns, such as echolalia (repeating phrases) or a monotone voice. Social communication challenges, like difficulty interpreting facial expressions or body language, are common across the spectrum. These variances highlight the need for tailored support. Speech therapists and educators often work closely with individuals to identify strategies that align with their strengths and needs. Ultimately, communication in autism is highly individualized. Embracing neurodiversity means recognizing that differences in expression are not deficits but unique ways of interacting with the world. Support should focus on accessibility, respect for autonomy, and fostering connection in ways that honor each personâ€™s preferred mode of communication.

He began using communication boards (we printed out and laminated simple picture sheets at home); he started pointing; and he seemed to understand and respond to our speech better and more often. A week or so after his fourth birthday I took him to our churchâ€™s Halloween party. Since he could point and generally respond to some simple questions I offered him a choice of which costume he wanted. He chose Iron Man. I had talked to him quite a bit about his costume. While we were at the party he suddenly, and spontaneously, looked up at me and said, â€œIron Manâ€. And I said, â€œYes! Thatâ€™s who you are!!!â€ I was so very excited. question: How can individuals with autism, particularly those who are non-verbal and have co-occurring conditions like ADHD, be treated?
answer: Individuals with autism, especially those who are non-verbal and have co-occurring conditions like ADHD, may benefit from a comprehensive and individualized treatment approach. Here are some considerations:Early Intervention:Early intervention programs are crucial for improving outcomes. Starting interventions in early childhood can address developmental delays and promote essential skills.Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA):ABA therapy is an evidence-based approach that focuses on reinforcing positive behaviors and teaching new skills. It can be tailored to address communication, social, and adaptive skills.Communication Support:Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) devices or communication boards can help non-verbal individuals express themselves. Speech therapy may also be beneficial.Occupational Therapy:Occupational therapy can address sensory sensitivities, motor skills, and daily living skills, promoting independence.Social Skills Training:Targeted interventions to improve social understanding and interaction can enhance relationships and communication.Medication Management:In cases where co-occurring conditions like ADHD impact daily functioning, consultation with a psychiatrist can be beneficial to explore medication options.Educational Support:Collaborating with schools to implement individualized education plans (IEPs) ensures that educational environments accommodate the specific needs of the individual.Family Support and Education:Providing families with education on autism, ADHD, and effective strategies for support is crucial. Support groups and counseling can also benefit families.Structured Environment:Creating a structured and predictable environment helps individuals with autism thrive. Consistent routines and clear expectations can reduce anxiety.Multidisciplinary Team Approach:A team comprising psychologists, speech therapists, occupational therapists, and other specialists can collaborate to address various aspects of the individual's development.Individualized Transition Planning:As individuals with autism grow older, transition planning becomes essential. This includes considerations for vocational training, independent living skills, and community integration.We must focus on the autistic individual's specific needs and strengths and the interventions should be tailored to the individual's specific needs and strengths. Regular reassessment and adjustments to the treatment plan are essential as the individual progresses. Collaborating with a healthcare team, including professionals with expertise in autism spectrum disorders, ensures a holistic and effective approach to treatment.

question: How difficult is it to be a parent of an autistic child?
answer: Extremely difficult. My son is 13, and is on the â€œmild" side or otherwise called Asperger's. He is my first born son, I have two. His younger brother is 10. I knew fairly early that there was something â€œnot right" with him. I knew when he was a babyâ€¦.but it took until he was in the 2nd grade until he was diagnosed and began to receive the help he needed. Raising my son has been the hardest, soul-searching, depression-inducing, panick attack every day, heart breaking, embarrassing, socially crushing, marriage in the dumpster time of my life. But he has given me more, taught me more than ANYTHING I have ever done. He has taught me that I have a voice, because I have had to fight for him more often than not; he has taught me that the littlest hurdle can be jumped. That there is more than one way to look at life. He has made laugh harder than anyone can. He has taught me how to push harder for change, against him and especially for him. He has taught me to never give up on anyone, this one is the hardest to do. My son is the most difficult journey, yet most rewarding, of my life. Don't get me wrong, I have on many occasions wished he was â€œnormal", for my sanity and his peace. But I somehow believe in my heart that he will be happy in his life. And he will have peace within himself. EDIT: I wanted to clarify, because I feel that I didn't do such a good job before. I don't want to sound like my son has ruined my life because he has Autism. Our lives have been more challenging because he has Autism but I don't feel he has ruined mine, his brother's, or any other family member's lives. Some days are far more challenging than others, but we are learning how to deal with these challenges as they come. I want note that he is in probably the best time of his life so far, other than when he was little and happy all the time! I meet with his teachers every week to go over any changes that need to be made, which has been years in the making! He struggled in school for a few years behaviorally, socially and academically. He still does. But there were a few years where it seemed like I was getting a call from his principal every day for something he did, or didn't want to do, or that he was acting out. It was so rough for him and he fell behind. He is slowly catching up. His social life is very limited and is hard for him to relate to the kids his age, but he still enjoys being around people. His father and I, though divorced now, try to work together to keep him engaged in his interests within reason! His relationship with his younger brother is strained, but we have found ways to work around this. I have often wondered if I made the right choice by having another baby because of some of the things his brother has had to deal with. There were many times that I had to deal with his behavior in the moment and felt like I was ignoring my younger son. It's hard to balance as a parent! So yes, it is very difficult to raise a child with Autism, even more so when you have more than one child. But I believe he is a gift, his brother is a gift and I take one day at a time!

question: What can a parent of an autistic child do to prepare their child for the future?
answer: My brother, who is 56, is autistic. My parents, who are both now deceased, did NOTHING to prepare my brother for the future, and I mean literally nothing. When my father died, my brother needed help with everything. Since 2009, thatâ€™s been my job. Hereâ€™s my advice:Unless your child is absolutely positively guaranteed going to be self-supporting upon adulthood, start the process of assessment for and application for SSI before theyâ€™re 18. It can take several years to get assessment done and go through the application process. Qualifying for SSI gives your child a safety net if they really are unable to support themselves. More important, it may make them eligible for counseling, job training programs, assistance from social services, and eligibility for medical insurance.You arenâ€™t going to live forever. If your child is not able to live independently, whatâ€™s going to happen to them after you die? Hint: the transition to whatever arrangement you think youâ€™re going to make will go a lot more smoothly if you, the parents, are alive to help! So if the plan is for the child to live with a sibling, start that transition ASAP. If the plan is for the child to live in a group home, start that transition ASAP. It may seem harsh and premature to start implementing such plans before you pass; trust me, itâ€™s not! If youâ€™re there to guide your child into their adult living situation, it will be easier than if it has to be done and youâ€™re gone.Get help from everyone you can. Check out support groups, advocacy groups, service organizations, government programs, educational/training opportunities. If they arenâ€™t a good fit for your child, fine, but maybe they can refer you to something thatâ€™s a better fit. Support groups can be great, because you can learn from other peopleâ€™s experiences and avoid mistakes. Donâ€™t try to do things alone if thereâ€™s help available.Be realistic about the future and do financial planning thatâ€™s realistic. If you have other children and theyâ€™re self-supporting or will be self-supporting, maybe your autistic child will need a larger share of the estate than they will. Maybe youâ€™ll have to save more money for your retirement if you intend to try to support your autistic child as an adult. If you love your child, sit down and figure out what you have to do.Try try TRY as hard as you can to prepare your autistic child for the future. Get them involved, if at all humanly possible, with mundane things helpful for independence. My brother had no idea you had to pay for electricity, water and gas. He didnâ€™t know how a checking account works. He didnâ€™t know how a debit card or gift card worked. He didnâ€™t know what to do if the toilet overflowed, how to go to the post office to pick up a package, how or where to get a money order. I could go on and on. My parents never involved him in those things, partly because they just didnâ€™t want the hassle, partly because my brother himself didnâ€™t want the hassle.Get your affairs in order: make sure you have a will, a living trust if you need one. Since Iâ€™m my brotherâ€™s caregiver, I went to a lawyer and together we created a special needs trust to provide for him if I pass before he does. Iâ€™ve worked with his social worker and the organization that provides services to autistic adults to make sure that whatever happens, my brotherâ€™s welfare is taken care of. (I have to add, my insistence on getting things put in order has not been entirely popular with all other members of my family.).TALK TO YOUR CHILD ABOUT LIFE AFTER YOUâ€™RE GONE. Parents predeceasing their children is the natural course of things! Some day you arenâ€™t going to be there for your child. That shouldnâ€™t be taboo to talk about. It isnâ€™t a big secret that we all die: help your child to understand that youâ€™re preparing them for that time.

question: How can parents minimize the chances of having an autistic child?
answer: There is a genetic predisposition to autism - it runs in families - but it is also believed that there are environmental triggers. Autism risk factors: genes, environment, and gene-environment interactions Here are two promising avenues of research regarding environmental factors that may influence autism. In my opinions there isn't enough evidence to support recommendations for specific practices, but I think these areas are worth keeping an eye on. The first is epigenetics, which looks at not only which genes are in a chromosome, but whether they are "activated" or not. Brain development, including in the womb, depends on complex sequences of gene activation/deactivation. The process of activation/deactivation is commonly through methylation, and certain compounds are known to be methylators. You can't (and shouldn't) avoid all methylators, but removing excessive and unnecessary methylators in the parent's and child's environment theoretically should reduce the number of genes that are switched into an unusual state. Google "autism methylation". The second is the gut biome. Google "autism gut brain connection". Clinicians have long noted that children with autism also often have digestive problems. Some children with autism have greatly reduced symptoms when they follow certain diets (e.g. eliminating certain foods, adding foods with live cultures). There is not a single diet that all children respond to, so most parents have to experiment. The diets may work because they encourage healthy flora and fauna in the gut, and there may be other practices needed to maintain a healthy biome, such as eliminating biofilms of unhealthy bacteria, or repopulating the gut properly after a course of oral antibiotics. There are some other suspected environmental triggers, such as childhood illnesses, that parents don't have much control over. When you have a child, though, you have to be ready to give up a certain amount of control over your life. There's a wonderful essay "Welcome to Holland" about the experience of raising a child with a disability that celebrates the beauty of the alternate journey, and about accepting how life will be different for you and your child because of that disability. Much of our joy and heartache comes from the way we perceive and react to the hand we are dealt. A Parent's Perspective

question: At what age does autistic child starts addressing the parents as Mom or Dad?
answer: All children develop at different rates. But when a child develops very differently from the neurotypical norm, parents and doctors get insight into whatâ€™s going on with that child. In the case of autistic children, they are on a huge spectrum and they may develop physical and mental characteristics and abilities at wildly disparate rates. This doesnâ€™t mean they are any less intelligent or capable in the long run, but during the 20-odd years of childhood that humans have, it can be frustrating for parents whose kid isnâ€™t doing what other kids are doing. An example: my grandson, very Aspergerâ€™s and extremely intelligent, didnâ€™t have the brain wiring for feeling or possibly for just expressing gratitude. The ability to say â€œthank youâ€ in a way that reflected his true feelings didnâ€™t come about until he was about 12. His parents, both on the spectrum and very high-functioning, didnâ€™t want him to learn how to parrot something that had zero meaning for him, so they didnâ€™t teach him a rote response. This devotion to just plain telling the truth is typical of autistic people. In fact, lying is, for many, extremely confusing and difficult. I vividly remember the day that the first spontaneous â€œthank youâ€ came from my grandson. Thatâ€™s how important that milestone was. Now this was a child who flew a plane by himself (his uncle as co-pilot), with banked turns and everything, on his fifth birthday. Go figure. So the ability to address the adult care-giving humanoids in their life as Mom or Dad means they have developed the wiring in the brain to make all those connections, cognitive and emotional. For some, like my grandson, calling people by their title instead of by their actual (true - not lying!) name is just plain stupid or baffling. So he doesnâ€™t. Iâ€™m guessing that most neurotypical grandparents would have a hard time not being called by the family term for â€œgrandmaâ€ or â€œgrandpa.â€ It took me quite awhile to feel okay with giving up â€œNanaâ€ - a name I associate with my own grandmother whom I loved dearly. See all the emotionality connected with this need to be called by something other than my own first name? This realm of emotion may be completely off the radar of your autistic child. If everyone else calls me Lonnie, why should my grandson be singled out and have to call me by a different moniker? In the long run, we have much bigger concerns than what a child calls us. Iâ€™m guessing that the connection you have with your child will be the same even if he or she calls you late to dinner. ;-)

question: What are the main difficulties with raising autistic children?
answer: I find all previous answers quite good and helpful, depending on what are you actually looking for, but I have to add my personal point of view. It is just something to think about and may be consider if it resonates. To me, the main problems that occur between autistic children and their adults are the pieces of the puzzle that are invisible. It is necessary to sort out the purely physical discomfort but apart from that there is a whole world of dynamics that Neurotypical people cannot comprehend because it never occur to them that it exist. For example, when humans communicate they need to be approximately at the same energy level for the transaction of information to happen smoothly. Autistic children are born with energy way above their parents and it feels like falling into a dark pit of depression when they are dragged to our level so we can communicate. They resist it, avoid it or, in their own way, will try to raise our levels to theirs (usually with the wrong means, shouting, hitting, provoking). In my work I push myself to do it voluntarily. Its not easy, and I find most people would not even try as it is just as painful for them to keep their spirits and energy high. The short moments when I succeed to match the childâ€™s level of energy, our understanding clicks like magic and we both end up transformed. Another dynamic, parents are not aware of is the Emotional Skin Deficiency (ESD) of their autistic child. Which means, that it is nearly imposible for those children to locate and manipulate their emotional boundaries, as we have learned to do. In a restrictive environment, the emotional â€œboxâ€ (as is the â€œno loud voices on the busâ€), hurts them. They lack the capacity to fit in, and when pushed forcibly, the â€œboxâ€ cuts through their emotional body. Parents need to teach their children how to manipulate their emotional body through modelling, but the problem is that they have never been taught this themselves. The problem for someone that has no emotional skin is that they cannot see otherâ€™s either. For them, in their world, we are puffs of floating emotional colors, exactly like themselves and, when a person comes near them, all the subconscious baggage would mix with theirs as if it was their own. Like a drop of ink in a glass of water. Depending on the person and their ability to close their open subconscious â€œprogrammesâ€ running on the background, the child would react to the invasion or not. What makes us who we are, our pains, sorrows, loves and exaltations, our black secrets hidden away in a drawer, our frustrations, achievements, glory and shame â€“ they perceive and live all of it, all at once, as if it was their own without realising what is going on. I hope I could explain what the existence in this world is like for our dear children. I believe it plays part of why some people, even complete strangers, happen to be accepted easily, and others â€“ even family, could be fiercely rejected. It is not the person that is being rejected, itâ€™s all the open wounds that they unconsciously carry, all the dark feelings, rigid principles and unresolved matters. Coping with this senseless world sometimes needs disconnecting strategies, like rocking back and forth for generating energy, repetitive movements, focusing narrowly on one thing for hours at a time, making noises to drown the noise in the head, anything that will make the pain go away or render the space unpleasant for the intruder. I see many more hidden dynamics unfolding in a relationship between parents, teachers, society and the autistic children, and that plays a big part of the difficulty of looking after them. It is just as difficult for them to be looked after by us too. Our world and theirs are like sliding doors, so close together and always missing each other, both longing for love and connection. I have the highest respect for the professionals, carers and relatives of people with autism. I do believe that, if any change in society towards the Future People is coming, it will start from them. No, scratch that. It is ALREADY starting with them. They instinctively figure out the lessons our children are teaching us and implement them inti their outside world. I have not seen a person more tolerant, understanding, patient and explaining, fun, open-minded and a hell of a multitasker than a mother of an autistic child.

question: How is your day as a parent of an autistic child?
answer: Every day with my young daughter was similar in these regards: (a retrospective)She was awake often during night, sitting up in bed staring at the dark for hours at a time.
