For many weeks cucumbers and hotdogs are the only tolerable items. She abhors any vegetable that â€œsqeaksâ€ on her teeth (zucchini, asparagus). Nothing mushy is acceptable, and through her adult days she prefers her food cold.My day is orchestrated around providing the routine and conditions that will avoid major upsets. I must travel the same traffic route each time we leave home. Sameness is important, displays in stores have been changed..this can be a problem. A blinking sign isn't blinking today..triggers a meltdown! I consider calling the store mgr. ahead to be sure the sign on, but decide I can't be going over the edge like that. So instead I try to avoid that route in the future in case the sign is off.The pediatrician supports my â€œ"searchâ€ for answers (Feingold diet, food elimination, etc.) . All he says is she's a â€œdifficultâ€ child and prescribes Benadryl to help her sleep. (Doesn't help) A later neurological evaluation identifies an Autistic like cluster, PDD-NOS. (No Asperger diag.back then).A long stroller walk in the afternoon, finds neighborhood is â€˜â€™the sameâ€™. There is her fascination with mailboxes and storm drains. I give her stones to drop in the storms drains. This becomes a fixed routine for every walk. I bring a scratcher to clean the leaves away from the drain in the fall, because any obstruction can cause agitation. Occasional mailboxes with lids hanging open cause great concern. But we are happy.. the routine is known and safe.Each afternoon I pour her bee-bees in a tin cookie tray. She rolls them back and forth, mesmerized. She rarely drops or spills a bee bee; at 3 years old she is meticulous. This is her fascination for a whole hour while I clean and fix supper. Regular toys do not appeal to her. I overcome my guilt with â€˜meaninglessâ€™ play, it soothes her and I know she will be content for an hour. She watches Sesame Street, always waiting for just for the ABC song she likes. Oh, but Sesame Street changes format all the time and she gets frustrated with the â€œvariety.â€ If there finally is the ABC songâ€¦ she is in bliss. Later she uses her tape recorder on which I've recorded her favorite tunes. She will pick one song and play it over and over. But she is content.. so I let go of my fears for her and share the contentment.Her love of routine slowly becomes my main reward! Iâ€™ve come to enjoy the â€œsamenessâ€ of our days and find new patterns/games that she attaches to. After many letters and word activities, it is not surprising she is an early reader and good in math. She goes on to excel academically, even though early school years bring unrelenting cruelty (back when bullying was â€˜acceptableâ€™) .She is a young woman now, living independently with a successful career in computer processing. I couldn't feel more blessed ! She reflects fondly on the long repetitive activities of her childhood. I am grateful that I had some â€˜inner wisdomâ€™ as a mother to accept her strange and exhausting ways. Her adult anxiety is frequent but manageable. I suspect her anxiety might have become disabling if she had been â€˜forced into a normal adjustment.â€™Thank you for reading.

question: What are some tips for autistic parents raising an autistic child?

Later this evening while in his bed he did it again, despite me checking in on him every five minutes to see if he had a dirty diaper. He has sensory issues that make smearing poop interesting, the same way that he likes playing with Play-doh. This is what autism is like and why it can be nearly impossible to relate to autistic children. The primary tip I have is patience. All parents of autistic children must learn to be patient, while their child struggles to figure out the things that come so naturally and easily to typical children like my eldest boy. We have TONS of situations like the one I just described. Learning to be patient is normally difficult for most people but the process is quickly expedited for parents of autistic children. My wife and I are trying hard to keep this aspect of their personalities, and know patience and understanding are critical in doing so.

question: What is the probability for a person with Asperger Syndrome to become a parent of an autistic child?

question: Will there be a chance that my child will be autistic if I am autistic?

question: How do parents handle dining out with their autistic child?
answer: There are several solutions here, depending on what works for your child:Only go to places that all of you want to attend.Leave your child at home if you want to go somewhere that they donâ€™t.Only go places that have â€œsafeâ€ menu items that you know theyâ€™ll eat, even if the rest of the menu isnâ€™t something theyâ€™ll eat.Picky eating with Autistics is often due to either sensory discomfort/overload, or a need for familiarity and routine (often to counteract the aforementioned overload.) For a personal anecdote, I was an extremely picky eater as a child, primarily due to sensory discomfort combined with a need for routine As an adult, Iâ€™ve become an adventurous eater not only compared to my childhood self, but also compared to my parents who for years bemoaned my pickiness! It took time to get there, and opportunities to branch out and try foods on my own without pressure and expectations from family. (Growing up and having the bitter taste senses die down a bit also helped.) My parents like to go out to dinner at places that I didnâ€™t care for as a kid, so they left me at home where I was much happier to do my own thing (and with a babysitter when I wasnâ€™t old enough to watch myself.) If my parents said to me â€œWeâ€™re going to [place you donâ€™t like], would you like to come with us, or stay home?â€ Iâ€™d be elated to stay home and that they gave me a choice at all. Your child is a part of the family, and thus his opinion about where they eat should be considered. They also have a neurodevelopmental disorder that makes it far more difficult to filter out painful sensory data, and likely modifiey their behaviour to avoid pain (hence the â€œpicky eatingâ€). Because of this, they canâ€™t â€œsuck it upâ€ the same way neurotypical children might be better equipped to do. question: What should a parent do or not do when their autistic child has a meltdown?
answer: A meltdown is the culmination of overstimulation and frustration at being unable to communicate needs. It is an involuntary reaction caused by massive amounts of stress, at its core, a little bit akin to a â€œstraw that breaks the camelâ€™s backâ€ situation. As such, the absolute last thing you want to do when your child is having a meltdown is hit them, yell at them, or otherwise try to â€œdisciplineâ€ them into stopping, because they literally cannot stop themselves once it starts. I know from both personal experience as well as second-hand accounts and professional materials that parents who take the authoritarian approach to dealing with meltdowns usually wind up with even worse problems down the line, ranging from the child having more frequent and intense meltdowns due to the additional stress, the child developing self-destructive behaviors (including self harm and suicidal ideation) and self-loathing due to being blamed for their involuntary reaction, the child becoming defiant due to losing trust in the parent, etc. Overall, just do not treat meltdowns as misbehavior. What you want to do is take the child out of the distressing situation, preferably somewhere that is relatively quiet, doesnâ€™t have a lot of people, not too visually stimulating, and familiar to the child. There, you can work on calming the child down, figuring out what was bothering them, and making this into a learning experience so they can tell you when theyâ€™re starting to feel overwhelmed. I think the best thing for an autistic child is helping them learn how to recognize when theyâ€™re at their limit, and encourage them to take breaks when they need it. The best way to deal with meltdowns is to teach the child how to avoid them in the future.

It is hours and hours of driving to different therapies and events and then trying to support your child the best you can through all of that when all of that is overwhelming and confusing on top of all the sensory information that is already overwhelming him. Add to that knowing that they are growing up in a world that mocks and for the most part refuses to work around their differences, well it is easy to see why people would not want to take that version of the parenting journey. I wouldnâ€™t want my boys to be anyone other than who they are, but I do wish they hadnâ€™t had to struggle as much to get as far as they have come. In comparison to parents with neurotypical children, the road to parenting autistic children is both different and more difficult, much like the difference between a nicely paved several lane main street and a narrow, windy, unpaved, precarious mountain road in a blizzard.

question: Why don't parents overindulge their autistic child? Isn't that bullying? The autistic child has the right to do things that comfort them.
answer: Hold your horses, both everyone seeing this question and the person asking the question himself. I sense a potential for disaster here, as this question is very poorly worded. Thereâ€™s two things we have to make sure happen here:Determine the sincerity of the question and the questioner.Mildly reword the question.Only then can we answer it. Letâ€™s start with step one thenâ€¦ itâ€™s step one after all. That makes sense, I donâ€™t know why I needed to clarify that *sighs*. You can see my credential, I am on the spectrum, you can imagine then that this is not the easiest job for me, but on the surface, Iâ€™d say itâ€™s really fifty-fifty. Either the OP is a confused person the spectrum who feels heâ€™s been robbed of something, or it is someone trying to bait people, hoping to get people ranting about how people on the spectrum are overindulged, and that you shouldnâ€™t actually do that. So, letâ€™s analyze Adrian Luk . On close inspection, both of questions and answers, Iâ€™d say the OP is sincere, and simply worded his question poorly. Maybe because thatâ€™s the term heâ€™s heard others use. Let me proceed by talking to Mr. Luk himself. Is it okay if I call you Adrian? Iâ€™ll proceed by calling you by your first name, as I want to establish trust, but do tell me if youâ€™re uncomfortable with that. Adrian, if I look at some of your other questions, you often have the feeling that people are trying to bully you. Now, I donâ€™t know if thatâ€™s true or not, but this question answered in a vacuum would necessitate a proper definition of what â€œbullyingâ€ means. Bullying is, in my opinion, an action performed with the (most times sadistic) intention to hurt. According to Oxford, it means to â€œseek to harm, intimidate, or coerce (someone perceived as vulnerable).â€ Many add the fact that it has to be a repeated offence, and performed by a group towards, an individual. I disagree with that extra requirement, but itâ€™s important to keep in mind. Now, here is where the question is poorly worded. To overindulge someone would be negative by default. Over means itâ€™s too much. Therefore, a parent or parents not overindulging their child (autistic or not) would not be bullying, in fact, itâ€™d be good parenting. Thatâ€™s not where it ends though, far from it. A child on the spectrum almost always needs more of some things than a neurotypical person. To indulge means to allow someone to enjoy something desired. In parenting, there always has to be a balance between letting your child enjoy themselves, making sure they are happy, and preventing them from expecting they will always get their way. Because, unfortunately, the world will not always give you what you want, especially as you get older. However, someone on the spectrum may need to be allowed to indulge more in some things, even if that may seem like overindulging if it was performed by a neurotypical. In fact, not letting the child on the spectrum indulge in some things may cause severe harm. This is probably what you have in mind. â€œThe things that comfort themâ€ are probably either what weâ€™d call coping mechanisms: Maybe itâ€™s tapping your feet on the floor, or not looking someone in the eyes, or one the other thousands of coping mechanisms that we may develop. It may also be fundamental needs that either a neurotypical doesnâ€™t have, or needs less of: time alone, a clear schedule, those things. And in both cases, the question would be: Why donâ€™t parents indulge their child on the Autism Spectrum? Isnâ€™t that bullying? The child with ASD has the right to do the things that comfort them. Youâ€™re absolutely right at the end there, they have the right. Those who restrict them by default are inflicting harm, potentially long lasting harm. (Of course there are coping mechanisms that are harmful to the child, some for example bash their head against the wall. This must be restricted and then a solution must be found. Or maybe there could be a rare situation where the child has to be restricted in some ways for the benefit of others, for example if someone in the room is sensitive to the tapping of feet, the child will unfortunately have to stop doing the things that severely annoy someone else. If itâ€™s the parent that is annoyed by the behavior however, a solution must be found. There must be an understanding that not tapping their feet may harm the child just as much or maybe more as hearing it harms the parent. Maybe make a clear rule in which rooms tapping of feet is allowed?.) Parenting is about avoiding harm, either by removing sources of harm, or teaching the child how to cope with harm. If the parent harms the child by restricting their ways of coping or not allowing certain needs to be met, thatâ€™s bad parenting. However, that is not necessarily bullying. Thereâ€™s always the possibility that itâ€™s simply a case of ignorance. The parent(s) doesnâ€™t (donâ€™t) know that their child has special needs, or needs those coping mechanisms to not go crazy. In this case, itâ€™s not bullying, itâ€™s harmful, yes, but the parent is not consciously trying to inflict pain. In this case simply teaching the parents about ASD is the solution. They may ignore that, or even say that they disagree with what specialists, other parents and children alike have said. Then, it becomes willful ignorance. Or they may even truly be sadists, and inflict what they know causes harm. In both cases, it is bullying. This isnâ€™t just bad parenting anymore, but actively being a bad person, in some cases maybe even evil. Soâ€¦ TL;DR: To not allow the child on the spectrum to indulge in certain things, meaning to have certain needs met or be allowed to perform certain actions, is either ignorance or bullying.

question: What are some tips for handling an autistic child's behavior at home and outside the house? How can parents teach their autistic child manners and respect?
answer: Be consistent, lead by example, encourage questions, be realistic and adapt your expectations, be patient and practice positive reinforcement consistently the same as you would with a neurotypical child. Take them to an occupational therapist one week, speech therapist the next week, so every week they have 1 appointment. Take them to a therapist with experience in autism and PDA. Treat them with the respect that you would like to be treated with. Explain things to them like you would an adult. "Because I said so" isn't an answer. Rules or behaviours need to be explained (and make sense) for them to be followed. "Because everyone else does it" isn't a reason. "Because you will stand out or look different" is NOT a reason. Ask yourself if it's important. You can't expect your child to clean their room if you own is messy. There has to be a reason for things and it has to be constant (we pick up our toys before we start a new game so there is more room on the floor/table) You can't ignore something one day and then enforce it the next. Imagine being at work one day and all of a sudden getting told off for something you have done every day. If there aren't rules that make sense and they are only rules sometimes then what do you expect? Manners: people learn by repetition and watching other people. If you are expecting them to say please and Thankyou and you aren't doing it yourself then again.. what do you expect. You earn respect. It's not taught.

question: What should an NT parent raising an autistic child keep in mind?
answer: What should an NT parent raising an autistic child keep in mind? Whether they are high functioning or not, please be aware that their sensory issues may be very real for them, and not a case of being fussy, difficult, spoiled, or any other behavioral problem they simply need to overcome. Donâ€™t turn it into a power struggle. Have compassion and try to find out what the underlying problem is, so you can address it from their perspective. Iâ€™m not saying there shouldnâ€™t be boundaries of behavior (depending on their capabilities), but I am saying that the sensory sensitivities may actually be painful or distracting beyond what they can tolerateâ€”literally (and I donâ€™t mean that word in the sense of figuratively). It could be something as simple as demanding to have the toe seam on their socks lined up exactly straight; or the part in their hair perfectly straight; or not being able to tolerate certain textures, aromas, touch sensations, lighting or sound issues, etc. Their issue may seem like no big deal to you, but it might be a very big deal to them, not a case of them being deliberately difficult. Their sensory sensitivities (in their brain) likely have not been pared down the way a neuro-typical brainâ€™s would be over time. Itâ€™s like the â€œvolumeâ€ of their sensitivities is at 90 (out of 100) all the time, where yours might be at 20. Show understanding and patience as much as possible. And, along those lines, if the sensitivities cause them to have a melt-down, be aware that is NOT the same thing as an NT child having a tantrum because they didnâ€™t get their way. It would not be wise or kind to punish them for behaving badly when you were trying to make them endure something that was physically unbearable to them. (Shopping trips can be a mine-field for someone with sensitivitiesâ€”the sights, the sounds, the smells, all the peopleâ€¦.) A shopping mall might be torturous. Same for an amusement park. If they do have sensitivities to aromas, please donâ€™t wear perfume around them or use scented cleaning supplies, especially on their clothing or bedding. Donâ€™t buy them any clothing (or bedding) that is scratchy or itchy or clingy or too tight in places, or colors they donâ€™t like. (Soft cotton is great.) Avoid (or remove) labels in their clothing. If they say they canâ€™t eat certain foods, they probably canâ€™tâ€¦ not wonâ€™tâ€”CANâ€™T (without gagging). If they wonâ€™t wear certain clothing or shoes, find out why it bothers them. If certain sounds or flickering lights or such things bother them, again, itâ€™s a real problem that needs addressing. Also, some autistic people are a little disconnected from the their bodies when it comes to moving about in the physical world. Itâ€™s not uncommon to be a bit more clumsy than usual, so donâ€™t blame them for that, or accuse them of not paying attention. If they donâ€™t want to play team sports, it might be because they feel uncoordinated, or/and they donâ€™t want to have to socialize with a whole team. Socializing can be quite difficult for certain people with ASD, no matter how high-functioning they may be. So, if theyâ€™d rather be engaging in some solo pursuit, maybe donâ€™t push them to join Little League or band or dance class (though some might love that). They may have an amazingly creative mind, you just canâ€™t see whatâ€™s going on in there. Iâ€™d keep some art supplies around, as well as lots of age- (or developmentally-) appropriate books. Patience and true understanding is key.

question: What did you wish your parents knew about you as an autistic child?

I always knew that I was â€œdifferentâ€ than other people, but I never figured out how to communicate the depth or nature of it in anything resembling a relatable manner in spite of trying to do so many times. My pain (and social) masking abilities and tendencies developed from an unusually young age, so accepting that others see the world differently and guessing what they wanted to hear a lot really became more of my life than I realized. question: Is it hard for NT parents to raise an autistic child?
answer: It can be, especially for the NT parent who gets little or no help from their often-undiagnosed Autistic biological co-parent. While it's possible for an Autistic child to get their Autism from a spontaneous genetic mutation, they're far more likely to get it from a biological parent who is Autistic, and often undiagnosed if the child's Autism is unexpected. That was my own experience. I was 57 when I unexpectedly discovered I had Asperger's Syndrome. question: My 17-year-old brother is severely autistic and exhibits extremely dangerous behaviors. What can my parents do to correct the behaviors? Keep in mind that they have already tried every method in the book for properly raising an autistic child.

Denial is the death-knell of effective advocacy - if you can't cope with the fact that your child is eg autistic, you will not be able to get them the supports they need. Like it or not, these things are tied to the 'label'. Lots of people have a little difficulty adjusting when they first get a diagnosis for their child, but you can't afford to wallow. Cry, drink a bottle of wine, have a messy night - and then wake up the next morning, wash your face, and deal with reality. Worse yet, some people resist going through the assessment process. Please don't do that. Your child cannot be helped if you refuse to do what is necessary to get them that help. Once the diagnosis is in and you've adjusted, and you've learned all you can about the condition (UK parents of autistic children, go on the Early Bird[1] course if you can), you're ready to advocate. Look at this as teamwork and negotiation. Hopefully, everyone around the table has the child's best interests at heart (if you don't believe this is the case, look into changing schools). However, everyone around the table also has secondary goals which need to be acknowledged and accommodated if possible. For instance, the school has legal obligations they need to meet, in addition to supporting your child. It is often helpful to acknowledge that the school's resources are limited, and to appreciate what they're already doing for your child in addition to asking for whatever further supports the child needs. Be as friendly as you can. Antagonistic advocacy is rarely the way forward - think of yourself as working alongside the school rather than in opposition to it. Go to every meeting. This probably goes without saying, but you should be the most focused, most enthusiastic person in the room. A parent who can't be bothered to show up won't be taken seriously as an advocate for their child. Every UK school has a person who is the special educational needs co-ordinator, usually abbreviated to SENCO or SENDCO. This person will be a key player. Connect with them. Avoid getting defensive. You will talk about difficulties your child is having, and sometimes difficulties that they're causing. Avoid the temptation to charge in with 'he wouldn't do that!' Work on problem-solving instead, unless you have very good reason to believe the school is lying (in which case, change schools). Be the parent who says 'what might have caused that? Could he be experiencing sensory overload?' rather than denying it could ever have happened. (Again, denial? Not your friend.) Assume good will. This goes back to my point about everyone having the child's best interest at heart. If your child is safe in that school, then you should all be working to the same goal. If your child isn't safe, get them out. If you need some additional support, there are often Parent Advocate groups or resources who can help you. I got some assistance from the Parent Advocate professional team in my area, simply because I didn't fully understand the process of transferring to a special school and needed someone to help me find my way through the system. These people can, if necessary, back you up against the school if things become confrontational. Sometimes you can't avoid confrontation. I can't give you any advice for that part, as I've never been there. I would urge you to do everything you can to avoid that and to stay on the same side as the school. They aren't the enemy - they are the ones who will work with you to achieve the best results for your child. I hope that helps. Let me know if there are any specific questions you have, and I'll amend my answer to cover them. (Experience: 7 years as the parent of an autistic child.)Footnotes[1] EarlyBird - NAS

question: Is it reasonable for a parent to request an autistic child or adult to clean a bedroom?
answer: It's reasonable to ask. Be prepared for a whole range of possible responses, many of which won't end in a clean room:Uh-oh, now somebody is mad at me.I don't want to do this.Hey, I remember this book!I don't want to put (this thing) away because then I won't remember why I had it out.I don't want to get rid of (this thing) because I used to like it, and I kind of still do.This room looks weird without my stuff where I'm used to having it.I could use (this thing) for something else later, so I don't want to get rid of it.I know I can't do all of it, so I'm afraid to try to do any of it.This is hard/boring, and I'd rather do anything else.Even if your child doesn't articulate any of these things, there's a pretty good chance these kinds of thoughts are going to be the hang-up. Autism isn't any one thing, but it can make changes harder to accept and it can make decisions and filtering harder. If it's just clutter, I strongly suggest considering whether closing the door and letting it be is a reasonable option. If the room really needs to be cleaner, here are a few things to try:Aim for cleaner rather than clean. One more day worth of dust and laundry settling really doesn't harm muchCorrect anything that's actually a health or safety problem, such as moisture where it shouldn't be, food that's getting moldy or attracting bugs, or blocked exits.Go in small pieces and suggest specific tasks.I'm about to run the dishwasher and I need a few more things. Can you bring out any dirty dishes that are in your room?It's trash day. Let's pick up all the trash and sort the recycling.Let's sort your sock drawer and donate the ones that don't fit and recycle the ones that have holes.Offer choices. Do you want to sort out your outgrown socks or clean out your school papers from last term?Get started, and help with the getting started.Do fifteen minutes at a time.Be tolerant of side tracks and plain old bad days.If decluttering is part of the task, offer to hang on to anything they're not sure about. Pack it up in a box, put a date on it, and keep it out of the way for a month or two. Knowing they can change their mind can make it a lot easier to make a decision.Don't second-guess their decisions. If they decide to let go of something and you just can't part with it, tuck it away in the basement or attic, somewhere out of the way.If boredom is a problem, offer or suggest music or podcasts. The right choice might actually help reduce distraction.Vacuum cleaners are really loud, which could be a sensory issue. You could vacuum for them when they're not there, get a quieter vacuum, install floors that can be swept or dust mopped, or get noise cancelling headphones.It is probably easier to get less stuff than to try to sort and organize stuff once it's acquired. Decluttering starts in the store.Ask if they like having their room cleaner. If they decide to do something, there's a much better chance of it getting done than if you just insist.Give good reasons. â€œIt will help me out if you gather up your laundry and sort it so I can run a couple loads" will probably go better than, â€œbecause I said so.â€

question: What are some of the less obvious 'hard moments' as the parent of an autistic child?
answer: I would say that dealing with "the system" is something most parents of autistic children struggle with on a daily basis. A couple of examples: Health insurers don't or won't cover therapy (they see autism as an educational issue, not a health issue), and so they make getting reimbursed an arduous process. When they do agree to pay, they often negotiate downward so significantly that the parents end up footing most of the bill. This assumes, of course, that you live in a state where insurers are mandated to pay for autism services, and that your particular provider is covered by that state's law (e.g., self-insured companies are often exempted from this requirement). School districts often take an openly antagonistic attitude toward the requirement that they offer a fair and adequate education â€” as mandated by law â€” to autistic children. (Previous NYC Mayor Michael Bloomberg, for example, hired legions of attorneys to fight parents, arguing disingenuously that autistic children deserved to be "mainstreamed" instead of put in an appropriate setting.) Families often have to tour dozens of schools and then negotiate with municipal bureaucracies just to secure an appropriate educational setting. If that doesn't work, then parents go broke paying for private schools willing and able to help their children.

question: How has being a Parent of an Autistic child made you a better person?
answer: It may well have been the arrogance of youth, or it may have been any number of other factors, but I attribute some very specific wisdom I've gained in the last decade to the birth and growth of my son, who is definitely autistic. From my son I learned several important parenting lessons: - Recognize that most of your planned traditions are for you, not for your kids. The first year we tried to take my son to a "Trunk or Treat" was an utter disaster. It was loud, filled with people, and the noise of the engines inflating the bounce house were even making ME cringe. He was very unhappy. We left, upset and unhappy with him and the situation. Then we realized that we were celebrating Halloween how WE wanted it, and not how HE might have wanted it. Halloween isn't an adult's holiday (well, at least not if you're bringing your kids along) but we were trying to make it about us. Recognizing the natural parental tendency towards vicarious living - and quashing it - has made both my wife and I much better parents. - Judge not lest ye be judged. There's a quote that I really enjoy by Steven Pinker: " If you aren't just brought up in your tribe but interact with other people either directly or vicariously, through journalism and literature, you see what life is like from other points of view and are less likely to demonize them or dehumanize others and more likely to empathize with them." As a teacher of gifted students who had VERY clear ideas about how *I* was going to parent, my son was a sharp rebuff to those ideas. Now I know why parents would allow children to "go out like that," or why parents "let their !@#% children scream like that" or [insert judgmental comment here]" ...because parenting is never simple or easy. I used to think - as many parents-to-be do - that parenting has clear lines you can choose to never cross. Hah! Any parent learns the truth of this - parents of autistic children get it seared into their flesh. - All accomplishments are noble. My son will learn most things later than other children - but he will learn them. Right now he's struggling mightily to beat Super Mario 1, Level 1-2, with the Nintendo I got him. When he succeeds, there will be mighty cheers in the house fit to shake the foundations, and I don't give a damn what the neighbors think. His accomplishments are no less great for him, and his struggles are no less real. Too many American parents measure their accomplishments on what other children and what other parents are doing. My son will never catch the winning pass in the high school football game. He will, however, try ten times harder and push ten times longer to accomplish his goals than I ever could - and he will accomplish them. When he does, I'm going to make sure he gets just as much recognition as the high school wide receiver. Accomplishments are a function of effort, not skill - and screw anyone who says otherwise. - Society's expectations are insidious, unfair, judgmental, and widespread. The number of times I've had to recognize that what I wanted for my son and what will happen for him didn't mesh are probably in the hundreds. Being a parent of an autistic child makes you very aware of "how things are supposed to go" that you might otherwise never recognize. Family pictures are not a given. Some babysitters are idiotic in their knee-jerk avoidances. People who talk to my son loudly (which, incidentally, is probably the worst thing you can do to get compliance from an autistic child) with the best of intentions...the list goes on. I'm lucky - I'm naturally, because of my intellect and upbringing, resistant to societal pressures. I'm not blind to them. I know your son is supposed to be just like ol' dad, get into trouble, get into fights with friends, kiss girls, drive cars too fast, play on the football team, blah blah blah. I know that any kid who doesn't do these things is likely to be looked on oddly - and my boy does none of them and probably never will. I also know none of these things actually matter. Society places importance on them, but you can choose whether or not they are important to you. Having the courage to make your own value judgments is, in my opinion, what truly makes the man or woman. tl;dr? I'm a far wiser person for the existence of my autistic son. Any set of new experiences will make you wiser. Autism is a long set of challenges and I'm not saying I wouldn't "fix" him if I had the chance - but I'm also saying that there's a great deal of wisdom to be learned, a great deal of beauty to be seen, and a great deal of love to be experienced. I used to be terrified of having a "handicapped" son, and now it's my reality. Y'know what? My life goes on. And so will his - and it will kick ass.

question: What is the one most important thing the parent of an autistic child should do to help their child grow up happy?
answer: In my opinion, the single most important thing the parent should do is to never treat their kid's autism as a problem or a disorder, and never compare your kid with anyone else. This will not be easy as you navigate the hard times for you ahead to give your kid the best possible experience at school and social situations. It will frustrate you to see your kid not being able to cope up at a school with neurotypical kids, and break your heart to see mundane things causing such a difficulty for your kid, but it is a test of acceptance that every parent must pass in order to provide a happy life to their child. Give your child your unconditional love, one that does not falter in the presence of other kids. Recognize the child's strengths and cater to them. As the child ages, he'll be quick to understand how he is different from his peers, and turn to you for gaining the confidence he needs. To allow him that confidence and self-esteem, BOTH the parents need to be rock-solid in their belief that this is not a handicap or a problem. This is his life, and you are an important part of how it shapes up. Raising an autistic child is a great lesson in loving someone completely unconditionally, and I believe such a love can only lead to happiness, for you as well as your child.

question: Can a parent spoil their autistic child too much? What are the potential consequences of this?
answer: Absolutely. Autistic children, in many ways, are just like neurotypical children. They will need boundaries too. What I would call spoiling your autistic child would be doing many of the things they are capable of doing on their own, for them. The best thing you can do for your autistic child is help them progress to become as functional a member of society as possible. Remember, autism is a condition where the connections between the right and left sides of the brain are rewired. Other senses become more predominant, and awareness of the social queues neurotypical people take for granted get lost in the shuffle. Donâ€™t take their lack of communication to be a mental disorder. Many autistic children are very intelligent. The challenge is to tap that intellect and find ways to connect with them. Doing too much for them to the point of spoiling them is locking them into a life where they will always depend on you. A doting mother might like the sound of that, but what happens when they become an adult? Grow to be 30 or 40 years old? What happens when you pass away and they still depend on you for everything? This is why you need to be very careful on how much to you do for your child. Granted, I can only speak for high functioning autism. Low functioning is a very different paradigm, and more attention is required. However even in this case there is a level of â€œspoilingâ€ that goes over the line. That being said here are things I strongly recommend to do for your child.Listen to the advice of your childâ€™s teacher, therapists, doctors and others who are in their support umbrella. Unreliable Facebook posts and amateur theories are no replacement for real, trained individuals who have a vested interest in your childâ€™s success.If they have a meltdown or tantrum because you arenâ€™t doing everything for them, redirect the focus. Focus their attention elsewhere, like ask what they were doing or how school was, bring up one of their interests (especially one that they love to talk about). There are lots of ways to redirect, and their teacher or therapist and help with some ides for that.Expose them to the world. The biggest mistake I see with many parents of autistic children is they have this sort of shame about their child, and are embarrassed being seen with them. This has to stop. Remember. IT IS NOT ABOUT YOU. Taking your autistic child to see the sights and experience the little joys of life has a very, VERY strong impact on them. In practical terms it gets them accustomed to the outside world and fills their brain with positive sensory inputs. On a human level you are taking your kid out to have memories with the family. This in many ways is better psychological therapy than what any doctor can provide.Challenge them. Get a feel for what they are capable of and look deeper into what potential they have. For example, is your child non-verbal? Get them speech therapy, and constantly communicate with them. They may start with signing or pointing to stuff, but with enough practice they will start to realize they can use their voice too. Of course, consult with your childâ€™s therapist, teacher and others involved in their ARD process to see where you can go with it.If they are physically capable give them activities. Household chores are a great start, since it also develops their independence. Start small, and help them step by step. Be patient, as you may need to help over and over, but eventually they will be able to things on their own. Cleaning their room, putting their clothes away, doing laundry, even some food preparation.Always encourage and be positive towards your autistic child. Your words carry weight with your kids, and for an autistic child it carries even more since many think literally. You say they are stupid, that becomes the truth instead of just a figurative insult you said in an angry rage. Recognize their accomplishments, and continue to encourage more.An autistic child will always need some sort of help, whether they are low functioning or high functioning. Itâ€™s the level of help that makes the difference between enabling your kid and keeping them held back.

question: Why do people divorce when they have children with autism or special needs?
answer: To succeed, marriage takes a lot of work. There is no situation on earth that will trigger you more often, or cause you to look more closely at your own "stuff" (emotional baggage still needing to be cleaned up) than a close relationship... and there are few relationships closer than a marriage or life partnership. Marriages and life partnerships come in 3 flavours:Destructive (partners are diminishing each other's capacity, through being silenced at best, or actively tearing each other down at worst; these couples achieve less together than they would separately).Neutral (partners are functioning in an adjacent way, but neither building each other's capacity, nor diminishing each other's capacity; these couples achieve slightly more together than they would separately through shared resources and coordinated communication) Constructive (partners are functioning in a collaborative way, each building the other's capacity so that together they can accomplish much more than they could as unpartnered individuals)Many couples stay in the first two types of marriages or partnerships "for the sake of the kids". Frankly, I know quite a number of these "kids" who wished their parents had separated and quit with the poisonous atmosphere a lot sooner. However, there are economic considerations that can make this choice really difficult. Children with special needs also take a lot of work. And each one of us human beings only has so much time and life energy to spend. If a marriage or partnership is already on the neutral or destructive end, the likelihood of it surviving the extra work of a child with special needs is low. Sometimes, neither parent is able to support the special needs child, who then ends up in the social services system. The main reason that couples end up in relationships that aren't constructive is our cultural lack of training around sustaining a loving connection with others, effective communication, and cleaning up old emotional baggage. But above and beyond that, there is very little support for parents in general, in North America. We've been torn from agricultural areas and smaller towns and villages to access employment that sometimes takes us far from friends, far from anyone we're close to who can help us. In the words of global addiction expert Bruce Alexander, we're "dislocated" from a supportive community context, and as a result of this, much more vulnerable to addictions, emotional turmoil, and any stress we may face in our lives. No couple sets out to break up. And the consequences of a break-up can be very difficult for a special needs child. But we've got to get a lot better at preparing couples for a constructive life together. The shame-blame-game does no-one any good!

I can say I've had to hold my son accountable for the times when he pretended he was not able to do/understand something, and used it as a means to use/abuse/mess with the people around him*. If the parents are being unreasonable, ignorant, and/or plain old mean, then I absolutely agree with the premise of the question. No, that behavior is unacceptable. If said autistic person is running a game on his/her parents, then it's not only okay for the parents to hold their child accountable, it's necessary and healthy. Though, either way, I'd say calling it a â€œlame excuseâ€ is pretty rude (and I do think children also deserve to be treated with manners)â€¦so yeah, rephrase. question: In what ways can parents support their autistic child's development and learning?
answer: Iâ€™ve had awesome success with my 2 kiddos thus far- they are 9 and 6, one HFASD, and the other with SPD. Hereâ€™s a list of some things that have really helped us. 1- Getting them into Speech, Occupational and Physical therapy. It took almost a year in my area of the US for an official diagnosis for my son, because you need to see a specialist. As soon as I got in to see the specialist, she asked why on earth our pediatrician hadn't referred us for those three services the minute ASD was even suspected- and Iâ€™ll tell you what, they are all absolutely amazing. Our speech therapist had an awesome program specifically to help those with autism to have successful social interactions. It was so helpful, especially because it helped communication between him and ME, so our relationship and my sanity improved by leaps and bounds. The PT helped immensely with physical issues such as body awareness and coordination. And the OT helped a lot with solving everyday problems, and helping me to understand how to meet sensory needs. I know Iâ€™m suggesting a lot of therapies here, so know you donâ€™t have to be enrolled in all of them at once. With therapies like these, your child may need it for 6 months, then be fine for a year or two and then need it again. Itâ€™s part of their growth process. Go with what is helping them right now. 2- Social stories. I learned how to use them and started drawing or making my own on the computer, and I tell you what, a well done social story may as well be gold. A social story is words and images that help to illustrate expected patterns of behavior. Sometimes ASD can cause a hiccup or disconnect in figuring out what to do next and how to do it. A social story helps them to visually see what steps they need to take to accomplish a task. To make a good social story, you figure out what step they are struggling with, and have the story show them the exact steps you bridge the gap. There are a few amazing television programs that do the same thing- Daniel Tiger was the most helpful one I found, with a story that clearly shows the steps to managing a particular situation- even a helpful jingle you can sing to help your child remember the story. We watched the potty episode a LOT. 3- Getting them an excellent therapist/counselor who has lots of experience with kids and autism. We had to fight our insurance about this one, but Iâ€™m telling you, it was one of the best things we ever did. Having autism can be frought with overwhelming experiences. A good therapist helps them to navigate theirs and others feelings and gives them loads of tools to help them manage. 4- Identify and remove food triggers. This was a lot more prevalent with my son. We discovered through a lot of trial and error that â€˜natural flavoringsâ€™ in some foods trigger meltdowns- like inconsolable screaming meltdowns. He has since grown out of it some, and by that, I mean he will still be overly emotional and more prone to having a meltdown, but with the support heâ€™s received from therapy, etc, he has enough skills that he can manage himself pretty well. From talking to others parents, trigger foods can vary widely- corn, sugar, food dyes and gluten are all things Iâ€™ve heard can be triggers. 5- Learn about and understand ASD, and try your best to figure out your child in particular and what works for them. My two are radically different and we have to parent then completely different from each other. Stop trying to make your child neurotypical, or treating them like they are. ASD is different- so you need to parent differently than your parents did with you. You will literally make both yourself and your child miserable if you donâ€™t. 6- Be their champion. Make sure they get what they need for success. Talk to your spouse, extended family, teachers, doctors, other parents, etc and help them understand your child and what they need from them. If a therapist, teacher or whoever isnâ€™t making progress, have frank discussions with them about your concerns, and if needed, ask for someone else. Get them a 504 or IEP for school, which in the US is a document that lays out accommodations that the school must make to help your child. Include in it that the teacher needs to use social stories (I made a set for my kids after getting a list of things they struggled with from the teacher), specific and individual discipline that works for your child, and other accommodations that they might need- like a calm down tent, noise canceling headphones, a quiet place to work etc. A couple of times Iâ€™ve had the option of either leaving a class, or teaching the teacher how to work with someone with ASD. I got some amazing advice that if I help the teacher instead of just pulling my kid out, I help a lot more kids that teacher comes in contact with. Since then, I have a meeting with every teacher before school starts. The results have been amazing, we have had some great teachers and they have all been supportive and respectful when I talk to them about what works for my kids. We did also seek out and get onto a good charter school, and our best teachers have been there. Charter schools often have more support for special needs, too. 7- Find ways to connect with your child, and show love to them the way that they need it. Each is different and it may take you some time but the effort Iâ€™ve put in has all been worth it a hundred times over. My kids are absolutely amazing, and they are both doing very well right now, which is something I never thought would be possible a few years back. Their hugs are priceless. 8- Get help and support for yourself. It can be very hard being an autism parent, and itâ€™s a 24/7 job. Take care of your own mental health, and find and teach trusted family or babysitters how to care for your child so you can take time off. Give both yourself and your kid lots and lots of grace. Best of luck to you on your journey, and God bless.

question: What are the telltale signs of high-functioning autism in adults?
answer: I’ve read a lot of the answers here- I have Autism, ASC1, (used to be called High Functioning or Aspergers)… and perhaps it’s just that my experience is different, but…I don’t visibly stim. I stim in my head with repetitive thoughts or scraps of songs that I like, or sayings- I’m a visual thinker and can kind of watch “memories” in my head if I’m stressed.I can make eye contact.My voice, albeit loud, is very expressive.Why are these things so different than what others have said? Because of a couple common key features of people with ASC 1, people at my end of the spectrum…We learn to “mask” and “camouflage”. We don’t want to be outcasts, we want to get along, and as there is a correlation between ASC1 and intelligence, we figure out what the “script” is for the “character” or “situation” we want to emulate “normality” in, and we learn to fake it, usually very effectively. That masking is absolutely characteristic of this end of the Autistic Spectrum. So, I don’t stim because I mask it.Not everyone with Autism struggles to make eye contact.As with masking, you can learn to control at least some elements of your voice- and as I was taught considerably through story telling (in the Native American part of my childhood) we were taught how to tell stories… so I learned more about how to use my voice.As with everyone who is not autistic, people with Autism are all individuals. How they learn to survive amongst the unkindnesses and intolerances of the NT world is as dynamic, diverse and individual as they are. Intelligence and verbal skills are variable amongst people with ASC 1 but they tend to be better than ASC 2 and 3 and the better they are, the easier many autistic people find it to cope and adapt. Culture, upbringing, personal choice and tastes, physical health, family dynamics, experiences, education, etc all make a huge difference to how an individual will manifest, and cope with, their autism. For me, I would sayA degree of dyspraxia or clumsiness is common amongst adults at the ASC 1 end of the spectrum.Extreme ability to know a *lot* about certain topics, and to exhibit a deep and thorough understanding to the degree that people say things like “Is there anything you don’t know about ‘Topic x’ ?”Anxiety about uncertainty and changeTendency to be visual thinkers and to express/ explain things in what are often seen as quite unique and original waysNoticing things that other people don’t, especially when those things are related to an area of interest.Social discomfort or inability to handle social interactions when under stressA black and white view of the world, and difficulty shifting to a new interpretation once one is set (clinging to a first impression).To many, rules and following rules is very important even when the rules might not make sense. You might even know the rule doesn’t make sense… but it’s a *rule*. Lots of times, the world and the people in it don’t make sense, and the closest thing we’re got to instructions are the “rules”. It causes me personally a lot of anxiety when others break simple rules- like- don’t cut the queue in front of me, trust me, it’s just not worth it.A unique way of relating things that others wouldn’t necessarily relate…Intolerances for certain types of fabric, sounds, lightings, sometimes even colours. I once had a lovely office chair but it was orange and had “squinchy” fabric… it was comfortable but I despised it. Orange is not a good colour (I told you, weird relationships…. a friend had a girlfriend who was nasty to me, and she always wore orange nail varnish; when I see orange, I see those nails, and feel the emotional destruction she did… so orange is not on my ‘favourite colours’ list).An odd way of organising things… one of my (autistic) friends organised her record collection (remember those?) first by type of music, and then… by the name of her favourite song on each album. Made sense to no one but her but it was her collection.Some people with Autism struggle to speak up. I struggle to shup up.I often struggle to get jokes. I have a good sense of humour, but in that my initial reaction with anything is to take it at face value, I need to get in a certain mindset to get jokes. For example - My hubby said “I bet they could take that to the bank” when someone on a TV show bought a vaulting horse. I was like “why do they need that in the bank?” and he said “Vault? Bank?” and I groaned. If I know to expect jokes, I do a bit better… like if we went to see a comedian. If Hubby had said “Hey, got a joke for you… “ and told me, I probably would have got the joke.I have superb spatial reasoning. You know these test questions? I love them, they are so easy I don’t even need to think about them. I love logic problems and find them easy to solve as I can “see” them in my mind. I have an excellent sense of direction. It’s all part of thinking visually. edit- For those who have asked … It cannot be A, as the two small squares and the large orange square cannot be side by side. B- the orange circle is on the opposite face as the three small spots, so they cannot be as this cube shows. In C, the three small dots are still on the opposite face as the large orange circle… so it can’t be C. D is then true, not only by exclusion but because the shown sides do relate to the flat image.If I am not interested in something I can get bored and distracted very eas… oh look! Something over there is SHINY!I don’t really have close friends. Everyone always seems to know me, but, I just don’t ‘get’ how relationships work. I don’t feel confident, I get nervous, and I don’t have a script to use for 1–1 relationships so I can’t mask. I have people who love me, and I love them, but I might not speak to them for ages- sometimes years- unless there is a reason to speak to them. “Hi Joan, thought I’d call, Im making a cake and need your icing recipe”. It might sound like I am using them, since I only call if there is a reason but … oh well. It’s very lonely sometimes, but I sincerely don’t know how it works. I know my “eccentricity” drives other people crazy, and I feel ashamed, so… that’s why we have QUora, right? So you have something else to do?Games. I love games. I not only play minecraft (for like 12+ years) I admin a minecraft server… so I can make people follow the rules! Muhahahaha cough cough cough So… the point of this is… you can’t tell (unless you are exceptionally skilled and know the person pretty well) if someone is Autistic based on ‘tells’ as we as individuals are usually quite good at being one of these…I’ve had people who on one hand have told me “You are so eccentric!” who will then say “Autistic? You can’t be autistic… you’re just…. really really you…” What they can’t see is how it’s *their* perception of my behaviour and nature that chalk me up as “eccentric” in their minds.

So suddenly, our son was surrounded by new people, who spoke a language he didn’t know, while he was already busy learning two other languages (French and English). So when he clammed up, we put it down to his being overwhelmed. When he regressed, we figured his brain was just struggling to adapt, and he just needed some time to adjust. When he went to pre-school and didn’t play with the other kids, we figured it was just because he still didn’t speak the language. And he was still so easy at home! As gentle and nice as ever. Oh, sure, he did things a bit weirdly sometimes, but it always made sense to me - maybe not to others, but always to me. I could easily explain why he did this or that; in fact, one of my recurrent sentences was, “Oh, I was like that as his age, so don’t worry, he’ll grow out of it!” (… Yes, I eventually realized that I most likely have Asperger’s, years later.) So how did we figure it out in the end? We didn’t. His first-year pre-school teacher was an ass who had no business being a pre-school teacher. (She literally told us he was just spoiled because we allowed him to do everything he wanted at home, for example.) But his second-year teacher was a real pro. And within two months, she had scheduled a meeting with us, where she gave us the address of the psycho-pediatric center, and told us to go there as soon as possible, because (I’ll never forget the words) “in 37 years in this job, I have never seen one like him.” So why did we ignore the signs of our son’s autism?Because he wasn’t exhibiting them for the first 18 months of his life,Because we didn’t know autism can take years to show up,Because we thought we were doing the right thing by not panicking when his social behavior changed as we moved to a completely new country.And because I most likely have a form of autism as well, and didn’t know it, so his autistic behavior actually made sense to me.(It ends well, though: turns out that country has one of the most awesome Special Needs education system ever, far better than what we could have had in France! The help my son has received has been nothing short of phenomenal, and he’s flourished into the most amazing teenager I could have dreamed of :) ! )

question: What are the symptoms of autism in girls?
answer: I'm “the obsessive fan girl.” I'm “the quiet girl in the corner.” I'm the girl who helps others with their homework. I'm the girl who's seen as a mom-friend to people a few years younger than me, but who doesn't have many friends my own age. I'm the “artsy” girl. I'm the girl who *always* wears leggings. I'm the girl who has snacks in her backpack. I'm the one who daydreams. The one who does quiz bowl. The one who reads all the books in the school library. The one who is clumsy. Autism in boys is often affectionately called “Little Professor Syndrome.” In girls, it is sometimes called “Little Philosopher Syndrome.” In reality, we have the same symptoms. It's just that society perceives them differently because of our genders. I am artsy and am picky about clothes, which was perceived by most outside folks as just a girl being a girl. My autistic brothers are also artistic and picky about clothes. That's seen as weird, because guys aren't “supposed” to care about those things. I've had special interests, and essentially have obsessed over things like Batman, animal healthcare, horses, plants, and various fictional worlds from books. However the voracious interest I demonstrate in such topics is labelled as “fan-girling” because girls are often stereotyped as obsessive fans anyhow. If a boy has a similar level of interest in topics (for example, one of my autistic brothers has a special interest in Minecraft) then it's seen as abnormal, because he expressed his excitement for it THE EXACT SAME WAY I express excitement about Stephanie Brown in the Batman Comics finally being put back into the canon where she belongs or things like that. So if you're looking for signs of autism in a girl, just ask yourself if you'd think a boy acting that way might be autistic. If the answer is yes, odds are good that the girl is also autistic.

question: What are subtle signs of autism and Asperger syndrome?
answer: Well, Asperger’s Syndrome is just autism, so we can get rid of the second half of the question. Thus, the question I’ll answer is: What are subtle signs of autism? There is the clinical, medical definition of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), and then there is the real, lived experiences that us autistics deal with all day, every day, and we’ve dealt with them our entire lives. And these signs are quite numerous, but be aware that not every autistic experiences these things, these are just the most common ones I’ve seen in my experience. So, here’s 63 subtle signs of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).Wearing bright colors/wearing subdued colors. We either crave stimulation, or we don’t want to be overwhelmed, so our clothes can be bright and attention seeking, or subdued. I insist on band shirts, jeans, and Vans.Hating phone calls. No, if I see a Rickenbacker bass that I want to buy, I will not call for a price, just let me know what it costs online.Not realizing you’re hungry or thirsty. Sometimes you just don’t feel or notice that you’re hungry or thirsty, even though you probably are very hungry or thirsty.Not replying to a text message. You want to choose your words carefully, so you think about it for a week, and then it’s too late to reply.Hating seams and tags in clothing. I hate clothing with tags or prominent seams. They feel stifling and itchy.Having an atypical sense of humor. Sometimes I say something I think is funny, but it just doesn’t land.Always telling the truth. I have a compulsive need for honesty, so I blurt out the truth even if it’s best for everyone if I keep my mouth shut.Feeling out of sync in groups. You always feel like an outsider in your friend groups.You have an aversion to or an obsession with popular culture. If pop culture is your special interest, you’ll be obsessed with it. If not, you just don’t “get” pop culture.Over-planning everything. You must schedule all tasks on a calendar, otherwise, nothing will get done. As someone that also has ADHD, this is a general feeling in ADHD as well, except it’s not for planning or setting schedules, it’s so you remember what you said you were going to do.Always feeling tired. Masking autism is mentally exhausting, so you always feel tired. Or you just feel tired all the time for no real reason.Don’t like being told what to do. We have a routine and schedule that works for us, don’t say it needs to be changed.You started reading at an early age. I was taught to read at 3 and a half years old.Finding comfort in repetition and routine. Routine is good. Routine is love. Routine is life. Except my ADHD wants something new and spontaneous too, so it’s a constant battle between the two.Struggling with crowds. You feel overwhelmed and overstimulated anywhere there’s a crowd.Seeing people as people. Because of how your brain is, you forget social expectations that other people have towards other people, and you default to treating people as people, regardless of who they are.Sensitive hearing. I’ve always had sensitive hearing, but I never found music to be triggering. In fact, I found it relaxing. I love music so much I decided to become a musician.High pain tolerance. I have a high pain tolerance. But the paradox is that I’m not indifferent to it, in fact, I feel pain more intensely, I just am able to tolerate it better.Over-apologizing. You apologize to people way too much over an issue because you perceive it’s due to you saying something and being misunderstood.Not caring what people think. The fun kind of autism where it’s just free and unmasked autism without a care in the world!Being really good at something that isn’t useful. I know a lot of dinosaur facts, data, and knowledge. I can give you the 100 million year evolutionary history of tyrannosauroids from memory, and if you’re lucky, with sources, but ask me to do my tax paperwork or expense reports and I fold like laundry. Another trait autism shares with ADHD, and for me, the two are reinforcing each other here.Being sarcastic. It’s not being sarcastic sometimes, you’re sarcastic all the time.Preferring face-to-face communication. Sometimes, people take a text message the wrong way, so you prefer discussing real matters face-to-face to avoid misunderstandings.Struggling to find appropriate gaps in conversation. You want to express your opinion on the subject, so you look for an opportunity, but none of them seem appropriate, and then the conversation moves on from that subject and you’re left there alone.Constant background anxiety. Masking autism or ADHD or any kind of neurodivergence breeds a specific kind of background anxiety that only people who are neurodivergent will understand. It’s more common than you think.Being overly empathic. In contrary to a popular myth, we autistic people actually have too much empathy and it becomes overwhelming to the point it comes off as overly literal or logical. We have so much empathy it creates so much emotion, that we have to use logic to make sense of it. That comes across as overly cold or logical, even when we may understand you and your situation more than you think we do.Relating to animals more than people. We love animals! I love all animals, but cats, dogs, lizards, and turtles are my favorites! They are completely non-judgmental, dogs and cats especially.Avoiding trying new things. Part of the rigid thinking pattern of autism. My routine works so well for me, why should I consider something new? That said, for me, it’s a constant battle between the autism wanting and craving the familiar, and my ADHD being curious and spontaneous and wanting something new and exciting. So how that ends up is that I spontaneously try something new, and if it works, I will make it a part of my routine, rigidly, and hate deviations from it.Eating the same food every day. We found the food we like, and it works for us. Some of us can be picky eaters, but again, my ADHD loves to try new things, so I’ve made food one of my special interests. How that looks is unless the food is meant to be mixed, it won’t be mixed and the food remains separate on my plate. That way I can try each individual thing on my own time. I’m like an autistic food critic. And yes, I loved the movie Ratatouille, why do you ask?Finding inappropriate things funny. I love Chris Tucker, Dave Chappelle, Monty Python, and Richard Pryor. I’d repeat their jokes, never understanding why repeating their jokes as a young, white, autistic and ADHD kid wasn’t appropriate. But I found them hilarious. Still do as an adult, quite frankly only now I learned there’s layers to the jokes they were telling that I didn’t see as a kid.Not liking to be touched. Only my wife, my family, and close friends can touch me. Everyone else must keep their distance, and stay out of my blood circle. For those that don’t know, the blood circle is a Scouting term that describes the area within the radius of the arm plus the length of a knife. Only a few people are allowed within my blood circle.Tendency to notice small details. For me, these are random, because, hey ADHD and autism linked up, so the small details I notice are small sounds that my brain fixates on and I have to respond to it.Hating florescent/down lights. I hate florescent lights. Even when other people don’t notice a flicker, I do, and it’s bothersome and overstimulating.Stimming. Flappy hands are happy hands. For me, my stims are cracking my knuckles, moving my leg rapidly, chewing my tongue, playing with my fidget cube, and squeezing my fists over and over.Always wanting to understand why. This is me with everything. Because of my logical thinking brain, everything happens due to some mechanism or reason, so my curiosity leads me to constantly ask questions. My ADHD side of me is also insanely curious, and since there’s no self-control, the two are reinforcing this curiosity.Enjoying repetition. When that dopamine hit from that new song hits, that song gets played on repeat for hours before I let Spotify continue on. Happened recently with the Zenith Passage’s song, “Synaptic Depravation.” That was on repeat for no less than three hours when I first heard it.Thinking in pictures. In other words, you’re a visual thinker and visual learner. You like to see something happen before you understand it. I’m an auditory thinker and learner myself, which isn’t shocking as I am a musician. But weirdly, I think in color when writing music, and unless music and optics are your special interests, that’s just going to seem weird to you, and a strange rabbit hole to fall down in. By the way, the note A is orange, and I won’t accept any counter-arguments on the matter.Having a flat affect. Otherwise known as “resting bitch face.” You have this look even if you’re just vibing. I don’t have this, personally.Preferring to pace around the room rather than sitting. Sitting can sometimes be weirdly painful, so we get up to move around. This is something that can overlap with ADHD, and in my case, having both, it just shows itself as that I can’t sit still and need to stim more.Imitating other people. Sometimes you learn something fun when imitating other people. I don’t do this anymore, but I did it as a kid all the time.Having a favorite thing. This thing you carry with you everywhere, no matter what. For me, it’s my fidget cube, but it used to be my $75 double action OTF knife, because I tend to always carry a knife on me, but it was confiscated when I went to my niece’s graduation, which bothered the hell out of me. I rather liked that knife a lot. There’s a whole other reason why I was bothered, but that’s personal stuff.Getting excited and interrupting people. Yeah, this is another trait autism and ADHD share, and yeah, the two don’t help each other out here. This leads to me info-dumping about my special interest for hours on end.Thinking over previous social interactions. You overthink about previous social interactions all the time.You see patterns in everything. Yep. For me it’s sonic patterns as I’m attuned to sound pretty strongly being a musician, so I perceive things as musical when they’re really random.You either have a good memory or a bad memory. You don’t have “normal” memory. Again, this is a trait autism shares with ADHD. For certain things, my mind’s like a steel trap, and nothing gets past it, but my working memory and executive functions aren’t the best, so I can lose my keys all the time and forget where I placed them.Preferring non-verbal communication. Some autistics are non-verbal, and may prefer to use other forms of communication, even if they can speak. I’m like the opposite, I can be a real motor mouth.Hating to brush your teeth. I hate to brush my teeth. I do it twice a day as dentists and doctors recommend, so my dental hygiene is good, but that doesn’t mean I like it. Admittedly, my Philips Sonicare toothbrush actually massages my gums, so that feels nice, but it still is part of the routine that is my least favorite. Showers? Love ‘em. Heeding nature’s call in the morning? Best part of the morning. Brushing my hair and styling my beard? Not as fun, but necessary, otherwise it gets unruly. But brushing my teeth? Nah, not the fun one, but I know it’s necessary.Having a monotone voice or a strange voice. Our voices can be strange at times.Difficulty identifying emotions/emotional dysregulation. A trait that autism also shares with ADHD. Our emotions can be overwhelming because it’s usually a combination of emotions at once, not one feeling. Worse yet, in my case, the ADHD leads me to be emotionally impulsive, so I just express emotion with no filter. The emotion is logical and rational, but there’s just no filter on it. This can make shutdowns and meltdowns worse, and easily, my least favorite part of being neurodivergent.Getting overwhelmed by too many tasks at once. This is an executive function challenge, something autism and ADHD share in common. The solution I’ve found is monotasking rather than multitasking. Focus on one task.Watching the same movies/TV shows all the time. There’s comfort in familiarity. There’s certain shows I go to that are comfort shows that put me in a better mood.Feeling awkward in groups. Social awkwardness is one of the quintessential autistic symptoms. Not that you’re not social, not that you don’t have friends, not that you’re introverted, you’re just a little socially awkward, and that can lead to misunderstandings.Thinking outside of the box. This is one of my favorite things about being autistic and ADHD is divergent thinking. Because the autism loves details my brain can come up with a detailed plan of action, and because the ADHD has millions of thoughts at once, those plans come out quickly, fully thought out, and detailed. Really a boon to creativity too, important for my job as a musician and songwriter.Having unique brilliant ideas. Same thing with problems, that divergent thinking also works with new and innovative ideas as well.Struggling to read between the lines. Socially, people don’t just say what they mean. Often, a lot of times, there’s a lot being said that’s not being said. I miss these all the time. For us autistic people, it’s a struggle because we think very logically and literally when it comes to communication. We’re assuming you’re saying what you’re actually saying, we don’t know if you meant something else between the words you said.Preferring written communication. Because it takes time and thought to write something out, some autistic people feel more comfortable with written communication.Two speed productivity. You’re either insanely productive you get 3 months worth of work done in 8 hours, or nothing gets attempted. There is no in between. This is a trait autism shares in common with ADHD.Compartmentalizing life experiences. We autistic people are really good with compartmentalizing everything, including our own life experiences.Comfortable being alone. You love the sweet embrace of solitude, because you can finally be yourself, no masks required.Happy with few material comforts. You love minimalism. You don’t need much, you don’t want much, and are happy with having few material comforts. Not a thing with me, as my autism came with ADHD, so my impulsivity came with special interest projects that… still need completing.Always finishing what you start. Hyperfixation and perseveration is real. This is something that autism shares in common with ADHD, when we’re hyper-productive, the project must get done start to finish, even though you should probably stop and take a break.Scripting conversations in advance. You have scripts that you practice for specific social interactions, or you think about hypothetical social situations and arguments and practice your responses to them.“How can someone so smart be so stupid?”. This isn’t what you think, but what others think of you. With my autism and ADHD I also was intelligent as a kid, and I still am intelligent as an adult, yet, there are so many strange and weird quirks about me, that my loved ones constantly think, “You’re so smart, why is this such an issue for you?” This points to the fact that, despite the positives of autism and ADHD, they really are disabilities, and they come with invisible struggles that no one sees.Hope this helps!EDIT: Two people took objection to me saying that Asperger’s Syndrome is just autism. Now, I’m coming from the DSM-V, because I’m from the United States, and one of the foremost authorities on mental conditions is the American Psychological Association. Here, Asperger’s is just a form of autism, as autism changed to become Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). In fact, there was other labels besides Asperger’s that further clouded the issue and lead to misunderstandings. I meant it quite literally that Asperger’s is just autism, and it’s to reflect that autism isn’t one thing. It was meant to be inclusive, as a lot of support aspies needed, weren’t all too dissimilar from ASD. So rather than have extra labels they just got rid of all those labels, including Asperger’s, PDD-NOS, Kanner Syndrome, and childhood disintegrative disorder (CDD). They realized these were all basically the same thing, so they’re all just Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). So that’s what I meant. I meant it in a very literal way that Asperger’s is just autism. Now, one commenter came at this very respectfully, intelligently, and clearly explained why they identify with the Asperger’s label. I’ve left their comments up for everyone to read, because they offered a unique perspective. Another commenter I deleted and blocked, something I don’t usually do, because he called autistic people the “R-word.” I don’t think I have to belabor the point that that’s offensive, it’s not speaking plainly or frankly, it’s just being an asshole for the sake of being an asshole, and doesn’t exactly encourage free and open discussion. So, I don’t usually block or delete someone’s comments. If you disagree, do what the other commenter did and just explain your point of view without insulting an entire group of people.Originally answered: What are subtle signs of autism and Asperger syndrome?
