question: Is picky eating a sign of autism?
answer: Picky eating can be a sign of autism. Autistic* folks can sometimes be averse to eating foods because of their colour, texture, taste, smell, or any other number of reasons. However, picky eating is also just a sign of being young and unwilling to try new things. If you suspect your child might be autistic because they’re a picky eater, and that’s the only sign you’re noticing, then your child most likely is not autistic. If you’re noticing other signs like a lack of eye contact, repetitive behaviours, echolalia (compulsively repeating what other people say, or noises that they’ve heard), uncontrollable tantrums, or stimming (the act of stimulating themself by flapping their hands, clapping, etc.) then you could talk to your doctor about it. However, picky eating on its own is not something to worry about. Just provide options at meal times and model good eating behaviour by enjoying the things your kid refuses to eat. *I wanted to add this footnote before I get a ton of comments complaining about my language. It used to be that we used person centred language when referring to disabled folks. “A child with autism” or “a person with a disability” has been the mutually agreed upon way to speak about disabled people without upsetting anyone Because you are focussing on the fact that they are a person, rather than focussing on their disability. However, these days we are seeing a shift towards identity centred language because the disabled community have advocated for this. Autistic people do not see themselves as living with a condition or a disease that they are living with, they see their autism as a part of their identity that’s worth celebrating. After all, I don’t tell people I’m “a man with homosexuality” I tell people I’m “a gay man” because “gay” is not something I’m living with, it is just who I am. Autistic adults are pushing more and more for this kind of language in order to alleviate the stigma surrounding autism. They don’t want to be viewed by neurotypical people as being burdened with a condition, they want to be viewed as people who are proud of their identity.

question: What signs of autism can be seen at 12 months of age?
answer: Some Early Signs of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Young Children By 6 months: The child has not learned to smile socially. By 12 months: The child is not pointing, making faces, babbling, or making other meaningful gestures. By 16 months: The child can not communicate with one word. By 24 months: The child has not learned two-word phrases. Poor eye contact is common among children on the autism spectrum. The child might not share interests with others. The child might have an unusually strong attachment to one specific toy or object. The child may not respond to sounds, voices, or their name. If the child experiences any loss of skills at any time. Children on the autism spectrum are less inclined or interested in pretend play (make-believe). If you have any concerns about whether or not your child has autism spectrum disorder, you should contact a pediatrician that specializes in autism spectrum disorder for an evaluation. We provide a wealth of information on autism on our website, AAPC Publishing.

question: Are autistic friends a sign of autism?
answer: Studies have shown that autistic people actually do not struggle with socialisation or communication. Autistic people struggle specifically with doing these things with allistic people. As allistic people also struggle to communicate and socialise with autistic people. While it's obviously not proof of anything, this 'double empathy problem' does mean if you find it easier to make friends with people you find out are autistic, it may indicate you are prone to some traits of autism, (if not affected to the level that it's useful to describe you as autistic) or that you may have some kind of “cousin condition” such as ADHD which tends your mindset towards certain norms If you suspect you have autism for other reasons, I would count it as ‘evidence' towards that theory if you have a large number of autistic friends, if you closest friends are mostly autistic, or if you find friendships with autistic people much faster and easier to establish. If you do not otherwise relate to autism as an experience, I would argue you're most likely just a straightforward, open, honest, and hopefully compassionate person, and autistic people are more likely to try to be your friends because we don't have many people who communicate openly enough to get on well with. Ie it could just be your personality and style of communication makes you “accessible” to autistic people and that leads to them seeking you out. I have friends like this. If you struggle to make friends who are *not* autistic, that would be a clearer indicator you could stand to read up on the symptoms of autism and think about wether they describe you *to the extent they impact your daily life recognisably*. .

question: What would be the signs of autism in a 2 years old?
answer: With two of my kids, speech delay and speech oddity were big. One learned words but did not use them, and quickly forgot them. Mostly, he would stand near what he wanted and scream. The other one spoke in “sentences” that had no actual words. Strangely, the whole family was able to understand him, even though most of the words in the sentence were “dup.” (His speech therapist said it was the oddest speech issue she had heard in 19 years.) Both really started making rapid language progress after enrollment in developmental preschool at age 3. Some other signs: (Bear in mind this is a list of signs I saw in any of my 5 with autism, so the list will be longer than the list for just one.) Favorite activities: building and taking apart. Dismantling evil genius. During nap time he completely dismantled his sister’s bed without tools and took one of the bars from it and broke the bedroom window. He broke through Every. Single. Lock. Even the “tot lock” which is supposed to be foolproof. He found a way out of his crib tent that we installed for his safety. He opened the lock to our cleaning supplies cupboard and poured out all the bleach from our child-safety-locked bottle. Outlet covers? Pfaw. All were removed and destroyed in about an hour. Sensory stuff. Two of them had obsessions with eggs. Specifically with cracking them all over the kitchen floor. They had, of course, busted through the fridge lock with ease. No smiling. Not a single tiny smile until 6 months. Laughing at a year. They did play imaginative games, and young. But they involved things, not people, and mostly blocks and other “building” toys. The mess. Oh, the mess. My daughter honestly did not understand the difference between toys and non toys. The laundry hamper and some metal cooking utensils were robot garb. Boxes were (and still are, at age 12) toys. Heaven help the person who throws out trash. It was her pet crayon! She once brought a plastic grocery bag to school, because it was her new friend. And of course, being hyperactive, the games were very fast, with the paraphernalia tossed wherever and new dishes or tools were her new toys. Difficulty potty training. Serious issues concerning waste products. I will not say more. Once they could talk all five were intensely literal. One, at age 27, knows how to identify and understand non-literal speech but there are still misunderstandings that lead to hurt feelings. The hardest thing is to convince a doctor that there is something going on. Especially if the child is extremely smart. With my son, the doctor didn’t believe he had speech difficulties because he could quote Caillou in response to questions, copying Caillou’s intonation and body language. If your doctor doesn’t see what you’re talking about, insist on a full evaluation. It shows more than a non specialist can identify. With a girl, the signs are often harder to identify, because they manifest in different ways. My daughter was a very early talker, and demanded attention. A lot of it. She wanted friends, and was always very social. But she didn’t have any, because she insisted on telling them the “right” way to play. Another daughter, on the other hand, was antisocial from birth. She hated being held. Hated it so much. She hated physical contact, and nursing was very difficult. I was able to bond with her only because she caught a cold and needed to be held to breathe. I once told my mother my daughter hated me, and she thought I was having sleep deprivation delusions. Now I realize it was touching that she hated, not me. But I was not imagining it. Ok, I could list more, but you get the idea. Sorry if I turned this into a vent. But just remember that no child has “all” the signs, and many times the “sign” is the opposite of the typical sign. Children doing something very late, or doing the same something very, very young.

question: Can someone show signs of autism and/or Asperger’s and not have autism?
answer: Yes. Someone can show some signs of almost any mental diagnosis and still not have it. Health conditions and traits, and especially these of brain and nervous system, are a complicated matter. The current categorization of them (DSM-5) is still far from perfect and many cases aren’t “clear-cut”. One possibility is that someone shows all or almost all kinds of signs of autism, but not strongly enough to be clinically significant - to notably affect/impair their life. Autism is a spectrum from not-at-all-autistic to severely autistic, and such people are close on it to the threshold for diagnosis, but still on the non-autistic side of that threshold. Or, the person is too young or too affected by something else to be reliably evaluated for autism at the time. If such a person is examined by a competent mental health professional, they may be diagnosed with (subclinical) autistic traits, or with nothing. (This is also how it works for most other mental health conditions - a person can also have subclinical borderline personality traits, obsessive-compulsive traits, etc.) Another thing is that there are many other conditions which share some traits with autism and can be mistaken with autism if the evaluation isn’t thorough enough and/or the person doing it doesn’t have enough knowledge. For example, most autistic people have some sensory sensitivities, but if the person doesn’t also have some other symptoms/traits which can’t be explained by that, a more appropriate diagnosis would most likely be sensory processing disorder. Or, the need to fidget due to ADHD can in some cases be confused for the need to stim due to autism. (It all also goes in the other direction, that is autistic people sometimes get misdiagnosed with such other conditions too - it is possible for the same person to have many conditions, but sometimes one more complex condition such as autism would be enough to explain all the behavior.) The exact diagnosis may or may not matter. A person may be harmed by misdiagnosis (or overdiagnosis, or lack of diagnosis) if given inappropriate treatment and/or denied appropriate help. But a person with subclinical autistic traits or a condition with some shared symptoms may still benefit from some kinds of advice, accommodations and treatment for autistic people. What matters is how to best help someone to live as well as possible - how their condition is called is just a tool to get there.

question: Does it mean that when an adult walks on their tip toes that they could have autism? Can it just be by habit?
answer: I’m autistic, but I feel I can actually give you a real answer on this topic, because the symptom of toe-walking, what really causes it, and the problems that are the result of it, are complex, multi-faceted, and as such, a real solution is similarly nuanced. Now, just to be clear, there are neurotypicals that toe-walk, and autistic people that don’t. But, why do so many of us autistic people toe-walk? In short, it’s caused by a misalignment of your posture, which itself is caused by a chronically overactive sympathetic nervous system, which is the nervous system that handles the fight, flight, freeze, and fawn responses. In other words, a chronically stressed out nervous system causes your body to compensate to change your posture in such a way that your center of gravity isn’t over the hips as it should be, but over the balls of your feet. In a proper system, your hips are aligned parallel to the ground. This places your center of gravity over the hips, and thus you feel weight over the middle arch of your foot where over millions of years of evolution, we adapted to do so. This is our natural tendency.This is proper posture. Now people who tend to toe-walk have an anterior pelvic tilt, meaning the hip tilts forward.This posture is bad, and it’s caused by a number of things, most commonly tension in the body, and weirdly enough, most commonly associated with nerve entrapment in the neck. A lot of issues with low back pain can actually be traced here, even if it’s not where you experience your symptoms, but not all back pain is caused by this. Just a fun little fact. Anyhow, with an anterior pelvic tilt, this shifts your upper body forward, which naturally changes your center of gravity from the center of the arches of your feet, to the balls of your feet. Tilting the hip in this manner also creates tension in the back of the legs, which causes the heels to lift off the ground somewhat. This can cause tight calves, tight hamstrings, low back pain, and make other things worse. But with this specific issue, the cause is nerve entrapment in the neck and this makes ischemia, which is restricted blood flow in the extremities, worse. So in this specific case, exercises to strengthen your core may make the issue worse, or help fix some aspects of your posture, but doesn’t address the underlying root cause. “But how can strengthening your core make this issue worse?” Well, with an anterior pelvic tilt, by necessity to maintain that posture, your muscles must always be contracting to hold you upright, and if this is your posture all the time, this leads to bad muscle tone. Not talking about getting ripped and shredded here, but how the muscles feel is important. Bad tone, is classified as spasticity or rigidity, and it’s characterized by an increased resistance to the passive movement of a joint. Bad tone, in so many words is passive tension in the muscle tissues. Healthy skeletal muscles feel tight when they’re contracting, and when not being in use, they should feel relaxed and floppy. If it’s firm or tense at rest, like when you feel knots in your back, that’s rigidity. When you’re just moving and you feel that muscle involuntarily resisting, like a muscle cramp, that’s spasticity. Both are bad tone. Bad tone is evidence of ischemia, nerve entrapment, and facilitation of efferent C-fibers, which are the nerve fibers associated with stress signal pathways in the sympathetic nervous system. In other words, if your back is chronically clenching all the time, how is strengthening your abs going to make it better? Chronic bad tone in the core muscles, which, if you have an anterior pelvic tilt you’ll feel constant tension in your core. Bad tone in the core, since all things are connected to everything in the body can lead to all sorts of things. But ultimately, the underlying problem is a chronically stressed out sympathetic nervous system, and autistic and ADHD people are more predisposed to this problem as a natural consequence of some symptoms of these conditions predisposing us to be sensitive to sensory stimuli, and due to stigmas and ableism about these conditions in our society. For some, they adopt this posture simply because the texture of the ground stresses out their feet, and want as minimal contact with the ground as possible, and walking on the toes is a good solution. As a result, we have a higher likelihood to have a chronically stressed out sympathetic nervous system, causing our body to compensate and change our posture, one of which is tilting the hip forward, putting the center of gravity over the balls of our feet, creating tension in the backs of our legs, which lift up our heels, leading to our backs chronically contracting all the time to hold our bodies upright, leading to the symptom of toe-walking. To address these issues is complex and multi-faceted. Physical therapy can help, but some exercises from some unqualified physical therapists won’t exactly address this issue, as this specific issue is multi-faceted and requires a neuromuscular therapist to address both the posture and underlying neurology, and requires a therapist to reduce the chronic stress that many of us who are neurodivergent are constantly experiencing, for any number of reasons. In short, us being predisposed to be more sensitive people predisposes us to be more chronically stressed, causing our body to compensate, leading to bad posture and toe-walking, and chronic tension in the core can lead to injuries and other medical issues. So where does one begin to start addressing this? Well, I suggest first figuring out your biggest stressors, and try to reduce them as much as you can, no matter how silly or minor they appear to be. If loud noises are stressful for you (as they are for me) then noise-cancelling headphones is a great way to help reduce stress. When you have a good idea of what your stressors are, and have found interventions or accommodations to address them, and you’re still toe-walking, it’s likely you need to talk to a neuromuscular specialist to address it, because there are some long term, chronic injuries caused by walking on your toes all the time, and having an anterior pelvic tilt. Plus, exercises and physical activity in general has actually been shown to be extremely helpful for us autistic and ADHD people, so physical therapy also isn’t out of the question, just do your homework and gauge how you feel in your physical therapy appointments. If you’re still in pain, or the exercises cause you a lot of pain, let them know, and see if they can address it properly. My physical therapist was fantastic, and did a combination of massage therapy, exercises, and electro-muscular stimulation therapy to help with nerve entrapment caused by a pulled muscle in my back that led to a bulging disc. In other words, to get the care you need, you have to stand up for yourself and be an advocate for yourself. You know yourself better than anyone else, study up, do your homework, and then choose the best therapy that works for your situation and aligns with your values. That’s being an advocate. Hope this helps!Originally answered: Does it mean that when an adult walks on their tip toes that they could have autism? Can it just be by habit?
comment_answer: That is a superb response, as far as I can tell. I don't understand why strengthening core is dismissed so readily, since I thought it relieved the spine and feet from some of the weight bearing…ie when engaging core muscles..but still. Was a good read!

question: What are some early signs of autism in toddlers?
answer: Baby may seem confused at times and cry when there doesn't seem to be anything wrong. Baby may not use as much eye contact as he should. Baby might get upset at unusual things: seeing a dog, hearing a song, the tone of someone's voice, a certain sound. Baby's facial expressions might seem unusual and when you look back at photos, you'll notice it more. You'll notice this more if you have experience with other babies or have had other children. Baby may be unusually undemanding at times (such as during the night and make noises rather than cry) but become demanding and unsettled during other parts of the day, (ie crying after he's been fed, changed and cuddled). Sometimes he just won't settle. As he grows there may be increasing differences in baby compared to his peers, ie: he might be slightly delayed in some or all of his milestones. He may not go past the chewing and banging toys stage without a lot of help. He may play in the same way with toys over and over - especially favourite toys. He may be fixed on certain things such as cars. He may be prone to temper outbursts over unlikely issues such as you buying a new sofa or moving his cot. He may seem confused when others outside his immediate family visit or when people make a fuss over him. He may do funny little movements with his hands, get excited and make sounds either for no reason or by seeing something although this usually develops as they grow. Some babies do not develop speech although they might use sounds. Others may have overall speech and language development delays. They may be slower to speak their first speech sounds (Dada, baba etc) and pick up words more slowly. These are all mostly things I noticed with my son who has ASD and some of these points may be exclusive to his development and not another child who goes on to have ASD as they are all different.

question: Is parroting a sign of autism?
answer: It can be; as many other answers mention, it is called “echolalia” in humans. An autistic person using this is likely trying to communicate, using a brain that partly works differently from allistics’ where words are concerned. I notice I still often have to do this word repetition internally; I review the spoken words and then get the meaning, during conversations. (Unfortunately the speaker may have said a bunch more stuff and I get behind.) It’s part of why I’m a little slower than some in following spoken language, and don’t do as well with lots of people gabbing at once, I suspect. I think maybe I started out doing more “obvious” echolalia, then developed a more complex way to use my slightly atypical verbal brain parts, but no one can tell me what I did as a young kid— my folks are gone now. But to the OP — please don’t assume development has to follow the “normal” track to be valid and functional for a person. Different developmental trajectories can often also end up with quite strong abilities as time goes on, though maybe not identical in strength everywhere. Folks with this verbal tendency might have other abilities that surpass the “average” in many cases. In my case, I’m an extremely fast reader; I used that to catch up in academic classes when in school, college, and university, — undiagnosed, and missing a lot of spoken lecture content. (I was only diagnosed 2 years ago and am in my 50s; this stuff only started being known recently, esp. for females.) I can still take in written info a lot faster than many people I know; useful for lots of stuff. The pluses that autistics can often bring to our societies are not studied nearly so well as the challenges we can have… not that that should determine whether different folks are treated well!

question: Is body rocking always a sign of autism?
answer: My opinion is not always. Frequently rocking back and forth isn’t in itself a sure sign of autism. Rocking is one of several repetitive behaviors that serve the purpose of soothing or pacifying us and helping with stress. That’s true for those on or off the Spectrum. From foot bouncing to finger strumming to twirling strands of hair, these repetitive motions help us pass the time, enjoy a moment, or deal with momentary anxiety. But the sudden onset of rocking back and forth is reserved for conditions when one is under extreme stress. It is common to see someone rocking upon receiving terrible news or having witnessed an horrific event. This behavior is seen in both children and adults. The person zones out, oblivious to their surroundings, and rocks back and forth for maybe several minutes. David, Givens, an author and researcher, points out in his Nonverbal Dictionary that the rocking action is similar to that of a mother rocking her baby to sleep. According to Givens, rocking “stimulates the vestibular senses and is therefore soothing” in a very primitive, but effective way. I rock myself and it is usually when I’m in meltdown country. It is true that rocking is one type of repetitive movement that can be seen in autism, but more than abnormal movement is required for an actual diagnosis. However, it is a recognizable clue that something is wrong and should prompt a discussion with a doctor.

question: What are subtle signs of autism and Asperger syndrome?
answer: Answering this from personal experience, these are my telltale signs: • Staring - being able to maintain eye contact but not blinking very often/staring through someone • Bad mental health - issues with anxiety/depression etc with no particular cause/unrelated to trauma • Freezing while being hugged/not enjoying being touched (mainly noticeable during childhood) • Disinterest in most school subjects and not wanting to revise, even when anxious about failing • Unusual interests for your gender (for example girls liking dinosaurs, football/ ‘manly sports’, gaming, cars/planes etc) • Not having FMO and being satisfied staying at home for long periods of time • Being interested in fantasy series such as Harry Potter, the Hobbit etc • Requiring alone time to feel happy and energised again • Rambling about special interests to family when you know they aren’t interested • Lack of imagination when interpreting a story - you take it at face value and don’t imagine backstories etc • Having interests in other cultures and languages (for example liking kpop/music in different languages) • Fearing teachers and school punishments, not engaging in class and giving short yet respectful answers when picked on • Not jumping at loud sounds or jump-scares in games or movies

question: Is being scared of everything a sign of autism?
answer: Not necessarily. Just because you are scared of everything doesn’t imply you have autism. According to Wikipedia, “Autism is a developmental disorder characterized by difficulties with social interaction and communication, and by restricted and repetitive behavior.” In other words, you don’t know when and how to behave, act and react when in certain situations and when around certain people. One having autism would have trouble speaking, is highly sensitive to certain scenarios like crowds, repetition of “weird” actions, etc. Autism is in another level than just being afraid of everything. A person who has suffered extreme trauma due to some unfortunate event would be scared of, well, most of everything, if not everything. That’s because they are scared that they will have to go through that pain again and they don’t want that to happen and they want to avoid that situation at all costs. Hope this helps…

question: My 7.5 month old daughter baby doesn't maintain eye contact. Is this a sign of autism?
answer: I know this is an old topic but I just wanted to reassure anyone that was feeling the same as me - as, despite what you may read elsewhere - it is perfectly possible for your baby to have poor eye contact in their first year and not have autism or other developmental issues. My son had poor eye contact and little engagement with us in his first 9 or so months of life, and I was extremely worried about him, and convinced he had autism. I made myself sick with anxiety, particularly when he was between 4 to 9 months old. However, he is now a very engaged, loving, chatty 2 year old who makes better eye contact than he did and loves making us laugh. He changed a huge amount between about 10 and 18 months. So I just want to reassure anyone that is worried about anything similar that it may be nothing - there really is a reason why most doctors won’t even think about diagnosing autism until 18 months at the very earliest: babies can change so much. And if you are feeling really anxious, I found it really helped me to speak to someone generally about how to best cope with the anxiety / fear of the unknown. That will help you to get through it to the point your child is old enough to know for sure (but remember that it’s perfectly possible for your child not to have ASD or any other developmental disorder at all - poorer eye contact and engagement in their first year may well not signify anything).

question: Is regression a sign of autism?
answer: Regression occurs in some cases of autism, but not others. Regression has nothing to do with vaccines. Regression has nothing to do with burnout, depression or meltdowns. Regression is not when a person with mild autism feels like staying in his room because he’s been bullied or mistreated. It’s not about getting bad grades in school because a person doesn’t feel like studying or just doesn't see the point of training for a career he doesn't want. Regressive autism is what some authors have called Childhood Disintegrative Disorder. Evidently they didn’t like the name of the disorder. It used to be in the category of Pervasive Developmental Disorders with Autism and Rett Syndrome. At some point, there was enough evidence of its similarity and then shared genetics and brain structure to autism, that it was subsumed under the diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder. Regression is a term that used to be used in psychology to refer to almost any behavioral problem in which a person behaved in an odd way. And, very strangely, some journalists have recently insisted ‘regression’ is VERY common in autism, even universal. Any difficulty, any time a person has trouble socializing, they call regression. They can only argue this by insisting on the older and unrelated definition of regression, or calling almost any difficulty ‘regression.’. Which they went right ahead and did! Have authors encouraged such weird stuff by describing symptoms of these disirders in too ‘politically correct,’ or sanitized, euphemised fashion? Has there been too much ‘vanilla-izing’ put into the descriptions of what these words mean? Or is this all just more of the internet denizen’s tendency to use words to mean whatever they feel like saying it means? I’m not sure, but many people are really not ‘getting what words like reggression and many other words mean. Part of the problem the recent journalists have is this onset of obvious autism symptoms at around 1 1/2. This is a lot about why people claim vaccines or some ingredient of vaccines cause autism(weeeelllll, that and the money involved…quack causes and cures are big, big money). They just can't understand what’s actually happening. All they need to do is read about it. Human brains go through much, even most of their development prior to birth, but there’s also a big spurt of development and change at 1 1/2. The symptoms of autism start when they do because that's how the brain develops. You could say the sutism symptoms are ‘genetically programmed’ to start at a specific time. And speaking in terms of the more relevant definition of regression, that's not actually regression so much as just change. In autism, regression means something very different than it does in older schools of psychology. In autism, regression is the loss of basic skills and behaviors which are related to very early childhood neurological, cognitive and intellectual development. Regression is when a person(usually a very Young child) loses basic, simple skills. For example, a 2 year old who has been speaking a few words, completely stops speaking or learning to speak entirely. A 2 1/2 year old who was potty trained suddenly is not. Regression usually is extreme and alarms parents greatly. It is very real and very neurological. And yes, very few people with mild autism show regression, either when symptoms start or even later. Unfortunately, some people with severe autism show what looks like regression in the teen or adult years. This could herald a completely different problem: the onset of severe mental illness. So for example, a 16 year old with severe autism has steadily been expanding his vocabulary since he began speaking at 11. He’s finally out of diapers, and he seems quite happy much of the time, and has his favorite people he loves to be with. He’s eating a variety of foods and getting much better nutrition, and he’s able to dress himself. Insidiously, this all gradually changes. He’s screaming in terror when he’s in the car. He’s back in the diapers. He’s hitting familiar people and screaming in abject terror when he sees unfamiliar people. He can't tolerate any change of routine at all. There are a number of different reasons he could be so upset - physical pain due to dental pain or other physical illness. Abuse. Neglect. Unfortunately, one other possibility is severe mental illness.

question: How do I recognize the signs of autism in a child?
answer: Method 1 of 4:Recognizing Social Differences 1. Interact with your baby.A typical infant is a social creature by nature and loves to make eye contact. An autistic infant may appear like they are not interacting with parents, or may look "inattentive" to non-autistic parents. Make eye contact. A typically developing baby can return eye contact by six to eight weeks of age. An autistic child may not look at you, or may avoid looking at your eyes. Smile at your baby. A non-autistic baby can smile and offer warm and happy expressions by six weeks of age or earlier. An autistic baby may not smile, even to a parent. Make faces at your baby. See if they mimic you. An autistic child may not participate in playing copycat. 2. Call your baby’s name.A typical baby will respond to it by nine months of age. Typically developing babies will be able to call you Mama or Dada in return by 12 months of age. 3. Play with your toddler.By ages two to three, a typical child will be very interested in playing games with you and others. An autistic toddler may appear disconnected from the world, or deep in thought. A non-autistic toddler will be involving you in their world by pointing, showing, reaching, or waving by 12 months of age. A typical child engages in parallel play until they are about three years old. When your toddler engages in parallel play, this means they play alongside other children and enjoy their company but do not necessarily engage in cooperative play. Don’t confuse parallel play with an autistic child not being socially engaged. 4. Examine differences of opinion.By around age five, a typical child can understand that you have a different opinion about things. An autistic child tends to have great difficulty in understanding that others have different points of view, thoughts, and feelings than their own. They often appear to lack empathy for others. If your child loves strawberry ice cream, tell your child that chocolate ice cream is your favourite, and see if they argue or get upset that you do not share the same opinion as them. Many autistic people understand this better in theory than in praxis. An autistic girl might understand that you like the color blue, but have no idea that it would upset you if she wandered off to check out the balloons across the street. An autistic child may experience meltdowns, or outbursts of extreme emotion that often resemble a temper tantrum. However, these are not voluntary and are extremely upsetting to the child. An autistic child experiences many challenges, and may attempt to "bottle up" emotions to please caregivers. Emotions may spiral out of control, and the child can become so frustrated that they engage in self-injury, such as banging their head against a wall or biting themselves. Autistic children may experience more pain due to sensory issues, mistreatment, and other problems. They may lash out more often in self-defense. Method 2 of 4:Watching for Communication Difficulties Listen for increasing sounds and babbling as they grow. Children usually become fully verbal by 16 to 24 months of age. A typical baby will be able to share sounds back-and-forth with you like sharing a conversation by nine months of age. An autistic baby may not be verbal at all or may have been verbal but then lost the skill. A typical child will be babbling by about 12 months of age. 2. Have a conversation.Talk together about your child’s favourite toy and listen to their sentence structure and conversation skills. Typically developing children will have many words by 16 months of age, can create their own meaningful, two-word phrases by 24 months of age, and have coherent sentences by age five. An autistic child tends to misplace words in sentence structure or simply repeat others’ phrases or sentences, called parroting or echolalia. They might mix up pronouns, saying "Do you want pancakes?" when they are trying to say that they want pancakes. Some autistic children pass over the "kid-speak" phase and have superior language skills. They may learn to speak early, and/or grow large vocabularies. They may converse differently than their peers do. 3. Try some expressions.Determine if your child takes phrases literally. An autistic child tends to misinterpret body language, tone of voice, and expressions. If you have a moment of sarcastic frustration and claim, "How wonderful!" when you find your autistic child has used his red marker all over the living room walls, they may think you literally mean their art is wonderful. 4. Check their facial expressions, tone of voice, and body language.Method 3 of 4:Identifying Repetitive Behaviours While all kids enjoy repetitive play to some degree, autistic children will exhibit strong repetitive behaviours such as rocking, hand-flapping, rearranging objects, or repeating sounds over and over again, called echolalia. These can be essential for self-calming and relaxation. All children partake in some verbal mimicry until the age of three. An autistic child may do this more often, and beyond the age of three Some repetitive behaviours are called self-stimulation or "stimming," meaning that they stimulate the child’s senses. An example of this is if your son wiggles his fingers in front of his eyes to stimulate his vision and amuse himself. Another example of stimming happens when the child hums to the exact or near-exact pitch of an external noise (also known as auditory stimulus or stimuli) of something that buzzes or hums that the child can hear, like a bumble bee, a lawn mower, a chainsaw, or even a vibrating cell phone. 2. Notice how your child plays.Autistic children may not engage in visible imaginative play, preferring to organize objects (e.g. organizing toys or building a city for their dolls instead of playing house). The imagination is occurring inside their head. Try breaking the pattern: rearranging the dolls they are lining up or passing in front of them while they are trying to walk in a circle. An autistic child will be noticeably bothered by you interfering. Autistic children may be able to engage in imaginative play with another child, especially if that child takes the lead; however, these children will usually not do it on their own. 3. Recognize special interests and favorite objects.Intense and unusual obsessions with everyday household objects (such as a broom or string) or, later, facts, may be a sign of autism. An autistic child may develop a special interest about a topic, and gain an extraordinary depth of knowledge. Examples include cats, baseball statistics, The Wizard of Oz, logic puzzles, and checkers. A child may "light up" or open up when asked about these subjects. A child may have one special interest at a time, or a few. They can change as the child learns and grows. 4. Notice a need for routine.Many autistic children have a strong need for routines and consistency, and may show exaggerated reactions or protests to changes in routines. For instance, if you always walk with your child to school taking the same route, try changing it up. An autistic child may become very resistant and upset by this change of routine. Routines may have to do with the order of daily tasks, but they may also be verbal (such as asking the same questions repeatedly), have to do with food (only eating foods of a certain color), clothing (only wearing clothes of a specific fabric or color), the location of furniture, and so on. Routines can be very comforting for an autistic person. The world can seem unpredictable, confusing, and scary to this person, and a routine can give them some sense of control and stability. 5. Look for heightened and diminished sensitivity to sensations.If your child shows unusual discomfort to light, textures, sounds, tastes, or temperatures, talk to your doctor. Autistic children may "overreact" to new sounds (e.g. a sudden loud noise or a vacuum cleaner), textures (e.g. an itchy sweater or sock), et cetera. This is because the particular sense is magnified, so it causes real discomfort or pain. Method 4 of 4:Assessing Autism Across the Ages 1. Know when autism may be noticed.Some symptoms are clear around two to three years of age. Beyond that, a child may be diagnosed at any age, especially during a transition (e.g. going to high school or moving house) or other stressful periods. Excessive life demands may cause an autistic person to "regress" in order to cope, causing concerned loved ones to seek a diagnosis. In some children, signs may be noticed in the first one to two years of life. Some are not diagnosed until college, when their developmental differences become especially obvious. 2. Know your childhood milestones.With some variation, most children meet developmental milestones following a specific pattern. Autistic children may meet these milestones later. Some may be precocious, and their parents may consider them a struggling or introverted gifted child. By age three, children are often able to walk stairs, work with simple dexterity toys, and play make-believe. By age four, a child can retell their favourite stories, scribble, and follow simple directions. By age five, a child can generally draw pictures, talk about their day, wash their hands, and focus on a task. Older autistic children and teens may exhibit strict adherence to patterns and rituals, engage passionately in special interests, enjoy things that are not typical of their age group, avoid eye contact, and be highly sensitive to touch. 3. Watch for loss of skills.Speak to your family doctor if you have concerns at any point in your child’s development. Do not delay if your child experiences a loss of speech, self-care skills, or social skills at any age. Most skills that are lost are still "there" and can be regained.

question: Can a child have signs of autism and not be autistic?
answer: Possibly, but it depends how many autism traits/symptoms you’re talking about. The thing is with autism, it’s a rather complex neurological condition, and really, there’s no single symptom that’s unique to autism. Every individual autistic symptom can also be a symptom of at least one other condition - and not just developmental disorders either. These can include anxiety disorders, mental illnesses - depression, bipolar disorder - personality disorders - especially avoidant personality disorder, dependent personality disorder and borderline personality disorder. It’s only when you put all the different aspects of ASD together - social difficulties, intense emotions, alexithymia, behavioural differences, etc. that you have ASD. So, it is possible for someone to have some autistic traits, but not the condition itself. But here’s how a diagnostician/psychiatrist/psychologist would determine whether someone has ASD or not: It can be argued that everyone - including neurotypicals [non-autistic people] has one or two symptoms of ASD. But people with ASD have a whole load of symptoms that fit the criteria for ASD. I’ve gone into this in more detail in other answers, but basically, it’s one or two, vs a lot. If someone has a lot of ASD characteristics, the chances are they’re autistic. If it’s just one or two, or they’re also displaying symptoms that might better fit an alternate diagnosis, i.e. ADHD, then it might not be ASD. And another big question is how are the x, y, z symptoms a person has impacting their life? If it’s impacting their life quite a lot, then ASD is likely. If the symptoms a person has isn’t impacting their life much, then ASD might not be likely.

question: Are there any physical signs of autism?
answer: Unveiling the Unseen: 10 Lesser-Known Physical Signs of Autism in Girls Introduction: Hello, everyone! Welcome back to The Aspie World. This could include actions like stimming (rocking, hand flapping, etc.), demonstrating a need for self-stimulation or comfort. 5. **Difficulty with Transitions:** Transitioning between environments can be particularly challenging for girls with autism. Changes from school to home or vice versa may evoke anxiety, leading to avoidance behaviors like pretending to be sick.6. **Eating Disorders:** Some autistic girls may exhibit eating disorders, experiencing challenges with food textures or succumbing to social and peer pressure surrounding food. Discomfort while walking on certain surfaces could be a factor. 10. **Hypertonia:** Hypertonia, characterized by low muscle density or tone, is a physical sign of autism in girls. This may affect their fine motor skills and lead to difficulties in holding small objects. Some might even receive a diagnosis of hypermobility. question: What are the signs of autism in adult women?
answer: Adult women and men may experience autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in different ways, and among women, ASD is frequently misdiagnosed or not recognised at all. Although the symptoms and indicators of autism in adult women might differ, the following traits and behaviours are frequently seen and maybe warning signals: Social difficulties: Women with autism may have trouble forming and maintaining friendships, interpreting social signs, and initiating or maintaining discussions. They could have social anxiety or have trouble comprehending unspoken social norms and expectations. Sensitivity to sensory stimuli: Many autistic women have heightened sensitivity to these stimuli. They could be more sensitive to specific textures, loud noises, strong odours, or bright lights. In some circumstances, this sensitivity may cause pain or distress. Similar to autistic males, autistic women may exhibit extreme interests in particular areas or themes. They could devote a lot of time to learning, researching, or partaking in pursuits connected to their particular interests. Challenges with routine and change: Women with autism may encounter difficulties with sudden occurrences or changes in routine. They can prefer a regimented, predictable environment and react negatively to changes in routine. Women with autism spectrum disorders may have trouble expressing and comprehending their feelings. They may struggle to recognise their own emotions as well as the emotions of others. This may make it difficult to establish and sustain connections. Using coping methods, such as "masking" or "camouflaging," many adult women with autism learn to blend in with their surroundings and fit in socially. To look more neurotypical, they could monitor and mimic the social signs and behaviours of others. This masking may be draining and have negative effects on one's mental and self-identity. Executive function challenges: Planning, organising, time management, and job prioritisation are just a few of the abilities needed for executive function. These executive function abilities may be difficult for women with autism, which presents difficulties in day-to-day tasks. It's crucial to remember that these symptoms and indicators do not prove that a person has autism. It is advised to obtain a professional examination from a licenced healthcare practitioner or expert with experience in identifying and assisting people with autism if you believe that you or someone you know may be on the autistic spectrum.

question: Are not following directions or focusing signs of autism?
answer: First I’ll give a short answer, although I’m not sure it’ll help too much! The answer is “sometimes, but not always”. As for focus, people (and kids) with autism tend to have either very strong focus, or be scattered. It’s not uncommon to have ADHD as well as ASD (I have both) so if you are concerned about someone (such as a child) having an ASD because they lack focus and/or don’t follow directions, my personal suggestion is to get an evaluation for ADD/ADHD first. Being on the autism spectrum has a whole host of other symptoms, so these two aren’t nearly enough to adequately screen for ASD. However, here is a screening tool you can access for free online. While those two things don’t mean someone has autism, someone with autism may have problems in those areas, yes. I actually wrote a kids’ book called A Little Learning Book About Following Directions (here is the bundled version) because teachers do have problems with students (including those with ASD) following directions in class. But, as one other person noted, the reason someone on the spectrum doesn’t follow directions is often different than for NT’s. There are many reasons a child (or adult) might not follow directions or lack skills focusing. Some have been mentioned, such as being distracted by a lot of activity, but another reason that spectrum individuals might not follow directions is if the directions don’t make sense to us. Because of the way our brains work, we easily think “out of the box”. For this reason, we might be inclined to improve upon the instructions. For instance, if someone is working in a clerical role (which is usually a horrible role for someone on the spectrum) and is instructed to complete a filing process in a way that seems to the person with autism to be more work than another way, it’s pretty likely that person will do it his/her way. If a teacher tells a student “you need to sit down”, a student with autism may reason to him or herself no, I need to stand up, because I want to get her attention. This is often seen as being problematic, but when people understand why the person modifies the directions, it’s easier to address that at the beginning. (A simple “If you have ideas on a better way to do it, let me know. For now, this is the way it needs to be done, because (whatever reason).” This is why, incidentally, people with autism may not follow directions but they do obey rules. A rule is arbitrary, and “because the rule exists” IS the reason to obey it. People with autism can be very focused on whatever they are doing. (Which makes them excellent employees, when in the right role!) Being focused to the point of “appearing to be deaf” can be a sign of autism. Note that this is not the same as ignoring someone. Not following directions and a lack of focus can be traits seen in someone with autism, but when you consider the bigger picture, there are other traits that are more “spectrumy” than either of these two. Good luck!

question: Is not listening a sign of autism?
answer: It can be a sign of a lot of things; ADHD and narcissism come to mind. Autism too, but less than the others, and for some reasons specific to autism. With ASD, it could be were so wound up with our obsessive thinking and hyper focus, that we failed to notice what else is going on. Or, it could be we are overwhelmed by stimuli coming at us, and feel a need to tune them out to keep from melting down or abruptly leaving the scene. This would probably be the most likely cause of an autistic person not listening. If this happens, we can say, “One thing at a time, please.” Or “Would you slow down a bit?” In other cases, we would have had painful experiences in the past, that the conversation reminded us of, so we would defensively tune out the other person. We might not know they were talking to us, because we failed to pick up the cues that would tell us this. Autistic people can miss social signaling cues that would be second nature to a normotypical person. What would less likely be true of the autistic person, is that we would tune them out to disparage or bully them. If we found ourselves doing that, we’d likely correct ourselves. OTOH, an ADHD person would fail to listen because their attention hops from one thing to another. Once they control their nerves and settle down, they would listen. Sometimes medication can assist them in this. A narcissist fails to listen to you because what (s)he says is so much more important than what you have to say (according to the narcissist). Of course, the non-listener might just be a normotypical arrogant bully. If an autistic person doesn’t listen, you’d have to consider autism-specific reasons for it, so as not to confuse their non-listening with other causes of non-listening. Does that help?

question: Why do people with autism commonly walk on their toes?
answer: Weak proprioception. Proprioceptors are your sense of body spatial awareness (knowing where your body is in space). Along with the traditional 5 senses everyone learns about: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, there are other senses including balance and acceleration, temperature, proprioception, etc. How Does Proprioception Work?Muscle spindles, the proprioceptors in the muscle, are long proteins that lay parallel to muscle fibers. Proprioception relies on the relationship between the body’s central nervous system and certain soft tissues, including muscles, tendons, and ligaments. Within these tissues are sensory organs called proprioceptors. Sensory nerve endings wrap around the proprioceptors to send information to the nervous system. The proprioceptors can sense when tissues are stretched or experience tension and pressure. For example, the proprioceptors in muscles are called muscle spindles. Muscle spindles are long proteins encapsulated in sheaths that lay parallel to muscle fibers. They work as follows:When a muscle is extended, muscle fibers are elongated and the coils of the muscle spindles are stretched. (Conversely, a contracted muscle causes muscle fibers and muscle spindles to shorten.)Nerve fibers in the muscle transmit information about the degree and rate at which the muscle spindle is stretched.The information is delivered to the nervous system, and a signal to contract or relax is sent to the muscle.The desired action is performed.How proprioception works in the muscle. The entire process takes less than a millisecond and, in some cases, it happens so quickly that it is referred to as a “reflex.” This feedback loop works continually; even when a person is sleeping the brain maintains some level of sensory input. This continual feedback loop is critical to everyone, especially athletes. For example, a runner can seamlessly transition from soft grass to hard concrete and back again, making unconscious, minor adjustments to stay upright and maintain balance. The runner does not have to think about changing leg and feet movements to accommodate the change in terrain. The proprioceptors in tendons are called Golgi Tendon Organs (GTOs), and they work similarly to muscle spindles. In ligaments, there is a neural feedback with our muscles that is still being studied and clearly defined by researchers. However, it is been understood that impaired/torn ligaments produce deficits in proprioceptive abilities. While you may be tiptoeing to maintain tension in the muscle to trigger a reflex, I believe your body is naturally substituting other senses from the vestibular (inner ear balance) and ocular-motor systems to navigate motion and position. In comparison, most birds cannot move their eyes, instead they adjust muscles in their necks to keep their steady gaze, for example: This Kestrel's Head Stabilization Skills Has To Be Seen To Be Believed. Tiptoeing is your brain and body compensating for a weakness with another system.

question: Are there any signs of autism that can only be detected by another autistic person?
answer: It helps to have a comprehensive understanding of the wide variety of autistic traits and how they can manifest in people differently, so that you know what you’re looking for explicitly and subconsciously. Autistic people often report a felt sense of resonance and ease of communication when talking to someone else who is also autistic or an ADHDer, which is why neurodivergent people tend to have neurodivergent friends and partners. This is the case regardless of whether someone knows what their neurotype is, and if someone doesn’t know they or the person they are talking with are autistic/ADHD, they may simply perceive this as rapport, without attributing it to neurotype. The combination of felt sense and explicit knowledge of neurodivergence enables ND people to identify each other as ND.

question: Is repeating words a sign of autism?
answer: It is important to know if this you mean in the context of a conversation, and what age the person is. 'Echolalia' is one of the traits that you look for when trying to find out if a person is autistic. So yes. If repeating words is the only habit in a person that does not show other behaviour that can indicate this person is autistic, probably not. Repeating some words or the question a person asked you in a conversation is a common way of gaining time to overthink your answer or make sure if you have understood right. Tricky: this technique can of course be used by autistic people as well, especially if the question involves for instance a phrase like 'how are you feeling (about) '. If a person seems to repeat a word ( or sound) without the intent of communicating it can be. We can become very fascinated by sounds and words. Repeating sounds and words is a normal phase in learning speech in children. it can be a sign of the different way the brain is developing in a child when the repeating does not evolve into speaking sentences. If the person is repeating words in a way that seems out of context and uncontrolled it can also be a sign of Tourette's.

question: Is nail biting a sign of autism?
answer: It can be sometimes, but not always as a rule. Anyone can have a nail biting habit, it’s not something exclusive to autism, but does seem to be exclusive to people with anxiety problems, which many people on the spectrum struggle with… so, I think the thing you can really say is that people with autism have a higher statistical chance of being a nail biter, but not an actual quality you can use as a diagnosis standard… unless you are diagnosing ANXIETY… in that case I think you can count it as a sign of anxiety for sure. I’m on the spectrum and chew my nails to an extreme. The therapist I see treats mostly people on she spectrum and she says most of her clients are nail biters as well. But on the other hand my son is also on the spectrum and does NOT bite his nails… he has well controlled anxiety though as I’ve home schooled him and kept him in a stresss free, trigger free environment most his life. For people on the spectrum I think nail biting is a form of stimming. Stimming is just a repetitive thing someone does in order to help them emotionally self regulate… and since nail biting is a “nervous habit” and done in order to sooth oneself it counts as one form of stimming, at least as far as I’m concerned.

question: Is moving your lips while reading a sign of autism?
answer: No. I would say it’s actually a sign of reading. I read out loud to myself to slow my reading down sometimes, but if I’m reading silently, then why would I move my lips and slow myself down? Forming each word as you read does slow your reading, and, if you’re short on books, that can be a good thing, but generally I’ve found that people who are enjoying a book move through it fairly quickly, without reading aloud or moving their lips while they read. The only people I’ve ever seen doing that are children whilst they’re learning to read. However, just because I haven’t seen adults doing it, doesn’t mean it doesn’t happen… but I have spent a great deal of my life surrounded by people with Autism and none of them have this particular behaviour.

question: What are some probable signs of autism in 9 months old babies?
answer: Ok, this is from a parent of preemie autistic twins. Autism is very difficult to diagnose before the 18 month mark. My twins were diagnosed with pervasive development disorder (PDD-NOS) at 14 months. They were officially diagnosed with autism after that, twice as they got older. There are the usual milestones that babies hit. The reason autism isn’t usually diagnosed so young is that the brain and body are both developing. Lack of eye contact could be poorly developed motor skills (yes, in the eyes), lack of social recognition, or some condition that prevents them focusing on people. At this age there are a variety of things that could be wrong. I would caution first time parents not to over react if their baby hasn’t hit milestones on time. Each kid is unique. Second piece of advice, if you trust your pediatrician, bring up your concerns with them. If you have a strong family history of anything, bring it with you. Keep notes on whatever it is that is causing your concern. Also, eating, sleeping and pooping notes can be helpful. Some allergies can effect babies early on. Now, having said all that, I will say this- odds are good that the baby is fine. So take a deep breathe and chill. My family has a history of issues. At the same time my twins were diagnosed, my oldest was also diagnosed at age 8. My brother and I also fit some of the parameters of Aspergers. We are the odd ones out. Statistically we are outliers and very unusual.

question: Are autistic friends a sign of autism?
answer: There is something to be said about the quality of one’s connection to autistic friends. I am autistic and, like many autists who have responded here, have both autistic and non-autistic friends. I could even say quantitatively that I have more non-autistic friends — probably by nature of there being more non-autistic people around. Notwithstanding, every time someone has appeared in my life who I can especially relate to, that person has turned out to be autistic, or at least neurodivergent. It hasn’t mattered if I have had lots of time with them or only heard them briefly from across the room. It hasn’t mattered how old they are, or if they are someone I meet socially or through work. It’s the magic and kinship that comes with the interaction. It’s the experience of coming away renewed and wishing to spend more time in their presence, rather than feeling drained. Even the non-autistic people to whom I am closest, I am almost certain, have autistic traits. I think doctors and psychologists should ask about the qualities in the people someone feels they can best relate to, if they are seeking to diagnosis autism. Not “Are your closest friends autistic?” but, “Tell me about the people you relate to the most.” It may be useful to know. Thank you for asking this question. I was happy to see and answer it!

question: Is staring into space a sign of autism?
answer: Autism is commonly characterized by certain repetitive behaviors and difficulties with social interaction and communication. According to the American Psychological Association the symptoms of autism include-Failure to engage in typical babbling or pointing in infancy.Failure to make eye contact beginning in infancy.Failure to respond to one’s own name.Loss of previously acquired language or social skills, usually during the second year of life.Unusual responses to sensory input.Unusual movements such as rocking, twirling or flapping arms.Difficulty playing with or interacting with peers.Difficulty talking about feelings.Difficulty understanding tone of voice, body language and gestures.Obsessive interest in a particular topic.Difficulty breaking from routineSo along with staring into space if the person exhibits any of the symptoms mentioned above then yes, they might be autistic but ‘staring into space’ alone is not a sign of autism. A person without autism might also stare into space.

question: Is pointing a sign of autism?
answer: “Is pointing a sign of autism?” Not in and of itself, no. But there are two possible reasons why an autistic person would point.Issues with speech. If a person cannot speak or has difficulty finding the right words, they will tend to use gestures to communicate. Autistic people who are nonverbal or who occasionally go nonverbal/semi-verbal will usually learn to use ASL (or their nation's equivalent sign language). In Deaf communities, it's perfectly acceptable to point. I won't explain why because I haven't learned ASL or about Deaf culture in the U.S. One reason could simply be that sign languages use gestures to convey ideas—and pointing is a gesture.Difficulty in learning social rules. Society is governed by rules which children learn from instruction by elders, and by watching and interacting with peers. It's more difficult for autistic people to learn social rules because we don't notice them as easily. It takes much more intentional effort on our part to learn which rule applies in a situation—but first, we have to realize that that situation even has a rule, or that we are breaking that rule. Also, even when we do become aware of a social rule, we are generally less likely to follow it if it doesn't make sense. Why can't I point? It's rude. Why is it rude? Because we've been told it is. Well, why were we told pointing is rude? Because it is. See? No logical reason for this rule. Some Autistic people find it extremely difficult to take such rules seriously.

question: Can temper tantrums be a sign of autism?

This is often confused with a behavior that some autistic children can have when they pass the body/mind limits on stress and their ability to cope with this stress becomes a behavior of neurological reaction - a subconscious reaction, and not a conscious behavior. They are often in a fight/flight reaction from a survival instinct. Its like jumping when there is a very loud and unexpected noise - You don’t think first you just react. This is how far their neurological system has been over stressed. What these kids need is to be in a place of no stress where they can let their mind/body find balance again so they can cope. There is no similarity between the two… Not that a NT child cannot be pushed to the same limits but they may not behave the same or recuperate the same either.

question: What would be the early symptoms of autism in an 8 year old kid?
answer: The word autism is derived from the Greek word autos which means self i.e. the difficulty of the person to relate to others or to understand the social or environmental cues. Symptoms of autism usually appear before the age of 3 and usually continues throughout the person's life. The signs or symptoms of autism can be broadly discussed under three headings -Social skills - Usually infants are interested in other people and their surrounding. They would response to other people by looking at them, use simple gestures such as social smile, clapping and waving bye. But a child with autism will have little in the people around him or her and will have difficulty in reciprocity. They will difficulty in initiating or maintaining social interaction with others. They will have difficulty in adequately responding to social or environmental cues. Mostly children with autism will like to remain aloof or engage in isolated play. They have difficulty in showing or talking about their feelings. Many are also very sensitive to being touched and might not want to be held or cuddled.Communication - Often children with autism will display delay in speech and language skills. They may use one word or two word sentences to express their needs. They may also repeat words or phrases over and over again which is known as echolalia. They may also use pronoun reversals in their communication ( saying You instead of I). They also have a hard time understanding non verbal gestures or body language of others.Restricted and repetitive behaviour and interests - these include repeated movements with objects motor mannerisms such as rocking of the body, hand flapping, spinning, jumping sensory sensitivities etc. Repeated behaviours means those actions or behaviours are repeated over and over again. They may involves one part of the body or the entire body or even an object. Children with autism also have difficulty when they notice a change in their routine as they like sticking to the same routine everyday.Apar from these children with autism can have co- morbid conditions such as they may display signs of ADHD - hyperactivity, impulsive and have short attention span. They can also display signs of self injury, throw temper tantrums and also have aggressive outbursts.

question: Is sensitivity to stimuli a sign of autism?
answer: It is a common trait for those on the Autism Spectrum to be sensitive to stimuli. Many of us on the spectrum have difficulty processing ordinary and daily sensory information. Any of our sensesmay be over- or under-sensitive, or both, at different times. This can be a daily battle in our life. For example, I was on a date with my tennis racket and ball at a campus practice wall when another meltdown started brewing. Someone showed up with a DVD player that was letting out a “stimuli” of a strong bass tone that felt like someone thumping at my ears. I felt a meltdown coming on. What does that feel like? A rumbling volcano comes to mind. I knew if I remained in the cage, I would feel like a caged animal and so I walked out of the cage. At least, I had the luxury of walking away from a meltdown trigger with a mile's worth of walking trail out of earshot range. The internal rumbling stopped somewhere along the trail. Eruption averted. After walking the entire lap, the tennis player with the DVD player had left. I didn't return to the cage because the humidity and walk had done me in. I used to have peculiar and frightening meltdowns at night. They would come on me suddenly and would feel like my bed pillows and sheets touching me were conspiring against me. I would get up out of frustration and throw the pillow down as if it was a bully. I'd sling the sheet/bed cover on the floor as if it was my worst enemy. The picture that came to mind was behaving like a cat with its tail caught underneath a rocking chair. It was something I had no control over and I just had to "rock" my way through it. As surely as it came over me, it left me after minutes passed. The minutes, however, seemed much longer than that. Sometimes meltdowns come upon me without any obvious trigger, but most of the time there is a stimuli. It can be a sound or smell that rises the tension in my body. It may be a pet peeve and my reaction is way out of bounds with it. If I can walk away from the annoyance, the odds improve of a lighter meltdown or not having one. If I can't, it'll be Mount St. Helens all over again.

question: How is it that some people can be diagnosed with high-functioning autism but interact with others and display no visible signs of autism to the casual observer?
answer: A lifetime of practice (it's called autistic masking). This masking does come at a VERY high life cost for most of us. Most of us learned to “live” normally, but in near-constant misery as adults with depression, chronic fatigue, and bouts of extreme exhaustion. Acceptance and success in the neurotypical world we all live in often comes at a rather obscene price. There may be mild outward signs too, but just not the kind most people would recognize. Often, the person might be accused of having a temper/“short fuse" or be rather uncomfortable around loud or crowded places. Frequent migraines are often common too. Many of us “middle-age” folks that grew up unaware of our ASD will eventually build up a long-term condition known as “autistic burnout” or “autistic regression” after living too many years of unknowingly increasingly masking. The eventual crash known as Autistic Burnout seems to involuntarily (instantaneously) erase many of our masking abilities that we didn't even “know” we were engaging in. It can happen out of the blue, and result in EXTREME confusion and “brain fog". Recovery can be very slow if autistic burnout gets that far, as it requires learning to deprioritize most masking behaviors and also learning how to be one's true self for the first time ever at a relatively old age. Brilliant careers are often cut rather painfully short by this phenomenon. Masking skills can return in time, but are rarely at the high level they were before. *** Children with ASD can often begin masking/socially camouflaging their own real needs and preferences long before they're even potty trained. Anyone ever knowing that they have ASD is not required! Learning to avoid invalidating and negative consequences as kids can begin to occur even at an insanely young age. Many born with with ASD learn from personal observation far better than they are able to communicate with others (even from their youngest age). Intellectual ability on the high end just further increases one's ability to mask.
