question: How do you spot signs of autism in teenagers?
answer: Part 1 of 2:Looking for Signs Autism is called a spectrum disorder because every autistic person is different, and some of them function better in certain areas than others. Some autistic people communicate nonverbally, while others are extremely good with verbal communication and may have a large vocabulary for their age. Some really struggle with executive dysfunction, while others have minimal issues transitioning from activity to activity and taking care of themselves. There are many "ways" to be autistic, and just as no non-autistic person is the same, no autistic person is the same, either. Watch out for using "subgroups" as well, such as describing someone as "high-functioning" or "low-functioning". Since everyone has their strengths and weaknesses, using these terms doesn't adequately describe an autistic person's experiences or strengths. 2. Analyze their childhood behaviors.Oftentimes, if a teenager is diagnosed with autism, it's because their behaviors weren't pervasive enough to significantly interfere with their development - for example, they're probably not going to communicate entirely non-verbally. However, some of the signs may actually become more obvious when the child reaches adolescence, such as trouble with social abilities. If you know anything about the teen's past, try looking back and seeing if you can recognize any of these signs from their early childhood. Did they learn to speak later than most children (for example, not saying two or three word sentences before the age of four)? Regardless of when they began speaking, did they exhibit unusual speech patterns, such as echolalia? Did they learn certain skills before most children would (such as reading at age two)? Did they have trouble dealing with transitions from one event to another, even if the transition seemed simple? For example, a simple "Come on, let's get in the car and go to Grandma's" could have spurned what seemed like a temper tantrum. Did they stim? While stimming isn't limited to autistic children, it's much more prevalent than in non-autistic children. Keep in mind that some autistic children may have been forced to stop stimming by non-autistic individuals; try to recall if they've ever started to stim, but then stopped. Did they play differently than other children would play? For example, an autistic teen may have not engaged in "playing pretend" as a child, or would have engaged in unusual play, such as feeling a doll's hair or stacking Lego bricks rather than using these toys in the way that one would expect them to be used. 3. Look for signs that may have carried on from childhood.Certain traits of autism can remain for quite a long time if the autistic teen has never received any form of treatment for it. These can be things that you might see in any child, such as stuttering or stammering, or something more significant, such as constant avoidance of eye contact. Consider the following questions when looking for signs that this teen may be autistic. Do they have special interests that they research constantly? Sometimes these special interests can be people, so they can become obsessed with a person to nearly stalker-like levels - whether the person is a celebrity or someone they know in person. Do they experience meltdowns (when they lose control over their emotions, scream, and in some cases, exhibit destructive behavior) or shutdowns (when they become more passive, retreat "into" themselves, and sometimes lose certain abilities, such as speaking)? Meltdowns may look like tantrums, especially in children, but a meltdown or shutdown is often a response to sensory overload or a sudden change in routine. Do they stim in not-so-obvious manners? This can be easy to overlook, as some stims may look like typical fidgeting that you'd see in just about any teenager. However, try to watch more closely and see how often they perform these behaviors. Do they tap their pencil or play with their hair frequently, for example? Do they stick to strict routines and get upset when the routine is altered in some way? For example, if an autistic teen is told, "You're not going to school today", they may become distressed and complain, even if they dislike school. Do they have sensory problems - for example, do they cover their ears and get visibly upset by loud noises, or have strange eating patterns, such as either eating bland food or overly spicy food? Some teens are hypersensitive to stimulation, while others are hyposensitive to it. Some teens may even have a mix of both. 4. Analyze long-lasting challenges and unusual aspects of the teen's social skills. Some teenagers may just be socially awkward and not have many friends. However, autism is much more than just "social awkwardness" - it involves some more serious problems with social skills than just teenage social problems. Search for trouble in the teen's social life and see if any of the following apply. Do they either make too much or too little eye contact? Infrequent eye contact is most commonly associated with autism, but some autistic people are considered "starers", and may rarely break eye contact. Do they have trouble understanding figurative language or sarcasm? For example, if an autistic teen is told, "Go jump in a lake!", their response might be, "Why? I can't swim" or "What lake? There's no lake here". Do they go on long-winded talks with barely a break to let the listener say something? These "rambles" or "infodumps" can be about anything, but you may hear about the autistic person's interests. Do they have few or no real friends? This may not apply in particularly accepting environments, but autistic teens may not realize that a fair-weather friend is not a real friend, even when the so-called friend tries to hint at this. Are they often a target for bullying or manipulation, and never seem to realize what's going on until it's too late? Some autistic people are extremely loyal, so you may also see them sticking with a "friend" who belittles them and treats them terribly. Are they most often alone? (This may be mistaken for being an introvert. Keep in mind that autistic people can be introverts, but they can also be extroverts or ambiverts.) Do they communicate in seemingly odd ways, such as speaking in a monotone or using very few gestures? 5. Watch for signs of alexithymia in the teen.Alexithymia is difficulty identifying and describing one's emotions. Autistic people can struggle with alexithymia, so if they're dealing with some sort of emotion, they may not recognize that they're feeling this emotion until it starts showing up in physical symptoms (e.g. sore throats, headaches). They may also have trouble identifying the emotions of others, and have a somewhat decreased empathy response, although it's important to understand that . While alexithymia isn't directly related to autism, it can be a sign of it. 6. Arrange for an autism assessment.At an appointment with your teen's doctor, explain that you suspect your teen to be autistic - or if your teen also suspects that they are autistic, allow them to communicate that if they so wish. You should be referred to someone who can assess your teen for autism. Don't ask for an assessment in front of your teen without your teen knowing that you're going to ask. This may shock and upset your teen, especially since you didn't keep them in the loop. Be aware that teenage girls may be at a higher risk of misdiagnosis. There are quite a few stories of autistic girls and women getting misdiagnosed for many reasons - whether it was because the doctor didn't believe a woman could be autistic, or because they identified comorbid conditions instead of autism signs. Some doctors or psychologists may diagnose an autistic girl with depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety, OCD, or any other psychological disorder that can account for some of their behaviors, but not the autism behaviors. Try to make sure that an autism assessment is in the picture, even if the doctor argues. 7. Keep an eye out for comorbid conditions.An autistic teen may have some comorbid conditions along with their autism. (However, keep in mind that if a teen was diagnosed with one of these initially, and then was later diagnosed with autism, that doesn't mean they have the comorbid condition.) Some conditions that occur more frequently in autistic people are: Depression ADHD Anxiety or OCD Sensory Processing Disorder (also known as Sensory Integration Disorder) Developmental coordination disorder Bipolar disorder Some autistic teenagers may have seizures. They may have epilepsy as well as autism, but some autistic people who are going through puberty and adolescence can experience seizures without having epilepsy. Part 2 of 2:Helping and Supporting 1. Presume competence.If your teen has been diagnosed as autistic, you may feel inclined to help them with everything. Don't. Autistic people are not incapable of taking care of themselves just because they're autistic. Every autistic person struggles with some things, but not with others. Ask your teen what they need help with, and help them only with what they tell you they need help with. If your teen doesn't say they need help with social situations and you jump in anyway, all you're going to do is aggravate them. Autistic people are not "high-functioning" or "low-functioning", and this label is hated by many autistic people. An autistic teen considered "low-functioning" because of his severe sensory problems and nonverbal communication may have incredible reading comprehension skills and be writing long novels. Another autistic teen considered "high-functioning" might have great social and communication skills, but have severe executive dysfunction, pull out her hair, and can't drive because she's hyposensitive and may miss important road signs or stoplights. Autistic people all have their own personal strengths and weaknesses, and it's impossible to define these by a functioning label. 2. Use identity-first language.Autism is part of a person's identity, and while it might be more inclining to say "person with autism" to be considered politically correct, this removes part of the autistic person's identity. Autistic people are autistic their whole lives, and saying "person with autism" makes it seem as though that person's autism isn't a part of them and it can just be "removed". Keep in mind that sometimes, this is a matter of personal preference. Some autistic people prefer to be referred to as a "person with autism", but if they haven't specified if they like this or not, stay on the safe side and refer to them as an autistic person. 3. Request an IEPParents can request an IEP for their teen, but the teen will have to be assessed to determine whether or not they qualify for an IEP. Under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, also known as IDEA, autistic children and teens are eligible for IEP services. An IEP can allow your teen some extra services - for example, permission to bring in stim toys, exercise balls to sit on, permission to leave the room if they're feeling overwhelmed, speech therapy, and more. Having an IEP in place can help your teen's teachers better understand how to support them in the classroom. Let your teen participate in the IEP meetings and communicate their needs. At high school age, autistic teens are not children and their parents should not be making the decisions for them. Make sure your teen gets some input on the services they're getting, even if it's just continuously asking, "Does that sound to you like it would help you?" Teachers can suggest to the parents of a teen that they request an IEP, but they do not have the power to call in an IEP request for the student without permission from the parents. You may want to discuss setting up a quiet spot for your teen at the school. If your teen is prone to meltdowns or shutdowns, especially at school, a prime point of the first IEP meeting should be finding a quiet place for them to calm down. 4. Try therapies for issues such as speech or motor problems.Some autistic teens have problems with their verbal communication, and speech therapy may benefit them greatly. Others have trouble with motor skills, and may need therapy for either gross motor skills or fine motor skills. Additionally, there are some sensory integration therapies that your teen can use to learn to cope with sensory problems. Try looking into these therapies and reviewing any potential therapists thoroughly. Be wary of ABA therapies. ABA therapy, also known as Applied Behavior Analysis, can work for some autistic teens who have trouble with motor skills, if the therapist is a good fit. However, there are also many, many stories of autistic people being abused in ABA therapy, and leaving the therapy with PTSD. Be extremely careful if you start looking into ABA therapies, and if your autistic teen starts becoming distressed with the therapy, don't force them to go. 5. Search for ways to make communication easier. Some autistic people are primarily nonverbal communicators, and others may lose the ability to communicate verbally when having a shutdown. While many teens that receive a late diagnosis of autism may communicate verbally, some of them may prefer nonverbal communication; work with them to find ways to communicate their needs. If the teen communicates primarily verbally, and only has infrequent cases of communicating nonverbally (for example, during shutdowns), it may be possible to figure out what stims show the teen's needs. For example, wringing their hands could mean, "It's too overstimulating and I need to leave". Consider sign language if the teen is primarily nonverbal, but doesn't have significant trouble with coordination and eye contact. How to Choose AAC for an Autistic Person may be a good article to look at if your teen has severe trouble with verbal communication or communicates (or prefers to communicate) nonverbally. 6. Assist the teen in finding ways of stimming if they want help.While this may seem confusing at first, there are actually many ways you can help an autistic teen find new ways of stimming. For example, you could help them find or make stim toys, or help them to redirect stims that they may not realize are disruptive. For example: "I've noticed you've been repeating phrases to yourself during tests. Do you think you could try playing with your ring or chewing on your necklace instead? Talking during tests can make it harder for the other students to focus, even if you're just whispering." Suggest to the teen that they read How to Stim, How to Stim Discreetly, and How to Replace Harmful Stims to help themselves with stimming. Do not try to stop the teen from stimming entirely. Stimming helps autistic people to focus and decrease sensory overload, and preventing them from stimming can cause them difficulty in focus and well-being - and forcing them to stop stimming by restraining them can lead to lifelong problems. It's okay to help them change harmful stims to non-harmful ones or suggest quieter stims to avoid disrupting people in public, but never try to stop them from stimming at all. Similarly, don't force a teen to engage in a quieter stim just because you don't want to be embarrassed. If your teen flaps their arms when they're happy or anxious, unless there's a legitimate reason to ask them to use a quieter stim (e.g. you're at airport security and currently have to undergo additional screening), don't ask them to use a quieter stim. This stifles them and teaches them that other people's feelings are more important than their own. 7. Show the teen support. Never apologize for them simply being autistic, or feel sad that they're autistic; autistic teens are capable of understanding you and being quite successful, even if they are nonverbal or struggle with executive dysfunction. Being autistic is not a curse, and right now, especially at this point in their life, an autistic teen will need your support and care more than ever. Show them support by caring for them unconditionally and not supporting organizations against autism (such as Autism Speaks). Instead, find organizations that support and are run by autistic individuals. Experience autistic culture with them. Autistic people have accomplished many things, with one example being writing books or blogs. Look at groups that don't demonize autism, such as the Autism Self-Advocacy Network (ASAN). These groups are run by autistic people. Support them during Autism Awareness Month. Autism Awareness Month, which takes place every April, can be very difficult for autistic people. Support Autism Acceptance Month instead. As a general rule, try to avoid organizations that use a puzzle piece for their logo. Autistic people are already complete; there is no missing piece from them. The puzzle piece is also often associated with Autism Speaks, which is often considered by autistic people to be a hate group disguised as an organization. Regardless of whether you and your teen actively support autism organizations, make sure they understand that you love them unconditionally - autism and all.

question: Can messy rooms be a sign of autism or Asperger's?
answer: Messy rooms can be a symptom of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), particularly in individuals with Asperger's syndrome, which is a form of high-functioning autism. People with Asperger's may have difficulty with organization and executive functioning skills, which can lead to a messy room or living space. However, it's important to note that a messy room alone is not indicative of autism or Asperger's, and it is not a diagnostic criterion for these conditions. Individuals with autism may have difficulty with organizational skills and executive functioning because they may have difficulties understanding the steps needed to tidy up, or may have difficulties prioritizing tasks. They may also have difficulty understanding the importance of maintaining an orderly living space. Additionally, some individuals with autism may have intense and restricted interests in specific topics or activities, which can lead to a cluttered room as they accumulate items related to those interests. It is important to note that not every person with autism or Asperger's will have difficulty with organizational skills and keeping a tidy room, and this symptom should be evaluated in the context of other symptoms, in consultation with a professional specialized in autism and developmental disorders.

They may seem to be behind in some areas of learning. For instance, speech or walking. •Seemingly advanced intellect in specific areas - Despite delays in some areas, their intellect or develop in other areas may well exceed that of other children. These areas of development are usually much more complex to the child and tend to be more associated with areas that most typical children struggle to grasp. They may be incredibly quick at picking up reading skills for example. •Sensory sensitivities - The child may like to make a great deal of noise, but dislike noise from elsewhere. They may cover their ears frequently or complain about certain textures. Lighting might hurt their eyes. •Awkwardness/anxiety - They may posses an odd posture, frequently tiptoe, struggle with eye contact, get restless or agitated easily and may be emotionally attached to one parent. question: Is late talking always a sign of autism or another disorder in toddlers?
answer: No. Autism always affects communication in some way, but does not always noticeably affect speech. The distinction is that “speech” is just the production of words using voice intelligibly. Many autistic people have motor control difficulty, which limits their ability to make and time the precise, rapid, yet smooth movements required to produce intelligible words, though they can use sign language or a voice output communication aid (VOCA). Here, speech and communication go hand in hand. I’m a level one autistic. I started talking at around 9 months old. I was a bit like Gerald McBoingBoing, echoing everything I heard. I understood what each word or sound was individually, and I constructed grammatical sentences, but the social context largely eluded me.I didn’t understand why I couldn’t go “BOOM!” like a big keg of powder. Other people make mouth sounds constantly. Why is it wrong when I do it? “Communication” is more broad than this, as is the Autism Spectrum. Communication includes everything that goes into speech, but also vocabulary, grammar, comprehension, and social context. This is why I prefer to say “non-speaking” rather than “non-verbal,” which to me implies no language at all, which is a different presentation entirely. A person who uses a VOCA has language and can understand what others say, even if their communication doesn’t look the way others expect. It works. There are many reasons someone might start talking later than average: prematurity, ear infections, illnesses, a sibling talking for/over them all the time, selective mutism, trauma, neglect, not understanding how words are used, or just being introverted. I’m a speech pathologist working primarily with children age 2–5, and these are only some of the reasons a child might talk late. If any one of these is affected, the child may talk later than expected, or not at all. Autistic people are often struggling with one or more of these foundational communication skills. I am a linguistic savant who speaks 10 languages; five fluently and the other five conversationally. I have more than enough language to express myself, but I struggle immensely with the social and nonverbal part of communication with people who are not also neurodivergent.

question: What are some typical signs of autism in a 4 year old?
answer: The signs that were, in combination and retrospectively, put together for the later diagnosis in my son, were actually first noticed at 4.Extremely developed, complex speech (this isn't some “proud mom" thing, it was noted by speech therapists he was visiting at the time)Refusal to deal with stuffed animalsCertain motor skills were delayed or absent (shoelaces, buttons, scissors, bicycle)Walking on tiptoes (13 now, still does it)Refusal to deal with any decorative elements (e.g. “I'm not going to draw in this activity book, it has flowers/stars/dinosaurs next to exercises")Extreme objections to change in something habitualRefusal to work with modeling clay (icky texture, won't touch)A tendency to become gradually overwhelmed during the day, leading to an emotional explosion at some point (what we later found out were meltdowns)A tendency to have everyone act according to his rules, which was also connected to his difficulty to make friendsEmotional and behavioral rigiditySpecific interests that were very deeply explored, and extensive memory about related details in those topicsKeen attention to when someone would make the mistake of “treating me like a child!!”Extreme choosiness in foodAgain, none of that was telling by itself, but all of these things were recalled during later assessment and were put together (along with those things that appeared later) in the “ah, now it all makes sense" conclusion. None of those signs was or should be “yeah, definite autism". Only together, only with other signs, and through a series of professional tests and conversations later. Other typical signs can be (we had them later, not at 4) echolalia, sensitivity to textures, stimming behavior, a mismatch between perceived emotional, physical, intellectual, and social age, lack of theory of mind (not understanding that other people are persons, too), etc.

question: Can there be signs of autism in healthy babies? For example stimming? My 8 month old is flapping his hand quite often, but otherwise does not show signs of autism. Should I be worried?

question: What are the signs of autism in a 18 year old?

question: What are the signs of autism in adults? Fifty years ago autism was unheard of.

They smile back when you smile to them. They give an excited expression when you try to tease them with a peek a boo. They cry when you pout. An autistic child does not give these specific reactions. The absence of reaction is one of the early signs of autism. An autistic child does not respond to loud noises. By the early years, normal children would have the ability to recognize their own names and to the common voices in their surroundings. Since they do not react to the sounds in the environment, autistic children at the early stages tend to be judged as hearing impaired. The ability to maintain eye contact is another way to know if the child may be suffering from autism. Normal kids can fairly stay and keep eye contact during communication. A child with autism tends to play alone, doesn't babble or smile during infancy, and tends to lag in language development skills. As a parent, you know that you have been instinctively guided to know what your child needs. And deep in your heart you also know that you will do anything to keep your child's life the best it can get. Detecting the early signs of autism will help you decide the right steps to take in ensuring that your child gets the best of care. question: What are the signs of autism in the workplace?
answer: Some autistic people find navigating social interactions difficult. Some autistic people may talk extensively about their special interest in a conversation without seeming to show interest in the other person’s interests. Some autistic people may not respond to their name, but I am not sure how prevalent this would be in working autistic adults. Some autistic people display palilalia (repeating a word or phrase that they say) or echolalia (repeating others’ words or phrases). Some autistic people may struggle to understand another person’s perspective. Some autistic people have difficulty reading the nonverbal language such as tone, facial expressions, and body language of typical people. Some autistic people do not make the typical amount of eye contact with people (which is okay, and they should not be made to). Some autistic people use less gestures than typical people, use less facial expressions than typical people or facial expressions that do not seem to match their words even if their words are literal, speak in a non-typical tone or monotone or in a tone that does not seem to match their words even if their words are literal. Some autistic people have difficulty understanding implied or indirect requests. Some autistic people have difficulty understanding figurative language such as idioms, metaphors, similes, hyperbole, irony, and jokes. Some autistic people have receptive and/or expressive language disabilities. Some autistic people have difficulty processing or understanding oral literal language. Some autistic people have difficulty remembering multiple oral instructions. Some autistic people at times or always need to use a method of communication other than speaking such as typing or writing. Some autistic people who are sometimes able to speak become unable to speak during times of high stress. Some autistic people stim such as rock back and forth or hand flap. Some autistic people have additional sensory processing needs due to being more and/or less sensitive than typical people to sensory input, and may need sensory processing tools such as preferential seating, noise-cancelling headphones, weighted blankets, and being allowed to listen to music while doing a task if safe to do so. Some autistic people have difficulty transitioning to different activities and/or coping with change, and need a visual timetable and transition cues such as a timer or area visual boundaries. Some autistic people have rigid routines or rituals. Some autistic people have special interests and find it difficult to focus on something that is not their special interest, but are able to focus intensely on a task related to their special interest. However, having some signs of being autistic does not mean being autistic, and other disabilities such as social communication disorder, a receptive and/or expressive language disorder, ADD/ADHD (attention deficit disorder/attention deficit hyperactivity disorder), schizophrenia, intellectual disability, and/or other disabilities may also cause signs similar to signs of autism.

question: Is head lag a sign of autism?
answer: Is head lag a sign of autism?Disclaimer: I am not a medical professional of any kind whatsoever, so my conclusions, such as they are, are based on a little research and reading, which I will cite. As far as I was able to discover, there is no definite connection between head lag and Autism Spectrum Disorder. According to one study, the presence of head lag in preterm infants is related to cerebral injury, to medical complications, and to neurobehavioural alterations (including low muscle tone, poor quality of movements, asymmetry, poor self-regulation, and poor reflex development). No associations were found between head lag and autism risk and social-emotional outcomes at age two. Nor were there any associations between head lag and language, cognitive, or motor scores, and no head lag or developmental delays were found in the two-year-old infants. [1][2] Please note that this doesn't mean that there is no association between head lag and ASD or developmental delay, but that there was no evidence of it found in the study. However, more testing needed to be done before any firm conclusions on the subject could be reached. Another study found that there was a link between motor difficulties (one of which was head lag) at 6 months of age and a later autism diagnosis. Those studied belonged to two cohorts: one group was composed of younger siblings of children with autism, and the other of infants with no family history of autism. Regardless of whether they were later diagnosed with autism, younger siblings of autists performed more poorly as a group on all the motor tests than did the group with no family history of autism. At two years of age, 11 out of 49 younger siblings of autists had been diagnosed with autism, while none of the 25 with no family history of autism were diagnosed with the condition. The authors of the study described the findings as ‘preliminary'. Note that in this study, a range of both fine and gross motor skills were tested, rather than head lag only. Additionally, siblings of autists are far more likely than average to be diagnosed with ASD. [3] In sum, I see little conclusive evidence that head lag (especially head lag alone) is a sign of autism.Footnotes[1] Head Lag in Infancy: What Is It Telling Us? - Life Sciences Journal[2] Head Lag in Infancy: What Is It Telling Us?[3] Motor problems in infancy may forecast autism | Spectrum | Autism Research News

question: Is it true that talking to everyone the same way is a sign of autism?
answer: It's not uncommon for autistic people to recognize authority differently compared to neurotypical people, so we speak to everyone similarly regardless of their position in the social hierarchy. There are exceptions, like when someone hurts us. We can quickly change how we speak to someone if they hurt us, but we’re likely to treat you the same as everyone else if you don't. Autistic people rely on logical reasoning to socialize, so we speak to everyone in the same way unless we can logically justify speaking to them differently. We tend to be nonconformists and independent thinkers too, so we may speak to everyone in the same way because we don’t like being told how to act or what to think. question: When do signs of autism usually appear in adults that are later diagnosed with the disorder?
answer: They appear in early childhood, the same as with those who are diagnosed in childhood. I cannot emphasize this enough: autism does not spontaneously appear at age 20 or 30. If it seems to do that, then it’s not autism. A requirement for the diagnosis is that the traits and deficits are present in early childhood. The reason that some people are not diagnosed until adulthood is because of 1. where those individuals fall on the spectrum, and 2. the time in which they were born. Both can make it very difficult to get a diagnosis. In the former case, if social skills are not a severe problem, and so a child can easily mask, and may not stim, then the child may come across, as just being somewhat odd, or quirky, or very set in their ways, and the fact that they have autism can be missed by teachers or doctors. In the latter case, people who were born before, and I’m being generous, the mid 1980s, probably did not get an autism diagnosis unless they were severely debilitated. No criteria for anyone else on the spectrum existed. So many people born before that time didn’t get that diagnosis until they were an adult, and it could be recognized in an assessment. But the signs of autism are the same for everyone, whether a child or adult, and those signs are present in early childhood. I’m at odds with a lot of people as to at what age autism can be easily recognized. I think we tend to go a bit too young, but, we can all agree that before age 7, autism is definitely clear. But the signs of autism never appear in adulthood when they were never there before. If they do, then, it’s a sign of a reaction to trauma, or the consequences of a personality disorder, or a possible brain injury, but if it’s autism, it’s been there since early childhood, and probably since birth. Some people may get the diagnosis later in life, but the signs of autism were always there.

question: How do I recognize the signs of autism in myself?
answer: Part 1 of 4:Observing the General Characteristics Autistic people have trouble understanding subtle social cues. This can make a variety of social situations difficult, from making friends to getting along with co-workers. Consider if you've experienced things like: Having trouble understanding how another person is feeling (e.g. wondering if they are too sleepy to talk or not) Being told that your behavior was inappropriate, awkward, strange, or impolite Not realizing that someone is bored of talking and wants to do something else Frequently feeling mystified by other people's behavior Having trouble making eye contact with others 2. Ask yourself if you have trouble understanding other people's thoughts. 3. Consider your responses to unexpected events. 4. Watch yourself to see if you stim. Stimming, or self-stimulatory behavior, is much like fidgeting, and it's a type of repetitive movement done for self-calming,focusing, expressing emotions, communication, and coping with difficult situations. While everyone stims, it's especially important and frequent for autistic people. If you haven't been diagnosed yet, your stims may be on the more subtle side. You may have also "unlearned" certain stims from childhood if your stimming was criticized. Flapping or clapping hands Rocking Hugging yourself tightly, squeezing your hands, or piling heavy blankets on yourself Tapping toes, pencils, fingers, etc. Crashing into things for fun Playing with hair Pacing, spinning, or jumping Looking at bright lights, intense colors, or moving GIFs Singing, humming, or listening to a song on repeat Smelling soaps or perfumes Many autistic people have Sensory Processing Disorder (also known as Sensory Integration Disorder), which means that the brain is overly sensitive, or not sensitive enough, to certain sensory input. You may find that some of your senses are amplified, while others might be dulled. Here are some examples: —Becoming overwhelmed by bright colors or moving objects, not noticing things like road signs, attraction to the sight of hustle and bustle —Covering ears or hiding from loud noises such as vacuum cleaners and crowded places, not noticing when people are talking to you, missing things that people say —Feeling disturbed or nauseated by smells that don't bother others, not noticing important smells like gasoline, loving strong scents and buying the strongest-smelling soaps and food available —Preferring to eat only bland or "kid food," eating extremely spicy and flavorful food while disliking anything bland, or disliking trying new foods —Being bothered by certain fabrics or clothes tags, not noticing when people touch you lightly or you are injured, or constantly running your hands along everything —Getting dizzy or sick in cars or on swing sets, or constantly running around and climbing things —Constantly feeling uncomfortable sensations in your bones and organs, bumping into things, or not noticing when you are hungry or tired 6. Consider whether you experience meltdowns or shutdowns. 7. Think about your executive function.Executive function is the ability to stay organized, manage time, and transition smoothly. Autistic people often struggle with this skill and may need to use special strategies (such as rigid schedules) in order to adapt. Symptoms of executive dysfunction include: Not remembering things (e.g. homework assignments, conversations) Forgetting to do self-care activities (eating, bathing, brushing hair/teeth) Losing things Procrastinating and struggling with time management Having difficulty starting a task and switching gears Struggling to keep your living space clean 8. Consider your passions.Autistic people often have intense and unusual passions, which are called special interests. Examples include fire trucks, dogs, quantum physics, autism, a favorite TV show, and writing fiction. Special interests are notable in their intensity, and finding a new special interest can feel like falling in love. Here are some signs that your passion is stronger than what non-autistics experience: Talking about your special interest for long periods of time, and wanting to share it with others Being able to concentrate on your passion for hours; losing track of time Organizing information for fun, such as charts, tables, and spreadsheets Being able to write/say long and detailed explanations of nuances of your interest, all off of the top of your head, perhaps even quoting passages Feeling excitement and bliss from enjoying your interest Correcting people who are knowledgeable about the subject Being wary of talking about your interest, for fear that you'll annoy people 9. Think about how easy it is for you to talk and process speech.Autism is often associated with difficulties related to spoken language, the degree of which greatly varies from person to person. If you're autistic, you may experience things like: Learning to speak later in life (or not at all) Difficulty speaking or losing the ability to speak, when overwhelmed Word-finding problems Long pauses in conversations so you can think Avoiding difficult conversations because you aren't sure you can express yourself Struggling to understand speech when the acoustics are different, such as in an auditorium or from a movie without subtitles Not remembering spoken information, especially longer lists Needing extra time to process speech (e.g. not reacting in time to commands like "Catch!") 10. Notice literal thinking.While autistic people are capable of abstract thought, they tend to be literal thinkers by nature. Sometimes this is very subtle, especially when the autistic person has developed workarounds and/or their loved ones show understanding. Here are some ways literal thinking can present itself: Not catching sarcasm or exaggeration, or being confused when others are not Misunderstanding figurative language, such as thinking "wrap it up" means "wrap up the package" when the speaker meant "I want you to finish up." Not picking up on subtext, such as when "I don't know if I have enough money" actually means "please pay for my food." Making literal jokes for the amusement of others, such as slapping the pavement when told, "it's time to hit the road." 11. Examine your appearance.One study found that autistic children have distinct facial characteristics—broad upper face, big wide-set eyes, a short nose/cheeks area, and a wide mouth—in other words, somewhat of a "baby face." You may look younger than your age or be told that you look attractive/adorable. Not every autistic child has each of these facial features. You may only have a few. Unusual airways (double branching of the bronchi) were also found in autistic people. The autistic people's lungs were completely typical, until the double branching at the end of the tubes. Part 2 of 4:Scouring the Internet 1. Search for autism quizzes online.Quizzes such as the AQ and RAADS can help give you a sense if you're on the spectrum. They are not a substitute for a professional diagnosis, but they are a useful tool. Some professional questionnaires are available online. 2. Turn to autism-friendly organizations.A truly autism-friendly organization is usually run partially or completely by autistic people, such as the Autistic Self-Advocacy Network and the Autistic Women and Nonbinary Network. These organizations provide a much clearer view of autism than organizations run exclusively by parents or family members do. Autistic people best understand their own lives and can offer the most insights. Avoid toxic and negative autism organizations. Some autism-related groups say terrible things about autistic people, and may push pseudoscience.Autism Speaks is a prominent example of an organization that uses disaster rhetoric. Look for organizations that provide a more balanced point of view, and empower autistic voices instead of excluding them. 3. Read the work of autistic writers. Many autistic people can be found in hashtags such as #ActuallyAutistic and #AskingAutistics. In general, the autistic community is very welcoming to people who are wondering if they are autistic, or who are self-diagnosed. 5. Start researching therapies.Part 3 of 4:Confronting Your Misconceptions Autism is mostly or completely genetic, and it begins in the womb (although behavioral signs don't become noticeable until toddler years or later). People are born autistic, and will always be autistic. However, this is nothing to be afraid of. Autistic people's lives can improve with the right support, and it's possible for autistic adults to lead happy, fulfilling lives. The most popular myth about autism causes is that vaccines cause autism, which has been disproven by over a dozen studies. This hoax was engineered by a single researcher who faked data and was hiding financial conflicts of interest. His work has been thoroughly disproven since, and he has lost his license for malpractice. Reported rates of autism aren't increasing because more autistic people are being born. Experts are becoming better at identifying autism, especially in girls and people of color (who have been historically overlooked). Autistic children become autistic adults. Stories of people who "recover" from autism either feature people who have learned to hide their autistic traits (and may suffer mental health problems as a result), or who were never autistic in the first place. Autistic people may struggle with the cognitive parts of empathy, while still being deeply caring and kind. While autistics may not understand someone's feelings, they generally experience average amounts of emotional empathy and above-average amounts of distress when they see someone who is upset. Autistic people may have a strong desire to help people, especially through concrete means such as organizing or giving them items they need. For example, an autistic person may be quick to offer tissues and a comfort object if they see someone crying. Some autistic people experience intense affective (emotional) empathy, sometimes to the point that it is painful. Experiences with empathy may vary with the presence of alexithymia, a condition that impacts someone's emotional understanding. 3. Don't assume that autistic people are lazy or intentionally rude. Autistic people have to try harder to conform to many social expectations of politeness. Sometimes they fail. They may realize it and apologize, or need someone to tell them that they missed their mark. Negative assumptions are the fault of the person who makes them, not of the autistic person. Rather than thinking "outside the box," autistic people do not see the box at all. Thus, they may not understand what is expected in social situations. This can result in a lot of guesswork. Some everyday situations can be uncomfortable or overwhelming for autistic people. This can make socializing more difficult. In this case, it's not any person who needs to change, but the environment. 4. Realize that autism is an explanation, not an excuse, for inappropriate behavior.Most times when autism is brought up after a disagreement, it is as an explanation for the autistic person's behavior, not an attempt to escape consequences. For example, an autistic person might say "I'm sorry I hurt your feelings. I didn't mean to imply that you aren't intelligent. Sometimes I struggle finding words that match what I really think. I think highly of you and my words didn't match my thoughts." Usually, people who complain about autistic people "using it as an excuse" either met one bad person, or are upset about autistic people showing signs of their disability. This isn't helpful or kind. 5. Don't believe the myths about autism and violence.While media speculation has sometimes blamed violent or harmful behavior on autism, the reality is that the large majority of autistic people are nonviolent. In fact, an autism diagnosis is associated with reduced violent behavior in childhood and adult years. When autistic children do lash out, it is usually in reaction to provocation. They are less likely to initiate violence than non-autistic children are. The average autistic person is very unlikely to hurt anyone and would probably be very upset if they accidentally did so. 6. Rid yourself of the idea that there's something wrong with stimming.Stimming is a natural mechanism that helps with self-calming, concentration, meltdown prevention, and expression of feelings. Preventing someone from stimming is damaging and wrong. There are only a few possible instances in which a stim is a bad idea: Head-banging, biting oneself, or hitting oneself, are all bad things. These can be replaced by a harmless stim, such as head-shaking and biting chewy bracelets. For example, playing with someone else's hair without their permission is a bad idea. Autistic or not, people need to respect others' personal space. It's good to be quiet in places where people work, such as schools, offices, and libraries. If people are trying to focus, it's good to stim subtly, or go to a place where quiet isn't necessary. 7. Recognize that people who catastrophize about autism are wrong.Autism is not a disease, not a burden, and not a life-destroying disorder. Many autistic people are capable of living worthwhile, productive, and happy lives. Autistic people have written books, founded organizations, run nationwide or worldwide events, and improved the world in many different ways. Even those who cannot live on their own or work can still improve the world through their kindness and love. Some organizations use gloom-and-doom scare tactics as a way to raise more money. Don't let it fool you. 8. Stop seeing autism as a puzzle to be solved.Autistic people are already complete. They add diversity and meaningful perspectives to the world. There is nothing wrong with who they are. Part 4 of 4:Consulting People You Know 1. Ask your autistic friends about it.(If you have no autistic friends, then go find some and come back.) Explain that you think you may be autistic, and that you're wondering if they've observed any signs of autism in you. They may ask you questions to better understand your experiences. Explain that you've been curious about your early childhood, and ask when you met different developmental milestones. It's normal for autistic children to hit their milestones late or out of order. See if they have any videos from your childhood that you could watch. Look for stimming and other signs of autism in children. Consider late childhood and teen milestones too, like learning to swim, ride a bike, cook, clean a bathroom, do laundry, and drive. 3. Show a close friend or family member an article on signs of autism (such as this one). Consider seeing a specialist to get diagnosed. Many health insurance plans will cover various therapies, such as speech, occupational, and sensory integration therapy. A good therapist can help you improve your skills to best adapt to a neurotypical world.

question: Do people with autism have introverted personalities as a rule?
answer: No. I have autism. I am definitely not introverted. In fact, I believe some people with autism are misinterpreted - people have a tendency to mistake shyness for introversion. Shyness often comes from a history of being made fun of and picked on, an unfortunately common occurrence for those with autism. This is how it was for me. When I first began public school in the fourth grade after being homeschooled, I was outgoing and happy to talk to anyone. However, just about everyone thought I was annoying and weird, and their jabs quickly shut my energetically social demeanor down. While I have started to bounce back ever since high school graduation, I still have a habit of analyzing situations before opening up, branding me as “the quiet one” to the collective mindset of the people I am around, such as a group of coworkers or college classmates. A lot of them would expect me to be introverted. The fact is, however, that I am energized from socialization and strongly prefer it to being alone. This is all it is. It’s how someone feels energy-wise upon periods of socialization versus isolation, not stereotypes such as shallow friendships, the need to be the center of attention, or an innate love of obnoxious parties and other typical social events. While it is quite possible that introversion is more common in people with autism, don’t mistake shyness for introversion. I am an extrovert through and through. I simply have an altered socialization pattern due to conditioning both at school and at home. I’m certain others are the same way.

question: As a child, I showed some traits of autism (restricted interests, unusual behavior, poor social skills) but I've grown up and I have absolutely no signs of autism. Is this possible?
answer: As a child, I showed some traits of autism (restricted interests, unusual behavior, poor social skills) but I've grown up and I have absolutely no signs of autism. Is this possible? It is possible that you have the “broad autism phenotype” (BAP), like many relatives of people with autism. For about half of the cases of autism, the cause is not a single mutation nor the deletion or duplication of a chunk of some chromosome (“copy number variation”), rather it is the accumulation of many genes, each one slightly “pro-autism”. This means that the relatives of such autistic people often have some of the same genes — and they also have some mild, autism-like characteristics — without being clinically “autistic”. They would not qualify for a diagnosis, rather they would be “sub-clinical”. Typically these people will score above average in autism screening tests, like the AQ Test, but probably not in the very high range where most diagnosed autistic fall. They have the “broad autism phenotype”, but not “autism” in the narrower, clinical sense. Of course, you may actually be autistic, and like many of us, you have learned to mask your autistic characteristics and survive — and even fool yourself. There are undiagnosed autistic people out there who are in denial about their autism: they have, through much hard work, managed to blend in. They don’t want the stigma of autism, which until recent times was regarded as severely disabling: the child in an institution who was intellectually disabled, couldn’t speak, had unregulated emotions and frequent meltdowns, frequently engaged in repetitive behaviours like rocking, and engaged in no social interaction. We now know that this is one part (an important part, but still only a part) of the wider autism spectrum. One of the tasks of a clinician is to decide between BAP and autism, although they might not put it in those terms. BAP is not a clinical designation, but rather a term used in some research projects to compare the relatives of autistic people with the relatives of non-autistic people. Autistic people are more likely to have relatives that score as BAP — and people who are BAP are more likely to have relatives who are autistic. This is what you expect if many cases of autism result from many genes working together, each contributing a small effect, rather than a few genes or even one gene causing autism (which also happens in some cases of autism).

question: When I'm overwhelmed, I rock back and forth. Is this a sign of autism?
answer: It’s a typical sign of autism! Not that autistics are the only people who would do this; but with them (us) it’s called a ‘stim.’ That is, a form of stereotypical behavior, one of the most recognizable patterns of autistic people. My brother, who is also autistic, used to do this. He would ‘bump’ against the back of the sofa when he was frustrated, and he was probably feeling overwhelmed at the time. We used to say, “Oh, he’s just bumping again.” Now, I’d call it ‘rocking.’ He doesn’t ‘bump’ anymore. What has taken the place of his ‘bumping’ is a habit of wringing his hands. It shows his anxiety. As for me, I may squirm, twitch or pick at my skin. Those are some of my stims. There are other stims I do, but am unaware of them til someone points them out. These vary with the person, and not all people on the spectrum have visible stims. If a person is autistic, they are likely to feel frustrated at their inability to do well with normal human activities, such as communicating. This could lead to a feeling of being overwhelmed. That’s when we engage in the activity of ‘stimming,’ to soothe ourselves. The ‘stimming’ is a form of self-stimulation or distraction, as one might attempt to calm or distract a child by patting or stroking them, except that the autistic person is doing it for themselves. Another stim is hand-flapping. It’s so typical as to be kind of an insider’s form of greeting among autistic people and their friends. “Oh, you’re one too? I’m one, too. Hello there, my autistic buddy!” (You’d need to have established some rapport and agreement beforehand if you try this, of course. If some random person comes up to me and starts flapping their hands, I’d react like, “What’s with this guy?” It makes me laugh a little to think of it.) A common, familiar example of this would be a person biting their fingernails. People who bite their nails are usually not autistic, but there is some similarity. This, too, might be a sign of nervousness or anxiety, though not usually so much overwhelm as with autistic people. Think what makes you feel overwhelmed. It might give clues whether you’re on the autism spectrum, if you don’t know it already.

question: Is a stutter a sign of autism?
answer: Not specifically, no. But it can be comorbid - which means it can occur alongside it. Many people with autism often have high anxiety, which can cause someone to stammer or have trouble getting their words out. Similarly, ADHD can cause a person to seem to stutter because their brain is working too fast for speaking to catch up. Medical literature says a stutter either develops with language development, or from a traumatic brain injury.

question: Is dwelling for a long time on other's criticism of you in the past a sign of autism or Asperger's?
answer: Not really. Dwelling or just remembering? It can seem to be a very fine distinction to perceive from the outside looking in on an autistic. It actually isn't all that hard to tell introspectively for an autistic that makes the effort. Usually it's NOT dwelling, but it's easy for such a misperception to occur. Asperger's on average have very good (above human average) memory and recall. Sometimes even more so if there was an impactful memorable situation, but that doesn't automatically mean that emotion is actually tied in. ** Unfair criticism of autistic motivations is extremely common, and in many situations can be extremely painful. In very rare circumstances, the memory in question might even have a minor but consistent trauma trigger associated that dregs up an emotion. Since emotion typically needs to be secondary to logic in autistic normal functioning, such triggers are a potential social hazard. To most autistics, such a trigger would be a bit annoying and anxiety generating, but not necessarily on a conscious level.

question: If you recognize early signs of autism in a child before his/her parents do, should you inform the parents?
answer: If you are a professional in the field and spend a lot of time with the child, and if you have a good relationship with the parents, it might be worth mentioning to them that you've noticed certain things that might indicate a developmental difference. Obviously you cannot diagnose autism based simply on casual observation, so you wouldn't say 'I think your kid is autistic'. But if you have a very high level of knowledge about neurodiversity and various developmental differences, and if you spend enough time with the child to make this possible judgment (note: this is a lot of time with the kid. If you only ever see it playing in the garden over the fence, you have no idea if it is autistic), then MAYBE mention it to the parents. But you need to be really sure there's something that needs investigating and you need to be making this observation with absolutely pure motives. Because if you're wrong, you will have caused the parents a degree of worry you cannot even imagine, not to mention trouble and expense to get the child checked out.

question: Do babies show signs of autism?
answer: As with any ASD question, it depends. Telling anything before 6 months is iffy. Probably the earliest is reluctance to be touched - hypersensitivity. This means that the touching is painful or at least an overload. This also appears as a reluctance to nurse and discomfort when being held. This typically doesn’t appear in newborns but shows up in a couple of months. There are also a number of possible reasons for this, not just ASD. The way to get around it (not to cure - that won’t happen) is deep pressure. Tight swaddling, firm touch, NO light touch, etc. For some reason deep pressure does not trigger the same aversion and pain. Note that not having early symptoms does not mean the child doesn’t have ASD. Since it is a developmental disorder, until the child reaches the typical age for doing something, you can’t use not doing it as a symptom. Talking is an example - until the child SHOULD be able to begin to talk (2+ years, sometimes longer) not talking is not a symptom.

question: Is chewing clothes a sign of autism?
answer: Not specifically or necessarily, but a connection is definitely possible. Nervous habits among neurotypicals and autistic stims are often perceived very similarly. Devices made to address nervous habit behavior originally made for one group are often quickly picked up on and used by others. Fidget spinners are a popular device that is a good example of that exact phenomenon. Oral nervous habits in non-autistics occur commonly enough that one should certainly NOT presume anything medically from such behavior! Pens, pencils, toys, smoking, candy, and a wide range of other possibilities have been historically been used by all human neurotypes in this manner. It is possible that in some cases chewing or suckling on clothes might be an autistic stimming behavior, but one definitely shouldn't make any medical label assumptions from so little evidence. ASD stims may very well include putting parts of clothes or fabric in one's mouth. Oral stimming isn't uncommon. Most oral stimulation habits whether autistic or not are relatively harmless, but may be less obvious publicly if channeled to more subtle objects. Fyi, various oral “stim” objects designed for both kids and adults are sold online(amazon carries several), but they may not be quite as effective as fabrics/clothes for that person's anxiety reduction if the habit is well established.

question: Can someone start showing signs of autism spectrum disorder later in childhood (later than the other autistic kids)?
answer: It all depends on the individual, we are all different with different development trajectories. Some would say that certain children would not show signs of autism till later as they are better at masking it, but I tend to disagree with that statement. Most children are not born with masking abilities but develop them later as they learn that certain behaviours are not acceptable to others. by the time they have the sophistication to mask the autism would already be showing itself. It’s more likely that they have been coping with the sensory load of autism with some success to begin with, but sooner or later the cumulative stress of being autistic catches up with them and they crash. Basically they cope until they can’t, and that's when the signs of their autism begin to appear. this usually happens in the infant years (0–4 years old), and is often the reason some parents think their child ‘caught autism’, because it can happen overnight. It’s also the reason so many parents are convinced that it is vaccines that are the cause, because often the crash can roughly coincide with the vaccine schedule. For some children that ability to cope can last longer than others, which is why it starts to become more visible later than for other autistic children. Of course as they get older they will certainly develop some masking skills to help them cope, but not during infancy.

question: Can repetitive hand-flapping be a sign of autism?
answer: As always when you group people by a single characteristic, the answer is “Maybe yes, maybe no”. Autism is not a cluster of symptoms, but rather a way of processing and interacting with the neurotypical world and people with neurological functioning; it’s a way of being human that is different from the average person. Someone may present with hand flapping as a sign of excitement or happiness. This happens with both neurotypical and neurodiverse brain functioning. It can also achieve a calming and re-organizing state. It could be something seen and imitated. It could be transient or more permanent. But it is not a “sign” of autism in and of itself. You need a full, comprehensive, preferably multi-disciplinary evaluation complete with parent, teacher, specialist input and medical history/evaluation to determine if someone has autism or does not have autism.

question: Has anyone realized that something they did in childhood was a symptom of autism and didn't realize it until they were an adult? I read license plates and looked through phone books obsessively. I've learned that's a sign of autism.
answer: I’m late diagnosed and still am still discovering the autistic behaviors that I could not understand all my life. What I’m saying here applies to many autistic people I’ve met but certainly not all. Those who are not autistic or who are, but unaware they are, may have a difficult time understanding how we can not know we have a different neurological system. Its hard to put into words.. Perception cannot perceive itself from outside of its own perception. People don’t “feel autistic” we just accept what we feel as our normal: and it is. Just as someone NT is feeling their normal self. Autistic people DO feel they are different - but since we cannot directly compare our life experience with someone else’s experience, it is natural to assume we all experience the same basic things in the same way. All people are pressured to conform to the “norms” of the those they are around. This pressures autistic people to change how they perceive and cope with their neurological differences. If my natural tendency in socialization / conversation is to emphasize detailed information when others naturally prefer general topics, there is a resistance or repulsion to detailed information in all conversations. I have two choices. Not talk about detailed information, or not engage in socialization/ conversations. A child who is autistic may then think to themselves… “I can play with these kids if I act the way they do!” This is how masking begins. But on even a more subtle level. It can be as a VERY young child and realizing some behavior gets a negative or no response. So they change their behavior… Its different than an NT child learning how to be NT.. For the autistic child they are learning how NOT to be autistic. We feel this strain and stress between our autistic self and the NT self we’ve cultivated and tried to develop. We have no logical reason or way to understand we naturally have different (autistic) needs and ways of fulfilling our needs. Instead, we have abandoned our true selves in order to feel connected with those around us. But this does not work because what we have done is disconnected from our selves. There can be no fulfilling connection if we have no self to connect to. So… all of our natural autistic tendencies tend to get defined from the NT perspective. What were my stims I called “things I do when nervous”. Or when I felt social strains or even rejections.. it was not because I was autistic but because I was doing something wrong.. When I should have told myself, MY ways are different than THEIR ways. I became very detached from my feelings.. Alexithymia it is called. Because I disconnected from my autistic self. Its a horrible state of mind you are in to cope with this. So when you finally do find out you are autistic, that false self you’ve tried to believe in is realized for what it is.. And all the behaviors you denied, avoided or changed you start to connect with and define from an autistic perspective. You finally are able to accept your true self. But much damage has been done in the underdevelopment of that true self. We have to go back through our lives and redefine all our experiences, rediscover our real self and understand how its all been twisted by this pressure to conform to standards that were not our own.

question: What are the signs of autism in a 20-month-old?
answer: The signs can be subtle and there are a lot of different signs, which not all will have. It isn’t generally until about age 3 or so that it becomes more obvious. We discovered later when he could talk that he did not ever want to walk along the same route. Another sign is that they may take awhile to begin to talk (and some won’t talk). When my son began to talk he spoke two syllable words. Most kids will always start with just one syllable words; usually Dad and Mum. When he got better at speech he learnt every letter in the alphabet, but did not link those letters to words and learning to read; the letters were a separate thing on their own. Once he began to play he would just line toys up in a row. He did not tend to play imagination games. Nor would he join in playing with other kids, but played on his own. This is just some small examples of the type of things he did which we discovered later were indicators of autism. I must also mention he was happy in his own company. He loved to color in pictures - even if not very well - and enjoyed us reading books to him and loved to look at them himself. He loved going grocery shopping and was good at telling me where items were and what we needed to buy. He learnt every flag in the world and learnt all road signs, which also helped us as we drove. He learnt how to use a computer himself very early. He was a totally gorgeous little kid and I love him dearly.

question: Is not liking eye contact a sign of Autism?
answer: It is one sign. It would have to coincide with other traits such as passion for limited interests (or passionate about one topic for a long period, then the next and the next and so on), sensory differences, naturally leans toward literal thinking. One example of my spectrum-ness is my fixation on language. You wrote ‘not liking’, whereas usually professionals will write ‘limited eye contact’ or ‘poor eye contact’. Limited/poor eye contact is very much an outsider’s perspective. But ‘not liking eye contact’ tells a different story. You may have just written that without thinking, but my literal orientated brain takes word choice very seriously when figuring out the answer. I do not like eye contact. When I am in my natural state I never make it. I am always looking off at the distance, noticing the nice things around me, staring up to the left to limit distractions so I can think. When I am socialising with people I am supposed to leave a good impression with (for example my daughter’s teacher or an interview), I will have previously worked myself up to eye contact. At some point in the conversation I will command myself to make eye contact. When I make the eye contact, I cannot hear or take in information. When I make eye contact, it seems as though time slows down and as if I am being sucked into the persons eyes. So you can imagine why I do not like it. I feel very intense feelings. I can feel intense ‘bad’ feelings or intense ‘good’ feelings. I’ll be honest and say that I usually determine whether I like a person based on these feelings. The hardest part is having intense good feelings with a person who is not a personal friend and it is socially inappropriate to have such intense feelings for this ‘acquaintance’. If I don’t keep myself under control, I will stare and stare and stare and enjoy the bliss. These people usually go on the good list. (Please note: the feelings are not of sexual nature- they are just a neurological response to a sensory experience, to me). I know that as an adult woman, sustained eye contact with a male acquaintance might be perceived as flirting. So I would say that yes, not liking eye contact is a sign of autism but there are other traits that the person would need to have to determine if they were or not. Other conditions can struggle with eye contact such as adhd, anxiety and even experiences such as shyness or low self esteem. I am not sure if these conditions ‘do not like’ eye contact though, in the same way some/many AS people dislike it.

question: Are elementary school teachers in the US trained to recognize signs of autism?
answer: Yes, elementary school teachers in the U.S. are trained to recognize signs of autism, but they are not always able to identify every sign. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a developmental disability that affects how a person communicates and interacts with others. It can also affect how a person sees and experiences the world around them. There is no one sign or symptom that can identify autism. However, there are some red flags educators can look for, such as difficulty with social interactions, lack of interest in interacting with others, poor eye contact, repetitive behaviors or speech patterns, and sensory sensitivities. If a teacher suspects that a student is displaying signs of ASD, they are encouraged to refer the student to a specialist doing ABA therapy in Port St. Lucie for further evaluation. In some cases, early intervention is critical for helping children with ASD achieve their fullest potential.

question: Can one have extraordinarily high logical intelligence and not have troubles socially/signs of autism?

(Also, I’ve yet to find a way for someone to talk about their own intelligence that isn’t even mildly grating.) I’ve been told I am fairly logical though. Perhaps you’ve seen the visual of a school of fish with one different colored fish swimming against the rest. That’s not me. I’d be swimming away on a completely different angle distracted by something shiny (and probably get eaten). Moving the question away from me, I believe an autistic will always have some signs of autism. That doesn’t mean it will be noticed or would ever be solid proof, but autism effects a person’s personality. The social aspect depends strongly on how you define it. For one thing, a ton of trouble for autistic people comes from simply being different. If someone with autism grows up around people that really get him or her, perhaps they’d never have any issues. Plenty of factors go into the individual as well. The ability and interest in cognitive empathy (mentally putting yourself in another’s shoes) goes a long way in avoiding social issues. Certain attitudes can also help, such as a tendency to take things as they come (roll with the punches life throws). I believe a better way to look at the situation is like this. People reflect both their genetic makeup and their life experiences (nature and nurture). People currently understand autism by symptoms, which are also the result of everything which makes up a person. This can come together to make a person who meets the “intelligence” and “autistic” criteria who doesn’t have many social issues stereotypically associated with either of those characteristics. However, that doesn’t mean “no social issues” and, if their experiences had been different, they might have had plenty of problems. Ramble done. question: What are some signs of autism in a 3 year old child?
answer: Start with your pediatrician, tell him about any symptoms you may have noticed which have you worried. If he agrees you have reason to be concerned, then you will be given a referral. question: Are signs of autism running into walls? How can this be treated?

Maybe contact the county health department/health & human services or something along those lines to get some direction on who to call to schedule an initial evaluation for him. In North Carolina the eval is free of charge for any child under the age of 3. We had my son’s eval when he was 21 or 22 months in Oct/Nov 2013 and he was receiving speech therapy twice each week at his daycare by Jan 2014. At age 3 the local school district evaluated him again, officially diagnosed him as autistic and he was enrolled in the public school’s pre-K program and began attending an EC (exceptional children) pre-K classroom with all autistic peers. It was the best thing that ever happened to him in terms of his development. Your nephew may not be autistic at all but put any worries you have to rest by getting him evaluated - that’s the only way to know for sure.
