question: What are the signs of autism? Can a person be diagnosed with autism just by appearance?
answer: Listed below are some common types of behaviors seen in people with Autism/ASD. Not all people with ASD will display all behaviors, but most will display some of the behaviors listed below. 1. Social communication/interaction behaviors may include: Infrequent or infrequent eye contact Does not seem to be looking at or listening to others Rarely shares interest, affection, or enjoyment of objects or activities (including rarely pointing to or showing things to others) Does not respond or is slow to respond to others’ names or other verbal requests for attention Has trouble having back-and-forth conversations Frequently talks at length about favorite topics without noticing that others are not interested or without giving others a chance to respond Exhibits facial expressions, movements, and gestures that are inconsistent with what is being said Unusual intonation of voice that may sound sing-song or flat and robotic Has trouble understanding others’ perspectives or anticipating or understanding their behavior Has trouble adjusting behavior to social situations Has trouble engaging in imaginative play or making friends 2. Restrictive/repetitive behaviors may include: Repeating certain behaviors or abnormal behaviors, such as repeating words or phrases (a behavior called echolalia) Persistent and intense interest in specific topics (such as numbers, details, or facts) Exhibits an overly focused interest, such as in moving objects or parts of objects Be disturbed by slight changes in daily life and have difficulty adapting to transitions Be more or less sensitive than others to sensory input (such as light, sound, clothing, or temperature) 3. Complications ASD is often accompanied by a variety of physical and mental illnesses: Feeding problems: eating disorders, anorexia nervosa, aversion to certain types of food, only eating foods with a specific taste/texture, which may cause abnormal weight, gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea and constipation, or lack of nutrition due to unreasonable eating Sleep disorders: sleep anxiety, tossing and turning, difficulty falling asleep, inability to lie flat to sleep, insomnia, repeated awakenings at night, sleepwalking and other abnormal sleep structures Gastrointestinal (GI) Problems: Gastroesophageal reflux, eosinophilic esophagitis, nausea and vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, flatulence, colitis, food intolerances Allergic Diseases: Asthma, nasal allergies, allergic diseases (immunoglobulin E mediated), food allergies and intolerances Toiletries: Difficulty learning to use the toilet during the day and night, not knowing when to use the toilet, communicating the need to use the toilet, being able to use the toilet independently or promptly, learning to use different and unfamiliar toilets, self-wiping, sensory differences (dislike of toilet noises, sensation of urination/feces, cold toilet seats or excessive concern about water in the toilet), fecal smearing, a range of specific continence difficulties including bowel or bladder control difficulties Abnormal responses to sensory stimuli: over-, under- or abnormal responses to environmental stimuli such as noise, touch, smell, taste or visual stimuli. For example, looking at objects out of the corner of the eye, focusing too much on edges, spinning objects, shiny surfaces, lights or smells, refusing or only eating foods with certain tastes/textures, being too obsessed with sniffing or licking non-food objects, tactile defense or resistance to being touched or being overly sensitive to certain types of touch; light touch may be painful, while deep pressure may be calming. They may resist wearing certain textures or colors of clothing next to their skin, be apparently indifferent to pain, strongly prefer and/or continue to touch certain materials, and strongly dislike other materials, and be highly sensitive to certain frequencies or types of sounds (such as fire trucks in the distance), but not respond to nearby sounds or sounds that would scare other children. For this type of auditory and visual abnormalities, please refer to previous articles: Symptoms related to autism, autism and CVI cranial neurological visual disorders Mental health problems: epilepsy, intellectual disability, learning disabilities, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), tics, anxiety and depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), personality and mood changes, hallucinations, phobias, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Headache and migraine: Some ASD patients will bang their heads because of headaches. The diagnosis of headaches and migraines requires the cooperation of the patient, and most ASD patients cannot cooperate, which makes the diagnosis a little difficult. Summary of types and complications of migraine Acute treatment and preventive treatment of migraine 4. Other clinical features: Motor defects: Children with ASD may have motor defects, including abnormal gait, clumsiness, walking on tiptoes, or other abnormal motor signs, such as hypotonia. Although motor defects are common, they are not the key features of ASD. Head deformity: About 15% of children with ASD have microcephaly, which is common in people with related diseases (such as Angelman syndrome and Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome). Among ASD children, about 1/4 of the head circumference is greater than the 97th percentile. Up to 70% of children with ASD have accelerated head growth in the first year of life, but these children do not necessarily become macrocephalic. People with ASD and macrocephaly may have mutations in the PTEN gene and are therefore at risk for hamartoma syndrome. Special skills: Some people with ASD have special skills (i.e., "scholar" skills) in areas such as memory, mathematics, music, art, or puzzles, despite having severe deficits in other areas. Other special skills include calendar calculation (calculating the day of the week on a given date) and precocious reading (spontaneous and premature mastery of single-word reading). This reading is usually formal, with little comprehension of meaning or understanding of the purpose of reading.

question: What are the signs of autism in adults, and how can one manage this mental disorder?
answer: Autism is a collection of characteristics some people inherit. I do not think it is a mental disorder as much as it is a collection of different characteristics of many people who are different from typical people in some similar ways to others who identify as autistic. But being autistic doesn't measure how intelligent you are or how successful you will be. If you think of autism as if a person's brain is a rubics cube, you can imagine a completed fully lined up rubics cube as being the typical conclusion someone is hoping to finish with. The autistic brain as a rubics cube might have everything lined up in a different way that sometimes, or in some cases, looks a bit chaotic. A different person, with autism, might finish with all red on one side, all yellow on another side, all blue on another side, until all six sides had only one color showing. That person might have done that because it looks interesting. They might be able to tell you mathematical facts sbout how many turns are needed to go from all one color sides to all one color stripes, or even complete two cubes at the same time. My impression of my own autism is that there is definitely something going on in my brain that has impacted me all of my life. It causes me to arrive at a literal understanding of language which requires me to translate it in order to know what is actually meant by the person speaking. What people see, however, is someone with a vast vocabulary and sophisticated skills in the English language, in reading, writing, literary criticism, who talks in an odd way, despite being conversant in four languages. But at the same time a person who finds printed forms of any kind to be in some ways incomprehensible, instructions baffling; a person who is often misunderstood by others or who misunderstands the point of certain verbal requests. I have gotten in trouble when using my judgement about random acts of creativity because my judgement evidently is weighted differently from what my supervisor’s judgement may have been, and some of my greatest successes have been viewed as coming from a place of deliberate transgression rather that intentional kindness and good will. But, if you were to meet me an hour from now you would likely never know that I am on the spectrum unless I wanted you to know. I generally don't make a point of mentioning it unless I sense that someone is misunderstanding something I do. I may mention that I am very poor at facial recognition; and I am not snubbing you. Once I hear you speak I will know who you are. I might avoid going to parties and give the impression that I don't care if I see friends or not. In reality, I know that parties will not give me a chance to converse about anything with a friend, and I will embarrass myself when I hide in the kitchen once I am overwhelmed and confused as to what I'm doing there. Autism is not something that people need to judge. The degree to which I am overwhelmed or stressed or confused is something I will deal with on my own and what you might see will be an ambiguous response to the situation, a pause to observe that helps me regain my equilibrium with society. If you want to be helpful, don't ask me to explain my behavior, and don't assume anything about it. if you need to know how I am feeling, just ask directly. Are you upset? Are you ok? May I join you? Would you like to go with me to lunch? If I say no thanks, I can't today. Don't assume it is a clear sign that I hate you. I will turn down invitations when I don't have the energy to behave typically at the same time as I am listening to a concert, or a lecture. I won't behave badly, but I will be focused on what's happening and not be great company. Anyway, that's my own view of how I try to manage my own version of the way I was born. I had no idea exactly what was different about me until I was around fifty. I wish I had known much earlier so I could have understood my own behavior and better understand what was going on, rather than feeling confused and broken.

question: Can babies show signs of autism or mental illness?
answer: Yes and no. Yes, there are certain signs of Autism (Autism Spectrum Disorder ASD) that can be detected fairly early. Stiffness when held and lack of social reciprocity are signs within the first few months that CAN be indicative of autism. The same is true for other disorders that are developmental in nature. ASD is caused by lack of development in certain regions of the brain. This can cause varying degrees of functioning that we do not define as neurotypical. The same is true of other cognitive ‘disabilities’ (controversial word, pick your own) such as down’s syndrome, PDD-NOS, or lowered IQ. That is because these ‘disorders’ are due to development of the brain, for better or for worse. What we classify as classic Mental Illness (Schizophrenia, Bipolar disorder, Dissociative identity disorder) will almost never be present in an infant. The reason for this is, these illnesses are caused by one of two things, both of which almost always happen later in life: Improper chemical balance And Trama DID, PTSD these illnesses all stem from trauma, I could talk all day about how and what but that’s not the question. Improper hormones are essential what cause Bipolar disorder and similar disorders, and they are more chemical imbalances. Not present as much in babies because simply it’s not as detectable and usually symptoms are exacerbated by puberty (that’s why the clinical onset of such disorders is early twenties to late teens…puberty is over and the patient realizes they should feel a certain way but don’t). Look in the DSM-V (Diagnostic Statistical Manual) for more information. Now, some children can have early onset of such illnesses that are chemical in nature, but because of the nature of the disease, it’s not going to be detectable until the child can start expressing themselves in words and actions. *******I am aware Body Dysphoric Disorder (I think they call it that now, they tend to change) is in the DSM-V as is Low-sex-drive in women. I personally do not believe that this is an actual illness. however, for the purposes of the question, BDD is present it is generally accepted from birth, however, the child is not aware of a sense of self until later in life, 3yrs and up, to be able to articulate how they feel about their body. Obviously something to do with sex-drive would not be apparent until after puberty. **Most people (including practitioners) don't consider these to be mental illness, but in order for insurance to pay for treatment, they must be kept in the manual to be diagnosable. There is anecodatal evidence to reflect that certain illness such as early onset schizophrenia and depression are experienced in infancy, with mothers and fathers reporting children that were very hard to soothe, or were obstinate, and unfeeling when held, that type of thing. question: What are the signs of autism in a 20-year-old girl?
answer: The signs of autism in adult women are really just the same sort of symptoms you normally see within autism. These can include: • Problems with direct eye contact • Preferring to be alone at times • Struggles with starting a conversation, or keeping one going • Sensory symptoms (Touch, Smell, hearing) • Having reserved/particular interests As you can see, autism in girls isn’t a whole lot different than autism in a boy for example; however, for years there has been a sort of social perception that autism in females is a lot rarer than in males. This may have very well been the case within data from around 10 to 20 years ago, and even findings from recent years have shown a ratio of 4:1 male to female autism diagnosis. However, current diagnostic methods have been found to misdiagnose many females with separate conditions such as ADHD and Bipolar disorder when, in actuality, they are autistic. It isn’t completely ludicrous as a disorder such as ADHD shares many mirroring symptoms with autism, however it is unfortunately a reason for why many adult women do not receive a correct diagnosis. In general, I’d say that the signs I’ve mentioned above prove that autism may be just as prevalent in females as it is in males, it’s just the historical studies that have falsely painted autism as a male-dominated condition. Hopefully, modern research can soon help to dispel this belief and provide some support to the autistic girls in our community.

question: Is being unaware of danger always a sign of autism?
answer: Autistic individuals are aware of danger. We fear just as much, if nor more so, than NTs. However, our lack of connectivity when we go into hyper focus (this blocks our communication completely at times) can cause us to disregard our environment completely. This includes danger. We are not ALWAYS unaware of danger, in fact a sign can actually be if there is an inappropriate amount of fear at times where there should be none at all. In example; Your daughter won't flush the toilet, or when she does, she runs from the bathroom crying afraid she will be sucked down... and she is 12 not 2 . Yet, she doesn't mind walking to the grocery store completely alone and buying her own lunch then walking back to school. That, she actually enjoys. It is more the social disconnect and the inability to perceive the surroundings that cause the indifference to danger. There are many reasons why someone would display these types of behaviors, however this is common amongst those who are on the spectrum.

question: My toddler just turned 16 months and he walks all the time on his tippy toes. Developmentally, he is looking well. He doesn’t show any signs of autism. Is there a cause for concern?
answer: Sometimes children with cerebral palsy walk this way, it's because the muscle tone in the back legs are high toned or too tight that they can't put their feet flat on the floor when they walk so they walk on tip toes. There could be lots reasons why a child walks this way but it's important to see your gp, get a referral to a neurologist who can run tests to confirm the cause of this walking. In certain cases, cerebral palsy can be seen on an MRI scan of the brain but usually a diagnosis of cerebral palsy is made by examination of muscle tone, reflexes and ruling out other medical conditions. Cerebral palsy itself is not a learning disability or social communication disorder, cerebral palsy is a physical condition that affects mobility. Other conditions can run alongside CP like autism, ADHD and dyspraxia but its important to not assume CP as a cognitive impairment. I have mild cerebral palsy alongside dyspraxia and global developmental delay as a child but I do normal activities, going to uni for teacher training and mostly independent.

question: Are contradictory thoughts a common sign of autism?
answer: The only contradictory thoughts for me, that I can think of, are when I'm forced to compliance to break a set of rules I've set for myself. I don't believe in any god or gods. I've been a boy scout, and a Sailor. I have a code and a set of morals that I do everything I possibly can to live by. I've been able to argue myself into compliance with my own convenient silver linings, and I don't like it at all. I can usually get by on just my rules, that I keep higher than someone could reasonably expect of me, but then there's always this expectation that I need to be like everyone else to do the bare minimum; absolutely no cherries on top (a metaphor for quality). I'm willing to “put the cherry on top" when no one's looking in secret, so that it seems I've broken my rule(s), and then things just continue functioning as they should. I don't want to solve the same problems again and again, just because someone won't let me do what I do. Given that, I'm betting that contradictory thought might be more a characteristic of “normies”, with a constant “but that's different" which looks to me like system discontinuity due to a lack of knowledge for their own set of completely arbitrary rules.

question: Can a child with ADHD have repetitive stimulating behaviours without also having autism? My child shows no other signs of autism besides stimming movements, which he stops if I ask, otherwise, he meets some criteria for ADHD.
answer: Both disorders can come with some sort of physical behavioral symptom, and can even be the same manifestation. BUT the cause & reasons for them are entirely different. ADHD people are often very fidgety and restless. Leg twitching, hair twirling, rocking and wiggling, etc. Often the twitching is a outlet for energy that would otherwise be spent running around, pacing, etc. The in-place restless behavior is necessary for them to stay seated and paying attention at all. It’s either twitch or get up and move around, they can’t stay still for long. So if it’s antsy, fidgety energy, then that’s just one more ADHD symptom. An absence of this does NOT rule out ADHD, as there are two types: the fidgeting and the daydreaming (and plenty who do both). The rest of the ADHD symptoms do overlap across both types. Autism ALSO can have a fidgeting-like behavior that can also be twitching, hair twirling, rocking, wiggling, etc. BUT in the case of Autism, it’s a self-soothing behavior. It’s a way for them to create their own internal stimulus as an attempt to counteract whatever external stimulus has overwhelmed them. So if the stimming behavior is them trying to calm down or block out the world, then it’s one more Autism symptom. Really it’s not always so clear cut, so I’d suggest you talk to a mental health professional specializing in diagnosing and treating things like ADHD and Autism. Only with a professional with experience in those two disorders can you have a definitive diagnosis. Also keep in mind that both of those are spectrum disorders. It’s possible to have them, but in such a mild form that no assistance or treatment is required. Autism and ADHD, like all other mental health issues, are only addressed when the condition negatively impacts the life of the person with the disorder or those around them.

question: Is not feeling comfortable or not wanting to talk to people all the time a sign of autism?
answer: It can be, but not necessarily. Let me introduce you to a couple of words. It sounds like you’re needing them. These words are shyness and introversion. Being shy and/or being an introvert are completely normal things, and they don’t mean you have autism. Not feeling comfortable around people and not wanting to talk to people all the time could just mean that you’re shy and introverted, as I said above. However, if you feel it goes beyond simple introversion, and you feel you’re having problems with it or it’s having an impact on your life, then it could be something, but it’s still not necessarily autism. So, what else could it be? Well, that would require a bit more information, but I’ll outline a few things for you.Depression - someone with clinical depression [that’s more than just feeling sad or having an off day or two, everyone has those. This is a mental health issue] might not want to be around people. If you’re used to being around people and enjoying it, and you’ve stopped enjoying it and stopped bothering with it all of a sudden, it could be the reason. However, you’d also have to have had other symptoms of depression for a minimum of two weeks. Ceasing to enjoy being around people and talking to people is just one of the many ways a depressed person may experience a change in habits.General Anxiety Disorder [GAD]. Again, this is more than ordinary worries, minor stresses, etc. and those with it can again see changes in their social and other parts of their day to day lives.Social Anxiety Disorder. Are you not being social because you fear rejection, or you’re anxious around crowds? If so, then it could be social anxiety.Avoidant Personality Disorder [AvPD]. Personality disorders are a little bit different from other mental illnesses. Most mental illnesses are due to chemical changes, or chemical differences in your brain. Personality disorders are to do with how you’re hardwired as a person and they develop with you through life. Avoidant Personality Disorder is one of the ‘anxious cluster’ or cluster C personality disorders and those who have it tend to avoid stressors and triggers as their main coping mechanism, and a big part of AvPD is similar to social anxiety disorder.So, I’ve outlined what else it could be, but now, back to autism. Autism is a huge spectrum and has a ton of different traits. It affects everyone on the spectrum differently from one person to the next, and there’s more than just one aspect to autism. What you’ve mentioned can be part of the social component of an autism spectrum disorder, but here’s what else you need to know as well:May have delayed speech [not all autistic people have this].Unable to relate to peers. May enjoy spending time with older or younger people.Indifferent to or rejects social norms. This can include behaviour, clothing, manners, etc.Has significant difficulties establishing and keeping friendships and relationships.May have echolalia [repeats words and phrases heard].May lack social/emotional reciprocity.May have special interests, which they can research and talk about at length.There are other aspects of autism as well, which you’d have to meet the criteria for as well, but that’s the social aspect. What you said can be to do with autism, but if it is, it may be that one of your traits is that you are anxious around people or it could be co-morbid social anxiety.

question: What are the signs of autism in children? How can you differentiate between autism and difficult behavior?

question: What are the signs of autism that nobody talks about?

question: Is getting attached to certain objects and concepts a sign of autism in children?
answer: Getting attached to certain objects and concepts can be a characteristic that is sometimes associated with autism in children, but it's important to note that not all instances of attachment to objects or concepts necessarily indicate autism. Autism, also referred to as Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), is a complex developmental condition that affects communication, social interaction, and behavior. It presents a wide range of symptoms and traits that can vary greatly from person to person. In some cases, individuals with autism may develop intense interests or fixations on specific objects, topics, or activities. This intense focus on certain things can sometimes be more pronounced than what is typically seen in neurotypical individuals. This can lead to behaviors such as repeatedly talking about a specific subject, having deep knowledge about a niche topic, or displaying a strong attachment to particular objects. However, it's important to recognize that attachment to certain objects or concepts is not exclusive to autism. Many children, both with and without autism, can develop strong attachments to things like comfort objects (like a favorite blanket or toy) or specific areas of interest. Diagnosing autism involves considering a range of behaviors and characteristics, not just attachment to objects or concepts. Other core features of autism include difficulties with social communication, repetitive behaviors, sensory sensitivities, and challenges in understanding and expressing emotions. If you suspect that a child might have autism, it's essential to consult with a qualified healthcare professional, such as a pediatrician or developmental specialist. A thorough evaluation is necessary to determine whether the child meets the criteria for an autism diagnosis and to provide appropriate support and interventions if needed.

question: How do teachers spot signs of autism that parents might miss?
answer: First of all, being a parent doesn’t come with instructions. Especially with your first child, you have no point of comparison—you don’t know what to expect. You’re often isolated, particularly if you’re a stay-at-home parent, possibly looking after a second child too, and you assume your child’s quirks and behaviours are what they should be. Even when you have another child to compare them to, you can still miss things—because every child is different. People around you constantly tell you there are many degrees of “normal”: some kids start talking at 6 months, others much later; some are picky eaters, others aren’t; some are very social, others shy. There’s also a massive difference between boys and girls. Talk to other parents and mention that a health visitor or paediatrician suggested your child might be on the spectrum. You’ll often get well-meaning but ignorant responses like, “Oh, don’t worry, he doesn’t look autistic.” That alone can make you doubt yourself and think you’re being overly cautious. You tell yourself your child has the right to develop in their own time, and eventually, they’ll catch up. Teachers, though, are in a different position. They have training, know what developmental milestones to expect, have worked with many children, and have a classroom full of peers to compare behaviours against. That gives them a clearer context to spot signs that a parent might dismiss as “normal differences.” Also, school can be a more stressful and revealing environment for an autistic child. Social interactions—one of the key areas where autistic traits often show—are much more demanding in a big, noisy classroom than in a familiar setting like a park or home, with just one or two well-known kids. The increased sensory input, pressure to follow group instructions, socialising in large numbers—all these things can make it harder for a child to mask their traits, so signs of autism can become more visible to an observant teacher. I’m not saying it’s “easy” for teachers to spot autism—they have a lot on their plates already—but they do have more tools, support, and opportunities to notice the signs than many parents, who are often just trying their best to get through the day without a roadmap. In short, it’s not about being a “better observer”—teachers and parents have different perspectives and experiences when noticing developmental differences.

question: Is expressive language disorder in a 4 to 5-year-old kid a sign of autism?
answer: Language impairment can be a stand alone diagnosis. In other words, you can have language impairment but nothing else. But children with autism have a range of language impairment. In fact, one of the diagnostic criteria for autism is language impairment. It's important to realize that language impairment is a blanket term. There is obviously a range of severity, but there are also 5 categories of language impairment.Pragmatics. This is our social use of language and is seen in children with autism. Examples include maintaining eye contact, topic introduction and maintenance, reading introduction and leave-taking cues, appropriate topics of conversation, etc.Syntax. This is best described as grammar, or the rules governing sentence structure in both spoken and written language.Semantics are the rules governing word knowledge, ie vocabulary.Morphology are the rules governing parts of words. For example, adding /s/ to the end to indicate a plural noun.Phonology are the rules governing the specific sounds of language. For example, knowing that a squiggly line makes the /s/ sound, and that sound comes through the middle of the mouth and not the sides.I suggest that you contact the school about your concerns. The speech language pathologist should be able to answer your specific questions. If that's not an option, most universities have a speech language pathology clinic where graduate level students are under supervision of a licensed SLP. Those clinics are usually run on a sliding scale pay rate.

question: What symptoms are present in an "autism spectrum disorder" diagnosis?
answer: In plain English, autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disability that can affect the ways a person interacts, communicates, and behaves. As I understand it, the spectrum itself exists on two axes:Deficits in social interaction and social communication. Known as Criterion A symptoms.Restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. Known as Criterion B symptoms.So, really, the autism spectrum itself looks like this:Less of a linear spectrum, and more like a pie chart. In all forms of ASD, the symptoms one is experiencing is rated by levels numbering 1–3. Level 3 requires very substantial support, level 2 requires substantial support, and level 1 requires support. This is where people get the idea of “low” and “high functioning” labels from, but that’s misleading. These merely just describe the levels of support this person might need with how they experience ASD. There is no low or high-functioning autism. There is just autism, and it’s important to understand that ASD requires support. Some only need a little, some need a lot. Remember, if you know someone that’s autistic, then you’ve met only one person that’s autistic. Everyone’s unique. The DSM-V describes the Criterion A symptoms as:Socially Awkward. Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, ranging, for example, from abnormal social approach and failure of normal back-and-forth conversation; to reduced sharing of interests, emotions, or affect; to failure to initiate or respond to social interactions.Strange Way of Interacting With People. Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction, ranging, for example, from poorly integrated verbal and nonverbal communication; to abnormalities in eye contact and body language or deficits in understanding and use of gestures; to a total lack of facial expressions and nonverbal communication.Overly Logical. Deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships, ranging, for example, from difficulties adjusting behavior to suit various social contexts; to difficulties in sharing imaginative play or in making friends; to absence of interest in peers.The DSM-V describes the Criterion B symptoms as:Stimming. Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech (e.g., simple motor stereotypes, lining up toys or flipping objects, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases).Love of Rules and Routines. Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, or ritualized patterns of verbal or nonverbal behavior (e.g., extreme distress at small changes, difficulties with transitions, rigid thinking patterns, greeting rituals, need to take same route or eat same food every day).Hyper-fixated Interests. Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus (e.g., strong attachment to or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessively circumscribed or perseverative interests).Sensitivity to Sensory Stimuli. Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g. apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement).The bold parts are a more simplified and practical view of the rather overly clinical way of describing the symptoms. So when observing someone you think might be autistic, you’re looking for someone that’s a bit socially awkward, has a strange way of interacting with people when they’re being social, they come off as a bit too literal and logical minded, leading to misunderstandings and issues, they engage in stimming behavior a lot, they crave schedules, routines, and rules, and changing them suddenly causes them distress, they have what we call special interests, or very laser focused interests that can sometimes lead to an uneven skill set, and finally, look for sensory issues. Not every autistic person is going to experience all of these symptoms, and some will be more intense than others. Think of the first three symptoms as how they interact with other people, and the final four symptoms as how they act when they’re by themselves. To meet the diagnostic criteria, the DSM-V requires that you meet all three Criterion A symptoms, and you meet two of the Criterion B symptoms. Also, for these to be classified as symptoms, they must be pervasive, the symptoms were present from early childhood, and they limit or impair everyday functioning. Those are the additional criteria for this to be considered Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). It’s up to the clinician to describe the severity of the symptoms, and every person is going to be unique, thus, that’s why autism is a spectrum disorder. Everyone experiences it a bit differently, and as a result, they’ll require different levels and kinds of support. Some will need a little support, some will need a lot. I know this was a bit more of a clinical way of looking at ASD, but the plain English way of looking at it is that an autistic person is:Socially awkward.They have a strange way of interacting with people.They come off as too logical or literal minded, leading to misunderstandings and issues.They engage in stimming behavior a lot.They love rules, routines, and structure, and any change causes distress.They have special interests that are very intense, sometimes to the point of them having an uneven skill set.They have sensory processing issues. They’re either really sensitive to sensory stimuli, or not sensitive at all to sensory stimuli.I hope that gives a very straightforward way of looking at autism. I know clinicians and us autistics tend to use clinical and precise language to describe the condition, but sometimes such language goes over people’s heads. Hope this helps!Originally answered: What symptoms are present in an "autism spectrum disorder" diagnosis?

question: I show some of the signs of autism, but not all of them. My brother shows these signs too. Should I be worried?
answer: First, regardless of whether you are autistic or not, you should not be worried about it. Autism is not a fate worse than death, it is a difference in brain wiring and brain chemistry that gives autistic people both strengths and weaknesses. Everyone, whether autistic or not, needs to learn how to manage their strengths and weaknesses to live the best life possible. Sometimes autistic people have very strong strengths, and very marked weaknesses, which means they can sometimes be exceptionally good at some things, and exceptionally poor at other things. The classic stereotype is the autistic person who is brilliant at mathematics, but clueless about relating to other people — but, like all stereotypes, only a few autistics are exactly like that. Autistic people can still live fulfilling lives, but their life will look a bit different to most other people’s. While about 1–2% of the general population are autistic — would qualify for a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) — quite a few more people have some autistic traits without being autistic. This is called the “broad autism phenotype” (BAP). BAP means that they have enough “autism” genes (pretty much everybody has some) to display a few autism-like traits, but not enough to make them clinically autistic — i.e. not enough to make them so different to the majority of people that they have experienced problems living in a world full of non-autistic people. (Look at the story of the “Ugly Duckling” to see how being different can be a major problem until you find out who you are and how to be yourself.) BAP is not a diagnosis, it is simply a research term. People with BAP are more likely to have autistic family members than people who are not BAP. One difference between BAP and autism (ASD) is whether you had significant clinical difficulties growing up or in adulthood as a result of your autistic traits. Autism is more than just being “unusual”. Another difference is whether you have enough autistic traits to qualify for a diagnosis: ASD is a syndrome — that is, a set of several behaviours. Unless you have a sufficient set of autistic behaviours, you are not autistic. No single autistic trait is enough to get you an autism diagnosis. An autistic diagnosis requires difficulties with reciprocity (back and forth interaction with non-autistic people), difficulties with forming relationships (with non-autistic people), difficulties with using and understanding non-verbal communication (with non-autistic people), and at least two types of behaviours from the following list:“stimming” (repetitive actions like rocking, swaying, pacing, flapping hands, and many other examples),“sameness” (e.g. a tendency to eat the same food, wear the same clothes, stick to a daily routine, hate changes, especially unexpected changes),“special interests” (an intense or unusual interest that may also dominate what you want to talk about with other [unwilling!] people), and …“sensory sensitivity” (an unusually heightened — or reduced — sensitivity to light, sounds, smells, tastes, touch, or other sensations).Whether you are autistic or simply BAP is not something random people on the internet can tell you. But either way, don’t worry. Try to understand yourself more, and learn how to use your strengths and manage your weaknesses — whatever they may be. There are quite a few autistic people on Quora who are married or in relationships, who have children, who have careers, even professional careers. There are autistic doctors, psychologists, social workers, teachers, lawyers, police … even an autistic admiral in the Royal Navy:Royal Navy Second Sea Lord reveals he is autistic | National Police Autism AssociationVice Admiral Nick Hine talks about his autism diagnosis and the need for neurodiversity in the Armed Forces In a candid interview with The Times ahead of World Autism Awareness Day, Vice Admiral Nick Hine has revealed that he is autistic. Vice Admiral Hine – as Second Sea Lord, the second highest ranking officer in […]https://www.npaa.org.uk/second-sea-lord-reveals-autism/Not only is Second Sea Lord a very senior naval position, the article is hosted on a website for the “National Police Autism Association” — in other words, there are enough autistic police officers in the UK to form an association with a website. No, autism is not something to worry about — but it is something to look into if you do have any difficulties in the areas I have mentioned above. Sometimes a diagnosis can help you understand yourself better and manage your life better. Many autistic people are actually relieved to gt a diagnosis — they finally understand why their lives have been so different to other people’s and why they have struggled with things that “other people” (i.e. non-autistic people) seem to do effortlessly. If you really are autistic, finding out should ultimately make your life better. But many of us have internalised so much of the stigma and stereotypes of autism from the non-autistic world around us that we can sometimes feel bad about ourselves when we get a diagnosis. This happened to me, but it did not last. I started tutoring autistic high school students, and soon realised that my autism was a positive qualification for working with them — I could help the students in a unique way because I was more like them than their teachers were. Non-autistic people grow up surrounded by a vast majority of non-autistic people, just like them. But autistic people usually grow up surrounded by people who are different to themselves, and this (like the baby swan in the story of the Ugly Duckling) can be very alienating. So giving autistic students the chance to interact with an autistic adult, doing fun autistic things — something I was very qualified to do — helped me get over the internalised stigma. I am not broken, I am the person I was meant to be.

question: I think my husband is autistic. How does an undiagnosed male present signs or symptoms of autism or asperger's?
answer: I recently sent a friend and her husband to a doctor for the ADOS-2 exam, and he ended up being diagnosed with ASD. I’ll list some of the main things to look for, but you will ultimately have to take him to a professional who specializes in autism. I’m not qualified to diagnose people, and I sometimes get things wrong (then again, the professionals misdiagnose people all the time). I’ll list common traits and behaviors, but they don’t necessarily apply to all aspies. Only the diagnostic criteria are common to everyone with ASD.Men with ASD tend to very attentive in the early stages of the relationship and then abruptly cut that off after winning the prize. This happens because he simply can’t maintain a high level of attentiveness indefinitely; it exhausts him and he falls back on old routines. The woman feels misled, which is understandable. However, I definitely wouldn’t call it deliberate false advertising.Deep absorption in a certain field of interest or study. It could anything from squirrels to the Akkadian Empire. Video games are common. Many men with ASD could be described as “nerdy” guys, such as the people you knew in high school who never left the computer lab to see the light of day, but that isn’t always the case. These special interests sometimes lead to lucrative jobs, although aspies aren’t particularly motivated by money alone.Egocentric. This isn’t the same as narcissism, so don’t get those mixed up. A narcissist is into himself, but men with ASD probably find themselves tiresome most of the time and they’re into whatever it is that interests them. Sometimes the egocentricity can be selfish, such as when he allows his routines to dominate her life and refuses to be flexible. However, a lot of this has to do with the psychological comfort derived from the routines, not pure selfishness. He might not remember things that you tell him about your life, such as your middle name. He might not ask questions about your life or seem to even care. He probably does love you very much, however. It’s just that those details might not interest him. I’m a pretty egocentric person myself, and an example from my life is the difficulty I have watching videos and reading articles that friends send me. It causes considerable stress to do it. Meanwhile, I send them links that interest me. I have a friend who is an aspie, and we basically ignore each other’s links most of the time. It’s ridiculous, I know. I know how she feels though when she sees that I’ve sent a link, so I don’t get upset. 4. Empathy deficit. I’m talking about empathy here, not compassion. Aspies are compassionate. Many have very kind hearts, too. By empathy I mean that he might not seem to notice when you’re under stress or when you’ve had a long day. Perhaps you even lost a loved one or something terrible happened, and he’ll carry on as he normally does. It’s not that he doesn’t care, but autistic people don’t seem to put themselves in other people’s shoes and then respond appropriately. If they are made aware of someone’s need for comfort, they prefer to do it in a practical way, not through emotional support or knowing what to say at the right moment. 5. Unusually honest. Men with ASD don’t lie as often. While they do sometimes lie, there’s a tendency to be blunt and sometimes brutally honest to the point of giving offense. They’re also less likely to have affairs, so there’s probably no need to hire a private investigator. Loyalty is definitely one of the benefits of an AS husband. Hard work is also common, and he’ll want to be appreciated for his practical contributions. 6. Storming out of the house during arguments. Aspies either leave or just completely shut down and go “walls up.” Explosive anger is common, but he usually won’t stay angry for a long time. 5 minutes later he could be back to normal again as if nothing happened. 7. Routines. As noted above, routines afford psychological comfort. 8. Gullible. He might have a genius IQ, but perhaps you’ve noticed that he’s easily tricked. This list isn’t exhaustive. If you aren’t sure, go to a professional who specializes in adults with autism. Again, I don’t do this for a living, but I do my best to pass information along.

question: What advice would you give to a teenager who is just starting to show signs of autism?
answer: Simply be proud of the person you are. Always remember that you are different. Difference is rarely a negative thing. Difference is fundamental to the diversity of thought of our society; it’s how new ideas are bred. I don’t mean to scare you, but the truth of the matter is that, if people catch on to these particular traits, they’re going to defer to psychiatrists. And if psychiatrists start to catch on to these traits, that’s when they’ll start to convince you that you’re disordered and wrong, simply for experiencing the world differently. I believe that is a horrible thing. However, I believe that it would be worse to disguise these aspects of yourself out of fear of psychiatry. Psychiatry is going to try to manipulate you into believing that you are “disordered”; there’s no sugar-coating that. However, manipulation feeds on doubt. Assuming you reject the notion that psychiatry is posing (which I certainly think you ought to, and if you don’t, you’ll soon start to), they can’t do a thing to you, so long as you remain resolute and truthful. Here’s an abbreviated version of my own experiences: I was diagnosed with autism at around 8 or 9 years old. I believed them at first, because until a certain age you just sort of believe everything that the grown-ups say. But I certainly was not happy about it. I wasn’t overjoyed and comforted by the fact that I “finally have an explanation”, despite how desperately psychiatry wanted me to accept that that was how was feeling. Rather, I felt deep sorrow and deep cynicism. I developed this peculiar sort of mistrust complex where I felt as though everybody was silently criticising me, because that was indeed what the psychiatrist was doing. So, when I left the school that diagnosed me and transitioned into secondary school, I was determined to disguise my diagnosis from my peers. However, one day, a few years back, I had a fascinating intellectual enlightenment and came to the conclusion that the medical model of autism has no logical nor moral basis. Sure, I experience the world differently, and I different thoughts, ideas, and behaviours; why should that equate to a disorder? Why can’t that simply be a difference, as it is with any other variation of character among humans? And, perhaps most importantly, why do I deserve to be treated this way? So, I became very vocal about being anti-psychiatry, and eventually confessed that I had been diagnosed with autism (which, evidently, I entirely reject). Again, I don’t mean to scare. But I don’t want to sugar-coat anything either. I simply want to make you aware of what the institution is going to attempt. Once you know this, you can deny anything the psychiatric industry tries to tell you. Or, you can go along with the whole rigmarole. We all know many have before. But as long as you have this information and the often silenced other side has been acknowledged, I have fulfilled my duty.

question: Is Einstein's mild autism the likely reason he was speech delayed and produced a schizophrenic son?
answer: We cannot determine if Einstein was autistic with any certainty. He was not diagnosed with autism, and definitely not with ASD as outlined in the DSM-5. But speech delay is one of the diagnostic criteria for ASD. It is also a diagnostic criterion for many other conditions. Further, there is a general trend to clump the neurodivergent attributes of the highly gifted in with ASD. This is a problem, because one of the great losses to current research is a lack of appreciation for the vast array of behavioural differences found in highly gifted people. Those differences, while similar to those found in people with ASD, donâ€™t have the same etiology (set of causes). This is my response to the question: Is Einsteinâ€™s mild autism the likely reason he was speech delayed and produced a schizophrenic son? There is research pointing out that schizophrenia differs significantly from autism. Some research has stated that people canâ€™t be both schizophrenic and autistic. I donâ€™t necessarily agree with this, but just because behaviours might overlap, it doesnâ€™t mean they have the same causes. I might jump around, shout and cry because I stubbed my toe, but I might equally jump around, shout and cry because I was caught speeding and got a ticket. Same behaviour, different causes. So, is autism the reason why it is reported Einstein had delayed speech? We will never really know because we cannot determine if he actually had any form of autism. It is popular to think he did, but we may yet develop a better understanding of highly gifted people and discover that his behaviour is peculiar to his intellect rather than possible autism. Could an autistic parent be causally responsible for producing schizophrenic off-spring? I think this is what you mean when you ask, â€œIs Einsteinâ€™s mild autism the likely reason he produced a schizophrenic son?â€ Research into the heritability of schizophrenia includes a longitudinal study from the mid-twentieth century that revealed that the sterilisation of schizophrenics (removal of schizophrenics from a population) did not reduce the prevalence of schizophrenia within the subsequent population. It is possible that we know less about the heritability of schizophrenia than we know about the heritability of autism, and that is a pretty damning thing to note. The most we can say is that family groups that contain people with autism also have been found to contain people with other conditions of the intellect, like ADHD, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. However, we also know that genius is part of that clustering, and so we tamper with those genealogies at the risk of damning our entire species. In other words, we donâ€™t know what is going on, and it is unlikely we will know what is going on in the immediate future. Personally, I think that creating environments where everyone can live their best lives, and allowing people who want to have children to have children, empowers humanity to create better societies and communities. Empowering our ability to nurture each other is our best chance at survival for our species. But that is my person belief. I wonâ€™t argue with anybody about it.

question: Can a person with autism and low IQ have no speech delay?
answer: Certainly, the spectrum of autism is vast and varied. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses a wide range of behaviors, abilities, and challenges. The term "spectrum" in ASD is significant, indicating that no two individuals with autism are alike, and the range of abilities can differ considerably from one person to the next. It is a common misconception that all individuals with autism will face challenges with verbal communication or will have delayed speech. While many individuals with autism do experience speech and language delays, not all do. Similarly, having a low IQ does not necessarily correlate with speech delays. It is entirely possible for someone with autism and a low IQ score to have typical speech development. It is crucial to differentiate between intelligence (as measured by IQ) and speech or language development. These are distinct areas of cognitive and developmental function. IQ tests primarily gauge problem-solving skills, logical reasoning, and certain types of memory, while speech development relates to the ability to produce and understand language. In practice, some individuals with autism might have fluent speech but struggle with other areas of communication, such as pragmatics (social use of language) or understanding non-literal language (like idioms or metaphors). Others might have challenges with speech production but have no difficulties with understanding or comprehension. In conclusion, while certain characteristics are commonly observed in individuals with ASD, the variability in presentation is vast. This underlines the importance of viewing each person as an individual and avoiding generalizations.

question: It seems that everyone has Aspergers. Should it be split from Autism?
answer: Asperger's (and autism spectrum disorder - ASD - in general) is diagnosed in about 1-2% of the population. It is probably under-diagnosed in women and girls. ASD is less common than ADHD and is a long way from being "everyone". Asperger's is more or less autism without speech delay or cognitive delay. Autism is more or less Asperger's with either speech delay or cognitive delay or both. There is no simple dividing line between the two. Both "speech delay" and "cognitive delay" can vary from barely noticeable to severely disabling. Speech delay by itself is not so useful as a basis for classification. Speech delay does not affect life outcomes in a major way if the person eventually learns fluent speech, as quite a few do. It would be more useful to classify autistic people according to their speech abilities at (say) age 10-12, rather than delays at age 3 (as stipulated in DSM-IV). These are some of the reasons for abolishing the distinction between Asperger's and autism in DSM5 - the prospects of autistic people can change over time as their abilities show (or fail to show) changes. Also, speech and cognitive abilities are only two of the characteristics of the autistic population. There are many other abilities and characteristics that autistic people have in quite varying degrees, from unimportant to very important: sensory sensitivity, emotional dysregulation, executive dysfunction, poor social intelligence, "stimming", etc. There is no single scale of "mild" to "severe" that encompasses all the different mixtures of strengths and weaknesses that are found among people on the autism spectrum.

question: Is it better for someone with Asperger's to say that they have Asperger's or that they're autistic?

Despite my (usually) good speech and practice with social scripts that allow me to "pass" most of the time, I have a lot of hidden impairments such as auditory processing difficulties and sensory sensitivities that are associated more with autism than Asperger's. Just in my online/real life circle of friends, I know people who had speech delays and classic autism who are doing better as adults than people diagnosed with Asperger's. it seems pretty common around here for young adults who received Asperger's diagnoses to end up living in group homes because they haven't mastered independent living skills. question: Do all people with Asperger Syndrome have high-functioning autism, but all people with high-functioning autism don't necessarily have Aspergerâ€™s Syndrome?
answer: Correct â€¦ with complications. Under DSM-IV, which was in force from 1994 to 2013, Aspergerâ€™s syndrome required that there be no significant delays in learning to speak nor in intellectual development. So these people were â€œhigh functioningâ€ by definition: they had average or above average intelligence and no delay in speech. Of course, they could be suicidal or completely unable to hold down a job because of problems with executive function â€” in other words, not functioning well at all â€” but they were â€œhigh functioningâ€ as narrowly defined by speech and intellectual ability. Autism, on the other hand, included people with intellectual delay â€” regardless of speech development â€” and also people with speech delay â€” regardless of intellectual ability. So some autistics had average or above average intelligence, but delayed or no speech. If such a person eventually developed full speech ability, say by age nine or ten, then they were described as â€œhigh functioning autisticâ€ â€” in their teen and adult years they had broadly similar issues to those who grew up with Aspergerâ€™s syndrome. What this indicated was a problem with the distinction between Aspergerâ€™s and autism. The official distinction depended on speech ability in early childhood (at age three, say), but this is not the best predictor of future life for autistic people. A better predictor is speech abilities around late childhood (age 9 or 10) rather than early childhood. Many autistic people learn speech slowly, but if they eventually develop full speech, then they are fairly similar to people with Aspergerâ€™s. If a person with speech delay is being diagnosed in early or mid childhood, it may not be clear how well they will eventually be able to speak. To complicate matters further, many clinicians would change the diagnosis from autism to Aspergerâ€™s if the autistic person acquired full speech ability. For example, I have heard Temple Grandin described as having â€œAspergerâ€™s syndromeâ€ even though she was clearly delayed in the development of speech â€” she can even remember being non-verbal. To complicate matters even further, if you followed the strict instructions of DSM-IV, most people diagnosed with Aspergerâ€™s syndrome should have been diagnosed with autism, as the manual stated that wherever a person met the criteria for both conditions, autism should take precedence as the diagnosis:â€œF. Criteria are not met for another specific Pervasive Developmental Disorder or Schizophrenia.â€ (DSM IV Criteria for Asperger's Disorder*)As autism was â€œanother specific Pervasive Developmental Disorderâ€, any one who met the criteria for autism should not have been diagnosed with Aspergerâ€™s. In practice, it was increasingly the other way: any autistic who had (eventually) developed speech and who had average or above intelligence was diagnosed with Aspergerâ€™s syndrome, not autism. This is one of the many reasons why Aspergerâ€™s syndrome was ditched as a separate category in DSM-5. Finally, the terms â€œhigh functioningâ€ and â€œlow functioningâ€ receive a lot of flak: autistics are notorious for having very uneven strengths and weaknesses, so a person with ability to pursue post-graduate study, say, may also lack the basic ability to manage their life, find their way around outside their home, and manage tasks that require planning. Each autistic person has a different profile of abilities and disabilities â€” and may be â€œhigh functioningâ€ one day, and â€œlow functioningâ€ the next. These days, we say â€œautism spectrum disorderâ€ (ASD) and can then add â€œwithâ€ or â€œwithout speech delayâ€ and â€œwithâ€ or â€œwithout cognitive delayâ€. Terms like â€œhigh functioningâ€ may be used colloquially, but they were never official terms and this remains the case in DSM-5.

question: What is stimming behavior? Is it okay for adults with ADHD to still engage in stimming behavior?
answer: Stimming behavior, also known as self-stimulatory behavior, refers to repetitive physical movements or vocalizations that individuals engage in to stimulate their senses, regulate emotions, or reduce anxiety or boredom. Common examples of stimming behavior include rocking back and forth, hand flapping, pacing, tapping fingers or feet, humming, and repeating words or phrases. Stimming behavior is particularly common among individuals with neurodevelopmental conditions, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and sensory processing disorder (SPD). However, stimming behavior is not exclusive to these conditions, and many people engage in some form of self-stimulation to regulate their sensory experiences or emotions. For individuals with ADHD, stimming behavior can serve as a coping mechanism to reduce hyperactivity, distractibility, and impulsivity. Engaging in stimming behavior can also help individuals with ADHD focus their attention on a task or relieve stress and anxiety. Therefore, it is generally considered okay for adults with ADHD to engage in stimming behavior as long as it is not harmful or disruptive to themselves or others. However, stimming behavior can also interfere with daily activities and social interactions, especially if it involves self-injury or disruptive vocalizations. In such cases, it may be helpful for individuals with ADHD to seek professional support to identify alternative coping strategies and reduce the impact of stimming behavior on their functioning.

question: Is stimming learned or innate?
answer: Learned, though with the proviso that they meet a biologically based sensory need. Differences in sensitvity to sensory stimuli are common in autism, and in the rather amorphous group of rather severe disabilities that get lumped into ‘profound and multiple learning disabilities’. They can take many forms and can be hyper of hypo sensitivities (over reaction or underreaction). One guy, N, I work with is hyposensitive to the often overlooked sense of proprioception (the sense that tells you about spatial relationships in the body without you having to actually look where you are). He likes spinning in a revolving office chair, it’s one of his ‘stims’, a way he has learned to deal with the lack of stimuli from normal movement, which (as far as we know) is due to his neurological make-up. L, a lady with PMLD I work with has the same hyposensitivity, but she likes pressing her hands together and dancing in her wheelchair (and will accidentally clobber anyone who gets too close, her eyesight isn’t great), and the best way of saying hello and getting her attention is to squeeze her hand. How much genetics has to do with a specific hyper or hypo sensitivity is unknown. Autism certainly appears to have a genetic cause, though there is nothing simple about the way it passes down through families, and nothing is known about how any genes that might be involved affect sensory input and processing. And this aspect of autism is widely variable and can affect a person to widely varying degrees and in different ways. N is hyspersensitive to light too, though other clients on the autistic spectrum I work with have no observable sensitivities or radically different ones. With L the case is a bit more clear cut, she has a rather rare single gene disorder that affects a wide range of central nervous system cells.

question: What is the difference between stimming behaviors in autism and other types of stimming behaviors? Are some stimming behaviors more acceptable than others?
answer: Naturally, some types of stimming behaviors are more acceptable than others. Humming on key — not so bad. But nose picking, head banging, hand flapping or repeating words over and over again — can be quite aggravating.Sometimes some people with ADHD do stimming such as hair twirling, toe tapping and nail biting.Stimming: autistic children and teenagersAbout stimming and autism Stimming – or self-stimulatory behaviour – is repetitive body movements or noises. Stimming might include: hand and finger movements – for example, finger-flicking and hand-flapping body movements – for example, rocking back and forth while sitting or standing posturing – for example, holding hands or fingers out at an angle or arching the back while sitting visual stimulation – for example, looking at something sideways, watching an object spin, or fluttering fingers near the eyes repetitive behaviour – for example, opening and closing doors or flicking switches vocal stimulation – humming, whistling, grunting, or repeating words or phrases chewing or mouthing objects listening to the same song or noise over and over. Many autistic children and teenagers stim, although stimming varies a lot among children . For example, some children just have small or occasional hand movements, whereas others spend a lot of time stimming. Stimming can also vary depending on the situation. For example, some autistic children and teenagers stim, or stim more, when they’re feeling stressed or anxious. Why autistic children and teenagers stim Stimming might help autistic children and teenagers cope with and manage strong emotions like anxiety, anger, fear and excitement. For example, stimming might help your autistic child to calm down because it focuses their attention on the stim or produces a calming change in their bodies. Stimming might also help autistic children and teenagers cope with and manage overwhelming sensory information . If your child is oversensitive to sensory information, stimming might reduce sensory overload because it focuses their attention on just one thing. If your child is undersensitive, stimming can stimulate ‘underactive’ senses. How stimming affects autistic children and teenagers Stimming isn’t a bad thing if it doesn’t hurt your autistic child or others. But some stimming can be self-injurious – for example, severe hand-biting. Stimming can also affect your child’s ability to learn in the classroom. For example, if your child is absorbed in watching their hands in front of their eyes, they might not be able to listen to their teacher or engage with their work. And stimming might lead to judgment or bullying by other people. We all use stimming sometimes. For example, some children suck their thumbs or twirl their hair for comfort, and others jiggle their legs while they’re working on a difficult problem or task. You might pace up and down if you’re anxious or fiddle with a pen in a boring meeting. Understanding and accepting stimming in autistic children and teenagers Many autistic people feel they should be allowed to stim because stimming helps them to manage emotions and overwhelming situations. Stopping autistic children and teenagers from stimming or reducing their stimming might make them feel more anxious, angry or sad. So it can be important to understand why your autistic child stims and show that https://raisingchildren.net.au/autism/behaviour/common-concerns/stimming-asd Stimming and Fidgeting Helps Some People with ADHD to Pay Attention - CHADDSelf-stimulatory and fidgeting behavior, often called “stimming," can be associated with ADHD and might actually help a child maintain focus.https://chadd.org/adhd-weekly/stimming-and-fidgeting-helps-some-people-with-adhd-to-pay-attention/

question: Do a lot of autistic people like repetitive and/or stimming behaviors?
answer: Do a lot of non-autistic people like repetitive and/or stimming behaviors? It’s a ridiculous question to ask, especially because “repetitive and/or stimming behaviors” is not something exclusively done by autistic people despite how we’re pathologized by psychologists and psychiatrists.Despite decades of intensive research, there is still no conclusive evidence that enables any of the major categories of mental disorder, including schizophrenia, depression,anxiety and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), to be considered a neurological condition in this way. The fact that there are some subtle group differences between people with some diagnoses and ‘normal controls’ in aspects of brain structure orfunction does not demonstrate the presence of a neurological disease. None of the findings are sufficiently specific or capable of differentiating between a person who is thought to have a particular mental disorder and one who is not. Diagnosis is still made on the basis of behaviour, thoughts and feelings that are reported by the individual or those around them and that depend, of course, on judgements about what is ‘normal’ and what is not. Moreover, the variations in brain structure or function that are detected,are most likely attributable to other differences between people who are labelled with psychiatric disorders and those who are identified as ‘controls’: differences in life experiences, social class, IQ and the use of psychiatric medication. [. . .] Historical analyses also reveal how psychiatry has evolved out of institutions developed to manage troubling behaviour or ‘deviance’. Productive interactions between people depend on the maintenance of social order. Confusion, despair, misunderstanding and dependency are all disruptive, though not necessarily unlawful. How they are understood and responded to is determined by prevailing social and political structures. Critical psychiatrists have highlighted how contemporary psychiatry is a current embodiment of the need to contain disruptions of social order, a perspective articulated by French philosopher Michel Foucault (Foucault 1965) and historian Andrew Scull (Scull 2015), as well as by Szasz. Foucault traced how attitudes to madness were transformed over the 17th and 18th centuries. As industrial society started to emerge, conformity and discipline became important. In France, the economically unproductive were brought together in the hôpitaux généreaux; Foucault identified this as the ‘Great Confinement’. In England, those without means were provided with minimal subsistence in the community under the Tudor Poor Laws, and then increasingly in the workhouse. Asylums reflected the segregation of ‘paupers’ into the ‘able-bodied’, who were kept in the workhouse and who could be obliged to work, and the incapacitated, who were moved to the workhouse hospital or the local asylum. Thus, the birthplace of institutional psychiatry can be considered arrangements for managing unproductive behaviour in a system of wage labour and industrial production. The growth of psychiatry in the 19th century legitimated this system by presenting it as a medical and therapeutic endeavour. From Foucault's perspective, ‘psychiatry is a moral practice, overlaid by the myths of positivism’ (Foucault 1965: p. 276). In the 20th century the medical framework became more strongly cemented, so that the social functions of mental institutions and services were further obscured.source: cambridge.org

question: What is autism? What causes it?
answer: Autism is a neurological disorder that can occur in developing brains that changes how the brain's nerve cells and their synapses connect and organize. There are a range of specific conditions that fall within the full spectrum of autism, but all are typically characterised by differing degrees of impaired social interaction, impaired verbal and non-verbal communication, and restricted and repetitive behavior. The exact cause or causes of autism are not fully understood and are still being widely researched. However, it is clear that there are a combination of genetic factors and environmental factors that have a causal effect. “Genetic factors” means a person’s susceptibility to the condition at the DNA level, given exposure to particular environmental conditions that may cause autism. It does not mean some people carry a gene that causes autism. It means that some people have genes that make them more susceptible to autism in the early stages of brain development. That susceptibility may be from an inherited genetic factor or a random mutation in their genes. “Environmental factors” means certain conditions that a person is exposed to as their brain develops that may act as triggers of autism where the person has genetic susceptibility. There is no agreed set of environmental conditions that are known to cause autism but some factors that have been found to be strongly linked include maternal gestational diabetes, maternal bleeding during pregnancy, certain maternal medications, maternal drug use (in particular exposure to intrauterine infections and first pregnancy. Autism has its roots in the early brain development that occurs during pregnancy. However, symptoms are often not obvious until between 12 and 18 months after birth due to the way the brain and behaviour continues to develop after birth. This leads some people to incorrectly conclude that a child has developed autism due to some event that has occurred during this later time period, such as when the child was immunised. Numerous scientific studies have concluded that there is no relationship between thimerosal-containing vaccines and autism. One promising field of reasearch is focussing on the link between particular gut bacteria found in some people, or more specifically, the complex compounds produced by the bacteria as a byproduct of their metabolization of food in the intestines. Some of these compounds enter the bloodstream and are able to penetrate the cell walls of certain brain cells. Once within the cell, they may be interacting with the cell at the DNA level to effectively switch off certain genes. Ironically, another study is looking at how the absence of a one specific species of gut bacteria causes social deficits in mice. It has been found that introducing this bacteria back into the guts of affected mice, some of the mice’s behavioral deficits, which are reminiscent of symptoms of autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) in humans, were reversed.

question: What are autism, Asperger's, and Autism Spectrum Disorder?
answer: Over the past 70 years, the medical community’s understanding of autism has evolved in both definition and implication. The public’s understanding of autism has changed as well, and though misconceptions persist, it’s now widely known that autism disorders exist along a wide spectrum of ability. Autism was most recently redefined in 2013, when the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) folded all subcategories of autism into one umbrella diagnosis called Autism Spectrum Disorder. It’s defined by two categories:impaired social communication and/or interactionrestricted or repetitive behaviorsThe autism spectrum can be a difficult one to interpret given its breadth and complexity. Rather than being limited to set characteristics and behavior, disorders along the spectrum can vary infinitely in combination and presentation, like colors on a prism. Though individuals share core symptoms, those with ASD range from severely challenged to extremely gifted and everywhere in between. The spectrum: a history Though autism by name is over a century old, the spectrum it encompasses is a very modern understanding of the diagnosis. The word autism was first used in 1908 to describe a certain subset of patients deemed schizophrenic, who were characterized by withdrawn and self-absorbed behavior. Then, in 1943 American child psychiatrist Leo Kanner published research describing highly intelligent children that displayed “a powerful desire for aloneness” and “an obsessive insistence on persistent sameness.” Kanner would call these traits early infantile autism; just a year later in 1944, Hans Asperger described the milder form of autism now known as Asperger’s Syndrome. In the 60s, misinformation prevailed when the “refrigerator mother” theory emerged, spreading claims that autism was caused by unloving parents. In 1977, scientists determined the cause to be a largely genetic one, and it wasn’t until 1980 that “infantile autism” was listed in the DSM. In 1987, the DSM replaced “infantile autism” with “autism disorder,” a more expansive definition closer resembling Autism Spectrum Disorder in function. Improved diagnosis capability and new types of behavioral therapy gave hope to parents, as did the emergence of special education in schools for children on the spectrum. After more progress (expansion of diagnosis) and missteps (a now-discredited 1998 study blaming vaccines for autism), 2013 brought about the current ASD definition and the spectrum as we know it today. ASD: What it encompasses Everyone along the autism spectrum embodies, to some level, core traits associated with autism. These include difficulty with social skills, empathy, flexible behavior and communication. Along the spectrum exist disorders that have more specific definitions. These are:Classic Autism: Also simply called “Autistic Disorder,” individuals with classic autism closely characterize traits associated with the disease such as language delays, trouble with communication, and unusual behaviors and interests.Asperger’s Syndrome: Individuals with Asperger’s display milder side effects of autism. They may have some social challenges as well as unusual behaviors and interests, but lack any impairment in language or intellectual development.Pervasive Developmental Disorder (Not Otherwise Specified): Also called “atypical autism,” individuals with PDD-NOS may meet some but not all of the traits associated with autism and Asperger’s. They typically display fewer or milder symptoms, causing challenges in one area rather than several.Individuals on the spectrum also range from low to high functioning. Those with Asperger’s or PDD are more likely to be high-functioning, and may even display extreme intellect or above average IQs. Low-functioning individuals may have severe to moderate learning disabilities that may or may not be overcome with therapy. Not under the spectrum but related to it are two rare but severe conditions: Rett syndrome and childhood disintegrative disorder. Is your loved one on the spectrum? If your child or family member exhibits difficulty with social interaction or communication, or displays abnormal behaviors and interests, there is a chance they are on the autism spectrum. Early signs include a lack of language skills or unusually obsessive behaviors. Children exhibiting these characteristics should be examined by a professional team with experience diagnosing autism. It may not be immediately apparent where on the spectrum they fall (if at all), but the sooner the diagnosis the closer you will be to providing the best possible emotional and physical support. To learn more, visit the SAILS Group online at http://sailsgroup.org/blog
