question: Why is autism considered a spectrum disorder?
answer: Autism is also known as a “spectrum” disorder because there's wide variation within the type and severity of symptoms people experience. Autism Spectrum disorder may occur in ethnic, racial, and economic groups. treatments and services can improve an individual's symptoms and skill to function. A diagnosis of Autism spectrum disorder now includes several conditions that wont to be diagnosed separately: Autistic disorder, Pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified (PDD-NOS), and Asperger syndrome. These conditions are now all called autism spectrum disorder.Symptoms are recognized between one and two years of age. It may vary with person to person. Children or adults with Autism spectrum disorder might: 1. Not point at objects to point out interest 2. Not check out objects when another person points at them 3. Avoid eye contact 4. Want to be alone. 5. Social interaction affected 6. Poor attention span 7. Poor concentration 8. Repeat or echo words or phrases said to them. 9. Have trouble expressing their needs using typical words or motions 10. Repeat actions over and over again 11. Have trouble adapting when a routine changes 12. Have unusual reactions to the way things smell, taste, look, feel, or sound Asperger's syndrome may be a condition on the autism spectrum, with generally higher functioning. Asperger syndrome (AS), also referred to as Asperger's, maybe a developmental disorder characterised by significant difficulties in social interaction and nonverbal communication, alongside restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests. As a milder autism spectrum disorder (ASD), it differs from other ASDs by relatively normal language and intelligence. Although not required for diagnosis, physical clumsiness and unusual use of language are common. Signs usually begin before two years aged and typically last for an individual's entire life. The syndrome is known as after the Austrian paediatrician Hans Asperger, who, in 1944, described children in his care who were clumsy, and lacking in nonverbal communication skills and understanding of others' feelings. The modern conception of Asperger syndrome came into existence in 1981 and went through a period of popularization. It became a standardized diagnosis in the early 1990s. Symptoms : Problems with social interactions, restricted and repetitive behaviour. PDD-NOS or pervasive developmental disorder-not otherwise specified, was one of the categories of an autism diagnosis.In the past, a diagnosis of PDD-NOS was given if an individual decided to possess some symptoms of autism but didn’t meet the complete diagnostic criteria for conditions like autistic disorder and Asperger’s syndrome. PDD-NOS was diagnosed when an individual had impairment in social skills, the inability to successfully interact with other people, problems with verbal or nonverbal communication, or stereotyped behaviour, interests, and activities. PDD-NOS only applied to people who didn’t have any of the following diagnoses: 1. Specific pervasive developmental disorder 2. Schizophrenia 3. Schizotypal personality disorder 4. Avoidant personality disorder PDD-NOS also included the diagnosis of atypical autism, which was used when an individual’s symptoms didn’t meet the full criteria for an autistic disorder diagnosis, either because the symptoms appeared or were diagnosed at an older age, they weren’t the typical symptoms of autism or both.

question: What is autism burnout, and how does it affect you?
answer: I had what I called a total breakdown about 15 years ago. The pivital moment was when I broke the cycle of unresolved disputes between me and my husband. I am choking up and tears are threateniing to burn my eyes. I had written myself off as a gonner. I had the biggest meltdown of my life. End of one life. Begining of seven years of hell on earth, and my gradual rebirth as someone I knew and recognised complete with Aspergers. Aspergers suddenly made sense of many mysteries that had puzzled me since my earliest years. I retreated inside myself. My stress levels were off the scale. At first my 15 yr old son was the only one who could communicate with me. He spent 6 weeks (summer holdays) with me 24 hrs a day, mostly in the bedsit we shared at the family hostel. When he got me so I could walk to the shop on my own and come back with milk or bread, he made that my special job. He prompted me to do everything I needed to do, but could not think of by myself. Then he said “I’ve got to go to school now Mum. I need you to look after me. Food, clean clothes, somewhere to live. You know, Mum, the whole deal.” He had given me respite, and then given me a purpose. I could make myself do things for my son, that I would not have done for myself. I still experienced:increased meltdowns and sensory sensitivityphysical pain and headaches, bewilderment, deep anxiety and depressionphysically shutting down, including the loss of speech. I was heartbroken.Autistic burnout affected all aspects of my life, and this makes it different from professional burnout, which is related to work. That was then and this is now. My work life had always been the successful part of my life. I am a good earner. I worked my socks off, and sent my son away to university when he was old enough. I told him it was his duty to himself. His rite of passage. I made sure he had a home to come back to. Free, like a bird. Free to fly away, and free to come home again. People like me. They make friends with me. I am now thriving and take my place to give a hand up in our mutual support network. I like myself, and will never feel I have to apologise for myself again. Burn out is burn out who ever you are. It will not happen to me again.

question: What is autism and how do you know if you have it?
answer: It's possible to have poor social skills without having autism. Some people didn't have the proper environment or opportunities to develop social skills, and some people are just not particularly good at this set of skills without being so bad that the problem is pathological. By way of comparison, some people are better at sports than others, but not all people who are not especially good at sports have something wrong with them, like cerebral palsy. At any rate, you need a professional to make a diagnosis. Someone like a clinical or developmental psychologist, a psychiatrist, or neurologist is the sort of professional you need. Start with your regular doctor (your GP) and ask for a referral. If you don't have a regular doctor, go to a clinic, explain your concerns, and say that you want a referral to a professional who can diagnose autism. Even if you don't get an autism diagnosis, you may still have maladaptive behaviors, but you can work on them. Ask for another referral to a clinical therapist, and explain to this person that you have difficulty with social skills, reading people's body language, and knowing what is expected in interpersonal situations. A therapist can give you a crash course in what you might have missed out on growing up, for whatever reason. If you want to explore the reasons, you can do that too, but it isn't necessary. It will be your choice. Actually, even if you do get an ASD diagnosis, you can still ask for a crash course in social skills and behaviors from a therapist.

question: What is the heritability of autism?
answer: This is a tricky question as it involves both genetics and epigenetics as well as clearly discernible evidence that autism is indeed passed along from one generation to the next. Let’s take a closer look. Genetics: A man or woman with autism who has children has a greater than average chance of having children with some kind of presentation of autism—ADHD, OCD, ADD, anxiety, sensory integration issues, learning disabilities or other diagnoses. Also, when one sibling is affected with autism, other siblings have a much greater chance of having some kind of diagnosis—maybe not as severe as the child on the spectrum, but something discernible and quantifiably different about them. This is especially true of male offspring. Females, perhaps due to their brain structures or extra leg of DNA (XX v. XY), seem to not present as often as their male counterparts. In addition, if a male child has a diagnosis of high functioning autism or HFA, subsequent male children have a greater than average chance of being more severely affected with autism. However, scientists have uncovered very few “autism genes” after parsing the DNA of thousands of individuals with autism. So, this is something that the scientific community is still working on. Epigenetics: Environmental insults such as alcoholism, trauma or even the age at which a parent gives birth can affect his or her offspring resulting in symptoms that are heritable for all future generations. Drug addicts who have children have a greater than average chance of having disabled children. Studies of Holocaust survivors found epigenetic traits such as depression and anxiety that have been passed down to grandchildren and great-grandchildren. There is a strong correlation between advanced paternal age and autism. Although 80% of all autism research is aimed at finding a gene or genes that confer autism on offspring, most autism researchers believe that many cases of autism that have no discernible origin are caused by epigenetic changes to a parent’s or child’s DNA. The parent may have been exposed to (for instance) pesticides, dry cleaning fluids, mercury or other brain-damaging chemicals. The child may have also been exposed in utero to pesticides, chemicals, alcohol, etc. The general idea is that these insults (trauma, environmental, etc.) change gene sequences within the individual’s DNA (consisting of amino acids ACGT). Certain “letters” drop off or are duplicated, making for copy number variations or CNVs. These changes, especially to particular areas known to affect brain function, cause an individual to exhibit autistic characteristics. Once a gene sequence has been changed, it does not repair itself in subsequent generations. This CNV will be passed along to future offspring. For many years, scientists and laypeople alike have observed that engineers, chess players, financial analysts, mathematicians, scientists and others in highly technical fields exhibit an appreciable number of spectrum characteristics including restrictive interests and social awkwardness. These individuals can, if given the right education and support, achieve great success in their fields of interest. A lot of their success has to do with pattern recognition and memory—signs of genius, really. Many of these successful professionals (and non-professionals) give birth to children who are on the spectrum—and not always at the high-functioning end. I hope this gives you a little insight into the “heritability” of ASD. It is complicated and shrouded in our lack of understanding of the brain, the gut (where more than 50% of neurotransmitter hormones are manufactured), DNA and the fact that autism is not really a disease but a cluster of symptoms that manifest across a broad range of brain differences.

question: What is autism train obsession?
answer: Many individuals with autism exhibit a profound interest in specific subjects, with trains being a common focus. This fascination, often referred to as a "train obsession," can be attributed to several factors: 1. Sensory Appeal: Trains provide rich sensory experiences through their movement, sounds, and visual patterns. The spinning wheels and rhythmic motion can be particularly captivating for those with sensory sensitivities. 2. Predictability and Structure: The structured nature of train schedules and routes offers a sense of predictability, which can be comforting for individuals who thrive on routine and order. 3. Detail-Oriented Interests: The intricate details of trains, such as their mechanics and design, align with the tendency of some autistic individuals to focus intensively on specific topics. 4. Cultural Associations: Media portrayals, like the "Thomas the Tank Engine" series, may also contribute to this interest by providing relatable characters and stories centered around trains. Understanding these factors can help caregivers and educators harness such interests for therapeutic and educational purposes, creating engaging learning opportunities that resonate with the individual's passions. *Note: While specific insights from Dr. Murli Singh, PhD, Chief Speech Therapist at Genesis Neurogen Neuro Rehabilitation Centre in Delhi, are not available in the provided sources, the information above reflects general observations regarding the affinity for trains among individuals with autism.*

question: What is autism, and how are people born with it?
answer: Autism is a social developmental disorder, at its core. That is, it’s a delayed (or perhaps “impaired”?) development in social skills. However, because it is such a pervasive difference in the brain itself, it is associated with many other common problems or strengths that vary greatly between people with autism. An autistic brain is larger, heavier, and has more neurons that are more interconnected. Different parts of the brain are larger or smaller than in a typical brain. For example, the amygdala (the emotional center of the brain) is much larger in autistic people, which I suppose could account for why autistic people appear to get so affected by emotions. (Referring to the work done by Simon Baron-Cohen, which is one of the leading experts on autism.) There is the low-functioning autism, non-verbal autism, or “classic autism”, then there is the high-functioning autism, and then there’s Asperger’s syndrome, characterized by having no delay in speech development and an average or higher level of intelligence (IQ testing). However, these have lately all been grouped into something called autism spectrum disorder, and those older terms are not used anymore. The only way for the brain to be so different is to have developed differently from the very start. It isn’t possible, for exmaple, that a vaccine could cause autism, as some nutjobs claim. If you tried to change a typical brain into an autistic brain, it would be such a drastic fundamental change that it’d kill you. You can’t damage a brain so that it becomes autistic, it needs to develop in a specific way from the start. It is highly genetic but appears to have more complicated reasons. It tends to run in families. Personally, I have autism, but my wife does not. We have two daughters, one of which is autistic, as well. In my extended family, there are at least two close relatives with autism on my father’s side. So it’s clear that it runs in families/lineages, even from my personal experience. But the exact cause of autism hasn't been determined, and it most likely has a few different causes, but still mainly tied to genetics. Last I read about this, geneticists have identified a section of 28 genes that appear to be related to autism. question: What is autism and what are its symptoms?
answer: Everything you need to know about autism What is autism? Autism spectrum disorder known as (ASD) is a broad term used to describe a group of neurodevelopment disorders. These disorders are characterized by problems with communication and social interaction. People with ASD often demonstrate restricted, repetitive, and stereotyped interests or patterns of behaviors. ASD is found in individuals around the world, regardless of race, culture, or economic background. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, known as (CDC), autism does occur more often in boys than in girls, with a 4 to 1 male - to - female with ASD. There are indications that instances of ASD are on the rise. Some attribute thin increase to environmental factors. However, experts debate whether there’s an actual increase in cases or just more frequent diagnoses. Compare autism rates in different states throughout the country. What are the different types of autism? The DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders) is published by the American Psychiatric Association (APA) and used by clinicians do diagnose a variety of psychiatric disorders. The fifth and most recent edition of the DSM was released in 2013. The DSM-5 currently recognizes five different ASD subtypes, or specifies. They are: with or without accompanying intellectual impairment with or without accompanying language impairment associated with a known medical or genetic condition or environmental factor associated with another neurodevelopment, mental, or behavioral disorder with catatonia Someone can be diagnosed with one or more specifies. Prior to the DSM-5, people on the autism spectrum may have been diagnosed with one of the following disorders: autistic disorder Asperser’s syndrome Pervasive development disorder-not otherwise specified (PDD-NOS) Childhood disintegrative disorder It’s important to note that a person who received one of these earlier diagnoses hasn’t lost their diagnosis and won’t need to be reevaluated. According to the DSM-5, the broader diagnosis of ASD encompasses disorders such as Asperser’s syndrome. What are the symptoms of autism? Autism symptoms typically become clearly evident during early childhood, between 12 and 24 months of age. However, symptoms may also appear earlier or later. Early symptoms may include a marked delay in language or social development. The DSM-5 divides symptoms of autism into two categories: problems with communication and social interaction, and restricted or repetitive patterns of behavior or activities. Problems with communication and social interaction include: issues with communication, including difficulties sharing emotions, sharing interests, or maintaining a back-and-forth conversation issues with nonverbal communication, such as trouble maintaining eye contact or reading body language Difficulties developing and maintaining relationships Restricted or repetitive patterns of behavior or activities include: Repetitive movements, motions, or speech patterns Rigid adherence to specific routines or behaviors An increase or decrease in sensitivity to specific sensory information from their surroundings, such as a negative reaction to a specific sound Fixated interests or preoccupations Individuals are evaluated within each category and the severity of their symptoms is noted. In order to receive an ASD diagnosis, a person must display all three symptoms in the first category and at least two symptoms in the second category. What causes autism? The exact cause of ASD is unknown. The most current research demonstrates that there’s no single cause. Some of the suspected risk factors for autism include: Having an immediate family member with autism Genetic mutations Fragile X syndrome and other genetic disorders Being born to older parents Low birth weight Metabolic imbalances Exposure to heavy metals and environmental toxins a history of viral infections Fetal exposure to the medications valproic acid (Depakene) or thalidomide (Thalomid) According to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), both genetics and environment may determine whether a person develops autism. Multiple sources, old and new, have concluded that the disorder isn’t caused by vaccines, however. A controversial 1998 study proposed a link between autism and the measles. However, that study has been debunked by other research and was eventually retracted in 2010. Read more about autism and its risk factors. What tests are used to diagnose autism? An ASD diagnosis involves several different screenings, genetic tests, and evaluations. Developmental screenings The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends that all children undergo screening for ASD at the ages of 18 and 24 months. Screening can help with early identification of children who could have ASD. These children may benefit from early diagnosis and intervention. The Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT) is a common screening tool used by many pediatric offices. This 23-question survey is filled out by parents. Pediatricians can then use the responses provided to identify children that may be at risk of having ASD. It’s important to note that screening isn’t a diagnosis. Children who screen positively for ASD don’t necessarily have the disorder. Additionally, screenings sometimes don’t detect every child that has ASD. Other screenings and tests Your child’s physician may recommend a combination of tests for autism, including: DNA testing for genetic diseases Behavioral evaluation Visual and audio tests to rule out any issues with vision and hearing that aren’t related to autism Occupational therapy screening Developmental questionnaires, such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) Diagnoses are typically made by a team of specialists. This team may include child psychologists, occupational therapists, or speech and language pathologists. Learn more about the tests used to diagnose autism. How is autism treated? There are no “cures” for autism, but therapies and other treatment considerations can help people feel better or alleviate their symptoms. Many treatment approaches involve therapies such as: Behavioral therapy Play therapy Occupational therapy Physical therapy Speech therapy Massages, weighted blankets and clothing, and meditation techniques may also induce relaxing effects. However, treatment results will vary. Some people on the spectrum may respond well to certain approaches, while others may not. Shop for weighted blankets here. Alternative treatments Alternative treatments for managing autism may include: High-dose vitamins Chelating therapy, which involves flushing metals from the body Hyperbaric oxygen therapy Melatonin to address sleep issues Research on alternative treatments is mixed, and some of these treatments can be dangerous. Before investing in any of them, parents and caregivers should weigh the research and financial costs against any possible benefits. Learn more about alternative treatments for autism. Can diet have an impact on autism? There’s no specific diet designed for people with ASD. Nevertheless, some autism advocates are exploring dietary changes as a way to help minimize behavioral issues and increase overall quality of life. A foundation of the autism diet is the avoidance of artificial additives. These include preservatives, colors, and sweeteners. An autism diet may instead focus on whole foods, such as: Fresh fruits and vegetables Lean poultry fish Unsaturated fats lots of water Some autism advocates also endorse a gluten-free diet. The protein gluten is found in wheat, barley, and other grains. Those advocates believe that gluten creates inflammation and adverse bodily reactions in certain people with ASD. However, scientific research is inconclusive on the relationship between autism, gluten, and another protein known as casein. Some studies, and anecdotal evidence, have suggested that diet can help improve symptoms of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), a condition similar to autism. Find out more about the ADHD diet. How does autism affect kids? Children with autism may not reach the same developmental milestones as their peers, or they may demonstrate loss of social or language skills previously developed. For instance, a 2 year old without autism may show interest in simple games of make-believe. A 4 year old without autism may enjoy engaging in activities with other children. A child with autism may have trouble interacting with others or dislike it altogether. Children with autism may also engage in repetitive behaviors, havedifficulty sleeping, or compulsively eat nonfood items. They may find it hard to thrive without a structured environment or consistent routine. If your child has autism, you may have to work closely with their teachers to ensure they succeed in the classroom. Many resources are available to help children with autism as well as their loved ones. Local support groups can be found through the national nonprofit The Autism Society. The organization Autism Speaks also provides targeted toolkits intended for the parents, siblings, grandparents, and friends of children with autism. Autism and exercise Children with autism may find that certain exercises can play a role in alleviating frustrations and promoting overall well-being. Any type of exercise that your child enjoys can be beneficial. Walking and simply having fun on the playground are both ideal. Swimming and being in water can serve as both exercise and a sensory play activity. Sensory play activities can help people with autism who may have trouble processing signals from their senses. Sometimes contact sports can be difficult for children with autism. You can instead encourage other forms of challenging yet strengthening exercises. Get How does autism affect girls? Because of its gender-specific prevalence, autism is often stereotyped as a boys’ disease. According to the CDC, ASDs are about 4 times more common in boys than in girls. However, this doesn’t mean that autism doesn’t occur in girls. In fact, the CDC estimates that 0.66 percent, or around 1 in every 152 girls, have autism. Autism may even present differently in women. In comparison to recent decades, autism is being tested earlier and more often now. This leads to higher reported rates in both boys and girls. How does autism affect adults? Families who have loved ones with ASD may worry about what life with autism looks like for an adult. A minority of adults with ASD may go on to live or work independently. However, many adults with ASD require continued aid or intervention throughout their lives. Introducing therapies and other treatments early in life can help lead to more independence and better quality of life. Sometimes people who are on the spectrum aren’t diagnosed until much later in life. This is due, in part, to a previous lack of awareness among medical practitioners. Seek help if you suspect you have adult autism. It’s not too late to be diagnosed. Why is autism awareness important? April is World Autism Month. It’s also been deemed National Autism Awareness Month in the United States. However, many advocates have rightly called for the need to increase awareness about ASDs year-round, and not just during 30 select days. Autism awareness also requires empathy and an understanding that ASDs are different for everyone. Certain treatments and therapies can work for some people but not others. Parents and caregivers can also have differing opinions on the best way to advocate for a child with autism. Understanding autism and people who are on the spectrum starts with awareness, but it doesn’t end there. Check out one father’s story on his “frustrations” with autism awareness. What’s the difference between autism and ADHD? Autism and ADHD are sometimes confused with one another. Children diagnosed with ADHD consistently have issues with fidgeting, concentrating, and maintaining eye contact with others. These symptoms are also seen in some people on the spectrum. Despite some similarities, ADHD isn’t considered a spectrum disorder. One major difference between the two is that people with ADHD don’t tend to lack socio-communicative skills. If you think your child has symptoms of hyperactivity, talk to their doctor about possible ADHD testing. Getting a clear diagnosis is essential to ensure that your child is receiving the correct treatment. It’s also possible for a person to have both autism and ADHD. Check out this article, which explores the relationship between autism and ADHD. What’s the outlook for people with autism? There are no cures for ASD. The most effective treatments involve early and intensive behavioral interventions. The earlier a child is enrolled in these programs, the better their outlook will be. Remember that autism is complex, and that it takes time for a person with ASD to find the program best suited for them.

question: On a cognitive level, what is autism?
answer: Have you ever seen a child’s mobile, the thing that hangs from the crib with several dangly things all nicely balanced? Well, a long time ago I learned that if you want to build a mobile, most people will start from the top, add two objects hanging from a bar, then try to hang other objects. It will be almost impossible to balance. I read that you need to start with the bottom elements first, not the top. Imagine the mobile as an upside down tree. In order to build the mobile, you don’t start with the trunk, you start with the leaves at the very ends of the tiniest branches! Take a quick peek here to see what I mean.How to Build / Make Mobiles / Kinetic SculpturesHow to Build / Make Mobiles / Kinetic Sculptures I’m a kinetic sculptor specializing in mobiles . I’ve received e-mails over the years asking to know how to make mobiles , which eventually prompted me to put together this page. It explains the basics about the balance structure that a mobile is made of, which is essentially a whippletree mechanism . It’s all about physics, which may seem complicated at first, but it’s actually really quite simple if you build the structure from the bottom to the top of the mobiles, just like Alexander Calder (who invented the art form of mobiles in the early 1930s) did. Look through the following four illustrations, then read the rest below. Part A weighs the same as part B – Balance point is right in the middle: Part A weighs more than part B – Balance point moves closer to part A, the heavier part: The following illustration might look more complex, but it’s really the exact same idea. All those lower parts marked as “B” count as just one part when it comes to the balance of the top part, it’s still only about the balance between part A and part B: And then it just goes on like that to the next level of the mobile: The trick is that you build the mobile from bottom to top . Start with connecting the first two elements at the bottom of the mobile and find the balance point between them. Then you connect the next upper element to that balance point, and again, find the balance point between the new element and the first two elements and so on. You can find the balance point by holding the connecting arm with your fingers and moving it back and forth, or if you want to be exact, tie a string around the connecting arm and move it back and forth until it balances. In Alexander Calder’s own words: “I begin with the smallest and work up. Once I know the balance point for this first pair of discs, I anchor it by a hook to another arm, where it acts as one end of another pair of scales, and so on up. It’s a kind of ascending scale of weights and counterweights.” – from Curtis Cate, Calder Made Easy, Horizon Magazine, vol. 9, no. 1 (Winter 1972). I would also recommend to take a look at a how-to article I wrote for Houzz: From the Artist: How to Make a Real Mobile Once you understand the basics on how to build this balance structure, anything goes from there. You can use whatever you like for the weights at the end of the arms, and you can play around with how you build the structure, make some arms longer than others, make some of them point in a more vertical direction than others, and so on. The possibilities are infinite. Oh, here’s something else to consider: There’s no need to understand this beyond what the above illustration shows, but if you’re interested in physics: there’s a balance point and a center of the mass (weight) for an object. If the center of mass of the object is above the balance point (meaning the majority of the weight is above the balance point), the object will fall over. If the center of masshttps://www.marcomahler.com/how-to-make-mobiles/As a general rule, folks with autism are said to “focus more on the details than the big picture.” This generalization bothered me for the longest time. “But, I have often have a much better big picture understanding of systems than most people. Why do they say I focus on the details?” And then I remembered the mobile. When I learn something, I find it difficult to start at the beginning of a textbook and learn anything in the order I’m “supposed to follow when learning.” What I realized is that I *do* focus on the little tiny details of a system. I learn about the things at the “bottom of the mobile” first because I can “achieve balance” at those levels. I may end up with dozens of separated pieces of a mobile and still have a giant black void in my mind when I try to see the big picture. Learning a brand new subject, where I have almost no context, is terrifying. It is like staring into a black void. I get anxious and worry that I won’t be able to learn how to do it. And so I read … and don’t understand. And then I look up words on Wikipedia and start to get an idea of how some of the smaller pieces fit together. Eventually … I get enough small pieces built … that they effing self-assemble in my mind and become a bigger picture. Because each individual piece is already balanced it is much easier for it to just snap into place where it belongs. I don’t build a whole picture. It is constantly building itself. The whole is something that is never quite complete in my mind. I don’t usually *see* the whole big picture, not even in my imagination. I often get “flashes” of it’s shape or how it moves but my visualization skills when I’m awake are almost non-existent. (My dreams are so real that they have been more vivid and real than waking reality, so this inability to visualize bugs the crap out of me!) The simulation of the whole exists as a constantly evolving structure in my mind. So, let’s say I helped develop a publishing workflow at my workplace. When my bosses come to me with an assignment I “look up and right” into my mind and they look “up and left” into the air next to my head to see what I’m thinking. (I’m not kidding. They never see it but they do wait for it!) I just realized at this moment, that when they give me the details of the assignment, those details snap onto the “bottom leaves” of the system and change how it balances. If there will be problems … I just wait for the Big Shape to start to break down … and as it does it “lights up” the branch where things fail. No, it’s not light. It’s invisible in my mind, I just get a “flash” and say “Um, this will need the Embassy Report but that’s not due until May and you want this out in April. That, and their budget feels way too small for 4-color slick print. Are we going to cut them a deal or will you need to talk them into cheaper paper stock?” If there are serious problems, piles and piles of them, I’ll have to go back to my office and “wait for the issues” to come up so I can write them all down. What am I writing down? Essentially … the leaves … where the details supplied in the request don’t match the details necessary for completion. So … my mind works almost entirely on balance. This is why neurotypical lies and/or sloppy communication can break my mind. I’m sure my mind isn’t exactly like all other autistic minds. I can see, however, why lies bother people on the spectrum more than neurotypicals. Autistic people need accurate data from the world in order to function. Lies are toxic to our minds. My mind literally will not solve problems if I have bad data. Actually, that’s not true. My mind will eventually realize the brain-balance is off … something I’ve been told doesn’t balance. This is another reason autistics may tend toward tech jobs. Technology is logical. Programming has strict rules that when followed produce results. A coding bug *has* a cause, therefore it can be logically hunted down. If a manager lies about what a piece of technology can do … they can be proven wrong. (They may still lie and say you don’t know what you are talking about. That is gaslighting and I endured more than a decade of it at work. It sucks.) Sometimes, my mind feels like I have a head full of buzzing bees and I can’t think. I’m not sure if that’s an autistic trait or part of my comorbid depression. Sometimes I can’t balance much of anything, can’t think straight, have trouble focusing and in general am not high-functioning anymore. I still *look* the same, though, which is annoying. “You are fine. You aren’t sick. Get back to work!” Sometimes I discover that the carefully constructed model that I have balanced … has some well balanced lies in it. And then I will freak out and have a meltdown. Yup. I’m a 50 something guy and when I am wronged or sense I’ve been led into a trap … anxiety starts, panic starts, anger starts … and I get furious and anger has been my undiagnosed autistic defense mechanism. I thought I was just rightfully pissed off. And loud. And, okay, blunt to the point of rudeness … “but they screwed me! And then they lied to my face! What am I supposed to do?” Anger meltdowns completely short-circuit my emotions and thought processes and my hand start moving and I start dropping F-bombs as they can often disarm other people … but it’s unprofessional and it sucks. I know this whole thing isn’t an objective cognitive description. It can’t be. People with autism often don’t look or act autistic! I’m such a Master Masker and I have gazillions of “neurotypically safe catch phrases” for all occasions! Everyone I’ve spent any time would say, “Oh, yeah. Dean is definitely Different.” But they wouldn’t guess I'm autistic. My own psychiatrist didn’t have a clue. There’s a lot more going on in my brain but I was only assessed Level 1 autistic in the past month, so I’m getting over “imposter syndrome” … “Nope, I’m not an imposter. I’m Autism Man!” Stay tuned. As I learn more about my own mind I will share.

question: Why has there been no cure for autism yet? If there is, what is it?
answer: I have high-functioning autism, and this means that I usually look normal on the outside. But I’m here to tell you that I am fundamentally different on the inside. By the time I hit adulthood, I learned to hide my autism to avoid unintentionally upsetting or insulting neurotypical people (our word for non-autistic). If I was standing next to you waiting for an elevator, I would make small talk and smile and you wouldn’t know I’m autistic. This is purposeful and requires significant intellectual investment, akin to taking an exam or solving a problem. I wish I could shout from the rooftops: You have no idea how hard I have to work to appear this way! Some neurotypical people try to relate to people with autism by saying things like, “I don’t like large parties either,” or “I can’t stand it when there’s a loud TV in the room.” I have no doubt this is true, but these neurotypical experiences are not like my autistic ones.You may not like large parties, but you are probably not in danger of having a meltdown in public. If there’s a loud TV, my brain cannot tune it out. Actually, I cannot tune out anything. Ever. That smell of popcorn from a co-worker’s desk? It hijacks my brain to the point that I have to take my work to another room if I am to have any hope of concentrating.Imagine having the acuity of your senses turned up to 11. Imagine being keenly aware of every single element of your environment, all the time, especially those you normally, reflexively ignore. Imagine that every time you walk out your front door, it is like being forced to walk too close to a wall of spikes that constantly threaten to impale you.Then imagine that, under this assault, you concentrate on maintaining an elaborate performance to relate to those around you while suppressing your natural mode of speaking and acting. Before I learned how to do this daily performance, people would cringe from my blank face, my monotone speech, my impatience with normal pleasantries.If it sounds exhausting and demoralizing, it is. But in trying to explain it to neurotypical acquaintances, I am often encouraged to just “be myself.” What they don’t realize is how dramatically different that self is from the bubbly, warm persona they know. Few are prepared for my taciturn way of speaking and my off-putting, emotionless facial expression. Few are prepared for literal responses to small talk.I have tried being myself, plenty of times, and the universally negative feedback I received from early childhood through college taught me that that self is not welcome in a neurotypical world. Neurotypical people claim to appreciate when someone is “being real,” but in my experience, giving people actual honest feedback is never the right response. In high school, I was told I “always know how to say the exact wrong thing.” I taught myself that whatever the first response was that came to my mind was inevitably wrong, so I would search for something nicer, even untruthful, to say.This performance, and the cognitive investment it entails, happens every time I leave the house. Otherwise, I’m at risk of being misunderstood and ostracized, something I and others like me have suffered many times throughout our lives.At one of my first long-term jobs, I ran into this same problem. After about six months, I was pulled aside by a supervisor and told “no one” wanted to work with me because of my “attitude.” This was feedback that took me completely off guard, and was humiliating and demoralizing, and again, I had no idea what she was talking about.I can’t describe how heartbreaking it is to hear that someone “can’t believe I didn’t know” that I had hurt them. A few years ago, a co-worker I had been close to abruptly stopped speaking to me. I begged her to tell me what was going on, but she adamantly refused. I left the job a couple of months later. I never found out what I had done to upset her.Sometimes people tell me I don’t “look” autistic (whatever that means). I am trapped in what I call the Autistic Paradox, too autistic to function comfortably in a neurotypical environment, but too apparently “normal” to get the sensory accommodations and solitude I need.The outside world is littered with things that could send an autistic person into a tailspin, like cellphones on speaker mode, flickering fluorescent lightbulbs and strong body sprays and air fresheners. When confronted with these overpowering sensations, my best option is to remove myself from the area — politely if possible, impolitely if not.This isn’t to say that there haven’t been small victories. There is a note in my file at the doctor’s office to let me wait for my appointment in the back, away from the noise of the TV. question: What is autism in females?
answer: Autism, or autism spectrum disorder [ASD], is a pervasive neurodevelopmental disorder, a type of neurological disorder. So, what this means is that an autistic person is born with a different brain wiring than non-autistic [neurotypical] people, it often affects their development and it affects multiple areas of their day to day lives. Areas affected by autism include: cognitive function, executive functioning, motor skills, speech/language skills, social skills, behaviour, emotions and sensory sensitivities. That’s a bit of an overview. Now, about gender differences, it’s been found by psychologists, doctors and scientists studying autism that autism often [but not always] manifests differently in males and in females, and this has led a lot of females to be missed until very recently. Seriously, not much was known about autistic females until the last five years or so. So, before then, it was thought that either autism was just something that affected boys, or that it was rare in girls. Now, it’s estimated that the ratio of autistic males to females could be around 2:1. Almost equal. Many of them still go undiagnosed and misdiagnosed with other conditions quite frequently as well, so this can mean autistic females are diagnosed later than boys - sometimes in the teenage years, sometimes in adulthood. Autistic traits in boys tend to be more obvious - they are more noticeably socially inept, they often don’t tend to be interested in socialising, they often prefer practical hobbies and interests such as building things out of Lego, and they tend to get noticed earlier on due to more behavioural differences and more obvious personality differences, such as being loud and domineering. Because of their tendency to be more interested in how things work than how people work, they often have the nickname “little professors”. This doesn’t apply to all autistic boys though - you can get boys on the spectrum with more subtle traits as well. Autistic traits in girls, however, tend to be more subtle - they are generally better at analysing neurotypical behaviour and masking their autistic traits and behaviours, they tend to be more interested in people, and when they can play with dolls to unpick social situations. Autistic girls also often prefer artistic hobbies, such as playing musical instruments, painting, drawing or writing stories and can often be very imaginative. They also have some differences in personality, but they’re more subtle differences. Whereas boys can be domineering, girls tend to be more passive. Because of their tendency to be more interested in how people work, they’re often called “little psychologists”. Again, this doesn’t apply to all autistic girls and you can get girls with more obvious autistic traits as well. You would have to: a. know quite a bit about autism in general b. know a fair amount about autism in females in order to know what to look for and c. be able to spend a lot of time with an autistic female to be able to get to know them in order to spot autism in females. You shouldn’t try to get a first impression from an autistic person anyway - first impressions usually aren’t accurate anyway, and especially in autism, they’re more likely to be inaccurate than in non-autistic people, especially if the autistic person you happen to be talking to happens to be good at masking their autism - that means they’re essentially putting on a persona in order to appear more “normal” to other people. So, you really need to spend time with the person to get to know them as who they are, rather than just meet them once and try to spot the traits your looking for from that one meeting - it’s highly unlikely to happen.

question: What does autism do to the brain? How is autism treated?
answer: Autism doesn't do anything to the brain, it is part of the brain. It is not a disease. People with autism are born that way. Autism is different in every individual, and there is no one-fits-all description of it. Some people with autism are more sensitive to certain stimuli (I cringe when I hear an electric toothbrush). Some of them have difficulties with social situations, with people on the less functional end sometimes never learning to talk. Lots of people with autism are not good at dealing with sudden changes, and instead prefer regularity. Personally, I am a control freak. There is also a tendency to become obsessed with certain topics - for some reason, most notably, trains. People with autism might also have some delay in developing their motoric skills, and some of them are bad at sports or clumsy. But autism spectrum disorder means that every individual with autism is just that - an individual with a disorder that can't be precisely described because it varies so much. Autism is generally treated by helping people understand who they are, what they find difficult, and what they are good at. Historically autism was "treated" by adapting the environment, but the current view is that although we can't cure autism, as it is not a disease, we can help people live with it better.

question: What is autism intervention?
answer: "Intervention", as far as I can tell, is an informal term that covers a wide range of activities designed to assist people on the spectrum (or in effect assist their parents, who may be the real customers). This page has a helpful explanation: Autism intervention for children with ASD Typically, an intervention will be a program undertaken with a professional or an agency that seeks to alter or develop behaviour in an autistic person that the person, or maybe their parents, believe will help them in life. There are many different kinds of programs: behavioural (e.g. psychology-based programs to directly alter or develop particular types of behaviour based on, say, Behaviourist theory); medical (e.g. diets; medication for associated conditions like anxiety disorders, depression, ADHD, etc); and relational (e.g. setting up special relationships, such as with a mentor, to give the autistic person practical experience in relationships, with structure and dependability). Some interventions may focus on a specific problem area - e.g. sensory sensitivity - rather than on the whole range of autistic characteristics. So an intervention is anything deliberate and (more or less) structured that is intended to reduce the difficulties (good) or differences (hmmm*) of an autistic person. Of course, someone may undergo intervention for something else, or just a generic rehab program, and find that it helps them - and then later learn that they are on the spectrum. In this case, the person realises in hindsight that they had autism intervention (I have seen this happen). * not all differences are bad, even though parents may not like them - e.g. special interests, especially in career-relevant fields like computer programming - may be helpful for the child with ASD, especially if they can be mentored by adults in the field and develop both social relationships and technical expertise at the same time that will help them get a skilled job. Autistic people do not have to turn into clones of non-autistic people in order to live happy, worthwhile lives. Just as some parents can place unrealistic expectations on non-autistic children, some parents will have unrealistic expectations of their children on the spectrum especially in terms of how "non-autistic" those children can or should become (or appear to become).

question: What is Autism level 1, 2, and 3?
answer: The DSM-5 states that there are three levels of autism, but as with any categorical classification they’re only a guide. I classify as Level 1 according this guide, and while I’m not the life and soul of a party I manage quite well with my wife and daughters to keep me on the straight and narrow. To use the late Terry Pratchett’s description of his final illness, as far as I’m concerned autism to me is an embuggerance, a fine autistic word, and official military slang for any obstacle (natural or artificial) that gets in the way of progress. The higher the level the more difficult it is for the individual to navigate such obstacles without support. In some cases it is a much more nuanced classification, an individual may be world class astrophysicist but be unable to navigate from home to university or be able to tie their own shoe laces. Level 1: Requiring support Level 1 is the least severe autism diagnosis. People in this category have social difficulties that require some support. They can find it difficult to initiate conversations with others and may respond inappropriately or lose interest quickly. As a result, it can be challenging for them to make friends, especially without the right support. People with level 1 autism may also show inflexible behaviours. It can be difficult for them to cope with changing situations or contexts, such as new environments. They may need help with organisation and planning. Level 2: Requiring substantial support People in this category need more support than those with a level 1 diagnosis. They have more severe social deficits that make holding a conversation very challenging. Even with support, they may struggle to communicate coherently and are more likely to respond inappropriately to others. They may speak in short sentences or only discuss very specific topics. These individuals may also have issues with nonverbal communication and might display behaviours such as facing away from the person with whom they are communicating. People with a level 2 diagnosis may also have inflexible behaviours that can interfere with daily functioning. They typically do not cope very well with changes, which can cause them significant distress. Level 3: Requiring very substantial support Level 3 is the most severe autism diagnosis. People with a level 3 diagnosis have significant impairments in their verbal and nonverbal communication. They will often avoid interactions with others, but they may interact in a limited way if they must respond to others or communicate a need. Their behaviours are highly inflexible and repetitive. They may react strongly to changes and become highly distressed in a situation that requires them to alter their focus or task.

question: What is autism, and how are people born with it?
answer: Autism is a neurotype. Think of it like this: Some people are born left handed, some right handed. Both can accomplish the same tasks, just slightly differently. Now history tells us that people were punished for being left handed. Why? because they were different. In modern day society we know there is nothing wrong with left handed people. Autism is much like this but society has not yet been educated enough to understand that we are not broken. We are just people how do things a little bit differently. How are we born with it? The current theory is synapses pruning. Every human fetus is born with excessive synapses connection in their brain, but at certain points in development the extra synapses become weak and finally disappear. The theory suggests that not enough synapses connections are pruned. This leads to a number of possible problems, and a number of possible advantages. Can autistics be successful? Well, lets see…. Einstein, Isaac Newton, Gretta Thrum burg, Elon Musk to name a few. In showbiz there is Dan Ackroyd and Sir Anthony Hopkins. Now autism was little understood before 1990 so any one prior to that is just “assumed or suspected” as being autistic. The point here is that autistics have value in human society. You can not claim were are all broken and disabled when some of the most influential people in history were also autistics. How are we different? Well it is a spectrum, we are not all the same just as normal people are not all the same. There are autistics who are disabled, and there are autistics who are not. This is no different with normal people, some being disabled and some who are not. The stereotypes we deal with suggest we are all versions of Rainman and that we are all broken. But there are common similarities, we tend to be introverts, but this may just be learned behavior from being bullied, dismissed and outcast by those who notice were different. We tend to think logically, and since most social norms have nothing to do with logic, we have difficulty understanding the social rules. Early on in life it is common to have difficulty looking people in the eye while speaking to them. Then as we grow we learn to over come these things. We tend to have overly acute senses. Certain textures are either heavenly or just completely irritating. For me I have to sleep on sheets made from tee shirt material because regular sheets are too scratchy. I remove the tags from all my shirts because it irritates me. Sometimes a when there is too much noise or light we can get overwhelmed by it. Earlier we talked about too many synapse connections. Sensory overload is a common issue with autistics. Some are more sever than others, and this can in itself be a cause for disability. This sensory overload causes us anxiety and frustration, this can lead to a meltdown or a shut down. When we are young we can have meltdowns which are very much like a Childs temper tantrum. Many of us are able to understand it is not acceptable behavior and over come this. But then we just tolerate it for long periods of time until we shut down. This is more or less our braking point, we just need some alone time to relax and refocus. Many of us learn to act “normal” while in social settings. The success of which usually only holds up for a short time. It is called masking and the longer we hold up the deception of being “one of you”, the more difficult it is. In the work place we might make it a few weeks before we do or say something that gives it away. Once we are identified as being different the usual outcome is that the normal people start acting like 8th graders. Social razzing and ridicule starts, then everyone else joins in. It is somehow acceptable from a grown adult to be out right rude, and behave this way. However it is not acceptable for an autistic to defend himself in a public or work setting against it. To us these double standard seem “irrational, illogical and emotional” nonsense. But it is the autistic community who is seen as different, so we are the ones who are expected to learn to tolerating normal people. Is it all bad? No, we tend to be Honest, Loyal, and efficient. I worked for a laser diode company. I was assigned to visual inspection and I consistently did 3x more work than my coworkers and even had a higher level of accuracy. How? I worked by myself on the night shift. The room lighting and temperature were acceptable and there were no distractions. I was able to “hyper focus” on my task. I was also the lowest paid worker. I did feel like I was being taken advantage of, however I was happy to have a decent paying job that accommodated my autism, and didn’t want to “rock the boat”. So I just did my work and drew as little attention to myself as possible. Well this is getting rather long. Autism is very complex and I’m just scratching the surface here. Thank you for taking the time to learn, I hope my answer was helpful..

question: What is Autism/Asperger syndrome , in layman's terms?
answer: Autism is a developmental disability, which is defined as a syndrome. A syndrome is simply a combination of signs or characteristics that can be used to identify a particular condition. Autism is a lifelong condition that has a combination of both developmental and behavioural features. Autism is often described as a spectrum. Classical Autism (sometimes referred to as Kanner's Autism after the psychiatrist who first described it in 1943) is at one end of the spectrum. It refers to people often described as ‘less able’. At the other end we have Asperger Syndrome. Hans Asperger was a paediatrician who wrote about autism. But his work did not achieve international recognition until after his death in 1980. People with Asperger Syndrome are usually seen to be quite able and articulate. While the autistic spectrum is a common framework for describing people with autism, it can cause some problems by assuming what is meant by mild or severe autism. Simply put, somebody with Asperger syndrome can be viewed as having less severe autism but may be very disabled by their condition. Similarly, people with classical autism are seen to have more severe autism but it does not necessarily follow that they are more disabled by it. Despite having this spectrum of autism, people anywhere on that spectrum all share three common sets of characteristics, called the “Triad of Impairments” (Triad is a group of three and an impairment is difficulty in carrying out certain activities): 1. Challenges of Language and Communication People with autism experience varying degrees of problems in social communication. Communication refers to both speech (verbal communication) or body language (non-verbal communication). Therefore people with autism experience difficulties with regard to the following: The non development or limited development of speech and body language tends to cut people off from everyone around them.Where speech does develop in a manner similar to others it can often be unusual or odd. Difficulty in understanding body language means that people struggle to understand or correctly use tone of voice, gestures, body posture, facial expressions.Unusual patterns of speech develop such as copying / repeating what others say, mixing up (pronouns) I, you, we, they, and talking constantly about one subject of interest. 2. Challenges of Social Interaction / Social Understanding People with autism have great difficulty in being able to relate to other people, which means: They exhibit inappropriate eye contact.They use laughter, or say things and behave in ways that are not suitable for the circumstances that they are in. They do not understand about relationships, especially in terms of friendships or meeting strangers. They frequently seem to be disinterested in others, by appearing aloof and distant.They appear to be withdrawn, remote and to have isolated themselves from others. 3. Challenges of Thought, Imagination and Behaviour Trying to make sense of the world means that we have to predict what might happen next or cope with new situations using our past experience. We must also be able to understand how other people think and feel. People with autism have great difficulty in doing these things as they have great problems with imagination. Instead they often rely on routines, or focus on special interests, to make sense of their world, which can become elevated to the status of rituals that have to be followed down to the smallest detail. Therefore the behaviour of people with autism can share certain characteristics: A dislike for variety and therefore a resistance to change.A tendency to be rigid and obsessive.A liking for repetitive patterns. Classic Autism (Kanner’s Autism) The person will have all three of the triad of impairments present in some form.The person will have some difficulty with social interaction, including an inability to understand other people’s reactions, one sided interactions and an apparent indifference to other people.The person will have difficulty with social communication, finding it hard to communicate using either words or gestures and having great difficulty in understanding tone of voice or facial expression. The person will have very limited imagination and is likely to engage in rigid activities and repetitive or obsessive behaviours. Asperger Syndrome Asperger Syndrome has the triad of impairments in common with classic autism. Therefore people with Aspereger Syndrome and Autism share difficulties in social relationships, limited imagination and problems in communicating. However, unlike in classic autism, in Asperger Syndrome there is: Normal development of speech and languageAn absence of a learning disabilityAverage or higher level intelligence

question: On a cognitive level, what is autism?
answer: In general, the cognitive style for autistic individuals (ASD) is more focused and concentrated than it is for others. This possibly accounts for the narrow range of special interest and talents that describe many ASD people. It also explains their preference for sameness, routine, accuracy, punctuality, and the pleasant repetition of familiar experience. Brain imaging studies explain these cognitive preferences in terms of brain development in which there is a greater density of neural connections in the close-point functions of the brain, and relatively weaker connectivity across brain regions and hemispheres. As such, the ASD brain functions optimally within a discrete focused field of attention and activity. In contrast, the broad and varied demands of social language create a difficult context for ASDs. Their close-point, concrete style relies on literal interpretation and factual knowledge, unsuited for the nuanced language of social gatherings. The ASD’s difficulty in making inferences, making connections between ideas, and seeing the ‘big picture’ may reflect a lack of robust connectivity across brain regions (frontal cortex, parietal regions, language and emotional regions). But the cognitive ‘trade off’ is the potential giftedness that comes with the ASD’s fascination for detail, tireless interest, and dogged pursuit of specific goals ( often in math, science and technology.) Note: This description of cognitive style is NOT representative of all ASD individuals. Those on the spectrum are quite diverse in every aspect ( intelligence, aptitude, ability, creativity, and sociability).

question: What is autism? More specifically, what is the autism spectrum score?
answer: What is autism? This is both a simple and excellent question. To answer it, I can only speak from my personal experiences. I was raised in a very poor, small town (legally a village) in the foothills of Appalachia. Because of this, few people around me were very aware of autism beyond its extreme manifestations of complete asociality, mutism, and severe compulsions. Weird kids were just that and nothing more. I suppose I can’t judge them too harshly- it was only the late ‘90s when I started school, and due to the less developed nature of the area it was more like the ‘80s. If I had instead been born in 2012 and started school in 2018, I’m fairly sure I’d have been diagnosed with mild to moderate autism. I had many noticeable traits which are associated with people on the spectrum-I was rather late-developing in terms of speech. At the age of two I was barely speaking and my mother was considering taking me to the doctor.Despite the first point, I learned to read remarkably quickly. By the age of two and a half I was reading children’s books aloud and upon entering kindergarten my mother demonstrated my knowledge to my teachers by having me read an encyclopedia entry.I had a special interest- reptiles, particularly snakes. By second grade I could tell someone about the difference between elapids and vipers, the difference between neurotoxic and hemotoxic venom, how the anaconda is the world’s only aquatic constrictor, or the function of the Jacobsen’s organ.I had an unusual speech pattern/inflection. Despite growing up in a rural, isolated area with no opportunities of travel, people frequently believed I had emigrated from a place far away.I was quite oblivious when it came to social skills. My first grade teacher developed a considerable aversion towards me when I corrected her for chewing with her mouth open at her desk. At the time it made sense- my mom corrected me for it, so it must have been wrong for everyone!I was often mistaken for being withdrawn. I very much enjoyed solitude and I would stay in my room with my books for hours at a time. In truth, I wasn’t depressed or antisocial- I just liked the comfort, quiet, and organization of my room.When I did go out to play, it was very structured. When I was 4, I used a Tonka bulldozer to build my own traffic network around the apple tree in the backyard. As my mom put it- “When Zack plays, he never “just plays”- he’s always working on something”I was a very literal person and didn’t understand most forms of sarcasm. Although I had a healthy sense of humor, I often couldn’t tell whether or not someone actually meant what they said. My mom would have to warn my teachers- “Zack is very smart, but be careful what you tell him because he’ll probably take it literally!”Due to the fact that I didn’t have a strong grasp of social subtleties, I was constantly bullied until my teenage years. To this day, I don’t understand many of the reasons my bullies did what they did or why they thought it was funny.Aside from the other “gifted weird kids”, I was essentially a loner. It took many years for me to develop the social skills required to function healthily among more neurotypical people.I often had trouble with the constant busywork assigned to us in class. A typical parent-teacher conference would be the teacher telling my mom- “I’m not sure exactly what’s going on with Zack- he’s making perfect scores on his tests but he has five missing worksheets” and my response to my mom would be that I already understood the material and would instead rather read on my own time. At the time it seemed logical- school was supposed to be a place of learning, so why grind over things I already knew?Despite my lack of “normal” social interaction, I had tremendous amounts of cognitive empathy. I would often embrace vegetarianism and nonviolence, to the point of opening windows and doors to let the flies out. I even attempted to convert to Buddhism, which my parents were open-minded enough to allow (even though none of us understood it completely).Due to the fact that I didn’t understand social barriers, I was often able to transcend them by simply not noticing them. One of my first friends in grade school was the one of the very few black kids in the school. A lot of the other kids were reluctant to be his friend, but I believe we got along well due to both the fact that we were both outsiders, and the fact that I wasn’t able to absorb the ambient racism around me.I’ve always been unusually conscious of rules and structure, even during my early years. Any transgressions on my part were usually due to either obliviousness or getting “caught up in the moment”, but I was always happy to correct myself when they were pointed out. This contrasts sharply with many of my peers, who were intentionally loud, disruptive, and cruel for reasons I didn’t understand.To this day, I have maintained many of these traits. Additionally, due to the freedom of adulthood, I have discovered that I have even more of them-I frequently find myself getting caught up in mild compulsions. The most notable one I’ve developed is recycling. Not only do I recycle everything I use, but I would often grab items from garbage cans to put them in their appropriate recycling bins. I have managed to fight the urge to do this, but it still infuriates me when I see someone throw a plastic bottle in a garbage can when a recycling bin is LITERALLY RIGHT BESIDE IT.I absolutely hate bright flashes of light and loud, sudden noises. question: What is autism in India?
answer: Many people have asked us: What is autism in India ‘like’? Does it look the same as autism in other places? What kinds of services are available? What do families do? Is the prevalence the same? These are all very intriguing and important questions. We can answer some of these from our experience of working with hundreds of families - for instance, we have a good idea of what the experience of autism is like for Indian families. However, without empirical research, there are many questions about autism in India (and other places in the world) that remain unanswered. Data released from the CDC in April 2014 placed the prevalence of autism in the U.S. at approximately 1 in 68 children. No data are available from India to provide an India-specific estimate of the prevalence, and it is unknown whether there are variations in this rate worldwide. Of note, however, is a study conducted in South Korea that found a prevalence rate of 1 in 38. read more about Research on Autism in India While the disorder is not rare, a multitude of people with autism in India have not been diagnosed and -- more critically -- do not receive the services they need. This problem occurs in many countries, but is especially true in India where there is a tremendous lack of awareness and misunderstanding about autism among the medical professionals, who may either misdiagnose or under diagnose the condition.Obtaining an accurate diagnosis is one of the major difficulties faced by parents of children with autism in India. A parent may take their child to a paediatrician only to be reassured that their child is just "slow." Unsatisfied, they may visit a psychologist, to be told their child is "mentally subnormal." Convinced that their child does not fit the typical picture of mental retardation, they may visit a psychiatrist, to be told that their child has attention deficit disorder, and must be put on medication to control hyperactivity. After months of sedation and unsatisfactory progress, they may again begin a cycle of searching for the correct name for their child’s problem. read more about Family Stories Fortunately, the process of obtaining a diagnosis of autism in India is improving in the major cities, as more paediatricians become aware of the condition. Some doctors may feel that nothing can be gained by a diagnosis of autism if the services are not available; yet, as more children are diagnosed as autistic and more awareness of the disorder spreads, there will be a demand for services. Schools will be forced to educate themselves if they find that more of the population they serve is autistic. Admittedly, there are not enough services to meet the needs of mentally retarded children and adults in India, let alone those who are autistic. Let this then be an impetus to create more services, and ensure that the special needs of autistic children are not ignored. There is also an urgent need to begin planning residences and centres for these children for when they become adults: people with autism have a normal life span and many will require considerable support after their parents’ death. Currently, the needs of autistic children in India are not being met in either the regular or special education systems. With an understanding teacher or possibly an aide, a more able autistic child can function very well in a regular school, and learn valuable social skills from his peers. However, even children with very high I.Q.’s are often not permitted in regular classes. Additionally, the rigidity and pressure of schools in India can make it difficult for an autistic child to cope without special allowances. Some children with higher support needs, who form the majority of autistic children, may attend special schools, but these schools often lack an understanding of effective methods of handling the challenging behaviours of autistic children. As one psychologist noted, "The kids just get ‘dumped’ or ignored at the special schools." Children with autism are frequently refused admission in these special schools because officials protest they are not equipped to handle autistic children, who are sometimes more challenging than children with mental retardation alone. We firmly believe that special schools need to invest in learning these techniques so that they can provide the necessary help to both the children and the families. Autism is still not recognized as a separate form of disability in the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995, the primary piece of legislation that provides for the rights of and benefits for persons with disabilities in India. However, advocacy movements, spearheaded primarily by AFA, succeeded in the inclusion of autism in the National Trust Bill – ‘National Trust for Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act 1999’. Persons with autism can receive certain benefits under this act, the first ever legislation to be passed in India that recognized autism as a distinct condition of its own. However, to get access to a majority of benefits, a disability certificate is required, and currently there is no disability certificate being issued just for autism. Those who want to avail of any schemes do opt to take the disability certificate for Autism with MR (Mental Retardation). read more about Legislation and Policy Autism in India also needs to be viewed in the context of attitudes toward disability more generally. Traditionally there has been stigma attached to disability— shame, embarrassment, concerns about inadequate parenting— perceptions that are shared by many countries worldwide. Autism comes with unusual behaviours, fuelling beliefs about what affected the children. Historically, stigma ensured that families hid their strange children. Since autistic children were not seen, they did not exist, which acted as a barrier to awareness. It isolated families, creating a cycle of ignorance and superstition. In recent years the stigma has lessened and there is greater acceptance. read more about the Role of the Media in spreading awareness. The autism movement in India has come a long way in the past two decades; identification and diagnoses are made at earlier ages, there are more services that cater to the needs of individuals with autism, there are also some changes in the awareness levels in the general population. But there is still a lot of work to be done. If people with autism are to have an opportunity to reach their maximum potential and have dignified futures, the community of parents, siblings, other relatives, and professionals will have to continue to work together as a team and advocate for the rights of this often marginalized and vulnerable sector. Till today, many parents of autistic children try to hide their child’s disability from the community, they are afraid to take their children to the parks, in fear that the onlookers will stare at them or may make fun of their conditions. The ignorance level about autism is very high in India and is considered a social stigma. The World’s Autism Awareness Day (WAAD), which is observed on April 2 every year, allows us to talk about autism in India – a health issue that is too often overlooked. Unless it is made aware, addressed, and accepted, there won’t be a way out and the sufferings of the patients and their loved ones will never end. The first WAAD was celebrated in 2008. The day highlights the need to help and improve the quality of life of those with autism so that they can lead full and meaningful lives as an integral part of society. Today, many organizations and communities around the world come together in recognition of the people with autism and their loved ones with kindness and acceptance to support them. However, any mental health condition in India is still considered taboo. India is a society that doesn’t understand mental health disorders, which may be due to lack of awareness and education, more superstitious beliefs, inability to accept the patients who suffer from them. Every person living here must be aware and be open to the basic understanding of the disease and its sufferers. Prevalence and incidence statistics about autism in India is 1 in 500 or 0.20% or more than 2,160,000 people. According to a study, an estimated three million people live with autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) on the Indian subcontinent. Autism is a pervasive developmental disorder (PDD), which is a frequent and debilitating neurological handicap in children – usually diagnosed in early childhood. Many doctors believe that genes play an important part in whether the child will be born with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) or not. For a majority of cases, there are no definitive biological markers of autism diagnosis depending on a range of behavioral signs. The major symptoms of autism involve problems with communication, social interaction, and repetitive behaviors. However, scientists believe that it may be associated with genetic or environmental factors. There’s no cure for ASD, but occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy, educational support, and several other interventions may help children and parents. The need for better services, acceptance, and understanding by the masses. There is a need to push back against stigma and provide acceptance and support to those living with autism, to dispel myths and spread awareness and knowledge. To make the masses understand what it is exactly and not. How to help those who are suffering, improve their living conditions in a society like ours. Autism can be prevented, though no one has yet figured out the main cause of autism. However, there are measures to prevent having a child with autism.
