question: What is autism? What is a spectrum?
answer: So, this is two questions. I've already answered the first question about autism, which you can read below.Chuck Kelbheu · 1yWhat does being autistic really mean?Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by issues in communication and sensory sensitivity, which differ from those of the larger population. Communication issues can vary from completely nonverbal to being verbal with a large vocabulary, but with difficulty around the nuance of typical communication, such as tone of voice, body language, metaphor, etc. Sensory issues can vary from being overwhelmed by sensory stimuli that others barely notice (like high pitched noises or florescent lights), to seeking out stimulation that others can find confusing (like repetitive movements or listening to the same song over and over again), and these issues can fluctuate over time. Many autistic people mask their symptoms due to social pressures, but the underlying issues for those symptoms are still there, and are often exacerbated by masking. So, an autistic person can appear neurotypical, but then seem to act differently “out of nowhere”. This is often due to the stress of masking becoming overwhelming to the point that they find masking difficult or even lose the ability to mask altogether. Autism is not a monolith, and every autistic person will have varying degrees of the previously mentioned issues. This is why autism is considered a spectrum. The autism spectrum isn't a gradient from “no autism” to “lots of autism”. A spectrum is like a color spectrum, red and blue are both equally colors, but they are clearly different. Autism is similar in that I'm clearly different from a nonverbal autistic person, but we're both equally autistic. Autism is not an intellectual disability, and while many autistic people can have an intellectual disability comorbid with their autism, many of us can also have average or higher than average intelligence. Autistic people have the same range of intelligence as the general population, but to different degrees than neurotypical people. It can be thought of as a learning disability in the context of social learning, but other than that it has little to do with intelligence. Autism is not a lack of emotion or empathy, and while we can often struggle to communicate our empathy and our emotions it doesn't mean that we don't have them. Some autistic people may have a comorbid condition that effects these areas like AsPD, but in general we have the normal range of empathy and emotions that we struggle to communicate with others. In fact, for many of us our emotions and empathy can be so strong that they're overwhelming to the point that we feel like we have to avoid situations where they're likely to be triggered. This can make us seem less empathetic than we actually are, especially when paired with our difficulties with communication. So, that's the gist of what autism is, with a bit of the common misconceptions of what it isn't for good measure. Hope that helps.As far as what a spectrum is, I think I touch on it a bit in my answer about autism, but I can talk about it a bit more here. So the best example of a spectrum is the light spectrum, also known as the color spectrum. The visible part of this spectrum is what we think of as the rainbow. You can think of autism as a spectrum, in the same way that color is a spectrum. Every autistic person is different from every other autistic person, but they're still autistic. In the same way that every color is different from every other color, but they're all still colors. Some may look similar, like red and orange, and some can look totally different, like yellow and blue, but they're all still colors. Likewise, the same can be said of autistic people. Some of us are very similar, and some of us are very different from each other, but that doesn't mean that we aren't autistic. Some people confuse spectrums with gradients. A gradient is like the shades of grey between black and white. Some people, making this mistake, think that autism being a spectrum means that everyone is a little bit autistic, some people are just in the light grey side of the gradient, and others are on the dark grey side of the gradient. That's not what a spectrum is. Autism is classified into three different levels of support, level 1 being the lowest support needs, and level 3 being the highest support needs. These levels are more like the shades of grey of a gradient. But just like you can have dark blue, medium blue, and light blue, which are all blue, the same is true of autism, and the levels. I hope this helps.

question: Is intellectual disability similar to autism?
answer: Is it possible that autism is actually the result of a general lack of intelligence? People used to think so. Many people with autism were misdiagnosed with intellectual disability, though their ability to learn was close to normal, or even in the gifted range. And many people with autism and intellectual disability were diagnosed with intellectual disability only, and their academic abilities and talents were ignored because they were assumed to be much worse at learning than they actually were. You see, when a person can’t talk very well, they have trouble telling neurotypicals what they are thinking. And, for neurotypicals—at least, for untaught, inexperienced neurotypicals—if it’s not communicated to them, it doesn’t exist. Luckily, we learned better. At first, there were just a few cases—Kanner’s boys, Asperger’s boys, practically always boys—that had such extreme autism, combined with relatively good speech, that they could show that they were good at learning and at the same time very poor at communicating and at dealing with uncertainty and at understanding other people’s non-verbal communication. Before that, “autism” had just been a symptom, that of turning inward and away from social contact as one tended to do with schizophrenia. After that, it became a diagnosis on its own. We discovered that autism and intellectual disability were different things. People could have autism and intellectual disability, but these people had different patterns of thinking and learning than those with intellectual disability alone. People could also have autism and be gifted, and had different ways of thinking than gifted neurotypicals did. The explosion in autism diagnosis has come along with a sharp decrease in intellectual disability diagnosis. Some people, institutionalized and thought to be profoundly developmentally delayed, were reevaluated and found to have autism instead, and finally given the intellectual challenges they were capable of—though because of the autism and the long stays in the institutions, they still needed a lot of help. Other people, who had been thought to be mildly developmentally delayed because of their behavior, were reevaluated and were able to show their ability to do the same schoolwork everybody else did; and these were the children whose teachers tried to get them mainstreamed so that they could have a regular education. Yet others, who had intellectual disability, were discovered to have autism too, and therapists who now had a more complete picture of how these people thought were able to start to teach them in the way they learned best. There were a lot of stops and starts along the way. There are a lot of things we still don’t know about how autistic people think, and neurotypicals are still learning to listen to us when we do our best to communicate. But what we have now—knowing the difference between ID and autism and how they occur together and apart—is a real advance on what we used to have.

question: What is autism therapy?
answer: Autism therapy refers to a range of interventions and strategies designed to support individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in developing skills, managing challenges, and improving their overall quality of life. There are various types of autism therapy, including:Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA): ABA therapy focuses on reinforcing positive behaviors and teaching new skills through structured interventions and rewards.2. Speech and Language Therapy: This therapy helps individuals with autism improve their communication and language skills through targeted exercises and techniques. 3. Occupational Therapy: Occupational therapists work with individuals with autism to develop skills necessary for daily living, such as self-care, fine motor skills, and sensory integration. 3. Social Skills Training: This therapy aims to improve social interaction and communication abilities, helping individuals with autism develop meaningful relationships and navigate social situations. 4. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): CBT helps individuals with autism identify and modify negative thought patterns and behaviors, allowing them to better manage anxiety, depression, and other mental health challenges. 5. Sensory Integration Therapy: This therapy focuses on addressing sensory processing difficulties commonly experienced by individuals with autism, helping them better understand and respond to sensory information. It's important to note that each person with autism is unique, and therapy should be tailored to their specific needs and strengths. Therapies can be combined or used individually based on the individual's goals and requirements.

question: How rare is autism?
answer: What are the odds of autism? The likelihood of autism — of having a child who is autistic or of being autistic yourself — is about 1–2%, depending on a variety of factors. That is the frequency at which autism, as currently diagnosed, appears in the general population. First, the likelihood is a little higher the older your father was when you were conceived. The likelihood is also a bit higher the older your paternal grandfather was when your father was conceived (my paternal grandfather was over 50 when my father was conceived, and I am the youngest child — so my father was older when I was conceived compared to my siblings). Second, the likelihood is much higher if there are already any autistic people in your family, such as a sibling, parent, or child. Quite a few parents are diagnosed when they get their children assessed for autism. It has always been observed since autism was first identified that family members of autistic people often have some autistic traits themselves, and maybe enough to be diagnosed. However, where autism occurred because of a mutation in a single gene or because of a “copy number variation”, it is possible for an autistic person to have no close autistic relatives, not even relatives with the “broad autism phenotype”. Third, the likelihood of you being autistic is very high if you have an identical twin who is autistic. Autism is a highly genetic condition, so identical twins are most likely to be both autistic or both non-autistic. There are other factors that can increase the likelihood of autism: e.g. where the mother experienced rubella or some other infections during the pregnancy, or where the mother used certain medications such as anti-depressants during the pregnancy. But overall, unless there are autistic people in your family, the likelihood of autism is under 2%, as those with existing autistic family members are more likely to produce the next generation of autistic people. But the likelihood of having autistic children does increase somewhat with the age of the father. Short answer: it varies, both from family to family and even over time in the same family, but generally less than 2% unless you have fairly close autistic relatives or are autistic yourself.

question: What is autism, and does it have a cure?
answer: Autism is one way a brain can develop in an individual. It can be called “neuro-divergent” because it differs from certain “norms”. Of course, being “different” in various ways is not necessarily “wrong”. It is just about what is commonly “expected”. And it is likely to render an individual at odds with certain environments. That can be “disabling” if it interferes with that person being able to accomplish certain goals. Though being autistic can result in some (often many) social, intellectual, and health challenges, the degree of these challenges differ greatly from one autistic person to another. But autism is not a disease to be “cured”. It is a brain difference that can originate from a number of causes. Scientists are increasingly identifying genetic variations responsible for different manifestations of autism. Look into UCLA research if you want more precise information. Not every autistic person would accept a “cure”, even if this was possible. How much “brain engineering” would society wish to undertake in the name of “conformity”? For instance, do we really want to forego the societal advantages that can result from “outsider perspectives”? Some autistic individuals feel stressed about the challenges they face in life and wish for an easier life. And I certainly cannot find fault with an autistic person's desire to better “fit in”. But that does not mean every autistic person wants to nullify their distinctions from broader human communities. I feel as if my “outsider status” has conferred on me certain talents— one of which is to be able to perceive ways in which human “flaws” (including my own) can be transmuted into assets. I possess a high degree of analytic ability that allows me to be quite adept at self-introspection. This permits me to grow psychologically in major ways that might be more difficult for others. I can readily check and recheck my approaches to life and make alterations in certain behaviors that do not serve me well. Not every autistic person possesses this ability. But I suspect that the way my unique traits have interacted with various environments has given rise to the development of this talent for introspection. Other autistics are likely to develop basic “gifts” that differ from my own. So, I harbor no desire to rid the world of autism! I don't want to live in a world where “neuro-divergences” are not incorporated into the “norms” of society. I am not prepared to lose the inadvertent “gifts” those differences might confer on our lives.

question: What is autism? What causes it, and how can I know that someone is suffering from autism?
answer: Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder. Neuro means having to do with the brain and nervous system(whose cells are called ‘neurons’). Developmental means the person is born with it, it forms and is having an effect before the person is born. Autism is caused by a group of small genetic errors, usually scattered across more than one gene. These genetic errors can be inherited, or pop up on their own. When the errors pop up on their own, most people call them ‘mutations.’ However, they are not caused by vaccines, radiation, modern life or industrialization. They just happen. No one has to do anything wrong for them to happen. Most of us have dozens of these ‘spelling errors.’ Most of these genetic errors don’t cause any problems. But specific spelling errors on specific genes that control brain development prior to birth, add up to what we call ‘autism.’ To be clear, genes are organized into chromosomes. A chromosome is like a neighborhood or town, with many houses. Each house representing one gene. Other disorders like Down Syndrome affect entire chromosomes, disrupting many genes on that chromosome. Autism isn’t like that. Instead, we are looking at much smaller errors in individual genes. But these do add up. I used the metaphor of houses…we nearly all have the same genes, but what matters is the spelling or coding each gene has. To give a very small example, we all have a gene for eye color. But our eye color is determined by the spelling or coding in that gene. We also have to remember that genes don’t just determine ‘traits’ and then just sit there and do basically nothing. Many genes are active all our lives. Many - most of the genes involved with autism - do most of their ‘work’ as that embryonic brain develops. Ultimately, each gene is a ‘recipe’ for a substance, usually a simple chemical. Each one has a job. If it’s misspelled, that gene might make a chemical that can’t quite do the job it’s intended for. Such as, say, nourishing embryonic nerve cells. That will affect how the nerves, brain develops prior to birth. All these tiny details of what genes really make, and how that chemical is used, are behind autism. Autism can be mild or severe or anything in between. People with mild autism have milder symptoms. People with severe autism have more severe symptoms. Let’s talk about what areas of thinking are affected by autism: 1.) Language 2.) Learning and using social rules 3.) Repetitive behavior and dealing with change of routine. As you can see, all three of these are more complicated kinds of thinking that involve multiple parts of the brain working together. So how would this affect a person? Well, I can give ‘teaching examples,’ but each person with autism is different, so not every person with autism will follow these examples perfectly. They just are not all the same. You need to get to know each autistic person as an individual. Example: mild autism:Language. Doesn’t ‘get’ slang, jokes, exaggeration, words with multiple meanings, shadings of meaning, etc.Dealing with social rules. Doesn’t ‘get’ dating rules, which are mostly unspoken and subtle and are different in different social groups.Dealing with change/repetitive behavior. Gets upset when school classes are canceled. It’s a change of routine. Most kids would cheer and go off to play, the autistic child will be upset and unsure what to do next. Repetitive behavior: Keeps on spinning a toy in class and the teacher complains.Example: severe autism:Language. Has a very hard time learning to speak and communicate. May never learn to speak if autism is very severe. Others, with lots of speech therapy will learn to speak some words, but still have lots of trouble communicating. May be able to learn to use picture cards or a computer tablet with pictures on it. Often has a very difficult time understanding what someone is saying to them.Dealing with social rules. Lots of trouble remembering and applying even very simple social rules, especially from one situation to another. For example, walks up to strangers and hugs them.Dealing with change. Frantic and panicky at even small changes of routine, such as when Dad arrives a bit late at home for dinner. Cries, sobs, hits self out of frustration and terror. Repetitive behavior. Stares all day at ceiling fan, screams and cries if forced to stop.In addition, with severe autism, many have Intellectual Disability. Intellectual Disability can really add to the person’s problems, as they could have more trouble learning, remembering and understanding, in the three areas of autism, but also just much more general problems learning, remembering and understanding.In addition, with severe autism, many have seizures. They must receive daily and possibly emergency medication if a seizure starts and will not stop.Some people with severe autism respond to psychiatric medications. These medications often don’t help people with mild autism.Some people with autism have what is loosely referred to as ‘sensory problems.’ This means loud noises hurt their ears, chaotic situations cause them distress, things like that are distressing. Some people with autism are real loners. They like to do their hobbies and stay to themselves and stick to a routine. Others are friendly and quite sociable, but are very unsure of what to do in different social situations. Many people with mild autism don’t feel they ‘suffer’ and don’t consider themselves to be disabled. They feel their worst problems are getting teased, bullied and later on, not getting hired at a job because they need some slight adaptations, such as to avoid loud noises and chaotic situations. People tend to think people with mild autism ‘should just act normal’ and ‘could do better if they just tried a little harder.’ This puts them in a difficult situation. They can make some changes and compromises, obviously, but it gets to be exhausting, stressful and painful after a point. With severe autism, the problems are different. Most will need lifelong care. With the language problems and possible Intellectual Disability, they may not recognize hazards, such as rapidly moving traffic or ponds. They may become very distressed and panicky at routine changes. They may not be able to tell someone when they feel pain or are sick or experience depression or anxiety. They may have ‘challenging behavior’ such as injuring themselves. Of course, while I talked about ‘mild’ and ‘severe,’ some people have a mix of some mild and some severe symptoms, some people have more moderate symptoms that are in between mild and severe…but that’s why we say ‘if you’ve met one person with autism, you’ve met one person with autism,’ meaning each person with this disorder will be different. You can also see a person with usually mild symptoms just have a ‘really bad day’ in one situation, and function really well in other situations. You can see a person with really severe autism who is ‘having a good day’ too. In certain situations that are familiar and routine, the person with severe autism may do rather well, and you don’t really see what limitations the person has. I used to go see my friend with severe autism for a few hours at a time, and it wasn’t until I took care of him for several days in a row, that I realized how much severe autism affected him.

Its being a developmental disorder means symptoms must be present from the early developmental stages. Autism has four main areas of difficulties - social/communication, emotional, behavioural and sensory. I don’t want to go into a huge amount of detail as that would make this an incredibly long answer, but I’ll just give you the gist of the four areas. Social/communication: Autistic people have differences in how they communicate with others. Quite often, autistic people use and interpret language used by others literally and can also be very blunt and say what they think of people even if it’s something they don’t want to hear. Autistic people often struggle reading social situations and are often unaware of social nuances. Emotional: Autistic people often have intense emotions and quite often struggle understanding them and putting them in speech. Behavioural: Autistic people often have patterns of repetitive behaviours (otherwise known as self-stimulators behaviours or stims). These can include hand-flapping, tapping, spinning around in desk chairs or on the floor. Autistic people often dislike changes to their routines and may also have obsessive special interests (these are subjects which they like to research for hours, make collections of or talk about for ages). Sensory: Autistic people have hypersensitive (over sensitive) or hyposensitive (under sensitive) reactions to sensory stimuli. Hypersensitive reactions are usually accompanied by sensory avoidant behaviours and hyposensitive reactions are usually accompanied by sensory seeking behaviours. Most autistics will have a spiky profile of hypersensitivities and hyposensitivities. I’ve written more about autism in other answers on Quora, which you are welcome to read, but I hope that’s given you a general idea of what autism is.

question: Is autism related to narcissism, what are the main differences?
answer: I’ll treat this as two questions - Is autism related to narcissism? Not really, but it depends how you’re using the word narcissism. Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder. Narcissism is a trait everyone has to some extent [healthy narcissism is like having a good self-esteem]. However, if you’re using narcissism to mean unhealthy narcissism, or NPD, then no, that has pretty much nothing to do with autism. NPD stands for narcissistic personality disorder, and as the name suggests, the category of conditions it’s in is personality disorders. It’s a Cluster B personality disorder [the other PDs in the same cluster as NPD include antisocial [ASPD], borderline [BPD] and histrionic [HPD] PDs]. What are the key differences? Well, I already mentioned a couple - narcissism is a trait, which can either be healthy or unhealthy, or someone can have narcissistic personality disorder [NPD], which is in a completely different category of conditions to autism. And autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder. Autism is thought to have mostly genetic and some environmental causes, but it’s always present from the earliest developmental stages - basically, you’re born autistic, or you’re born not autistic. Autism isn’t the only different neurotype out there - there are plenty of other ways people can potentially have different neurological wiring from the norm [the norm is called neurotypical]. Personality disorders, on the other hand, develop over time and aren’t diagnosed until the person’s in their late teens to early twenties at least. Another difference is self-esteem. Assuming you’re talking about NPD, those with NPD have inflated self-esteem. Autistics, on the other hand, tend to have low self-esteem. Also, autistic people are very much known for being socially inept. This is due to the fundamental differences in how their brains are wired, so autistics and non-autistics frequently misunderstand each other. Narcissists [people with NPD] on the other hand, have excellent social skills [this is how they’re able to manipulate people - they’re master manipulators, and this requires expert knowledge of how neurotypicals think and communicate with each other]. Autistic people have different ways of attempting to interact with people [or not], which I’ve written more about in other answers, but the only way in which autistic people are in any way similar to narcissists is if as a result of constant isolation, they act like they’re better than those shunning them in order to boost their terribly low self-esteem. This is a learned interaction style, rather than a natural one [something I’ve also covered in the answers I’ve written more about autistic interaction styles in], and it doesn’t apply to all or even most autistics. Besides this, autistics and narcissists have nothing in common.

question: Is autism ever going to be seen for what it really is?

question: How is autism diagnosed, and what sort of tests or evaluations are involved?
